xq.q: Starting from the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\tfrac12(e^{x}+e^{-x})\) and \(\sinh x=\tfrac12(e^{x}-e^{-x})\), show that \(\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1\). Then use \(\cos jx=\cosh x\) and \(\sin jx=j\sinh x\) to explain how this identity relates to \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\).
xq.a: cosh²x = (\(e^{2x}\)+2+\(e^{-2x}\))/4 and sinh²x = (\(e^{2x}\)-2+\(e^{-2x}\))/4. Subtracting gives 4/4 = 1. Putting θ = jx in cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 gives cosh²x + (j sinh x)² = cosh²x - sinh²x = 1, since j² = -1. This is why the hyperbolic identity has a minus sign.
s: Substitute θ = jx in the circular identity
Use j² = -1 to get the minus sign

units.name: 3.3 Circular and hyperbolic functions of complex arguments
units.ov: This material extends sine and the hyperbolic functions to complex arguments z = x + jy by using addition formulas together with the imaginary-argument identities \(\cos jy=\cosh y\) and \(\sin jy=j\sinh y\). The result is that circular and hyperbolic functions are two faces of the same exponential-based family, and a complex function is evaluated by splitting it into real and imaginary parts. Note that p8 and p9 write the same result in different term orders, and that sin z is unbounded in modulus, unlike the real sine.
must: \(\sin(x+jy)=\sin x\cosh y+j\cos x\sinh y\): real part \(\sin x\cosh y\), imaginary part \(\cos x\sinh y\). (p9 writes the j term as \(j\sinh y\cos x\), which is the same thing.)
\(\cos jy=\cosh y\) and \(\sin jy=j\sinh y\): these are the key identities used to derive the result.
\(\cosh jx=\cos x\) and \(\sinh jx=j\sin x\): the reverse links between hyperbolic and circular functions.
Derivation method: apply the addition formula \(\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B\) with \(A=x\), \(B=jy\), then substitute the imaginary-argument identities.

The addition formula \(\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y\) is used for the hyperbolic function of a complex argument. By analogy with sin, expect \(\sinh(x+jy)=\sinh x\cos y+j\cosh x\sin y\); derive it yourself to confirm.
Do not drop the j: \(\sinh(j4)=j\sin 4\), not \(\sin 4\), otherwise the imaginary part is lost.
\(|\sin z|\le 1\) does NOT hold for complex z, because \(\cosh y\) grows with \(|y|\).
Use radians for all trig arguments on the calculator, and for hyperbolic functions use the actual real values of x and y.
Final answers should be given in Cartesian form \(a+jb\), with numerical values for the real and imaginary parts.
Mapping view: \(w=\sin z\) sends a rectangular grid in the z-plane to a curvilinear grid, so it is not a rigid transformation.
conn: Complex trig links to hyperbolic functions through \(\cos jy=\cosh y\) and \(\sin jy=j\sinh y\), so a question on one often needs the other.
Evaluating \(\sin(x+jy)\) combines the compound-angle formulas with the hyperbolic identities and Cartesian real/imaginary separation.
Real and imaginary parts feed into modulus and argument (polar form), so questions can ask for \(|\sin z|\), and it can be shown that this exceeds 1 for large y.
The mapping picture links to solving equations such as \(\sin z=w\), by equating real and imaginary parts.
exq: Derive \(\sin(x+jy)=\sin x\cosh y+j\cos x\sinh y\) from the addition formula and the identities for \(\cos jy\) and \(\sin jy\).
Evaluate \(\sin(5+j4)\) in the form \(a+jb\), working in radians and giving 3 significant figures.
Show that \(\sinh(x+jy)=\sinh x\cos y+j\cosh x\sin y\), and hence evaluate \(\sinh(2+j3)\).
Explain why \(|\sin z|\le1\) fails for complex z, and find \(|\sin(\pi/2+j3)|\).
Find the real and imaginary parts of \(\sin z\) along the line \(x=\pi/4\) and describe the image of this line under the map \(w=\sin z\).

notes.t: Circular and hyperbolic functions of complex arguments: sin z
pts: Expand sin of a complex argument using the sine addition formula, splitting z = x + jy into real and imaginary parts.
Imaginary-argument trig identities convert to hyperbolic functions: cos jy becomes cosh y, and sin jy becomes j sinh y.
The final form of sin z separates into a real part sin x cosh y and an imaginary part cos x sinh y.
The mapping diagram shows a rectangular grid in z being transformed by sin z into a curvilinear grid, illustrating that sin z is not a simple rigid transformation.
eqs: Sine of a complex argument in Cartesian form
\sin z = \sin x\cosh y + j\cos x\sinh y
z = complex argument (dimensionless); x = real part of z (dimensionless, radians); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not forget the factor j on the sinh term: sin jy = j sinh y, so the imaginary part of sin z carries a j in front of sinh y.
sin z is not bounded by 1 in modulus for complex z; cosh y grows with |y|, so do not assume |sin z| ≤ 1.
rq: Why does cos jy reduce to cosh y rather than to a cosine of a real number?
Because cos(jy) = (\(e^{j·jy}\) + \(e^{-j·jy}\))/2 = (\(e^{-y}\)+\(e^{y}\))/2 = cosh y, so the imaginary argument turns the periodic cosine into the hyperbolic cosine.
What would change in the result if y = 0?
sinh 0 = 0 and cosh 0 = 1, so sin z reduces to sin x, the familiar real sine, as expected.

notes.t: Circular and hyperbolic functions of complex arguments
pts: Sine of a complex argument splits into a real part using sinh and cosh of the imaginary part.
Hyperbolic sine of a complex argument uses the addition formula for sinh.
For imaginary arguments, sinh(jx) gives j sin x and cosh(jx) gives cos x.
Evaluating a complex function means expanding it into real and imaginary parts, then computing numerically.
defs: Circular function of complex argument
sin(x + jy) = sin x cosh y + j sinh y cos x, obtained by expanding with the compound-angle formula and the hyperbolic relations for jy.
Hyperbolic function of imaginary argument
sinh(jx) = j sin x and cosh(jx) = cos x, linking hyperbolic and circular functions.
eqs: x = real part of argument (rad); y = imaginary part of argument (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Keep track of the j factor: sinh(j4) = j sin 4, not sin 4, otherwise the imaginary part is lost.
Argument units: trigonometric functions use radians, so 5 and 4 must be treated as radians in calculators.
rq: Why does sin(5 + j4) have a real part involving cosh 4 rather than cos 4?
Because the real-part formula is sin x cosh y, where y is the imaginary part (4), so cosh 4 appears; cos enters only through the imaginary part term with x.
What if you tried to apply sinh(x+y) directly to sinh(5+j4) without expanding the jy term?
You would still need sinh(j4) and cosh(j4), which must be converted with sinh jx = j sin x and cosh jx = cos x before numerical evaluation.

xq.q: For the complex number \(z=2+j1\) (real part in radians), use \(\sin z=\sin x\cosh y+j\cos x\sinh y\) with \(z=x+jy\) to find the modulus \(|\sin z|\). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
Which of the following is the value of \(\sin(j2)\)? Take the argument in radians.
xq.w: With x = 0 and y = 2, sin z = j cos 0 sinh 2 = j sinh 2 = j3.627; the traps are using sin 2 (option 0), using cosh 2 (option 1) and a sign error (option 2).
s: Put x = 0, y = 2 in sin z = sin x cosh y + j cos x sinh y

xq.q: Starting from the compound-angle formula for sine, show that \(\sin(x+jy)=\sin x\cosh y+j\cos x\sinh y\) for real \(x,y\). Hence explain why \(|\sin z|\le 1\) does not hold for complex \(z\).
xq.a: sin(x+jy) = sin x cos jy + cos x sin jy. Using cos jy = cosh y and sin jy = j sinh y gives sin x cosh y + j cos x sinh y. For x = π/2 the real part is cosh y, which grows without bound as |y| increases, so |sin z| can exceed 1.
s: Compound angle: sin(x+jy) = sin x cos jy + cos x sin jy
Substitute sin jy = j sinh y
Result: sin x cosh y + j cos x sinh y
cosh y is unbounded, so |sin z| can exceed 1, e.g. at x = π/2

units.name: 3.4 Logarithm of a complex number
units.ov: This material defines the logarithm of a complex number by writing z in polar/Euler form, \(z=|z|e^{j\theta}\), so that \(\ln z\) splits into a real part \(\ln|z|\) and an imaginary part \(j\theta\). Because the argument is only defined up to multiples of \(2\pi\), the logarithm is multivalued. The principal value fixes this by restricting \(\theta\) to \((-\pi,\pi]\), and the general solution adds \(2n\pi j\).
must: Principal value: \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j\theta\) with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\); the real part is the log of the modulus, the imaginary part is the argument.
General solution: \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j(\theta\pm2n\pi)\) for integer n (include n=0 and negative n); always give this when asked for 'all values'.
Modulus: \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), real and non-negative; it alone determines the real part of \(\ln z\).

Find \(\theta\) by quadrant: \(\arctan(y/x)\) alone is wrong for \(x<0\); add \(\pi\) (second quadrant) or subtract \(\pi\) (third quadrant), and handle the axes separately (e.g. \(\pm\pi/2\) on the imaginary axis).
Multivalued because \(e^{j\theta}=e^{j(\theta+2n\pi)}\); one z gives infinitely many logs differing by \(2\pi j\).
Worked example: \(\ln(5+j4)=\ln\sqrt{41}+j(0.67\pm2n\pi)\), with \(\theta=\arctan(4/5)\approx0.675\) rad, principal value \(\approx1.857+0.675j\).
Angles must be in radians in \(j\theta\); never use degrees.
Log rules (product, quotient, power) carry over, but with multivalued logs they hold only up to \(2n\pi j\), so be careful with principal values.
Check the argument is within \((-\pi,\pi]\) before quoting the principal value; negative real numbers have \(\theta=\pi\), e.g. \(\ln(-1)=j\pi\).
conn: Euler's form \(z=|z|e^{j\theta}\) links polar representation to the logarithm: take ln of both sides to get \(\ln|z|+j\theta\).
Periodicity of sine and cosine leads directly to the \(\pm2n\pi\) term and hence multivaluedness and the principal-value restriction.
Quadrant determination of the argument (arctan with \(\pm\pi\) corrections) feeds directly into the imaginary part, so errors in the argument propagate to the log.
Complex logs combine with solving equations such as \(e^z=w\), and with powers \(z^w=e^{w\ln z}\), where branch choice matters.
exq: Find the principal value of \(\ln(-3+j4)\), giving the answer to 3 d.p. (note the second-quadrant argument).
Write the general solution of \(\ln(5+j4)\) and state the value for n = 0 and n = 1.
Evaluate \(\ln(-2j)\) and \(\ln(-5)\), stating the principal argument used in each case.
Solve \(e^{z}=1+j\sqrt{3}\) for all complex z, expressing the result in the form \(a+j(b+2n\pi)\).
Explain why \(\ln z\) is multivalued, and show that the principal values of \(\ln(z_1z_2)\) and \(\ln z_1+\ln z_2\) can differ by \(2\pi j\), using \(z_1=z_2=-1+j\) as an example.

notes.t: Logarithm of a complex number
pts: A complex number can be written in polar form using its modulus and argument, so its natural logarithm splits into a real part and an imaginary part.
The principal value of the logarithm uses the real logarithm of the modulus plus j times the principal argument.
Log rules (product, quotient, power) carry over to complex logarithms, as they do for real logarithms.
Because sine and cosine are periodic, adding any integer multiple of 2π to θ leaves z unchanged, so the argument is not unique.
The argument θ must be chosen by the quadrant of (x, y), using arctan(y/x) with corrections of ±π or ±π/2 on the axes.
defs: Modulus of z
The distance of z = x + jy from the origin, |z| = √(x² + y²), always real and non-negative.
Argument of z
The angle θ = arg(x + jy) that the vector from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, chosen according to the quadrant.
Principal value of the logarithm
The standard single-valued form ln z = ln|z| + jθ, using the principal argument of z.
eqs: Natural logarithm of a complex number (principal value)
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = principal argument of z (rad); j = imaginary unit
x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); |z| = modulus (dimensionless)
Euler's form of a complex number
|z| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Use the quadrant rule for θ: arctan(y/x) alone gives the wrong angle for x < 0; add or subtract π accordingly.
Angles are in radians, so the imaginary part jθ must use θ in rad, not degrees.
rq: Why does the logarithm of a complex number have infinitely many values, and which one is the principal value?

Adding any integer multiple of 2π to θ does not change z because cos and sin are periodic; the principal value uses the principal argument, the one in the range −π < θ ≤ π (given by the quadrant rule).
Why is the real part of ln z ln|z| rather than something involving x and y directly?
The modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is the magnitude, and ln of a product or power reduces to sums of logs of moduli; the imaginary part only carries the angle, so the real part depends only on |z|.
What if x = 0 and y = 0 — could you still compute θ?
No. The argument is undefined at the origin because there is no direction from the origin, so ln z is not defined for z = 0.

notes.t: Logarithm of a complex number
pts: The complex logarithm is a multivalued function, so one input z gives infinitely many values of ln z.
The general solution adds the angle term j(θ ± 2nπ) for integer n, reflecting the periodicity of the argument.
The principal value is obtained by restricting the argument to a single branch, giving a unique answer.
The principal argument is restricted to the interval (−π, π], which fixes which value of arg z is used.
defs: Multivalued function
A function that assigns more than one output to a single input; for the complex logarithm each z yields infinitely many values of ln z differing by multiples of 2πj.
Principal value of ln z
The single value of the complex logarithm obtained by taking the argument in the range −π < arg z ≤ π, written ln z = ln|z| + j arg z.
eqs: General solution of the complex logarithm (all branches)
z = complex number (dimensionless); \(|z|\) = modulus of z (dimensionless); \(\theta\) = argument of z (rad); n = integer branch index (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Principal value of the complex logarithm
z = complex number (dimensionless); \(|z|\) = modulus of z (dimensionless); \(\arg z\) = principal argument of z (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Forgetting that ln z is multivalued: always state the general solution or specify the branch used.
Using arg z outside (−π, π] for the principal value; check the range before writing ln|z| + j arg z.
rq: Why does adding 2nπ to the argument leave the value of z unchanged, and what does this imply for ln z?
Because angles differing by 2π describe the same point in the complex plane, so \(e^{j(θ+2nπ)}\) = \(e^{jθ}\); hence ln z acquires the extra term j·2nπ, giving infinitely many logarithms.
Why is the restriction −π < arg z ≤ π needed for the principal value?
Without a fixed range the argument could take any value differing by 2π, so the logarithm would not be a single well-defined function; the interval selects exactly one branch.

notes.t: Logarithm of a complex number
pts: Write the complex number in polar/exponential form first; the modulus gives the real part of the log.
The log of z splits into ln|z| (real part) plus j times the argument θ (imaginary part).
The principal value uses the principal argument θ between −π and π.
Adding multiples of 2nπ gives the general solution, since the argument is only defined up to 2π.
defs: Principal value of ln z
The single value of the complex logarithm obtained using the principal argument θ of z, giving ln z = ln|z| + jθ.
General solution of ln z
All values of the complex logarithm, obtained by adding 2nπj for integer n to the principal value.
eqs: z = complex number; |z| = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad)
tips: Mistake: forgetting the ±2nπ term when asked for the general solution; the principal value alone is not the full answer.
Check the argument lies in the principal range (−π, π] before reading off θ, or the imaginary part will be wrong.
rq: Why does the logarithm of a complex number have infinitely many values?
Because the argument θ is only defined up to multiples of 2π, so adding 2nπj for any integer n gives another valid logarithm.
Why is the real part of ln z equal to ln|z| rather than |z|?
Because the log of a product becomes a sum, and the modulus is the magnitude; the real part is the natural log of that magnitude.

xq.q: For \(z=-3+j4\), find the magnitude of the principal value of \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j\arg z\), where \(-\pi<\arg z\le\pi\) in radians. That is, find \(\sqrt{(\mathrm{Re}\ln z)^2+(\mathrm{Im}\ln z)^2}\). Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
s: z is in the second quadrant: arg z = π - arctan(4/3) = 3.1416 - 0.9273 = 2.2143 rad

xq.q: What is the principal argument of \(z=-2-j2\), in radians?
xq.w: z is in the third quadrant, so arg z = arctan(1) - π = -3π/4 on the principal range (-π, π]; arctan alone gives π/4, the wrong sign gives 3π/4, and 5π/4 lies outside the principal range.
s: x < 0 and y < 0, so subtract π: -3π/4

xq.q: Find the principal value and the general solution of \(\ln(-5)\). Explain why the complex logarithm is multivalued.
xq.a: For z = -5, |z| = 5 and arg z = π, so the principal value is ln 5 + jπ = 1.609 + j3.142. The general solution is ln 5 + j(π ± 2nπ) with n an integer. The logarithm is multivalued because z = |z|\(e^{jθ}\) is unchanged when 2nπ is added to θ, so infinitely many logarithms differ by 2πj.
s: |z| = 5, so the real part is ln 5 = 1.609
arg(-5) = π, which is in (-π, π], so the principal value is 1.609 + j3.142
General solution: ln 5 + j(π ± 2nπ), n an integer
The argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π, hence ln z is multivalued

units.name: 3.5 Powers of complex numbers and De Moivre's theorem
units.ov: This material covers De Moivre's theorem, which gives integer powers of a complex number by raising the modulus to the power n and multiplying the argument by n. It follows from the product rule (moduli multiply, arguments add) applied repeatedly, and it is equivalent to the exponential form \(z^n=r^ne^{jn\theta}\) because \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\). The standard method is: Cartesian to polar, apply the theorem, then convert back to Cartesian.
must: De Moivre: \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)\) for integer \(n\), where \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\)
Exponential form: \(z=re^{j\theta}\Rightarrow z^n=r^ne^{jn\theta}\), using \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\)
The modulus is raised to the power \(n\) (\(r^n\)); the argument is multiplied by \(n\) (\(n\theta\)). Do not swap these.
Convert \(a+jb\) to polar first: \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), and \(\theta=\arctan(b/a)\) with the quadrant checked. The theorem does not apply directly to Cartesian form.
Product rule: \(z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)]\). Repeating it gives the power rule, so squaring squares the modulus and doubles the argument.
Keep angle units consistent. Use radians in the exponential form and when evaluating cos and sin on a calculator.
Final step: evaluate \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\) to return to \(a+jb\). Simplify exact values where possible (e.g. at multiples of \(\pi/6\) or \(\pi/4\)).
Reduce \(n\theta\) by multiples of \(2\pi\) to a principal value (\(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\)) when stating the argument.
conn: Cartesian to polar conversion (finding \(r\) and the correct quadrant for \(\theta\)) is the first step of every De Moivre power question.
The exponential form \(re^{j\theta}\) links De Moivre to Euler's formula, and the power rule becomes \((e^{j\theta})^n=e^{jn\theta}\).
The product rule for multiplication leads to the power rule, and also to division (moduli divide, arguments subtract) and to negative powers.

De Moivre is the basis for finding roots of complex numbers, and for trigonometric identities such as \(\cos3\theta\) and \(\sin3\theta\), by expanding the binomial and equating real and imaginary parts.
exq: Express \(z=1+j\sqrt3\) in polar form and use De Moivre's theorem to find \(z^6\) in Cartesian form.
Evaluate \((\sqrt3-j)^5\), giving the answer in both polar form and the form \(a+jb\).
Use exponential form to calculate \((2e^{j\pi/6})^4\) and give the result as \(a+jb\).
Find \((-1+j)^{8}\), taking care over the quadrant of the argument and the \(r^n\) calculation.
Use De Moivre's theorem with \(n=3\) to derive expressions for \(\cos3\theta\) and \(\sin3\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\).

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers: De Moivre's theorem
pts: De Moivre's theorem gives the nth power of a complex number written in polar form by raising the modulus to n and multiplying the argument by n.
In polar form a complex number z with modulus r and argument θ is written as r(cos θ + j sin θ), so its nth power keeps the same angle structure with nθ.
Using exponential form z = \(re^{jθ}\), raising to the power n simply multiplies the modulus by \(r^{n}\) and the exponent by n, giving \(z^{n}\) = \(r^{n}\) \(e^{j(nθ)}\).
The two forms are equivalent because \(e^{jθ}\) = cos θ + j sin θ, so the polar and exponential results agree.
defs: De Moivre's theorem
For a complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) and integer n, \(z^{n}\) = \(r^{n}\)(cos nθ + j sin nθ).
eqs: De Moivre's theorem in polar form (nth power of a complex number)
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Exponential form of a complex number
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
z = complex number; r = modulus; θ = argument (rad); n = integer power
tips: The formula applies with θ in radians when using the exponential form; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong angles.
Remember the modulus is raised to the power n (\(r^{n}\)), not multiplied by n; the argument is multiplied by n, not raised to n.
rq: Why does raising z to the power n multiply the argument by n rather than adding n to it?
Because \(z^{n}\) = \(r^{n}\) \(e^{jθ}\) multiplied n times, and exponents add when bases are multiplied: \(e^{jθ}\)·\(e^{jθ}\)… gives \(e^{jnθ}\), so the angle accumulates as nθ.
What happens to the modulus when you raise a complex number to a power n?
It becomes \(r^{n}\), since each multiplication multiplies the moduli together.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers and De Moivre's theorem
pts: Squaring a complex number squares its modulus and doubles its argument.
Multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
Repeating the product rule gives the power rule: the modulus is raised to n and the argument is multiplied by n.
defs: De Moivre's theorem
For any complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) and integer n, zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + j sin nθ).
eqs: Product of two complex numbers in polar form
De Moivre's theorem (power of a complex number)
z = complex number; r = |z| modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless)
tips: Angles must be in consistent units (radians or degrees) when applying nθ; mixing them gives wrong results.
Apply De Moivre only to polar form z = r(cos θ + j sin θ); it does not directly apply to Cartesian a + jb without converting first.
rq: Why does the argument get multiplied by n while the modulus gets raised to the power n?
Multiplying moduli is multiplicative (rⁿ), while multiplying complex numbers adds their arguments, so n copies add nθ.
What happens to z² if |z| = 1?
Its modulus stays 1, so z² = cos 2θ + j sin 2θ, a point on the unit circle at angle 2θ.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers and De Moivre's theorem
pts: Write the complex number in polar form, z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), finding r and θ first.
Raise the modulus to the power n and multiply the argument by n to get the power of a complex number.
Convert the final polar result back to Cartesian form, a + jb, using the cos and sin values of the angle.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem: power of a complex number in polar form
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Use the modulus r = √(a²+b²), not r², when raising to a power: (√10)^3 = (10)^{3/2}, not \(10^{3.}\)
Ensure the angle θ is in radians when using cos and sin on a calculator; a degree/radian mix-up gives a wrong answer.
rq: Why is the modulus raised to the power 3 in this example, giving (10)^{3/2}, rather than just multiplying the argument by 3?
The modulus r = √10 is raised to n = 3, so \(r^{3}\) = (√10)^3 = (10)^{3/2}; the argument is multiplied by n, which is a separate operation applied to θ.
What would change in the result if the argument were not reduced into the principal range before multiplying by 3?
Nothing in the final point would change, because cos and sin are periodic with period 2π, but the intermediate angle would be larger and harder to check.

xq.q: Let \(z = 1 + j\sqrt{3}\). Using De Moivre's theorem, find the real part of \(z^{6}\).
xq.a: 64 (\(z^{6}\) = 64, purely real)

xq.q: The complex number \(z = \sqrt{3} + j\) is raised to the power 3. Which is \(z^{3}\)?
xq.w: r = 2, θ = π/6, so z³ = 8(cos π/2 + j sin π/2) = 8j; the traps are cubing r wrongly as 2·3 = 6 or 3 (giving 2j or 24j-type errors) and sign errors.

xq.q: Show using De Moivre's theorem that \((-1 + j)^{4} = -4\). State the modulus and argument you use and explain why the angle must be chosen in the correct quadrant.
xq.a: z = -1 + j has r = √2 and lies in the second quadrant, so θ = 3π/4 (arctan(-1) = -π/4 would be wrong, add π). Then z⁴ = (√2)⁴(cos 3π + j sin 3π) = 4(-1 + 0j) = -4. Using -π/4 would give +4.
s: z⁴ = r⁴(cos 4θ + j sin 4θ) with r⁴ = 4

units.name: 3.6 nth roots of complex numbers
units.ov: This material finds the n roots of a complex number \(z\), meaning the solutions of \(w^n=z\). It uses two routes. The algebraic route factorises \(w^3-j=0\) and solves the factors. The geometric route places the roots at equal angles \(2\pi/n\) apart on a circle of radius \(|z|^{1/n}\). Both give the same answers for the cube roots of \(j\), and polar form generalises to any \(n\).
must: A non-zero \(z\) has exactly \(n\) distinct nth roots, which are the solutions of \(w^n=z\).
General formula: for \(z=re^{j\theta}\), \(w_k=r^{1/n}e^{j(\theta+2\pi k)/n}\) for \(k=0,\dots,n-1\).
The roots are equally spaced by \(\Delta\theta=2\pi/n\) and lie at the vertices of a regular n-gon on the circle \(|w|=r^{1/n}\).
Cube roots of \(j\): \(|j|=1\) and \(\arg j=\pi/2\), so the roots are \(e^{j\pi/6}\), \(e^{j5\pi/6}\), \(e^{-j\pi/2}\). Equivalently, \(\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\) and \(-j\).
Algebraic method: \(w^3-j=(w+j)(w^2-jw-1)\). The linear factor gives \(w=-j\), and the quadratic formula gives \(w=\frac{j\pm\sqrt3}{2}\).
Use \(j^2=-1\) carefully: \((-j)^2=-1\), so the discriminant is \(-1+4=3\).
Modulus and argument: \(|w|=|z|^{1/n}\) and \(\arg w=(\arg z+2\pi k)/n\). Keep arguments in \((-\pi,\pi]\) and be consistent about radians versus degrees.
Check every root by cubing it, or by confirming that \(n\theta_k\equiv\arg z \pmod{2\pi}\) and \(|w|^n=|z|\).

Caution on the notes: the notes call \(-j\) the principal root, but the principal root is the one with the smallest argument magnitude from \(\arg z/n\). For \(j^{1/3}\) that is \(e^{j\pi/6}\). \(-j\) is just one of the three roots.
conn: Polar/exponential form and De Moivre's theorem: converting \(z\) to \(re^{j\theta}\) turns root-finding into dividing the angle by \(n\) and adding \(2\pi k/n\).
Polynomial equations and the fundamental theorem of algebra: \(w^n=z\) has \(n\) roots, which links to factorisation and the quadratic formula with complex coefficients.
Roots of unity and the Argand diagram: all roots are rotations of one another, so one root can be found and the rest generated by multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/n}\).
Engineering applications: phasors, AC analysis and vibration (complex characteristic equations) use roots in rectangular and polar form.
exq: Find all cube roots of \(j\). Give them in both Cartesian and polar form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Solve \(w^4=-16\). Express the roots in the form \(a+jb\) and show that they form a square.
Factorise \(w^3+8=0\) as a linear factor times a quadratic. Solve it algebraically and confirm the roots using polar form.
Find the fifth roots of \(1+j\) in the form \(re^{j\theta}\) with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\), and state the angular separation between roots.
Show that \(w=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\) satisfies \(w^3=j\). Hence find the other two cube roots by rotating through \(2\pi/3\).

notes.t: nth roots of complex numbers (heuristic approach)
pts: The nth root of z is the complex number w satisfying \(w^{n}\) = z, so the problem becomes solving a polynomial equation.
Rewrite \(w^{3}\) = j as \(w^{3}\) − j = 0 and factor it to split the solutions into simpler equations.
Factoring gives a linear factor (w + j) and a quadratic factor; each factor set to zero yields roots.
The quadratic factor is solved with the quadratic formula, treating j as the imaginary unit with \(j^{2}\) = −1.
defs: nth root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that \(w^{n}\) = z; there are n such roots for z ≠ 0.
eqs: w = complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Remember \(j^{2}\) = −1 when squaring terms such as (−j)^2, which equals −1, not +1.
Do not forget that an nth root of a complex number has n distinct solutions, not just the principal one.
rq: Why does \(w^{3}\) − j = 0 have three solutions rather than one?
A degree-3 polynomial has three roots over the complex numbers (fundamental theorem of algebra); the factorisation shows one linear root (w = −j) and two from the quadratic.
Why is w = −j a solution even though it is not written as a square root?
Substituting gives (−j)^3 = −\(j^{3}\) = −(−j) = j, so it satisfies \(w^{3}\) = j.

notes.t: nth roots of complex numbers (geometric interpretation of \(j^{1/3}\))
pts: The three cube roots of j are all unit-modulus complex numbers, spaced evenly around the unit circle.
Each successive root is obtained by adding the angle 2π/3 to the previous one, giving rotations of 120° between roots.
In polar form the roots are written as \(e^{jθ}\), so their arguments are the angles measured from the positive real axis.
Geometrically, the roots of \(j^{1/3}\) = w lie at the vertices of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle.
The principal root \(w_{1}\) = −j sits at argument −π/2, and the others follow by rotating it through multiples of 2π/3.
defs: Argument of a complex number
The angle θ = arg(z) measured from the positive real axis to the vector representing z in the complex plane, usually taken in (−π, π].
Modulus of a complex number
The distance |z| of the point z from the origin in the complex plane; for a root of unity-type result on the unit circle, |w| = 1.
eqs: Polar (exponential) form of a unit complex number used for roots
\(w_{k}\) = k-th root (dimensionless); θ_k = argument of \(w_{k}\) (rad); j = imaginary unit
Angular spacing between successive nth roots
Δθ = angle between adjacent roots (rad); n = order of the root (dimensionless)
tips: Check the modulus: when taking roots of j (|j| = 1), every root has modulus 1, so do not forget to state it.
Keep arguments in the principal range when reading a root off the diagram; adding 2π/3 may give angles like 5π/6 that need no further reduction, but mixing degrees and radians is a common error.
rq: Why do the three cube roots of j lie exactly 120° apart rather than at arbitrary angles?
Because they are obtained by repeatedly multiplying by \(e^{j2π/3}\), and the nth roots of a complex number are always separated by 2π/n around the circle.
What would change in the picture if you asked for the square roots of j instead?
There would be only two roots, separated by 180° (π) and both on the unit circle, forming a diameter instead of a triangle.

xq.q: The three cube roots of \(j\) all have modulus 1. If one root has argument \(-\pi/2\), what are the arguments of the other two?
xq.w: Roots are spaced 2π/3 apart: -π/2 + 2π/3 = π/6 and π/6 + 2π/3 = 5π/6; the traps are using spacing π/2 or π/3.

xq.q: Show that \(w = -j\) is a cube root of \(j\), then use the factorisation \(w^{3} - j = (w + j)(w^{2} - jw - 1)\) to find the other two cube roots.

units.name: 3.7 Preview of Lecture 4
units.ov: The notes are only a short preview of Lecture 4. It covers De Moivre's theorem (the second part of section 3.3.1), then how to express powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles (section 3.3.2). The two connect because De Moivre's theorem, \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\), links powers of complex numbers to multiple angles. That link gives identities for \(\cos^n\theta\), \(\sin^n\theta\), \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\). The notes give no worked detail, so the points below rely on standard results for these topics and should be checked against the full lecture notes.
must: De Moivre's theorem: \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\), and the equivalent form \((e^{i\theta})^n = e^{in\theta}\)
Polar form: \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = re^{i\theta}\), so \(z^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)\)

Multiple-angle formulae: expand \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\) with the binomial theorem and equate real and imaginary parts to get \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\) as polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\)
Define \(z = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\). Then \(z^n + z^{-n} = 2\cos n\theta\) and \(z^n - z^{-n} = 2i\sin n\theta\)

Powers of trig functions: write \((2\cos\theta)^n = (z + z^{-1})^n\) or \((2i\sin\theta)^n = (z - z^{-1})^n\), expand, and pair terms \(z^k\) with \(z^{-k}\) to get sums of \(\cos k\theta\) or \(\sin k\theta\)
Know the binomial coefficients (Pascal's triangle) and apply them accurately, including the signs and powers of \(i\)
Use \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) to convert between forms, for example writing \(\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\)
Roots of complex numbers: \(z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n} + i\sin\frac{\theta + 2\pi k}{n}\right]\) for \(k = 0,\dots,n-1\)
The reduction identities are useful for integrating powers of trig functions, e.g. \(\cos^2\theta = \tfrac12(1 + \cos 2\theta)\)
conn: De Moivre's theorem and the binomial expansion: expanding \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\) and equating real and imaginary parts gives the multiple-angle formulae
\(z^n \pm z^{-n}\) and the exponential form: these give the expressions for \(\cos^n\theta\) and \(\sin^n\theta\) as sums of multiple angles, which is the reverse of the multiple-angle expansion
Powers-to-multiple-angles identities and integration: reducing \(\cos^n\theta\) to a sum of \(\cos k\theta\) makes \(\int\cos^n\theta\,d\theta\) straightforward
De Moivre's theorem and roots of unity: solving \(z^n = w\) uses the polar form, and the roots lie at equal angles on a circle in the Argand diagram
exq: Use De Moivre's theorem to show that \(\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\) and find a similar expression for \(\sin 3\theta\).
Express \(\cos^4\theta\) in terms of \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\cos 4\theta\), then use the result to evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta\,d\theta\).
Express \(\sin^5\theta\) as a combination of \(\sin\theta\), \(\sin 3\theta\) and \(\sin 5\theta\).
Evaluate \((1 + i\sqrt3)^8\) in the form \(a + ib\) using polar form and De Moivre's theorem.
Find all cube roots of \(-8\) and plot them on an Argand diagram. Then express \(\cos 5\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) only.

notes.t: Preview of Lecture 4: De Moivre's theorem and powers of trigonometric functions
pts: Lecture 4 continues with De Moivre's theorem, the second part of section 3.3.1.
Lecture 4 then covers expressing powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles, section 3.3.2.

units.name: 4.1 Recap of complex numbers and circular/hyperbolic links
units.ov: This material recaps complex numbers in Cartesian, polar and exponential form (modulus, quadrant-correct argument, Euler's formula). It then uses these forms for multiplication, division, powers (De Moivre) and the multi-valued logarithm, and links circular and hyperbolic functions through imaginary arguments. Everything rests on \( e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta \): polar form, De Moivre and the logarithm all follow from it.
must: Modulus and argument: \( |z|=r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \), and \( \theta=\arg z \) is measured from the positive real axis
Quadrant correction of the argument: \( \arctan(y/x) \) is only correct for \( x>0 \); add \( \pi \) if \( x<0, y\ge0 \), subtract \( \pi \) if \( x<0, y<0 \); \( x=0 \) gives \( \pm\pi/2 \)
Euler's formula: \( e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta \), so \( z=re^{j\theta}=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta) \)
Products and quotients in polar form: moduli multiply or divide, arguments add or subtract, \( z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)] \)
De Moivre's theorem: \( z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta) \), i.e. power the modulus and multiply the argument by n
Complex logarithm: \( \ln z=\ln|z|+j(\theta\pm2n\pi) \); the principal value uses n = 0, and the \( 2n\pi \) term must be kept when all values are asked for
Circular-hyperbolic links: \( \cos jx=\cosh x \) and \( \sin jx=j\sinh x \) (do not drop the j)
Work in radians throughout for polar form, Euler, De Moivre and logarithms unless told otherwise
Always sketch or locate the point in the Argand plane to check the argument and the quadrant
conn: Euler's formula underlies polar form, De Moivre's theorem and the complex logarithm: \( \ln(re^{j\theta})=\ln r+j\theta \)
The quadrant-corrected argument feeds into every polar calculation, so a wrong argument gives wrong products, powers and logs
De Moivre with fractional n gives roots, and the \( 2n\pi \) periodicity generates all the distinct roots, as with the multi-valued log
Writing \( \cos jx \) and \( \sin jx \) via Euler's exponentials shows the hyperbolic links; these can be combined with \( \sin(a+jb) \) expansions to separate real and imaginary parts
exq: Express \( z=-3+4j \) and \( w=-1-j \) in polar form, giving the arguments in radians in the correct quadrants, then find \( zw \) and \( z/w \) in polar form.
Use De Moivre's theorem to evaluate \( (1-j\sqrt{3})^6 \), giving the answer in Cartesian form.
Find all values of \( \ln(-2+2j) \) and state the principal value.
Show using Euler's formula that \( \cos jx=\cosh x \) and \( \sin jx=j\sinh x \), then evaluate \( \sin(j\ln 2) \) and \( \cos(j\ln 3) \).
Write \( z=2e^{j\pi/3} \) in Cartesian form and find \( z^5 \) and \( \ln z \).

notes.t: Modulus, argument and polar form of complex numbers
pts: The modulus of a complex number is its distance from the origin in the Argand plane, found from its real and imaginary parts.
The argument is the angle from the positive real axis, and its value depends on the quadrant, so the arctan result must be corrected by adding or subtracting π.
Polar form writes a complex number using its modulus and argument, which makes multiplication and division simpler.
In polar form, moduli multiply and arguments add when multiplying; for division, moduli divide and arguments subtract.
Euler's formula links the exponential form to trigonometry, giving the compact exponential form of a complex number.
defs: Modulus
The modulus |z| of a complex number z = x + jy is its distance from the origin, equal to √(x² + y²).
Argument
The argument of a complex number is the angle θ between the positive real axis and the line joining the origin to the point representing the number, measured with the correct quadrant.
Polar form
The representation z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) of a complex number using its modulus r and argument θ.
eqs: x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless)
\theta = \arg(x+jy)=\begin{cases}\arctan(y/x) & x>0\\ \arctan(y/x)+\pi & x<0,\ y\ge 0\\ \arctan(y/x)-\pi & x<0,\ y<0\\ +\pi/2 & x=0,\ y>0\\ -\pi/2 & x=0,\ y<0\end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x = real part; y = imaginary part
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
Product of complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
Quotient of complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
tips: Check the quadrant before finalising the argument: a calculator's arctan(y/x) gives the wrong angle when x < 0, so add or subtract π.
Angles must be in radians when used in Euler's formula and polar form unless the question specifies otherwise; mixing degrees and radians is a common error.
rq: Why must the argument formula be adjusted by ±π depending on the quadrant, rather than using arctan(y/x) alone?
Because arctan returns angles only between −π/2 and π/2, so points in the left half-plane (x < 0) would be given the wrong angle; adding or subtracting π places them in the correct quadrant.
Why does dividing in polar form subtract the arguments rather than add them?
Dividing by z₂ is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal, whose argument is −θ₂, so the arguments combine as θ₁ − θ₂ while moduli divide.
What happens to the argument if x = 0 and y = 0?
The argument is undefined, since the origin has no direction from the positive real axis.

notes.t: Circular and hyperbolic links, complex logarithm and De Moivre's theorem
pts: Circular functions of imaginary arguments equal hyperbolic functions, with a factor j on sin and sinh.
The complex logarithm is multi-valued: its imaginary part repeats every 2π, so the argument carries ±2nπ.
De Moivre's theorem raises a complex number to a power by powering the modulus and multiplying the argument by n.
defs: Logarithm of a complex number
For z with modulus |z| and argument θ, ln z = ln|z| + j(θ ± 2nπ), n ∈ ℕ; the principal value uses n = 0.
eqs: x = real argument (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
x = real argument (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer ∈ ℕ (dimensionless)
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus \(|z|\) (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless)
tips: Forgetting the factor j in sin jx = j sinh x is a common error; sinh alone is not equal to sin jx.
Angles in De Moivre and the logarithm must be in radians, and the ±2nπ term must not be dropped when asked for all values.
rq: Why does the complex logarithm have infinitely many values, and what fixes it to one?
Adding any multiple of 2π to the argument θ gives the same point in the complex plane, so ln z has terms ±2nπ; choosing n = 0 gives the principal value.
Why does the sine link need a factor j but the cosine link does not?
sin jx = j sinh x because the Taylor series of sin has odd powers, each bringing a factor j³ or j, while cos has even powers that give real signs matching cosh.

xq.q: Express \(z = -3 - j3\) in polar form and find its argument in radians in the range \((-\pi, \pi]\).
s: x<0, y<0 so subtract π: θ = π/4 - π = -3π/4 = -2.356 rad

xq.q: Which is the correct value of \(\sin(j2)\)?
xq.a: \(j\sinh 2\)
o: \(\sinh 2\)
\(j\sinh 2\)
\(-j\sinh 2\)
\(j\sin 2\)
xq.w: sin jx = j sinh x; the trap is dropping the factor j or using sin instead of sinh.

xq.q: \(z_1 = 6(\cos 50° + j\sin 50°)\) and \(z_2 = 2(\cos 20° + j\sin 20°)\). Find the modulus and argument in degrees of \(z_1/z_2\); give the argument.
xq.a: 30° (modulus 3)

units.name: 4.2 De Moivre for rational powers and heuristic root finding
units.ov: This material defines rational powers of complex numbers as \(z^{m/n}=\sqrt[n]{z^m}\), which gives n distinct values, and shows a heuristic way to find nth roots by solving \(w^n=z\) as a polynomial, using the cube roots of j as the example. It leads to the polar-form De Moivre method, which gives all roots systematically, and then to powers of trig functions and multiple angles.
must: An nth root of z is any w with \(w^n=z\); for \(z\neq0\) there are exactly n distinct roots.
\(z^{m/n}\) is defined as \(\sqrt[n]{z^m}\) and has n distinct values, so state all of them.
Do not simply take \(z^m\) to the power \(1/n\) as one value: the principal root alone misses the other roots.
Heuristic method: write \(w^n-z=0\), factor it, and solve each factor (linear, then quadratic formula).
Cube roots of j: \(w^3-j=0\) factors with the linear factor \((w+j)\), so \(w=-j\) is a root; the quadratic factor gives \(w=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\).
Always use \(j^2=-1\); for example \((-j)^2=-1\), not +1, which matters inside the discriminant.
Check answers by cubing: \(\left(\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac j2\right)^3=j\) and \((-j)^3=j\).
The n roots of z lie equally spaced on a circle of radius \(|z|^{1/n}\), separated by angle \(2\pi/n\), which motivates the polar/De Moivre method.
Heuristic factoring works only for simple cases; for general z, use polar form and De Moivre.
conn: Polar form and De Moivre's theorem generalise the heuristic factoring: the same cube roots of j come out as angles \(\pi/6,\,5\pi/6,\,3\pi/2\) on the unit circle.
Rational powers combine roots with integer powers: compute \(z^m\) in polar form, then take the n roots, giving n values.
Roots of unity and polynomial factorisation: solving \(w^n=z\) links to the fundamental theorem of algebra, with n roots counted via factors and the quadratic formula.
De Moivre's theorem for roots leads to powers of trig functions and multiple-angle formulae, which are often tested in the same question.
exq: Find all cube roots of j by factorising \(w^3-j=0\), give them in Cartesian form, and verify one by cubing.
Evaluate \(z^{2/3}\) for \(z=1+j\): give all distinct values in polar form with modulus and argument.
Solve \(w^4=-16\) and plot the roots on an Argand diagram, stating the spacing between them.
Explain why \(z^{1/n}\) taken as a principal value is insufficient, using the cube roots of j as an example.
Show that \((w+j)\) is a factor of \(w^3-j\), find the quadratic factor, and solve it to obtain the remaining two roots.

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem (2): powers with rational exponents
pts: For a rational exponent m/n, the power \(z^{m/n}\) is defined as the n-th root of \(z^{m.}\)
The lecture poses the question of how to evaluate \(z^{m/n}\) once it is written as an n-th root of \(z^{m}\), which is the starting point for using polar form and De Moivre's theorem.
The page lists the next topic, powers of trigonometric functions and multiple angles, which follows from De Moivre's theorem.
eqs: Rational power of a complex number written as an n-th root
z = complex number (dimensionless); m = integer exponent (dimensionless); n = positive integer root index (dimensionless)
tips: Remember that \(z^{m/n}\) generally has n distinct values, not a single value, so state all roots when asked to evaluate it.
Do not treat \sqrt[n]{\(z^{m}\)} as \(z^m\) to the power \(1/n\) without checking the branch: the principal root may not give all the values.
rq: Why can \(z^{m/n}\) be written as the n-th root of \(z^{m}\), and why does this make the answer multi-valued?
Because the rational exponent m/n is defined through the n-th root of \(z^{m}\); an n-th root of a non-zero complex number has n distinct values, so \(z^{m/n}\) has n values.

notes.t: nth roots of complex numbers (heuristic approach)
pts: The nth root of z is the complex number w satisfying \(w^{n}\) = z, so the problem becomes solving a polynomial equation.
Rewrite \(w^{3}\) = j as \(w^{3}\) − j = 0 and factor it to split the solutions into simpler equations.
Factoring gives a linear factor (w + j) and a quadratic factor; each factor set to zero yields roots.
The quadratic factor is solved with the quadratic formula, treating j as the imaginary unit with \(j^{2}\) = −1.
defs: nth root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that \(w^{n}\) = z; there are n such roots for z ≠ 0.
eqs: w = complex root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Remember \(j^{2}\) = −1 when squaring terms such as (−j)^2, which equals −1, not +1.
Do not forget that an nth root of a complex number has n distinct solutions, not just the principal one.
rq: Why does \(w^{3}\) − j = 0 have three solutions rather than one?
A degree-3 polynomial has three roots over the complex numbers (fundamental theorem of algebra); the factorisation shows one linear root (w = −j) and two from the quadratic.
Why is w = −j a solution even though it is not written as a square root?
Substituting gives (−j)^3 = −\(j^{3}\) = −(−j) = j, so it satisfies \(w^{3}\) = j.

xq.q: Find the cube roots of \(w^3 = j\) by the heuristic factorisation method: \(w^3 - j = 0\) factors as \((w + j)(w^2 - jw - 1) = 0\), where \(j^2=-1\). Solve the quadratic factor with the quadratic formula, and hence give the real part of the root in the first quadrant (dimensionless).
In the heuristic solution of \(w^3 = j\), the quadratic factor is \(w^2 - jw - 1\) and its discriminant is \((-j)^2 - 4(1)(-1)\). What is its value?
xq.w: Since \(j^2=-1\), \((-j)^2=-1\) and \(-1+4=3\); the trap is taking \((-j)^2=+1\), giving 5.

xq.q: Explain why \(z^{m/n}\) generally has n distinct values rather than one, and illustrate by finding all values of \(1^{1/3}\) in the form \(e^{j\theta}\) with \(\theta\) in radians.
xq.a: \(z^{m/n}\) is the n-th root of \(z^m\), i.e. any w with \(w^n=z^m\), and the equation \(w^n=c\) has n solutions for \(c\neq0\). For \(1^{1/3}\): \(w^3=1\), arguments \(2\pi k/3\), giving \(1, e^{j2\pi/3}, e^{-j2\pi/3}\).
s: Definition as n-th root of \(z^m\), so solves \(w^n=z^m\)

units.name: 4.3 Cube roots of j: geometry and De Moivre method
units.ov: This material finds the three cube roots of \(j\) by two routes: a geometric picture (equally spaced points on the unit circle) and an algebraic De Moivre calculation solving \(w^3=j\). Both give \(|w|=1\) and arguments \(\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6,\ -\pi/2\), which form an equilateral triangle on the unit circle. The key idea is that taking roots divides the argument by n and adds the 2π/n spacing from the 2πk ambiguity.
must: The three cube roots are \(e^{j\pi/6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\), \(e^{j5\pi/6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{j}{2}\), and \(e^{-j\pi/2}=-j\)
De Moivre: \(w^n=|w|^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)\), so moduli are raised to the power n and arguments multiplied by n
Modulus: \(|w|^3=|j|=1\) so \(|w|=1\); always state it
The roots are spaced by \(\Delta\theta=2\pi/n=120^\circ\) and form an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle
Only n distinct nth roots exist; k beyond 0..n−1 repeats points
Equate \(\cos3\phi=0,\ \sin3\phi=1\) to get \(3\phi=\pi/2+2\pi k\), and divide the whole expression, including \(2\pi k\), by 3
Use radians consistently and keep arguments in \((-\pi,\pi]\) (e.g. \(-\pi/2\) rather than \(3\pi/2\))
Check answers by cubing: \((-j)^3=-j^3=j\)
conn: Roots of j link polar/exponential form to the unit circle diagram: algebraic angles map directly to vertices of a regular polygon
Solving \(z^n=a\) generalises to any complex a: take \(r^{1/n}\) for modulus and \((\theta+2\pi k)/n\) for the arguments
Converting between polar and Cartesian form to give the roots as \(a+jb\), then factorising \(w^3-j\) using the known roots
Cube roots of j connect to roots of unity through rotation: multiply the principal root by \(e^{j2\pi k/3}\)
exq: Find all solutions of \(w^3=j\) using De Moivre's theorem, giving answers in polar and Cartesian form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Show that the three cube roots of j sum to zero and state the geometric reason.
Solve \(z^3=-8j\) and state the modulus and arguments of each root, marking them on the complex plane.
Given that \(w_1=-j\) is one cube root of j, find the other two by rotating through \(2\pi/3\), and verify by cubing one of them.
Explain why \(k=3\) gives no new root of \(w^3=j\), and find the fourth roots of j for comparison.

notes.t: nth roots of complex numbers (geometric interpretation of \(j^{1/3}\))
pts: The three cube roots of j are all unit-modulus complex numbers, spaced evenly around the unit circle.
Each successive root is obtained by adding the angle 2π/3 to the previous one, giving rotations of 120° between roots.
In polar form the roots are written as \(e^{jθ}\), so their arguments are the angles measured from the positive real axis.
Geometrically, the roots of \(j^{1/3}\) = w lie at the vertices of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle.
The principal root \(w_{1}\) = −j sits at argument −π/2, and the others follow by rotating it through multiples of 2π/3.
defs: Argument of a complex number
The angle θ = arg(z) measured from the positive real axis to the vector representing z in the complex plane, usually taken in (−π, π].
Modulus of a complex number
The distance |z| of the point z from the origin in the complex plane; for a root of unity-type result on the unit circle, |w| = 1.
eqs: Polar (exponential) form of a unit complex number used for roots
\(w_{k}\) = k-th root (dimensionless); θ_k = argument of \(w_{k}\) (rad); j = imaginary unit
Angular spacing between successive nth roots
Δθ = angle between adjacent roots (rad); n = order of the root (dimensionless)
tips: Check the modulus: when taking roots of j (|j| = 1), every root has modulus 1, so do not forget to state it.
Keep arguments in the principal range when reading a root off the diagram; adding 2π/3 may give angles like 5π/6 that need no further reduction, but mixing degrees and radians is a common error.
rq: Why do the three cube roots of j lie exactly 120° apart rather than at arbitrary angles?
Because they are obtained by repeatedly multiplying by \(e^{j2π/3}\), and the nth roots of a complex number are always separated by 2π/n around the circle.
What would change in the picture if you asked for the square roots of j instead?
There would be only two roots, separated by 180° (π) and both on the unit circle, forming a diameter instead of a triangle.

notes.t: Cube roots of j using De Moivre's theorem
pts: Write w in polar form, then raise to the 3rd power: moduli cube and arguments triple.
Equate real and imaginary parts of \(w^{3}\) = j with the polar form of j; the modulus gives |w| = 1 since \(cos^{2}\) + \(sin^{2}\) = 1.
Solve cos 3φ = 0, sin 3φ = 1 to get 3φ = π/2 + 2πk, then divide by 3 to obtain distinct roots.
Only three distinct cube roots arise (k = 0, 1, 2); further k values repeat the same points on the unit circle.
Geometrically the three roots are equally spaced by 2π/3 on the unit circle, at angles π/6, 5π/6 and -π/2.
defs: De Moivre's theorem
For w = |w|(cos φ + j sin φ), \(w^{n}\) = |w|^n (cos nφ + j sin nφ) for integer n.
Cube root of j
A complex number w satisfying \(w^{3}\) = j, i.e. w = cube roots of the imaginary unit.
eqs: Argument of the cube roots of j
\phi = argument of w (rad); k = integer index of root (dimensionless)
w = complex number; |w| = modulus (dimensionless); n = integer power; θ = argument (rad)
tips: Forgetting to divide the whole angle 2πk by 3 when solving for φ, leaving the wrong argument.
Mixing up degrees and radians: π/2 must be used consistently as radians when adding 2πk.
rq: Why does taking the modulus of both sides of \(w^{3}\) = j force |w| = 1?
Since |j| = 1, |w|^3 = 1, so |w| = 1 for real positive modulus; the squared-sum identity \(cos^{2}\) + \(sin^{2}\) = 1 gives the same result.
Why are only three roots obtained even though k can be any natural number?
Angles differing by multiples of 2π describe the same point, so k = 3 gives the same root as k = 0; the roots repeat with period 3.

xq.q: The cube roots of \(j\) have unit modulus and arguments \(\phi_k=\frac{1}{3}\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{2\pi k}{3}\), k=0,1,2. Find the real part of the root with k=1 (dimensionless).
Which set gives the arguments (rad) of the three cube roots of \(j\) on the unit circle?
xq.w: Start at \(\pi/6\) (=\(\pi/2\) divided by 3) and add \(2\pi/3\); the trap is not dividing the angle by 3, or listing \(\pi/2\) itself.

xq.q: Use De Moivre's theorem to show that the cube roots of \(j\) all have modulus 1 and find their arguments in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
xq.a: Let \(w=R(\cos\phi+j\sin\phi)\). Then \(w^3=R^3(\cos3\phi+j\sin3\phi)=j\). Squaring and adding real and imaginary parts: \(R^6=1\), so R=1. Then \(\cos3\phi=0,\ \sin3\phi=1\), so \(3\phi=\pi/2+2\pi k\), \(\phi=\pi/6+2\pi k/3\). k=0,1,2 give \(\pi/6, 5\pi/6, 3\pi/2\equiv-\pi/2\).

units.name: 4.4 General nth roots via polar and exponential form
units.ov: This material shows how to find all n solutions of \(w^n = z\) by writing z in polar or exponential form, taking the nth root of the modulus, and dividing the angle (plus \(2\pi k\)) by n. The roots all share the modulus \(r^{1/n}\) and are spaced \(2\pi/n\) apart, so they form a regular n-gon on a circle. This ties together de Moivre's theorem, the periodicity of the argument and Argand-diagram geometry.
must: Roots of \(z = re^{j\theta}\): \(w_k = r^{1/n}e^{j(\theta+2\pi k)/n}\), \(k=0,1,\dots,n-1\)
Equating \(w^n=z\) gives \(R^n = r\) and \(n\phi = \theta + 2\pi k\), so \(R = r^{1/n}\) (real positive) and \(\phi = \theta/n + 2\pi k/n\)
Divide the angle \(\theta\) by n before adding \(2\pi k/n\); forgetting to divide, or forgetting the \(2\pi k\) term (which gives only one root), are the commonest errors
There are exactly n distinct roots for \(z\neq 0\); k beyond \(n-1\) only repeats earlier roots, so never list more than n
All roots have the same modulus \(|z|^{1/n}\) and lie on a circle centred at the origin; only the arguments differ
Consecutive roots differ by the factor \(e^{j2\pi/n}\), i.e. \(w_{k+1}=w_k e^{j2\pi/n}\), an angular step of \(2\pi/n\) (not \(2\pi\))
Joining the roots gives a regular n-gon, e.g. an equilateral triangle for cube roots
First find the correct \(\theta\) in radians (principal argument in \((-\pi,\pi]\)); wrap final angles back into range, e.g. \(3\pi/2 \to -\pi/2\)
Worked cases: cube roots of 1 are \(1, e^{j2\pi/3}, e^{j4\pi/3}\); cube roots of j have modulus 1 and arguments \(\pi/6 + 2\pi k/3\)
Always use radians in exponential formulas; mixing degrees with \(2\pi\) gives wrong roots
conn: De Moivre's theorem \(w^n = R^n(\cos n\phi + j\sin n\phi)\) is the engine for the root formula, and the same polar and exponential conversions are used for powers and products
Periodicity of the argument (\(\theta + 2\pi k\)) explains why exactly n roots exist and why k repeats after \(n-1\)
Argand-diagram geometry: equal angular spacing gives a regular polygon, so one found root plus rotation by \(e^{j2\pi/n}\) yields the rest
Roots of unity link to solving polynomial equations \(w^n = a\) and factorising \(w^n - 1\) into linear and quadratic factors; converting final answers to Cartesian form needs trig values
exq: Find all cube roots of \(j\) (i.e. solve \(w^3 = j\)), give them in exponential form with arguments in \((-\pi,\pi]\) and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Solve \(w^4 = -16\). Give the roots in polar and Cartesian form and state the shape they form.
Write \(z = 1 - j\sqrt{3}\) in exponential form and find all its fifth roots, giving modulus and argument of each.
Given that one cube root of a complex number z is \(2e^{j\pi/9}\), use rotation by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) to find the other two roots and the value of z.
Show that the n roots of \(w^n = z\) all have modulus \(|z|^{1/n}\), that their arguments are in arithmetic progression with step \(2\pi/n\), and explain why \(k=n\) repeats \(k=0\).

notes.t: General nth roots of a complex number via polar form
pts: The nth roots of a unit-modulus number lie on the unit circle and are equally spaced by angle 2π/n.
Each root's argument is the principal angle divided by 3 plus a multiple of 2π over 3, giving distinct roots for k = 0 to |n|−1.
Adding 2πk/3 for successive k rotates the root to the next vertex of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle.
Wrapping angles outside (−π, π] back into range gives the same point, e.g. 3π/2 equals −π/2.
defs: nth root of a complex number
A complex number w such that \(w^{n}\) equals the given number z; for n ≥ 1 there are exactly n distinct nth roots.
Principal argument
The angle φ of a complex number in polar form, usually taken in the interval (−π, π].
eqs: Argument of the k-th nth root of a unit complex number
\phi = argument of root (rad); k = integer index (dimensionless); n = exponent (dimensionless)
tips: Divide the principal angle by n before adding 2πk/n; forgetting to divide the angle is a common error.
Only the first |n| values of k give distinct roots; do not list more than n roots.
rq: Why do the nth roots of a complex number all have the same modulus?
Because if \(w^{n}\) = z with |z| = 1, then |w|^n = 1, so |w| = 1; all roots therefore sit on the same circle.
What if you used k = 3 in the formula?
You get φ = 3π/6 + 2π = 5π/2, which is the same point as π/6; k beyond |n|−1 just repeats existing roots.

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem for roots: \(z^{1/n}\)
pts: To find the n-th root w of z, write w = \(z^{1/n}\) and equate moduli and arguments of \(w^{n}\) and z.
Write w in polar form with |w| = R and arg w = φ; then \(w^{n}\) = \(R^{n}\)(cos nφ + j sin nφ).
Matching real and imaginary parts of \(w^{n}\) and z gives \(R^{n}\) = r and nφ = θ (up to multiples of 2π).
The example \(w^{3}\) = j is solved by rewriting it as w = \(j^{1/3}\), i.e. taking the cube root of j.
defs: Argument of a complex number
The angle θ that z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) makes with the positive real axis, measured in radians.
Modulus of a complex number
The distance r = |z| of z from the origin in the Argand diagram.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for n-th roots (modulus and argument of w)
R = |w| (dimensionless); φ = arg w (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
r = |z| (dimensionless); θ = arg z (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Remember that nφ = θ holds only up to multiples of 2π, so all n roots must be listed by adding 2kπ to θ before dividing by n.
Use radians for arguments in the exponent formulas; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong roots.
rq: Why do we equate both the modulus and the argument when solving \(w^{n}\) = z, rather than just one of them?
A complex number is fixed by both its modulus and argument; equating only one would not determine w uniquely, so \(R^{n}\) = r and nφ = θ must both hold.
Why does the argument of the root come out as θ/n plus multiples of 2π/n rather than just θ/n?
Angles differing by 2π represent the same complex number, so nφ = θ + 2kπ, giving n distinct roots for k = 0,…,n−1.

notes.t: General nth roots via polar and exponential form
pts: Equate real and imaginary parts of \(w^{n}\) = z after writing both in polar form; squaring and adding removes the angle to give the modulus relation.
Equating angles gives nφ = θ + 2πk, so the angle is periodic and only finitely many distinct roots arise.
The modulus of the nth root is the nth root of the modulus of z, so |w| = \( |z|^{1/n} \).
Distinct roots are obtained by letting k run from 0 to n−1; larger k repeat earlier roots.
defs: nth root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that \( w^n = z \); for z ≠ 0 there are exactly n distinct such w.
eqs: Principal set of nth roots of z = r \(e^{jθ}\)
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer root order; k = integer index; j = imaginary unit
tips: Use θ in radians consistently with 2πk; mixing degrees with 2π gives wrong roots.
Take the modulus root as the real positive \( r^{1/n} \) only; the rotation comes from the angle term with k.
rq: Why does the angle equation nφ = θ + 2πk produce only n distinct roots rather than infinitely many?
Because substituting k and k+n gives angles differing by 2π, so the points repeat around the circle; only k = 0,…,n−1 give distinct roots.

notes.t: Roots of complex numbers (de Moivre's theorem for \(z^{1/n}\))
pts: The nth roots of z are found from the modulus-argument form with k = 0, 1, …, n−1, giving exactly n distinct roots.
Values of k beyond n−1 repeat earlier roots: k = n gives the same root as k = 0, k = n+1 as k = 1, and so on.
The n roots lie equally spaced on a circle of radius \(r^{1/n}\) centred at the origin of the Argand diagram.
Arguments of successive roots increase in arithmetic progression, so joining the roots gives a regular polygon inscribed in the circle.
defs: nth root of a complex number z
A complex number w such that wⁿ = z; for z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) there are exactly n such roots.
eqs: nth roots of a complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ)
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = positive integer; k = integer 0, 1, …, n−1; j = imaginary unit
tips: Only use k = 0 to n−1; larger k values repeat roots, so listing more gives duplicates.
Make sure θ is the correct argument (in radians, within the chosen branch) before dividing by n, otherwise the root arguments are wrong.
rq: Why does taking k = n give the same root as k = 0?
Adding 2πn to the argument (2πk/n with k = n adds 2π) rotates the point back to the same position, since cos and sin are periodic with period 2π.
Why must the roots of \(z^{1/n}\) all have the same modulus?
Each root has modulus \(r^{1/n}\), because taking the nth root of the modulus r of z gives the modulus of every root.

notes.t: General nth roots via polar and exponential form
pts: The n roots of a complex number lie equally spaced on a circle of radius |z|^(1/n), so joining them forms a regular polygon inscribed in that circle.
The arguments of successive roots increase in arithmetic progression, each step being 2π/n.
The nth-root equation can be written in exponential form, generating each root by multiplying the previous one by e^(j2π/n).
defs: nth roots of a complex number z
The set of n complex numbers w such that \(w^{n}\) = z; they are equally spaced on a circle centred at the origin.
eqs: \(w_{k}\) = k-th root of z (dimensionless complex number); n = number of roots (dimensionless integer); j = imaginary unit
tips: Students often forget that all n roots share the same modulus |z|^(1/n); only the arguments change.
Check that the angle step is 2π/n (not 2π) when generating roots with e^(j2π/n).
rq: Why does multiplying by e^(j2π/n) move from one root to the next rather than changing the modulus?
e^(j2π/n) has modulus 1, so it only rotates the point by angle 2π/n and keeps |w| = |z|^(1/n) unchanged.
Why do the roots form a regular polygon, and how many sides does it have for n = 6?
The roots are equally spaced in argument by 2π/n on a common circle, so the polygon is regular; for n = 6 it is a hexagon with six vertices \(w_{1}\) to \(w_{6}\).

notes.t: General nth roots via polar and exponential form
pts: The n roots of a complex number z are generated by repeatedly multiplying the first root by the factor \(e^{j2π/n}\).
Writing z in polar form r \(e^{jθ}\) gives all n roots at once: magnitude \(r^{1/n}\) with angles spaced equally by 2π/n.
Only the k values 0 to n−1 give distinct roots; larger k repeats the same roots.
For z = 1 (r = 1, θ = 0) the cube roots of unity are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\).
defs: nth root of a complex number
A complex number w such that \( w^n = z \); a complex number z ≠ 0 has exactly n distinct nth roots.
Exponential (polar) form
Representation of a complex number as \( z = r e^{jθ} \), where r is the modulus and θ the argument in radians.
eqs: General nth roots of z in polar form
\( r \) = modulus of z (dimensionless); \( \theta \) = argument of z (rad); \( n \) = root order (integer); \( k \) = root index (integer)
\( w_k \) = k-th root of z (complex, dimensionless); \( n \) = root order
tips: Express z in exponential form first and include the full angle θ + 2πk; forgetting the 2πk term gives only one root.
Angles in \( e^{j\theta} \) are in radians; using degrees for the 2π/n spacing is a common error.
rq: Why does k only need to run from 0 to n−1 rather than to infinity?
Because \( e^{j2\pi k/n} \) repeats with period n in k, so k = n gives the same root as k = 0, producing no new roots.
Why does the root spacing equal 2π/n in angle?
The n roots are equally spaced on a circle of radius \( r^{1/n} \), so the full 2π is shared equally among n roots.

xq.q: Find the modulus and the argument (rad, principal root, k=0) of a fourth root of \(z=16e^{j2\pi/3}\). Give the argument.
xq.a: \(\pi/6\approx0.524\) rad (modulus 2)

xq.q: Find the root with k=2 of \(w^3=8e^{j\pi/2}\) and give its argument in radians within \((-\pi,\pi]\).
xq.a: \(-\pi/2\approx-1.571\) rad

xq.q: The 6th roots of a complex number z with \(|z|=64\) are plotted on an Argand diagram. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: Six points on a circle of radius 2, spaced \(\pi/3\) apart
o: Six points on a circle of radius 2, spaced \(\pi/3\) apart
Six points on a circle of radius 2, spaced \(\pi/6\) apart
Six points on a circle of radius 10.7, spaced \(\pi/3\) apart
Twelve points on a circle of radius 2, spaced \(\pi/6\) apart
xq.w: Radius is \(64^{1/6}=2\) and spacing is \(2\pi/6=\pi/3\); the traps are dividing the modulus by 6 (10.7) or using \(\pi/n\) spacing.

units.name: 4.5 Roots of unity and cube roots of unity
units.ov: This material covers the cube roots of unity, the three solutions of \(z^3=1\). They sit equally spaced (120° apart) on the unit circle of the Argand diagram, and can be written in exponential, polar and Cartesian forms. The central idea is that multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) rotates a point anticlockwise by 120°, which generates each root from the previous one.
must: The cube roots of unity are the solutions of \(w^3=1\): \(1,\ e^{j2\pi/3},\ e^{j4\pi/3}\).
Geometrically they are equally spaced on the unit circle, \(2\pi/3\) (120°) apart, forming an equilateral triangle.
Successive roots: \(w_{n+1}=w_n e^{j2\pi/3}\); multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) is an anticlockwise rotation of 120°.
Three rotations return to the start: \(w_3 e^{j2\pi/3}=1\), equivalent to \(e^{j2\pi}=1\).
Cartesian form: \(w_2=-\tfrac12+j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(w_3=-\tfrac12-j\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\); the imaginary part is \(\sqrt3/2\), not \(1/2\).
Polar form: \(w_2=\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+j\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\), \(w_3=\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{3}+j\sin\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\).
\(w_2\) and \(w_3\) are complex conjugates, and \(w_3=e^{j4\pi/3}=e^{-j2\pi/3}\) by periodicity (don't confuse \(4\pi/3\) with \(-4\pi/3\)).
Use radians in exponential form (\(2\pi/3\), not 120) unless working wholly in degrees.
The sign of the exponent sets the rotation direction: \(e^{-j2\pi/3}\) rotates clockwise, giving the other pair of roots in the opposite order.
conn: Solving \(z^3=1\) by de Moivre or Euler's formula links to general \(n\)th roots of any complex number: take the modulus root and divide the argument by \(n\) plus multiples of \(2\pi/n\).
Converting between exponential, polar and Cartesian forms uses \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) of \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\), so exact trigonometric values and quadrant signs matter.
The Argand rotation picture links multiplication by a unit complex number to phasor rotation, as in AC and vibration problems with three phases 120° apart.
The conjugate pair property links to factorising \(z^3-1=(z-1)(z^2+z+1)\), whose quadratic roots are \(w_2\) and \(w_3\).
exq: Solve \(z^3=1\) and give all roots in exponential, polar and Cartesian form. Sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Show that \(w_2=e^{j2\pi/3}\) satisfies \(w_2^3=1\) and \(1+w_2+w_2^2=0\), and hence deduce that the three roots sum to zero.
Starting from \(w_1=1\), use \(w_{n+1}=w_n e^{j2\pi/3}\) to find \(w_2\) and \(w_3\), and verify that \(w_3e^{j2\pi/3}=1\). Describe the rotation geometrically.
Solve \(z^3=8\) using the cube roots of unity, giving answers in Cartesian form.
Explain why \(e^{j4\pi/3}\) and \(e^{-j2\pi/3}\) are the same number, and find \(w_2\cdot w_3\) and \(w_2^2\) in terms of \(w_2\) and \(w_3\).

notes.t: Cube roots of unity (Argand diagram)
pts: The three cube roots of unity are equally spaced on the unit circle, each 2π/3 apart.
Successive roots are obtained by multiplying the previous one by \(e^{j2π/3}\).
Multiplying by \(e^{j2π/3}\) rotates a point anticlockwise by 120° on the Argand diagram.
Going round the circle three times returns to the start, so w3 · \(e^{j2π/3}\) = 1.
defs: Cube root of unity
A complex number w satisfying w³ = 1; the three solutions are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\).
eqs: \(w_{n}\) = nth root of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Exponential form of the second root
tips: Watch the sign: \(e^{j2π/3}\) rotates anticlockwise; using \(e^{-j2π/3}\) gives the other pair of roots.
Angles must be in radians in the exponential form (2π/3, not 120) unless working purely in degrees.
rq: Why do the three cube roots of unity lie at 120° intervals on the unit circle?
Because they satisfy w³ = 1, so their modulus is 1 and their arguments are 0, 2π/3 and 4π/3; these are spaced 2π/3 apart.
What happens if you multiply w3 = \(e^{j4π/3}\) by \(e^{j2π/3}\) again?
You get \(e^{j2π}\) = 1 = w1, so the sequence cycles back to the start.

notes.t: Cube roots of unity: exponential, polar and Cartesian forms
pts: The cube roots of unity are 1, w₂ and w₃, found as the three solutions of z³ = 1.
Using the exponential form, w₂ and w₃ are rotations of the unit circle by 2π/3 and 4π/3.
The same roots can be written in polar form using cosine and sine of 2π/3 and 4π/3.
In Cartesian form, w₂ and w₃ are complex conjugates with real part −1/2 and imaginary parts ±√3/2.
defs: Cube root of unity
A complex number w satisfying w³ = 1; the three cube roots of unity are 1, \(e^{j2π/3}\) and \(e^{j4π/3}\).
eqs: Exponential form of the non-real cube roots of unity
\(w_{2}\), \(w_{3}\) = complex cube roots of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit; π = pi (dimensionless)
Cartesian form of the non-real cube roots of unity
\(w_{2}\), \(w_{3}\) = complex cube roots of unity (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Be careful with angle conversion: 4π/3 is not the same as −4π/3 in the exponential form unless you account for periodicity.
Cartesian imaginary parts carry a factor √3/2, a common place to lose marks by writing 1/2 instead.
rq: Why do w₂ and w₃ have the same modulus, and what does that tell you about their position?
Both have modulus 1 (they are unit-circle points), so they lie on the unit circle, spaced 2π/3 apart.
What happens if you cube w₂ = \(e^{j2π/3}\)? Why does this confirm it is a root?
w₂³ = \(e^{j2π}\) = 1, so it satisfies z³ = 1.

xq.q: Let \(w=e^{j2\pi/3}\) be the non-real cube root of unity with \(w^3=1\). Using the Cartesian forms of \(w\) and \(w^2\), evaluate \(5w^2+3w\) and state its real part.
xq.a: 5w²+3w = −4 − j√3, so the real part is −4

xq.q: The real number 3 is represented by a point on the Argand diagram. It is multiplied by the cube root of unity \(w_3=e^{j4\pi/3}\). Which is the resulting complex number?
xq.w: w₃ = −1/2 − j√3/2, so 3w₃ = −1.5 − j2.60; the traps are using w₂ (sign of the imaginary part), writing 1/2 instead of √3/2, and a sign error on the real part.

xq.q: Let \(w=e^{j2\pi/3}\). (a) Show using the Cartesian form of w that \(1+w+w^2=0\). (b) Hence, or otherwise, evaluate \(w^{100}+w^{200}\).
xq.a: (a) w = −1/2 + j√3/2 and w² = −1/2 − j√3/2, so 1+w+w² = 1 − 1/2 − 1/2 + j(√3/2 − √3/2) = 0. (b) Since w³ = 1, w¹⁰⁰ = (w³)³³·w = w and w²⁰⁰ = (w³)⁶⁶·w² = w². Therefore w¹⁰⁰ + w²⁰⁰ = w + w² = −1.
s: Write w and w² in Cartesian form
Add real parts to get 0 and imaginary parts to get 0, so the sum is 0

units.name: 4.6 Powers and roots z^(m/n) and square roots in quadratics
units.ov: This material extends De Moivre's theorem to fractional powers and roots of complex numbers. A complex number is put in polar form \(r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\), the modulus is raised to the power, and the argument is scaled with the \(2\pi k\) branch term. The result is n equally spaced values on a circle. The same nth-root method evaluates the complex square roots that appear in the quadratic formula when the discriminant is complex.
must: nth roots: \(z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}\left[\cos\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}+j\sin\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right]\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\), giving exactly n distinct values
Rational powers: \(z^{m/n}=r^{m/n}\left[\cos\frac{m}{n}(\theta+2\pi k)+j\sin\frac{m}{n}(\theta+2\pi k)\right]\). Add \(2\pi k\) to the argument before multiplying by \(m/n\)
Always convert to polar form first (find \(r=|z|\) and the principal argument \(\theta\), using the correct quadrant). Never take roots of the real and imaginary parts separately

All n roots lie on a circle of radius \(r^{m/n}\). For \(z^{1/n}\) they are spaced \(2\pi/n\) apart (120° for cube roots). In general k steps rotate by \(2\pi m/n\), so with \(m/n\) in lowest terms the n values are still distinct
k runs only from 0 to \(n-1\); larger k just repeats earlier roots. Reduce \(m/n\) to lowest terms first
Work in radians throughout (mixing degrees with \(2\pi\) gives wrong roots), and keep a negative exponent in the modulus \(r^{m/n}\)
Square roots (\(n=2\)) give two values that are negatives of each other: \(k=0\) and \(k=1\) differ by a factor \(e^{j\pi}=-1\)

Complex quadratics: use \(z=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\), evaluate \(\sqrt{\text{discriminant}}\) via polar form, and keep the \(\pm\) so you get both roots. With complex coefficients the roots need not be conjugates

Worked example: \(z=-\tfrac12(5+j4)\pm\tfrac12\sqrt{37+j12}\). Here \(|37+j12|\approx38.9\) and \(\arg\approx0.314\) rad, so \(\sqrt{37+j12}\approx\pm(6.16+j0.98)\) and \(z\approx0.58-j1.51\) or \(-5.58-j2.49\)
Do not confuse the branch index k with the imaginary unit j. Check answers by squaring or substituting back
conn: Polar form and De Moivre's theorem underlie everything. Finding arguments (quadrants, radians) comes first, and errors there carry through to every root

Complex quadratics combine algebra (discriminant \(b^2-4ac\) with complex coefficients) with the square-root method. Expect to compute the discriminant, convert to polar, take both roots, then simplify to Cartesian form
Roots plotted on an Argand diagram form a regular n-gon centred at the origin. Questions often ask for sketches, or for sums and products of the roots (the n roots of \(z^n=w\) sum to zero)
Solving \(z^n=w\) or factorising polynomials such as \(z^3+8=0\) uses the nth-root family, and the roots can then be used to build factors or conjugate pairs
exq: Find all cube roots of \(-8\) in polar and Cartesian form, and plot them on an Argand diagram.
Find all values of \(z^{2/3}\) for \(z=1+j\sqrt3\), giving modulus and argument (radians) for each. State why only three distinct values arise.
Solve \(z^2+(5+j4)z+(-7+j7)=0\). Evaluate the discriminant \(37+j12\), find its square roots in polar form, and give both roots as \(a+jb\) to 2 d.p.
Solve \(z^4=-16\) and write the roots in the form \(a+jb\). Hence factorise \(z^4+16\) into real quadratic factors.
Find the principal value and all other values of \((-1+j)^{1/3}\). Show that the roots lie on a circle and give its radius and the angular spacing.

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem and roots/powers z^(m/n)
pts: Taking the nth root of z=r(cos θ + j sin θ) gives n distinct roots, obtained by adding 2πk/n to the argument for k = 0,1,…,(n−1).
A rational power \(z^{p}\) with p = m/n is found by first taking the nth root and then raising to the mth power.
Raising to the mth power multiplies the modulus exponent and the argument, giving the general form for z^(m/n).
The result for \(z^{p}\) carries the same family of values indexed by k, so non-integer powers are multi-valued.
defs: Modulus and argument form
A complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) is written with modulus r = |z| and argument θ.
eqs: nth root of a complex number (principal family over k)
