z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = positive integer root index; k = 0,1,…,(n−1); j = imaginary unit
p = m/n (dimensionless); m, n = integers; r = modulus; θ = argument (rad); k = 0,1,…,(n−1)
tips: Remember k runs only from 0 to (n−1); using k up to m or beyond double-counts roots.
Use the same argument convention (e.g. θ in radians) throughout; mixing degrees with 2π gives wrong roots.
rq: Why does z^(m/n) produce n different values rather than one?
Because the argument of z is defined only up to multiples of 2π, and dividing by n yields n distinct arguments 2πk/n shifts for k = 0,…,(n−1).
What happens if p = m/n is written as an integer multiple, e.g. m = n?
Then the factor 2πkp = 2πk·m/n becomes a multiple of 2π, so all n values collapse to the single value \(z^{m}\), consistent with ordinary De Moivre's theorem.

notes.t: Powers z^(m/n) of complex numbers: finding n roots
pts: For z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), the power z^(m/n) has n distinct values obtained by varying k in the formula; these are spaced evenly around a circle.
The modulus of the result is r^(m/n), so all n roots lie on the same circle of radius r^(m/n).
Changing k by 1 rotates the answer by 2π·m/n, so the roots are equally spaced by angle 2π/3 when n = 3.
Angles are computed from the principal argument θ plus 2πk, then multiplied by the exponent m/n.
defs: Principal argument θ
The angle of a complex number measured from the positive real axis, in radians, usually taken in the range -π to π.
eqs: Powers of a complex number (all n roots of z^(m/n))
z = complex number; r = modulus \(|z|\) (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); m, n = integers; k = root index (dimensionless)
tips: Forgetting to add 2πk inside the bracket before multiplying by m/n gives the wrong angles; the 2πk term is multiplied by the exponent too.
Keep the modulus as \(r^{m/n}\) with the sign of the exponent: a negative power means the modulus is less than 1 when r > 1.
rq: Why does the formula give only n different answers even though k can be any integer?
Values of k differing by a multiple of n make the angle differ by a full turn times m, so they repeat the same n roots; only k = 0 to n−1 are distinct.
What would change if the exponent were 2/3 instead of −2/3?
The modulus would become \(r^{2/3}\) (greater than 1 here) instead of \(r^{-2/3}\), and the angles would be multiplied by +2/3, moving the roots to different positions on a larger circle.

notes.t: Powers and roots z^(1/n) and square roots in quadratics
pts: The quadratic formula gives the roots of a quadratic with complex coefficients, leaving a square root of a complex number to evaluate.
A complex number under a root is converted to polar form, then its root is found by taking the root of the modulus and dividing the argument by n.
The n distinct nth roots are found by adding 2πk/n to the argument for k = 0, 1, …, n−1.
defs: Principal and other nth roots of a complex number
For z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), the nth roots are r^(1/n)[cos((θ+2πk)/n) + j sin((θ+2πk)/n)], k = 0,1,…,n−1, giving n distinct values.
eqs: Quadratic formula for roots of az² + bz + c = 0
z = unknown root (dimensionless); a, b, c = coefficients (complex or real, dimensionless)
nth roots of a complex number in polar form
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = root order (integer); k = 0,1,…,n−1 (integer)
tips: Convert the complex number to polar form (modulus and argument) before applying the root formula; do not take roots of the real and imaginary parts separately.
Remember to give all n roots, using k = 0 to n−1, and check the angle is in radians (0.31 rad) when using cos and sin.
rq: Why must the angle be divided by n but 2πk/n added, rather than just dividing the angle?
Adding 2πk before dividing by n generates all n distinct roots spaced evenly around the circle, since the same complex number has many arguments differing by 2π.
Why does the square root of 37 + j12 give two answers, and how are they related?
Taking k = 0 and k = 1 gives two roots equal in modulus and opposite in direction (differing by π), so they are negatives of each other.

notes.t: Square roots of complex numbers and solving quadratics with complex roots
pts: A complex square root has two values, one the negative of the other; the k index labels the two branches.
The quadratic formula gives complex roots by adding and subtracting half the square root of the discriminant term.
Both roots of the quadratic are found by applying the ± sign to the square root, so the two roots are z₁ and z₂.
Roots of a quadratic with complex coefficients need not be complex conjugates; they are plotted as separate points on the complex plane.
defs: Principal square root of a complex number
The two square roots of a complex number are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign; the k = 0 and k = 1 branches give these two values.
eqs: Roots of a quadratic with complex coefficients
z = root of the quadratic (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Forgetting the ± sign in the quadratic formula, which loses one of the two roots.
Confusing the j index k of the square-root branches with the imaginary unit j.
rq: Why does the ± sign in the quadratic formula give two roots even when the coefficients are complex?
Because the square root of a complex number has two values that differ by a sign; each sign choice gives one root.
What if you took only the k = 0 root of the square root and ignored k = 1?
You would find only one root of the quadratic, missing the second solution z₂.

xq.q: Let \(z=8j\). Write z in polar form and find the three cube roots of z. Give the real part of the root obtained with \(k=1\) in the formula \(z^{1/3}=r^{1/3}[\cos((\theta+2\pi k)/3)+j\sin((\theta+2\pi k)/3)]\).
xq.a: Real part = −√3 ≈ −1.732 (the k=1 root is −√3 + j)
s: z = 8(cos π/2 + j sin π/2), so r = 8 and θ = π/2
Root = 2(cos 5π/6 + j sin 5π/6) = −√3 + j, so the real part is −1.732

xq.q: Solve the quadratic \(z^2-2z+4-4j=0\) for complex z. Give both roots and state the modulus of the root that has non-zero real part.
xq.a: Roots z = 2+2j and z = −2j; the modulus of 2+2j is 2√2 ≈ 2.83
s: Polar form: r = 20, θ = π − arctan(4/3) = 2.214 rad

xq.q: A complex number is \(z=27(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\) with \(\theta=\pi/3\). Which statement correctly describes all values of \(z^{2/3}\)?
xq.a: Three distinct values, all of modulus 9, equally spaced by 2π/3 on a circle
o: Three distinct values, all of modulus 9, equally spaced by 2π/3 on a circle
Three distinct values, all of modulus 18, equally spaced by 2π/3
Two distinct values, all of modulus 9, spaced by π
Three distinct values, all of modulus 3, equally spaced by 2π/3
xq.w: The modulus is \(27^{2/3}\) = 9 and the denominator n = 3 gives three values; the traps are multiplying 27 by 2/3, using m = 2 as the number of roots, and taking only the cube root.
s: The number of distinct values is n = 3, with k = 0, 1, 2
Adjacent values are spaced by 2π/3 on the circle of radius 9

units.name: 4.7 Powers of trig functions and multiple angles
units.ov: This material uses Euler/de Moivre with unit-modulus \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta=e^{j\theta}\) to get \(z^n\pm z^{-n}\) as \(2\cos n\theta\) or \(2j\sin n\theta\). Expanding a power such as \((z+z^{-1})^k\) with the binomial theorem then converts powers of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) into sums of multiple-angle terms. The worked example \(\cos^2 3\theta=(1+\cos 6\theta)/2\) shows the method on its simplest case.
must: De Moivre: \(z^n=\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta\) for \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) with \(|z|=1\)
Negative power: \(z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-j\sin n\theta\); the sign of the sine term flips
\(z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta\), so \(\cos n\theta=\tfrac12(z^n+z^{-n})\)
\(z^n-z^{-n}=2j\sin n\theta\), so \(\sin n\theta=\tfrac{1}{2j}(z^n-z^{-n})\)
Method for \(\cos^k\theta\): write \((2\cos\theta)^k=(z+z^{-1})^k\), expand binomially, pair \(z^m\) with \(z^{-m}\) terms
Squaring \((z^n+z^{-n})^2=z^{2n}+z^{-2n}+2\), so \(4\cos^2 n\theta=2\cos 2n\theta+2\)
Reduced power formula: \(\cos^2 3\theta=\tfrac{1+\cos 6\theta}{2}\) (general: \(\cos^2 n\theta=\tfrac{1+\cos2n\theta}{2}\))
Do not drop the constant +2 cross term (middle binomial term) when squaring
Divide by the correct factor: \(2^k\) for cosine powers, and \((2j)^k\) for sine powers, taking care with \(j^k\)
Euler forms: \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=re^{j\theta}=r\angle\theta\); angles in radians, \(n\) an integer
conn: Binomial theorem + de Moivre: expansion of \((z+z^{-1})^k\) with coefficients from Pascal's triangle gives the multiple-angle sum
Reduced power formulae link to integration: \(\int\cos^k\theta\,d\theta\) becomes a sum of simple cosine integrals
Reverse direction: expanding \(\cos n\theta\) or \(\sin n\theta\) via \((\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^n\) and equating real and imaginary parts
Engineering use: power in AC/vibration signals (\(\sin^2\omega t\) average) and harmonic decomposition in Fourier series
exq: Show that \(z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta\) and hence prove \(\cos^2 3\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos6\theta)\).
Express \(\cos^4\theta\) in the form \(a\cos4\theta+b\cos2\theta+c\) by expanding \((z+z^{-1})^4\).
Express \(\sin^3\theta\) in terms of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\sin3\theta\), using \((z-z^{-1})^3=(2j\sin\theta)^3\).
Express \(\sin^5\theta\) as a combination of \(\sin5\theta,\sin3\theta,\sin\theta\), and use it to evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi}\sin^5\theta\,d\theta\).
Use de Moivre to find \(\cos 3\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\), then verify with \(\theta=\pi/3\).

notes.t: Powers of Trigonometric Functions and Multiple Angles
pts: Euler's form writes a complex number as a modulus times cos plus j sin of its angle, so powers of z follow directly from de Moivre's result.
Raising z to the power n multiplies the angle by n, giving cos nθ + j sin nθ.
Negative powers give the conjugate-angle result, since z^(-n) reverses the sign of the sine term.
Adding and subtracting \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) isolates cos nθ and sin nθ, which is the basis for expressing powers of sin θ and cos θ in terms of multiple angles.
defs: Euler's formula (polar form)
For a complex number z with modulus r and argument θ, z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) = re^(jθ) = r∠θ.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for powers of z
z = unit-modulus complex number (dimensionless); θ = angle (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Sum of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) giving cosine of multiple angle
z = unit complex number; θ = angle (rad); n = integer (dimensionless)
Difference of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) giving sine of multiple angle
z = unit complex number; θ = angle (rad); n = integer (dimensionless)
tips: Check the sign of the sine term: z^(-n) = cos nθ − j sin nθ, not + j sin nθ; dropping the minus sign flips the result.
Remember the factor of 2 when isolating cos nθ or sin nθ: \(z^{n}\) + z^(-n) = 2cos nθ, so divide by 2 (and by 2j for sine).
rq: Why does z^(-n) have the sine term with a negative sign, and what does this tell you about z^(-n) compared with \(z^{n}\)?

Because z^(-n) = 1/\(z^{n}\), which corresponds to the angle −nθ; cos is even and sin is odd, so the sine term changes sign while the cosine term stays the same. Thus z^(-n) is the complex conjugate of \(z^{n}\) when |z| = 1.
How would you use \(z^{n}\) + z^(-n) = 2cos nθ to express cos³θ in terms of cosines of multiple angles?
Write cos θ = (z + z^(-1))/2, cube it to get (z³ + 3z + 3z^(-1) + z^(-3))/8 = (2cos 3θ + 6cos θ)/8, so cos³θ = (cos 3θ + 3cos θ)/4.
What if you needed sin²θ instead of cos²θ — which combination of \(z^{n}\) and z^(-n) would you use?
Use sin θ = (z − z^(-1))/(2j), square it, and apply the result that z² + z^(-2) = 2cos 2θ, giving sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2.

notes.t: Powers of trig functions and multiple angles
pts: Use z = cos θ + i sin θ so that \(z^{n}\) + z^(-n) = 2 cos nθ, then square to reduce cos² nθ
Squaring (\(z^{n}\) + z^(-n)) gives z^(2n) + z^(-2n) + 2, which turns a squared cosine into a cosine of double the angle
Applying the identity with n = 6 gives 2 cos 6θ + 2 = 2² cos² 3θ, so cos² 3θ = (1 + cos 6θ)/2
eqs: Multiple-angle identity used to expand powers of cosine
z = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta (dimensionless complex number); n = integer; \theta = angle (rad)
tips: Do not forget the constant +2 produced by the cross term when squaring; dropping it gives the wrong answer for cos² 3θ.
Check the factor: 2² cos² 3θ must equal 2 cos 6θ + 2, so divide by 4, not by 2, to obtain (1 + cos 6θ)/2.
rq: Why does squaring \(z^{3}\) + z^(-3) produce a term in cos 6θ rather than cos 3θ?
Squaring adds exponents: (\(z^{3}\))^2 = \(z^{6}\), so the cross term gives \(z^{6}\) + z^(-6), which equals 2 cos 6θ.
How would you expand cos⁴θ using the same method?
Square the identity twice: (z + z^(-1))^4 = \(z^{4}\) + 4z^2 + 6 + 4z^(-2) + z^(-4), giving cos⁴θ = (3 + 4cos 2θ + cos 4θ)/8.

xq.q: Using \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) and the result \(\cos^2 3\theta=(1+\cos 6\theta)/2\), evaluate \(\cos^2 3\theta\) when \(\theta=\pi/18\) rad.
Let \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) and \(\theta=\pi/9\) rad. What is the value of \(z^3-z^{-3}\)?
xq.w: By de Moivre, z³ − z⁻³ = 2j sin 3θ = 2j sin(π/3) = j√3; the traps are dropping the j, forgetting the factor 2, and getting the sign of the sine term wrong.

xq.q: Let \(z=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\). By squaring \(z^3+z^{-3}\), show that \(\cos^2 3\theta=\tfrac12(1+\cos 6\theta)\).
xq.a: By de Moivre, z³ + z⁻³ = 2cos 3θ. Squaring: 4cos²3θ = z⁶ + 2 + z⁻⁶. Since z⁶ + z⁻⁶ = 2cos 6θ, this gives 4cos²3θ = 2cos 6θ + 2. Dividing by 4 gives cos²3θ = (1 + cos 6θ)/2.
s: Square: z⁶ + 2 + z⁻⁶ = 4cos²3θ (the cross term gives +2)
Divide by 4 to obtain the result

units.name: 5.1 De Moivre's theorem: powers and roots
units.ov: De Moivre's theorem expresses powers of a complex number in polar form: the modulus is raised to the power n and the argument is multiplied by n. Extending it with the 2πk shift in the argument gives all n distinct nth roots, which sit equally spaced on a circle and form a regular n-gon. Rational powers \(z^{m/n}\) combine both ideas: take the nth root, then raise to the mth power.
must: De Moivre: \( z^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + j\sin n\theta) \) for \( z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta) \), with \( r=|z| \) and \( \theta=\arg z \) in radians
nth roots: \( z^{1/n} = r^{1/n}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right)+j\sin\left(\frac{\theta+2\pi k}{n}\right)\right],\ k=0,\dots,n-1 \)
Exponential form: \( z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}e^{j(\theta+2\pi k)/n} \), which is quicker to write and manipulate
Always include the \( 2\pi k \) term, because \( \theta \) is defined only modulo \( 2\pi \); omitting it gives one root instead of n
The n roots all have modulus \( r^{1/n} \) and are spaced \( 2\pi/n \) apart on a circle, forming a regular n-gon (e.g. 60° apart for n = 6)
Convert to polar form first: find \( r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \) and \( \theta \) in the correct quadrant (check the sign of x and y)
Rational powers: \( z^{m/n}=(z^{1/n})^m \), so take the nth root (n branches via k = 0..n−1) and then raise to the mth power, keeping the \( 2\pi k \) terms
Sanity checks: the roots sum to zero for n ≥ 2, and each root raised to the nth power returns z
Give the final answers in the requested form (polar, exponential or Cartesian), with the argument usually in \( (-\pi,\pi] \) for principal values
conn: Cartesian to polar conversion (modulus and argument, quadrant) is the first step of every power or root question, and an error in \( \theta \) carries through to all the answers
Roots of unity and solving \( z^n = w \) link De Moivre's theorem to polynomial equations, with the roots found geometrically on an Argand diagram
Expanding \( (\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^n \) binomially and equating real and imaginary parts gives multiple-angle identities such as \( \cos 3\theta \) and \( \sin 3\theta \)
The exponential form \( re^{j\theta} \) links to Euler's formula and to phasors and rotating vectors in vibrations and AC analysis
exq: Express \( z=-1+j\sqrt{3} \) in polar form and use De Moivre's theorem to find \( z^{8} \) in the form \( a+jb \)
Find all the cube roots of \( 8(\cos 90^\circ + j\sin 90^\circ) \), give them in polar and Cartesian form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram
Solve \( z^6 = 1 \), plot the roots and state the geometric shape they form; then solve \( z^4=-16 \)
Find all values of \( (1+j)^{3/4} \) in exponential form, taking the 4th root first and then cubing
Use De Moivre's theorem with the binomial expansion to derive an expression for \( \cos 4\theta \) in terms of \( \cos\theta \)

notes.t: De Moivre's theorem: powers and roots of complex numbers
pts: De Moivre's theorem gives the nth power of a complex number directly from its modulus and argument, with the modulus raised to the power n and the argument multiplied by n.
The nth roots of a complex number are found by taking the nth root of the modulus and dividing the argument by n, with the k-shift producing n distinct roots.
The n distinct nth roots lie equally spaced on a circle of radius the nth root of the modulus, forming a regular n-gon (shown for n = 6).
Raising a number to a rational power m/n is done by first taking the nth root and then raising the result to the mth power.
defs: Modulus and argument form
A complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) is written in polar form, with r = |z| its modulus and θ its argument.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem for integer powers
z = complex number; r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless)
nth roots of a complex number (trigonometric form)
\(r^{1/n}\) = modulus of each root (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); k = 0, 1, …, n−1 (integer); n = root index (dimensionless)
nth roots of a complex number (exponential form)
\(r^{1/n}\) = modulus of each root (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); k = integer index 0 to n−1; n = root index
p = m/n (dimensionless); r = modulus of z; θ = argument of z (rad); k = integer 0 to n−1; m, n = integers
tips: Argument θ is only defined modulo 2π; forgetting the 2πk term when finding roots gives only one root instead of n.
For \(z^{m/n}\), take the nth root first (giving n branches via k) and then raise to the mth power; do not treat the exponent as simply multiplying the argument without including the 2πk terms.
rq: Why does taking the nth root of a complex number produce n answers, while a real number's nth root in ordinary arithmetic is usually one?

Because the argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π, so adding 2πk to θ before dividing by n gives n different angles (k = 0, …, n−1) that all satisfy the equation, spaced 2π/n apart around the circle.
What happens to the roots' positions if n = 6 and the modulus of z is increased?
All six roots remain at equal angular spacing of 60° (2π/6) but move onto a larger circle, since the radius is the nth root of |z|.

xq.q: Let \(z=\sqrt{3}+j\). Use De Moivre's theorem to find \(z^{6}\), giving your answer as a single real number.
xq.a: \(z^{6}\) = -64 (a real number, -64)
s: Modulus r = √(3+1) = 2, argument θ = arctan(1/√3) = π/6

xq.q: The cube roots of \(z=-8\) are found using \(z^{1/3}\). Which option gives the modulus and argument of the root with the smallest positive argument?
xq.a: modulus 2, argument π/3
o: modulus 8/3, argument π/3
modulus 2, argument 3π
modulus 2, argument π/3
modulus 2, argument 2π/3
xq.w: Here r = 8 and θ = π, so the modulus is \(8^{1/3}\) = 2 and the smallest argument is θ/3 = π/3 (k = 0); the traps are dividing the modulus by 3, multiplying the argument by 3, or mishandling θ/3.

xq.q: Find all four fourth roots of \(z=-16\). Give each in the form \(a+jb\) with exact values of \(a\) and \(b\), and state where they lie in the Argand diagram.
xq.a: Write -16 = 16(cos π + j sin π). Then \(z^{1/4}\) = 2[cos(π/4+πk/2) + j sin(π/4+πk/2)], k = 0,1,2,3. The roots are √2+j√2, -√2+j√2, -√2-j√2, √2-j√2. They lie equally spaced (90° apart) on a circle of radius 2 centred at the origin, forming a square.
s: Roots equally spaced on circle radius 2 (a square)

units.name: 5.2 Loci as straight lines (Re, arg, Im conditions)
units.ov: This material shows how conditions on a complex variable z = x + jy describe straight-line loci in the Argand diagram. Re(z) = c gives a vertical line, arg(z − z₀) = θ gives a ray, |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| gives a perpendicular bisector, and Im[kz] = c reduces to a line in x or y. The common method is to translate the condition into x and y, simplify to a linear equation, then interpret it geometrically.
must: A locus is the set of points satisfying a condition. State the property first, then convert it to algebra, and keep the set of points distinct from its equation.
\(\mathrm{Re}(z)=c\) gives the vertical line \(x=c\), with y unrestricted. \(\mathrm{Im}(z)=c\) gives the horizontal line \(y=c\). Do not mix them up.
\(\arg(z-z_0)=\theta\) is a half-line (ray) starting at \(z_0\), not a full line. Its parametric form is \(z=z_0+r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta),\ r\ge 0\).
In an argument locus, \(z_0\) fixes the starting point (excluded from the ray, since arg 0 is undefined) and \(\theta\) fixes the direction, measured from the positive real axis.
\(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\).
Method for modulus loci: put \(z=x+jy\), write each modulus as a real distance, square both sides to remove the roots, and expand carefully. The quadratic terms cancel, leaving a linear equation.
Example: \((x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=(x-2)^2+y^2\) simplifies to a straight line. Watch the cross-terms such as \(-2x\) and \(-4x\) when expanding, because sign slips change the line.
Im conditions: expand the expression in z = x + jy and take the imaginary part. For example \(\mathrm{Im}[-jz]=-x\), so \(\mathrm{Im}[-jz]=\sqrt2\) gives the vertical line \(x=-\sqrt2\).
Multiplying by \(-j\) rotates by \(-\pi/2\) and swaps the roles of the real and imaginary parts: \(-j(x+jy)=y-jx\).
Sketch the locus on an Argand diagram with axes labelled and key points marked, such as intercepts, the apex of a ray and the two fixed points. State 'for any real y' or the allowed range of r.
conn: Modulus loci: \(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) as a perpendicular bisector links to midpoint and gradient geometry. The bisector passes through \((z_1+z_2)/2\) with gradient \(-1/m\), which checks the algebra.
Argument loci link to polar form and the rotation of complex numbers. Converting \(z_0\) to \(r(\cos\phi+j\sin\phi)\) and using principal arguments determines the ray direction and quadrant.
Im and Re conditions on expressions like \(-jz\) or \(1/z\) combine complex multiplication or division with the line loci. You must expand first, then identify the line.

Questions may ask for the intersection of two loci, such as a ray and a bisector or a vertical line. This means solving simultaneous linear equations and checking that the point lies on the ray (r ≥ 0).
exq: Sketch the locus \(\arg(z-(1+j))=-\pi/3\) on an Argand diagram. Give its parametric form and state the starting point and direction.
Find the Cartesian equation of the locus \(|z-(1+j)|=|z-2|\). Show that it is a straight line in the form \(y=mx+c\) and sketch it with the two fixed points.
Show that \(\mathrm{Im}[-jz]=\sqrt2\) represents a vertical line. Find its equation and sketch it.
Find where the line \(\mathrm{Re}(z)=2\) meets the ray \(\arg(z-(1+j))=-\pi/3\)? Give the intersection point in the form \(x+jy\).
Describe in words and algebraically the locus of points equidistant from \(z_1=-1+2j\) and \(z_2=3-j\). Identify the midpoint and the gradient of the line.

notes.t: Loci in the complex plane
pts: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a specified property, which may be given in words or algebraically.
A circle is the locus of points in a plane a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
The Argand diagram represents complex numbers as points in a plane, allowing complicated loci to be written concisely in terms of a complex variable.
Loci arise widely in engineering, e.g. safety guards around machinery, aircraft wing sections, and water percolation through dams.
defs: Locus (plural loci)
The set of points in a plane (or space) that have a specified property.
tips: Do not confuse the locus (the set of points) with the equation describing it; state the property clearly before converting to algebra.
Check whether the property is given in words or algebraically, and translate words such as 'fixed distance' into a modulus condition.
rq: Why is the Argand diagram useful when describing a locus that would be awkward in Cartesian form?
Because a point can be represented by a single complex variable z, so a complicated locus can be written as a concise equation in z, simplifying the analysis.
What is the locus of points at fixed distance r from a fixed point c in the complex plane, and why?
A circle with centre c and radius r, since the distance |z − c| is fixed at r for all points on it.

notes.t: Straight lines: loci defined by Re(z) = constant
pts: Writing z = x + jy, the condition Re(z) = x = constant fixes the horizontal coordinate, so the locus is a vertical line.
The value y is unrestricted, so the line extends infinitely up and down through the Argand diagram.
The locus is parallel to the imaginary axis and crosses the real axis at the given Re(z) value.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane (Argand diagram) satisfying a given condition on z.
Real part Re(z)
For z = x + jy, Re(z) = x, the horizontal (real-axis) coordinate of the point representing z.
eqs: Vertical line locus for a fixed real part
x = real part of z (dimensionless); c = fixed real constant (dimensionless); z = x + jy
tips: Do not confuse Re(z) = constant (vertical line) with Im(z) = constant (horizontal line).
The line is infinite: state 'for any real y' rather than giving a finite segment unless a range is specified.
rq: Why does the condition Re(z) = −√2 produce a line rather than a single point?
Only the real part is constrained; y can be any real number, so infinitely many points with x = −√2 form a vertical line.
What would change if the condition were Im(z) = −√2 instead?
The locus would be a horizontal line y = −√2, parallel to the real axis, since the imaginary part is fixed and x is free.

notes.t: Straight lines as loci: arg(z − z₀) = θ
pts: The locus arg(z − (1+j)) = −π/3 is a half-line starting at the point 1+j, not a full line, because r is restricted to be non-negative.
Writing z − z₀ = r(cos θ + j sin θ) turns an argument condition into a parametric form with fixed direction θ and varying modulus r.
The point z₀ = 1+j is the starting point (apex) of the ray; the ray points in the direction of angle −π/3 measured from the positive real axis.
Converting 1+j to polar form, √2(cos π/4 + j sin π/4), gives an alternative description of the starting point via its modulus and argument.
defs: Locus
The set of all points z in the Argand plane satisfying a given condition, such as a fixed argument or modulus.
eqs: Parametric form of an argument locus
z = complex variable (dimensionless); \(z_{0}\) = fixed starting point (dimensionless); r = modulus of z − \(z_{0}\) (dimensionless); θ = fixed argument in radians (rad)
tips: Forgetting the condition r ≥ 0 and describing the answer as a whole line instead of a half-line (ray).
Confusing the fixed point z₀ with the direction θ; the point sets the starting position, the angle sets the direction.
rq: Why is the locus arg(z − (1+j)) = −π/3 a ray rather than a full straight line?
Because the modulus r = |z − (1+j)| is non-negative, so z only covers points in one direction from 1+j; a full line would need r to take negative values as well.
What would change if the condition were arg(z − (1+j)) = 2π/3 instead?
The ray would start at 1+j but point in the direction 2π/3, i.e. up and to the left, so the parametric form would use θ = 2π/3.

notes.t: Straight lines as loci in the complex plane (|z−z₁|=|z−z₂|)
pts: Substitute z = x + jy and rewrite each modulus as a real distance in the x–y plane
A locus where distances to two fixed points are equal is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them
Squaring both sides removes the square roots and leaves a linear equation in x and y, i.e. a straight line
Rearranging the linear equation gives the line in slope–intercept form
defs: Locus
The set of all points satisfying a given geometric or algebraic condition, here expressed in the complex plane.
eqs: Equal-distance condition for a straight-line locus
z = complex point, \(z_{1}\), \(z_{2}\) = fixed complex points (dimensionless)
Resulting straight line from squaring the modulus condition
x, y = real and imaginary parts of z (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget to square both sides: leaving the square roots in place hides the linear form of the locus.
Watch the sign when expanding \( (x-1)^2 \) and \( (x-2)^2 \); a dropped cross-term such as −4x changes the final line.
rq: Why does squaring both sides of the modulus equation produce a straight line rather than a circle?
The x² and y² terms appear on both sides and cancel, leaving only linear terms in x and y, which describes a line.
Why must the locus be the perpendicular bisector of the two points?
Every point on it is equidistant from z₁ and z₂, and that property defines the perpendicular bisector.

notes.t: Loci as straight lines (Im condition)
pts: Write z = x + jy and multiply out the expression inside Im[ ] to split it into real and imaginary parts.
Multiplying by −j swaps real and imaginary roles: the real part becomes y and the imaginary part becomes −x.
Taking the imaginary part of the product gives a condition on x alone, so the locus is a vertical line.
Setting the imaginary part equal to a constant gives a straight line parallel to the imaginary axis.
The locus is the line x = −√2, plotted as a vertical line in the Argand diagram.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane whose coordinates satisfy a given condition.
eqs: Cartesian form of a complex number
z = complex number; x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Imaginary part of −jz giving the locus
x = real part of z (dimensionless); Im = imaginary-part operator
tips: Watch the sign: Im[−jz] = −x, not +x, so the line is x = −√2 (on the left of the origin).
The condition involves only x, so the locus is a vertical line; don't mistakenly give a horizontal line.
rq: Why does multiplying z by −j turn the condition into one on x only?
Because −j·(x + jy) = y − jx, so the imaginary part is −x, which contains no y.
What would the locus be if the condition were Re[−jz] = √2 instead?
Re[−jz] = y, so y = √2, a horizontal line parallel to the real axis.

xq.q: A point \(z\) lies on the locus \(\arg\big(z-(1+j)\big)=-\pi/3\) and has real part \(\mathrm{Re}(z)=3\). Find \(\mathrm{Im}(z)\) to 3 decimal places.
Which description fits the locus \(|z-(1+j)|=|z-2|\)?
xq.a: The line y = x − 1
o: The line y = x + 1
The line y = x − 1
The line y = −x + 1
A circle with centre 1+j and radius 1
xq.w: Squaring gives (x−1)²+(y−1)² = (x−2)²+y², which simplifies to y = x − 1; the traps are a sign slip when expanding, a wrong slope, or confusing a bisector with a circle.

xq.q: Show that the locus \(|z-(1+j)|=|z-2|\) is a straight line, find its equation, and explain geometrically why it is a line.
xq.a: Let z = x + jy. Then |z−(1+j)|² = (x−1)²+(y−1)² and |z−2|² = (x−2)²+y². Equating: x²−2x+1+y²−2y+1 = x²−4x+4+y², so 2x − 2y = 2, i.e. y = x − 1. Geometrically the points are equidistant from (1,1) and (2,0), so the locus is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them (slope 1, passing through the midpoint (1.5, 0.5)).
s: Substitute z = x + jy and square both sides
Quadratic terms cancel leaving 2x − 2y = 2, so y = x − 1
Equidistant from two fixed points means perpendicular bisector

units.name: 5.3 Loci as circles and perpendicular bisectors
units.ov: This material describes loci in the Argand plane defined by modulus conditions. |z − z₁| = R is a circle, |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| is a perpendicular bisector (a line), and |z − z₁| = k|z − z₂| with k ≠ 1 is an Apollonius circle. All three come from the same method: substitute z = x + jy, square the modulus condition, and read the geometry from the Cartesian equation.
must: \(|z-z_1|=R\) is the circle with centre \(z_1\) and radius \(R\), because \(|z-z_1|\) is the distance from z to \(z_1\)
Cartesian form: \((x-x_1)^2+(y-y_1)^2=R^2\). Use \(R^2\) on the right, and the centre is \((x_1,y_1)\) with the signs reversed in the brackets
Parametric form: \(z=z_1+Re^{jt}\), \(-\pi<t\le\pi\)
Modulus: \(|a+jb|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). Always square the modulus condition to remove the root, and square both sides, including any factor k
\(|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(z_1\) and \(z_2\), so it is a straight line. Two fixed points with k = 1 means a line

Method for the bisector: find the midpoint and the slope of the segment, then use the negative reciprocal slope, or just expand the squared equation (the x² and y² terms cancel). Example: \(z_1=1+j,\ z_2=2\) gives \(y=x-1\)

\(|z-z_1|=k|z-z_2|\) with \(k\neq1\) is an Apollonius circle. Square to get \(|z-z_1|^2=k^2|z-z_2|^2\), collect the x², y², x and y terms, divide by \(k^2-1\), and complete the square to read off the centre and radius
Completing the square gives \(R^2\) on the right. Check the arithmetic, then take the square root to get R. In the worked example, ratio \(\sqrt2\) gives centre \((3,-1)\) and radius 2, so \(R^2=4\)
Read points like \(2+j0\) as \((2,0)\). Misreading a point changes the midpoint and the line
Sanity-check any result: the bisector must be equidistant from \(z_1\) and \(z_2\), and the Apollonius circle must satisfy the original ratio condition at a test point
conn: The bisector is the k = 1 special case of the Apollonius circle. The x² and y² terms cancel on expansion, leaving a line, whereas for k ≠ 1 they survive and give a circle
Every locus question reduces to the same pipeline: modulus as distance, then squaring, then expansion, then completing the square, then geometry. The algebraic and geometric views check each other
The parametric form \(z_1+Re^{jt}\) links loci to complex exponentials and phasors. It is useful when a question asks for points at specific angles on the circle

Loci combine with intersections: a circle and a bisector line, or two circles, are solved simultaneously. This gives quadratics, with 0, 1 or 2 intersection points, and can also bring in inequalities (inside or outside the circle)
exq: Sketch the locus \(|z-(3-j)|=2\), give its Cartesian equation, and write down a parametric form for z.
Find the Cartesian equation of the locus \(|z-1-j|=|z-2|\) and show it is \(y=x-1\). Identify the geometric meaning, including the midpoint and slope used.
Show that \(|z-4|=2|z-1|\) is a circle and find its centre and radius. (Answer: centre 0, radius 2.)
Show that \(|z-2|=\sqrt2\,|z|\) is a circle, and find its centre and radius. (Answer: centre \((-2,0)\), radius \(2\sqrt2\).)
Find where the line \(y=x-1\) meets the circle \(|z-(3-j)|=2\). State the number of intersection points and describe the region \(|z-(3-j)|<2\).

notes.t: Circles in the Argand plane: loci of the form |z − z₁| = R
pts: A circle is the locus of points at constant distance R from a fixed centre z₁.
Writing z − z₁ = \(Re^{jt}\) with −π < t ≤ π parametrises the circle by angle t.
The modulus condition |x + jy − x₁ − jy₁| = R converts to Cartesian form by taking the square root of a sum of squares.
defs: Circle locus in the Argand diagram
The set of points z satisfying |z − z₁| = R, i.e. all points a fixed distance R from the centre z₁ = a + jb.
eqs: Locus of a circle with centre z₁ and radius R
z = x + jy (dimensionless complex coordinate); z₁ = a + jb (centre); R = radius (dimensionless, same units as the plane)
x, y = coordinates of P; x₁, y₁ = coordinates of centre; R = radius
t = angle of radius to the x-axis (rad), −π < t ≤ π
tips: Do not confuse the centre z₁ = a + jb with the point P(z = x + jy) lying on the circle.
Use R² (not R) on the right-hand side of the Cartesian equation after squaring.
rq: Why does the modulus |z − z₁| = R describe a circle rather than a line?
Because every point is the same distance R from the fixed centre z₁, which in the plane is the defining property of a circle.
What does the angle t represent in z − z₁ = \(Re^{jt}\), and why is it restricted to −π < t ≤ π?
t is the angle the radius from the centre makes with the positive x-direction; the interval covers exactly one full turn once, so each point on the circle is counted once.

notes.t: Locus of a circle in the complex plane: |z − z₁| = R
pts: Write z = x + iy and the centre z₁ = x₁ + iy₁; subtracting gives the real and imaginary parts of z − z₁.
The modulus |z − z₁| is the distance between the points z and z₁ in the Argand plane, so |z − z₁| = R describes all points a fixed distance R from the centre.
Applying the modulus formula to (x − x₁) + i(y − y₁) gives a square root of a sum of squares, which is then squared to remove the root.
The result is the Cartesian equation of a circle with centre (x₁, y₁) and radius R.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = a + ib, |z| = √(a² + b²), the distance of the point from the origin in the Argand plane.
eqs: Locus of points at constant distance R from centre z₁ (circle in Argand plane)
z = complex variable (dimensionless); z₁ = centre (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless, same units as the plane)
x, y = coordinates of z (dimensionless); x₁, y₁ = centre coordinates (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse |z − z₁| with z − z₁ itself; the modulus must be taken before squaring.
Remember the centre is (x₁, y₁) with signs reversed in the bracket: (x − x₁), not (x + x₁).
rq: Why does squaring both sides of √((x−x₁)²+(y−y₁)²) = R not introduce extra solutions here?
Because R is a non-negative distance, so both sides are non-negative and squaring is reversible; the result is equivalent to the original.
What does the locus |z − z₁| = R become if R = 0?
Only the single point z = z₁ satisfies it, a degenerate circle of zero radius.

notes.t: Loci as perpendicular bisectors
pts: The equation |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| describes points equidistant from two fixed points z₁ and z₂.
Equidistance from two points means the locus is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
Here z₁ = 1 + j and z₂ = 2 + j0, so the locus is a line through the midpoint of these two points.
The line through the points (1,1) and (2,0) that is perpendicular to their joining segment has slope 1, giving the locus y = x − 1.
defs: Locus
The set of all points in the complex plane satisfying a given geometric condition.
Perpendicular bisector
The line perpendicular to a segment passing through its midpoint; every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
eqs: Locus of points equidistant from two complex numbers z₁ and z₂
z = variable complex point (dimensionless); z₁, z₂ = fixed complex points (dimensionless)
Resulting Cartesian locus for this example
x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| (a line) with |z − z₁| = r (a circle); the presence of two fixed points signals a bisector.
Remember z₂ = 2 + j0 means the imaginary part is zero, so the point is (2,0); misreading it changes the midpoint and the line.
rq: Why does |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| give a line rather than a circle?
Because the condition is equal distances to two points, which defines the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them; a circle arises when the distance is fixed to one point, |z − z₁| = r.
How can you check that y = x − 1 is correct for z₁ = 1 + j and z₂ = 2?
Substitute a point on the line, e.g. z = 0 − j (x=0, y=−1): |z−z₁| = |−1−2j| = √5 and |z−z₂| = |−2−j| = √5, so the distances match.

notes.t: Loci as circles (Apollonius locus)
pts: A locus of points whose distances to two fixed points have a constant ratio \( |z-z_1| = k|z-z_2| \) is a circle when \( k \neq 1 \)
Substitute \( z = x + jy \) and square both sides to convert the complex modulus condition into a Cartesian equation
Expanding and collecting terms gives the standard circle form, from which the centre and radius are read off
Here the ratio \( \sqrt{2} \) gives centre \( (3,-1) \) and radius 2, and the dashed line is the perpendicular bisector case that arises only when the ratio is 1
defs: Locus
The set of all points satisfying a given geometric or algebraic condition, here expressed as a modulus equation in the complex plane.
eqs: Standard equation of a circle with centre \( (x_c,y_c) \) and radius \( R \)
x, y = Cartesian coordinates (dimensionless); \(x_{c}\), \(y_{c}\) = centre coordinates (dimensionless); R = radius (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the ratio case \( k \neq 1 \) (circle) with \( k = 1 \) (perpendicular bisector, a straight line).
Take the square root of the right-hand side carefully: the constant 4 on the right comes from dividing through after expanding, so check the arithmetic before reading off \( R \).
rq: Why does squaring both sides of \( |z-z_1| = \sqrt{2}|z-z_2| \) turn the condition into a circle rather than a line?

Squaring gives \( (x-1)^2+(y-1)^2 = 2[(x-2)^2+y^2] \), where the coefficients of \( x^2 \) and \( y^2 \) are both 1 on the left and 2 on the right, so the quadratic terms do not cancel and the result is a circle.
What would change if the ratio were 1 instead of \( \sqrt{2} \)?
The \( x^2 \) and \( y^2 \) terms would cancel, leaving a linear equation: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \( z_1 \) and \( z_2 \).

xq.q: A complex number \(z\) lies on the circle \(|z-(3+4j)|=2\). Find the greatest possible value of \(|z|\).
s: Centre is 3+4j, with distance from origin √(9+16) = 5
Largest |z| occurs at the point on the circle furthest from the origin, in line with the centre

xq.q: The locus \(|z+2-3j|=4\) is a circle in the Argand diagram. What are its centre and radius?
xq.a: Centre (−2, 3), radius 4
o: Centre (2, −3), radius 4
Centre (−2, 3), radius 16
Centre (2, 3), radius 4
Centre (−2, 3), radius 4
xq.w: Rewrite as |z−(−2+3j)| = 4, so the centre is −2+3j with radius 4; the traps are reversing the signs of the centre or using R² as the radius.

xq.q: Show that the locus \(|z|=2|z-3|\) is a circle, and find its centre and radius.
xq.a: With z = x + jy, squaring gives x²+y² = 4[(x−3)²+y²] = 4x²−24x+36+4y². So 3x²+3y²−24x+36 = 0, i.e. x²+y²−8x+12 = 0. Completing the square: (x−4)²+y² = 4. This is a circle with centre (4, 0) and radius 2.
s: Substitute z = x + jy and square both sides

units.name: 5.4 General loci: mapped unit circle and ellipse
units.ov: This material finds loci of complex-plane curves in two ways. For a mapping, you substitute a parametrised input curve, \(z=e^{j\theta}\), into \(w=f(z)\). For a modulus condition, you convert it to a Cartesian equation in \(x,y\) and identify the conic. Both turn a geometric description into an explicit curve, one parametric and one algebraic, and both need careful expansion of complex squares.
must: Parametrise the unit circle as \(z=e^{j\theta}\), \(0\le\theta<2\pi\), substitute into \(w=f(z)\), and separate real and imaginary parts.
For \(w=(z+1)^2\): \(w=(1+2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta)+j\,2(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta\). Expand fully, using \(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=\cos2\theta\) and \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\).

Shortcut and check: \(z+1=2\cos(\theta/2)e^{j\theta/2}\), so \(w=2(1+\cos\theta)e^{j\theta}\), i.e. \(r=2(1+\cos\theta)\). This is a cardioid, the special limaçon, with a cusp at \(w=0\) (\(\theta=\pi\)) and \(w=4\) at \(\theta=0\).
A full period of \(\theta\) gives the whole closed locus; a partial range gives only an arc.

\(|z-z_1|+|z-z_2|=k\) is an ellipse with foci \(z_1,z_2\), provided \(k>|z_1-z_2|\). Here the foci are \(j\) and \(1\), \(k=2>\sqrt2\). If \(k=|z_1-z_2|\) the locus is the segment between the foci, and if \(k<|z_1-z_2|\) it is empty.

Method for modulus loci: set \(z=x+jy\) and write each modulus as a square root. Isolate one root and square, then repeat. A quicker route is to use \(A^2-B^2\) to get \(A-B\), then combine with \(A+B=2\).
Result: \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\). Keep the cross term \(2xy\) and watch the signs.
Conic test: \(b^2-4ac<0\) means an ellipse. Here \(4-36=-32<0\).

Ellipse geometry: the centre is \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\) and the axes lie along \(y=x\) and \(y=-x\). Semi-major axis \(a=1\), semi-minor \(b=1/\sqrt2\), focal distance \(c=\sqrt2/2\), with \(b^2=a^2-c^2\). The locus passes through the origin and \((1,1)\)... check: \((1,1)\) gives \(3+3+2-8=0\), so yes.
Rotating by \(u=(x+y)/\sqrt2,\ v=(x-y)/\sqrt2\) removes the cross term and gives \(2(u-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2})^2+v^2=1\).
conn: Parametric versus Cartesian loci: the mapped circle is found parametrically, while the ellipse is found by eliminating roots. Know both, and know when to convert (e.g. \(r=2(1+\cos\theta)\) to Cartesian form).
Modulus and argument form versus real and imaginary form: \(z+1=2\cos(\theta/2)e^{j\theta/2}\) simplifies \(w\) and checks the double-angle expansion.
Geometric definition of an ellipse (sum of distances to the foci) links to the algebraic conic and the discriminant test, and to \(a,b,c\) from the rotated standard form.
Validity checks (\(k\) versus the focal separation, special points such as the cusp at \(w=0\)) are used to confirm the algebra.
exq: Find the image of \(|z|=1\) under \(w=(z+1)^2\) in parametric form. Show that \(w=2(1+\cos\theta)e^{j\theta}\), sketch it, and state the values of \(w\) at \(\theta=0,\pi/2,\pi\).
Show that \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\) leads to \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\). Use \(b^2-4ac\) to classify the conic.
For the ellipse \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\), find the centre, the semi-axes and the directions of the axes. Rotate coordinates to reach \(2(u-\sqrt2/2)^2+v^2=1\).
Determine for which values of \(k\) the locus \(|z-j|+|z-1|=k\) is an ellipse, a line segment, or empty, and justify your answer.
Find the image of \(|z|=1\) under \(w=(z-1)^2\) or \(w=z^2+2z\), and identify any cusps.

notes.t: More general loci: mapping the unit circle by \(w=(z+1)^2\)
pts: Points on the unit circle \(|z|=1\) are parametrised as \(z=e^{j\theta}\), so the mapped locus is found by substituting this into \(w=(z+1)^2\).
Expanding \((\cos\theta+j\sin\theta+1)^2\) gives real and imaginary parts that are both functions of \(\theta\), tracing a parametric curve as \(\theta\) runs over one full turn.
Varying \(\theta\) over \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) traces the complete image of the unit circle under the mapping; the resulting shape is a limaçon.
defs: Locus (of a mapping)
The set of image points \(w\) obtained when the input \(z\) traverses a given curve in the complex plane under the mapping \(w=f(z)\).
eqs: Parametric image of the unit circle under \(w=(z+1)^2\)
\(w\) = image point in the complex plane (dimensionless); \(\theta\) = angle parameter (rad)
tips: Do not forget to expand the square fully: \((\cos\theta+1+j\sin\theta)^2\) must produce the \(\cos(2\theta)\) and \(\sin(2\theta)\) terms, not just \(\cos^2\theta\).
Use \(\theta\) over a full period \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) so the whole closed locus is captured; a partial range gives only an arc.
rq: Why can we write the unit circle as \(z=e^{j\theta}\) rather than \(z=x+jy\) with \(x^2+y^2=1\)?
Because \(|e^{j\theta}|=1\) for every \(\theta\), so a single real parameter \(\theta\) covers the whole circle, making substitution and expansion into a parametric form straightforward.
Why does the curve pass through the origin, and what does that tell you about \(z\)?
At \(z=-1\) (θ = π) we get \(w=(-1+1)^2=0\), so the origin is the image of the point on the circle where \(z+1=0\).

notes.t: General loci: ellipse from sum of distances (|z−j|+|z−1|=2)
pts: Write z = x + jy and split each modulus into real and imaginary parts to get a Cartesian equation in x and y.
Remove square roots by squaring both sides, isolating one root first; this gives a quadratic curve.
The resulting general conic has the form ax² + bxy + cy² + dx + fy + g = 0; the discriminant b² − 4ac < 0 identifies an ellipse.
The locus is the set of points whose total distance to the two foci (j and 1) equals 2, which is the defining property of an ellipse.
defs: Locus
The set of all points z in the Argand diagram satisfying a given geometric condition or equation.
eqs: Cartesian equation of the locus from modulus condition
\(x\) = real part of \(z\) (dimensionless); \(y\) = imaginary part of \(z\) (dimensionless)
\(a,b,c\) = coefficients of \(x^{2}, xy, y^{2}\) in the conic (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget the cross term 2xy when expanding squares of the form (x + ...)² with complex parts; sign errors here change b and the conic type.
Check validity: the sum of distances (2) must exceed the distance between the foci (√2 here); otherwise the locus is empty or a line segment.
rq: Why must you square the equation twice-style (isolate one root, then square) rather than squaring both roots at once?
Squaring a sum of two square roots directly leaves a cross term with a root; isolating one root first lets squaring remove it cleanly, leaving a single root to handle in a second squaring.
Why does the sum of distances to two fixed points give an ellipse, and what would change if the constant were less than the distance between the foci?

The sum of distances to two foci is constant on an ellipse; if the constant is less than the focal separation (here separation is 1 and constant is 2 so it is valid), no points satisfy the condition and the locus is empty.
How can you check that the derived equation is correct without plotting?
Substitute a simple point on the curve, such as z = 0 (x = 0, y = 0), which satisfies both the modulus condition and 3x²+3y²+2xy−4x−4y=0.

xq.q: The unit circle \(|z|=1\) is mapped by \(w=(z+1)^2\), with \(z=e^{j\theta}\) and \(\theta\) in rad. The image has parametric form \(w=(1+2\cos\theta+\cos 2\theta)+j\,2(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta\). Find the real and imaginary parts of the image point at \(\theta=\pi/3\), and hence its distance \(|w|\) from the origin of the \(w\)-plane (dimensionless).

The locus \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\) leads to the conic \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\), where \(z=x+jy\). Using the test \(b^2-4ac\) for the coefficients of \(x^2\), \(xy\), \(y^2\), what is the value of the discriminant, and what does it show?
xq.a: \(-32\): an ellipse
o: \(+32\): a hyperbola
\(-35\): an ellipse
\(-32\): an ellipse
\(-5\): an ellipse
xq.w: Here a=3, b=2, c=3, so b²−4ac = 4−36 = −32 < 0, an ellipse; the traps are a sign slip, using b=1, or using b²−ac.

xq.q: Let \(z=x+jy\). Show that the locus \(|z-j|+|z-1|=2\) has Cartesian equation \(3x^2+3y^2+2xy-4x-4y=0\). Explain why the locus is a genuine ellipse and not empty or a line segment.
xq.a: Let A=|z−j|=√(x²+(y−1)²) and B=|z−1|=√((x−1)²+y²). Then A=2−B, so A²=4−4B+B², giving A²−B²=4−4B. A²−B²=(x²+y²−2y+1)−(x²−2x+1+y²)=2x−2y, so B=(2−x+y)/2. Squaring: 4(x²−2x+1+y²)=(2−x+y)², i.e. 4x²−8x+4+4y² = x²+y²+4−4x+4y−2xy. Collecting terms: 3x²+3y²+2xy−4x−4y=0. The foci are j and 1, a distance √2 apart. The sum of distances is 2 > √2, so the locus is a real ellipse, and b²−4ac=−32<0 confirms this.
s: Isolate one modulus: A=2−B and square
Square again and expand, including the cross term −2xy

units.name: 5.5 Complex functions and transformations (w = z³ on a strip)
units.ov: This material covers complex functions w = f(z) as mappings from the z-plane to the w-plane, using the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 under w = z³ as the worked example. The method is to expand (x+jy)³, separate real and imaginary parts u and v, and trace the images of the boundary lines x = 1 and x = 2. The modulus/argument view (|w| = |z|³, arg w = 3 arg z) provides a quick check on the shape of the image.
must: Expansion of \(w=(x+jy)^3\) gives \(u = x^3 - 3xy^2\) and \(v = 3x^2y - y^3\); be able to derive it using \(j^2=-1,\ j^3=-j\)
Image of a region = image of its boundary curves; substitute the boundary line (here \(x=1\) and \(x=2\)) with \(y\) as the free parameter
Boundary \(x=1\): \(u = 1-3y^2,\ v = 3y - y^3\); boundary \(x=2\): \(u = 8-6y^2,\ v = 12y - y^3\), both parametric curves in \(y\)
Polar form: \(|w| = |z|^3\) and \(\arg w = 3\arg z\), so angles triple and moduli cube; use this to check the image
w = z³ is non-linear: lines become curves (parabola-like), not strips, so do not read off boundaries without computing \(u\) and \(v\)
The notation is \(z=x+jy\) (z-plane) and \(w=u+jv\) (w-plane); do not confuse \(u,v\) with \(x,y\)
Eliminating \(y\) where possible gives a Cartesian equation for the image curve; otherwise sketch from the parametric form by plotting key points (\(y=0\) gives \(u=1\) or \(8\), \(v=0\))
Symmetry: \(y\to -y\) gives \(u\to u,\ v\to -v\), so the image is symmetric about the real axis; use it to halve the work
Check which side of the boundary curves the interior maps to by testing a point, e.g. \(z=1.5\) gives \(w=3.375\)
conn: Binomial expansion and \(j^2=-1\) algebra feed into the real/imaginary separation, so sign errors there ruin the whole image
Cartesian-parametric form (\(u(y),v(y)\)) links to polar form (\(r^3,3\theta\)); questions often ask you to verify one with the other
The strip method carries over to other maps (examples 3.30 and 3.31): same boundary-line parameterisation with a different \(f(z)\)
Sketching the image combines curve sketching with checking interior points to determine the correct region between the two curves
exq: Find \(u\) and \(v\) for \(w=z^3\) with \(z=x+jy\), and hence find the parametric equations of the images of the lines \(x=1\) and \(x=2\).
Sketch the image in the w-plane of the strip \(1\le x\le 2\) under \(w=z^3\), marking the points where the boundary curves cross the real axis (\(u=1\) and \(u=8\)) and indicating the region.
Find the image of the point \(z=1+j\) under \(w=z^3\) using both the expansion and polar form (\(|w|=2\sqrt2,\ \arg w=3\pi/4\)), showing they agree (\(w=-2+2j\)).
Show that the line \(x=1\) maps to a curve with \(u=1-3y^2\), \(v=3y-y^3\), and find where it crosses the imaginary axis (\(y=\pm1/\sqrt3\)) and the corresponding \(v\) values.
Determine the image of the strip \(1\le x\le 2\), \(0\le y\le 1\) under \(w=z^3\), and find the range of \(|w|\) and \(\arg w\).

notes.t: Functions of a complex variable
pts: A complex function maps a complex independent variable z = x + jy to a dependent variable w = u + jv, so both real and imaginary parts of the output generally change.
By convention the dependent variable is written w, with real part u and imaginary part v.
Finding the image of a region means applying w = f(z) to the boundary lines of the region in the z-plane and tracing the resulting curves in the w-plane.
defs: Function of a complex variable
A rule that assigns to each complex number z = x + jy in a set a unique complex number w = f(z); the output w = u + jv is generally complex even when the input is complex.
eqs: w = u + jv = f(z), \quad z = x + jy
z = complex independent variable (dimensionless); w = complex dependent variable (dimensionless); x, y = real parts of z; u, v = real and imaginary parts of w
tips: Do not assume a real-valued function output: f(z) is generally complex, so keep both u and v when converting w = f(z).
Remember the strip is between two vertical lines x = 1 and x = 2 in the z-plane; the boundary images, not individual points, define the answer.
rq: Why must the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 be mapped by considering its two boundary lines x = 1 and x = 2 rather than by testing single points?
The strip is an infinite region; its image is bounded by the images of its edges, so mapping the boundary lines x = 1 and x = 2 (and checking the interior) determines the image region.

notes.t: Complex transformation w = z³ on a vertical strip
pts: Write z as x + jy, so the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 is parameterised by real x with y free.
Substitute z into w = z³ and expand the cube using binomial expansion, separating real and imaginary parts.
The image is written as w = u + jv, with u and v real functions of x and y.
Identify u as the real part and v as the imaginary part of the transformed point.
Use the same parameterisation method as examples 3.30 and 3.31 for other strip transformations.
eqs: Real and imaginary parts of w = z³ for z = x + jy
\(x\) = real part of z (dimensionless); \(y\) = imaginary part of z (dimensionless); \(u\) = real part of w (dimensionless); \(v\) = imaginary part of w (dimensionless)
tips: Remember that \(j^2 = -1\) and \(j^3 = -j\) when expanding \((x + jy)^3\); sign errors here are the most common mistake.
Do not confuse \(u\) and \(v\) with the parameters \(x\) and \(y\); \(u\) and \(v\) are the coordinates in the w-plane.
rq: Why does the expansion of (x + jy)³ produce the −3xy² term in the real part but not in the imaginary part?

Because j² = −1, the terms with an even power of j (3x y² j² and y³ j³ with j³ = −j) fall into the real part with a minus sign, while odd powers of j (3x²y j and j³ y³) contribute to the imaginary part.
What happens to the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 under w = z³ if y is free to vary?
The strip maps to a curved region in the w-plane, since u and v depend on both x and y, and the image boundaries follow the curves given by x = 1 and x = 2.

notes.t: Image of a strip under w = z³
pts: The transformation w = z³ maps the vertical strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 to a region in the w-plane found by substituting z = x + iy into w = z³ and separating real and imaginary parts.
The real and imaginary parts of w are found by expanding (x+iy)³ and collecting terms, giving polynomial expressions in x and y.
The image of the strip is plotted in the w-plane to visualise how the strip is distorted by the cubic map, forming sector-like shaped regions.
defs: Image of a set under a transformation
The set of all values w = f(z) obtained as z ranges over the given set; here the image of the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 under w = z³.
eqs: Real part of z³ with z = x + iy
x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless); Re(w) = real part of w (dimensionless)
Imaginary part of z³ with z = x + iy
x = real part of z (dimensionless); y = imaginary part of z (dimensionless); Im(w) = imaginary part of w (dimensionless)
tips: Do not treat w = z³ as linear: the image of the strip is curved, not a strip, so avoid simply reading off boundaries without computing Re(w) and Im(w).
Remember that the modulus cubes and the argument triples under w = z³, which is the quickest check on the shape of the image.
rq: Why does the strip 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 not map to a simple strip under w = z³?

Because z³ is non-linear; the cube of a complex number changes both modulus (|w| = |z|³) and argument (arg w = 3 arg z), so vertical lines are mapped to curves and the strip is distorted into sector-like regions.
What happens to the argument of z when z is mapped by w = z³?
The argument triples: arg(w) = 3 arg(z), so the angular extent of the image is three times that of the original.

xq.q: The vertical strip \(1\le x\le 2\) in the \(z\)-plane (\(z=x+jy\)) is mapped by \(w=z^3=u+jv\). Using \(u=x^3-3xy^2\) and \(v=3x^2y-y^3\), find the image of the point \(z=1.5+2j\) and hence its distance \(|w|\) from the origin of the \(w\)-plane (dimensionless).
The point \(z=1+j\sqrt{3}\) lies on the boundary line \(x=1\) of a strip. What is its image under \(w=z^3\)?
xq.w: |z|=2 and arg z=60°, so w has modulus 8 and argument 180°, giving −8; the traps are squaring instead of cubing, cubing only the argument, or a sign error with j³.

xq.q: Let \(z=x+jy\) and \(w=z^3=u+jv\). Expand \((x+jy)^3\) to show that \(u=x^3-3xy^2\) and \(v=3x^2y-y^3\). Hence find the images of the points \(z=2\) and \(z=2+j\) on the line \(x=2\), and explain why the image of the strip \(1\le x\le 2\) is not itself a strip.
xq.a: (x+jy)³ = x³ + 3x²(jy) + 3x(jy)² + (jy)³ = x³ + 3jx²y − 3xy² − jy³, since j²=−1 and j³=−j. So u=x³−3xy², v=3x²y−y³. For z=2: w=8. For z=2+j: u=8−6=2, v=12−1=11, so w=2+11j. The image of x=2 is the curve u=8−6y², v=12y−y³, which is curved, not a straight line. Since the modulus is cubed and the argument tripled, the boundary lines map to curves, so the image is a curved, sector-like region.
s: Separate real and imaginary parts to get u and v
z=2 gives w=8; z=2+j gives w=2+11j
Boundary image is a curve (u=8−6y², v=12y−y³), so not a strip

units.name: 5.6 Engineering Maths Challenge: NAVIGATE
units.ov: This challenge applies complex-number multiplication to a navigation problem. A transmitter location \(z = X + Yj\) is transformed by a complex factor \((\beta + \alpha j)\), and a real navigation key is extracted from the real and imaginary parts of the result. It tests accurate algebra with \(j^2=-1\), separating real and imaginary parts, and giving the answer in exact form.
must: Signal transformation: \(w = (\beta + \alpha j)z\) with \(z = X + Yj\), so \(w\) comes from complex multiplication
\(j^2 = -1\): this is the step where sign errors most often occur
Expansion: \((\beta+\alpha j)(X+Yj) = (\beta X - \alpha Y) + (\alpha X + \beta Y)j\)
Read off \(\operatorname{Re}(w) = a = \beta X - \alpha Y\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(w) = b = \alpha X + \beta Y\); the \(j\) is not part of the imaginary part
Navigation key: \(K = \operatorname{Im}(w) - \operatorname{Re}(w) = b - a\), a real number
Substituting gives \(K = (\alpha X + \beta Y) - (\beta X - \alpha Y) = (\alpha-\beta)X + (\alpha+\beta)Y\)
Give the answer exactly, as fractions and surds with no decimals, and simplify surds and rationalise denominators where needed
Order matters in the subtraction: imaginary minus real, so check the sign of \(K\)
Quantities are dimensionless, except that \(z\) carries the units of metres from the coordinates; state this if asked
Check the result by substituting simple values or recomputing the product a second way
conn: Complex multiplication links to rotation and scaling in the Argand plane: \(\beta+\alpha j\) has modulus \(\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}\) and argument \(\arctan(\alpha/\beta)\), so \(w\) is a rotated and scaled copy of \(z\)
Exact surds arise when \(\alpha,\beta\) or \(X,Y\) are given in polar form or contain roots, which links to exact trigonometric values such as \(\cos 30^\circ=\sqrt3/2\)
Finding \(z\) from a given \(w\) requires complex division and conjugates: \(z = w/(\beta+\alpha j)\)
Equating real and imaginary parts connects this to solving simultaneous equations for unknown \(X, Y\) or \(\alpha, \beta\)
exq: Given \(z = 3 + 2j\) and factor \((1+2j)\), find \(w\) and the key \(K = \operatorname{Im}(w)-\operatorname{Re}(w)\).
Show that for general \(X, Y, \alpha, \beta\), \(K = (\alpha-\beta)X + (\alpha+\beta)Y\).
Take \(\beta = \sqrt3\), \(\alpha = 1\), \(z = 2 + \sqrt3 j\). Find \(K\) exactly, with no decimals.
If \(w = 5 - j\) and the factor is \((2+j)\), find the transmitter location \(z\) and then \(K\).
For \(\alpha=\beta\), find \(K\) in terms of \(X, Y, \alpha\). Interpret the result and find the condition on \(X, Y\) for \(K=0\).

notes.t: Challenge 3: NAVIGATE — transforming a complex signal
pts: The transmitter location is written as a complex number z = X + Yj, with X and Y as its coordinates.
The navigation system multiplies z by the complex factor (β + αj), so w is found by complex multiplication.
Once w is expanded as a + bj, the key is the difference of its imaginary and real parts.
The answer must be exact: keep fractions and surds rather than rounding to decimals.
defs: Navigation key K
For w = a + bj, K = Im(w) − Re(w) = b − a, a real number obtained from the transformed complex signal.
eqs: w = transformed signal (dimensionless); β, α = real transformation constants (dimensionless); z = X + Yj = transmitter location as a complex number (m)
K = navigation key (dimensionless); Im(w) = imaginary part of w; Re(w) = real part of w
tips: Expanding (β + αj)(X + Yj) requires j² = −1; forgetting this sign error changes Re(w).
Give K in exact form (no decimals), as the question explicitly forbids decimal approximations.
rq: Why must w be written in the form a + bj before the key can be found?
Because the key is defined using the separate real part a and imaginary part b, so they must be identified explicitly.
What happens to K if you multiply out (β + αj)z and accidentally swap the real and imaginary parts?
The sign of K reverses, since K = b − a becomes a − b, giving the wrong answer.

xq.q: A navigation system transforms the transmitter location \(z=X+Yj\) (coordinates in m) into \(w=(\beta+\alpha j)z\), with \(\beta=\tfrac12\) and \(\alpha=\tfrac32\). For \(X=6\) and \(Y=4\), find the navigation key \(K=\mathrm{Im}(w)-\mathrm{Re}(w)\) (dimensionless).
A signal is transformed by \(w=(2+j)z\) with \(z=3+2j\). What is the navigation key \(K=\mathrm{Im}(w)-\mathrm{Re}(w)\)?
xq.w: w=(6−2)+(4+3)j=4+7j, so K=7−4=3; the traps are taking j²=+1 (giving −1), swapping the order (−3), or adding the parts (11).

xq.q: For \(w=(\beta+\alpha j)(X+Yj)\) with real \(\alpha,\beta,X,Y\), show that the navigation key \(K=\mathrm{Im}(w)-\mathrm{Re}(w)\) equals \((\alpha-\beta)X+(\alpha+\beta)Y\). Hence find \(K\) in the special case \(\alpha=\beta\).
xq.a: Expanding: w = βX + βYj + αXj + αYj² = (βX − αY) + (βY + αX)j, using j²=−1. So Re w=βX−αY and Im w=αX+βY. K = αX+βY−βX+αY = (α−β)X + (α+β)Y. If α=β the X term vanishes and K = 2αY.
s: Re w = βX − αY, Im w = αX + βY

units.name: 6.1 AC through R, C, L: phase relationships
units.ov: This module shows how sinusoidal current i = i₀ sin ωt produces different voltage responses in R, C and L, taking current as the phase reference. The responses follow from the element laws v = Ri, i = C dv/dt and v = L di/dt. Phasors (rotating vectors) represent amplitude and phase, so the in-phase, lagging and leading relationships can be drawn and combined in AC networks.
must: Resistor: \(v_R = R i_0 \sin\omega t\), so voltage is in phase with current
Capacitor: \(v_C = \frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t - \pi/2)\); voltage lags current by \(\pi/2\), so current leads voltage
Inductor: \(v_L = \omega L i_0 \sin(\omega t + \pi/2)\); voltage leads current by \(\pi/2\), so current lags voltage
Reactances: \(X_L = \omega L\) (numerator) and \(X_C = 1/(\omega C)\) (denominator), both in Ω; the amplitude is \(V_0 = X i_0\)
Origin of the phases: \(i = C\,dv/dt\) and \(v = L\,di/dt\); differentiating a sine gives a cosine, i.e. a \(\pi/2\) shift
Memory aid with current as reference: inductor voltage leads (+π/2), capacitor voltage lags (−π/2); swapping them is the commonest error

Phasor: a rotating vector whose length is the amplitude and whose angle is the phase; freezing it at one instant gives a static diagram. \(v_L\) is drawn at +π/2 and \(v_C\) at −π/2 relative to the current phasor at angle \(\omega t\)
Use \(\omega = 2\pi f\) in rad/s; using f in Hz gives wrong reactances
Dependence on frequency: \(X_L\) rises with \(\omega\), \(X_C\) falls with \(\omega\), and R is independent of frequency
Instantaneous values follow from the sine forms: the voltage and current amplitudes are in the ratio R, \(X_L\) or \(X_C\), with the stated phase
conn: Element laws (v=Ri, i=C dv/dt, v=L di/dt) → calculus of sinusoids → phase shifts of 0, −π/2, +π/2
Phasor diagrams → series RLC analysis: \(v_L\) and \(v_C\) are antiphase (π apart) and partly cancel, giving net reactance \(X_L - X_C\) and impedance \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}\)
Reactance and ω → resonance, where \(\omega L = 1/(\omega C)\) and the voltages cancel, giving \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\)
Phase between v and i → power: average power is zero in ideal L and C and nonzero only in R
exq: A current i = 2 sin(100πt) A flows through a 50 Ω resistor, a 20 μF capacitor and a 0.5 H inductor in turn. Find the voltage amplitude and phase relative to the current for each element.
Derive from v = L di/dt the voltage across an inductor carrying i = i₀ sin ωt, and state whether the voltage leads or lags the current. Repeat for a capacitor using i = C dv/dt.

Draw the phasor diagram at t = 0 for a series R, L, C circuit with current i₀ sin ωt, showing \(v_R\), \(v_L\) and \(v_C\). Find the total voltage amplitude and phase for R = 30 Ω, \(X_L\) = 80 Ω, \(X_C\) = 40 Ω and i₀ = 1 A.

A 10 μF capacitor and a 0.2 H inductor are each driven at 50 Hz and then at 500 Hz with the same current amplitude. Calculate the reactances and voltage amplitudes, and explain how each changes with frequency.
A student writes \(v_C = \omega C i_0 \sin(\omega t + \pi/2)\) for a capacitor with the current as reference. Identify all the errors and give the correct expression.

notes.t: AC through R, C, L: phase relationships
pts: Current is taken as the reference: i = i₀ sin ωt for the generator.
Resistor voltage is in phase with current (\(v_{R}\) = R i₀ sin ωt).
Capacitor voltage lags current by π/2, since its amplitude is i₀/(ωC) and it is written with a sin(ωt − π/2) form.
Inductor voltage leads current by π/2, shown by the sin(ωt + π/2) form.
defs: Resistor relation
Ohm's law applied instantaneously: voltage is proportional to current, v = Ri.
Capacitor relation
Current is proportional to the rate of change of voltage across the capacitor, i = C dv/dt.
Inductor relation
Voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current through the inductor, v = L di/dt.
eqs: Instantaneous voltage across a resistor carrying sinusoidal current
\(v_{R}\) = resistor voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
Instantaneous voltage across a capacitor with sinusoidal current
\(v_{C}\) = capacitor voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s)
Instantaneous voltage across an inductor with sinusoidal current
\(v_{L}\) = inductor voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
tips: Forgetting that the capacitor amplitude has ωC in the denominator while the inductor has ωL in the numerator (units: Ω for both reactances).
Confusing lead and lag: inductor leads, capacitor lags, when current is the reference.
rq: Why does the capacitor voltage lag the current by π/2 even though the voltage equation has a 1/(ωC) factor?
Because i = C dv/dt means voltage is the integral of current; integrating sin ωt gives −cos ωt = sin(ωt − π/2), so the voltage peaks a quarter cycle after the current.
What happens to the inductor voltage amplitude if frequency doubles while i₀ stays fixed?
It doubles, since \(v_{L}\) amplitude = ωL i₀ is proportional to ω; the inductor's opposition to current grows with frequency.
Why does the resistor voltage have no phase shift?
Ohm's law v = Ri is instantaneous with no derivative or integral, so \(v_{R}\) has the same sin ωt phase as i.

notes.t: Alternating currents in electrical networks: phasors and phase relationships
pts: Current through the circuit is taken as the reference: i = i₀ sin ωt
Resistor voltage is in phase with the current
Capacitor voltage lags the current by π/2
Inductor voltage leads the current by π/2, with amplitude ωL·i₀
A phasor is a rotating vector: length gives amplitude, angle gives phase; freezing rotation at one instant gives a time-invariant picture
defs: Phasor
A complex number or rotating vector representing a sinusoid, whose length is the amplitude and whose angle is the phase; used to analyse AC circuits in steady state.
eqs: Voltage across a capacitor for sinusoidal current i = i₀ sin ωt
\(v_{C}\) = capacitor voltage (V); i₀ = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s)
Voltage across an inductor for sinusoidal current i = i₀ sin ωt
\(v_{L}\) = inductor voltage (V); L = inductance (H); i₀ = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
Voltage across a resistor for sinusoidal current i = i₀ sin ωt
\(v_{R}\) = resistor voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); i₀ = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
tips: Check the sign of the phase shift: capacitor lags (−π/2), inductor leads (+π/2); swapping them is a common error.
Angular frequency ω must be in rad/s; using Hz without multiplying by 2π gives wrong reactances.
rq: Why does the capacitor voltage lag the current by π/2 while the inductor voltage leads it by π/2?
Current into a capacitor charges it, so voltage builds up only after current has flowed (lag); an inductor opposes changes in current, so its voltage peaks before the current does (lead).
What happens to the capacitor's voltage amplitude if the frequency doubles?
It halves, since amplitude is i₀/(ωC) and ω doubles, so the capacitor's impedance falls with frequency.
Why is the resistor voltage the only one with no phase shift?
Ohm's law v = Ri holds instantaneously for a resistor, so voltage and current rise and fall together with zero phase difference.

notes.t: AC through R, C, L: phase relationships
pts: In a resistor, voltage and current are in phase; the voltage across R follows the current directly.
Across a capacitor the voltage lags the current by π/2, so the current leads the voltage.
Across an inductor the voltage leads the current by π/2, so the current lags the voltage.
The phasor diagram shows \(v_{L}\) rotated by +π/2 and \(v_{C}\) rotated by −π/2 relative to the current phasor at angle ωt.
eqs: \(v_R\) = instantaneous voltage across R (V); \(R\) = resistance (Ω); \(i_0\) = peak current (A); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(t\) = time (s)
\(v_C\) = instantaneous voltage across C (V); \(C\) = capacitance (F); \(i_0\) = peak current (A); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(t\) = time (s)
\(v_L\) = instantaneous voltage across L (V); \(L\) = inductance (H); \(i_0\) = peak current (A); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(t\) = time (s)
tips: Do not confuse the sign of the phase shift: capacitor uses −π/2 (current leads) and inductor uses +π/2 (current lags).
Check that ω is in rad/s when computing ωL and 1/(ωC); using frequency in Hz gives wrong amplitudes.
rq: Why does the capacitor voltage lag the current while the inductor voltage leads it?
A capacitor's voltage builds up only as charge accumulates from the current, so it lags by π/2; an inductor opposes changes in current, so its voltage peaks before the current, leading by π/2.
What happens to the capacitor voltage amplitude as frequency increases, and why?
It decreases, since the amplitude is \(i_{0}\)/(ωC) and ω appears in the denominator.

xq.q: A generator drives a current \(i = i_0\sin\omega t\) through an inductor \(L = 40\ \text{mH}\) in series with a capacitor \(C = 50\ \mu\text{F}\), where \(i_0 = 0.50\ \text{A}\) is the peak current and \(\omega = 1000\ \text{rad/s}\). Using the phase relationships of each element, find the instantaneous voltage across the L–C series combination (in V) at the instant when \(\omega t = \pi/3\).
s: Inductor: \(v_L = \omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2) = 20\cos\omega t\) V

xq.q: A sinusoidal current \(i = i_0\sin\omega t\) flows through a capacitor of capacitance C. Which expression gives the voltage across the capacitor?
xq.a: \(\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)\)
o: \(\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\)
\(\omega C i_0\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)\)
\(\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)\)
\(\frac{i_0}{\omega C}\sin\omega t\)
xq.w: The capacitor voltage lags the current by \(\pi/2\) and its amplitude has \(\omega C\) in the denominator; the traps are swapping lead and lag, putting \(\omega C\) in the numerator, or treating it like a resistor.

xq.q: An inductor L carries a current \(i = i_0\sin\omega t\), where \(i_0\) is the peak current and \(\omega\) the angular frequency. Starting from \(v = L\,di/dt\), show that the voltage across the inductor is \(v_L=\omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\) and explain what this means for the phase relationship between voltage and current.
xq.a: Differentiate: \(di/dt = \omega i_0\cos\omega t\), so \(v_L = L\omega i_0\cos\omega t\). Since \(\cos\omega t=\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\), \(v_L=\omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\). The voltage reaches its peak a quarter cycle before the current, so it leads the current by \(\pi/2\); amplitude \(\omega L i_0\) with \(\omega L\) in ohms.
s: Voltage leads current by \(\pi/2\) (current lags voltage)

units.name: 6.2 Phasors and complex exponential representation
units.ov: This material shows how sinusoidal currents and voltages can be written as the imaginary part of a rotating complex exponential, so that AC circuit analysis becomes complex algebra. Each component (R, C, L) is assigned a complex impedance Z that links voltage and current through V = ZI. The phase relationships (in phase, lag 90°, lead 90°) follow directly from multiplying by 1, -j or +j.
must: Euler's formula: \( e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta \), and a sinusoid is \( i=i_0\sin\omega t=\operatorname{Im}[i_0e^{j\omega t}] \)
Generalised Ohm's law in phasor form: \( V=ZI \) with \( I=i_0e^{j\omega t} \)
Resistor: \( Z_R=R \), real, voltage in phase with current
Capacitor: \( Z_C=-j/(\omega C) \), voltage lags current by 90°, impedance falls with frequency
Inductor: \( Z_L=j\omega L \), voltage leads current by 90°, impedance grows with frequency
Multiplying by \( j \) rotates a phasor by +90° (advance); multiplying by \( -j \) rotates it by -90° (lag)
Use \( \omega=2\pi f \) in rad/s, never f in Hz, when computing reactances
Phasor amplitudes are peak values \( i_0 \) unless RMS is stated; RMS changes the amplitude factors by \( \sqrt2 \)
Impedance has a real part (resistance) and an imaginary part (reactance); the physical quantity is recovered by taking Im[ ] of the complex result
Check signs: \( 1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C) \), and a wrong sign gives the wrong phase
conn: Phasors and impedance link to circuit analysis: series R, L, C impedances add as complex numbers, giving total \( Z=R+j(\omega L-1/\omega C) \), whose magnitude and phase give the amplitude and phase of the current
Euler's formula links to the time-domain result: the physical voltage is the Im[ ] of \( Z i_0 e^{j\omega t} \), with the phase of Z shifting the sine wave
Frequency dependence of \( Z_C \) and \( Z_L \) connects to resonance and to filter behaviour (low/high-pass), where reactances cancel or dominate
Phase rotation by ±j relates to differentiation and integration of sinusoids: \( L\,di/dt \) gives \( j\omega L \), and \( \frac1C\int i\,dt \) gives \( -j/\omega C \)
exq: A current \( i=2\sin(1000t) \) A flows through a 10 mH inductor. Find \( Z_L \), the complex voltage phasor, and write the instantaneous voltage \( v_L(t) \), stating its phase relative to the current.
A 50 µF capacitor carries a current of amplitude 0.5 A at f = 50 Hz. Calculate \( \omega \), \( Z_C \), the peak voltage and the phase of the voltage relative to the current.
Starting from \( I=i_0e^{j\omega t} \) and \( V=ZI \), derive the voltage across each of R, C and L and sketch the corresponding phasors on an Argand diagram.
A 20 Ω resistor and a 0.1 H inductor are in series with a current \( 3\sin(200t) \) A. Find the total complex impedance, its magnitude and phase angle, and the peak supply voltage.

Explain why using \( 1/(j\omega C) \) without simplification can give the wrong phase, and show that it equals \( -j/(\omega C) \). Then explain what changes if the given current value is RMS rather than peak.

notes.t: Phasors and complex exponential representation of sinusoids
pts: A sinusoidal current can be written as the imaginary part of a complex exponential, so sine waves become rotating phasors.
Resistor voltage is in phase with current, so multiplying by R simply scales the complex amplitude.
Capacitor voltage lags current by 90°; in phasor form this corresponds to multiplying by -j and dividing by ωC.
Inductor voltage leads current by 90°; in phasor form this corresponds to multiplying by +jωL.
