Multiplication by j rotates a phasor by +90° (advance) and by −j rotates it by −90° (lag).
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at a fixed frequency, used to convert time-domain sinusoidal analysis into algebra.
eqs: θ = phase angle (rad); j = imaginary unit
Sinusoid as imaginary part of complex exponential
i = instantaneous current (A); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
\(v_{C}\) = capacitor voltage (V); C = capacitance (F); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A)
\(v_{L}\) = inductor voltage (V); L = inductance (H); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); \(i_{0}\) = peak current (A)
tips: Do not confuse −j/(ωC) with +j: capacitors lag (−90°) and inductors lead (+90°).
Phasor amplitudes use peak values \(i_{0}\) unless stated; using RMS values changes the amplitude factors.
rq: Why does multiplying a phasor by j shift a sinusoid by 90° rather than changing its amplitude?
Because |j| = 1, so the magnitude is unchanged; j = \(e^{jπ/2}\) only adds a phase angle of +π/2.
Why is the capacitor voltage written with 1/(ωC) while the inductor voltage has ωL?
Capacitor impedance is 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) and inductor impedance is jωL, so the amplitude scaling follows from these reactances.
What would change if the current were a cosine instead of a sine?
The phasor would be \(i_{0}\) with no imaginary-part shift needed; the same 90° rules apply to the voltages relative to the current's phase.

notes.t: Complex impedances in exponential (phasor) form
pts: Switching to capital letters denotes quantities written in exponential form, so the current is a complex exponential with amplitude \(i_{0}\).
For a resistor the voltage is in phase with the current and its complex impedance is simply the resistance R.
For a capacitor the complex impedance is -j/(ωC), a purely imaginary quantity that depends inversely on frequency.
For an inductor the complex impedance is jωL, a purely imaginary quantity that grows with frequency.
In every case the voltage is the complex impedance multiplied by the current, so V = Z I.
defs: Complex impedance (Z)
The ratio of the complex voltage phasor to the complex current phasor for a circuit element, generalising resistance to AC circuits; it has real part (resistance) and imaginary part (reactance).
eqs: \( I \) = complex current (A); \( i_0 \) = current amplitude (A); \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad/s); \( t \) = time (s); \( j \) = imaginary unit
Voltage across resistor as complex impedance times current
\( V_R \) = complex voltage across R (V); \( Z_R \) = complex impedance of R (Ω); \( I \) = complex current (A)
\( Z_C \) = complex impedance (Ω); \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad/s); \( C \) = capacitance (F)
\( Z_L \) = complex impedance (Ω); \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad/s); \( L \) = inductance (H)
tips: Watch the sign and the \( j \) in \( Z_C = -j/(\omega C) \); forgetting the minus sign or writing \( 1/(j\omega C) \) without checking gives a wrong phase.
Use angular frequency \( \omega \) in rad/s, not frequency f in Hz; \( \omega = 2\pi f \).
rq: Why does the capacitor impedance \( -j/(\omega C) \) decrease as frequency increases, while the inductor's \( j\omega L \) increases?

Capacitor impedance is inversely proportional to \( \omega \), so higher frequency lets charge flow more easily; inductor impedance is proportional to \( \omega \), so higher frequency induces a larger opposing back-EMF.
Why is the resistor impedance a real number with no \( j \) term while the other two are purely imaginary?

A resistor dissipates energy and keeps voltage in phase with current, whereas capacitors and inductors store and release energy, shifting voltage out of phase by 90°, which the \( j \) factor represents.

xq.q: A current \(I = i_0 e^{j\omega t}\) with \(i_0 = 0.20\ \text{A}\) and \(\omega = 2000\ \text{rad/s}\) flows through an inductor \(L = 15\ \text{mH}\) in series with a capacitor \(C = 25\ \mu\text{F}\). Using complex impedances, find the amplitude of the physical voltage across the series L–C pair (in V).
A capacitor \(C = 20\ \mu\text{F}\) carries a sinusoidal current at angular frequency \(\omega = 500\ \text{rad/s}\). What is its complex impedance \(Z_C\)?
o: \(100\ \Omega\) (real)
xq.w: \(Z_C=-j/(\omega C)=-j/(0.01)=-j100\ \Omega\); the traps are using \(\omega C\) instead of its inverse, dropping the minus sign, or treating it as a resistance.

xq.q: Using Euler's formula, show that multiplying a phasor by \(j\) advances it by \(90^\circ\). Hence show that for \(I=i_0e^{j\omega t}\) the inductor voltage \(V_L = j\omega L I\) has physical part \(\omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\).
xq.a: Euler: \(e^{j\pi/2}=\cos\pi/2+j\sin\pi/2=j\), so \(jA=e^{j\pi/2}A\) adds \(\pi/2\) to the phase. Then \(V_L=j\omega L i_0e^{j\omega t}=\omega L i_0e^{j(\omega t+\pi/2)}\). Taking the imaginary part gives \(\omega L i_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\), so the voltage leads the current by \(90^\circ\).
s: Multiplying by j adds \(\pi/2\) to the phase
Im part gives \(\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\): lead of \(90^\circ\)

units.name: 6.3 Impedance and voltage amplitude of a series circuit
units.ov: This material develops the complex impedance of a series RLC circuit, \(Z = R + j(\omega L - 1/\omega C)\), and uses it to find the voltage amplitude and phase for a given current. It then examines how \(|Z|\) varies with frequency, with a minimum equal to \(R\) at resonance, which is the basis of frequency selection. The ideas connect as follows: phasor addition gives \(Z\), \(Z\) gives \(|Z|\) and \(\phi\), and these give \(v_0\) and the phase shift.
must: Series impedance: \(Z = R + jX\) with net reactance \(X = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\); the inductor contributes \(+j\omega L\) and the capacitor \(-j/(\omega C)\), so they partially cancel
Magnitude: \(|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L - 1/\omega C)^2}\); combine in quadrature, never add \(R + X_L + X_C\) directly and never omit the square root
Phase angle: \(\tan\phi = \frac{\omega L - 1/(\omega C)}{R}\), \(\phi = \arg Z\) (valid for \(R>0\)); \(\phi>0\) means inductive and voltage leads current, \(\phi<0\) means capacitive
Voltage amplitude: \(v_0 = |Z|\, i_0\), and the instantaneous voltage is \(v = i_0|Z|\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)
Complex form: \(V = ZI\), and the physical voltage is the imaginary part (the sine convention used here)
Phasor diagram: voltage leads the current by \(\phi\); \(\phi\) is the phase difference between applied voltage and current
Resonance: \(\omega L = 1/(\omega C)\) gives \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\), \(|Z|_{min} = R\), \(\phi = 0\) and maximum current
Frequency dependence: \(|Z|\) is large at low \(\omega\) (capacitor dominates) and high \(\omega\) (inductor dominates), so the circuit passes frequencies near \(\omega_0\)
Units: use \(\omega = 2\pi f\) in rad/s; the resonant frequency in Hz is \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\)
conn: Complex impedance gives both magnitude and phase: \(|Z|\) sets the amplitude relation \(v_0 = |Z| i_0\), while \(\arg Z\) sets the time shift in \(\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)
Resonance links the impedance formula to the phase: at \(\omega_0\) the reactance is zero, so \(|Z| = R\), \(\phi = 0\) and the current peaks, which is the basis of tuning and filtering
The frequency dependence of reactance (\(\omega L\) rising, \(1/\omega C\) falling) explains both the sign of \(\phi\) and the shape of the \(|Z|\)-versus-\(\omega\) curve
The RLC circuit is analogous to a damped driven oscillator: \(L\) is like mass, \(1/C\) like stiffness and \(R\) like damping, so resonance appears in both
exq: A series circuit has \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 0.2\,\text{H}\), \(C = 20\,\mu\text{F}\) and is driven at \(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\). Calculate \(\omega\), the net reactance, \(|Z|\) and \(\phi\), and state whether the circuit is inductive or capacitive.
For the circuit above with current amplitude \(i_0 = 0.4\,\text{A}\), find the voltage amplitude \(v_0\) and write the expression \(v(t)\), given the current's phase.

Derive the resonant angular frequency and the resonant frequency in Hz for \(L = 10\,\text{mH}\), \(C = 100\,\text{nF}\). State \(|Z|\) and \(\phi\) at resonance, and the current amplitude for a 5 V amplitude source with \(R = 20\,\Omega\).
Sketch \(|Z|\) against \(\omega\) for a series RLC circuit, labelling the minimum value and its frequency, and explain physically why the circuit blocks low and high frequencies.
A student calculates \(|Z|\) as \(R + \omega L - 1/(\omega C)\). Explain why this is wrong, give the correct expression, and show by a numerical example how large the error can be.

notes.t: Impedance and voltage amplitude of a series RLC circuit
pts: Series RLC impedance is the sum of the element impedances, so the total voltage is the sum of the component voltages for the same current.
Inductor contributes +jωL and capacitor contributes −j/(ωC); the reactances partially cancel, leaving a net reactance X = ωL − 1/(ωC).
Impedance is written in polar form with magnitude |Z| and phase φ, where the phase gives the phase difference between voltage and current.
The magnitude of impedance combines resistance and net reactance as a right-triangle (Pythagorean) sum, not a simple addition.
The phase angle follows from the ratio of net reactance to resistance, and the arg function applies to a complex number with R > 0.
defs: Impedance Z
The complex ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current in an AC circuit, Z = R + jX, combining resistance and reactance.
Phase angle φ
The argument of the complex impedance, arg(Z) = φ, giving the phase shift between the applied voltage and the current.
eqs: Total impedance of series RLC circuit
Z = total impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
|Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
φ = phase angle (rad or °); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not add |Z| values of components directly; reactances combine vectorially with a 90° phase difference, so use the Pythagorean form.
Ensure ω is angular frequency (rad/s), i.e. ω = 2πf, not frequency f in Hz, when substituting into ωL and 1/(ωC).
rq: Why does the capacitor term enter the impedance with a negative sign while the inductor term is positive?
Inductor reactance is +jωL (voltage leads current by 90°), while capacitor reactance is −j/(ωC) (voltage lags current by 90°), so their imaginary parts have opposite signs.
What happens to |Z| when ωL = 1/(ωC), and why does this matter?
The reactive term vanishes, so |Z| = R is at its minimum; this is resonance, where current amplitude is maximal for a given voltage.
Why can't you find |Z| by simply adding R, ωL and 1/(ωC) directly?
Because the components are out of phase by 90°, so they must be combined as complex numbers, giving the square-root form.

notes.t: Impedance and voltage amplitude of a series RLC circuit
pts: Voltage across the series circuit is found by multiplying the complex impedance by the complex current, V = ZI.
The real, physical voltage is the imaginary part of the complex phasor V.
The voltage amplitude equals the current amplitude times the magnitude of impedance, and the phase φ shifts the voltage relative to the current.
In phasor diagrams, the voltage vector V leads the current vector ωt by the angle φ.
defs: Impedance Z
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, generalising resistance to include reactance; its magnitude |Z| sets the voltage amplitude for a given current amplitude.
eqs: Instantaneous voltage across a series RLC circuit
v = instantaneous voltage (V); \(i_{0}\) = current amplitude (A); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); t = time (s); φ = phase angle (rad)
\(v_{0}\) = voltage amplitude (V); |Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); \(i_{0}\) = current amplitude (A)
tips: Do not forget the square root: |Z| = √(R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²), not R + (ωL − 1/ωC).
Ensure ω is in rad/s when computing ωL and 1/(ωC), otherwise reactances have wrong units.
rq: Why must we take the imaginary part of V rather than the real part to get the physical voltage?
Because the exponential \(e^{j(ωt+φ)}\) is used as a rotating phasor representation, and the sine wave corresponds to its imaginary component: Im[\(e^{jθ}\)] = sin θ.
What happens to the voltage amplitude when ωL equals 1/(ωC)?
The reactance term vanishes, so |Z| = R and the voltage amplitude is minimised at \(i_{0}\) R, the resonance condition.

notes.t: Impedance of a series LCR circuit and its frequency dependence
pts: The impedance magnitude depends on angular frequency ω, combining resistance with the net reactance of L and C.
Impedance reaches its minimum (equal to R) when the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, i.e. at resonance.
At low and high frequencies the circuit blocks current, while frequencies near the resonant value are passed.
The resonant frequency sets the frequency band the circuit passes, giving the basis of frequency selection.
defs: Resonant angular frequency
The angular frequency at which inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, giving minimum impedance equal to R.
eqs: Magnitude of impedance of a series LCR circuit
|Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Impedance is not simply R + \(X_{L}\) + \(X_{C}\); the reactances are subtracted and combined in quadrature, so use the square-root formula.
Keep ω in rad/s: the resonant frequency in hertz is 1/(2π√(LC)), not 1/√(LC).
rq: Why does the impedance have its minimum value exactly at ω = 1/√(LC), and what is the impedance there?
At that frequency ωL = 1/(ωC), so the reactance term cancels to zero and |Z| = R.
What happens to |Z| as ω tends to zero or infinity, and why does this make the circuit block those frequencies?
|Z| grows large because the capacitive reactance 1/(ωC) dominates at low ω and the inductive reactance ωL dominates at high ω, limiting current.

xq.q: A series circuit has \(R = 80\ \Omega\), \(L = 0.20\ \text{H}\) and \(C = 50\ \mu\text{F}\), driven by a current of amplitude \(i_0 = 0.30\ \text{A}\) at angular frequency \(\omega = 500\ \text{rad/s}\). Find the amplitude of the voltage across the whole series circuit (in V).
A series LCR circuit has \(L = 0.10\ \text{H}\) and \(C = 10\ \mu\text{F}\). At what angular frequency is the impedance a minimum (equal to R)?
o: \(1\times10^{6}\ \text{rad/s}\)
\(159\ \text{rad/s}\)
xq.w: Resonance needs \(\omega L=1/(\omega C)\), so \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=1/\sqrt{10^{-6}}=1000\) rad/s; the traps are using \(1/(LC)\), multiplying by \(2\pi\), or quoting the frequency in Hz (159 Hz) as rad/s.

xq.q: For a series LCR circuit with resistance R, inductance L and capacitance C driven at angular frequency \(\omega\), show that the impedance magnitude has its minimum value R at \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\), and explain why the circuit passes frequencies near \(\omega_0\) but blocks very low and very high frequencies.
xq.a: \(|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L-1/\omega C)^2}\). The square term is never negative, so \(|Z|\) is minimum when it is zero: \(\omega L=1/(\omega C)\), giving \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(|Z|=R\). At low \(\omega\), \(1/(\omega C)\) is large; at high \(\omega\), \(\omega L\) is large; either way the net reactance is large, \(|Z|\) is large and the current for a given voltage is small. Near \(\omega_0\) the reactances cancel and the current is largest.
s: Minimum when reactance term is zero: \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\), \(|Z|=R\)
High \(\omega\): \(\omega L\) dominates, large \(|Z|\); current large only near \(\omega_0\)

units.name: 6.4 Complex impedance of series R–L and RLC circuits
units.ov: This material covers the complex impedance of series R–L and R–L–C circuits in AC analysis. Impedances of R, L and C add in series, giving Z = R + jX, whose magnitude and phase angle determine the current amplitude and the voltage–current phase shift. All of it rests on converting f to ω and using consistent SI units.
must: Series impedances add: \( Z = Z_R + Z_L + Z_C \), with \( Z_R = R \), \( Z_L = j\omega L \), \( Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C} = -\frac{j}{\omega C} \)
Series R–L: \( Z = R + j\omega L \); series R–L–C: \( Z = R + j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right) \)
Magnitude: \( |Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2} \), where \( X = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \) is the net reactance
Phase angle: \( \phi = \tan^{-1}(X/R) \); this is the phase by which voltage leads current (positive for inductive, negative for capacitive)
Always use \( \omega = 2\pi f \), never f itself, e.g. at 100 Hz \( \omega = 200\pi \) rad s⁻¹
Convert units before calculating: mH → H (\(10^{-3}\)), µF → F (\(10^{-6}\))
Phasor diagram: R on the real axis, L on the positive imaginary axis, C on the negative imaginary axis, and Z is their vector sum
Rectangular \( R + jX \) and polar \( |Z|e^{j\phi} \) forms are interchangeable; be able to convert between them
Z = V/I, so \( I = V/Z \): the current amplitude is \( V/|Z| \) and its phase is \( -\phi \) relative to the voltage
Sign care: the capacitor term is subtracted in the imaginary part, and X = 0 (\( \omega = 1/\sqrt{LC} \)) gives purely resistive Z, minimum |Z| (resonance)
conn: Impedance with Ohm's law for phasors: \( I = V/Z \) gives current amplitude and phase, and then the component voltages \( V_R = IR \), \( V_L = I j\omega L \), etc.
Reactance sign and resonance: when \( \omega L = 1/(\omega C) \), the imaginary parts cancel, so φ = 0 and |Z| = R, linking impedance to resonant frequency
Frequency dependence: because X depends on ω, changing f changes |Z| and φ, so questions often ask for these at several frequencies or whether the circuit is inductive or capacitive
Complex number skills (rectangular/polar conversion, arctan quadrant choice) connect to power and phase calculations, e.g. power factor \( \cos\phi = R/|Z| \)
exq: A coil with R = 20 Ω and L = 41.3 mH is connected in series and driven at 100 Hz. Calculate Z in rectangular and polar forms, |Z| and the phase angle φ.
For the same R–L circuit with a 10 V rms supply at 100 Hz, find the rms current and its phase relative to the voltage, and state whether it lags or leads.
A series circuit has R = 50 Ω, L = 0.2 H and C = 40 µF at 50 Hz. Find the net reactance, |Z| and φ, and state whether the circuit is inductive or capacitive.
For the R–L–C circuit above, find the frequency at which the impedance is purely real, and give |Z| there.
Sketch the impedance phasor diagram for a series R–L–C circuit where \( \omega L < 1/(\omega C) \), labelling \(Z_{R}\), \(Z_{L}\), \(Z_{C}\), Z and φ, and explain the sign of φ.

notes.t: Complex impedance of series R–L circuits
pts: Series impedances add, so the total complex impedance is the sum of the resistive and inductive parts.
An inductor's impedance is \( j\omega L \), which is purely imaginary and so shifts the phase of the current.
The magnitude of impedance is found by Pythagoras on the real and imaginary parts, and the phase angle by an arctangent.
On an impedance phasor diagram, \( Z_R \) lies on the real axis and \( Z_L \) on the imaginary axis, with \( Z \) as their vector sum.
Angular frequency is \( \omega = 2\pi f \); at 100 Hz, \( \omega = 2\pi \times 100 \) rad s⁻¹.
defs: Complex impedance
The ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current in an AC circuit, written as a complex number with real part resistance and imaginary part reactance.
Phase angle φ
The angle of the impedance phasor relative to the real axis, given by \( \phi = \tan^{-1}(X/R) \); it gives the phase difference between voltage and current.
eqs: Impedance of a series R–L circuit
Z = complex impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H); j = imaginary unit
|Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H)
φ = phase angle (rad); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); L = inductance (H); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not forget to convert frequency to angular frequency: use ω = 2πf, not ω = f.
Check units: L given in mH must be converted to H (41.3 mH = 41.3 × 10⁻³ H) before multiplying by ω.
rq: Why does the inductor's term carry a factor j, and what does that do to the phase of the voltage relative to the current?
The factor j represents a 90° phase rotation; the inductor's voltage leads its current by 90°, so the term sits on the imaginary axis.
If the frequency doubled while R and L stayed the same, what would happen to |Z| and φ?
ωL doubles, so the imaginary part grows, |Z| increases and φ increases toward 90°.

notes.t: Complex impedance of series R–L–C circuits
pts: Total impedance of a series circuit is the sum of the individual impedances of R, L and C.
The inductor contributes a positive imaginary part \(j\omega L\), while the capacitor contributes a negative imaginary part \(1/(j\omega C)\).
The resistor is purely real, so it only sets the real part of Z.
Impedance can be written in rectangular form \(R + jX\) or polar form \(|Z|e^{j\phi}\); the phase angle follows from \(\tan\phi\).
Angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\) must be used, not f itself, in reactance formulas.
defs: Complex impedance Z
The ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current in an AC circuit, Z = V/I, with real part resistance and imaginary part reactance.
Angular frequency ω
ω = 2πf, the rate of phase change of a sinusoidal signal in radians per second.
eqs: Total series impedance of R, L and C
Z = complex impedance (Ω); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
|Z| = impedance magnitude (Ω); R (Ω); ω (rad/s); L (H); C (F)
φ = phase angle (rad or °); ω (rad/s); L (H); C (F); R (Ω)
tips: Do not substitute f for ω in \(j\omega L\) or \(1/(j\omega C)\); convert with \(\omega = 2\pi f\) first.
Keep sign carefully: capacitive term is subtracted in the imaginary part, and use the same units (H, F, Ω) throughout, e.g. 40 µF = 40 × 10⁻⁶ F.
rq: Why does the capacitor's impedance have a negative imaginary part while the inductor's is positive?
Inductor voltage leads current by 90°, giving +jωL; capacitor current leads voltage, so its reactance 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) is negative.
What happens to the imaginary part of Z when ωL = 1/(ωC)?
The reactances cancel, the imaginary part is zero, and the circuit is purely resistive (resonance).

xq.q: A series R–L circuit has \(R = 30\ \Omega\) and \(L = 50\ \text{mH}\). It is driven by a sinusoidal supply of angular frequency \(\omega = 800\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\) and peak voltage 100 V. Find the peak current in the circuit.

A series RLC circuit has \(R = 15\ \Omega\), \(L = 0.20\ \text{H}\) and \(C = 25\ \mu\text{F}\), and is driven at \(\omega = 500\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). Find the phase angle \(\phi\) of the total impedance, in degrees.
xq.a: φ = 53.13° (voltage leads current)

xq.q: A series RLC circuit is driven at a frequency where \(\omega L < 1/(\omega C)\). Which statement about the phase angle \(\phi = \tan^{-1}(X/R)\) of the total impedance is correct?
xq.a: φ is negative, so the current leads the voltage
o: φ is positive, so the voltage leads the current
φ is zero, because the inductor and capacitor cancel exactly
φ is negative, so the current leads the voltage
φ is −90° regardless of the value of R
xq.w: The net reactance \(\omega L - 1/(\omega C)\) is negative, so \(\phi\) is negative and the current leads; the traps are to ignore the sign, to assume exact cancellation, or to ignore R, which sets φ only to −90° when R = 0.
s: tan φ = X/R < 0, with |φ| < 90° for R > 0

units.name: 6.5 Series and parallel impedance combinations
units.ov: This material covers combining complex impedances in series (add directly) and in parallel (add reciprocals, then invert). Networks are solved by reducing series and parallel groups step by step from the innermost combination, using complex arithmetic and rationalisation to give results in the form a + jb. It extends resistor combination rules to AC circuits, where impedances are complex.
must: Series: \(Z = Z_1 + Z_2 + \dots\); elements carry the same current, so impedances add (real and imaginary parts separately)
Parallel: \(\frac{1}{Z} = \frac{1}{Z_1} + \frac{1}{Z_2}\); elements share the same voltage across the same two nodes
Two-element parallel shortcut: \(Z = \frac{Z_1 Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}\), which is equivalent to the reciprocal rule
Always invert the final reciprocal sum for parallel networks; never add the impedances directly or stop at \(1/Z\)
Rationalise by multiplying by the complex conjugate: \(\frac{1}{a+jb} = \frac{a-jb}{a^2+b^2}\) to get the form \(a + jb\)
Reduce networks from the innermost group outward, e.g. \(Z = Z_1 + (1/Z_2 + 1/Z_3)^{-1}\) for \(Z_1\) in series with \(Z_2 \parallel Z_3\)
Watch sign errors in the j-terms (e.g. \(1-j\), \(5+j5\)); a wrong sign changes the final answer
Use \(j^2 = -1\) when multiplying complex numbers, and keep real and imaginary parts separate
Units of impedance are ohms (Ω); state the answer in Cartesian form, and polar form (magnitude and phase) if asked
conn: Impedance combination feeds Ohm's law for AC: once \(Z\) is found, \(I = V/Z\) gives the current magnitude and phase
Complex arithmetic (conjugates, polar-Cartesian conversion) underpins the algebra; many lost marks come from arithmetic, not circuit method
Series and parallel reduction links to voltage and current dividers: same current in series, same voltage in parallel, used to find individual element quantities after reduction
Resistor, inductor (\(j\omega L\)) and capacitor (\(1/j\omega C\)) impedances are combined in the same way, so questions often start by deriving each \(Z\) at a given frequency
exq: Find the equivalent impedance of \(Z_1 = 2 + j3\ \Omega\) in series with \(Z_2 = 4 - j1\ \Omega\), and give its magnitude and phase angle
Two impedances \(Z_1 = 1 + j\ \Omega\) and \(Z_2 = 5 + j5\ \Omega\) are in parallel. Find \(Z\) in the form \(a + jb\), showing rationalisation
A network has \(Z_1 = 3\ \Omega\) in series with the parallel combination of \(Z_2 = j4\ \Omega\) and \(Z_3 = 6 - j2\ \Omega\). Find the total impedance, then the current drawn from a 10 V supply
A resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C are in parallel at angular frequency \(\omega\). Write the equivalent impedance and find the frequency at which the imaginary part of the admittance is zero
Explain why adding parallel impedances directly gives the wrong answer, and show with a numerical example the error in a two-element parallel circuit

notes.t: Series and parallel impedance combinations
pts: Impedances in series add directly, so the total is the sum of the individual impedances.
Impedances in parallel combine through their reciprocals: the reciprocal of the total equals the sum of the reciprocals.
Complex impedances are added and inverted using complex arithmetic, so rationalising the denominator (multiplying by the complex conjugate) is needed to express results in the form a + jb.
A combined network is solved by reducing series and parallel groups step by step, starting from the innermost combination.
defs: Series impedance combination
Two or more impedances connected end to end carry the same current; their equivalent impedance is the sum of the individual impedances.
Parallel impedance combination
Impedances connected across the same two terminals share the same voltage; the reciprocal of the equivalent impedance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual impedances.
eqs: Equivalent impedance of two series elements
Equivalent impedance of two parallel elements
tips: Do not invert each impedance and then add the results as if they were resistances in the wrong form; always take the reciprocal of the final sum for parallel networks.
Keep track of the j-terms carefully when rationalising, since sign errors in \( 1-j \) or \( 5+j5 \) are common and change the final answer.
rq: Why can we simply add impedances in series but must add reciprocals in parallel?
Series elements share the same current, so voltages add; parallel elements share the same voltage, so currents add, and admittances (reciprocals of impedance) add.
Why must the denominator be rationalised when computing \( \frac{1}{1+j} \)?
Multiplying numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \( 1-j \) makes the denominator real, giving the result in standard form \( a+jb \).
What happens to the total impedance if one parallel branch is an open circuit?
The reciprocal of the open branch impedance is zero, so the equivalent reduces to the other branch alone.

notes.t: Series and parallel impedance combinations
pts: Impedances in series add directly, so the total equals the sum of the individual impedances.
For elements in parallel, the reciprocal of the total impedance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual impedances.
Complex impedances must be combined using complex arithmetic (separate real and imaginary parts).
A network can be solved by reducing parallel groups first, then adding series elements to get the total.
defs: Series combination
Elements connected end to end so the same current flows through each; equivalent impedance is the sum of the individual impedances.
Parallel combination
Elements connected across the same two nodes so the same voltage appears across each; the reciprocal of the equivalent impedance is the sum of the reciprocals.
eqs: Z = total impedance (Ω); \(Z_1, Z_2\) = individual impedances (Ω)
Z = total impedance (Ω); \(Z_1, Z_2\) = individual impedances (Ω)
Network impedance of Figure 3.23 (\(Z_{1}\) in series with \(Z_{2}\) ∥ \(Z_{3}\))
Z = total impedance (Ω); \(Z_1, Z_2, Z_3\) = element impedances (Ω)
tips: Do not add impedances in parallel directly; invert each impedance first, add, then invert back.
Keep track of complex arithmetic: \(1/(a+jb)\) must be rationalised, and the \(j\) terms must not be dropped.
rq: Why must you invert the sum of reciprocals rather than add the impedances directly for the parallel branches \(Z_{2}\) and \(Z_{3}\)?
Parallel elements share the same voltage, so currents add; admittances (1/Z) add, so the combined impedance is the reciprocal of their sum.
What would happen to the total impedance if \(Z_{3}\) were removed (open circuit)?
Only \(Z_{2}\) would remain in that branch, so the total would become \(Z_{1}\) + \(Z_{2}\) = (1+j) + (5−j5) = 6 − j4 Ω.
Why is the parallel result (0.3 − j0.3)^−1 = 1.67 + j1.67 Ω smaller in magnitude than either branch alone?
Parallel combination always gives a total impedance smaller than the smallest individual branch impedance, since more current paths reduce opposition.

xq.q: A network consists of \(Z_1 = 4 + j3\ \Omega\) in series with a parallel pair, \(Z_2 = 10\ \Omega\) and \(Z_3 = -j10\ \Omega\). Find the magnitude of the total impedance.
Two branches are connected in parallel across a supply. Branch A has impedance \(4 + j3\ \Omega\) and branch B has impedance \(4 - j3\ \Omega\). Find the equivalent impedance of the combination.
xq.a: 3.125 Ω (purely resistive)
s: Z = 25/8 = 3.125 Ω, with zero imaginary part

xq.q: A resistor of \(10\ \Omega\) is connected in parallel with an inductor of impedance \(j10\ \Omega\). Show that the equivalent impedance is \(5 + j5\ \Omega\), and state its magnitude and phase angle.
s: Parallel rule: Z = Z₁Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂) = j100/(10 + j10)
Rationalise with the conjugate (1 − j): j10(1 − j)/2

units.name: 6.6 Parallel LC circuit and resonance
units.ov: This material analyses an ideal parallel LC circuit using phasor impedance. Admittances of the capacitor (jωC) and inductor (1/jωL) add, giving Z₁ = jωL/(1−ω²LC). The impedance diverges at ω₀ = 1/√(LC), and normalising with x = ω/ω₀ collapses every LC pair onto one universal curve.
must: Parallel elements add admittances: \(1/Z_1 = j\omega C + 1/(j\omega L)\), never add impedances directly
Equivalent impedance: \(Z_1 = j\dfrac{\omega L}{1-\omega^2 LC}\)
Resonant frequency: \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\) in rad/s, and \(f_0=\omega_0/2\pi\) in Hz
Normalised form: \(Z_1(x)=\dfrac{j\omega_0 L\,x}{1-x^2}\) with \(x=\omega/\omega_0\), a universal curve for any L and C
At \(x=1\) the denominator vanishes, so \(|Z_1|\to\infty\) (the reactances cancel; real circuits are limited by losses)
Resonance condition: capacitive and inductive reactance magnitudes are equal, \(\omega_0 L = 1/(\omega_0 C)\)
Behaviour either side of resonance: for \(x<1\) Z is positive imaginary (inductive); for \(x>1\) it is negative imaginary (capacitive); \(Z\to0\) as \(x\to0\) and as \(x\to\infty\)
Use ω in rad/s, not Hz; using f shifts the resonance by a factor of 2π
Practical context: LC resonant structures are used in quantum computing hardware, and the ideal infinite peak is tempered by resistance
conn: Complex impedance and phasors (\(Z_L=j\omega L\), \(Z_C=1/j\omega C\)) feed directly into the admittance-sum derivation of the parallel result
Parallel LC resonance contrasts with series LC resonance: parallel gives an impedance maximum (infinite), series gives a minimum (zero), though both occur at \(1/\sqrt{LC}\)
Normalisation \(x=\omega/\omega_0\) links to the analogy with the mechanical mass-spring system, where natural frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\) and frequency ratio are used in the same way
Real losses (a resistor) turn the infinite peak into a finite peak with a quality factor and bandwidth, which questions combine with resonance
exq: Derive the equivalent impedance of a parallel L and C starting from admittances, and show it equals \(j\omega L/(1-\omega^2LC)\).
For L = 10 mH and C = 100 nF, calculate ω₀ and f₀, and find the impedance magnitude at ω = 0.5ω₀ and ω = 2ω₀.
Show that \(Z_1(x)=j\omega_0 L x/(1-x^2)\) and sketch its magnitude and sign for 0 < x < 3, labelling the behaviour as inductive or capacitive on each side of resonance.
A student calculates the resonance using f in Hz in the formula \(1/\sqrt{LC}\). By what factor is the result wrong, and why?
Explain physically why the parallel LC impedance becomes infinite at resonance, and what happens in a real circuit with coil resistance.

notes.t: Parallel LC circuit and resonance
pts: Parallel LC impedance: admittances add, so 1/Z₁ equals the sum of capacitor and inductor admittances.
Impedance of the parallel LC combination peaks sharply at the resonant frequency, where the reactances cancel.
Normalising frequency by resonance, x = ω/ω₀, gives a single universal curve for any L and C.
At x = 1 the denominator vanishes, so the impedance theoretically becomes infinite (limited only by losses in practice).
The LC circuit is the basis of resonant structures used in quantum computers.
defs: Resonant frequency ω₀
The angular frequency at which the capacitive and inductive reactances of a parallel LC circuit are equal, ω₀ = 1/√(LC).
Normalised angular frequency x
The ratio of operating angular frequency to resonant angular frequency, x = ω/ω₀, used to make impedance curves dimensionless in frequency.
eqs: Equivalent impedance of parallel LC circuit
\(Z_{1}\) = equivalent impedance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
ω₀ = resonant angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
Z₁(x) = impedance (Ω); ω₀ = resonant angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); x = ω/ω₀ (dimensionless)
tips: Parallel circuits: add admittances (1/Z), not impedances; mixing these up gives the wrong expression for Z₁.
Keep units consistent: ω in rad/s, not Hz; using f instead of ω shifts the resonance by a factor of 2π.
rq: Why does the impedance blow up at resonance even though each individual component has finite impedance?
At ω₀ the capacitor and inductor currents are equal and opposite, so the total current from the source is near zero; since Z = V/I, the impedance becomes very large.
Why is it useful to plot against x = ω/ω₀ rather than ω?
It collapses all LC combinations onto one curve with the peak at x = 1, so the shape of the response can be compared independent of the specific L and C values.

xq.q: A parallel LC circuit has \(L = 10\ \text{mH}\) and \(C = 1\ \mu\text{F}\). Find the magnitude of its equivalent impedance at \(\omega = 8000\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\).
xq.a: |Z₁| ≈ 222 Ω (inductive)
s: |Z₁| = 80/0.36 = 222 Ω, and it is positive imaginary so inductive

xq.q: A parallel LC circuit with \(L = 1\ \text{mH}\) and \(C = 10\ \mu\text{F}\) is operated at half its resonant angular frequency. Find the magnitude of its impedance in ohms.

Starting from \(Z_1 = j\omega L/(1-\omega^2 LC)\) for a parallel LC circuit, show that \(Z_1(x) = j\omega_0 L\,x/(1-x^2)\), where \(x=\omega/\omega_0\) and \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\). Explain what happens to the impedance as \(x \to 1\).
xq.a: Since ω₀² = 1/(LC), ω²LC = ω²/ω₀² = x². Also ωL = ω₀xL. Substituting gives Z₁ = jω₀Lx/(1 − x²). As x → 1 the denominator tends to zero, so |Z₁| tends to infinity. The inductor and capacitor currents cancel, so the circuit draws no net current and acts as an open circuit. In practice losses limit the peak.
s: Substitute to get Z₁ = jω₀Lx/(1 − x²)
At x = 1 the denominator is 0, so |Z₁| → ∞ (resonance)
In practice losses keep the impedance finite

units.name: 7.1 3D coordinates, position vector length and direction cosines
units.ov: This material places a point P(x,y,z) in a right-handed Cartesian system and treats the position vector OP as the space diagonal of a rectangular box, so its length follows from 3D Pythagoras. Direction cosines l, m, n are the coordinates divided by r. They give the angles to the axes and satisfy l²+m²+n²=1, which gives a check and lets you find a missing component or angle.
must: Length of the position vector: \( r=|OP|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \), always non-negative, with units (m).
Direction cosines: \( l=\cos\alpha=x/r,\; m=\cos\beta=y/r,\; n=\cos\gamma=z/r \). Compute r first, then divide.
Unit-length identity: \( l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \). Use it to check answers and to get the third cosine.
Third cosine from two: \( n^2=1-(l^2+m^2) \). The sign of n is ambiguous, so use the geometry to choose it.
Direction cosines are dimensionless and keep the sign of the coordinate, e.g. \( m=-2/\sqrt{17} \). Squaring removes signs only inside r.
Angles come from \( \alpha=\cos^{-1}(l) \) etc., measured from the positive axes and lying in [0, π]. Check radian/degree mode.
The inverse cosine can give more than one candidate, e.g. \( \cos\gamma=\sqrt3/2 \) in [0, 2π). Use the geometry to select the right one.
Right-triangle projections: each coordinate is the adjacent side and r the hypotenuse. In the theodolite setup, \( |TP|=|OT|\tan(\pi/2-\gamma) \).

Components of the position vector are the coordinates, so \( \mathbf r = x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+z\mathbf k = r(l\mathbf i+m\mathbf j+n\mathbf k) \). Use a right-handed axis convention and consistent units.
conn: Magnitude and direction cosines: r is needed before any cosine can be found, and l²+m²+n²=1 then checks both.
Direction cosines and angles: given two angles or cosines, the unit-length condition gives the third, and the inverse cosine ambiguity must be resolved geometrically.
Position vector to trigonometry in surveying: a theodolite angle and a known distance give a horizontal offset via tan, which leads to coordinates and then r and the cosines.
Unit vector link: l, m, n are the components of the unit vector along OP, which feeds into later work on resolving forces and vectors in 3D.
exq: Point P has coordinates (3, −2, 6) m. Find |OP|, the direction cosines, and the angles α, β, γ to the axes. Verify that l²+m²+n²=1.

A line makes angles α=60° with the x-axis and β=45° with the y-axis. Find the possible values of the third direction cosine n and the angle γ, and explain which is appropriate if P lies above the xy-plane.
A point has m = −2/√17 and r = √17 m with x = 3 m. Find y, then the possible values of z and the corresponding direction cosines l and n.

A theodolite at T is a distance |OT| = 50 m from O, and the line to P makes an angle γ with the z-axis where cos γ = √3/2. Find γ and the horizontal offset |TP|, then state the coordinates and |OP| if the offset lies along the x-axis.
Show that for any point (x,y,z) the direction cosines satisfy l²+m²+n²=1, and use this to show whether the values (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) can be the direction cosines of a line.

notes.t: Cartesian coordinates and position vector magnitude
pts: A point P in 3D space is located by its coordinates along three mutually perpendicular axes (x, y, z) measured from the origin O.
The position vector r runs from the origin O to the point P, and its length equals the straight-line distance from O to P.
Right-angled construction: projecting P onto each axis gives the components x, y, z, which form the sides of a rectangular box whose space diagonal is r.
The same geometry applies with generic axis labels x1, x2, x3, so coordinates may be written with subscripts for indexed notation.
The right-hand figure shows a screw-like rotation about the x axis, indicating the handedness (right-handed) convention of the axis system.
defs: Cartesian coordinates
An ordered set of perpendicular distances (x, y, z) from the origin to a point, measured along three mutually perpendicular axes that meet at the origin O.
Position vector
The vector r from the origin O to a point P, whose components are the Cartesian coordinates of P.
eqs: Magnitude (length) of the position vector r from origin to P(x,y,z)
r = distance from origin O to P (m); x = coordinate along x axis (m); y = coordinate along y axis (m); z = coordinate along z axis (m)
tips: Squaring removes signs, so r is always non-negative; do not drop the square root when stating the magnitude.
Keep consistent units (e.g. metres) across x, y, z before computing r, and state the unit in the answer.
rq: Why does the formula for r come from Pythagoras applied twice rather than once?
First, the diagonal in the xy-plane gives \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); then this diagonal and z form a right-angled triangle, so \(r=\sqrt{(x^2+y^2)+z^2}\).
What would happen to r if one coordinate were negative, e.g. P(3, -4, 0)?
Nothing changes in magnitude because the coordinates are squared, so \(r=\sqrt{9+16}=5\); the sign only indicates the side of the axis.
Why must the axes be mutually perpendicular for the simple formula to hold?
Right angles make the projections form rectangular sides, allowing Pythagoras to apply; non-perpendicular axes would require a different distance formula.

notes.t: Direction cosines of line OP in 3D
pts: Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the x, y and z axes, giving l, m, n.
Each direction cosine is the ratio of the corresponding coordinate to the length r of the position vector OP.
Direction cosines of any line satisfy a sum-of-squares identity that always equals 1.
The projection of OP onto each axis forms a right triangle with hypotenuse r, which is how the cosine ratios arise.
defs: Direction cosines
The cosines of the angles between a line and the positive x, y and z axes; for position vector OP they are l = x/r, m = y/r, n = z/r.
Position vector length r
The magnitude of OP from the origin O to point P(x, y, z), given by r = √(x² + y² + z²).
eqs: l = direction cosine (dimensionless); α = angle to x-axis (rad or °); x = x-coordinate (m); r = length of OP (m)
Direction cosines with y and z axes
m, n = direction cosines (dimensionless); β, γ = angles to y- and z-axes (rad or °); y, z = coordinates (m); r = length of OP (m)
tips: Direction cosines are dimensionless: do not attach units to l, m or n.
Remember that r = √(x² + y² + z²) must be computed first; using x instead of r gives a wrong cosine.
rq: Why must l² + m² + n² always equal 1, regardless of where P lies?
Because l² + m² + n² = (x² + y² + z²)/r², and r² = x² + y² + z² by Pythagoras in 3D, so the ratio is exactly 1.
If you know only l and m for a line, how would you find n?
Use n = ±√(1 − l² − m²); the sign depends on whether the line points above or below the xy-plane.

notes.t: 3D coordinates, position vector length and direction cosines
pts: The length of OP is found from the squared sum of its coordinate components (Pythagoras in 3D).
Direction cosines are each coordinate divided by the length r, giving the cosine of the angle with each axis.
The three direction cosines of a line satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1, which provides a check on the answer.
Angles α, β, γ are found by taking the inverse cosine of each direction cosine.
defs: Direction cosines
The cosines of the angles a directed line OP makes with the positive x, y and z axes, equal to x/r, y/r and z/r.
Length of position vector r
The distance from the origin O to the point P(x, y, z), given by r = √(x² + y² + z²).
eqs: r = length of OP (m); x, y, z = coordinates of P (m)
l = direction cosine (dimensionless); α = angle to x-axis (rad or °); x = x-coordinate (m); r = length (m)
m = direction cosine (dimensionless); β = angle to y-axis (rad or °); y = y-coordinate (m); r = length (m)
n = direction cosine (dimensionless); γ = angle to z-axis (rad or °); z = z-coordinate (m); r = length (m)
tips: Keep the sign of each coordinate when squaring; squaring removes it for r, but the direction cosines keep the sign (e.g. m = −2/√17).
Give angles in the required unit and check your calculator is in the correct mode (radians vs degrees).
rq: Why must the direction cosines of OP always square and add to 1, and how can you use this to check your answer?
Because (x²+y²+z²)/r² = 1 by definition of r, so l²+m²+n² = 1; computing (3/√17)²+(−2/√17)²+(−2/√17)² = 17/17 = 1 verifies the result.
What happens to the direction cosine along an axis if the point lies in the plane perpendicular to that axis?
Its coordinate on that axis is zero, so the direction cosine is zero and the angle with that axis is 90°.
Why does the example give β and γ identical values?
Because the y- and z-coordinates of P are both −2, so their direction cosines are equal and hence the angles are equal.

notes.t: Direction cosines and position vector from a theodolite setup
pts: Direction cosines l, m, n give the cosines of the angles a line makes with the x, y, z axes; their squares sum to 1.
Given two direction cosines, the third follows from the unit-length condition, giving its angle.
The horizontal offset |TP| from a known distance |OT| and an elevation-type angle is found with a tangent relation.
defs: Direction cosines
The cosines of the angles between a line and the coordinate axes x, y, z; for a unit direction vector they are the components l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ.
Unit-length condition for direction cosines
For any direction, l² + m² + n² = 1, equivalently (x²+y²+z²)/r² = 1 where r is the length of the position vector.
eqs: l, m, n = direction cosines (dimensionless); \(r\) = position vector length (m)
Third direction cosine from the other two
n = cos γ (dimensionless); l, m = cos α, cos β (dimensionless)
|TP| = horizontal/target offset (m); |OT| = distance from O to T (m); γ = azimuth-related angle (rad)
tips: Direction cosines are dimensionless; do not attach units to l, m, n.
Check the range of the inverse cosine: cos γ = √3/2 has more than one solution in [0, 2π), so use the geometry to choose.
rq: Why does the calculation give n = √3/2 but then γ = π/6, not 5π/6?
cos γ = √3/2 has solutions γ = π/6 and 11π/6 (in [0, 2π)); the physical setup with the vertical z-axis and the device's azimuth restricts γ to the acute value π/6 for the stated geometry.
What if β were not π/2, so m ≠ 0?
Then m² > 0 reduces n² = 1 − (l² + m²), so n and hence γ change; the direction cosines must still satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1, so the result depends on m.

xq.q: A point P on a machine frame has Cartesian coordinates \(x = 3\) m, \(y = -4\) m, \(z = 12\) m measured from the origin O. Find the direction cosine \(n\) of OP with the z-axis, and hence the angle \(\gamma\) between OP and the positive z-axis, in degrees.
The line OP has direction cosines \(l = 2/7\) and \(m = -3/7\) with the x and y axes, and makes an acute angle with the positive z-axis. What is \(n\)?
o: \(\sqrt{36}/7 = 6/7\) with a negative sign, \(-6/7\)
xq.w: Use \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\): \(n^2 = 1 - 4/49 - 9/49 = 36/49\), and acute means positive, so \(n = 6/7\); the traps are choosing the wrong sign, or adding the cosines without squaring.

xq.q: Point P has coordinates \((x, y, z)\) and r is the length of OP. Show that the direction cosines of OP satisfy \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\). Then find the direction cosines of the line from O to \(P(2, -1, -2)\) m and verify the identity.
s: Each direction cosine is coordinate divided by r (1 mark)
Sum of squares = (x²+y²+z²)/r² = 1 since r² = x²+y²+z² (2 marks)
l = 2/3, m = −1/3, n = −2/3, signs kept (1 mark)

units.name: 7.2 Scalars, vectors and basic properties (equality, scalar multiples, parallel)
units.ov: This material introduces scalars (magnitude only) and vectors (magnitude and direction), shows how to represent vectors in Cartesian components and as position vectors, and defines equality, scalar multiplication and parallelism. These ideas build on each other: equality is componentwise, scalar multiplication scales every component, and parallelism is the statement that one vector is a scalar multiple of another. They are the algebraic foundation for describing forces in mechanics.
must: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector needs both magnitude and direction, so anything with direction must be treated as a vector
Position vector \(\vec{OA}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\) runs from the origin O to the point \(A(a_1,a_2,a_3)\); its components are the coordinates of A
Magnitude in 3D needs all three components: \(|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}\); the xy-projection has length \(\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}\) by Pythagoras
Equality: \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}\iff a_1=b_1,\ a_2=b_2,\ a_3=b_3\), i.e. same modulus, direction and sense, wherever located
Equal magnitude does not imply equal vectors; matching only the magnitude or only two components does not prove equality
Scalar multiplication \(\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{b}\) gives \((\lambda b_1,\lambda b_2,\lambda b_3)\) with magnitude \(|\lambda||\mathbf{b}|\); use \(|\lambda|\), not \(\lambda\)
\(\lambda>0\) keeps the direction; \(\lambda<0\) reverses it
Parallel: \(\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{b}\) for some real \(\lambda\); \(\lambda>0\) same direction, \(\lambda<0\) antiparallel (antiparallel is still parallel)
To prove parallelism, show the component ratios \(a_1/b_1=a_2/b_2=a_3/b_3=\lambda\) are all equal
Write scalar multiplication by juxtaposition (\(\lambda\mathbf{b}\)), never with \(\cdot\) or \(\times\), which denote dot and cross products; always state both magnitude and direction in answers
conn: Equality of vectors gives component equations, so finding unknown constants in a vector identity reduces to solving simultaneous equations
Parallel condition combines scalar multiplication with componentwise equality: set \(\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{b}\) and solve for \(\lambda\) and any unknown component
Position vectors plus magnitude formulas give lengths and directions of forces, and scaling by \(\lambda\) (including negative) models reversing or changing the size of a force
Collinearity of points A, B, C can be tested by checking that \(\vec{AB}\) is parallel to \(\vec{AC}\)
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=(2,-4,6)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,2,-3)\), show they are parallel, find \(\lambda\) with \(\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{b}\), and state whether they are parallel or antiparallel.
Find the value of \(p\) and \(q\) such that \((3,p,2q)\) is parallel to \((6,-4,10)\), and give the scalar multiple.
Point A is (2,3,6). Write the position vector \(\vec{OA}\), find its magnitude, and the length of its projection onto the xy-plane.
Vectors \(\mathbf{a}=(x+1,\,2y,\,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(4,\,6,\,z-2)\) are equal. Find x, y, z. Explain why two vectors of equal magnitude need not be equal.
A force \(\mathbf{F}=(3,-4,12)\) N is multiplied by \(\lambda=-2.5\). Give the new vector, its magnitude, and its direction relative to \(\mathbf{F}\).

notes.t: Scalars and vectors: definitions
pts: A scalar is fully specified by a magnitude (numerical value) alone
A vector needs both a magnitude and a direction to be fully specified
Vector mathematics is essential for describing forces
defs: Scalar
A quantity completely described by its magnitude (numerical value) alone, with no direction.
Vector
A quantity completely described by both a magnitude and a direction.
tips: Do not confuse a scalar with a vector: a quantity that has a direction must be treated as a vector, even if you quote only its size.
Always give both magnitude and direction when stating a vector result in an exam answer.
rq: Why is a force described as a vector rather than a scalar?
A force has a size (magnitude) and acts in a particular direction, and its effect depends on both, so a single number is not enough to describe it.
What would be lost if you treated a velocity of 10 m/s as just a scalar speed?
The direction of motion would be lost, so you could not tell where the object is heading or combine it correctly with other velocities.

notes.t: Vector Representation: Cartesian components and position vector OA
pts: A vector from the origin O to a point A is the position vector, written OA with an arrow over it.
A point A(a1,a2,a3) gives the position vector's components along the x, y and z axes.
The vector is written as an ordered triple of its Cartesian components, or as a single bold letter.
The projection of the vector onto the xy-plane has length √(a1²+a2²), found by Pythagoras.
defs: Position vector
The vector OA from the origin O to a point A, whose components are the coordinates of A.
Cartesian representation
Writing a vector as an ordered triple (a1, a2, a3) of its components along the mutually perpendicular x, y and z axes.
eqs: Magnitude of the vector in the xy-plane projection
tips: Do not confuse the scalar components a1, a2, a3 with the magnitude of the vector; the magnitude in 3D needs all three components.
Keep the order of the triple consistent with the x, y, z axes when reading the diagram.
rq: Why does the length of the diagonal drawn in the base plane equal √(a1²+a2²) rather than a1+a2?
Because the two perpendicular components form a right-angled triangle in the xy-plane, so Pythagoras applies; components add as squares under a square root, not linearly.
If the z-component a3 were zero, where would the vector A lie and what would its representation look like?
A would lie in the xy-plane, so the vector would be (a1, a2, 0) with no vertical height.

notes.t: Vector equality
pts: Two vectors are equal when they have the same modulus, direction and sense, regardless of where they are located.
In Cartesian form, equality of vectors means each corresponding component is equal.
defs: Equality of vectors
Vectors a and b are equal (a = b) if and only if they have the same modulus, the same direction and the same sense.
eqs: Condition for equality of two vectors in Cartesian form
\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = i-th Cartesian components of vectors a and b (dimensionless or same unit as the vector quantity)
tips: Do not confuse equal vectors with equal magnitudes: vectors with the same length but different direction are not equal.
Check all three components; matching only the magnitude or only two components does not establish equality.
rq: Why does equality of vectors not depend on where the vectors are drawn?
Because a vector is defined only by its modulus, direction and sense (its free-vector nature); position does not change it, so equal components imply equal vectors wherever they are placed.
If two vectors have equal magnitudes but opposite sense, can they be equal?
No. Equality requires the same sense as well as the same modulus and direction, so opposite sense means the vectors are not equal (they are negatives of each other).

notes.t: Multiplication by a Scalar
pts: Multiplying a vector by a scalar λ scales its magnitude by |λ|, giving a new vector parallel to the original.
If λ is positive, the result points in the same direction as the original vector.
If λ is negative, the result points in the opposite direction, with magnitude |λ| times that of the original vector.
Multiplication by a scalar is written by juxtaposition, not with a dot or cross symbol, since those denote other operations in vector algebra.
defs: Scalar
A quantity with magnitude only (a real number) that is used to multiply a vector, changing its magnitude and possibly reversing its direction.
eqs: \mathbf{a} = resultant vector (same units as \mathbf{b}); \lambda = scalar (dimensionless); \mathbf{b} = original vector (units of \mathbf{b})
tips: Do not write a·b or a×b when meaning scalar multiplication; those symbols denote the dot and cross products.
For negative λ, the magnitude uses |λ|, not λ; forgetting the modulus gives a negative length.
rq: Why does a negative λ reverse the direction of a vector, even though the magnitude is still scaled by |λ|?
Because the sign of λ sets the sense of the vector: a negative factor flips it to point the opposite way, while |λ| sets the length, which is always non-negative.
What would the result be if λ = 0?
The zero vector: its magnitude is 0 and it has no defined direction.

notes.t: Parallel Vectors
pts: Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other.
The scalar λ is a real number, not a vector; it may be positive or negative.
If λ > 0, the vectors point in the same direction, so they are parallel.
If λ < 0, the vectors point in opposite directions, so they are antiparallel.
defs: Parallel vectors
Vectors a and b are parallel if a = λb for some scalar λ, with λ > 0 meaning they point in the same direction.
Antiparallel vectors
Vectors a and b are antiparallel if a = λb with λ < 0, meaning they point in opposite directions.
eqs: a = vector; b = vector; λ = scalar (dimensionless or same units ratio)
tips: Do not confuse antiparallel with 'not parallel': antiparallel vectors are still parallel, just pointing in opposite directions.
The scalar λ must be a real number; a check that one vector is a multiple of the other (ratio of components equal) is needed to prove parallelism.
rq: Why does the sign of λ determine direction rather than just whether the vectors are parallel?
Both cases satisfy a = λb, so they are both parallel lines; the sign of λ only tells whether the direction is the same (λ > 0) or reversed (λ < 0).
If a = 0 (zero vector), can it be parallel to b?
Yes, since 0 = 0·b for any b, the zero vector is parallel to every vector under this definition.

xq.q: Forces are given as vectors in newtons: \(\mathbf{a} = (2, -6, 4)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (-3, 9, p)\), where p is a constant. Given that \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) are parallel, find p, and state whether they are parallel or antiparallel.
xq.a: \(p = -6\) N; antiparallel since \(\lambda = -3/2 < 0\)

xq.q: Vectors \(\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 3)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (3, 2, 1)\) are compared. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: They are not equal because the corresponding components differ
o: They are equal because they have the same modulus
They are parallel because they contain the same numbers
They are not equal because the corresponding components differ
They are antiparallel because the components are reversed in order
xq.w: Equality requires every corresponding component to match; equal modulus (√14 each) only gives equal length, not equal direction.

xq.q: Explain, using the definition of parallel vectors, why \(\mathbf{a} = (2, 1, -3)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (-6, -3, 9)\) are parallel, and decide whether they are parallel or antiparallel. Find the ratio of their moduli \(|\mathbf{b}|/|\mathbf{a}|\).
xq.a: b = λa with λ = −3 for all three components (−6=−3×2, −3=−3×1, 9=−3×(−3)). So b is a scalar multiple of a, hence parallel. λ < 0 so they point in opposite directions: antiparallel. |b| = |λ||a| = 3|a|, so the ratio is 3.

units.name: 7.3 Modulus, unit vectors and normalisation
units.ov: This material defines the modulus (length) of a vector as a non-negative scalar, and the unit vector as a dimensionless vector of length 1 that carries direction only. Normalisation divides a non-zero vector by its modulus to give its unit vector, and any vector can be rebuilt as modulus times unit vector. The null vector, with zero length and no direction, cannot be normalised.
must: Modulus of a 2D vector: \( |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2} \); in 3D add \( a_z^2 \) under the root (the notes only give the 2D form)
Normalisation: \( \hat{\mathbf{a}} = \mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}| \) gives length 1 in the same direction as \( \mathbf{a} \)
Reconstruction: \( \mathbf{a} = |\mathbf{a}|\,\hat{\mathbf{a}} \), so magnitude and direction are separated
The modulus is a scalar and is always \( \ge 0 \); never confuse \( \mathbf{a} \) with \( |\mathbf{a}| \)
Unit vectors are dimensionless; the units of a vector sit entirely in its modulus
Divide by the modulus \( |\mathbf{v}| \), not by a single component
The null vector \( \mathbf{0} \) has zero length and no defined direction, so it cannot be normalised (division by 0)
Standard unit vectors \( \hat{\mathbf{i}}=(1,0) \) and \( \hat{\mathbf{j}}=(0,1) \) lie on the unit circle
Do not forget the square root: e.g. \( |\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{5} \), not 5
conn: Components and modulus: the modulus comes from Pythagoras on the components, and the unit vector then has components \( a_x/|\mathbf{a}| \) and \( a_y/|\mathbf{a}| \), which are direction cosines
Unit vector times a magnitude gives a vector in a stated direction, as in a force of given size along a given line (mechanics resolution of forces)

Normalisation links to \( \hat{\mathbf{i}} \), \( \hat{\mathbf{j}} \) notation: a vector \( a_x\hat{\mathbf{i}}+a_y\hat{\mathbf{j}} \) has modulus from its coefficients, and dividing gives a unit vector on the unit circle
Vector addition or subtraction (e.g. \( \overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \)) is usually followed by finding the modulus (distance) and then the unit vector (direction)
exq: Given \( \mathbf{a} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} \), find \( |\mathbf{a}| \) and the unit vector \( \hat{\mathbf{a}} \), then verify that \( |\hat{\mathbf{a}}|=1 \).
Points A(1,2) and B(4,6) are given. Find \( \overrightarrow{AB} \), its modulus, and the unit vector in the direction from A to B.

A force has magnitude 50 N and acts in the direction of \( \mathbf{v}=2\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}} \). Write the force as a vector using \( \mathbf{F}=|\mathbf{F}|\hat{\mathbf{v}} \), and state the units of each part.
Find a vector of modulus 10 parallel to \( 5\hat{\mathbf{i}}+12\hat{\mathbf{j}} \). Explain why the same method fails for the null vector.
Find the value(s) of \( k \) for which \( \mathbf{a}=k\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{\mathbf{j}} \) is a unit vector.

notes.t: Vector modulus, unit vectors and the null vector
pts: The modulus (length or magnitude) of a vector is written |a| or |OA|, and is a scalar quantity.
A unit vector has modulus of one and is used to indicate direction only.
Any non-zero vector can be expressed as its modulus multiplied by its unit vector, and the unit vector is found by dividing by the modulus.
The null vector is a vector of zero length and is written as a bold zero.
defs: Modulus (magnitude)
The length of a vector, a non-negative scalar, written |a| or |OA|.
Unit vector
A vector with modulus equal to one, used to represent direction; denoted with a hat, e.g. â.
Null vector
The vector with zero magnitude and no defined direction, written as the bold zero 0.
eqs: Vector expressed as modulus times unit vector
a = vector; |a| = modulus of a (m, or the unit of a); â = unit vector in the direction of a (dimensionless)
Unit vector in direction of a
â = unit vector (dimensionless); a = vector; |a| = modulus of a
tips: Do not confuse the vector a with its modulus |a|; the modulus is a scalar and is always non-negative.
The unit vector is dimensionless, so units of a vector are carried entirely by its modulus.
rq: Why does dividing a vector by its modulus give a vector of length one, and why is this useful?
Dividing by |a| scales every component by the same positive factor, so the length becomes |a|/|a| = 1 while the direction is unchanged; this lets us separate magnitude from direction.
What would happen if you tried to compute the unit vector of the null vector 0?
It is undefined, because |0| = 0 and division by zero is not allowed; the null vector has no direction, so it has no unit vector.

notes.t: Modulus and unit vectors
pts: The modulus of a vector is found from the square root of the sum of squares of its components.
A unit vector is obtained by dividing a vector by its modulus, giving length 1 in the same direction.
Normalisation keeps the direction of a vector while scaling its length to one.
The modulus is always non-negative, so the unit vector direction matches the original vector's direction.
defs: Unit vector
A vector of magnitude 1 pointing in the same direction as a given non-zero vector, found by dividing the vector by its modulus.
Modulus (magnitude) of a vector
The length of a vector, equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.
eqs: \widehat{a} = unit vector (dimensionless); \mathbf{a} = vector (same unit as a); |\mathbf{a}| = modulus of a (same unit as a)
|\mathbf{a}| = modulus (same unit as components); \(a_{x}\) = x-component; \(a_{y}\) = y-component
tips: Unit vectors are dimensionless; do not carry units of the original vector into \widehat{a}.
Remember to take the square root when finding the modulus, e.g. |a| = √5 not 5.
rq: Why does dividing a vector by its modulus produce a vector of length 1 without changing its direction?

Dividing by the positive scalar |a| only rescales the length; the modulus of the result is |a|/|a| = 1, and the direction is unchanged because the components are all scaled by the same positive factor.
What would happen to the unit vector if you divided by the square of the modulus instead?
The result would have modulus 1/|a|, not 1, so it would not be a unit vector although it would still point in the same direction.

notes.t: Unit vectors: definition and normalisation
pts: A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1 and carries only direction information.
Any non-zero vector can be normalised by dividing it by its own length to give a unit vector in the same direction.
The standard Cartesian unit vectors are i-hat (1,0) along x and j-hat (0,1) along y, lying on the unit circle.
defs: Unit vector
A vector of magnitude exactly 1 that points in the same direction as a given vector; used to express direction without magnitude.
eqs: Unit vector in the direction of v (normalisation)
\hat{u} = unit vector (dimensionless); \vec{v} = given vector (units of \vec{v}); |\vec{v}| = magnitude of \vec{v} (same units as \vec{v})
tips: Normalising requires dividing by the magnitude |v|, not by a component of v; the zero vector cannot be normalised because its length is 0.
A unit vector is dimensionless in magnitude, so do not confuse \hat{u} with a vector carrying physical units of \vec{v}.
rq: Why does dividing a vector by its own magnitude produce a vector of length 1 while keeping its direction?
Dividing by the scalar |v| scales every component by the same positive factor 1/|v|, so the direction is unchanged, and the new length is |v|/|v| = 1.
What would happen to the unit vector if you divided by 2|v| instead of |v|?
Its direction would be unchanged, but its magnitude would be 1/2, so it would no longer be a unit vector.

xq.q: A displacement vector is \(\mathbf{v} = (2, -3, 6)\) m. Find its unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\) and hence the displacement vector of length 35 m in the same direction. Give the z-component of that vector in metres.
xq.a: |v| = 7 m, unit vector (2/7, −3/7, 6/7); 35 m vector = (10, −15, 30) m, z-component 30 m

xq.q: The vector \(\mathbf{a} = (3, -4)\) N is normalised to give \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\). Which is correct?
xq.a: \((3/5, -4/5)\), dimensionless
o: \((3/5, -4/5)\), dimensionless
xq.w: |a| = √(9+16) = 5 N, so â = (0.6, −0.8) with no units; traps are keeping units, forgetting the square root (dividing by 25), or dividing by a component.

xq.q: Show that \(\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}|\) has modulus 1 for any non-zero vector \(\mathbf{a}\). Hence find the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a} = (4, -3)\) m and write \(\mathbf{a}\) as modulus times unit vector. Explain why the null vector cannot be normalised.
xq.a: |â| = |a|/|a| = 1 since scaling by 1/|a| > 0 scales length by 1/|a|. For a = (4,−3): |a| = 5 m, â = (4/5, −3/5), a = 5 m × (0.8, −0.6). The null vector has |0| = 0, so division by zero is undefined (and it has no direction).
s: Scalar 1/|a| is positive so direction unchanged, modulus scaled to 1 (2 marks)
Zero modulus means division by zero (1 mark)

units.name: 7.4 Vector addition and subtraction (triangle and parallelogram laws)
units.ov: This material introduces vector addition by the triangle law (head-to-tail) and the parallelogram law (tail-to-tail diagonal), the algebraic laws these obey, and subtraction as addition of the negative. It extends to chains of vectors, closed polygons summing to zero, and component-based resultants such as the sailing-boat displacement. All of it rests on one idea: a vector sum depends on direction as well as magnitude, so it must be built geometrically or by components.
must: Triangle law: place vectors head-to-tail and the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last, \(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}=\vec{AC}\)
Parallelogram law: draw a and b tail-to-tail from O; the diagonal from O is \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\)
Magnitudes do not add: \(|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|\le|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|\), with equality only if a and b are parallel in the same direction
Subtraction is addition of the negative: \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}+(-\mathbf{b})\), where \(-\mathbf{b}\) has the same magnitude and opposite direction

Algebraic laws: \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}\), \((\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})+\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a}+(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})\), \(\lambda(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b}\)
Reversing a vector changes its sign: \(\vec{CB}=-\vec{BC}\), and \(\vec{CB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OC}\) by going via the common origin
Polygon rule: a closed loop of vectors traversed head-to-tail sums to zero, e.g. \(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}+\vec{CD}+\vec{DA}=\mathbf{0}\); use it to solve for an unknown side
Chain addition: \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}+\dots+\mathbf{k}\), with order irrelevant to the resultant
Components for a leg of length r at angle θ from north: \(\vec r=(r\sin\theta,\,r\cos\theta)\); sum the components to get \(\vec R\)

Displacement is not distance travelled: the resultant is the straight-line vector from start to finish (shorter than the 21 km path in the sailing example); only add vectors with the same units and a consistent angle reference
conn: Triangle and parallelogram laws give the same resultant, and both are the graphical form of adding components
Subtraction via the negative links to the common-origin identity \(\vec{AB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OA}\), which links to the polygon rule for finding unknown sides in geometry problems
Scalar multiples (\(\lambda\vec{OB}\), negative λ reversing direction) combine with addition in expressions like \(\vec{OA}-\lambda\vec{OB}\) and in the distributive law
Compass bearings or angles from north feed into component form, so navigation problems combine chain addition, component resolution and magnitude/direction of the resultant
exq: A boat sails 10 km NE, then 6 km NW, then 1 km due west. Using components with angles measured from north, find the resultant displacement from the start: its magnitude and bearing. State how it differs from the total distance travelled.

In quadrilateral OABC, OA = a, OB = b and OC = c. Express \(\vec{AB}\), \(\vec{CB}\) and \(\vec{AC}\) in terms of a, b and c. Then use the polygon rule to find \(\vec{DA}\) if D completes a closed loop.

Two vectors of magnitude 5 m and 8 m are at 60° to each other. Find \(|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|\) and \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) using the parallelogram/triangle construction, and explain why neither equals 13 m or 3 m.
Prove graphically and algebraically that vector addition is commutative and associative, using \(\vec{AB}\), \(\vec{AC}\), \(\vec{AD}\) drawn in different orders.
Given \(\vec{OA}\) and \(\vec{OB}\) with λ = −2, sketch and compute \(\vec{OA}-\lambda\vec{OB}\) for \(\vec{OA}=(3,1)\) m and \(\vec{OB}=(1,4)\) m. State its magnitude and direction.

notes.t: Addition of vectors (triangle law)
pts: Adding vectors head-to-tail: OA = a then AC = b gives the resultant OC = a + b.
The order of addition does not change the resultant (commutativity), so the same vector a + b is reached by starting with b.
Directions are given by compass bearings: N is up, E is to the right, and NNE lies between N and E.
defs: Resultant vector
The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors applied in succession; for a and b placed head-to-tail it runs from the tail of the first to the head of the second.
eqs: Resultant of two vectors placed head to tail
a = first displacement vector (m); b = second displacement vector (m); OC = resultant vector (m)
tips: Do not add magnitudes directly; vector addition must account for direction, so |a + b| is generally not |a| + |b|.
Check that vectors are placed head-to-tail consistently before reading off the resultant.
rq: Why does the resultant a + b point from O to C rather than from A to B?
Because the resultant joins the start of the first vector (O) to the end of the second vector (C) when they are placed head-to-tail.
What would happen to the resultant if b were drawn starting at O instead of at A?
The shape would be a parallelogram and the diagonal from O would still give a + b, so the result is unchanged.

notes.t: Parallelogram rule for vector addition
pts: Vector sum a + b is found by forming a parallelogram with a and b as adjacent sides.
The resultant a + b is the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the common origin O.
Vectors a and b share the starting point O, and their tails are joined to form the other two sides (OA and OB, with C completing the figure).
defs: Resultant (sum) of two vectors
The single vector a + b obtained by placing a and b tail-to-tail and taking the diagonal of the parallelogram they generate.
tips: Draw both vectors from the same origin; if they are not tail-to-tail the parallelogram is not formed correctly.
Adding vectors is not the same as adding magnitudes: |a + b| is generally less than |a| + |b| unless a and b are parallel.
rq: Why must a and b be placed tail-to-tail at O rather than tip-to-tail when using the parallelogram rule?

Tail-to-tail placement makes a and b adjacent sides of the same parallelogram, so the diagonal from O gives a + b directly; the tip-to-tail (triangle) construction gives the same result but uses a different geometric picture.
What happens to the resultant if b is reversed in direction?
The parallelogram collapses toward a difference, and the diagonal represents a − b (the other diagonal represents a + b), so the sign of b matters.

notes.t: Vector addition: triangle law
pts: Two vectors can be added by placing them tail-to-tip; the sum is the vector drawn from the tail of the first to the tip of the second.
The resultant a + b is the closing third side of the triangle, giving both magnitude and direction.
Order of the sides matters for the path taken, but the closing side (the sum) is the same vector regardless of order.
defs: Triangle law of vector addition
If two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the two sides of a triangle taken in order, their sum is represented in magnitude and direction by the closing third side.
tips: Keep the arrows head-to-tail when drawing; joining two tails or two tips gives the wrong resultant.
The resultant points into the closing side's arrowhead (from start to finish), so check the direction of the sum arrow.
rq: Why does the sum point from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the second rather than the other way round?
Because the vectors are chained tail-to-tip, so the resultant must start at the first tail and finish at the last tip; reversing the closing arrow would reverse the sum to −(a + b).

notes.t: Tail-to-tip vector addition
pts: Vectors can be added by placing them head to tail; the resultant runs from the start of the first vector to the tip of the last.
The resultant r joins the origin O to the final point K, so it is the sum of all the successive vectors a, b, c, …, k.
The order of addition does not change the resultant, since vector addition is commutative.
defs: Resultant vector
The single vector that has the same effect as a set of vectors added together; it is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last.
eqs: Resultant of a chain of vectors by tail-to-tip addition
\mathbf{r} = resultant vector (same unit as the component vectors); \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\dots,\mathbf{k} = successive displacement/vector quantities (same unit each)
tips: Keep the direction of each vector: adding vectors head-to-tail requires following their arrows, not just adding magnitudes.
Vector addition only works when all quantities share the same units; do not add a displacement to a velocity.
rq: Why does the resultant r point from O to K rather than from K back to O?
Because r is defined as the displacement from the starting point O to the final tip K, following the head-to-tail chain of vectors.
What happens to r if the vectors are added in a different order, e.g. c before a?
The resultant is unchanged, because the total displacement from start to end depends only on the endpoints, not the order of the steps.

notes.t: Vector Algebra: Laws of Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication
pts: Vector addition is commutative: the order of the two vectors does not change the sum.
Vector addition is associative: when adding three vectors, the grouping can be changed without affecting the result.
Scalar multiplication distributes over vector addition: a scalar multiplying a sum equals the sum of the scalar multiplied by each vector.
eqs: a, b = vectors (any units of the physical quantity they represent)
a, b, c = vectors (any units of the physical quantity they represent)
Distributive law of scalar multiplication over vector addition
λ = scalar (dimensionless or same unit as the scaling quantity); a, b = vectors
tips: Vector laws hold for vectors, not for their magnitudes: |a + b| is generally not equal to |a| + |b|.
Do not confuse the distributive law λ(a + b) = λa + λb with the non-existent rule for distributing over products of vectors; only scalars distribute in this way.
rq: Why does the commutative law hold geometrically when adding two vectors head-to-tail?
Both orders form the same parallelogram (diagonal is the resultant), so the resultant vector is identical either way.
What would change if you applied λ to only one term, i.e. λa + b, when trying to distribute?
It is not equal to λ(a + b); the scalar must multiply every vector in the sum for the distributive law to hold.

notes.t: Vector subtraction as addition of the negative
pts: Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative, so a difference can be built with the triangle law.
Scalar multiples of a position vector are found by scaling its length; λOB gives a parallel vector of length |λ| times |OB|.
The negative of a vector has the same magnitude but opposite direction, shown by the dashed arrow.
OA − λOB is the vector from the tip of λOB' to A, i.e. the result of adding OA and −λOB.
defs: Vector subtraction
