The difference a − b of two vectors is defined as the sum of a and the negative of b: a − b = a + (−b).
Negative of a vector
The vector −b has the same magnitude as b but points in the opposite direction.
eqs: Vector subtraction as addition of the negative
a = first vector; b = vector being subtracted (same units as a)
Subtracting a scalar multiple of a position vector
OA, OB = position vectors (m); λ = real scalar (dimensionless)
tips: Keep the direction of −b opposite to b; using the same direction gives the wrong resultant.
Check that λ is a scalar: multiplying a vector by λ scales its length by |λ| and reverses direction if λ < 0.
rq: Why can subtraction be rewritten as addition, and what does this let you do geometrically?
Because a − b = a + (−b); you can then use the triangle law by drawing −b (same length, opposite direction) and joining it head-to-tail to a.
What happens to the diagram if λ is negative in λOB?
λOB points in the opposite direction to OB, so the scaled vector reverses direction and −λOB then points along OB.

notes.t: Vector addition and subtraction from a diagram (Example 4.4)
pts: Express an unknown side vector by adding or subtracting known vectors that form a closed path through a triangle.
Vector subtraction: \(\overrightarrow{CB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OC}\) follows from going via the common origin O.
The polygon rule: a closed loop of vectors around a quadrilateral sums to zero.
Reversing a vector's direction changes its sign, so a vector traversed against its arrow contributes a negative term.
Solving the closed-loop equation gives the unknown side in terms of the others.
defs: Polygon rule
For a closed polygon of vectors traversed head-to-tail, the vector sum of all sides is the zero vector.
eqs: vectors AB, AO, OB (m if position vectors in metres)
vectors CB, OB, OC (same SI unit as the vectors, e.g. m)
vectors CD, DA, AB, BC (same SI unit)
tips: Watch direction: a vector written in reverse order (e.g. CB instead of BC) changes sign.
Keep track of signs when reading a loop; forgetting the minus on a reversed side gives a wrong answer.
rq: Why does \(\overrightarrow{CB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OC}\) rather than \(\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}\)?
Going from C to B means going back from C to O (that is −OC) then from O to B (OB), so the vectors are subtracted because OC points the opposite way to the path.
What if you traverse a side of a closed loop against its arrow?
Its vector changes sign, so you write it with a minus, e.g. −h, as done for side h in the loop CBAD.

notes.t: Vector addition: tail-to-tip method for a sailing boat's displacement
pts: Each leg of the journey is a displacement vector with magnitude and direction; the total displacement is the vector sum of the legs.
In the tail-to-tip method, each vector starts where the previous one ends, and the resultant runs from the initial tail to the final tip.
Angles are measured from the north direction (or a horizontal reference), so the NE leg at π/3 and the NW leg at π/4 are given relative to the north axis.
The final 1 km leg points due west, so it is horizontal and only changes the east–west component.
defs: Displacement vector
A vector giving the straight-line change in position from a starting point to an end point, with magnitude equal to the distance in a straight line and a direction.
Resultant vector
The single vector equal to the sum of several vectors, joining the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last.
eqs: Cartesian components of a leg of length \(r\) at angle \(\theta\) from north (positive east/north)
\(r\) = leg length (km); \(\theta\) = angle from north (rad); \(\vec{r}\) = displacement vector (km)
\(\vec{r}_i\) = displacement of leg \(i\) (km); \(\vec{R}\) = total displacement from A to the arrival point (km)
tips: Measure angles consistently from the north (or the horizontal) axis; mixing reference directions gives wrong components.
Keep units in km throughout and check that the final arrival point is expressed as a displacement from A, not as a distance travelled (total distance is 21 km, but displacement is shorter).
rq: Why does the final 1 km leg towards the west not affect the north–south position of the boat?
A westward displacement is perpendicular to north, so it has zero north component and only changes the east–west coordinate.
How would the tail-to-tip result change if the legs were added in a different order?
The resultant vector is the same, because vector addition is commutative; only the intermediate points change.

notes.t: Vector addition and subtraction (triangle and parallelogram laws)
pts: Adding vectors head-to-tail: the sum \(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}\) is the single vector from the start of the first to the end of the second.
Graphically, the commutative and associative laws of vector addition can be verified by drawing the vectors in different orders and comparing the resultant.
Vector addition is commutative and associative, so the order of grouping and of summands does not change the resultant vector.
defs: Triangle law of vector addition
If two vectors are placed head-to-tail, their resultant is the vector joining the tail of the first to the head of the second.
eqs: Vector sum by triangle law (chaining displacements)
\overrightarrow{AB}, \overrightarrow{AC}, \overrightarrow{AD} = vectors (same unit as the quantity they represent)
tips: Keep the head-to-tail order when chaining vectors; reversing a vector changes its sign.
Check that both sides of an associativity or commutativity check use identical vectors, not just similar-looking ones.
rq: Why does the triangle law give the same resultant regardless of which vector is drawn first?
Because vector addition is commutative: \(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}\) and \(\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{AB}\) produce the same diagonal, so the resultant is unchanged by order.
What if the vectors are not joined head-to-tail when you apply the triangle law?
The construction no longer gives the resultant; you must translate vectors so the head of one meets the tail of the next before joining start to end.

xq.q: A drone flies three successive horizontal displacements: \(\mathbf{a}\) = 11 m due East, \(\mathbf{b}\) = 8 m due North, then \(\mathbf{c}\) = 5 m due West. Using tail-to-tip addition, find the magnitude of the resultant displacement \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\) from the start point.
Two forces of magnitude 5 N and 12 N act at the same point at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
o: 7 N
xq.w: The resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram (a right-angled triangle), so |a+b| = √(5²+12²) = 13 N; adding magnitudes (17) ignores direction.

xq.q: Using the triangle law, explain why \(|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|\) is in general less than \(|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|\), and state the condition under which equality holds.
xq.a: Place a and b head-to-tail; the resultant a+b is the closing third side of the triangle. One side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two, so |a+b| < |a|+|b|. If a and b are parallel and in the same direction, the triangle collapses into a straight line and the resultant length equals |a|+|b|.
s: Draw a then b head-to-tail with a+b as closing side (1)
Closing side of a triangle shorter than sum of other two sides (2)
Magnitudes add directly only if a, b parallel in same direction (triangle degenerates) (1)

units.name: 7.5 Resultant magnitude: laws of cosines and sines
units.ov: This material finds the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors using the law of cosines (magnitude) and the law of sines (direction), with Pythagoras on resolved components as the underlying derivation. The central difficulty is deciding which angle goes into the formula, because the sign of the cosine term depends on it. A worked navigation-style example (two 10 km legs, angle 7π/12, |V| ≈ 12.18 km) then shows how to chain resultants and use right-triangle checks.
must: Resultant magnitude: \( V^2 = V_1^2 + V_2^2 + 2V_1V_2\cos\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail
Triangle form: with the interior angle \( \pi-\theta \) of the head-to-tail triangle, the sign flips to \( V^2 = V_1^2 + V_2^2 - 2V_1V_2\cos(\pi-\theta) \); the two forms are equivalent
Direction of the resultant by the law of sines: \( \alpha = \arcsin\left[\frac{V_2}{V}\sin\theta\right] \), where \( \alpha \) is measured from \( V_1 \)
Derivation: resolve \( V_2 \) into \( (V_2\cos\theta,\ V_2\sin\theta) \), add to \( V_1 \), and apply Pythagoras: \( V^2=(V_1+V_2\cos\theta)^2+(V_2\sin\theta)^2 \)
A resultant is the single vector equivalent to the head-to-tail sum of the vectors
Worked example: \( \theta = \pi/3+\pi/4 = 7\pi/12 \) with \( V_1=V_2=10 \) km gives \( |V|\approx 12.18 \) km
For three or more vectors, add step by step, e.g. \( (AB+AC)+AD \), drawing each vector from the tip of the previous one
Use Pythagoras only for right-angled triangles, e.g. \( \sqrt{12.18^2-1^2}=12.14 \) km; otherwise use the cosine law
Keep units consistent and the calculator in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians)
The arcsin gives only an angle in the range \( \pm 90^\circ \), so check the result is sensible for obtuse cases
conn: Law of cosines and component resolution give the same result: \( V^2 \) expands from Pythagoras on the \( \cos\theta \) and \( \sin\theta \) components, so either can be used to check the other
The magnitude from the cosine law feeds directly into the sine law for direction, so any error in \( V \) or in the angle convention carries through to \( \alpha \)
Force resultants (N) and velocity or displacement resultants (m/s, km) use identical vector addition, so statics, relative-velocity and navigation problems all reduce to this triangle
Multi-vector problems chain two-vector resultants, with a right-triangle (Pythagoras) check used for the final magnitude
exq: Two forces of 80 N and 120 N act at a point with 50° between them (tail-to-tail). Find the resultant magnitude and its angle to the 80 N force using the cosine and sine laws.
Show, by resolving \( V_2 \) into components and applying Pythagoras, that \( V^2=V_1^2+V_2^2+2V_1V_2\cos\theta \), then explain the sign change when the interior angle \( \pi-\theta \) is used.

A walker travels 10 km on one bearing then 10 km on a second bearing, with \( \theta = 7\pi/12 \) between the directions. Calculate the magnitude of the displacement and state which angle goes into the formula.

Three displacements AB, AC and AD are added in sequence. Find the intermediate resultant AB + AC with the cosine law, then add AD. Verify with a right-triangle calculation such as \( \sqrt{12.18^2-1^2} \).

A student gets a resultant larger than \( V_1+V_2 \). Identify the likely error (angle convention or calculator mode) and correct the calculation for \( V_1=5 \) m/s, \( V_2=7 \) m/s, \( \theta=120^\circ \).

notes.t: Resultant magnitude: laws of cosines and sines
pts: The magnitude of the resultant of two vectors follows from the law of cosines, with the angle between them entering as cos θ.
Resolving V₂ into components (V₂ cos θ, V₂ sin θ) and applying Pythagoras gives the resultant magnitude V.
The law of sines relates the sides of the vector triangle to the sines of their opposite angles, and is used to find the direction α of the resultant.
Using the supplementary angle π − θ in the cosine law gives the form with a minus sign, which is equivalent when θ is the interior angle of the triangle.
defs: Resultant
The single vector V that has the same effect as the sum of the vectors V₁ and V₂ acting together.
eqs: Magnitude of resultant (law of cosines, angle θ between V₁ and V₂)
V = resultant magnitude (N or m/s, same unit as inputs); V₁ = magnitude of first vector (same unit); V₂ = magnitude of second vector (same unit); θ = angle between V₁ and V₂ (rad or °)
α = angle between V₁ and the resultant V (rad or °); V₂ = magnitude of second vector (same unit); V = resultant magnitude (same unit); θ = angle between V₁ and V₂ (rad or °)
tips: Check whether the angle θ is measured between the two vectors tail-to-tail or head-to-tail; using the wrong one flips the sign of the cosine term.
Ensure V₁, V₂ and V are in the same units and the calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) before applying arcsin.
rq: Why does the cosine term change sign when the angle is written as π − θ, and when would you prefer that form?
cos(π − θ) = −cos θ, so the minus-sign form is used when θ is the interior angle of the triangle formed by the vectors head-to-tail; both give the same V.
What happens to V if θ = 0° and if θ = 180°?
At θ = 0°, V = V₁ + V₂ (maximum); at θ = 180°, V = |V₁ − V₂| (minimum), since cos θ = 1 or −1.

notes.t: Resultant magnitude via the law of cosines (vector addition with angle between components)
pts: The resultant of two vectors of given magnitudes is found by adding them tail-to-head; the angle between them determines the resultant's magnitude.

For two vectors of length 10 km meeting at an interior angle, the law of cosines gives the magnitude of the sum, using the supplementary angle form when the angle is taken between the vectors' extensions.
The angle used in the cosine term is the angle between the two vector directions as drawn, here π/3 + π/4 = 7π/12, giving |V| ≈ 12.18 km.
defs: Resultant vector
The single vector equal to the vector sum of given vectors, obtained by placing them head-to-tail.
eqs: Magnitude of the resultant of two vectors (law of cosines)
|V| = resultant magnitude (km); |\(V_{1}\)|, |\(V_{2}\)| = component magnitudes (km); θ = angle used in the cosine term (rad)
tips: Check which angle the cosine uses: the angle between the vectors as placed tail-to-tail, not an exterior angle, or the sign of the cross term will be wrong.
Keep angles in radians consistently when evaluating cos(7π/12) on a calculator set to degrees gives a wrong result.
rq: Why does the cosine term become a plus sign in the formula here, when the vectors are 10 km each?

Because the cosine is taken over the angle 7π/12 between the directions as set up, and since cos(7π/12) is negative the term in the bracket shows the combined effect; the cross term sign follows the chosen angle.

notes.t: Resultant magnitude of vectors: law of cosines (worked example)
pts: The resultant of two vectors is found by adding them tip-to-tail; their sum is shown as a single arrow from the common origin.
When the resultant is combined with a third vector, the sum (AB + AC) + AD is built up step by step, with each added vector drawn from the tip of the previous one.
A right-angle triangle formed by the resultant, a horizontal component and a vertical component lets the magnitude be found with Pythagoras' theorem.
The small green horizontal arrow represents the perpendicular offset of one vector relative to the other, and its length is 1 km in the worked calculation.
eqs: Magnitude of the resultant from a hypotenuse and a perpendicular leg
12.18 = length of the hypotenuse (km); 1 = length of the perpendicular leg (km); 12.14 = resulting magnitude (km)
tips: Check the units of every length (here km) before and after the square-root step.
Only apply Pythagoras when the triangle is genuinely right-angled; for general angles use the law of cosines.
rq: Why does the calculation subtract the square of 1 from the square of 12.18 rather than adding it?
Because 12.18 is the hypotenuse and 1 is a perpendicular leg, so Pythagoras gives leg² = hypotenuse² − other leg², i.e. the unknown side is the one opposite the right angle's partner.
What would happen to the magnitude if vectors were added in the reverse order?
The resultant is the same, since vector addition is commutative; only the intermediate construction path changes.

xq.q: Two forces \(V_1\) = 7 N and \(V_2\) = 8 N act at a point with an angle \(\theta\) = 60° between them. Find the magnitude \(V\) of the resultant and the angle \(\alpha\) between \(V_1\) and the resultant, in degrees. Give \(\alpha\) as your final answer.
Two forces of 5 N each act at a point with 120° between them (tail-to-tail). What is the magnitude of the resultant?
xq.a: 5 N
o: 5 N
0 N
xq.w: V² = 25+25+2(25)cos120° = 25, so V = 5 N; using cos120° with the wrong sign gives 8.66 N and ignoring angle gives 10 N.

xq.q: Two vectors \(\mathbf{V}_1\) and \(\mathbf{V}_2\) have magnitudes \(V_1\), \(V_2\) and angle \(\theta\) between them. Take \(\mathbf{V}_1\) along the x-axis and resolve \(\mathbf{V}_2\) into components to show that the resultant magnitude satisfies \(V^2 = V_1^2 + V_2^2 + 2V_1V_2\cos\theta\).
xq.a: With V1 along x, V2 = (V2 cosθ, V2 sinθ). The resultant has components (V1 + V2 cosθ, V2 sinθ). By Pythagoras V² = (V1 + V2cosθ)² + (V2 sinθ)² = V1² + 2V1V2cosθ + V2²cos²θ + V2²sin²θ = V1² + V2² + 2V1V2cosθ, using cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

units.name: 7.6 Cartesian components and component-wise vector algebra
units.ov: This material introduces Cartesian representation of vectors using the perpendicular unit vectors \( \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k} \), so a position vector has the coordinates of its endpoint as components. All vector algebra (addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, finding magnitudes and unit vectors) then reduces to ordinary arithmetic on each component separately. These tools underpin later work on dot and cross products, forces and kinematics.
must: Cartesian form: \( \mathbf{r}=x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}+z\mathbf{k} \), where x, y, z are the coordinates of P and the scalar components carry units (m) while i, j, k are dimensionless
Magnitude: \( |\mathbf{r}|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \) (3D Pythagoras, built from the base-plane diagonal then the height z)
Unit vector: \( \hat{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{u}/|\mathbf{u}| \) has magnitude 1 and the same direction as u (u must be non-zero)
Addition and subtraction are component-wise: \( \mathbf{a}\pm\mathbf{b}=(a_1\pm b_1,\,a_2\pm b_2,\,a_3\pm b_3) \); never add magnitudes
Scalar multiplication scales every component: \( \lambda\mathbf{b}=(\lambda b_1,\lambda b_2,\lambda b_3) \); distributive law \( \lambda(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b} \)
Equality of vectors needs all three components equal; this turns one vector equation into three scalar equations
Subtraction is not commutative: \( \mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}=-(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \) (every component changes sign)
Zero vector \( \mathbf{0}=(0,0,0) \) is the additive identity
Distinguish the scalar component x from the vector \( x\mathbf{i} \)
Evaluate combined expressions in order: brackets, then scalars, then subtraction; keep surds exact, e.g. \( (3-2\sqrt2)/4 \)
conn: Unit vector with magnitude: to find a vector of given length m in the direction of u, compute \( m\,\mathbf{u}/|\mathbf{u}| \), combining the magnitude formula with scalar multiplication
Equality with unknown scalars: setting a = λb or equating two expressions gives three simultaneous component equations (e.g. parallel vectors, finding unknown constants)
Position vectors and displacement: the vector from A to B is \( \mathbf{r}_B-\mathbf{r}_A \), so subtraction links to magnitude (distance) and unit vector (direction)
These component methods carry into forces, resultants and equilibrium (sum of components = 0) and later dot/cross products
exq: Given a = 2i − j + 3k and b = i + 4j − k, calculate 3(a + b) − 2a, then find its magnitude.
Find the unit vector in the direction of u = 3i − 4j + 12k and then a vector of magnitude 5 parallel to it.
Points A(1, 2, 3) and B(4, −2, 15): find the vector AB, its length and the unit vector from A towards B.
Find the scalars λ and μ such that λ(i + 2j) + μ(3i − k) = 5i + 4j − 2k, or show that none exist.
Simplify the unit vector of (1+√2)i + j − k, keeping surds exact, and verify that its magnitude is 1.

notes.t: Cartesian components of vectors
pts: A position vector from the origin can be resolved along the three perpendicular unit vectors i, j, k, so its components are its coordinates.
The displacement OM is built in two steps: first along x and y in the base plane, then the height z is added along k to reach P.
Components can be written as an ordered triple, with each component paired with a unit basis vector.
The magnitude of a vector is found from its components using Pythagoras extended to three dimensions.
defs: Position vector r
The vector from the origin O to a point P, whose Cartesian components are the coordinates of P.
Unit vectors i, j, k
Mutually perpendicular unit vectors pointing along the x, y and z axes respectively, forming the basis of the Cartesian representation.
Cartesian components
The scalar multiples x, y, z of the unit vectors i, j, k that together make up a vector.
eqs: Cartesian form of a position vector
x, y, z = coordinates / components (m); i, j, k = unit vectors along the axes (dimensionless)
|r| = length of the vector (m); x, y, z = components (m)
tips: Do not confuse the component x with the vector xi; the scalar is the length, the vector is the scalar times the unit vector.
Units: components and |r| carry the length unit (m), while the unit vectors i, j, k are dimensionless.
rq: Why is the vector OM written as xi + yj with no k term?
M lies in the base plane (the x–y plane), so its z-coordinate is zero; only the x and y components contribute.
What if the point P were below the x–y plane?
Then z would be negative, so the k component is −|z|k; the magnitude formula still works because z² is positive.

notes.t: Basic Properties of Vectors in Cartesian Form
pts: A vector in 3D is written as an ordered triple of components, one per axis.
Two vectors are equal only when every corresponding component is equal.
The zero vector has all three components equal to zero.
Vectors are added component by component, giving another vector of the same dimension.
defs: Zero vector
The vector whose three Cartesian components are all zero, written 0 = (0, 0, 0); it is the additive identity for vector addition.
Equality of vectors
Two vectors are equal if and only if their corresponding Cartesian components are equal: a1 = b1, a2 = b2 and a3 = b3.
eqs: a, b = vectors; a1, a2, a3 and b1, b2, b3 = their Cartesian components (same units as the quantity represented)
tips: Do not add magnitudes or only one component when adding vectors; every component must be added, e.g. a + b needs a1 + b1, a2 + b2 and a3 + b3.
Equality needs all three components to match; checking only the first component is insufficient.
rq: Why must two vectors have the same number of components before you can add them?
Addition is defined component by component, so each component of a must pair with exactly one component of b; mismatched dimensions leave some components with no partner.
If a = (2, -1, 4) and b = (2, -1, 4), what can you conclude and why?
Since every corresponding component matches, a = b; equality requires all three components to agree, not just some of them.

notes.t: Basic Properties of Vectors (2): Scalar Multiplication, Distributive Law, Subtraction
pts: Multiplying a vector by a scalar scales each component by that same scalar.
Scalar multiplication distributes over vector addition, so λ(a + b) = λa + λb.
Vector subtraction is performed component by component.
defs: Scalar
A single real number (no direction) that multiplies a vector to scale its magnitude, written λ in a = λb.
eqs: Multiplication of a vector by a scalar
\mathbf{a} = \lambda \mathbf{b} \Rightarrow a_1 = \lambda b_1,\ a_2 = \lambda b_2,\ a_3 = \lambda b_3
λ = scalar (dimensionless or same unit as scaling quantity); \(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = Cartesian components of vectors a and b (units of the vector quantity)
Distributive law for scalar and vector addition
λ = scalar; a, b = vectors (units of the vector quantity)
\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = Cartesian components of vectors a and b (units of the vector quantity)
tips: Do not treat a scalar as a vector: λ only scales, it has no components of its own.
Subtraction order matters: a − b ≠ b − a; the sign of every component flips when reversing the order.
rq: Why must the scalar λ multiply every component rather than just one?
Scaling a vector changes its length but not its direction; this only holds if every component is multiplied by the same λ.
Why does subtraction work component by component, and what would go wrong if you subtracted magnitudes instead?
Components are the independent directional parts; subtracting magnitudes ignores direction and gives a wrong resultant.
What happens to a vector when λ is negative?
Its components all change sign, so the vector keeps its line but reverses direction.

notes.t: Component-wise vector algebra (addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, unit vectors)
pts: Vectors are added or subtracted by combining their corresponding Cartesian components.
Multiplying a vector by a scalar multiplies every component by that scalar.
Subtracting a vector means adding its negative, so each component changes sign.
Combined expressions are evaluated by first forming the sum inside brackets, then applying scalars, then subtracting componentwise.
A unit vector is found by dividing a vector by its magnitude.
defs: Component-wise operation
An operation on vectors performed separately on each Cartesian component (x, y, z) of the vectors involved.
Unit vector
A vector with magnitude 1 pointing in the same direction as a given non-zero vector, obtained by dividing the vector by its magnitude.
eqs: \(a_{x}\), \(a_{y}\), \(a_{z}\) = Cartesian components of a (dimensionless or as given); \(b_{x}\), \(b_{y}\), \(b_{z}\) = components of b
\hat{u} = unit vector (dimensionless); u = vector; |u| = magnitude of u (same unit as u)
tips: Do not add or subtract vectors with different components as if they were scalars; apply the operation to each component separately, and watch signs when subtracting.
Keep surds exact (e.g. 3 − √2 ... rather than decimals) and simplify fractions carefully, as in (3 − 2√2)/4.
rq: Why must you compute the sum inside the brackets before multiplying by 1/2 and subtracting 5a?
Order of operations: the scalar 1/2 multiplies the whole bracketed vector sum, and 5a is a separate vector term subtracted afterwards.
What happens to the components of c if you compute 0 - c instead of subtracting c from 2b?
Every component of c changes sign, giving -c = (√2, 2, -1).

xq.q: Two position vectors are \(\mathbf{a}=(4,\,1,\,3)\) m and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,\,-1,\,0)\) m. Find the magnitude of \(\mathbf{c}=2\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\).
xq.a: 9 m

xq.q: What is the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}=(2,\,-3,\,6)\) m?
xq.w: |v| = √(4+9+36) = 7, so divide each component by 7; dividing by |v|² or by the sum of components, or flipping a sign, are the traps.

xq.q: The vectors \(\mathbf{a}=(2p,\;q+1,\;3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(p+2,\;3q-5,\;3)\) are equal. Find \(p\) and \(q\), justifying your method, and then write down \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\).
xq.a: Equal vectors need all corresponding components equal: 2p = p+2 gives p = 2; q+1 = 3q−5 gives q = 3; third components 3 = 3 consistent. Then a = (4, 4, 3) = b, so a − b = (0, 0, 0), the zero vector.
s: Equality requires every component to match (1)

units.name: 7.7 Magnitude and unit vector in Cartesian form
units.ov: This material covers finding the magnitude of a Cartesian vector with \( |\vec{a}|=\sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2+a_z^2} \), and using it to build a unit vector \( \hat{u}=\vec{a}/|\vec{a}| \). Questions often involve a combination such as \( \tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})-5\vec{a} \) or components containing surds. The combination must first be reduced to a single component vector, then the magnitude is found and the vector is normalised. The result is verified by checking that its magnitude is 1.
must: Magnitude: \( |\vec{a}|=\sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2+a_z^2} \), which is always non-negative and has the same units as the vector.
Unit vector: \( \hat{u}_{\vec{a}}=\vec{a}/|\vec{a}| \). It has magnitude 1, is dimensionless, and gives direction only. It is defined only for a non-zero vector.
Normalising scales every component by the same factor \( 1/|\vec{a}| \), so the direction is unchanged.
For a combination such as \( \tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})-5\vec{a} \), reduce it to one vector first by adding and scaling component by component, and only then take the magnitude.
Scalar multiples act on every component, so \( -5\vec{a} \) flips the sign of all components and multiplies them by 5. Sign errors are the most common mistake.
Square surd components fully: \( (3+\sqrt{2})^2=9+6\sqrt{2}+2=11+6\sqrt{2} \). The cross term is not dropped.
Collect like terms (rational parts and surd parts) before simplifying under the square root, and leave the answer in exact form unless a decimal is requested.
Verification: compute \( |\hat{u}| \) and confirm it equals 1. This catches arithmetic errors.
Do not take the square root term by term, because \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\neq a+b+c \).
conn: Vector algebra and magnitude: a linear combination of vectors must be simplified to components before \( |\vec{v}| \) is found. Taking magnitudes of the separate vectors and then combining them is wrong, since \( |\vec{b}+\vec{c}|\neq|\vec{b}|+|\vec{c}| \).
Unit vectors and force or position vectors: a force in a given direction is \( \vec{F}=F\hat{u} \), and \( \hat{u} \) is found from the position vector between two points divided by its length.
Unit vectors and dot product: \( \hat{u} \) gives the direction for projections and for angles, using \( \cos\theta=\hat{a}\cdot\hat{b} \).
Surd algebra and vector magnitude: exact answers need careful expansion and simplification, and the unit vector components may then require rationalising the denominator.
exq: Given \( \vec{a}=(3+\sqrt{2})\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k} \), expand and simplify \( |\vec{a}| \) exactly, giving the result as a single surd, then find the unit vector in the direction of \( \vec{a} \).

Given \( \vec{a}=(1,-2,3) \), \( \vec{b}=(4,0,-2) \) and \( \vec{c}=(2,6,2) \), compute \( \vec{v}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})-5\vec{a} \), find \( |\vec{v}| \) and the unit vector \( \hat{u} \), and verify that \( |\hat{u}|=1 \).
Find the unit vector in the direction from point A(1,2,3) to B(4,-2,15), then write a 260 N force along AB in Cartesian form.
Find the values of \( k \) for which \( \vec{v}=(k,2k,-2) \) has magnitude 6.
Show that \( \hat{u}=\vec{v}/|\vec{v}| \) always has magnitude 1 for any non-zero vector \( \vec{v} \), and explain why it cannot be defined for the zero vector.

notes.t: Magnitude and unit vector in Cartesian form
pts: The magnitude of a Cartesian vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.
A unit vector in the direction of a vector is found by dividing the vector by its magnitude.
Expanding squared components carefully (including surds) is needed before simplifying the magnitude.
The unit vector is the vector divided by its magnitude, giving components that are each scaled by the same factor.
defs: Unit vector
A vector with magnitude 1 that indicates direction only, obtained by dividing a vector by its magnitude.
eqs: \(a_x, a_y, a_z\) = Cartesian components of the vector (dimensionless or same unit as the vector); \(|\vec{a}|\) = magnitude (same unit as the vector)
Unit vector in the direction of a vector
tips: Do not forget to square the surd term: \((3+\sqrt{2})^2 = 9+6\sqrt{2}+2\), not \(9+2\).
Check that the final unit vector has magnitude 1 as a verification step.
rq: Why does dividing each component by the magnitude produce a unit vector?
Because the magnitude of the result becomes \(|\vec{a}|/|\vec{a}| = 1\), so only the direction is kept.
Why must \(\sqrt{57}/2\) be simplified rather than left as \(\sqrt{49/4+2}\)?
Simplifying to a single fraction under one root reveals the exact magnitude, making the components of the unit vector easier to write exactly.

notes.t: Magnitude and unit vector of a vector combination (Cartesian components)
pts: The magnitude of a Cartesian vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.
A unit vector is found by dividing the vector by its magnitude, giving a vector of length 1 in the same direction.
Combined vectors such as \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})-5\vec{a}\) must first be reduced to a single Cartesian component vector before taking the magnitude.
defs: Unit vector
A vector with magnitude 1 pointing in the same direction as a given non-zero vector, obtained by dividing that vector by its magnitude.
eqs: \(v_x,v_y,v_z\) = Cartesian components of the vector (dimensionless or same unit as the vector); \(|\vec{v}|\) = magnitude (same unit as the vector)
Unit vector in the direction of \(\vec{v}\)
\(\vec{v}\) = non-zero vector; \(|\vec{v}|\) = its magnitude; \(\hat{u}\) = unit vector (dimensionless)
tips: Watch sign errors when combining components (e.g. \(-5\vec{a}\) changes the sign of each component of \(\vec{a}\)).
Check that the unit vector has magnitude 1 as a verification step.
rq: Why must the magnitude be calculated from the final combined vector rather than from each vector separately?
Magnitude is not linear: \(|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|\neq|\vec{b}|+|\vec{c}|\), so the vector must be fully combined into components first.
What happens to the unit vector if you divide by the magnitude of a different vector?
It no longer has length 1 and points in the wrong direction unless the divisor is the magnitude of that same vector.

xq.q: Three force vectors, in newtons, are \(\vec{a}=(1,2,-2)\), \(\vec{b}=(10,4,-3)\) and \(\vec{c}=(4,10,-5)\). A resultant is formed as \(\vec{r}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})-5\vec{a}\). Find the magnitude \(|\vec{r}|\) in N.
xq.a: 7 N

xq.q: A vector is \(\vec{a}=(2+\sqrt{3},\;2-\sqrt{3},\;\sqrt{2})\). Find the x-component of the unit vector \(\hat{u}\) in the direction of \(\vec{a}\), to 3 decimal places.
A displacement is \(\vec{d}=(4,-4,2)\) m. Which expression gives the unit vector in the direction of \(\vec{d}\)?
xq.w: \(|\vec{d}|=\sqrt{16+16+4}=6\), so each component is divided by 6; dividing by 36 or by the sum of components 2, or dropping a sign, gives wrong results.

units.name: 8.1 Vector space axioms
units.ov: This material defines a vector space as a set V with vector addition and scalar multiplication over a field F (the reals for a real vector space), subject to eight axioms. The axioms fall into three groups: addition (commutativity, associativity, identity, inverse), distributivity (over vector and scalar addition), and scalar compatibility (including the scalar identity). Verifying that a given set is a vector space means checking these axioms, together with closure, rather than relying on a quick closure check.
must: A vector space is a set \(V\) with addition and scalar multiplication over a field \(F\) satisfying eight axioms for all \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\in V\) and \(\lambda,\mu\in F\)
Real vector space: the scalar field is \(F=\mathbb{R}\)
Addition axioms: commutative \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}\) and associative \((\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})+\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a}+(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})\)
Additive identity: there is a \(\mathbf{0}\in V\) with \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{a}\)
Additive inverse: for each \(\mathbf{a}\) there is \(-\mathbf{a}\) with \(\mathbf{a}+(-\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{0}\)
Distributivity over vector addition: \(\lambda(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b}\)
Distributivity over scalar addition: \((\lambda+\mu)\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\mu\mathbf{a}\)
Compatibility of scalar multiplication: \(\lambda(\mu\mathbf{a})=(\lambda\mu)\mathbf{a}\), and the scalar identity gives \(1\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{a}\)
To show a set is a vector space, check closure under both operations and all eight axioms; closure alone is not enough
Keep scalars (from \(F\)) distinct from vectors (from \(V\)); the zero vector \(\mathbf{0}\) is not the scalar 0
conn: Closure and the axioms feed into subspace tests: a subset needs the zero vector and closure under addition and scalar multiplication, and it inherits the other axioms
The axioms underpin the usual properties of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) vectors, such as component-wise addition and scaling in statics and mechanics
Function and matrix sets (for example \(2\times2\) matrices, polynomials of degree at most \(n\)) are vector spaces, and they lead on to linear independence, basis and dimension
Showing that a set fails the axioms (no zero vector, no inverse, or not closed) is the usual way to disprove a vector space claim
exq: List the eight vector space axioms for a real vector space and state which involve only addition, which involve only scalars, and which mix the two.
Show that the set of all \(2\times2\) real matrices with matrix addition and scalar multiplication is a real vector space, identifying \(\mathbf{0}\) and \(-\mathbf{a}\).
Determine whether \(S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2: y\ge 0\}\) is a vector space under the usual operations. Which axiom fails, and for which \(\lambda\)?
Let \(V=\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual addition but scalar multiplication \(\lambda(x,y)=(\lambda x,0)\). Which axiom fails? Justify with a specific counterexample.
Prove from the axioms that the additive identity \(\mathbf{0}\) is unique, and that \(0\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}\) for every \(\mathbf{a}\in V\).

notes.t: Definition of a Vector Space
pts: A vector space V over scalar field F must satisfy the listed axioms for all vectors a, b, c in V and scalars λ, μ in F.
When the scalar field F is the real numbers, the vector space is called a real vector space.
Vector addition must be commutative and associative, with an additive identity 0 and additive inverse −a for each a.
Scalar multiplication must distribute over vector addition and over scalar addition.
Scalar multiplication must be compatible with scalar multiplication, and multiplying by the scalar identity leaves a unchanged.
defs: Vector space
A set V with vector addition and scalar multiplication over a scalar field F, satisfying the eight listed axioms for all a, b, c in V and λ, μ in F.
Real vector space
A vector space whose scalar field F is the real numbers.
eqs: Distributivity of scalar over vector addition
λ = scalar in F; a, b = vectors in V
a = vector in V; 0 = zero vector
tips: Check all eight axioms when verifying a set is a vector space; checking closure alone is not enough.
Do not confuse the scalar field F with the vector set V; scalars λ, μ come from F, vectors a, b, c from V.
rq: Why must the scalar identity 1a = a be an axiom rather than following from the other axioms?
Without it, scalar multiplication could collapse vectors (e.g. 1a = 0), so it fixes the scalar 1 as a genuine identity for scaling.
What would fail if scalar multiplication did not distribute over scalar addition?
The axiom (λ + μ)a = λa + μa would fail, so scaling would not be linear in the scalar and combinations would not behave consistently.

xq.q: Let S be the set of all vectors \((x,y)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(x\ge 0\), with the usual addition and scalar multiplication over the real numbers. Is S a real vector space?
xq.a: No, because multiplying by a negative scalar takes vectors out of S, so \(-\mathbf{a}\) is not in S
o: Yes, because addition is commutative and associative
Yes, because S is closed under addition and contains \((0,0)\)
No, because vector addition in S is not commutative
No, because multiplying by a negative scalar takes vectors out of S, so \(-\mathbf{a}\) is not in S
xq.w: For \(\mathbf{a}=(1,0)\), \(-\mathbf{a}=(-1,0)\) has \(x<0\), so the additive inverse axiom and closure fail; checking closure under addition and zero alone is not enough.

xq.q: Let \(S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2 : y=1\}\) with the usual vector addition and scalar multiplication over \(\mathbb{R}\). Show that S is not a real vector space, giving two distinct reasons.
xq.a: S fails the axioms in two ways. (1) Closure under addition: \((1,1)\) and \((2,1)\) are in S but their sum \((3,2)\) has \(y=2\), so is not in S. (2) The zero vector \((0,0)\) has \(y=0\ne1\), so S has no additive identity (and \(\mathbf{a}+(-\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{0}\) cannot hold within S). Hence S is not a vector space.
s: Pick two members of S, e.g. \((1,1),(2,1)\) [1]
Sum \((3,2)\) not in S, so not closed [1]
Conclude additive identity/inverse axiom fails, so not a vector space [1]

xq.q: In a real vector space, \(\lambda=2\), \(\mu=3\) and \(\mathbf{a}=(1,-1)\). Using the axiom for distributivity of scalar multiplication over scalar addition, what is \((\lambda+\mu)\mathbf{a}\)?
xq.w: \((\lambda+\mu)\mathbf{a}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\mu\mathbf{a}=(2,-2)+(3,-3)=(5,-5)\); multiplying the scalars, scaling only one component, or flipping the sign are the traps.

units.name: 8.2 Complex numbers as vectors
units.ov: This material treats a complex number z = x + jy as a position vector in the Argand plane, so addition, subtraction, modulus and distance become vector operations. Multiplication by j is a 90° anticlockwise rotation, which links algebra to geometry. The scalar (dot) product is then introduced for general vectors, giving a component formula and a geometric formula that together yield magnitudes and angles.
must: A complex number \(z = x + jy\) is the position vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}\); the real part is the horizontal component and the imaginary part (the coefficient of j) is the vertical component
Addition \(z_3 = z_1 + z_2\) is vector addition, the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by \(OP_1\) and \(OP_2\)
Subtraction \(z_1 - z_2 = z_1 + (-z_2)\) is the vector from \(z_2\) to \(z_1\); it is not commutative, and reversing the order reverses the direction
Modulus \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) is the distance of P from the origin
The distance between two points is \(|z_1 - z_2| = \sqrt{(a_1-a_2)^2+(b_1-b_2)^2}\): the modulus of the difference, not the difference of the moduli
Multiplying by j rotates a point 90° anticlockwise about the origin (\(z_{n+1} = jz_n\)); the powers of j cycle every 4 steps, with \(j^2 = -1\)
When expanding \(j(a+jb) = -b + ja\), do not lose the sign from \(j^2 = -1\); for example \(j(-1+j2) = -2 - j\)
Dot product in components: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3\), and the result is a scalar
Dot product geometrically: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) with \(0\le\theta\le\pi\), measured tail-to-tail; rearrange to find \(\theta\)
The dot product uses cos θ and gives a scalar; the cross product uses sin θ and gives a vector, so do not confuse them
conn: Repeated multiplication by j generates points on a circle about the origin (a square for four points), and the side and diagonal lengths come from the modulus of differences, which combines rotation with the distance formula

Vector subtraction gives the side vector between two Argand points, and the modulus of that vector gives its length, so geometry problems such as triangles and parallelograms reduce to complex algebra
The component and geometric forms of the dot product can be equated to find the angle between two vectors, with magnitudes taken from the same square-root formula as the complex modulus
Treating complex numbers as 2D vectors lets the dot product be applied to them, for example to test perpendicularity: a·b = 0 matches a rotation by j, which gives perpendicular vectors
exq: Given \(z_1 = 3 + j2\) and \(z_2 = -1 + j4\), draw \(z_1\), \(z_2\), \(z_1+z_2\) and \(z_1-z_2\) on an Argand diagram, state the vector joining \(z_2\) to \(z_1\), and find its modulus

Starting from \(z_1 = -1 + j2\), generate \(z_2 = jz_1\), \(z_3 = jz_2\) and \(z_4 = jz_3\). Show that all four points lie on a circle centred at the origin, give its radius, and find \(|z_1 - z_2|\) and \(|z_1 - z_3|\)
Simplify \(j(-1+j2)\) and \(j^{15}\), and describe the geometric effect of multiplying by j
Find \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) for \(\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 3)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (4, -1, 2)\), then find the angle between them
Find the value of k for which \(\mathbf{a} = (2, k, 1)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (3, -2, 4)\) are perpendicular, and explain why a student who gets an angle outside 0 to π has made an error

notes.t: Complex numbers as vectors: point P, addition and subtraction
pts: A complex number z = x + jy is represented as a position vector from the origin O to the point P(z) in the Argand plane.
The real part x is the horizontal (x-axis) component and the imaginary part y is the vertical (y-axis) component of the vector OP.
Adding complex numbers corresponds to vector addition: the sum z₃ = z₁ + z₂ is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by OP₁ and OP₂.
Subtracting z₂ is equivalent to adding −z₂, which is the reflection of z₂ through the origin, so z₃ = z₁ − z₂ is the vector joining z₂ to z₁.
defs: Position vector of P
For a point P(z), z = \(\overrightarrow{OP}\), the vector from the origin O to P, whose components are the real and imaginary parts of z.
eqs: Complex number in rectangular form (vector components)
z = complex number (dimensionless); x = real part / x-component (dimensionless); y = imaginary part / y-component (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (√−1)
tips: Subtraction is not commutative: z₁ − z₂ points from z₂ to z₁, so reversing the order reverses the direction of the resulting vector.
Keep the imaginary unit j distinct from the real components when reading coordinates; the y-coordinate is the coefficient of j, not j itself.
rq: Why does adding complex numbers graphically look exactly like adding vectors?
Because a complex number x + jy has components (x, y) along the axes, and vector addition adds components, so real parts add and imaginary parts add.
What geometric transformation does −z₂ represent, and why does this make subtraction a vector joining two points?
−z₂ is the reflection of z₂ through O (same length, opposite direction); adding it to z₁ gives the vector from z₂ to z₁.

notes.t: Complex numbers as vectors: multiplication by j as rotation
pts: Multiplying a complex number by j rotates it 90° anticlockwise about the origin, so each successive z is a rotated copy of the previous one.
Powers of j cycle every four steps (\(j^{2}\) = -1), which is used to simplify expressions such as j(-1+j2).
The four points \(z_{1}\) to \(z_{4}\) lie on a circle centred at the origin, forming a square-like closed quadrilateral; distances between them are found as modulus of differences.
The modulus of a difference of two complex numbers gives the distance between their points in the Argand diagram.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = a + jb, |z| = \( \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), the distance of the point from the origin in the Argand plane.
eqs: \( z_n \) = nth complex number (dimensionless); \( j \) = imaginary unit
Distance between two points in the Argand diagram
\( a_k, b_k \) = real and imaginary parts of \( z_k \) (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget \( j^2 = -1 \) when expanding j(a+jb); the real term sign is easy to lose.
When computing a distance, take the modulus of the difference, not the difference of moduli.
rq: Why does multiplying by j rotate a point rather than stretch it?
Because \( |j| = 1 \), so the modulus is unchanged; j as a unit vector multiplies the argument by 90°, i.e. a rotation.
Why are all four points the same distance from the origin?
Each step multiplies by j, which has modulus 1, so \( |z_n| = |z_1| = \sqrt{5} \) for all n.

notes.t: Scalar (or Dot) Product
pts: The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar, computed by multiplying corresponding components and summing them.
Geometrically, the dot product equals the product of the magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between the vectors.
The angle θ used in the geometric definition is restricted to the range 0 to π.
defs: Scalar (dot, inner) product

For vectors a = (\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\)) and b = (\(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\)), the scalar product is a·b = \(a_{1b}_{1}\) + \(a_{2b}_{2}\) + \(a_{3b}_{3}\), which equals |a||b|cos θ where θ is the angle between them.
eqs: \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a (dimensionless or units of a); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b (units of b)
|a|, |b| = magnitudes of vectors (units of a, b); θ = angle between the vectors (rad)
tips: Do not confuse the dot product (scalar result) with the cross product (vector result); the dot product uses cos θ, the cross product uses sin θ.
Ensure the angle θ is the angle between the two vectors when they are placed tail-to-tail, not an external or reflex angle outside 0 to π.
rq: Why does the dot product of two perpendicular vectors equal zero?
Because θ = π/2, so cos θ = 0 and a·b = |a||b|·0 = 0.
What does a negative dot product tell you about the angle between two vectors?
The angle θ lies between π/2 and π, so the vectors point in broadly opposite directions.

xq.q: In an Argand diagram the complex numbers are \(z_1=3+j4\) and \(z_2=-1+j2\). Find the distance between the points \(P(z_1)\) and \(P(z_2)\), to 3 significant figures.
For \(z=x+jy\), show that multiplying by \(j\) rotates the position vector of \(z\) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Use the dot product and the modulus in your argument.
xq.a: \(jz=jx+j^2y=-y+jx\), so \(\overrightarrow{OP}=(x,y)\) maps to \((-y,x)\). The dot product is \((x,y)\cdot(-y,x)=-xy+xy=0\), so the vectors are perpendicular (\(\cos\theta=0\)). The modulus is \(\sqrt{y^2+x^2}=|z|\), unchanged. For example \(z=1\) (along +x) goes to \(j\) (along +y), which is anticlockwise, so the rotation is 90° anticlockwise.
s: Direction check, e.g. \(1\to j\), shows anticlockwise [1]

xq.q: Two vectors are \(\mathbf{a}=(3,0,4)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,-2,1)\). Find the angle \(\theta\) between them in degrees, to 1 decimal place.

units.name: 8.3 Scalar (dot) product definition and work done
units.ov: This module defines the scalar (dot) product in two equivalent forms: the component sum \(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\) and the geometric form \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\). The equivalence is proved with the cosine rule. The main application is mechanical work, \(W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}\), where only the force component along the displacement does work.
must: Dot product, component form: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\), which gives a scalar, not a vector
Dot product, geometric form: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail
Work done by a constant force: \(W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=F_xd_x+F_yd_y\), measured in joules (J)
Only the force component along the displacement does work: \(W=|\mathbf{F}||\mathbf{d}|\cos\theta\). A perpendicular component does zero work.
Angle between vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}\). Perpendicular vectors have \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\).
Sign of the dot product: it is positive for acute \(\theta\), zero at 90°, and negative for obtuse \(\theta\) (e.g. friction does negative work).
Derivation: apply the cosine rule \(AB^2=OA^2+OB^2-2(OA)(OB)\cos\theta\) to the triangle with sides \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\). This shows the two forms are equal.
Resolving an angled force: \(F_x=|\mathbf{F}|\cos\theta\) and \(F_y=|\mathbf{F}|\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the x-axis (the displacement direction)
Dot only between two vectors, never scalar·vector. \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2\), and the dot product is commutative.
Don't confuse work (a scalar, J) with torque (a vector, N·m). Don't use the full force magnitude when the force is at an angle.
conn: Dot product and angle finding: compute \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) from components, then equate it to \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) to find \(\theta\). Questions often ask for the angle between two force vectors or members.
Work and vector resolution: find the force components from trigonometry, then take the dot product with a displacement given in component form (or use \(Fd\cos\theta\) directly) to get W.

Zero dot product and perpendicularity: show that two vectors are perpendicular, or find an unknown component so that they are. The same idea explains why normal forces and perpendicular components do no work.
Projection: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) gives the component of a along b. This links work, resolving forces along a slope and the later vector topics.
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=4\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\), calculate \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and the angle between them. State whether it is acute or obtuse.
A 50 N force acts at 30° above the horizontal and drags a crate 12 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the force. Then state the work done by the vertical component and by the weight.
A force \(\mathbf{F}=(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\) N moves a particle from (1,2) to (5,5) m. Find the displacement vector, the work done, and the angle between F and the displacement.
Find the value of \(p\) for which \(\mathbf{a}=p\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k}\).
Using the cosine rule on the triangle formed by vectors a and b, derive \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) from the component definition.

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product: geometric and component definitions
pts: The scalar product of two vectors is equivalent to the geometric definition via the cosine rule, linking component form and magnitude-angle form.
Establishing the equivalence uses the cosine rule for a triangle formed by the two vectors.
The scalar product of two vectors gives a number (scalar), not a vector.
The scalar product is defined only between two vectors, so the dot must be written explicitly between them.
defs: Scalar (dot) product
For vectors a and b, a·b is the scalar a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃, equal to |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between them.
eqs: Scalar product in component and geometric form

\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = vector components (dimensionless or units of a, b); |a|, |b| = magnitudes of a and b (same units as the vectors); θ = angle between a and b (rad or degrees); result is a scalar (units of a × units of b)
Cosine rule for a triangle (used in the derivation)
AB, OA, OB = side lengths (m or any consistent length unit); θ = included angle at O (rad or degrees)
tips: The scalar product is only defined between two vectors; do not use the dot between a scalar and a vector.
Check the angle: θ is the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail, and cos θ can be negative (obtuse angle).
rq: Why does expanding (a−b)² in the cosine-rule derivation produce the dot product?
The squared terms a₁², b₁², etc. cancel against the magnitudes, leaving −2(a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃) = −2|a||b|cos θ, so the cross terms define a·b.
What would happen if you omitted the dot and wrote a b for two vectors?
ab is undefined or ambiguous; the dot signals the scalar product of two vectors, and it is not defined between a vector and a scalar or other quantities.

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product and work done by a force
pts: Work done by a force is the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector.
Resolve the force into components; only the component along the displacement does work.
The perpendicular component (here the y-component) contributes zero work because its dot product with the displacement is zero.
Components of an angled force are found with cosine (x) and sine (y) of the angle from the x-axis.
defs: Work (dot product form)
Work done by a constant force is the scalar product of the force vector and the displacement vector, W = F·d, a scalar quantity measured in joules.
eqs: Work done by a force via dot product
W = work (J); \(\vec{F}\) = force vector (N); \(\vec{d}\) = displacement vector (m)
Components of an angled applied force
\(|\vec{F}|\) = force magnitude (N); \(\theta\) = angle from displacement direction (rad)
tips: Do not use the full force magnitude in W = F·d when the force is at an angle; use only the component along the displacement (F cos θ).
Work is a scalar in joules (J = N·m); do not leave it as a vector or confuse it with the N·m of torque.
rq: Why does the vertical component of the pulling force \(F_y\) do no work on the wagon in this example?
Because the wagon's displacement is purely along x (\(\vec{d}=(100\,\text{m})\hat{i}\)), so the dot product \(F_y \cdot 0 = 0\); only the component parallel to displacement transfers energy.
What would the work be if the handle were held horizontal (\(\theta = 0\)) with the same 20 N force?
\(W = 20\,\text{N}\times 100\,\text{m} = 2000\,\text{J}\), since \(\cos 0 = 1\) makes the full force parallel to displacement.

xq.q: A crate is pulled along level ground by a rope. The rope force has magnitude \(|\vec F| = 50\) N and acts at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal. The crate is displaced 12 m horizontally. Using the scalar product, find the work done by the rope force.
s: \(W \approx 519.6\) J (the vertical component does no work)

xq.q: A constant force \(\vec F = (4\mathbf i - 3\mathbf j + 2\mathbf k)\) N moves a particle through displacement \(\vec d = (2\mathbf i + 5\mathbf j - \mathbf k)\) m. Find the angle between the force and the displacement, in degrees.
A force of magnitude 20 N acts at \(60^\circ\) to the direction of a straight displacement of 5 m. What is the work done by the force?
xq.w: Only the component along the displacement does work, so \(W = 20\times5\cos60^\circ = 50\) J; 100 J ignores the angle, 86.6 J uses sin instead of cos, and −95.2 J puts the angle in radians.

units.name: 8.4 Properties and algebraic rules of the dot product
units.ov: This section sets out the algebraic rules of the dot product: it is commutative, distributes over addition, and pulls out scalar multiples. Together with a·a = |a|², these rules let you expand expressions like |a±b|², which gives the vector form of the cosine rule. The component form and the magnitude-angle form are two views of the same scalar, and exam work moves between them.
must: Two equivalent definitions: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \); the result is a scalar, not a vector
Commutative: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a} \)
Distributive over addition: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c} \), so brackets expand like ordinary algebra
Scalar multiples: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(\lambda\mathbf{b})=(\lambda\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{b}=\lambda(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}) \)
Self dot product: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2 \) (it is the squared magnitude, not \( |\mathbf{a}| \)), because \( \cos 0=1 \)
Unit vectors: \( \mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}=1 \)
Sum: \( |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2+2|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \)
Difference: \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2-2|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta \); watch the sign of the cross term
Associativity does not apply: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c} \) is undefined because \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} \) is a scalar
θ must be the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail, not the angle of the resultant
conn: Expanding \( (\mathbf{a}\pm\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}\pm\mathbf{b}) \) combines distributivity, commutativity and \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2 \) to give the cosine rule

Component form and magnitude-angle form together give \( \cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} \), so you can find angles and test for perpendicularity (\( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \))
Resultant of two forces: the magnitude of \( \mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2 \) uses the sum formula, and the tail-to-tail angle must be checked
Dot product versus cross product: scalar versus vector result, and commutative versus anticommutative, so don't mix the rules
exq: Given \( \mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k} \) and \( \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k} \), compute \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} \), the angle between them, and verify \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a} \).
Two forces of 30 N and 50 N act at 60° tail-to-tail. Use \( |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|^2 \) to find the magnitude of the resultant, then find \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}| \).
Prove, using the distributive and commutative laws, that \( |\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2-2\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} \), and state the geometric meaning (cosine rule).
Expand and simplify \( (2\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}) \) given \( |\mathbf{a}|=2 \), \( |\mathbf{b}|=3 \) and \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=4 \).
Explain why \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c} \) is meaningless. Find \( \lambda \) such that \( \mathbf{a}+\lambda\mathbf{b} \) is perpendicular to \( \mathbf{a} \) for given vectors.

notes.t: Basic rules and properties of the scalar product
pts: The scalar product is commutative: swapping the two vectors gives the same result.
The scalar product can be computed from components or from magnitudes and the angle between the vectors.
Associativity does not apply to the scalar product because a·b is a scalar, so a·b·c is undefined.
defs: Commutative law (scalar product)
For vectors a and b, a·b = b·a: the order of the two vectors in a dot product does not change the result.
eqs: Scalar (dot) product in component form and magnitude-angle form

a₁,a₂,a₃ and b₁,b₂,b₃ = vector components (dimensionless or in the units of the vector); |a|, |b| = vector magnitudes (same units as the vectors); θ = angle between a and b (rad or degrees); result is a scalar
tips: Do not write a·b·c as if it were associative; the triple dot product is not defined in this context.
Check that θ is the angle between the vectors placed tail-to-tail when using the magnitude-angle formula.
rq: Why is a·b·c not defined, even though multiplication of numbers is associative?
Because a·b is a scalar, and the dot product requires two vectors, so there is no valid second dot product with c; associativity needs three objects of the same type that can be grouped.
If a·b = b·a, why can't we say the same about the order in a·b·c?
Commutativity concerns swapping two vectors in one dot product; grouping in a·b·c is not meaningful at all, so the question of order of grouping does not arise.

notes.t: Scalar (dot) product: distributive laws
pts: Multiplying a dot product by a scalar λ can be applied to either vector or to the product itself; all give the same result.
The dot product distributes over vector addition, so a·(b+c) can be expanded term by term.
The proof works componentwise: expand each aᵢ(bᵢ+cᵢ) and regroup the sums.
The dot product can be computed from components or from magnitudes and the angle between vectors.
defs: Scalar product (dot product)
For vectors a and b, the scalar a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between them; the result is a number, not a vector.
eqs: λ = scalar (dimensionless); a, b = vectors (units of their quantity)
aᵢ, bᵢ = components of a and b (same units as each vector)
tips: Do not confuse the dot product (scalar result) with the cross product (vector result).
Ensure the angle θ in |a||b|cos θ is measured between the vectors tail-to-tail.
rq: Why does the dot product of two vectors give a scalar rather than a vector?
Each term aᵢbᵢ is a number, and the three numbers are summed; equivalently |a||b|cos θ is a scalar, so no direction remains.
If a·b = 0 for nonzero vectors, what can you conclude about their geometry?
cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°: the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).

notes.t: Powers of a vector: dot product of a vector with itself
pts: The dot product of a vector with itself equals the sum of the squares of its components.
Because the angle between a vector and itself is zero, a·a equals the squared magnitude of the vector.
The unit vectors i, j, k each square to 1 under the dot product.
eqs: Square of a vector's magnitude via the dot product
a = vector; a₁, a₂, a₃ = components of a (dimensionless or same unit as a); |a| = magnitude of a (same unit as a)
Unit vector squares under dot product
i, j, k = unit basis vectors (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse a·a = |a|² with a·a = |a|; the dot product gives the squared magnitude.
Remember cos 0 = 1 when simplifying a·a, otherwise the result is wrong by a factor.
rq: Why does a·a give the magnitude squared rather than just the magnitude?
The dot product of a vector with itself is |a||a|cos 0 = |a|²; it returns the squared length, so a square root is needed to recover |a|.
Why is the angle term cos 0 in a·a?
A vector makes zero angle with itself, and cos 0 = 1, so the product reduces to |a|².

notes.t: Dot product: magnitude expansion of a+b and a−b via the cosine rule
pts: The square of the magnitude of a sum of vectors expands into the squared magnitudes plus a cross term involving the angle between them.
For a difference, expand (a−b)·(a−b) using distributivity; the cross terms appear with a minus sign.
Since a·b = b·a, the two cross terms combine into −2a·b, giving the law of cosines for vectors.
Writing a·b = |a||b|cos θ turns the dot product into a geometric (angle-based) form.
defs: Dot product (scalar product)
For vectors a and b, a·b = |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between them; the result is a scalar.
eqs: Magnitude of a sum of two vectors
a, b = vectors (N, m, or any consistent unit); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same unit as a, b)
Magnitude of a difference of two vectors
a, b = vectors; θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same unit)
tips: Watch the sign: the cross term is +2|a||b|cos θ for a+b but −2|a||b|cos θ for a−b.
Use the angle θ between the vectors tail-to-tail, not the angle of the resultant with one vector.
rq: Why does the cross term change sign between |a+b|² and |a−b|²?
Expanding (a−b)·(a−b) gives −a·b − b·a, which is −2a·b, whereas (a+b)·(a+b) gives +2a·b, so the sign of the cosine term flips.
What does the sign of cos θ tell you about the size of |a+b|?
If θ is acute, cos θ > 0 and |a+b| is larger than when vectors are perpendicular; if θ is obtuse, cos θ < 0 and |a+b| is smaller.
How is the difference formula related to the triangle in the figure?
a−b is the third side of the triangle formed by a and b, so the formula is the law of cosines applied to that triangle.

xq.q: Two forces \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) act at a point, with \(|\mathbf a| = 4\) N and \(|\mathbf b| = 3\) N. The angle between them (tail-to-tail) is \(60^\circ\). Find the magnitude of the resultant \(\mathbf a + \mathbf b\).
s: \(|\mathbf a+\mathbf b|^2 = |\mathbf a|^2+|\mathbf b|^2+2|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\)

xq.q: Starting from \((\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\cdot(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\), show that \(|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|^2 = |\mathbf a|^2+|\mathbf b|^2-2|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\). Name each property of the dot product you use.
xq.a: Since \(|\mathbf v|^2=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v\), \(|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|^2=(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\cdot(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\). By distributivity this is \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b\). Commutativity gives \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a\), so the cross terms combine to \(-2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\). With \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a=|\mathbf a|^2\), \(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf b|^2\) and \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\), the result follows.
s: Use \(|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|^2=(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\cdot(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\) (a·a = |a|²)
Expand by the distributive law into four terms
Commutativity combines the cross terms into \(-2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\)
Substitute \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\) to reach the result

xq.q: Vectors \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c\) satisfy \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = 3\) and \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c = -5\). What is \(\mathbf a\cdot(2\mathbf b-\mathbf c)\)?
xq.w: By the distributive laws \(\mathbf a\cdot(2\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=2(3)-(-5)=11\); the traps are dropping the sign of \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c\) (giving 1), multiplying the whole bracket by 2 (giving 16) and reversing the overall sign (giving −11).
s: \(\mathbf a\cdot(2\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c\)

units.name: 8.5 Magnitudes and angles using the dot product
units.ov: This material uses the dot product to get lengths and angles of combined vectors. It starts from the law-of-cosines identity \(|\mathbf{u}\pm\mathbf{v}|^2=|\mathbf{u}|^2+|\mathbf{v}|^2\pm2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) and the formula \(\cos\theta=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|)\). It then applies these to the angle between two composite vectors such as \(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}\) and \(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\), to perpendicularity, and to the fact that dot products cannot be cancelled.
must: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), so \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}\) for nonzero vectors
\(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{|\mathbf{u}|^2+|\mathbf{v}|^2+2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta}\), and the cross term is \(-\) for \(|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|\)
Scalars scale magnitudes: \(|k\mathbf{a}|=|k||\mathbf{a}|\), so use \(|2\mathbf{b}|=2|\mathbf{b}|\) and \(|3\mathbf{a}|=3|\mathbf{a}|\) when substituting

Worked data: \(|\mathbf{a}|=3,\ |\mathbf{b}|=2,\ \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=5\) gives \(\cos\theta=5/6\), \(|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5\) and \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{85-30}=\sqrt{55}\)
Wrong sign on the cross term gives \(\sqrt{115}\) instead of \(\sqrt{55}\), a classic error

Angle between composite vectors: expand the numerator \((\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b})\cdot(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})=3|\mathbf{a}|^2+5\,\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}-2|\mathbf{b}|^2=44\) using bilinearity, then divide by the two composite magnitudes
Simplify the denominator: \(\sqrt{45}\sqrt{55}=\sqrt{2475}=15\sqrt{11}\), so \(\cos\varphi=\dfrac{44}{15\sqrt{11}}=\dfrac{4\sqrt{11}}{15}\approx0.884\) and \(\varphi\approx27.9^\circ\)
Perpendicular iff \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\) with both vectors nonzero; a positive dot product means an acute angle and a negative one means an obtuse angle

Never cancel in dot products: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}\iff\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})=0\), so \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\) need not be equal (equal projections onto \(\mathbf{a}\))
Check calculator mode (degrees or radians) when evaluating \(\cos^{-1}\)
conn: Magnitude of a sum or difference and the angle formula combine: \(\cos\theta\) from \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) feeds the cross term in \(|\mathbf{a}\pm k\mathbf{b}|\)
Angle between composite vectors needs three pieces together: expanded dot product by bilinearity, both composite magnitudes via \(\sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\), then surd simplification

Perpendicularity condition links to the non-cancellation result: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})=0\) means \(\mathbf{a}\perp(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})\), and solving for an unknown scalar such as \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}+\lambda\mathbf{c})=0\) uses the same idea

Component form and \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) form are interchangeable; use components when given coordinates and the magnitude form when given lengths and angles, as in force-resolution and work problems
exq: Given \(|\mathbf{a}|=3\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=2\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=5\), find \(\cos\theta\) and the exact value of \(|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}|\).
With the same data, find \(|3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) and the angle between \(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}\) and \(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\), giving the answer in degrees to 1 d.p.
For \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,-1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,\lambda,3)\), find \(\lambda\) so that \(\mathbf{a}\perp\mathbf{b}\), and the angle between them when \(\lambda=1\).

Show that \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}\) with \(\mathbf{a}\neq\mathbf{0}\) does not imply \(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c}\). Give a numerical counterexample with \(\mathbf{a}=(1,0,0)\).
Two forces of 10 N and 6 N act at an angle of 60° between them. Find the magnitude of their sum and of their difference, and state which sign of the cross term applies to each.

notes.t: Magnitudes and angles using the dot product
pts: The magnitude of a sum of two vectors follows from the law of cosines with the angle between them.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors is the dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes.
Scalar multiples scale the magnitude: |2b| = 2|b|, so substitute the scaled magnitude into the formula.
Compute |a+2b| by expanding the squared magnitudes plus the cross term 2|a||2b|cos θ.
Here a·b = 5 gives cos θ = 5/6, so |a+2b| = √45 = 3√5.
defs: Dot product angle formula
For nonzero vectors a and b, cos θ = (a·b)/(|a||b|), where θ is the angle between them.
eqs: u, v = vectors; θ = angle between u and v (rad or °); magnitudes in the units of the vectors
Cosine of angle between vectors via dot product
a, b = vectors; a·b = dot product (same units as |a||b|); θ = angle between them
tips: Use |2b| = 2|b| (not |b|) when substituting into the sum formula; forgetting the scalar is a common error.
Check the sign of the cross term: the cos θ term must be included with + for the sum and - for the difference |a − b|.
rq: Why does the sign of a·b tell you whether the angle is acute or obtuse?
Because cos θ has the same sign as a·b (magnitudes are positive): a·b > 0 means θ < 90°, a·b < 0 means θ > 90°.
Why is the factor 2 in front of the cross term 2|u||v|cos θ?
It comes from expanding (u+v)·(u+v) = u·u + v·v + 2u·v, and u·v = |u||v|cos θ.

notes.t: Scalar product: finding the magnitude of 3a − b
pts: The magnitude of a difference of vectors follows from the law of cosines using the angle between them.
Scaling a vector by k multiplies its magnitude by |k|, so |3a| = 3|a|.
The cross term uses the angle θ between a and b; its cosine is taken from the scalar product value.
eqs: Magnitude of the difference of two vectors (law of cosines form)
|3a − b| = magnitude of resultant vector (m or same unit as a, b); |3a| = magnitude of 3a (same unit as a); |b| = magnitude of b (same unit as b); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °)
tips: Do not write |3a| = 3 — the scalar multiplies the magnitude, giving 9 here.
Check the sign of the cross term: the subtraction gives −2|3a||b| cos θ; forgetting the minus sign gives the wrong answer (√(81+4+30)=√115).
rq: Why does |3a| equal 9 rather than 3 when |a| = 3?
Multiplying a vector by the scalar 3 multiplies its length by 3, so |3a| = 3 × |a| = 3 × 3 = 9.
What would change in the final result if the angle θ were 90° instead of the value used here?
cos 90° = 0, so the cross term −2·9·2·cos θ vanishes and the magnitude becomes √(81 + 4) = √85.

notes.t: Angle between two vectors using the scalar product
pts: The angle between two vectors follows from the scalar product divided by the product of their magnitudes.
Magnitudes of combined vectors must be found first, using the square root of the dot product with itself.
Square roots of products can be combined under a single root, which simplifies the denominator.
eqs: Cosine of the angle between two vectors via scalar product
φ = angle between the vectors (rad or °); a, b = vectors; · = scalar product; |v| = magnitude of v (same units as the vector components)
tips: Do not forget to expand the vectors (e.g. 3a − b) before taking the magnitude; magnitudes are of the combined vectors, not of a and b separately.
Check the denominator simplification: √5·√55 = √275 is valid, but leaving the answer unsimplified or mis-multiplying the coefficient 3 is a common slip.
rq: Why must the scalar product be divided by both magnitudes rather than just one?
The scalar product equals |u||v|cos φ, so dividing by both magnitudes isolates cos φ and makes the result independent of vector lengths.
What would the value of cos φ tell you if it came out greater than 1?
It signals an arithmetic error, since cosine of any real angle lies between −1 and 1.

notes.t: Magnitudes and angles using the dot product
pts: The dot product of two vectors can be computed from their components or from their magnitudes and the angle between them.
Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero.
A non-zero dot product means the vectors are not perpendicular; the sign depends on whether the angle is acute or obtuse.
defs: Perpendicular vectors
Two non-zero vectors a and b are perpendicular if and only if their dot product equals zero, i.e. the angle between them is 90°.
eqs: Dot product in component form and in terms of magnitude and angle

\(a_i, b_i\) = vector components (dimensionless or in the unit of the vector); \(|\mathbf{a}|, |\mathbf{b}|\) = magnitudes of the vectors (same unit as the vectors); \(\theta\) = angle between the vectors (degrees or radians)
\(a_i, b_i\) = vector components; valid for \(\mathbf{a}\) and/or \(\mathbf{b} \neq 0\)
tips: Perpendicularity requires both vectors to be non-zero; a zero vector gives a dot product of zero trivially.
Check that the angle is in the correct mode (degrees vs radians) when using cos θ on a calculator.
rq: Why does a·b = 0 imply perpendicularity even though the formula is written as |a||b|cos θ?
Because cos θ = 0 only when θ = 90°, so with non-zero magnitudes the product vanishes only for perpendicular vectors.
What happens to the dot product if the angle between a and b is obtuse?
cos θ is negative, so a·b is negative.

notes.t: Dot product: cancellation does not hold for vectors
pts: Dot product equality a·b = a·c does not imply b = c, unlike cancelling scalars.
Rearranging gives a·(b − c) = 0, so a is perpendicular to (b − c), not that b and c are equal.
Equal dot products can hold when a is zero or when a is perpendicular to the difference of b and c.
The diagram shows two different vectors b and c with the same projection onto a, so their dot products with a match.
eqs: Condition for equal dot products with a common vector
\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} = vectors (dimensionless or units of their physical quantity)
tips: Do not cancel vectors in a dot product equation; instead move terms and factor to get a·(b − c) = 0.
Equal dot products do not mean the vectors are equal; check whether a is zero or perpendicular to (b − c).
rq: If a·b = a·c, why can't we conclude b = c, and what extra condition would make it true?
Because a·(b − c) = 0 only says a is perpendicular to (b − c); b = c requires a ≠ 0 with the difference (b − c) to vanish, i.e. the vectors are equal, not merely having the same projection onto a.
What does the zero vector case a = 0 tell you about the dot-product equation?
If a = 0 then both sides are zero for any b and c, so the equality holds trivially without b = c.

xq.q: Two displacement vectors \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) have \(|\mathbf a| = 5\) m, \(|\mathbf b| = 3\) m and \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b = 9\) m². Find the magnitude of \(\mathbf a - 2\mathbf b\).
xq.a: 5 m

xq.q: Vectors \(\mathbf a = 2\mathbf i - \mathbf j + 2\mathbf k\) and \(\mathbf b = \mathbf i + 2\mathbf j - 2\mathbf k\) are given. Find the angle between them in degrees.
The vectors \(\mathbf p = 2\mathbf i + k\mathbf j - \mathbf k\) and \(\mathbf q = 3\mathbf i + 4\mathbf j + 2\mathbf k\) are perpendicular. What is the value of \(k\)?
