xq.w: Perpendicular means \(\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q = 6+4k-2 = 0\), so \(k=-1\); the traps are a sign slip on the \(\mathbf k\)-term (giving 1 or −1.5) or adding instead of subtracting 2 (giving −2).

units.name: 8.6 Unit vectors i, j, k and dot products
units.ov: This material introduces the orthonormal unit vectors \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) along the x, y, z axes and uses them to write any 3D vector in component form. Because the unit vectors are mutually perpendicular with magnitude 1, expanding a dot product collapses to a sum of matching-component products, giving a scalar result. The notes do not cover the geometric form \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), but the component formula is the computational route to it.
must: Unit vectors \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) have magnitude 1 and point along the +x, +y, +z axes; any vector is \(\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}\)
Component formula: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\)
The dot product is a scalar (a number), not a vector; do not confuse it with the cross product
Orthonormality: \(\mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}=1\)
Orthogonality: \(\mathbf{i}\cdot\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{i}=0\)
Derivation: expand the 9 terms of \((a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k})\cdot(b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k})\); the 6 cross terms vanish, leaving 3
Match components by position (x with x, y with y, z with z) and keep signs for negative components
Dot with itself gives the squared magnitude: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2\)
Zero dot product between nonzero vectors means they are perpendicular (use this to find unknown components)
A unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\) is \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}|\)
conn: Dot product with \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) gives the angle between vectors: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}\)
Work done \(W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}\) and resolved components (projection of a force onto a direction using a unit vector) in mechanics
Perpendicularity tests (\(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\)) combine with solving for unknown constants, and with the cross product to build orthogonal sets or normals to planes
Magnitude and normalisation link unit vectors and dot products: \(|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}}\), then \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{a}/|\mathbf{a}|\)
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=4\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k}\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and state whether the vectors are perpendicular.
Find the value of \(p\) such that \(\mathbf{u}=3\mathbf{i}+p\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k}\).

Show by expanding that \((a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k})\cdot(b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k})=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\, ,\) stating which unit-vector products equal 0 and which equal 1.

A force \(\mathbf{F}=(3\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k})\) N moves a particle through displacement \(\mathbf{d}=(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+4\mathbf{k})\) m. Calculate the work done and the angle between \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(\mathbf{d}\).
Find the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\) and the component of \(\mathbf{b}=3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) along it.

notes.t: Unit vectors i, j, k and the scalar (dot) product
pts: The unit vectors i, j and k are mutually perpendicular, so each pair has zero dot product.
Each unit vector dotted with itself gives 1, while dot products between different unit vectors give 0.
Expanding the product of two component-form vectors and using the orthogonality rules reduces the scalar product to the sum of products of matching components.
defs: Unit vector
A vector of magnitude 1 used to indicate a direction; i, j and k are the unit vectors along the x, y and z axes.
Scalar (dot) product
For vectors a and b, the scalar product is the sum of products of corresponding components, giving a scalar result.
eqs: Scalar product of two vectors in component form
a₁, a₂, a₃ = components of vector a (dimensionless or same unit as a); b₁, b₂, b₃ = components of vector b (same unit as b)
tips: Do not confuse the scalar product (result is a number) with the vector/cross product (result is a vector).
Ensure the components are matched in the same position (x with x, y with y, z with z) before summing.
rq: Why does the dot product of i with j vanish, and what does this tell us geometrically?
i and j are mutually perpendicular, and a·b = |a||b|cos θ with θ = 90°, so cos 90° = 0.
Why do only the terms a₁b₁, a₂b₂ and a₃b₃ survive in the expansion?
Every cross term such as a₁b₂ i·j contains a dot product of two different unit vectors, which is zero, while i·i = j·j = k·k = 1.

xq.q: Two vectors are given by \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}+p\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\), where \(p\) is a constant. Using the orthogonality of \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\), find the value of \(p\) for which \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) are perpendicular.
For \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\), what is \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\)?
o: \(3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}\)
xq.w: a·b = 3 − 2 − 2 = −1; ignoring signs gives 7, a sign slip gives 1, and keeping the component products as a vector confuses the dot product with a vector result.

xq.q: Let \(\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{b}=b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k}\). Show, using the dot products of the unit vectors, that \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\).
xq.a: Expanding gives nine terms of the form \(a_{i}\) \(b_{j}\) (\(e_{i}\)·\(e_{j}\)). Since i·i = j·j = k·k = 1 and i·j = j·k = i·k = 0 (mutually perpendicular unit vectors), only the matching terms survive, leaving a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3.
s: Expand the product into nine terms \(a_{i}\) \(b_{j}\) (\(e_{i}\)·\(e_{j}\))
Same-vector dot products: i·i = j·j = k·k = 1
Different unit vectors are perpendicular so their dot products are 0
Remaining terms give a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3

units.name: 9.1 Dot product and orthocenter proof
units.ov: This material covers the dot product in component form, its use for lengths (\(|\mathbf{a}|^2=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}\), \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) by expansion) and for testing perpendicularity. It then applies these to prove that a triangle's three altitudes meet at one point (the orthocenter), by placing the origin at the intersection of two altitudes and showing the third passes through it. The link is that 'perpendicular' becomes 'dot product = 0', so a geometric proof reduces to algebra.
must: Component form: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\) gives a scalar, not a vector.
\(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=|\mathbf{a}|^2\), so \(|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}\) (square the components first, then sum, then take the root).
Perpendicularity test: non-zero \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\) are orthogonal iff \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\). Always state the non-zero condition.
\(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})=|\mathbf{a}|^2-2\,\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}+|\mathbf{b}|^2\), using distributivity and commutativity.
Orthocenter proof setup: put the orthocenter O at the origin, with position vectors \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\) for A, B, C.
An altitude is perpendicular to the opposite side, and the side vector is a difference of positions (e.g. \(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{b}\) for BC), not a position vector itself.
Altitude conditions: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{b})=0\) (from A, perpendicular to BC) and \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})=0\) (from B, perpendicular to AC).

Adding the two conditions cancels \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and leaves \(\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=0\). So OC is perpendicular to AB, the third altitude passes through O, and the three altitudes are concurrent.

Check labelling: the notes pair \((\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0\) with the altitude from C. That expression is actually the altitude from A, and \((\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\) is from B. The algebra still works, but label it correctly in an exam.
Handle degenerate cases: if a vector is zero (e.g. O coincides with a vertex in a right-angled triangle), the zero dot product no longer implies perpendicularity, so say so.
conn: Magnitude and perpendicularity: Pythagoras emerges from \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2\) when \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\), so a question may ask you to verify a right angle from side lengths.
Side vectors from positions: finding \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\) feeds directly into the dot-product test for altitudes and into \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) for side lengths.
Concurrency proofs: choosing the origin at a special point (orthocenter) and combining two dot-product equations to derive a third is a pattern reusable for other triangle-center proofs.
Engineering use: the dot product gives the component of a force along a direction and tests for zero work (force perpendicular to displacement).
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(1,4,-2)\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\), decide whether they are orthogonal, and find \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) using \((\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\).
Find the value of \(k\) for which \((k,2,-1)\) is perpendicular to \((3,-1,4)\).

Prove that the three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent, by placing the orthocenter at the origin and using \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{b})=0\) and \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})=0\) to deduce \(\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=0\).

Show that \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|^2=|\mathbf{a}|^2-2\,\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}+|\mathbf{b}|^2\). Then, for \(|\mathbf{a}|=3\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=4\), \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\), find \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\).
Explain why \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\) does not always imply perpendicular vectors, and give an example.

notes.t: Dot product: calculation and |a−b| via dot product
pts: The dot product of two vectors is found by multiplying matching components and summing them.
A zero dot product means the two vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).
The magnitude of a vector difference can be found by expanding (a−b)·(a−b) as a dot product.
The dot product of a vector with itself equals the square of its magnitude.
defs: Dot product
For vectors \(\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)\), the scalar \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\).
Orthogonal vectors
Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) if and only if their dot product is zero.
eqs: \(a_i,b_i\) = vector components (dimensionless or same unit as the vector); \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) = scalar
Magnitude of a difference of vectors
\(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) = length of the difference vector (same unit as \(\mathbf{a}\))
tips: Do not forget to square the components before summing when finding \(|\mathbf{a}|\); the magnitude is the square root of the sum, not the sum of roots.
A zero dot product only implies perpendicularity when both vectors are non-zero.
rq: Why does a·b = 0 in the example even though a and b look unrelated?
Because the component products \(1(-2)+1(0)+2(1)=0\) cancel exactly, so the vectors are perpendicular.
Why do the cross terms vanish when expanding (a−b)·(a−b) for perpendicular a and b?
Since \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\), the terms \(-\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and \(-\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a}\) are zero, leaving \(|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2\).

notes.t: Dot product and orthocenter proof
pts: Place the orthocenter O at the origin and let position vectors of A, B, C be a, b, c
Altitude from C is perpendicular to AB, so (b − c)·a = 0 (vector AB direction is b − a; the altitude through O gives orthogonality conditions)
Similarly the altitude from A gives (c − a)·b = 0
Adding the two orthogonality conditions and simplifying shows c·(b − a) = 0, i.e. the third altitude passes through O
defs: Orthocenter
The point where the three altitudes of a triangle intersect
eqs: a, b, c = position vectors of vertices A, B, C from O (m); \(\cdot\) = dot product
tips: Do not confuse the side vector b − a with the position vector b; the orthogonality is with the side direction.
The dot-product zero condition only implies perpendicularity when neither vector is the zero vector.
rq: Why does choosing O as the origin simplify the proof?
Because the position vectors a, b, c then directly represent the vertices, so perpendicularity of a side and an altitude reduces to a dot product equal to zero.
What does a dot product of zero tell you about two vectors?
They are perpendicular (orthogonal), provided both are nonzero.

xq.q: Position vectors of two points relative to an origin are \(\mathbf{a}=(4,1,3)\) m and \(\mathbf{b}=(1,5,-2)\) m. By expanding \((\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\), find the distance \(|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|\) between the points.
Which of the following vectors is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{u}=(2,-1,3)\)?
xq.w: u·(1,5,1) = 2 − 5 + 3 = 0; (−2,1,−3) is antiparallel to u (dot −14), not perpendicular, and the others give 12 and 9.
s: Compute the dot product with each option

xq.q: Triangle ABC has its orthocentre O at the origin, and A, B, C have position vectors \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\). The altitudes from C and from A pass through O, giving \((\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0\) and \((\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\). Show that the altitude from B also passes through O, i.e. \(\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=0\).
xq.a: Expand: b·a − c·a = 0 and c·b − a·b = 0. Add: b·a − c·a + c·b − a·b = 0. Since a·b = b·a, this gives c·b − c·a = c·(b−a) = 0. So OC is perpendicular to AB (both non-zero), meaning the third altitude passes through O.
s: Expand both conditions using the dot product
Add them; b·a and a·b cancel
Conclude OC ⟂ AB, so the third altitude passes through O

units.name: 9.2 Cross product definition, magnitude and right-hand rule
units.ov: This material defines the cross (vector) product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), whose magnitude comes from the sine of the included angle and whose direction comes from the right-hand rule. Its magnitude gives the area of a parallelogram (and half of it the area of a triangle), and its anticommutative nature and perpendicularity to both inputs underpin later uses such as moments and rotation.
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is a vector, not a scalar.
Magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\), with \(0\le\theta\le\pi\), so it is never negative.
Direction: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), so \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) form a right-handed set.
Right-hand rule: curl the fingers from the first vector to the second through the smaller angle \(\theta\); the thumb gives the direction.
Anticommutative: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\); same magnitude, opposite direction, so order always matters.
Parallel vectors (\(\theta=0,\pi\)) give the zero vector; perpendicular vectors (\(\theta=\pi/2\)) give the maximum magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\).
Parallelogram area \(=|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) (base × perpendicular height); triangle area \(=\tfrac12|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\).

\(\theta\) is the included angle between the vectors with tails joined; using the exterior angle is wrong in general, though \(\sin\theta=\sin(\pi-\theta)\) so the magnitude is unaffected by the supplement while the direction logic is.
Take the magnitude before quoting an area; units are the product of the input units (e.g. m²).
Do not confuse with the dot product (scalar, \(\cos\theta\)); the cross product uses \(\sin\theta\) and gives a vector.
conn: Cross product magnitude and geometry: the area of a parallelogram or triangle defined by position vectors such as \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{AD}\) is found from \(|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AD}|\).

Cross product and dot product: the dot product gives \(\cos\theta\) (projection, parallel test) while the cross product gives \(\sin\theta\) (perpendicular test, area); together they determine the angle between vectors.

Right-hand rule and anticommutativity: the sign/direction of a result (e.g. a moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\)) depends on the order of the vectors, so a swapped order gives a reversed direction.
Zero cross product and parallelism: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}\) is a test for parallel vectors, linking to collinearity of points.
exq: Vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) have magnitudes 4 m and 6 m with an angle of 30° between them. Find \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\), and state the magnitude and direction of \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\) relative to \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\).
Parallelogram ABCD has \(|\vec{AB}|=5\) m, \(|\vec{AD}|=3\) m and included angle 120° at A. Find the area of the parallelogram and of triangle ABD, explaining why using 60° gives the same magnitude.

Using the right-hand rule, state the direction of \(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j}\), \(\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{i}\), and explain the sign change when the order is reversed.

Explain why \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), and for what angles \(\theta\) its magnitude is zero and maximum, giving the maximum value for \(|\mathbf{a}|=2\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=7\).
A triangle has area 12 m² and two sides of lengths 6 m and 8 m meeting at a vertex. Find the included angle \(\theta\) between them.

notes.t: Vector (Cross) Product
pts: The cross product of two vectors a and b is a vector, not a scalar.
Its magnitude is |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between a and b, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.
Its direction is along the unit vector n̂, perpendicular to both a and b, such that a, b, n̂ form a right-handed set.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the direction of n̂, so the cross product is not commutative.
defs: Vector (cross) product
The product a × b of two vectors, equal to |a||b| sin θ n̂, which is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
Unit vector n̂
A vector of length 1 perpendicular to both a and b, defining the direction of the cross product.
eqs: Magnitude and direction of the vector (cross) product of a and b

a, b = vectors; |a|, |b| = magnitudes (dimensionless if a, b are unitless, otherwise their units); θ = angle between a and b (rad), 0 ≤ θ ≤ π; n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the cross product with the scalar (dot) product; the cross product result is a vector, while the dot product is a scalar.
Order matters: b × a = −(a × b), so reversing the vectors flips the direction of n̂.
rq: Why does the cross product give a vector perpendicular to both a and b rather than a scalar?
Because it is defined to point along n̂, which is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b; its magnitude |a||b| sin θ is the area of the parallelogram they span.
What happens to a × b if a and b are parallel?
θ = 0 or π gives sin θ = 0, so a × b = 0 (the zero vector).

notes.t: Cross product: definition, magnitude and right-hand rule
pts: The cross product of two vectors a and b is a vector c, whose magnitude is |a||b| sin θ and whose direction is perpendicular to both.
The direction of the cross product is given by the unit vector n̂, normal to the plane containing a and b.
Using the right-hand rule: fingers sweep from the first vector to the second through angle θ, and the thumb points along the result.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the direction of the cross product, so B × A = −(A × B).
The magnitude |c| depends only on the angle θ between the vectors, being zero when they are parallel and maximal when perpendicular.
defs: Cross product (vector product)
The vector product of a and b, written a × b, is a vector perpendicular to both a and b with magnitude |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between them, and direction given by the right-hand rule.
Right-hand rule
Curl the fingers of the right hand from the first vector towards the second through the smaller angle θ; the extended thumb gives the direction of the cross product.
eqs: Vector cross product, magnitude and direction

c = cross product vector (same units as a·b); a, b = input vectors; |a|, |b| = magnitudes of a and b; θ = angle between a and b (degrees or radians); n̂ = unit vector normal to the plane of a and b (dimensionless)
|c| = magnitude of the cross product (product of units of a and b); |a|, |b| = magnitudes of the vectors; θ = angle between them
tips: Students often forget that the angle θ is between the vectors when tails are joined; using the wrong angle (e.g. supplement) changes the magnitude sign or value.
The cross product is only defined for 3D vectors and is not commutative; always state the order when writing a × b.
rq: Why is the magnitude of a × b zero when the two vectors are parallel?
Because the angle between them is θ = 0° or 180°, and sin θ = 0, so no area is spanned and the vectors give no perpendicular component.
What happens to the direction of a × b if you swap a and b?
It reverses: b × a = −(a × b), since the right-hand rule now sweeps in the opposite sense.
Why is the result perpendicular to both input vectors?
The right-hand rule defines the direction as normal to the plane containing both vectors, so it has zero dot product with each of them.

notes.t: Area of parallelogram and triangle using the cross product
pts: Area of a parallelogram equals base times perpendicular height, which can be written as the magnitude of a cross product of two adjacent side vectors.
The magnitude of a × b equals |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between the two vectors.
The area of triangle ABD is half the area of the parallelogram formed by the same two adjacent sides.
The cross product a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, with direction given by the unit normal n̂.
defs: Cross product magnitude
For vectors a and b with angle θ between them, |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ, which equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b.
Unit normal n̂
A unit vector perpendicular to both a and b, giving the direction of the cross product a × b.
eqs: Area of parallelogram ABCD from adjacent sides
\vec{AD}, \vec{AB} = adjacent side vectors (m); θ = angle between them (rad or °); Area (m²)
AD, AB = side lengths (m); θ = included angle; Area (m²)
tips: Use the included angle θ between the two vectors meeting at the same vertex; using the exterior or wrong angle gives the wrong sine.
Area results are in square units (m²) while the cross product is a vector; take magnitude before quoting an area.
rq: Why is the triangle's area exactly half the parallelogram's area when both use sides AD and AB?
The diagonal BD splits the parallelogram into two congruent triangles ABD and BCD of equal area, so each is half.
What happens to |a × b| if a and b are parallel, and why?
θ = 0 or π, so sin θ = 0 and |a × b| = 0; parallel vectors span no area.

xq.q: In a parallelogram frame, adjacent side vectors \(\vec{AD}\) and \(\vec{AB}\) have lengths 7 m and 4 m, and the included angle between them (tails joined) is \(150^\circ\). Find the area of triangle ABD.
xq.a: 7 m²
s: Area of triangle = ½|AD||AB| sin θ

xq.q: Two vectors satisfy \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=12\mathbf{k}\). What is \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\)?
xq.a: \(-12\mathbf{k}\)
o: \(12\mathbf{k}\)
\(\mathbf{0}\)
\(-12\mathbf{k}\)
xq.w: Reversing the order reverses the direction of the cross product, so b×a = −12k; assuming commutativity gives 12k, and dropping k gives a scalar.

xq.q: Explain, using base times perpendicular height, why the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) (angle \(\theta\) between them) equals \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\), and deduce the area of the triangle formed by the same two sides.
xq.a: Take |a| as the base. The perpendicular height of the parallelogram is |b| sin θ. So area = |a||b| sin θ = |a × b|. The triangle formed by the same two sides is half the parallelogram, so its area is ½|a × b|.
s: Triangle = half the parallelogram = ½|a × b|

units.name: 9.3 Algebraic properties: anti-commutativity, non-associativity, distributivity
units.ov: This material covers the algebra of the vector (cross) product: anti-commutativity, non-associativity, and the scalar and distributive laws. It then applies these to the unit vectors i, j, k to give the Cartesian form. All of it follows from the definition \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) and the right-hand rule, which fix both the sign behaviour and the direction of every result.
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), where \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is perpendicular to both vectors and given by the right-hand rule; the result is a vector, so always keep \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\).
Anti-commutativity: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=-(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a})\); swapping the order flips the sign but not the magnitude.

Non-associativity: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\neq(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) in general, so \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) without brackets is ambiguous and must never be written.
Geometry of triple products: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) lies in the plane of b and c, while \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) lies in the plane of a and b.
Distributive law: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c}\); keep the order of the factors when expanding.
Scalar law: \(\mathbf{a}\times(\lambda\mathbf{b})=\lambda(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})=(\lambda\mathbf{a})\times\mathbf{b}\).

Unit vector products: \(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k},\ \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i},\ \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}\) (cyclic), and the reversed order gives a minus sign, e.g. \(\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{i}=-\mathbf{k}\).
Parallel vectors: \(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}\), because \(\sin 0=0\); this is a zero vector, not the scalar 0.
Set the calculator to the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) when evaluating \(\sin\theta\).
conn: Distributivity plus the unit vector table gives the component (determinant) form of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\): expand term by term, then use the cyclic rule and anti-commutativity for the signs, with the parallel terms vanishing.
Anti-commutativity combined with \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}\) links to parallel-vector tests and to the area of a parallelogram, \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\).

Non-associativity and the plane-membership argument underlie the vector triple product, which links to the dot product and to mechanics, e.g. moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\), where the order of r and F determines the sign of the moment.
The right-hand rule fixes both \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) in the definition and the sign pattern of the i, j, k products, so the geometric and Cartesian approaches must agree.
exq: Show that \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\neq(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) using \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{j}\), and state which plane each result lies in.
Expand \((2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})\times(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{k})\) using the distributive law and the unit vector products, giving the answer in components.

Given \(|\mathbf{a}|=4\), \(|\mathbf{b}|=3\) and an angle of \(30^\circ\) between them, find \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) and \(|\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}|\), and describe how the directions of the two products differ.

Prove, using the definition and the right-hand rule, that \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\), and explain why \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) is not a valid expression.
Simplify \(\mathbf{a}\times(\lambda\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})-\lambda(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\) and justify each step by naming the law used.

notes.t: Vector/Dot Product Properties: Anti-commutativity and Non-associativity of the Vector Prod
pts: The vector (cross) product is anti-commutative: swapping the order reverses the sign of the result.
The vector product is non-associative: bracketing changes the result in general.
b×c is perpendicular to both b and c, so a×(b×c) is perpendicular to a and (b×c), meaning it lies in the plane of b and c.
a×b is perpendicular to both a and b, so (a×b)×c lies in the plane of a and b.
Because of non-associativity, a triple product written without brackets is ambiguous and must never be written.
eqs: a, b = vectors (dimensionless as symbols; magnitude in their own units)
Non-associativity of the vector product (general case)
Magnitude and direction of the vector product
|a|, |b| = magnitudes (same units as a, b); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless)
tips: Unit trap: the cross product magnitude uses sin θ, so θ must be in the correct angle mode (radians vs degrees) on your calculator.
Do not assume a×b×c can be evaluated left-to-right like ordinary multiplication; always insert brackets first.
rq: Why must the brackets be included in a×(b×c) when you compute a triple vector product?
Because the vector product is non-associative, so a×(b×c) and (a×b)×c generally give different vectors; without brackets the expression is ambiguous.
If a×(b×c) always lies in the plane of b and c, what does this imply when b and c are parallel?
b×c = 0, so a×(b×c) = 0; the result is the zero vector, consistent with lying in a 'plane' of parallel vectors.
What happens to a×b if you swap a and b, and why?
It changes sign: b×a = −(a×b), because the unit normal n̂ reverses direction by the right-hand rule while the magnitude is unchanged.

notes.t: Distributive laws of the vector product
pts: The vector product a × b has magnitude |a||b| sin θ and direction n̂ perpendicular to both vectors.
A scalar can be pulled out of a vector product, so scalar multiplication commutes with the cross product.
The vector product distributes over vector addition, so the second vector can be expanded term by term.
eqs: Magnitude and direction of the vector product
a, b = vectors; θ = angle between a and b (rad or°); n̂ = unit vector perpendicular to a and b (dimensionless); |a|, |b| = magnitudes (same units as a, b)
Scalar multiplication law for the vector product
tips: Do not treat the cross product as commutative; a × b = −(b × a).
The result of a × b is a vector, not a scalar; keep the unit vector n̂ in your final answer.
rq: Why does the cross product give a vector perpendicular to both a and b, and what happens if a and b are parallel?
n̂ is defined perpendicular to both a and b; if they are parallel, θ = 0 or π so sin θ = 0 and a × b = 0.
Why is the order of the vectors important for the cross product?
Reversing the order flips the direction of n̂ (right-hand rule), so b × a = −(a × b); the product is not commutative.

notes.t: Cartesian form of the vector product
pts: The cross product of a with b has magnitude |a||b|sin θ and points along the unit normal n̂, perpendicular to both vectors.
The cross product of any unit vector with itself is zero, since the angle between parallel vectors is zero.
The unit vectors i, j, k form a right-handed set; cross products of them follow a cyclic pattern, so order matters.
Cross product is anti-commutative: swapping the order reverses the sign, so i × j = k but j × i = −k.
defs: Cross (vector) product
The vector product a × b is a vector whose magnitude is |a||b|sin θ, where θ is the angle between a and b, and whose direction n̂ is perpendicular to both a and b following the right-hand rule.
Unit vectors i, j, k
Three mutually perpendicular unit vectors parallel to the x, y and z coordinate axes respectively.
eqs: Magnitude/direction form of the cross product
a, b = vectors (m or other units of the quantities); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °); n̂ = unit normal vector (dimensionless)
i, j, k = orthogonal unit vectors (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the order: a × b = −b × a, so swapping vectors flips the sign of the result.
The cross product gives a vector, not a scalar; keep the direction n̂ from the right-hand rule and don't drop it.
rq: Why must i × i equal the zero vector rather than a unit vector?
Because the angle between identical vectors is θ = 0, so sin θ = 0 and the magnitude |i||i|sin 0 vanishes.
What happens to the sign if the order of the cyclic pair is reversed, e.g. j × i?
It reverses: j × i = −k, showing the cross product is anti-commutative.

xq.q: Two position vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) have magnitudes \(|\mathbf{a}|=6\) m and \(|\mathbf{b}|=4\) m, and the angle between them is \(\theta=150^\circ\). Using the scalar multiplication law and the magnitude formula for the vector product, find the magnitude of \((3\mathbf{a})\times(-2\mathbf{b})\).
xq.a: 72 m²
s: Scalar law: \((3\mathbf{a})\times(-2\mathbf{b}) = -6(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\), so the magnitude is \(6|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) (the minus sign only reverses direction).

xq.q: The unit vectors \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) form a right-handed set. Evaluate \(\mathbf{i}\times(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j})\).
xq.a: \(-\mathbf{j}\)
o: \(\mathbf{0}\)
\(-\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{k}\)
xq.w: \(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}\), then \(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{k}=-(\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{i})=-\mathbf{j}\); the traps are assuming the answer is zero by bracketing as \((\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i})\times\mathbf{j}\), and dropping the sign from anti-commutativity.

xq.q: (a) Explain, using the direction of the vector product, why \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) lies in the plane of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\). (b) Take \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{j}\) and show that the vector product is not associative.
xq.a: (a) \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) is perpendicular to the plane of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\). The vector \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\), so it must lie in the plane of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\). (b) \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{i}\times(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j})=\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{k}=-\mathbf{j}\), but \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}=(\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i})\times\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{0}\). The results differ, so the product is not associative.
s: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) is perpendicular to the plane of b and c.
The outer product is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\), hence in the plane of b and c.

units.name: 9.4 Computing cross products with determinants
units.ov: The cross product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) of two 3D vectors is a vector perpendicular to both. Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram they span, and its direction follows the right-hand rule. It is computed by expanding a 3×3 determinant with rows \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\); \(\mathbf{a}\); \(\mathbf{b}\) along the first row, using 2×2 minors with signs +, −, +. Row order matters, which gives anticommutativity: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\).
must: Determinant set-up: row 1 is \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\), row 2 is \(\mathbf{a}\), row 3 is \(\mathbf{b}\), in that order.
Expansion: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\mathbf{i}-(a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\mathbf{j}+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\mathbf{k}\).
The j-component carries a minus sign. Forgetting it is the commonest error.
Anticommutativity: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\), because swapping rows flips the sign. It is not commutative.
The result is a vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), with direction given by the right-hand rule. The dot product is a scalar.
Magnitude: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\), which equals the parallelogram area. The triangle area is half of this.
Worked example: \(\mathbf{a}=(3,2,1)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1)\) gives \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(-1,2,-1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=(1,-2,1)\).
Check any answer by taking dot products with both inputs, which must give 0. For the example, \((-1,2,-1)\cdot(3,2,1)=0\).
The cross product is defined only for 3D vectors. The mnemonic/diagonal method gives the same result as the determinant, with the same sign pattern.
conn: Cross product and area: compute \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), then take \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) for parallelogram or triangle area, e.g. from three points via two edge vectors.

Cross product and dot product: the cross product gives \(\sin\theta\) and the dot product gives \(\cos\theta\). Combining them gives the angle, and a zero dot product with the result verifies perpendicularity.

Cross product and mechanics: moment \(\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) and the direction of the torque vector depend on the order of the operands, so a sign error reverses the moment direction.
Determinants and parallel vectors: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}\) exactly when the vectors are parallel, and swapping rows (anticommutativity) is the same as the determinant sign change.
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(1,4,-2)\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) using the determinant method and verify that it is perpendicular to both vectors.

For \(\mathbf{a}=(3,2,1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1)\), find \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\). State the relationship between them and find the magnitude (\(\sqrt6\)).
Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1,0,0), B(0,2,0), C(0,0,3) using a cross product.
A force \(\mathbf{F}=(0,5,-2)\) N acts at position \(\mathbf{r}=(2,1,3)\) m. Calculate the moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) about the origin and explain what changes if the order is reversed.
Find a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,0)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(0,1,3)\).

notes.t: Vector product: determinant method and graphic (mnemonic) method
pts: The vector product a × b is computed by expanding a 3×3 determinant whose first row is the unit vectors i, j, k.
Each component of a × b is a 2×2 minor, with signs alternating +, −, + along the first row.
The graphic method lists a1 a2 a3 and b1 b2 b3 in rows; the diagonal products give the i, j, k components, with red (+ve) and blue (−ve) crossing lines.
defs: Vector (cross) product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span and whose direction follows the right-hand rule.
eqs: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a (dimensionless or units of a); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b (units of b); i, j, k = unit basis vectors (dimensionless)
Expanded component form of the vector product
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a; \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b; i, j, k = unit basis vectors
tips: Remember the middle (j) term is subtracted; forgetting this flips the j-component's sign.
Keep the row order a then b in the determinant; reversing rows changes the sign of the result.
rq: Why does the j-term carry a minus sign while the i and k terms are positive?
Cofactor expansion along the first row alternates signs (+, −, +), so the j-component's minor is subtracted.
What happens to a × b if you swap a and b?
The sign reverses: b × a = −(a × b), because the determinant changes sign when two rows are swapped.

notes.t: Computing cross products with determinants
pts: The cross product a × b is computed as the determinant of a 3×3 matrix whose first row is the unit vectors i, j, k.
Expanding the determinant along the first row gives the three components via 2×2 minors with alternating signs.
Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the sign of the cross product, so b × a = −(a × b).
Worked example: with a = (3,2,1) and b = (−1,−1,−1), the cross product is (−1, 2, −1).
eqs: Cross product components of a × b
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = components of a (dimensionless or units of a); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = components of b (units of b); i, j, k = unit basis vectors
tips: Watch the minus sign on the j-component: it is −(\(a_{1b}_{3}\) − \(b_{1a}_{3}\)), not +.
Cross products only apply to 3D vectors; the result is a vector, not a scalar, and is perpendicular to both inputs.
rq: Why does swapping a and b flip the sign of the result, and what does that say about the direction of a × b?

Each minor's rows swap, flipping every component's sign, so b × a = −(a × b); the result is perpendicular to both vectors with a direction given by the right-hand rule, which reverses when the order is reversed.
Why are there minus signs on the j-component but not on i and k?
The cofactor expansion along the first row alternates signs (+, −, +) because the j position is the middle entry of the row, giving the −(a1b3 − b1a3) term.

notes.t: Cross product of vectors: anticommutativity and component calculation
pts: Swapping the order of the vectors reverses the direction of the cross product, so \( \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \).
The cross product is computed with a 3×3 determinant whose first row is the unit vectors \( \hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k} \) and whose other rows are the vector components.
The result of a cross product is a vector perpendicular to both original vectors, shown in the diagram as the green (a × b) and orange (b × a) arrows pointing in opposite directions.

For the worked example \( \mathbf{a}=(3,2,1) \) and \( \mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1) \), the result \( \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = (1,-2,1) \) is the negative of \( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = (-1,2,-1) \).
defs: Cross product
A vector operation on two vectors in three dimensions producing a third vector perpendicular to both, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span.
Anticommutativity
Property of the cross product that reversing the order of the operands changes the sign of the result: \( \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \).
eqs: \( \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \) = input vectors (dimensionless components); \( \hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k} \) = unit vectors along x, y, z
tips: Keep the row order of the determinant consistent with the operand order; swapping rows flips the sign of the answer.
Do not confuse the cross product (a vector) with the dot product (a scalar) when computing components.
rq: Why does swapping a and b flip the sign of the cross product rather than leaving it unchanged?
The determinant has rows a and b; swapping two rows of a determinant changes its sign, so \( \mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a} = -(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}) \).
What would happen to the cross product if b were parallel to a?
The cross product would be the zero vector, since parallel vectors span no area.

xq.q: Two edge vectors of a triangular bracket are \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,0)\) m and \(\mathbf{b}=(0,2,1)\) m. Use the determinant method to find \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), and hence the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\).
xq.a: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(2,-1,2)\) m², so the area is 3 m²

xq.q: For \(\mathbf{a}=(3,2,1)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,-1)\) it is found that \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(-1,2,-1)\). What is the \(\mathbf{j}\)-component of \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\)?
xq.w: Swapping the order reverses the sign, so \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=(1,-2,1)\); the trap is quoting the \(\mathbf{j}\)-component of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) without reversing the sign.

xq.q: Let \(\mathbf{a}=(1,-1,2)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(3,0,1)\). Evaluate \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}\) using determinants, and show that \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\).
xq.a: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(-1,5,3)\) and \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=(1,-5,-3)\), which is the negative of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\).
s: Each component is the negative of the corresponding component of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), so anticommutativity is confirmed (swapping the rows of the determinant flips the sign).

units.name: 9.5 Cross product and unit normal to a plane
units.ov: This material introduces the cross product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) as a vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), with magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) equal to the area of the parallelogram they span. It is computed with a 3×3 determinant and normalised to give the unit normal to the plane containing the two vectors. The geometric definition (magnitude, right-hand rule), the component calculation and the normalisation step all feed into one routine: find two in-plane vectors, cross them, then divide by the magnitude.
must: Definition: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), direction by the right-hand rule
Unit normal: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|}\); always normalise, since the raw cross product is not unit length
Determinant form: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\a_x&a_y&a_z\\b_x&b_y&b_z\end{vmatrix}\) with unit vectors in the first row
The j component carries a minus sign in the expansion: \(-(a_xb_z-a_zb_x)\hat j\), the most common slip
Anticommutativity: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\), so swapping the order reverses the normal
Magnitude \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta\) equals the parallelogram area; the triangle area is half of this
The cross product is zero when the vectors are parallel (\(\sin\theta=0\)), so they define no plane
Simplify by factoring out a common scalar from the cross product before normalising, to keep the arithmetic clean
Plane normals: take two in-plane vectors, e.g. differences of points \(\mathbf{AB}\) and \(\mathbf{AC}\), and cross them
Check the answer: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{a}=0\), \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\) and \(|\hat{\mathbf{n}}|=1\)
conn: Cross product and area: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) gives the parallelogram or triangle area, and the same vector gives the normal direction, so one calculation answers both
Dot product check: a correct normal has zero dot product with both in-plane vectors, which verifies the determinant arithmetic
Points to plane: build \(\mathbf{AB}\) and \(\mathbf{AC}\) from coordinates, find \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), then use it for the equation of the plane or for resolving forces normal to a surface
Mechanics: moment \(\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) uses the same determinant, and the right-hand rule and order dependence set the direction of the moment
exq: Given \(\mathbf{a}=2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k\) and \(\mathbf{b}=\hat i+4\hat j-2\hat k\), compute \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) by determinant and find the unit normal to the plane containing them.
Points A(1,0,2), B(3,1,1) and C(2,4,0) lie in a plane. Find \(\mathbf{AB}\times\mathbf{AC}\), the unit normal and the area of triangle ABC.
Vectors of magnitude 5 m and 3 m are at 30° to each other. Find \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|\) and the parallelogram area, and state how the normal changes if the order is reversed.
Show that \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{a}\) for general components, then verify it numerically for a chosen pair of vectors.
A force \(\mathbf{F}=(10,-5,2)\) N acts at position \(\mathbf{r}=(1,2,3)\) m. Compute \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) and its magnitude, and give the unit vector along the moment axis.

notes.t: Cross product and unit normal to a plane
pts: The cross product a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, so it defines the normal direction of the plane they span.
The unit normal is obtained by dividing the cross product by its magnitude.
The cross product is evaluated as a 3×3 determinant using the unit vectors i, j, k in the first row.
The cross product is anticommutative: swapping a and b reverses the direction of the normal.
defs: Cross product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector with magnitude |a||b| sin θ, direction perpendicular to both a and b following the right-hand rule.
Unit normal vector
A vector of length 1 perpendicular to a plane, obtained as n̂ = (a × b)/|a × b|.
eqs: a, b = vectors (m or N as applicable); θ = angle between a and b (rad); n̂ = unit normal vector (dimensionless)
\(a_{x}\), \(a_{y}\), \(a_{z}\) = components of a; \(b_{x}\), \(b_{y}\), \(b_{z}\) = components of b (same units as a, b)
n̂ = unit normal (dimensionless); a × b = cross product vector
tips: Watch the sign of the j component: the j term in the determinant expansion carries a minus sign.
A cross product vector is not automatically unit length; always normalise before giving n̂.
rq: Why does dividing a × b by its magnitude give a unit normal, and what would go wrong if you skipped this step?
Dividing by the magnitude scales the vector to length 1 while keeping its direction; skipping it gives a normal of the wrong length, so it is not a unit vector.
For a = (2,0,1) and b = (2,2,1), what is a × b and why does it lie perpendicular to both?
a × b = −2i + 4k; the dot product with a and with b is zero, so it is perpendicular to both.

notes.t: Cross product and unit normal to a plane
pts: The cross product a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, so it gives a normal direction to the plane they span.
Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by a and b, since it scales with sin θ.
Normalise the cross product by dividing by its magnitude to obtain a unit normal vector.
Compute the components of a × b as a determinant of the unit vectors and the components of a and b.
Simplify the unit normal by factoring out the scalar, leaving a clean direction vector.
defs: Cross product
For vectors a and b, a × b is a vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude |a||b|sin θ and direction given by the right-hand rule.
Unit normal vector
A vector of length 1 perpendicular to a plane, found as the cross product of two in-plane vectors divided by its magnitude.
eqs: Magnitude of the cross product (area of parallelogram)
a, b = vectors (dimensionless or same units as the vectors); θ = angle between a and b (rad or °)
Unit normal to the plane of a and b
n̂ = unit normal vector (dimensionless); a × b = cross product vector
tips: Forgetting to divide by |a × b| leaves a vector that is perpendicular but not of unit length.
Check the sign of components carefully when expanding the determinant, since a × b reverses sign if the order of a and b is swapped.
rq: Why must the unit normal be divided by |a × b| rather than just taking a × b directly?
Because a unit vector must have length 1; dividing by the magnitude removes the length while keeping the perpendicular direction.
What happens to a × b if a and b are parallel?
sin θ = 0, so a × b is the zero vector and no unique plane or unit normal exists.

xq.q: A triangular plate has two edge vectors from one corner, \(\mathbf{a}=(1,1,0)\) m and \(\mathbf{b}=(0,1,2)\) m. Find \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) and hence the area of the triangular plate.
xq.a: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(2,-2,1)\) m², so the area is 1.5 m²
s: Triangle area is half of this: 1.5 m².

xq.q: Two vectors in a plane give \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(4,0,-3)\). What is the unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|}\) for this order of vectors?
xq.w: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{16+9}=5\), so divide each component by 5; the traps are not normalising, reversing the sign (swapped order), and a sign slip on the k-component.

xq.q: A flat panel contains the vectors \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,0)\) m and \(\mathbf{b}=(0,3,4)\) m. Find the unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) to the panel in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\), and explain what happens to the normal if the order of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is reversed. State also the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\).
xq.a: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(0,-8,6)\) m², magnitude 10 m², so \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}=(0,-0.8,0.6)\). Reversing the order gives \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\), so the normal points the opposite way, \((0,0.8,-0.6)\). The parallelogram area is 10 m².
s: \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{64+36}=10\) m², which is the parallelogram area.
Reversing the order flips the sign (anticommutativity), so \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) reverses direction.

units.name: 10.1 Cross product recap and navigation
units.ov: This material recaps the three-dimensional cross product: the component formula, the geometric meaning (a vector perpendicular to both inputs, with magnitude equal to the parallelogram area), and the sign rule when the order is reversed. It then uses the resulting vector in a navigation-style problem, where its components are summed to give a scalar key R. The notes are brief and do not define R or give the navigation context, so check the full module notes for those.
must: Component formula: \(\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q}=(d_2q_3-d_3q_2,\; d_3q_1-d_1q_3,\; d_1q_2-d_2q_1)\)
\(\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q}\) is a vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{d}\) and \(\mathbf{q}\)
Magnitude \(|\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q}|=|\mathbf{d}||\mathbf{q}|\sin\theta\), which equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors
Order matters: \(\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{d}=-(\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q})\), so reversing the order flips every sign
The cross product is zero when the vectors are parallel (\(\sin\theta=0\))
Scalar key: sum the components of \(\mathbf{n}\), \(R=n_1+n_2+n_3\), keeping their signs
Check the result: \(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}=0\) and \(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{q}=0\)
The middle component has the pattern \(d_3q_1-d_1q_3\), which is the reverse of the cyclic order. This is the usual place to slip.
The direction follows the right-hand rule.
conn: Cross product and dot product: the dot product gives a zero-check for perpendicularity, and the cross product gives the perpendicular vector itself.
Cross product and geometry: \(|\mathbf{n}|\) gives parallelogram area, half of it gives triangle area, and the unit normal \(\mathbf{n}/|\mathbf{n}|\) gives a plane's normal direction.
Cross product and mechanics: moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) uses the same formula, and the order and sign convention determine the moment direction.
Vector result to scalar key: errors in the signs of components pass straight into R, so sign care in the cross product decides the final answer.
exq: Given \(\mathbf{d}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(1,4,-2)\), compute \(\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q}\), verify that it is perpendicular to both vectors, and find \(R=n_1+n_2+n_3\).
For the same vectors, compute \(\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{d}\) and state how R changes. Explain why.
Find the area of the parallelogram and of the triangle spanned by \(\mathbf{d}=(1,0,2)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(3,1,1)\). Then give a unit vector normal to their plane.
Show that \(\mathbf{d}=(2,4,6)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(1,2,3)\) are parallel using the cross product. What does this say about the parallelogram area?
A force \(\mathbf{F}=(0,5,2)\) N acts at position \(\mathbf{r}=(1,2,0)\) m. Calculate the moment \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\) and its magnitude.

notes.t: Vectors: cross product and navigation key
pts: The cross product of two vectors gives a new vector perpendicular to both.
Components of the cross product are found from the determinant-style formula using the components of d and q.
The result of the cross product is a vector, so its components can be summed to give a scalar key.
defs: Cross product
For vectors d and q in three dimensions, d × q is a vector perpendicular to both d and q, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram they span.
eqs: d, q = input vectors (dimensionless here); n = resultant vector; \(n_{1}\), \(n_{2}\), \(n_{3}\) = components of n
tips: Keep the order of vectors in the cross product; reversing them changes the sign of the answer.
Check that the components are summed with their signs preserved when computing R.
rq: Why must the cross product be computed in component order rather than swapping d and q?
Because the cross product is anticommutative: q × d = −(d × q), so swapping the order flips the sign of every component and changes R.

xq.q: Two vectors are \(\mathbf{d}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(1,4,-2)\). The vector \(\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{d}\times\mathbf{q}\) has components \((n_1,n_2,n_3)\). A navigation key is defined as \(R=n_1+n_2+n_3\). Calculate R, keeping the signs of the components.
xq.a: R = 6 (dimensionless)

xq.q: For \(\mathbf{d}=(1,2,0)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(3,1,0)\), what is \(\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{d}\)?
xq.w: Only the third component is non-zero: for d×q it is 1·1 − 2·3 = −5, and reversing the order flips the sign to +5; the traps are keeping the d×q order, adding the products instead of subtracting, and putting the result in the wrong component.

xq.q: For \(\mathbf{d}=(2,-1,3)\) and \(\mathbf{q}=(1,4,-2)\), the cross product is \(\mathbf{n}=(-10,7,9)\). Show that \(\mathbf{n}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{d}\) and \(\mathbf{q}\), and find the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{d}\) and \(\mathbf{q}\).
xq.a: n·d = -20 - 7 + 27 = 0 and n·q = -10 + 28 - 18 = 0, so n is perpendicular to both. The area equals |n| = √(100+49+81) = √230 ≈ 15.2.
s: Area = |n| because the magnitude of d×q is the parallelogram area

units.name: 10.2 Scalar triple product as parallelepiped volume
units.ov: This material introduces the scalar triple product \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}\) as the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by three vectors, and contrasts it with the triple vector product. The cross product supplies the base area vector, the dot product with \(\boldsymbol{c}\) supplies the height, and so the result is a scalar. Cyclic invariance, the dot/cross interchange and the zero (coplanar) condition follow directly from this geometric picture.
must: Scalar triple product \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}\) is a scalar; its magnitude is the volume of the parallelepiped with edges \(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}\) (units m³ if the vectors are in m).

Geometric derivation: \(|\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b}|=|\boldsymbol{a}||\boldsymbol{b}|\sin\theta\) = area of parallelogram OACB, direction along the unit normal \(\boldsymbol{k}\); dotting with \(\boldsymbol{c}\) gives area \(\times|\boldsymbol{c}|\cos\phi\) = area \(\times\, h\).

Volume = \(|(\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}|\); the sign is positive for a right-handed set \(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}\) and negative for a left-handed set, so take the absolute value when asked for a volume.

Cyclic invariance and dot/cross interchange: \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{a}\cdot(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})=\boldsymbol{b}\cdot(\boldsymbol{c}\times\boldsymbol{a})=\boldsymbol{c}\cdot(\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\).
A non-cyclic reordering (swapping two vectors) changes the sign of the triple product but not its magnitude.
Zero condition: \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}=0\) if and only if the vectors are coplanar, which includes two being parallel or one being zero.
A zero triple product does not mean all the vectors are zero. Use it as the coplanarity test.

\((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{a}=0\) and \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{b}=0\), because \(\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b}\) is perpendicular to both \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

Triple vector product \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\times\boldsymbol{c}\) is a vector lying in the plane of \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\); it is not associative, so \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\times\boldsymbol{c}\neq\boldsymbol{a}\times(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})\) in general, and the brackets must be kept.
Always state the result type: the scalar triple product is a scalar (volume), the triple vector product is a vector. Evaluate the cross product first and the dot product last.
conn: Cross product (area vector, magnitude \(|\boldsymbol{a}||\boldsymbol{b}|\sin\theta\)) combined with dot product (projection \(|\boldsymbol{c}|\cos\phi\)) gives the volume. Questions often ask you to compute each step.
Coplanarity test: a zero triple product links to linear dependence, to parallel vectors, and to whether a point lies in a given plane.

Determinant evaluation: the triple product in components equals a 3×3 determinant of the rows \(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b},\boldsymbol{c}\), and row swaps explain the sign change and cyclic invariance.
Triple scalar and triple vector products appear together in mechanics, e.g. moments about an axis \(\boldsymbol{\hat n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}\times\boldsymbol{F})\) versus vector moments.
exq: Given \(\boldsymbol{a}=2\boldsymbol{i}+\boldsymbol{j}\), \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{j}+3\boldsymbol{k}\), \(\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{i}+\boldsymbol{j}+\boldsymbol{k}\) (m), compute \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}\) and state the volume of the parallelepiped, with units and the handedness of the set.

Show that \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{a}\cdot(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})\) using the parallelepiped volume argument, and state what happens to the sign if \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) are swapped.
Find the value of \(\lambda\) for which \(\boldsymbol{a}=(1,2,3)\), \(\boldsymbol{b}=(0,1,\lambda)\), \(\boldsymbol{c}=(2,1,1)\) are coplanar, and justify the method.

Explain why \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{a}=0\) for any \(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\). Then show with a numerical example that \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\times\boldsymbol{c}\neq\boldsymbol{a}\times(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})\).

A parallelepiped has base edges \(|\boldsymbol{a}|=3\) m, \(|\boldsymbol{b}|=4\) m at 30° to each other, and a third edge \(|\boldsymbol{c}|=5\) m at 40° to the base normal. Find the base area, the height and the volume.

notes.t: Triple products
pts: The triple scalar product gives a scalar value, the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors.
The triple vector product gives a vector and is generally not associative, so brackets must be placed carefully.
defs: Triple scalar product
The scalar obtained by taking the cross product of two vectors and dotting the result with a third vector; its magnitude equals the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors.
Triple vector product
The vector obtained by crossing the cross product of two vectors with a third vector; the result lies in the plane of the first two vectors.
eqs: Triple scalar product (scalar volume of parallelepiped)
tips: The triple vector product is not associative: \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\times\boldsymbol{c} \neq \boldsymbol{a}\times(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})\) in general, so always keep the brackets.
Do not confuse the triple scalar product (a scalar) with the triple vector product (a vector) when stating units or result type.
rq: Why does the triple scalar product give zero when the three vectors are coplanar?
Because the parallelepiped they span has zero volume, so the cross product \(\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b}\) is perpendicular to \(\boldsymbol{c}\), making the dot product zero.
Why must brackets be used in the triple vector product?
Because the cross product is not associative, so \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\times\boldsymbol{c}\) generally differs from \(\boldsymbol{a}\times(\boldsymbol{b}\times\boldsymbol{c})\).

notes.t: Triple scalar product as volume of a parallelepiped
pts: The cross product a × b is a vector whose magnitude equals the area of parallelogram OACB and whose direction is k.
Dotting that area vector with c gives the height projection, so the triple scalar product equals the volume of the parallelepiped.
Because the result is a volume, the triple scalar product is a single number (scalar), and it is zero when a, b, c are coplanar.
defs: Triple scalar product
The scalar (a × b)·c, equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c.
Parallelepiped
A three-dimensional solid whose six faces are parallelograms, spanned by three edge vectors from a common vertex.
eqs: \(|\boldsymbol{a}|\), \(|\boldsymbol{b}|\) = vector magnitudes (m); \(\theta\) = angle between a and b (rad); \(\boldsymbol{k}\) = unit normal vector (dimensionless)
\(h\) = height of the parallelepiped (m); \(\phi\) = angle between k and c (rad); area in m²
tips: Do not confuse the scalar triple product with a vector result: \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}\) gives a scalar with units of volume (m³), not a vector.
The volume is the absolute value of the triple product; the sign depends on whether a, b, c form a right-handed set.
rq: Why does the triple scalar product become zero when a, b and c lie in one plane?
Coplanar vectors span no volume, so the height \(h\) is zero and \((\boldsymbol{a}\times\boldsymbol{b})\cdot\boldsymbol{c}=0\).
What does the cos φ factor represent geometrically in the derivation?
It projects c onto the normal k, so \(|\boldsymbol{c}|\cos\phi\) is the perpendicular height h of the parallelepiped above the base OACB.

notes.t: Triple scalar product: interchanging dot and cross
pts: In a triple scalar product the dot and cross can be interchanged, since both measure the same parallelepiped volume.
Keeping the same cyclic order of a, b, c gives three equal forms of the triple product.
The triple product equals the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b, c.
defs: Triple scalar product
The scalar \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) \), whose magnitude is the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors.
eqs: Interchange of dot and cross and cyclic invariance of the triple product
\( \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \) = vectors (dimensionless or their physical units); result is a scalar volume (\(m^{3}\) if vectors are in m)
tips: Only the cyclic order (a,b,c)→(b,c,a)→(c,a,b) preserves the sign; reordering non-cyclically changes the sign.
The triple product gives a volume only in magnitude; take the absolute value when a volume is asked for.
rq: Why does swapping the dot and cross leave the value unchanged?
Both \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c} \) and \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) \) equal the same signed parallelepiped volume spanned by a, b, c.
What happens to the triple product if you reverse the cyclic order, e.g. \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{b}) \)?
The sign flips, since swapping two vectors reverses the cross product; the magnitude (volume) is unchanged.

notes.t: Scalar triple product: zero conditions
pts: If two of the vectors are parallel, the parallelepiped collapses to a plane, so the scalar triple product is zero.

Consequently the triple product vanishes whenever \( \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} \) is perpendicular to the third vector, which holds in particular for \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0 \) and \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \).
If the three vectors are coplanar, the triple product is zero by the same volume argument.
Conversely, a zero triple product implies that one vector is zero, two vectors are parallel, or the three vectors are coplanar.
eqs: Triple product zero when vectors are parallel or coplanar
\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} = vectors (dimensionless or consistent units); \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c} \) = scalar triple product
Vector perpendicular to its own cross product
tips: Do not conclude that a triple product of zero requires all vectors to be zero; it only requires parallel, coplanar, or a zero vector.
Remember the triple product is a scalar, so \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c} \) must be evaluated with the dot product last, not the cross product of a scalar.
rq: Why does a zero triple product imply the three vectors are coplanar or that two are parallel?
Because the triple product equals the volume of the parallelepiped they span; zero volume means the parallelepiped is flat, i.e. the vectors lie in one plane or two are parallel.
Why is \( (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{a}=0 \) true even when a and b are not parallel?
The cross product \( \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} \) is perpendicular to both a and b, so its dot product with a (or b) is zero.

xq.q: A parallelepiped has edges from one vertex given by \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,1)\) m, \(\mathbf{b}=(1,3,0)\) m and \(\mathbf{c}=(0,1,4)\) m. Find its volume.
xq.a: 25 m³

xq.q: Three vectors satisfy \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}=8\) m³. What is \((\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{a}\)?
xq.a: -8 m³
o: 8 m³
0 m³
-8 m³
16 m³
xq.w: (c×b)·a = a·(c×b) = −a·(b×c) = −8, because swapping b and c is a non-cyclic reordering that flips the sign; the trap is assuming any reordering of the same three vectors keeps the value.

xq.q: The vectors \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\) are related by \(\mathbf{c}=2\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\). Show that \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}=0\) and explain the result geometrically.
xq.a: (a×b)·c = 2(a×b)·a − (a×b)·b. Since a×b is perpendicular to both a and b, both dot products are zero, so the triple product is 0. Geometrically, c lies in the plane of a and b, so the parallelepiped has zero height and zero volume (the vectors are coplanar).
s: Substitute c = 2a − b and expand the dot product
a×b is perpendicular to a and to b, so (a×b)·a = 0 and (a×b)·b = 0
c lies in the plane of a and b, so the parallelepiped is flat with zero volume

units.name: 10.3 Scalar triple product as a determinant
units.ov: The scalar triple product \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) combines the cross and dot products into a single number. It equals the 3×3 determinant whose rows are the components of \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\). Its magnitude is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors, and it is zero exactly when the vectors are coplanar. The determinant form, the cyclic and sign properties, and the coplanarity test are all consequences of this one definition.
must: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\begin{vmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{vmatrix}\), with rows in the order a, b, c
Coplanarity test: three vectors are coplanar \(\iff\) \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}=0\) (determinant = 0)
Geometric meaning: \(|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})|\) is the volume of the parallelepiped; the sign gives the handedness (signed volume)
Cyclic invariance: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\)
Swapping any two vectors (a non-cyclic reordering, i.e. swapping two rows) flips the sign, e.g. \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})=-\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\)
The dot and cross can be swapped: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}\)
Cross product as a determinant: \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\mathbf{i}-(a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\mathbf{j}+(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\mathbf{k}\), with cofactor signs \(+,-,+\)
Expanded six-term form: \(a_1b_2c_3-a_1b_3c_2-a_2b_1c_3+a_2b_3c_1+a_3b_1c_2-a_3b_2c_1\)
Method for unknown parameter \(\lambda\): set the determinant to zero and solve the resulting linear equation, taking care over signs

The scalar triple product is a number; the vector triple product \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) is a vector, so don't confuse them. Also, \(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}\) is a scalar, so \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c})\) is meaningless.
conn: Determinant properties link to the triple product: swapping two rows flips the sign, and two equal or proportional rows give zero (so a repeated vector gives a triple product of 0).

Coplanarity links to linear dependence: if \(\mathbf{c}=\alpha\mathbf{a}+\beta\mathbf{b}\), the determinant is zero, so questions on a point lying in a plane or on three vectors being independent reduce to the same test.

Volume of a parallelepiped is \(|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})|\), and a tetrahedron has volume one sixth of that. This can be combined with the base area \(|\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}|\) to find a height.
Cross product geometry links to the triple product: \(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}\) is normal to the plane of b and c, so dotting with a measures how far a lies out of that plane.
exq: Find the value of \(\lambda\) for which \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(2,-1,\lambda)\), \(\mathbf{c}=(0,1,4)\) are coplanar. Show the determinant expansion and state what \(\lambda\) means geometrically.

Calculate \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) for \(\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\), \(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\), \(\mathbf{c}=-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\). Hence state the volume of the parallelepiped and the value of \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})\).
Prove from the six-term expansion that \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a})\). Explain why swapping two vectors changes the sign.
Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices O(0,0,0), A(1,0,2), B(3,1,0), C(0,2,1) using a triple product.

Explain the difference between \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) and \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\). Compute both for simple vectors, and say which can be written as a single determinant.

notes.t: Scalar triple product in Cartesian form
pts: The scalar triple product equals the determinant of the matrix whose rows are the three vectors.
The scalar triple product is cyclic: swapping the cyclic order of the three vectors leaves its value unchanged.
The cross product a × b is itself computed as a 3×3 determinant using the unit vectors i, j, k in the first row.
defs: Scalar triple product
The scalar a · (b × c), whose magnitude is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b and c.
eqs: Scalar triple product as a determinant
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}
\(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = Cartesian components of \(\mathbf{a}\) (dimensionless or units of \(\mathbf{a}\)); \(b_i\), \(c_i\) = components of \(\mathbf{b}\), \(\mathbf{c}\)
Expanded form of the scalar triple product
\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\), \(c_{i}\) = Cartesian components of the vectors (units of the vectors multiplied together)
Cross product a × b in Cartesian form
\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = Cartesian components of \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\); \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) = unit basis vectors
tips: Watch the order of vectors: swapping any two changes the sign of the triple product, so \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) and \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})\) differ by a minus sign.

Do not confuse the scalar triple product (a number) with the vector triple product \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\); the cross product in row one of the determinant must be expanded with the \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) signs \(+,-,+\).
rq: Why does swapping the two rows of the determinant change the sign of the triple product, and what does this imply about \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) versus \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c})\)?
A row swap changes the sign of a determinant, so \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c}) = -\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\); the order of the vectors matters for sign.
How can the triple product be used to test whether three vectors are coplanar?
If \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = 0\), the three vectors lie in one plane (the parallelepiped has zero volume).

notes.t: Scalar triple product as a 3×3 determinant
pts: The scalar triple product a·(b×c) is invariant under cyclic permutation of a, b, c.
Expanding the cross product gives the components of a×b, which are then dotted with c.
The scalar triple product equals the determinant of the matrix whose rows are the vectors a, b, c.
Expanding the determinant along the first row reproduces the same six-term expression as the dot-product route.
defs: Scalar triple product
The scalar a·(b×c), the dot product of a with the cross product of b and c; its magnitude is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b, c.
eqs: Scalar triple product as a determinant
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}
\(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\), \(c_{i}\) = components of vectors a, b, c (dimensionless if vectors are dimensionless; otherwise product of their units)
Cyclic invariance of the triple product
tips: Keep the row order a, b, c consistent; swapping rows flips the sign of the result.
Do not confuse the scalar triple product with the vector triple product a×(b×c), which is a vector.
rq: Why does swapping two rows of the determinant change only the sign of the triple product?
Swapping two rows of a determinant changes its sign, so the triple product changes sign; equivalently a·(b×c) = −b·(a×c).
Why can the triple product be zero even when all three vectors are non-zero?
If a, b, c are coplanar (linearly dependent), the determinant has dependent rows and equals zero, so the parallelepiped has zero volume.

notes.t: Coplanar vectors via scalar triple product
pts: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product is zero.
Compute the cross product of two vectors first, then dot it with the third vector.
Setting the triple product to zero gives a linear equation in the unknown parameter λ.
defs: Scalar triple product
The dot product of one vector with the cross product of two others, (a × b)·c; it equals the signed volume of the parallelepiped they span.
eqs: Condition for three vectors to be coplanar
a, b, c = the three vectors (dimensionless components here); × = cross product; · = dot product
tips: Watch the signs in the cross-product determinant; a single sign error changes the value of λ.
Make sure to use the cross product result (a × b) before dotting with c, not a × (b · c).
rq: Why does a zero scalar triple product imply the three vectors are coplanar?
The triple product equals the volume of the parallelepiped they span; zero volume means they lie in one plane, so the parallelepiped is flat.
