The vector from the origin O to a point; a is the position vector of a fixed point A in the plane and r that of a generic point P.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane (point–normal form)
\mathbf{r} = position vector of generic point P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of known point A in the plane (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector (dimensionless direction)
\mathbf{r} = position vector of P (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector; p = constant \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} (m)
tips: Do not confuse the normal vector n with a direction vector lying in the plane; n must be perpendicular to every in-plane direction.
Watch that p in r·n = p equals a·n as a scalar, so it depends on the chosen n; scaling n also scales p.
rq: Why does the dot product (r − a)·n = 0 describe every point of the plane rather than just one point?
Because any point P in the plane gives a vector AP lying in the plane, which is perpendicular to n, so its dot product with n is zero; points off the plane give a nonzero dot product.
What happens to the plane if you multiply n by 2 without changing a?
The equation (r − a)·2n = 0 is equivalent to (r − a)·n = 0, so the same plane is described; only the length of the normal changes, not its direction.

notes.t: Vector Equation of a Plane
pts: A plane is fixed by a point A on it and a normal vector n perpendicular to the plane.
Any point P lies on the plane exactly when the vector AP is perpendicular to n, giving r·n = a·n.
If n is a unit vector, p is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
Writing n = (α, β, γ) turns the vector form into the Cartesian equation αx + βy + γz = p.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A non-zero vector perpendicular to every vector lying in the plane.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane (scalar product form)

\mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of a known point A on the plane (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector to the plane (dimensionless direction if unit); p = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} (m when n is a unit vector)
\alpha, \beta, \gamma = components of the normal \mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma); x, y, z = coordinates of P (m); p = constant (m when n is a unit vector)
tips: Only when \( \mathbf{n} \) is a unit vector does \( p \) equal the perpendicular distance from the origin; otherwise divide by \( |\mathbf{n}| \).
Use the normal components \( (\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \) directly as coefficients of x, y, z in the Cartesian form.
rq: Why does the dot product r·n equal a constant for every point on the plane?
Because AP = r − a lies in the plane and is perpendicular to n, so (r − a)·n = 0, meaning r·n = a·n is fixed.
What if n is not a unit vector: does p still give the distance from the origin?
No; p = a·n then equals the distance times |n|, so the distance is p/|n|.

xq.q: A plane passes through the point A with position vector \(\mathbf a=(2,1,3)\) m and has normal vector \(\mathbf n=(2,-1,2)\). Find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
xq.a: 3 m

xq.q: A plane has Cartesian equation \(3x-4y+12z=26\), with x, y, z in metres. What is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane?
xq.a: 2 m
o: 2 m
xq.w: n = (3,−4,12) is not a unit vector (|n| = 13), so the distance is p/|n| = 26/13 = 2 m; quoting p gives 26 m, inverting gives 0.5 m, and dividing by |n|² gives 0.15 m.

xq.q: A plane contains the point A(1,2,−1) and has normal vector \(\mathbf n=(3,-2,4)\). Starting from the condition that \(\overrightarrow{AP}\) is perpendicular to n for any point P(x,y,z) on the plane, derive the Cartesian equation of the plane and show that P(1,4,0) lies on it.
xq.a: P is on the plane when (r − a)·n = 0, i.e. r·n = a·n. Here a·n = 3 − 4 − 4 = −5, so the plane is 3x − 2y + 4z = −5. For P(1,4,0): 3 − 8 + 0 = −5, so P satisfies the equation. Equivalently AP = (0,2,1) and AP·n = 0 − 4 + 4 = 0, so AP is perpendicular to n.
s: Substituting P(1,4,0): 3 − 8 + 0 = −5, so P is on the plane

units.name: 12.1 Vector equation of a plane (point and normal)
units.ov: A plane in 3D is fixed by one point A on it and a normal vector n. Requiring that AP is perpendicular to n gives the point-normal form (r−a)·n = 0. This rearranges to the scalar form r·n = p and then to the Cartesian form αx+βy+γz = p, where p links to the distance from the origin when n is a unit vector.
must: Point–normal form: \( (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{n}=0 \), meaning AP is perpendicular to n for every point P on the plane
Scalar form: \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p \), where p is a constant found by substituting the known point
Cartesian form: with \( \mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \), the plane is \( \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p \), so the coefficients of x, y, z are the components of n
The normal vector n is nonzero and perpendicular to every direction in the plane; it fixes the plane's orientation
Perpendicular distance from the origin is p only if n is a unit vector; in general it is \( |p|/|\mathbf{n}| \)
p depends on the chosen n: scaling n by k scales p by k, but the plane stays the same
Do not confuse n with an in-plane direction vector; n·d = 0 for any direction d lying in the plane
Position vectors r = OP and a = OA are measured from the origin; the units of r, a and p are metres
Method: pick n, pick a known point A, compute p = a·n, then write the plane equation in vector or Cartesian form
conn: Dot product and perpendicularity: the plane equation is just the condition a·b = 0, so any test of 'is this point on the plane' reduces to substituting into r·n = p
Normalising n links the plane equation to distance calculations: dividing by |n| gives the distance from the origin, and the same idea extends to the distance from a point to the plane
Cartesian and vector forms are interchangeable: read n from the coefficients, or convert back to find a point and a normal
Normals and cross products: if the plane is given by three points or two in-plane directions, find n by a cross product, then use point–normal form
exq: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the plane through A(1, 2, −1) with normal n = (2, −3, 4). State p and check that the point (3, 1, 1) lies on it or not.
The plane 3x − 4y + 12z = 26 is given. Write down a normal vector, convert to a unit normal, and find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
Show that scaling n = (1, 2, 2) to 3n changes p but not the plane, for the plane through (2, 0, 1). Give both equations of the plane.
A plane has the equation r·(1, −1, 2) = 5. Find three points on it, and show that the vector between any two of them is perpendicular to n.
Find the plane through the point (0, 1, 2) that is perpendicular to the vector from the origin to (2, −1, 2), and give the distance of the plane from the origin.

notes.t: Vector equation of a plane
pts: A point P belongs to the plane if the vector from a known point A in the plane to P is perpendicular to the normal vector n.
Using the position vector r of P and a of A, the condition becomes a dot-product equation; the normal vector n fixes the orientation of the plane.
Perpendicularity is expressed by a zero dot product, which gives the plane's vector equation.
Rearranging gives the compact form where p is the constant a·n, the perpendicular distance term for the plane.
defs: Normal vector n
A nonzero vector perpendicular to every direction lying within the plane; it defines the plane's orientation.
Position vector
The vector from the origin O to a point; a is the position vector of a fixed point A in the plane and r that of a generic point P.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane (point–normal form)
\mathbf{r} = position vector of generic point P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of known point A in the plane (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector (dimensionless direction)
\mathbf{r} = position vector of P (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector; p = constant \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} (m)
tips: Do not confuse the normal vector n with a direction vector lying in the plane; n must be perpendicular to every in-plane direction.
Watch that p in r·n = p equals a·n as a scalar, so it depends on the chosen n; scaling n also scales p.
rq: Why does the dot product (r − a)·n = 0 describe every point of the plane rather than just one point?
Because any point P in the plane gives a vector AP lying in the plane, which is perpendicular to n, so its dot product with n is zero; points off the plane give a nonzero dot product.
What happens to the plane if you multiply n by 2 without changing a?
The equation (r − a)·2n = 0 is equivalent to (r − a)·n = 0, so the same plane is described; only the length of the normal changes, not its direction.

notes.t: Vector Equation of a Plane
pts: A plane is fixed by a point A on it and a normal vector n perpendicular to it; any point P on the plane has AP perpendicular to n.
Using position vectors from the origin O, the plane condition is that the dot product of the position vector r with n equals the dot product of a with n.
If n is a unit vector, the constant p gives the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
Writing n = (α, β, γ) turns the vector equation into the Cartesian form αx + βy + γz = p.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A nonzero vector perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane; it fixes the orientation of the plane.
Position vector r
The vector from the origin O to a general point P on the plane, so that r = OP.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane (normal form using a point)
r = position vector of a general point on the plane (m); n = normal vector (dimensionless direction, or with magnitude as given); a = position vector of a fixed point A on the plane (m)
Vector equation of a plane with scalar constant
r = position vector (m); n = normal vector; p = scalar constant (m when n is a unit vector)
\(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) = components of n (dimensionless); \(x,y,z\) = coordinates of a point on the plane (m); p = scalar constant (m)
tips: Only read p as the distance from the origin when n is a unit vector; otherwise divide by |n|.
Keep consistent units: a, r and p are lengths (m), while n is a direction whose magnitude must be stated.
rq: Why does the condition r · n = a · n describe every point on the plane rather than just one point?
Because AP = r − a lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to n; (r − a)·n = 0 holds for every point P in the plane.
What happens to p if n is not a unit vector?
p is no longer the perpendicular distance from the origin; the distance is p divided by the magnitude of n.

xq.q: A flat roof panel is modelled as a plane passing through the point \(A\) with position vector \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)\) m. The vector \(\mathbf{n}=(2,-1,2)\) is normal to the panel. Write the plane in the form \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p\), where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the position vector of a general point on the plane, and hence find the perpendicular distance from the origin \(O\) to the plane.
xq.a: p = 6, |n| = 3, so the distance is 6/3 = 2 m
s: n is not a unit vector, so distance = p/|n| = 6/3 = 2 m

xq.q: A plane passes through the point with position vector \(\mathbf{a}=(3,-1,2)\) m and has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(1,2,-2)\). Which is its Cartesian equation?
xq.w: p = a·n = 3 − 2 − 4 = −3; the traps are a sign slip in the dot product (3 or 5) or using a as the normal (14).
s: Components of n are the coefficients: x + 2y − 2z = −3

xq.q: A plane has equation \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=14\) with \(\mathbf{n}=(2,3,6)\), where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the position vector of a general point (in m). Show that the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane is 2 m, and explain why replacing \(\mathbf{n}\) by \(2\mathbf{n}\) does not change this distance.
xq.a: |n| = √(4+9+36) = 7, so the unit normal is n̂ = (2,3,6)/7. Dividing r·n = 14 by 7 gives r·n̂ = 2, so p = 2 with a unit normal and the distance is 2 m. With 2n, the equation becomes r·(2n) = 28 and |2n| = 14, so the distance is 28/14 = 2 m. Scaling n scales p by the same factor, so p/|n| is unchanged.
s: Divide the equation by 7: r·n̂ = 2, so the distance is 2 m (p is the distance only for a unit normal)
With 2n: p = 28 and |2n| = 14, so the distance is 28/14 = 2 m
Scaling n scales p equally, so the ratio p/|n| is unchanged

units.name: 12.2 Plane through three points using cross product
units.ov: This module shows how to find the equation of a plane through three non-collinear points. Form two in-plane vectors by subtracting position vectors, take their cross product (via a 3×3 determinant) to get a normal, then use (r − a)·n = 0 to get the Cartesian form. The worked example uses a=(2,0,0), b=(0,2,0), c=(0,0,2), giving the normal (1,1,1) and the plane x+y+z=2.
must: A plane is fixed by one point and one normal vector: \( (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{n}=0 \iff \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} \)
Normal from three points: \( \mathbf{n}=(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\times(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}) \), where both vectors lie in the plane
The three points must be non-collinear; if the difference vectors are parallel the cross product is zero and no unique plane exists
Cross product by determinant: expand along the row \( \hat i,\hat j,\hat k \) with cofactor signs +, −, +, so the j-component carries a minus sign
The cross product is anti-commutative: reversing the order flips the normal, which is fine as long as you stay consistent
Cartesian form: \( \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p \) with \( (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=\mathbf{n} \) and \( p=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} \), using the same n you computed
Worked example: \( \mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}=(2,-2,0) \), \( \mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}=(2,0,-2) \), \( \mathbf{n}=(4,4,4)\propto(1,1,1) \), plane \( x+y+z=2 \)
The normal can be scaled by any non-zero factor (e.g. divide by 4), but rescale p consistently
The normal is perpendicular to the plane, not lying in it; \( |\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}| \) equals the parallelogram area spanned by u and v
Check the answer by substituting all three points into the final equation; each must satisfy it
conn: Cross product and determinants: the normal is computed by a 3×3 determinant, so sign errors in the minors (especially j) propagate straight into the plane equation
Dot product and perpendicularity: (r − a)·n = 0 expresses that every in-plane vector is perpendicular to n, linking to the Cartesian equation
Cross product magnitude and area: |n| gives the parallelogram area, so half of it is the triangle area abc, often asked alongside the plane
Plane equation with distance and intersection: the normal n and constant p feed into point-to-plane distance and line-plane intersection problems
exq: Find the equation of the plane through A(1,0,2), B(3,1,0) and C(0,2,1). Give your answer in Cartesian form and verify that all three points satisfy it.
Points a=(2,0,0), b=(0,2,0), c=(0,0,2) lie on a plane. Compute (a−b)×(a−c) by determinant, simplify the normal, and write the plane as r·n = p.
Show that the points (1,2,3), (2,4,6) and (3,6,9) do not define a unique plane, using the cross product.
Find the area of triangle ABC for A(2,0,0), B(0,2,0), C(0,0,2) using the cross product, and then the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane through them.
A student computes (a−c)×(a−b) instead of (a−b)×(a−c). Explain how the normal and plane equation change, and whether the final plane is the same.

notes.t: Equation of a plane through three points using vectors
pts: Form two direction vectors lying in the plane by subtracting position vectors of the points
A normal to the plane is found by the cross product of the two in-plane vectors
The three points a, b, c are not collinear, so the difference vectors are independent and define a unique plane
defs: Position vector
A vector from the origin to a point, here a = (2,0,0), b = (0,2,0), c = (0,0,2).
eqs: Direction vector between two points on the plane
a, b = position vectors of points (m); result is a direction vector (m)
Second direction vector between two points on the plane
a, c = position vectors of points (m); result is a direction vector (m)
tips: Ensure the two difference vectors are not parallel; otherwise the cross product is zero and no plane exists.
Keep track of signs when subtracting position vectors, e.g. a − c has third component −2, not +2.
rq: Why do we subtract position vectors rather than use the points directly to find the plane's orientation?
Subtracting gives a vector lying within the plane, which is independent of the origin's position and is needed to build the normal via the cross product.
What would happen if the three points were collinear, e.g. a, b and (1,1,0)?
The difference vectors would be parallel, their cross product would be zero, and no unique plane would be defined.

notes.t: Cross product of vectors via determinant
pts: The cross product n = (a − b) × (a − c) is found by expanding a 3×3 determinant with unit vectors i, j, k in the first row.
Expanding along the first row gives the components as 2×2 minors, with the middle term carrying a minus sign.
The resulting normal vector can be simplified by factoring out a common scalar, giving the direction (1, 1, 1).
eqs: Cross product of two vectors via determinant (normal vector to the plane through the points a, b, c)
\mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}) \times (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}

\(\mathbf{n}\) = normal vector (dimensionless in this example); \(\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}\) = unit vectors along x, y, z (dimensionless); components of the difference vectors \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}\) (length units, e.g. m)
tips: Watch the sign of the j-component: the cofactor pattern is +, −, + along the first row, so forgetting the minus flips the normal's y-component.
The cross product is anti-commutative, so the order of the two vectors determines the sign of the normal.
rq: Why does the middle term of the expansion pick up a minus sign?
The cofactor sign pattern for expansion along the first row alternates +, −, +, so the j-term is subtracted.
What would change if the two vectors were swapped in the cross product?
The sign of n would reverse, since the cross product is anti-commutative; the direction is opposite but the line is the same.

notes.t: Equation of a plane using a normal vector
pts: A plane is the set of points r such that (r − a) is perpendicular to the normal n, giving a dot-product condition.
Rearranging gives r · n = a · n, so the plane is fixed by a point a and normal n.
Expanding the dot products in components turns the vector equation into a Cartesian plane equation.
Dividing the common factor out of both sides simplifies the plane to a clean Cartesian form.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A non-zero vector perpendicular to every direction lying within the plane; it fixes the orientation of the plane.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane through point a with normal n
\vec{r} = position vector of a general point (m); \vec{a} = position vector of a known point on the plane (m); \vec{n} = normal vector (dimensionless in this example)
\alpha, \beta, \gamma = components of the normal \vec{n}; x, y, z = coordinates (m); p = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{n} (constant)
tips: Watch the constant p: it must equal \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{n}\) computed with the same normal, not just the coordinates of a.
Do not forget that the normal is perpendicular to the plane, not a direction lying in it.
rq: Why can we divide both sides of 4x + 4y + 4z = 8 by 4 without changing the plane?
Dividing by a non-zero constant scales the equation but keeps the same solution set, so the plane is unchanged; the normal is only defined up to a scalar multiple.
What happens to the plane if the normal vector is multiplied by a constant?
The orientation is unchanged, so the plane is the same; only the scaling of the coefficients and p changes consistently.

notes.t: Equation of a plane through three points using vector algebra
pts: A plane needs a point on it and a normal vector perpendicular to it.
The normal vector is found as the cross product of two in-plane vectors, here (a−b) and (a−c).
The general plane equation is (r−a)·n = 0, equivalent to r·n = a·n, where r is any generic point on the plane.
The cross product is evaluated by expanding a 3×3 determinant along the first row using 2×2 minors.
defs: Normal vector
A non-zero vector perpendicular to every direction lying within a plane; it fixes the plane's orientation.
Cross product
For vectors u and v, u × v is a vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane through point a with normal n
\mathbf{r} = position vector of generic point (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of known point on plane (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector (dimensionless direction, any scale)
\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} = position vectors of the three points (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector (m²)
tips: Keep the cross product order consistent: (a−b)×(a−c) and (a−c)×(a−b) give opposite normals, which is fine but must not be mixed mid-calculation.
Watch the signs when computing 2×2 minors, especially the middle j-component which carries a minus sign.
rq: Why can any scalar multiple of n be used as the normal vector without changing the plane?
Scaling n by a non-zero constant keeps it perpendicular to the same plane, and the equation r·n = a·n remains satisfied by the same set of points.
What happens if (a−b) and (a−c) are parallel?
Their cross product is the zero vector, so no normal is defined; the three points are collinear and do not determine a unique plane.

xq.q: A triangular glass panel has vertices at \(\mathbf{a}=(1,0,0)\) m, \(\mathbf{b}=(0,2,0)\) m and \(\mathbf{c}=(0,0,3)\) m. Find a normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\times(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})\), write the plane of the panel as \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p\), and hence find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
s: p = a·n = 6, so the plane is 6x+3y+2z = 6

xq.q: Points have position vectors \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,0)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(0,2,0)\), \(\mathbf{c}=(0,0,2)\) (m). Taking the vectors in the order \((\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})\times(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})\), what is the resulting normal vector?
xq.w: The cross product is anti-commutative, so reversing the order flips (4,4,4) to (−4,−4,−4); the traps are ignoring the order, dropping the minus on the j-term, or using the dot product, which gives a scalar.

xq.q: Show that the plane through the points \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,0)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(0,2,0)\), \(\mathbf{c}=(0,0,2)\) (in m) has Cartesian equation \(x+y+z=2\).
xq.a: Two in-plane vectors are a−b = (2,−2,0) and a−c = (2,0,−2). Their cross product, expanded as a determinant, is n = (4,4,4), which is perpendicular to the plane, and can be simplified to (1,1,1). Then p = a·n = (2,0,0)·(1,1,1) = 2. So r·n = a·n gives x + y + z = 2. Check: b and c also satisfy 0+2+0 = 2 and 0+0+2 = 2.
s: Cross product via determinant gives n = (4,4,4), simplified to (1,1,1)
p = a·n = 2 using the same normal
Plane: x + y + z = 2, with b and c checked
Marks for the minus sign on the j-term and the consistent p

units.name: 12.3 Scalar product form r·n = a·n
units.ov: This material covers the scalar product (normal) form of a plane, \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\), where \(\mathbf{n}\) is perpendicular to the plane and \(\mathbf{a}\) is a known point on it. Expanding the dot product with \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) gives the Cartesian form \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\), where \(p=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\). The key link is that the normal's components are the coefficients of \(x,y,z\), so you can move freely between the vector and Cartesian forms.
must: Vector equation of a plane: \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\), with \(\mathbf{a}\) a known point on the plane and \(\mathbf{n}\) the normal
Cartesian form: \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) with \(p=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\)
The normal \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) is read directly off the coefficients of \(x,y,z\)
The normal is perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane
Compute \(p\) using the point \(\mathbf{a}\) and the normal, not the normal alone: e.g. \((2,0,0)\cdot(4,4,4)=8\), not 2
Scaling \(\mathbf{n}\) by a factor scales \(p\) by the same factor, so divide both sides consistently to simplify (e.g. \(4x+4y+4z=8\to x+y+z=2\))
Any point on the plane can serve as \(\mathbf{a}\); the resulting equation is the same plane
Units: \(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}\) and coordinates are lengths in m; \(p\) carries the units of \(\mathbf{n}\) times m
conn: Cross product and planes: given two direction vectors in the plane or three points, \(\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\), then use \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\) to get the plane equation
Parametric (vector) form of a plane vs scalar product form: convert between them by eliminating parameters or by finding \(\mathbf{n}\) from the direction vectors

Line-plane intersection: substitute the line \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{d}\) into \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p\) to solve for \(t\); \(\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}=0\) means parallel or lying in the plane
Distance from a point to a plane and the angle between planes both use \(\mathbf{n}\) (unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), and \(\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2\))
exq: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the plane through \(A=(2,0,0)\) with normal \(\mathbf{n}=(4,4,4)\), and give it in simplest form.
Write the plane \(3x-2y+6z=12\) in the form \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\), stating a unit normal and a suitable point \(\mathbf{a}\).
Find the plane through \(P(1,2,3)\), \(Q(2,0,1)\), \(R(0,1,4)\) in the form \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p\) using a cross product to find \(\mathbf{n}\).
Find where the line \(\mathbf{r}=(1,0,2)+t(2,1,-1)\) meets the plane \(x+2y+z=7\).
Show that the planes \(2x+y-z=3\) and \(4x+2y-2z=10\) are parallel, and find the distance between them.

notes.t: Vector equation of a plane: r·n = a·n
pts: Take the dot product of the position vector r with the normal n and set it equal to a·n, where a is a known point on the plane.
Expanding r·n with n = (α, β, γ) gives the Cartesian form αx + βy + γz = p, with p = a·n.
A non-unit normal can be scaled; dividing the whole equation by a common factor gives the simplest form of the plane.
defs: Normal vector n
A vector perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane; its components (α, β, γ) are the coefficients of x, y, z in the Cartesian equation.
eqs: r = position vector of a general point (m); n = normal vector (dimensionless if unit, otherwise its own units); a = position vector of a known point on the plane (m)
General Cartesian form of a plane
α, β, γ = components of n; x, y, z = coordinates (m); p = a·n (m·|n|)
tips: Watch the dot product: a·n uses the point a, not the normal alone; using (2,0,0)·(4,4,4) gives 8, not 2.
Scaling the normal changes p by the same factor, so keep the right-hand side consistent when dividing through.
rq: Why can we divide 4x + 4y + 4z = 8 by 4 without changing the plane?
Dividing both sides by the same nonzero constant gives an equivalent equation; the set of points satisfying it is unchanged, only the normal's length is rescaled.
What does the constant p represent geometrically?
p = a·n measures the (signed) distance of the plane from the origin, scaled by the length of n.

xq.q: A plane passes through the point \(A\) with position vector \(\mathbf{a}=(1,-2,3)\) m and has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(2,3,-1)\). Using \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\), find the Cartesian equation of the plane and hence the z-coordinate of the point where the plane meets the z-axis.
xq.a: Plane: 2x + 3y − z = −7; it meets the z-axis at z = 7 m
s: On the z-axis x = y = 0, so −z = −7

xq.q: A plane passes through the point \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,0)\) m and has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(4,4,4)\). What is its simplest Cartesian equation?
xq.a: x + y + z = 2
o: x + y + z = 8
x + y + z = 4
x + y + z = 2
xq.w: p = a·n = 8, so 4x+4y+4z = 8, and dividing both sides by 4 gives x+y+z = 2; the traps are using p = 2 without scaling it, or dividing only the left-hand side.
s: Divide both sides by 4: x + y + z = 2

xq.q: A plane passes through \(A=(1,2,0)\) m with normal \(\mathbf{n}=(3,-1,2)\). Show that its equation is \(3x-y+2z=1\), and verify that the point \(P=(0,-1,0)\) lies on it by showing that \(\overrightarrow{AP}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{n}\).
xq.a: The plane is r·n = a·n. Here a·n = 3 − 2 + 0 = 1, and r·n = 3x − y + 2z, so the plane is 3x − y + 2z = 1. For P = (0,−1,0): 0 + 1 + 0 = 1, so P lies on the plane. Also AP = (−1,−3,0) and AP·n = −3 + 3 + 0 = 0, so AP is perpendicular to n, as required for a point on the plane.

units.name: 12.4 Line of intersection of two planes
units.ov: This material shows how to find the line where two planes \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}_1=p_1 \) and \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=p_2 \) meet. The direction comes from the cross product of the normals, and a point on the line comes from solving the two plane equations simultaneously. Combining them gives the vector equation \( \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_0+t(\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2) \), which converts to parametric form. The worked example uses \( x+y+z=5 \) and \( 4x+y+2z=15 \), with point (0,−5,10) and direction (1,2,−3).
must: Direction of the line of intersection: \( \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2 \), because the line lies in both planes and so is perpendicular to both normals
Vector equation of the line: \( \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}_0+t(\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2) \), where \( \mathbf{r}_0 \) is a point on the line and \( t \) is a scalar parameter

Finding \( \mathbf{r}_0 \): set one coordinate to a convenient value (often 0) and solve the resulting 2×2 system, so that \( \mathbf{r}_0\cdot\mathbf{n}_1=p_1 \) and \( \mathbf{r}_0\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=p_2 \)
Compute the cross product via the 3×3 determinant, taking care with the minus sign on the \( \mathbf{j} \) component
Worked example: for \( \mathbf{n}_1=(1,1,1) \) and \( \mathbf{n}_2=(4,1,2) \), \( \mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2=(1,2,-3) \), giving \( \mathbf{r}=(0,-5,10)+t(1,2,-3) \)
Verify by substituting the point into BOTH plane equations; for t = 1, (1,−3,7) gives 1−3+7=5 and 4−3+14=15
Parametric form: \( x=t,\ y=-5+2t,\ z=10-3t \); watch the signs
Check first that the planes are not parallel: if \( \mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2=\mathbf{0} \) there is no unique line of intersection
Any non-zero scalar multiple of \( \mathbf{d} \) is a valid direction, and any point on the line is a valid \( \mathbf{r}_0 \), so answers can look different yet be equivalent
Use the cross product, not the dot product, for the direction; the dot product gives a scalar
conn: Cross product and determinants: the direction vector comes from expanding a 3×3 determinant, so cofactor sign errors carry straight into the line equation
Simultaneous linear equations: finding \( \mathbf{r}_0 \) means solving an underdetermined 2-equation, 3-unknown system by fixing one variable, which links to the parametric solution
Vector equation, parametric form and two-point form: \( \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \) can be used once two points on the line are found, for example t = 0 and t = 1
Plane equation \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p \) and the dot product: verification and point-finding rely on dotting position vectors with normals
exq: Find the vector equation of the line of intersection of the planes \( x+y+z=5 \) and \( 4x+y+2z=15 \). Show the cross product and a point on the line, and verify the point in both equations.

Planes \( 2x-y+3z=4 \) and \( x+2y-z=3 \) intersect in a line. Find \( \mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2 \), find a point with z = 0, write the line in vector and parametric form, and check the point at t = 1.
Show that the planes \( x+2y-z=1 \) and \( 2x+4y-2z=5 \) do not meet in a line, using the cross product of the normals. Explain geometrically what this means.
Given the line \( \mathbf{r}=(0,-5,10)+t(1,2,-3) \), write the parametric equations and find the point where t = 1. Show it lies on both planes \( x+y+z=5 \) and \( 4x+y+2z=15 \).

Two students find the line of intersection of the same two planes and get different-looking vector equations. Explain why both can be correct, and state how to test whether two such lines are the same.

notes.t: Line of intersection of two planes: direction and vector equation
pts: The line of intersection lies in both planes, so its direction is perpendicular to both normal vectors, giving the cross product direction.
Any point a on the line can be taken as r₀, a position vector satisfying both plane equations; the line is then r = r₀ + t(n₁ × n₂).
Find a point on the line by solving the two plane equations simultaneously, then use the cross product of the normals as direction vector.
defs: Vector equation of a line
A line through a fixed point with position vector r₀ in direction d is r = r₀ + t d, where t is a scalar parameter.
eqs: Direction of line of intersection of two planes
n₁, n₂ = normal vectors of the planes (dimensionless direction vectors)
Vector equation of the line of intersection
r = position vector (m); r₀ = point on line satisfying both planes (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Check the two planes are not parallel before using n₁ × n₂; a zero cross product means no unique line.
When finding r₀, the point must satisfy both plane equations; choosing one coordinate to be zero and solving the 2×2 system is a common method.
rq: Why must the direction of the line be the cross product n₁ × n₂ rather than either normal alone?

A normal is perpendicular to its own plane, so a line in that plane is perpendicular to it; the line lies in both planes, so it must be perpendicular to both normals, which is exactly what the cross product gives.
What if n₁ and n₂ are parallel?
Then n₁ × n₂ = 0, the planes are parallel (coincident or disjoint), and there is no line of intersection.

notes.t: Line of intersection of two planes (vector form)
pts: The line of intersection of two planes is perpendicular to both normal vectors, so its direction is the cross product of the normals.
To find a point on the line, set one coordinate to zero and solve the resulting two equations in the other two unknowns.
The vector equation of a line uses a point r0 on the line plus a multiple t of the direction vector.
The equation of a line can also be written from two points a and b as r = a + t(b − a).
defs: Line of intersection of two planes
The set of points satisfying both plane equations simultaneously; its direction is parallel to the cross product of the two normal vectors.
eqs: Direction of the line of intersection of two planes
Vector equation of a line through point r0 with direction n1 × n2
\boldsymbol{r} = position vector (m); \boldsymbol{r}_0 = point on line (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Check the cross product components carefully: a sign error in the determinant (e.g. the j component) gives the wrong direction vector.
Verify that the chosen point r0 satisfies both plane equations before writing the line equation.
rq: Why must the direction of the line be the cross product of the two normals rather than either normal alone?
The line lies in both planes, so its direction must be perpendicular to both normals; the cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both.
Why can we set x = 0 to find a point on the line?

Setting one coordinate to zero reduces the 3-variable system to 2 equations in 2 unknowns, which can be solved for a specific point on the line (valid provided the line is not parallel to the plane x = 0).

notes.t: Testing a specific parameter value t = 1 in a vector system
pts: Substitute the chosen value of t into the vector sum to get a specific vector result
The vector sum is computed component by component: first, second and third coordinates are added separately
The resulting vector components are then used as x, y, z in the linear system; each equation can be checked by direct substitution
eqs: Component-wise vector addition used to test the system at t = 1
Linear system satisfied by the test point (x, y, z) = (1, −3, 7)
tips: Keep signs carefully when adding negative components, e.g. −5 + 2 = −3 and 10 + (−3) = 7.
Substitute the full result back into every equation of the system to confirm the check, not just one.
rq: Why is substituting one specific value of t a useful check before solving in general?
It quickly verifies that the computed vector satisfies the system at that t, catching arithmetic or setup errors before a general derivation.
Why must the components be added separately rather than as a single number?
Vectors add component by component, so each coordinate of the result depends only on the matching coordinates of the summands.

notes.t: Line of intersection of two planes: direction via cross product
pts: The direction of the line of intersection is perpendicular to both plane normals, so it is found using the cross product.
A line is written in vector form using a point on the line and a direction vector with a scalar parameter.
Substituting the direction d = n₁ × n₂ into the point-direction form gives the line of intersection.
The point r₀ can be any vector satisfying both plane equations, usually found by setting one coordinate to a convenient value.
defs: Line of intersection
The set of points lying in both planes r·n₁ = p₁ and r·n₂ = p₂; it is perpendicular to both normals n₁ and n₂.
Cross product
The vector operation n₁ × n₂ that yields a vector perpendicular to both n₁ and n₂.
eqs: Vector equation of the line of intersection of two planes

\mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point on the line (m); \mathbf{r}_0 = any point on the line satisfying both plane equations (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless); \mathbf{n}_1, \mathbf{n}_2 = normal vectors of the planes (dimensionless if unit, otherwise as given)
\mathbf{r} = position vector (m); \mathbf{r}_0 = point on the line (m); \mathbf{d} = direction vector (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Do not use the dot product n₁ · n₂ to find the direction; the direction requires the cross product n₁ × n₂.
Check that the chosen r₀ satisfies both plane equations before writing the final line equation.
rq: Why must the direction of the intersection line be the cross product rather than the dot product of the normals?
The dot product gives a scalar, not a vector perpendicular to both normals; the cross product n₁ × n₂ gives a vector orthogonal to both, which is the required direction.
Why can any point r₀ satisfying both plane equations be used in the line equation?
Every such point lies on the intersection line, and the direction vector alone fixes the line's orientation, so any common point works.

notes.t: Line of intersection of two planes: direction via cross product and a point on the line
pts: A point on the intersection line must satisfy both plane equations simultaneously
The direction vector of the intersection line is the cross product of the two normal vectors
A specific point on the line is found by solving the two plane equations, e.g. by fixing one coordinate arbitrarily
Expanding a 3×3 determinant along the first row gives the components of the cross product
defs: Direction vector of intersection line
The cross product of the two plane normals, \(n_{1}\) × \(n_{2}\), is parallel to the line where the planes intersect.
eqs: Conditions for a point \(r_{0}\) on both planes
\(r_{0}\) = position vector of a point on the line (m); \(n_{1}\), \(n_{2}\) = plane normal vectors (dimensionless here); \(p_{1}\), \(p_{2}\) = plane constants
Direction vector of line of intersection
d = direction vector of the line; \(n_{1}\), \(n_{2}\) = plane normal vectors
tips: Do not confuse the cross product (vector, for direction) with the dot product (scalar); using the dot product gives no direction.
Check the sign of each cofactor term when expanding the determinant, e.g. the middle j-component carries a minus sign.
rq: Why must the direction vector be the cross product of the normals rather than their dot product?
The cross product yields a vector perpendicular to both normals, which lies in both planes and so is parallel to their line of intersection; the dot product is a scalar.
Why can we arbitrarily set x = 0 when finding a point on the line?
Two planes intersect in a line (infinitely many points), so any single coordinate can be fixed to obtain one valid point, provided the reduced system remains solvable.

notes.t: Vector equation of a line in 3D
pts: A line is fixed by a point on it, \( \mathbf{r}_0 \), and a direction vector \( \mathbf{d} \); every point is reached by adding a multiple of \( \mathbf{d} \).
A point on the line can be checked by dotting it with the given normal-type vectors; a correct point gives the stated scalar products.
The vector equation converts directly to three parametric equations, one per coordinate.
defs: Direction vector of a line
A non-zero vector parallel to the line; any scalar multiple of it is also a valid direction.
eqs: Vector equation of a line through \( \mathbf{r}_0 \) with direction \( \mathbf{d} \)

\( \mathbf{r} \) = position vector of a general point (m); \( \mathbf{r}_0 \) = position vector of a known point (m); \( t \) = real parameter (dimensionless); \( \mathbf{d} \) = direction vector (dimensionless in direction)
tips: Do not confuse the direction vector with a point on the line; \( \mathbf{d} \) gives direction only, \( \mathbf{r}_0 \) gives position.
Keep signs right when converting to parametric form, e.g. \( z = 10 - 3t \) not \( 10 + 3t \).
rq: Why can the direction vector \( \mathbf{d} = (1,2,-3) \) be replaced by \( (2,4,-6) \) without changing the line?
Because \( (2,4,-6) = 2\mathbf{d} \) is parallel to \( \mathbf{d} \); only the direction matters, and rescaling \( t \) absorbs the factor.
How would you check whether the point \( (1,-3,7) \) lies on this line?
Solve \( x=t \) to get \( t=1 \); then check \( y=-5+2(1)=-3 \) and \( z=10-3(1)=7 \). All match, so it lies on the line.

xq.q: Two planes have equations \(x+y+z=5\) and \(4x+y+2z=15\) (coordinates in m). The point \((0,-5,10)\) lies on both planes. Find the direction vector of their line of intersection, and hence write down its vector equation. Use it to find the z-coordinate of the point on the line where \(x=4\).
s: z = 10 − 3(4) = −2 m (check point (4,3,−2) satisfies both planes)

xq.q: Plane 1 is \(2x-y+z=3\) and plane 2 is \(x+y-z=1\). Which vector is parallel to their line of intersection?
xq.w: The direction is n₁×n₂ = (2,−1,1)×(1,1,−1) = (0,3,3); (3,0,0) comes from adding normals, (0,−3,3) from a sign error in the j component, and (2,−1,−1) from multiplying components element by element.

xq.q: Show that every point of the line \(\mathbf{r}=(0,-5,10)+t(1,2,-3)\) lies in both planes \(x+y+z=5\) and \(4x+y+2z=15\), and explain why the direction vector of the line is perpendicular to both plane normals.
xq.a: Points on the line are x=t, y=−5+2t, z=10−3t. Plane 1: t+(−5+2t)+(10−3t)=5 for all t. Plane 2: 4t+(−5+2t)+2(10−3t)=4t−5+2t+20−6t=15 for all t. So the whole line lies in both planes. The line lies in both planes, so its direction is perpendicular to each normal, so it is parallel to n₁×n₂ = (1,1,1)×(4,1,2) = (1,2,−3), which is the direction used. Check: (1,2,−3)·(1,1,1)=0 and (1,2,−3)·(4,1,2)=4+2−6=0.
s: Write parametric coordinates x=t, y=−5+2t, z=10−3t
Substitute into plane 1: result 5 for all t
Substitute into plane 2: result 15 for all t
Line lies in both planes so direction is perpendicular to both normals, i.e. n₁×n₂
Dot product checks with both normals give zero

units.name: 12.5 Angle between two planes
units.ov: This material shows how to find the angle between two planes from their normal vectors. Read each normal from the plane's coefficients, apply the dot product formula, and take the absolute value so the angle is acute. It combines plane equations, vector magnitudes, the dot product and inverse cosine.
must: The angle between two planes equals the acute angle between their normal vectors.
For \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\), the normal is \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), read directly from the coefficients.
Formula: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2|}{\|\mathbf{n}_1\|\,\|\mathbf{n}_2\|}\).
Always include the absolute value on the dot product; without it you may get the obtuse angle \(\pi-\theta\).
The constant \(p\) does not enter the normal. It only fixes the plane's position, not its orientation.
Dot product: \(\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=\alpha_1\alpha_2+\beta_1\beta_2+\gamma_1\gamma_2\).
Magnitude: \(\|\mathbf{n}\|=\sqrt{n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2}\).
Take \(\theta=\arccos(\cdot)\) and check the calculator mode. The notes call for radians, but give degrees if the question asks for them.
Check your answer: an acute angle satisfies \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\). \(\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=0\) means perpendicular planes, and parallel normals mean parallel planes.
conn: Plane equations and normals: rearrange to the form \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) first (for example, collect all x, y, z terms on one side) before reading off the normal.
Dot product and magnitude: the angle formula is the dot product definition \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) applied to normals.
Line of intersection: the cross product \(\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2\) gives the direction of the line where the planes meet, and the angle between planes is the angle between the normals.

Perpendicularity and parallelism tests: \(\mathbf{n}_1\cdot\mathbf{n}_2=0\) gives perpendicular planes, and \(\mathbf{n}_1=k\mathbf{n}_2\) gives parallel planes. Questions often ask you to find an unknown coefficient this way.
exq: Find the acute angle between the planes \(2x-y+2z=5\) and \(x+2y-2z=3\). Give the answer in radians and in degrees.
Find the angle between \(x+y+z=1\) and \(x-y+2z=4\). Explain why the absolute value is needed, and what angle you get without it.
Find the value of \(k\) for which the planes \(3x+ky-z=2\) and \(x+2y+5z=7\) are perpendicular.
Find the angle between the plane \(2x+3y-6z=12\) and the plane \(z=0\) (the xy-plane).

Find the angle between two planes, given in a different form, by first rearranging them to \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\). Then find the direction of their line of intersection using \(\mathbf{n}_1\times\mathbf{n}_2\).

notes.t: Angle between two planes via normal vectors
pts: The angle between two planes is found from the angle between their normal vectors.
Each plane \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), read directly from the coefficients.
Use the dot product formula to get the cosine of the angle between the normals.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A vector perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane; for \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) it is \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\).
eqs: Angle between two planes from their normal vectors
\(\theta\) = angle between normals (rad or °); \(\vec{n}_1,\vec{n}_2\) = normal vectors (dimensionless coefficients); \(|\vec{n}|\) = magnitude of normal
tips: The formula gives the angle between normals, which may be obtuse; take the acute angle by using the absolute value of the dot product, i.e. \(|\cos\theta|\).
Read the normal from the coefficients of x, y, z only; the constant term \(p\) does not affect the orientation.
rq: Why does the formula use the normal vectors rather than the planes' direction vectors directly?
A plane has infinitely many in-plane directions, but a single normal vector characterises its orientation completely, so the angle between normals determines the angle between planes.
If the normals are perpendicular, what is the angle between the planes?
cos θ = 0, so the planes meet at 90°.

notes.t: Angle between two planes via normal vectors
pts: The angle between two intersecting planes is the acute angle between their normal vectors.
A plane \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) read directly from its coefficients.
Taking the absolute value of the dot product ensures the acute angle is found.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
For the plane \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\), the normal vector is \(\mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), perpendicular to the plane.
eqs: Cosine of the acute angle between two planes
\(\mathbf{n}_1,\mathbf{n}_2\) = normal vectors of the planes (dimensionless coefficients); \(\theta\) = acute angle between the planes (rad or degrees)
tips: Use the coefficients of x, y, z only; the constant on the right-hand side does not enter the normal vector.
Forgetting the absolute value can give an obtuse angle instead of the required acute angle.
rq: Why must we take the absolute value of the dot product when finding the angle between planes?
Because the normals may point in opposite senses, giving a negative cosine; the absolute value guarantees the acute angle between the planes is returned.

notes.t: Angle between two planes using normal vectors
pts: The magnitude of a vector is found from the square root of the sum of the squares of its components.
The acute angle between two planes is found from the normal vectors via the dot product and magnitudes.
Taking the absolute value of the dot product ensures the angle returned is acute.
The arccos function returns the angle directly in radians.
defs: Acute angle between planes
The smaller of the two angles formed where two planes intersect, found from their normal vectors.
eqs: Cosine of the acute angle between two planes
\theta = acute angle between planes (rad); \mathbf{n}_1, \mathbf{n}_2 = normal vectors of the planes (dimensionless here); \|\mathbf{n}\| = magnitude of normal vector
tips: Forgetting the absolute value on the dot product gives an obtuse angle rather than the required acute angle.
Ensure the calculator is in radian mode, since arccos returns radians directly and degrees are not wanted here.
rq: Why must the dot product be wrapped in absolute value when finding the angle between two planes?
Because the normals can point in opposite directions, and the absolute value ensures the result is the acute angle, which lies between 0 and 90 degrees.
Why is the result \(\cos\theta = 4/21\) positive even though the dot product sign depends on the normal orientations?
The absolute value removes the sign, so only the acute angle is returned regardless of how the normals are oriented.

xq.q: Two planes have equations \(2x-y+2z=5\) and \(x+2y-2z=3\). Find the acute angle between the planes, in degrees to 1 decimal place.
Plane A is \(x+2y+2z=9\) and plane B is \(-z=4\). What is the acute angle between them?
xq.w: n₁=(1,2,2) with |n₁|=3 and n₂=(0,0,−1) give cosθ=|−2|/3=2/3, so θ=48.2°; 131.8° omits the absolute value, 41.8° uses arcsin instead of arccos, and 77.2° forgets the square root in |n₁| (using 9).

xq.q: Show that the acute angle between the plane \(x+y+z=2\) and the plane \(z=0\) is \(\arccos(1/\sqrt{3})\approx 54.7^\circ\). Explain why the constants 2 and 0 do not affect the answer.
xq.a: Normals are n₁=(1,1,1) and n₂=(0,0,1). n₁·n₂=1, |n₁|=√3, |n₂|=1. So cosθ=|1|/(√3·1)=1/√3=0.5774 and θ=arccos(0.5774)=54.7°. The constants only fix where each plane sits in space (translate it); they do not change the normal direction, so the angle between the planes is unchanged.
s: Constants only translate the planes, not their orientation

units.name: 13.1 Vector and Cartesian equations of a line
units.ov: This material develops the equation of a line in 3D from two points A and B, using the position vector a plus a scalar multiple of the direction b − a. The vector form expands component-wise into parametric equations, and eliminating the parameter t gives the symmetric Cartesian form. Converting fluently between the three forms, and choosing a point and a direction vector, underlies all line problems.
must: Vector equation of a line through A and B: \( \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \)
Equivalent symmetric form: \( \mathbf{r} = (1-t)\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b} \), with t = 0 giving A and t = 1 giving B
The direction vector is \( \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \), not \( \mathbf{b} \); the position vector a only fixes a point on the line
Parametric equations: \( x = a_1 + t(b_1-a_1),\; y = a_2 + t(b_2-a_2),\; z = a_3 + t(b_3-a_3) \)
Cartesian (symmetric) form: \( \frac{x-a_1}{b_1-a_1} = \frac{y-a_2}{b_2-a_2} = \frac{z-a_3}{b_3-a_3} \), obtained by eliminating t
In the Cartesian form the numerators use the point a (x − a₁), and the denominators are the direction components (b₁ − a₁)
t is a real, dimensionless scalar; t ranging over all reals sweeps out the whole infinite line, while 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 gives only the segment AB
A line has many valid representations: any point on it and any parallel direction vector work (e.g. reparametrising with t = x + 1 gives the same line)
To parametrise a Cartesian line, set a free variable as the parameter, e.g. \( z=0,\; y=1+2x \) gives \( (x,y,z)=(t,\,1+2t,\,0) \); keep the zero z-component in the direction vector
Keep units consistent (metres) so that direction components are correct
conn: Two points → direction vector b − a → vector equation → parametric equations → symmetric Cartesian form: questions often ask you to move through the chain, or to go backwards from Cartesian to vector form
A zero direction component (e.g. z = 0 for all t) means the symmetric form has a zero denominator, so write that coordinate as a separate equation such as z = 0
Parametric form is used to test whether a point lies on the line (solve for t consistently in all three components) and to find intersections of two lines or of a line with a plane
The direction vector from the line equation feeds into later topics such as the angle between lines (dot product) and the shortest distance from a point to a line (cross product)
exq: Find the vector equation of the line through A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, −1, 4), then write its parametric and Cartesian forms.
Does the point P(5, −4, 5) lie on the line through A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, −1, 4)? If so, state the value of t.
Write the line \( y = 1 + 2x,\; z = 0 \) in vector parametric form, and give a second, different parametrisation (e.g. with \( t = x+1 \)) of the same line.
Convert \( \frac{x-2}{3} = \frac{y+1}{-2} = \frac{z-4}{1} \) to vector form and state a point and a direction vector.
Two lines are given in parametric form with parameters t and s. Determine whether they intersect, and if so find the point of intersection.

notes.t: Vector Equation of a Line
pts: A line through points A and B can be reached by starting at A and moving along the direction of AB; the position vector of any point P on the line is OA plus a multiple of AB.
Since AP is a multiple of AB, the position vector r of a general point on the line is the position of A plus a scalar multiple of AB.
Substituting AB = b − a turns the equation into a form using only the position vectors of two known points on the line.
Varying the parameter t over all real numbers sweeps out the whole infinite line, with t = 0 giving A and t = 1 giving B.
defs: Position vector
A vector from the origin O to a point, e.g. OA = a means a is the position vector of A.
Parameter t
A real scalar that scales the direction vector b − a; each value of t gives one point on the line.
eqs: Vector equation of a line through two points A and B
\mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of A (m); \mathbf{b} = position vector of B (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
Equivalent form starting at A along direction AB
\mathbf{r} = position vector of P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of A (m); \mathbf{b} = position vector of B (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the position vector b with the direction vector AB; the direction is b − a, not b.
Remember t is a dimensionless scalar, so it cannot be treated as a vector or carry units.
rq: Why does the equation still describe the line when t is negative or greater than 1?
Because the line extends infinitely in both directions along AB; t < 0 gives points beyond A and t > 1 gives points beyond B, which still lie on the same line.
What would the equation describe if t were restricted to 0 ≤ t ≤ 1?
Only the finite line segment from A to B, not the whole infinite line.

notes.t: Vectors: Cartesian Form of a Line
pts: A line through points a and b is written as a position vector r plus a scalar multiple t of the direction b − a.
Expanding the vector equation component-wise gives three parametric equations, one for each coordinate.
Eliminating the parameter t from the parametric equations gives the symmetric Cartesian form of the line.
The direction components (b₁ − a₁, b₂ − a₂, b₃ − a₃) appear as denominators in the Cartesian form.
defs: Position vector r
The vector from the origin O to a general point P(x, y, z) on the line.
Parameter t
A real scalar that varies over all real numbers to sweep out every point on the line.
eqs: Vector equation of a line through a and b
\mathbf{r} = position vector of point P (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of point A (m); \mathbf{b} = position vector of point B (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
x, y, z = coordinates of P (m); \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = coordinates of A (m); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = coordinates of B (m); t = parameter (dimensionless)
x, y, z = coordinates of point on line (m); \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) = coordinates of point A (m); \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\), \(b_{3}\) = coordinates of point B (m)
tips: Watch the sign and order: the numerator is (x − a₁) with the point a, not b, while the denominator uses (b₁ − a₁).
All variables must be in consistent SI units (metres); mixing mm and m inside the ratios gives wrong direction components.
rq: Why must the three denominators in the Cartesian form all be non-zero, and what does a zero denominator mean geometrically?
A zero denominator (e.g. b₁ − a₁ = 0) means the line has no change in x; the equation becomes x = a₁ with the other ratios still equal, i.e. the line lies in a plane parallel to a coordinate plane.
Why is the parameter t needed at all, and what happens to a point when t = 0 and t = 1?
t links every coordinate to one shared scalar so the three coordinates move together; t = 0 gives point A and t = 1 gives point B.

notes.t: Parametric equations of a line in 3D
pts: A line in Cartesian form can be converted to parametric form by introducing a parameter t and expressing each coordinate in terms of it.
Given two points A and B on the line, the parametric form uses the displacement (b − a) as the direction.
Setting z = 0 and y = 1 + 2x means x can be chosen freely as the parameter, so the line lies in the plane z = 0.
eqs: Parametric equations of a line through point A and point B
\(t\) = parameter (dimensionless); \(a_1, a_2, a_3\) = coordinates of a point on the line (m); \(b_1, b_2, b_3\) = coordinates of a second point (m)
tips: Choosing a different parameter (e.g. t = x + 1) changes the point and direction but not the line; any valid point and parallel vector is acceptable.
Do not forget the z-component: here z = 0 for all t, so the z-component of the direction vector is 0, not omitted.
rq: Why can x be used directly as the parameter for the line y = 1 + 2x, z = 0?
Because x can take any real value and determines y uniquely via y = 1 + 2x, with z fixed at 0, so setting t = x gives x = t, y = 1 + 2t, z = 0.
What point and direction vector follow from x = t, y = 1 + 2t, z = 0?
The point (0, 1, 0) lies on the line (t = 0) and the direction vector is (1, 2, 0), read from the coefficients of t.

xq.q: A straight cable passes through points A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, −2, 7), with coordinates in m. Write its vector equation and find the z-coordinate of the point where the cable crosses the plane \(y=0\).
xq.a: z = 5 m (point (2, 0, 5) at t = 0.5)

xq.q: Which is the Cartesian equation of the line through A(2, −1, 3) and B(5, 1, 2)?
xq.w: The direction is b − a = (3, 2, −1) and the numerators use the point A; option 0 uses b as the direction, option 1 flips the signs of the point, option 2 loses the minus sign in the z component.

xq.q: A line lies in the plane \(z=0\) and satisfies \(y=1+2x\). Write down parametric equations for the line using \(x=t\). Then show that choosing the parameter \(s=x+1\) gives a different parametrisation of the same line.
xq.a: With x=t: x=t, y=1+2t, z=0, i.e. r=(0,1,0)+t(1,2,0). With s=x+1, x=s−1, y=1+2(s−1)=2s−1, z=0, i.e. r=(−1,−1,0)+s(1,2,0). The direction (1,2,0) is the same, and the point (−1,−1,0) satisfies y=1+2x (−1=1−2) and z=0, so it lies on the first line (t=−1). Hence both describe the same line; the z-component of the direction is 0, not omitted.
s: Base point (−1,−1,0) lies on the first line at t=−1
Conclude same line, z-component kept as 0

units.name: 13.2 Converting lines to parametric/vector form (worked examples)
units.ov: This material shows how to convert a line given by Cartesian equations (e.g. y = 1 + 2x, z = 0) into parametric and vector form by setting x = t. The constant terms give a point a on the line and the coefficients of t give the direction vector b − a, so the line is r = a + t(b − a). The same ideas apply whether a line is specified by two points or by Cartesian equations.
must: Vector equation of a line: \( \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \), with a a point on the line and b − a the direction
Converting from Cartesian form: set \( x = t \), express y and z in terms of t, then read off constants (point a) and coefficients of t (direction)
Direction vector between two points: \( \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} = (b_1-a_1,\ b_2-a_2,\ b_3-a_3) \); it is non-zero and parallel to the line
Do not confuse the point a (constant terms) with the direction vector (coefficients of t)
Include every coordinate, writing e.g. \( z = 0 + 0t \), so that no direction component is lost
Substituting values of t gives points on the line: \( t=0 \to (0,1,0) \), \( t=-1 \to (-1,-1,0) \)
Watch signs of constants: from \( y=1+2x \), \( a_2 = 1 \), not −1
The parameter t is real and dimensionless; each value of t gives exactly one point, and r varies with t
The representation is not unique: any point on the line and any non-zero multiple of the direction vector works
conn: Two-point line construction and Cartesian conversion are the same object: the direction b − a can be checked by taking two points found from different values of t
Parametric lines feed into line intersection and parallel/skew tests: equate components, solve for the parameters, and compare direction vectors
Direction vectors link to the dot product (angle between lines) and the cross product (shortest distance, or perpendicular direction)
Parametric form extends to motion: r(t) with t as time gives a particle moving at constant velocity equal to the direction vector
exq: Write the line \( y = 1+2x,\ z=0 \) in parametric and vector form. Give the points at \( t=0 \) and \( t=-1 \), and a unit direction vector.
Find the vector equation of the line through A(1, 2, 3) and B(4, 0, −1), and state whether the point (7, −2, −5) lies on it.
Convert \( \mathbf{r} = (2,-1,3) + t(1,4,0) \) to Cartesian equations, and explain why the z-component of the direction is zero.
Show that the lines \( \mathbf{r}_1 = (0,1,0)+t(1,2,0) \) and \( \mathbf{r}_2 = (1,0,0)+s(2,4,0) \) are parallel, and decide whether they coincide.
A line has Cartesian equations \( y = 3 - 2x,\ z = 5 \). Using \( x=t \), find its vector equation and the angle it makes with the x-axis.

notes.t: Vector equation of a line in 3D (worked example)
pts: A line given as Cartesian equations can be rewritten in parametric form by letting x = t.
Parametric form gives each coordinate as a linear function of the parameter t, with a constant part and a direction part.
Substituting specific values of t gives points on the line, e.g. t = 0 gives (0,1,0) and t = −1 gives (−1,−1,0).
The direction vector of the line is found as the difference of two points on it, b − a.
The vector equation of a line through point a in direction (b − a) is r = a + t(b − a).
defs: Parameter
An auxiliary variable t that runs over the real numbers, each value giving one point of the line.
Direction vector
A non-zero vector parallel to a line; for a line through two points a and b it is b − a.
eqs: Vector (parametric) equation of a line through a with direction b − a
\mathbf{r} = position vector of any point on the line (m); \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} = position vectors of two known points on the line (m); t = real parameter (dimensionless)
Parametric equations of the line y = 1 + 2x, z = 0
x, y, z = Cartesian coordinates (m); t = parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the parameter t with a coordinate; t is dimensionless and the vector r varies with it.
When writing parametric form, make sure every coordinate is included (z = 0 + 0t), otherwise the direction vector components are lost.
rq: Why can we choose x = t as the parameter, and what would change if we chose y = t instead?
Any variable that can vary freely along the line works; with y = t you would solve x = (t − 1)/2 and get a different but equivalent parametrization of the same line.
Why does the vector (1, 2, 0) point along the line y = 1 + 2x?
Its components give the change in x, y, z per unit step in t; the slope 2 matches Δy/Δx = 2 and Δz = 0 because z is fixed.
What if a and b were chosen as two different points on the same line?
The equation r = a + t(b − a) still describes the same line, since b − a remains parallel to it, only the reference point and parameter scaling change.

notes.t: Parametric equations of a line in space (vector approach)
pts: A line is fixed by a point A with position vector a and a direction vector b − a, joining A to another point B.
Any point on the line is reached by adding a multiple of the direction vector to a, with parameter t.
For a Cartesian system where x is free, set x = t, then read off the constant terms (point a) and the coefficients of t (direction vector).
The constants \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), \(a_{3}\) give the position vector of a point on the line; the coefficients of t give the direction vector.
defs: Parametric form of a line

A set of equations x = \(a_{1}\) + t(\(b_{1}\) − \(a_{1}\)), y = \(a_{2}\) + t(\(b_{2}\) − \(a_{2}\)), z = \(a_{3}\) + t(\(b_{3}\) − \(a_{3}\)) giving every point of the line as t varies over the real numbers.
Direction vector
A non-zero vector parallel to a line, obtained as the difference of position vectors of two points on it, b − a.
eqs: Vector equation of a line through A and B
\mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of point A (m); \mathbf{b} = position vector of point B (m); t = parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the sign of the constant term: from y = 1 + 2x the point has \(a_{2}\) = {{1}}, not −1.
Direction vector components are differences \(b_{i}\) − \(a_{i}\); do not confuse the point (a) with the direction vector (b − a).
rq: Why can we set x = t when the line is given as y = 1 + 2x, z = 0?
Because x is free (any real value gives a point on the line), so using it as the parameter makes y and z depend on t, giving a valid parametrisation.
Why is the parameter t not unique, and what does changing it do?
Any non-zero scalar multiple of the direction vector gives the same line; a different choice of t (e.g. t → 2t) changes the speed/spacing of points but not the line traced.

notes.t: Vector equation of a line: finding a point and direction vector
pts: Let the parameter equal x (t = x), then substitute into the other equations; z stays constant.
Rewrite parametric equations as constant term plus coefficient of t to read off the position vector a.
The constant terms give a point on the line (position vector a).
The coefficients of t give the direction vector b − a.
The vector line equation is r = a + t(b − a).
eqs: Vector equation of a line through a point with direction b − a
\mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point (m); \mathbf{a} = position vector of a point on the line (m); \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} = direction vector (m); t = parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Don't confuse the position vector a with the direction vector: a is the constant term, b − a is the coefficient of t, and a zero coefficient (like z = 0 + 0t) means no change in that direction.
rq: Why must the parametric equations be rewritten as constant + coefficient·t before reading off a and b − a?
Because the general form r = a + t(b − a) matches each component's constant term to a and each coefficient of t to b − a; without this matching the components are easy to mix up.

xq.q: A straight cable lies along the line given by \(y = 3 - 2x\), \(z = 4\) (coordinates in m). Setting \(x = t\), it is written as \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{d}\), where \(\mathbf{a}\) is the position vector of the point at \(t=0\) and \(\mathbf{d}\) is the direction vector given by the coefficients of t. Find the position vector of the point on the cable at \(t = 2.5\) and give its distance from the origin.
xq.a: The point is (2.5, −2, 4) m, so the distance from the origin is 5.02 m (to 3 s.f.)

xq.q: The line \(y = 1 + 2x\), \(z = 0\) is parametrised by \(x = t\). Which vector equation is correct?
o: \(\mathbf{r} = (0,1,0) + t(1,2)\) with the z-component omitted, giving direction (1,2,0) lost
xq.w: Constants give the point (0,1,0) and the coefficients of t give the direction (1,2,0); the traps are the sign of the constant and swapping the point with the direction.

xq.q: A line passes through A(1, 2, −1) and B(3, 1, 2) (coordinates in m). Find its vector equation. Then show that the point C(5, 0, 5) lies on the line and state the value of t at C.
s: Check y = 0 and z = 5 are satisfied, so C lies on the line

units.name: 13.3 Perpendicular lines via direction vectors and dot product
units.ov: This material tests whether two lines in 3D are perpendicular. Each line's direction vector is found by subtracting the position vectors of two points on it (end minus start), and the dot product of the two direction vectors is then computed. The lines are perpendicular exactly when that dot product is zero, which follows from \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) with \(\theta=90^\circ\).
must: Perpendicular lines have direction vectors with \(\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=0\) exactly.
Direction vector from two points: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\) (end minus start), kept consistent for each line.
Dot product: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\).
Test the direction vectors (endpoint differences), never the endpoint position vectors themselves.
Worked example: (2,3,4)→(1,2,3) gives \((-1,-1,-1)\); (1,0,2)→(2,3,−2) gives \((1,3,-4)\); dot product \(-1-3+4=0\), so the lines are perpendicular.
Reversing a direction vector (a−b instead of b−a) flips its sign but does not change whether the dot product is zero.
Take care with signs when subtracting negative coordinates, e.g. \((2,3,-2)-(1,0,2)=(1,3,-4)\).
Orthogonality means a zero dot product (a scalar), not a zero vector; the vectors must be non-zero.
A nonzero dot product means the lines are not perpendicular, and \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\big(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|)\big)\) gives the angle between them.
conn: Dot product and angle: the zero test is the special case \(\cos\theta=0\) of \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\). Questions often ask for a general angle between lines.

Position vectors and direction vectors: the direction vector comes from subtracting position vectors. Questions often start from point coordinates, and the same vectors are reused for line equations \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{d}\).
Unknown parameter problems: setting \(\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=0\) gives a linear equation to solve for an unknown coordinate or constant.
Perpendicular lines (zero dot product) versus parallel lines (direction vectors are scalar multiples, or zero cross product): questions may ask you to classify a pair of lines.
exq: Line 1 passes through (2,3,4) and (1,2,3); line 2 passes through (1,0,2) and (2,3,−2). Find both direction vectors and show that the lines are perpendicular.
Points A(1,2,0), B(3,−1,k), C(0,1,2), D(2,2,1). Find k so that AB is perpendicular to CD.

Determine whether the line through P(0,1,2) and Q(3,3,1) is perpendicular to the line through R(1,0,0) and S(2,−1,4). Justify with a dot product, and if not perpendicular, find the angle between them.
Explain why reversing the direction vector of a line does not affect the perpendicularity test, and why you must use direction vectors rather than position vectors of the endpoints.
Show that \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0\) implies perpendicularity using \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\), stating the condition on the vectors.

notes.t: Perpendicular lines via direction vectors (dot product)
pts: Find the direction vector of each line by subtracting the coordinates of its two endpoints.
Two lines are perpendicular exactly when their direction vectors have zero dot product.
Line 1 runs from (2,3,4) to (1,2,3), giving direction (−1,−1,−1); Line 2 runs from (1,0,2) to (2,3,−2), giving direction (1,3,−4).
The dot product of (−1,−1,−1) and (1,3,−4) is −1−3+4 = 0, so the lines are perpendicular.
defs: Dot product (scalar product)
For vectors a=(a₁,a₂,a₃) and b=(b₁,b₂,b₃), a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃; it equals |a||b|cos θ and is zero when the vectors are perpendicular.
eqs: a, b = direction vectors of the two lines (dimensionless components); \(a_{i}\), \(b_{i}\) = components of each vector
p, q = position vectors of points P and Q (m); PQ = vector from P to Q (m)
tips: Use direction vectors (endpoint differences), not the endpoint position vectors, when testing perpendicularity of lines.
Watch signs when subtracting negative coordinates, e.g. (2,3,−2)−(1,0,2) = (1,3,−4).
rq: Why does subtracting endpoint coordinates give a direction vector for the line rather than a point on it?
The difference q−p is the displacement from P to Q, which is parallel to the line; the endpoints themselves are positions, not directions.
What would the dot product be if the two lines were parallel, and why?
Parallel direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other, so the dot product is nonzero (equal to ±|a||b|), not zero.

notes.t: Direction vectors from two points and perpendicularity via dot product
pts: The vector joining point A (position a) to point B (position b) is found by subtraction.
Two lines are perpendicular exactly when their direction vectors have zero dot product.
The vector AB is parallel to the line joining the two points and serves as its direction vector.
defs: Direction vector
A vector parallel to a line, obtained as the difference of position vectors of two points on the line.
Orthogonal vectors
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) if and only if their dot product equals zero.
eqs: Vector from point A to point B
\mathbf{a} = position vector of A (m); \mathbf{b} = position vector of B (m)
\mathbf{d}_1 = direction vector of first line; \mathbf{d}_2 = direction vector of second line
tips: Compute the direction vector as end point minus start point (b − a), not a − b; the sign does not affect perpendicularity but keep it consistent.
Perpendicularity requires the dot product to be exactly zero; check each component carefully when multiplying and summing.
rq: Why does subtracting position vectors give a vector along the line joining the points?
Because b − a is the displacement from A to B, which travels along the line joining them, so it is parallel to that line.
What if the dot product of the two direction vectors is nonzero?
Then the lines are not perpendicular; they meet at some other angle (not 90°).

notes.t: Checking perpendicularity of two lines using direction vectors
pts: A direction vector for a line through two points is found by subtracting the position vectors of the points (end minus start).
Two lines are perpendicular when their direction vectors have a zero dot product.
The dot product is computed component by component and summed.
defs: Direction vector of a line
A vector parallel to the line, obtained as the difference of position vectors of two points on it.
Orthogonal vectors
Two non-zero vectors whose dot product is zero, meaning they meet at a right angle.
eqs: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} = position vectors of the points (m); \mathbf{d} = direction vector (m)
\mathbf{d}_1, \mathbf{d}_2 = direction vectors (m); result is dimensionless scalar in these units
tips: Compute direction vectors as end point minus start point (b − a), not a − b, to keep the sign convention consistent.
Perpendicularity requires a zero dot product, not a zero vector; check each component sign carefully when multiplying negatives.
rq: Why is subtracting the points in the order start-to-end essential when forming the direction vector?
Reversing the order only flips the sign of the vector, which still gives a parallel direction, but the consistent order (end minus start) is the standard convention for AB = b − a.
What would it mean if the dot product of the two direction vectors were non-zero?
The lines would not be perpendicular; the non-zero value indicates the angle between them is not 90°.

xq.q: Line 1 passes through P(2, 1, −3) and Q(4, 0, 1). Line 2 has direction vector \(\mathbf{d}_2 = (k, 6, 1)\), where k is a constant. Coordinates are in m. Find k so that the two lines are perpendicular.
Line A has direction vector \((2,-1,3)\). Which of the following is a direction vector of a line perpendicular to A?
xq.w: (2)(1)+(−1)(5)+(3)(1) = 0; (−2,1,−3) is parallel (dot product −14), (1,2,1) gives 3, and (3,0,2) gives 12, from sign or arithmetic slips.
s: Compute dot product with each option

xq.q: Line 1 runs from A(2, 3, 4) to B(1, 2, 3). Line 2 runs from C(1, 0, 2) to D(2, 3, −2). Show that the lines are perpendicular, and explain why using the position vectors of the endpoints directly would be wrong.
xq.a: AB = (−1,−1,−1) and CD = (1,3,−4). Dot product = −1 − 3 + 4 = 0, so the lines are perpendicular. The position vectors of endpoints depend on the origin and do not give the line's direction; only the differences do.
s: Endpoint position vectors are not parallel to the lines, so a zero dot product of those would say nothing

units.name: 13.4 Forms of a line in space (planes intersection, Cartesian, parametric)
units.ov: This material covers three ways to describe a line in 3D: as the intersection of two planes (Cartesian/implicit), as parametric equations, and in vector form \(\vec r=\vec r_0+t\vec d\). It then applies these to find the shortest distance between two skew lines via the common perpendicular. Converting between forms gives a point and a direction vector, which feed into the orthogonality conditions used to find the closest points.
must: Vector form of a line: \(\vec r=\vec r_0+t\,\vec d\), with \(\vec r_0\) a known point and \(\vec d\) the direction vector
Read \(\vec d\) from the coefficients of the parameter, watching signs (e.g. \(y=1-s\) gives \(d_y=-1\))
A line in 3D needs two plane equations (Cartesian form); a single equation gives a plane, not a line
Convert Cartesian (two planes) to parametric: set one variable equal to a parameter and solve for the others, or use \(\vec d=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2\)
Representations are not unique: a different point, parameter or scalar multiple of \(\vec d\) gives an equivalent line, so check equivalence
Shortest segment between skew lines is the common perpendicular: \(\overrightarrow{P'Q'}\cdot\vec d_1=\overrightarrow{P'Q'}\cdot\vec d_2=0\)
