Method for skew-line distance: take \(P(t)\) on \(l_1\) and \(Q(s)\) on \(l_2\), form \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\), impose both dot-product conditions, solve the 2×2 system for \(t,s\)
Use different parameters (\(t\) and \(s\)) for the two lines, otherwise the system cannot be solved
The answer is the length \(|\overrightarrow{P'Q'}|\), so take the magnitude after solving
Check by substituting \(t=0\) and \(t=1\), and verify the points lie on the original lines
conn: Cross product and planes: \(\vec d=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2\) links the plane-intersection form to the direction vector of the line
Dot product orthogonality gives a pair of linear equations in \(t,s\), which links vector geometry to solving simultaneous equations
Skew-line distance can also be found with \(|(\vec r_2-\vec r_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|/|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|\), which checks the parametric method
Deciding whether lines intersect, are parallel or are skew (compare directions, then solve for a common point) comes before the distance calculation
exq: Line \(l\) is the intersection of the planes \(x+y+z=3\) and \(x-y+2z=1\). Find a direction vector, write the line in parametric and vector form, and verify that your point lies on both planes.
Given \(l_2: x=2+s,\ y=1-s,\ z=-1+s\), state its direction vector and a point on it, then find a Cartesian form as the intersection of two planes.
Lines \(l_1:\vec r=(1,0,2)+t(1,2,-1)\) and \(l_2:\vec r=(2,1,-1)+s(1,-1,1)\) are given. Show they are skew, and find the closest points \(P'\) and \(Q'\) and the shortest distance between the lines.
Find the shortest distance between two skew lines using the common perpendicular method, then confirm the result using the cross-product formula.

notes.t: Shortest segment between two skew lines (perpendicular distance)
pts: The segment P'Q' joining the two lines must be perpendicular to both direction vectors, so it is the common perpendicular.
Write general points P on l1 and Q on l2 using parameters, then form the vector PQ in terms of both parameters.
Impose the two orthogonality conditions PQ·d1 = 0 and PQ·d2 = 0 to solve for the parameters giving P' and Q'.
The required length is the magnitude of the vector P'Q' once P' and Q' are found.
defs: Common perpendicular
The unique shortest segment between two skew lines, perpendicular to both lines; its endpoints are the closest points on the lines.
eqs: Orthogonality condition for the common perpendicular
\(\overrightarrow{P'Q'}\) = connecting vector (m); \(\vec{d}_1, \vec{d}_2\) = direction vectors of the lines (dimensionless)
tips: Use different parameters (e.g. t and s) for the points on l1 and l2; reusing one parameter loses the freedom needed to solve.
The answer is the length |P'Q'|, not the coordinates; remember to take the magnitude of the vector after solving.
rq: Why must the shortest segment between two skew lines be perpendicular to both lines?
Any displacement along a line that is not perpendicular to it could be shortened by sliding the endpoint along the line, so the minimum occurs when the dot product with each direction vector is zero.

notes.t: Vectors: Cartesian and vectorial forms of a line in space
pts: A line in space can be written as the intersection of two planes, giving its Cartesian (implicit) form.
The Cartesian parametric form expresses each coordinate as a function of a real parameter t, with each coordinate equal to a constant plus a multiple of t.
The vectorial form writes a generic point P on the line as position vector r = r0 + t d, where r0 is a point on the line and d is the direction vector.
The direction vector can be read directly from the coefficients of t in the parametric equations.
defs: Direction vector of a line
A non-zero vector parallel to the line; its components are the coefficients of the parameter t in the parametric equations.
Parametric form of a line
A description of the line by expressing x, y, z each as a function of a real parameter t ∈ ℝ.
eqs: Vectorial (vector parametric) equation of a line through r0 with direction d

\vec{r} = position vector of a generic point (m); \vec{r}_0 = position vector of a known point on the line (m); t = real parameter (dimensionless); \vec{d} = direction vector (dimensionless in this example)
tips: Do not confuse the two forms: the vector equation uses r0 + t d, while the Cartesian form is a system of two plane equations; check the direction vector by substituting t = 0 and t = 1 back into the equations.

Parametric solutions are not unique: a different choice of parameter, point or scalar multiple of d gives an equivalent but different-looking answer, so verify equivalence rather than matching the textbook form exactly.
rq: Why can the same line have many different parametric forms?

Because the choice of point r0 on the line and of direction vector d (any non-zero multiple of the original) is not unique; any point on the line and any vector parallel to it will generate the same set of points.
How do you get the direction vector from the Cartesian (two-plane) form?
Solve the system for x, y, z in terms of one free variable t; the coefficients of t give the direction vector d.

notes.t: Equations of a line in space (Cartesian, parametric, vectorial forms)
pts: A line in space can be written as the intersection of two planes, giving a Cartesian system of two equations.
The parametric form expresses each coordinate as a point plus a multiple of the direction vector, with parameter s real.
The vectorial form writes a generic point Q on the line as the position vector r equal to r0 plus s times the direction vector d.
The direction vector can be read directly from the coefficients of the parameter s in the parametric equations.
defs: Direction vector of a line
A nonzero vector parallel to the line; its components are the coefficients of the parameter in the parametric equations.
Generic point of a line
A point Q whose coordinates are written in terms of a free parameter s, so that every point of the line is obtained by varying s over the reals.
eqs: Vectorial equation of a line through point r0 with direction d

\vec{r} = position vector of a generic point (m); \vec{r}_0 = position vector of a known point on the line (m); s = real parameter (dimensionless); \vec{d} = direction vector (dimensionless components)
x = 2 + s,\quad y = 1 - s,\quad z = -1 + s
x, y, z = coordinates of a point (m); s = real parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the Cartesian form (two plane equations) with the parametric form; a single equation of a line in 3D does not exist.
Watch the signs when reading the direction vector: from y = 1 − s the y-component is −1, not +1.
rq: Why does the direction vector (1, -1, 1) come straight from the parametric equations?
Each coordinate is a constant plus the coefficient of s times s, so the coefficients 1, -1, 1 of s give the components of a vector parallel to the line.
How can you check that the Cartesian system x + y = 3, x - z = 3 really describes the same line as the parametric form?
Substitute x = 2+s, y = 1-s, z = -1+s: x+y = 3 and x−z = 3 hold for every s, so the parametric points satisfy both planes.

xq.q: Line \(l_1\): \(\mathbf{r} = (0,0,0) + t(1,0,0)\) and line \(l_2\): \(\mathbf{r} = (0,0,3) + s(0,1,0)\) (coordinates in m) are skew. Let P = (t,0,0) on \(l_1\) and Q = (0,s,3) on \(l_2\). Using the conditions that PQ is perpendicular to both direction vectors, find the shortest distance between the lines.
xq.a: 3 m

xq.q: A line is given in Cartesian parametric form by \(x = 2 + s\), \(y = 1 - s\), \(z = -1 + s\). What is a direction vector of the line?
o: \((-1,1,-1)\) with the point (2,1,−1) taken as the direction
xq.w: The direction vector is the coefficients of s, (1,−1,1); the traps are using the constants (the point) or dropping the sign of y.
s: Constants (2,1,−1) are a point, not the direction

xq.q: Lines \(l_1\): \(\mathbf{r} = (1,0,0) + t(1,1,0)\) and \(l_2\): \(\mathbf{r} = (0,0,2) + s(0,1,1)\) are given (m). Write the vector PQ between a general point P on \(l_1\) and a general point Q on \(l_2\), and write the two equations that give the closest points. Solve them for t and s.
xq.a: P = (1+t, t, 0), Q = (0, s, 2+s), PQ = (−1−t, s−t, 2+s). PQ·(1,1,0) = −1 − t + s − t = 0 gives s − 2t = 1. PQ·(0,1,1) = s − t + 2 + s = 0 gives 2s − t = −2. Solving: from the first, s = 1 + 2t; then 2 + 4t − t = −2, so t = −4/3, s = −5/3.
s: Use different parameters t and s

units.name: 13.5 Shortest distance between skew lines
units.ov: This material finds the shortest distance between two skew lines (non-parallel, non-intersecting lines in 3D). Method 1 takes generic points P(t) and Q(s), forms PQ, imposes PQ·d₁ = PQ·d₂ = 0, solves the 2×2 linear system and takes |P′Q′|. Method 2 uses the common normal n = d₁ × d₂ and the scalar triple product. Both methods give the same worked-example answer, √2/2 m, so each can check the other.
must: Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting; the shortest distance is the length of the unique common perpendicular segment P′Q′
Read direction vectors \(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2\) correctly from the symmetric form, watching the signs of the y and z components
Form \(\overrightarrow{PQ}=Q-P\) with generic points using distinct parameters (t for l₁, s for l₂), and keep the sign convention consistent
Impose both conditions \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\mathbf{d}_1=0\) and \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\mathbf{d}_2=0\); using only one gives wrong endpoints
Solve the resulting 2×2 linear system for s and t, then substitute back to get P′ and Q′
Distance is \(|\overrightarrow{P'Q'}|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\), the positive root, in metres; do not confuse the vector with its length
Formula method: \(d=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\mathbf{d}_1\times\mathbf{d}_2)|}{|\mathbf{d}_1\times\mathbf{d}_2|}\) with A on l₁ and B on l₂
The normal \(\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{d}_1\times\mathbf{d}_2\) may be scaled by any nonzero constant, but the denominator must be the magnitude of the same scaled vector
Worked example: both methods give \(|P'Q'|=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\) m, with \(\overrightarrow{PQ}=(2+s-t,\,-1-s+t,\,-3+s+t)\)
Take the absolute value of the scalar triple product so the distance is non-negative
conn: Dot product (orthogonality) leads to a linear system in two parameters, which gives the points and then the distance via a vector magnitude
Cross product gives the common normal direction, and projecting AB onto it (scalar triple product) replaces solving the system

Converting lines between symmetric and parametric form is needed to get direction vectors and generic points; a distance of zero means the lines intersect, and parallel lines (d₁ × d₂ = 0) need a different method
Both methods should agree, so use one as a check on the other
exq: Two lines are given in symmetric form. Find their direction vectors, show they are skew, and find the shortest distance between them by parametrising generic points P and Q and imposing PQ·d₁ = PQ·d₂ = 0.
Using the same lines, verify the distance with \(d=|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\mathbf{d}_1\times\mathbf{d}_2)|/|\mathbf{d}_1\times\mathbf{d}_2|\), choosing suitable points A and B.
Given \(\overrightarrow{PQ}=(2+s-t,\,-1-s+t,\,-3+s+t)\) and suitable d₁ and d₂, derive the two linear equations in s and t, solve them, and find P′, Q′ and \(|P'Q'|\) (expected √2/2 m).
Show that simplifying (scaling) the normal vector n does not change the shortest distance, and explain what happens if d₁ × d₂ = 0.
Explain why using only one perpendicularity condition fails to give the shortest distance, and find the coordinates of the feet of the common perpendicular for a given pair of lines.

notes.t: Shortest distance between two skew lines: perpendicular vector PQ
pts: The vector PQ joining generic points on the two lines is built from the difference of their position vectors
The shortest distance is found when PQ is perpendicular to both direction vectors of the lines
Perpendicularity is imposed as two dot-product conditions, one for each line's direction vector
defs: Generic points on the lines
Points P and Q whose positions depend on free parameters s and t, one parameter per line, so that PQ can be expressed in terms of s and t.
eqs: Vector joining generic points P and Q (difference of position vectors)
s, t = line parameters (dimensionless); components of \overrightarrow{PQ} in metres (m)
Perpendicularity conditions fixing the shortest-distance points
\vec{d}_1, \vec{d}_2 = direction vectors of l1 and l2 (dimensionless); \overrightarrow{PQ} = connecting vector (m)
tips: Do not confuse the vector from P to Q with its length; the dot-product equations give the parameters, and the distance is then the magnitude of PQ.
Keep the sign order consistent when subtracting the second point's position from the first (PQ = Q − P vs P − Q changes signs of components).
rq: Why must the connecting vector PQ be perpendicular to both lines, rather than just one, to give the shortest distance?
The distance between skew lines is minimised only when PQ is orthogonal to both directions; any component of PQ along either line could be reduced by moving P or Q along that line.
Why does the difference Q − P use the parameters s and t instead of fixed numbers?
Because P and Q can slide along their lines, so the shortest connection is found by optimising over s and t via the two perpendicularity conditions.

notes.t: Perpendicular distance between skew lines via orthogonal projection
pts: The connecting vector PQ is perpendicular to both direction vectors, so its dot product with each direction vector must be zero.
Setting both dot products to zero gives a linear system in parameters s and t that is solved to locate the common perpendicular's endpoints P′ and Q′.
Once P′ and Q′ are found, the shortest distance is the length of the vector P′Q′.
defs: Orthogonal (perpendicular) vectors
Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product equals zero.
eqs: \overrightarrow{PQ} = connecting vector between points on the two lines (m); \vec{d}_1 = direction vector of first line (dimensionless)
tips: Make sure both dot products are set to zero, not just one; using only one condition gives the wrong endpoints.
Check the vector P′Q′ is computed from the correct parameter values before taking its magnitude.
rq: Why must the connecting vector be perpendicular to both direction vectors to give the shortest distance?
The shortest segment between two skew lines is the common perpendicular; any other connecting segment is longer, so its direction must be orthogonal to both lines.
What does the system s − 3t + 6 = 0 and 3s − t = 0 tell you about the endpoints?
It fixes the parameter values s and t that place P′ and Q′ on the lines so the connecting segment is perpendicular to both.

notes.t: Shortest distance between skew lines: perpendicular segment P'Q'
pts: P' and Q' are generic points on l₁ and l₂, parameterised by t and s
The connecting vector P'Q' is perpendicular to both lines, so its dot product with each direction vector must vanish
Direction vectors are read off from the symmetric form of each line
Once P' and Q' are found, the segment length is the magnitude of the connecting vector
defs: Skew lines
Two lines in 3D that are neither parallel nor intersecting.
Shortest distance between skew lines
The length of the unique segment perpendicular to both lines, joining a point on each line.
eqs: P' = point on l₁ (m); Q' = point on l₂ (m)
d₁, d₂ = direction vectors of l₁, l₂ (dimensionless components)
tips: Direction vectors come from the symmetric form: for x−2 = s the x-component of d₂ is 1, but a sign error in y or z changes the answer.
Keep parameters distinct (t for l₁, s for l₂) when forming the connecting vector to avoid mixing variables.
rq: Why must the dot product with both direction vectors be zero rather than just one?
The shortest segment must be perpendicular to both lines; perpendicularity to only one line leaves the segment free to be shortened along the other.
Why are parameters t and s used for the two lines rather than the same letter?
Each point moves independently along its own line, so two different parameters are needed to describe all pairs of points.

notes.t: Perpendicularity conditions and distance between points P' and Q'
pts: A vector joining two points must be orthogonal to both direction vectors of the lines, so its dot product with each direction vector is zero.
Each perpendicularity condition gives a linear equation in the parameters s and t, forming a 2×2 system solved by substitution.
Once the parameters are found, substitute them back into the line equations to get the points P' and Q'.
The distance between two points is the magnitude of the vector joining them, computed from the square root of the sum of squared components.
defs: Orthogonal vectors
Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) when their dot product equals zero.
eqs: Perpendicularity condition between the connecting vector and a direction vector
\(\overrightarrow{P'Q'}\) = vector from P' to Q' (m); \(\mathbf{d}_1\) = direction vector of the first line (dimensionless)
tips: Watch signs when expanding the dot product, e.g. the term (−s + t − 1)(−1) is easy to mis-sign.
Distance is a magnitude, so always take the positive square root and keep the unit of length.
rq: Why must the dot product of the connecting vector with each direction vector be zero?
Because the connecting vector is the common perpendicular to both lines, so it is orthogonal to each direction vector.
Why does the system of two linear equations in s and t have a unique solution here?
Because the two equations are independent (their coefficient matrix is non-singular), so substitution gives one value each for s and t.

notes.t: Shortest distance between skew lines (alternative method)
pts: The shortest distance between skew lines equals the projection of AB onto the common normal direction, computed with a scalar triple product over the magnitude of the cross product.
The normal vector n = d₁ × d₂ can be scaled by any nonzero constant without changing the distance, so simplifying n is allowed.
The result is cross-checked against the step-by-step method, giving the same distance |P′Q′| = √2/2.
defs: Skew lines
Two lines in three-dimensional space that are neither parallel nor intersecting.
eqs: Shortest distance between two skew lines

d = shortest distance (m); \(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2\) = direction vectors of the lines (dimensionless); \(A\in l_1,\ B\in l_2\) = points on each line; \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) = vector from A to B (m)
tips: Use the magnitude of the cross product in the denominator; forgetting it or using a non-normalised normal gives a wrong distance.
Take the absolute value of the scalar triple product so the distance is non-negative.
rq: Why can the normal vector (−2, −2, 0) be replaced by (1, 1, 0) without changing the answer?
Because the distance formula is a ratio in which any nonzero scalar multiple of the normal cancels between numerator and denominator.

xq.q: Line \(l_1\) is \(\mathbf{r}=(0,0,0)+t(1,1,0)\) and line \(l_2\) is \(\mathbf{r}=(1,0,2)+s(0,1,1)\), with coordinates in metres and \(s,t\) dimensionless. Let P be a general point on \(l_1\) and Q a general point on \(l_2\). Find the values of \(t\) and \(s\) for which \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) is perpendicular to both lines, and hence find the shortest distance between the lines.
xq.a: \(\sqrt{3}\approx1.73\) m

xq.q: Two skew lines have direction vectors \(\mathbf{d}_1=(1,2,2)\) and \(\mathbf{d}_2=(2,1,-2)\). Which vector is parallel to the common perpendicular joining the lines?
xq.w: The common perpendicular is perpendicular to both directions, so it is parallel to d1×d2=(−6,6,−3)∝(2,−2,1); adding or subtracting the directions, or multiplying components, does not give a vector orthogonal to both.

xq.q: Line \(l_1\) is \(\mathbf{r}=(t,0,0)\) and line \(l_2\) is \(\mathbf{r}=(2,s,1)\), where \(s,t\) are dimensionless and coordinates are in metres. Show that the lines are skew and find the shortest distance between them.
xq.a: Directions (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) are not parallel. Equal points would need z: 0=1, impossible, so no intersection; the lines are skew. With P=(t,0,0), Q=(2,s,1), PQ=(2−t,s,1). PQ·d1=2−t=0 gives t=2; PQ·d2=s=0 gives s=0. PQ=(0,0,1), so the shortest distance is 1 m.
s: Directions not scalar multiples, so not parallel
z-coordinates 0 and 1 never match, so no intersection, hence skew
PQ=(2−t,s,1); both dot products zero give t=2, s=0

units.name: 13.6 Vector equation of a plane
units.ov: A plane is defined by a point A (position vector a) and a normal vector n. Any point P on the plane satisfies AP·n = 0, which gives the dot-product form r·n = a·n. This rearranges to the scalar form r·n = p and the Cartesian form αx+βy+γz = p. When n is a unit vector, p is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
must: Vector equation of a plane: \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} \), where a is a known point on the plane and n is the normal
Derivation: P lies in the plane exactly when \( \overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a} \) is perpendicular to n, so \( (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{n}=0 \)
Scalar form: \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p \) with \( p=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} \)
Cartesian form: for \( \mathbf{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \), \( \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p \). The coefficients of x, y, z are the components of the normal
Distance from the origin: p is the perpendicular distance only if n is a unit vector. Otherwise use \( p/|\mathbf{n}| \), with \( |\mathbf{n}|=\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2} \)
Normalising: \( \hat{\mathbf{n}}=\mathbf{n}/|\mathbf{n}| \); divide both sides of the plane equation by \( |\mathbf{n}| \) to get the unit-normal form
The normal must be perpendicular to the whole plane, i.e. to every direction in it, not just to one line drawn in it
Use the difference vector \( \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a} \), which lies in the plane, and not the position vectors themselves, in the perpendicularity condition
Scaling n by any nonzero constant gives the same plane (the constant p scales with it). Sign and direction of n only change which side is 'positive'
conn: Dot product and perpendicularity: the plane equation is just \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \) applied to the vector \( \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a} \) and n
Cross product: when the normal is not given, find it from two in-plane vectors, \( \mathbf{n}=\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC} \), for a plane through three points

Vector equation of a line: intersecting a line \( \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{d} \) with a plane (substitute into \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p \) and solve for t), and the angle between a line and a plane or between two planes (via normals)
Distance and projection: the distance from a point to a plane uses the unit normal and the projection of a vector onto n, which links to mechanics problems with surfaces and forces normal to them
exq: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the plane through A(1, 2, 3) with normal \( \mathbf{n}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k} \). Then find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
Find the equation of the plane through A(1,0,0), B(0,2,0) and C(0,0,3), giving the answer in the form \( \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n}=p \) and in Cartesian form.
The plane \( 3x-4y+12z=26 \) is given. Write it in unit-normal form and state the distance from the origin. Does the point (2, 1, 2) lie on it?
Find where the line \( \mathbf{r}=(1,1,1)+t(2,-1,3) \) meets the plane \( \mathbf{r}\cdot(1,2,-1)=4 \), and find the angle between the line and the plane.
Show that \( (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{n}=0 \) leads to \( \alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p \), and explain why p is a distance only for a unit normal.

notes.t: Vector Equation of a Plane
pts: A plane is fixed by a point A with position vector a and a normal vector n perpendicular to the plane.
Any point P in the plane gives a vector AP = r − a that lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to n.
The perpendicularity condition is a zero dot product, which rearranges to a scalar form of the plane equation.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A vector perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane; it fixes the plane's orientation.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane (dot product form)
\mathbf{r} = position vector of any point P in the plane (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector (dimensionless direction or N if scaled); \mathbf{a} = position vector of a known point A in the plane (m)
Scalar form of the plane equation
\mathbf{r} = position vector of point P (m); \mathbf{n} = normal vector; \(p\) = constant equal to \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}\) (m for unit normal)
tips: Do not confuse position vectors with the vector AP = r − a; the equation uses the difference vector lying in the plane.
The normal n must be perpendicular to the plane, not to a line drawn within it.
rq: Why does the dot product (r − a)·n equal zero for every point P in the plane?
Because r − a is the vector AP, which lies in the plane, and n is perpendicular to the plane, so the angle between them is 90° and cos 90° = 0.
What would change if you used a different point A in the plane?
The vector a changes, but a·n stays the same, so the constant p is unchanged; the equation describes the same plane.

notes.t: Vector Equation of a Plane (2)
pts: A plane is fixed by a point A with position vector a and a normal vector n; any point P with position vector r lies on the plane when AP is perpendicular to n.
Taking the dot product of r with the normal n gives the general form of the plane's equation.
If n is a unit vector, the constant p equals the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
Writing n = (α, β, γ) turns the vector form into a Cartesian equation in x, y, z.
defs: Normal vector n
A vector perpendicular to every direction lying within the plane.
eqs: Vector equation of a plane through point A with normal n
r = position vector of a general point on the plane (m); a = position vector of a fixed point A on the plane (m); n = normal vector (dimensionless direction if unit)
Plane with unit normal, distance from origin
p = perpendicular distance from origin to plane (m); n = unit normal vector
α, β, γ = components of n (dimensionless); x, y, z = coordinates (m); p = distance from origin (m)
tips: Only the unit-normal form r · n = p gives p as a distance; for a non-unit normal divide by |n|.
Check that the normal is perpendicular to the plane, not parallel to a line lying in it.
rq: Why does the dot product r · n equal the same constant for every point on the plane?
Because the vector AP lies in the plane and is perpendicular to n, so (r − a) · n = 0, making r · n = a · n constant.
What happens to p if the normal n is not a unit vector?
p no longer equals the perpendicular distance from the origin; the distance must be found as p divided by the magnitude of n.

xq.q: A plane passes through the point A with position vector \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,3)\) m and has normal vector \(\mathbf{n}=(2,-1,2)\). Find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
xq.a: 2 m

xq.q: A plane passes through A with position vector \(\mathbf{a}=(2,0,1)\) m and has normal \(\mathbf{n}=(1,-2,2)\). Which is its Cartesian equation?
xq.w: The constant is a·n=2+0+2=4; adding the components of a gives 3, a sign slip gives −4, and using a as the normal gives 2x+z=5.

xq.q: A plane has Cartesian equation \(2x-2y+z=9\) with x, y, z in metres. Show that it can be written as \(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}=p\) with \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) a unit normal, and hence find the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane.
xq.a: The plane is r·n=9 with n=(2,−2,1). |n|=3, so n̂=(2/3,−2/3,1/3) and dividing by 3 gives r·n̂=3. Only for a unit normal is the constant the distance from the origin, so the distance is 3 m.
s: Read off n=(2,−2,1) from the Cartesian form, r·n=9
Divide both sides by 3: r·n̂=3 with n̂ a unit vector
So p=3 m is the distance from the origin

units.name: 13.7 Line–plane intersection
units.ov: This material covers the parametric (vector) equation of a line in 3D, \(\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{d}\), and how to find where it meets a plane \(ax+by+cz=d\). The method is to substitute the line's parametric coordinates into the plane equation, solve the resulting linear equation for \(t\), and substitute back to get the point. The number of solutions for \(t\) tells you whether the line crosses, is parallel to, or lies in the plane.
must: Parametric line: \(\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{d}\), which expands to \(x=a_1+td_1,\ y=a_2+td_2,\ z=a_3+td_3\)
A line is fixed by a point on it plus a non-zero direction vector; any scalar multiple of \(\mathbf{d}\) is also a valid direction
Worked example line: point \((1,2,4)\), direction \((1,1,2)\), so \(x=1+t,\ y=2+t,\ z=4+2t\)
Intersection method: substitute \(x(t),y(t),z(t)\) into \(ax+by+cz=d\), giving one linear equation in \(t\)
Solve for \(t\), then substitute it into all three parametric equations to get the full point \((x,y,z)\)
Example plane \(x+3y-4z=5\): substituting gives \((1+t)+3(2+t)-4(4+2t)=5\), so \(-9-4t=5\) and \(t=-7/2\), giving the point \((-5/2,\,-3/2,\,-3)\)
Classify the result: a unique \(t\) means a single intersection point; no solution (\(0=k\), \(k\ne0\)) means the line is parallel to the plane; an identity (\(0=0\)) means the line lies in the plane
Always check the answer by putting the point back into the plane equation
Common errors: not distributing signs when expanding brackets such as \(-4(4+2t)\), and confusing the parameter \(t\) with the coordinates
The plane's coefficients \((a,b,c)\) form its normal vector; the line is parallel to the plane exactly when \(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}=0\)
conn: Dot product and normal vector: the substitution gives \(t(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d})=d-\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{a}\), so \(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}=0\) is the parallel or in-plane case
Angle between a line and a plane: use \(\sin\theta=|\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}|/(|\mathbf{n}||\mathbf{d}|)\), usually asked right after finding the intersection point
Line through two points: build \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\) first, then intersect with a plane (for example a plane through three points found by a cross product)
Linear systems: the intersection is a 3-equation, 3-unknown system, with unique, none or infinite solutions matching the three geometric cases
exq: Find the line through \((1,2,4)\) with direction \((1,1,2)\) in parametric form and its intersection with the plane \(x+3y-4z=5\). Verify your answer.
Show that the line \(\mathbf{r}=(2,0,1)+t(1,2,-1)\) is parallel to the plane \(x+y+3z=4\). Determine whether it lies in the plane or not.
A line passes through \(A(1,0,2)\) and \(B(3,4,-2)\). Find where it meets the plane \(2x-y+z=7\) and the angle between the line and the plane.
For what value of \(k\) does the line \(\mathbf{r}=(1,1,1)+t(2,k,1)\) lie in the plane \(x-y-2z=-2\)? Explain what happens for other values of \(k\).

notes.t: Parametric equation of a line and intersection with a plane
pts: A line is defined by a point on it and a direction vector; the point (1, 2, 4) and direction (1, 1, 2) give its parametric form.
To find where the line meets a plane, substitute the parametric coordinates of the line into the plane equation and solve for the parameter.
The intersection point is found by substituting the parameter value back into the line's parametric equations.
defs: Direction vector of a line
A non-zero vector parallel to the line; any scalar multiple of it is also a valid direction.
eqs: Parametric equation of a line through point \(\mathbf{a}\) with direction \(\mathbf{d}\)
\(\mathbf{r}\) = position vector (m); \(\mathbf{a}\) = position vector of given point (m); \(\mathbf{d}\) = direction vector (dimensionless in this example); \(t\) = scalar parameter (dimensionless)
tips: Keep the parameter \(t\) distinct from coordinate variables when substituting into the plane equation.
Check the intersection point satisfies the plane equation before final answer.
rq: Why must you substitute the line's parametric x, y, z into the plane equation rather than intersecting using the point alone?

Because the point (1, 2, 4) is only one point on the line; the intersection point is a different point on the line, found by determining the specific parameter \(t\) that satisfies the plane equation.
What happens if the direction vector is perpendicular to the plane's normal \((1, 3, -4)\)?
The line is parallel to the plane; substituting gives a contradiction (no solution) unless the line lies in the plane, then infinitely many solutions.

notes.t: Equation of a line and intersection with a plane
pts: A line in 3D is defined by a point on it and a direction vector parallel to it.
The vector equation r = r₀ + t d expands into parametric equations for x, y and z.
To find an intersection with a plane, substitute the parametric equations of the line into the plane's Cartesian equation to get an equation in t alone.
After solving for t, substitute back into the line's equations to get the intersection point coordinates.
defs: Direction vector
A non-zero vector parallel to a line, which determines the line's orientation in space.
eqs: \mathbf{r} = position vector of a general point (m); \mathbf{r}_0 = position vector of a known point on the line (m); t = scalar parameter (dimensionless); \mathbf{d} = direction vector (dimensionless in this example)
tips: If the substituted equation in t has no solution, the line is parallel to the plane; if every t works, the line lies in the plane.
Substituting t back must be done into all three parametric equations to obtain the full coordinates of the intersection point.
rq: Why must the direction vector be non-zero, and what would happen to the line if it were zero?
A zero direction vector gives no direction, so the equation r = r₀ + t·0 describes only the single point r₀, not a line.
Why does substituting the parametric equations into the plane equation produce a single equation in t?
Each of x, y, z is written in terms of t, so the plane equation becomes one linear equation in t; solving it gives the unique parameter value where the line meets the plane.

notes.t: Intersection of a line with a plane (substitution method)
pts: Substitute the parametric expressions for x, y and z of the line into the plane equation to get a single equation in the parameter t.
Solve the resulting linear equation for t, then substitute back into the parametric equations to get the intersection point.
Verify the intersection point by plugging its coordinates back into the original plane equation.
eqs: x, y, z = Cartesian coordinates (m); 5 = constant term (dimensionless here)
tips: Be careful when expanding brackets such as −4(4 + 2t); the sign of every term must be distributed correctly.
Substitute the value of t back into all three parametric equations, not just one, to obtain the full point (x, y, z).
rq: Why does substituting the line's parametric form into the plane equation give exactly one value of t when the line is not parallel to the plane?
The substituted equation is linear in t with a non-zero coefficient (here −4), so it has a unique solution; a zero coefficient would mean the line is parallel to the plane.
How can you check an intersection point without redoing the whole calculation?
Substitute the point's coordinates into the plane equation; if the left side equals the right side, the point lies on the plane.

xq.q: A cable lies along the line \(\mathbf{r}=(1,2,4)+t(1,1,2)\) (coordinates in m, t dimensionless). It meets a flat panel with equation \(2x+y-z=7\). Find the point of intersection and the distance along the cable from the point (1, 2, 4) m to the panel.
xq.a: Intersection at (8, 9, 18) m; distance 7√6 ≈ 17.15 m

xq.q: The line \(\mathbf{r}=(0,1,2)+t(2,1,-1)\) and the plane \(x+y+3z=3\) are given. What happens when the line's parametric equations are substituted into the plane equation?
xq.a: The t terms cancel and the equation is inconsistent (7 = 3), so the line is parallel to the plane and does not meet it
o: The line meets the plane at t = 0
The line meets the plane at t = −4
The line lies in the plane
The t terms cancel and the equation is inconsistent (7 = 3), so the line is parallel to the plane and does not meet it
xq.w: Substituting gives 2t+(1+t)+3(2−t)=7, independent of t, and 7≠3 so there is no solution; the trap is treating the leftover constants as a value of t or assuming it lies in the plane.
s: 7=3 is impossible, so no intersection (d·n=0, parallel)

xq.q: A line is given by \(\mathbf{r}=(2,0,1)+t(1,-1,2)\) and a plane by \(x+y+z=7\), with coordinates in metres. Find the point where the line meets the plane and verify your answer.
xq.a: x=2+t, y=−t, z=1+2t. Substituting: 2+t−t+1+2t=3+2t=7, so t=2. Point is (4, −2, 5) m. Check: 4−2+5=7 ✓.
s: Write parametric equations x=2+t, y=−t, z=1+2t
Substitute t=2 into all three equations: (4, −2, 5)

units.name: 13.8 Distance from a point to a plane and plane conversions
units.ov: This material covers finding the shortest distance from a point to a plane by dropping a perpendicular line onto the plane and measuring the length of that segment. It also covers converting a plane's Cartesian equation to vector form \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\) and finding where a line meets a plane. The ideas connect through the normal vector, which gives the plane's orientation, the direction of the perpendicular line and the dot product used to solve for the parameter \(t\).
must: The shortest distance from a point to a plane is measured along the normal, so the perpendicular line through P has direction \(\boldsymbol{n}\).
For \(ax+by+cz=d\), the normal is \(\boldsymbol{n}=(a,b,c)\); never use the constant \(d\) (e.g. 13) as a component.

The vector form of a plane is \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\), where \(p=\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\) for any known point \(\boldsymbol{a}\) on the plane, so the Cartesian constant equals \(p\).
The perpendicular line through P is \(\boldsymbol{r}=\overrightarrow{OP}+t\boldsymbol{n}\).
To find the foot Q, substitute the general point of the line into the plane equation and solve for \(t\): \(t=\dfrac{p-\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}}{\boldsymbol{d}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}}\).
Expand \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\) fully, including the \(t(\boldsymbol{d}\cdot\boldsymbol{n})\) term; forgetting the direction vector's dot product is the commonest error.
Substitute \(t\) back into the line to get \(\overrightarrow{OQ}=\overrightarrow{OP}+t\boldsymbol{n}\), the foot of the perpendicular.
Distance \(=|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=|\overrightarrow{OP}-\overrightarrow{OQ}|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}\); give a positive scalar with units.
Shortcut check: when the line direction is \(\boldsymbol{n}\), distance \(=|t|\,|\boldsymbol{n}|\), and \(t\) is the same one found from the substitution.
Sanity-check by substituting Q back into the plane equation, and check that \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) is parallel to \(\boldsymbol{n}\).
conn: Dot products link plane equations to lines: \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\) turns a line-plane intersection into a single linear equation in \(t\).
The normal vector serves as both the plane's orientation and the direction of the perpendicular line, so point-plane distance reduces to a line-plane intersection followed by a vector magnitude.
Cartesian and vector plane forms are interchangeable, and questions often ask you to convert between them before finding the intersection.
Vector subtraction and magnitude (\(\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}\)) finish the problem, so arithmetic and sign errors in \(t\) feed directly into the final distance.
exq: Find the distance from P(1, 2, 3) to the plane \(2x+y+2z=13\). Give the foot of the perpendicular Q and \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\).
Write the plane \(3x-2y+z=7\) in the form \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\), using a point on the plane to verify \(p\).
Find where the line \(\boldsymbol{r}=(1,0,2)+t(2,1,2)\) meets the plane \(x+2y+2z=13\), and state the value of \(t\).
Show that the line through P(0, 0, 0) in direction \(\boldsymbol{n}=(2,1,2)\) meets \(2x+y+2z=9\) at the point where \(t=1\), and hence find the distance from P to the plane.

notes.t: Distance from a point to a plane using a perpendicular line and projection point Q
pts: The shortest distance from a point to a plane is measured along the normal direction, so find the line through P perpendicular to the plane.
The normal vector of the plane is read from the coefficients of x, y, z in the plane equation.
Q is the intersection of the perpendicular line with the plane; the distance equals the length of segment PQ.
The required distance is the magnitude of the vector from P to Q, equivalently of OP minus OQ.
defs: Normal vector to a plane
A vector perpendicular to every direction lying in the plane; for ax+by+cz=d it is (a,b,c).
Foot of the perpendicular
The point Q on a plane where the line through a given point P perpendicular to the plane meets the plane.
eqs: Distance from point P to plane via perpendicular foot Q
\overrightarrow{OP} = position vector of P (m); \overrightarrow{OQ} = position vector of foot Q (m)
tips: Use the coefficients of the plane equation as the normal direction; do not use the constant 13 as a component.
Distance is a length: take the magnitude of PQ, and check the result is non-negative.
rq: Why must the line used be perpendicular to the plane rather than any other line through P?
Only the perpendicular gives the shortest path from P to the plane; any other segment to the plane is longer by Pythagoras.
How can Q be found directly once the normal vector is known?
Parametrise the line as P + t·n with n = (1,2,2), substitute into x+2y+2z=13, solve for t, then substitute t back to get Q.

notes.t: Converting a plane's Cartesian equation to vector form and finding where a line meets a pl
pts: A plane \(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z=p\) has normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), so its vector form is \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\).
The constant \(p\) equals \(\boldsymbol{a}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\) for any point \(\boldsymbol{a}\) lying on the plane.
A line in vector form is \(\boldsymbol{r}=\overrightarrow{OP}+t\boldsymbol{n}\), where \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) is the position vector of a point on the line and \(\boldsymbol{n}\) is its direction.
The intersection of a line and a plane is found by substituting the line's general point into the plane equation and solving for the parameter \(t\).
eqs: Vector form of a plane with normal \(\boldsymbol{n}\)

\(\boldsymbol{r}\) = position vector of a general point (m); \(\boldsymbol{n}\) = normal vector (dimensionless components here); \(p\) = constant (scalar, same units as \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\))
\(\boldsymbol{r}\) = position vector (m); \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) = position vector of a fixed point (m); \(t\) = scalar parameter (dimensionless); \(\boldsymbol{n}\) = direction vector
tips: Do not confuse the constant \(p\) with a coordinate; it is found by dotting a known point on the plane with the normal, not read off directly.

When solving for the intersection, carefully expand \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}\) including the \(t\)-term, since the direction vector's dot product with \(\boldsymbol{n}\) is often forgotten.
rq: Why is the normal vector \(\boldsymbol{n}=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) read directly from the coefficients of \(x,y,z\)?

Because the dot product \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z\) must reproduce the left-hand side of the Cartesian equation, so the coefficients form the vector perpendicular to the plane.
What if the line's direction vector were parallel to the plane's normal vector — would the line meet the plane?

Not necessarily in general; the line is perpendicular to the plane, so it always meets the plane at exactly one point, unless the line's starting point is not handled; the substitution gives a unique \(t\).
How would you find \(t\) once you substitute the line into the plane equation?

notes.t: Line-plane intersection and distance from a point to a plane using vectors
pts: Substitute the parametric line into the plane equation and solve for the parameter t to find the intersection point Q.
The position vector of Q is found by adding t times the direction vector to the point on the line.
The displacement from P to Q is the difference of position vectors, and its magnitude gives the distance.
The length of a vector is found from the square root of the sum of squares of its components.
defs: Parametric line
A line written as r = a + t·d, where a is a point on the line, d is its direction vector, and t is a scalar parameter.
Unit normal vector
A vector perpendicular to a plane with magnitude 1, indicating the plane's orientation.
eqs: Parameter of intersection of line with plane
\mathbf{a} = point on line (m); \mathbf{d} = direction vector (–); \mathbf{n} = plane normal (–); t = line parameter (–)
tips: Do not forget the factor from the direction vector when computing d·n; the result t = 1 depends on the full dot product 9.
Distance is a magnitude, so always give a positive value with units (e.g. 3 m) rather than a signed vector.
rq: Why does the dot product of the line equation with the normal (1, 2, 2) reduce the problem to a single linear equation in t?
Because the plane condition is r·n = 13, so substituting the line gives a dot product that is linear in t, which can be solved directly.
Why is PQ = OQ − OP and not OP − OQ?
Because the vector from P to Q points from the start point P to the end point Q, which equals the position of Q minus the position of P.

xq.q: A plane has Cartesian equation \(2x+y+2z=13\) and a point P has position vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}=(0,-1,-2)\) m. The line through P perpendicular to the plane meets the plane at the foot Q. Find the position vector of Q and hence the shortest distance from P to the plane.
xq.a: Q = (4, 1, 2) m; shortest distance PQ = 6 m
s: Normal n = (2,1,2), so the line is r = (0,-1,-2) + t(2,1,2)
Substitute into the plane: 2(2t)+(-1+t)+2(-2+2t) = 9t-5 = 13, so t = 2

xq.q: A line is r = (1,0,2) + t(2,1,1) with lengths in m, and a plane is x + 2y + 2z = 11. At what value of the parameter t does the line meet the plane?
xq.w: Substituting gives 5 + 6t = 11 because d·n = 2+2+2 = 6, so t = 1; dropping d·n gives 6, using the sum of d's components (4) gives 3/2, and a sign slip gives −1.

xq.q: A plane has Cartesian equation \(3x-2y+z=7\). (a) Write down its vector form \(\boldsymbol{r}\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=p\), finding \(p\) by using the point A(1, 0, 4) on the plane. (b) Explain why \(p\) is not simply read off as a coordinate of A.
xq.a: (a) n = (3,−2,1). A lies on the plane since 3(1) − 0 + 4 = 7. Then p = a·n = (1,0,4)·(3,−2,1) = 3+0+4 = 7, so r·(3,−2,1) = 7. (b) p is the dot product of any point on the plane with the normal, a scalar that is the same for every point on the plane. A coordinate of A is just one component of one point.
s: p comes from dotting a plane point with n, not from a coordinate

units.name: 1 Block 3 overview and course outline
units.ov: The supplied notes are only title and outline slides for Engineering Mathematics 1, Block 3: Matrix Algebra, Sequences, Series and Limits. They contain no worked content, definitions or formulae, so the report below reflects the standard syllabus for these topics and is not drawn from the notes themselves. The block links matrix methods for linear systems with the analysis of sequences, series and limits, which together underpin later engineering modelling.
must: Matrix operations: addition, multiplication (non-commutative, \(AB\neq BA\)), transpose and \((AB)^T=B^TA^T\)
Determinants and inverses: \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}(A)\), exists only if \(\det A\neq0\); \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\)
Solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) by Gaussian elimination, and the cases of unique, no or infinitely many solutions (rank)
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors: solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\), then \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0\)
Sequences: definition, convergence to a limit \(L\), and the behaviour of \(r^n\) and \(1/n\)
Limit laws and techniques: algebraic manipulation, squeeze theorem, L'Hôpital's rule for \(0/0\) and \(\infty/\infty\)
Series: partial sums \(S_n\), geometric series \(\sum ar^k=\frac{a}{1-r}\) for \(|r|<1\), and the divergence test
Convergence tests: ratio test, comparison test, and the p-series and harmonic series
Power series and Taylor/Maclaurin expansions, e.g. \(e^x=\sum x^n/n!\), with radius of convergence
conn: Gaussian elimination and the determinant both decide whether \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a unique solution; \(\det A=0\) means a zero eigenvalue and a singular matrix
Series convergence is a limit of partial sums, so limit techniques such as L'Hôpital and the ratio limit feed directly into convergence tests
Matrix powers \(A^n\) via diagonalisation give sequences whose convergence depends on whether eigenvalues satisfy \(|\lambda|<1\)
Taylor series use limits and sequences of polynomial approximations, with the error assessed through convergence
exq: Given a 3×3 matrix \(A\), find \(\det A\) and \(A^{-1}\), then use it to solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) and verify the answer.
Use Gaussian elimination to solve a 3×3 system containing a parameter \(k\), and state for which values of \(k\) there is a unique solution, none, or infinitely many.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and state the diagonalisation.
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x - x}{x^3}\) and \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3n^2+1}{5n^2-n}\), justifying each method.
Determine whether \(\sum \frac{n!}{3^n}\) and \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2+1}\) converge, naming the test used, and find the radius of convergence of \(\sum \frac{x^n}{n2^n}\).

units.name: 1 Block 3 overview and recap of determinants
units.ov: This material recaps determinants, minors and cofactors for square matrices, the first stage of Block 3 on matrix algebra. A determinant is a single scalar summarising a matrix, for example whether it is invertible. Minors and cofactors are the building blocks for computing determinants by expansion, and they lead directly to the matrix inverse covered next.
must: A determinant is a single scalar (no units) computed from a square matrix only; it indicates whether the matrix is invertible (\(\det A\neq 0\))
Minor \(M_{ij}\): the determinant of the submatrix left after deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\)
Cofactor \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\); the sign is set by the position of the entry
The checkerboard sign pattern \(\begin{pmatrix}+&-&+\\-&+&-\\+&-&+\end{pmatrix}\); forgetting it is the most common error
Cofactor expansion along any row or column: \(\det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}\)
Exploit matrix properties (zeros, triangular or diagonal form, etc.) and expand along the row or column with the most zeros to save work
2x2 determinant: \(\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc\)
A minor is a determinant of a smaller matrix, not a matrix entry; do not confuse the two
Minors and cofactors lead to the cofactor matrix, the adjugate and the inverse \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}(A)\)
conn: Cofactors link to the inverse: the cofactor matrix, transposed, gives the adjugate, which is divided by \(\det A\). Questions often ask for a determinant first and then an inverse.
\(\det A=0\) means no inverse (singular), which links to whether a linear system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a unique solution.
Choosing a row or column with zeros for expansion combines property-spotting with cofactor signs, so sign errors and arithmetic slips become the main risk.
Determinants of larger matrices reduce through minors to 2x2 determinants, so recursive expansion ties the definitions together.
exq: Calculate the determinant of a given 3x3 matrix by cofactor expansion along the row or column of your choice, and justify your choice.
For a 3x3 matrix, find the minor \(M_{23}\) and the cofactor \(C_{23}\), stating the sign factor used.
Find the value of a parameter \(k\) for which a matrix such as \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&k\\0&3&1\\2&k&1\end{pmatrix}\) is singular.
Evaluate the determinant of a triangular or sparse 4x4 matrix quickly by exploiting its structure, and explain the property used.
Compute the full cofactor matrix of a 3x3 matrix and use it to begin finding the inverse, checking that \(\det A\neq 0\).

notes.t: Summary of Lecture 2: determinants, minors and cofactors
pts: Determinants, minors and cofactors are useful numbers that can be calculated for a given matrix.
Properties of a matrix can sometimes be exploited to compute determinants quickly.
These quantities are the stepping stone to computing the inverse of a matrix, covered in the next lecture.
defs: Determinant
A single number calculated from a square matrix that summarises certain of its properties, such as whether it is invertible.
Minor
The determinant of the submatrix obtained by deleting one row and one column of a square matrix.
Cofactor
A minor multiplied by a sign \((-1)^{i+j}\) depending on the position of the entry in the matrix.
tips: Watch the sign pattern for cofactors: \((-1)^{i+j}\) alternates across the matrix, and forgetting it is a common error.
A determinant is a scalar with no units; do not confuse a minor (a determinant of a smaller matrix) with a single matrix entry.
rq: Why would exploiting matrix properties (for example, a row of zeros or a triangular form) make a determinant quicker to compute?
Many entries are zero, so most terms in the expansion vanish; for a triangular matrix the determinant is just the product of the diagonal entries.
How are minors and cofactors related to the determinant, and why do we need them for the inverse?
Cofactors are used in cofactor expansion of the determinant and form the matrix of cofactors, whose transpose (divided by the determinant) gives the inverse.

xq.q: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&4&1\\1&2&5\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Find the cofactor \(C_{12}\). (b) Hence, or otherwise, evaluate \(\det A\) by expanding along the first row.
xq.a: C12 = 1 and det A = 25

xq.q: For \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&10\end{pmatrix}\), what is the cofactor \(C_{23}\)?
xq.w: Delete row 2 and column 3 to get the minor 1·8 − 2·7 = −6, then multiply by (−1)^{2+3} = −1 to get 6; forgetting the sign gives −6, deleting the wrong row and column gives −11, and adding the products gives 22.

xq.q: For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\2&5&1\\4&1&2\end{pmatrix}\), evaluate \(\det M\) using cofactors and explain why expanding along the first row is the efficient choice.
xq.a: Expanding along row 1: det M = 3·C11 + 0·C12 + 0·C13. C11 = +(5·2 − 1·1) = 9, so det M = 27. The zeros make the other two cofactor terms vanish, so only one 2×2 minor is needed.
s: Expand along row 1 because it has two zero entries
Zero entries multiply their cofactors to 0

units.name: 1 Course introduction, outcomes and logistics
units.ov: This introductory material sets out the outcomes for Block 3 of Engineering Mathematics 1, which has two strands: matrix algebra (operations, determinants, inverses, simultaneous equations, eigenvalues) and sequences, series and limits (sums, convergence tests, power series). The two strands are tied together by using algebraic structure to solve engineering problems exactly and by checking when a method is valid (an inverse exists, a series converges). The page also covers logistics, including the Maths Challenge, which draws on Blocks 1-3 and carries answers forward.
must: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: \(AB \neq BA\) in general, so keep factor order, e.g. \(AX=B \Rightarrow X=A^{-1}B\), not \(BA^{-1}\)
Add, subtract and multiply matrices: dimensions must be compatible, and an \((m\times n)(n\times p)\) product is \(m\times p\)
Evaluate determinants and use their properties (row operations, zero rows, factoring) to simplify the work
The inverse \(A^{-1}\) exists only if \(\det A \neq 0\) (A non-singular); always state this condition
Solve simultaneous equations in matrix form \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) and interpret the cases of a unique solution, none, or infinitely many
Eigenvalues come from \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\); do not forget the \(-\lambda I\) term
Know the definitions of a sequence and a series, and sum arithmetic and geometric series
The geometric series converges only for \(|r|<1\), with sum to infinity \(\frac{a}{1-r}\)
Test convergence with comparison and ratio tests; \(a_n\to 0\) is necessary but not sufficient (e.g. harmonic series diverges)
Recognise the power series of common functions such as \(e^x,\sin x,\cos x,\ln(1+x),(1+x)^n\)
conn: Determinants link inverses, simultaneous equations and eigenvalues: \(\det A=0\) means no inverse, no unique solution, and \(\lambda=0\) is an eigenvalue
Ratio test and geometric series: the ratio test compares a series to a geometric one, so the condition \(|r|<1\) becomes \(\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|<1\)
Power series connect series convergence to function approximation, where the radius of convergence comes from the ratio test
The Maths Challenge combines techniques from Blocks 1-3, so an early error propagates through later answers
exq: Given \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(AB\) and \(BA\) and show they differ, then find \(A^{-1}\) and state when it exists.
Find the values of \(k\) for which a 3x3 system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has no unique solution, using \(\det A\), and solve it for one other value of \(k\).
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\) from \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).
Determine whether \(\sum \frac{n!}{3^n}\) and \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2+1}\) converge, naming the test used and justifying it.
Find the sum to infinity of the geometric series \(5+\frac{5}{2}+\frac{5}{4}+\dots\), and the range of \(x\) for which \(\sum (x/3)^n\) converges.

notes.t: Learning outcomes: Matrix Algebra
pts: Matrix algebra lets you turn engineering problems into equations involving matrices.
You must be able to add, subtract and multiply matrices.
Determinants are evaluated and their properties exploited to simplify work.
An inverse matrix must be found, and you must state when one exists.
Matrices are used to solve simultaneous equations.
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: \( AB \neq BA \) in general, so keep the order of factors when solving matrix equations.
Eigenvalues come from \( \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \); forgetting the \( -\lambda I \) term is a common error.
rq: Why does a matrix need a nonzero determinant before its inverse can exist?
A zero determinant means the matrix is singular (rows or columns are linearly dependent), so the system has no unique solution and no inverse exists.

notes.t: Learning outcomes: sequences, series and limits
pts: Know the formal definitions of a sequence and of a series.
Be able to sum arithmetic, geometric and other simple series.
Find limits of sequences and series, and test convergence using comparison and ratio tests.
Recognise the power series expansions of common functions.
tips: Do not conclude convergence just because \( a_n \to 0 \); the terms must go to zero fast enough.
Check the conditions of the geometric series formula: it only converges when \( |r| < 1 \).
rq: Why must a series' terms tend to zero for the series to converge, yet this condition alone does not guarantee convergence?
Necessary condition: if \( \sum a_n \) converges then \( a_n \to 0 \). Not sufficient: the harmonic series \( \sum 1/n \) has terms tending to zero but diverges.
What does a ratio test limit of exactly 1 tell you, and why is the test inconclusive?
If \( \lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| = 1 \) the test gives no information, since series with terms behaving like \( 1/n \) (divergent) and \( 1/n^2 \) (convergent) both give limit 1.

notes.t: Engineering Maths Challenge (introduction)
pts: The challenge has six problems spread across three blocks leading to one final answer.
Each challenge yields information needed for later challenges, so every answer must be kept.
The mathematics draws on Blocks 1–3 but problems may be presented differently from class questions.
Teams must have at least three members; the winning team receives £150 in Amazon vouchers.
tips: Do not discard intermediate answers; later challenges depend on them, so an early error propagates through the whole challenge.
Problems may not resemble class questions, so identify the underlying Block 1–3 technique rather than matching the wording.
rq: Why is it important to keep every answer in a multi-stage challenge like this?
Because each challenge unlocks information that is required to solve later challenges and the final answer.
Why might a problem drawn from Blocks 1–3 look unfamiliar even though the underlying mathematics is the same?
The question may be reframed or set in a different context, so students must recognise the underlying method rather than the surface form.

notes.t: Course format and delivery
pts: Lecture slides are posted on Moodle one day before each lecture.
Worked examples are given during lectures and students should copy them down.
Skills are practised through tutorials and homework exercises.
Students are invited to give feedback on what is good or bad about the block's delivery.
tips: Do not rely only on the posted slides; the worked examples given live in lectures are not all contained in them.
rq: Why is it more useful to copy down the worked examples during lectures than to rely on the slides posted beforehand?
Writing the worked steps yourself forces you to follow the reasoning actively, and the slides are only a summary, so the handwritten working is what you will reproduce in exams.
How should tutorials and homework be used to build the skills taught in lectures?
They provide the practice needed to turn worked examples into independent problem-solving, so each lecture's methods should be rehearsed on similar problems.

units.name: 2 Lecture 1 recap and Lecture 2 objectives
units.ov: These notes recap Lecture 1 (matrices as arrays of numbers, their special names, and the rules for addition, subtraction and multiplication) and set the objectives for Lecture 2: computing determinants, minors and cofactors, applying determinant properties, and recognising shortcuts. The notes give only objectives and general tips, not worked methods, so the formulas below come from standard theory and should be checked against the lecture slides. The ideas connect because minors lead to cofactors, cofactors give the cofactor-expansion definition of the determinant, and the properties and shortcuts reduce that work.
must: A matrix is an array of numbers; know its order \(m\times n\) and the special names (square, identity, zero, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, transpose), because exam questions use the terms directly
Addition and subtraction need matrices of the same order and work element by element
Multiplication \(AB\) needs columns of \(A\) = rows of \(B\), and in general \(AB\neq BA\); ordinary arithmetic rules do not carry over automatically
Minor \(M_{ij}\) is the determinant left after deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\)
Cofactor \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\), using the checkerboard sign pattern \(+,-,+,\dots\)
Determinant by cofactor expansion along any row or column: \(\det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}\)
\(2\times2\): \(\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc\); for \(3\times3\), expand along a row or column

Properties: \(\det A^T=\det A\); \(\det(AB)=\det A\det B\); swapping two rows changes the sign; a row of zeros or two identical or proportional rows gives \(\det=0\); multiplying one row by \(k\) multiplies \(\det\) by \(k\), so \(\det(kA)=k^n\det A\); adding a multiple of one row to another leaves \(\det\) unchanged
Shortcuts: for triangular or diagonal matrices the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries; expand along the row or column with the most zeros
\(\det A=0\) means the matrix is singular (no inverse), which matters for solving equations
conn: Cofactors and the determinant: the cofactor matrix and determinant lead to the adjugate and the inverse \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}A\)
Determinant properties and row operations: reduce a matrix to triangular form to get the determinant quickly, tracking sign changes from row swaps and any scaling
Determinant and linear systems: \(\det A\neq0\) gives a unique solution of \(Ax=b\) (Cramer's rule), while \(\det A=0\) means no solution or infinitely many
Multiplication rules with determinants: \(\det(AB)=\det A\det B\) and \(\det(A^T)=\det A\) can avoid computing the product
exq: Find the minors and cofactors of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&4&-1\\5&2&0\end{pmatrix}\), then compute \(\det A\) by expanding along the second row, and check by expanding along a column
Without expanding, explain why \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}=0\), and state the effect on the determinant of swapping two rows
Given \(\det A=5\) for a \(3\times3\) matrix, find \(\det(2A)\), \(\det(A^T)\) and \(\det(A^2)\)
Find the values of \(k\) for which \(\begin{pmatrix}k&1&0\\2&k&1\\0&1&k\end{pmatrix}\) is singular
Compute the determinant of an upper-triangular \(4\times4\) matrix and state the property used; then give the result when two rows are interchanged

notes.t: Matrices: summary of Lecture 1
pts: A matrix is simply an array of numbers, and matrices appear throughout computing, algorithms and equation solving.
Matrix work involves a lot of terminology, and certain matrices have special names that must be learned.
Basic operations on matrices (addition, subtraction, multiplication) must follow specific rules.
Fluency with matrices comes from regular practice.
tips: Do not assume ordinary arithmetic rules apply to matrices; always check the specific rules for each operation.
Learn the special names of matrices, since exam questions often use the terminology directly.
rq: Why must matrix addition, subtraction and multiplication follow specific rules rather than the ordinary rules of arithmetic?

Because a matrix is an array of numbers arranged by rows and columns, so operations act on entries in structured ways; for example, addition needs matrices of the same size and multiplication needs the number of columns of the first to equal the number of rows of the second.

notes.t: Learning objectives: determinants, minors and cofactors
pts: Learning goal: understand and compute determinants, minors and cofactors
Learning goal: understand determinant properties and apply them
Learning goal: spot when the determinant can be computed quickly

units.name: 2 Lecture 3 introduction and objectives
units.ov: This lecture develops the adjoint (adjugate) matrix, the inverse, and their link through the determinant, then applies the inverse to solving linear systems written as \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\). The central idea is that \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}(A)\), so invertibility depends on a non-zero determinant, and that one formula gives both the 2×2 and 3×3 inverses and the solution of square systems. Note: the supplied notes contain only learning objectives and two tips, so details such as the adjoint construction are standard results rather than quotes from the slides.
must: Inverse formula: \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}(A)\); the adjoint alone is NOT the inverse, so never forget the \(1/\det A\) factor
Invertibility: \(A\) is invertible (non-singular) iff \(\det A\neq 0\); if \(\det A=0\) it is singular and has no inverse
Adjoint construction: \(\mathrm{adj}(A)\) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, \(\mathrm{adj}(A)_{ij}=C_{ji}\) with \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\)
Key adjoint identity: \(A\,\mathrm{adj}(A)=\mathrm{adj}(A)\,A=\det(A)\,I\)

2×2 shortcut: for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\); swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones, do not swap the off-diagonal ones
Definition of inverse: \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\); the inverse is unique and only exists for square matrices; check answers by multiplying back
3×3 inverse procedure: minors, then cofactor signs (checkerboard), transpose to get adjoint, compute \(\det A\), divide
Matrix form of linear systems: write as \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\); if \(\det A\neq0\) the unique solution is \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\) (multiply on the left)
If \(\det A=0\) the system has either no solution or infinitely many, so the inverse method fails
conn: Determinant ↔ adjoint ↔ inverse: the cofactors used to expand \(\det A\) are the same ones that build \(\mathrm{adj}(A)\), and \(A\,\mathrm{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\) yields the inverse formula
Determinant ↔ solvability: \(\det A=0\) means singular, which means no unique solution of \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\); questions often ask for the parameter value that makes the system singular
Inverse ↔ matrix products: solving \(AX=B\) or \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\) relies on left-multiplication and non-commutativity, and \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\) reverses order
Linear systems in engineering (e.g. equilibrium or circuit equations) lead to \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\), solved via the inverse as an alternative to Gaussian elimination
exq: Find the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\5&2\end{pmatrix}\) and verify that \(AA^{-1}=I\).
For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\\2&0&1\end{pmatrix}\), compute the cofactor matrix, \(\mathrm{adj}(A)\), \(\det A\) and hence \(A^{-1}\).
Determine the value(s) of \(k\) for which \(\begin{pmatrix}k&2\\3&k+1\end{pmatrix}\) is not invertible, and explain what that means for the corresponding linear system.
Write \(x+2y=5,\;3x+y-z=2,\;2y+z=4\) as \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) and solve using \(A^{-1}\).
Prove that \(A\,\mathrm{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\) for a 2×2 matrix and deduce the formula for \(A^{-1}\); state \(\det(A^{-1})\) in terms of \(\det A\).

notes.t: Learning objectives: adjoint, inverse matrices and linear systems
pts: Form the adjoint matrix and know its key results
Know what an inverse matrix is and decide whether a matrix is invertible
Relate the inverse, adjoint and determinant to each other
Compute inverses of 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
Write linear systems as a matrix equation and solve them
tips: Do not forget the factor 1/det(A) when writing the inverse; the adjoint alone is not the inverse.
For a 2×2 matrix, swap the diagonal entries and change the sign of the off-diagonal entries; do not swap the off-diagonal entries themselves.
rq: Why does a matrix with determinant zero have no inverse?
Because the inverse formula A⁻¹ = (1/det A)·adj(A) requires dividing by det A, which would be division by zero, so the matrix is singular and not invertible.
How do the four cases (unique, trivial, no solution, infinitely many) relate to the determinant of the coefficient matrix?
If det A ≠ 0 there is a unique solution (trivial if b = 0); if det A = 0 there are either no solutions or infinitely many solutions, depending on consistency.

units.name: 2 Why matrices matter: applications and PageRank
units.ov: This introductory material motivates matrices as a compact way to organise and manipulate many interrelated variables, then sets out the basic vocabulary (order, special types, trace, transpose) and operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication). Applications range from structures, aircraft, circuits and robot arms to Google's PageRank, where importance scores come from repeated matrix multiplication on a link matrix. The ideas connect as follows: state the relationships first, represent them as a matrix, then manipulate the matrix using the algebra rules.
must: Order is rows × columns: a \(2\times 3\) matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns, which is not the same as its number of entries (6).
Product \(AB\) is defined only if columns of \(A\) = rows of \(B\); an \(m\times n\) times \(n\times p\) matrix gives an \(m\times p\) matrix.
Transpose \(A^T\) swaps rows and columns, so an \(m\times n\) matrix becomes \(n\times m\).
Symmetric means \(A=A^T\); skew-symmetric means \(A^T=-A\), which forces zero diagonal entries.
Trace is the sum of the diagonal entries and is defined only for square matrices.
Know the special types: square, zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric and skew-symmetric, and recognise each from its entries.
Addition and subtraction require matrices of the same order and work entry by entry; the transpose obeys rules such as \((A+B)^T=A^T+B^T\).
Matrices are a bookkeeping and modelling tool: write down the relationships first, then put the many coupled equations into one matrix equation such as \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\).
PageRank: the web is a link matrix, importance is recursive (important pages linking to you raise your score), and scores are found by repeated multiplication until the relative values settle.
PageRank scores are relative, not link counts, and are only one signal in search ranking.
conn: Order and the multiplication compatibility rule: check dimensions before multiplying, and use them to predict the order of the result and of any transpose.
Symmetric and skew-symmetric definitions combine with transpose rules and trace, for example showing that a skew-symmetric matrix has zero trace.
PageRank links the link matrix to repeated multiplication and convergence of relative values, which leads to the idea of a steady-state vector.
Engineering applications (structures, circuits, robot arms) rely on writing many coupled equations as one matrix equation, which then uses matrix multiplication.
exq: Given \(A\) (\(2\times 3\)) and \(B\) (\(3\times 2\)), state whether \(AB\) and \(BA\) are defined, give their orders, and compute \(AB\).
For a given \(3\times 3\) matrix, find its trace and transpose, and decide whether it is symmetric, skew-symmetric or neither. Justify your answer.
Prove that every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero, and show that \(A+A^T\) is symmetric for any square \(A\).
A small web of 4 pages has given links. Write the link matrix, perform two iterations of multiplication from an equal starting vector, and rank the pages. Comment on what the scores mean.
Three coupled linear equations describe loads on a truss. Write them in the form \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\), identify the order of each matrix, and explain why the matrix form is useful.

notes.t: Learning objectives: matrix algebra basics
pts: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, described by its rows and columns, and its entries (elements) are identified by position.
The order of a matrix is given by its number of rows and columns; special types include square, zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
Basic properties include the trace (sum of diagonal entries) and the transpose (rows and columns swapped).
Basic matrix algebra covers addition, subtraction and multiplication, governed by rules for addition and transpose.
defs: Matrix
A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.
Order of a matrix
The size of a matrix written as number of rows × number of columns.
Trace
The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix.
Transpose
The matrix obtained by interchanging the rows and columns of a matrix.
Symmetric matrix
A square matrix equal to its own transpose.
Skew-symmetric matrix
A square matrix whose transpose equals its negative.
tips: Do not confuse order (rows × columns) with the number of entries; a \(2\times 3\) matrix has order 2 by 3, not 3 by 2.
Matrix multiplication requires the number of columns of the first matrix to equal the number of rows of the second; check this before multiplying.
rq: Why must two matrices have the same order before they can be added or subtracted?
Addition and subtraction act entry by entry, so corresponding entries must occupy the same row and column positions, which requires identical orders.
How does the transpose of a product relate to the transposes of its factors?
\((AB)^T = B^T A^T\): the order of the factors reverses, which is why matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

notes.t: Why we need matrices
pts: Engineering problems often describe relationships between many quantities or variables at once.
Large numbers of variables mean large amounts of data must be handled efficiently.
Matrices provide a compact way to organise and manipulate such data.
tips: Matrices are a bookkeeping and manipulation tool for many variables, not a method that by itself solves a problem; state the relationships first, then represent them in matrix form.
rq: Why does a system with many variables make hand-by-hand manipulation impractical, and how does a matrix help?

Each variable and relationship must be tracked individually, which is error-prone and lengthy; a matrix stores all the data in one organised array so that operations can be applied to the whole set at once.

notes.t: Google's PageRank Algorithm
pts: The web is modelled as a matrix where rows and columns are webpages and entries record links between them.
A page's importance is determined recursively: it is more important if other important pages link to it.
Importance scores are estimated by repeated matrix multiplication until the relative values stabilise.
The importance score is one signal used to rank pages in search results, not the sole factor.
defs: PageRank
An algorithm that scores the relative importance of webpages from the pattern of hyperlinks between them, used by Google to rank search results.
tips: PageRank importance is a relative ranking, not an absolute measure; do not claim the scores equal the number of links.
The importance score is only one signal in search ranking, so do not state that it alone determines search result order.
rq: Why does repeated matrix multiplication allow the importance of pages to be estimated, even though each page's importance depends on the importance of the pages linking to it?

Each multiplication propagates importance one link step further through the network; repeating it lets the scores converge to a stable set of relative values, so the circular definition is resolved iteratively.
What would happen to a page's rank if it received many links from unimportant pages compared with a few links from highly important pages?
Under the algorithm, links count in proportion to the importance of the linking page, so a few links from important pages can outweigh many links from unimportant ones.

notes.t: Matrices as a tool for engineering problems
pts: Matrices are used across all engineering disciplines to model, analyse and solve complex, interconnected problems.
Large systems of equations describe how civil structures such as bridges behave under loads.
Matrices describe the coupled dynamics of an aircraft moving in three dimensions.
In electrical circuits and control systems, multiple interacting variables are solved together using matrices.
Mechanical systems such as robot arms are analysed by modelling forces, motion and vibration with matrices.
tips: Matrices here are a modelling tool; exam questions will expect you to set up a system as a matrix equation, not just describe applications.
Do not confuse 'large systems of equations' with a single equation: the matrix form compresses many coupled equations into one expression.
rq: Why does a system where several variables affect each other naturally call for matrix methods rather than solving each variable separately?
Because the variables are coupled, so each equation contains several unknowns; writing the system as one matrix equation lets all unknowns be solved together.
What do the matrices in a biomedical hip-replacement model represent, and why does this matter for predicting stress?
