rq: Why must the order be reversed when transposing a product, i.e. why is (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ rather than AᵀBᵀ?

Because the entry in row i, column j of (AB)ᵀ is the entry in row j, column i of AB, which is a dot product of row j of A with column i of B; this equals a dot product of row i of Bᵀ with column j of Aᵀ, giving BᵀAᵀ. AᵀBᵀ generally has incompatible sizes or different values.
Does multiplying by the identity matrix require the identity to be the same size as A?
Not the same size, but compatible: Iₘ must be m×m to multiply A on the left and Iₙ must be n×n to multiply on the right, so the sizes must match the rows and columns of A respectively.

notes.t: Matrix products: possibility and evaluation
pts: A product XY is only defined when the number of columns of X equals the number of rows of Y; check dimensions before multiplying.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so AB and BA can differ or one may be undefined.
Transposing swaps rows and columns, which can make an otherwise impossible product possible.
Show that a polynomial identity holds for matrices, noting that the identity matrix I is needed for the constant term and that products of A with itself and with I commute.
Matrix algebra does not behave like scalar algebra when matrices fail to commute, so expanding (A+B)(A+2B) requires care with the order of factors.
defs: Matrix product
For A (m×n) and B (n×p), the product AB is the m×p matrix whose (i,j) entry is the sum over k of \(a_{\text{ik}}\) \(b_{\text{kj}}\).
Transpose
The transpose Aᵀ of a matrix A is formed by interchanging its rows and columns, so an m×n matrix becomes n×m.
eqs: m, n, p = number of rows/columns (dimensionless)
tips: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: \(AB \neq BA\) in general, so keep the order of factors.
Check inner dimensions before multiplying; \(A^2\) requires a square matrix, and \(C^4\) is impossible for a 1×4 matrix.
rq: Why is \(AB\) possible for \(A\) (2×2) and \(B\) (2×2) but \(CD\) is not possible for \(C\) (1×4) and \(D\) (4×1)?
Actually \(CD\) is possible: \(C\) is 1×4 and \(D\) is 4×1, so the inner dimensions match and the result is 1×1; \(DC\) is 4×1 times 1×4, giving a 4×4 matrix.
What if \(A\) and \(B\) commute, i.e. \(AB = BA\)? Does \((A+B)(A+2B)\) then expand like ordinary algebra?
Yes; if AB = BA, the cross terms combine and \((A+B)(A+2B) = A^2 + 3AB + 2B^2\) holds.

xq.q: Let \(\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&3\\0&4&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\-2&0\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}\). Find the matrix product \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{AB}\) and give the sum of all four entries of \(\mathbf{C}\).
xq.a: C = [[13, 1],[-5, -1]], so the sum of entries is 8
s: A is 2×3 and B is 3×2, so AB exists and is 2×2

xq.q: Matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) is 2×3 and matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) is 3×4. Which statement about the products is correct?
xq.a: \(\mathbf{PQ}\) exists and is 2×4, but \(\mathbf{QP}\) does not exist
o: \(\mathbf{QP}\) exists and is 4×2
\(\mathbf{PQ}\) exists and is 3×3
\(\mathbf{PQ}\) exists and is 2×4, but \(\mathbf{QP}\) does not exist
\(\mathbf{PQ}\) exists and is 2×4, and \(\mathbf{QP}\) exists and is 4×2
xq.w: PQ has inner dimensions 3 and 3 so is 2×4, whereas QP needs 4 columns of Q to equal 2 rows of P, which fails; the trap is assuming both orders exist.

xq.q: Let \(\mathbf{A}\) be an m×n matrix and \(\mathbf{B}\) an n×p matrix. Show that \((\mathbf{AB})^T=\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{A}^T\) is dimensionally consistent, and explain why \(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{B}^T\) is generally not defined. Illustrate with m=2, n=3, p=4.
xq.a: AB is m×p so its transpose is p×m. \(B^{T}\) is p×n and \(A^{T}\) is n×m, so \(B^{T}\) \(A^{T}\) is conformable (inner n) and gives p×m, matching (AB)^T. \(A^{T}\) \(B^{T}\) is (n×m)(p×n), which needs m=p to be conformable. For m=2, n=3, p=4: (AB)^T is 4×2, \(B^{T}\) \(A^{T}\) is (4×3)(3×2)=4×2, but \(A^{T}\) \(B^{T}\) is (3×2)(4×3), not conformable since 2≠4.
s: AB has size m×p so (AB)^T is p×m
\(B^{T}\) is p×n, \(A^{T}\) is n×m, product is p×m, consistent

units.name: 6 Singular and homogeneous systems
units.ov: This material covers linear systems \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) where the coefficient matrix is singular (\(|A|=0\)), so no inverse exists and solving by inversion fails. It separates the non-homogeneous case (\(\mathbf{b}\neq\mathbf{0}\): no solution or infinitely many) from the homogeneous case (\(\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}\): always the trivial solution, with non-trivial solutions exactly when \(|A|=0\)). The determinant is the single test that links these cases.
must: A square matrix is singular if \(|A|=0\); it then has no inverse, so \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\) cannot be used
Non-homogeneous system (\(\mathbf{b}\neq\mathbf{0}\)) with \(|A|=0\): either no solution (inconsistent) or infinitely many (dependent equations)
Homogeneous system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) has a non-trivial solution \(\iff |A|=0\)
If \(|A|\neq0\), a homogeneous system has only the trivial solution \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\)
\(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) is always a solution of \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\), so a homogeneous system is never inconsistent
Inconsistent equations contradict each other, so no vector \(\mathbf{x}\) satisfies all of them
\(|A|=0\) alone does not decide between no solution and infinitely many; you must check consistency by elimination or row reduction
Infinitely many solutions are written with a free parameter (e.g. \(x=t\)), with the other unknowns expressed in terms of \(t\)
Find the values of a parameter (e.g. \(\lambda\)) that make \(|A|=0\) by solving the determinant equation, then solve for the non-trivial solutions
conn: Determinants and inverses: \(|A|\neq0\) gives a unique solution via \(A^{-1}\), while \(|A|=0\) leads to the singular cases above
Gaussian elimination: a row of zeros with a zero right-hand side means infinitely many solutions, while a zero row with a non-zero right-hand side (\(0=c\)) means inconsistent

Parameter problems: set \(|A|=0\) to find the special parameter value, then substitute it back to find the non-trivial solution; this is the same method used later for eigenvalues and eigenvectors, \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\)

Engineering applications such as equilibrium of forces, circuit loops and vibration modes: a non-trivial solution of a homogeneous system corresponds to a special condition such as resonance, buckling or a mode shape
exq: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), show \(|A|=0\). Determine whether \(A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}\) have no solution or infinitely many, and give the general solution where it exists.
Find the value(s) of \(k\) for which \(\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) has a non-trivial solution, and find that solution in terms of a parameter.
Given a 3×3 system with \(|A|=0\), use row reduction to decide whether it is inconsistent or has infinitely many solutions, and write the solution set in terms of a free parameter.
Explain why a homogeneous system can never be inconsistent, and state the condition on \(|A|\) for non-trivial solutions to exist. Apply it to a 3×3 system containing an unknown \(\lambda\).
True or false, with justification: 'If \(|A|=0\) then \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has no solution.'

notes.t: Singular systems Ax = b: no solution or infinitely many
pts: If the determinant of A is zero, the inverse does not exist, so Ax = b cannot be solved by inversion.
With b ≠ 0 and |A| = 0, the system may be inconsistent and have no solution.
With b ≠ 0 and |A| = 0, the system may instead have infinitely many solutions when the equations are dependent.
defs: Inconsistent equations
A system of linear equations with no common solution; the equations contradict each other so no vector x satisfies all of them.
eqs: Condition for the inverse of A to exist (singular case when zero)
|A| = determinant of the coefficient matrix A (dimensionless); \(A\) = square coefficient matrix
tips: Do not assume \(|A| = 0\) means no solution; it may also give infinitely many solutions when the equations are multiples of each other.
Remember the condition \(b \neq 0\): for a homogeneous system \(Ax = 0\) with \(|A| = 0\), there is always at least the trivial solution, which is a different case.
rq: Why can't we solve Ax = b by computing \(A^{-1}b\) when \(|A| = 0\), and what does this tell us about the rows of A?
Because \(A^{-1}\) does not exist when \(|A| = 0\); this means the rows (equations) of A are linearly dependent, so the system is either inconsistent or has infinitely many solutions.
How could you tell from the equations themselves whether a singular system has no solution or infinitely many?

If one equation is a multiple of another and the right-hand sides are in the same ratio, there are infinitely many solutions; if the left sides are proportional but the right-hand sides are not, the equations are inconsistent and there is no solution.

notes.t: Homogeneous systems and singular matrices
pts: If the inverse of \(A\) does not exist, the determinant is zero, so \(A\) is singular.
When \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\) and \(A\) is singular, the system \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) has infinitely many solutions.
A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution exactly when the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero.
defs: Singular matrix
A square matrix whose determinant is zero, so it has no inverse.
Non-trivial solution
A solution \(\boldsymbol{x}\) of \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) that is not the zero vector.
eqs: Homogeneous system with a non-trivial solution condition
\(A\) = square coefficient matrix (dimensionless); \(\boldsymbol{x}\) = unknown vector (depends on problem); \(|A|\) = determinant of \(A\) (dimensionless for a unitless matrix)
tips: Do not confuse \(\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{0}\) with \(A\) singular: infinitely many solutions require both conditions; with \(|A|=0\) but \(\boldsymbol{b}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\) the system may have no solution.
The zero vector \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) is always a solution of a homogeneous system, so it is not the 'non-trivial' one being asked about.
rq: Why does a zero determinant allow infinitely many solutions to \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\) rather than just the zero vector?

Because \(A\) has no inverse, so \(\boldsymbol{x}=A^{-1}\boldsymbol{0}\) cannot be used to force a unique answer; the columns of \(A\) are linearly dependent, allowing non-zero \(\boldsymbol{x}\) that map to zero.
If \(|A|\neq 0\), what is the only solution of \(A\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\)?
The trivial solution \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}\), since \(A^{-1}\) exists and \(\boldsymbol{x}=A^{-1}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}\).

xq.q: The system \(x_1+2x_2+kx_3=0\), \(2x_1+x_2+x_3=0\), \(x_1+x_2+2x_3=0\) has a non-trivial solution only for a particular value of the constant \(k\). Find \(k\).
For a 2×2 system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) with \(\mathbf{b}\neq\mathbf{0}\) and \(|A|=0\), which statement is correct?
xq.a: There are either no solutions or infinitely many solutions, depending on whether the equations are consistent
o: There is always a unique solution \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\)
There is always exactly the trivial solution
There are either no solutions or infinitely many solutions, depending on whether the equations are consistent
There are always infinitely many solutions
xq.w: With |A|=0 the inverse does not exist, and the outcome depends on whether the right-hand side matches the dependence of the rows; assuming always no solution or always infinite is the trap.
s: |A|=0 means no inverse, so no unique solution
Consistent dependent equations give infinitely many, otherwise none

xq.q: Explain why a homogeneous system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) with square \(A\) always has a solution, and show that it has non-trivial solutions exactly when \(|A|=0\). Illustrate with \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\).
xq.a: x=0 always satisfies A0=0, so the trivial solution always exists. If |A|≠0, \(A^{-1}\) exists and x=A^{-1}0=0 is the only solution. If |A|=0, A is singular, the equations are dependent and infinitely many solutions exist, so non-trivial ones exist. For the example |A|=4-4=0; both equations give x1+2x2=0, so x=t(-2,1) for any t, non-trivial.

units.name: 6 Summary of determinants, minors and cofactors
units.ov: This material summarises determinants, minors and cofactors, which are numbers calculated from square matrices. Minors are determinants of submatrices, and cofactors are minors with an alternating sign attached. Cofactor expansion is used to compute determinants, and the same ideas feed directly into finding the matrix inverse in the next lecture. Note: the source notes are only a brief summary page, so the specific formulas below are standard results that you should check against your lecture notes.
must: Determinants, minors and cofactors are defined only for square matrices; applying them to a non-square matrix is an error
Minor \(M_{ij}\) is the determinant of the matrix left after deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\)
Cofactor \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\), so the sign pattern is \(+\,-\,+\,\dots\) in a checkerboard layout
Always apply the alternating sign pattern; dropping it is the most common mistake
Determinant by cofactor expansion along any row or column: \(\det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}\)
For a \(2\times2\) matrix, \(\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc\)
Matrix properties can shorten the work: expand along the row or column with most zeros, and triangular or diagonal matrices have determinant equal to the product of the diagonal entries
A row or column of zeros, or two identical rows or columns, gives \(\det A=0\) (standard result)
These quantities lead to the inverse: \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A)\), where the adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so \(\det A\neq0\) is needed (next lecture)
conn: Cofactor expansion links minors, signs and determinants: you compute minors, attach signs to get cofactors, then sum along a row or column to get the determinant
Determinant and inverse: the cofactor matrix, its transpose (the adjugate) and the determinant combine to give \(A^{-1}\). A zero determinant means the matrix is singular and has no inverse
Choosing the expansion row or column cleverly, using zeros or the properties above, reduces the arithmetic and the chance of sign errors
A nonzero determinant is linked to systems of linear equations having a unique solution (standard result, e.g. Cramer's rule)
exq: Find the minors and cofactors of the \(3\times3\) matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&4&-1\\5&2&0\end{pmatrix}\) and use them to compute \(\det A\) by expansion along the first column
Compute the determinant of a \(4\times4\) matrix containing several zeros by choosing the best row or column to expand along, and justify your choice
Explain why the determinant is not defined for a \(2\times3\) matrix, and state what a zero determinant tells you about a square matrix
Write down the cofactor sign pattern for a \(4\times4\) matrix and find \(C_{23}\) and \(C_{32}\) for a given matrix
Given a \(3\times3\) matrix, form the matrix of cofactors and use it to start finding \(A^{-1}\), checking that \(\det A\neq0\)

notes.t: Summary: Determinants, Minors and Cofactors
pts: Determinants, minors and cofactors are useful numbers that can be calculated for a given matrix.
Properties of a matrix can sometimes be exploited to compute determinants quickly.
These ideas are used in the next lecture to compute the inverse of a matrix.
tips: Determinants, minors and cofactors are only defined for square matrices; attempting them on non-square matrices is an error.
Check the sign pattern (+ − + …) when applying cofactors, as dropping the alternating sign is a common mistake.
rq: Why might exploiting properties of a matrix (such as zeros or triangular structure) make computing its determinant faster?
Special structure lets many terms vanish or reduces the problem to a product of diagonal entries, so fewer cofactor expansions or row operations are needed.
How are minors and cofactors related to the determinant, and why do they lead to computing the matrix inverse?
The determinant is built from entries multiplied by their cofactors (minors with sign); the inverse uses the transpose of the cofactor matrix divided by the determinant.

units.name: 7 2×2 system examples and elimination methods

notes.t: Solving 2×2 linear systems of equations (Examples 6)
pts: Solve each 2×2 system for x₁ and x₂ by elimination or Cramer's rule; a zero determinant signals a singular system.
A homogeneous system (right-hand sides all zero) always has the trivial solution x₁ = x₂ = 0.
If the two equations are proportional on the left but not on the right, the system has no solution.
If the left-hand sides are proportional and the right-hand sides match in that ratio, there are infinitely many solutions.
eqs: Determinant of a 2×2 coefficient matrix (test for unique solution)
a, b, c, d = coefficients of the system (dimensionless)
tips: Check consistency of proportional rows: matching coefficient ratios alone does not guarantee a solution; the right-hand sides must match the same ratio.
Do not forget the trivial solution x₁ = x₂ = 0 for homogeneous systems when stating the solution set.
rq: Why does system 2 (both right-hand sides zero) always have x₁ = x₂ = 0 as a solution, and when could it have more?
Substituting zeros satisfies every homogeneous equation; non-zero solutions exist only when the determinant ad − bc = 0.
How can you tell from the coefficients alone whether system 3 and system 4 differ in the number of solutions?
Both have proportional left-hand sides (−3 : 6 = 1 : −2); the right-hand sides 15 and −5 are consistent with ratio −3 (infinite solutions), while 10 and −5 are not (no solution).

notes.t: Elimination methods
pts: When the inverse of a matrix is not known explicitly, it may be difficult to compute, so solving \(Ax=b\) directly without forming \(A^{-1}\) is needed.
tips: Do not assume \(A^{-1}\) exists or is easy to compute; elimination works on \(Ax=b\) directly, and the matrix must be invertible for a unique solution.
rq: Why might we avoid computing \(A^{-1}\) explicitly when solving \(Ax=b\)?
Computing the inverse is often expensive or difficult; elimination methods solve for x directly from A and b without needing \(A^{-1}\).

xq.q: Solve the system \(3x_1+2x_2=7\), \(x_1-4x_2=7\) for \(x_1\) using Cramer's rule. Give the value of \(x_1\).
Consider \(x_1+2x_2=3\) and \(2x_1+4x_2=7\). What is the nature of the solution?
xq.a: No solution, because the left sides are proportional (determinant 0) but the right sides are not in the same ratio
o: Unique solution \(x_1=1,x_2=1\)
Infinitely many solutions because the left-hand sides are proportional
No solution, because the left sides are proportional (determinant 0) but the right sides are not in the same ratio
Only the trivial solution \(x_1=x_2=0\)
xq.w: The determinant is 1·4-2·2=0 and the second left side is 2× the first but 7≠2·3, so the equations contradict; the trap is stopping at proportional coefficients.

xq.q: For the system \(2x_1-x_2=4\), \(-6x_1+3x_2=-12\), show that the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero, decide whether solutions exist, and describe the solution set.
xq.a: det = 2(3) - (-1)(-6) = 6 - 6 = 0, so the matrix is singular. The second equation is -3 times the first on both sides (-3·4 = -12), so the equations are consistent and dependent. There are infinitely many solutions: x2 = 2x1 - 4, with x1 arbitrary.

units.name: 7 Summary of matrix algebra basics
units.ov: This material is a summary of matrix algebra basics: what matrices are, the terminology and named special matrices, and the rules for addition, subtraction and multiplication. The notes are brief, so the key ideas are that every operation depends on matrix dimensions, and that multiplication behaves differently from scalar multiplication. Fluency in these basics is the foundation for later work such as solving systems of equations.
must: Dimension rule for addition and subtraction: matrices must have identical size \( m\times n \), and the operation is done entry by entry
Dimension rule for multiplication: \( A_{m\times n}B_{n\times p} \) is defined and gives \( C_{m\times p} \); the inner dimensions must match
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: \( AB \neq BA \) in general, and \( BA \) may not even be defined
Computing a product: entry \( c_{ij} \) is the dot product of row \( i \) of \( A \) with column \( j \) of \( B \)
Always check dimensions first; if they are mismatched, the operation is undefined
Know the terminology and special named matrices (e.g. square, identity, zero, diagonal, transpose, symmetric) and their definitions
The identity matrix \( I \) satisfies \( AI = IA = A \), the matrix analogue of multiplying by 1
Be able to carry out addition, subtraction and multiplication quickly and accurately; this comes from repeated practice
Transposing a product reverses the order: \( (AB)^T = B^T A^T \) (standard rule, not stated in the notes)
conn: Dimension checking links addition and multiplication: before any combined expression such as \( AB + C \), the product size must equal the size of \( C \)
Non-commutativity affects algebra with matrices: expanding \( (A+B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2 \), not \( A^2+2AB+B^2 \) unless \( AB=BA \)
Special matrices (identity, zero, diagonal) simplify multiplication and give shortcuts in calculations
Matrix multiplication is how systems of linear equations are written as \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \), connecting these basics to equation solving
exq: Given \( A \) (2×3) and \( B \) (3×2), state the sizes of \( AB \) and \( BA \), compute both, and show that \( AB \neq BA \)
For \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix} \) and \( B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \), calculate \( A+B \), \( A-B \), \( AB \) and \( BA \), and comment on the results
Explain, using dimensions, why \( A_{2\times3}+B_{3\times2} \) is undefined while \( A_{2\times3}B_{3\times2} \) is defined
Define the identity, diagonal and symmetric matrices, give a 3×3 example of each, and verify \( AI=A \) for a given \( A \)
Expand \( (A+B)^2 \) for 2×2 matrices and state under what condition it reduces to \( A^2+2AB+B^2 \)

notes.t: Matrices: summary of matrix algebra basics
pts: Matrices are arrays of numbers that appear across computing, algorithms and equation solving.
Matrix work involves much terminology, and certain matrices have special names that must be learned.
Basic operations such as addition, subtraction and multiplication must follow specific rules.
Fluency with matrix operations comes from repeated practice.
tips: Check dimensions before adding or multiplying matrices; mismatched sizes make the operation undefined.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, so \( AB \neq BA \) in general.
rq: Why must the rules for matrix addition and multiplication be followed strictly rather than treated like ordinary number arithmetic?

Matrix operations are not generally commutative and require compatible dimensions (e.g. addition needs equal sizes, multiplication needs inner dimensions to match), so applying scalar rules gives wrong results.

units.name: 8 Lecture 3 summary
units.ov: This lecture summarises how the inverse matrix \( A^{-1} \) is used to solve linear systems \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \), and when it can and cannot be used. The inverse gives \( \mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b} \) but exists only for square, non-singular matrices, and computing it is often impractical, so direct methods such as Gaussian elimination are needed. The notes are brief, so the core ideas are existence (via the determinant), use, and practicality.
must: A linear system is written in matrix form \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \); if \( A^{-1} \) exists, the solution is \( \mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b} \)
The inverse exists only if \( A \) is square and non-singular, i.e. \( \det(A)\neq 0 \)
Definition of the inverse: \( AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I \)
If \( \det(A)=0 \) the matrix is singular: there is no unique solution (either none or infinitely many)
Computing \( A^{-1} \) is often impractical for large systems, so do not assume it is the best route
Alternative direct methods (e.g. Gaussian elimination / row reduction) solve the system without forming \( A^{-1} \)
For a 2x2 matrix, \( A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix} \) with \( \det A=ad-bc \)
Order matters: multiply by \( A^{-1} \) on the left, since matrix multiplication is not commutative
Always check a solution by substituting back into \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \)
conn: Determinant and invertibility: \( \det(A)\neq 0 \) tests whether a unique solution exists before any solving is attempted
Inverse method versus Gaussian elimination: both solve \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \), but elimination is more efficient for larger systems and also reveals singular cases
Engineering applications: equilibrium of forces in trusses and circuit analysis give linear systems, where a singular \( A \) signals a mechanism or an indeterminate structure
exq: Given a 2x2 matrix \( A \) and vector \( \mathbf{b} \), find \( \det(A) \), compute \( A^{-1} \), and solve \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \) for \( \mathbf{x} \).
For which value of \( k \) is the matrix \( \begin{pmatrix}2&k\\4&6\end{pmatrix} \) singular? State what this means for the solutions of the corresponding system.
Explain why computing \( A^{-1} \) may be impractical for a large system, and name an alternative method, solving a 3x3 example with it.
Solve a 3x3 system of equations by Gaussian elimination and verify the result by substitution.
State the conditions under which \( A^{-1} \) exists and give an example of a matrix that has no inverse.

notes.t: Summary: inverse matrices and solving linear systems
pts: The inverse matrix can solve systems of linear equations quickly and efficiently.
Computing the inverse is sometimes not easy or practical, so alternative methods are needed.
tips: Do not assume the inverse is always the best route: computing \( A^{-1} \) is often impractical, so direct methods may be needed.
The inverse only exists for a square, non-singular matrix, i.e. when \( \det(A) \neq 0 \).
rq: Why might computing the inverse of a matrix be impractical even when a solution to a linear system exists?
For large or ill-conditioned matrices, finding the inverse is computationally expensive and can be numerically unstable, so alternative methods (e.g. direct elimination) are preferred.

rep.ov: So far the module covers two halves. The DC half starts with voltage, current, resistance, Ohm's law and power. It then adds Kirchhoff's laws and series-parallel reduction, followed by Thévenin/Norton equivalents, maximum power transfer, superposition and star-delta conversion, and finally mesh-current analysis. The AC half starts with sinusoids, phasors and complex numbers. It builds up to the impedances of R, L and C (jωL, 1/(jωC)), voltage-divider transfer functions, dB and Bode plots, and RC, LR and LCR filters. It also introduces ideal op-amp golden rules. Each topic reuses the previous one: Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws underpin the network theorems and mesh analysis, and the same divider and equivalence ideas carry over to complex impedances and filters.
must: Ohm's law \( V=IR \) and power \( P=VI=I^2R=V^2/R \); keep units consistent (mA, kΩ) and check component power ratings, not just equivalent resistance
KCL (\( \sum I_{in}=\sum I_{out} \)) and KVL (\( \sum v=0 \)) with consistent sign conventions
Series/parallel reduction: \( R_{eq}=R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2) \) for two parallel resistors; voltage divider \( V_{R2}=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V \) and current divider (branch current uses the opposite resistor)
Thévenin/Norton: \( V_T=V_{oc} \), \( R_T \) from zeroing sources (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened), \( I_N=V_T/R_T \), \( R_N=R_T \)
Maximum power transfer: \( R_L=R_T \), \( P_{max}=V_T^2/(4R_T) \); superposition applies to voltages and currents only, never to power
Star-delta conversion for bridge networks: each star arm = product of the two adjacent delta resistors over the sum of all three

Mesh-current analysis: one KVL equation per mesh, written as \( R\,I=V \) with shared resistors off-diagonal and negative; solve by elimination or Cramer's rule; a current source on an outer branch fixes the mesh current

Sinusoids and phasors: \( V(t)=V_0\sin(\omega t+\phi) \), \( \omega=2\pi f \), \( T=1/f \); \( j^2=-1 \) and multiplying by j rotates by 90°; magnitude \( |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \) and phase \( \arctan(b/a) \)

Component impedances: \( Z_R=R \), \( Z_L=j\omega L \), \( Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C) \); the capacitor current leads the voltage by 90° (\( I=C\,dV/dt \)) and the inductor current lags (\( V=L\,dI/dt \))
Series/parallel rules for L and C: inductors in series add, capacitors in series use reciprocals (the reverse of resistors)

RC/LR first-order filters as impedance dividers: low-pass \( \frac{1}{1+j\omega RC} \), high-pass \( \frac{1}{1+1/(j\omega RC)} \), cut-off \( \omega_0=1/RC \) or \( R/L \); at cut-off the gain is \( 1/\sqrt2 \), which is −3 dB

Decibels: \( 20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in}) \) for voltage and \( 10\log_{10} \) for power; Bode plots; the series LCR band-pass with output across R peaks at \( \omega_0 \); op-amp golden rules (\( V_-=V_+ \), zero input current) hold only with negative feedback
conn: Thévenin resistance, voltage dividers and series/parallel reduction combine in maximum power questions: find \( V_T \) and \( R_T \), set \( R_L=R_T \), then compute \( P_{max} \)

Mesh analysis versus superposition or Thévenin: the same circuit can be solved several ways, so an exam may ask you to use one method and check with another; star-delta is the fix when series/parallel reduction fails

The voltage-divider idea carries from resistors to impedances: RC, LR and LCR transfer functions are \( Z_{out}/Z_{total} \), and the complex-number algebra (conjugates, magnitude) turns them into gain in dB and phase

Capacitor and inductor behaviour (\( I=C\,dV/dt \), \( V=L\,dI/dt \), 90° phase) leads directly to \( Z_C \), \( Z_L \), the phasor diagram and the high-pass versus low-pass behaviour; at DC a capacitor is open and an inductor is a short
Combining a high-pass RC and a low-pass LR gives the band-pass crossover, linking the filter lectures to the speaker application and to Bode plots
exq: A network has a 28 V source with 4 Ω, a 7 V source with 1 Ω and a 2 Ω load. Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the load, the load current, and the power in the load.
For a source with \( V_T=20 \) V and \( R_T=50\ \Omega \), find the load resistance for maximum power and \( P_{max} \). What is the load power if \( R_L=100\ \Omega \)?

Write mesh equations for a two-mesh circuit with \( R_1=470\ \Omega \), \( R_2=820\ \Omega \), \( R_3=220\ \Omega \), \( V_A=10 \) V and \( V_B=5 \) V. Solve for \( i_1 \), \( i_2 \) and the current in \( R_3 \) using Cramer's rule.
Use delta-star conversion to find the equivalent resistance of a bridge network between two terminals.
An RC low-pass filter has \( R=1\ \text{k}\Omega \) and \( C=100 \) nF. Derive \( V_o/V_{in} \), find the cut-off frequency in Hz, and give the gain in dB and the phase at \( f=3 \) kHz.

A series LCR circuit has the output across R. Derive its transfer function, find the centre frequency \( \omega_0 \), and sketch the Bode magnitude plot. State the filter type and why it is second order.
Find the impedance of a series R-C circuit at 1 kHz in rectangular and polar form, and the phase between voltage and current.
weak: Complex-number algebra in transfer functions: rationalising complex denominators with conjugates, then finding magnitude and phase, goes wrong over sign errors, \( j^2=-1 \), and forgetting \( \omega=2\pi f \)
Mesh analysis sign conventions and current sources: shared-resistor signs, source polarity relative to the loop direction, and handling meshes fixed by current sources cause most errors

Choosing the output and recognising the filter type: output across C or R (low-pass versus high-pass), the capacitor/inductor phase direction, and the dB conventions (20log versus 10log, −3 dB only at cut-off)

units.name: 1.1 Voltage and current basics
units.ov: This material introduces the two basic electrical quantities, voltage (energy per unit charge) and current (rate of charge flow), and links them through Ohm's law for resistors. It also covers the physical picture of current as electron drift in a conductor and the conventional current direction, which is the foundation for analysing AC waveforms later in the lecture.
must: Voltage is energy transferred per unit charge between two points: \( V = E/q \), with 1 V = 1 J/C
Current is the rate of flow of charge: \( I = \frac{dQ}{dt} \), with 1 A = 1 C/s
Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), valid for ohmic components at constant temperature
Voltage and current are different quantities: J/C versus C/s; current is not charge
Conventional current is the direction positive charge would flow, opposite to electron motion in a metal
In a copper wire the charge carriers are free electrons drifting through the lattice when a voltage drives them
The source pushes charge around a closed loop, and the voltage drop across a resistor is set by the current through it
Use consistent SI units (V, A, Ω, C, s, J) and rearrange: \( I = V/R \), \( R = V/I \), \( Q = \int I\,dt \)
Individual electrons drift slowly; the energy and signal propagate quickly, so do not say carriers travel fast along the wire
conn: Charge, current and voltage: \( I = dQ/dt \) and \( V = E/q \) combine to give energy and power, since \( E = qV \) and \( P = VI \)

Ohm's law with the current definition: a time-varying current \( i(t) \) through a resistor gives \( v(t) = i(t)R \), so the voltage waveform has the same shape as the current waveform (key for AC waveforms)
Current direction and sign convention: the conventional current arrow and the voltage polarity must be defined consistently, or the sign of \( V = IR \) and of the energy transfer will be wrong
Microscopic and circuit views: electron drift in the conductor (opposite to the arrow) explains the macroscopic current \( I \) used in circuit equations
exq: A charge of 12 C passes through a cross-section of a wire in 4 s. Calculate the current. How much energy is transferred if the potential difference across the component is 9 V?
A 220 Ω resistor carries a current of 15 mA. Find the voltage across it and the charge that flows through it in 2 minutes.
Define voltage and electric current, giving SI units and the relation of each to joules, coulombs and seconds.
In a copper wire, electrons move from left to right. State the direction of conventional current and explain why the two directions differ.
The charge passing a point is \( Q(t) = 3t^2 \) coulombs, with t in seconds. Find the current at t = 2 s, and the voltage across a 10 Ω resistor carrying this current at that instant.

notes.t: Voltage: energy per unit charge and Ohm's law
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge moving between two points in a circuit.
Voltage is measured in volts (V), where 1 V equals 1 joule per coulomb.
In a circuit, charges (electrons) are pushed around a loop by the source, and the voltage drop across a resistor is related to the current through it by Ohm's law.
defs: Voltage (potential difference)
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts, where 1 V = 1 J/C.
eqs: Voltage as energy per unit charge
V = voltage (V); E = energy transferred (J); q = charge (C)
Ohm's law: voltage across a resistor
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not confuse voltage (energy per unit charge, V = E/q) with current (charge per unit time); the units are J/C versus C/s.
Ohm's law V = IR applies to ohmic components at constant temperature; use consistent SI units (volts, amps, ohms).
rq: Why does a higher voltage not automatically mean more charge flows, and what else must you know?
Current depends on both voltage and resistance (I = V/R); the same voltage across a larger resistance gives less current.
If the charge q doubles while the energy E stays the same, what happens to V?
V = E/q halves, since voltage is inversely proportional to the charge moved for a fixed energy.

notes.t: What is current?
pts: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, not the charge itself.
defs: Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-section of a conductor, measured in amperes (A), where 1 A equals 1 coulomb of charge passing per second.
eqs: Current as rate of charge flow
I = current (A); Q = charge (C); t = time (s)
tips: Do not confuse current (A) with charge (C); 1 A = 1 C/s, so a charge in coulombs must be divided by time in seconds to find current.
rq: Why is current defined as a rate of charge flow rather than as the amount of charge itself?

Because a conductor can carry a large or small amount of charge at any instant; what determines how strongly a circuit is driven is how quickly charge moves past a point, so current measures flow per unit time.

notes.t: Electric current as flow of charge carriers in a conductor
pts: Current in a copper wire is the drift of negatively charged electrons (carriers) along the conductor.
The arrow shows the direction of conventional current, which is opposite to the direction electrons actually move.
Free electrons are shown moving through the lattice of a copper wire, so charge flows when a voltage drives them along the wire.
defs: Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor cross-section, measured in amperes.
Conventional current direction
The direction in which positive charge would flow, taken as opposite to the motion of electrons.
tips: Do not confuse electron drift direction with conventional current direction; always state which convention you use.
Current is the rate of charge flow (A = C/s), not the charge itself; the carriers themselves do not travel quickly along the wire.
rq: Why does the arrow point right while the negative charges in the wire are drawn moving the opposite way?
Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would flow, which is opposite to electron motion.
What would change in the picture if the current were alternating?
The carriers would periodically reverse direction, oscillating back and forth rather than drifting steadily one way.

xq.q: A charge of 90 C passes through a cross-section of a conductor in 5 minutes. The conductor is a 150 Ω resistor. Find the voltage across the resistor using V = IR.
A source transfers 36 J of energy to 12 C of charge moving through a resistor of 6 Ω. What is the current in the resistor?
o: 3 A
xq.w: V = E/q = 3 V, then I = V/R = 0.5 A; the trap is stopping at 3 or multiplying instead of dividing.

xq.q: Explain why the conventional current direction in a copper wire is opposite to the direction in which the electrons move, and explain why a current of 1 A does not mean that electrons travel quickly along the wire.
xq.a: Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would flow. Electrons are negative, so they drift opposite to this. Current is the rate of charge flow, I = dQ/dt, 1 A = 1 C/s; it is the charge passing a cross-section per second, and the carriers themselves drift slowly.
s: Conventional current = direction of positive charge flow
I = dQ/dt, rate of charge flow, 1 A = 1 C/s
Carriers drift slowly; current is charge per second not carrier speed

units.name: 1.2 Course intro, HiFi systems and loudspeaker waveforms
units.ov: This introductory material frames AC circuits through HiFi audio. A system has three blocks: a source producing a small signal, an amplifier boosting its power, and a loudspeaker converting the AC electrical signal into sound. The loudspeaker example motivates AC waveforms: a time-varying current in a voice coil sitting in a permanent magnet's field makes the cone oscillate and produce pressure waves.
must: HiFi chain: source (small signal, mV) \(\rightarrow\) amplifier (raises power, measured in W) \(\rightarrow\) loudspeaker (transducer to sound)
Source (e.g. turntable cartridge, CD player) converts physical or stored information into a small time-varying electrical signal
Amplifier increases voltage, current and/or power without changing the waveform shape, so it can drive a load
Speaker is a transducer: alternating electrical signal \(\rightarrow\) acoustic pressure waves via cone/diaphragm motion
Loudspeaker mechanism: voice coil carrying current in a constant permanent-magnet field experiences a force (\(F = BIL\)), which moves the cone
Current reversal reverses the force, so the cone moves back and forth; DC gives only a steady displacement and no sustained sound
The magnet supplies a constant field; the varying current drives the motion
Waveform shape (e.g. sinusoidal) is distinct from frequency; frequency sets the perceived pitch
Distinguish the small source output from the large amplifier output delivered to the speaker
conn: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (\(F = BIL\)) links the loudspeaker to electromagnetism, and the same principle works in reverse in microphones and guitar pickups
Amplifier gain links signal levels (mV at the source) to power (W) at the speaker, which leads to power calculations with AC voltage and current
Frequency and waveform of the current determine the cone's oscillation and hence the pitch of the sound, linking electrical waveforms to acoustics
The block-diagram view (source, processing, transducer) carries over to the other applications, such as radar and heart rate monitors
exq: Draw a block diagram of a HiFi system, naming the three main blocks and stating the type and approximate magnitude of the signal at each stage.
Explain, with a labelled sketch, how an alternating current in a voice coil produces sound. Why would a steady DC current not produce sustained sound?

A voice coil of length 5 m in a field of 1 T carries a current of 2 A. Calculate the force on the coil, and describe how this force varies if the current is sinusoidal at 440 Hz. What is the cone's oscillation frequency?
Distinguish between the waveform shape and the frequency of a signal. Which determines the pitch heard, and what does the amplifier change and not change?
Define source, amplifier and speaker, and give an example of each. Explain why the amplifier is needed between a turntable cartridge and a loudspeaker.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits – course introduction
pts: The course covers the basics of electronics and how they relate to several types of technology.
Application examples used to illustrate the course include HiFi audio systems, guitar pickups and microphones, radar systems, and heart rate monitors.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - HiFi Systems
pts: A HiFi system is built from three main blocks: a source that produces a small signal, an amplifier that boosts it, and a speaker that converts the electrical signal into sound.
The source (e.g. a turntable with a cartridge) converts the physical groove modulations of a record into a small, time-varying electrical signal.
The amplifier increases the power of the signal from the source so it can drive the speakers; its power level meters show output in watts.
The speaker converts the amplified alternating electrical signal back into sound waves by moving its cone/diaphragm.
defs: Source
The part of a HiFi system that produces the original low-level electrical signal representing the music, such as a turntable or CD player.
Amplifier
A circuit that increases the amplitude (voltage, current and/or power) of an input signal without changing its waveform, so it can drive a load such as a loudspeaker.
Speaker
A transducer that converts an alternating electrical signal into acoustic (sound) pressure waves.
tips: Do not confuse the source's output (a small signal, often millivolts) with the amplifier's output (large power delivered to the speaker).
Remember that the signal is alternating: the speaker responds to the varying AC waveform, not a steady DC level.
rq: Why is an amplifier needed between the source and the speaker rather than connecting the source directly to the speaker?
The source signal is far too small in power to move the speaker cone audibly; the amplifier increases the signal's power so the speaker can produce loud sound.
What would happen to the sound quality if the amplifier changed the shape of the waveform rather than only its size?
The sound would be distorted, because the speaker would reproduce a different waveform from the original signal; a good amplifier preserves the waveform while increasing its amplitude.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms
pts: This slide is an introduction to AC waveforms, motivated by how loudspeakers reproduce music, which is an alternating signal.
tips: Do not confuse the waveform's shape (e.g. sinusoidal) with its frequency, which determines the perceived pitch of the sound.
rq: Why does a loudspeaker need an alternating (rather than steady) current to produce sound?

A steady current gives a constant cone position, producing no pressure variation; sound requires the cone to oscillate back and forth, so the current must alternate in direction and amplitude, following the waveform of the music.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms (loudspeaker example)
pts: An alternating current supply drives the loudspeaker's voice coil, which sits in the field of a permanent magnet.
The alternating current reverses direction periodically, so the force on the coil reverses and the cone moves back and forth.
Moving the cone pushes and pulls the air, producing pressure waves that we hear as sound.
The magnet provides a constant magnetic field; the varying current is what makes the coil and cone oscillate.
tips: Do not confuse the permanent magnet (constant field) with the time-varying current that actually drives the motion.
Remember that the cone moves in both directions only because the current reverses; a DC supply gives no sustained sound.
rq: Why does a loudspeaker need an alternating rather than a steady (DC) current to produce sound?
A steady current gives a constant force, so the cone would just sit displaced; only a current that reverses direction makes the cone oscillate and push air back and forth to create sound waves.
What would happen to the sound if the frequency of the alternating current were doubled?
The cone would oscillate twice as fast, so the sound would have double the frequency (higher pitch), while the wave shape determines the tone quality.

units.name: 1.3 Period, frequency and combining waves
units.ov: This material introduces periodic AC waveforms and the reciprocal link between period and frequency, \(f = 1/T\). It then shows how waves of different frequency combine by superposition (adding instantaneous values), which explains how chords and music arise from many frequencies. Amplitude, frequency and phase are the three descriptors that must be kept distinct.
must: Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\) and \(f = \frac{1}{T}\)
Period \(T\) is the time of one complete cycle (in seconds), read from the horizontal time axis, not from the voltage axis
Frequency \(f\) is cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz); higher frequency means shorter period and more tightly packed cycles
UK mains is about 50 Hz, so \(T = \frac{1}{50} = 20\ \text{ms} = 0.02\ \text{s}\)
Convert units before calculating: ms to s (and kHz to Hz) so that \(f\) is in Hz and \(T\) in s
Amplitude (peak value, e.g. ±1.0 V) is independent of frequency; changing \(f\) does not change peak height
Superposition: when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements, \(y = y_1 + y_2\); interference is the same process
Add instantaneous values at each time point, never peak amplitudes of waves with different frequencies; same-sign values reinforce, opposite-sign values reduce
Phase difference is the horizontal offset between waves, not a difference in peak height; in phase reinforces, out of phase cancels
Musical pitch is set by frequency (e.g. 440 Hz sounds higher than 240 Hz), and chords and music come from combinations of different frequencies
conn: Period and frequency conversion is often combined with unit handling: a period read from a graph in ms must be converted to s before finding \(f\) in Hz
Superposition depends on both frequency and phase: waves of different frequency drift in and out of phase, so the combined waveform is not a simple sinusoid and its shape changes over time
Amplitude, frequency and phase are separate properties; questions often ask which one changes when a graph is altered (e.g. tighter cycles means higher \(f\), same amplitude)
The mains example links the abstract \(T = 1/f\) to real engineering AC: 50 Hz gives 50 cycles per second and a 20 ms period, which sets the time scale on an oscilloscope trace
exq: A waveform on an oscilloscope has successive peaks 4 ms apart. Calculate its period and frequency, stating the units, and explain why the 1.0 V peak value is not the period.
UK mains is 50 Hz. Calculate the period in ms, and state how many complete cycles occur in 0.5 s. A US supply has a period of 16.7 ms; find its frequency.
Three sinusoids of equal amplitude have frequencies 240 Hz, 340 Hz and 440 Hz. Find each period, state which is highest in pitch, and explain why their peak heights are identical.

Two sinusoidal waves, each between +1.0 and −1.0, have different frequencies. Explain using superposition how to sketch the combined waveform, and state the possible range of the resultant at an instant when one wave is +0.6 and the other is −0.8.

Explain the difference between amplitude, frequency and phase difference when two waves are superimposed, and describe how the combined amplitude differs when they are in phase and when they are out of phase.

notes.t: AC Waveforms and the Period
pts: A periodic waveform repeats its shape at regular intervals; the time for one full repetition is the period T.
The period is measured between two identical points on consecutive cycles, such as successive peaks.
The plotted waveform is a voltage (V) varying with time, oscillating between +1.0 V and −1.0 V about zero.
defs: Period (T)
The time taken for a waveform to repeat itself exactly; the duration of one complete cycle, measured in seconds.
tips: Read the period from the time axis in the correct time units; the period is a time, not a voltage, so do not use the 1.0 V peak value as T.
Do not confuse the period with the amplitude: the amplitude here is 1.0 V, while T is the horizontal duration of one cycle.
rq: Why is the distance between two successive peaks, rather than between a peak and a zero crossing, used to define the period?

Successive peaks are identical points on consecutive cycles, so the interval between them is exactly one full repetition. A peak and a zero crossing are not equivalent points (one is a maximum, the other is rising or falling), so they do not define a full period.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Frequency and Period
pts: Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz, and is the inverse of the period.
One period is the time taken for one complete repetition of the waveform, shown as the distance between successive peaks.
UK mains supply is AC at approximately 50 Hz, so the waveform repeats 50 times per second.
Substituting f = 50 Hz into T = 1/f gives a period of 20 ms for mains voltage.
defs: Frequency (f)
The number of complete cycles of a periodic waveform per second, measured in hertz (Hz); the reciprocal of the period.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform, measured in seconds.
eqs: Period of mains voltage at 50 Hz
tips: Convert units before calculating: a period given in ms must be converted to seconds (20 ms = 0.02 s) when used with f in Hz.
Do not confuse the period with the frequency: the period is the time for one cycle, while frequency counts cycles per second.
rq: Why does doubling the frequency of an AC supply halve the period, and what would this do to the number of cycles in one second?
Since T = 1/f, doubling f halves T; the waveform then completes twice as many cycles per second, e.g. 100 Hz gives T = 10 ms.
If the time axis of the graph were read in milliseconds, how would you find the period from the peak-to-peak distance?
Measure the time between two successive peaks on the time axis; that interval is T, and f = 1/T gives the frequency.

notes.t: AC Waveforms and Frequency
pts: An AC signal is a sinusoidal waveform that repeatedly reverses direction, oscillating between positive and negative peaks.
Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz; higher frequency means more cycles in the same time.
The three waveforms have the same amplitude (peaks at ±1.0) but different frequencies, so they look different only in how tightly the cycles are packed.
In audio terms, frequency determines perceived pitch: the 440 Hz signal has the most cycles and sounds highest, while 240 Hz sounds lowest.
defs: Frequency (f)
The number of complete cycles of a periodic waveform per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a waveform; it is the reciprocal of frequency.
tips: Do not confuse frequency (Hz) with amplitude (peak value); changing frequency does not change the peak height of the waveform.
Remember that period and frequency are reciprocals; using T = f instead of T = 1/f is a common error.
rq: Why does the 440 Hz waveform look 'compressed' compared with the 240 Hz waveform if both have the same peak amplitude?
Because it completes more cycles per second, so each cycle occupies a shorter time interval; amplitude is unchanged, only the period is shorter.
What would happen to the perceived tone if the frequency of a signal doubled, and why?
The tone would be perceived an octave higher, since pitch increases with frequency.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms (Superposition and Interference)
pts: Music heard is a combination of many different waves, not a single wave.
Each guitar string vibrates at its own frequency; the waves combine as they travel through air to produce the sound of a chord.
When waves overlap, their displacements add together; this combining process is superposition, also called interference.
defs: Superposition
The principle that when two or more waves overlap in the same medium, the resulting displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual wave displacements.
Interference
The effect produced when overlapping waves combine, reinforcing or cancelling each other depending on their relative phase; another name for superposition.
tips: Superposition adds displacements algebraically (with sign), not magnitudes; waves in phase reinforce and out of phase cancel.
Superposition and interference are the same process here; do not treat interference as a separate phenomenon.
rq: Why does a single guitar chord sound different from a single string played alone, even though each string is a wave?
Each string produces a wave at its own frequency; when these waves superpose, the combined waveform is more complex, which the ear perceives as a chord with a distinct timbre.
What would happen to the combined wave if two component waves were exactly out of phase with equal amplitudes?
They would cancel by destructive interference, giving zero net displacement at every point.

notes.t: AC waveforms and combining frequencies
pts: Two sinusoidal waves of different frequency are plotted against time; the one with the shorter period completes more cycles in the same interval, so it has the higher frequency.
When two waveforms are superimposed, their instantaneous values add: where both are positive the combined amplitude is increased (+), and where they have opposite signs it is reduced (−).
Both waves swing between +1.0 and −1.0, so they share the same peak amplitude but are out of step with each other, meaning they are not in phase.
defs: Frequency
The number of complete cycles of a periodic waveform per second, measured in hertz (Hz); higher frequency corresponds to a shorter period.
tips: Do not add the peak amplitudes of waves of different frequency; add the instantaneous values at each point in time.
Phase difference is the horizontal offset between the waves, not a difference in their peak heights.
rq: Why does superposing two waves of different frequencies produce a complex waveform rather than a single sinusoid?
Their instantaneous values add at each moment, and because the frequencies differ the peaks and troughs drift in and out of alignment, producing a repeating but non-sinusoidal pattern.
What would you expect to hear if the two waves in the figure had identical frequencies and phases?
A single pure tone at double the amplitude, since the waves would reinforce each other at every instant.

xq.q: A sinusoidal signal has a period of 0.25 ms. Find its frequency, and the number of complete cycles in 20 ms.
A waveform is observed to have successive peaks 8 ms apart. What is its frequency?
xq.a: 125 Hz
o: 8 Hz
125 Hz
1.25 kHz
xq.w: f = 1/T = 1/0.008 = 125 Hz; the traps are using f = T, or forgetting to convert ms to s.

xq.q: Two sinusoidal voltages of different frequencies are added in a circuit. Explain how the instantaneous value of the combined waveform is found, and state what happens at an instant when one wave is +0.6 V and the other is −0.4 V.
xq.a: By superposition the instantaneous values add algebraically, with sign. At that instant the sum is 0.6 + (−0.4) = +0.2 V, so the combined amplitude is reduced because the signs are opposite. When both are positive the combined value is increased.
s: Opposite signs reduce, same signs reinforce

units.name: 1.4 Non-sinusoidal waveforms (sawtooth, square)
units.ov: This module extends AC analysis beyond sinusoids to periodic waveforms such as the sawtooth (linear ramp 0 to 1 V then abrupt drop) and the square wave (switching between +1 V and -1 V). Every periodic waveform is described by its period T, frequency and amplitude, but its shape determines the relation between peak, average and RMS values. The notes give only qualitative detail, so a top-grade student should derive the quantitative results from the definitions of average and RMS.
must: Period \(T\) is the time for one complete cycle and frequency is \(f=1/T\); read T from the time axis, checking its scale first.
Waveform shape, amplitude and frequency are independent properties: two waves can share a shape but differ in size or repetition rate.
Sawtooth: linear rise from 0 to 1.0 V over T, then an abrupt drop to 0 V. Its equation is \(v(t)=V_{pk}\,t/T\) for \(0\le t<T\).
Square wave: abrupt switching between two fixed levels (here +1.0 V and -1.0 V) with constant peak values, used in digital signalling.
Symmetric square wave (±V): \(V_{RMS}=V_{pk}\) because \(v^2\) is constant, and the average over a full cycle is 0.
General definitions: \(V_{avg}=\frac1T\int_0^T v\,dt\) and \(V_{RMS}=\sqrt{\frac1T\int_0^T v^2\,dt}\). Use these for any waveform.
Sawtooth 0 to 1 V (derived from the definitions): \(V_{avg}=0.5\) V and \(V_{RMS}=1/\sqrt3\approx0.577\) V. Note it is not \(V_{pk}/\sqrt2\).
The sinusoid relations \(V_{RMS}=V_{pk}/\sqrt2\) and \(V_{avg}=0.637V_{pk}\) (half-cycle) do not apply to other shapes; the ratio of peak to RMS depends on shape (form and crest factors).
Sawtooth and square waves are harmonically rich, whereas a sine wave is single-frequency. This explains their different sound in synthesisers.
Applications: sawtooth for TV raster scanning and oscilloscope time bases; square wave for digital signals; sine, sawtooth and square from oscillators in synthesisers.
conn: RMS and power: RMS gives the equivalent DC heating value, so \(P=V_{RMS}^2/R\). A ±1 V square wave across R dissipates \(1/R\), while a 0 to 1 V sawtooth dissipates only \(1/(3R)\).
Average versus RMS: the sawtooth has a non-zero average (DC offset) while the symmetric square wave averages zero. This matters when AC-coupling or when reading a meter that assumes a sine wave.
Period and frequency with the oscilloscope: the time-base sawtooth sweeps the trace, and you read T from the time-axis scale to find f and then compare it with amplitude.
Waveform shape and harmonic content: abrupt edges (the sawtooth drop and square-wave switching) imply high-frequency harmonics, which links to Fourier ideas and to circuit bandwidth.
exq: A sawtooth rises linearly from 0 to 1.0 V over T = 2 ms then drops to 0 V. Find its frequency, average value and RMS value by integration.
A symmetric square wave of ±1.0 V and period 10 µs is applied across a 50 Ω resistor. Determine f, \(V_{\text{RMS}}\) and average power. Compare with a 1 V peak sinusoid.
Derive the RMS value of the sawtooth \(v=V_{pk}t/T\) and explain why it is not \(V_{pk}/\sqrt2\). Calculate the crest factor.

From an oscilloscope trace showing 4 divisions per cycle at 0.5 ms/div and 2 V/div peak amplitude, state T, f and the peak, average and RMS values if the waveform is (a) a ±V square wave, (b) a 0 to V sawtooth.
A sawtooth (0 to 1 V) and a square wave (±1 V) have equal period. Compare their average and RMS values and the power dissipated in the same resistor, and explain the differences.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Non-Sinusoidal Waveforms (Sawtooth)
pts: AC circuits are not limited to sinusoidal voltages; other periodic waveforms can be used.
The sawtooth waveform rises linearly from 0 V to 1.0 V over each period and then drops abruptly back to 0 V, repeating every period T.
Sawtooth waveforms are used in TV raster scanning and in oscilloscope time bases.
defs: Sawtooth waveform
A periodic waveform that increases linearly over one period and then falls abruptly to its starting value, repeating each period T.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform before it repeats.
tips: Do not assume AC means sinusoidal: the period T is the same for all periodic waveforms, but the shape determines the relationship between peak and average values.
rq: Why is a sawtooth waveform useful for a TV raster scan or an oscilloscope time base?
Its linear rise sweeps the beam across the screen at a constant rate, and the abrupt drop resets it quickly to the start for the next sweep.
How does the sawtooth differ from a sinusoid in terms of the rate of change of voltage?
A sawtooth has a constant rate of change (constant slope) during its rise, whereas a sinusoid's rate of change varies continuously with time.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Non-Sinusoidal Waveforms (Square Wave)
pts: AC circuits do not have to use sinusoidal waveforms; other waveform shapes are possible.
The square wave switches abruptly between two fixed voltage levels, here +1.0 V and −1.0 V, with a period T.
Square waves are widely used in digital signals, where the voltage is either high or low.
defs: Square wave
A periodic waveform that alternates abruptly between two constant voltage levels with equal-or-specified durations, widely used in digital signalling.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform before the pattern repeats.
tips: Do not assume every AC waveform is sinusoidal; read the voltage–time graph to find peak values and period.
Remember that the peak values for a square wave are constant, unlike a sinusoid, so RMS calculations differ (RMS equals the peak value for a symmetric square wave).
rq: Why might a circuit designer choose a square wave rather than a sinusoid for a digital system?
Square waves have abrupt transitions between two defined levels, which map directly onto binary high and low states and are easy to detect reliably.
If the square wave in the figure has a period of T, what fraction of each period is it at +1.0 V?
From the plot, the signal is at +1.0 V for half the period (T/2) and at −1.0 V for the other half, so the duty cycle is 50%.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms
pts: This page introduces AC waveforms, which are the periodic signals that alternating current circuits use; the page itself shows only a video link rather than explanatory content.
tips: The page only links to an external video; the content relevant to exams (waveform shapes, period, frequency, amplitude) must be learned from the video or following slides, not assumed from this page alone.
rq: Why might a video be used to introduce waveforms before any equations are given?
Watching how voltage or current varies over time builds an intuitive picture of periodic waveforms (shape, repetition, amplitude) that makes later mathematical descriptions easier to understand.

notes.t: Alternating current waveforms: sine, sawtooth and square
pts: Waveforms such as sine, sawtooth and square are alternating signals that vary periodically over time.
Synthesisers and electronic music generate these common waveform shapes using oscillators.
The sine wave is the smooth, single-frequency waveform that repeats its shape each cycle.
The sawtooth wave rises linearly and then drops sharply, giving a bright, harmonically rich sound.
The square wave switches abruptly between two fixed levels, alternating between positive and negative values.
defs: Waveform
The shape of a signal plotted as a function of time, describing how its value varies over each cycle.
tips: Do not confuse waveform shape with amplitude or frequency; two waves can share a shape but differ in size or rate of repetition.
Read the time axis scale on waveform plots before estimating period or frequency.
rq: Why does a square wave sound harsher than a sine wave when played on a synthesiser?
A square wave contains sharp transitions and strong higher-frequency harmonics, whereas a sine wave is a pure single frequency with no harmonics.
What would you expect to change in the sawtooth waveform if its frequency were doubled?
The waveform would repeat twice as often, so each cycle would occupy half the time while its amplitude stays the same.

xq.q: A symmetric square wave alternates between +5.0 V and −5.0 V with period T = 2 ms. What are its RMS value and frequency?
xq.a: 5.0 V and 500 Hz
o: 2.5 V and 500 Hz
5.0 V and 500 Hz
3.5 V and 2 kHz
5.0 V and 2 kHz
xq.w: For a symmetric square wave the voltage magnitude is always 5 V so RMS equals the peak, and f = 1/T = 500 Hz; the traps are using 1/√2 (sine) or 1/(T in ms).

xq.q: A sawtooth waveform rises linearly from 0 V to 1.0 V over each period and then drops abruptly to 0 V. It is used as an oscilloscope time-base with a repetition frequency f = 250 Hz. Find the period T, and hence the time at which the voltage first reaches 0.60 V after a drop to zero.
xq.a: 2.4 ms

xq.q: A square wave switches between +1.0 V and −1.0 V with period T. Explain why its RMS value equals its peak value, whereas a sinusoid of the same peak value has a smaller RMS value. Sketch one period of the square wave to support your answer.
xq.a: The square wave has |V| = 1.0 V at all times, so V² = 1.0 V² throughout the period. The mean of V² is 1.0 V², and its square root is 1.0 V = peak. A sinusoid only reaches its peak momentarily; V² is smaller for most of the cycle so the mean of V² is less than the peak squared, giving an RMS below the peak.
s: Sketch: levels +1 V and −1 V, abrupt switching, labelled period T
V² constant at 1 V² for square wave
Sinusoid spends most time below peak so RMS < peak

units.name: 1.5 Sine and cosine from circular motion
units.ov: This material builds sine and cosine from right-angled triangle ratios, then places the triangle inside a circle so that the radius is the hypotenuse and its horizontal and vertical projections give cosine and sine. A point rotating around the circle then traces sinusoidal waveforms, with one revolution equal to one period. These ideas underlie later work on harmonic motion, phasors and AC signals.
must: Right-triangle definitions: \(\sin\theta = o/h\) and \(\cos\theta = a/h\), so \(o = h\sin\theta\) and \(a = h\cos\theta\)
Identify opposite and adjacent relative to the angle \(\theta\), not by their position on the page; swapping them is the commonest error
In the circle, the hypotenuse is the radius \(r\): horizontal projection \(x = r\cos\theta\), vertical projection \(y = r\sin\theta\)
For a unit circle (\(r=1\)), \(\cos\theta\) is the x-coordinate and \(\sin\theta\) is the y-coordinate of the rotating point
Plotting a projection against angle (or time) gives a sinusoid that oscillates between \(+r\) and \(-r\); the amplitude equals the radius
One full revolution (\(360^\circ = 2\pi\) rad) equals one period \(T\) of the waveform
Key cosine values: maximum 1 at \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), minimum -1 at \(180^\circ\), zero at \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\); sine is the same wave shifted by \(90^\circ\)
Amplitude (radius) and frequency (rotation speed) are different things: radius sets the height, rotation rate sets how quickly the wave repeats
Keep the calculator in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) and use one unit consistently throughout
conn: Vector resolution in statics and dynamics: a force or velocity of magnitude \(h\) at angle \(\theta\) has components \(h\cos\theta\) and \(h\sin\theta\), which is the same projection idea as the circle
Rotating point to waveform: with \(\theta = \omega t\), the projection becomes \(A\cos(\omega t)\), linking angle, angular frequency, period \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) and simple harmonic motion
Degrees versus radians: converting a revolution to \(2\pi\) rad connects the period, arc length and angular velocity, and calculator mode errors affect all of these
Sine and cosine as phase-shifted versions of one wave leads to phase angles and phasor representations of oscillating quantities
exq: A ladder of length 4.0 m rests at \(65^\circ\) to the horizontal. Find the height it reaches up the wall and the horizontal distance of its foot from the wall, stating which side is opposite and which is adjacent to the angle.

A point moves around a circle of radius 0.5 m, starting at \(\theta = 0\). Find its horizontal and vertical positions at \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(120^\circ\) and \(225^\circ\), and sketch the vertical projection against angle for one revolution.

A crank of radius 150 mm rotates at constant speed. Write the expression for the vertical displacement of its end, state the amplitude, and give the angles in one revolution where the displacement is maximum, minimum and zero.
Explain why one revolution of a rotating point corresponds to one period of the cosine wave. If the point completes a revolution in 0.02 s, find the period and the angular speed in rad/s.
A force of 200 N acts at \(35^\circ\) above the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal and vertical components, and show how the answer changes if the calculator is wrongly set to radians.

notes.t: Origin of sine and cosine from a right-angled triangle
pts: Sine and cosine are ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to an angle θ.
The opposite side equals the hypotenuse multiplied by sin(θ).
The adjacent side equals the hypotenuse multiplied by cos(θ).
defs: Hypotenuse (h)
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Opposite side (o)
The side across from the angle θ in a right-angled triangle.
Adjacent side (a)
The side next to the angle θ that is not the hypotenuse.
eqs: Opposite side from hypotenuse and angle
o = opposite side (m); h = hypotenuse (m); θ = angle (rad or °)
Adjacent side from hypotenuse and angle
a = adjacent side (m); h = hypotenuse (m); θ = angle (rad or °)
tips: Check the angle mode: θ must be in radians or degrees consistently with your calculator setting.
Identify o and a relative to θ, not by position; swapping them gives the wrong sine/cosine.
rq: Why does dividing the opposite side by the hypotenuse give a value that depends only on θ?
Similar right-angled triangles with the same angle have proportional sides, so the ratio o/h is fixed by θ alone.
If θ is fixed and h doubles, what happens to o and a?
Both o and a double, since each is h multiplied by a constant depending only on θ.

notes.t: Origin of sine and cosine from a right-angled triangle in a circle
pts: Sine and cosine describe the side ratios of a right-angled triangle formed by a radius at angle θ within a circle.
The hypotenuse h is the radius of the circle; the adjacent side a is the horizontal projection of h, so a = h·cos(θ).
The opposite side o is the vertical projection of h, giving o = h·sin(θ) and linking sine to height on the circle.
defs: Cosine (cos θ)
Ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle: cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
Sine (sin θ)
Ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
eqs: Horizontal (adjacent) component of a vector of length h at angle θ
a = adjacent side (m or same unit as h); h = hypotenuse / radius (m); θ = angle from horizontal (rad or °)
tips: Check which side is adjacent to θ before choosing sine or cosine; mixing them up is the most common error.
Ensure the calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) when evaluating cos θ.
rq: Why does the adjacent side equal h·cos(θ) rather than h·sin(θ)?
Cosine is defined as adjacent/hypotenuse, and the adjacent side lies next to the angle θ measured from the horizontal axis.
What happens to a and o as θ increases from 0° towards 90°?
a = h·cos θ decreases from h to 0, while o = h·sin θ increases from 0 to h.

notes.t: Rotation around a circle (sinusoid from circular motion)
pts: A point rotating around a unit circle has its horizontal projection following the cosine of the angle and its vertical projection following the sine.
The vertical projection of the rotating point traces a sinusoidal waveform between +1 and -1 as the angle increases.
The amplitude of the resulting waveform equals the radius of the circle, here 1.
tips: Do not confuse the radius of the rotating circle (the amplitude) with the frequency of rotation, which determines how fast the waveform repeats.
rq: Why does the vertical projection of a rotating point produce an AC waveform rather than a constant value?
Because the vertical coordinate of the point changes continuously with the angle as it rotates, giving \( \sin\theta \), which oscillates periodically between -1 and +1.

notes.t: Rotation around a circle and the sinusoidal waveform
pts: A point rotating once around a unit circle through 360° traces one full cycle of a cosine wave when its horizontal position is plotted against angle.
One complete revolution of the rotating point corresponds to one period (T) of the waveform on the right.
The vertical value of the waveform equals the projection of the rotating point onto the horizontal axis, which ranges between -1 and 1.
The waveform reaches its maximum value of 1 at 0° and 360°, and its minimum value of -1 at 180°.
defs: Period (T)
The time or angle taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform; for a rotation this is one full revolution of 360°.
tips: Do not confuse the horizontal axis of the waveform (angle or time) with the vertical axis, which shows the projected amplitude between -1 and 1.
Ensure the angle is measured consistently in degrees or radians when relating a full rotation to the period.
rq: Why does the plotted waveform return to its starting value after 360°?
Because the rotating point completes one full revolution and returns to its original position on the circle, so its projection repeats.
What would happen to the period if the point rotated twice as fast around the circle?
The period would halve, since one full cycle would be completed in 180° of rotation-equivalent time instead of 360°.

xq.q: A point rotates around a circle of radius 12 V-units (amplitude 12 V) so that the vertical projection gives V = 12 sin θ. When the radius has turned to θ = 150° from the horizontal, find the instantaneous value V and the horizontal projection a = 12 cos θ, and hence give the magnitude of a.
A point moves at constant speed around a circle of radius 3 V-units, starting at the horizontal position (angle 0). Its horizontal projection is plotted against angle. Which describes the waveform?
xq.a: A cosine of amplitude 3 with maximum at 0° and 360° and minimum at 180°
o: A sine of amplitude 3 starting from zero at 0°
A cosine of amplitude 1 because the circle is a unit circle
A cosine of amplitude 3 with maximum at 0° and 360° and minimum at 180°
A cosine of amplitude 3 with minimum at 0° and maximum at 180°
xq.w: Horizontal projection is 3cosθ, giving 3 at 0°, −3 at 180°; the traps are confusing it with sine, using the unit radius, or inverting the sign.

xq.q: A rotating radius of length h makes angle θ with the horizontal. Show how the sinusoidal waveform V = h sin θ arises from this circular motion, and state what determines the amplitude and what determines how quickly the waveform repeats.
xq.a: The vertical projection of the radius is the opposite side of a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse h, so o = h sin θ. As the point rotates, θ increases and the projection traces a sine wave between +h and −h. The amplitude equals the radius h. The rate of rotation sets how fast one revolution (one period) is completed, i.e. the frequency.
s: Right-angled triangle with hypotenuse = radius h
Opposite side o = h sin θ is the vertical projection
Projection varies between +h and −h as θ increases: sinusoid
Amplitude = radius; frequency set by rotation rate, one revolution = one period

units.name: 1.6 Radians, angular frequency and phase
units.ov: This material defines the radian as the ratio of arc length to radius (so 2π rad = 360°), then uses it as the natural angle unit for sinusoids. Angular frequency \(\omega\) links period T, frequency f and the sine argument, and phase offsets \(\phi\) are shifts along the angle axis that are equivalent to time shifts \(\Delta t\). Everything ties together through one cycle = 2π rad = one period T.
must: Radian definition: \(\theta = s/r\), dimensionless; one full turn is \(2\pi r/r = 2\pi\) rad
Conversions: \(\pi\) rad = 180°, \(\theta_{rad}=\theta_{deg}\times\pi/180\); never confuse π rad with π degrees
Sinusoid: \(V=V_o\sin(\omega t)\), with amplitude \(V_o\) (peak value) and the argument \(\omega t\) in radians
\(\omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f\), so \(T=2\pi/\omega = 1/f\); \(\omega\) in rad/s, f in Hz
Write in terms of frequency as \(V=V_o\sin(2\pi f t)\); never put f directly into \(\sin(\omega t)\) without the 2π
Phase shift: \(y=\cos(\omega t+\phi)\); positive \(\phi\) shifts the curve left, so the wave leads (e.g. \(\cos(\theta+\pi/2)\) leads by a quarter cycle)
Phase and time shift: \(\phi=\omega\Delta t = 2\pi\Delta t/T\) and \(\Delta t=\phi T/2\pi\)
Phase difference \(\Delta\phi\) between two waves of the same frequency is usually all that matters, not absolute phase
Check the calculator is in radian mode when \(\omega t\) is in rad; 2π ≈ 6.28 rad, and one period = 360° = 2π rad
Keep units consistent: s and r in the same units, \(\Delta t\) and T in the same units (ms with ms)
conn: Frequency, period and angular frequency: converting between f, T and \(\omega\) is needed before evaluating \(\sin(\omega t)\) or finding a phase
Phase shift and time shift: \(\phi=\omega\Delta t\) turns an oscilloscope time offset into a phase angle in rad or degrees, and back
Radians and calculator mode: evaluating \(V_o\sin(\omega t+\phi)\) at a given time needs \(\omega t\) and \(\phi\) in radians, so degree/radian conversion matters
