For ω << ω0 the term ω0/(jω) is very large so the gain tends to 0: low frequencies are blocked. For ω >> ω0 the term tends to 0 so the gain tends to 1: high frequencies pass.
s: Divide by R and use -j = 1/j to get 1/(1+1/(jωCR))

units.name: 3.8 Band-pass filters, speaker crossovers and summary
units.ov: This material covers how passive RC/LC filters (low-pass, high-pass and their combination, the band-pass) are used in loudspeaker crossovers to split audio between drivers, and how Bode plots describe them. The key ideas are the -3 dB cut-off point, the 20 dB/decade first-order roll-off, and the fact that a band-pass response needs a high-pass and a low-pass section together, which is why the mid-range driver is the hardest to filter.
must: At the characteristic (cut-off) frequency of a first-order RC filter, \( V_{out}/V_{in}=1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707 \), which is -3 dB.
Power ratio at cut-off is \( P_{out}/P_{in}=1/2 \); use \( 10\log_{10} \) for power and \( 20\log_{10} \) for voltage, giving -3 dB either way.
First-order roll-off is 20 dB per decade; state the sign explicitly (negative slope for low-pass, positive for high-pass below cut-off).
Cut-off frequency is set by choosing R and C: \( \omega_c = 1/RC \), so \( f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) \) (design R and C for a target \( f_c \)).
Capacitors pass high frequencies and block low; inductors pass low frequencies and block high.
A band-pass filter passes a band around the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and attenuates above and below; the Bode magnitude plot peaks at \( \omega_0 \) and rolls off on both sides.
A band-pass response needs a high-pass and a low-pass section combined; no single component can achieve it.
A crossover is a passive network (R, L, C) that divides the signal into bands and routes each to the right driver; the mid-range driver needs a band-pass, so is hardest to filter.
Read the actual peak gain from the Bode plot: 0 dB means unity gain, and the band-pass peak is at 0 dB only in the ideal case.
conn: The -3 dB point links the transfer function, the Bode plot and the power-halving idea. The cut-off frequency defines the band edges of both the high-pass and the low-pass sections of a band-pass filter.

Cascading a high-pass RC (sets lower cut-off) with a low-pass RC (sets upper cut-off) gives the band-pass; the 20 dB/decade slope applies on each side, and component choices set both corner frequencies.

Crossover design combines the capacitor/inductor frequency behaviour with the chosen \( f_c \) for each driver (woofer low-pass, tweeter high-pass, mid-range band-pass), and dB conversions are used to check the attenuation at given frequencies.
exq: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Calculate its cut-off frequency, the output/input voltage ratio and the gain in dB at that frequency, and the attenuation one decade above.
Explain why power ratio ½ and voltage ratio 1/√2 both correspond to -3 dB, showing the calculations with 10log10 and 20log10.
Design a first-order RC high-pass filter for a tweeter with a cut-off of 3 kHz given C = 10 nF. Find R and sketch the Bode magnitude plot, labelling the slope in dB/decade.
Describe how a band-pass filter for a mid-range driver is built from high-pass and low-pass sections. For band edges of 400 Hz and 4 kHz, sketch the Bode plot and state the roll-off on each side.
State which of a capacitor and an inductor passes high frequencies and which blocks them, and use this to explain how a simple two-way crossover routes signals to a woofer and a tweeter.

notes.t: Filter circuits in speaker crossovers
pts: Mid-range drivers need a bandpass filter so they only reproduce a limited band of frequencies.
A crossover uses passive components (resistors, capacitors, inductors) to split the audio signal between drivers by frequency.
Mid-range is the hardest driver to filter because it needs both a high-pass and a low-pass action at once.
defs: Bandpass filter
A circuit that passes signals within a defined frequency range and attenuates frequencies above and below that range.
Crossover
A filter network that divides an audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate loudspeaker driver.
tips: Do not confuse which element passes which frequencies: capacitors pass highs and block lows, inductors pass lows and block highs.
Bandpass behaviour needs a combination of high-pass and low-pass sections; a single component cannot achieve it.
rq: Why can a single capacitor or inductor not produce the mid-range band on its own?
A single reactive element gives only one cutoff, a high-pass or low-pass slope; a mid-range driver needs both a lower and an upper cutoff, so high-pass and low-pass sections must be combined.
Why do inductors (coils) block high frequencies while capacitors block low frequencies?
An inductor's reactance increases with frequency, so it impedes highs; a capacitor's reactance decreases with frequency, so it impedes lows.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Bandpass Filter Bode Plot
pts: A bandpass filter passes signals near a central frequency and attenuates signals on both sides of the peak.
The Bode magnitude plot peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \), where the gain is at its maximum (0 dB reference).
Bandpass filters are widely used across many engineering disciplines and will be revisited for different applications.
defs: Bandpass filter
A filter whose Bode magnitude plot curves down on both sides of a central frequency, passing a band of frequencies near \( \omega_0 \) while attenuating frequencies above and below it.
tips: Do not confuse the plot's dB axis: 0 dB means unity gain, and the bandpass peak is at 0 dB only in an ideal case; read the actual peak value from the plot.
A bandpass filter must roll off on both sides; a plot that falls off on only one side describes a low-pass or high-pass filter instead.
rq: Why does a bandpass filter's gain fall off on both sides of \( \omega_0 \) rather than just one side?

It must reject both low frequencies (below the band) and high frequencies (above the band), so it combines a high-pass-like roll-off at low frequency with a low-pass-like roll-off at high frequency, giving a peak in between.
What does the value 0 on the vertical axis of the plot represent for \( V_{out}/V_{in} \) in dB?
A gain of 0 dB, meaning \( V_{out} = V_{in} \); the peak of a bandpass filter reaches this level so signals at \( \omega_0 \) pass unattenuated.

notes.t: Summary of first-order RC filters: -3 dB point, roll-off, design, high-pass and band-pass
pts: At the characteristic frequency a first-order RC filter gives Vout/Vin = 1/√2, i.e. power ratio Pout/Pin = ½, which is -3 dB.
The roll-off of a first-order filter is 20 dB per decade; the slope is negative for a low-pass filter.
An RC filter can be designed for a chosen cut-off (characteristic) frequency by selecting R and C appropriately.
An RC high-pass filter was demonstrated, and a band-pass filter passes only a selected band of frequencies.
defs: -3 dB attenuation
The point where output voltage falls to 1/√2 (≈0.707) of input voltage, or output power is half the input power.
Roll-off
The rate at which the gain of a filter falls (or rises) beyond the cut-off frequency; for a first-order filter it is 20 dB per decade.
Band-pass filter
A filter that passes frequencies within a selected band and attenuates frequencies outside it.
eqs: Voltage gain at the characteristic frequency of a first-order RC filter
Power ratio at the characteristic frequency
tips: Do not mix up the 3 dB power and voltage rules: power ratio ½ uses 10 log10, voltage ratio 1/√2 uses 20 log10.
A low-pass filter has a negative slope in the roll-off; state the sign explicitly in answers.
rq: Why does a power ratio of ½ correspond to -3 dB rather than -6 dB?

Decibels for power use 10 log10(\(P_{\text{out}}\)/\(P_{\text{in}}\)) = 10 log10(0.5) ≈ -3 dB, whereas voltage ratios use 20 log10, which would give -6 dB for a voltage ratio of ½; here the voltage ratio is 1/√2, so 20 log10(1/√2) ≈ -3 dB.
Why is the roll-off of a first-order filter 20 dB per decade?
A first-order RC filter has one reactive element, so its gain falls as 1/f beyond the cut-off; 20 log10 of a tenfold frequency change gives 20 dB per decade.
How does a band-pass filter differ from a low-pass filter in its frequency response?
A low-pass filter passes frequencies below cut-off and attenuates above it, while a band-pass filter passes frequencies within a selected band and attenuates both below and above that band.

xq.q: A mid-range loudspeaker driver must only reproduce a limited band of frequencies. Which filter arrangement achieves this, and what does its Bode magnitude plot look like?
xq.a: A high-pass section combined with a low-pass section, giving a plot that peaks and falls on both sides of a central frequency
o: A single capacitor in series, giving a plot that rises and stays flat
A single low-pass RC section, giving a plot that falls on one side only
A high-pass section combined with a low-pass section, giving a plot that peaks and falls on both sides of a central frequency
A single inductor in series, giving a plot that is flat at low frequency and falls at high frequency
xq.w: A band-pass response needs both high-pass and low-pass action so the gain rolls off on both sides; a single component or section gives only one-sided roll-off.

xq.q: A first-order RC filter has a power ratio \(P_{out}/P_{in}\) = 1/2 at its characteristic frequency. The input signal power to the filter is 8.0 W at that frequency. Calculate the output power in W, and the gain in dB at that frequency using the power ratio, \(10\log_{10}(P_{out}/P_{in})\).
xq.a: Output power = 4.0 W; gain = -3.0 dB

xq.q: Explain why a first-order low-pass RC section alone cannot be used to filter a mid-range speaker driver, and describe, with a sketch of the Bode magnitude plot, how a band-pass filter is built and how its response behaves around the central frequency \(\omega_0\).
xq.a: A mid-range driver needs to pass only a band, so frequencies below and above must both be attenuated. A single low-pass section attenuates only high frequencies and a single high-pass section only low frequencies. Cascading a high-pass section and a low-pass section gives a band-pass filter. Sketch: log frequency axis, gain in dB; the curve rises on the low side, peaks at ω0 (near 0 dB in the ideal case), and falls on the high side, rolling off on both sides at 20 dB per decade for first-order sections.
s: Single section rolls off on one side only
Sketch peak at ω0 with roll-off on both sides
Peak near 0 dB for ideal case; first-order slopes of 20 dB per decade

units.name: 4.1 Bandpass filters and speaker crossovers (recap)
units.ov: This recap covers passive loudspeaker crossovers built from resistors, capacitors and inductors, focusing on the bandpass filter needed for mid-range drivers. A bandpass response is made by combining high-pass and low-pass action, and it is read from a Bode plot of gain in dB against angular frequency, with a peak at \( \omega_0 \) and roll-off on both sides. The links to understand are component frequency behaviour, cascaded filter sections, cut-off frequencies and the Bode plot shape.
must: A bandpass filter passes a band of frequencies and attenuates those both below and above it; its Bode plot peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \).
A mid-range driver needs a bandpass filter because it must be bounded at both ends of the band, unlike a woofer (low-pass) or tweeter (high-pass).
A bandpass can be built by cascading a high-pass section (sets the lower cut-off) and a low-pass section (sets the upper cut-off); both cut-offs must be defined.
Capacitors pass high frequencies and block low ones, since \( X_C = 1/(\omega C) \) falls as \( \omega \) rises.
Inductors pass low frequencies and block high ones, since \( X_L = \omega L \) rises with \( \omega \).
A crossover is a filter network that splits the audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate driver.
Bode plot: gain \( 20\log_{10}(V_{out}/V_{in}) \) in dB against \( \omega \) (log scale); the peak is near 0 dB and attenuation appears as negative dB.
Distinguish the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) (the peak) from the cut-off frequencies on either side, where gain is down 3 dB (\( 1/\sqrt{2} \) of the peak voltage gain).
Passive crossovers use only R, L and C, with no power gain, so the output can never exceed the input.
conn: Impedance of C and L vs frequency determines whether each section acts as high-pass or low-pass, which sets the overall bandpass shape.
Cascading high-pass and low-pass sections links the cut-off frequencies \( \omega_{c1} \) and \( \omega_{c2} \) to the bandwidth and the position of \( \omega_0 \) on the Bode plot.
Potential-divider analysis of the RC or RL circuits gives \( V_{out}/V_{in} \), which is converted to dB for the Bode plot.
The crossover design links to the driver layout: woofer low-pass, mid-range bandpass and tweeter high-pass must overlap sensibly around their cut-offs.
exq: Explain why a mid-range driver requires a bandpass filter and sketch a block diagram of a three-way crossover showing the filter type for each driver.

Design a passive bandpass filter for a mid-range driver passing about 500 Hz to 5 kHz using a high-pass RC and a low-pass RC section; calculate the component values given \( R = 8\,\Omega \) using \( f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) \).
Sketch the Bode plot (gain in dB vs \( \omega \)) of a bandpass filter, label \( \omega_0 \), the cut-off frequencies and the -3 dB points, and state the gain in dB at the cut-offs.

State and justify which of a capacitor and an inductor blocks low frequencies, using reactance expressions, and calculate their reactances at 100 Hz and 10 kHz for \( C = 10\,\mu F \) and \( L = 1\,mH \).
A bandpass filter has a voltage gain of 0.5 at a given frequency relative to a peak gain of 1; express this in dB and say whether this frequency is inside or outside the passband.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Passive Speaker Crossovers
pts: Mid-range drivers need a bandpass filter so they only receive a limited band of frequencies, rejecting both very low and very high signals.
A passive crossover in a loudspeaker is built from resistors, capacitors and inductors (coils), each shaping which frequencies reach each driver.
Mid-range speakers are the trickiest to filter because they must be bounded at both ends of the band, requiring combined high-pass and low-pass action.
defs: Bandpass filter
A circuit that passes signals within a specific range of frequencies while attenuating frequencies outside that range.
Crossover
A filter network that divides an audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the appropriate loudspeaker driver.
tips: Do not confuse which component blocks which band: capacitors pass high frequencies and block low, inductors do the opposite.
A mid-range bandpass is usually formed by cascading high-pass and low-pass sections; check that both cut-off frequencies are defined.
rq: Why can't a single capacitor or single inductor alone isolate the mid-range driver's band?

A single reactive element only cuts off on one side (high-pass with a capacitor in series, low-pass with an inductor in series); a band needs both a high-pass and a low-pass section to bound the frequencies at both ends.
Why do capacitors block low frequencies while inductors block high frequencies?
A capacitor's reactance 1/(2πfC) falls as frequency rises, so it passes highs; an inductor's reactance 2πfL rises with frequency, so it passes lows.

notes.t: Filter Circuits: Bandpass Filter Bode Plot
pts: A bandpass filter passes a band of frequencies around a central frequency and attenuates signals on either side of the peak.
On the Bode plot, the gain curve peaks at the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and falls off on both sides.
The output-to-input voltage ratio is plotted in decibels against angular frequency \( \omega \).
Bandpass filters are widely used across many engineering disciplines.
defs: Bandpass filter
A filter circuit whose Bode plot has a peak at a central frequency \( \omega_0 \) and attenuates frequencies both above and below that band.
tips: Gain is plotted in dB, so the peak is at 0 dB reference and attenuation appears as negative dB values below it.
Do not confuse the central frequency \( \omega_0 \) (the peak) with the cut-off frequencies on either side of the band.
rq: Why does a bandpass filter's Bode plot fall off on both sides of \( \omega_0 \) rather than only on one side?

A bandpass filter must reject both low-frequency and high-frequency signals, so it combines a high-pass response (attenuating low frequencies) with a low-pass response (attenuating high frequencies), producing a peak between them.

xq.q: A passive crossover for a mid-range loudspeaker driver is built by cascading a high-pass section and a low-pass section. Which choice correctly describes the components and the resulting frequency response?
xq.a: A series capacitor blocks low frequencies, a series inductor blocks high frequencies, and the gain peaks at a central frequency \( \omega_0 \) with attenuation on both sides
o: A series inductor blocks low frequencies, a series capacitor blocks high frequencies, and the gain peaks at \( \omega_0 \)
A series capacitor blocks low frequencies, a series inductor blocks high frequencies, and the gain peaks at \( \omega_0 \) with attenuation on both sides
A series capacitor blocks high frequencies and a series inductor blocks low frequencies, so the gain has a minimum at \( \omega_0 \)
A single high-pass section is enough, since a capacitor alone limits the band at both ends
xq.w: A capacitor passes high frequencies and blocks low, an inductor does the opposite, so combining them bounds the band at both ends; swapping the roles is the common trap.
s: Cascade gives a peak at the central frequency with roll-off either side

xq.q: Sketch the Bode plot (gain in dB against angular frequency \( \omega \)) of a bandpass filter used for a mid-range loudspeaker driver. Label the central frequency \( \omega_0 \), and explain why a mid-range driver needs both a high-pass and a low-pass action, and how the central frequency differs from the cut-off frequencies.
xq.a: The plot shows gain in dB against \( \omega \) with a peak at \( \omega_0 \) (0 dB reference) falling to negative dB values on both sides. A mid-range driver must reject very low frequencies (which could damage it and belong to the woofer) and very high frequencies (which belong to the tweeter), so it needs high-pass action to remove the low end and low-pass action to remove the high end, usually from cascaded sections. The central frequency \( \omega_0 \) is the peak of the response, whereas the cut-off frequencies lie on either side of the peak and mark the edges of the passband.
s: Sketch: peak at \( \omega_0 \), falling on both sides, axes labelled dB and \( \omega \)
Peak at 0 dB, attenuation shown as negative dB
High-pass removes low frequencies, low-pass removes high frequencies
Cascaded sections bound both ends of the band
\( \omega_0 \) is the peak, distinct from the cut-offs either side

xq.q: On the Bode plot of a bandpass filter, the output-to-input voltage ratio is plotted in dB. At frequencies well away from the passband the plotted values are:
xq.a: Negative dB values, below the 0 dB peak
o: Positive dB values, above the peak
Negative dB values, below the 0 dB peak
Exactly 0 dB, because the signal is only delayed
Zero on a linear scale, which appears as 0 dB
xq.w: Attenuation means the output is smaller than the input, giving negative dB; zero output on a linear scale would be minus infinity dB, not 0 dB.
s: The peak is the 0 dB reference
Attenuated signals have a ratio less than 1, so negative dB

units.name: 4.2 Faraday's law, magnetic fields and Lenz's law
units.ov: This material covers how a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces a voltage (Faraday's law), how the direction of the induced current is fixed by Lenz's law, and how currents in wires and coils create magnetic fields. These ideas link together in generators: mechanical work moves a magnet or coil, the flux changes, a voltage and current are induced, and the induced field opposes the motion, so mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy.
must: Faraday's law: induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, \( \varepsilon = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} \), where N is the number of turns
Induction needs changing flux, not just the presence of a field; a steady field or a static magnet in a coil induces no voltage
Lenz's law: the induced current creates a field that opposes the change in flux that caused it; this is the origin of the minus sign
Magnetic flux: \( \Phi = BA\cos\theta \), the field passing through a surface; flux can change through B, A or θ
Energy conservation: work done against the opposing force on the magnet becomes electrical energy; it is not created from nothing
Right-hand rule: the field around a straight wire forms concentric loops following the current direction; do not confuse current direction with field direction
A solenoid's loop fields add inside the coil, giving a strong, nearly uniform axial field; the coil acts as a magnet with N and S poles
Method for Lenz's law: (1) state whether flux increases or decreases, (2) state the opposing field direction, (3) use the right-hand rule to find the current direction
Closed loop is needed for a current; an open coil still has an induced emf but no current flows
conn: Faraday and Lenz together: the magnitude of the emf comes from \( d\Phi/dt \) and the direction from the opposing field, which is found with the right-hand rule for coils
Solenoid fields and induction: the induced current in a coil makes its own solenoid field, whose poles oppose the approaching or retreating magnet
Lenz's law and energy conservation: the opposing force explains why mechanical work is needed and why generators convert mechanical power to electrical power
Generators: the speed of the moving magnet or rotating coil sets \( d\Phi/dt \), so it sets the emf amplitude and frequency
exq: A bar magnet is pushed north pole first into a coil. State the direction of the induced current, as seen from the magnet side, and the polarity of the coil end facing the magnet. Justify using Lenz's law.

A coil of 200 turns and area \(5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2\) lies perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.8 T to 0.2 T in 0.1 s. Calculate the induced emf and say which way the induced field points relative to the original.
Explain why a stationary magnet inside a coil produces no electrical energy, and why pushing a magnet into a closed coil requires more force than into an open one.
Sketch the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire and a solenoid. Mark the directions with the right-hand rule and identify the poles of the solenoid.
A flat coil rotates at constant angular speed in a uniform field. Sketch the flux and induced emf against time, and explain how doubling the speed changes the peak emf.

notes.t: Generators and Faraday's law of induction
pts: A changing magnetic flux through a coil induces a voltage in the coil.
If the coil forms a closed loop, the induced voltage drives a current, which creates its own magnetic field opposing the change (Lenz's law).
Power generation works because a moving magnet inside a coil induces a voltage; the flux must change, since a static magnet in a coil produces no energy.
defs: Magnetic flux
A measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area.
tips: Induction depends on changing flux, not on the presence of a magnetic field; a steady field gives no induced voltage.
Lenz's law sign: the induced current opposes the change, so the induced voltage is a sign reversal of the rate of change of flux.
rq: Why can't a stationary magnet sitting inside a coil generate energy?
Induction requires a changing magnetic flux; with a stationary magnet the flux is constant, so no voltage is induced.
Why does the induced current create a field that opposes the change rather than reinforcing it?
Lenz's law: opposing the change is required by conservation of energy; reinforcing it would create energy from nothing and runaway growth.

notes.t: Magnetic field around current-carrying wires and coils
pts: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field that circles the wire.
Field lines around a straight wire form concentric loops whose direction follows the current (right-hand rule).
Coiling a current-carrying wire makes the field from each loop add in the same direction inside the coil.
A current-carrying coil therefore behaves like a magnet, with a north and south pole at its ends.
defs: Magnetic field B
A vector field describing the magnetic force influence around a current-carrying conductor or magnet; its field lines form closed loops.
Solenoid (coil)
A helical winding of wire carrying current whose individual loop fields reinforce inside the coil, producing a strong, nearly uniform axial magnetic field.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of current with the direction of the field; use the right-hand rule to determine the field direction around a wire.
The field lines in the coil diagram are drawn as closed loops; the field inside a coil is strongest and most uniform along its axis.
rq: Why does the field inside a coil add up, while the field outside the coil largely cancels?

Inside the coil the loop fields all point along the axis in the same direction, so they add; outside, the return paths of the field run in opposite directions and tend to cancel, weakening the external field.
If the current in a coil is reversed, what happens to the magnet's poles?
The magnetic field direction reverses, so the north and south poles swap positions.

notes.t: Changing magnetic flux and induced current (Lenz's law)
pts: A moving magnet changes the magnetic flux through the coil, which induces a current in the coil.
The induced current produces a field that opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused it.
Work must be done against this opposing field to push the magnet into the coil; this work is converted into electrical energy.
tips: Energy conservation: the electrical energy output comes from the mechanical work done, not from nowhere; the opposing force is what makes the work necessary.
The induced effect acts to oppose the change in flux, so do not state that it reinforces or assists the motion.
rq: Why does pulling the magnet out of the coil require work just as pushing it in does?

Withdrawing the magnet also changes the flux, so the induced current opposes the change in both directions; the opposing force must be overcome either way, so mechanical work is needed to keep the magnet moving.
What would happen to the induced current if the magnet were held stationary inside the coil?
The flux would not change, so no current would be induced and no opposing field would be produced.

xq.q: A bar magnet is held stationary inside a coil connected to a voltmeter. The magnet produces a strong, steady field through the coil. What does the voltmeter read, and why?
xq.a: Zero, because the flux is not changing
o: A large constant voltage, because the field is strong
Zero, because the flux is not changing
A large voltage with reversed sign, as given by Lenz's law
A small voltage that decays, because the field gradually weakens
xq.w: Induction depends on changing flux, not on the presence of a field; a steady field induces nothing.
s: Flux is constant so the voltage is zero

xq.q: A bar magnet is pushed north pole first into a closed coil. Explain, using Lenz's law, the direction of the induced field and why the person pushing the magnet has to do work. State where the electrical energy comes from.
xq.a: Pushing the magnet in increases the flux through the coil, which induces a current. By Lenz's law the induced current creates a field opposing the change, so the coil's end facing the magnet acts as a north pole and repels it. The person must therefore push against this repulsive force, doing mechanical work. This work is converted into electrical energy in the coil, so energy is conserved and nothing comes from nowhere.
s: Moving magnet changes flux and induces a current
Induced field opposes the increase in flux (repels the north pole)
Work must be done against the opposing force
Mechanical work is converted to electrical energy

xq.q: A straight wire carries a current. Which statement about its magnetic field is correct, and what mistake does it avoid?
xq.a: The field forms concentric closed loops around the wire, with direction given by the right-hand rule
o: The field points along the wire in the same direction as the current
The field forms concentric closed loops around the wire, with direction given by the right-hand rule
The field lines start at the wire and radiate outward like an electric field
The field circles the wire but its direction is independent of the current direction
xq.w: Field lines circle the wire and reverse if the current reverses; the trap is confusing the field direction with the current direction.
s: Field lines are closed concentric loops
Direction follows the right-hand rule with the current

units.name: 4.3 Self-inductance and inductors
units.ov: This module introduces self-inductance: a changing current in a coil changes its own magnetic flux, which induces a voltage that opposes the change (Lenz's law). An inductor is a coil, often on an iron core, that exploits this effect and stores energy in its magnetic field. The notes give only the qualitative picture and definitions, so the standard quantitative relations (\(v=L\,di/dt\), \(E=\tfrac12 LI^2\), \(L=N\Phi/I\)) should be learned alongside them.
must: Self-inductance: a changing current changes the coil's own flux and induces a voltage in that same coil, opposing the change (Lenz's law).
The induced voltage opposes the change in current, not the current itself; the coil 'fights' changing currents.
Steady DC through an ideal inductor gives zero induced voltage, so it acts like a short circuit (a plain wire) in steady state.
Inductance \(L\) relates flux linkage to current, \(L=N\Phi/I\), and measures how strongly the inductor opposes changes in current.
Voltage-current law (beyond the notes): \(v=L\,\frac{di}{dt}\) (equivalently \(v=-L\,di/dt\) as an induced emf). A larger rate of change of current gives a larger voltage.
Unit of inductance is the henry (H), where 1 H = 1 V·s/A. Do not confuse it with farads (capacitance) or ohms (resistance).
An iron (high-permeability) core strengthens the magnetic field and increases \(L\). \(L\) also grows with more turns (\(L\propto N^2\)) and larger cross-sectional area.
Energy is stored in the magnetic field: \(E=\tfrac12 LI^2\). It is released when the current falls, so an inductor stores energy rather than dissipating it.
Current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, since that would need infinite voltage. This is the key to switching and transient problems.
conn: Faraday's and Lenz's laws lead to \(v=L\,di/dt\): the induced emf is \(-N\,d\Phi/dt\) and flux is proportional to current, so \(N\Phi=Li\).

Inductor and capacitor are duals: the capacitor stores energy in an electric field and resists changes in voltage, while the inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and resists changes in current. Compare \(\tfrac12 CV^2\) and \(\tfrac12 LI^2\).
Inductance in RL circuits with a switch: the continuity of current gives the time constant \(\tau=L/R\) and exponential growth or decay \(i=I_0(1-e^{-t/\tau})\).
Coil geometry and core material (turns \(N\), area, length, permeability) link magnetic circuits and electromagnet design to the value of \(L\).
exq: A 50 mH inductor carries a current that rises uniformly from 0 to 2 A in 10 ms. Calculate the induced voltage across it, and state its polarity relative to the current.
Explain why a steady DC current through an ideal inductor produces no induced voltage, but switching the current on or off can produce a large voltage spike. Include Lenz's law.
Calculate the energy stored in a 0.2 H inductor carrying 3 A. If the current is halved, by what factor does the stored energy change?
A coil of \(N=500\) turns produces a flux of 0.4 mWb when the current is 2 A. Find its inductance, and explain how inserting an iron core would change \(L\) and the energy stored at the same current.

Define self-inductance and the henry. Describe why an inductor in series with a resistor, switched onto a DC supply, takes time to reach its final current, and give an expression for the time constant.

notes.t: Self-inductance
pts: A changing current produces a changing magnetic flux through the coil, which in turn induces a voltage in that same coil.
The coil behaves as if a magnet were being moved into it: the induced voltage opposes the change that caused it.
The induced voltage resists changes in current, so the coil 'fights against changing currents'.
Self-inductance opposes the change in current, not the current itself; a steady current produces no induced voltage.
defs: Self-inductance
The property of a coil whereby a changing current through it induces a voltage across the same coil that opposes the change in current (Lenz's law).
tips: Self-inductance opposes the change in current, not the current itself; a steady DC current through an ideal coil induces zero voltage.
Remember the induced voltage direction follows Lenz's law: it opposes the change that produced it.
rq: Why does a coil oppose a change in current but not a steady current?

A steady current gives a constant magnetic flux, so there is no change in flux and no induced voltage (\( v = 0 \)). Only a changing flux, i.e. a changing current, induces a voltage that opposes the change.
What would happen to the induced voltage if the current were increasing rapidly rather than slowly?
A faster rate of change of current produces a larger rate of change of flux and therefore a larger induced voltage opposing the change.

notes.t: Inductor
pts: An inductor is a coil of wire, often wrapped around an iron core; current through it generates a magnetic field.
The iron core strengthens the magnetic field, intensifying the effect.
Inductors resist changes in electrical current.
Energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor.
defs: Inductor

A component, typically a coil of wire (sometimes around a core), that generates a magnetic field when current flows through it, opposing changes in that current and storing energy in the magnetic field.
Inductance (L)
The property of an inductor that relates the magnetic flux linkage to the current; it quantifies how strongly the component opposes changes in current.
tips: Inductance is measured in henrys (H), not farads or ohms; do not confuse it with capacitance.
An inductor opposes changes in current, not current itself: steady DC current flows freely through an ideal inductor.
rq: Why does adding an iron core to a coil increase its effect?
The iron core has a much higher magnetic permeability than air, so it concentrates and strengthens the magnetic field produced by the current.
Why can an inductor not change its current instantly?
A changing current changes its magnetic field, inducing a voltage that opposes the change, so the current can only change gradually.

xq.q: A steady DC current of 2 A flows through an ideal inductor of inductance L = 10 mH. What is the voltage induced across the inductor?
xq.a: 0 V
o: 20 mV
0 V
5 V
xq.w: Self-inductance opposes changes in current, not the current itself, so a steady current gives zero induced voltage; multiplying L by I is the trap.
s: Induced voltage depends on rate of change of current

xq.q: A current through a coil is increased rapidly. Explain, with reference to flux and Lenz's law, why the coil is said to 'fight against changing currents', and state what happens to energy in the inductor.
xq.a: The increasing current increases the magnetic flux through the coil itself, which induces a voltage in the same coil. By Lenz's law this voltage opposes the change that caused it, so it acts to oppose the rise in current. The coil therefore resists changes in current, not the current itself. Energy supplied by the source against this opposition is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor.
s: Changing current gives changing flux in the same coil
Opposes change in current, not current itself
Energy is stored in the magnetic field

xq.q: An iron core is inserted into an air-cored coil. What is the effect, and which unit is used for the property involved?
xq.a: The magnetic field is strengthened, increasing the inductance, measured in henrys
o: The magnetic field is strengthened, increasing the inductance, measured in farads
The magnetic field is weakened, decreasing the inductance, measured in henrys
The magnetic field is strengthened, increasing the inductance, measured in henrys
The inductance is unchanged because the current is the same
xq.w: The iron core intensifies the field so inductance rises, and inductance is measured in henrys, not farads.
s: Core strengthens the field, so L increases

units.name: 4.4 Inductor voltage, phase and complex impedance
units.ov: This material shows that an inductor's voltage depends on the rate of change of current, \(V=L\,dI/dt\). For a sinusoidal current this gives a voltage amplitude of \(\omega L I_0\) and a 90° phase shift, which is captured by the complex impedance \(Z_L=j\omega L\). The calculus derivation, the phase relationship and the phasor/impedance form are three views of the same result, and the phasor form is what you use in AC circuit analysis.
must: Inductor law: \(V=L\,\frac{dI}{dt}\). Voltage depends on the rate of change of current, not the current itself, so steady DC gives \(V=0\).
Derivation: for \(I=I_0\sin\omega t\), \(V=\omega L I_0\cos\omega t\). The factor \(\omega\) comes from the chain rule, and \(V_0=\omega L I_0\).
Phase: in an ideal inductor voltage leads current by 90° (\(\pi/2\)), equivalently current lags voltage. For a capacitor it is the reverse (the mnemonic is ELI the ICE man).
Complex impedance: \(Z_L=V/I=j\omega L\). It is purely imaginary, with no resistive part.
Magnitude (reactance): \(|Z_L|=X_L=\omega L=2\pi fL\). It rises linearly with frequency, so an inductor passes DC (\(X_L=0\)) and opposes high frequencies.
Phasor interpretation: multiplying by \(j\omega L\) rotates the current phasor by +90° and scales it by \(\omega L\), so \(V=\omega L|I|\angle 90^\circ\) when the current is the reference.
Always use \(\omega\) in rad/s, converting with \(\omega=2\pi f\). Using Hz gives an error of a factor of \(2\pi\).
Units: L in henries, \(dI/dt\) in A/s, Z and \(X_{L}\) in ohms. Impedance is not a plain real resistance, so state the phase and the magnitude.
Physical reason: the changing current changes the magnetic field, which induces a voltage opposing the change.
conn: Calculus and phasors: differentiating \(\sin\omega t\) gives \(\omega\cos\omega t\), which is the same result as multiplying the phasor by \(j\omega\). Exam questions ask for both routes.
Impedance and phase: \(Z=j\omega L\) gives the magnitude \(\omega L\) and the phase +90° at once. This links to the voltage and current waveforms and to the phasor diagram.

Inductor, capacitor and resistor: series and parallel combinations use \(Z_R=R\), \(Z_L=j\omega L\) and \(Z_C=1/(j\omega C)\). Total impedance, current and phase angle follow from complex arithmetic, and the inductor and capacitor phases are opposite.
Frequency dependence: \(X_L\propto f\) links to filter behaviour and to resonance with a capacitor, where \(\omega L=1/(\omega C)\).
exq: A 50 mH inductor carries \(I=2\sin(314t)\) A. Find the reactance, write the instantaneous voltage \(V_L(t)\), and state the peak voltage and its phase relative to the current.
Starting from \(V=L\,dI/dt\) and \(I=I_0\sin\omega t\), derive \(Z_L=j\omega L\). Explain where the \(j\) and the factor \(\omega\) come from.
Calculate the impedance of a 10 mH inductor at 50 Hz and at 5 kHz. Express each in the form \(j\omega L\), and say what happens to the current for a fixed voltage amplitude.
A current phasor of \(0.5\angle 0^\circ\) A flows through a 20 mH inductor at 1 kHz. Find the voltage phasor in magnitude and phase, and sketch the phasor diagram.
Explain why a steady DC current of 10 A through an ideal inductor gives zero voltage, whereas a 10 A peak AC current does not. Compare the phase behaviour with that of a capacitor.

notes.t: Inductor: voltage across an inductor in an AC circuit
pts: An inductor carrying an alternating current develops a voltage across its terminals.
The induced voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current through the inductor, not to the current itself.
Because the voltage depends on the rate of change, a steady DC current produces no induced voltage, while a changing AC current does.
defs: Inductance (L)
The property of a component that opposes changes in current by producing a voltage proportional to the rate of change of current; measured in henries (H).
eqs: Voltage across an inductor as a function of the rate of change of current
V = voltage across the inductor (V); L = inductance (H); \(\frac{dI}{dt}\) = rate of change of current (A/s)
tips: Do not treat the voltage as proportional to current; the relationship uses \(dI/dt\), so a large steady current gives zero voltage.
Keep units consistent: with L in henries and I in amperes, \(dI/dt\) must be in A/s so that V comes out in volts.
rq: Why does a DC current produce no voltage across an ideal inductor, even though the inductor is in the circuit?
Because a constant DC current has zero rate of change, \(dI/dt = 0\), so \(V = L\,dI/dt = 0\).
What happens to the voltage across an inductor if the AC frequency is doubled while the current amplitude stays the same?
The rate of change of current increases (it is proportional to frequency for a sinusoid), so the voltage amplitude roughly doubles.

notes.t: Inductor: phase relationship between voltage and current
pts: Current through an inductor produces a magnetic field; changes in current change this field and induce a voltage.
The magnetic field takes time to react to a change in current, so the voltage effect is delayed relative to the current change.
In an inductor the current waveform lags the voltage waveform by the phase angle \( \phi \).
On the phasor/waveform plot, the voltage peaks occur earlier than the current peaks by the angle \( \phi \), showing a quarter-cycle (90°) lag in ideal inductors.
defs: Phase angle (\( \phi \))
The angular difference between the voltage and current waveforms of the same frequency; for an inductor, current lags voltage.
tips: Remember the direction: for an inductor current lags voltage, whereas for a capacitor current leads voltage — do not swap them.
Phase angle \( \phi \) must be read as a time/angle difference between corresponding peaks; state its sign and units (radians or degrees) clearly.
rq: Why does the current lag the voltage in an inductor rather than the two being in step?
Because the magnetic field built up by the current takes time to respond to a change in current, so the resulting effect on the circuit's electrical potential (voltage) is delayed.
What would you expect to see on the plot if the inductor were replaced by a pure resistor?
Voltage and current would rise and fall together (in phase, \( \phi = 0 \)), since no energy-storing magnetic delay exists.

notes.t: Deriving the complex impedance of an inductor
pts: The voltage across an inductor is proportional to the rate of change of its current, so differentiating the sinusoidal current gives the voltage.
Differentiating a sine function gives a cosine, and the chain rule brings out a factor of ω from the argument ωt.
The voltage leads the current by 90°, since the cosine term is a sine shifted by a quarter cycle; the amplitude of the voltage is ωL times the current amplitude.
The peak voltage amplitude V₀ = ωLI₀ gives the inductor's opposition to current, which leads to the reactance \(X_{L}\) = ωL.
defs: Inductor voltage
The induced voltage across an inductor equals L multiplied by the rate of change of current through it.
eqs: \(V_{L}\) = voltage across the inductor (V); L = inductance (H); I = current (A); t = time (s)
\(I_{L}\) = instantaneous current (A); \(I_{0}\) = peak current (A); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
\(V_{L}\) = instantaneous voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(I_{0}\) = peak current (A); t = time (s)
\(V_{0}\) = peak voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(I_{0}\) = peak current (A)
tips: Forgetting the chain rule: the factor ω comes from differentiating ωt inside the sine, so omitting it gives the wrong voltage amplitude.
Unit trap: ω must be in rad/s (not Hz) when calculating ωL, otherwise the reactance is wrong by a factor of 2π.
rq: Why does the derivation produce a factor of ω in the voltage amplitude but not in the current amplitude?
Because the chain rule applied to sin(ωt) differentiates the argument ωt, giving a factor ω; the current itself is not differentiated, so no ω appears in its amplitude.
What would happen to the peak voltage across an inductor if the frequency doubled while the peak current stayed the same?
The peak voltage would double, since V₀ = ωLI₀ is directly proportional to ω.
Why does the voltage waveform use cosine while the current uses sine?
Differentiating sin(ωt) gives cos(ωt), so the voltage is 90° ahead of the current (the voltage leads the current).

notes.t: Complex impedance of an inductor
pts: The voltage across an inductor leads its current by 90°, so the phase change of π/2 is represented by the factor j.
The magnitude of the impedance of an inductor is the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude, which equals ωL and grows with frequency.
Complex impedance combines magnitude and phase: the inductor's impedance is purely imaginary, meaning it has no resistive part.
Current is taken as the reference sinusoid \(I_{L}\) = \(I_{o}\) sin(ωt), and the voltage amplitude is ω\(LI_{o}\).
defs: Complex impedance
The ratio of the phasor voltage to the phasor current across a circuit element, Z = V/I, expressed in complex form with magnitude giving the amplitude ratio and phase giving the phase difference.
eqs: |\(Z_{L}\)| = impedance magnitude (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H)
\(Z_{L}\) = complex impedance (Ω); \(V_{L}\) = voltage phasor (V); \(I_{L}\) = current phasor (A); j = imaginary unit; ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H)
\(V_{L}\) = voltage phasor (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); \(I_{o}\) = current amplitude (A)
tips: Do not confuse the phasor form \(V_{L}\) = jωL \(I_{o}\) with the time-domain form; the π/2 phase shift is the voltage leading the current.
Impedance is in ohms (Ω) and depends on angular frequency ω in rad/s, not frequency f in Hz, unless you convert using ω = 2πf.
rq: Why does multiplying by j correspond to a phase shift of π/2 rather than a change in magnitude?
Because j has magnitude 1 and represents a rotation of 90° in the complex plane, so it shifts phase without altering amplitude. Here it makes the voltage lead the current by π/2.
What would happen to |\(Z_{L}\)| if the frequency were doubled, and why?
It would double, since |\(Z_{L}\)| = ωL is directly proportional to ω; inductors oppose changing current more strongly at higher frequencies.

notes.t: Inductor impedance and phasor voltage-current relationship
pts: An inductor's impedance is purely imaginary and proportional to frequency, so it has no resistive part.
In phasor form, the voltage across an inductor leads the current by 90°: the current phasor lies on the real axis while the voltage phasor lies on the imaginary axis.
Multiplying the current phasor by the impedance j\omega L rotates it by +90° and scales its magnitude by \omega L, giving the voltage phasor.
defs: Impedance of an inductor
The ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current for an inductor, Z = j\omega L, which is purely imaginary and increases linearly with angular frequency.
eqs: Z = impedance (\Omega); j = imaginary unit; \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H)
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (\Omega); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H)
tips: Do not confuse the phase relationship: for an inductor voltage leads current by 90°, whereas for a capacitor current leads voltage.
Angles must be in consistent units; ensure \omega is in rad/s when computing \omega L, not Hz.
rq: Why does the voltage phasor sit at +90° relative to the current phasor for an inductor, and what would change if the element were a resistor?
The factor j in Z = j\omega L rotates the phasor by 90° (+90°), so V leads I by 90°. For a resistor, Z is real (Z = R), so there is no rotation and V is in phase with I.
If the frequency doubles while the current amplitude stays the same, what happens to the voltage amplitude across the inductor?
The voltage amplitude doubles, since |V| = \omega L|I| is proportional to \omega.

notes.t: Impedance of an inductor in AC circuits
pts: For AC signals we must know the impedance of an inductor, not just its inductance.
Inductor impedance is directly related to the inductance L and is expressed using a complex (j) term.
The impedance of an inductor is purely imaginary, so it introduces a 90° phase shift between voltage and current.
defs: Impedance (Z)
The complex generalisation of resistance for AC circuits, relating the phasor voltage to the phasor current across a component.
eqs: Z = impedance (\Omega); j = imaginary unit; \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H)
tips: Use angular frequency ω = 2πf (rad/s), not the frequency f in Hz, when substituting into Z = jωL.
Impedance is measured in ohms (Ω) and is complex; do not treat it as a simple real resistance.
rq: Why does the impedance of an inductor increase as the frequency of the AC source increases?
Because |Z| = ωL is proportional to angular frequency ω, so higher frequency gives larger impedance (the inductor opposes rapid changes in current more strongly).
What would the impedance of an inductor be in a DC circuit, and why?
At DC, ω = 0, so Z = 0: the inductor acts as a short circuit (ideal wire).

xq.q: A sinusoidal current of peak value \(I_0\) = 20 mA and frequency f = 5 kHz flows through an ideal inductor L = 47 mH. The voltage across the inductor is \(V_L = L\,dI/dt\). Calculate the peak voltage \(V_0\) across the inductor.
An ideal inductor carries a steady DC current of 3 A. Which statement about the voltage across it is correct?
xq.a: It is zero, since dI/dt = 0 for a steady current
o: It is 3L volts, since voltage is proportional to current
It is zero, since dI/dt = 0 for a steady current
It is infinite, since the inductor opposes any current
It is ωL×3 volts with ω = 2π×50 rad/s
xq.w: V = L dI/dt and a steady current has dI/dt = 0, so V = 0; the trap is treating V as proportional to I itself.

xq.q: The current through an ideal inductor L is \(I_L = I_0\sin(\omega t)\). Show that the voltage across the inductor has peak value \(\omega L I_0\) and state the phase relationship between voltage and current.
xq.a: \(V_{L}\) = L dI/dt = L d/dt[I0 sin(ωt)] = ωL I0 cos(ωt) = ωL I0 sin(ωt + π/2). The peak voltage is V0 = ωL I0, so the magnitude of the impedance is V0/I0 = ωL. Since cos is sin shifted by a quarter cycle, the voltage leads the current by 90° (current lags voltage), which is represented by the factor j in Z = jωL.
s: Differentiate, chain rule gives factor ω: \(V_{L}\) = ωL I0 cos(ωt)
cos(ωt) = sin(ωt+π/2): voltage leads current by 90°

units.name: 4.5 Series and parallel inductors
units.ov: This material shows how to combine inductors into a single equivalent inductance. Series inductors add directly, because impedances in series add and inductive impedance \(Z=j\omega L\) is proportional to \(L\). Parallel inductors follow the reciprocal rule, exactly as for resistors. Both rules assume there is no mutual coupling between the coils.
must: Series inductors: \(L_{total}=L_1+L_2\) (extends to any number of inductors)
Parallel inductors: \(\frac{1}{L_{total}}=\frac{1}{L_1}+\frac{1}{L_2}\), so \(L_{total}\) is smaller than the smallest individual \(L\)
Two inductors in parallel: \(L_{total}=\frac{L_1L_2}{L_1+L_2}\) (product over sum)
Series and parallel impedances combine like resistances: \(Z_{total}=Z_1+Z_2\) in series, and reciprocals add in parallel
Why the rules work: \(Z_L=j\omega L\) is proportional to \(L\) at a given frequency, so impedance rules carry over to inductance
Series inductors carry the same current; parallel inductors share the same voltage
Never add inductance directly to capacitance or resistance; only combine impedances (complex values) for mixed elements
The rules assume no mutual inductance; coupled coils need a different treatment
Sanity check: a series result must be larger than the largest \(L\), and a parallel result smaller than the smallest \(L\)
For mixed networks, reduce step by step, with parallel groups first and then series, as for resistor networks
conn: Inductor rules mirror resistor rules (series adds, parallel by reciprocals), while capacitors are the reverse, so questions mix up the three to test you
Impedance \(Z_L=j\omega L\) links equivalent inductance to AC circuit analysis: find \(L_{total}\), then the current \(I=V/(j\omega L_{total})\)
Combining inductors with resistors or capacitors requires complex impedances, not simple addition of component values
Equivalent inductance feeds into time-constant problems such as \(\tau=L/R\) in RL circuits, and into resonance calculations
exq: Inductors of 10 mH and 40 mH are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel. Find the equivalent inductance in each case and explain why (b) is less than 10 mH.
Three inductors of 6 mH, 12 mH and 4 mH are in parallel. Find \(L_{total}\), then the impedance magnitude of the combination at 50 Hz.
A 20 mH inductor is in series with a parallel pair of 30 mH and 60 mH inductors. Find the equivalent inductance and the current drawn from a 12 V, 1 kHz source.
Starting from \(Z_L=j\omega L\) and the rule that series impedances add, derive the series inductance formula. Explain what changes if the two coils are magnetically coupled.
A 5 mH inductor needs to be changed to 8 mH using one additional inductor. Should it be placed in series or in parallel, and what value is needed?

notes.t: Inductors in series: total impedance and inductance
pts: Impedances of series elements add just like resistances, so the total impedance is the sum of each inductor's impedance.
Because inductive impedance is proportional to inductance at a given frequency, adding impedances in series means adding inductances in series.
The source voltage \(V_{I}\) drives the same current through both inductors, so the series combination behaves as one larger inductor.
eqs: Total impedance of impedances in series
\(Z_{\text{total}}\) = total impedance (Ω); \(Z_{1}\), \(Z_{2}\) = impedances of each element (Ω)
Total inductance of inductors in series
tips: Only the inductances add directly when the impedances are both inductive at the same frequency; do not add inductance to capacitance or resistance values.
Remember that adding inductances in series is the reverse of the parallel rule, where reciprocals add instead.
rq: Why can we simply add the inductances here, when the phase of each inductor's impedance is the same?

Each inductor has impedance jωL, so \(Z_{\text{total}}\) = jω\(L_{1}\) + jω\(L_{2}\) = jω(\(L_{1}\) + \(L_{2}\)); the common factor jω (same frequency, same phase of 90°) lets the inductances add directly.
What would happen to the total inductance if the two inductors were connected in parallel instead?
Their reciprocals would add: 1/\(L_{\text{total}}\) = 1/\(L_{1}\) + 1/\(L_{2}\) (for non-coupled inductors), so the total is smaller than either individual inductance.

notes.t: Inductors in parallel
pts: Inductors in parallel combine with the reciprocal rule, the same form as resistors in parallel, so the total inductance is less than the smallest individual inductance.
The rule is a guess from the resistor case: the reciprocals of the inductances add, not the inductances themselves.
eqs: Total inductance of two inductors in parallel
\(L_{\text{total}}\) = equivalent total inductance (H); \(L_{1}\) = first inductance (H); \(L_{2}\) = second inductance (H)
tips: Do not add inductances directly in parallel; you must add their reciprocals and then invert, which is a common slip.
This rule assumes no mutual inductance between the coils; coupled inductors need a different treatment.
rq: Why does adding a second inductor in parallel always reduce the total inductance below the smallest value?
Each inductor provides an extra path for current, so the reciprocal sum 1/\(L_{\text{total}}\) is larger than 1/\(L_{1}\) or 1/\(L_{2}\) alone, giving a smaller \(L_{\text{total}}\).
How would you find the total inductance of three inductors in parallel?
Extend the rule: 1/\(L_{\text{total}}\) = 1/\(L_{1}\) + 1/\(L_{2}\) + 1/\(L_{3}\), then invert the sum.

xq.q: Two inductors, \(L_1\) = 30 mH and \(L_2\) = 60 mH, are connected in parallel (no mutual inductance). This combination is then connected in series with a third inductor \(L_3\) = 15 mH. Calculate the total inductance \(L_{total}\).
xq.a: \(L_{\text{total}}\) = 35 mH

xq.q: Two inductors of 12 mH and 4 mH are connected in parallel with no mutual coupling. What is the equivalent inductance?
xq.a: 3 mH
o: 16 mH
3 mH
8 mH
xq.w: 1/L = 1/12 + 1/4 = 4/12 so L = 3 mH; adding them directly gives 16 mH, and the result must be below the smallest value.

xq.q: Explain why inductors in series have a total inductance \(L_1 + L_2\), starting from the addition of impedances, and state how the parallel rule differs. Give one condition needed for the parallel rule to hold.
xq.a: The same current flows through both inductors in series, so the voltages add and \(Z_{\text{total}}\) = Z1 + Z2. With Z = jωL at the same ω, jω\(L_{\text{total}}\) = jωL1 + jωL2, so \(L_{\text{total}}\) = L1 + L2. In parallel the reciprocals add, 1/\(L_{\text{total}}\) = 1/L1 + 1/L2, giving a total smaller than the smallest inductor. The rule requires no mutual inductance between the coils.
s: Substitute Z = jωL and cancel jω: \(L_{\text{total}}\) = L1 + L2

units.name: 4.6 First-order LR filters and cut-off frequency
units.ov: This material covers first-order passive RC and LR filters, treated as impedance voltage dividers. It derives the transfer function, the cut-off (corner) frequency and the −3 dB point. In the LR low-pass the output is taken across R, and in the high-pass across L. Both share ω₀ = R/L. Their magnitude responses, the 1/√2 gain at cut-off and the 20 dB/decade roll-off all follow from the same normalised form.
must: LR cut-off angular frequency is \(\omega_0 = R/L\) (rad/s); in hertz \(f_0 = R/(2\pi L)\). Always include the 2π and never write L/R.
LR low-pass (output across R, L in series): \(V_{out}/V_{in} = R/(R+j\omega L) = 1/(1+j\omega/\omega_0)\).
LR high-pass (output across L, R in series): \(V_o/V_{in} = 1/(1+\omega_0/(j\omega))\), which equals \(j\omega L/(R+j\omega L)\).
Magnitudes: low-pass \(1/\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_0)^2}\), high-pass \(1/\sqrt{1+(\omega_0/\omega)^2}\).
At \(\omega=\omega_0\) the gain is \(1/\sqrt{2}\approx0.707\) of the passband value (−3 dB), which is half power. This is the definition of the cut-off.
Start from the divider \(V_{out}=\frac{Z_{out\ element}}{Z_R+Z_L}V_{in}\) with \(Z_R=R\) and \(Z_L=j\omega L\). Which element the output is taken across decides low-pass or high-pass.
RC comparison: \(\omega_0 = 1/RC\) and \(f_0=1/(2\pi RC)\). The LR and RC low-pass or high-pass pairs share the same form, and only the formula for ω₀ differs.
The cut-off frequency, characteristic frequency and Bode corner frequency are the same point (ω₀ = ω_c) for first-order filters. The stopband roll-off is 20 dB/decade.
Check units: Ω/H = 1/s, so R/L gives rad/s. The 20 dB/decade and simple corner results apply only to first-order filters, not higher-order ones.
Physical reasoning: \(Z_L=j\omega L\) grows with frequency. Across R the output is attenuated at high ω (low-pass), and across L it is attenuated at low ω (high-pass).
conn: Complex impedance and the voltage divider lead to the transfer function, then to the magnitude and phase, then to the −3 dB cut-off. Questions often ask for the whole chain.

Cut-off frequency links to Bode plots: the corner is at ω₀, the passband is 0 dB, and the slope above it is −20 dB/decade for the low-pass. Straight-line asymptotes and the actual −3 dB point at the corner are often combined.
The RC and LR filters are compared by swapping roles: ω₀ = 1/RC against R/L. Questions may ask you to design either one to hit a target f₀, which needs the rad/s to Hz conversion.
The low-pass and high-pass versions are complementary: the same R and L give the same ω₀. Their outputs across R and across L are related by the divider, and their magnitudes at ω₀ are both 0.707.
exq: An LR low-pass filter has R = 470 Ω and L = 50 mH, with the output taken across R. Find ω₀ and f₀, and the gain magnitude in dB at 20 kHz.

Derive the transfer function \(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) for an LR filter with the output across R, and write it in the normalised form 1/(1+jω/ω₀). Identify ω₀ and show that the gain is 1/√2 at ω = ω₀.
Design an LR high-pass filter with a cut-off of 1 kHz using a 10 mH inductor. Find R, sketch the Bode magnitude plot, and state the gain at 100 Hz and at 10 kHz.
For an LR low-pass filter with ω₀ = 2000 rad/s, calculate the magnitude and phase of the output relative to the input at 500 Hz. State how much the gain changes per decade well above cut-off.
Compare an RC low-pass filter with R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF against an LR low-pass with R = 1 kΩ and L = 100 mH. Find f₀ for each and explain the reason for the swapped R roles in the formulas.

notes.t: First-order LR filter: transfer function and cut-off frequency
pts: The output is taken across the resistor R in parallel with the output terminals, so the divider ratio is \(Z_{R}\)/(\(Z_{R}\)+\(Z_{L}\)).
Substituting \(Z_{R}\) = R and \(Z_{L}\) = jωL gives a transfer function with a low-pass character: the inductor's impedance grows with frequency, reducing the output.
Rewriting in normalised form, the characteristic frequency is ω₀ = R/L, which sets the cut-off point of the filter.
Dividing through by R shows the transfer function as 1 over (1 + j ωL/R), a standard first-order form.
defs: LR filter
A passive first-order filter made of a series inductor and a shunt resistor whose output is taken across the resistor.
Cut-off frequency (ω₀)
The frequency at which the magnitude of the transfer function falls to 1/√2 of its passband value; for an LR filter ω₀ = R/L.
eqs: Output voltage of the LR divider
\(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); \(Z_{R}\) = resistor impedance (Ω); \(Z_{L}\) = inductor impedance (Ω)
Transfer function of the LR filter
R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H); ω = angular frequency (rad/s)
ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); R = resistance (Ω)
ω₀ = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H)
tips: Be careful that the cut-off is ω₀ = R/L (angular frequency in rad/s), not f = R/L; convert with f = ω/2π when a frequency in Hz is asked.
The output is across R (the shunt element), not across L; using the inductor voltage gives a high-pass result and the wrong answer.
rq: Why does the output fall as frequency increases in this circuit?
Because the inductor's impedance \(Z_{L}\) = jωL increases with ω, so more of the input drops across the series inductor and less appears across the shunt resistor.
What happens to the cut-off frequency if L is doubled while R is kept constant?
ω₀ = R/L halves, so the filter cuts off at a lower frequency and passes less of the mid-band signal.

notes.t: First-order LR low-pass filter and cut-off frequency
pts: The LR low-pass places the inductor in series with the input and the resistor in shunt to ground, so the output is taken across R.
The filter's corner (cut-off) angular frequency is set by the ratio R/L, with \(f_{0}\) obtained by dividing by 2π.
Normalising the transfer function by ω_0 gives a magnitude that falls off once ω exceeds ω_0, which is the low-pass behaviour.
At ω = ω_0 the magnitude of the gain is 1/√2 (about −3 dB) of the passband value.
defs: Cut-off frequency (ω_0, \(f_{0}\)) of an LR low-pass
The frequency at which the output magnitude falls to 1/√2 of its low-frequency value; for the LR filter ω_0 = R/L and \(f_{0}\) = R/(2πL).
eqs: Transfer function of the first-order LR low-pass filter
\(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); R = resistance (Ω)
Cut-off angular frequency of the LR filter
ω_0 = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H)
\(f_{0}\) = cut-off frequency (Hz); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H)
Magnitude of the normalised transfer function
|\(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\)| = gain magnitude (dimensionless); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω_0 = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
tips: Do not confuse angular frequency ω_0 = R/L (rad/s) with \(f_{0}\) = R/(2πL) (Hz); the 2π factor is a common error.
Check units: L in henries and R in ohms give ω_0 in rad/s, so convert to Hz by dividing by 2π before quoting a frequency.
rq: Why does the output fall at high frequency in this circuit?
At high frequency the inductor's impedance jωL becomes large relative to R, so the series inductor drops most of the input and little voltage reaches the output across R.
What happens to the gain if the inductance L is doubled, with R unchanged?
ω_0 = R/L halves, so the cut-off frequency is lowered by a factor of two and the filter rolls off earlier.

notes.t: First-order LR high-pass filter
pts: In the LR high-pass filter the resistor is in series with the input and the inductor is shunt to ground, swapped relative to the low-pass arrangement.
The filter's corner (cut-off) frequency is set by the ratio R/L; below it the output is attenuated, above it the output passes with little loss.
The magnitude of the transfer function is 1 over the square root of one plus (ω0/ω) squared, giving the gain roll-off with frequency.
The cut-off frequency can be stated in hertz as f0 = R/(2πL), converting from angular frequency.
defs: Cut-off frequency (ω0) of an LR high-pass filter
The angular frequency at which the output magnitude falls to 1/√2 (about 0.707) of the passband value, equal to R/L for this circuit.
eqs: Magnitude of voltage transfer function of the LR high-pass filter
\(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(\omega\) = angular frequency of input (rad/s); \(\omega_0\) = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
Complex transfer function of the LR high-pass filter
\(V_o\) = output voltage phasor (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage phasor (V); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(\omega_0\) = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); \(j\) = imaginary unit
tips: Do not confuse ω0 (rad/s) with f0 (Hz): f0 = ω0/2π, so use f0 = R/(2πL) when a frequency in hertz is asked.
In the low-pass filter the inductor is in series and the resistor is shunt; in the high-pass they are swapped, so do not reuse the low-pass formula directly.
rq: Why does the output of an LR high-pass filter fall to zero at low frequency?
At low frequency the inductor's reactance ωL is small, so it shunts the output to ground and most of the input voltage drops across R; the output tends to zero as ω→0.
What happens to |Vo/Vin| when ω is much greater than ω0, and why does this make it a high-pass filter?
The ratio ω0/ω tends to 0, so |Vo/Vin| tends to 1; high frequencies pass unattenuated, hence high-pass.

notes.t: Passive first-order RC and LR filters: cut-off frequency
pts: First-order RC and LR filters each have one reactive element, giving a single characteristic (cut-off) frequency that sets where the response changes.
At the characteristic frequency the gain is 3 dB below the pass-band gain (about 0.707 of the pass-band voltage ratio).
Low-pass and high-pass versions of the same RC or LR pair share the same characteristic frequency; the difference is only the position of the reactive element.
The RC network has ω₀ = 1/RC, while the LR network has ω₀ = R/L; the R and L are swapped in roles compared with RC.
The cut-off frequency is often written as ω_c instead of ω₀.
defs: Characteristic (cut-off / corner) frequency
The frequency at which the filter output power falls to half the pass-band value, i.e. the gain is −3 dB relative to the pass-band gain.
eqs: Low-pass transfer function of a first-order filter (normalised)
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = characteristic/cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
High-pass transfer function of a first-order filter (normalised)
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω₀ = characteristic/cut-off angular frequency (rad/s)
Characteristic angular frequency of an RC filter
ω₀ = angular cut-off frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
Characteristic frequency of an RC filter in Hz
f₀ = cut-off frequency (Hz); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
Characteristic angular frequency of an LR filter
ω₀ = angular cut-off frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H)
Characteristic frequency of an LR filter in Hz
f₀ = cut-off frequency (Hz); R = resistance (Ω); L = inductance (H)
tips: Do not confuse ω₀ (rad/s) with f₀ (Hz): f₀ = ω₀/2π, so include the 2π when a frequency in hertz is asked for.
For LR filters the formula is R/L, not L/R; check units (Ω/H = 1/s) to avoid inverting the ratio.
rq: Why does the RC low-pass and RC high-pass share the same cut-off frequency?
Both use the same R and C; the cut-off comes from the RC time constant, and the filter type only changes whether the output is taken across the resistor or the capacitor.
Why is the LR cut-off R/L rather than 1/(LR)?
The inductor's impedance jωL grows with frequency, so the ratio of reactance to resistance gives ω₀ = R/L, which has units of rad/s (Ω/H = 1/s).
What happens to the gain at ω = ω₀ compared with the pass-band?
The magnitude is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 of the pass-band gain, i.e. −3 dB.

notes.t: First-order RC and LR filters: cut-off (corner) frequency
pts: For first-order RC and LR filters, the characteristic frequency, cut-off frequency and Bode corner frequency are all the same point.
At the cut-off frequency the gain is 3 dB below the passband gain.
The stopband roll-off of a first-order filter is 20 dB per decade.
The result for RC and LR first-order filters does not automatically carry over to higher-order filters.
The angular characteristic frequency defines the cut-off or corner frequencies.
defs: Cut-off (corner) frequency
The frequency at which the filter output power falls to half the passband value, i.e. the gain is −3 dB relative to the passband; it marks the transition between passband and stopband.
Characteristic (angular) frequency
The angular frequency \( \omega_0 \) that defines the cut-off or corner frequency of a first-order RC or LR filter.
eqs: Angular cut-off frequency of a first-order RC filter
\( \omega_o, \omega_c \) = angular cut-off (characteristic) frequency (rad/s); \( R \) = resistance (Ω); \( C \) = capacitance (F)
Angular cut-off frequency of a first-order LR filter
\( \omega_o, \omega_c \) = angular cut-off (characteristic) frequency (rad/s); \( R \) = resistance (Ω); \( L \) = inductance (H)
tips: Do not confuse angular frequency ω (rad/s) with frequency f (Hz); \(f_{c}\) = ω_c/2π.
The 20 dB/decade roll-off and the simple corner-frequency formulas apply only to first-order RC/LR filters, not to higher-order filters.
rq: Why does a first-order filter's gain fall by exactly 3 dB at its corner frequency, and how does this relate to power?
At the corner frequency the magnitude ratio is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, so gain is 20log10(0.707) ≈ −3 dB; this is the point where output power is half the passband power.
If a first-order RC filter's cut-off doubles, what change in R or C achieves this?
Since ω_c = 1/(RC), doubling ω_c requires halving RC, e.g. halving R or halving C.
Why can't the 20 dB/decade roll-off be assumed for a higher-order filter?
Higher-order filters have steeper roll-offs (e.g. 40 dB/decade for second order) and their corner frequency does not simply equal the RC/LR expression, so the first-order relationships do not hold.

xq.q: An LR low-pass filter has the inductor L = 10 mH in series with the input and the output taken across a resistor R = 2.2 kΩ. Calculate (a) the cut-off frequency \(f_0\) in Hz and (b) the gain magnitude \(|V_{out}/V_{in}|\) at f = 70 kHz. Give your final answer for (a).
An LR filter has R = 1 kΩ and L = 100 mH. A student quotes the cut-off frequency as 10 kHz. What is the correct value?
xq.a: 1.59 kHz
o: 10 kHz
1.59 kHz
62.8 kHz
0.1 kHz
xq.w: ω0 = R/L = 10⁴ rad/s, and f0 = ω0/2π ≈ 1.59 kHz; the trap is quoting rad/s as Hz.

xq.q: For the first-order LR low-pass filter with output taken across R, show that \(V_{out}/V_{in} = 1/(1 + j\omega L/R)\), and hence show that the gain magnitude is \(1/\sqrt{2}\) at \(\omega_0 = R/L\).
xq.a: Potential divider: Vout/Vin = \(Z_{R}\)/(\(Z_{R}\)+\(Z_{L}\)) = R/(R + jωL). Dividing top and bottom by R gives 1/(1 + jωL/R). The magnitude is 1/√(1+(ωL/R)²) = 1/√(1+(ω/ω0)²) with ω0 = R/L. At ω = ω0 this is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB), so this is the cut-off.
s: Divide by R to get normalised form

units.name: 4.7 Series LCR band-pass filter
units.ov: This material builds a series LCR band-pass filter by combining an RC high-pass stage and an LR low-pass stage, with the output taken across R. It treats the circuit as a voltage divider of complex impedances, giving a second-order transfer function whose magnitude peaks at the centre frequency \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\), where the reactances cancel. Gain falls away on both sides, and R controls the width of the band but not its centre.
must: Circuit is a voltage divider with output across R: \( \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=\frac{Z_R}{Z_C+Z_L+Z_R} \)
Impedances: \(Z_R=R,\ Z_L=j\omega L,\ Z_C=\frac{1}{j\omega C}\); keep the j and the signs consistent
Rearranged transfer function: \( \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}=\frac{R}{R+j(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C})} \), using \(1/j=-j\)
Magnitude: \( |V_{out}/V_{in}|=\frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L-1/(\omega C))^2}} \)
Centre frequency: set \(\omega L=1/(\omega C)\), so \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(f_0=\omega_0/2\pi\); R does not appear
At \(\omega_0\) the impedance is purely resistive, the gain is a maximum of 1 (0 dB) and the phase is 0
\(\omega_0\) is the peak, not a −3 dB cut-off; the −3 dB points lie either side of it where gain is \(1/\sqrt2\)
The circuit is second order (an \(\omega^2\) term, two energy-storing components), so it is a higher-order filter
Gain in dB is \(20\log_{10}|V_{out}/V_{in}|\); the response is a peak, and the band width depends on R, not a flat passband
Use ω in rad/s in \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\); convert with \(\omega=2\pi f\)
conn: RC high-pass plus LR low-pass cascade gives band-pass: the C sets the lower roll-off and the L sets the upper roll-off, and both are first-order ideas combined into a second-order result
Complex impedance and voltage divider: the transfer function comes directly from the impedance ratio, and its magnitude follows from the modulus of the complex expression
Reactance cancellation gives resonance: \(X_L=X_C\) leads to \(\omega_0\), maximum gain and zero phase, so the denominator is minimised and the magnitude is 1
Limiting behaviour: at low ω the capacitor dominates (acts as open circuit) and at high ω the inductor dominates, so gain falls on both sides and the dB plot has a peak shape
exq: Derive the transfer function \(V_{out}/V_{in}\) of a series LCR circuit with the output across R, and hence its magnitude. State the gain at very low and very high frequency.
A series LCR band-pass has \(L=10\) mH, \(C=100\) nF and \(R=100\ \Omega\). Calculate \(\omega_0\) and \(f_0\), and state the gain at \(\omega_0\) in dB.
For the circuit above, calculate the gain magnitude and its value in dB at \(\omega=0.5\omega_0\) and \(\omega=2\omega_0\). Explain why the response is a peak and not a flat passband.
Explain why \(\omega_0\) does not depend on R. State what changing R does to the shape of the gain curve and the band width.
Explain why this circuit is second order. Show how it is built from an RC high-pass and an LR low-pass, and distinguish \(\omega_0\) from a −3 dB cut-off frequency.

notes.t: Combining RC high-pass and LR low-pass into a series LCR band-pass
pts: Cascading a high-pass stage and a low-pass stage gives a filter that passes only a band of frequencies around a centre frequency.
The series LCR band-pass takes the capacitor from the RC high-pass and the inductor from the LR low-pass, with R across the output.
The gain \(V_{\text{out}}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) in dB is near zero at the peak ω₀ and falls off on both sides, so the response is a peak shape.
defs: Band-pass filter
A filter that passes frequencies within a band around a centre frequency ω₀ and attenuates frequencies below and above that band.
tips: Do not read the peak as a flat passband; the gain is only maximal at ω₀ and the band width depends on R.
Plot gain in dB (20 log₁₀ of the ratio), so the peak is at 0 dB only for an ideal, lossless-output case.
rq: Why does the response fall at both very low and very high frequencies in the series LCR circuit?
At low frequency the capacitor's reactance 1/(ωC) is large and blocks the signal (high-pass behaviour); at high frequency the inductor's reactance ωL is large and blocks it (low-pass behaviour).
What happens to the output if the component values are changed so that ω₀ moves?
The peak moves to the new resonant frequency, since ω₀ depends on L and C, so the passband shifts along the ω axis.

notes.t: Series LCR band-pass filter transfer function
pts: The series LCR band-pass circuit is just a voltage divider, with the output taken across R.
To find the transfer function, treat the circuit as three impedances in series (C, L, R) and substitute each impedance's expression before rearranging for Vout/Vin.
Because the circuit contains more than one energy-storing component (inductor and capacitor), it is a higher-order filter.
Rearranging the transfer function produces an ω² term, which indicates the filter order.
eqs: Output voltage of the voltage divider across R
\(V_{out}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(Z_{R}\) = impedance of resistor R (Ω); \(Z_{C}\) = impedance of capacitor C (Ω); \(Z_{L}\) = impedance of inductor L (Ω)
R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Use the complex impedances (\(Z_{L}\) = jωL, \(Z_{C}\) = 1/(jωC)) consistently; forgetting the j or the sign of the reactance terms is a common error.
Remember the output is across R only, so the denominator must include all three impedances in series while the numerator is \(Z_{R}\) alone.
rq: Why is the output taken across R rather than across L or C, and what type of filter does this give?
