Taking the output across R gives a band-pass response: the reactances of L and C cancel near resonance, so the voltage across R peaks at the resonant frequency and falls off on either side.
What happens to the magnitude |Vout/Vin| when ωL = 1/(ωC)?
The imaginary term vanishes, so |Vout/Vin| = R/R = 1; the filter passes the signal unattenuated at resonance.

notes.t: Centre frequency of a series RLC bandpass filter
pts: For a series RLC bandpass filter, the centre frequency is found where the reactances cancel, i.e. the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal.
At the centre frequency the impedance is purely resistive, so the gain is maximum and equal to 1 (for this output across R).
The centre frequency is not a cut-off or -3dB point; it is the peak of the response, and it differs from the cut-off logic used for first-order circuits.
Setting the reactance term to zero gives ωL = 1/(ωC), which rearranges to ω² = 1/(LC).
defs: Centre frequency (ω₀)
The angular frequency at which the reactive components of a bandpass filter cancel, giving maximum gain and a purely resistive impedance.
eqs: Magnitude of voltage gain of series RLC filter (output across R)
R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F); \(V_{\text{out}}\), \(V_{\text{in}}\) = output and input voltage (V)
ω₀ = centre angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Do not treat ω₀ as a cut-off or −3dB frequency; it is the central peak frequency.
Use angular frequency ω (rad/s) in ω₀ = 1/√(LC), not frequency f in Hz, unless converting with ω = 2πf.
rq: Why does the gain peak at the centre frequency, and what is the magnitude of the gain there?
The reactance term (ωL − 1/(ωC)) becomes zero, so the denominator reduces to R, giving |Vout/Vin| = 1, the maximum gain.
Why can't ω₀ be found by locating the −3dB points as with first-order circuits?
The bandpass response is a peak defined by reactance cancellation, not a single cut-off; the −3dB points are on either side of ω₀ and are used to find bandwidth, not the centre frequency.

notes.t: Band-pass filter: central frequency and gain response
pts: A series RLC band-pass filter passes frequencies near a central frequency and attenuates those well above or below it.
The central frequency is set by L and C alone, not by R.
At the central frequency the output-to-input gain peaks, and the magnitude curve falls away on either side in dB.
defs: Central frequency (ω₀)
The angular frequency at which the reactances of the inductor and capacitor cancel, giving maximum output-to-input voltage ratio in a band-pass filter.
eqs: Central (resonant) angular frequency of the band-pass filter
ω₀ = central angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
Magnitude of output-to-input voltage ratio versus frequency
|Vout/Vin| = gain (dimensionless); R = resistance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Do not confuse ω (angular frequency, rad/s) with f (Hz); ω₀ = 2πf₀ when converting.
The central frequency depends only on L and C; do not include R in the ω₀ formula.
rq: Why does the gain peak exactly at ω₀, and what happens to the reactance term at that point?
At ω₀ the inductive reactance ωL equals the capacitive reactance 1/(ωC), so the reactive term (ωL − 1/ωC) is zero and the gain reduces to |Vout/Vin| = 1, its maximum.
What happens to the bandwidth if R is increased, given the gain formula?
A larger R makes the denominator's reactive term relatively smaller compared with R, so the response is flatter and the pass band widens; a smaller R gives a sharper peak.
Why is the response symmetric-looking on a linear frequency axis but not exactly symmetric?
The gain depends on (ωL − 1/ωC), which is not symmetric in ω, so the curve is only approximately symmetric about ω₀ and is more accurately viewed on a logarithmic frequency scale.

xq.q: A series LCR band-pass filter has the output taken across the resistor R = 100 Ω, with L = 10 mH and C = 100 nF (100×10⁻⁹ F). Calculate the centre frequency f₀ of the filter in kHz.
xq.a: f₀ ≈ 5.03 kHz

xq.q: A series LCR band-pass filter has R = 50 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 100 nF, with the output across R. The input is a sinusoid of angular frequency ω = 2.0×10⁴ rad/s. Calculate the magnitude of the gain |Vout/Vin| (a number, not dB).
For a series LCR band-pass filter with the output taken across R, the resistance R is doubled while L and C are unchanged. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: The centre frequency ω₀ is unchanged, and the peak gain is still 1 at ω₀
o: The centre frequency ω₀ doubles because R is in the denominator of the gain
The centre frequency ω₀ is unchanged, and the peak gain is still 1 at ω₀
The centre frequency ω₀ halves, and the peak gain falls to 0.5
The centre frequency ω₀ is unchanged, but the peak gain doubles to 2
xq.w: ω₀ = 1/√(LC) depends only on L and C, and at ω₀ the reactances cancel so |Vout/Vin| = R/R = 1; the trap is thinking R sets the centre frequency.

units.name: 4.8 Complex impedance and phasors in AC circuits
units.ov: This module extends resistance to complex impedance \(Z = R + jX\), so that sinusoidal steady-state AC circuits can be analysed with phasors and the same algebra as DC circuits. Resistors, inductors and capacitors each have a characteristic impedance, and \(V = IZ\) gives both the magnitude and the phase relationship between voltage and current. Series and parallel combinations then follow the DC rules, with complex arithmetic (conjugates, rectangular and polar forms) needed to simplify the results.
must: Impedance is \(Z = R + jX\): the real part is resistance and the imaginary part is reactance. It is the complex ratio \(Z = V/I\) of phasor voltage to phasor current.
Component impedances are \(Z_R = R\), \(Z_L = j\omega L\) and \(Z_C = \dfrac{-j}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{j\omega C}\).
AC Ohm's law is \(V = IZ\). The voltage phasor's magnitude is \(|I||Z|\) and its phase is the current phase plus \(\arg Z\).

Signs of reactance: an inductor gives \(+jX\), so voltage leads current (by 90° for a pure inductor). A capacitor gives \(-jX\), so voltage lags current (by 90° for a pure capacitor). A resistor gives no phase shift.
Series impedances add directly. Parallel impedances combine as \(\dfrac{1}{Z_T} = \sum \dfrac{1}{Z_n}\); take reciprocals first, then invert the total.
Simplify complex denominators by multiplying top and bottom by the complex conjugate: \(\dfrac{1}{a+jb} = \dfrac{a-jb}{a^2+b^2}\). Also use \(1/j = -j\).

Convert between rectangular and polar form: \(|Z| = \sqrt{R^2+X^2}\) and \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(X/R)\). Use polar form for multiplication and division, and rectangular form for addition and subtraction.
Use \(\omega\) in rad/s, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\), never Hz. Keep peak and RMS values consistent, and keep degrees and radians consistent.
Impedance is not simply resistance. It depends on frequency through \(\omega\), and the units are ohms for all three components.
conn: Complex numbers and phasors: rectangular and polar conversion and conjugates are the tools used to evaluate \(V = IZ\) and parallel combinations.

Impedance angle and waveforms: \(\arg Z\) is the phase by which voltage leads current in the phasor diagram, and it appears as the time shift between the sinusoids. The sign of \(X\) tells you whether the circuit is inductive or capacitive.

DC circuit laws and AC analysis: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws, series/parallel reduction and divider rules all carry over with \(R \to Z\). Questions often combine reducing a network to \(Z_T\) with finding the source current and then branch voltages.
Frequency dependence: \(\omega\) sets \(X_L = \omega L\) and \(X_C = 1/(\omega C)\), so changing frequency changes the impedance, its phase and the current magnitude.
exq: Find the impedance of a 6 Ω resistor in series with a 20 mH inductor at 50 Hz. Give the answer in rectangular and polar form and state the phase angle by which voltage leads current.
A 6 Ω resistor and a j8 Ω inductor in series form one branch, in parallel with a capacitive branch of −j5 Ω. Find \(Z_T\) in rectangular form, then find the supply current for a 100∠0° V source.

A current \(I = 3 + j4\) A flows through \(Z = 2 - j5\,\Omega\). Calculate the voltage phasor in rectangular and polar form, its magnitude and its phase relative to the current. State whether the load is inductive or capacitive.
A 10 µF capacitor is driven at 1 kHz. Calculate its impedance. Explain why using f instead of \(\omega\), or omitting the minus sign, gives wrong results, and sketch the phasor diagram.
Using the conjugate method, simplify \(\dfrac{1}{3+j4} + \dfrac{1}{-j2}\), and use the result to find the equivalent impedance of the parallel combination.

notes.t: Impedances of R, L and C using complex numbers
pts: Impedance generally combines a real resistive part and an imaginary reactive part, written as Z = R + jX.
A resistor's impedance is purely real, so it changes only the amplitude of the current relative to the voltage, not the phase.
An inductor's impedance is purely imaginary and positive, so it introduces a phase change between voltage and current.
A capacitor's impedance is also purely imaginary but negative, introducing a phase change opposite to that of an inductor.
defs: Impedance
The complex generalisation of resistance in an AC circuit, Z = R + jX, relating phasor voltage to phasor current; its real part is resistance and its imaginary part is reactance.
eqs: Z = impedance (\Omega); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); L = inductance (H); j = imaginary unit
Z = impedance (\Omega); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); C = capacitance (F); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not confuse the impedance of a capacitor, -j/(ωC), with the inductor's jωL; the sign difference determines the opposite phase shifts, and forgetting the minus sign gives wrong phase answers.
Impedance is measured in ohms (\Omega) for all three components; ω must be in rad/s, not Hz, when substituting into jωL or 1/(ωC).
rq: Why does the capacitor's impedance carry a negative imaginary sign while the inductor's is positive?

Current leads voltage across a capacitor (phase lag of voltage by -90°), whereas voltage leads current across an inductor (+90°); the j factor encodes this 90° phase shift, with 1/j = -j giving the opposite sign.
What happens to the capacitor's impedance as frequency increases, and why does this matter?
Its magnitude 1/(ωC) decreases, so the capacitor passes high frequencies more easily and blocks low (DC) frequencies more strongly.

notes.t: Phasors, impedance and phasor voltage in AC circuits
pts: Current is represented as a phasor in the complex plane, written in rectangular form with real part a and imaginary part b.
Impedance is a complex number that can include contributions from inductance, resistance and capacitance.
The voltage phasor is found by multiplying the current phasor by the impedance, so the voltage and current phasors differ in magnitude and phase.
In the phasor diagram the voltage phasor leads the current phasor by an angle set by the impedance angle, which is what produces the phase difference seen in the sinusoidal waveforms.
The phasor representation lets sinusoidal steady-state AC circuits be analysed with the same algebra used for DC resistive circuits.
defs: Phasor
A complex number representing a sinusoidal quantity by its magnitude and phase angle, allowing AC steady-state analysis using algebra.
Impedance
The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor in an AC circuit, generalising resistance to include the effects of inductance and capacitance.
eqs: Rectangular form of the current phasor
I = current phasor (A); a = real part (A); b = imaginary part (A); j = imaginary unit
Voltage phasor from Ohm's law for AC
V = voltage phasor (V); I = current phasor (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
tips: Impedance Z is complex and in general not equal to R; include the reactive terms from L and C, and do not treat Z as a simple resistance.
Keep phasors in complex (rectangular or polar) form consistently; mixing peak and RMS values or degrees and radians gives wrong phase angles.
rq: Why can the same algebra used for DC resistive circuits be applied to AC circuits once phasors are used?
Because for sinusoidal steady state all voltages and currents share the same frequency, so they can be represented as complex phasors and Ohm's law generalises to V = IZ.
What happens to the phase relationship between V and I if the impedance Z has a non-zero angle?
The voltage phasor is rotated relative to the current phasor by the angle of Z, so V and I are out of phase and the waveforms are shifted in time.

notes.t: Simplifying parallel impedances with complex denominators
pts: Impedances in parallel combine by adding reciprocals, so the parallel combination is found from the reciprocal sum of the branch impedances.
The 6 Ω resistor and j8 Ω inductor are in series in one branch, giving a branch impedance of 6 + j8 Ω.
The capacitive branch has impedance −j5 Ω, so its reciprocal introduces a complex denominator that must be simplified before adding.
Simplifying a complex denominator requires a technique (such as multiplying by the complex conjugate) before the result can be expressed in rectangular form.
eqs: Reciprocal impedance of two branches in parallel
\(Z_{T}\) = total parallel impedance (Ω); 6 + 8j = series R–L branch impedance (Ω); −j5 = capacitive branch impedance (Ω)
tips: Do not add parallel impedances directly; take reciprocals first, then invert the total.
Watch the sign of the reactance: an inductor gives +jX Ω and a capacitor gives −jX Ω.
rq: Why can't we simply add the two branch impedances 6 + j8 and −j5 to find the parallel combination?
Impedances in parallel combine as reciprocals, so 1/\(Z_{T}\) = 1/Z₁ + 1/Z₂; adding the impedances directly only applies to series branches.
What does the j in the 6 + j8 branch tell us about the element that produces it?
The positive imaginary part (+j8 Ω) indicates an inductive reactance, so that branch is inductive.

xq.q: In the op-amp circuit below, the source voltage has form \( v_s = 4\sin(200t) \) Volts. The circuit consists of a voltage source \( v_s \) feeding a 20 kΩ resistor, then a node with a 0.25 µF capacitor to ground, then a second 20 kΩ resistor into the inverting (−) input of an ideal op-amp. A 10 kΩ feedback resistor connects the op-amp output back to the inverting input. The non-inverting (+) input is connected to ground. A 33 kΩ load resistor is connected across the output \( v_o \). Calculate the form of the output voltage \( v_o \) across the 33 kΩ resistor. Assume the op-amp is ideal.
s: The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the second 20 kΩ resistor connects the node to 0 V. The load on the output of an ideal op-amp has no effect.
The node impedance to ground is \(Z = 20\text{k} \parallel (-j20\text{k}) = 10\text{k}(1-j)\) Ω.
The node voltage is \(V_x = V_s Z/(20\text{k}+Z) = V_s (1-j)/(3-j) = V_s(0.4 - j0.2)\).
The op-amp stage is inverting with gain \(-R_f/R = -10/20 = -0.5\). The overall gain is \(-0.5(0.4 - j0.2)\), with magnitude 0.2236 and phase \(180° - 26.6° = 153.4°\).

xq.q: A series circuit consists of a resistor R = 30 Ω, an inductor of reactance +j40 Ω and a capacitor of reactance −j8 Ω at the operating frequency. A current phasor I = 2 + j0 A (amplitude) flows. Calculate the magnitude of the voltage phasor V = IZ across the whole series circuit, in V.
A capacitor C = 2 µF is connected across a sinusoidal supply of frequency f = 100 Hz. What is its impedance Z?
xq.w: Z = −j/(ωC) with ω = 2π×100 = 628.3 rad/s gives −j796 Ω; the traps are the wrong sign, using ωC, or using f in place of ω.

xq.q: A branch consisting of a 6 Ω resistor in series with an inductor of reactance 8 Ω is connected in parallel with a capacitor of reactance 5 Ω at the operating frequency. Write down the impedance of each branch and show that the reciprocal of the total impedance, 1/\(Z_{T}\), is 0.06 + j0.12 S.

units.name: 4.9 Complex number algebra: squaring, conjugates, complex denominators
units.ov: This material covers squaring complex numbers, the complex conjugate, and using the conjugate to rationalise complex denominators. The key identity \(zz^*=a^2+b^2=|z|^2\) is real and non-negative. It connects the rectangular and polar forms and is applied to parallel impedances such as \(1/Z_T=1/(6+8j)+1/(-j5)\).
must: Conjugate: \(z=a+jb \Rightarrow z^*=a-jb\); only the sign of the imaginary part changes, not the real part
\(zz^*=(a+jb)(a-jb)=a^2+b^2=|z|^2\), which is real and positive
Rationalising a denominator: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator
Squaring: \((a+jb)^2=a^2-b^2+2abj\); the imaginary part is \(2ab\), and the \(-b^2\) comes from \(j^2=-1\)
Magnitude: \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), and \(|z|^2\) is real, so do not confuse it with the complex \(z^2\)
Polar form: \(Z=|Z|\angle\theta\Rightarrow Z^*=|Z|\angle(-\theta)\); the conjugate is the reflection in the real axis, and \(ZZ^*=|Z|^2\angle0^\circ\)
Reciprocal of an imaginary number: \(1/(-j)=j\), so \(1/(-j5)=j/5\)
Parallel impedances: \(1/Z_T=1/Z_1+1/Z_2\); rationalise each term, then combine over a common denominator
The conjugate trick gives \(|Z|^2\), not \(|Z|\); do not forget to square
conn: Conjugate multiplication links rectangular and polar forms: \(a^2+b^2=|Z|^2\) with zero angle, so you can check an answer in either form
Rationalisation is the tool for parallel impedance and admittance problems: reciprocals, sums, then a final conjugate step to get \(Z_T\) in the form \(a+jb\)
Squaring and magnitude are linked: \(|z^2|=|z|^2\), so compare \(z^2\) (complex) with \(zz^*\) (real) to catch sign errors
Reciprocal of a capacitive impedance \(-j5\) gives \(+j/5\), which is a positive imaginary admittance (susceptance)
exq: Expand \((3-4j)^2\) and find \(|(3-4j)^2|\). Check that it equals \(|3-4j|^2\).
Write \((2+5j)/(3-2j)\) in the form \(a+jb\) by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator.
Find the total admittance \(1/Z_T\) for \(Z_1=6+8j\,\Omega\) in parallel with \(Z_2=-j5\,\Omega\), giving the answer as a single fraction over 100. Then find \(Z_T\) in rectangular form.
Given \(Z=10\angle30^\circ\), write down \(Z^*\) and compute \(ZZ^*\). Convert \(Z\) to rectangular form and verify \(a^2+b^2\).
Find the real and imaginary parts of \(z^2\) when \(z=a+jb\), and find \(z\) such that \(z^2\) is purely imaginary. Explain the sign-error traps.

notes.t: Squaring complex numbers and complex conjugates
pts: Squaring a complex number expands to a real part plus an imaginary part, with the imaginary term 2ab j.
The complex conjugate of z flips the sign of the imaginary part.
Multiplying a complex number by its complex conjugate gives its squared magnitude, which is a real, non-negative value.
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = a + jb, the complex conjugate z* = a − jb; it has the same real part and the opposite sign of imaginary part.
Magnitude of a complex number
The distance of z = a + jb from the origin in the complex plane, equal to the square root of a² + b².
eqs: |z| = magnitude of z (dimensionless); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
|z|² = squared magnitude (dimensionless); a = real part; b = imaginary part
z = a + jb (dimensionless); a = real part; b = imaginary part; j = imaginary unit
Product of z and its conjugate
z = a + jb; z* = a − jb (complex conjugate); |z|² = squared magnitude
tips: Do not forget j² = −1 when expanding (a + jb)²; the term −b² is negative and the imaginary term is 2abj, not 2ab.
The squared magnitude |z|² is a real number, so do not confuse it with z² which is complex.
rq: Why does multiplying z by z* remove the imaginary part entirely?
The cross terms +jab and −jab cancel, and j² = −1 turns the −(jb)² term into +b², leaving only a² + b².
Why is z² not equal to |z|² in general, even though both involve a² and b²?
z² contains the cross term 2abj and a² − b² (which can be negative), whereas |z|² = a² + b² is always real and non-negative.

notes.t: Squaring complex numbers continued: complex conjugate trick
pts: A complex number and its conjugate have the same magnitude but opposite angles, reflected about the real axis.
Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate gives a real, positive result equal to the magnitude squared, with zero angle.
This identity is used to remove complex numbers from denominators by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate.
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = a + jb, the conjugate is z* = a − jb; in polar form, if Z = |Z|∠θ then Z* = |Z|∠(−θ).
eqs: Product of a complex number and its conjugate (magnitude squared)
Z = complex number; Z* = complex conjugate of Z; |Z| = magnitude of Z (dimensionless or same unit as Z)
Polar form of a complex number
Z = complex number; |Z| = magnitude (same unit as Z); θ = phase angle (degrees or radians)
Z* = complex conjugate; |Z| = magnitude; θ = phase angle (degrees or radians)
tips: Only the sign of the imaginary part changes in the conjugate: a − jb, not −a − jb or a + jb with a changed angle.
Remember that the conjugate trick gives |Z|², the magnitude squared, not |Z|; forgetting to square is a common error.
rq: Why does multiplying a complex number by its conjugate produce a real number?
The angles θ and −θ cancel, leaving zero phase, so the product is |Z|², a real non-negative number.
Why is the conjugate trick useful when dividing complex numbers?
Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator makes the denominator real, so it is simpler to evaluate.

notes.t: Simplifying equations with complex denominators
pts: To remove a complex number from a denominator, multiply top and bottom by its complex conjugate.
The product of a complex number and its conjugate is always real: (a+jb)(a−jb) = a²+b².
Reciprocal of a purely imaginary number: 1/(−j) = j, so 1/(−j5) = j/5.
Impedances in parallel combine via the sum of reciprocals, 1/\(Z_{T}\) = 1/Z₁ + 1/Z₂.
Final result is written over a common denominator of 100, giving the combined admittance as a single complex fraction.
defs: Complex conjugate
For a complex number a+jb, its conjugate is a−jb; multiplying a complex number by its conjugate gives a real number a²+b².
eqs: Product of a complex number and its conjugate
a = real part (Ω); b = imaginary part (Ω); j = imaginary unit
\(Z_{T}\) = total impedance (Ω); 6+8j = series branch impedance (Ω); −j5 = capacitor impedance (Ω)
tips: Sign error trap: the conjugate of 6+8j is 6−8j; keep the minus sign on the imaginary part when expanding.
Remember j² = −1 when expanding products such as (6+8j)(6−8j) = 36+64 = 100, not 36−64.
rq: Why do we multiply by the conjugate of the denominator rather than just the same number?
Multiplying by the conjugate produces a real denominator (a²+b²), so the complex number is isolated in the numerator and the fraction can be split into real and imaginary parts.
Why does 1/(−j) equal j?
Since 1/(−j) = (1/(−j))·(j/j) = j/(−j²) = j/1 = j, using j² = −1.

xq.q: Given z = 3 + j4, calculate the real part of z² and the value of zz*, where z* is the complex conjugate of z. Give the value of zz* as your final answer.
xq.a: zz* = 25 (and Re(z²) = −7)

xq.q: An impedance Z = 6 + j8 Ω is connected across a source. Find the real part of the admittance Y = 1/Z in siemens by multiplying top and bottom by the complex conjugate of Z.
What is the value of (6 + 8j)(6 − 8j)?
xq.w: The product of a number and its conjugate is a² + b² = 36 + 64 = 100, since j² = −1; the traps are using 36 − 64, forgetting to square the magnitude (giving 10), or expanding incorrectly.

units.name: 4.10 Lecture summary
units.ov: This material covers inductors, which oppose changes in current, and how their behaviour in AC circuits is described using complex impedance. It then applies this to first-order LR filters, which pass or attenuate signals depending on frequency, and to the idea of a band-pass filter. Complex numbers are the common tool: they give magnitude and phase of impedance, and so the gain and phase shift of each filter. Note that the source notes are a brief summary, so the formulas below are standard results and not quoted from the notes.
must: Inductors oppose changes in current: \( v = L\,\frac{di}{dt} \), so a steady DC current gives zero voltage across an ideal inductor.
Inductor impedance: \( Z_L = j\omega L \), with magnitude \( \omega L \) increasing with frequency (short circuit at DC, open circuit at very high frequency).
Phase: current LAGS voltage by \( 90^\circ \) in an inductor (voltage leads). This is the opposite of a capacitor, so check the direction (a common error).
Series impedance adds as a complex number: \( Z = R + j\omega L \), with \( |Z| = \sqrt{R^2+\omega^2L^2} \) and phase \( \phi = \arctan(\omega L/R) \).
First-order LR filter as a potential divider: \( H(j\omega) = \frac{Z_{out}}{Z_{in}} \), with gain \( |H| \) and phase \( \arg H \) found from the complex ratio.
Time constant and cut-off: \( \tau = L/R \), \( \omega_c = R/L \), \( f_c = R/(2\pi L) \); at cut-off \( |H| = 1/\sqrt{2} \) (−3 dB) and the phase is \( \pm45^\circ \).
Low-pass vs high-pass: output across R gives low-pass (inductor in series), output across L gives high-pass; sketch the gain behaviour at \( \omega \to 0 \) and \( \omega \to \infty \).
A band-pass filter passes a range of frequencies and rejects those above and below, so it needs both low- and high-frequency attenuation (e.g. combining high-pass and low-pass stages).
Complex number skills: rectangular and polar forms, \( j^2=-1 \), modulus, argument, multiplication/division, and converting between forms and to \( \cos(\omega t+\phi) \).
conn: Complex impedance + potential divider: the filter transfer function is a complex ratio, so gain comes from the modulus and phase shift from the argument.

Inductor phase lag + filter phase: the \( 90^\circ \) lag of the inductor becomes the \( 0^\circ \) to \( \pm90^\circ \) phase shift of the filter as frequency changes, with \( \pm45^\circ \) at cut-off.
Time domain and frequency domain: \( \tau = L/R \) governs step response and also sets \( \omega_c = 1/\tau \).
Low-pass and high-pass combined: a band-pass response arises by cascading the two, with the cut-off frequencies setting the passband edges.
exq: An inductor \( L = 50\,\text{mH} \) carries a current \( i = 2\sin(1000t)\,\text{A} \). Find its impedance, the voltage across it, and state the phase relationship between voltage and current.
A series LR circuit has \( R = 100\,\Omega \) and \( L = 20\,\text{mH} \). Calculate the time constant, cut-off frequency, and the gain and phase of the output across R at \( f = 10\,\text{kHz} \).
Derive the transfer function \( H(j\omega) \) for an LR high-pass filter (output across L). Sketch the magnitude and phase against frequency, marking the −3 dB point.
Express \( \frac{3+j4}{1-j2} \) in polar form, and use it to find the amplitude and phase of the current in a circuit with \( V = 5\angle0^\circ \) V and \( Z = R + j\omega L \).
Explain how a band-pass filter could be built from first-order stages, and estimate the passband for chosen component values.

notes.t: Summary: inductors, LR filters and complex numbers
pts: Inductors oppose changes in current, which is the defining behaviour of inductance.
For an inductor the current lags the voltage across it, a phase relationship captured by its complex impedance.
LR first order filters are simple circuits built from an inductor and a resistor that pass or attenuate signals depending on frequency.
A band-pass filter passes a range of frequencies while rejecting those above and below it.
Working with complex numbers is essential for handling AC impedances and phase in these circuits.
tips: Check the phase direction: the current lags the voltage across an inductor, the opposite of a capacitor.
rq: Why does the current through an inductor lag the voltage across it?
Because the voltage across an inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, so the current reaches its peak a quarter cycle (90°) after the voltage does.

units.name: Analogue Electronics - Lecture 7 -originalNamingScheme

notes.t: Operational Amplifiers: the two golden rules
pts: With negative feedback, the inverting input voltage is forced to equal the non-inverting input voltage, so the op-amp acts to make the difference zero.
An ideal op-amp draws no current into either input terminal, so the inputs can be treated as open circuits when analysing a circuit.
The two rules together allow fast analysis of op-amp circuits: use the virtual short (V- = V+) and zero input current to find currents and voltages.
defs: Inverting terminal
The op-amp input marked with a minus sign (−); signals applied here appear inverted (180° out of phase) at the output.
Non-inverting terminal
The op-amp input marked with a plus sign (+); signals applied here appear at the output without inversion.
eqs: Virtual short condition under negative feedback
\(V_{-}\) = voltage at the inverting input (V); \(V_{+}\) = voltage at the non-inverting input (V)
tips: The virtual short (V- = V+) only holds with negative feedback; without feedback (open loop or positive feedback) the rule does not apply.
Do not confuse a virtual short with a real short circuit: no current flows through it, so the two inputs are at equal voltage but not connected by a conductor.
rq: Why must the inputs of an ideal op-amp draw zero current, and what would break if they did?

An ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, so no current flows in; if current flowed, the input currents would change the circuit's node equations and the golden-rule analysis (using zero input current) would give wrong results.
Why does negative feedback make V- equal V+?

The huge open-loop gain means any small difference between V+ and V- is amplified enormously; the feedback path routes the output back to the inverting input so the output adjusts until the difference is essentially zero.

notes.t: Ideal Operational Amplifier Properties
pts: An op-amp has an inverting (−) input, a non-inverting (+) input and one output terminal.
An ideal op-amp is assumed to draw no current into its inputs, so its input impedance is infinite.
An ideal op-amp output acts as a perfect voltage source, so its output impedance is zero and the output is unaffected by the load.
An ideal op-amp has the potential for infinite voltage gain, which is why negative feedback is almost always used to make circuit behaviour predictable.
defs: Operational amplifier (op-amp)
A high-gain differential voltage amplifier with two inputs (inverting and non-inverting) and one output, whose behaviour is set by external components.
Inverting terminal
The op-amp input marked (−) whose signal is inverted in phase at the output.
Non-inverting terminal
The op-amp input marked (+) whose signal appears at the output without phase inversion.
Input impedance
The opposition an amplifier presents to the signal source; for an ideal op-amp it is infinite, so no input current flows.
Output impedance
The internal opposition to current seen at the output; an ideal op-amp has zero output impedance.
tips: Do not confuse the ideal assumptions (infinite gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance) with real op-amp values; real devices have finite, though very large, gain and input impedance.
The inverting terminal is marked (−) and the non-inverting terminal (+); mixing these up reverses the sign of the output in circuit analysis.
rq: Why does an ideal op-amp's infinite input impedance mean no current flows into its input terminals?
Current \( I = V/Z_{in} \) tends to zero as \( Z_{in} \to \infty \) for any finite voltage, so the inputs draw no current.
What would happen to the output voltage if the op-amp had non-zero output impedance and a load was connected?
Part of the output voltage would be dropped across the internal impedance, so the output would fall as load current increases.

notes.t: Open loop gain of an op-amp
pts: Open loop gain A is the amplification with no feedback, typically around \(10^{5}\) to \(10^{6.}\)
Output is the gain multiplied by the difference between the two input voltages, so tiny inputs produce large outputs.
Because the gain is so large, even a 10 mV input would drive the output far beyond the supply rails, so the output saturates at the supply voltage limit.
With ±15 V supplies, the output is clipped to between +15 V and −15 V.
defs: Open loop gain
The voltage gain of an op-amp with no feedback connected between output and input; very large (about \(10^{5}\) to \(10^{6}\)), so the output saturates easily.
Saturation
The condition in which the op-amp output reaches its maximum (or minimum) value set by the supply voltages and can no longer increase with the input.
eqs: Op-amp output voltage in open loop
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); A = open loop gain (dimensionless); \(V_{in}\) = differential input voltage (V)
\(V_{in}\) = differential input voltage (V); \(V_{+}\) = voltage at non-inverting input (V); \(V_{-}\) = voltage at inverting input (V)
tips: Do not compute \(V_{o}\) = \(AV_{in}\) and quote the result as the answer when it exceeds the supply; the output is clipped to the supply rails (±15 V here).
Watch the sign of \(V_{\text{in}}\): it is V_+ − V_- (non-inverting minus inverting), so swapping the inputs reverses the output polarity.
rq: Why does a 10 mV input not give a 10 mV-scale output when the gain is \(10^{6}\)?
Output would be \(V_{o}\) = \(10^{6}\) × 10 mV = 10 kV, which is far beyond the supply, so the op-amp saturates at about ±15 V.
What would happen to the output if the inverting and non-inverting inputs were at exactly the same voltage?
\(V_{\text{in}}\) = 0 so \(V_{o}\) = 0; in practice the output sits at a value near 0 V, with a tiny input offset able to push it to saturation.

notes.t: Negative feedback: voltage follower / voltage buffer
pts: Negative feedback connects the output directly to the inverting input, forcing the two op-amp inputs to be equal.
The voltage follower has a gain of 1, so the output voltage equals the input voltage.
Because an ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance, it draws no current and does not load the source it is connected to.
Because the output impedance is zero, the buffer drives any load without dropping voltage across its own output, as in Thevenin analysis.
defs: Voltage follower / buffer
An op-amp circuit with output fed back to the inverting input, giving unity gain (\( V_o = V_{in} \)) with very high input impedance and very low output impedance, used to isolate stages.
eqs: \( V_o \) = output voltage (V); \( V_{in} \) = input voltage (V)
tips: Do not confuse the voltage follower's gain of 1 with having no purpose: its value is in impedance transformation (high input, low output), not voltage amplification.
Assumes an ideal op-amp; with real devices the input impedance is finite and output impedance is small but non-zero.
rq: Why does connecting the output directly to the inverting input make the two inputs equal?
Negative feedback: if V− differs from V+, the op-amp's large open-loop gain drives the output so as to reduce the difference, settling when V− = V+ (and V− = Vin here).
Why is a buffer useful if its voltage gain is only 1?
It has very high input impedance so it draws almost no current from the source, and very low output impedance so it delivers voltage to a load without voltage drop; it isolates stages.

notes.t: Negative feedback: voltage follower / voltage buffer
pts: Output is fed directly back to the inverting input, so the op-amp drives V- to equal Vin and the output follows the input.
Gain is unity and the circuit isolates the source from the load while passing the same voltage.
The follower only works while the input stays within the supply/rail limits; outside them the output saturates.
defs: Voltage follower (buffer)
An op-amp circuit with 100% negative feedback from output to inverting input and the signal applied to the non-inverting input, giving unity voltage gain and a high input/low output impedance.
eqs: Output voltage of the voltage follower
\(V_{max}\) = positive supply/rail saturation voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V)
tips: Do not assume Vo = Vin for all inputs; the relation only holds for \(-V_{max} < V_{in} < V_{max}\), otherwise the output saturates at the rail.
Remember the buffer has unity gain (no voltage amplification); its purpose is impedance transformation, not amplifying the signal.
rq: Why does setting V- = Vin force Vo = Vin in this circuit?
The op-amp's large open-loop gain drives its output to whatever value makes the difference between the inputs approximately zero, so the output must equal the voltage fed back, which is Vin.
What happens to Vo if Vin is larger than Vmax?
The output cannot exceed the supply rail, so it saturates at about Vmax and the follower no longer tracks the input.

notes.t: Non-inverting amplifier: gain and linear region
pts: Feedback resistor \(R_{f}\) and \(R_{1}\) form a voltage divider in the feedback loop, which sets the closed-loop gain of the circuit.
The gain of a non-inverting op-amp is always at least 1, because the input signal is applied to the + terminal and the output is not inverted.
While the output has not reached the supply rail voltage (not saturated), the circuit operates in the linear region and the gain formula applies.
defs: Linear region
The operating range in which the op-amp output is not saturated, i.e. it has not reached the rail voltage, so the output is proportional to the input and the closed-loop gain formula holds.
Voltage divider (feedback)
The network of \(R_{f}\) and \(R_{1}\) that feeds back a fraction of the output voltage to the inverting input, setting the gain.
eqs: Closed-loop gain of a non-inverting amplifier
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistance (Ω); \(R_{1}\) = resistance to ground from the inverting input (Ω)
tips: Do not use the inverting formula \(V_{o}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) = -\(R_{f}\)/\(R_{1}\); the non-inverting gain has the leading 1 and no minus sign.
The gain formula is only valid in the linear region; check that \(V_{o}\) has not reached ±15 V before applying it.
rq: Why can the gain of a non-inverting amplifier never fall below 1, even if \(R_{f}\) is made very small?

With \(R_{f}\) = 0 the gain is 1 + 0/\(R_{1}\) = 1; \(R_{f}\) cannot be negative in practice, so the gain is minimum 1 (unity-gain follower). The '1' term comes from the input applied directly to the + terminal.
What happens to the output if \(V_{\text{in}}\) is increased until the output reaches the +15 V rail?
The output saturates at the rail voltage and leaves the linear region; the gain formula no longer predicts \(V_{o}\), which stays clipped at about 15 V.

notes.t: Operational amplifier gain boost of a filtered signal by 10 dB
pts: The non-inverting amplifier stage built earlier can be reused to raise the filtered signal level by 10 dB.
The filter (R and C) feeds the non-inverting (+) input, so the op-amp output follows the filtered source voltage scaled by the feedback network.
The gain is set by the feedback resistors \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) in the negative-feedback path to the inverting (-) input.
defs: Decibel gain
A voltage gain expressed in dB is 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of output to input voltage amplitude.
eqs: Voltage gain in dB required for a 10 dB boost
\(G_{dB}\) = gain in decibels (dB); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_s\) = input voltage (V)
\(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_s\) = input voltage (V); \(R_1\) = 100 Ω; \(R_2\) = 216 Ω
tips: Do not confuse dB with linear gain: 10 dB is not a gain of 10; convert using \(10^{G_{dB}/20}\).
Non-inverting configuration gain is \(1+R_2/R_1\), not \(-R_2/R_1\); the sign is positive because the signal enters the + input.
rq: Why does a 10 dB boost correspond to a linear voltage gain of about 3.16 rather than 10?
Because dB is logarithmic: 10 dB = 20 log₁₀(\(V_{o}\)/\(V_{s}\)), so \(V_{o}\)/\(V_{s}\) = 10^(10/20) ≈ 3.16.
Using \(R_{1}\) = 100 Ω and \(R_{2}\) = 216 Ω, does this amplifier give the required 10 dB boost?
Gain = 1 + 216/100 = 3.16, which equals 10 dB, so yes it matches the requirement.

notes.t: Cascaded Amplifier Gain and Decibels
pts: Overall voltage gain of cascaded stages is the product of individual stage gains.
Converting each stage gain to dB allows the total gain to be found by addition instead of multiplication.
A gain below 1 (attenuation) gives a negative dB value, e.g. 0.1 gives −20 dB.
The overall example gives a voltage ratio of 10, i.e. +20 dB, from 1 V in to 10 V out.
This analysis assumes loading between stages has been mitigated.
defs: Decibel (dB) voltage gain
A logarithmic measure of voltage ratio given by 20 log₁₀ of the ratio of output to input voltage.
eqs: Overall gain of cascaded stages (voltage ratio)

\(V_{\text{out}}\) = overall output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = overall input voltage (V); \(V_{out1}\), \(V_{in1}\) = output and input voltage of stage 1 (V); \(V_{out2}\), \(V_{in2}\) = output and input voltage of stage 2 (V)
R = voltage gain (dB); \(V_{\text{out}}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V)
Total dB gain of cascaded stages
\(R_{\text{total}}\) = overall gain (dB); \(R_{1}\) = gain of stage 1 (dB); \(R_{2}\) = gain of stage 2 (dB)
tips: Do not add raw voltage ratios; only add dB values, and convert each stage to dB first.
Remember the cascade formula assumes loading between stages has been mitigated; otherwise the simple product is not valid.
rq: Why can dB gains be added when voltage gains must be multiplied?
Because dB is a logarithm, and log(a × b) = log a + log b, so multiplying ratios becomes adding their dB values.
What happens to the dB value if a stage has a gain less than 1?
The dB value is negative, meaning the stage attenuates the signal rather than amplifies it.
Why does the example total of +20 dB correspond to a voltage ratio of 10?
Because 20 log₁₀(10) = 20 dB, so the dB value maps back to the voltage ratio 10.

notes.t: RC low-pass filter Bode magnitude plot
pts: A first-order RC low-pass filter passes low frequencies with 0 dB gain and attenuates high frequencies.
Above the corner frequency the gain falls off at roughly -20 dB per decade on a log frequency axis.
Adding a constant 10 dB gain shifts the whole magnitude curve up by 10 dB without changing its shape or corner frequency.
The magnitude is plotted in decibels, so the curve is flat at low frequency and sloped at high frequency.
defs: Corner (cut-off) frequency
The frequency at which the filter gain has dropped by 3 dB (about 0.707 of its passband value); it marks the transition from flat passband to roll-off.
tips: Decibel offsets add: a 10 dB gain shifts the curve by +10 dB, not by a multiplicative factor of 10 in the dB plot.
Remember the log frequency axis: the roll-off slope is quoted per decade, not per octave, and the -3 dB point is not the same as zero gain.
rq: Why does adding 10 dB gain move the whole curve up but leave the corner frequency unchanged?
A constant gain multiplies the transfer function by a fixed factor, which in dB is an additive offset; it does not change the pole location that sets the corner frequency.
What happens to the high-frequency slope if the filter were second-order instead of first-order?
The roll-off would double to about -40 dB per decade, since each RC stage contributes about -20 dB per decade.

notes.t: High-pass RC filter: transfer function and cut-off frequency
pts: A series capacitor blocks low frequencies, so the output across R follows high-frequency input.
The output is taken across the resistor R, shunted to ground, so \(V_{o}\) is the resistor voltage.
The gain tends to 1 as ω becomes much greater than ω_o, and to 0 as ω tends to 0.
The cut-off (corner) frequency is set by the product of R and C.
defs: High-pass filter
A filter that passes frequencies above a cut-off frequency and attenuates frequencies below it.
Cut-off frequency ω_o
The frequency at which the filter gain falls to 1/√2 (≈0.707) of its passband value, given by ω_o = 1/RC.
eqs: Transfer function of the high-pass RC filter
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage across R (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω_o = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); j = imaginary unit
ω_o = cut-off angular frequency (rad/s); R = resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
tips: Do not confuse the high-pass output (across R) with the low-pass configuration (across C); the output here is taken across the resistor.
Check units: ω_o in rad/s, so \(f_{c}\) = ω_o/2π in Hz; using RC directly gives angular, not ordinary, frequency.
rq: Why does the output go to zero at very low frequencies?
At low frequency the capacitor's reactance 1/(ωC) is very large, so almost all the input voltage drops across the capacitor and little reaches R.
What happens to the gain if ω is much larger than ω_o?
ω_o/(jω) becomes negligible, so \(V_{o}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) tends to 1: high frequencies pass unattenuated.

notes.t: High-pass RC filter with a load: is the transfer function still valid?
pts: The transfer function derived for the unloaded high-pass RC filter is only valid when no load is attached across the output.
The corner frequency is set by the R and C values, which define where the response transitions from blocking to passing.
Attaching \(R_{L}\) across the output changes the effective impedance seen by the filter, so the given expression must be re-examined rather than assumed.
defs: High-pass filter
A circuit that passes signals above a cut-off frequency and attenuates signals below it.
eqs: Voltage transfer function of the high-pass RC filter (unloaded)
\(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(\omega\) = angular frequency (rad/s); \(\omega_o\) = corner angular frequency (rad/s)
tips: Do not apply \(\omega_o = 1/RC\) blindly to a loaded filter; the true R seen by the capacitor is the parallel combination with \(R_L\).
Check the condition of validity: the standard transfer function assumes negligible output current, i.e. \(R_L\) very large.
rq: Why can't the expression \(V_o/V_{in}=1/(1+\omega_o/j\omega)\) be assumed unchanged when \(R_L\) is connected?
Because \(R_L\) draws current and loads the R–C network, altering the effective resistance and so the output voltage divider; the derivation assumed no output current.
What would you expect to happen to the corner frequency if \(R_L\) is much smaller than \(R\)?
The effective parallel resistance falls, so the apparent corner frequency shifts; the simple \(\omega_o=1/RC\) no longer gives the true cut-off.

notes.t: High-pass RC filter with a resistive load
pts: Adding a load resistor \(R_{L}\) in parallel with R lowers the effective resistance, so the total resistance \(R_{T}\) is less than R.
If \(R_{L}\) is very large, \(R_{T}\) is approximately R, so the load has negligible effect on the filter.
If \(R_{L}\) = R, then \(R_{T}\) = R/2, and the cutoff frequency doubles because ω_o is inversely proportional to \(R_{T}\).
The cutoff frequency depends on the parallel combination R//\(R_{L}\) and C, so loading changes the filter's response.
defs: Parallel resistance (R//\(R_{L}\))
The equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel, given by the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals, which is always smaller than either resistor alone.
eqs: Voltage transfer function of the high-pass filter
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); ω_o = cutoff angular frequency (rad/s); j = imaginary unit
ω_o = cutoff angular frequency (rad/s); \(R_{T}\) = equivalent parallel resistance (Ω); C = capacitance (F)
Equivalent resistance of two parallel resistors
\(R_{T}\) = equivalent resistance (Ω); R = resistor (Ω); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (Ω)
tips: Do not add resistances in parallel directly; use 1/\(R_{T}\) = 1/R + 1/\(R_{L}\), not \(R_{T}\) = R + \(R_{L}\).
Remember ω_o is angular frequency in rad/s; convert to \(f_{o}\) = ω_o/2π in Hz when asked for frequency in Hz.
rq: Why does connecting a load resistor change the cutoff frequency of a high-pass filter?
The load is in parallel with R, reducing the total resistance \(R_{T}\); since ω_o = 1/(\(R_{T}\) C), a smaller \(R_{T}\) gives a higher cutoff frequency.
What happens to the cutoff frequency if \(R_{L}\) is much larger than R, and why?
\(R_{T}\) ≈ R, so the cutoff frequency is essentially unchanged because the load draws very little current.

notes.t: Parallel resistors
pts: If one resistor is much larger than the other, the total resistance is approximately equal to the smaller resistor.
With \(R_{L}\) = 10 × R, the total resistance is about 91% of R, so the parallel combination barely changes R.
eqs: Total resistance of two resistors in parallel (reciprocal rule)
\(R_{T}\) = equivalent total resistance (\(\Omega\)); R = first resistor (\(\Omega\)); \(R_{L}\) = load resistor (\(\Omega\))
tips: Do not add parallel resistances directly; use the reciprocal formula \(1/R_T = 1/R + 1/R_L\) and invert at the end.
Watch units: keep R and \(R_{L}\) in the same units (e.g. kΩ) before combining, and give the final answer with the correct unit.
rq: Why does a very large \(R_{L}\) have almost no effect on the total resistance in parallel with R?
Because its conductance 1/\(R_{L}\) is tiny, so almost all current paths go through R and \(R_{T}\) ≈ R.
If R = 1 kΩ and \(R_{L}\) = 10 kΩ, what is \(R_{T}\) and why is it less than 1 kΩ?
\(R_{T}\) = 9.1 kΩ; adding a parallel path always lowers the total resistance below the smallest branch.

notes.t: Cascaded first-order RC filters and loading effects
pts: Cascading a high-pass RC stage with a low-pass RC stage gives a band-pass response, but only if the stages do not load each other.
Ideal separate-filter predictions overstate the passband: the actual band-pass peak is well below 0 dB, around -6 to -7 dB.
Significant loading of the second stage changes the first stage's frequency response, so the overall corner frequencies shift and the peak gain drops.
The -5 dB reference line shows that the real cascaded filter's gain may never reach the -5 dB level expected from naive design.
defs: Loading effect
The interaction between cascaded stages where the input impedance of the following stage draws current from the preceding stage, altering its transfer function.
Band-pass filter
A filter that passes frequencies within a band between a lower and upper cutoff while attenuating frequencies outside that band.
tips: Do not multiply the individual filter transfer functions of cascaded RC stages unless loading is negligible or a buffer isolates them.
The peak of the real band-pass response is below 0 dB; do not read the ideal separate-filter curves as the actual cascaded response.
rq: Why does the measured band-pass peak fall below the 0 dB level predicted from separate filters?

Because the low-pass stage loads the high-pass stage (its input impedance draws current from the high-pass output), so the stages no longer behave as independent ideal filters and the gain is reduced.
What would you do to make the cascaded response match the ideal product of the two separate responses?
Use a buffer (e.g. a voltage follower op-amp with very high input and low output impedance) between the stages, or make the second stage's impedance much larger than the first stage's.

notes.t: Preventing loading in cascaded RC filters (method 1)
pts: Cascading an RC high-pass stage directly into an RC low-pass stage causes loading, altering the response away from the ideal.
Inserting a series resistor R2 between the stages isolates the low-pass stage; a larger R2 brings the response closer to ideal.
On this course, R2 ≥ 10 × R1 is accepted as an adequate loading mitigation strategy.
With R2 = 10 × R1 the passband gain dips slightly below the ideal curve, while R2 = 100 × R1 essentially overlays the ideal response.
defs: Loading
The interaction between cascaded filter stages where the following stage draws current from the preceding stage, changing its transfer function from the value predicted for an isolated stage.
eqs: Loading mitigation condition for the isolating resistor
\(R_2\) = isolating series resistor (\(\Omega\)); \(R_1\) = high-pass shunt resistor (\(\Omega\))
tips: The 10× rule is a course-specific design guideline, not a universal law; state it as an acceptable mitigation rather than an exact requirement.
Remember that the gain curves are only close to ideal; with R2 = 10 × R1 there is still a small deviation in passband gain.
rq: Why does increasing R2 relative to R1 reduce loading between the stages?

A larger series resistor draws less current from the high-pass stage, so the low-pass stage's impedance has a smaller effect on the high-pass output and the cascade behaves more like the ideal product of the two transfer functions.
What would happen to the passband gain if R2 were made equal to R1?
Loading would be severe: the low-pass stage would load the high-pass output significantly, lowering and distorting the gain relative to the ideal curve.

notes.t: Preventing loading in cascaded filters using a voltage follower
pts: A voltage follower (unity-gain op-amp buffer) placed between filter stages isolates them so the second stage does not load the first.
An ideal op-amp's infinite input impedance draws no current from the first stage, so the first stage's R1 behaves as if unloaded.
The op-amp's zero output impedance means the full output voltage is delivered to the second filter stage regardless of its load.
defs: Voltage follower

An op-amp configured with the output fed back directly to the inverting input, giving a voltage gain of 1 with very high input impedance and very low output impedance; used as a buffer to isolate circuit stages.
Loading
The effect where a following stage draws current from a preceding stage, altering its voltage and frequency response; avoided by using a buffer with high input impedance.
tips: A voltage follower has unity gain, so it isolates stages but does not amplify the signal; do not expect any voltage gain from this buffer.
Real op-amps have finite input and non-zero output impedance, so the ideal assumptions only hold approximately; check the op-amp's datasheet values for accurate design.
rq: Why does the input impedance need to be much larger than \( 10 \times R_1 \) rather than just larger than \( R_1 \)?

Loading is negligible only when the load impedance is at least about ten times the source impedance; otherwise a noticeable fraction of the signal current and voltage is diverted and the filter response shifts.
What would happen to the cutoff frequency of the first stage if a non-buffered second stage were connected directly to it?

The second stage's resistor and capacitor would draw current from the first stage, changing its effective resistance and loading the filter so its cutoff frequency and gain no longer match the design values.

notes.t: Preventing loading in cascaded filters – method 1
pts: Loading between cascaded first-order RC filters can be reduced by making the second-stage resistance much larger than the first-stage resistance.
The approach is cheap and simple because it uses only passive components.
Isolation is not perfect: the actual corner frequencies differ from those of the individual first-order filters.
A large R2 may force an impractical capacitor value to set the second-stage cut-off, such as a tiny capacitance that is hard to control accurately.
eqs: Design rule to reduce loading between cascaded filter stages
\(R_{2}\) = resistor value in the second stage (\(\Omega\)); \(R_{1}\) = resistor value in the first stage (\(\Omega\))
tips: Even with R2 ≥ 10 × R1, the combined corner frequencies are not exactly those of the individual first-order filters, so the calculated cut-offs must be checked.
Check that the chosen R2 does not force an impractically small capacitor or large inductor for the second-stage cut-off.
rq: Why does making R2 large reduce loading of the first stage by the second stage?
A large second-stage resistance draws little current from the first stage, so the first stage's output is not significantly altered by the load it drives.
If R2 is made very large to avoid loading, what problem can arise when choosing the second-stage capacitor?
The cut-off frequency \(1/(2\pi R_2 C_2)\) forces \(C_{2}\) to be very small, which is impractical because tiny capacitances are hard to control accurately.

notes.t: Preventing loading in cascaded filters using a voltage follower
pts: A voltage follower (unity-gain buffer) placed between stages isolates them so each stage does not load the previous one.
With an ideal op-amp the isolation is perfect, so each stage can be designed independently.
Component values in each stage can be chosen freely because stages no longer interact.
The cost is that the op-amp is an active component requiring a power supply, adding complexity and cost.
defs: Voltage follower

An op-amp circuit with output fed directly back to the inverting input and the signal applied to the non-inverting input, giving a voltage gain of 1 with very high input impedance and very low output impedance.
tips: The voltage follower has gain exactly 1 (not zero or infinite); students often confuse it with an amplifier of non-unity gain.
The perfect isolation holds only for an ideal op-amp; real op-amps have finite input impedance and non-zero output impedance, and limited bandwidth.
rq: Why does a voltage follower prevent loading between two filter stages?
Its very high input impedance draws almost no current from the previous stage, and its very low output impedance drives the next stage without its load affecting the earlier stage.
What trade-off makes this method less attractive than a passive solution for a simple low-cost design?
It needs an active device with a power supply, which adds complexity, power consumption and cost compared with a purely passive network.

notes.t: Cascaded RC filters and first-order approximation
pts: Cascading a high pass and a low pass RC stage technically gives a higher-order filter.
If loading effects are designed out, the cascade can be treated as two separate first-order filters.
Each stage's cut-off (corner) frequency can be designed separately as a good-enough approximation.
defs: Loading effect
The interaction between cascaded stages where the second stage draws current from or changes the impedance seen by the first, altering its transfer function.
Higher-order filter
A filter whose transfer function has a denominator polynomial of degree greater than one, such as that produced by cascading first-order stages without loading effects being neglected.
eqs: Corner (cut-off) frequency of an RC first-order stage
tips: Treating the stages as independent is only valid when loading effects are designed out; otherwise the overall cut-off is not simply the product of the individual stage responses.
Keep corner frequency units consistent: R in ohms and C in farads give f in hertz only with the factor 2π.
rq: Why does cascading two RC stages not simply give the product of their individual transfer functions?
Because loading: the second stage's input impedance draws current from the first, changing its behaviour, so the stages interact unless designed to minimise this.
What design rule lets you treat the cascade as two independent first-order filters?
Make the second stage's input impedance much larger than the first stage's output impedance, so loading is negligible.

notes.t: Designing an RC bandpass filter from separate high-pass and low-pass first-order stages
pts: A bandpass is built by cascading an RC high-pass stage (sets the lower corner) with an RC low-pass stage (sets the upper corner).
Each stage's -3 dB corner is set independently by its own RC product, so the two stages can be designed separately.
Separate first-order approximations are only valid if loading is mitigated, e.g. R2 ≥ 10 × R1 or by a voltage follower.
The high-pass stage uses C1 in series with the input and R1 to ground; the low-pass stage uses R2 in series with C2 to ground.
defs: Bandpass filter
A filter that passes frequencies between a lower and an upper cut-off frequency while attenuating frequencies outside this band.
-3 dB cut-off frequency
The frequency at which the output power falls to half its passband value, i.e. the gain drops by 3 dB (about 0.707 of the passband voltage gain).
Loading

The effect on one filter stage's transfer function when it drives or is driven by the next stage; it is avoided by making the following stage's impedance much larger (≥10×) or by buffering with a voltage follower.
eqs: Lower -3 dB corner of the high-pass stage (C1 with R1)
\(\omega_{c1}\) = high-pass corner angular frequency (rad/s); \(R_1\) = shunt resistor (Ω); \(C_1\) = series capacitor (F)
Upper -3 dB corner of the low-pass stage (R2 with C2)
\(\omega_{c2}\) = low-pass corner angular frequency (rad/s); \(R_2\) = series resistor (Ω); \(C_2\) = shunt capacitor (F)
tips: Convert kHz to angular frequency: the formulas use \(\omega = 2\pi f\), so 1.2 kHz gives \(2\pi \times 1200\) rad/s; forgetting the 2π or mixing Hz and rad/s is a common error.
Only use the simple 1/(RC) corner formulas when loading is mitigated; ignoring loading gives incorrect cut-off frequencies.
rq: Why must R2 be at least 10 times R1 (or a voltage follower used) before you can design the two stages independently?
Otherwise the low-pass stage's resistor R2 loads the high-pass node, changing the high-pass corner so the simple 1/(RC) formulas no longer give the true -3 dB frequencies.
If you increase C2 while keeping R2 fixed, what happens to the upper cut-off and why?
The upper cut-off \(\omega_{c2}=1/(R_2C_2)\) decreases, so the passband narrows from the top because the low-pass stage rolls off at a lower frequency.
What determines the bandwidth of this bandpass?
The difference between the two corners, \(2\pi(2.4-1.2)\) kHz, set by the two independent RC products.

notes.t: High-pass and low-pass filter attenuation at each other's cut-off frequency
pts: Each filter attenuates frequencies between its cut-off and the pass band, so the -3 dB point of one filter lies in the other's transition region.
At the cut-off frequency of the high-pass (1.2 kHz) the low-pass gain is only about -1 dB, while at the low-pass cut-off (2.4 kHz) the high-pass gain is about -1 dB.
The mutual attenuation is a property of the filter response shape, not a loading effect between stages.
defs: Cut-off frequency (-3 dB point)
The frequency at which the output gain of a filter has fallen to about -3 dB (half power, about 0.707 of the passband voltage gain).
tips: Do not assume a filter passes everything below or above its cut-off; the roll-off means partial attenuation near the cut-off of the other filter.
Cascaded attenuations add in dB, so combined gain is the sum of the individual dB values, not a simple -3 dB.
rq: Why does a low-pass filter with a 2.4 kHz cut-off still reduce a 1.2 kHz signal, even though 1.2 kHz is below its cut-off?
Its gain falls gradually; the transition region lies below the -3 dB point, so at 1.2 kHz the low-pass gain is only about -1 dB, not zero attenuation.
If the two filters were cascaded with cut-offs at 1.2 kHz and 2.4 kHz, what would you expect to see at 2.4 kHz in the combined response?
The high-pass contributes about -1 dB at 2.4 kHz and the low-pass contributes -3 dB there, so the combined attenuation is roughly -4 dB, not simply -3 dB.

notes.t: Combined ideal band-pass filter: loading and cut-off approximation
pts: Two first-order filter stages are isolated, so their gains in dB simply add.
Each stage's attenuation at the other stage's cut-off adds extra attenuation, beyond the nominal -3 dB at each cut-off.
This extra attenuation is larger when the two cut-off frequencies are closer together, and shrinks as they are moved further apart.
At either nominal cut-off the total gain is about -3.98 dB, not -3.01 dB, even with zero loading.
Strictly, the combined filter passes nothing with less than 3 dB attenuation, but the first-order cut-off approximation was permitted by the question, so the approach is valid.
eqs: Combined gain of two isolated stages in dB
\(G_{\text{total}}\) = overall gain (dB); \(G_{1}\), \(G_{2}\) = gains of stage 1 and stage 2 (dB)
tips: Do not assume the -3 dB points of a combined band-pass are at the nominal cut-offs; the stages interact and add attenuation.
Remember that the first-order cut-off approximation is only valid because the question permits it; strictly the combined filter gives less than -3 dB at each nominal cut-off.
rq: Why does the attenuation at each cut-off get worse when the two cut-off frequencies are close together?
Each stage's roll-off reaches the other stage's cut-off frequency while still significant, so each stage adds extra attenuation there; when cut-offs are close, this overlap is greater.
What if the cut-off frequencies are moved far apart?
The extra attenuation from each stage at the other's cut-off becomes small, so the gain at each cut-off approaches the nominal -3 dB.

notes.t: Adding gain to everything (non-inverting amplifier stage)
pts: The filter output drives the non-inverting (+) input, so the signal passes through unchanged in polarity and gain is set by the feedback resistor network.
R1 connects the inverting (-) input to ground, and R2 feeds the output back to the inverting input, forming negative feedback.
The filtered signal is amplified as a whole, so filter and gain stage are cascaded blocks.
eqs: Closed-loop voltage gain of the non-inverting amplifier stage
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = filter output voltage applied to + input (V); \(R_{1}\) = resistor from inverting input to ground (\Omega); \(R_{2}\) = feedback resistor (\Omega)
tips: Do not use the inverting-amplifier gain \(-\frac{R_2}{R_1}\); here the sign is positive because the signal enters the + input.
Assumes an ideal op-amp (infinite gain, no current into inputs) and that the output does not saturate; check the supply rail limits.
rq: Why does the gain depend only on \(R_{2}\) and \(R_{1}\) and not on the op-amp's open-loop gain?

With negative feedback and a very large open-loop gain, the op-amp drives the inverting input to virtually the same voltage as the non-inverting input, so the feedback ratio sets the closed-loop gain.
What would happen to the gain if \(R_{2}\) were shorted to ground instead of connected to the output?
The gain would become 1 (voltage follower-like behaviour is lost); with \(R_{2}\) = 0 the formula gives \(V_{o}\) = \(V_{in}\), i.e. unity gain.

notes.t: Inverting op-amp: virtual earth and ideal op-amp assumptions
pts: The non-inverting (+) input is connected to 0 V (ground), so V+ = 0.
The very high open-loop gain forces the two inputs to be equal, so V- is also 0 V; the inverting node is a 'virtual earth'.
The large input impedance means no current flows into the inverting input, so all of the input current passes through R2.
defs: Virtual earth
A node held at 0 V by negative feedback, even though it is not physically connected to ground; the op-amp's inputs are at equal potential and no current enters the inputs.
eqs: Closed-loop voltage gain of the inverting amplifier (from current through R1 equal to current through R2)
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{1}\) = input resistor (Ω); \(R_{2}\) = feedback resistor (Ω)
tips: Do not confuse the virtual earth with a real ground connection: the inverting node is at 0 V only because of feedback and high gain, and it can be checked with the ideal assumptions.
The gain \( -R_2/R_1 \) is only valid under the ideal assumptions (infinite gain, infinite input impedance) and while the op-amp is operating linearly, not saturated.
rq: Why does the inverting input sit at 0 V even though it is not connected to ground?
Because the op-amp's very high gain with negative feedback forces V- to equal V+ = 0 V, creating a virtual earth.
What would happen to the current through R1 if the op-amp did draw current into its inverting input?

The current through R1 would split between R2 and the amp input, so the ratio \(V_{o}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) would no longer be simply -R2/R1; the zero-input-current assumption is what makes all of \(I_{\text{in}}\) flow through R2.

notes.t: Inverting op-amp: current through R1 (virtual earth)
pts: The inverting input is at virtual earth, so its voltage is 0 V (the non-inverting input is grounded).
Current through R1 is found from the voltage across it, which is \(V_{\text{in}}\) minus the node-1 voltage (0 V).
Because the op-amp input draws no current, the current through R1 must flow through R2 instead.
defs: Virtual earth
A node in an op-amp circuit held at 0 V by negative feedback without being physically connected to ground, because the inverting input is at the same potential as the grounded non-inverting input.
eqs: \(I_{1}\) = current through \(R_{1}\) (A); \(V_{\text{in}}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{1}\) = input resistor (Ω); 0 = voltage at node 1 (virtual earth) (V)
tips: Do not treat node 1 as physically grounded; the 0 V comes from virtual earth, so the voltage across \(R_{1}\) is \(V_{\text{in}}\) − 0 = \(V_{\text{in}}\).
Keep units consistent: V in volts and R in ohms gives I in amps; watch for kΩ and mA conversions.
rq: Why can we replace the voltage at node 1 with 0 V even though it is not connected to ground?
Negative feedback forces the inverting input to the same potential as the grounded non-inverting input (virtual earth), and the op-amp draws no input current.
If the op-amp input draws no current, where does the current \(I_{1}\) go?
It flows entirely through \(R_{2}\) to the output, so \(I_{2}\) = \(I_{1}\).

notes.t: Operational amplifier: current through feedback resistor R2
pts: Node 1 is the inverting input; with ideal op-amp behaviour its voltage is held at the non-inverting node voltage (0 V), so the current through R2 is set by the output voltage across R2.
The current through R2 is found from the voltage difference across it, between node 1 (at 0 V) and the output \(V_{o}\).
eqs: Current flowing through feedback resistor \(R_{2}\) (from node 1 to output)
\(I_2\) = current through \(R_{2}\) (A); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(R_2\) = feedback resistance (\(\Omega\))
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: the direction of \(I_2\) must match the voltage difference used (0 − \(V_{o}\)), otherwise the output sign will be wrong.
Remember the virtual-earth assumption (node 1 ≈ 0 V) only holds under negative feedback with an ideal op-amp.
rq: Why can node 1 be taken as 0 V even though it is not connected to ground?
With an ideal op-amp (high gain, negative feedback), the inverting input is forced to the same voltage as the non-inverting input, which is grounded at 0 V (a virtual earth).
Why is the current through \(R_{2}\) written with a voltage difference of (0 − \(V_{o}\)) rather than (\(V_{o}\) − 0)?

Current is defined as flowing from node 1 to the output; the voltage drop across \(R_{2}\) goes from 0 V at node 1 to \(V_{o}\) at the output, so the sign convention gives \(I_{2}\) = (0 − \(V_{o}\))/\(R_{2}\) in this direction.

notes.t: Inverting operational amplifier: current balance at node 1
pts: No current flows into the op-amp inputs, so the current through R1 must equal the current through R2.
Applying Kirchhoff's current law at the inverting input (node 1) gives the closed-loop relationship between output and input voltage.
Node 1 is held at virtual ground (0 V) because the non-inverting input is at 0 V, so both resistor voltage drops are measured relative to 0.
defs: Virtual earth (virtual ground)

A node in a negative-feedback op-amp circuit that is held at 0 V without being directly connected to ground, because the op-amp drives its inverting input to the same potential as the grounded non-inverting input.
eqs: Current balance at the inverting input (gives closed-loop gain)
\(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(R_1\) = input resistor (\(\Omega\)); \(R_2\) = feedback resistor (\(\Omega\))
tips: The sign matters: the current balance uses \(0 - V_o\) for R2, so the closed-loop gain \(V_o/V_{in} = -R_2/R_1\) is negative.
Only valid under ideal op-amp assumptions (infinite input impedance, negative feedback so node 1 is at virtual earth); check negative feedback exists before using this equation.
rq: Why can we set the voltage at node 1 to 0 V even though it is not physically connected to ground?
The op-amp has high gain and negative feedback through R2, so it drives the inverting input to the same voltage as the non-inverting input, which is grounded (0 V). This is the virtual earth.
Why does the current in R1 have to equal the current in R2?
The op-amp draws no current into its inputs, so all current from \(V_{\text{in}}\) through R1 must continue through R2 to the output.

notes.t: Inverting Operational Amplifier: Voltage Gain
pts: No current flows into the op-amp inputs, so the current through R1 equals the current through R2.
The inverting input is a virtual earth at the same potential as the non-inverting input (node 2, grounded), so the input current is set by \(V_{\text{in}}\) across R1.
The output is the input scaled by the ratio of feedback to input resistance and inverted in sign (phase shift of 180°).
defs: Inverting amplifier

An op-amp circuit where the input signal is applied to the inverting (−) terminal through R1 and negative feedback is applied through R2, giving an output that is the inverted, scaled version of the input.
eqs: Current balance at the inverting node (input current = feedback current)
\(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(R_1\) = input resistor (Ω); \(R_2\) = feedback resistor (Ω)
Closed-loop voltage gain of the inverting amplifier
\(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_2\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_1\) = input resistor (Ω); gain is dimensionless
tips: The minus sign means a 180° phase inversion; forgetting it gives the wrong polarity of \(V_o\).
Only use this formula when the op-amp is in negative feedback with ideal assumptions (no input current, equal input voltages).
rq: Why does the gain depend only on resistor ratio and not on the op-amp's internal gain?
With negative feedback and a very large open-loop gain, the op-amp keeps the inputs at the same potential and draws no current, so the closed-loop gain is set by the external resistors R2/R1.
What would happen to the output if R2 were doubled while \(V_{\text{in}}\) and R1 stayed the same?
The gain magnitude doubles, so \(V_o\) doubles in magnitude and remains inverted in sign.

notes.t: Inverting operational amplifier
pts: The voltage gain of the circuit depends only on the ratio of the resistors around the op amp.
Input is applied to the inverting (-) terminal through R1, with R2 feeding back from the output, so the output is 180° out of phase with the input.
The non-inverting (+) input is connected to ground (0 V), so the amplifier is an inverting amplifier.
defs: Inverting amplifier

An op-amp configuration where the input signal is applied to the inverting terminal via a resistor and the output is fed back to the same terminal, producing an output voltage that is negative (phase-inverted) relative to the input, with gain set by resistor ratio.
eqs: Closed-loop voltage gain of the inverting amplifier
\(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_1\) = input resistor (Ω); \(R_2\) = feedback resistor (Ω)
tips: Do not forget the minus sign: the gain of an inverting amplifier is negative, so \(V_o\) and \(V_{in}\) have opposite polarity.
Make sure you identify the feedback resistor correctly: \(R_2\) goes from output to the inverting node, and \(R_1\) is the input resistor, so the ratio is \(R_2/R_1\), not \(R_1/R_2\).
rq: Why does the negative sign in the gain expression mean the output is inverted?
The gain \(-R_2/R_1\) is negative, so for a positive input the output is negative and vice versa; the signal is shifted by 180° in phase.
What would happen to the gain if R2 were made larger than R1?
The magnitude of the gain \(R_2/R_1\) would exceed 1, so the output amplitude is larger than the input, while remaining inverted.

notes.t: Non-inverting and inverting op-amp amplifiers with negative feedback
pts: Negative feedback forces the two op-amp inputs to be equal, so the inverting input follows the input signal (non-inverting case) or sits at ground (inverting case).
In the non-inverting amplifier the input is applied to the + terminal and the output is fed back via \(R_f\) to the − terminal, so \(V_- = V_+ = V_{in}\).
In the inverting amplifier the input drives \(R_1\) into the − terminal while the + terminal is grounded, creating a virtual ground at the − input (\(V_- = V_+ = 0\)).
The non-inverting gain is always at least 1 and has the same sign as the input; the inverting gain is negative (phase reversed).
defs: Virtual ground

A point in an op-amp circuit held at 0 V by negative feedback, even though it is not physically connected to ground; the inverting input of an inverting amplifier is a virtual ground because \(V_- = V_+ = 0\).
Negative feedback
Connecting the output back to the inverting (−) input so that the op-amp drives its inputs toward equality, which makes \(V_- = V_+\) in a linear circuit.
Non-inverting amplifier
An op-amp configuration where the input is applied to the + terminal; the output has the same polarity as the input and gain \(1 + R_f/R_1\).
Inverting amplifier
An op-amp configuration where the input is applied through \(R_1\) to the − terminal; the output is inverted with gain \(-R_f/R_1\).
eqs: Closed-loop voltage gain of the non-inverting amplifier
\(A_v\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_f\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_1\) = resistor to ground from the − input (Ω)
Closed-loop voltage gain of the inverting amplifier
\(A_v\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_f\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_1\) = input resistor (Ω)
tips: Watch the sign: the inverting amplifier gain is negative, the non-inverting gain is positive and at least 1.
Virtual ground (\(V_- = 0\)) is not a real connection to 0 V; do not confuse it with the grounded + terminal, and only use these formulas when negative feedback is present.
rq: Why does the inverting amplifier's gain depend only on resistor ratio and not on the op-amp's open-loop gain?

Negative feedback makes the closed-loop gain set by external resistors; with a very large open-loop gain, the input difference is driven to nearly zero, so the currents through \(R_1\) and \(R_f\) determine \(V_o/V_{in}\).
What would happen to the inverting amplifier's gain if the + terminal were not grounded?
The virtual-ground condition \(V_- = V_+ = 0\) would no longer hold, so the simple formula \(-R_f/R_1\) would not apply; the circuit would behave differently.
Why can the non-inverting gain never be less than 1?
Because \(R_f\) and \(R_1\) are positive, \(1 + R_f/R_1 \ge 1\); the output always follows the input with at least unity gain.

notes.t: Connecting source circuits to op-amp amplifiers: effect of source resistance
pts: In a non-inverting amplifier, no current flows into V+, so \(R_{\text{TH}}\) has no influence on gain for an ideal op-amp.
In an inverting amplifier, the source resistance \(R_{\text{TH}}\) is in series with \(R_{1}\) and so adds to the input resistance, changing the gain.
Current flowing to the virtual ground changes because of \(R_{\text{TH}}\), so the effective input resistor becomes \(R_{1}\) + \(R_{\text{TH}}\).
