The non-inverting gain is unchanged by \(R_{\text{TH}}\) because the input draws no current, whereas the inverting gain is reduced in magnitude.
defs: Virtual ground
The inverting input of an ideal op-amp in negative feedback, held at the same potential as the non-inverting input (ground) while drawing no current.
eqs: \(A_{v}\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_{1}\) = resistor to ground (Ω)
\(A_{v}\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_{1}\) = input resistor (Ω)
Modified inverting amplifier voltage gain with source resistance

\(A_{v}\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(R_{1}\) = input resistor (Ω); \(R_{th}\) = source Thévenin resistance (Ω)
tips: Only add \(R_{\text{TH}}\) to \(R_{1}\) for the inverting configuration; the non-inverting gain stays 1 + \(R_{f}\)/\(R_{1}\) regardless of source resistance.
Remember the gain is negative for the inverting amplifier; dropping the minus sign when substituting \(R_{1}\) + \(R_{\text{th}}\) is a common error.
rq: Why does \(R_{\text{TH}}\) affect the inverting amplifier but not the non-inverting one?

In the inverting circuit \(R_{\text{TH}}\) sits in series with \(R_{1}\) carrying the input current into the virtual ground, whereas in the non-inverting circuit the ideal op-amp draws no current into V+, so \(R_{\text{TH}}\) carries no current and has no effect.
What happens to the magnitude of the inverting gain if \(R_{\text{TH}}\) is large compared with \(R_{1}\)?
The denominator \(R_{1}\) + \(R_{\text{th}}\) grows, so the gain magnitude falls, approaching zero as \(R_{\text{th}}\) becomes very large.

notes.t: Summing amplifier
pts: Inverting op-amp with virtual earth at the negative input (0 V), so each input current equals its input voltage divided by its resistor.
All input currents flow through the feedback resistor, so the feedback current equals the sum of the input currents.
The output is the negative weighted sum of the inputs; each input is weighted by \(R_{F}\) divided by its own resistor.
defs: Virtual earth
The inverting input of an ideal op-amp held at 0 V (through negative feedback) without being physically connected to ground, so input currents can be found directly from input voltages and resistors.
eqs: \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(V_1, V_2, V_3\) = input voltages (V); \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) = input resistors (Ω); \(R_F\) = feedback resistor (Ω)
Input current through each input resistor
\(I_n\) = input current (A); \(V_n\) = input voltage (V); \(R_n\) = input resistor (Ω)
\(I_F\) = feedback current (A); \(V_o\) = output voltage (V); \(R_F\) = feedback resistor (Ω)
tips: Keep the minus sign: the summing amplifier is inverting, so the output is the negative of the weighted sum.
Ensure all resistances are in consistent units (Ω) and do not confuse the feedback resistor \(R_F\) with the input resistors when weighting each term.
rq: Why can the input currents be calculated as \(V_{n}\)/\(R_{n}\) even though the inverting input is not connected to ground?
Negative feedback holds the inverting input at virtual earth (0 V), so each input resistor sees a voltage drop of \(V_{n}\) across it.
What would happen to the output if all three inputs were made equal to 1 V with \(R_{1}\) = \(R_{2}\) = \(R_{3}\) = \(R_{F}\)?
Each input contributes -1 V, so \(V_{o}\) = -3 V: the output is the negative sum of the inputs.

notes.t: Summing amplifier
pts: An inverting op-amp with several input resistors sums the input voltages, with the output being a weighted, inverted sum.
The inverting input is a virtual earth, so each input current is set by its own input voltage and resistor.
All input currents flow through the feedback resistor \(R_{F}\), giving the output voltage.
With equal input resistors, the output is the negative scaled sum of the inputs.
eqs: Output voltage of a summing amplifier with three inputs
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{1}\), \(V_{2}\), \(V_{3}\) = input voltages (V); \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) = input resistors (\Omega); \(R_{F}\) = feedback resistor (\Omega)
Output voltage with equal input resistors
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{1}\), \(V_{2}\), \(V_{3}\) = input voltages (V); R = common input resistance (\Omega); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistance (\Omega)
tips: The output is negative (inverted); forgetting the minus sign is a common error.
Only with equal input resistors does the gain ratio \(R_{f}\)/R apply uniformly to every input; with unequal resistors each input has its own weight \(R_{f}\)/\(R_{i}\).
rq: Why is the inverting input called a virtual earth, and why does this let each input current be found as V/R?
The op-amp's high gain drives the inverting input to nearly 0 V (the + input is grounded), so each input resistor sees its input voltage across it with the other end at 0 V, giving I = V/R.
What happens to the output if \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\) and \(R_{3}\) are not equal?
Each input is weighted by 1/\(R_{i}\), so the output becomes a weighted sum of the inputs rather than a plain sum; the equal-resistor formula no longer applies.

notes.t: Mixing multiple audio sources
pts: Multiple microphones are mixed by feeding each through its own preamp, then into a common mixer amplifier.
Each channel has a volume pot (R1–R5) that sets how much of that source reaches the mixer.
Capacitors C1–C5 block DC offsets so only the audio signal passes to the mixer input.
The mixer amplifier sums the channels; its feedback resistor Rf sets the closed-loop gain.
The mixed output drives a power amplifier (U7) that feeds the loudspeaker SPK1.
defs: Mixer amplifier
An op-amp summing amplifier that adds several input signals together into one output, with gain set by feedback resistor Rf.
Preamplifier
A low-gain amplifier placed directly after a microphone to boost its weak signal before mixing or further processing.
eqs: Closed-loop gain of inverting summing mixer (output for N inputs)
\(V_{out}\) = output voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (Ω); \(V_{i}\) = input voltage of channel i (V); \(R_{i}\) = input resistor of channel i (Ω)
tips: Remember the inverting summing amplifier gives a negative sign; each channel's gain is \( -R_f/R_i \), not simply \( R_i/R_f \).
Coupling capacitors form high-pass filters with input resistances; check the cutoff \( f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) \) so low bass frequencies are not lost.
rq: Why are coupling capacitors (C1–C5) placed in series with each channel before the mixer?
They block DC offsets from the preamps so only the AC audio signal is summed, preventing bias voltages from interfering with the mix.
What would happen to the mix if one channel's input resistor were made much smaller?
That channel would contribute a larger share of the output, since the gain for input i is inversely proportional to \(R_{i}\).

notes.t: Common question forms for op-amp gain design
pts: A gain specified in dB must first be converted to a linear voltage gain before choosing resistors.
Whether the amplifier is inverting or non-inverting determines which gain formula to use.
After finding the required gain, select resistor values that achieve it.
Check whether the output is limited by rail/supply voltages (saturation); this can be ignored if the question states the amplifier is in the linear operating region.
If rail voltages are not given, assume saturation will not occur.
eqs: Voltage gain of a non-inverting op-amp amplifier

\(A_{v}\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (\Omega); \(R_{1}\) = resistor from inverting input to ground (\Omega)
Voltage gain of an inverting op-amp amplifier
\(A_{v}\) = voltage gain (dimensionless); \(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{in}\) = input voltage (V); \(R_{f}\) = feedback resistor (\Omega); \(R_{1}\) = input resistor (\Omega)
tips: Using the inverting formula for a non-inverting circuit (or vice versa) gives the wrong sign or wrong gain; check the circuit configuration first.
Forgetting the 20 in the dB conversion (using dB/10 or dB directly) gives a badly wrong voltage gain.
rq: Why must a dB gain be converted to a linear voltage gain before using these formulas?
The formulas give the ratio \(V_{o}\)/\(V_{\text{in}}\) as a plain number, whereas dB is a logarithmic scale; use \(A_{v}\) = 10^(dB/20) for voltage gain.
What would happen to the output if you chose gain that requires a larger output than the rail voltage allows?
The op-amp saturates, so the output clips at the rail voltage and the ideal gain formula no longer applies.
How can you tell from the gain formula alone whether the output is in phase or out of phase with the input?
The non-inverting formula gives a positive gain (in phase); the inverting formula has a minus sign (180° out of phase).

notes.t: Summary of Analogue Electronics Lecture 7: Op-amps, Loading and Filters
pts: Ideal op-amp and open-loop vs closed-loop gain were recapped
Cascading passive first-order filters causes loading effects between stages
Loading is mitigated by making the next stage's resistance much larger (R2 ≥ 10·R1) or by isolating stages with voltage followers/buffers
Gain can be added to cascaded filters to create a bandpass configuration
Inverting amplifiers were introduced and contrasted with non-inverting amplifiers
tips: Do not ignore loading: cascaded RC stages do not simply multiply their individual transfer functions unless loading is accounted for or isolated.
Remember that an inverting amplifier introduces a 180° phase inversion, whereas a non-inverting amplifier does not.
rq: Why does the rule R2 ≥ 10·R1 reduce loading between cascaded filter stages?
A much larger input resistance of the following stage draws only a small current from the preceding stage, so the preceding stage's transfer function is barely altered.
What is the trade-off of using a voltage follower to isolate filter stages instead of a purely resistive design?
The buffer removes loading and gives isolation, but it adds cost, complexity and power consumption, and has its own limitations (e.g., finite bandwidth and supply constraints).

xq.q: An op-amp has open loop gain \(A = 2\times10^{5}\) and is powered from ±15 V supplies. It has no feedback, so \(V_o = A(V_+ - V_-)\) up to the supply limits. The inverting input is held at \(V_- = 2.000\) V and the non-inverting input is at \(V_+ = 2.050\) mV above this, i.e. \(V_+ = 2.00005\) V. Calculate the output voltage \(V_o\).
s: 10 V is within ±15 V so no clipping

xq.q: An op-amp with open loop gain \(A = 10^{5}\) and ±15 V supplies has no feedback. The non-inverting input is at \(V_+ = 1.00\) V and the inverting input is at \(V_- = 1.01\) V. What is the output voltage?
o: 0 V
xq.w: \(V_{\text{in}}\) = V+ − V- = −10 mV, and A·\(V_{\text{in}}\) = −1000 V far exceeds the supply, so the output saturates at −15 V; the traps are quoting the unclipped value, swapping the inputs, or applying a virtual short without feedback.

xq.q: An op-amp circuit uses negative feedback. Explain how the two golden rules (the virtual short and zero input current) arise from the ideal op-amp properties, and explain why the virtual short cannot be used when the op-amp is in open loop. Include in your answer the reason why an open loop op-amp with a 10 mV input saturates.
xq.a: With open loop gain A about \(10^{5}\) to \(10^{6}\), \(V_{o}\) = A(V+ − V-) is finite only if V+ − V- is tiny. Negative feedback adjusts the output so the difference is driven to zero, giving V- = V+ (virtual short). The infinite input impedance means no current enters the inputs. In open loop there is no feedback to correct the difference, so V+ and V- can differ; a 10 mV input times a gain of \(10^{5}\) gives 1000 V, far beyond the ±15 V rails, so the output saturates.
s: High gain means the differential input must be nearly zero for finite output
Negative feedback forces V- = V+ (virtual short)
Infinite input impedance gives zero input current
Without feedback nothing forces the inputs equal, so rule fails
A×10 mV exceeds supply so output clips at the rail

units.name: 1.1 Course introduction, presenter and administration
units.ov: This material is an administrative introduction to Analogue Electronics 1 (ENG1003). It covers the course aims (DC analysis, then AC analysis with complex impedance, filters and ideal op-amps), why the course matters as a prerequisite for later electronics modules, and the four-part assessment. The notes contain almost no technical content, so top marks depend on knowing the course structure and assessment rules precisely and on recognising the technical topics the course will examine later.
must: Assessment is four components of 25% each: continuous assessment, labs, online midterm theory exam, and December design exam.
All four components must be attempted to receive course credit; missing any one means no credit, however high the other marks.
Continuous assessment (25%) is lecture questions plus online quizzes, and all of them must be completed to pass.
Labs (25%) are the component simulation lab (10%) and the filter circuits and design lab (15%); attendance is mandatory.
Lab deadlines differ: simulation lab due 1 week after the session, filter circuits lab 2 weeks after.
The midterm is online, 90 minutes, with randomised questions on fundamental theory; cheating is reported to the school.
The December design exam has two circuit-design questions and can draw on any course content, including midterm concepts.
DC outcomes: electrical quantities, Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws, nodal analysis, Norton and Thevenin theorems (non-time-varying sources).
AC outcomes: complex impedance (\(Z\) combines resistance and reactance, complex-valued), low and high pass filters, and ideal op-amp voltage gain.

Ideal op-amp gain results are valid only under the ideal assumptions. Analogue Electronics 1 is a prerequisite for Analogue Electronics 2, Power Electronics 2, Embedded Processors 2 and ENG3034 Instrumentation and Data Systems 3, depending on the degree programme.
conn: DC methods (Ohm, Kirchhoff, nodal analysis, Thevenin/Norton) carry over to AC analysis once resistance is replaced by complex impedance \(Z\).
Complex impedance of R, L and C underpins the filter labs, so filter design questions combine impedance with frequency response.
Midterm theory topics (DC fundamentals) can reappear in the December design exam, so design questions need theory to justify component choices.
Lectures 2 and 3 (Wheatstone bridge and sensing) apply circuit laws and link to ENG3034 Instrumentation and Data Systems 3.
exq: State the four assessment components, their weightings, and the consequence of not attempting one of them.
Explain the difference between impedance and resistance, and say why inductors and capacitors behave differently in DC and AC analysis.
List the DC analysis techniques covered in the course and state which type of source they assume.
A student gets 90% on the midterm, labs and exam but skips the online quizzes. Do they receive course credit? Justify your answer using the assessment rules.
Explain what is assumed in an ideal op-amp voltage gain calculation and why the result is only valid within that idealisation.

notes.t: Presenter background and research context (UofG)
pts: Presenter holds an MEng in EEE from the University of Glasgow.
Presenter completed a PhD on silicon photonic devices.
Presenter is developing chip-scale atomic devices for the UK Quantum Enabled Position, Navigation and Timing Hub, part of the UK NQTP.
tips: This slide is not from DC circuits lecture notes; check that the correct file or page was attached before studying from it.

notes.t: Analogue Electronics 1 (ENG1003) course overview and intended learning outcomes
pts: The course teaches analysis of networks of resistors, inductors and capacitors under both direct and alternating voltages and currents.
DC outcomes cover fundamental electrical quantities, Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, nodal analysis, and Norton's and Thevenin's theorems.
AC outcomes cover complex impedance representation, low and high pass filters, and ideal op-amp voltage gain.
tips: Do not confuse the DC outcomes (non-time-varying sources) with the AC outcomes (complex impedance), since inductors and capacitors behave differently in each case.
Ideal op-amp gain calculations assume ideal properties, so results are only valid within that idealisation.
rq: Why does the course treat Thevenin's and Norton's theorems as tools for simplification rather than new physics?

They are equivalent ways of replacing a complicated linear network, seen from two terminals, with a simple source plus resistance, which makes later analysis far easier without changing the terminal behaviour.
Why is complex impedance needed to analyse AC networks instead of plain resistance?
Inductors and capacitors make current and voltage vary in time with phase differences, so their opposition to current depends on frequency and must be represented as a complex quantity.

notes.t: Why Analogue Electronics Is Relevant
pts: Analogue Electronics 1 is a prerequisite for several second-year courses, including Analogue Electronics 2, Power Electronics 2 and Embedded Processors 2.
Analogue Electronics 1 is also a prerequisite for the third-year course Instrumentation and Data Systems 3.
Which courses require Analogue Electronics 1 depends on the degree programme, so students should check their own programme list.
tips: Prerequisite lists depend on the degree programme; do not assume a course is compulsory for every student without checking the programme's list.
rq: Why would a Mechanical student need Analogue Electronics 1 if they never plan to design circuits?

Because Power Electronics 2 (ENG2045) and Instrumentation and Data Systems 3 (ENG3034) list Mechanical programmes as eligible students and require Analogue Electronics 1 as a prerequisite, so the foundation is needed to progress in those courses.
Why might Embedded Processors 2 require analogue knowledge even though it is a computing course?
Embedded systems interface with real-world sensors and actuators, which produce and need analogue signals, so analogue electronics underpins that interfacing.

notes.t: Electronics throughout the degree program: prerequisites
pts: Analogue Electronics is a prerequisite for ENG3034 Instrumentation and Data Systems 3 in 3rd year
Prior knowledge needed covers passive components, impedance, DC/AC quantities and circuit laws
Lectures 2 and 3 cover the Wheatstone bridge and sensing configurations
defs: Complex impedance
The generalised resistance of a circuit to alternating current, combining resistance and reactance as a complex quantity.
tips: Do not confuse impedance with resistance: impedance applies to AC circuits containing L and C, and is complex-valued.
rq: Why does Ohm's law alone not suffice for analysing AC circuits containing inductors and capacitors?
Inductors and capacitors introduce reactance that varies with frequency and causes phase shifts, so impedance (a complex quantity) is needed rather than resistance alone.

notes.t: Assessment structure and requirements
pts: Final grade is weighted across four components, and all four must be attempted to receive course credit.
Continuous assessment is 25% and includes lecture questions and online quizzes; all of them must be completed to pass.
Lab work is 25%, comprising a component simulation lab (10%) and a filter circuits and design element lab (15%), with mandatory attendance and deadlines after each session.
A 25% online midterm theory exam covers fundamental course theory, is timed at 90 minutes, and uses randomised questions with cheating reported to the school.
A 25% December design exam requires two circuit-design questions and can draw on any part of the course, including midterm concepts.
tips: Missing any one of the four assessment components means no course credit, even with high marks elsewhere.
Lab deadlines differ: the Component Simulation lab is due 1 week after the session, the Filter Circuits lab 2 weeks after.
rq: Why might a student who scores well on the midterm still need to revisit midterm concepts for the December exam?
Midterm concepts may reappear as part of a larger design-focused question in the final design exam, so they remain examinable.
What is the risk of skipping a single online lecture question or quiz, given the assessment rules?
Failing to complete any continuous assessment item means the student does not pass the course, regardless of other marks.

units.name: 1.2 Lecture aims and basic circuit components
units.ov: This material introduces DC circuit notation and the basic building blocks: voltage sources, conductors, switches and resistances, using a car headlight circuit as the worked model. It defines current, voltage and resistance and links them through Ohm's law \(V = IR\), with power calculated from these quantities. The ideas connect because a source's voltage drives current through resistive elements joined by conductors in closed loops.
must: Ohm's law: \(V = IR\), with V in volts, I in amperes and R in ohms; rearrange to \(I = V/R\) or \(R = V/I\)
Current is the rate of flow of charge, \(I = dQ/dt\), measured in amperes
Voltage is the driving force (potential difference) that pushes charge round a circuit
Resistance opposes current and converts electrical energy to heat or light; it is measured in ohms (\(\Omega\))
Power is calculated from voltage, current and resistance: \(P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R\)
An ideal voltage source holds a fixed voltage across its terminals regardless of the current drawn (it models the battery)
A circuit is elements joined in closed paths by low-resistance conductors; current flows only in a complete loop
Conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to electron flow; keep this consistent when labelling
A switch is an open or closed path, not a resistor, and it controls whether current flows
Parallel branches across a source each see the full source voltage (12 V for each headlamp); convert to base units before calculating
conn: Ohm's law and power: substituting \(V = IR\) into \(P = VI\) gives \(P = I^2R = V^2/R\), so one calculation can often replace another
Circuit diagram and analysis: translating the physical layout into ideal symbols (source, switch, resistors) is the first step before applying \(V = IR\)
Parallel connection and voltage: each parallel headlamp has the full battery voltage, so the current in each is \(V/R\) and the total current is the sum of the branch currents
Current direction and sign convention: labelling conventional current wrongly leads to sign errors in voltage and power calculations
exq: Two identical headlamps, each of resistance 6 \(\Omega\), are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Calculate the current in each lamp, the total battery current and the total power dissipated.
Draw the circuit diagram for a car headlight system (battery, switch, two parallel lamps) from its physical layout, labelling each element and the direction of conventional current.
A lamp draws 2.5 A from a 12 V source. Find its resistance and power, then find the new current and power if the voltage drops to 10 V, assuming constant resistance.
Define electrical resistance and electric current, giving units. Explain why a switch is not a resistor and what an ideal voltage source implies about current.
A resistance is given as 4.7 k\(\Omega\) with a current of 3 mA. Calculate the voltage across it and the power dissipated, showing consistent unit conversion.

notes.t: Learning Outcomes from lecture: DC circuits
pts: The lecture covers circuit notation, showing how sources and circuit elements are drawn.
Resistance is a property of materials that opposes the flow of electrons.
Current describes the flow of electrons through a material.
Voltage is the quantity to be understood as the driving force behind current flow.
Voltage, current and resistance are linked by Ohm's law, and power is defined and calculated from them.
defs: Electrical resistance
A property of a material that opposes the flow of electric current through it, measured in ohms.
Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge (electrons) through a material, measured in amperes.
eqs: Ohm's law (relation between voltage, current and resistance)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (\(\Omega\))
tips: Keep units consistent: resistance in ohms, current in amperes, voltage in volts before applying \(V = IR\).
rq: Why must the same three quantities (voltage, current, resistance) be related by one law rather than treated independently?
Because current through a resistor depends on both the driving voltage and the opposition of the material; knowing any two determines the third via Ohm's law.

notes.t: Basic Circuit of Headlights in an Automobile
pts: A car's headlights are modelled as a simple circuit: the battery acts as a voltage source, the wires as conductors, the switch controls the current, and the headlamps as resistances.
The physical configuration (a) is translated into a circuit diagram (b) by replacing each real component with its ideal circuit symbol.
The two headlamps are connected in parallel across the battery, so each receives the full 12 V supply.
defs: Voltage source
An ideal two-terminal element that maintains a fixed voltage across its terminals regardless of the current drawn; here it models the car battery.
Resistance
A circuit element that opposes the flow of current and converts electrical energy into heat or light; here it models each headlamp.
tips: Do not confuse the switch symbol with a resistor: the switch is an open or closed path, not an element that limits current.
rq: Why are the two headlamps drawn side by side between the same two conductors rather than one after the other?
They are in parallel, so each lamp has the same 12 V across it and one lamp failing does not switch off the other.

notes.t: Basic Components in an Electrical Circuit
pts: An electrical circuit is circuit elements joined in closed paths by conductors.
Conductors are the connecting wires in a physical circuit.
A voltage source creates forces that drive charge through conductors and other elements.
defs: Electrical circuit
A set of circuit elements connected in closed paths by conductors, through which charge can flow.
Conductor
An element (connecting wire) that provides a low-resistance path linking the other circuit elements in a closed loop.
tips: Conventional current flows from positive to negative terminals, opposite to the direction of electron flow; do not mix the two directions when labelling a circuit.
rq: Why must the conductors form a closed path for current to flow in the circuit?
Charge can only circulate continuously if it returns to its starting point; an open path has no return route, so steady current cannot exist.

xq.q: A car's two identical headlamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery, which is modelled as an ideal voltage source. Each lamp is modelled as a resistance of 2.4 Ω. Calculate the total power drawn from the battery, using \(V = IR\) and \(P = VI\).
xq.a: Total power = 120 W
s: Current per lamp I = V/R = 12/2.4 = 5 A

xq.q: A headlamp modelled as a resistor draws 4.0 A from a 12 V battery. The lamp resistance \(R\) in ohms is:
xq.w: R = V/I = 12/4 = 3.0 Ω; the traps are inverting the formula (I/V = 0.33) or multiplying V×I (48).

xq.q: In the headlamp circuit the two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Explain why parallel connection is used, and describe the direction of conventional current and of electron flow in the circuit when the switch is closed.
xq.a: In parallel each lamp is connected directly across the battery so each receives the full 12 V, and if one lamp fails the other still works. Conventional current flows from the positive terminal through the lamps to the negative terminal, whereas electrons drift in the opposite direction, from negative to positive.
s: Parallel: each lamp sees full 12 V

units.name: 1.3 Electron flow and conduction in materials
units.ov: This material introduces how electric current arises from the motion of free electrons in a conductor, using copper as the example. It links atomic structure (loosely bound outer electrons) to the bulk properties of conductivity and resistivity, and then to the net drift of charge under an applied voltage. Materials span a huge range of conductivity, from copper to fused quartz.
must: Resistivity and conductivity are reciprocals: \( \rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} \), with \( \rho \) in Ω·m and \( \sigma \) in S/m.
Copper has \( \sigma \approx 10^{7} \) S/m and \( \rho \approx 10^{-7} \) Ω·m, so it is an excellent conductor.
Fused quartz has \( \sigma \approx 10^{-14} \) S/m, so it is a near-perfect insulator; conductivity spans about 21 orders of magnitude.
Copper has 29 protons and 29 electrons; its loosely bound outermost electron is free to move and carries the current.
With no applied voltage, free electrons move randomly and there is no net charge flow, so no current.
With a battery connected, electrons drift from the negative towards the positive terminal, giving a net flow of charge.
Current is the organised net movement of charge carriers (the rate of charge flow) caused by a potential difference, \( I = \frac{dQ}{dt} \).
Conventional current flows from positive to negative, opposite to the electron drift; state the convention explicitly.
High conductivity means low resistivity: do not confuse the two. Compare powers of ten and check units (S/m vs Ω·m).
conn: Atomic structure to conductivity: loosely bound outer electrons give many free carriers, which gives high \( \sigma \) and low \( \rho \).
Conductivity to current: a higher \( \sigma \) gives a larger drift current for the same applied voltage, which links to Ohm's law and resistance \( R = \rho L/A \).
Random motion versus drift: thermal random motion gives zero net current, and an applied field superimposes a net drift, so current is the net flow.
Electron flow versus conventional current: questions on circuit direction often need both to be stated consistently.
exq: Copper has \( \sigma \approx 10^{7} \) S/m. Calculate its resistivity and state the units. Then compare it with fused quartz (\( 10^{-14} \) S/m) as a ratio of conductivities.
Explain, using the atomic structure of copper (29 protons and 29 electrons), why copper is a good conductor.
Describe the motion of free electrons in a copper wire (a) with no voltage applied and (b) when connected to a battery. Why is there a current in only one case?
State the direction of conventional current and of electron flow in a simple circuit with a battery and a lamp, and explain why they differ.
Define electrical conductivity and resistivity, give their units, and explain why a material with a very large \( \sigma \) is not one with a large \( \rho \).

notes.t: Electron flow through a material: copper and conductivity
pts: Copper has 29 protons and 29 electrons, arranged in shells around the nucleus; its outermost electron is loosely bound and can move freely.
Copper has very high electrical conductivity (about \(10^{7}\) S/m), meaning electrons flow through it very easily.
Copper has very low resistivity (about \(10^{-7}\) Ω·m), the reciprocal of its conductivity, so it offers little opposition to current.
Materials span a huge range of conductivity: copper sits at the top, while fused quartz (about \(10^{-14}\) S/m) is a near-perfect insulator.
defs: Electrical conductivity (σ)
A measure of how easily a material allows electric current to flow; the reciprocal of resistivity, measured in siemens per metre (S/m).
Resistivity (ρ)
A material property describing how strongly it opposes current flow, measured in ohm-metres (Ω·m); the reciprocal of conductivity.
tips: Conductivity and resistivity are inversely related: do not confuse a large conductivity value with a large resistivity value.
Check units: conductivity is in S/m and resistivity in Ω·m; the table gives orders of magnitude, so compare powers of ten rather than exact values.
rq: Why does copper, with its loosely bound outer electrons, conduct so much better than fused quartz?
Copper's outer electrons are weakly bound and free to drift under an applied field, whereas in fused quartz electrons are tightly bound in covalent bonds with no free charge carriers.
If a material's conductivity is \(10^{-7}\) S/m, what is its resistivity and how does it compare to copper?
Resistivity is 1/\(10^{-7}\) = \(10^{7}\) Ω·m, which is about \(10^{14}\) times larger than copper's \(10^{-7}\) Ω·m, so it is a far poorer conductor.

notes.t: Electron flow through a material
pts: Free electrons in a material move randomly when no voltage is applied, so there is no net flow of charge.
When a battery is connected, electrons drift from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal, giving a net flow of charge.
The moving electrons transfer energy between circuit elements, and this organised movement constitutes an electric current.
defs: Current flow
The organised (net) movement of charge carriers, such as free electrons, through a conductor caused by a potential difference; it is the rate of charge flow.
tips: Conventional current is taken to flow from positive to negative, opposite to the direction of electron flow; state the convention clearly in exam answers.
Random electron motion does not constitute current; only the net drift of electrons does.
rq: Why does the random motion of free electrons produce no current, while a battery makes them produce one?
Random motions in all directions cancel out, giving zero net charge transfer; the battery's potential difference biases the motion so electrons drift in one direction, giving a net flow.

xq.q: Copper has electrical conductivity \(\sigma = 6\times10^{7}\) S/m. A piece of fused quartz has conductivity \(\sigma_q = 10^{-14}\) S/m. Using \(\rho = 1/\sigma\), calculate the ratio of the resistivity of quartz to that of copper.
A material has conductivity \(\sigma = 5\times10^{6}\) S/m. Its resistivity is:
xq.w: ρ = 1/σ = 2×\(10^{-7}\) Ω·m; the traps are treating conductivity as resistivity, or only flipping the exponent's sign without inverting the 5.

xq.q: Explain, in terms of free electrons, why no current flows in a copper wire when it is not connected to a battery, even though the electrons are moving, and why current flows when a battery is connected.
xq.a: Free electrons in copper move randomly, so over time there is no net movement of charge in any direction and hence no current. When a battery is connected, the potential difference makes the electrons drift from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal, giving a net flow of charge, which is the current. The electrons transfer energy between circuit elements.
s: Random motion gives zero net charge flow
Net drift of electrons gives current

units.name: 1.4 Resistance, conductance and resistivity
units.ov: This section defines resistance (Ω) and its reciprocal, conductance (S), then links resistance to a conductor's physical properties through resistivity using \( R = \rho l / A \). Most of the marks come from careful unit handling (kΩ to Ω, mm² to m²) and from knowing how R and G scale with length, area and temperature.
must: Resistance of a uniform conductor: \( R = \frac{\rho l}{A} \), with R in Ω, ρ in Ω·m, l in m and A in m²
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: \( G = 1/R \), unit siemens (S). It is undefined at R = 0 (a zero-resistance path has infinite conductance)
Unit conversion: \( 1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2 \) and \( 1\,\text{k}\Omega = 1000\,\Omega \). Leaving area in mm² gives an answer 10⁶ times too small
Proportionality: \( R \propto l \) and \( R \propto 1/A \). Doubling the length doubles R, and doubling the area halves R. Since \( A = \pi d^2/4 \), halving the diameter multiplies R by 4
Resistivity ρ is a material property: the resistance of unit length and unit cross-section. It is constant only at a fixed temperature, so state the temperature
Worked example: a 40 kΩ resistor has \( G = 1/40\,000 = 25\,\mu\text{S} \). Lower R gives higher G
Worked example: a 100 m copper wire of 2.5 mm² has \( R \approx 0.688\,\Omega \), which implies \( \rho_{Cu} \approx 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m} \). Check the power of ten on the calculator
Distinguish resistance (a property, in Ω) from a resistor (the component). Resistors limit current and divide voltage, and their heating is usually unwanted
Parallel resistors each have the full battery voltage across them and the current splits between branches. Identify series or parallel before applying equivalent-resistance formulas
Check units by dimensional analysis: \( \Omega\text{m} \times \text{m} / \text{m}^2 = \Omega \)
conn: Resistivity, length and area give R, and G = 1/R then gives conductance. Questions often ask for both from the wire dimensions
Unit conversions (mm² to m², kΩ to Ω, µS prefixes) run through every calculation, so a single slip carries into all later parts
Parallel circuits link to conductance: in parallel, conductances add, \( G_{total} = G_1 + G_2 + \dots \). Two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel give 500 Ω, or 2 mS
Temperature changes ρ and therefore R, so a wire's resistance at a different temperature differs from the value calculated from a tabulated ρ
exq: Calculate the resistance of a 100 m length of copper wire with cross-sectional area 2.5 mm², given \( \rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m} \). Then find its conductance in siemens.
A 40 kΩ resistor is replaced by one with twice the conductance. State the new resistance and the conductance in µS.
A wire has resistance R. It is drawn out to twice its length at constant volume, so its area halves. Find the new resistance in terms of R and justify your answer using \( R = \rho l/A \).

Two 1 kΩ resistors are connected in parallel across a battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the equivalent conductance. Explain how the current splits and what the voltage is across each resistor.
A wire of diameter 1.8 mm and length 50 m has resistance 0.34 Ω. Determine the resistivity of the material and suggest which metal it is. Comment on the temperature condition on your answer.

notes.t: Resistance and Resistors
pts: Resistance is the property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons.
Resistance is measured in ohms, symbolised by the Greek letter omega.
A resistor is a component deliberately designed to have a specific resistance.
Resistors are used to limit current, divide voltage, and sometimes generate heat or light.
defs: Resistance (R)
The property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons; measured in ohms (Ω).
Resistor
A component specifically designed to have a certain amount of resistance.
tips: Do not confuse resistance (a property of a material or component, measured in Ω) with resistor (the physical component designed to have that resistance).
Resistors can limit current and divide voltage, but their heating effect is usually unwanted; only in certain cases is heat or light the intended purpose.
rq: Why would a circuit designer deliberately insert a resistor rather than rely on the resistance of the wires?
Wire resistance is very small and unplanned; a resistor provides a known, controlled resistance to limit current or set voltage levels.
Why does a resistor used to divide voltage need to be placed in series with other resistors?
Voltage divides across series components in proportion to their resistances, so series placement is what creates the split.

notes.t: Resistance and Conductance
pts: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance and measures how easily current flows.
Conductance is symbolised by G and its SI unit is the siemens (S).
Resistance is analogous to the restriction water experiences flowing through a pipe.
defs: Conductance
The reciprocal of resistance, G = 1/R, measuring the ease with which a component allows current to pass; its SI unit is the siemens (S).
eqs: G = conductance (siemens, S); R = resistance (ohm, Ω)
tips: Do not confuse conductance (siemens, S) with resistance (ohms, Ω); the unit of G is S, not Ω.
Remember G = 1/R only holds for R ≠ 0; a zero-resistance path has infinite conductance.
rq: Why does a larger resistance give a smaller conductance?
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance (G = 1/R), so as R increases, 1/R decreases; a more opposed path conducts less readily.
If a resistor has R = 4 Ω, what is its conductance and in what unit is it expressed?
G = 1/4 = 0.25 S (siemens).

notes.t: Resistance and Resistor
pts: A resistor opposes the flow of current; the simulated circuit shows two 1 kΩ resistors connected in parallel across the battery.
In a parallel arrangement, each resistor has the same voltage across it as the battery, while the total current splits between the branches.
defs: Resistance
The opposition a component or material offers to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω).
Resistor
A circuit component designed to provide a specific resistance, used to limit current or divide voltage.
tips: Watch units: 1k means 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω, not 1 Ω; convert before calculating.
Check whether resistors are in series or parallel before applying resistance formulas, since the circuit topology determines the equivalent resistance.
rq: Why do both 1 kΩ resistors have the same voltage across them even though the current through each may differ?
They are connected in parallel directly across the same two nodes of the battery, so they share the battery's voltage.

notes.t: Conductance of a resistor
pts: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so a lower resistance gives a higher conductance.
Substitute the resistance in ohms (40 kΩ = 40 000 Ω) and the result is in siemens.
A 40 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 25 µS.
defs: Conductance
The measure of how easily current flows through a component; it is the reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemens (S).
eqs: G = conductance (siemens, S); R = resistance (ohms, Ω)
G = conductance (siemens, S); R = 40 kΩ = 40 000 Ω
tips: Unit trap: 40 kΩ must be treated as 40 000 Ω, giving 25 µS, not 25 S or 0.025 S.
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so do not divide R by 1 or confuse G = 1/R with G = R.
rq: Why must the resistance be converted to ohms before calculating conductance?
Because the SI unit of conductance, the siemens, is defined from ohms; using kΩ directly gives a result in kS (or µS after conversion), which is only correct if units are handled consistently.

notes.t: Resistance and Resistor
pts: Resistance of a wire depends on the material, its length and its cross-sectional area.
Resistance is directly proportional to the length of the wire: longer wire, greater resistance.
Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area: thicker wire, lower resistance.
Resistivity is a material property that stays constant only at a given temperature.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length of a unit cross-sectional area of that material; it is constant at a fixed temperature.
Cross-sectional area (A)
The area of a slice taken perpendicular to the length of the conductor through which the current flows.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity of material (Ω·m); l = length of wire (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert area to m² (e.g. mm² × 10⁻⁶) before using R = ρl/A with ρ in Ω·m.
Resistivity ρ is only constant at a fixed temperature; resistance changes if temperature changes, so state the temperature condition.
rq: Why does doubling the wire's diameter reduce its resistance to one quarter?
Area A = πd²/4 scales with d², so doubling d multiplies A by 4; since R ∝ 1/A, R becomes one quarter of its original value.
What happens to resistance if the length is doubled and the area is also doubled?
R = ρl/A: length doubles (×2) and area doubles (÷2), so R stays the same.

notes.t: Resistance of a conductor from resistivity, length and cross-sectional area
pts: Resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the material constant.
Resistivity is a material property, so the same formula applies to any conductor once ρ, l and A are known.
Area must be converted from mm² to m² before substituting, since resistivity is in Ω·m.
Checking units (Ω·m × m / m² = Ω) confirms the formula gives resistance in ohms.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-sectional area of that material; measured in Ω·m.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Unit trap: leaving area in mm² gives a result that is 10⁶ times too small; always convert to m².
The answer for the 100 m copper wire is about 0.688 Ω; check the powers of ten when entering 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ on a calculator.
rq: Why must the area be converted from mm² to m² before calculating?
Because resistivity is given in Ω·m, so every quantity must be in SI base units for the result to be in ohms; 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m².
What would happen to the resistance if the wire were doubled in length and its diameter doubled?
Length doubling doubles R, but doubling diameter quadruples area so R is divided by 4; net effect R → R/2.

xq.q: A uniform copper wire has length l = 25 m and circular cross-section of diameter d = 0.50 mm. The resistivity of copper at the operating temperature is \(\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m}\). Calculate the resistance R of the wire, and hence its conductance G, in millisiemens (mS).
A resistor of resistance R = 8 kΩ is connected in parallel with a resistor of resistance 8 kΩ. What is the total conductance of the pair?
xq.a: 250 µS
o: 250 µS
125 µS
4 kΩ
xq.w: Each has G = 1/8000 = 125 µS and parallel conductances add to 250 µS; halving gives the wrong value 125 µS, forgetting units gives 0.25 S, and 4 kΩ is a resistance, not a conductance.

xq.q: A wire of resistance R has the same material and temperature changed to a new wire of twice the length and twice the diameter. Show, using \(R=\rho l/A\), how the resistance changes, and explain why the temperature must be stated.
xq.a: Area scales with diameter squared, so A becomes 4A. Length becomes 2l. New R' = ρ(2l)/(4A) = R/2. The resistance halves. Resistivity is only constant at a fixed temperature, so if temperature changed ρ and hence R would change too.
s: ρ constant only at fixed temperature, so state it

units.name: 1.5 Resistor types and colour codes
units.ov: This material classifies resistors as linear (ohmic) or nonlinear, and as fixed or variable, then shows how to read a four-band colour code to get nominal resistance and tolerance. The link is that colour codes apply to fixed linear resistors, where Ohm's law \(V=IR\) holds with constant \(R\). Nonlinear devices (thermistors, LDRs) and variable ones (potentiometers, rheostats) change R, so the circuit analysis differs.
must: Colour code formula: \(R=(10d_1+d_2)\times10^{n}\ \Omega\), where band 3 gives \(n\), the number of zeros
Digit chart: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9
Tolerance band: gold = ±5%, silver = ±10%; it is never a digit and is read last, so start from the end opposite it
Band 3 is a power of ten, not a multiplying value: brown-black-red = \(10\times10^2=1\,\text{k}\Omega\), not \(10\times2\)
Tolerance range: actual \(R\) lies in \(R_{nom}(1\pm t)\), giving minimum and maximum values
Linear (ohmic) resistors have constant R, so V and I are directly proportional; \(V=IR\) applies only to these
Nonlinear resistors change R with a physical condition: a thermistor with temperature, an LDR with light (LDR resistance falls as intensity rises)
Potentiometer = 3 terminals, voltage divider; rheostat = 2 terminals (one fixed, one sliding contact), current control
Fixed linear types: carbon film, thick film, thin film
Convert prefixes carefully: 27,000 Ω = 27 kΩ; 5,600,000 Ω = 5.6 MΩ
conn: Colour code reading feeds directly into tolerance calculations, which give the range of current or voltage in an Ohm's law problem
Linear versus nonlinear decides whether Ohm's law can be used with a constant R or whether an I–V graph or a value at given conditions is needed
Potentiometer (voltage divider) with an LDR or thermistor gives a light- or temperature-sensing circuit whose output voltage changes with the condition
Rheostat current control combines with \(V=IR\): changing R changes I for a fixed supply
exq: A resistor has bands yellow, violet, orange, gold. Find its nominal resistance in kΩ and its minimum and maximum possible values.
A resistor is coded green-blue-green-silver. Give its resistance in MΩ with tolerance, and the current range when 10 V is applied.
Explain with I–V sketches why a thermistor is nonlinear whereas a carbon film resistor is linear, and state whether \(V=IR\) applies to each.
Distinguish a rheostat from a potentiometer by terminals and function, and say which you would use to vary the current in a series circuit and which to provide an adjustable output voltage.
A student reads a resistor from the gold end as brown-black-red and gets 1 kΩ. Explain why this is wrong, give the correct reading procedure, and describe how an LDR's resistance changes with light.

notes.t: Resistors: classification by type
pts: Resistors split into linear (ohmic) and nonlinear types; linear resistors have constant resistance across voltage changes.
Fixed linear resistors are made as carbon film, thick film or thin film types, each with a fixed value.
Variable linear resistors include the potentiometer (voltage divider use) and the rheostat (current control use), with adjustable resistance.
Nonlinear resistors change resistance with a physical condition: thermistors respond to temperature and LDRs respond to light.
defs: Linear resistor
A resistor whose resistance stays constant as the voltage across it (or current through it) changes, so V and I are directly proportional.
Nonlinear resistor
A resistor whose resistance changes with a physical quantity such as temperature or light intensity, so V and I are not directly proportional.
Potentiometer
A variable resistor with three terminals used as a adjustable voltage divider.
Rheostat
A variable resistor with two terminals (one fixed, one sliding contact) used to control current in a circuit.
Thermistor
A nonlinear resistor whose resistance changes significantly with temperature.
LDR (light-dependent resistor)
A nonlinear resistor whose resistance decreases as the intensity of incident light increases.
tips: Do not confuse a rheostat (two terminals, current control) with a potentiometer (three terminals, voltage division).
Ohm's law V = IR only applies to linear resistors; nonlinear resistors such as thermistors and LDRs do not have constant R.
rq: Why is a thermistor classed as a nonlinear resistor while a carbon film resistor is linear?
A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, so V and I are not proportional; a carbon film resistor keeps a constant resistance over the operating range, so it obeys Ohm's law.
How does a rheostat differ from a potentiometer in a circuit?
A rheostat uses two terminals to vary resistance and control current; a potentiometer uses three terminals to act as a variable voltage divider.

notes.t: Resistor Colour Coding
pts: The first band (nearest one end) gives the first digit of the resistance; never start from a gold or silver band.
The second band gives the second digit of the resistance value.
The third band is the multiplier: the number of zeros following the second digit.
The fourth band gives the percent tolerance and is usually gold (±5%) or silver (±10%).
defs: Percent tolerance
The permitted percentage deviation of a resistor's actual value from its stated (coded) value, shown by the fourth band: gold = ±5%, silver = ±10%.
Multiplier
The power of ten (number of zeros) appended to the two significant digits of a resistor's colour code, given by the third band.
eqs: Resistance from colour bands (first two digits and multiplier)
R = resistance (\Omega); \(d_{1}\) = first digit (band 1); \(d_{2}\) = second digit (band 2); n = number of zeros (band 3 multiplier)
tips: Read the bands from the end nearest the first band, not the tolerance band; reading from the gold/silver end gives the wrong value.
The multiplier band gives a number of zeros (a power of ten), not the multiplier value itself; e.g. brown-black-red = 10 × 10² = 1 kΩ, not 10 × 2.
rq: Why must you never start reading the colour code from a gold or silver band?
Gold and silver are not digit colours; they are used only for tolerance, which sits at the end, so starting from them would misread the value.
A resistor has bands yellow, violet, orange, gold. What is its value and tolerance?
Digits 4 and 7, multiplier ×10³: 47 kΩ (47 000 Ω) with ±5% tolerance.

notes.t: Reading resistor colour codes: resistance value and tolerance
pts: The first two bands give the two significant digits of the resistance.
The third band gives the power-of-ten multiplier as the number of zeros appended.
The fourth band gives the tolerance; gold means ±5% and silver means ±10%.
The colour chart maps each colour to a digit: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9.
Read the bands from the end without the wider gap or gold/silver tolerance band, then combine digits and zeros into the resistance.
defs: Tolerance
The maximum allowed percentage deviation of a resistor's actual value from its marked nominal value.
Colour code
A system of coloured bands on a resistor body that encodes its nominal resistance in ohms and its tolerance.
eqs: Resistance from colour bands (band 1 and 2 digits, band 3 multiplier)
\(d_{1}\) = first digit (band 1); \(d_{2}\) = second digit (band 2); m = number of zeros (band 3) (dimensionless); R = resistance (Ω)
tips: Watch units: 5,600,000 Ω is 5.6 MΩ, and 27,000 Ω is 27 kΩ; convert prefixes carefully.
Do not read the tolerance band as a digit; the gold or silver band is always the tolerance.
rq: Why does the 4th band of 27,000 Ω ± 10% mean the true value could be 24,300 Ω to 29,700 Ω?
Tolerance is a percentage of the nominal value: 10% of 27,000 Ω is 2,700 Ω, so R lies in 27,000 ± 2,700 Ω.
What if the 3rd band of the green-blue-green resistor were brown instead of green?
The multiplier would be \(10^{1}\) instead of \(10^{5}\), giving 56 Ω instead of 5,600,000 Ω.

xq.q: A resistor has colour bands brown, black, orange, silver, read from the end nearest the first band. Find its nominal resistance and the range of values it may actually have, giving the maximum value in kΩ.
xq.a: Nominal 10 kΩ, tolerance ±10%, range 9 kΩ to 11 kΩ; maximum 11 kΩ
s: Brown 1, black 0, orange 3 zeros: 10 000 Ω = 10 kΩ

xq.q: A resistor is coloured yellow, violet, red, gold. What is its nominal resistance and tolerance?
xq.w: Yellow 4, violet 7, red = two zeros gives 4700 Ω, gold is ±5%; treating red as ×2 gives 47×2 Ω-type errors, and silver/gold are confused for ±10%.

xq.q: Explain why Ohm's law \(V=IR\) with a single constant R describes a carbon film resistor but not a thermistor or an LDR, and state how a potentiometer differs from a rheostat in construction and use.
xq.a: A carbon film resistor is linear: its R is constant so V and I are proportional. A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature and an LDR's decreases as light intensity increases, so R is not constant and V–I is not a straight line. A potentiometer has three terminals and acts as an adjustable voltage divider; a rheostat has two terminals (one fixed, one sliding) and controls current.

units.name: 1.6 Electric current: definition and notation
units.ov: This material defines electric current as the time rate of flow of charge (1 A = 1 C/s) and shows how current is described as a function of time (DC, AC, other waveforms). It also covers reference-direction notation, which fixes the sign of a current, and the current source symbol. The ideas connect because \(I=Q/t\) is the constant-current special case of \(i=dq/dt\), and the sign of any current only has meaning relative to its reference arrow.
must: Current is the rate of flow of charge: \(i(t)=\frac{dq}{dt}\); unit ampere, 1 A = 1 C/s
For constant current only, \(I=Q/t\); for time-varying current use \(i=dq/dt\) or \(Q=\int i\,dt\)
Charge (C) is not current (A): current is charge per unit time
Reference direction is an assumed positive direction shown by an arrow; a negative value means flow opposite to the arrow, not zero current
Reversing the reference direction negates the current: \(i_{ab}=-i_{ba}\)
DC is constant in magnitude and direction, e.g. \(i_a(t)=2\) A
AC varies sinusoidally and periodically reverses, e.g. \(i_b(t)=2\cos(2\pi t)\) A: amplitude 2 A, \(\omega=2\pi\) rad/s, \(f=1\) Hz, \(T=1\) s
Other time-varying waveforms (triangular, square) are also valid currents; read their values and signs from the graph

Current source symbol: circle with an arrow giving the direction of the current; reversing the arrow flips the sign. Parallel sources in the same direction are equivalent to one source with the same current as stated in the notes
One coulomb is about \(6\times10^{18}\) electrons, each with charge \(-1.6\times10^{-19}\) C; use consistent units (C, s) and radians in cos
conn: Charge–current calculus: differentiate \(q(t)\) to get \(i(t)\), and integrate a waveform (area under an \(i\)-\(t\) graph) to get the charge transferred, which is common for square or triangular waveforms
Reference direction with waveform sign: for AC, the sign of \(i(t)\) at an instant tells you whether actual flow is with or against the arrow, linking notation to \(\cos\) phase and period
Electron charge with the coulomb: converting between number of electrons, charge Q and current via \(I=Q/t\), remembering that electron flow is opposite to conventional current direction
Current source direction with KCL-style circuit analysis: the arrow and sign convention determine what current enters or leaves a node
exq: A charge of 20 C passes a point in a wire in 5 s at constant current. Find the current, and the number of electrons passing per second.
The charge through a device is \(q(t)=3t^2-2t\) C. Find \(i(t)\) and the current at \(t=2\) s, stating the units.
A current is \(i(t)=2\cos(2\pi t)\) A. State the amplitude, frequency and period, evaluate \(i\) at \(t=0.25\) s and \(t=0.5\) s, and find the charge passed from \(t=0\) to \(t=0.25\) s.
A square-wave current is +3 A for 2 s then -3 A for 2 s. Sketch it and find the net charge passed over one period and over the first 3 s.
Given \(i_{ab}=-4\) A, find \(i_{ba}\) and explain in words the actual direction of flow. How does this change if the reference arrow of a current source is reversed?

notes.t: Electrical Current Forms & Notations
pts: DC current has constant value over time; here a constant 2 A.
AC current varies sinusoidally with time, here a cosine with 1 Hz frequency (period 1 s).
Triangular and square currents are examples of time-varying current waveforms.
Current direction notation: reversing the reference direction changes the sign of the current.
defs: Direct current (DC)
Current whose magnitude and direction remain constant with time.
Alternating current (AC)
Current that periodically reverses direction, typically varying sinusoidally with time.
Time-varying current
Current whose value changes with time, such as triangular or square waveforms.
Reference direction
The assumed positive direction of current flow, marked by an arrow; reversing it negates the current value.
eqs: \(i_{a}\)(t) = current in branch a at time t (A); constant value 2 A
\(i_{b}\)(t) = current at time t (A); t = time (s); amplitude 2 A; angular frequency 2π rad/s
\(i_{ab}\) = current from a to b (A); \(i_{ba}\) = current from b to a (A)
tips: Mind the reference direction: a negative value means current flows opposite to the arrow, not that it is absent.
Check units: the amplitude is in amperes (A), and the argument of cos must be in radians, so t is in seconds with 2π rad.
rq: Why does the AC current \(i_{b}\)(t) = 2 cos 2πt A have a period of 1 s even though the amplitude is 2 A?
The period is set by the angular frequency: cos(2πt) repeats every t = 1 s, since T = 2π/(2π) = 1 s; amplitude only sets peak height.
If the arrow for branch ab is reversed, what happens to the numerical value of the measured current, and why?
Its sign flips: \(i_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(i_{\text{ba}}\), because the current flows the opposite way relative to the reference direction.
What distinguishes a DC current from an AC current in terms of how it changes with time?
DC is constant in magnitude and direction; AC periodically changes direction and magnitude (sinusoidally here).

notes.t: Electrical Current Form & Notations
pts: A current source is drawn as a circle with an arrow showing the direction of current flow through it
The symbol labelled I with an arrow indicates the source supplies current I in the arrow's direction
Two current sources in parallel with the same direction are equivalent to a single source with the same current
tips: Always check the arrow direction on a current source, since reversing it flips the sign of the current.
rq: Why does the arrow direction matter when drawing a current source?
The arrow sets the reference direction of the current I; reversing it changes the sign of the current.

notes.t: Electrical Current: Definition, Units and Notation
pts: Electrical current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a conductor or circuit element.
The SI unit of current is the ampere, equal to one coulomb per second.
A constant current of 1 A means 1 C of charge passes a cross-section each second.
Current is the derivative of charge with respect to time, so it generalises to time-varying current.
One coulomb corresponds to roughly 6 × \(10^{18}\) electrons, each carrying charge −1.6 × 10^−19 C.
defs: Electrical current (I)
The time rate of flow of electrical charge through a conductor or circuit element.
Ampere (A)
The SI unit of electrical current, equal to one coulomb of charge passing a point per second.
eqs: I = current (A); Q = charge transferred (C); t = time interval (s)
I = current (A); q(t) = charge as a function of time (C); t = time (s)
tips: Do not confuse charge (coulombs) with current (amperes): current is charge per unit time, so 1 A = 1 C/s.
Use Q/t only for constant current; for time-varying current you must integrate or use I = dq/dt.
rq: Why does the instantaneous form dq/dt reduce to Q/t when the current is constant?
For constant current the charge rises linearly with time, so the derivative equals the total charge divided by the elapsed time: I = Q/t.
If 0.5 A flows for 10 s, how much charge has passed, and how many electrons is that?

notes.t: Electric current as rate of charge flow
pts: Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a wire.
Current is found by dividing charge transferred by the time taken.
Worked example: 20 C in 5 s gives a current of 4 A.
defs: Electric current
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor; the charge passing a given point per unit time.
eqs: Electric current from charge and time
I = current (A); Q = charge transferred (C); t = time taken (s)
tips: Ensure charge is in coulombs and time in seconds before dividing; ampere = coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
Current is a rate, so do not confuse it with total charge Q; the answer is the quotient, not the charge itself.
rq: Why does the same 20 C of charge produce a larger current if it flows in 2 s instead of 5 s?
Current is charge divided by time, so a shorter time for the same charge means a larger rate of flow: I = 20/2 = 10 A.

xq.q: The charge passing a point in a wire is \(q(t)=0.2t^{2}+3t\) coulombs, where t is in seconds. Find the current at t = 5 s, and the average current over the interval from t = 0 to t = 5 s.
xq.a: I(5) = 5 A; average current = 4 A (Q = 20 C in 5 s). Instantaneous value is 5 A.

xq.q: A current \(i_{ab}\) = 3 A flows from node a to node b. Which statement about \(i_{ba}\) and the charge delivered in 10 s is correct?
xq.a: \(i_{ba}\) = −3 A and 30 C flows from a to b
o: \(i_{ba}\) = +3 A and 30 C flows from a to b
\(i_{ba}\) = −3 A and 30 C flows from a to b
\(i_{ba}\) = −3 A and 0.3 C flows from a to b
\(i_{ba}\) = 0 A because the current is reversed
xq.w: Reversing the reference direction negates the current, so \(i_{ba}\) = −3 A, while Q = It = 30 C still moves from a to b; the traps are ignoring the sign change and dividing instead of multiplying.
s: Q = It = 3×10 = 30 C from a to b

xq.q: A constant current I = 40 mA flows in a wire for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge transferred, and the approximate number of electrons passing a cross-section, taking the electron charge magnitude as \(1.6\times10^{-19}\) C. Give the number of electrons.

units.name: 1.7 Voltage and current/voltage sources
units.ov: This material introduces voltage as energy transferred per unit charge between two points, and shows how it is measured across elements and labelled with polarity. It then applies the idea to ideal voltage sources and to real bench supplies that set a voltage and a current limit. The ideas connect through V = W/Q, sign conventions, and the contrast between voltage across an element and current through it.
must: Voltage is energy per unit charge: \(V = W/Q\), with \(1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}\)
Rearrangements: \(W = QV\) and \(Q = W/V\). Worked example: 80 J moving 20 C gives 4 V
Voltage is measured across an element's two ends; current flows through it. Never mix them up
Uniform-field relation: \(V = El\), so \(W = QEl\), with E in V/m and l in m
Reference reversal: \(v_{ab} = -v_{ba}\). Voltage is always relative to a chosen reference point
Source polarity: the + terminal is at higher potential, and V is the potential of + relative to −. Reversing the markings flips the sign of V
Circle and battery symbols both denote an ideal voltage source. Use the +/− markings for polarity, not the plate lengths
An ideal voltage source holds a specified V regardless of the current drawn
On a bench supply, the set current limit is a maximum. The load determines the actual current, up to that limit
Check units and convert prefixes (mC, kJ) before substituting. Voltage is not energy (J), current (charge per time) or power (energy per time)
conn: \(V = W/Q\) combines with current (\(I = Q/t\)) to give power \(P = VI\), so energy questions chain voltage, charge, current and time
Polarity and \(v_{ab} = -v_{ba}\) underpin sign conventions in later circuit analysis (KVL, passive sign convention)
\(V = El\) links circuit voltage to electric field and work done on a charge, so field problems can be converted into energy problems
The ideal voltage source (fixed V, any current) contrasts with a real bench supply with a current limit, so questions ask what the load actually draws
exq: A source transfers 150 J of energy to move 30 C of charge between two terminals. Find the voltage, and the energy needed to move 0.5 C across the same terminals.
A charge of 5 mC moves through a 12 V potential difference. Calculate the energy transferred in joules, taking care with units.
A uniform electric field of 200 V/m acts over a 5 cm length. Find the voltage across it and the work done moving 2 µC along it.
If \(v_{ab} = 6\,\text{V}\), state \(v_{ba}\). A 9 V source is redrawn with its +/− labels swapped. What is its voltage relative to the original reference, and why?
A bench supply is set to 5 V with a 1 A current limit and connected to a 10 Ω resistor. What current flows? What happens if the load is changed to 2 Ω? Explain the role of the limit.

notes.t: Voltage
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge as charge moves between two points in a circuit.
Voltage is measured across the two ends of a circuit element, whereas current measures charge flowing through the element.
In a battery-driven headlight, stored chemical energy is converted by the headlight into heat and light.
Voltage across an element reverses sign when the reference direction is reversed: \(v_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(v_{\text{ba}}\).
defs: Voltage (V)
The energy transferred per unit of charge when charge moves from one point in an electrical circuit to a second point; measured in volts (V = J/C).
eqs: Voltage as energy per unit charge
V = voltage (V); W = energy (J); Q = charge (C)
Voltage as electric field times length
V = voltage (V); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
W = energy (J); Q = charge (C); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
\(v_{\text{ab}}\) = voltage at a relative to b (V); \(v_{\text{ba}}\) = voltage at b relative to a (V)
tips: Units trap: voltage is in volts (J/C), not joules; do not confuse energy W with voltage V.
Do not confuse voltage (measured across an element) with current (measured through an element); mixing these up loses marks.
rq: Why does reversing the reference polarity of a voltage change only its sign rather than its magnitude?
Voltage is a potential difference between two points, so swapping which point is the reference gives the same magnitude with opposite sign: \(v_{\text{ab}}\) = −\(v_{\text{ba}}\).
If a charge of 2 C gains 10 J of energy passing through a headlight, what is the voltage across it, and what would happen if the charge was doubled while the energy stayed the same?
V = W/Q = 10/2 = 5 V; doubling the charge to 4 C with the same energy would halve the voltage to 2.5 V.
Why is voltage not the same thing as current, even though both relate to a circuit element?
Voltage is energy per unit charge across the element's ends, while current is the rate of charge flow through the element; they measure different quantities.

notes.t: Electrical Voltage Form & Notations
pts: A voltage source is drawn as a circle (or battery symbol) with a + and − terminal marking its polarity.
Circle symbol and battery symbol represent the same ideal voltage source V; the + terminal is the higher-potential end.
Voltage V is labelled beside the source and its polarity is given by the +/− signs.
defs: Voltage source
An element that maintains a specified voltage V between its two terminals, independent of the current drawn through it.
Polarity (+/−)
The marking on a source terminals showing which end is at higher electric potential; V is the potential of the + terminal relative to the − terminal.
tips: Watch the polarity: reversing the + and − signs changes the sign of V, a common source of sign errors in circuit analysis.
Do not confuse the battery symbol's long/short plates with polarity; always use the + and − markings to determine direction.
rq: Why can the circle symbol and the battery symbol be used interchangeably for the same source?
Both represent an ideal voltage source with the same V and polarity; the battery symbol is just a traditional graphic for the same element.
What would change if the + and − markings were swapped on the source?
The voltage would have the opposite sign relative to the chosen reference direction, reversing the direction of potential difference and current flow.

notes.t: Voltage as energy per unit charge
pts: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge moved between two points in a circuit.
Worked example: 80 J to move 20 C gives a voltage of 4 V, i.e. 4 J of energy per coulomb.
defs: Voltage (potential difference)
The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge moved between two points: V = W/Q, measured in volts (1 V = 1 J/C).
eqs: Voltage from work done and charge moved
V = voltage (V); W = energy/work done (J); Q = charge moved (C)
tips: Keep units consistent: energy in joules and charge in coulombs give volts directly; watch for mC or kJ inputs needing conversion.
Do not confuse voltage (energy per charge, V = W/Q) with current (charge per time) or power (energy per time).
rq: Why does the calculation divide energy by charge rather than multiply?
Voltage is energy per unit charge, so the energy supplied is shared across each coulomb; more charge for the same energy means a lower voltage.
What would the voltage be if the same 80 J moved 40 C of charge?
V = 80/40 = 2 V, half the original voltage, since the energy is spread over twice the charge.

notes.t: Current and Voltage Sources
pts: Bench power supplies act as voltage sources or current sources, and can be set to a required output voltage and current limit.
The example bench supply displays set voltage (V) and current (A), with output terminals and controls for setting values.
A programmable DC supply lets the user set the output voltage and current limit before connecting to a circuit.
tips: Do not confuse the displayed current limit with the current the circuit actually draws; the load determines the actual current, up to the set limit.
rq: Why does a DC power supply have both a voltage setting and a current setting?
The voltage setting determines the output potential difference, while the current setting limits the maximum current the supply can deliver, protecting the circuit and supply from overload.

xq.q: A battery does 540 J of work moving 45 C of charge through a headlight lamp. The lamp has a resistance of 6 Ω. Calculate the current through the lamp, assuming the voltage is constant.
xq.a: I = 2 A

xq.q: The voltage across an element is measured as \(v_{ab}\) = +9 V, where a is the first-named terminal. A student reverses the meter leads and records \(v_{ba}\). What does the student record, and what does it mean?
xq.a: −9 V; terminal b is 9 V lower in potential than terminal a
o: +9 V; the element now supplies energy instead of absorbing it
0 V; reversing the leads removes the potential difference
−9 V; terminal b is 9 V lower in potential than terminal a
−9 V; the element's resistance has changed sign
xq.w: Reversing the reference direction gives \(v_{ba} = -v_{ab}\), and the physical potential difference is unchanged, only its labelling; the trap is thinking the sign change alters the element.

xq.q: A 12 V ideal voltage source is connected first across a 4 Ω resistor and then across a 12 Ω resistor. Explain, with calculations, what is meant by saying the source maintains a specified voltage independent of the current drawn. Also state how the energy transferred per coulomb compares in the two cases.
xq.a: An ideal voltage source keeps 12 V across its terminals whatever the load. With 4 Ω the current is 12/4 = 3 A; with 12 Ω it is 12/12 = 1 A. The current is set by the load, but the voltage stays 12 V. Since V = W/Q, each coulomb gains/transfers 12 J in both cases.
s: Voltage fixed at 12 V in both cases
I = V/R gives 3 A and 1 A
Load determines current, not the source
V = W/Q so 12 J per coulomb in both cases

units.name: 1.8 Ohm's Law and its history
units.ov: This module covers Ohm's law in its circuit form (V = IR, with conductance G = 1/R) and its material or field form (J = σE, E = ρJ), together with a short history of Georg Ohm. The two forms are linked through geometry: R = ρl/A, E = V/l and J = I/A convert the macroscopic law into the microscopic one. The law holds only for linear (ohmic) components at constant temperature, so recognising when it fails is as important as applying it.
must: Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), with \( I = V/R \) and \( R = V/I \). Be fluent in all three rearrangements.

Validity: it holds only for a fixed linear resistance at constant temperature. The V–I graph is a straight line through the origin, and real or non-ohmic devices (diodes, heating filaments) give curves.
Resistance from geometry: \( R = \rho l / A \), so \( V = I\rho l/A \). R is proportional to l and ρ, and inversely proportional to A.
Conductance: \( G = 1/R \) (siemens), so \( V = I/G \). Conductivity is \( \sigma = 1/\rho \) (S/m).
Field form: \( J = \sigma E \), equivalently \( E = \rho J \). This is the material-level statement of Ohm's law.
Definitions and units: \( E = V/l \) (V/m), \( J = I/A \) (A/m²), ρ in Ω·m, σ in S/m. Do not confuse J with I, or ρ with R.
Derive the field form from the circuit form: \( V = El \), \( I = JA \), and substituting into \( V = IR = I\rho l/A \) gives \( E = \rho J \).
Graph shapes: V against I is a straight line with gradient R. At constant V, I against R is a decreasing hyperbola \( I = V/R \).
Unit discipline: convert mA, kΩ, mm and mm² to base SI before substituting. Errors in area units (mm² to m²) cause errors of orders of magnitude.
History: Georg Ohm formulated the proportionality between voltage and current. Be ready to state the law in words, with its constant-temperature condition.
conn: Geometry links circuit and field forms: R = ρl/A combined with E = V/l and J = I/A turns V = IR into E = ρJ, so questions often ask you to move between them.
Temperature and linearity: heating changes resistivity and hence R, so a non-linear V–I curve for a real resistor or filament can be explained by Ohm's law failing, not by V = IR being wrong.
Reciprocal pairs (R and G, ρ and σ) let you solve the same problem in either form, and the inverse I–R hyperbola follows from I = V/R.
Resizing a wire (stretching, changing diameter) changes l and A together, so R = ρl/A is combined with a constant-volume condition.
exq: A copper wire of length 50 m and diameter 1.0 mm has resistivity \( 1.7\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m} \). Calculate its resistance, the current when 3 V is applied, and the current density in the wire.
Starting from \( V = IR \) and \( R = \rho l/A \), derive the field form \( J = \sigma E \). State the units of each quantity.
A 4.7 kΩ resistor carries 2.5 mA. Find the voltage across it and its conductance. What happens to the current if the voltage is doubled, if the component is ohmic?
A V–I graph of a filament lamp is curved but that of a resistor is straight. State Ohm's law, explain the difference, and sketch both graphs plus the I–R curve at constant voltage.
A wire is drawn out to three times its original length at constant volume. By what factor does its resistance change, and what is the effect on E and J for a fixed current?

notes.t: Ohm's Law
pts: At constant temperature, current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the voltage across it, so V ∝ I.
Resistance is the constant of proportionality between V and I; the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin for an ideal resistor.
Real resistors deviate from the ideal straight line, shown by the practical curves, because temperature and material effects change resistance.
Conductance G is the reciprocal of resistance, so V = I/G is an equivalent form of Ohm's law.
At constant voltage, current is inversely related to resistance, so the I–R graph is a decreasing hyperbola.
defs: Ohm's Law
At constant temperature, the current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the voltage across it.
eqs: V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); \rho = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length of conductor (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); G = conductance (S)
tips: Ohm's law only holds at constant temperature and for a linear (fixed) resistance; a non-linear or heating component will give a curved V–I graph.
Keep units consistent: length in metres and area in m² when using \( R = \rho l / A \), otherwise the resistance will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
rq: Why does the ideal V–I graph pass through the origin, and what does a curved 'practical' line tell you about the resistor?
