Zero voltage gives zero current, since V = IR with R constant; a curved line means R is not constant, typically because the resistor heats up and its resistance changes.
If the resistance R doubles while the voltage stays constant, what happens to the current, and why?
The current halves, because I = V/R, so I is inversely proportional to R at constant V.

notes.t: Ohm's Law
pts: Voltage across a component equals current through it multiplied by its resistance.
The triangle (V, I, R) is a memory aid: cover the unknown quantity to see the formula needed.
Current is voltage divided by resistance, so current falls as resistance rises for a fixed voltage.
Resistance is voltage divided by current, giving the ratio of voltage to current for a component.
eqs: Ohm's Law: voltage from current and resistance
tips: Keep units consistent: volts, amps and ohms; convert mA or kΩ to A or Ω before substituting.
Ohm's Law applies to ohmic (linear) components at constant temperature; it does not hold for all devices such as diodes.
rq: Why does the triangle show V on top, with I and R below?
V is the product of I and R, so it is written on top and the other two are the divisors/factors that can be covered to isolate the unknown.
If the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles, what happens to the current?
The current doubles, since \(I = V/R\) and R is constant.

notes.t: Ohm's Law
pts: Ohm's Law is presented as a cartoon: Volt pushes Amp through a resistance controlled by Ohm, showing the relationship between voltage, current and resistance.
tips: Ohm's Law itself is not shown explicitly on this page; the relation V = IR and its units (V, A, Ω) must be recalled from the surrounding notes rather than from this image.
rq: Why does the cartoon show Ohm as the one holding back the flow between Volt and Amp?
Resistance (Ohm) opposes the flow of current driven by voltage, so for a given voltage a larger resistance gives a smaller current.

notes.t: Ohm's Law in Field Form (Resistivity, Conductivity, E and J)
pts: Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its length and resistivity, and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Voltage across a conductor equals electric field times length, so E is voltage per unit length.
Resistivity is the reciprocal of conductivity, linking the two material properties.
Current density is current per unit area, and in the field form the current density is proportional to the electric field.
The field-form Ohm's law J = σE is the material-level statement of Ohm's law.
defs: Electric field E
The voltage drop per unit length along a conductor, measured in V/m.
Current density J
Current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of a conductor, measured in A/m².
Conductivity σ
A material's ability to conduct current, the reciprocal of resistivity, measured in S/m.
Resistivity ρ
A material property giving resistance per unit length and area, measured in Ω·m.
eqs: Resistance of a conductor from resistivity
R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
Electric field from voltage and length
E = electric field (V/m); V = voltage (V); l = length (m)
J = current density (A/m²); σ = conductivity (S/m); E = electric field (V/m)
Resistivity from electric field and current density
E = electric field (V/m); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); J = current density (A/m²)
J = current density (A/m²); I = current (A); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Check units: ρ is in Ω·m (not Ω), and σ is in S/m; mixing these with R (Ω) gives wrong results unless length and area are included.
Do not confuse J (current density, A/m², per area) with I (total current, A); divide by area A when converting between them.
rq: Why does doubling the wire's length double its resistance, but doubling its cross-sectional area halve it?
R = ρl/A: resistance is directly proportional to length (more material to push current through) and inversely proportional to area (a wider path offers less opposition).
If two materials carry the same electric field, how does their current density compare when one has twice the conductivity?
From J = σE, the current density is doubled, since J is directly proportional to σ at fixed E.

xq.q: A copper wire of length 50 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² (1.5×10⁻⁶ m²) has resistivity ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m. A voltage of 2.0 V is applied across its ends. Calculate the current in the wire.
A conductor of cross-sectional area 2.0×10⁻⁶ m² and length 4.0 m carries a current of 5.0 A. Its conductivity is σ = 5.0×10⁷ S/m. Using J = σE, calculate the voltage across the conductor.
A resistor's V–I graph is measured as the current is increased and the resistor heats up. The graph curves away from a straight line. What is the correct conclusion?
xq.a: Ohm's law no longer holds because the resistance changes with temperature
o: The voltage is falling, because current is inversely proportional to resistance
Ohm's law no longer holds because the resistance changes with temperature
The conductance is zero at high current
Ohm's law always holds, so the graph must be a measurement error
xq.w: Ohm's law requires constant temperature; heating changes R so the graph curves, and the trap is assuming V = IR holds for any component under any conditions.
s: Ohm's law needs constant temperature and linear resistance

units.name: 1.9 Power, energy and lecture summary
units.ov: This material covers the basic DC circuit quantities (charge, voltage, current, resistance, conductance, energy and power) and how Ohm's law links V, I and R. Combining Ohm's law with P = VI gives the three power formulae, so any two known quantities fix the other two. It closes Lecture 1 and leads into Kirchhoff's laws.
must: Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), \( I = V/R \), \( R = V/I \)
Three power forms: \( P = VI = I^{2}R = V^{2}/R \); each follows from substituting Ohm's law into \( P = VI \)
Choose the power formula by the known pair: \( I^{2}R \) for current and resistance, \( V^{2}/R \) for voltage and resistance, \( VI \) for voltage and current
Any two of V, I, R, P determine the other two, so solve by selecting the equation that contains the two knowns
Units and symbols: V (volt), I (ampere), R (ohm, Ω), P (watt), Q (coulomb), W (joule)
Conductance \( G = 1/R \) is measured in siemens (S)
Convert prefixes before substituting: mA to A (\(\times10^{-3}\)) and kΩ to Ω (\(\times10^{3}\))
Definitions: power is the rate of energy transfer (\( P = dW/dt \), so energy in joules = power × time); voltage is energy per unit charge; current is the rate of flow of charge
Symbol and unit clashes: W is the symbol for energy but also the unit abbreviation for watts, and A is the unit for amps. Quantity symbols are italic and units upright
conn: Ohm's law with the power equations: eliminate V or I to get \( I^{2}R \) or \( V^{2}/R \), which is used in resistor power rating and heating questions
Power with energy: \( W = Pt \), so a power calculation is often followed by energy used or cost over a time period
Resistance with conductance: \( G = 1/R \) is used later for parallel combinations, where conductances add
Lecture 1 quantities with Kirchhoff's laws: Ohm's law supplies the voltage-current relation for each element, and KCL and KVL give the circuit equations
exq: A 330 Ω resistor carries 25 mA. Find the voltage across it and the power dissipated, and state which power formula you used and why.
A 12 V supply is connected across a 470 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the power. How does the power change if the voltage doubles?
A 0.25 W resistor of 1 kΩ is used in a circuit. Find the maximum voltage and maximum current it can take without exceeding its rating.
A heater rated at 2 kW operates at 230 V. Find its current and resistance, and the energy in joules and kWh used in 3 hours.
Convert a 200 Ω resistance to conductance. A component has G = 5 mS and carries 2 mA. Find the voltage across it and the power dissipated.

notes.t: Power and Energy: Ohm's Law Relationships
pts: Power, voltage, current and resistance are linked so any two known quantities determine the other two.
Voltage is measured in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms and power in watts.
Power can be found from voltage and current, or from current and resistance, or from voltage and resistance.
defs: Power (P)
The rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted, measured in watts (W).
Voltage (V)
The electric potential difference driving charge around a circuit, measured in volts (V).
Current (I)
The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A).
Resistance (R)
The opposition to current flow in a component, measured in ohms (Ω).
eqs: P = power (W); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
P = power (W); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
P = power (W); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω)
Voltage from current and resistance (Ohm's law)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
Current from voltage and resistance (Ohm's law)
I = current (A); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω)
Resistance from voltage and current (Ohm's law)
R = resistance (Ω); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert mA to A and kΩ to Ω before substituting into the power and Ohm's law equations.
Do not confuse the power formulas: P = I²R applies to current and resistance, while P = V²/R applies to voltage and resistance.
rq: Why can the power equation P = V²/R be used instead of P = V × I when only voltage and resistance are known?
Because substituting I = V/R (Ohm's law) into P = V × I gives P = V²/R, so current need not be measured.
What happens to the power dissipated in a fixed resistor if the voltage doubles?
Power quadruples, since P = V²/R and doubling V multiplies V² by four.

notes.t: Summary of DC circuit terms and quantities
pts: Circuit notation and element depiction give the basic language for drawing DC circuits.
Resistance, current and voltage are the core quantities introduced in this lecture.
Each quantity has a standard symbol, SI unit and unit abbreviation that must be used consistently.
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance and is measured in siemens.
Power and energy are linked to electrical quantities and measured in watts and joules.
defs: Resistance
Opposition to current flow in a circuit element, measured in ohms (Ω) with symbol R.
Conductance
The reciprocal of resistance, a measure of how easily current flows, measured in siemens (S) with symbol G.
Electric charge
A fundamental property of matter measured in coulombs (C) with symbol Q.
Electric potential
Electric potential energy per unit charge, measured in volts (V) with symbol V.
Energy
The capacity to do work, measured in joules (J) with symbol W.
Power
The rate at which energy is transferred or converted, measured in watts (W) with symbol P.
tips: Do not confuse the quantity symbol A (current) with the unit abbreviation A (amp); keep quantity symbols italic and units upright.
Watts (W) and ohms (Ω) use different symbols; do not mix up the power symbol P with the unit abbreviation W for watt, or the energy symbol W with watts.
rq: Why is the symbol for current A while the unit abbreviation is also A, and how could this cause confusion?

Current uses the symbol A in the table, which is also the abbreviation for amp; context must show whether a letter denotes the quantity or its unit, so write quantities in italics and units in roman type.
Why are conductance and resistance both needed if they describe the same property?
They are reciprocals; conductance is more convenient for parallel elements where conductances add, while resistance is more convenient for series elements where resistances add.

notes.t: DC Circuits Lecture 1 Summary
pts: Lecture 1 covered circuit notation, element depiction, and the core quantities resistance, current and voltage.
A formulae sheet is provided for each lecture to support revision.
A Moodle test quiz is available to practise before real quizzes begin after the next lecture.
The next lecture moves on to Kirchhoff's laws.
tips: Practise on the Moodle test quiz before the real quizzes start, since those will count toward assessment.
rq: Why is the next topic, Kirchhoff's laws, a natural follow-on from resistance, current and voltage?
Kirchhoff's laws describe how current and voltage behave across connected elements in a circuit, so they build directly on the three quantities introduced in Lecture 1.

xq.q: A heater element of resistance 23 Ω is connected to a 230 V d.c. supply for 2.0 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in kWh.
xq.a: P = 2300 W, so energy = 4.6 kWh
s: W = P t = 2.3 kW × 2.0 h = 4.6 kWh

xq.q: A resistor dissipates 0.5 W when 5 V is across it. The voltage is doubled to 10 V with the resistance unchanged. What is the new power dissipated?
xq.a: 2 W
o: 1 W
1.0 W, because P = VI doubles when V doubles
2 W
xq.w: P = V²/R so doubling V quadruples P to 2 W; the trap is treating power as proportional to V.

xq.q: A 330 Ω resistor carries a current of 40 mA. Show that the power dissipated is the same whether calculated using \(P = I^2R\) or \(P = V^2/R\), and state the value.
s: P = V²/R = 0.528 W, so they agree

units.name: Formula sheet DC lecture 1
units.ov: This sheet covers the basic DC circuit quantities (resistance, current, voltage and power) and the relationships linking them. Resistance comes from material geometry (\(R=\rho l/A\)). Ohm's law relates voltage to current through R, and power \(P=IV\) follows from energy per charge times charge per time. Together these form the toolkit for all later circuit analysis.
must: Ohm's law: \(V = IR\), valid only for a fixed linear resistance at constant temperature
Resistance of a conductor: \(R = \rho l / A\) (ρ in Ω·m, l in m, A in m²)
Power: \(P = IV\), and by substituting Ohm's law \(P = I^2R = V^2/R\)
Current is charge per unit time: \(I = Q/t\), with 1 A = 1 C/s
Voltage is energy per unit charge: \(V = W/Q\), and \(V = El\) for a uniform field (E in V/m)
Voltage is measured across an element; current is measured through it
Conductance: \(G = 1/R\) in siemens (S)
Slope of an I vs V graph gives \(1/R\) (conductance), not R; a straight line indicates ohmic behaviour
Unit hygiene: convert mA, cm² and mm² to SI before calculating; 1 W = 1 J/s
Combined form: \(V = I\rho l/A\), so doubling length doubles R and doubling area halves R
conn: Resistivity formula plus Ohm's law: geometry changes (stretching or changing wire diameter) alter R, which changes the current for a given V
Ohm's law plus power: substitute to get \(P=I^2R\) or \(V^2/R\) when only two of V, I, R are known (heating, fuse and rating problems)
Charge-time and current relations: \(Q = It\) combined with \(W = QV = Pt\) gives energy delivered over a time period
Electric field and voltage: \(V = El\) links field strength across a conductor to its potential difference and thus to current via \(R=\rho l/A\)
exq: A copper wire of length 50 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² has resistivity \(1.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}\). Calculate its resistance and the current when 12 V is applied.
A 230 V heater draws 10 A. Find its resistance, power, and the energy used in 3 hours in joules and kWh.
A charge of 120 C passes through a resistor in 40 s while the voltage across it is 9 V. Find the current, resistance, and power dissipated.
A wire is drawn to twice its length with constant volume and resistivity. By what factor does its resistance change, and what happens to the current at fixed voltage?
An I vs V graph for a component is a straight line through the origin with I = 0.25 A at V = 5 V. Find R and G, and explain why Ohm's law might fail if the component heats up.

notes.t: DC circuits: resistance, current, voltage, Ohm's law and power
pts: Resistance is the property of a material that restricts electron flow; it is measured in ohms and depends on resistivity, length and cross-sectional area.
Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor or circuit element, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).
Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points and is measured across a circuit element, whereas current is measured through it.
At constant temperature, current through a fixed linear resistance is directly proportional to the applied voltage; the slope of an I vs. V graph gives R.
Power is the rate of electrical energy transfer, measured in watts, where one watt is one joule per second.
defs: Resistance
The property of a material that restricts the flow of electrons; measured in ohms (Ω).
Current (I)
The time rate of flow of electrical charge through a conductor or circuit element; measured in amperes (A), where 1 A = 1 C/s.
Voltage (V)
The energy transferred per unit charge when a charge moves from one point in an electrical circuit to a second point; measured in volts.
Power
The rate of electrical energy transferred within a circuit; measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
Resistor
A component with a value of resistance.
eqs: resistivity = material resistivity (Ω·m); length = conductor length (m); area = cross-sectional area (m²)
Conductance = reciprocal of resistance (siemens, S); Resistance = (Ω)
I = current (A); Q = charge (C); t = time (s)
V = voltage (V); W = energy (J); Q = charge (C); E = electric field (V/m); l = length (m)
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = area (m²)
P = power (W); I = current (A); V = voltage (V)
tips: Ohm's law (V = IR) requires constant temperature and a fixed linear resistance; do not apply it blindly to temperature-dependent components.
Keep units consistent: resistivity in Ω·m with length in m and area in m² gives resistance in Ω; watch for mA or cm² conversions.
rq: Why does the I vs. V graph of a fixed linear resistor have a steeper slope when the resistance is lower?
Since I = V/R, slope = 1/R; lower resistance gives a larger slope, so the line is steeper.
If a resistor's temperature rises, what happens to the proportionality between I and V, and why does the formula's condition matter?
Ohm's law only holds at constant temperature because resistance changes with temperature, so the proportionality breaks down.
Why is voltage measured across a component while current is measured through it?
Voltage is an energy-per-charge difference between two points, so it needs two connection points; current is charge flow, so it must pass through the element.

xq.q: A copper cable of length \(l = 200\) m has a uniform cross-sectional area \(A = 0.50\) mm². The resistivity of copper is \(\rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m. A steady current \(I = 2.5\) A flows along the cable. Calculate the power dissipated in the cable.
A steady current of 250 mA flows through a resistor for 2 minutes. How much charge passes through the resistor?
xq.w: \(Q = It = 0.25\ \text{A}\times120\ \text{s} = 30\) C; the traps are leaving time in minutes, leaving the current in mA, and dividing instead of multiplying.
s: Convert 250 mA = 0.25 A and 2 min = 120 s

xq.q: A fixed linear resistor R is connected across a supply of voltage V. Show that the power dissipated is \(P = V^2/R\), and hence explain what happens to the power when V is doubled, assuming R stays constant.
xq.a: Start from P = IV. Ohm's law gives I = V/R, so P = (V/R)V = V²/R. If V is doubled, P becomes (2V)²/R = 4V²/R, so the power quadruples. This assumes R is constant (constant temperature, linear resistor).
s: Substitute \(I = V/R\) (Ohm's law) to get \(P = V^2/R\)
Power increases by a factor of 4, assuming R is constant

units.name: Mentimeter Questions Lecture1
units.ov: This is a short set of lecture-1 Mentimeter notes covering course logistics (formula sheet, quiz weighting, no need to memorise the resistor colour code) and one core technical idea: the resistance of a uniform conductor, R = ρl/A. The technical content is mostly about using SI units correctly, especially converting mm² to m², and checking dimensional consistency. The notes contain very little technical content, so a top-grade student should master this formula and its unit handling thoroughly.
must: Resistance of a uniform conductor: \( R = \frac{\rho l}{A} \), with R in Ω, ρ in Ω·m, l in m and A in m²
R is proportional to resistivity and length, and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (doubling l doubles R; doubling A halves R)
Resistivity ρ is a material property: the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-section of the material, in Ω·m
Copper resistivity is given as \( 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m} \)
Area conversion: \( 1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2 \), because the length factor \( 10^{3} \) is squared to give \( 10^{6} \)
Convert everything to SI base units (m, m²) before substituting, otherwise the answer can be off by orders of magnitude
Dimensional check: \( \Omega\,\text{m}\times\text{m}/\text{m}^2=\Omega \), which confirms the formula is consistent
Different resistor symbols (zigzag or rectangle) represent the same component; read the label R and its value

Admin: the formula sheet is on Moodle and the resistor colour code need not be memorised; the Moodle quizzes allow unlimited attempts, the highest grade counts, and together they are worth 5% of the module
conn: Resistivity and geometry link to Ohm's law: calculate R = ρl/A first, then use V = IR to find the current or voltage drop across a wire

Unit conversion and the resistance formula appear together: a wire diameter or area given in mm² must be converted to m² before use, and a diameter must first be turned into area with \( A=\pi d^2/4 \)
Dimensional analysis can be used to check any rearrangement of R = ρl/A, for example making ρ or l the subject
Wire resistance feeds into circuit analysis: a wire's R can be treated as a resistor in series or parallel with other components, with the symbol having no effect on the analysis
exq: A copper wire (ρ = 1.72×10⁻⁸ Ω·m) is 50 m long with cross-sectional area 2.5 mm². Calculate its resistance, stating the unit conversion used.
A copper conductor of length 100 m must have a resistance no greater than 0.5 Ω. Find the minimum cross-sectional area in mm².
A wire has resistance R. It is replaced by a wire of the same material with twice the length and twice the diameter. Find the new resistance in terms of R.
Show by dimensional analysis that \( R=\rho l/A \) gives units of ohms, and explain why using A in mm² without conversion gives an error of a factor of 10⁶.
A 20 m copper cable of diameter 1.8 mm carries 10 A. Calculate its resistance and the voltage drop along it.

notes.t: Resistor circuit symbols
pts: Two different resistor symbols are shown, and either can be used in a circuit diagram.
The zigzag and rectangular symbols both represent a resistor with resistance R; the answer to whether it matters is no.
tips: Do not treat different circuit symbols for the same component as different components; check the label (R) and value instead.
rq: Why does it not matter which resistor symbol is used, even though the drawings look different?
Both symbols represent the same component, a resistor with resistance R; the symbol is only a convention, and the circuit behaviour depends on the resistance value, not the drawing style.

notes.t: Unit conversion of area (mm² to m²) and resistance of a wire
pts: Converting mm² to m² requires a factor of a million, because each metre is 1000 mm and area is squared.
Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its resistivity and length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Resistivity of copper is given as 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, so all lengths and areas must be in metres and metres squared before substitution.
The unit of resistance works out as Ω·m × m / m² = Ω, confirming the formula is dimensionally consistent.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit length and unit cross-sectional area of the material; measured in ohm-metres (Ω·m).
eqs: Resistance of a conductor of uniform cross-section
R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Unit trap: a factor of 10³ is used for length conversions (mm to m) but the area conversion must be squared, giving 10⁶.
Always convert all quantities to SI base units (m, m²) before substituting into R = ρl/A to avoid an answer off by orders of magnitude.
rq: Why does converting 2.5 mm² to m² give 10⁻⁶ rather than 10⁻³?
Because 1 m = 1000 mm, so 1 m² = (1000)² mm² = 10⁶ mm²; the area is squared, so the factor is a million, not a thousand.
What happens to the resistance if the wire's cross-sectional area is doubled, with length and material unchanged?
The resistance halves, since R = ρl/A is inversely proportional to area.

xq.q: A copper supply cable of length \(l = 30\) m has a uniform cross-sectional area \(A = 2.5\) mm². The resistivity of copper is \(\rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m. A current of 10 A flows through the cable. Calculate the voltage drop along the cable.
A conductor has a cross-sectional area of 4 mm². What is this area in m², for use in \(R = \rho l/A\)?
o: 4×10⁶ m²
xq.w: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶ m²; the trap is using the length factor unsquared.

xq.q: A wire of resistance R is replaced by a wire of the same material that is twice as long and has half the cross-sectional area. Show that the resistance of the new wire is 4R, and explain the physical reason for each change.
xq.a: R = ρl/A. New wire: R' = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4ρl/A = 4R. Doubling the length doubles the path that restricts electron flow; halving the area halves the cross-section available for current, which doubles the resistance again. Resistivity is unchanged because the material is the same.
s: R is proportional to l and inversely proportional to A; ρ is unchanged

notes.t: Unit conversion of area (mm² to m²) and resistance of a wire
pts: Area conversion from mm² to m² uses the square of the length factor, not the length factor itself, because 1 mm = 10⁻³ m gives 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².
Resistance of a uniform conductor is proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.

defs: Resistivity (ρ)
A material property giving the resistance of a unit-length, unit-area sample of the material; units Ω·m.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); ρ = resistivity (Ω·m); l = length (m); A = cross-sectional area (m²)
tips: Do not convert mm² to m² by multiplying by 10⁻³; square the linear conversion factor to get 10⁻⁶.

rq: Why does converting 2.5 mm² to m² give a factor of 10⁻⁶ rather than 10⁻³?

If the wire's cross-sectional area doubled, what would happen to its resistance, and why?

xq.q: A coil of copper wire has a measured resistance \(R = 0.86\) Ω and a uniform cross-sectional area \(A = 1.5\) mm². The resistivity of copper is \(\rho = 1.72\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m. Calculate the length of the wire.
A wire has resistance R. A second wire of the same material has half the length and twice the cross-sectional area of the first. What is its resistance?
o: R
4R
xq.w: \(R\propto l/A\), so halving l and doubling A each halve R, giving R/4; the traps are applying only one change or inverting the dependence on A.

xq.q: (a) Show that the resistance formula \(R = \rho l/A\) is dimensionally consistent, given that ρ is in Ω·m, l in m and A in m². (b) A student substitutes an area of 2 mm² into the formula as 2×10⁻³ m². By what factor is the calculated resistance in error, and in which direction?
xq.a: (a) Units of ρl/A = Ω·m × m / m² = Ω, which matches the unit of resistance. (b) The correct area is 2×10⁻⁶ m² because 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². Using 2×10⁻³ m² makes A too large by a factor of 10³, so R is too small by a factor of 1000.
s: Correct conversion: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², so A = 2×10⁻⁶ m²
The student's area is 10³ times too large
R ∝ 1/A, so the calculated R is 1000 times too small

units.name: 2.1 Lecture intro, recap and learning outcomes
units.ov: This material recaps circuit notation and Ohm's law (V = IR) and sets out Lecture 2's outcomes: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, series and parallel resistor networks with voltage and current dividers, and power in these circuits. Ohm's law applies to single components, and Kirchhoff's laws link components together, so together they form the basis of all later circuit analysis.
must: Ohm's law: \( V = IR \), with the rearrangements \( I = V/R \) and \( R = V/I \); use the triangle as a memory aid
Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the sum of currents into a node is zero, which expresses conservation of charge
Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero, which expresses conservation of energy
Do not confuse KCL (node, charge) with KVL (loop, energy); name the correct law and apply it to the correct node or loop
Ohm's law applies to one component and the voltage across that component; do not mix up voltages across different branches
Convert units before calculating: mA to A, k\(\Omega\) to \(\Omega\)
Series and parallel resistor combinations are analysed with voltage dividers (series) and current dividers (parallel)
Power in series and parallel circuits, using \( P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R \) (standard relations, not in these notes), is the third learning outcome
Know the circuit symbols: voltage source (battery), switch, conductor (wire), resistance (load such as a headlamp)
conn: Ohm's law with KVL: write the loop equation, substitute \( V = IR \) for each resistor, and solve for the current
Ohm's law with KCL: at a parallel junction the branch currents (each \( V/R \)) sum to the supply current, which leads to the current divider
KVL in a series circuit gives the voltage divider, because the source voltage splits in proportion to resistance
Power calculations need the voltages and currents found by Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws, and the total power supplied equals the total power dissipated
exq: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 k\(\Omega\) resistor. Find the current in mA and the power dissipated, converting units correctly.

Three resistors of 100 \(\Omega\), 220 \(\Omega\) and 330 \(\Omega\) are in series with a 9 V source. Use KVL to find the current and the voltage across each resistor, and check that the voltages sum to 9 V.
At a node, currents of 3 A and 2 A flow in and one current of 1.2 A flows out. Use KCL to find the remaining current and its direction.

Two resistors of 6 \(\Omega\) and 12 \(\Omega\) are in parallel across a 24 V supply. Use a current divider to find each branch current and the total power, then compare with the power in the equivalent single resistor.
Explain the physical principle behind KCL and KVL, and describe a common mistake made when applying Ohm's law to a multi-branch circuit.

notes.t: Previous Lecture: Circuit Notation, Voltage, Current, Resistance and Ohm's Law
pts: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols: a voltage source represents the battery, a switch controls the circuit, conductors represent wires, and resistances represent loads such as headlamps.
Voltage, current and resistance are the three linked quantities of a circuit, and Ohm's law relates them.
The triangle diagram is a memory aid for Ohm's law: cover the quantity you want to find and the remaining positions give its formula.
eqs: Ohm's law: voltage across a resistor from current and resistance
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (\Omega)
Current from voltage and resistance (rearranged Ohm's law)
I = current (A); V = voltage (V); R = resistance (\Omega)
Resistance from voltage and current (rearranged Ohm's law)
R = resistance (\Omega); V = voltage (V); I = current (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert milliamps to amps and kilo-ohms to ohms before applying \( V = IR \).
Ohm's law applies to the resistance of a single component across which the voltage is measured; do not mix up the voltage across different branches of a circuit.
rq: Why does the triangle diagram show V on top with I and R underneath?

V is the product of I and R, so it sits above; I and R are the quantities that are multiplied together, while the single line shows division, so covering V leaves I × R and covering I or R leaves V ÷ the other quantity.
What happens to the current in the circuit if the resistance of a headlamp doubles while the 12 V supply stays the same?
By I = V/R, the current halves, since the voltage is fixed and the resistance is doubled.

notes.t: Learning Outcomes: Kirchhoff's Laws, Series-Parallel Circuits
pts: This lecture covers Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws as the foundation of circuit analysis.
Resistors in series and parallel are analysed using voltage dividers and current dividers.
Power in series and parallel circuits is the third learning outcome.
tips: Do not confuse Kirchhoff's current law (node/charge conservation) with the voltage law (loop/energy conservation).
rq: Why are Kirchhoff's laws listed before resistor divider rules?
Divider rules are derived from Kirchhoff's laws applied to series (voltage) and parallel (current) connections, so the laws come first.

xq.q: A series circuit has a single 12 V source and two resistors. The current is measured as I = 2.5 mA. The voltage across resistor \(R_1\) is 7.5 V. Find the resistance of the second resistor \(R_2\), in kΩ.
A student wants to find the resistance of a resistor R when the voltage across it is 6 V and the current through it is 15 mA. Which value is correct?
xq.w: R = V/I = 6/0.015 = 400 Ω; the traps are inverting the ratio and forgetting to convert mA to A.

xq.q: Explain why the voltage in Ohm's law \(V = IR\) must be the voltage measured across the same resistor that carries the current I, and illustrate with a series circuit of a 10 V source with \(R_1 = 1\) kΩ and \(R_2 = 4\) kΩ, finding the voltage across \(R_2\).
xq.a: Ohm's law relates the current through a component to the voltage across that same component, so using the source voltage for one resistor of a series pair is wrong. Total R = 5 kΩ, I = 10/5000 = 2 mA, and V across R2 = 2 mA × 4 kΩ = 8 V, not 10 V.
s: Ohm's law applies to a single component's own voltage
Series total R = 5 kΩ, I = 2 mA
\(V_{R2}\) = IR2 = 8 V (not the 10 V source voltage)

units.name: 2.2 Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
units.ov: This module introduces Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL), which says charge is conserved at any node, so the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. It is applied first to general nodes with a sign convention, then to parallel circuits where \(I_{T}\) = \(I_{1}\) + \(I_{2}\) + \(I_{3}\), and finally to a ladder-style circuit where unknown currents are found by working node by node (X then Y). Together these give a systematic method for finding unknown branch currents.
must: KCL statement: \(\sum I_{IN} = \sum I_{OUT}\), equivalent to the algebraic sum of currents at a node being zero; this expresses conservation of charge
A node is any point where two or more circuit elements join, so identify nodes before writing equations
Sign convention: currents entering are positive and leaving are negative (or the reverse), applied consistently in every node equation, e.g. \(i_1 + i_2 - i_3 = 0\)
Parallel circuits: \(I_T = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\), because the source current splits across the branches
Finding an unknown branch current: \(I_2 = I_T - I_1 - I_3\)
Convert all currents to the same units (mA or A) before adding or subtracting, e.g. 100 − 30 − 20 = 50 mA
Parallel branches share the same voltage but divide the current, whereas KCL concerns currents at a node and KVL concerns voltages around a loop; do not mix them up
A negative result for a current means its true direction is opposite to the one assumed; it is not an error
conn: KCL with Ohm's law: branch currents in parallel are \(I = V/R\) at a common voltage, so \(I_T = V(1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3)\), which gives the equivalent resistance and the current divider
KCL with KVL: nodal and loop equations together solve circuits with several unknowns, and the sign convention must be consistent across both
Sequential nodes (X then Y): the output current from one node becomes the input to the next, so errors propagate down the chain
KCL with ammeter readings: ammeters in series read branch current, so questions give some readings and ask for the others by applying KCL
exq: A node has currents \(i_1 = 4\) A and \(i_2 = 3\) A entering and \(i_3\) leaving. Write the KCL equation with a stated sign convention and find \(i_3\). Then find the current in a further branch if \(i_3\) splits into 2 A and an unknown.
A source supplies \(I_T = 100\) mA to three parallel resistors. \(I_1 = 30\) mA and \(I_3 = 20\) mA. Find \(I_2\). If the supply is 10 V, calculate \(R_1\), \(R_2\) and \(R_3\).
In the ammeter circuit, A1 reads 5 mA and A2 reads 1.5 mA at node X, and A4 reads 1 mA at node Y. Find the readings of A3 and A5, showing the KCL equation at each node.
A node has three branch currents with directions marked: \(i_5 + i_6 + i_7 = 0\). Given \(i_5 = 2\) A and \(i_6 = -5\) A, find \(i_7\) and state its actual direction relative to the node.
Explain the difference between KCL and KVL. State which one you would use at a junction and which around a loop, and explain why parallel branches share a voltage but not a current.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
pts: At any node, the total current flowing in equals the total current flowing out, so charge is conserved.
A node is any point where two or more circuit elements are joined together.
Currents entering a node are taken as positive and leaving as negative when writing the node equation as a sum equal to zero.
In a parallel branch arrangement, the total current from the source splits across the branches so the total equals the sum of the branch currents.
defs: Node
A point in an electrical circuit at which two or more circuit elements are joined together.
Kirchhoff's Current Law
The sum of the currents entering a node equals the sum of the currents leaving that node.
eqs: KCL in summation form: total current entering a node equals total current leaving it
\(I_{IN}\) = current entering the node (A); \(I_{OUT}\) = current leaving the node (A)
KCL at node a: net current into the node is zero
\(i_1\), \(i_2\) = currents entering node a (A); \(i_3\) = current leaving node a (A)
KCL at node b: net current into the node is zero
\(i_5\), \(i_6\), \(i_7\) = branch currents at node b with signs set by direction (A)
Total source current split across parallel branches
\(I_T\) = total current from source (A); \(I_1, I_2, I_3\) = branch currents (A)
tips: Be consistent with sign convention: currents entering are positive and leaving negative (or vice versa) in every node equation; mixing conventions gives wrong results.
Do not confuse KCL (currents at a node) with Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (voltages around a loop).
rq: Why does KCL follow from conservation of charge?
Charge cannot accumulate at a node, so the charge arriving per unit time must equal the charge leaving per unit time; hence incoming and outgoing currents balance.
If a node has three currents, two entering at 2 A and 3 A, what is the leaving current?
Leaving current = 2 A + 3 A = 5 A, since entering current equals leaving current.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Current Law in a Parallel Circuit
pts: In a parallel circuit the total current entering a junction equals the sum of the branch currents leaving it.
An unknown branch current can be found by subtracting the known branch currents from the total current.
Branch currents divide the total current; each branch with its own resistor carries its own share of \(I_{T}\).
defs: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
The algebraic sum of currents entering a node equals the sum of currents leaving it; in a parallel circuit, the total current equals the sum of the branch currents.
eqs: Total current in a parallel circuit (KCL)
\(I_{T}\) = total source current (A); \(I_{1}\), \(I_{2}\), \(I_{3}\) = branch currents through \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) (A)
\(I_{2}\) = current through \(R_{2}\) (A); \(I_{T}\) = total current (A); \(I_{1}\) = current through \(R_{1}\) (A); \(I_{3}\) = current through \(R_{3}\) (A)
tips: Keep units consistent: 100 mA - 30 mA - 20 mA must all be in mA before subtracting (or convert to A).
Do not confuse KCL (currents add at a node) with KVL (voltages around a loop sum to zero); branches in parallel share the same voltage but split the current.
rq: Why can we find \(I_{2}\) by subtraction rather than using Ohm's law on \(R_{2}\)?

Because in a parallel circuit the total current splits among the branches, so KCL gives \(I_{2}\) directly from \(I_{T}\), \(I_{1}\) and \(I_{3}\) without needing \(R_{2}\)'s value or the source voltage.
What would happen to \(I_{2}\) if \(I_{3}\) were removed from the circuit?
\(I_{2}\) would increase to 70 mA, since the 20 mA branch no longer takes its share of the 100 mA total (100 - 30 = 70 mA).

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Current Law applied to nodes X and Y
pts: Kirchhoff's current law: the algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero, so the current entering a node equals the current leaving it.
At node X the 5 mA supplied by ammeter A1 splits: 1.5 mA goes down branch R1 (measured by A2) and the remainder flows on through ammeter A3.
At node Y the 3.5 mA arriving through A3 splits: 1 mA goes down branch R2 (measured by A4) and the rest flows through ammeter A5.
Working through the nodes in order, each unknown branch current is found by subtracting the known branch currents from the total current into the node.
defs: Node
A junction point in a circuit where two or more branches are connected; current entering and leaving a node is governed by Kirchhoff's current law.
eqs: Kirchhoff's current law applied at node X to find the current through ammeter A3
\(I_{A3}\) = current through ammeter A3 (mA); \(I_{X,in}\) = total current into node X (mA); \(I_{A2}\) = current through ammeter A2 (mA)
Kirchhoff's current law applied at node Y to find the current through ammeter A5
\(I_{A5}\) = current through ammeter A5 (mA); \(I_{Y,in}\) = total current into node Y (mA); \(I_{A4}\) = current through ammeter A4 (mA)
tips: Use the correct sign convention: currents entering the node are positive and currents leaving are negative when writing the KCL equation.
Keep units consistent (all in mA) before subtracting; mixing mA and A gives wrong answers.
rq: Why does the current through A3 equal 3.5 mA rather than 5 mA?
Current divides at node X: 1.5 mA leaves through branch R1 (A2), so only 5 − 1.5 = 3.5 mA continues through A3, because charge cannot accumulate at a node.
What would happen to \(I_{A5}\) if ammeter A4 read 2 mA instead of 1 mA?
\(I_{A5}\) would fall to 3.5 − 2 = 1.5 mA, since the current left for A5 is whatever remains after all branches off node Y.

xq.q: A source supplies a total current \(I_T = 120\) mA to three parallel branches. The currents in branches 1 and 3 are \(I_1 = 35\) mA and \(I_3 = 0.045\) A. Find the current \(I_2\) in branch 2, in mA.
xq.a: I2 = 40 mA

xq.q: At a node, \(i_1 = 4\) mA and \(i_2 = 3\) mA enter, and \(i_3\) leaves. Using KCL, what is \(i_3\)?
xq.a: 7 mA
o: 1 mA
12 mA
7 mA
-7 mA
xq.w: Current out equals current in, so i3 = 4 + 3 = 7 mA; subtracting the entering currents is the sign trap.
s: Sum in = sum out: i3 = 4 + 3 = 7 mA

xq.q: In a circuit, ammeter A1 reads 8 mA into node X. A branch through R1 carries 2.5 mA. The remaining current passes on to node Y, where a branch through R2 carries 1.5 mA and the rest flows through ammeter A5. Find the reading of A5, in mA.

units.name: 2.3 Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) and energy conservation
units.ov: This module covers Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero. It shows how to write loop equations with a consistent sign convention, apply KVL to series circuits to find source voltages and unknown resistances, and derive KVL from energy conservation (power absorbed sums to zero). Ohm's law and the power relation \(p=vi\) link KVL to practical calculations.
must: State KVL: \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} v_k = 0\) around any closed loop, which expresses conservation of energy
Sign convention: going + to − across an element adds its voltage; going − to + subtracts it. Pick one traversal direction and use it for every element in the loop
Series loop with a source: \(-V_S + \sum V_k = 0\), so \(V_S = V_{R1}+V_{R2}+\dots\) (e.g. 5 V + 10 V = 15 V; 6.6 V + 5.4 V = 12 V)
In a series loop the same current flows through every resistor, so \(V_R = IR\) gives each drop
Finding an unknown resistance: use KVL to get \(V_4 = V_S - V_1 - V_2 - V_3\), then \(R_4 = V_4/I\). Convert units first, e.g. 10 mA = 0.01 A
Power absorbed by an element is \(p = vi\) with the passive sign convention. The sign is + only if current enters the + terminal, and reversed polarity gives \(p=-vi\)
Energy conservation: \(p_a+p_b+p_c=0\). Factoring out the common current \(i\) gives KVL, \(v_a - v_b + v_c = 0\), which is valid only because the same \(i\) flows through every element
Closed loop: a path that starts and ends at the same node and passes through no node more than once. An outer loop equation is a combination of the inner loop equations, so it is not independent
KVL uses voltage polarity only, not current direction. Voltages are measured across components, not through them
conn: KVL + Ohm's law: write the loop equation, substitute \(V=IR\) for each resistor, then solve for the unknown current, voltage or resistance
KVL + power: the sum of power absorbed equals the sum of power delivered, so a power-balance check can verify KVL results and the sign of each element
KVL + KCL: in multi-loop circuits the current differs between branches, so KCL gives the branch currents that go into the KVL loop equations
Independent loops: choose only independent loops (inner loops) for simultaneous equations, because an outer loop adds no new information
exq: A 12 V source drives a series loop of R1, R2 and R3. The drops across R1 and R2 are 3.5 V and 4.5 V. Use KVL to find the voltage across R3, and its resistance if the loop current is 20 mA.

Write the KVL equations for two adjacent loops that share an element, with loop 1 containing elements a, b, c and loop 2 containing c, d, e. Then write the outer-loop equation and show it is dependent on the other two.
A series circuit has a 24 V source and four resistors. The known drops are 4 V, 6 V and 8 V and the current is 10 mA. Find \(R_4\) and give the answer in ohms and kΩ.

Elements A, B and C carry the same current \(i\) in one loop, with B's polarity reversed relative to the current. Write \(p_a\), \(p_b\) and \(p_c\), show that \(p_a+p_b+p_c=0\) leads to KVL, and explain why \(i\) can be factored out.

A loop has a source \(V_S\) and resistors with measured drops of 5 V and 10 V. Find \(V_S\), then calculate the power delivered by the source and absorbed by each resistor for \(I = 0.5\) A, and verify power balance.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
pts: In any closed loop, the algebraic sum of voltages is zero, so the voltage rises and drops around a loop cancel out.
Sign convention: moving from + to − across an element adds its voltage; moving from − to + subtracts it.
Each loop equation is written by traversing the loop in one direction and applying the sign convention to every element met.
Loop 3 is an outer loop that passes around the whole circuit, so its equation is a combination of the inner loop equations and is not independent of them.
defs: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
In any closed loop of an electrical circuit, the algebraic sum of all voltages around the loop is zero.
Closed loop
A path through a circuit that starts and ends at the same node, passing through no node more than once.
eqs: \(v_{k}\) = voltage across the k-th element in the loop (V); n = number of elements in the loop
tips: Be consistent with the traversal direction: every element in one loop must be signed using the same direction of travel.
Do not confuse the sign convention for voltage with current direction; KVL uses voltage polarity (+/−) only.
rq: Why does a voltage drop receive a negative sign when the loop is traversed in the direction shown?

Because travelling from + to − across an element means adding its voltage per the convention, while the loop equation sums with the sign set by the traversal direction; a drop opposite to the traversal direction is subtracted, so the sign depends on the direction of travel relative to the + terminal.
What if you traversed Loop 1 in the opposite (anticlockwise) direction?
Every sign in the equation would reverse, giving \(v_{a}\) − \(v_{b}\) − \(v_{c}\) = 0 ... equivalently the same equation multiplied by −1, so the physical result is unchanged.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) in a series loop
pts: Around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of voltage rises and drops is zero; the source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops across the resistors.
Voltages measured across each resistor in series add up to the total supplied voltage, as shown by the meters reading 6.6 V + 5.4 V = 12 V.
The sign of each voltage depends on whether it is a rise or a drop when travelling around the loop in one chosen direction.
defs: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
The algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
eqs: KVL for a closed loop with a source and drops
\(v_{s}\) = source voltage (V); \(v_{k}\) = individual voltage drops across loop elements (V)
Total voltage for series resistors (applied to the example)
tips: Keep a consistent sign convention: a voltage rise and a voltage drop must be given opposite signs when writing the loop equation.
Voltages are measured across components, not through them; do not confuse the meter reading with the current through the resistor.
rq: Why must the voltage drops around the loop add to the source voltage, rather than being independent of it?
Energy is conserved: the source supplies energy per charge equal to the energy dissipated across the resistors as the charge completes one loop, so the voltages must balance.
What would change in the sign of the equation if you traversed the loop in the opposite direction?
Every term flips sign, but the equation still equals zero, so the physical result is unchanged.

notes.t: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: finding source voltage from voltage drops
pts: Around a closed loop, the sum of voltage rises and drops is zero (KVL).
With the source as a rise and resistors as drops, the source voltage equals the sum of the drops in the loop.
Here the two resistor drops are 5 V and 10 V, so the source must supply 15 V.
eqs: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law applied to the loop (sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero)
\(V_{S}\) = source voltage (V); \(V_{R1}\) = voltage drop across \(R_{1}\) (V); \(V_{R2}\) = voltage drop across \(R_{2}\) (V)
Source voltage as the sum of the series resistor voltage drops
\(V_{S}\) = source voltage (V); \(V_{R1}\) = voltage drop across \(R_{1}\) (V); \(V_{R2}\) = voltage drop across \(R_{2}\) (V)
tips: Keep a consistent loop direction and sign convention; a drop traversed in the direction of current is negative when moving around the loop.
Voltage drops in a series loop add to give the source voltage only when all drops are taken with the same sign convention; mixing signs gives wrong answers.
rq: Why does the source voltage equal the sum of the drops rather than their difference?
Because the source is a voltage rise around the loop, and KVL requires rises to balance drops, so the drops add up to the source voltage.
What would happen to \(V_{S}\) if the polarity of \(R_{2}\)'s voltage were reversed in the loop direction you traversed?
That drop would become a rise in your sign convention, so \(V_{S}\) would equal \(V_{R1}\) − \(V_{R2}\) = −5 V, meaning the sign convention must be applied consistently.

notes.t: Finding an unknown resistance using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law in a series loop
pts: In a series loop the same current flows through every resistor, so each voltage drop is found with Ohm's law, V = IR.
Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of all voltage rises and drops around a closed loop is zero, so the source voltage balances the drops.
Once the unknown voltage across R4 is known from KVL, its resistance follows from Ohm's law using the loop current.
defs: Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)
In any closed loop of a circuit, the sum of the voltage rises equals the sum of the voltage drops, so the net voltage around the loop is zero.
eqs: Voltage drop across a resistor (Ohm's law)
\(V_{R}\) = voltage across the resistor (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop
\(V_{S}\) = source voltage (V); \(V_{1}\)…\(V_{4}\) = voltage drops across each resistor (V)
Unknown resistance from voltage and current
\(R_{4}\) = resistance (Ω); \(V_{4}\) = voltage across \(R_{4}\) (V); I = loop current (A)
tips: Keep signs consistent: source voltage is a rise, resistor drops are falls, so write -\(V_{S}\) + ... = 0 and do not drop the minus sign.
Convert units before dividing: 10 mA must be used as 0.01 A to give ohms, or the result is in kΩ when using mA with kΩ.
rq: Why can we find each resistor's voltage drop directly with V = IR without knowing the voltage of the other resistors?
Because the resistors are in series, so the same current I = 10 mA flows through each, and each drop depends only on its own resistance.
What would happen to the calculated R4 if the source voltage were recorded as 40 V instead of 50 V?
V4 would be 24.3 V, so R4 = 24.3 V / 10 mA = 2.43 kΩ; the result depends directly on the source voltage.

notes.t: Energy Conservation Using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
pts: Power absorbed by each element is the product of its voltage and the current through it, with sign set by the passive reference convention; for element B the sign flips because its reference polarity is opposite to the assumed current direction.
Summing the power of all elements in a closed loop gives zero, so the power delivered equals the power absorbed (energy conservation).
Because the same current i flows through every element in the loop, the common factor i can be factored out, leaving Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop.
defs: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
The algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
Power (P)
The rate at which an element absorbs or delivers energy, equal to the product of voltage across the element and current through it.
eqs: \(p_{a}\) = power absorbed by A (W); \(v_{a}\) = voltage across A (V); i = current through A (A)
\(p_{b}\) = power absorbed by B (W); \(v_{b}\) = voltage across B (V); i = current through B (A)
\(p_{c}\) = power absorbed by C (W); \(v_{c}\) = voltage across C (V); i = current through C (A)
\(p_{a}\), \(p_{b}\), \(p_{c}\) = power absorbed by elements A, B, C (W)
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law for the loop
\(v_{a}\), \(v_{b}\), \(v_{c}\) = voltages across elements A, B, C (V)
tips: Watch the sign convention: an element's power is +v·i only when current enters at the + terminal; reversed polarity introduces a minus sign.
Factoring out i is only valid because the same current flows through all elements in the single loop; in multi-loop circuits check the current in each element.
rq: Why does the power of element B carry a minus sign while A and C do not?

Element B's assumed polarity (+ at top) is opposite to the direction of the reference current i relative to its voltage convention, so its absorbed power is −\(v_{b}\) i; the sign follows the passive sign convention.
Why must the total power in the loop sum to zero?
Energy is conserved: the power delivered by sources equals the power absorbed by the loop elements, so the net power over the loop is zero.
What happens to the KVL result if the current direction through B is reversed?
The sign of the B term in the power sum changes, but the loop relation is still a KVL-type sum of voltages with signs set by the reference polarities of each element.

xq.q: A series loop contains a 24 V source and three resistors. The voltage drops across the first two resistors are 7.2 V and 9.6 V. The loop current is 4 mA. Find the resistance of the third resistor \(R_3\), in kΩ.

Applying KVL to a loop, traversed from the source's negative terminal to its positive terminal and then around through resistors \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) with drops \(V_{R1}\) and \(V_{R2}\), which equation is correct, where \(V_S\) is the source voltage?
xq.w: The source is a rise and the resistor drops are opposite in sign, so \(V_{S}\) = \(V_{R1}\) + \(V_{R2}\); giving all terms the same sign or omitting the source breaks KVL.
s: Rise and drops carry opposite signs

xq.q: Two meters across the two series resistors of a circuit read 6.6 V and 5.4 V. Use KVL to find the source voltage and explain, in terms of energy, why the voltages must add in this way.
xq.a: Take the loop with the source as a rise: -Vs + 6.6 + 5.4 = 0, so Vs = 12 V. KVL expresses energy conservation: the energy gained per unit charge from the source equals the energy lost per unit charge in the resistors around a closed loop, so the net voltage is zero.
s: Energy per charge gained = energy per charge lost around the loop

units.name: 2.4 Series circuits, resistors in series and voltage divider
units.ov: This material covers series circuits, where a single current path means every element carries the same current and the voltages differ. It builds from Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law to the equivalent resistance \(R_T=\sum R_i\), then to the voltage divider, where each resistor takes a share of the source voltage in proportion to its resistance. The ideas connect because a common current turns Ohm's law applied to the whole string into a ratio rule for any single resistor.
must: Series elements share one current path, so the current is identical through each; voltage differs. Parallel elements share the same voltage and the current splits.
Equivalent series resistance: \(R_T = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n\)
KVL for a series loop: \(V_B = V_1 + V_2 + \cdots = I(R_1+R_2+\cdots)\), with consistent polarity signs.
Circuit current by Ohm's law on the whole string: \(I = \dfrac{V_B}{R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n}\)
Voltage divider rule: \(V_k = V_B\dfrac{R_k}{R_T}\). The numerator is the resistor of interest, and the denominator is the total of every resistor in the series path.
Ratio of voltages across series resistors: \(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}=\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}\). This holds only because the current is common. The larger resistor takes the larger voltage drop.
Method: find \(R_T\), then \(I\), then \(V=IR\) for each resistor. Check that the drops sum to \(V_B\) (for example, 9 V across 6 kΩ out of 15 V).
Keep units consistent: all in Ω or all in kΩ within a ratio, and V, A, Ω in \(V=IR\).
Identify series from how the ends are joined (end to end, no branch point), not from how the drawing looks. Never use the series sum or the divider rule for parallel resistors.
conn: KVL and Ohm's law together give the divider: \(V_B=I R_T\) and \(V_k=IR_k\) combine to \(V_k=V_B R_k/R_T\).
The series current rule (same \(I\)) is the reason the divider ratio \(V_1/V_2=R_1/R_2\) works. It fails once a parallel branch or a load draws extra current from the divider node.
Mixed circuits: reduce parallel groups to an equivalent resistance, treat it as one resistor in the series chain, then apply the divider and expand back to find branch currents.
Power links in as well: \(P=I^2R\) in series means the largest resistor dissipates the most power, and the total power is \(V_B I\).
exq: Three resistors of 2 kΩ, 3 kΩ and 5 kΩ are connected in series across a 20 V supply. Find the equivalent resistance, the current, and the voltage across each resistor. Verify with KVL.
A 15 V source drives four series resistors, and R4 = 6 kΩ drops 9 V. Find the total resistance and the current. If R1 drops 1.5 V, what is R1?
Design a voltage divider from a 12 V supply to give 5 V across R2 using standard resistor values. State the ratio \(R_1/R_2\) required and the current drawn if \(R_2 = 10\,\text{k}\Omega\).
Explain why the divider formula gives the wrong output when a load resistor is connected across R2. Calculate the actual output for \(R_1=R_2=10\,\text{k}\Omega\), \(V_B=10\) V and a 10 kΩ load.
Two resistors in series have \(V_1/V_2 = 3\) and a total of 24 V across them. Find V1 and V2. If \(R_1+R_2=8\,\text{k}\Omega\), find R1, R2 and the current.

notes.t: Series and Parallel Circuits (Kirchhoff's and Ohm's laws)
pts: Elements in series are connected end to end, so they share one current path and carry the same current.
Elements in parallel have both ends connected to corresponding ends of the other element, giving multiple current paths.
In a series circuit the current is the same through each element, but the voltage across each differs.
In a parallel circuit the voltage across each element is the same, but the current splits between the branches.
defs: Series connection
Circuit elements are connected end to end so that they form a single current path and carry the same current.
Parallel connection
Elements are connected such that both ends of each element connect directly to corresponding ends of the other, providing multiple current paths with the same voltage across each.
tips: Do not confuse the two rules: series means same current, different voltage; parallel means same voltage, split current.
Identify connections by how the ends are joined (end to end vs. corresponding ends), not by how the drawing looks.
rq: Why does a series circuit have one current path but a parallel circuit have several?
In series, elements are chained end to end so charge has only one route; in parallel, each element connects across the same two nodes, giving separate branches for the current to take.
If two identical resistors are connected in parallel across a battery, what is the same in each, and what differs?
The voltage across each resistor is the same (equal to the battery voltage), while the current divides between them.

notes.t: Series Circuits
pts: In a series circuit there is only one path for current to flow, so the current is the same at every point in the circuit.
Components in series are connected end to end along a single route between terminals A and B, so the same current passes through each one in turn.
Adding more components in series (as in panels a to e) does not create new paths; the total path from A to B remains a single route.
defs: Series circuit
A circuit in which components are connected in a single chain so that there is only one path for current, meaning the same current flows through every component.
tips: Do not assume components in series share the voltage equally; the current is equal, but voltage divides according to resistance.
Do not confuse the number of loops or drawn bends with the number of paths; a series circuit has one path even if drawn in a zigzag.
rq: Why must the current be identical at every point in a series circuit, even if the components have different resistances?
Charge cannot accumulate or leak away at a point in a steady state, and with only one path all charge passing one component must pass every other component, so the current is the same throughout.
What would happen to the current in a series circuit if one component were removed or broke open?
The single path would be broken, so no current could flow anywhere in the circuit.

notes.t: Resistors in Series
pts: Series elements carry the same current but have different voltages across them.
Ohm's law gives the voltage across each resistor as the current times its resistance.
KVL says the source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops across the series resistors.
Series resistances add directly to give the equivalent resistance.
eqs: Voltage across each series resistor (Ohm's law)
V_1 = I R_1, \quad V_2 = I R_2
\(V_{B}\) = source voltage (V); \(V_{1}\), \(V_{2}\) = voltage drops (V); I = current (A); \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\) = resistances (\(\Omega\))
Equivalent resistance of resistors in series
tips: Voltage drops across series resistors add to the source voltage (KVL) only with consistent polarity; do not add them as magnitudes when signs differ.
Do not add resistances in parallel as if they were in series; series resistances simply sum, parallel ones do not.
rq: Why must the current be identical through every resistor in a series string?
There is only one path for charge, so charge cannot accumulate or disappear at any point; the current entering one resistor must equal the current leaving it.
If \(R_{1}\) = 2 \(\Omega\) and \(R_{2}\) = 4 \(\Omega\) carry 3 A, what fraction of \(V_{B}\) appears across \(R_{2}\)?
\(V_{2}\) = 3 × 4 = 12 V and \(V_{B}\) = 3 × 6 = 18 V, so \(R_{2}\) takes 2/3 of the source voltage, matching its share of the total resistance.
Why does adding a resistor in series always increase the total resistance?
Since \(R_{T}\) = \(R_{1}\) + \(R_{2}\) + ..., each added positive resistance increases the sum, so the equivalent resistance is always larger than any single component.

notes.t: Resistors in Series and the Voltage Divider
pts: Resistances in series add directly: the total resistance is the sum of all individual resistances.
The same current flows through every resistor in a series string, so the current is common to R1 and R2.
In a voltage divider, the source voltage is shared across series resistors; each resistor's voltage is its share of the total resistance.
Ohm's law applied to the whole string gives the current, which is then used to find the voltage across any single resistor.
Because the current is common, the voltage across R2 equals I multiplied by R2, which is the source voltage times R2 over the total resistance.
defs: Series circuit
A circuit in which components are connected end to end in a single path, so the same current flows through each component.
Voltage divider
A series arrangement of resistors that splits the source voltage among them in proportion to their resistances.
eqs: Total resistance of n resistors in series
Source voltage across two series resistors
Current in a series circuit (Ohm's law)
Equivalent resistance of two series resistors
tips: Do not add resistances in parallel as if they were in series; only add directly for series connections.
Keep units consistent: voltage in V, current in A, and resistance in \(\Omega\) when applying \(V = IR\).
rq: Why is the current the same through R1 and R2 in a series circuit, and what would change if a branch split off between them?
There is only one path, so charge cannot accumulate or divert; a branch would split the current, so the series rule would no longer hold.
If R2 is much larger than R1, which resistor carries the larger voltage drop and why?
R2, because the voltage divides in proportion to resistance and the current is common, so V = IR is larger across the larger resistor.

notes.t: Resistors in Series and the Voltage Divider
pts: Resistances in series add directly, so the total (equivalent) resistance of n resistors is the sum of all of them.
Resistors in series share the same current I, and the source voltage \(V_{B}\) is divided among them in proportion to their resistances (voltage divider).
The voltage across any series resistor equals the source voltage multiplied by its resistance divided by the total resistance.
The ratio of voltages across two series resistors equals the ratio of their resistances, since they carry the same current.
defs: Series resistors
Resistors connected end to end in a single path so that the same current flows through each of them.
Voltage divider
A series arrangement in which the source voltage is shared among resistors, each receiving a fraction of \(V_{B}\) equal to its resistance divided by the total resistance.
eqs: Total resistance of n resistors in series
Ratio of voltages across two series resistors
Equivalent resistance of two series resistors
tips: Do not add resistors in parallel using the series formula; series addition applies only when resistors share the same current path.

In voltage divider questions, the ratio \(V_{1}\)/\(V_{2}\) = \(R_{1}\)/\(R_{2}\) holds only when the same current flows through both resistors, and the answer must keep the correct units (V for voltage, Ω for resistance).
rq: Why is the current the same through every resistor in a series circuit, and why does this lead to the voltage divider rule?

There is only one path for charge, so current is identical through each resistor; since V = IR, the voltage across each resistor is proportional to its resistance, so the larger resistance takes the larger share of \(V_{B}\).
What happens to the voltage across \(R_{1}\) if \(R_{2}\) is made much larger, with \(V_{B}\) fixed?
\(V_{1}\) = \(V_{B}\)·\(R_{1}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\)) decreases, because the denominator grows while the numerator stays fixed, so \(R_{1}\) receives a smaller fraction of the source voltage.
Why does adding a resistor in series always increase the total resistance?
\(R_{T}\) is the sum of all resistances, and each resistance is positive, so adding any extra resistor makes the sum larger.

notes.t: Voltage Division for Three Resistors in Series
pts: In a series circuit the equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
The same current flows through every series resistor, found by dividing the source voltage by the equivalent resistance.
Each resistor's voltage is its share of the total resistance multiplied by the total voltage, so larger resistors take larger voltage drops.
defs: Voltage division
The process by which a total source voltage is split among series resistors in proportion to their resistances, since the same current flows through each.
eqs: Equivalent resistance of three series resistors
I = current (A); \(V_{\text{total}}\) = source voltage (V); \(R_{\text{eq}}\) = equivalent resistance (\(\Omega\))
V_1 = R_1 I = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2 + R_3} V_{total}
V_2 = R_2 I = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2 + R_3} V_{total}
V_3 = R_3 I = \frac{R_3}{R_1 + R_2 + R_3} V_{total}
tips: Do not use the voltage divider formula for resistors in parallel; it only applies to series elements carrying the same current.
Make sure the numerator uses the resistor of interest (e.g. \(R_{2}\) for \(V_{2}\)), not \(R_{1}\), and that \(V_{\text{total}}\) is the source voltage in volts.
rq: Why does the resistor with the largest resistance get the largest voltage drop in a series string?
The same current I flows through all series resistors, so by Ohm's law V = IR the voltage is proportional to resistance; a larger R gives a larger share of \(V_{\text{total}}\).
If R2 were doubled while R1 and R3 stayed the same, what happens to \(V_{1}\)?
\(V_{1}\) decreases, because the denominator R1 + R2 + R3 grows while the numerator R1 stays fixed, so \(V_{1}\) = R1·\(V_{\text{total}}\)/(R1+R2+R3) falls.
Why can you not simply use the formula with the total voltage if the resistors are in parallel?
Parallel resistors share the same voltage and split the current, so the series voltage divider formula applies only when resistors are in series carrying the same current.

notes.t: Voltage division in a series circuit
pts: In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor, so the total voltage divides across the resistors in proportion to their resistance.
The voltage across a resistor equals its resistance times the common series current, which equals its share of the total resistance times the source voltage.
The larger the resistor, the larger the share of the source voltage it drops; here R4 = 6 kΩ takes 9 V of the 15 V supply.
The voltages across all resistors in a series string add up to the total source voltage (1.5 V + ... + 9 V = 15 V for the full set).
defs: Series circuit
A circuit in which components are connected end to end in a single path, so the same current flows through each component.
Voltage divider
A series arrangement of resistors that splits a source voltage into fractions proportional to each resistance.
eqs: Voltage across resistor R1 in a series circuit (voltage divider)
V_1 = R_1 I = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + R_4} V_{total}
\(V_{1}\) = voltage across R1 (V); \(R_{1}\) = resistance of R1 (Ω); I = series current (A); \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\), \(R_{4}\) = other resistances (Ω); \(V_{total}\) = source voltage (V)
Voltage across resistor R4 in a series circuit
V_4 = R_4 I = \frac{R_4}{R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + R_4} V_{total}
\(V_{4}\) = voltage across R4 (V); \(R_{4}\) = resistance of R4 (Ω); I = series current (A); \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) = other resistances (Ω); \(V_{total}\) = source voltage (V)
tips: Use the same resistance units (all in Ω or all in kΩ) in the ratio; mixing units gives wrong voltages.
Remember the total resistance in the denominator must include every resistor in the series path, not just the ones of interest.
rq: Why is the voltage across R4 (6 kΩ) larger than across R1 (1 kΩ) even though they carry the same current?
Because voltage equals current times resistance (V = IR); with the same current, the 6 kΩ resistor has six times the voltage drop of the 1 kΩ resistor.
What would happen to V1 if R4 were doubled to 12 kΩ, with everything else unchanged?
The total resistance rises, so the current falls and V1 = R1/\(R_{\text{total}}\) × 15 V decreases; V1 becomes 1000/19000 × 15 ≈ 0.79 V.
How can you check that your voltage-divider answers are correct?
Add all the resistor voltages; they must sum to the source voltage (here 1.5 V + 1.5 V + 3 V + 9 V = 15 V).

xq.q: A voltage divider is built from two resistors in series, \(R_1 = 4.7\) kΩ and \(R_2 = 3.3\) kΩ, connected across a d.c. supply \(V_B = 12\) V. Calculate the voltage across \(R_2\) in volts.
Two resistors \(R_1 = 1\) kΩ and \(R_2 = 3\) kΩ are connected in series across a 8 V supply. What is the voltage across \(R_1\)?
xq.a: 2 V
o: 6 V
2 V
4 V
xq.w: The current is common, so \(V_{1}\) = 8 × 1/(1+3) = 2 V; the trap is giving \(R_{1}\) the larger share (6 V) or assuming equal sharing (4 V).

xq.q: Two resistors \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are connected in series across a source \(V_B\). Show that the voltage across \(R_2\) is \(V_2 = V_B R_2/(R_1+R_2)\), and explain why the voltages across the two resistors are not equal even though they carry the same current.
xq.a: The same current I flows through both resistors, so by KVL and Ohm's law \(V_{B}\) = I(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\)), giving I = \(V_{B}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\)). The voltage across \(R_{2}\) is \(V_{2}\) = I \(R_{2}\) = \(V_{B}\) \(R_{2}\)/(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\)). The current is common, so the voltage across each resistor, V = IR, is proportional to its resistance; unequal resistances give unequal voltages.
s: Same current in series; KVL: \(V_{B}\) = I(\(R_{1}\)+\(R_{2}\))
V = IR with common I means voltage proportional to R, so drops differ

units.name: 2.5 Voltage sources in series and series breaks
units.ov: This material covers how voltage sources combine in series, where polarity decides whether voltages add or subtract, and how a series circuit behaves when a break (open circuit) occurs. Both ideas rest on Kirchhoff's voltage law and on the fact that a series string carries a single common current. An open element stops that current and so takes the whole supply voltage.
must: Series sources combine by signed sum: \(V_{total}=\sum \pm V_k\), with + for aiding polarity and − for opposing polarity
Aiding polarity means + to − connected end to end, so the voltages add (three 9 V sources give 27 V)
An opposing (reversed) source is subtracted, e.g. a 1.5 V result rather than 4.5 V; always assign a sign before summing
Series circuit: components are connected in a single path, so the same current flows through every component
Kirchhoff's voltage law for a series string: \(V_S=V_1+V_2+\dots+V_6\), so the drops sum to the supply
An open circuit is a break that allows no current, so the ammeter reads zero everywhere in the loop
With a break, \(I=0\), so every intact resistor drops \(V=IR=0\) V
The open element carries the full supply voltage: \(V_4=V_S-V_1-V_2-V_3-V_5-V_6=V_S\), since the other drops are 0
Do not assume the open component's voltage is zero; the break takes the full source voltage
Watch signs when rearranging KVL, and check polarity consistency before adding or subtracting voltages
conn: Source polarity and KVL: the net EMF from signed series sources is the \(V_S\) that must equal the sum of the drops around the loop
Open circuit and Ohm's law: \(I=0\) makes every intact resistor drop \(IR=0\), so KVL forces the full \(V_S\) across the break
Series current and fault-finding: a zero ammeter reading together with voltmeter readings across components locates the open element
Opposing sources reduce net EMF, so they reduce the current \(I=V_{net}/R_{total}\) and every drop in the loop
exq: Three 9 V cells are in series, with one reversed. Find the net voltage and its polarity. Then find the current through a 10 Ω resistor connected across the combination.
A 1.5 V cell is connected in series with two others, giving a net of 1.5 V. Deduce the cell values and orientations, e.g. two 1.5 V cells aiding and one 1.5 V cell opposing.
A string of six resistors is connected to a 12 V supply. The ammeter reads 0 A. State what has happened, and give the voltage across each resistor and across the faulty one.
In a series string with supply \(V_S=24\) V, a voltmeter reads 24 V across resistor \(R_4\) and 0 V across all the others. Explain why, and use KVL to prove it.
Explain why the voltage across an open element equals the source voltage even though no current flows, and describe how reversing one source in a series chain changes this.

notes.t: Voltage Sources in Series
pts: Voltage sources in series combine like resistors in series, but the polarity of each source must be checked.
Sources connected with aiding polarity (+ to − end to end) add their voltages, giving the total as the sum.
A source connected with opposing polarity subtracts its voltage from the total, reducing the net EMF.
In the 9 V example, three aiding 9 V sources in series give a net 27 V with the + terminal at the top.
eqs: Net voltage of series sources (sum of signed voltages)
\(V_{\text{total}}\) = net terminal voltage (V); \(V_{k}\) = magnitude of the k-th source voltage (V); ± = + for aiding polarity, − for opposing polarity
tips: Mixing up polarity: a reversed source must be subtracted, not added (panel b gives 1.5 V, not 4.5 V).
Do not sum voltage-source values as you would resistances without first assigning each source a sign according to its orientation.
rq: Why does the 1.5 V cell reversed in panel (b) give 1.5 V instead of 4.5 V?
The reversed cell opposes the other two, so its +1.5 V is subtracted: (1.5 + 1.5) − 1.5 = 1.5 V.
How does series connection of voltage sources differ from series resistors when polarity is mixed?
Resistances always add, but voltage sources must be summed with signs according to their polarity.

notes.t: Series circuits and breaks (open circuits)
pts: In a complete series circuit current flows through every component in turn, so the same current passes through each.
If one component is open (e.g. an open filament), the loop is broken, current stops everywhere and the ammeter reads zero.
In a series circuit the source voltage is shared among the resistors (Kirchhoff's voltage law): the sum of the drops equals the supply.
With an open resistor and no current, the open element carries the full supply voltage across its terminals while the other resistors drop 0 V.
defs: Open circuit
A break in a conducting path so that no current can flow; the voltage across the break equals the source voltage.
Series circuit
A circuit in which components are connected end to end in a single path, so the same current flows through each component.
eqs: Kirchhoff's voltage law for a series string
\(V_{S}\) = source voltage (V); \(V_{1}\)…\(V_{6}\) = voltage drops across each component (V)
