Check that the mesh-current direction is applied consistently around every loop when setting up the equations.
rq: Why does mesh analysis need fewer equations than branch-current analysis?
Because each mesh current is one unknown, and there is one KVL equation per mesh, so the number of unknowns equals the number of meshes, whereas branch-current analysis uses one unknown per branch.
In a circuit with 3 meshes and 6 branches, how many unknowns and equations does each method need?
Mesh analysis: 3 unknowns and 3 equations. Branch-current analysis: 6 unknowns and 6 equations.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: writing loop equations for a multi-loop circuit
pts: Each loop (mesh) gets its own clockwise loop current; the equations are written by applying KVL around every loop.
Rule for each loop equation: sum of resistors in the loop times the loop current, minus shared resistors times adjacent loop currents, equals the source voltage in that loop.
A resistor shared by two loops appears with a minus sign in the neighbouring loop's equation, because the two loop currents flow in opposite directions through it.
A voltage source is placed on the right-hand side with a sign set by its polarity relative to the loop direction; a source opposed to the loop current gives a negative term.
Three meshes give three simultaneous equations, which can be written in matrix form and solved for i1, i2 and i3.
defs: Mesh (loop) current
A fictitious current circulating around a single mesh of a circuit; the actual branch current in a shared element is the algebraic sum of the mesh currents flowing through it.
eqs: KVL for loop 1 (mesh with R1, R2 and \(V_{A}\))
KVL for loop 2 (mesh with R2, R3 and \(V_{B}\))
KVL for loop 3 (outer mesh with R1, R3, R4)
tips: Keep track of source polarity: a voltage source whose polarity opposes the chosen loop direction contributes a negative term, and the sign of \(V_B\) in the equation above reflects this.
Use the same direction convention for all mesh currents; mixing clockwise and counter-clockwise loops produces sign errors in the coupling terms.
rq: Why does the shared resistor R2 carry a negative sign in loop 1's equation but a negative sign in loop 2's equation as well?
Because the two mesh currents i1 and i2 flow in opposite directions through R2, so the voltage drop due to the neighbouring loop current subtracts from the drop due to the loop's own current.
What would change if the loop 2 current were defined counter-clockwise instead of clockwise?

The signs of the coupling terms (e.g. -R2 i1 and -R3 i3) would flip to +, since the shared resistor would then carry currents in the same direction; the solution for the branch currents would be unchanged.
Why is the right-hand side of the outer loop equation zero?
Because the outer mesh contains no voltage source, so the sum of voltage drops around it must equal zero by KVL.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: resolving element currents from mesh currents
pts: Each element current is the algebraic sum of the mesh currents flowing through it; shared branches carry the difference of adjacent mesh currents.
Mesh currents are i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A and i₃ = 2 A, taken clockwise in each loop.
The 20 Ω resistor R₁ lies only in mesh 1 (plus mesh 3 on its top branch), so its current is i₁ − i₃ = 2 A.
The 10 Ω resistor R₂ is shared by meshes 1 and 2, so its current is i₁ − i₂ = 3 A.
The 12 Ω resistor R₃ carries i₂ − i₃ = 1 − 2 = −1 A relative to mesh 2; the page lists magnitude 2 A, so direction must be checked against the reference sign convention.
defs: Mesh current
A fictitious current circulating around a closed loop (mesh) of a planar circuit; it is used as the unknown in mesh-current analysis.
Branch current
The actual current in a single element, found by superposing the mesh currents of all meshes that share that element.
eqs: Current in a shared resistor between meshes k and m
\(I_{R}\) = element current (A); \(i_{k}\), \(i_{m}\) = mesh currents of adjacent meshes (A)
Current in an outer-branch resistor of a single mesh
\(I_{R}\) = element current (A); \(i_{k}\) = mesh current of the only mesh containing the element (A)
tips: Watch the sign: a branch current is the difference of mesh currents with respect to the chosen reference direction; a negative result means the true current flows opposite to the assumed direction.
Do not add mesh currents on a shared branch; only subtract them, and only use the single mesh current for outer branches.
rq: Why does the 10 Ω resistor current equal a difference of mesh currents rather than a single mesh current?
Because it is shared by meshes 1 and 2, which circulate in opposite senses through it, so the net current is i₁ − i₂.
If the mesh current directions were all reversed, how would the element currents change?
Every mesh current changes sign, so each element current changes sign too; the magnitudes stay the same.

xq.q: In a three-mesh circuit, mesh 1 contains a source \(V_{B1} = 12\) V, a resistor \(R_1 = 100\,\Omega\), and a resistor \(R_2 = 200\,\Omega\) shared with mesh 2. The KVL equation for mesh 1 is \(-V_{B1} + R_2(I_1 - I_2) + I_1 R_1 = 0\). The mesh current in mesh 2 is \(I_2 = 20\) mA. Find the mesh current \(I_1\) and the current in \(R_2\), both in mA. Give \(I_1\) as the final answer.
xq.a: I1 ≈ 53.3 mA (the current in R2 is 33.3 mA)

xq.q: A planar circuit has five branches and three meshes (windows). Compared with the branch-current method, how many unknowns and simultaneous equations does mesh-current analysis need?
xq.a: 3 mesh currents and 3 equations, compared with 5 for the branch-current method
o: 5 mesh currents, one per branch
5 mesh currents, one per node
3 mesh currents, but 5 equations are still needed
3 mesh currents and 3 equations, compared with 5 for the branch-current method
xq.w: Mesh analysis uses one unknown loop current per mesh (window), not per branch or per possible closed path, so it needs fewer equations.
s: Mesh analysis has one unknown per mesh, so 3.
The branch-current method has one unknown per branch, so 5.
Each mesh gives one KVL equation, so 3 equations are enough.

xq.q: In a three-mesh circuit, mesh 2 contains resistors \(R_3\) (carrying only \(I_2\)), \(R_2\) (shared with mesh 1) and \(R_4\) (shared with mesh 3). Write the KVL equation for mesh 2 using the mesh currents \(I_1, I_2, I_3\). Rearrange it into the standard form and explain why the shared resistances appear with negative signs.
xq.a: KVL for mesh 2: R2(I2 − I1) + R4(I2 − I3) + R3 I2 = 0. This rearranges to −R2 I1 + (R2+R3+R4) I2 − R4 I3 = 0. The shared resistors appear with negative signs because the neighbouring mesh currents flow through them in the opposite direction to I2, so they reduce the voltage drop in mesh 2.
s: R2 carries I2 − I1 and R4 carries I2 − I3.
Sum of drops: R2(I2 − I1) + R4(I2 − I3) + R3 I2 = 0.
Collect terms: −R2 I1 + (R2+R3+R4) I2 − R4 I3 = 0.
Own-mesh resistances multiply I2; shared resistances multiply the neighbouring currents with a minus sign.
The minus sign arises because the two clockwise loop currents oppose each other in a shared branch.

units.name: 5.7 Mesh-current analysis with current sources
units.ov: This material covers mesh-current analysis when a circuit contains current sources. A current source fixes its branch current but not its voltage, so a mesh current through it is known, which reduces the unknowns, and KVL is written only for the remaining meshes. The ideas connect through consistent sign conventions, correct mutual-resistor terms and substitution of the known current into the remaining equation.
must: A current source fixes the current through its branch, but its terminal voltage is unknown and set by the rest of the circuit; never assume \(V=0\).
A current source on the outer edge of only one mesh sets that mesh current directly, e.g. \(i_1=\pm I_s\); no KVL is needed for that mesh.
Do not write KVL through a mesh with a current source on its own, because its voltage is an unknown; use the known current instead.
Sign of the constraint depends on the source arrow relative to the chosen (clockwise) mesh direction: opposing gives \(i_1=-5\) A, not +5 A.
The shared resistor gives a mutual term \(R(i_2-i_1)\), not \(Ri_2\) alone; dropping \(-i_1\) is the commonest error.
KVL form: sum of resistor drops = sum of source rises, with voltage-source signs matched to the mesh direction (e.g. \(10(i_2-i_1)+5i_2-100=0\)).
Expand and rearrange: \(15i_2-10i_1=100\), then substitute the known \(i_1\). With \(i_1=-5\): \(i_2=\frac{100-50}{15}=3.33\) A.
Check the algebra: \(15i_2=100+10i_1\), so with \(i_1=-5\) the right side is 50, so keep the sign of \(i_1\) when substituting.
A current source shared between two meshes needs a supermesh: combine the two meshes into one KVL loop that excludes the source, plus a constraint equation from the source current.
Unknown source voltage can be recovered afterwards by applying KVL to a mesh that contains it.
conn: Current-source constraint plus mutual-resistor KVL: the known \(i_1\) is substituted into the mesh 2 equation, so sign errors in the constraint propagate to the answer.
Supermesh analysis links mesh analysis to KCL: the shared source gives a constraint such as \(i_a-i_b=I_s\) alongside the single supermesh KVL.
Mesh analysis with current sources parallels nodal analysis with voltage sources (supernodes): each uses the source's known quantity as a constraint and avoids writing the unknown one.
After finding mesh currents, branch currents, resistor voltages and power (including power delivered or absorbed by the current source, using its found voltage) are asked for together.
exq: Meshes 1 and 2 share a 10 Ω resistor; mesh 2 has a 5 Ω resistor and a 100 V source, and mesh 1 contains a 5 A current source opposing the clockwise direction. Find \(i_1\), \(i_2\) and the voltage across the 10 Ω resistor.
Explain why the voltage across an ideal current source cannot be assumed to be zero, and show how it is found in a two-mesh circuit once \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) are known.
In a circuit with a 2 A current source on the outer branch of mesh 1 and a 10 V source in mesh 2 with 10 Ω shared and 5 Ω resistors, write the KVL for mesh 2 and solve for \(i_2\).
A 3 A current source lies in the branch shared by two meshes. Set up the supermesh equation and constraint equation, then solve for both mesh currents.
Calculate the power absorbed or supplied by the current source in a given two-mesh circuit, stating the sign convention used and checking that total power balances.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis with current sources
pts: A current source forces a specified current through its terminals, but the voltage across it is not fixed in advance.
The voltage across a current source is set by the rest of the circuit it is connected to, so it must be solved for.
Do not assume a current source has zero voltage across it; this is a common beginner error.

In mesh analysis, a mesh current is assigned to each loop, and a branch carrying a current source fixes the mesh current through it, so the source's voltage becomes an unknown to be found from the other mesh equations.
defs: Current source
An ideal element that forces a specified current to flow through its terminals, independent of the voltage across it; its terminal voltage is determined by the connected circuit.
tips: Do not set the voltage across a current source to zero; treat it as an unknown voltage and include it in the KVL equation of the mesh(es) it belongs to.
A current source on the outer edge of a mesh fixes that mesh current directly (e.g. i₁ = 2 A), but a current source shared between two meshes requires a supermesh-style treatment.
rq: Why can't we assume the voltage across a 2 A current source is zero when writing the mesh equations?
Because the voltage across a current source is determined by the circuit it is connected to, so it is an unknown that must be solved for, not zero.
In this circuit, what fixes the value of i₁ directly, and why does that simplify the mesh analysis?
The 2 A source lies on the outer branch of mesh 1, so i₁ is forced to 2 A, reducing the number of unknown mesh currents.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis with current sources
pts: Avoid writing KVL for meshes containing a current source; its voltage is unknown, so use the known current directly.
A current source fixes the mesh current directly, so i1 is known and only the remaining mesh needs a KVL equation.
Apply KVL to the mesh not containing the current source; the shared 10 Ω resistor gives a term proportional to (i2 − i1).
The presence of a current source simplifies the solution because it reduces the number of unknown mesh currents.
defs: Mesh current
A current assumed to circulate around the perimeter of an individual mesh (loop with no internal branches) in a planar circuit.
eqs: Known mesh current from the current source
\(i_{1}\) = mesh current through the current source (A)
\(i_{2}\) = mesh 2 current (A); \(i_{1}\) = mesh 1 current (A); 10 = resistance in the shared branch (Ω); 5 = resistance in mesh 2 (Ω); 10 = source voltage (V)
tips: The shared resistor term in KVL is multiplied by (i2 − i1), not i2 alone; forgetting the mesh 1 contribution is a common error.
Keep sign conventions consistent: the 10 V source sign must match the chosen clockwise direction of i2.
rq: Why can we write i1 = 2 A without any KVL equation?
Because the branch carrying mesh current i1 is a current source, which forces that current to be 2 A regardless of the rest of the circuit.
Why is it wise to avoid writing KVL around a loop containing a current source?
That loop's KVL would contain an unknown voltage across the current source, adding an extra unknown that must be solved for.

notes.t: Mesh-current analysis: writing KVL equations for mesh currents with a current source
pts: A mesh current that flows through an independent current source is fixed by that source, so it needs no KVL equation.
Mesh currents shared by a resistor are subtracted around that resistor, giving the mutual term in each loop equation.
Apply KVL around each mesh: the sum of voltage drops across resistors equals the sum of source voltage rises.
Rearranging the loop equation gives a linear equation in the unknown mesh current, which is then solved by substitution.
defs: Mesh current
A current assumed to circulate around a single independent loop (mesh) of a planar circuit, used as the unknown in mesh analysis.
eqs: \(i_2\) = mesh current in loop 2 (A); \(i_1\) = mesh current in loop 1 (A); 10 = resistance shared by the meshes (Ω); 5 = resistance in loop 2 (Ω); 100 = source voltage (V)
tips: Check the direction of each mesh current relative to the source arrow: a current source pointing against the mesh direction gives \(i_1 = -5\) A, not +5 A.
Keep the shared-resistor term with the correct sign (\(i_2 - i_1\)) when expanding; dropping the \(-i_1\) term is a common error.
rq: Why is no KVL equation written for loop I1 even though it is a mesh?
Because it contains a current source whose current fixes \(i_1\) directly, so \(i_1 = -5\) A is the constraint.
What is the sign of the shared-resistor term, and why?
It is \(10(i_2 - i_1)\): the current in the shared resistor is the difference of the two mesh currents, taking loop 2's direction as positive.

xq.q: A planar circuit has two meshes with clockwise mesh currents \(i_1\) and \(i_2\). Mesh 1 contains an ideal current source that forces \(i_1 = 2\) A. Mesh 1 shares a resistor \(R_{sh} = 6\ \Omega\) with mesh 2. Mesh 2 also contains a resistor \(R = 4\ \Omega\) and a voltage source \(V = 30\) V whose polarity aids \(i_2\). Find the power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor.

In a two-mesh circuit, an ideal current source in mesh 1 points against the clockwise direction of \(i_1\), so \(i_1 = -5\) A. The shared resistor is 10 Ω. Mesh 2 contains a 5 Ω resistor and a 100 V source aiding \(i_2\). What is \(i_2\)?
xq.w: KVL for mesh 2 is 10(i2 + 5) + 5 i2 = 100, so i2 = 50/15 = 3.33 A; the traps are using i1 = +5 A (giving 10 A) or dropping the i1 term (giving 6.67 A).

xq.q: Mesh 1 of a two-mesh circuit contains an ideal 2 A current source on its outer edge, so \(i_1 = 2\) A. It shares a 10 Ω resistor with mesh 2. Mesh 2 contains a 5 Ω resistor and a 10 V source, and its KVL equation is \(10(i_2 - i_1) + 5 i_2 + 10 = 0\). Explain why no KVL equation is written for mesh 1, and why the voltage across the current source is not taken as zero. Then find \(i_2\).
xq.a: The current source fixes i1 = 2 A, so mesh 1 needs no equation. Its terminal voltage is set by the rest of the circuit and is an unknown, so it is not zero. Writing KVL for mesh 1 would add an unknown without being needed. Mesh 2: 10(i2 − 2) + 5 i2 + 10 = 0, so 15 i2 = 10 and i2 = 0.667 A.
s: The current source fixes i1 = 2 A, so there is no unknown in mesh 1 to solve for
Its voltage is unknown and set by the circuit, so a KVL for mesh 1 would only add an unknown

units.name: 5.8 Mesh-current method recap and summary
units.ov: This recap covers the mesh-current method, a systematic way to analyse arbitrary planar resistive circuits. Each mesh is given a mesh current, KVL is applied around each mesh with an unknown current, and Ohm's law expresses resistor voltages in terms of those currents. The result is a smaller linear system that is solved for the mesh currents, and sign conventions on shared branches are the main source of error.
must: A mesh is a loop with no other loops inside it; not every loop is a mesh.
Identify all meshes first, then assign one mesh current per mesh (use a consistent direction, e.g. all clockwise).
Apply KVL \( \sum V = 0 \) around each mesh whose current is unknown.
Write resistor voltages with Ohm's law, \( V = RI \), in terms of mesh currents.
On a shared branch the resistor current is the difference of the two mesh currents, e.g. \( R(I_1 - I_2) \) in mesh 1, with the sign reversed in mesh 2.
A current source on an outside branch of a mesh fixes that mesh current, so no KVL equation is needed for that mesh.
With n unknown mesh currents you need n independent equations, which are solved as a linear system (substitution, elimination, or matrix form \( \mathbf{R}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{V} \)).
Check the reference direction of each mesh current before writing KVL; sign errors are the most common mistake.
The method reduces the number of unknowns and simultaneous equations, and works on circuits that cannot be simplified into series/parallel combinations.
Finish by checking results: recompute a KVL loop, or check power supplied equals power dissipated.
conn: Mesh current method combines KVL with Ohm's law: KVL gives the loop equations, and Ohm's law turns resistor voltages into expressions in the mesh currents.
Series/parallel reduction versus mesh analysis: reduce first where possible, then use mesh currents on what remains.
Current sources and meshes: a source on an outer branch fixes a mesh current and removes an equation, which links to counting unknowns and independent equations.
Mesh results feed into branch currents, voltages and power calculations, e.g. a shared-resistor current is \( I_1 - I_2 \) and its power is \( R(I_1-I_2)^2 \).
exq: A two-mesh circuit has a 12 V source and resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω (shared) and 3 Ω. Assign clockwise mesh currents, write the KVL equations, solve for both currents, and find the current in the shared resistor.

A three-mesh circuit has a 2 A current source on the outer branch of the right-hand mesh. State which mesh current is known, how many KVL equations are needed, and solve for the remaining currents given the resistor values.
Explain the difference between a loop and a mesh, and identify the meshes in a given bridge-type circuit that cannot be reduced by series/parallel combinations.
Write the mesh equations in matrix form \( \mathbf{R}\mathbf{I}=\mathbf{V} \) for a given three-mesh circuit and solve for the mesh currents. Then calculate the power dissipated in a chosen resistor.

A student's mesh solution gives an incorrect answer because a shared branch was written as \( R(I_1+I_2) \). Identify the error, correct the equations, and explain how the reference directions determine the sign.

notes.t: Mesh-current method
pts: Identify every individual mesh in the circuit before doing anything else.
Assign one mesh current per mesh; a mesh current is already known if a current source sits on an outside branch of that mesh.
Apply KVL around each mesh with unknown current to write a loop equation, then use Ohm's law to express resistor voltages in mesh currents.
With n unknown mesh currents you need n independent equations; solve the resulting linear system to find the mesh currents.
tips: Only meshes with unknown currents need a KVL loop equation; meshes fixed by a current source do not.
Write resistor voltages as R times the mesh current with correct sign for the direction you assigned, especially for shared branches.
rq: Why does a mesh whose outside branch contains a current source not need a KVL equation?
Its mesh current is fixed by the source, so it is no longer an unknown; only meshes with unknown currents need loop equations.
Why must the number of independent equations equal the number of unknown mesh currents?
A unique solution requires as many independent linear equations as unknowns; fewer gives no unique answer, and extra ones are redundant.

notes.t: Summary: Mesh-Current Analysis
pts: Mesh-current analysis can solve arbitrary circuits, not just simple ones.
It works even when circuits cannot be easily reduced to series or parallel combinations.
Using mesh currents reduces the number of unknowns and simultaneous equations needed.
tips: Do not confuse a mesh with any loop: a mesh is a loop that contains no other loops inside it.
Always check the reference direction of each mesh current before writing KVL, since sign errors are a common source of wrong answers.
rq: Why does mesh-current analysis usually need fewer simultaneous equations than applying KVL and KCL to every branch current?
Because each mesh current is defined once and automatically satisfies KCL at every node, so only one KVL equation per independent mesh is needed, reducing the number of unknowns.
What type of circuit would make you choose mesh-current analysis over simple series/parallel reduction?
A circuit with multiple sources and interconnected loops that cannot be reduced to simple series or parallel combinations.

units.name: Formulae sheet lecture 5
units.ov: This material covers mesh (loop) current analysis of resistive DC circuits. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law is applied to each independent mesh to give a set of simultaneous linear equations, which are then solved with Cramer's rule (determinants). The ideas connect as a pipeline: identify meshes, write KVL in standard form, build the resistance matrix, solve, then recover branch currents.
must: Mesh currents are mathematical loop quantities, not necessarily physical currents; branch currents are found from them, e.g. \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\)
Number of independent KVL equations = number of meshes (open areas), giving as many equations as unknown loop currents
KVL: \(\sum V = 0\) around a closed loop; go clockwise in every mesh and take resistor voltages as positive (\(+iR\))
Standard-form loop 1: \((R_1+R_3)i_1 - R_3 i_2 = V_A\)
Standard-form loop 2: \(-R_3 i_1 + (R_2+R_3)i_2 = -V_B\) (sign of source depends on its polarity relative to the clockwise direction)
Quick rule: (sum of resistors in loop)×(loop current) − (shared resistor)×(adjacent loop current) = source voltage in loop
Shared-resistor terms are negative because adjacent clockwise loop currents oppose each other through that resistor
Cramer's rule: \(I_i = \det(R_i)/\det(R)\), where \(R_i\) has column i replaced by the source-voltage vector
2×2 determinant: \(|A| = ad - bc\)
Keep units consistent (Ω, V, A) and convert mA carefully, e.g. 13.9 mA = 0.0139 A; check results by substituting back
conn: KVL to matrix form: writing the mesh equations in standard form gives \([R][I]=[V]\), which is directly solvable by Cramer's rule
Mesh currents to branch currents: the current in a shared resistor is the difference of the two loop currents (\(i_1 - i_2\)), which then feeds into voltage drops \(V=IR\) and power \(I^2R\)
Source polarity and clockwise convention: sign of \(V_A\), \(V_B\) on the right-hand side determines sign of the answers; a negative current means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed one
Mesh analysis versus nodal/KCL methods: the substitution \(i_3=i_1-i_2\) is essentially KCL built into the loop definition
exq: A two-mesh circuit has \(R_1=10\,\Omega\), \(R_2=20\,\Omega\), shared \(R_3=30\,\Omega\), \(V_A=12\) V and \(V_B=6\) V opposing. Write the mesh equations in standard form and solve for \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) using Cramer's rule.
For the same circuit, find the current in the shared resistor \(R_3\), its direction, the voltage across it and the power dissipated.
Explain why the number of independent KVL equations equals the number of meshes and why loop currents need not be physical currents.
Evaluate \(\det(R)\) for \(\begin{bmatrix}40 & -30\\ -30 & 50\end{bmatrix}\) and use it to find both loop currents when the source vector is \([12, -6]^T\) V; give answers in mA.
Derive the standard-form loop equations for a two-battery, three-resistor network from KVL, showing how \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\) is used to eliminate a variable.

notes.t: Mesh Current Analysis and Solving Simultaneous Equations
pts: Loop currents are mathematical quantities used to simplify circuit analysis, not necessarily physical currents.
The number of independent KVL equations equals the number of open areas (meshes) in the network layout.
Write KVL for each mesh going clockwise, always taking resistor voltages as positive so resistor voltages are added.
Substitute branch current i3 as i1 − i2 so the unknowns match the number of equations.
A quick rule writes loop equations directly: (sum of loop resistors)×(loop current) − (shared resistor)×(adjacent loop current) = source voltage in loop.
defs: Loop (mesh) current
A mathematical circuit current assumed to circulate around one independent mesh, used to simplify nodal/mesh analysis; it is not necessarily a physical current.
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
The sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is zero.
Determinant method (Cramer's rule)
A matrix-algebra method for solving simultaneous linear equations where each unknown equals the ratio of two determinants.
eqs: \(I_{i}\) = unknown loop current (A); det(R) = determinant of the resistance (coefficient) matrix; det(\(R_{i}\)) = determinant with column i replaced by the source-voltage vector (V)
a, b, c, d = matrix entries (dimensionless for coefficient matrices); |A| = determinant
tips: Watch the sign of shared-resistor terms: they appear with a negative sign in the loop equations because the loop currents oppose each other through that resistor.
Keep units consistent: resistances in ohms and voltages in volts give currents in amps, so convert mA carefully when checking answers (e.g. 13.9 mA = 0.0139 A).
rq: Why do we treat resistor voltages as positive when going clockwise around each mesh, and what does that imply for the signs in the KVL equation?

It is a consistent convention: with clockwise loop current, each resistor voltage is taken as a drop in the direction of the loop, so all resistor terms are added; only source signs depend on their polarity relative to the loop.
Why does the shared resistor R3 appear with a negative sign in the equation for loop 1 but as a positive term in its own loop?
The shared resistor carries i1 and i2 in opposite directions relative to its own loop, so the current from the adjacent loop subtracts from the self-term.
What would go wrong if you substituted i3 = i1 + i2 instead of i1 − i2?
The sign convention for i3 would be inconsistent with the chosen loop directions, giving incorrect loop equations and wrong currents.

xq.q: A two-mesh circuit has clockwise loop currents \(i_1\) and \(i_2\). Loop 1 contains \(R_1 = 10\ \Omega\) and source \(V_A = 10\) V. Loop 2 contains \(R_2 = 30\ \Omega\) and source \(V_B = 5\) V. The resistor \(R_3 = 20\ \Omega\) is shared. The standard-form equations are \((R_1+R_3)i_1 - R_3 i_2 = V_A\) and \(-R_3 i_1 + (R_2+R_3) i_2 = -V_B\). Use Cramer's rule to find the current \(i_3 = i_1 - i_2\) in \(R_3\).

In a two-mesh circuit, loop 1 has \(R_1 = 2\) kΩ, loop 2 has \(R_2 = 3\) kΩ and the shared resistor is \(R_3 = 6\) kΩ. The sources are \(V_A = 12\) V in loop 1 and \(V_B = 6\) V in loop 2, with the standard-form equations \((R_1+R_3)i_1 - R_3 i_2 = V_A\) and \(-R_3 i_1 + (R_2+R_3) i_2 = -V_B\). Find the voltage across \(R_3\).
xq.a: V = 8 V
s: 8 i1 − 6 i2 = 12 and −6 i1 + 9 i2 = −6 (i in mA, R in kΩ)

xq.q: The loop equations of a circuit are \(30 i_1 - 20 i_2 = 10\) and \(-20 i_1 + 50 i_2 = -5\), with resistances in Ω. What is the determinant of the coefficient matrix used in Cramer's rule?
xq.w: det = ad − bc = 30×50 − (−20)(−20) = 1500 − 400 = 1100, because the product of two negative shared terms is positive and is subtracted; adding it gives 1900, and ignoring it gives 1500.

units.name: extended tutorial solutions
units.ov: This material covers DC and AC linear circuit analysis: series/parallel reduction, Thévenin equivalents and maximum power transfer, then phasor impedance of RC circuits and nodal analysis of an ideal op-amp with a capacitor. The unifying idea is to reduce a network to a simple equivalent (resistance, impedance or Thévenin source) while remembering what the equivalent does and does not preserve. DC methods carry over to AC by replacing R with complex impedance.
must: Series: \( R_T=R_1+R_2+R_3 \); parallel: \( R=\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} \) (product over sum for two resistors, reciprocal sum in general)
Equivalent resistance is \( R=V/I \) at the terminals only; it does not guarantee that individual component current/power ratings are respected (e.g. a 20 Ω branch carries only \( I/2 \))
Thévenin voltage \( V_T \) = open-circuit voltage across A–B (use the voltage divider; no current means no drop in a series resistor)
Thévenin resistance \( R_T \): short voltage sources (replace with a wire, don't remove), then reduce series/parallel as seen from A–B
Load power \( P=\frac{V_T^2R_L}{(R_L+R_T)^2} \) is maximised at \( R_L=R_T \), giving \( P_{max}=V_T^2/4R_T \)
For a given fraction of peak power (e.g. 75%), set P equal to the target to get a quadratic in \( R_L \) and state both roots (e.g. 40/3 Ω and 120 Ω for \( R_T=40\,\Omega \))
Practical source: ideal \( V_T \) in series with internal \( R_T \); two load cases give simultaneous equations for \( V_T \) and \( R_T \)

Capacitor impedance \( X_C=-j/(\omega C) \), \( \omega=2\pi f \); series impedances add as complex numbers, parallel uses \( Z=\frac{RX_C}{R+X_C} \) rationalised with the conjugate, and branch currents add as phasors
Ideal op-amp with negative feedback: \( V_+=V_- \) (virtual earth, 0 V here), no input current; apply nodal analysis at the inverting node
Solve complex nodal equations in rectangular form, convert to polar, then to a time-domain \( v(t)=V\sin(\omega t+\phi) \) keeping degrees/radians consistent
conn: Thévenin reduction feeds maximum power transfer: find \( V_T,R_T \), then write \( P(R_L) \) and optimise or solve for given power levels
Equivalent resistance by \( V/I \) links to practical source modelling: two measured load cases give \( V_T \) and \( R_T \) by simultaneous equations or a quadratic
Series/parallel reduction extends from resistors to RC impedances, using the same formulae with complex arithmetic and phasor currents
Op-amp virtual earth combined with capacitor impedance gives a complex nodal equation whose result is converted to a time-domain output
exq: Reduce a series-parallel network (e.g. 20 Ω∥20 Ω in series with 8, 3 and 9 Ω) to a single resistance between A and B, then check whether a single 20 Ω component rating is adequate in the original circuit.

A network has \( R_1+R_2 \) and \( R_1R_2 \) given by two conditions; form and solve the quadratic for the resistor values, and find \( V_T \) and \( R_T \) of a practical source from two load measurements.
Find the Thévenin equivalent between A and B of a circuit with 12 Ω and 24 Ω resistors and a source, then determine the load resistance for maximum power and the power delivered (e.g. 25/8 W at 8 Ω).
For \( R_T=40\,\Omega \), find the two load resistances that dissipate 75% of the maximum power.
At 1 kHz, find the impedance magnitude and phase of a resistor and capacitor in series and in parallel, and the total current phasor from a given supply.
For an op-amp circuit with C = 0.25 µF at \( \omega=200 \) rad/s (\( X_C=-j20\,k\Omega \)) and a 4∠0° V input, use nodal analysis to find \( V_o \) in polar form and as a time-domain expression.

notes.t: Series-parallel resistor network simplification and current-rating check
pts: Parallel resistors combine by reciprocal sum; two 20 Ω branches in parallel give 10 Ω, and 8 Ω + 3 Ω + 9 Ω combine in series
Equivalent resistance is found by repeatedly reducing series and parallel groups until a single resistor remains between terminals A and B
An equivalent resistance can match the terminal behaviour of a circuit but still fail to carry the internal branch currents of the original network
Replacing a network by one resistor is only valid for the terminal voltage-current relation; the individual component current ratings must still be checked
In the original circuit the current splits so that the 20 Ω branch carries only \( I/2 \), which a single 20 Ω part can safely handle
defs: Equivalent resistance
The single resistance that, between two terminals, draws the same current for the same applied voltage as the original network.
eqs: Equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel
\( R_1, R_2 \) = branch resistances (\(\Omega\)); \( R \) = equivalent resistance (\(\Omega\))
Total resistance of resistors in series
\( R_1, R_2, R_3 \) = series resistances (\(\Omega\)); \( R_T \) = total resistance (\(\Omega\))
tips: Do not assume a single equivalent resistor is safe; check the power rating (current through each physical component) in the original circuit.
Watch the units: each resistance is in \(\Omega\) and parallel combination requires reciprocals before adding.
rq: Why can a single 20 Ω resistor replace the whole network without guaranteeing that it survives in practice?

Equivalence only preserves the voltage-current relationship at terminals A and B; the 20 Ω equivalent must carry the full current I, which exceeds what the 20 Ω part rated for, so internal component currents (I/2) must be checked separately.
Why does the current through the 20 Ω branch equal I/2 in the original circuit?
The current entering the parallel node divides between the parallel branches in inverse proportion to their resistances; here the two branches are equal (20 Ω each), so the current splits equally.

notes.t: Resistor combinations and equivalent resistance from circuit solutions
pts: Series resistors: the equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances, with the same current through each.
Parallel resistors: the equivalent resistance is the product over the sum, equivalently the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals.
Equivalent resistance of a circuit is found from Ohm's law as voltage divided by current.
Two conditions (sum and product of R1 and R2) give a quadratic whose roots are the resistor values.
A practical voltage source is modelled as an ideal source VT in series with an internal resistance RT; solving two cases simultaneously gives VT and RT.
defs: Equivalent resistance
The single resistance that draws the same current from a source at the same voltage as the original network.
eqs: Equivalent resistance from voltage and current
\(R_{T}\) = equivalent resistance (Ω); V = voltage across network (V); I = current through network (A)
\(V_{T}\) = source EMF (V); \(R_{T}\) = internal resistance (Ω); I = current (A)
tips: Watch the sign when factorising: x² − 6x − 8 = 0 is not (x−4)(x−2); check the expansion before using roots.
Keep units consistent: the 4/3 Ω and 6 Ω values are in ohms, and R1R2 is in Ω².
rq: Why can R1 = 4 Ω and R2 = 2 Ω be found by inspection once R1 + R2 = 6 Ω and R1R2 = 8 Ω² are known?
Two numbers summing to 6 with product 8 must be 4 and 2, since they are the roots of x² − 6x − 8 = 0... (note: factorising gives roots 2 and 4).
Why do we subtract the two source equations to find RT?
Both equal VT, so eliminating VT leaves a single equation in RT (2 − 2RT = 0), giving RT = 1 Ω.

notes.t: Thévenin equivalent and maximum power transfer
pts: Thévenin voltage found as the open-circuit voltage between terminals A and B, with B taken as 0 V
Thévenin resistance found by shorting the voltage sources and combining the resistors in parallel
Load power is maximised when the load resistance equals the Thévenin resistance
Load voltage found by voltage divider across the Thévenin resistance and load
defs: Thévenin resistance
Equivalent resistance seen between two terminals with all independent voltage sources set to zero (shorted).
eqs: Thévenin resistance of two resistors in parallel
Power in load resistor from voltage divider
tips: Shorting voltage sources (not open-circuiting them) is required when finding the Thévenin resistance.
Check units: resistances in ohms and power in watts; power at \(R_{L}\) = 8 Ω is 25/8 ≈ 3.1 W.
rq: Why does the maximum power occur when \(R_{L}\) equals \(R_{T}\) rather than when \(R_{L}\) is as small as possible?
Small \(R_{L}\) draws large current but gets little voltage across it; large \(R_{L}\) gets voltage but little current. The product of V and I peaks when \(R_{L}\) = \(R_{T}\).

notes.t: Maximum power transfer and Thevenin equivalent circuit
pts: Thevenin voltage found by treating the open terminals; a resistor with no current flow drops no voltage, so the Thevenin voltage equals the voltage across the 20Ω resistor by the voltage divider rule.
Thevenin resistance found by shorting the voltage source and looking back between the terminals A and B, combining resistors in series and parallel.
Power in the load is P = V²/R; for a fixed source, power peaks when the load equals the Thevenin resistance (40Ω here), and the load voltage splits equally across equal resistances.
To find load values giving a given power (75% of peak), set the power expression equal to the target and solve the resulting quadratic in \(R_{L}\), taking both roots.
defs: Thevenin equivalent circuit
A linear network replaced by a single voltage source in series with a single resistor that gives identical behaviour at the load terminals.
eqs: P = power (W); V = voltage across load (V); R = load resistance (\(\Omega\))
Power delivered to load \(R_{L}\) from Thevenin source of voltage \(V_{T}\) and resistance \(R_{T}\)
\(V_{T}\) = Thevenin voltage (V); \(R_{T}\) = Thevenin resistance (\(\Omega\)); \(R_{L}\) = load resistance (\(\Omega\)); P = power (W)
tips: Both roots of the quadratic (40/3 Ω and 120 Ω) give 75% of peak power; state both unless the question restricts \(R_{L}\).
Shorting a voltage source means replacing it with a wire (zero resistance), not removing it.
rq: Why does the 24Ω resistor not affect the Thevenin voltage, but does affect the Thevenin resistance?
No current flows through it when the terminals are open, so it drops no voltage; but it is still in series with the network seen from A and B, so it adds to \(R_{T}\).
Why does the load power peak at \(R_{L}\) = 40Ω rather than at the largest or smallest load?
Power is zero for \(R_{L}\) = 0 (no voltage) and for \(R_{L}\) → ∞ (no current); maximum power transfer occurs when \(R_{L}\) equals \(R_{T}\) = 40Ω.

notes.t: RC circuit impedance at 1 kHz: series and parallel
pts: Capacitor reactance at a given frequency is found from \( X_c = -j/\omega C \), with \( \omega = 2\pi f \).
In series, impedances add: the resistor and capacitor reactance combine as a complex sum, and the magnitude and phase are then taken in polar form.
In parallel, the combined impedance is \( RX_c/(R+X_c) \), computed by rationalising the complex denominator.
Branch currents in parallel add as phasors (vector addition), giving the total current magnitude and angle.
eqs: \( X_c \) = reactance (Ω); \( \omega \) = angular frequency (rad \(s^{-1}\)); \( C \) = capacitance (F)
\( Z \) = impedance (Ω); \( R \) = resistance (Ω); \( X_c \) = capacitive reactance (Ω)
tips: Keep the sign of j when inverting: \( 1/(1-j1.59) \) must be rationalised by multiplying by the complex conjugate.
Watch units: convert kΩ and mA consistently when computing current \( I = V/Z \).
rq: Why does the series case give a larger impedance magnitude than the resistor alone?
Because the capacitive reactance (–j1.59 kΩ) is added as a quadrature component, so \( |Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + X_c^2} \) exceeds R.
Why does the source voltage of 2 V split into \(V_{R}\) + \(V_{C}\) that sum to 2 V in both phasor and magnitude sense?
Because the same current flows through series elements, and the phasor voltages add vectorially, satisfying Kirchhoff's voltage law.

notes.t: Op-amp nodal analysis with a capacitor at ω = 200 rad/s
pts: For an ideal op-amp the inputs are at the same potential, so V+ = V− = 0 and nodal analysis is applied at the inverting node.
Capacitor impedance is \(X_{C}\) = −j/(ωC); at ω = 200 rad/s with C = 0.25 µF it gives −j20 kΩ.
Phasor source voltage is written in rectangular form before solving: 4∠0° V = 4 + 0j V.
Complex-valued nodal equations are solved algebraically, then converted to polar form and finally to a time-domain sinusoid.
defs: Virtual earth (ideal op-amp)
With negative feedback and ideal (infinite gain) op-amp, V+ = V− so the inverting input sits at the non-inverting input's potential, here 0 V.
eqs: \(X_{C}\) = impedance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); C = capacitance (F)
\(V_{o}\) = output voltage (V); \(V_{x}\) = voltage at top of capacitor (V)
tips: Keep phase angles in radians vs degrees consistent: 153° ≈ 2.68 rad when writing sin(200t + φ).
Multiplying through by 20 kΩ clears denominators but the −j20 kΩ term must keep its sign and j factor.
rq: Why can V− be set to 0 V when analysing the op-amp circuit?
Because the ideal op-amp has V+ = V− (with V+ grounded), so the inverting node is at 0 V.
Why is the final answer converted from rectangular to polar form?
Polar form gives magnitude and phase directly, which converts easily to a sinusoid \(V_{o}\) = A sin(ωt + φ).

xq.q: A network is connected across a supply. A 30 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of a 20 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor. The network draws a total current I = 0.8 A. Find (a) the equivalent resistance of the network and (b) the power dissipated in the equivalent resistor, using P = I²R, with I the total current.

A network of resistors has equivalent resistance 40 Ω and draws a total current I = 0.8 A. It contains a 20 Ω resistor in a branch that carries I/2. A student replaces the whole network with a single 40 Ω resistor rated 5 W. What is the correct judgement?
xq.a: Not safe, because P = 0.64 × 40 = 25.6 W exceeds 5 W
o: Safe, because the 20 Ω branch carries only I/2
Safe, because 40 Ω is larger than any resistor in the network
Not safe, because P = 0.64 × 40 = 25.6 W exceeds 5 W
Not safe, because P = 0.8 × 40 = 32 W exceeds 5 W
xq.w: The equivalent resistor carries the total current, so P = I²R = 25.6 W; the traps are using only the branch current or using P = IR.

rep.ov: So far the module covers the machine elements and systems that make up basic mechanical and fluid equipment: valves (Week 2), positive displacement and centrifugal pumps (Week 3), pumps in systems (Week 4), heat exchangers (Week 5), clutches (Week 6), and machinery mountings, gearboxes, fluid-system drawing standards and concept selection (Week 7). Each topic follows the same pattern of purpose, design principles, types and their pros and cons, and the topics build on one another. Valves and pumps feed into system curves and operating points, clutches lead into torque and power, and gearbox design links thermal, structural and lubrication principles. Assessment is coursework only (30% set exercises, 70% design project), so the aim is to apply this material in quizzes and the project, with the standard drawing conventions and the concept-selection method supporting both.
must: Pump classification: positive displacement (PD) pumps enclose a fixed volume, so flow is set by speed and pressure by the system. Centrifugal pumps never enclose the fluid, so flow is set by the system, and head falls as flow rises.

Operating point = intersection of the pump curve and the system curve, plotted on the same head-flow axes. The system curve is \(H = H_{static} + \) friction head, and the friction part is proportional to \(Q^2\). With no static head the curve starts at the origin.

Static head = suction head + discharge head (elevation only, in metres of fluid, independent of density and flow). Dynamic head adds friction. TDH = static + dynamic. System curves are bounded by best-case and worst-case valve settings.

Theoretical suction lift \(H = \frac{P}{\rho g}\approx 10\) m for water. Practical lift is lower because of vapour pressure, friction, leakage and cavitation (NPSH). Scale by specific gravity for other fluids, e.g. diesel at SG 0.86.

PD piston pump flow \(\dot{v} = (AK - V)S\). A single piston gives pulsed, half-wave-rectifier-like output, which is smoothed with multiple pistons or an accumulator. Centrifugal pump parts: the impeller adds energy, and the volute/casing converts kinetic energy to pressure. Know the BEP, the allowable flow range, the affinity laws (\(Q\propto N\), \(H\propto N^2\)), and that impeller diameter shifts the curve.

Valve types and duty: globe (linear, throttling, S-shaped flow path, flow enters under the seat, gland packing, plug lift \(h = D/4\) from \(\pi R^2 = 2\pi R h\)); gate (on/off only, low pressure drop when fully open, thrust collar, guides can jam under pressure drop); butterfly (quarter-turn); relief and non-return valves. Know the four functions: on/off, flow rate, pressure and direction.

Heat exchanger conduction \(\frac{Q}{t} = \frac{kA\Delta T}{d}\). Design needs large area, thin wall, high conductivity, strength, corrosion resistance, and no fluid mixing. Compare plate exchangers (compact, cleanable, expandable, but with short-lived seals) with shell-and-tube (differential expansion, floating end with O-rings and tell-tale, tube plates, headers).

Parallel-flow vs counter-flow: counter-flow is more efficient (the cold outlet can approach the hot inlet temperature) but gives a higher pressure drop. Heat transfer uses \(Q = UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\) with LMTD = \(\frac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}\). Also know plate materials (304/316 stainless, titanium, Hastelloy), seal materials (NBR, EPDM), vents at high points, drains at low points, and sacrificial anodes.

Clutch classification: positive contact (dog/jaw, align before engaging, no slip), friction (drum/centrifugal, disc, with wet multi-disc clutches adding discs to offset the lower \(\mu\)), overrunning (ratchet and pawl, roller, sprag), and fluid coupling (always has slip, which becomes heat). Know the engagement/disengagement conditions of each.

Clutch torque and power: \(P = T\omega\) with \(\omega\) in rad/s. Inertial torque \(T = mk^2\alpha\). Gearbox speed reduction raises torque at constant power, so the clutch goes on the high-speed, low-torque side. Engagement heat depends on the speed difference and on \(\alpha\).

Gearbox and mounting design: beam deflection depends on the support configuration (simply supported, cantilever, fixed), so use the correct formula. Heat transfer by Fourier \(Q=-K\,dT/dx\) and Newton cooling \(Q=hA\Delta T\). Gearboxes need lubrication to reduce wear and remove heat (sump vs pumped oil), and must carry axial end-thrusts from helical and worm gears.

Communication and method: SI units with a full stop as the decimal point and no thousands commas. Fluid diagrams follow BS 5070-3, BS 1553 and BS ISO 1219-1. Drawings use orthographic views with tolerances and stated dimensions (never scaled). Concept selection uses a weighted decision matrix with 5-10 concepts and criteria taken from the PDS.
conn: Valves + system curves: opening and closing globe or gate valves changes system resistance, which moves the system curve (best and worst cases) and so shifts the pump operating point.

Pump selection + suction lift + NPSH: the static suction head, vapour pressure and \(H=P/\rho g\) limit the practical lift, and NPSHR rises with flow on the pump curve. A question may ask for the operating point and then check cavitation risk.
Clutches + gearbox: \(P=T\omega\) decides where to place the clutch relative to the gearbox, and \(T=mk^2\alpha\) gives the engagement torque and heat, which links to gearbox lubrication and cooling.

Heat exchanger conduction + enclosure cooling: the same conduction and convection ideas (\(kA\Delta T/d\), \(hA\Delta T\)) apply to exchanger walls, gearbox enclosures and oil coolers, as does the choice of material and thickness.
Fluid system drawings + valves/pumps: symbols and standards (BS 1553, BS 5070) are used to draw pump-valve circuits, and concept selection with the PDS ties these into the Semester 2 project.
exq: A pump must lift water 6 m on the suction side and 14 m on the discharge side. The friction head is 5 m at 20 m³/h and scales with \(Q^2\). Sketch the system curve, give the static head, and find the operating point on a given pump curve.
A pump is to draw diesel (SG 0.86) from a tank. Using \(H=P/\rho g\), find the theoretical maximum suction lift, and explain why the practical lift is lower.
A single-acting piston pump has piston area 0.002 m², stroke 0.1 m, leakage 5×10⁻⁶ m³ per stroke and speed 300 rpm. Calculate the flow rate in m³/s, and describe how to reduce pressure ripple.

Compare plate and shell-and-tube heat exchangers for a seawater cooling duty. Cover materials, differential expansion, cleaning, vents/drains and corrosion protection, and explain why counter-flow is preferred, with an LMTD calculation for given terminal temperatures.

A motor drives a load of inertia mk² through a clutch and gearbox. Explain where to put the clutch, and calculate the engagement torque for a given \(\alpha\) and the power transmitted at a given torque and speed (rpm to rad/s). Compare a dog clutch, a multi-plate wet clutch and a sprag clutch for this duty.
Explain, with sketches, how a globe valve and a gate valve work. State which is suited to throttling and which to isolation, and calculate the plug lift for a 50 mm bore.
weak: Constructing system curves with static head and finding operating points: students mix up static, suction, discharge and dynamic head, forget that friction scales with \(Q^2\), and mishandle units (m³/h vs m³/s, head vs pressure).

Clutch torque, power and engagement analysis: the rpm to rad/s conversion, the squared radius of gyration, and the reasoning about which side of the gearbox to put the clutch on. Distinguishing the overrunning clutch types, and reading the sprag and ratchet direction from sketches, is also hard.

Heat exchanger flow configurations and LMTD: choosing the correct \(\Delta T_1\) and \(\Delta T_2\) at each end for parallel vs counter-flow, and explaining the trade-offs (efficiency vs pressure drop, expansion) rather than just listing them.

units.name: 1.2 Purpose, engineering skills and course aims
units.ov: This introductory material sets out why the course exists, which skills engineers need, and what the course will teach. It frames engineering as creative, systematic problem solving that combines technical and non-technical skills. The specific aims (design process, sustainability and ethics, basic fluid machines, engineering drawing, group project) show how lectures feed into the collaborative design project. The notes contain no equations or calculations, so questions will probably be descriptive or applied.
must: Engineering is more than maths and physics: it is creative problem solving applied to real needs.
Design follows a systematic, learnable process, and the course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within design, so iteration and refinement are part of the process.
Core engineering skills span technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills (teamwork, communication, leadership) are as essential as technical ones.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail underpin sound engineering judgement.
A capacity for lifelong learning lets engineers keep pace with evolving technology.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed, not optional add-ons.
Basic fluid machines are studied through their design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
Students must be able to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings; the group project applies lecture knowledge to a real design problem.
conn: The systematic design process links to the group project: the project is where the process is applied and where mistakes and iteration serve as learning.
Sustainability and ethics apply to every design decision, including the design and operation of fluid machines.
Sketches and engineering drawings are the means of communicating design ideas, which links technical skill to teamwork and communication in the project.
Fluid machines serve as the worked example in which design, construction, operation and drawing skills come together.
exq: Describe the stages of a systematic engineering design process and explain how iteration and learning from mistakes improve the final design.
Discuss why non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are as important as technical knowledge for a mechanical engineer. Give examples from a group design project.
Explain how sustainability and ethical considerations could influence the design of a basic fluid machine such as a pump. Give at least three specific design decisions affected.
Sketch a simple fluid machine (e.g. a centrifugal pump) and label its main components. State what information an engineering drawing must convey so that it can be built.

notes.t: Purpose of the course
pts: Engineering is broader than just maths and physics; it involves creative problem solving.
Students learn common engineering solutions to recurring problems.
Design follows a systematic process that can be learned and applied.
Imagination and personal ideas are encouraged, and students get hands-on design opportunities.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within the design process.
tips: This page states course aims rather than technical content, so exam questions are unlikely to ask for these points verbatim; focus on the technical topics that follow.
rq: Why does the course stress that engineering is more than maths and physics?
Because real engineering design also requires creativity, practical judgement, and the ability to choose sensible solutions, not just solve equations.
What might be the benefit of following a defined design process rather than designing ad hoc?
It structures the work into repeatable steps, making problems easier to define, solutions easier to evaluate, and errors easier to find and correct.

notes.t: What are engineering skills?
pts: Engineering requires a set of core skills spanning technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are equally essential for engineers.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail support sound engineering judgement.
A capacity to learn lets an engineer keep pace with evolving technology throughout a career.
rq: Why might a graduate with strong technical knowledge still struggle in an engineering job?
Because engineering work also depends on teamwork, communication, management and leadership, which technical knowledge alone does not provide.

notes.t: Specific course aims
pts: The course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed.
Basic fluid machines are studied in terms of their design, construction and operation.
Students learn to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings.
A collaborative project applies lecture knowledge to a real engineering design problem.
tips: Note that the course covers fluid machines as "basic machines" focused on design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
rq: Why does the course pair technical design processes with sustainability and ethics?
Engineering designs affect society and the environment, so sustainability and ethical considerations must be built into design decisions from the start, not added afterwards.

must: Mechanical Design 1 covers the more unique elements of design; Design and Manufacture 1 covers the more repetitive elements. Do not swap them.
The two courses are deliberately designed as partners and should be treated as complementary, not separate.
Mechanical Design 1 has two parts: (1) design and functionality of fundamental machines and systems, and (2) the design process leading to a completed real-world design project.
Semester 1 is mainly the taught side: fundamental machines and systems, with the course schedule on the timetable page.
Semester 2 centres on the Design Project, which applies the design process; check the timetable for milestone dates.
Know your own timetable: deadlines, session types and locations. The extracted notes give no specifics, so take these from the original slides or Moodle.
This page has no formulae or definitions. Credit comes from understanding structure and how the parts fit together, not from calculation.
conn: Fundamental machines and systems (part 1) provide the technical knowledge applied in the part 2 design project.

The Semester 1 schedule feeds the Semester 2 project timetable: skills learned early are assessed through project deliverables later.

The slide describes course structure only; do not expect technical formulae or definitions from this page.
rq: Why are Mechanical Design 1 and Design and Manufacture 1 taught as partner courses rather than as one course?
Mechanical Design 1 covers the unique, non-routine aspects of design, while Design and Manufacture 1 covers the repetitive, routine aspects; together they give a complete view of engineering design.
How does the second part of Mechanical Design 1 differ from the first part?

The first part teaches the design and functionality of fundamental machines and systems, whereas the second part focuses on the overall design process that leads to completing a real-world design project.

must: The course has no exams: all assessment is coursework, so check deadlines and submission details on Moodle
Set Exercises are worth 30% of the credit and the Design Project 70%, so \(30\%+70\%=100\%\)
Set Exercises consist of two Moodle quizzes and one hand-written in-class exercise
Design Project (70%) = 50% project report + 20% poster presentation, both group-marked
Group marks are adjusted per student by 20% peer weighting, so individual contribution affects your final mark
Knowledge a professional engineer must know without looking it up is assessed by timed online quizzes

conn: Assessment type matches knowledge type: recall is tested by timed quizzes, creation by report and poster quality and process, and source use by proof of use
Peer weighting links the group-marked report and poster (70% of credit) to your individual contribution and so to your final mark

Recognising strengths reinforces effective practice and keeps the student motivated, while errors are then addressed constructively and targeted for improvement.

rq: Why might basing the design project on a real-world competition like EWB's be valuable compared with a textbook exercise?
A real problem has ill-defined requirements, constraints from cultures and environments, and cannot be solved by a single known method, so it develops practical engineering judgement.

units.name: 1.6 AI caution, ethics and expectations of engineers
units.ov: This material covers the University of Glasgow grading scheme (A–H, CR and grade points), cautions on using AI tools without misconduct, the four engineering ethical principles from the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering, and the wider expectations of 21st-century engineers. The ideas connect through professional integrity: honest acknowledgement of AI use, verifying information with engineering judgement and maintaining high standards all reflect ethical practice and meet what industry and academia expect.
must: The four ethical principles (Engineering Council/RAEng): honesty and integrity; respect for life, law, the environment and public good; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication
Principle 2 bundles four concepts: life, law, the environment and public good; name them all
AI use is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as your own is misconduct and plagiarism, with severe penalties
AI output may be inaccurate: verify it with your own research and engineering judgement, and cite software-generated information using the guidance
Why ethics matters: safety (protecting people from harm), public trust, reputation of organisations, sustainability, quality and professional standards
Ethics is more than legal compliance, so cover safety, sustainability, quality and trust in answers
Core expectations of engineers: technical knowledge, work ethic, teamwork, ethics, organisation and independence; industry seeks skilled, reliable, industrious people
Grading: A (Excellent) down to H; D (Satisfactory) is the minimum acceptable attainment of intended learning outcomes; E–G are deficient; H is no convincing evidence
Grade points run 0–22 with higher meaning better (A1 = 22, H = 0); don't reverse the direction
CR (Credit Refused) is a compliance outcome for failing to meet course requirements without good cause or for serious breach of regulations, not a measure of academic ability
conn: AI caution and ethical principles: undeclared AI use breaches honesty and integrity, and unverified AI output breaches accuracy and rigour
Ethics and professional expectations: ethical conduct underpins public trust and reputation, which industry demands alongside reliability and work ethic
Grading and misconduct: academic misconduct or non-compliance can lead to CR regardless of content knowledge, so grade points reflect attainment while CR reflects compliance
Engineering judgement links AI verification, accuracy and rigour, and independence as an expected skill
exq: List and briefly explain the four fundamental principles of ethical engineering behaviour defined by the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering.

Discuss four reasons why ethical behaviour is important in engineering, beyond legal compliance.

Outline the skills and attitudes expected of a 21st-century engineer beyond technical knowledge, and explain why industry values them.

notes.t: Grading scheme
pts: Grades run from A (Excellent) down to H, with CR meaning credit refused.
Each primary grade has secondary bands with numeric grade points, higher points indicating stronger attainment.
Grade D (Satisfactory) is the minimum acceptable attainment of intended learning outcomes.
Grades E to G indicate deficient attainment, with H meaning no convincing evidence of attainment.
CR (Credit Refused) applies to failure to comply with course requirements or serious breach of regulations, not to academic performance alone.
defs: Credit Refused (CR)
Outcome given for failure to comply, without good cause, with published course or programme requirements and/or a serious breach of regulations.
Primary grade
The top-level letter band (A–H, CR) describing overall attainment of intended learning outcomes, each subdivided into secondary bands.
Grade point
Numeric score (0–22) attached to each secondary band, with A1 = 22 the highest and H = 0 the lowest.
tips: Do not confuse grade point scale direction: higher numbers mean better performance (A1 = 22, H = 0), not the reverse.
CR is a compliance outcome, not a measure of academic ability; a student can be CR despite strong content knowledge.
rq: Why does a grade of D count as a pass while E does not, even though both indicate imperfect attainment?

D denotes acceptable attainment with a minimally sufficient range of materials and reasonable analytical grasp, whereas E denotes deficient attainment of specific outcomes with weak argument deployment.
What is the difference between a grade of H and a grade of CR?

H reflects academic performance with no convincing evidence of attainment; CR reflects non-compliance with course or programme requirements or serious regulation breaches, regardless of academic content.

notes.t: Notes of caution about AI
pts: AI tools like ChatGPT are increasingly used in universities
Use of AI is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as your own is misconduct and plagiarism
Penalties for academic misconduct are severe, so do not risk it
AI-generated information may be inaccurate, so you must verify it with your own research and engineering judgement
Cite information generated from software using the guidance linked on the page
tips: Do not assume AI-generated information is correct; always check it against your own research and engineering judgement.
Undeclared AI use counts as misconduct even if the AI use itself is not prohibited; always acknowledge and cite AI-generated content.
rq: Why is spellchecking considered a form of artificial intelligence in a strict sense?
Because it uses automated algorithms to process and correct text, which falls under the broad definition of AI.
What would make the use of an AI tool become academic misconduct, even though AI use itself is allowed?
Failing to acknowledge how the AI was used, or presenting AI-generated output as your own work.

notes.t: Ethical principles in engineering
pts: Ethical principles sit at the forefront of modern engineering practice.
The UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering define four fundamental principles of ethical behaviour.
Principle 1: honesty and integrity.
Principle 2: respect for life, law, the environment and public good.
Principles 3 and 4: accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication.
defs: Ethical principles (engineering)
Fundamental standards of ethical behaviour defined for the engineering profession by the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering, guiding professional conduct.
tips: Know all four principles by name; exam questions often ask you to list or briefly explain them.
Principle 2 bundles several concepts (life, law, environment, public good); name them all when describing it.
rq: Why might respect for the environment and public good be listed alongside respect for law as a single principle?
Engineering decisions affect society and the environment beyond the client, so professional duty extends to public welfare, not just legal compliance.
What could go wrong if an engineer had accurate calculations but poor communication?
Correct analysis could still be misunderstood or ignored, leading to unsafe decisions; leadership and communication ensure results are acted on properly.

notes.t: Ethical principles in engineering
pts: Ethics underpins safe engineering practice, protecting people from harm.
Ethical conduct sustains public trust in the engineering profession.
Ethical behaviour protects the reputation of companies and organisations.
Ethics encourages sustainable engineering practices and maintains quality and professional standards.
Adhering to ethics ensures high quality work and a high standard of professional engineer.
tips: Ethics is about more than legal compliance; it covers safety, sustainability, quality and public trust, so answers should cover several of these.
rq: Why might a company's reputation depend on the ethical conduct of its engineers?
Unethical or unsafe work can lead to failures, legal action and loss of client and public trust, damaging the organisation's commercial standing.
How does ethical practice relate to public confidence in engineering?
When engineers consistently act safely, honestly and responsibly, the public trusts that engineered products and infrastructure are reliable.

notes.t: Expectations of engineers in the 21st century
pts: Engineers are expected by both industry and academia to meet a range of skills and attitudes beyond pure technical knowledge.
The core expectations include technical knowledge, work ethic, teamwork, ethics, organisation and independence.
Industry actively seeks skilled, reliable and industrious people, so maintaining high standards is key.
rq: Why might communication and teamworking matter as much as technical accomplishment for an engineer's career?
Engineering projects are collaborative and engineers must explain and coordinate their work with others, so technical skill alone is rarely sufficient in industry.
What might happen to an engineering organisation if individuals lacked ethics, openness and honesty?
Trust, safety and reliability would be undermined, leading to errors being hidden, poor decisions and damage to reputation or public safety.

xq.q: A student with strong coursework marks is awarded grade CR for a course after a serious breach of regulations. Which statement about this outcome is correct?
xq.a: CR is a compliance outcome, so it can be given even if the student's content knowledge is strong.
o: CR is the lowest academic grade, equal to H with 0 grade points, so it reflects weak content knowledge.
CR is a compliance outcome, so it can be given even if the student's content knowledge is strong.
CR is a secondary band of grade D, the minimum acceptable attainment.
CR is awarded when a student scores between grade points 1 and 5, in the E to G range.
xq.w: CR is given for failure to comply with requirements or a serious breach of regulations, not for academic performance; confusing it with H is the trap.
s: CR = Credit Refused, a compliance outcome
It does not measure academic ability

xq.q: A student uses an AI tool to produce a calculation of the pressure drop in a pipe and submits it as their own work without checking it or declaring the tool. Explain why this is unacceptable, referring to both academic regulations and the engineering ethical principles.
xq.a: Using AI is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as one's own is misconduct and plagiarism, which carries severe penalties. AI output may be inaccurate, so it must be verified using one's own research and engineering judgement; not checking breaches the principle of accuracy and rigour. Presenting it as own work breaches honesty and integrity. Wrong calculations in practice could harm people, breaching respect for life and public good. The correct approach is to declare and cite the AI-generated content and verify it.
s: Undeclared use or passing off output as own is misconduct/plagiarism with severe penalties
AI may be inaccurate: must verify with research and judgement (accuracy and rigour)
Dishonest presentation breaches honesty and integrity
Should declare and cite the use

xq.q: Explain why adherence to ethical principles matters in engineering, giving four distinct benefits, and name the four fundamental principles of ethical behaviour defined by the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering.
xq.a: The four principles are: honesty and integrity; respect for life, law, the environment and public good; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication. Ethics matters because it protects people from harm by underpinning safe practice, sustains public trust in the profession, protects the reputation of companies and organisations, and encourages sustainable practice while maintaining quality and professional standards.
s: Sustainability, quality and standards (any four benefits)

units.name: 1.7 Course introduction and contents (summary notes)
units.ov: This is the introduction to Basic Machine Elements. It outlines the course topics: valves and pumps, pumps in systems, heat exchangers, clutches, machinery mountings and gearboxes, plus basic fluid systems and engineering drawing. It also sets the conventions for communicating technical information (SI units, number formatting). The notes are only an outline, so the technical content below comes from what the contents pages list and from standard knowledge of these topics.
must: Use SI units throughout and convert every quantity before substituting into formulas; unit errors give answers wrong by orders of magnitude
Number format: decimal point is a full stop, and no commas as thousands separators (write 12500 or 12.5, not 12,500)
Pump-system matching: the operating point is where the pump curve intersects the system curve
System curve: \(H_{sys}=H_{static}+kQ^2\), so with static head it starts at a non-zero height on the head axis; check for static head first
Suction lift and static head both affect the pump duty and must be included in the system analysis
Heat exchanger types: plate and shell-and-tube, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials, so be ready to compare and justify a choice
Clutch types by purpose: dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, fluid coupling
Clutch analysis separates steady state (\(P=T\omega\), torque balance) from accelerating conditions (\(T-T_{load}=I\alpha\), which must include inertia)
Machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes: transmitting power loads the gearbox, so consider the effects of the transmitted torque and power
conn: Pump curve with system curve (static head plus friction) gives the operating point, and suction lift limits where the pump can be placed
Clutch torque, power and speed link to gearbox loading: \(P=T\omega\) sets the torque transmitted through the gearbox and onto its mountings
Accelerating clutch engagement needs inertia, \(T=I\alpha\), and the slipping energy dissipated is a heating problem, which links to thermal management
Unit consistency underlies all of these calculations (pressure to head, rpm to rad/s, kW to W)
exq: A pump delivers water through a pipe system with 15 m static head and friction losses \(kQ^2\). Given the pump curve data, plot both curves and find the operating flow rate and head.
Explain how suction lift affects pump selection and positioning, and state what changes in the system curve when static head is added.
Compare plate and shell-and-tube heat exchangers in terms of advantages, disadvantages and materials, and recommend one for a stated application.

A friction clutch connects a motor of known power and speed to a load of known inertia. Calculate the steady-state torque transmitted, then the torque needed to accelerate the load to speed in a given time.
Describe how a sprag clutch (overrunning) and a fluid coupling work and give one suitable application for each.

notes.t: Table of contents: Pumps in Systems, Heat Exchangers, Clutches, Machinery Mountings
pts: The notes cover pump-system matching, including system curves and pump curves, with static head and suction lift considered.
Heat exchangers are split into plate type and shell and tube type, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials.
Clutches are organised by purpose and type, including dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, and fluid couplings.
Torque, power and speed are treated separately for steady state and accelerating conditions in clutch analysis.
The final section covers machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, including the effects of transmitting power on a gearbox.
tips: Do not confuse the steady-state and accelerating torque conditions; accelerating analysis must include inertia effects.
Check whether a pump problem includes static head before drawing the system curve, as the curve starts at a different height.
rq: Why would a dog clutch be unsuitable for engaging while the shafts are rotating at different speeds?
Dog clutches have interlocking teeth that must align; with a speed difference the teeth would clash and cause shock loading and damage, so they are engaged at rest or near matched speed.
What is the key difference between steady-state and accelerating torque in a clutch?
Steady-state torque is what the clutch transmits at constant speed; accelerating torque additionally includes the torque needed to change the rotating inertia's speed.

notes.t: Communicating Technical Information in this Course
pts: Always use SI units, whatever is customary in your home country.
Write the decimal point as a full stop, not a comma.
Do not use commas to separate thousands in numbers, to avoid confusion with European decimal commas.
tips: Unit trap: convert all quantities to SI units before substituting into formulas, otherwise answers will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
Number formatting: write 12500 or 12.5 rather than 12,500 or 12,5 so markers read values unambiguously.
rq: Why does a comma used as a thousands separator cause problems in an international engineering context?
Because in many European countries the comma is the decimal point, so 1,500 could be read as 1.5 rather than 1500, risking a serious numerical error.

units.name: 2.1 Course intro and learning outcomes
units.ov: The material is only the intro and learning outcomes page for the Week 2 'Valves' topic of Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016). It sets out what must be learned: the engineering principles behind valve design, the types of valve, their key components, and the advantages and limitations of each type. The notes give no technical detail, so the lecture content is needed, especially for the Moodle quiz.
must: The course notes are only a basic version of the lectures; the Moodle quiz needs the lecture content, so revise from both
Be able to explain the engineering principles used in valve design (the notes do not list them, so take them from the lectures)
Be able to identify the different types of valve, by name and from a diagram
Be able to identify and name the key components of a valve (e.g. body, seat, closure element, stem or actuator; confirm the exact list in the lectures)
For each valve type, know its advantages and its limitations
Be able to compare valve types and choose the right one for a given application, justifying the choice
Use correct terminology and sketch labelled diagrams, as quiz questions are likely to test recognition
conn: Valve type and key components: each type's design (how the closure element moves and seals) determines its advantages and limitations
Design principles and application choice: selecting a valve means matching its strengths and limits to the operating requirements
Components and function: knowing what each part does lets you explain why a valve works and how it can fail or leak
Course notes and lecture content: the notes give the framework and the lectures give the detail the quiz tests
exq: Name and sketch three different types of valve and label their key components.
Compare two valve types, giving two advantages and two limitations of each.
Given a described application, select the most suitable valve type and justify your choice using the engineering principles of valve design.
Describe the function of each key component in a named valve and explain what happens if one fails.
Explain the engineering principles that govern how a valve controls or isolates flow.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes (valves)
