Turning the threaded spindle raises or lowers the gate (plug) against a matching seat; the thrust collar is trapped by the cover so it cannot move axially.

Guides on either side of the gate slide in channels in the casing to stop it rotating; high pressure drop can push the gate against these guides, so their bearing surfaces must be smooth and low-friction.
defs: Gate valve
A valve in which a parallel or wedge-shaped gate (plug) is raised or lowered by a threaded spindle to open or close the flow path against a matching seat, used mainly for on/off isolation.
tips: Do not select a gate valve for flow regulation; it is designed only as an ON/OFF valve.
A gate valve's low pressure drop applies only when fully open; partial opening causes large losses and vibration.
rq: Why must the guide and channel surfaces be smooth and made of suitable materials?
A large pressure drop can force the gate sideways against the guides; rubbing surfaces with high friction would cause jamming and wear, so smooth, low-friction materials are needed.
Why does a gate valve require extra height in the system?
The plug must lift fully out of the flow stream to avoid obstructing flow and causing pressure drop when open, which needs vertical clearance.

notes.t: Butterfly Valves: Design Points and Aspects
pts: A butterfly valve's basic purpose is as a simple ON/OFF valve, though it can also be used to control flow.
A butterfly valve can achieve a 100% seal, but sealing becomes harder to maintain over time.
Any butterfly valve causes some resistance to flow, even when fully open.
Full closure is difficult because the disc often must push against a rubber seat, and the disc can jam in the closed position.
The handle length sets the opening or closing torque that can be generated, so long handles are often needed.
tips: Do not confuse the handle length with the flow rate: handle length governs the force needed to operate the valve, not how much fluid passes.
Butterfly valves cannot be made one-way only, so do not propose them where strict non-return flow is required.
rq: Why does a longer valve handle make the valve easier to operate?
The handle acts as a lever arm; a longer arm gives a greater moment (torque) for the same hand force, so a larger opening or closing force can be generated.
Why might a butterfly valve that seals 100% when new later leak?
The rubber seat wears and the disc repeatedly pushes against it, so the seal degrades over time and full closure becomes harder.

notes.t: Butterfly valve construction
pts: A butterfly valve regulates flow with a disc rotated on a stem inside the body.
The disc sits against a seat in the body; the seat may be rubber or metal.
The stem passes through packing, bushing and stem retainer, sealed by a thrust washer and retaining ring.
Two principal versions exist: rubber-seated and metal-seated.
defs: Butterfly valve
A quarter-turn valve in which a circular disc, mounted on a rotating stem, controls flow when turned against a seat within the body.
Disc
The circular closure element of a butterfly valve that rotates on the stem to open or shut the flow path.
Seat
The sealing surface in the body against which the disc closes, either rubber or metal.
Stem
The shaft connecting the actuator to the disc, passing through the body and sealed by packing.
tips: Do not confuse the disc (the rotating closure) with the seat (the fixed sealing surface in the body).
Identify the seat type (rubber or metal) before stating leakage or temperature limits.
rq: Why does the stem need packing, bushing and a stem retainer rather than passing straight through the body?
Packing seals against leakage, the bushing supports the stem and reduces friction, and the retainer locates the stem axially so it cannot be pushed out under pressure.
What trade-off would you expect between a rubber-seated and a metal-seated butterfly valve?
Rubber seats give tight, bubble-tight shut-off at lower pressures and temperatures but wear and degrade; metal seats tolerate high temperatures and pressures and are more durable but may leak more.

notes.t: Relief (safety) valves – construction and design
pts: Relief valves prevent excess pressure building up in pipe systems by opening automatically.
The valve disc is held closed by a spring arrangement on the stem; spring compression sets the opening pressure.
The spring setting must be tamper-proof yet still allow the valve to be tested in service.
The shape of the valve plug determines how the valve lifts: proportionally to over-pressure, or fully lifted with hysteresis-like staying open until pressure falls well below the set value.
Two main types exist: proportional-lift safety valves and high-lift safety valves.
defs: Relief valve
A pressure-activated valve that opens when system pressure exceeds a set value to vent fluid and prevent over-pressurisation of a pipe system.
Proportional-lift safety valve
A safety valve whose disc lift is proportional to the amount by which pressure exceeds the set (opening) pressure.
High-lift safety valve
A safety valve designed to fully lift once over-pressure is detected and to remain open until pressure drops significantly below the over-pressure value.
tips: Do not confuse the set (opening) pressure with the over-pressure value; the high-lift valve reseats only well below the over-pressure level.
Be clear that the spring compression, not the plug shape alone, sets the pressure at which the valve begins to open.
rq: Why must the spring setting be tamper-proof but still testable?
Tamper-proofing prevents unauthorised changes to the set pressure, which could allow dangerous over-pressure; testability ensures the valve is confirmed to open correctly in service.
What would happen if the valve plug shape were changed to a high-lift design on a system needing gradual pressure relief?
The valve would fully open at set pressure and stay open until pressure drops well below it, causing a larger, abrupt discharge rather than a proportional release.

xq.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two globe valve types SDSL and SDNR?
xq.a: In SDSL the disc is fixed to the spindle so it is positively raised and lowered, whereas in SDNR the disc is free and only opens when upstream pressure exceeds downstream pressure
o: In SDNR the disc is fixed to the spindle, so it is positively lifted
In SDSL the disc is free and closes under reverse pressure
In SDSL the disc is fixed to the spindle so it is positively raised and lowered, whereas in SDNR the disc is free and only opens when upstream pressure exceeds downstream pressure
Both are free-disc valves, differing only in the gland material
xq.w: The SDSL spindle is joined to the disc, while the SDNR disc is unattached so it acts as a non-return valve; swapping the two is the common error.

xq.q: In a globe valve the liquid is directed to enter from below the valve seat. Explain the benefit of this arrangement when the valve is closed, and state the main drawback of the globe valve compared with a gate valve.
xq.a: With flow entering below the seat, when the disc is closed the upstream pressure acts on the underside of the disc and the chamber above the seat is not pressurised. This reduces the load on the gland and bonnet, so sealing the spindle is easier and the bonnet is less stressed. The main drawback is a large pressure drop, because the internal passages give high flow resistance, whereas a fully open gate valve adds almost no resistance.
s: Inlet below seat means the upper chamber is not pressurised when closed
Reduced load on gland and bonnet
Globe valve has high flow resistance and large pressure drop
A fully open gate valve gives negligible extra pressure drop

xq.q: A designer needs a valve for isolating a section of pipe with the least possible pressure drop when open, and with flow possible in either direction. Which valve is the best choice?
xq.a: Gate valve, because fully open it is unobstructed and multidirectional
o: Globe valve, because it seals completely and throttles accurately
SDNR valve, because it prevents backflow
Butterfly valve, because the disc rotates 90°
Gate valve, because fully open it is unobstructed and multidirectional
xq.w: A fully open gate valve gives almost no extra resistance and passes flow either way; the trap is choosing the globe valve, which has high flow resistance and is unidirectional.

units.name: 3.1 Pump purpose, machine elements and background principles
units.ov: This material introduces why pumps are used (circulating fluid, moving it, raising pressure and increasing flow rate) and the machine elements they are built from (shafts, seals, bearings, gears, crankshafts). It then sets out the background principles: pressure (static) head and dynamic (friction) head from fluid mechanics, and the gas laws from thermodynamics. These provide the tools for sizing a pump against a system and for distinguishing positive displacement from centrifugal pumps.
must: Pressure head: \( H = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} \), in metres; P in Pa, \( \rho \) in kg/m³, g in m/s²
Head depends on fluid density: the same pressure gives a different head for different liquids
Static (pressure) head is the potential energy per unit weight of fluid at rest; dynamic head is the head loss from friction that the pump must overcome in addition

Pump duties: circulate fluid in a closed loop, transfer fluid between locations, raise pressure, increase volumetric flow rate; pumps add energy to a liquid (unlike compressors for gases or fans for small pressure rises)
Centrifugal pump flow depends strongly on the system head curve, not just speed; do not treat the two pump families alike (positive displacement vs centrifugal)
Machine elements: shafts transmit rotation and torque, bearings support shafts and reduce friction, gears/crankshafts transmit and convert motion, seals prevent leakage
Seal types: dynamic (between moving parts) vs static (between stationary parts)
Boyle's law: \( P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \) at constant T; Charles's law: \( V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2 \) at constant P
Avogadro's law: \( V_1/n_1 = V_2/n_2 \) at constant T and P; ideal gas law: \( PV = nRT \)
Use absolute temperature (K) and consistent SI units (Pa, m³) in gas law calculations; °C is a common error
conn: Total pump head requirement = static head (from \( P/\rho g \)) plus dynamic head (friction losses); this sets the duty point where the pump curve meets the system head curve, which determines centrifugal pump flow
Pressure head conversion links fluid mechanics to pump selection: a pressure rise in Pa converts to metres of head only via the fluid's density
Gas laws apply where a gas is present (e.g. a compressible pocket or a compressor/fan comparison); Boyle's law for compression, Charles's for heating, PV = nRT combining them
Machine elements connect to pump type: crankshafts and gears convert motion in positive displacement mechanisms, while shafts, bearings and dynamic seals serve the rotating parts of centrifugal pumps
exq: A pump must raise a pressure of 300 kPa in water (\( \rho = 1000 \) kg/m³). Calculate the pressure head in metres, and the head if the fluid were oil with \( \rho = 850 \) kg/m³.
Explain the difference between static (pressure) head and dynamic head, and state how each contributes to the total head a pump must deliver.
Distinguish between positive displacement and centrifugal pumps, explaining why flow in a centrifugal pump depends on the system head curve.
Describe the roles of shafts, bearings, gears/crankshafts and seals in a pump, and distinguish dynamic from static seals with examples.

A gas at 100 kPa and 20 °C occupies 0.5 m³. It is compressed isothermally to 300 kPa, then heated at constant pressure to 80 °C. Find the final volume, stating the laws used and converting temperatures to kelvin.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes: pumps
pts: Distinguish positive displacement pumps from centrifugal pumps
Understand the engineering principles used in pump design
Identify the different types of pump
Identify key pump performance characteristics
tips: Do not confuse the two pump families: flow in a centrifugal pump depends strongly on the system head curve, not just on speed.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump deliver a roughly constant flow regardless of outlet pressure, whereas a centrifugal pump's flow falls as pressure rises?

A positive displacement pump traps a fixed volume each cycle and forces it out, so flow depends on speed and geometry (leakage aside). A centrifugal pump relies on impeller-generated head, so its delivered flow varies with the system resistance it works against.

notes.t: What pumps are used for
pts: Pumps circulate a fluid around a closed system, such as a heating or cooling loop.
Pumps move a fluid from one location to another, e.g. supplying water to a point of use.
Pumps raise the pressure of the fluid within a system.
Pumps increase the volumetric flow rate of the fluid through a system.
tips: Pumps add energy to a fluid; do not confuse their function with that of a compressor, which handles gases, or a fan, which produces only small pressure rises.
rq: Why does a fire hydrant or a tyre-inflating pump need to increase pressure rather than just move fluid?

Delivering water to a height or through hoses needs enough pressure to overcome gravity and friction losses; air in a tyre must be pressurised to a set value to support the load, so pressure rise, not just transfer, is the purpose.
In a circulating system such as a heating loop, why is a pump needed even though the fluid returns to where it started?
Friction losses in pipes and components continuously dissipate energy, so the pump must add energy to keep the fluid moving around the loop.

notes.t: Machine elements required in pumps
pts: Pumps, like valves, are assemblies made up of smaller machine elements.
Shafts transmit rotational motion and torque between components within the pump.
Seals prevent leakage and come in two types: dynamic (between moving parts) and static (between stationary parts).
Gears and crankshafts are used to transmit and convert motion within pump mechanisms.
Bearings support rotating shafts and reduce friction.
tips: Distinguish clearly between dynamic seals (moving interfaces) and static seals (stationary interfaces) when naming seal types.
rq: Why are dynamic seals and static seals treated differently in pump design?

Dynamic seals must handle relative motion between surfaces (e.g. rotating shaft), so they face wear and friction; static seals sit between stationary faces and only need to resist pressure and leakage.
What would happen to a pump if its shaft were not properly supported by bearings?
Misalignment, excessive friction, vibration and wear would occur, leading to seal failure and eventual breakdown.

notes.t: Engineering design principles
pts: Pressure (static) head is the height of a liquid column that corresponds to a given pressure.
Suction head and dynamic head are further fluid-mechanics quantities that must be considered in pump design.
Dynamic head is generated by friction in the system, so losses must be accounted for alongside static head.
Thermodynamic gas laws (Boyle's, Charles's, Avogadro's, Ideal Gas) underpin the behaviour of gases in engineering systems.
Mechanics design considers friction and machine elements (moving parts) as core design principles.
defs: Static / pressure head (H)
The height of a liquid column that produces a given pressure P, measured in metres.
Dynamic head
The head loss generated by friction in the system, which must be overcome by the pump in addition to static head.
eqs: H = pressure head (m); P = pressure (Pa); \rho = fluid density (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
tips: Pressure head is in metres only after dividing by ρg; check that P is in Pa (N/m²) and ρ in kg/m³.
Head depends on the liquid's density, so the same pressure gives different heads for different fluids.
rq: Why does dividing pressure by ρg convert pressure into a height, and what would change if the liquid were denser?
Pressure equals weight per area, ρgH; rearranging gives H = P/(ρg). A denser liquid gives a smaller head for the same pressure.

notes.t: Fluid mechanics: static/pressure head
pts: Static (pressure) head is the static pressure in a pipe, channel or duct, representing the potential energy of fluid at rest.
Head has units of length: it is the flow-work per unit weight of fluid, so it is expressed in metres.
Pressure head equals the height of a liquid column that produces a given pressure at the base of its container.
Dynamic head is generated by friction in the system, distinct from static head.
defs: Static (pressure) head
The height of a liquid column that corresponds to the static pressure in a fluid system; the potential energy per unit weight of fluid at rest, measured in metres.
Dynamic head
Head loss in a fluid system generated by friction, which must be overcome by a pump in addition to static head.
eqs: Pressure head from pressure of a liquid column
h = pressure head (m); p = pressure (Pa); \rho = fluid density (kg \(m^{-3}\)); g = gravitational acceleration (m \(s^{-2}\))
tips: Head is a length (m); do not confuse it with pressure in Pa unless converting via \( \rho g \).
Static head describes fluid at rest/potential energy; dynamic head is friction-related and is not the same quantity.
rq: Why is pressure head measured in metres rather than in pascals, and what does that tell you about its physical meaning?
Dividing pressure by \( \rho g \) (units Pa / (kg \(m^{-3}\) · m \(s^{-2}\)) = m) gives a length; it represents the energy per unit weight of fluid, i.e. the height the fluid could be raised to.
Two pipes carry the same water pressure, but one contains oil of lower density. Which has the greater pressure head, and why?
Both have the same pressure head only if the fluid is the same; for the same pressure, the lower-density oil has a greater head since \( h = p/\rho g \) is inversely proportional to density.

notes.t: Thermodynamics: gas laws
pts: At constant temperature, gas volume falls as pressure rises (inverse relation).
At constant pressure, gas volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
Equal volumes of all gases at the same T and P contain the same number of molecules.
The ideal gas law combines the individual gas laws into one equation of state.
defs: Boyle's Law
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional, so P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Charles's Law
For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
Avogadro's Law
Equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
Ideal Gas Law
An equation of state for an ideal gas relating pressure, volume, amount of substance and absolute temperature: PV = nRT.
eqs: P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); subscripts 1 and 2 denote two states
V = volume (m³); T = absolute temperature (K); subscripts 1 and 2 denote two states
V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); subscripts 1 and 2 denote two gases/states
P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = universal gas constant (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); T = absolute temperature (K)
tips: Temperature must be absolute (K) in Charles's Law and PV = nRT; using °C is a common error.
Keep units consistent (Pa, m³) and check whether the question wants the ideal gas constant with n in moles.
rq: Why must temperature be in kelvin, not °C, when using Charles's Law or the ideal gas law?

Both laws assume volume or pressure is proportional to temperature, which only holds on an absolute scale where zero means zero thermal energy. In °C, the ratios would give wrong results (e.g. doubling 10 °C is not doubling the energy).
What happens to the product PV if you double the temperature of a fixed amount of gas in a sealed rigid container?
V is fixed, so PV = nRT implies P doubles (P ∝ T). Pressure rises with temperature at constant volume.
Why does Avogadro's Law let us compare gases using volume alone?
At the same T and P, equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, so volume directly measures the amount of gas (moles), regardless of gas identity.

xq.q: A pump raises the pressure of water in a heating loop. Gauge readings are 40 kPa at the inlet and 236.2 kPa at the outlet. Take water density \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³ and \(g = 9.81\) m/s². (a) Find the head the pump produces, using \(H = P/(\rho g)\). (b) The loop is refilled with oil of density 800 kg/m³ and the pump gives the same pressure rise. Find the head in metres of oil.
xq.a: (a) 20 m of water; (b) 25 m of oil
s: (b) \(H = 196200/(800\times9.81) = 25.0\) m, higher because the oil is less dense

xq.q: The static pressure in a pipe carrying a liquid of density 800 kg/m³ is 200 kPa (\(g = 9.81\) m/s²). What is the pressure head?
xq.w: \(H = P/(\rho g) = 200000/(800\times9.81) = 25.5\) m; 250 m omits g, 20.4 m uses the density of water, and 0.0255 m uses kPa without converting to Pa.

xq.q: A pump must deliver water to a tank at a given height through a long pipe. Explain what is meant by static head and dynamic head, say why the pump must overcome both, and say why the same pressure corresponds to a different head for a different liquid.
xq.a: Static (pressure) head is the height of liquid column that gives the pressure, \(H = P/(\rho g)\), the potential energy per unit weight of fluid at rest. Dynamic head is the head lost to friction in the pipework and fittings. The pump must supply energy to lift or pressurise the fluid (static head) and also to overcome friction losses (dynamic head), so the total head required is larger than the static head alone. Because \(H = P/(\rho g)\), a denser liquid gives a smaller head for the same pressure.
s: Static head defined as column height, \(H = P/(\rho g)\)
Dynamic head defined as head loss from friction
Pump must overcome both, so total head is greater than static alone
Head depends on \(\rho\), so the same P gives different H for different liquids

units.name: 3.2 Pump types: positive displacement vs centrifugal
units.ov: This material classifies pumps as positive displacement (PD) or centrifugal, based on whether the fluid is completely enclosed at some point in the cycle. It then describes PD pump behaviour: flow is set by pump speed and pressure by the system. These ideas explain why stopped-pump behaviour, performance characteristics and safety protection differ between the two types.
must: Classification test: a pump is PD if the fluid is completely enclosed at least once per cycle; otherwise it is centrifugal
PD pumps draw in a fixed volume, enclose it, then force it out of the outlet
Centrifugal pumps spin the fluid at high speed to give it kinetic energy, and the liquid is never enclosed
Stopped-pump behaviour: PD pumps block flow when stopped; centrifugal pumps let fluid flow back through
PD pump flow rate is set by pump speed, not by the connected system, so \(Q \propto N\) approximately
PD pump outlet pressure is set by the downstream system, not by the pump
PD pumps give low flow rates but medium to high outlet pressure
A PD pump needs a relief valve, because closing the outlet does not stop the flow and the pressure can rise dangerously
Do not classify by having an inlet and outlet, since every pump has both
Several PD types exist with different internal arrangements, but all share the enclosure principle
conn: Enclosure test and stopped-pump behaviour: enclosed fluid is what blocks backflow in a PD pump, while an open flow path in a centrifugal pump allows it
Flow set by speed and pressure set by the system: a blocked or restricted outlet makes the pressure rise without limit, which is why a relief valve is needed
Energy transfer mechanism and performance: a centrifugal pump adds kinetic energy to the fluid, while a PD pump forces a trapped volume out, which explains their different flow and pressure ranges
exq: Define a positive displacement pump and a centrifugal pump. State the test used to classify an unfamiliar pump and apply it to a described design.

A pump has an inlet and an outlet, and its fluid is fully enclosed once per cycle. Classify it and justify the answer. What happens to flow through it when it is stopped, and how does that differ from a centrifugal pump?
A PD pump runs at constant speed and its outlet valve is slowly closed. Describe what happens to flow rate and outlet pressure, and explain why a relief valve is needed.
Explain why a PD pump's flow rate depends on its speed while its outlet pressure depends on the system. If the speed doubles, what happens to flow and pressure?
Compare PD and centrifugal pumps in terms of mechanism, flow rate, pressure and stopped-pump behaviour, and suggest which suits a high-pressure, low-flow duty.

notes.t: Pump types: positive displacement vs centrifugal
pts: Every pump is either positive displacement or centrifugal, distinguished by how it moves the fluid.
Positive displacement pumps draw in a fixed volume, enclose it, then force it out of the outlet.
Centrifugal pumps spin the fluid at high speed to give it kinetic energy; the liquid is never enclosed.
Positive displacement pumps block flow when stopped, whereas centrifugal pumps let fluid flow back through when stopped.
The key test for classification is whether the fluid is completely enclosed at some point in the cycle.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that traps a fixed volume of fluid, encloses it, and forces it out of the outlet, with the fluid completely enclosed at least once per cycle.
Centrifugal pump
A pump that spins fluid at high speed to impart kinetic energy, never enclosing the liquid.
tips: Do not classify by whether the pump has an inlet and outlet; the test is whether the fluid is completely enclosed at some point in the cycle.
Remember the stopped-pump behaviour: positive displacement pumps block flow when stopped, centrifugal pumps do not.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump stop the flow when it is switched off, while a centrifugal pump does not?

A positive displacement pump relies on enclosing and displacing a fixed volume, so its mechanism seals the flow path; a centrifugal pump has an open flow path with no enclosure, so fluid can pass through it by gravity or pressure difference.
If a pump imparts energy by spinning the fluid but never traps it, what category does it belong to and why?
Centrifugal, because the defining principle is spinning fluid to give kinetic energy, and the liquid is never enclosed.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: characteristics and types
pts: Positive displacement pumps deliver low flow rates but can produce medium to high outlet pressure.
Flow rate is set by pump speed, not by the connected system.
Outlet pressure is set by the system the pump feeds, not by the pump itself.
Many different internal arrangements exist, giving several pump types.
tips: Do not confuse flow rate with outlet pressure: flow is set by pump speed, pressure by the system.
Positive displacement pumps must be protected by a relief valve, since closing the outlet does not stop the flow and pressure can rise dangerously.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump's flow rate depend on speed rather than on the system resistance?
Each cycle traps and displaces a fixed volume of fluid, so flow equals displaced volume per cycle times cycles per second; resistance only changes the pressure needed to push that fixed volume out.
What would happen to the outlet pressure if a blocked outlet valve were closed on a running positive displacement pump?
Pressure would rise sharply, since the fixed displaced volume cannot escape; without a relief valve this can damage the pump or pipework.

xq.q: A running positive displacement pump has its outlet valve closed by mistake and no relief valve is fitted. What happens?
xq.a: Flow continues to be forced into the closed outlet, so pressure rises until something fails
o: Flow falls to zero and the pressure stays at its normal value, as in a centrifugal pump
Flow continues to be forced into the closed outlet, so pressure rises until something fails
The pump speed automatically falls so that the pressure stays constant
Fluid flows backwards through the pump because the fluid is not enclosed
xq.w: A positive displacement pump traps and forces out a fixed volume per cycle, so its pressure is set by the system, which here is a dead end; the first option wrongly applies centrifugal behaviour.
s: Fixed volume is displaced each cycle regardless of the outlet
Pressure is set by the system, so it rises dangerously

xq.q: A pump has an inlet and an outlet and fluid passes through it. Explain how you would decide whether it is a positive displacement or a centrifugal pump, and describe how each type behaves when it is stopped.
xq.a: Having an inlet and outlet does not decide the type. The test is whether the fluid is completely enclosed at some point in the cycle. If a fixed volume is drawn in, enclosed and forced out, the pump is positive displacement. If the fluid is spun at high speed to give it kinetic energy and is never enclosed, it is centrifugal. When stopped, a positive displacement pump blocks flow, whereas a centrifugal pump lets fluid flow back through it.
s: Inlet and outlet are not the test
Test: is the fluid fully enclosed at some point in the cycle?
Positive displacement: encloses a fixed volume and forces it out; centrifugal: spins the fluid and never encloses it
Stopped: positive displacement blocks flow, centrifugal allows flow through

xq.q: A positive displacement pump feeds a fixed system. Its speed is doubled and the system is unchanged. Which statement is best?
xq.a: The flow rate roughly doubles, and the outlet pressure is still set by the system
o: The flow rate stays the same because the system sets the flow
The outlet pressure doubles because the pump sets the pressure
The flow rate roughly doubles, and the outlet pressure is still set by the system
The flow rate halves because the fluid has less time to be enclosed
xq.w: Flow is set by pump speed and pressure by the system; the other options swap these roles or invent an inverse relation.
s: Flow is proportional to speed for a positive displacement pump
Pressure is determined by the connected system

units.name: 3.3 Piston pumps: single and double acting
units.ov: This material covers positive displacement piston pumps, from the simple single-acting pump to the double-acting pump, and the auxiliary components they need (valves, seals, relief valve, accumulator). Flow is set by piston geometry and speed, reduced by leakage, and is largely independent of discharge pressure. That is why pressure pulsation, safety relief and smoothing devices become central design issues.
must: Flow rate of a simple piston pump: \(\dot{v} = (AK - V)S\), with \(A\) the piston crown area (m²), \(K\) the stroke (m), \(V\) the leakage per stroke (m³) and \(S\) the speed (s⁻¹); leakage always reduces flow
Unit discipline: \(A\) in m², \(K\) in m, \(S\) in rev/s (convert RPM by dividing by 60) gives \(\dot{v}\) in m³/s
Definition: a positive displacement pump delivers a fixed volume per cycle, so flow is set by geometry and speed, not by discharge pressure
Operation of the simple pump: on the backward stroke, pressure falls, the discharge valve closes and the suction valve opens; on the forward stroke the reverse happens and fluid is expelled

Double acting pump: fluid acts on both sides of one piston with two sets of check valves, so every stroke delivers fluid (intake on one side while exhausting on the other); drawbacks are more parts, harder maintenance and a larger footprint
A relief valve is mandatory because the pump delivers flow regardless of downstream resistance and would otherwise over-pressurise the system
The accumulator (gas or bladder vessel) absorbs pressure pulses, like a capacitor smoothing voltage, and stores energy for low-demand periods so a smaller pump can be used; it does not generate flow
Seals: dynamic seals (piston rings) seal the moving piston to the cylinder wall, static seals are where the rod passes through the body; the cross-head converts crank rotation to linear reciprocation
Leakage paths (piston–bore, valve seats, joints) reduce volumetric efficiency, whereas dead (unswept) volume reduces compression and compactness; keep the two distinct
Applications and versatility: suited to viscous fluids, fluids with solids and high consistent pressure (e.g. irrigation); they can also compress gases, not only move liquids
conn: Flow equation and leakage: leakage paths (seals, valve seats) set \(V\), so seal quality directly determines volumetric efficiency and delivered flow
Fixed displacement and relief valve: because flow does not fall as pressure rises, a blocked outlet causes pressure to climb, hence the mandatory relief valve
Reciprocating motion and the accumulator: the cyclic, pulsating delivery (large in a single-acting pump, reduced in a double-acting pump) causes pressure variation, which the accumulator smooths

Double acting vs simple: the effective swept volume per revolution roughly doubles, so adapt \(\dot{v}\) accordingly (taking account of rod area on one side), at the cost of complexity, more seals and a larger footprint
exq: A simple piston pump has a piston of diameter 80 mm, stroke 120 mm, speed 300 rpm and leakage of 5 cm³ per stroke. Calculate the volumetric flow rate in m³/s and in L/min, and the volumetric efficiency.
Explain with sketches how a double acting piston pump operates. State two advantages and three drawbacks compared with a simple single acting pump.
Why must a positive displacement pump be fitted with a relief valve? Describe what happens to pressure and flow if the discharge is blocked without one.
Describe the function of an accumulator in a reciprocating pump circuit. How does it smooth pulsations and allow a smaller pump to be used?
Distinguish between dynamic and static seals in a double acting piston pump, giving the location of each, and between leakage and dead volume in terms of their effect on pump performance.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: simple piston pump
pts: A simple piston pump has a discharge valve (upper) and a suction valve (lower) acting on the cylinder.
Backward piston motion lowers cylinder pressure, closes the discharge valve and draws fluid into the cylinder through the suction valve.
Piston pumps can be arranged in different configurations and can be motorised or hand-powered.
The theoretical flow rate depends on piston crown area, stroke, speed, and is reduced by leakage per stroke.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by mechanically displacing it within a sealed chamber, so flow is set by geometry and speed rather than by pressure.
Piston stroke
The distance the piston travels from one end of the cylinder to the other in a single movement.
Leakage volume per stroke
The volume of fluid that slips past the piston or valves each stroke, reducing the effective delivered flow.
eqs: Volumetric flow rate of a simple piston pump
\(\dot{v}\) = flow rate (m³/s); \(A\) = area of piston crown (m²); \(K\) = piston stroke (m); \(V\) = leakage volume per stroke (m³); \(S\) = speed, e.g. revolutions per second (s⁻¹)
tips: Keep units consistent: \(A\) in m², \(K\) in m and \(S\) in s⁻¹ give flow in m³/s; RPS must not be mixed with RPM.
Remember that \(V\) is subtracted, so leakage always reduces the theoretical flow.
rq: Why does moving the piston backwards cause the discharge valve to close and fluid to enter the cylinder?

Backward motion increases the cylinder volume, reducing pressure below the suction side pressure; the higher pressure above pushes the discharge valve shut and the lower pressure opens the suction valve, drawing fluid in.
What happens to the flow rate predicted by the equation if the pump leaks more badly?
V increases, so (AK − V) decreases and the actual flow rate falls, since leakage subtracts from the swept volume delivered per stroke.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: simple piston pump
pts: A piston pump uses a cylinder in a casing with a piston attached to a connecting rod; the high-pressure seal reciprocates with the piston.
Piston pumps can move liquids or compress gases, and high pressure can be reached without a strong drop in flow rate.
Down-strokes create pressure differentials that fill the pump chamber; up-strokes force the fluid out for use.
Suited to viscous media and fluids containing solid particles, and to systems needing high, consistent pressure such as water irrigation or delivery.
Because pressure varies widely over each cycle, a safety mechanism (e.g. a relief valve) is required.
defs: Positive displacement pump

A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a chamber and mechanically displacing it, so flow is set by the swept volume and cycle rate rather than by the discharge pressure.
tips: Positive displacement pumps are not restricted to liquids: piston pumps can also compress gases, so do not state that they only move liquids.
Always include a pressure safety/relief device when describing piston pumps, since pressure variations are large.
rq: Why does a piston pump keep its flow rate roughly constant when the discharge pressure rises?
Each stroke displaces a fixed swept volume, so the delivered volume per cycle is set by geometry, not by the resistance against it; only leakage (slip) reduces flow at high pressure.
What would happen to the pump if the outlet were blocked and the piston kept moving?
Pressure would rise sharply because the fixed volume cannot escape, so the pump, pipework and seals could fail; this is why a safety (relief) mechanism is required.

notes.t: Characteristics of piston pumps (positive displacement pumps)
pts: Piston pumps are positive displacement machines: a piston draws fluid into a cylinder and then pushes it out through valves, so each stroke delivers a fixed volume.
Inlet and outlet check valves control flow direction; if the pump is inverted, valves must be retained (e.g., by springs, retainers or housing geometry) so they do not fall out.
Leakage paths exist between the piston and cylinder bore, around valve seats and at joints, and these reduce volumetric efficiency.
Seals are needed where the moving piston or rod passes through the housing and at valve seats to prevent leakage and loss of pressure.
Space usage should be judged: the dead volume around the cylinder and valve passages reduces efficiency and compactness of the design.
tips: Do not confuse the valves' purpose: check valves allow one-way flow, and their retention in an inverted pump is a mechanical design issue, not a flow issue.
Leakage paths and dead (unswept) volume are distinct: leakage reduces delivered flow, while dead volume reduces compression and space efficiency.
rq: Why does inverting a piston pump put the valves at risk, and what would you do to retain them?
Gravity acts on the valve elements, so they can drop out of their seats or housing; retain them with springs, caps, or a captive housing design.
Why must leakage be minimised in a positive displacement pump even though it still moves fluid?
Leakage lets fluid slip back past the piston or valves, so the actual delivered flow falls below the swept-volume flow, lowering volumetric efficiency.

notes.t: Double acting piston pump
pts: A double acting piston pump has two sets of check valves, with fluid acting on both sides of the piston.
Moving the piston in both directions completes a full pumping cycle, so each stroke delivers fluid.
While one side of the piston is intaking fluid, the other side is exhausting fluid simultaneously.
Drawbacks are more parts, difficult maintenance, and a large physical footprint.
defs: Double acting piston pump
A positive displacement pump in which fluid is drawn in and discharged on both sides of the piston, using two sets of check valves, so every stroke pumps.
tips: Do not confuse double acting with double-headed or two-cylinder pumps; the defining feature is fluid on both sides of one piston with two sets of check valves.
rq: Why does a double acting pump deliver fluid on both strokes, while a single acting pump delivers only on one?
Because fluid acts on both faces of the piston, so the side that is moving away from the inlet is simultaneously exhausting while the other side intakes, giving a discharge on each stroke.
What is the trade-off in choosing a double acting pump over a simpler design?
It gives higher, smoother output per cycle but needs more parts, more valves, more maintenance and more space.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: double acting piston pump and accumulator
pts: Dynamic seals (piston rings) seal the moving piston against the cylinder wall, while static seals are where the piston rod passes through the body.
A cross-head converts the rotary motion of the crank into linear reciprocating motion of the piston rod.
A relief valve is mandatory on a positive displacement pump, because the pump delivers flow regardless of downstream resistance and would otherwise over-pressurise the system.
An accumulator absorbs pressure pulses caused by large pressure variations, acting like a capacitor smoothing voltage fluctuations.
An accumulator stores energy for later use during low demand, which allows a smaller pump to be used.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping and mechanically displacing it, so flow is largely independent of discharge pressure.
Accumulator
A pressure vessel containing a gas (air bladder) that absorbs hydraulic pressure pulses and stores energy for later use.
tips: Do not confuse dynamic seals (moving, e.g. piston rings) with static seals (stationary interfaces, e.g. where the rod passes through the body).
An accumulator stores energy but does not generate flow; it only smooths pulses and supplies stored energy during low demand.
rq: Why must a relief valve always be fitted to a positive displacement pump, even if the system has other protection?
Because the pump forces a fixed volume per stroke regardless of resistance, so with a blocked outlet pressure would rise until the pump or pipework fails; the relief valve limits this pressure.
What would happen to pressure in the discharge line if the accumulator were removed, and why does a smaller pump become possible with it fitted?
Pressure would fluctuate strongly with each piston stroke; the accumulator smooths these pulses and stores energy during low demand, so the pump only needs to meet average rather than peak demand.

xq.q: A simple piston pump has a piston crown area \(A = 3.0\times10^{-3}\) m², a stroke \(K = 0.12\) m and a leakage volume \(V = 2.0\times10^{-5}\) m³ per stroke. It runs at 90 rev/min. Using \(\dot v = (AK - V)S\), find the volumetric flow rate in m³/s.

A piston pump must deliver \(6.0\times10^{-4}\) m³/s. The piston crown area is \(A = 4.0\times10^{-3}\) m², the leakage is \(V = 4.0\times10^{-5}\) m³ per stroke and the speed is \(S = 2.0\) s⁻¹. Using \(\dot v = (AK - V)S\), find the stroke \(K\) required in metres.
Explain how a double acting piston pump differs from a simple piston pump in the way it delivers fluid, and give two drawbacks of the double acting design.
xq.a: A simple piston pump delivers fluid on only one direction of piston travel. A double acting pump has two sets of check valves and fluid acts on both sides of the piston. While one side intakes fluid, the other side discharges it, so every stroke pumps and a full cycle uses movement in both directions. Drawbacks: more parts, more difficult maintenance and a larger physical footprint.
s: Simple pump: delivery on one stroke direction only
Double acting: two sets of check valves, fluid acts on both piston sides
One side intakes while the other exhausts, so every stroke delivers
Drawbacks: more parts, harder maintenance, larger footprint (any two)

units.name: 3.4 Pressure ripple, accumulators and PD pump characteristics
units.ov: This module covers why positive displacement (PD) pumps produce pulsating discharge pressure, how single- and double-acting piston pumps differ, and how an accumulator smooths the ripple. It also covers the PD pump pressure-flow characteristic. The ideas are linked by electrical analogies (rectifier and smoothing capacitor, mass-inertia, compliance), which let pulsation and smoothing be treated as circuit behaviour.
must: PD pump definition: it traps and displaces a fixed volume per cycle, so flow is set by speed and geometry rather than by pressure.
Single-acting piston pump: pressure is delivered only on the delivery half-cycle, giving positive humps separated by zero-pressure gaps (analogue of half-wave rectification).
Double-acting piston pump: it delivers on both strokes, so there are no gaps, and the pulse frequency is twice that of a single-acting pump (analogue of full-wave rectification).
Accumulator: it charges during delivery and discharges more slowly, lengthening the pressure-decay periods and reducing ripple (analogue of a smoothing capacitor).
The accumulator does not raise the peak pressure and does not remove pulses; it only reduces fluctuation about the mean.
Accumulator absorbs part of the pump flow, so the system outlet flow is not the full pump flow; real delivery is also reduced by volumetric and mechanical efficiency below 100%.
PD pump characteristic: the discharge pressure vs flow curve is steep and nearly vertical, unlike the rising head-flow curve of a centrifugal pump.
The curve leans backwards because internal leakage (slip) increases with discharge pressure; higher speed shifts the whole curve to higher flow.
Flow is proportional to the pressure differential across the system, not to pressure alone.

Mechanical-electrical analogies map by role: voltage to force/pump, current to flow/velocity, resistance to friction, capacitance to compliance (accumulator), inductance to mass/inertia, transformer to lever.
conn: The rectifier analogy (half-wave, full-wave, three-phase) links pump type to ripple frequency and shape, and the accumulator acts as the smoothing capacitor on that waveform.
Accumulator compliance (capacitance) together with line inertia (inductance) and friction (resistance) forms an RLC-type circuit that determines how much ripple is attenuated.
Slip and efficiency link the characteristic curve to real delivered flow: leakage rises with pressure, so delivered flow falls, and the accumulator then diverts some of it from the outlet.
Pump speed sets the flow (shifts the curve) and also sets the pulse frequency, which affects ripple.
exq: Sketch the discharge pressure waveform for a single-acting and a double-acting piston pump over two revolutions, and state the ripple frequency of each at a given speed, e.g. 1200 rpm.
Explain with an electrical analogy how an accumulator reduces pressure ripple. Why does it not change the peak pressure? Draw the waveform with and without it.
Draw the pressure-flow characteristic of a PD pump and compare it with a centrifugal pump. Explain the backward lean and show the effect of doubling the speed.
Draw the hydraulic-electrical analogy table (pump, turbine, diaphragm, pipe friction, lever) and use it to build an equivalent circuit for a pump-accumulator-pipe system.
A PD pump has a theoretical flow of 20 L/min and a volumetric efficiency of 92%. Estimate the actual delivered flow, and discuss how the accumulator affects the mean and instantaneous outlet flow.

notes.t: Mechanical-electrical analogies
pts: In a pipe system, electrical current corresponds to the flow of fluid.
An inductor can be modelled by a turbine, since both resist changes in flow through inertia.
A voltage source can be modelled by a pump that drives the fluid.
A capacitor can be modelled by a diaphragm inside the pipe that stores displaced fluid.
Voltage maps to force, current to velocity, resistance to friction, capacitance to compliance, inductance to mass and transformer to lever.
tips: Analogies map quantities by role, not by units: voltage (V) is not the same unit as force (N), so keep the correspondence conceptual.
Inductance maps to mass (inertia), not to friction; confusing resistance with inertia is a common error.
rq: Why does a turbine behave like an inductor in the fluid analogy?
Its rotating mass resists changes in flow rate, just as an inductor opposes changes in current, so inertia corresponds to inductance.
Why is a diaphragm a sensible analogue for a capacitor?
It stores fluid by deflecting and resists pressure build-up, just as a capacitor stores charge and voltage builds up across it.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: discharge pressure characteristics
pts: A single-piston pump delivers pressure only during one half of each revolution; the other half is intake (suction) with no output pressure.
The discharge pressure waveform of a piston pump is a series of positive hump pulses separated by zero-pressure gaps, one hump per piston stroke.
The pulsed output of a piston pump is analogous to a half-wave rectified electrical signal, which is why it is useful to model it with rectifier ideas.
To analyse the waveform, imagine the piston is at the middle of its stroke when considering the cycle.
defs: Positive displacement pump

A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it and mechanically displacing it, so discharge is driven by the moving boundary (e.g. a piston) rather than by continuous kinetic energy transfer.
tips: Do not assume the piston pump gives a continuous output pressure; the waveform is zero during intake, so average and peak pressures must be treated separately.
Remember the waveform is shown in arbitrary units for both pressure and time, so only the shape and relative behaviour are meaningful, not numerical values.
rq: Why does a single-piston pump's output pressure drop to zero for half of each revolution, and what does this imply for smoothing the flow?

During the intake half-cycle the piston draws fluid in and nothing is pushed out, so there is no discharge pressure. The pulsating output means a single piston gives a pulsed, non-continuous flow, so multi-piston arrangements or accumulators are needed to smooth it, just as a half-wave rectifier needs a smoothing capacitor.
How is the piston pump's output waveform analogous to a half-wave rectifier, and what does the 'missing' half represent in each system?

A half-wave rectifier passes only the positive half of an AC cycle and blocks the negative half. Similarly the pump only delivers pressure during the discharge half-stroke; the intake half produces no output, playing the role of the blocked half-cycle.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: discharge pressure of a double-acting piston pump
pts: A double-acting piston pump delivers fluid on both strokes, so the discharge pressure has no gaps between pulses.
The discharge pressure waveform is a series of repeated humps that drop to zero twice per cycle, assuming both sides run at the same speed.
The output pressure pattern is analogous to full-wave rectification of an AC signal, so the pulse frequency is double that of a single-acting pump.
tips: The waveform shows pulses dropping to zero only at the points where the strokes change over; do not assume a constant pressure output.
The analogy to rectification describes the pulse pattern only; the pressure values are arbitrary units on this page.
rq: Why does a double-acting piston pump produce a smoother discharge than a single-acting pump?
Because it pumps fluid on both the forward and return strokes, so there is a delivery pulse on every stroke and no interval of zero flow, giving twice as many pulses per revolution.
What would the output waveform look like if only one side of the piston delivered fluid?
It would resemble half-wave rectification: a series of humps separated by gaps at zero pressure, with half as many pulses per cycle.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: accumulator effect on output pressure ripple
pts: An accumulator smooths the pulsating output pressure of a positive displacement pump, analogous to voltage smoothing after rectification.
Without an accumulator the pressure pulses sharply; with one, it charges during each delivery stroke and then discharges more slowly, producing a ripple.
The accumulator does not change the peak pressure; it reduces the fluctuation between peaks by lengthening the decreasing-pressure periods.
The response resembles three-phase rectification, where output pulses overlap to give a smoother waveform than single-phase rectification.
Ripple arises from alternating charging (pressurisation) and longer discharging (pressure decrease) phases.
tips: Do not claim the accumulator increases peak pressure; the peak is the same with or without it, only the ripple changes.
Ripple is a time-varying pressure about a mean; state that the smoothing effect comes from longer discharge periods, not from removing the pulses entirely.
rq: Why does adding an accumulator not raise the peak output pressure of a positive displacement pump?

The peak is set by the pump's delivery and the load/relief conditions; the accumulator only stores fluid during the peak and releases it later, so it flattens the variation between peaks rather than increasing the maximum.
Why would a hydraulic system need smoother pressure, e.g. in a braking or control circuit?
Pressure ripple causes vibration, noise, inconsistent actuator motion and wear; a steadier pressure gives more precise, predictable control and safer braking.

notes.t: Positive displacement pump characteristics and accumulator effect
pts: Pump output pressure rises when flowrate is increased; the pressure profile is pulsating because of the piston strokes.
Flow is directly proportional to the pressure differential across the pump system.
The accumulator absorbs part of the pump delivery, so the system outlet never receives the full pump flowrate.
Real pumps deliver less than the theoretical flow because mechanical and volumetric efficiencies are below 100%.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it and forcing it out, e.g. a piston pump.
Accumulator
A pressure storage device that absorbs pressure peaks from the pump and releases stored fluid, smoothing the output pressure and flow.
tips: Do not assume the theoretical pump flow equals the system outlet flow; account for accumulator storage and volumetric/mechanical efficiency losses.
Flow is proportional to pressure differential, not to pressure alone; check which difference is being used in calculations.
rq: Why does the accumulator make the system flowrate lower than the pump's maximum flowrate, even though the pump is delivering fluid continuously?
Part of the pump output is diverted into the accumulator to charge it during pressure peaks, so less fluid reaches the system outlet at that moment.
Why does a real pump never deliver the theoretical flow?
Internal leakage (volumetric losses) and friction (mechanical losses) mean efficiencies are below 100%, so actual delivered flow is less than the calculated displacement flow.

notes.t: Positive displacement pump characteristics
pts: For a positive displacement pump, discharge pressure is plotted as a function of flow rate, giving a steep curve.
The curve is classic positive displacement: the flow is almost fixed by pump speed and geometry, so the curve is nearly vertical rather than rising with head like a centrifugal pump.
The curve leans backwards (flow falls slightly as pressure rises) because internal leakage (slip) increases with discharge pressure.
Turning the pump faster increases the displaced volume per unit time, shifting the whole curve to higher flow rate.
tips: Do not confuse the positive displacement curve (near-vertical, flow almost independent of pressure) with the rising head-flow curve of a centrifugal pump.
Do not assume the backwards lean is caused by friction alone; it is due to internal leakage (slip) increasing with discharge pressure.
rq: What happens to the pump curve if you turn the pump faster, and why?
The curve shifts to higher flow rate at each pressure, because more fluid is displaced per revolution per unit time, so volumetric flow scales with pump speed.
Why does a positive displacement pump's flow barely change as discharge pressure rises?
Each cycle traps and displaces a fixed volume; only internal leakage (slip) past clearances increases with pressure, so flow falls only slightly.

xq.q: A single-acting piston pump delivers fluid only on its delivery stroke, and the intake stroke gives zero discharge pressure. Which statement correctly compares its discharge pressure waveform with that of a double-acting pump running at the same speed?
xq.a: The double-acting pump has twice the pulse frequency and no zero-pressure gaps between pulses, like full-wave rather than half-wave rectification
o: The double-acting pump has twice the pulse frequency and no zero-pressure gaps between pulses, like full-wave rather than half-wave rectification
The double-acting pump has half the pulse frequency because each side shares the load, like half-wave rectification
The double-acting pump has a constant, ripple-free pressure because both strokes deliver
The double-acting pump has the same waveform but a doubled peak pressure
xq.w: Both strokes deliver, so the pulse rate doubles and gaps vanish (full-wave rectification); the trap is thinking pulses disappear or peaks double.
s: Single-acting: one hump per revolution with a gap, half-wave
Double-acting: a hump on each stroke, so double frequency, full-wave

xq.q: A piston pump feeds a hydraulic system through an accumulator. Explain how the accumulator changes the output pressure waveform, stating what it does and does not change, and use the electrical analogy.
xq.a: During each delivery stroke the pump output charges the accumulator, which absorbs part of the delivery. Between strokes the accumulator discharges into the system more slowly, so the pressure falls over a longer period. This gives a ripple about a mean pressure instead of sharp pulses separated by gaps. The peak pressure is unchanged; only the fluctuation is reduced and the pulses are not removed entirely. It is analogous to a smoothing capacitor after a rectifier (the overlapping pulses of three-phase rectification give a smoother output).
s: Charges on delivery stroke, discharges slowly after
Lengthens pressure-decrease periods so ripple replaces sharp pulses
Peak pressure unchanged, pulses not eliminated

xq.q: Using the mechanical-electrical analogy (voltage-force, current-velocity), which mapping is correct for modelling a mass-spring-damper system?
xq.a: Mass to inductance, compliance (spring) to capacitance, friction to resistance
o: Mass to inductance, compliance (spring) to capacitance, friction to resistance
Mass to resistance, compliance to inductance, friction to capacitance
Mass to capacitance, friction to inductance, spring to resistance
Mass to inductance, friction to capacitance, spring to resistance
xq.w: Inductance maps to mass (inertia), capacitance to compliance and resistance to friction; the common error is confusing resistance with inertia.

units.name: 3.5 Rotary PD pumps: gear, lobe, vane and screw
units.ov: This material covers rotary positive displacement (PD) pumps: gear (spur, helical, herringbone), lobe, sliding vane and screw. Each traps a fixed volume of fluid in chambers and carries it from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed and is largely independent of discharge pressure. The ideas connect through displacement per revolution, slip and leakage through small clearances, and axial thrust and its balancing.
must: Definition of a PD pump: traps a fixed volume and forces it from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed and is largely independent of discharge pressure, apart from leakage/slip

Ideal gear pump flow: \(\dot{v} = A\,l\,N\,S\), with \(A\) the area between two teeth and the casing (m²), \(l\) tooth length (m), \(N\) number of teeth and \(S\) speed (rev/s). Keep units consistent and state that real flow is lower

Gear pump operation: fluid is carried round the outside of the gears in the casing on the side where the teeth unmesh (suction), not squeezed through the mesh. Clearances are microns, so wear or contamination raises slip and cuts efficiency
Gear pump types and thrust: spur, helical, herringbone and planetary. Helical is smoother and quieter than spur but gives axial end-thrust. Herringbone cancels the thrust with opposed helix angles
Lobe pump: a gear-pump variant with non-contacting lobed rotors, usually driven through external timing gears. Suited to viscous or shear-sensitive fluids

Sliding vane pump: eccentric rotor in a stator, with vanes sliding radially in slots. The eccentric geometry, not the spinning alone, changes chamber volume. Vanes are held against the wall by springs, pressure or centrifugal force, and vane wear and leakage are key failure modes
Vane material is matched to the fluid: steel for hydraulic oil pumps, graphite for air compressors

Screw pump: fluid moves axially in cavities formed by meshing screws and is discharged at the outlet. Flow is low-pulsation, quiet and reliable, and suits lubricating fluids. This differs from the radial flow of a centrifugal pump

Screw pump thrust balancing: a single screw needs a thrust bearing, usually in the motor. Two opposite-hand screws with suction at both ends and central discharge cancel the axial thrust. Location bearings are still needed
Auxiliary components: the relief valve is a pressure-limiting safety device that returns fluid to suction, not a flow control. The mechanical or lip seal stops leakage along the shaft
conn: Slip and leakage link every pump type: small clearances (gear), vane-to-wall contact (vane), and screw cavity sealing all set the gap between ideal flow \(A l N S\) and real flow, and so volumetric efficiency and wear

Axial thrust recurs in helical gears and screw pumps. The cure is symmetry: opposed helix angles (herringbone) and opposite-hand screws with double-ended suction. Questions ask why a thrust bearing is or isn't needed
Because flow is fixed per revolution, blocking the outlet makes pressure rise without limit, so a relief valve is needed. This links the PD definition to safety and circuit design
Fluid properties drive pump choice: viscous fluids suit gear and lobe pumps, lubricating fluids suit screw pumps, and the fluid type sets the vane material
exq: A gear pump has tooth-space area 40 mm² between two teeth and the casing, tooth length 25 mm, 12 teeth and speed 1500 rpm. Calculate the ideal volumetric flow rate in m³/s and L/min. If the measured flow is 85% of ideal, find the volumetric efficiency and the slip flow.
Explain, with a sketch, how a gear pump draws in and delivers fluid. State on which side of the mesh the fluid is carried and why the clearances must be so small.
Compare spur, helical and herringbone gears in a gear pump in terms of noise, smoothness and axial thrust. Explain how herringbone gears cancel end-thrust.

Describe the operation of a sliding vane pump. Explain how the eccentric rotor produces pumping, how the vanes stay in contact with the wall, and why vane material differs between hydraulic oil pumps and air compressors.
Explain how a double-ended screw pump with opposite-hand threads avoids needing a thrust bearing. State what the bearings in the drawing do, and the role of the relief valve and mechanical seal.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: gear pump
pts: A gear pump uses meshing gears to move fluid; it is a positive displacement pump.
Gear pumps suit viscous fluids because the sealed gear chambers carry the fluid positively.
As gears separate at the intake, a void forms and generates suction.
Fluid is carried round the outside of the gears in the casing from intake to exit, not squeezed through the mesh.
Internal clearances are very small, around microns, which limits leakage and slip.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that traps a fixed volume of fluid in a chamber and forces it from the inlet to the outlet, giving a flow largely independent of discharge pressure.
tips: Determine suction from the direction of rotation: fluid is carried round the casing on the side where the teeth unmesh, not where they mesh.
Gear pump clearances are microns, so contamination or wear quickly increases slip and reduces efficiency.
rq: Why does a gear pump deliver fluid even when the outlet is blocked (a relief valve is needed)?
Because it is positive displacement: it traps a fixed volume per revolution and pushes it regardless of pressure, so pressure rises until a relief valve opens or the pump is damaged.
What would happen to suction if the gears turned in the opposite direction?
The inlet and outlet would swap roles: the side where the teeth separate becomes the suction side, so the flow reverses direction.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: gear pump
pts: A gear pump is a positive displacement pump: fluid trapped between gear teeth and the casing is carried from inlet to outlet, so flow is set by geometry and speed.
The drawing shows the driven gear and idler gear meshing inside a body, with a lip seal and seal cover on the shaft and white metal bushes supporting the gears.
Ideal volumetric flow rate is proportional to the trapped area, tooth length, number of teeth and shaft speed; real pumps deliver less because of leakage and slip.
The question asks what may be wrong with the drawing, so the student should check the gear meshing and the sealing/bearing arrangement against how a real gear pump works.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that delivers a fixed volume of fluid per revolution or cycle by trapping it in cavities and forcing it out, so output is largely independent of outlet pressure apart from leakage.
Idler gear
The gear that is not directly driven but meshes with the driven gear, transferring fluid in the gear pump and rotating in the opposite direction.
eqs: Ideal volumetric flow rate of a gear pump

\(\dot{v}\) = volumetric flow rate (m³/s); \(A\) = area enclosed between two gear teeth and the casing (m²); \(l\) = length of gear tooth (m); \(N\) = number of gear teeth (–); \(S\) = speed, e.g. rev/s (s⁻¹)
tips: Keep units consistent: with \(S\) in rev/s, \(\dot{v}\) comes out in m³/s only if \(A\) is in m² and \(l\) in m; mixing mm and m gives errors of 10⁹.
The equation gives the ideal flow; always state that real flow is lower due to slip/leakage.
rq: Why does doubling the shaft speed double the ideal flow rate, but not the pressure developed?
Flow is proportional to speed (\(\dot{v}=AlNS\)) because more fluid is trapped and moved per second; pressure depends on the load/outlet resistance, not on the geometry-set displacement.
What would make the actual flow lower than the ideal value given by \(\dot{v}=AlNS\)?
Internal leakage (slip) past the teeth and casing clearances, and fluid compressibility or cavitation, reduce delivered flow; higher outlet pressure increases leakage.

notes.t: Gear pumps: types of positive displacement gear pump
pts: Gear pumps are positive displacement pumps; the main types are spur, helical, double-helical (herringbone) and planetary.
Helical gears give smoother and quieter operation than spur gears, but they produce an axial end-thrust that must be carried by bearings.
Double-helical (herringbone) gears reduce noise and produce no resultant end-thrust, because the opposing helix angles cancel the axial forces.
defs: Gear pump
A positive displacement pump in which meshing gears trap fluid between teeth and casing and carry it from inlet to outlet, delivering a flow largely independent of outlet pressure.
Helical gear
A gear whose teeth are cut at an angle to the axis, giving smoother, quieter meshing than spur gears but producing axial (end) thrust.
Herringbone (double-helical) gear
A gear with two opposed sets of helical teeth on one hub, which cancels axial thrust and reduces noise.
tips: Do not state that helical gears have no end-thrust; it is herringbone gears that cancel it.
Planetary gear pumps are listed as a type but no detail is given on this page; avoid inventing operating details for them.
rq: Why do helical gears need thrust bearings while herringbone gears do not?
The angled teeth of a helical gear push the gear axially; a herringbone gear's two opposed helices produce equal and opposite axial forces that cancel, so no net end-thrust arises.
Why are helical gears preferred in cars despite the extra bearing requirement?
Their smoother, quieter meshing outweighs the added cost of bearings to support the end-thrust load.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: lobe pump
pts: A lobe pump is a positive displacement pump that works as a variation on the gear pump, with two rotating lobed rotors trapping and carrying fluid from inlet to outlet.
Lobe pumps are well suited to highly viscous fluids because the fluid is displaced mechanically rather than relying on pressure-driven flow.
defs: Lobe pump

A positive displacement pump in which two (or more) meshing, non-contacting lobed rotors rotate in a casing, transferring fixed volumes of fluid from the suction to the discharge side; suited to viscous or shear-sensitive media.
tips: Do not confuse a lobe pump with a gear pump: lobe rotors do not contact each other and typically use timing gears externally.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump like a lobe pump handle highly viscous fluids better than a centrifugal pump?

A positive displacement pump traps and mechanically pushes a fixed volume of fluid each revolution, so its output is largely independent of viscosity-driven losses, whereas a centrifugal pump relies on kinetic energy transfer that viscosity greatly reduces.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: rotary sliding vane pump
pts: A rotary sliding vane pump has a rotor mounted eccentrically inside a stator, so chamber volume changes as it turns.
Sliding vanes seal off each chamber; spring-loading them helps the vanes stay in contact at slower pump speeds.
The eccentricity of the rotor produces the changes in chamber volume that give the pumping action.
Vane material must be chosen according to the fluid being pumped.
Steel vanes are used for hydraulic oil pumps; graphite vanes are used for air compressors.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in chambers whose volume is cyclically changed, rather than relying on velocity head.
Eccentric rotor
A rotor whose axis is offset from the axis of the surrounding stator, so the gap between them varies around the circumference and creates chambers of changing volume.
Sliding vane
A blade that slides radially in slots in the rotor and seals the chambers between rotor and stator, maintaining contact with the stator wall as the rotor turns.
tips: Do not confuse the rotor's eccentricity with its rotation: it is the offset geometry, not the spinning, that changes chamber volume.
Vane material must be matched to the fluid; the page's examples (steel for hydraulic oil, graphite for air) are not interchangeable.
rq: Why does the pump need the rotor to be eccentric rather than concentric with the stator?

With a concentric rotor the gap between rotor and stator would be constant, so no chamber volume change would occur and no pumping action would result. Eccentricity makes the volume of each chamber expand (drawing fluid in) and then shrink (expelling fluid).
What would happen to the sealing of the chambers if the pump runs slowly and the vanes are not spring-loaded?

At low speed centrifugal force on the vanes is small, so they may not be pressed firmly against the stator, causing leakage between chambers and reduced efficiency; spring-loading keeps them in contact.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: rotary / sliding vane pumps
pts: A sliding vane pump has a rotor set eccentrically inside a casing; vanes slide radially in slots and trap fluid in chambers that change volume as the rotor turns, displacing fluid from inlet to outlet.
Vanes must stay in contact with the casing wall, so they are pushed outward (by springs or pressure/centrifugal force) and wear is a key failure mode over time.

The vanes do not jam at the ports because the rotor is eccentric and the ports sit where vanes are moving radially, with the casing shaped so vanes slide along the wall rather than catching on the port edges.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a chamber and forcing it from inlet to outlet, giving a flow largely independent of outlet pressure.
tips: Positive displacement pumps deliver a near-constant flow per revolution; leakage past vanes reduces the effective delivered flow, so wear matters.
Do not confuse a sliding vane pump (vanes slide radially) with a gear pump (teeth mesh); sealing relies on vane-to-wall contact.
rq: Why does the eccentric position of the rotor matter for a sliding vane pump?
Eccentricity makes the chamber volume between vanes grow on the inlet side and shrink on the outlet side, so fluid is drawn in and then expelled.
What would happen if the vanes were not pushed outward against the casing?
Chambers would leak between vanes and the casing, lowering volumetric efficiency and pumping capacity, especially at low speed or high pressure.
How could the vanes be extended by hand without springs?
Use a manually operated mechanism such as a lever or cam, or rotate the vanes/rotor by hand so that the vane is pushed out by hand against the casing wall.

notes.t: Positive displacement pumps: screw pump
pts: Fluid is drawn in at the inlet, carried axially along the meshing screws by the rotating central screw, and discharged at the outlet, so flow moves along the pump axis.
The central (yellow) screw is the driven element, normally turned by a motor via the shaft, while meshing screws/collars seal and carry the fluid in cavities.
Fluid enters a suction manifold and passes through the meshing screws to the discharge, trapped in cavities that advance together as the screws turn.
Screw pumps are quiet and reliable because the smooth, continuous meshing motion gives low pulsation and low noise.
Screw pumps suit lubricating fluids, which are transported well by the sealed screw cavities without damage to the fluid.
defs: Positive displacement pump
A pump that moves a fixed volume of fluid per cycle by trapping it in a cavity and forcing it through the outlet, giving a flow largely independent of discharge pressure.
Meshing collars
Intermeshing features on the screws that form sealed cavities between the screw flights and the casing, preventing backflow and carrying fluid axially.
Relief valve
A pressure-limiting safety device that opens to return fluid to the suction side when discharge pressure exceeds a set value, protecting the pump and circuit.
Mechanical seal
A rotating shaft seal that prevents fluid leakage along the drive shaft where it passes out of the pump casing.
tips: Do not confuse the flow direction: in a screw pump fluid moves axially (along the shaft), not radially as in a centrifugal pump.
Remember the relief valve is a safety device for pressure limiting, not a flow-control device.
rq: Why does a screw pump's flow stay nearly constant even if the discharge pressure rises?
Because it is a positive displacement pump: each revolution traps a fixed volume in the screw cavities, so pressure rise mainly increases leakage slightly, not the displaced volume.
What would happen to the pump if the outlet were blocked and no relief valve were fitted?
Pressure would rise rapidly since the fixed volume cannot escape, risking overload of the casing, seals and motor; the relief valve prevents this by bypassing fluid to suction.

notes.t: Screw pump: thrust balancing and bearings
pts: A single-screw arrangement produces an axial end thrust that must be absorbed by a thrust bearing, usually in the motor.
Using two screws with opposite-hand threads, suction at both ends and discharge in the centre, lets the axial forces cancel so no thrust bearing is needed.
In the double-ended design the suction is at both ends of the screws with a central discharge, so the pressure loads on each end oppose one another.
The drawing shows only location bearings, which fix the shaft radially and axially in position but do not carry a net thrust load.
tips: Only the thrust is balanced by opposite threads and symmetric suction; location bearings are still needed to position the shaft.
Remember the drawing is of the balanced double-screw type, so its absence of a thrust bearing is not an omission.
rq: Why does a single-screw pump need a thrust bearing but the double-ended, opposite-hand design does not?

In a single-screw pump the discharge pressure acts on the screw end creating a net axial force. In the double-ended design the two screws have opposite-hand threads and suction at each end, so the axial forces from the two halves are equal and opposite and cancel, leaving no net thrust.
What would happen to the balanced design if the two screws had threads of the same hand?
The axial forces would no longer be opposed in the correct sense, so the thrust would add rather than cancel, and a thrust bearing would again be required.

xq.q: An ideal gear pump has gears with \(N = 12\) teeth. The area enclosed between two teeth and the casing is \(A = 40\ \text{mm}^2\), the tooth length is \(l = 25\ \text{mm}\), and the shaft speed is \(S = 24\ \text{rev/s}\). Using \(\dot{v} = A l N S\), calculate the ideal volumetric flow rate in litres per minute. (1 m³ = 1000 L.)
xq.a: 17.28 L/min

xq.q: In a gear pump, the teeth unmesh on the inlet side. Where is the fluid carried from inlet to outlet?
xq.a: Around the outside of the gears between the teeth and the casing
o: Around the outside of the gears between the teeth and the casing
Through the meshing region between the two gears
Through the centre of the idler shaft
Through the lip seal cover
xq.w: Fluid is trapped between teeth and casing and carried round the outside; a common mistake is thinking it is squeezed through the mesh.
s: Unmeshing creates a void and suction
Fluid is carried in tooth spaces along the casing

xq.q: Compare spur, helical and herringbone (double-helical) gears for a gear pump in terms of noise and axial end-thrust, explaining why herringbone gears behave as they do.
xq.a: Helical gears mesh more smoothly and quietly than spur gears but their angled teeth produce an axial end-thrust that the bearings must carry. Herringbone gears have two opposed sets of helical teeth, so the axial forces from the opposing helix angles cancel, giving no resultant end-thrust while keeping the low noise.
s: Herringbone: opposed helix angles cancel thrust

units.name: 3.6 Centrifugal pump operation, casings and impellers
units.ov: This module covers how a centrifugal pump works: the impeller adds velocity to the fluid and the casing (volute or diffuser) converts that velocity to pressure. It then compares impeller types (enclosed, open, semi-open, shrouded, double-entry) and casing types, and covers operating limits, seals, bearings and wear rings. The unifying idea is that each design choice trades efficiency, solids handling, suction performance, stability and leakage control against the others.
must: Energy path: the impeller imparts rotational energy and velocity, fluid enters at the eye and leaves through the vane tips, and the casing slows it to convert kinetic energy to pressure
Impeller = rotating, adds energy; casing = stationary, guides flow and converts velocity to pressure (do not mix these up)
