If two pumped systems have identical elevation and pressure differences but one has much longer pipework, which has the higher TDH and why?
The longer pipework has the higher TDH, because the greater pipe length produces greater friction loss \(h_{f}\), which adds to the total head.
Why must the velocity term use \(V_{2}^{2}\) - \(V_{1}^{2}\) rather than just \(V^{2}\)?
The term represents the change in kinetic energy head between outlet and inlet, so only the difference in velocity heads contributes to the pump's required head.

notes.t: Key terminology for pumps in systems
pts: Static head is the total vertical distance a pump raises fluid, and total dynamic head combines static, pressure, velocity and friction components.
Static lift and static discharge are measured from the pump centre-line: lift to the fluid level when the pump is off, discharge to the final exit elevation.
Total dynamic head is the pressure difference between pump inlet and outlet while the pump is running, and equals the sum of static, pressure, velocity and friction heads.
Suction head applies when inlet pressure is above atmospheric; suction lift applies when it is below atmospheric.
Friction head is the pressure loss caused by friction in the system.
defs: Static Head
The total vertical distance through which a pump raises fluid.
Static Lift
The vertical distance between the pump centre-line and the fluid elevation when the pump is not operating.
Static Discharge
The vertical distance between the pump centre-line and the final exit elevation.
Total Dynamic Head
The total pressure difference between the inlet and outlet of an operating pump, equal to static head + pressure (operating) head + velocity head + friction loss.
Suction Head
Pump inlet pressure when it is above atmospheric pressure.
Suction Lift
Pump inlet pressure when it is below atmospheric pressure.
eqs: Total dynamic head of an operating pump

\(H_{TDH}\) = total dynamic head (m); \(H_{static}\) = static head (m); \(H_{pressure}\) = pressure (operating) head (m); \(H_{velocity}\) = velocity head (m); \(H_{friction}\) = friction loss/head (m)
tips: Do not confuse static head (geometric height) with total dynamic head (pressure difference across a running pump); they are not interchangeable.
Suction head and suction lift are defined by inlet pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, not by the height of the fluid source alone.
rq: Why is static lift measured only when the pump is not operating, while total dynamic head requires the pump to be running?

Static lift is a purely geometric height of fluid relative to the pump centre-line, which exists regardless of flow. Total dynamic head depends on pressure and velocity differences that only develop when fluid is moving through the pump.
What would happen to the classification of an inlet condition if a pump's inlet pressure dropped from above atmospheric to below atmospheric?
It would change from suction head to suction lift, because the classification depends on whether inlet pressure is above or below atmospheric pressure.

xq.q: A pump transfers water (\(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³, \(g = 9.81\) m/s²) between two points. The outlet is 18 m above the inlet. The outlet pressure is 150 kPa higher than the inlet pressure. The water velocity is \(V_1 = 1.0\) m/s at the inlet and \(V_2 = 3.0\) m/s at the outlet. The friction head loss in the pipework is \(h_f = 4.5\) m. Calculate the total dynamic head (TDH) the pump must supply.
xq.a: TDH ≈ 38.2 m

xq.q: A pump lifts fluid through a vertical distance of 12 m from source to discharge point. The fluid is changed from water to a brine of relative density 1.2, and the pipework and elevations stay the same. What is the static head of the system with brine?
xq.w: Static head is a height of fluid in metres set only by the elevation difference, so it is independent of density; multiplying by 1.2 confuses head with pressure.
s: Static head = elevation difference = 12 m regardless of density

xq.q: A technician says: "The pump lifts water 25 m, so the total dynamic head is 25 m." Explain why this statement is incomplete. Name the four components of TDH for an operating pump and state which of them changes with flow rate.
xq.a: The 25 m is only the static head (elevation difference). TDH = static head + pressure head + velocity head + friction head. Pressure head is (P2 − P1)/ρg, which is the difference in pressure converted to metres. Velocity head is (V2² − V1²)/2g. Friction head is the loss in pipes and fittings. Friction head grows with flow rate, so TDH is larger than 25 m whenever there is flow, and it varies with the flow rate. Static head is only the geometric part.
s: 25 m is only the static (elevation) head [1]
TDH = static + pressure + velocity + friction head [1]
Pressure head and velocity head defined as (P2−P1)/ρg and (V2²−V1²)/2g [1]
Friction head increases with flow rate, so TDH exceeds the static head and depends on flow [1]

units.name: 4.4 System curves without static head, pipe size and valves
units.ov: This material covers system curves for piping with no static head, where the curve starts at the origin and the head demand is purely friction (and fitting) losses that rise roughly with \(Q^2\). It shows how pipe diameter and valves (globe vs gate) change resistance and steepen or shift the curve. It then links the system curve to the pump curve through the operating point, with TDH = static head + friction head.
must: System curve = head the system demands vs flow rate; it is not the pump curve (the pump curve is what the pump supplies)
With no static head the curve passes through the origin: \(Q=0 \Rightarrow H=0\)
Friction head rises roughly with the square of flow: \(H_f \propto Q^2\) (via \(v^2\)), giving a parabolic curve, \(H = kQ^2\)
Total dynamic head: \(TDH = H_{static} + H_{friction}\); static head is constant and friction head varies with flow
Operating point = intersection of pump curve and system curve, which gives the actual flow and head
Higher resistance gives a steeper system curve (more head for the same flow, or less flow for the same head); narrower pipe, extra fittings and valves all do this
Globe valve resistance is greater than gate valve resistance, so it moves the curve further left (steeper); a wider pipe lowers resistance
Flow depends on pressure, roughness, fluid type, laminar/turbulent regime, orientation and viscosity; hold all others constant when comparing diameters
Static head is the height difference between surfaces or discharge and suction points, independent of flow
Check units: flow in m³/hr on the axis vs head in m; convert consistently (1 m³/hr = 1/3600 m³/s) before calculating
conn: Pipe diameter and friction: a smaller bore raises velocity and \(H_f\), steepening the system curve and moving the operating point to lower flow on a given pump curve
Valves as added resistance: throttling with a globe or gate valve changes \(k\) in \(H=kQ^2\), which shifts the intersection with the pump curve and so the duty point
Static vs no static head: the same friction curve is shifted up by \(H_{static}\) when there is a lift, so the curve no longer starts at the origin and TDH must be split into its parts
Flow regime and viscosity: laminar vs turbulent flow changes how friction scales with \(Q\), so the parabolic assumption holds mainly for turbulent flow
exq: Sketch the system curve for a pipe with no static head and explain why it passes through the origin and is parabolic. Then add the curve for a narrower pipe and explain the difference.
A system with no static head needs 12 m of head at 30 m³/hr. Assuming \(H=kQ^2\), find k and the head required at 45 m³/hr. If a pump delivers 20 m at that flow, what happens to the operating point?
Explain, with a sketch, how fitting a globe valve versus a gate valve changes the system curve and the operating point on a given pump curve.
Define total dynamic head. For a system with 8 m static head and friction head of 5 m at 20 m³/hr, calculate TDH at 20 m³/hr and at 40 m³/hr, and state which component changes with flow.
List the factors that influence flow rate in a piping system and explain why other parameters must be held constant when comparing the effect of pipe diameter.

notes.t: System curve for no static head
pts: With no static head, the system curve starts at the origin: zero flow requires zero head.
The head required rises with flow rate in a curved (approximately parabolic) shape, because friction losses increase with the square of velocity.
Each point on the curve gives the head needed to drive a given flow through the system at a fixed point.
defs: System curve
A graph of the head a pump must provide against the flow rate required to overcome the frictional and other losses in a piping system.
Static head
The difference in height between the liquid surfaces (or discharge and suction points), independent of flow; a system with no static head has its curve pass through the origin.
tips: Do not read the system curve as the pump curve; it shows the head the system demands, not what the pump supplies.
Check units: flow is in m³/hr on the axis while head is in metres, so convert flow units consistently before calculating.
rq: Why does the system curve pass through the origin when there is no static head?
At zero flow there are no friction losses and no elevation difference to overcome, so the required head is zero.
If the flow rate doubles, why does the required head rise by roughly four times?
Friction head loss is proportional to velocity squared, and velocity is proportional to flow rate, so head scales with flow squared.

notes.t: System curve for 'no static head'
pts: With no static head, pipe flow resistance alone determines the system curve; a wider pipe lowers resistance and a narrower pipe raises it, all else constant.
Flow rate in a system depends on pressure, pipe roughness (friction), fluid type, flow regime (turbulent or laminar), pipe orientation and fluid viscosity.
Adding fittings such as globe valves or gate valves increases the system's flow resistance and so changes the system curve.
tips: Keep all other parameters constant when comparing pipe diameters, otherwise the comparison is invalid.
Remember that the system curve shows head versus flow rate; a higher resistance means a steeper curve, not a higher flow rate.
rq: Why does a narrower pipe shift the system curve upwards when there is no static head?
Smaller diameter increases friction losses for a given flow, so more head is needed to drive each flow rate, raising the head–flow curve.
Which flow-rate factors change the system curve, and which do not?
Pipe roughness, fluid viscosity, flow regime and fittings change friction losses; pipe orientation affects the static contribution, not the pure friction curve.

notes.t: System curves and the influence of valves
pts: A globe valve offers more resistance to flow than a gate valve, shifting the system curve further left.
A wider pipe reduces resistance to flow, while a narrower pipe increases it, changing the system curve.
The operating point is where the pump curve intersects the system curve; total dynamic head splits into static head and friction head.
defs: Total Dynamic Head (TDH)
The sum of static head and friction head that the pump must supply to move fluid through the system at a given flow rate.
Static head
The vertical height difference the fluid must be lifted, independent of flow rate.
Friction head
The head lost to fluid friction in pipes, valves and fittings, which increases with flow rate.
tips: Friction head rises with flow rate, whereas static head is constant; do not treat the whole head as flow-independent.
Read the operating point from the intersection of the pump and system curves, not from the static head line.
rq: Why does a globe valve move the system curve to the left rather than the right?
A globe valve adds more resistance, so for a given flow rate more head is needed (friction head rises), making the curve steeper and shifting it left.
What would happen to the operating flow rate if a narrower pipe were installed?
Friction head increases, the system curve rises, and it intersects the pump curve at a lower flow rate.

xq.q: A closed-loop pipe circuit has no static head, so its system curve is \(H = kQ^2\), where \(H\) is the head (m) and \(Q\) the flow rate (m³/hr). The pump must supply 8.0 m of head to drive 30 m³/hr through the circuit. Find the constant \(k\), then calculate the head required to drive 45 m³/hr.
xq.a: H = 18 m at 45 m³/hr (k ≈ 0.00889 m/(m³/hr)²)

xq.q: A gate valve in a no-static-head piping system is replaced by a globe valve of the same nominal size, with everything else unchanged. Which statement about the system curve is correct?
xq.a: The curve becomes steeper, so more head is needed for the same flow rate
o: The curve is unchanged because the pipe diameter has not changed
The curve becomes less steep because the globe valve gives a higher flow
The curve becomes steeper, so more head is needed for the same flow rate
The curve is shifted upward and no longer passes through the origin
xq.w: A globe valve has higher flow resistance than a gate valve, so more friction head is needed at each flow and the curve is steeper; it still passes through the origin because no static head has been added.
s: Globe valve has higher resistance than a gate valve
Higher resistance means a steeper curve, and with no static head it still starts at the origin

xq.q: Sketch the system curves for a pipe system with no static head for two pipe diameters, a wide pipe and a narrow pipe, on the same axes of head (m) against flow rate (m³/hr). Explain the shape of the curves and the relative positions of the two curves, stating which condition must be satisfied for the comparison to be valid.
xq.a: Both curves start at the origin because there is no static head, so zero flow needs zero head. They rise in a roughly parabolic shape because friction losses increase with the square of velocity. The narrow pipe has higher resistance, so its curve is steeper and lies above the wide-pipe curve, requiring more head for the same flow. The wide pipe curve is flatter. The comparison is only valid if all other parameters (fluid, roughness, fittings, length) are kept constant.
s: Sketch: two curves from the origin, head on y-axis and flow on x-axis [1]
Parabolic shape because friction rises with velocity squared [1]
Narrow pipe curve steeper, above the wide-pipe curve [1]
Origin because there is no static head [1]

units.name: 4.5 System curves with static head
units.ov: This module covers the static head component of a pump system curve: the elevation difference the pump must lift fluid through, independent of flow rate. It sets the non-zero intercept of the system curve, and friction and velocity losses that grow with flow are added on top. The operating point is found where the pump curve intersects this system curve.
must: Static head is the vertical elevation difference between source and discharge free surfaces, and is independent of flow rate: \( H_{st} = z_d - z_s \)
Total static head is the algebraic sum \( H_{TSH} = H_{SDH} + H_{SSH} \), with signs kept, where both are measured from the pump centreline datum

Sign convention for the suction side: SSH is positive if the source surface is above the pump centreline (flooded suction) and negative if it is below (a lift). Check this against the source's own definitions, because the notes' wording is inconsistent here

Equivalent form: the lift below the pump and the lift above it add as magnitudes, so \( H_{st} = \text{lift below} + \text{lift above} \) when the source is below the pump, and it is reduced when the source is above
System curve: \( H_{sys}(Q) = H_{st} + H_{friction}(Q) \), where friction \( \propto Q^2 \) (\( H_f = kQ^2 \)), so the curve starts at \( H_{st} \) at \( Q=0 \) and steepens with flow
The static part plots as a constant horizontal offset, and the system curve must never be drawn through the origin when static head is present
Friction losses in pipes and fittings are not part of static head; they are the dynamic, flow-dependent part of the curve
The operating point is the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve, giving the flow and head the pump actually delivers
Units: head is in m of fluid and flow must be consistent (m³/hr vs m³/s). Convert head to pressure with \( p = \rho g H \)
Static head is measured between free surfaces, so pressurised tanks need an extra pressure-head term \( \Delta p/\rho g \)
conn: Static head plus the friction term \( kQ^2 \) builds the full system curve, and a question usually gives the head at one flow to find \( k \)
The system curve intersecting the pump curve gives the operating point, so changing the static head (e.g. a tank level change) shifts the whole system curve vertically and moves the operating point
Head and pressure conversion \( p=\rho g H \) links static head to pressure gauge readings at the pump inlet and outlet
Sign convention for suction head (flooded suction vs suction lift) determines the total static head, which then sets the minimum head the pump must supply at zero flow
exq: A pump draws water from a tank whose surface is 3 m below the pump centreline and discharges to a tank 12 m above the pump centreline. Calculate the total static head and sketch the system curve, labelling the intercept at \( Q=0 \).

For the system above, the friction head is 4 m at \( 0.02\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \). Find \( k \) in \( H_f=kQ^2 \), write the system curve equation, and find the head required at \( 0.03\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \).
The pump in the previous question has the curve \( H_p = 30 - 5000Q^2 \) (H in m, Q in m³/s). Find the operating flow rate and head.

The source tank is moved so its surface is 2 m above the pump centreline (flooded suction), with the discharge height unchanged at 12 m above the pump. Recalculate the total static head, and explain the effect on the system curve and operating point.
Explain why static head is independent of flow rate whereas friction head is not, and convert a static head of 10 m of water to pressure in kPa.

notes.t: Static head in a pump system curve
pts: Static head is the physical vertical height a fluid must be lifted by the pump, independent of flow rate.
Static head is the sum of two parts: suction head and discharge head, added together because head/pressure is a scalar quantity.
Suction head is the vertical elevation difference from the fluid source to the pump.
Discharge head is the vertical elevation difference from the pump to the outlet.
defs: Static head
The total vertical height through which a fluid must be lifted by a pump, equal to the sum of suction head and discharge head; it does not depend on flow rate.
Suction head
The vertical elevation difference between the fluid source (free surface) and the pump inlet.
Discharge head
The vertical elevation difference between the pump outlet and the final discharge point.
eqs: \(H_{static}\) = total static head (m); \(H_{suction}\) = suction head (m); \(H_{discharge}\) = discharge head (m)
tips: Static head is measured as vertical height only; do not include pipe friction losses, which belong to the dynamic part of the system curve.
Use consistent units (metres of fluid head) when adding suction and discharge heads.
rq: Why is static head added as a simple sum rather than a vector or a difference?
Head/pressure is a scalar quantity, so both elevation components act in the same lifting sense and their magnitudes simply add.
If the fluid source sits below the pump, how does the suction head contribute to the total static head?
The pump must lift the fluid up from the source, so the suction elevation difference is still a positive lift and is added to the discharge head.

notes.t: System curve for static head
pts: A system curve plots the head a pump must overcome against flow rate; here it rises from a non-zero value at zero flow, showing a static head component.
Static head is the constant elevation difference the pump must lift fluid through, present even when flow is zero.
Head increases with flow rate because friction and velocity losses grow, making the curve steepen as flow increases.
The pump operating point is where the pump curve intersects this system curve.
defs: System curve
A graph of the total head required to drive a given flow rate through a piping system, including static head and losses that vary with flow.
Static head
The vertical height difference between the fluid's source and discharge levels, which the pump must overcome regardless of flow rate.
tips: Do not assume the system curve starts at zero head; the static head offset must be included.
Keep units consistent: flow rate is in m³/hr while head is in m, so convert if combining with pump data in m³/s.
rq: Why does the system curve not pass through the origin?
Because even at zero flow the pump must still raise fluid through the static head (elevation difference), so a non-zero head is required.
What would happen to the curve if the discharge tank were raised higher?
The static head would increase, shifting the whole curve upward while keeping its shape largely the same.

notes.t: Static head in pump system curves
pts: Static head is the elevation difference the pump must overcome, independent of flow rate.
If the pump sits below the fluid surface, the static lift is negative, reducing the head required.
Total static head is found by adding suction and discharge static heads with their signs.
Total static head sets the minimum pressure (head) the pump must supply, before friction losses are added.
defs: Static suction head (SSH)
Vertical distance from the pump centreline to the free surface of the source liquid; positive if the surface is above the pump, negative if below.
Static discharge head (SDH)
Vertical distance from the pump centreline to the free surface of the receiving tank, measured with the pump as datum.
Total static head (TSH)
Algebraic sum of static discharge head and static suction head, giving the net elevation head the pump must provide.
Resistance to flow
Head loss caused by friction in pipes and fittings, which adds to static head to form the system curve.
eqs: Total static head of a pumped system
\(H_{TSH}\) = total static head (m); \(H_{SDH}\) = static discharge head (m); \(H_{SSH}\) = static suction head (m, negative if the pump is below the source surface)
tips: Keep the sign of static suction head: a pump below the source surface gives a negative SSH, so do not add its magnitude.
Static head is a height in metres of fluid; do not confuse it with pressure in Pa unless multiplied by density and gravity.
rq: Why does a pump located below the source liquid level have a lower required head?
Because the negative static suction head subtracts from the discharge head, so the pump only has to lift the liquid the net elevation difference, and gravity helps supply the suction side.
What happens to the system curve if the receiving tank level rises while the source stays fixed?
Static discharge head increases, so total static head increases and the system curve shifts upward, with the pump needing more head at every flow rate.

notes.t: Static head in pumped system curves
pts: Static head is the elevation difference the pump must lift fluid, independent of flow rate.
Static suction head is measured from the lower (inlet) tank surface to the pump centreline; static discharge head from the pump centreline to the outlet tank surface.
Total static head is the sum of suction and discharge static heads, giving a flat (constant) horizontal line on the system curve.
Because static head does not vary with flow, the static component of the system curve is a horizontal offset; friction losses add the flow-dependent part on top.
defs: Static head
The vertical elevation difference between the fluid surfaces at the suction and discharge ends of a pumped system, independent of flow rate.
Static suction head
Height of the source fluid surface above (or below) the pump centreline, which a pump either receives as positive suction head or must lift against.
Static discharge head
Vertical height from the pump centreline to the free surface of the receiving tank.
eqs: Total static head of the system
\(H_{st}\) = total static head (m); \(z_{d}\) = elevation of discharge surface (m); \(z_{s}\) = elevation of suction surface (m)
tips: Do not let flow rate change the static head; only friction head varies with \(Q\) and must be added on top of the static offset.
Keep sign conventions consistent: suction head is positive when the source surface is above the pump centreline and negative when it is a lift.
rq: If the pump were moved down to the level of the lower tank, what would happen to the static suction head and the total static head?

Moving the pump down to the lower tank increases the static suction lift (suction head becomes negative/lift increases), so the total static head that the pump must overcome increases by the same amount of lowering, while the discharge head is unchanged. Practically this reduces available NPSH risk concerns and changes the system curve's static offset.
Why does adding parallel branches to a pipe system not change the static head portion of the system curve?

Static head depends only on elevation difference between fluid surfaces, not on pipe layout or flow split. Parallel branches reduce friction losses at a given total flow, lowering the dynamic (friction) part of the curve, but the horizontal static offset remains the same.

xq.q: A pump sits on the ground. The free surface of the source tank is 3 m above the pump centreline, so the static suction head is \(H_{SSH} = -3\) m (negative because the pump is below the source surface). The receiving tank surface is 22 m above the pump centreline. Friction head in the system is 5.0 m at 40 m³/hr and varies with the square of flow rate. Calculate the total static head and the total head the pump must supply at 60 m³/hr.
xq.a: TSH = 19 m; total head at 60 m³/hr = 30.25 m

xq.q: A pump centreline is 2 m below the free surface of the source tank. The free surface of the discharge tank is 10 m above the pump centreline. What is the total static head of the system?
xq.a: 8 m
o: 2 m
8 m
xq.w: A pump below the source surface has a negative static suction head (−2 m), so TSH = 10 + (−2) = 8 m; adding the magnitude gives the wrong value of 12 m.

xq.q: Sketch a system curve for a pump system with static head, showing the pump curve and the operating point. Explain why the system curve does not start at the origin and why it steepens as flow rate increases.
xq.a: The sketch shows head against flow rate. The system curve starts at a non-zero head on the vertical axis equal to the total static head and rises, getting steeper with flow. The pump curve falls with flow and crosses the system curve at the operating point. The curve does not start at the origin because the pump must lift the fluid through the elevation difference even at zero flow; static head is independent of flow. It steepens because friction and velocity losses grow with flow rate (approximately with the square of velocity), and these are added on top of the constant static head.
s: Sketch: system curve starting at static head on the head axis, rising and steepening [1]
Pump curve crossing it at the operating point [1]
Non-zero start because static head is independent of flow and present at zero flow [1]
Friction/velocity losses increase with flow, added to the constant static head, so the curve steepens [1]

units.name: 4.6 Pump curves and pump–system matching (operating point)
units.ov: This material covers pump curves (head vs flow rate) and how a pump is matched to a piping system. The pump curve is intersected with the system curve, which comes from friction and static head, to give the operating point. Centrifugal pumps have head falling with flow, whereas positive displacement pumps give nearly fixed flow whatever the head.
must: Operating point = intersection of pump curve and system curve; it gives the actual flow \(Q\) and head \(H\) at which the system runs
Head is energy per unit weight of fluid, \(H = p/\rho g\) (+ elevation/velocity terms), expressed in metres of fluid column, not as a pressure unit
A pump curve plots head \(H\) (m) against flow rate \(Q\) (m³/hr); read the axes carefully and check units
Centrifugal pump: head falls as flow rises (downward-sloping curve), so head and flow change together
Positive displacement (steep or near-vertical) curve: flow is almost fixed, and a small change in head barely changes it
System curve rises with flow because friction losses increase (roughly \(H_{sys} = H_{static} + kQ^2\)); do not confuse it with the falling pump curve
A falling pump curve and a rising system curve cross at only one point, giving a stable operating point
Design workflow: determine the required flow or pressure first, then select a pump whose curve passes through or near that duty point
If the system changes (e.g. a valve is throttled, which raises \(k\)), the system curve moves and so does the operating point; the pump curve stays the same
conn: Friction losses (Darcy–Weisbach, \(h_f \propto Q^2\)) build the system curve, which is then overlaid on the pump curve to find the operating point
Bernoulli/energy equation with pump head: \(H_{pump}\) equals static lift plus friction and minor losses, so the operating point is where the energy balance is satisfied
Pump type (centrifugal vs positive displacement) determines how sensitive the operating flow is to changes in system resistance, e.g. throttling a valve
Unit consistency: converting m³/hr to m³/s when computing velocity, \(Re\) and friction, then converting back to read the graph
exq: Sketch a centrifugal pump curve and a system curve with static head 10 m on the same axes, mark the operating point, and explain why it is the only possible steady running condition.

A system has \(H_{sys} = 15 + 0.002Q^2\) (H in m, Q in m³/hr) and a pump curve is given. Find the operating point graphically and calculate the head and flow, then state the effect of partly closing a valve.
Compare the curves of a centrifugal pump and a positive displacement pump. How does the operating point of each respond to a rise in system resistance?
Explain what is meant by 'head' as a height of fluid. Convert a pump head of 25 m of water into a pressure in kPa (\(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³, \(g = 9.81\) m/s²).
Given a required duty of 40 m³/hr at 20 m head, describe how you would select a suitable pump from a set of curves and check that the resulting operating point is acceptable.

notes.t: Pump curves: head vs flow rate
pts: Each line on a pump curve plots the head a pump delivers against the flow rate it passes; the curve describes how the pump behaves.
The red line is steep, so flow is almost fixed whatever the head; a small change in head barely changes the flow, as with a positive displacement-type or near-constant-flow characteristic.
The green line slopes down: as flow rises, head falls, and both change together, which is the typical characteristic of a centrifugal pump.
The operating point of a pump in a system is where its curve crosses the system curve, which is where the pump's head matches the head required by the system.
defs: Head
The energy per unit weight of fluid delivered by a pump, expressed as a height of fluid column (metres), that the pump can raise the fluid through.
Pump curve
A graph of the head a pump produces against flow rate, showing how the pump's performance varies with flow.
tips: Read the axes carefully: head is in metres and flow rate in m³/hr, so do not confuse the two when reading the curve.
A steep curve means flow is nearly independent of head; a sloping curve means both head and flow change together.
rq: Why does the red line lean backwards (negative slope with head falling as flow rises) rather than sloping the other way?

Increasing flow through a pump requires less head to be developed, because the pump's losses and the energy it imparts shift; the curve therefore falls as flow increases, and the steepness of the red line means flow hardly changes with head.
If a pump's curve were the red line and the system resistance increased, what would happen to the flow?
Because the red curve is almost vertical, flow stays nearly constant; the head rises to meet the higher resistance while the flow changes very little.

notes.t: Pump and system matching
pts: A balanced system operates at the point where the system curve crosses the pump curve.
In design, the required flow or pressure is usually known first, and a pump is then selected to deliver it.
A centrifugal pump's head falls as flow rises, while the system (friction) head rises with flow, so the two curves intersect at one operating point.
A positive displacement pump has a near-vertical flow curve, so its operating point is set mainly by flow rather than by head.
defs: System curve
A plot of the head required to drive fluid through a piping system against flow rate, typically rising with flow because friction losses increase.
Operating point
The intersection of the pump curve and the system curve, giving the actual flow rate and head at which the system runs.
tips: Do not confuse the system curve (rising with flow, from friction) with the pump curve (falling head with flow for a centrifugal pump); the operating point is their intersection.
Read flow in m³/hr and head in m from the axes; head is a height of fluid, not a pressure unit.
rq: Why does a centrifugal pump's operating point shift when its impeller diameter is reduced?
Reducing impeller diameter lowers the pump curve (less head at each flow), so it intersects the system curve at a lower flow and head, which reduces power and can match a system needing less duty.
How could you make a positive displacement pump operate at the same point as a centrifugal pump?
Use a bypass or relief valve to divert excess flow, or adjust pump speed or stroke length, so the delivered flow and pressure match the system curve at the intersection point.

xq.q: A centrifugal pump has head–flow curve \(H_p = 30 - 0.002Q^2\), where \(H_p\) is in m and \(Q\) is flow rate in m³/hr. It serves a system with static lift 10 m and friction head rising with flow, giving system curve \(H_s = 10 + 0.003Q^2\) (m, with \(Q\) in m³/hr). Find the flow rate at the operating point.
xq.a: The operating point flow is 2.0×10¹ m³/hr, i.e. Q = 63.2 m³/hr

xq.q: For the pump curve \(H_p = 30 - 0.002Q^2\) and system curve \(H_s = 10 + 0.003Q^2\) (both in m, \(Q\) in m³/hr), the operating flow is \(Q = 63.2\) m³/hr. Calculate the head at the operating point, and the fraction of this head that is used to overcome friction.
xq.a: Head = 22 m; friction fraction = 12/22 = 0.545 (about 54.5%)

xq.q: A centrifugal pump is connected to a piping system. The system valve is partly closed, increasing friction losses so the system curve becomes steeper. What happens to the operating point?
xq.a: Flow rate falls and the head delivered rises, moving up the pump curve to a new intersection
o: Flow rate rises and head falls, because the pump curve falls with flow
Flow rate falls and the head delivered rises, moving up the pump curve to a new intersection
Flow rate stays the same because the pump sets the flow
Both flow rate and head fall, because friction removes energy from the pump
xq.w: A steeper system curve crosses the falling centrifugal pump curve at lower flow and higher head; the trap is thinking friction lowers the head the pump delivers or that flow is fixed (that applies to positive displacement pumps).

units.name: 4.7 Suction lift limits, vapour pressure and practical lift
units.ov: This material explains why a pump cannot lift liquid by suction beyond a limit. Atmospheric pressure supports a finite liquid column (~10.33 m for water, less for dense liquids). In practice, losses, wear and above all vapour pressure and cavitation cut this to about 5-7 m for water at 25 °C. The ideas connect through one pressure balance: the available pressure difference (atmospheric minus vapour pressure) converts to a height via \( h = \Delta p/\rho g \).
must: Theoretical max suction lift: \( H = \frac{p_{atm}}{\rho g} \), obtained by equating column weight \( \rho A H g \) to pressure force \( pA \); about 10.3 m for water at 101.3 kPa
Check: \( \frac{101300}{1000\times 9.81} = 10.33 \) m, with P in Pa, \( \rho \) in kg/m³, g in m/s²
Specific gravity \( SG=\rho/\rho_{water} \) is dimensionless; lift is \( h_{max}=10.33/SG \) m (e.g. diesel, SG 0.86: about 12.0 m)
10 m assumes a perfect vacuum and no losses; it is an idealised upper bound and never a design value
Practical limits for water at 25 °C: about 7 m for a reciprocating pump and about 5 m for a centrifugal pump
Reasons for reduced practical lift: imperfect vacuum, worn seals, inlet friction (dynamic losses), and vaporisation/cavitation at low pressure
Vapour pressure is the pressure of a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature; it rises steeply and non-linearly with temperature

A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure, so the boiling point depends on pressure (water boils at 100 °C at 101.3 kPa); lowering the inlet pressure lowers the boiling temperature
Hotter or more volatile liquids (e.g. propanone) have higher vapour pressure, so less vacuum is permissible and less lift is available

Method: take the vapour pressure at the actual liquid temperature, work in absolute pressure, then convert the allowable vacuum (\( p_{atm}-p_v \)) to a height; do not mix gauge and absolute, or bar and kPa
Design consequence: place pumps low, close to or below the free surface, to keep suction lift small
conn: Hydrostatic pressure balance and vapour pressure: the usable lift is \( (p_{atm}-p_v)/\rho g \), not \( p_{atm}/\rho g \), so temperature reduces lift via \( p_v \)
Specific gravity and lift: a lighter liquid (SG<1) has a higher theoretical lift, but a volatile one has a higher \( p_v \), which can cancel or outweigh this gain
Boiling and cavitation: reducing inlet pressure to \( p_v \) causes vaporisation at the pump inlet, linking the vapour pressure curve to the practical limits of 5-7 m
Pump type and losses: friction, seal wear and pump type reduce the idealised lift, so practical design uses the lower figures
exq: Derive the maximum theoretical suction lift for water by equating the weight of a column to the force from atmospheric pressure, and calculate it for \( p_{atm}=101.3 \) kPa, \( \rho=1000 \) kg/m³.
Calculate the theoretical maximum suction lift for diesel with SG = 0.86 and compare it with water. Why can this value not be used as a design lift?

Using a vapour pressure curve, find the vapour pressure of water at 80 °C. Calculate the percentage vacuum and the maximum height of a pump above the liquid surface. Repeat for propanone at 50 °C and comment.
List four reasons why the practical suction lift of a pump is less than 10 m, and state typical values for reciprocating and centrifugal pumps drawing water at 25 °C.
Explain why water can boil at room temperature at a pump inlet, and what this implies for pump positioning.

notes.t: Theoretical pump suction lift
pts: Atmospheric pressure can only support a finite column of water; the maximum height is reached when the weight of the column balances the force from air pressure.
The weight force of the water column is its mass times gravitational acceleration, with mass = density × volume = d × A × H.
The force from air pressure acting on the water surface is pressure times area.
Equating the two forces gives the theoretical maximum suction lift, which is about 10 m for water under standard conditions.
defs: Suction lift
The maximum vertical height a pump can draw water up from a free surface on its suction side, limited by atmospheric pressure.
eqs: Maximum theoretical suction lift (height of water column supported by air pressure), from balancing weight and air pressure force
H = height of water column (m); P = air pressure (Pa); d = density of water (kg·m⁻³); g = gravitational acceleration (m·s⁻²)
tips: Check units: P in Pa (N·m⁻²), d in kg·m⁻³ and g in m·s⁻² give H in metres; forgetting to convert pressure or density units gives wrong answers.
This is a theoretical maximum; real pumps achieve less lift due to vapour pressure, friction losses and cavitation, so do not treat ~10 m as the practical limit.
rq: Why does the area A cancel out when we find the maximum suction lift?
Because the weight force is ρAHg and the air force is PA; both forces are proportional to A, so dividing by A leaves H = P/(ρg), independent of the pipe or container area.
What would happen to the maximum suction lift if the liquid were mercury (density about 13,600 kg·m⁻³) instead of water?
The lift would fall to roughly 0.76 m, since H = P/(ρg) is inversely proportional to density.

notes.t: Theoretical pump lift and specific gravity
pts: Specific gravity is the ratio of a fluid's density to the density of water, so it is dimensionless.
Diesel's specific gravity of 0.86 means it is less dense than water, which sets the theoretical suction lift a pump can achieve from a tank below it.
In a perfect world, the maximum theoretical suction lift is limited by atmospheric pressure acting on the fluid surface, so it depends on the fluid's density.
defs: Specific gravity
The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at a stated reference temperature; it is dimensionless.
eqs: Theoretical maximum suction lift of a pump for a liquid of specific gravity SG
\(h_{max}\) = maximum suction lift (m); \(p_{atm}\) = atmospheric pressure (Pa); \rho = fluid density (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); SG = specific gravity (dimensionless)
tips: Specific gravity is dimensionless; do not attach units such as kg/m³ to it.
The theoretical lift is a perfect-world limit; real pumps, vapour pressure and friction losses reduce the practical suction height well below this value.
rq: Why does a lower specific gravity allow a higher theoretical lift for the same pump?

Atmospheric pressure supports a column of fluid with height inversely proportional to density, so a less dense fluid such as diesel (SG 0.86) gives a taller column, about 10.33/0.86 ≈ 12 m of diesel, compared with about 10.33 m for water.

notes.t: Theoretical pump lift (suction limit)
pts: A pump's inlet suction can only lift water about 10 m; beyond this, gravity overcomes the suction effect.
The 10 m figure assumes a perfect vacuum with no losses, so it is an idealised upper bound that cannot be reached in practice.
Lift is driven by atmospheric pressure acting on the water surface, pushing water up the inlet pipe into the low-pressure region created by the vacuum.
Practical design consequence: locate pumps low down in a system, close to or below the free water surface, to keep suction lift small.
eqs: Theoretical maximum suction lift of water (approximately)
\(h_{max}\) = maximum suction lift (m); \(p_{atm}\) = atmospheric pressure (Pa); \rho = density of water (kg/m³); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
tips: The 10 m value is a theoretical ideal assuming a perfect vacuum and no losses; do not quote it as achievable in practice.
Suction lift depends on atmospheric pressure and fluid density, so the limit changes for liquids other than water.
rq: Why does a real pump lift water less than the theoretical 10 m?
Real pumps cannot create a perfect vacuum and suffer losses (friction, cavitation, vapour pressure, imperfect seals), so the achievable suction lift is well below 10 m.
What would happen to the lift limit if the water were replaced by a liquid of higher density, such as mercury?
The maximum lift scales inversely with density (h = \(p_{\text{atm}}\)/ρg), so it would drop to roughly 0.76 m for mercury.
Why is it the atmosphere, not the pump, that ultimately pushes water up the inlet pipe?
The pump only lowers pressure in the inlet; the higher atmospheric pressure on the water surface pushes the water into that low-pressure region.

notes.t: Practical pump lift
pts: Theoretical suction lift of about 10 m for water is never reached in practice because pumps cannot create a perfect vacuum.
Pump wear weakens internal seals, reducing the vacuum the pump can achieve and so lowering the achievable lift.
Friction in the pump inlet causes dynamic losses that reduce the usable suction lift.
Lowering the liquid pressure at the inlet lowers its boiling temperature, so the liquid can vaporise (cavitate) before the theoretical lift is reached.
Typical practical maximum lift for water at 25 °C is about 7 m for a reciprocating pump and about 5 m for a centrifugal pump.
tips: Do not use the theoretical 10 m (atmospheric pressure head) as the design value for suction lift; apply the practical limits of roughly 5 m to 7 m.
The practical lift values apply to water at 25 °C; lift reduces for warmer liquids because of their higher vapour pressure.
rq: Why does a centrifugal pump achieve a lower maximum suction lift than a reciprocating pump?
Centrifugal pumps are not positive displacement and cannot create as strong a vacuum at the inlet, so their practical lift is limited to about 5 m versus about 7 m for a reciprocating pump.
What would happen to the achievable lift if the water were much hotter, say near boiling?
Water at higher temperature has a higher vapour pressure, so it vaporises at a smaller inlet pressure drop; the achievable suction lift falls well below the 25 °C values.

notes.t: Vapour pressure of liquids
pts: Vapour pressure rises steeply and non-linearly as temperature increases for every liquid shown.
At a given temperature, more volatile liquids (e.g. propanone) have higher vapour pressure than less volatile ones (e.g. ethanoic acid).
Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure; atmospheric pressure of 101.3 kPa (1 bar) is the reference line.
Water reaches atmospheric pressure at about 100 °C, the normal boiling point at 1 bar.
defs: Vapour pressure
The pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid (or solid) at a given temperature in a closed system.
tips: Read vapour pressure in kPa against atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa (1 bar); do not confuse bar and kPa when comparing values.
Boiling point is not a fixed property of a liquid; it is the temperature at which the curve crosses the applied pressure.
rq: Why does a liquid boil when its vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure, rather than at a fixed temperature?

Boiling is the formation of vapour bubbles throughout the liquid; bubbles can only form and grow when the internal vapour pressure equals or exceeds the external pressure, so the boiling temperature depends on the surrounding pressure.
What would happen to water's boiling point at high altitude where atmospheric pressure is lower than 101.3 kPa?
Water would boil at a lower temperature, because its vapour pressure reaches the lower ambient pressure at a smaller temperature on the curve.

notes.t: Discussion questions: suction lift and vapour pressure limits in pumps
pts: A pump's maximum suction lift is limited by the vapour pressure of the liquid at its operating temperature, since the liquid boils when pressure drops below vapour pressure.
Hotter liquids have higher vapour pressure, so they allow less vacuum at the pump inlet and less height above the liquid level.
The pump's allowable height above the liquid level depends on the percentage vacuum it can safely draw, which is set by the liquid's vapour pressure.
Propanone (acetone) is far more volatile than water, so at 50 °C its vapour pressure is high and the permissible vacuum is small.
tips: Use the vapour pressure at the liquid's actual temperature (e.g. 80 °C, 100 °C, 50 °C), not the ambient or room temperature value.
Convert the vapour pressure to a percentage vacuum relative to atmospheric pressure before converting to a height; mixing absolute and gauge pressures is a common error.
rq: Why does a hot water supply system allow less vacuum at the pump inlet than cold water does?
Hotter water has a higher vapour pressure, so cavitation/boiling begins at a smaller pressure drop, leaving less room for vacuum.
What would happen to the allowable pump height if the water were heated from 80 °C to 100 °C?
It would fall further, because vapour pressure rises with temperature, reducing the permissible vacuum and hence the suction height.

xq.q: Atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa. Water has density 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². Calculate the theoretical maximum suction lift for water, and then for diesel of specific gravity 0.86.
A centrifugal pump draws water at 25 °C from a sump. The pump site is 8 m above the water surface. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: It will not work reliably, since the practical centrifugal limit is about 5 m due to vapour pressure, inlet friction and imperfect vacuum
o: It will work, since 8 m is below the theoretical 10 m limit
It will work, since centrifugal pumps can lift about 7 m and 8 m is close enough
It will not work reliably, since the practical centrifugal limit is about 5 m due to vapour pressure, inlet friction and imperfect vacuum
It will not work, since the theoretical limit is 8 m for water
xq.w: Practical lift for a centrifugal pump is about 5 m; the trap is using the idealised 10 m (or the 7 m reciprocating value) as a design limit.

xq.q: Show that the theoretical maximum suction lift of a liquid is \(H = P/(dg)\), where \(P\) is air pressure, \(d\) liquid density and \(g\) gravitational acceleration. Then explain three reasons why the practical lift achieved is lower.
xq.a: Column of cross-section A and height H has weight = mass×g = dAHg. Air pressure force on the surface = PA. At the limit these balance: dAHg = PA, so H = P/(dg). Practical lift is less because: wear weakens seals so a perfect vacuum cannot be formed; friction in the pump inlet causes losses; reduced pressure lowers the boiling temperature so the liquid vaporises (cavitates) before the theoretical height, worse for warm liquids.
s: Low pressure lowers boiling point, cavitation

units.name: 4.8 Summary of pumps in systems
units.ov: This summary covers how pumps are matched to the systems they serve. The system sets the required head, which is the static lift plus friction losses (dynamic head), and the pump's own characteristic curve must meet that requirement. Real pumps fall short of theoretical lift for several practical reasons, so selection is always a compromise.
must: The system dictates the pump requirement: choose or design the pump from the system's demands, not the other way round
Static head \(H_s\) is the purely physical vertical lift, independent of friction and flow rate
Dynamic (total) head is the static lift plus friction losses: \(H_d = H_s + h_f\); this is the true pump duty
Using static head alone underestimates the required pump duty; always include friction losses
Head is a height of the fluid in metres, not a pressure; convert with \(H = \frac{p}{\rho g}\) before comparing with pump curves
Each pump has its own characteristic curve (head vs flow), so matching to the system usually means compromise
Theoretical (perfect) pump lift is never reached because of imperfect sealing and vacuum, wear, inlet friction loss, and the effect of reduced pressure on boiling temperature
Reduced inlet pressure lowers the liquid's boiling temperature, which limits suction lift (vapour formation/cavitation risk)
conn: System curve and pump curve: the system curve (static head plus friction rising with flow) intersects the pump characteristic curve at the operating point, so friction losses from pipe flow directly shift duty
Pressure-to-head conversion links fluid statics (\(p=\rho g h\)) to pump selection: suction lift is limited by atmospheric pressure, which sets the theoretical maximum lift
Suction-side limits (inlet friction, vapour pressure/boiling) combine with wear and sealing to explain the gap between theoretical and actual lift
Pipe friction (velocity, diameter, length) feeds the dynamic head, so changing pipe size changes the pump needed
exq: Define static head and dynamic head. A pump lifts water 12 m through a pipe with friction loss equivalent to 3 m of head. What dynamic head must it supply, and why would choosing a pump on static head alone be inadequate?
A system requires a delivery pressure of 250 kPa for a fluid of density 900 kg/m³. Convert this to head in metres and state how you would use it with a pump characteristic curve.
Explain four reasons why the actual lift of a pump is less than the theoretical lift, including the effect of reduced pressure on boiling temperature.
Describe how a pump is selected for a given system, and discuss the compromises required when the pump characteristic curve does not exactly match the system requirement.
Calculate the theoretical maximum suction lift of water at atmospheric pressure (101.3 kPa) and discuss why the practical value is considerably lower.

notes.t: Summary: Pumps in Systems
pts: Pump selection or design is driven by the characteristics of the system it will serve; the system dictates the pump's required characteristics.
Static head is the physical lift height, while dynamic head is the equivalent height the pump must supply once friction losses in the system are included.
Each pump has its own characteristic curve, so selecting a pump usually involves compromises to match it to the system.
Theoretical (perfect) pump lift is never achieved in practice because of imperfect sealing and vacuum, wear, inlet friction loss, and the effect of reduced pressure on boiling temperature.
defs: Static head
The vertical physical height through which a fluid must be lifted by a pump, independent of friction.
Dynamic head
The equivalent height a fluid must be pumped to overcome both the static lift and the friction losses in the system.
tips: Do not confuse static head (physical height only) with dynamic head (includes friction); using static head alone underestimates the required pump duty.
Head is expressed as a height in metres of the fluid, not as a pressure; convert pressure to head using the fluid density and gravity before comparing with pump curves.
rq: Why must a pump selected for a system be matched to that system's characteristics rather than chosen only by its rated maximum lift?
Because the pump operates at the point where its characteristic curve intersects the system curve (head vs. flow); a mismatch gives poor efficiency or inability to deliver the required flow.
What would happen to the practical lift of a pump if the liquid were pumped at a higher temperature, and why?
The practical lift falls, because lowering the liquid's pressure at the inlet lowers its boiling temperature, causing vapour formation (cavitation) and loss of suction.

xq.q: A pump must lift water through a vertical height of 12 m (static head). Friction losses in the pipework at the design flow are equivalent to 4.5 m of water. The delivery pressure at the outlet is atmospheric. Find the dynamic head the pump must supply, and the pressure rise it must produce if \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³ and \(g = 9.81\) m/s².
xq.a: Dynamic head = 16.5 m; pressure rise = 162 kPa

xq.q: A designer selects a pump using only the 12 m vertical lift of a system, ignoring pipe friction equivalent to 5 m. What is the consequence?
xq.a: The pump duty is underestimated, because the dynamic head is 17 m, not 12 m
o: The pump is oversized, because friction helps push the fluid
The pump duty is underestimated, because the dynamic head is 17 m, not 12 m
The pump is correct, since head is only the physical height
The pump duty is overestimated, because friction losses are included twice
xq.w: Dynamic head = static head + friction head = 17 m; the trap is using static head alone, which underestimates the required duty.

xq.q: Explain the difference between static head and dynamic head, and explain why a pump must be selected using the system curve rather than static head alone. Include a sketch description of how the operating point is found for a centrifugal pump.
xq.a: Static head is the physical vertical height the fluid is lifted, independent of friction. Dynamic head is the equivalent height including friction losses as well, so it is larger and rises with flow. Using static head alone underestimates the pump duty. The system curve (head required against flow) rises with flow because of friction, starting at the static head at zero flow. The centrifugal pump curve falls with flow. Plot both on axes of head (m) against flow (m³/hr); they cross at one point, the operating point, giving actual flow and head.
s: System curve rises with flow from static head

units.name: 4.9 Pumps in systems and suction lift (summary notes)
units.ov: This material covers how a pump is chosen and matched to a pipe system using system curves, pump characteristic curves and the operating point. It then covers suction lift: the theoretical limit of about 10 m set by atmospheric pressure, and the lower practical limit set by vapour pressure, friction and pump type. The two halves connect because the system fixes the head and flow required, while suction conditions limit where the pump can be placed and whether it can run without vaporising the liquid.
must: The system defines the pump: establish the system curve (head required vs flow-rate) before selecting a pump.
System curve shape depends on pipe diameter, surface finish and flow restrictions. Valve positions shift it, so use best-case and worst-case curves.
With static head the curve starts above zero at zero flow; with none it passes through the origin.
The operating point is the intersection of the system curve and the pump curve. It is where the system actually runs, not necessarily at the flow-rate you marked.
Pump curve types: positive displacement gives a near-vertical (constant flow) line; centrifugal gives a falling head-flow curve.
Matching procedure: draw the system curve, mark the target flow-rate, then choose a pump curve through or closest to that point.
Head is energy per unit weight, in metres of fluid. Check the axis units (head in m, flow in m³/hr).
Theoretical suction lift: \( H = \frac{P}{dg} \) (from \( F_p = PA = F_g = AHdg \)). For water this gives about 10 m, independent of pipe area. Use SI units, e.g. \( P \approx 101300\,\text{Pa} \).

Practical lift is always below theoretical because of vapour pressure, pipe friction and pump condition. The lowest allowable inlet pressure is the liquid's vapour pressure, and the pump is damaged if it pumps vapour.
Practical limits for water at 25°C are about 7 m for reciprocating pumps and 5 m for centrifugal pumps. They apply only to water at 25°C; other liquids or temperatures need the vapour-pressure curve.
conn: System curve and pump curve combine at the operating point. Changing a valve moves the system curve and so shifts the flow and head delivered.
Static head raises the system curve, and suction lift is part of that static head. A pump placed too high above the reservoir cannot work, whatever its curve.
Inlet friction and vapour pressure link the pipe-system ideas to suction lift. Inlet losses reduce the pressure available, which cuts the usable lift below 10 m.
Pump type affects both halves: centrifugal pumps have falling curves and a lower lift limit (5 m), while reciprocating or positive displacement pumps give near-constant flow and a higher limit (7 m).
exq: Calculate the theoretical maximum suction lift of water, with density 1000 kg/m³, at atmospheric pressure 101300 Pa. Then explain why the practical lift is lower and give the typical values for centrifugal and reciprocating pumps at 25°C.

A pipe system has a static head of 8 m plus a friction head that rises with flow. Sketch the system curve, and show the operating point for a centrifugal pump curve. Explain what happens to the operating point when a valve is partly closed.
Derive \( H = P/(dg) \) by equating the gravity force on a water column to the air pressure force. State why the result is independent of pipe cross-sectional area.
A pump is to deliver a specified flow-rate in m³/hr. Describe the steps for selecting a suitable pump, and explain why best-case and worst-case system curves are needed.
Explain why a liquid pump must not operate below the liquid's vapour pressure at the inlet. How would raising the liquid temperature change the allowable suction lift?

notes.t: Pumps in Systems: System Curves
pts: The system must be known before a pump can be chosen, since the system defines the pump.
Every pipe system has a characteristic curve of head required against flow-rate.
Curve shape depends on pipe diameter, surface finish, and number of flow-restricting items.
System curves change as valves open and close, so a system is often bounded by a best and worst case curve.
With no static head the curve passes through the origin; with static head it starts above zero at zero flow.
defs: System curve
A plot of the head required by a pipe system against the flow-rate needed to achieve that flow-rate; its shape depends on pipe diameter, surface finish and flow restrictions.
Static head
The fixed elevation head component that the pump must overcome regardless of flow-rate, shifting the system curve upward.
tips: Do not choose a pump before the system curve is known; the system defines the pump.
Check whether a system includes static head: curves without it start at the origin, those with it do not.
rq: Why would a system with static head have a system curve that does not pass through the origin?
Because at zero flow the pump must still overcome the fixed static (elevation) head, so the required head is greater than zero.
Why is a best and worst case curve needed for one system?
Because valve positions change the flow restriction, so the required head at a given flow varies and the pump must work across that range.

notes.t: Pump Curves and Pump-System Matching
pts: A pump's characteristic curve plots head against flow-rate; positive displacement pumps give a near-vertical (constant flow) line, while centrifugal pumps give a falling curve.
Matching a pump to a system: draw the system curve, mark the desired flow-rate, select a pump curve passing through (or closest to) that point.
The operating point of the system is where the system curve and the pump curve intersect.
Flow-rate is usually specified rather than pressure, because it is more common in industry to require a flow-rate.
defs: Head
The energy per unit weight of fluid delivered by a pump, expressed as a height (m) of the fluid column; it is the pressure value expressed in metres.
Operating point
The intersection of the system curve and the pump characteristic curve, at which the system will actually run.
tips: Head is measured in metres of fluid, not pressure in Pa; always check units when reading the vertical axis (m) against flow-rate in m³/hr.
Flow-rate is the fixed design target; do not assume the pump delivers the flow you marked unless the curves actually intersect there.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump's curve appear almost vertical while a centrifugal pump's curve falls with increasing flow?

A positive displacement pump delivers an essentially fixed volume per cycle regardless of head, so flow stays nearly constant as head changes; a centrifugal pump's head falls as flow increases, giving a downward-sloping curve.
What happens to the operating point if the system curve steepens (more resistance) while the pump curve is unchanged?
The intersection moves to a point of lower flow-rate and higher head, so the delivered flow falls.

notes.t: Theoretical Pump Suction Lift
pts: A water column is held up by atmospheric pressure; the limit is reached when the weight of the column equals the air pressure force.
Equating gravity force to air pressure force gives the maximum theoretical suction height of about 10 m, independent of pipe area.
A covered glass turned upside down keeps its water because air pressure exceeds the downward gravity force, provided the cover stays sealed.
A vacuum in the inlet pipe removes air pressure above the liquid, so atmospheric pressure on the reservoir surface pushes water up the pipe.
defs: Theoretical pump suction lift
The maximum height a water column can be raised by atmospheric pressure acting on the free surface, about 10 m for water, when the pipe above is a complete vacuum.
eqs: Force due to gravity on water column
A = water surface area (\(m^{2}\)); H = height of water column (m); d = density of water (kg·\(m^{-3}\)); g = gravitational acceleration (m·\(s^{-2}\))
P = atmospheric air pressure (Pa); A = water surface area (\(m^{2}\))
Maximum suction height of water column
H = maximum column height (m); P = air pressure (Pa); d = water density (kg·\(m^{-3}\)); g = gravity (m·\(s^{-2}\))
tips: Use consistent SI units: pressure in Pa (not bar, 1.013 bar ≈ 101300 Pa) and density in kg·\(m^{-3}\) when computing H = P/(dg).
The 10 m limit is theoretical; real pumps lift less because of imperfect vacuum, friction and vapour pressure.
rq: Why does the area A cancel when finding the maximum suction height?
Both the gravity force (AHdg) and the air pressure force (PA) are proportional to A, so dividing through by A leaves Hdg = P, making H independent of the surface area.
What would happen to the maximum lift height if the liquid were mercury instead of water?
Mercury's density (about 13,600 kg·\(m^{-3}\)) is much greater, so H = P/(dg) would be roughly 0.76 m instead of 10 m.

notes.t: Practical Pump Lift
pts: Practical pump lift is always less than theoretical lift because of pump condition, vapour point and pipe friction.
A liquid flashes to vapour when the pressure reduced at the pump inlet drops its boiling point below ambient temperature; this boiling point is pressure-dependent and liquid-specific.
The lowest allowable inlet pressure is the vapour pressure of the liquid at the expected temperature, since a liquid pump will be damaged if it pumps vapour.
Inlet pipe friction requires extra force to overcome, further reducing the achievable lift.
For water at 25°C, practical lift limits are about 7 m for reciprocating pumps and 5 m for centrifugal pumps.
defs: Vapour pressure
The pressure at which a liquid is in equilibrium with its own vapour at a given temperature; the lowest inlet pressure a pump may safely reach.
tips: Practical lift must always be lower than theoretical lift; do not use the theoretical value as the design limit.
Lift limits given (7 m, 5 m) apply to water at 25°C only; do not apply them to other liquids or temperatures without reading the vapour-pressure curve.
rq: Why would a centrifugal pump be limited to a lower lift than a reciprocating pump for water at 25°C?
A centrifugal pump relies on the liquid pressure at the inlet and is more sensitive to cavitation/vapour formation, so its practical maximum lift is lower (5 m versus 7 m).
What would happen to the allowable lift if the liquid were hotter?
Vapour pressure rises with temperature, so less vacuum can be tolerated before the liquid flashes to vapour, reducing the practical lift.

xq.q: A pump draws water from an open reservoir through a vertical inlet pipe, and the pipe above the water is a perfect vacuum. Atmospheric pressure is \(P = 101300\) Pa, water density is \(d = 1000\) kg·m⁻³ and \(g = 9.81\) m·s⁻². Show how the maximum theoretical suction height follows from equating the weight of the water column to the air pressure force, and calculate it.
s: Gravity force \(F_{g}\) = A H d g equals pressure force \(F_{p}\) = P A

xq.q: A centrifugal pump has a falling head-flow curve. A system has static head and a system curve that starts above zero at zero flow. You mark the desired flow-rate on the system curve, but the pump curve passes below that point. What happens?
xq.a: The system runs at the intersection of the two curves, at a lower flow than desired
o: The pump delivers the marked flow because flow-rate is the design target
The system runs at the intersection of the two curves, at a lower flow than desired
The system runs at the intersection, at a higher flow than desired
The pump delivers the marked flow but at a lower head
xq.w: The operating point is where the curves intersect; a pump curve below the system curve at the target flow means the intersection is at a lower flow, so the target is not assumed to be delivered.
s: Pump curve falls with flow and is below the system curve at the target, so the intersection is at lower flow

xq.q: Explain why the practical suction lift of a centrifugal pump pumping water at 25°C (about 5 m) is much less than the theoretical lift of about 10 m. Give three distinct reasons.
xq.a: Theoretical lift assumes a perfect vacuum in the inlet pipe. In practice the pump cannot produce a perfect vacuum because of its condition. The inlet pressure cannot fall below the vapour pressure of the liquid at its temperature, otherwise the liquid flashes to vapour and the pump is damaged. Friction in the inlet pipe consumes part of the available pressure difference, reducing the lift further.
s: Inlet pressure limited by vapour pressure; liquid boils and vapour damages pump (2)
Inlet pipe friction needs extra force, reducing lift (1)

units.name: 5.1 Course intro and learning outcomes
units.ov: The notes only give the intended learning outcomes for the Week 5 Heat Exchangers topic of Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016); they contain no technical content such as equations or worked examples. The outcomes link four ideas: classifying heat exchanger types, the design considerations behind each type, the strengths and weaknesses of each, and maintenance. A strong answer treats these as a checklist applied to every type discussed. Anything beyond that must come from lectures, so the points below are a framework to fill in.
must: Be able to classify the main heat exchanger types (e.g. shell-and-tube, plate, double-pipe, finned/air-cooled) and say what distinguishes each; confirm the exact list against the lecture slides
For each type, state the design considerations that drive the choice (e.g. operating pressure and temperature, fluid properties, fouling tendency, size and cost, flow arrangement)
For each type, give both strengths and weaknesses, and compare types directly rather than describing them in isolation
Know how each type is maintained (cleaning, inspection, fouling control, leak or corrosion checks) and how its design affects ease of maintenance
Use the learning outcomes as a four-part answer template: type, design drivers, pros and cons, maintenance
Link design choice to application: justify why a given type suits a given duty
Basic heat transfer vocabulary likely to be needed: \(Q = UA\Delta T_{lm}\) relates duty, area and temperature difference (check whether the module uses it)
Do not rely only on memorised lists; the exam rewards structured, comparative reasoning
conn: Design considerations and maintenance: fouling-prone fluids favour designs that are easy to clean, which affects type selection
Strengths/weaknesses and classification: compactness, pressure capability and cost follow from the construction of each type, so compare types on these criteria
Heat transfer fundamentals and design choice: the area required for a duty (\(Q = UA\Delta T_{lm}\)) influences whether a compact or a large-volume type is chosen
exq: Classify the main types of heat exchanger and describe the construction of two of them.
For a given duty (e.g. cooling oil with water at high pressure), select a suitable heat exchanger type and justify your choice in terms of design considerations.
Compare shell-and-tube and plate heat exchangers, covering strengths, weaknesses and typical applications.
Describe the maintenance a heat exchanger needs and explain how the type affects ease of cleaning and inspection.
Discuss how fouling influences both the design choice and the maintenance regime of a heat exchanger.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes – Heat Exchangers
pts: Learning goals: classify the main types of heat exchanger
Know the design considerations that drive engineering choices for each type
Compare the strengths and weaknesses of each heat exchanger type
Understand how heat exchangers are kept in working order through maintenance
tips: Do not treat the learning outcomes as content to memorise; use them as a checklist of what each exam answer on heat exchangers should address for every type discussed.
rq: Why is it useful to compare heat exchanger types by both advantages and disadvantages rather than by performance alone?

Because each type trades off cost, size, pressure capability, fouling tolerance, and ease of cleaning, so the best choice depends on the application's constraints, not just heat transfer effectiveness.

units.name: 5.2 What heat exchangers are and everyday examples
units.ov: This introductory material defines a heat exchanger as a device that transfers heat between fluids (or places) across a separating boundary, mainly by conduction, without mixing. It applies the idea to three everyday cases: freezers (two exchangers, internal and external), car engine radiators, and hot water cylinders with one or two heat sources. The common thread is to identify the heat source, the heat sink and the direction of heat flow, then judge the design against practical constraints.
must: Definition: a heat exchanger transfers heat from one fluid to another (or place to place) across a boundary, with no mixing or direct contact needed
Main mechanism is conduction through the separating wall, so wall material, area and thickness matter: \( \dot{Q} = UA\Delta T \)
Fluid pairings can be liquid-liquid, gas-gas or liquid-gas; do not assume the fluids mix or touch
Purpose: either remove heat to keep a system working (radiator) or form the core function of the system (hot water cylinder, freezer)
Freezer: the internal exchanger takes heat from cabinet air into the refrigerant; the external (rear) exchanger rejects heat from the refrigerant to room air. Keep the two directions straight
Freezer design problems should be named specifically: airflow around the rear coil, frost build-up on the internal coil, heat rejection into a hot or confined room
Car radiator: the heat source is engine combustion and the cooling medium is air; constraints include space, weight, airflow, and reliability under vibration and temperature variation

Hot water cylinder: the heat source (boiler or solar collector) heats the stored water without mixing; the cylinder design must match the number of heat sources (single-source versus dual-source with solar)

Coil position in the cylinder has no single fixed answer: reason from heat delivery to the water and from thermal stratification (hot water rises, so heat from below mixes the tank by natural convection)
Answer design questions in a structure: identify source, sink, direction of heat flow, then constraints, then specific problems
conn: Conduction through the wall links the definition to design: the heat transfer rate depends on \( U \), area and \( \Delta T \), so the space and weight limits in cars compete with the need for a large surface area

Freezer and cylinder examples both rely on heat direction and temperature difference: the rear freezer coil needs a cooler surroundings to reject heat, just as a cylinder coil needs to be hotter than the water

Stratification and natural convection connect the cylinder coil position to the choice between boiler-only and solar-plus-boiler systems: a solar coil is usually placed low to heat the cold bottom water, and the boiler coil higher
Radiator design combines the heat source (combustion), the coolant loop and air-side airflow, so it links exchanger sizing to vehicle packaging and operating conditions
exq: Define a heat exchanger and explain, with a sketch, how heat is transferred between two fluids without them mixing. State the main heat transfer mechanism.

A domestic freezer has an internal exchanger and an external exchanger on the back. State the fluids and direction of heat flow in each, and identify three design problems with this layout, with the physical reason for each.

Explain the heat source, cooling medium and four design constraints for a car engine radiator. Estimate how the required heat rejection rate would change if the engine power output doubled, assuming \( \dot{Q} = UA\Delta T \).

Why does a hot water cylinder for a boiler plus solar thermal collector differ from a single-source cylinder? Discuss where each heat exchanger coil should be placed and justify it using stratification.
Compare liquid-liquid, gas-gas and liquid-gas heat exchangers, giving an everyday example of each and commenting on how the fluid type affects the surface area needed.

notes.t: Heat exchangers
pts: A heat exchanger transfers heat from one place (often a fluid) to another, without the fluids needing to touch.
A basic heat exchanger can be a simple plate separating two fluids at different temperatures.
Heat exchangers can work with liquids, gases, or a mix of both.
The main heat transfer mechanism is usually conduction through the separating wall.
Heat exchangers either remove heat to keep a system working or form a core part of a system's function.
defs: Heat exchanger
A device that transfers heat from one fluid to another (or from one place to another) across a boundary, usually by conduction, without the fluids mixing or needing to be in direct contact.
tips: Do not assume the fluids must mix or touch; heat is transferred through a separating surface.
Remember heat exchangers can handle liquid-liquid, gas-gas, or liquid-gas combinations.
rq: Why does a heat exchanger not need the two fluids to be in contact to work?
Heat flows by conduction through the separating wall (plate) from the hotter fluid to the cooler one, so only the wall needs to be in contact with each fluid.
What would happen to a system that has no means of removing its heat?
Its temperature would rise, potentially causing it to stop working or fail, which is why heat exchangers are used to remove heat.

notes.t: Heat exchangers in freezers: example and design problems
pts: A domestic freezer uses two heat exchangers, each handling a different fluid pairing.
The internal exchanger removes heat from the air inside the cabinet by transferring it to the refrigerant.
The external exchanger on the back rejects heat from the refrigerant to the surrounding room air.
The design is posed as a question: students are asked to identify its problems, so the page invites critical evaluation of the layout.
tips: Identify the direction of heat flow in each exchanger (inside vs. back) before judging the design; mixing up the two exchangers loses marks.
Name the specific problem (e.g. airflow, frost build-up, heat rejection to a hot room) rather than vaguely saying the design is 'bad'.
rq: Why must the back-mounted exchanger reject heat to the room air for the freezer to keep working?

The refrigerant absorbs heat from inside the cabinet and must release that heat (plus the work input) somewhere at higher temperature; the room air at the back is the heat sink, so without it the refrigerant cannot be recondensed and the cycle stops.
What might go wrong if the internal evaporator coil has poor airflow over its surface?
Heat transfer from the cabinet air to the refrigerant falls, the refrigerant evaporates less, the coil frosts and the freezer runs warmer and less efficiently.

notes.t: Example 2: Cars – heat exchangers in automobiles
pts: Cars contain heat exchangers, such as the engine radiator, which remove waste heat from the engine.
The heat is generated by combustion in the engine, so the heat source must be identified before designing the exchanger.
