Design must address constraints such as limited space, airflow, weight, and reliability under vibration and varying temperatures.
tips: Identify the heat source (engine combustion) and the cooling medium (air) clearly when answering design questions.
Consider space, weight, airflow and vibration as key design constraints, not just heat transfer rate.
rq: Why is the radiator placed at the front of the car, behind the grille?
It receives the largest airflow from the vehicle's motion and fans, which increases convective heat transfer to the air.
What would happen to the engine if the radiator's coolant flow stopped?
Heat would not be removed from the engine, so its temperature would rise, risking overheating and damage.

notes.t: Hot water cylinders as heat exchangers
pts: The blue hot water cylinder is a heat exchanger for a traditional system with only one heat source, the boiler.
The grey cylinder is designed for a system with two heat sources: a solar thermal collector and a traditional boiler.
Cylinder design depends on the number of heat sources, so the choice of cylinder must match the system.
The position of the heat exchanger coil inside the cylinder is a design question that may affect how heat is delivered and stored.
defs: Heat exchanger (hot water cylinder context)
A device in which heat is transferred from a heat source, such as a boiler or solar thermal collector, to stored water without the two fluids mixing.
tips: Match the cylinder to the number of heat sources; a single-source cylinder should not be assumed to work with two sources.
Do not confuse the coil position question with a fixed answer; reason about heat transfer to the water and stratification.
rq: Why would a cylinder designed for one heat source be unsuitable for a solar thermal plus boiler system?
It is designed around a single heat input, so it may not have the coil arrangement or heat-exchange capacity needed to accept and combine two separate heat sources effectively.
What might change if the coil is placed near the top of the cylinder rather than at the bottom?

Heat from the source is delivered to the upper water first, so hot water is available sooner at the top, while the lower water heats more slowly, affecting stratification and which heat source can be used efficiently.

units.name: 5.3 Heat exchanger properties, constraints and material selection
units.ov: This module covers what a heat exchanger wall must do: conduct heat well, resist pressure, corrosion and erosion, and keep the two fluids separate. It quantifies conduction through the wall with \(Q/t = kA\Delta T/d\), then uses that equation with strength, corrosion and fluid compatibility to select materials. The central theme is a trade-off. The best conductors are not always the strongest or most durable, so selection is a balance and not a single-property choice.
must: Conduction through the wall: \(\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{kA\Delta T}{d}\). The rate rises with \(k\), \(A\) and \(\Delta T\), and is inversely proportional to wall thickness \(d\).
Use SI units (\(d\) in m, \(A\) in m², \(k\) in W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), and use \(\Delta T\) as the difference across the wall, not absolute temperatures.
Design aims: large surface area, short heat-flow path (thin wall), high \(k\), allowance for thermal expansion, and never letting the fluids mix.
Material constraints: impermeable (some polymers leak), strong enough for the pressures of both fluids, chemically resistant, and thick enough to allow for wear over the design life.
Corrosion is chemical or electrochemical degradation by the fluid. Erosion is mechanical wear from particles or debris (e.g. seawater). Do not confuse them.
Strength and conductivity trade off. Silver and copper have the highest \(k\), while stainless steel is low (12–45 W/m°C).

Alloying usually lowers conductivity. Pure Al is better than alloy 5052, and Cu-Ni falls from 59 to 29 W/m°C as Ni rises because Ni atoms disrupt electron flow. Cu-Ni has \(k\) below both pure metals but excellent corrosion resistance.
Aluminium corrodes below pH 7 and releases hydrogen, so it is unsuitable for potable or untreated water.
Brass suffers galvanic (dezincification) corrosion. Zn is the most anodic, so it dissolves and leaves porous copper, which limits brass to inert fluids.
Selection must never rest on conductivity alone. Weigh strength, corrosion resistance, fluid compatibility and service life. Quote \(k\) with units W/m°C.
conn: Wall thickness works in two opposing ways: a thin wall raises \(Q/t\) because \(Q/t\propto 1/d\), but the wall must be thick enough for pressure and for wear allowance, so the minimum thickness is set by strength and corrosion or erosion rates.
Conductivity versus strength and corrosion resistance: Cu-Ni lowers \(k\) but gains corrosion resistance, so you must justify the trade-off with the \(Q/t\) equation.
Fluid choice drives material choice: pH or water type (aluminium), seawater erosion and corrosion (Cu-Ni), or inert fluids (brass).
Surface area and thickness are geometric design levers, while \(k\) is the material lever. All three appear together in the rate equation.
exq: A copper wall (\(k\approx 400\) W/m°C) has area 2 m², thickness 2 mm and a 30 K temperature difference across it. Calculate \(Q/t\). Then find the new rate if the wall thickness is doubled, or if the material is changed to stainless steel (\(k=15\)).
Explain the difference between corrosion and erosion in a seawater-cooled heat exchanger, and state which material properties help resist each.
Why is aluminium unsuitable for tubes carrying potable or untreated water, and why is brass limited to inert fluids? Define galvanic corrosion in your answer.

Cupronickel's conductivity falls from 59 to 29 W/m°C as nickel content increases. Explain why this happens, why the alloy is still used, and how much the heat transfer rate changes for the same geometry.
Discuss the trade-offs in selecting a heat exchanger wall material, covering conductivity, strength, thickness, permeability, corrosion and fluid compatibility.

notes.t: Properties of heat exchangers
pts: Heat exchanger materials must conduct heat well (adequate thermal transfer properties).
A large heat transfer area increases the rate of heat transfer between fluids.
Wall thickness must be low so heat can pass through the wall efficiently.
The wall must be strong enough to withstand fluid pressures, and resist corrosion and erosion.
Heat transfer rate depends on area and conductivity, and falls as wall thickness rises.
eqs: Rate of heat transfer through the exchanger wall (conduction)

\(Q/t\) = heat transferred per unit time (W); \(k\) = thermal conductivity of wall material (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹); \(A\) = heat transfer surface area (m²); \(\Delta T\) = temperature difference between the two fluids (K); \(d\) = wall thickness (m)
tips: Heat transfer is inversely proportional to thickness d, not proportional; check units are SI (m for d, K for ΔT) before substituting.
The equation uses the temperature difference ΔT across the wall; using absolute temperatures instead of a difference gives wrong results.
rq: Why does doubling the wall thickness halve the heat transfer rate, all else being equal?
Because the rate is inversely proportional to thickness d, so Q/t ∝ 1/d; doubling d halves Q/t.
Why must a heat exchanger wall resist corrosion and erosion even if it conducts heat well?
Fluid flow and chemical attack can thin or degrade the wall over time, increasing thickness of material or creating leaks, which reduces performance and safety.

notes.t: Design constraints of heat exchangers
pts: A heat exchanger must transfer heat, so different parts of it get hot.
Design aims for as large a surface area as possible to maximise heat transfer.
A short heat flow path reduces resistance to heat transfer.
Materials need high thermal conductivity, and the design must allow for thermal expansion and keep the two fluids from mixing.
Three key considerations are thermal conductivity, erosion (e.g. from seawater) and corrosion.
tips: Do not confuse design constraints with the physics: a short heat flow path and large surface area both help, but a thicker wall does not.
Remember the requirement that the two fluids must never mix, which is separate from heat transfer.
rq: Why would a high surface area and a short heat flow path both improve a heat exchanger's performance?
Heat flow rate increases with area and decreases with conduction path length, so both raise the rate of heat transfer between the fluids.
Why must the design accommodate thermal expansion of the materials?
Different parts heat up and expand at different rates; without allowance, thermal stresses can cause cracking, leaks or fluid mixing.

notes.t: Constraints on the materials of heat exchangers
pts: Heat exchanger materials must be impermeable, since some polymers allow fluid to pass through them.
Walls must be thick enough to allow for wear over the design lifespan so that no hole forms in the plate or tube.
The material must be strong enough to resist the pressure of both fluids without collapsing.
The material must be chemically resistant to the fluids being used.
Corrosion must be considered, especially when water is the cooling fluid.
defs: Corrosion
Gradual chemical or electrochemical degradation of a material caused by reaction with its environment, such as the fluids in a heat exchanger.
Erosion
Wearing away of material surfaces caused by abrasive action of debris or particles carried in the flowing fluids.
tips: Corrosion and erosion are different: corrosion is chemical attack by the fluid, while erosion is mechanical wear from debris in the fluid.
Strength requirements apply to both fluids, since the wall separates two pressurised streams.
rq: Why might a polymer be unsuitable for a heat exchanger plate even if it is cheap and corrosion-resistant?
Some polymers are permeable, so fluid could pass through the wall, which the heat exchanger material must prevent.
Why does the wall need extra thickness beyond what the pressure load alone requires?
To allow for wear and erosion over the expected lifespan so that the wall never thins to the point of forming a hole.

notes.t: Thermal conductivity of metals and material selection
pts: Thermal conductivity values vary widely between metals, with silver and copper among the highest.
Strong materials tend to have low thermal conductivity, so strength and conductivity trade off against each other.
Pure aluminium conducts heat far better than its alloy 5052, showing alloying reduces conductivity.
Increasing nickel content in cupronickel sharply reduces thermal conductivity (59 to 29 W/m°C).
Stainless steel has a low and variable conductivity range of 12–45 W/m°C.
defs: Thermal conductivity
The rate at which a material conducts heat through it per unit thickness and temperature difference, measured in W/m°C.
tips: Always quote conductivity with units W/m°C; forgetting units loses marks.
Do not assume a strong metal is a good conductor; the table shows the trade-off reverses for many metals.
rq: Why does material selection for a heat exchanger become difficult when strength is needed?
Because the strongest materials generally have low thermal conductivity, so a strong material may transfer heat poorly, while a good conductor may be too weak.
What would you expect to happen to conductivity if you add nickel to copper to make cupronickel, and why?
Conductivity falls, since alloying adds atoms that scatter electrons and phonons, reducing heat transport.

notes.t: Constraints on the materials of heat exchangers
pts: Heat exchanger surfaces must conduct heat well, which usually means a metal
Copper-nickel alloys have lower thermal conductivity than either constituent, because Ni atoms disrupt electron flow, but they resist corrosion very well
Aluminium tubes corrode below pH 7.0 and release hydrogen, so they are unsuitable for potable or untreated water
Brass corrodes galvanically because zinc is the most anodic metal, leaving a pure copper matrix; it is only suitable in inert fluids
Material choice balances thermal conductivity against mechanical strength, corrosion resistance and service life, not conductivity alone
defs: Galvanic corrosion
Preferential corrosion of the more anodic (less noble) metal when two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in an electrolyte; in brass, zinc is dissolved, leaving porous copper.
tips: Do not select a heat exchanger material on thermal conductivity alone; corrosion resistance, strength and fluid compatibility must also be considered.
Alloying does not always raise thermal conductivity: Cu-Ni alloys have values below both pure metals.
rq: Why might a copper-nickel alloy be chosen even though its thermal conductivity is lower than pure copper?
Its excellent corrosion resistance gives a longer service life, which can outweigh the reduced conductivity in a corrosive environment.
Why is brass acceptable in some heat exchangers but not in others?
Zinc corrodes galvanically, so brass is only suitable where the fluid is inert and will not drive dezincification.

xq.q: A flat stainless steel heat exchanger wall has area \(A = 2.0\) m², thickness \(d = 2.0\) mm and conductivity \(k = 16\) W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. The fluids on either side differ in temperature by \(\Delta T = 25\) K. Using \(Q/t = kA\Delta T/d\), find the heat transfer rate, and the rate if the wall is replaced by a 4.0 mm thick wall of the same material.
xq.a: With 2.0 mm: 400 kW; with 4.0 mm: 200 kW
s: Doubling d halves the rate: 200000 W

xq.q: Which statement correctly describes the difference between corrosion and erosion in a heat exchanger?
xq.a: Corrosion is chemical or electrochemical degradation by the fluid; erosion is mechanical wear from particles carried in the flow
o: Corrosion is mechanical wear from debris; erosion is chemical attack
Corrosion is chemical or electrochemical degradation by the fluid; erosion is mechanical wear from particles carried in the flow
Both are chemical attack, erosion being the faster form
Both are mechanical wear, corrosion occurring only in seawater
xq.w: Corrosion is chemical attack by the environment while erosion is abrasive wear by debris; the first option swaps them.

xq.q: Explain why strength and thermal conductivity conflict when choosing a heat exchanger wall material, and why brass is only suitable in inert fluids. Use cupronickel as an example of the trade-off.
xq.a: Strong materials tend to have low thermal conductivity, so a material chosen for strength conducts heat poorly. Alloying reduces conductivity: raising nickel content in cupronickel cuts conductivity from 59 to 29 W/m°C because Ni atoms disrupt electron flow, though it resists corrosion very well. Brass corrodes galvanically because zinc is the most anodic metal, leaving a pure copper matrix, so it suits only inert fluids.
s: Strong materials tend to have low conductivity (1)
Cupronickel: Ni lowers conductivity 59 to 29 W/m°C but gives corrosion resistance (2)
Brass: zinc anodic, galvanic corrosion, so only inert fluids (2)

units.name: 5.4 Types of heat exchanger and plate heat exchanger basics
units.ov: This material introduces the two main heat exchanger types, plate and shell and tube, and then looks at the construction and operation of gasketed plate heat exchangers (PHEs). Corrugated thin plates, gaskets and a clamped frame combine to give compact, continuous heat transfer between hot and cold streams that never mix. The notes are descriptive, so top marks depend on precise terminology and on avoiding the common confusions flagged in the tips.
must: The two main types of heat exchanger are plate and shell and tube; hybrids exist but are harder to install and maintain, so name only the two main types unless asked about hybrids.
A PHE is a stack of many corrugated pressed plates separated by gaskets/seals, clamped together in a frame by end-plates.
Gaskets/seals route the hot and cold fluids into alternate channels and keep them separate so they never mix; they do not transfer heat.
The plates are the heat transfer surface: thin plates with small gaps give good thermal conductivity and compact heat transfer.
Corrugations do three jobs: they increase turbulence, increase heat transfer area, and stiffen the large flat plates against pressure differences.
Inlet and outlet branches for both fluids are fitted to one end-plate.
Mechanical layout: plates hang from a carry bar, are aligned by a guide bar, and are clamped into a plate stack.
Operation is continuous: the hot fluid temperature falls and the cold fluid temperature rises along the exchanger, so do not reverse these in calculations.
PHEs handle both liquids and gases (not liquids only) and need few parts.
Heat exchanger types (plate, shell and tube) are equipment categories and must not be confused with the heat transfer mechanisms they use.
conn: Corrugation geometry links turbulence, heat transfer area and mechanical stiffness, so a single design feature explains both thermal performance and pressure capability.
Thin plates plus small gaps give good conduction and compactness, which links to the heat transfer rate for a given size and to the number of plates needed.
Gasket arrangement determines the alternate-channel flow pattern, which links to keeping fluids separate and to the temperature changes of the hot and cold streams along the exchanger.
Equipment type (plate versus shell and tube) links to installation and maintenance, where hybrids are the harder case.
exq: Name the two main types of heat exchanger and state one reason why hybrid types are less favoured. (3 marks)
Describe the construction of a gasketed plate heat exchanger, naming the plates, gaskets, end-plates, carry bar and guide bar, and say where the inlet and outlet branches are located. (6 marks)
Explain the three functions of corrugations on PHE plates, and explain why the gaskets are essential to the flow arrangement. (5 marks)
Sketch the temperature variation of the hot and cold fluids along a PHE, labelling which rises and which falls, and state whether the process is continuous or batch. (4 marks)
A student says a PHE can only be used for liquids and that gaskets help transfer heat. Identify and correct both errors. (4 marks)

notes.t: Types of heat exchanger
pts: There are two main types of heat exchanger: plate and shell and tube.
Hybrid types exist but are harder to install and maintain than the two main types.
tips: Name only the two main types (plate, shell and tube) unless the question asks about hybrids; do not confuse heat exchanger types with the heat transfer mechanisms they use.
rq: Why might an engineer choose a standard plate or shell-and-tube design over a hybrid exchanger?
Standard designs are simpler to install and maintain, so hybrids are only justified when their performance benefits outweigh the extra complexity.

notes.t: Plate heat exchangers
pts: A plate heat exchanger is built from many corrugated pressed plates separated by seals.
The plates are clamped together in a frame by end-plates.
Inlet and outlet branches for both fluids are fitted to one end-plate.
Seals direct the hot and cold fluids through alternate channels so they never mix.
Corrugations enhance heat transfer and stiffen the large flat plate surfaces.
defs: Corrugation
A pressed wavy pattern on each plate that increases turbulence and heat transfer area while supporting the plate against pressure differences.
tips: Do not confuse the seals' role: they route fluids through alternate channels and keep the two streams separate, rather than allowing them to mix.
The statement that plate heat exchangers work for liquids or gases means they are not limited to one fluid phase; do not state they are only for liquids.
rq: Why do the corrugations both improve heat transfer and provide structural support?
Wavy patterns create turbulent flow and extra surface area for heat transfer, and their ridges act as supports that stop the large flat plates from deforming under pressure.
Why are the inlet and outlet branches for both fluids placed on a single end-plate?
It makes the connections compact and convenient, since the seals already route each fluid through alternate channels between the plates.

notes.t: Plate heat exchangers
pts: This page is a video slide introducing how plate heat exchangers (PHE) work, supported by an image of a gasketed plate heat exchanger.

notes.t: Plate heat exchangers
pts: Thin plates separated by small gaps give good thermal conductivity and compact heat transfer.
Gaskets keep the hot and cold fluids apart and direct each fluid into alternate channels.
Plates are hung from carry bars and clamped into a plate stack, with a guide bar for alignment.
The process is continuous: hot fluid cools while cold fluid heats up along the exchanger.
Few parts are needed, and both liquids and gases can be accommodated.
tips: Remember the gaskets separate the two fluids; they are not there to transfer heat, and the plates provide the heat transfer surface.
Hot fluid temperature falls and cold fluid temperature rises along the exchanger; do not reverse these in calculations or explanations.
rq: Why are the plates kept thin and the gaps between them small?
To maximise thermal conductivity and heat transfer area per unit volume, so heat passes quickly between the fluids through the plate walls.
What would happen if the gaskets failed on one side of the stack?
Hot and cold fluids would mix or leak into each other's channels, so heat transfer would be lost and the fluids could contaminate one another.

units.name: 5.5 Plate heat exchanger materials and plate features
units.ov: This module covers why plate heat exchangers use particular materials (metal plates, elastomer gaskets), what properties the plates need, and how pressed chevron corrugations and gaskets work. The ideas connect through trade-offs: thin, ductile plates give high heat transfer and formability, while corrugations restore stiffness and add turbulence at the cost of pressure drop.
must: Plate materials: stainless steel 304/316, titanium, Hastelloy, chosen for strength, corrosion resistance and temperature suitability
Why low carbon steel fails (weak, rusts) and why pure aluminium fails (too soft for pressure and handling loads); never just say 'aluminium is bad'
Gasket materials are elastomers: NBR and EPDM most common; also silicone, butyl, chloroprene. Chosen for sealing and chemical compatibility, not strength
Plate property requirements: thin (high heat transfer coefficient), ductile (pressed into shape without cracking), creep resistant (thin plates must not stretch under own weight over time)
Core trade-off: formability/ductility conflicts with strength and stiffness needed to withstand clamping load, so justify a choice as a compromise, not 'strongest is best'
Definitions: ductility = large plastic deformation before fracture (not stiffness or hardness); creep = slow time-dependent permanent deformation under sustained load, worse at high temperature
Chevron corrugations: create turbulence (break up laminar flow, mix near the wall), increase surface area, raise heat transfer coefficient, and stiffen the plate
Corrugations allow thinner plates, so less material and lower cost, and also raise pressure drop; always state this trade-off
Gaskets around edges and ports seal the channels so hot and cold fluids flow in alternate channels without mixing; this is distinct from the function of corrugations
Maintenance: a cracked plate is fixed by removing only two plates, so repair is simple
conn: Thin plates for a high heat transfer coefficient demand ductility for pressing, but thinness reduces strength and creep resistance; corrugations stiffen the plate and resolve this
Corrugations raise heat transfer through turbulence and area but also raise pressure drop (pumping power), so design balances thermal gain against hydraulic cost
Plate metal selection (corrosion, temperature) and gasket selection (elastomer compatibility with fluid and temperature) must both suit the same duty, but are chosen for different reasons
Material property definitions (ductility, creep) link to rejection of materials: pure aluminium (too soft) and low carbon steel (weak, rusts)
exq: Explain why low carbon steel and pure aluminium are unsuitable for heat exchanger plates, and name two suitable materials with the properties that make them suitable. [4 marks]
List four material property requirements for plates and discuss why formability and clamping strength conflict. Suggest how a designer resolves this. [6 marks]
State the functions of chevron corrugations on a plate and explain the penalty they bring. Why do they permit thinner plates? [5 marks]
Distinguish the roles of the plate material and the gasket material, naming two common gasket elastomers and describing what the gasket does on a plate. [4 marks]
Define creep and ductility, and explain why each matters for a thin pressed plate operating at elevated temperature. [4 marks]

notes.t: Plate heat exchangers: materials
pts: Plates are typically made from corrosion-resistant metals such as stainless steel 304/316, titanium or Hastelloy, chosen for strength and resistance to the fluids and temperatures involved.
Low carbon steel is unsuitable for plates because it is not very strong and it rusts.
Pure aluminium is unsuitable for plates because it is too soft to withstand the pressure and handling loads.
Gaskets/seals are elastomers; nitrile rubber (NBR) and EPDM are the most common, with alternatives such as silicone, butyl and chloroprene rubber.
Material choice for a plate depends on the required properties: strength, corrosion resistance and high-temperature suitability.
defs: Hastelloy
A nickel-based alloy that is corrosion resistant and suited to high-temperature service, used for heat exchanger plates.
NBR (nitrile rubber)
A synthetic elastomer commonly used as a gasket/seal material in plate heat exchangers.
EPDM
Ethylene propylene diene monomer rubber, a common elastomeric seal material in plate heat exchangers.
tips: Do not confuse the plate material (metal, chosen for strength and corrosion resistance) with the seal material (elastomer, chosen for sealing and chemical compatibility).
Stating 'aluminium is bad' is incomplete; specify that pure aluminium is too soft, not that it is unsuitable for all uses.
rq: Why is pure aluminium rejected for plates even though it resists corrosion well?
Because it is too soft; plates must carry pressure and handling loads without deforming, so strength is required alongside corrosion resistance.
Why would low carbon steel be a poor choice even though it is cheap and strong enough for many structures?
It is not strong enough for thin pressed plates and it rusts, so it fails the corrosion-resistance requirement in a fluid-handling heat exchanger.

notes.t: Plate heat exchangers: material property requirements
pts: Plates need a high heat transfer coefficient, which favours a material that can be made very thin.
Plates must be ductile so they can be pressed into complex shapes without cracking.
Good creep resistance stops the thin plates stretching under their own weight over time.
The clamped stack must be strong enough not to deform under clamping load, which conflicts with formability.
Formability (ductility) and strength/stiffness pull in opposite directions, so material choice is a trade-off.
defs: Ductility
The ability of a material to undergo large plastic deformation (e.g. stretching or pressing) without fracturing.
Creep resistance
The ability of a material to resist slow, time-dependent permanent deformation under a sustained load, especially at elevated temperature.
tips: Formability and clamping strength conflict: justify a material choice as a trade-off, not as 'strongest is best'.
Ductility is about plastic deformation before fracture; do not confuse it with stiffness or hardness.
rq: Why can't a plate simply be made as strong as possible to resist clamping forces?
Greater strength and hardness reduce formability, so the plate would crack or be impossible to press into the corrugated pattern; the material must balance strength against ductility.
What would happen to a very thin, low-creep-resistance plate after long service?
It would slowly stretch or sag under its own weight and thermal/operating loads, changing the flow channel geometry and reducing heat transfer and sealing.

notes.t: Plate heat exchanger plate features
pts: The image shows two gasketed plates of a plate heat exchanger, with corrugated (chevron) patterns pressed into the surface.
The corrugations (chevrons) create turbulence, increasing heat transfer coefficient and providing mechanical rigidity to the plate.
The raised dark ridge/gasket around the plate edge and port holes seals the flow channels so the hot and cold fluids do not mix and flow in alternate channels.
defs: Chevron (herringbone) corrugation
Pressed pattern on a heat exchanger plate that induces turbulent flow, enhancing heat transfer and stiffening the plate.
tips: Do not confuse the gasket (sealing) with the corrugations (heat transfer enhancement); they have different functions.
Corrugations increase pressure drop as well as heat transfer, so the trade-off must be mentioned in answers.
rq: Why do the plates have a chevron pattern rather than a flat surface?
Chevrons induce turbulence and increase heat transfer area and coefficient, and also add mechanical strength so the thin plates can withstand pressure.
What would happen if the gasket around the edges failed?
Hot and cold fluids would leak or mix across channels, causing contamination and loss of thermal performance.

notes.t: Plate features in plate heat exchangers
pts: Cracks in a plate are fixed by removing only two plates, which makes repair simple.
Corrugations disrupt the flow so it does not stay laminar, improving mixing near the wall.
Corrugations increase the surface area and turbulence, which raises heat transfer.
Corrugations add rigidity, so the plate structure is stiffer.
Because corrugations add strength, thinner plates can be used, reducing material and cost.
tips: Corrugations improve heat transfer but also increase pressure drop; state this trade-off when discussing plate design.
Do not confuse the stiffening effect of corrugations with the sealing role of gaskets.
rq: Why does a corrugated plate give higher heat transfer than a flat plate?
Corrugations break up laminar flow and create turbulence and extra surface area, thinning the boundary layer and improving convective heat transfer.
Why can corrugated plates be thinner than flat plates for the same pressure duty?
The corrugations stiffen the plate, so it resists deformation and bending without needing extra thickness.

xq.q: A designer proposes pure aluminium for plate heat exchanger plates because it conducts heat well. What is the correct objection?
xq.a: It is too soft to withstand pressure and handling loads
o: It is too soft to withstand pressure and handling loads
It is not ductile enough to be pressed
It is an elastomer so it cannot seal
It has too high a creep resistance
xq.w: Pure aluminium is too soft for the pressure and handling loads; the trap is assuming good conductivity is enough.
s: Plates need strength and corrosion resistance

xq.q: Explain the functions of the chevron corrugations pressed into a plate heat exchanger plate and state the main disadvantage. Explain how they allow thinner plates.
xq.a: Corrugations disrupt the flow so it does not stay laminar, creating turbulence that increases the heat transfer coefficient, and they increase surface area. They add rigidity to the plate, so thinner plates can be used, reducing material and cost and improving heat transfer through the wall. The disadvantage is increased pressure drop.
s: Turbulence and larger area raise heat transfer (2)
Added rigidity allows thinner plates, lowering cost (2)

xq.q: Which pair of requirements for plate material conflict with each other?
xq.a: Ductility for pressing and strength to resist clamping load
o: Corrosion resistance and impermeability
Ductility for pressing and strength to resist clamping load
High heat transfer coefficient and thin plates
Creep resistance and strength
xq.w: Formability (ductility) pulls against strength and stiffness needed to avoid deforming under clamping; the other pairs are compatible.
s: Ductile materials are easy to press but weaker

units.name: 5.6 Flow configurations, LMTD and parallel vs counter-flow
units.ov: This material compares parallel-flow, counter-flow and cross-flow arrangements in plate heat exchangers, then introduces the LMTD method for sizing them. Flow configuration sets the end-to-end temperature differences \(\Delta T_1\) and \(\Delta T_2\), the LMTD averages these into an effective driving force, and \(Q = UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\) gives the heat duty or required area.
must: LMTD definition: \(\mathrm{LMTD}=\dfrac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}\), the log-averaged hot-cold temperature difference between the two ends of the exchanger
Heat transfer rate: \(Q=UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\) (W). Rearrange for A (required size), for Q, or for U

Correctly identify \(\Delta T_1\) and \(\Delta T_2\) as the hot-cold differences at each end. In parallel-flow the ends are inlet-inlet and outlet-outlet; in counter-flow they are hot in/cold out and hot out/cold in

Counter-flow: more uniform thermal gradient across each plate, less thermal shock, thermally efficient (larger LMTD for the same terminal temperatures), but with a significant pressure-drop penalty. State both when comparing
Parallel-flow: simple, steady thermal gradients, but may need a physically larger structure (smaller LMTD, so larger A)
Cross-flow: suited to single-pass systems, gases and complex configurations; generally less effective than counter-flow but not always the worse choice
U is the overall heat transfer coefficient in W/m²K; A is the heat transfer area in m²
Temperature differences in °C and K are numerically equal, but any absolute temperatures must be in K
LMTD limitations: it assumes uniform, steady conditions, so it is unreliable for turbulent or non-steady flow. It ignores heat loss to the surroundings, phase change and pressure drop
Turbulence can be advantageous in heat exchangers, but it conflicts with the LMTD model's simplifying assumptions
conn: Configuration determines the end temperature differences, which determine LMTD, which determines required area A via \(Q=UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\). Counter-flow's larger LMTD means a smaller exchanger for the same duty
Efficiency versus pressure drop: counter-flow gives better thermal performance but higher pumping cost. Questions often ask for a justified choice of configuration
Turbulence raises U (better heat transfer) but undermines LMTD's assumptions and increases pressure drop
Model assumptions versus real behaviour: heat loss, phase change and pressure drop are ignored by the basic LMTD method, so calculated A or Q may be inaccurate
exq: Hot fluid enters a heat exchanger at 90°C and leaves at 60°C; cold fluid enters at 20°C and leaves at 50°C. Calculate the LMTD for parallel-flow and for counter-flow, and comment on the difference.
Using \(Q=UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\), find the area needed to transfer 50 kW with \(U=1500\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}\) and the LMTD you calculated. State which configuration needs less area and why.
Compare parallel-flow, counter-flow and cross-flow in plate heat exchangers, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each, and recommend a configuration for a gas, single-pass application.
Explain why counter-flow is thermally more efficient than parallel-flow yet may not always be chosen. Include the effects on thermal gradients and pressure drop.
State the assumptions and limitations of the LMTD method. Give two real-world effects it neglects and explain how turbulent or non-steady flow affects its reliability.

notes.t: Fluid flow configurations in plate heat exchangers
pts: Parallel-flow is simple with steady thermal gradients but may need physically larger structures.
Counter-flow reduces thermal shock and improves thermal gradient uniformity across each plate, and is thermally efficient, though it can cause significant pressure drops.
Cross-flow suits single-pass systems, gases, or complex configurations, but is generally less effective than counter-flow.
Turbulence may be advantageous in heat exchangers.
Heat transfer, and hence required heat exchanger size, is determined using the LMTD approach.
defs: Logarithmic Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD)
A log-averaged temperature difference between hot and cold fluids along a heat exchanger, used to calculate heat transfer rate and required exchanger size.
tips: Do not assume cross-flow is always worse; it is useful for gases and single-pass systems, even though it is generally less effective than counter-flow.
Counter-flow's efficiency benefit comes with a pressure-drop penalty; state both when comparing configurations.
rq: Why is counter-flow usually preferred over parallel-flow even though both have similar simplicity?
Counter-flow gives a more uniform thermal gradient across each plate, reducing thermal shock, and achieves higher thermal efficiency, though at the cost of greater pressure drop.
What trade-off does counter-flow introduce compared with parallel-flow?
Higher thermal efficiency and better gradient uniformity, but significant pressure drops that can lower the flow rate.

notes.t: The LMTD approach
pts: LMTD gives the average (log-mean) temperature difference driving heat transfer between two flowing fluids in a heat exchanger.
ΔT₁ and ΔT₂ are the hot-cold temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger; the log form weights them correctly for a changing temperature difference.
Heat exchanged is found from Q = UA·LMTD, with LMTD in Kelvin.
LMTD method is simplistic: it assumes uniformity or homogeneity and is less reliable for turbulent or non-steady flow.
Real exchangers can lose heat to the environment, change fluid phase and suffer pressure drops, which the basic LMTD model ignores.
defs: LMTD (log mean temperature difference)
The logarithmic average of the temperature differences between hot and cold fluids at the two ends of a heat exchanger, used as the effective driving temperature difference for heat transfer.
Heat transfer coefficient U
The overall rate of heat transfer per unit area per unit temperature difference between the fluids, in W/m²K.
eqs: LMTD = log mean temperature difference (K); ΔT₁ = hot–cold temperature difference at one end (K); ΔT₂ = hot–cold temperature difference at the other end (K)
Q = heat transfer rate (W); U = overall heat transfer coefficient (W/m²K); A = heat transfer area (m²); LMTD = log mean temperature difference (K)
tips: LMTD must be in Kelvin; a temperature difference in °C gives the same value numerically, but absolute temperatures used elsewhere must be in K.
LMTD is unreliable for turbulent or non-steady flow and when phase change or heat loss occurs, so do not apply it blindly to such cases.
rq: Why is a logarithmic mean used instead of the simple arithmetic mean of ΔT₁ and ΔT₂?
Because the temperature difference between the fluids changes continuously along the exchanger, and the log mean gives the correct average driving force for the exponential temperature profile.
What happens to the heat transfer estimate if ΔT₁ = ΔT₂?
The logarithm is undefined as a ratio of 1 yields ln(1)=0 in the denominator, so the limit is taken: LMTD equals that common ΔT value.

xq.q: A counter-flow heat exchanger cools oil from 150 °C to 90 °C using water that enters at 30 °C and leaves at 70 °C. The overall heat transfer coefficient is \(U = 500\) W/m²K and the heat transfer area is \(A = 2.0\) m². Using the LMTD method, where \(Q = UA\,\mathrm{LMTD}\), calculate the heat transfer rate in kW.
xq.a: Q ≈ 69.5 kW (LMTD ≈ 69.5 K)
s: Counter-flow ends: ΔT₁ = 150 − 70 = 80 K, ΔT₂ = 90 − 30 = 60 K

xq.q: A counter-flow exchanger must transfer \(Q = 120\) kW. Hot fluid enters at 90 °C and leaves at 50 °C. Cold fluid enters at 20 °C and leaves at 40 °C. The overall heat transfer coefficient is \(U = 800\) W/m²K. Find the heat transfer area \(A\) required, in m².
s: Counter-flow ends: ΔT₁ = 90 − 40 = 50 K, ΔT₂ = 50 − 20 = 30 K
Rearrange Q = UA·LMTD: A = Q/(U·LMTD) = 120 000/(800 × 39.15) = 3.83 m²

xq.q: A designer compares flow configurations for a plate heat exchanger. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: Counter-flow is thermally efficient and gives more uniform thermal gradients across each plate, but can cause a significant pressure drop.
o: Cross-flow is always more effective than counter-flow, so it should be chosen for every duty.
Counter-flow is thermally efficient and gives more uniform thermal gradients across each plate, but can cause a significant pressure drop.
Parallel-flow gives the most uniform thermal gradients and always needs the smallest physical structure.
Counter-flow has no pressure-drop penalty, so it is always the best choice.
xq.w: Counter-flow improves efficiency and reduces thermal shock at the cost of a larger pressure drop, whereas cross-flow is generally less effective but still suits gases and single-pass systems.
s: Counter-flow: efficient, reduced thermal shock, pressure-drop penalty
Cross-flow is generally less effective but useful for gases and single-pass duties
Parallel-flow is simple but may need larger structures

units.name: 5.7 Plate heat exchanger applications, pros/cons and cleaning
units.ov: This module covers plate heat exchangers (PHEs) in practice: their use in a distillery to cool wort, their advantages and disadvantages, and the procedure for cleaning and reassembling them. The ideas connect because the features that make PHEs compact and flexible (thin plates, gaskets, a clamped stack) also create the maintenance demands: sealing, gradual compression, and the fittings needed for safe isolation and monitoring.
must: Construction: thin plates clamped into a stack form alternating channels for hot and cold fluids, with entry and exit ports. This is not a simple parallel-plate flow.
Process purpose: in the distillery, wort must be cooled before yeast is added, so temperature control is essential.
Advantages: large heat transfer area in a small volume, less space than other types, and both fluid sides cleaned at once.
Flexibility: capacity can be changed at any time by adding or removing plates, and damaged plates can be replaced or removed individually.
Disadvantages: expensive plate metal, long cleaning and reassembly, space needed to open the unit, and a short-lived edge seal (the shortest lifetime of any component).
Damaged plates are hard to locate. Replacing a plate is easy, but finding the faulty one is not.
Pre-opening: close the inlet and outlet valves, drain both sides, and log inlet and outlet temperatures to detect fouling. Measure the stack length at each clamp bolt before release.
Opening and cleaning: release the bolts, spread the plates along the guide rail (this needs floor space), clean gently with a soft brush or water spray, and inspect all seals before reassembly.
Reassembly: tighten the bolts gradually and evenly back to the original stack length, not to a single torque in one go. Over-compression crushes plates and reduces flow; under-compression leaks.
Recommissioning and minimum fittings: flood the unit, vent air, and monitor for leaks. Minimum fittings are 4 isolating valves, 4 thermometers, 2 drain valves and 2 air vents.
conn: Temperature logging links to fouling: a falling heat transfer performance (a smaller temperature change at the same flows) signals when cleaning is needed, which triggers the whole cleaning procedure.
The large area and compactness advantage trades off against gasket seals: more plates and seals mean more potential leak paths, and the edge seal has the shortest life.
Stack length measurement links to compression: the recorded length sets the correct compression on reassembly, balancing leakage against crushed plates and reduced flow.
Fittings link to procedure: isolating valves and drains enable safe opening, air vents enable flooding, and thermometers enable performance tracking.
exq: List four advantages and four disadvantages of a plate heat exchanger compared with other types, and explain why the edge seal is a limiting factor.
Describe, in order, the procedure for opening, cleaning and reassembling a plate heat exchanger. Explain why the stack length is measured at each clamp bolt beforehand.
State the minimum number of isolating valves, thermometers, drain valves and air vents needed to allow cleaning, and justify each.
Explain the consequences of over-tightening and under-tightening the clamp bolts, and why the bolts must be tightened gradually and evenly.

A distillery uses a plate heat exchanger to cool wort before yeast is added. Explain how logged inlet and outlet temperatures could show fouling, and how the unit's capacity could be changed if more cooling were needed.

notes.t: Real-world example: plate heat exchanger in a distillery
pts: A compact plate heat exchanger, about 1 m tall, is used in a distillery to cool wort.
Thin plates are compressed together, creating alternating channels for the two fluids.
Fluid entry and exit ports allow the hot and cold streams to pass through the stack.
Wort is cooled before yeast is added in the distillation process, so the cooling step is essential to the process.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of fluid flow in the plate stack with a simple parallel-plate arrangement; the channels alternate between hot and cold fluid.
Remember the process reason for cooling: wort must be cooled before yeast is added, so temperature control is critical.
rq: Why is a plate heat exchanger so compact compared with a shell-and-tube design of the same duty?
Thin corrugated plates give a very large heat transfer area per unit volume, and the fluids flow in thin channels that promote high heat transfer coefficients.
Why must the wort be cooled before yeast is added?
Yeast would be killed or damaged by hot wort, so the liquid must be brought down to a suitable temperature first.

notes.t: Benefits and drawbacks of plate heat exchangers
pts: Plate heat exchangers offer a large heat transfer surface in a small volume, and need less space than other types.
Both fluid sides can be cleaned at the same time, and damaged plates can be replaced or removed individually.
The overall size can be changed at any time by adding or removing plates, making them flexible.
Main drawbacks are cost of plate metal, cleaning and reassembly effort, and space needed to open the unit.
The plate edge seal has the shortest lifetime, and damaged plates can be hard to locate.
tips: Do not confuse the ease of replacing a damaged plate with the ease of finding one; locating damage is actually difficult.
Remember that cleaning is advantageous in being simultaneous but disadvantageous in being long and requiring space to open the unit.
rq: Why does the ability to clean both sides simultaneously matter, and why does it become a drawback?
Both sides fouling together is convenient for maintenance, but because both sides must be opened and cleaned together, the cleaning takes a long time and requires space to open the unit.
Why can a plate heat exchanger achieve a large heat transfer area in a small volume?
Thin corrugated plates are stacked closely together, so many heat transfer surfaces fit into a compact frame.

notes.t: Cleaning plate heat exchangers
pts: Before opening, close inlet and outlet valves and drain both fluid sides so no liquid is trapped or spilled.
Record inlet and outlet temperatures in a log to track performance and detect fouling over time.
Measure the plate stack length at each clamp bolt before release so the stack can be correctly reassembled to the same compression.
Release clamp bolts and spread plates along the guide rail, which requires sufficient floor space.
Clean plates gently with a soft brush or water spray to avoid damaging the plate surfaces, then inspect all seals for damage before reassembly.
tips: Always close valves and drain both sides before opening; trapped pressure or fluid is a safety hazard.
Check all seals for damage before reassembly, as damaged gaskets are a common cause of leakage.
rq: Why must the plate stack length be measured at each clamp bolt before the bolts are released?
So the stack can be reassembled to the same compression; uneven or excessive compression can cause leaks at the seals or distort the plates.
Why is a soft brush or low-pressure water spray preferred over a hard scraper?
Plate surfaces are thin and corrugated; hard tools can scratch or deform them, reducing heat transfer and creating leak paths, and damaging the gaskets.

notes.t: Cleaning plate heat exchangers
pts: Plates are reassembled by sliding them together and replacing the clamp bolts; over-compression crushes plates and reduces flow, while too little compression causes leaks.
Clamp bolts must be tightened gradually and evenly until the original stack length is restored, not forced to a set torque in one go.
After reassembly the exchanger is flooded and air drained off before leaks are monitored, confirming the stack is sealed and ready for use.
The minimum fittings that allow cleaning need to be identified are 4 isolating valves, 4 thermometers, 2 drain valves and 2 air vents.
tips: Over-tightening is as harmful as under-tightening: it crushes plates and reduces flow, while too loose a stack leaks.
Remember the minimum fittings count: 4 isolating valves (two inlets, two outlets), but only 2 drain valves and 2 air vents.
rq: Why must the clamp bolts be tightened gradually and evenly rather than all at once?
Uneven or abrupt tightening can distort or crush plates and misalign the gaskets, causing flow restriction or leaks; gradual even tightening restores the correct stack length uniformly.
What would happen if the stack were clamped too loosely after cleaning?
Insufficient pressure on the stack gives leaks at the gaskets, so fluid escapes between plates and the exchanger cannot be safely pressurised.

units.name: 5.8 Parallel vs counter-flow comparison activity
units.ov: This activity compares parallel-flow and counter-flow heat exchangers for the same fluids and terminal temperatures. Flow direction sets the temperature difference profile along the exchanger, which sets the log-mean temperature difference (LMTD), and so the heat transfer \(Q=UA\,\Delta T_{lm}\) and the outlet temperatures that can be achieved. Counter-flow keeps a more uniform driving temperature difference and lets the cold fluid approach the hot inlet temperature, so it is generally preferred.
must: Counter-flow is generally more effective than parallel flow for the same fluids, area and inlet temperatures, because the temperature difference stays larger and more uniform along the length.

In counter-flow the cold outlet can approach (even exceed) the hot outlet temperature, so \(T_{c,out}\) can approach \(T_{h,in}\). In parallel flow both outlets converge towards a common temperature, so \(T_{c,out}<T_{h,out}\).
Heat transfer rate: \(Q=UA\,\Delta T_{lm}\), with \(\Delta T_{lm}=\dfrac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}\).

Define \(\Delta T_1\) and \(\Delta T_2\) at the two ends consistently. Parallel: \(\Delta T_1=T_{h,in}-T_{c,in}\), \(\Delta T_2=T_{h,out}-T_{c,out}\). Counter: \(\Delta T_1=T_{h,in}-T_{c,out}\), \(\Delta T_2=T_{h,out}-T_{c,in}\).
Energy balance: \(Q=\dot m_h c_{p,h}(T_{h,in}-T_{h,out})=\dot m_c c_{p,c}(T_{c,out}-T_{c,in})\). Use it to find unknown temperatures or flow rates.
For the same four terminal temperatures, \(\Delta T_{lm,counter}\ge\Delta T_{lm,parallel}\), so counter-flow needs less area for the same duty \(Q\) (or gives more \(Q\) for the same \(A\)).
Only temperature differences matter, so use K or °C consistently in differences. Use absolute units only if a formula needs them.
If \(\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2\), the LMTD formula gives 0/0. In that case \(\Delta T_{lm}=\Delta T_1\).
Parallel flow does have a niche: it gives a more uniform wall temperature and is useful when the cold fluid must not be overheated. Its limit is that the cold outlet can never exceed the hot outlet.
conn: Energy balance with LMTD: the energy balance gives unknown outlet temperatures and \(Q\); LMTD then gives the required area \(A=Q/(U\Delta T_{lm})\).

Temperature profiles with effectiveness: the shape of the T–x plot (converging in parallel, roughly parallel lines in counter-flow) explains why the maximum effectiveness differs between the two arrangements.
Heat capacity rates: \(C=\dot m c_p\) determines which fluid has the larger temperature change, and so the slopes of the profiles and which fluid limits the duty.
Overall coefficient \(U\) with exchanger sizing: thermal resistances (convection and conduction) give \(U\), which then combines with LMTD in a design question.
exq: Hot oil enters at 120 °C and leaves at 70 °C. Water enters at 20 °C and leaves at 60 °C. Calculate \(\Delta T_{lm}\) for parallel and counter-flow, and state which needs the smaller area for a duty of 50 kW with \(U=300\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}\). Find that area.
Explain with sketched T–x profiles why the cold fluid outlet temperature can exceed the hot fluid outlet temperature in counter-flow but not in parallel flow.
For the same inlet temperatures and flow rates, determine whether parallel or counter-flow transfers more heat in an exchanger of fixed area. Justify using \(\Delta T_{lm}\) and energy balances.
A counter-flow exchanger has \(\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2=30\ \mathrm{K}\). Explain why the LMTD formula fails and give \(\Delta T_{lm}\). Describe what this implies about the heat capacity rates.

Given \(\dot m_c c_{p,c}\), the cold inlet and outlet temperatures and the hot inlet temperature, find the hot outlet temperature and then the area required in each configuration, stating the end definitions you use.

notes.t: Parallel vs counter-flow heat exchanger comparison (activity)
pts: Counter-flow lets the cold fluid leave near the hot inlet temperature, so it can be heated more closely to the hot fluid's inlet temperature.
In parallel flow both fluids exit at similar temperatures, limiting the achievable heat transfer.
Compare the given inlet and outlet temperatures to judge which flow arrangement transfers more heat for the same fluids.
Consider the flow directions of the two fluids when deciding which configuration is preferential.
tips: Keep consistent definitions of hot and cold ends when computing temperature differences for each configuration.
Temperatures must be in consistent units (K or °C differences); the temperature difference, not the absolute temperature, drives heat transfer.
rq: Why does the cold outlet temperature in a counter-flow exchanger can approach or even exceed the hot outlet temperature, which is impossible in parallel flow?

In counter-flow the fluids move in opposite directions, so the cold fluid exits next to the hot inlet, allowing its outlet temperature to be close to \(T_{\text{HI}}\); in parallel flow the outlet temperatures converge toward a common value, so the cold outlet cannot exceed the hot outlet.
Using the given values, what is the temperature difference at the hot end and cold end of the exchanger?

Hot end: \(T_{\text{HI}}\) − \(T_{\text{CO}}\) = 90 − 50 = 40 °C; cold end: \(T_{\text{HO}}\) − \(T_{\text{CI}}\) = 55 − 20 = 35 °C, so the temperature differences are similar and large, favouring counter-flow.
Why is the cold outlet (50 °C) close to the hot inlet (90 °C) a sign of good performance?
It shows the cold fluid is heated to nearly the hot inlet temperature, meaning most of the available temperature difference is exploited, which is characteristic of counter-flow.

units.name: 5.9 Shell and tube heat exchanger construction and internals
units.ov: This module introduces the construction of shell and tube heat exchangers: a tube bundle inside a cylindrical shell, with one fluid inside the tubes and another outside. It covers the main components (shell, tubes, tube plates, headers, baffles, turbulators), pass arrangements, materials, and the logic for allocating fluids to the tube or shell side. Each component's function follows from the need to keep the fluids separate, enhance heat transfer, and allow cleaning and thermal movement.
must: Basic layout: tube bundle inside a shell; one fluid flows inside the tubes (tube side) and the other flows around them (shell side), with heat transferred through the tube walls, which are the heat-transfer surface
Tube plates (tube sheets) hold the tubes at each end and seal them, separating tube-side from shell-side fluid
Headers (end covers) enclose the tube plates and direct tube-side fluid into and out of the tubes; in multi-pass designs they reverse the flow
Baffles are perpendicular to the tubes; they support the tubes and force shell-side fluid to flow across the bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer, but they do not seal
The shell is a pressure vessel containing the shell-side fluid, typically cast iron or mild steel, as are the headers
Fluid allocation: the cleanest fluid goes on the shell side and the dirtiest goes through the tubes, where it is easier to access and clean
Single-pass means the tube fluid traverses the shell length once; double-pass means out and back, with the headers reversing the flow. Passes refer to the tube side, not to baffles or shells
Materials: tubes of brass, aluminium brass, titanium, stainless steel or Hastelloy (corrosion resistance and conductivity); tube plate of naval brass (resists seawater)
Turbulators inserted in tubes promote turbulence and raise the tube-side heat transfer rate
The diagram shows a fixed tube plate and an expansion tube plate, plus sea water and oil inlets and outlets; identify and label each component and say what it does
conn: Fluid allocation (dirty fluid in tubes) links to cleaning access, fouling, and the choice of tube material for corrosive fluids such as seawater
Baffles and turbulators both raise turbulence, so they increase heat transfer but also pressure drop and pumping power
Number of passes links header design to the tube-side flow path, velocity, and effective heat transfer area
Material choice per component (naval brass tube plate, steel shell, corrosion-resistant tubes) links to corrosion, cost, and the pressure-vessel function
exq: Sketch and label a double-pass shell and tube heat exchanger with sea water in the tubes and oil in the shell, and state the function of each labelled component.
Explain why the dirtier fluid is normally routed through the tubes and the cleaner fluid through the shell. What are the consequences for cleaning and maintenance?
Distinguish between single-pass and double-pass tube stacks. How do the headers produce a double pass, and what happens to the flow path and velocity?
Describe the role of baffles and turbulators in improving heat transfer. What is the penalty of using them?
State suitable materials for the tubes, tube plate, shell and end covers of a seawater-cooled oil cooler, and justify each choice.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: A shell and tube heat exchanger is built from a stack of tubes fitted inside an outer shell.
Two fluids are used: one flows inside the tubes and the other flows around the outside of the tubes, within the shell.
Tubes are sealed into tube plates at each end, which keeps the two fluids apart and gives the tubes a defined path for the cooling fluid.
Headers fit over the tube plates at each end, enclosing the shell and directing fluid into and out of the tubes.
defs: Shell and tube heat exchanger

A heat exchanger consisting of a bundle of tubes fitted inside an outer shell, in which one fluid flows through the tubes and a second fluid flows around the outside of the tubes so that heat is transferred between them.
Tube plate
A plate at each end of the tube bundle into which the tubes are sealed, separating the tube-side fluid from the shell-side fluid.
Header
A chamber fitted over each tube plate that encloses the end of the shell and distributes the tube-side fluid into and out of the tubes.
tips: Do not confuse the tube side with the shell side: the fluid inside the tubes and the fluid outside them are the two separate streams that exchange heat.
Describe the tube plates and headers as the components that seal and direct flow, not as the heat-transfer surface itself, which is the tube wall.
rq: Why must the tubes be sealed into the tube plates at both ends rather than simply left open?

Sealing prevents the two fluids from mixing, so the tube-side fluid stays inside the tubes and the shell-side fluid stays outside, while the tubes still provide a defined conduit for the cooling fluid.
What would happen to heat transfer if the two fluids were both passed through the tubes instead of one through the tubes and one around the outside?

Heat would not be transferred between the fluids in the intended way, because the shell-side fluid, which is the one that surrounds the tubes and exchanges heat through their walls, would be absent; the design depends on one fluid inside and one outside the tubes.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: A shell and tube heat exchanger is a common industrial design in which one fluid flows through a bundle of tubes while another fluid flows around them inside a cylindrical shell.
The image shows the external form: a cylindrical shell with inlet and outlet nozzles on each fluid side, flanged end covers, and support feet/brackets.
tips: Do not confuse the shell-side and tube-side fluids; state clearly which fluid is inside the tubes when calculating heat transfer or pressure drop.
The image is only a photograph of the external hardware; internal tube layout and baffles are not shown on this page.
rq: Why are the ends of a shell and tube heat exchanger flanged and bolted rather than welded?
Bolted flanged covers allow the tube bundle to be removed for inspection, cleaning and maintenance of the tubes and shell side.
Why do shell and tube exchangers use multiple nozzles on the shell, as seen in the image?
Separate nozzles allow the shell-side fluid to enter and leave the shell, and the nozzle positions set the fluid flow path around the tubes.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: The shell is a pressure vessel housing the tube bundle, pressurised to match the shell-side fluid.
Cold fluid flows through the tubes while hot fluid passes around them on the shell side.
Baffles support the tubes and force shell-side fluid to flow across the tubes, improving heat transfer.
Tube sheets fix the tubes at each end and seal them from the shell side.
Turbulators inserted in tubes increase turbulent flow and so raise the heat transfer rate.
defs: Shell
The outer housing of a shell and tube heat exchanger, acting as a pressure vessel that contains the shell-side fluid.
Baffles
Plates inside the shell that support the tubes and direct shell-side fluid across the tube bundle.
Tube sheet
A plate fixed at each end of the tube bundle that holds the tubes in position and seals them from the shell.
Turbulator
An insert placed inside tubes to induce turbulent flow and enhance convective heat transfer.
tips: Do not confuse the sides: the cold fluid is on the tube side and the hot fluid is on the shell side in this description.
Baffles improve heat transfer and support tubes; they do not seal the shell, which is the job of the tube sheets.
rq: Why are baffles needed on the shell side rather than letting the shell fluid flow straight along the tubes?
Baffles force the shell-side fluid to cross the tubes, increasing velocity and turbulence around them, which improves heat transfer; they also support the tubes against vibration and misalignment.
Why must the shell be designed as a pressure vessel?
The shell contains a fluid at pressure, so its walls must withstand that pressure; it is pressurised to match the shell-side fluid to avoid large stress or leakage between the two fluids.

notes.t: Internals of shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: In double-pass tube stacks, the end covers (headers) must route the liquid so it flows through the correct tubes on each pass.
Tubes are typically made from brass, aluminium brass, titanium, stainless steel or Hastelloy, chosen for corrosion resistance and heat transfer.
The tube plate is typically made of naval brass, which resists seawater corrosion.
End covers/headers and the shell are typically cast iron or mild steel, which are cheaper structural materials.
defs: Double-pass tube stack
A tube bundle in which the fluid travels along the tubes twice, out and back, with end covers reversing the flow between passes.
Single-pass tube stack
A tube bundle in which the fluid flows through the tubes once, from one end to the other, without reversal.
Tube plate
The perforated plate into which the ends of the heat exchanger tubes are fixed and sealed, separating the tube side from the shell side.
tips: Do not confuse the tube plate material (naval brass) with the shell/header material (cast iron or mild steel); the question may ask which material suits which part.
Remember that double-pass means two passes through the tubes, so the flow path is reversed by the end covers, not by the shell.
rq: Why must the end covers direct the flow correctly in a double-pass stack?
Without correct routing, fluid could bypass tubes or mix between passes, so the fluid would not follow the intended counter-/parallel-flow path, reducing heat transfer and performance.
Why is naval brass used for the tube plate while cast iron is used for the shell?
Naval brass resists corrosion from seawater at the tube joints, whereas the shell and headers carry structural loads cheaply and are not as exposed to the same corrosive attack.

notes.t: Internals of shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: Baffle plates are positioned perpendicular to the tubes and force the shell-side fluid to flow across all the tubes, improving heat transfer.
Cleanest fluid is routed around the outside of the tubes (shell side), while the dirtiest fluid is routed through the tubes so it can be cleaned.
Turbulence induced by baffles and tube flow aids cleaning and heat transfer; dirtier fluid inside tubes allows easier access for cleaning.
Double-pass and single-pass arrangements describe how many times the tube-side fluid passes along the shell length.
Labelled components in the diagram include shell, tubes, baffles, fixed tube plate, expansion tube plate, end covers, and inlets/outlets for sea water and oil.
defs: Baffle plate
A plate placed perpendicular to the tubes in a shell and tube heat exchanger that directs shell-side fluid across the tube bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer.
Shell side
The space outside the tubes inside the shell, through which the cleaner fluid flows in a shell and tube heat exchanger.
Tube side
The fluid path inside the tubes, typically used for the dirtier fluid so it can be cleaned and so fouling is easier to manage.
Double-pass
A shell and tube configuration in which the tube-side fluid makes two passes along the shell length, doubling the path and increasing heat transfer area use.
Single-pass
A shell and tube configuration in which the tube-side fluid flows once along the full length of the shell.
tips: Do not confuse the shell side and tube side: the cleaner fluid is normally on the shell side, the dirtier fluid inside the tubes.
Single-pass and double-pass refer to tube-side passes, not the number of baffles or shells.
rq: Why are baffle plates placed perpendicular to the tubes rather than parallel to them?

Perpendicular baffles force the shell-side fluid to cross the tube bundle repeatedly, creating turbulence and better heat transfer, whereas parallel flow would leave much of the tube surface poorly contacted.
Why is the dirtiest fluid usually sent through the tubes rather than around them?
Tube interiors are easier to clean (mechanically or chemically) and fouling is confined there, while the shell side is harder to access for cleaning.

xq.q: During commissioning of a shell and tube exchanger, shell-side fluid is found contaminating the tube-side fluid. Inspection shows leakage at the ends of the tubes. Which feature has most likely failed?
xq.a: The tube plate (tube sheet) joints, because they seal the tubes and separate tube-side from shell-side fluid.
o: The baffles, because they seal the shell and keep the two fluids apart.
The turbulators, because they stop shell-side fluid entering the tubes.
The tube plate (tube sheet) joints, because they seal the tubes and separate tube-side from shell-side fluid.
The header, because it forms the heat-transfer surface between the fluids.
xq.w: Tube plates hold the tubes and seal them from the shell side; baffles only support the tubes and direct flow, and headers only direct tube-side fluid.
s: Tube plate fixes the tube ends and separates the two fluids
Baffles support tubes and direct flow, they do not seal
Headers direct flow, and the heat-transfer surface is the tube wall

xq.q: A seawater-cooled shell and tube exchanger is being specified. Which material choice is most appropriate for the listed parts?
xq.a: Tube plate in naval brass to resist seawater corrosion, with shell and end covers in cast iron or mild steel.
o: Tube plate in cast iron, shell in naval brass, to save cost on the shell.
Tube plate in naval brass to resist seawater corrosion, with shell and end covers in cast iron or mild steel.
Everything in mild steel, since structural strength is the only requirement.
Tubes in cast iron, because it resists corrosion and transfers heat best.
xq.w: The tube plate is in contact with seawater so naval brass is used, while the shell and headers are cheaper structural parts; tubes use corrosion-resistant, conductive materials such as titanium, brass or stainless steel.
s: Tube plate: naval brass for seawater corrosion resistance
Shell and headers: cast iron or mild steel, cheaper structural materials
Tubes: brass, titanium or stainless steel for corrosion resistance and heat transfer

xq.q: Explain how baffles and turbulators each increase the heat transfer rate in a shell and tube heat exchanger. State on which side of the exchanger each is located and one other function of the baffles.
xq.a: Baffles are plates in the shell, on the shell side. They force the shell-side fluid to flow across the tube bundle rather than along it, which increases heat transfer, and they also support the tubes. Turbulators are inserts placed inside the tubes, on the tube side. They induce turbulent flow in the tube fluid, which raises the convective heat transfer rate. The sealing between the fluids is done by the tube sheets, not by the baffles.
s: Baffles are on the shell side and force cross-flow over the tubes, raising heat transfer (1.5)
Turbulators are inside the tubes, on the tube side (1)
Turbulators induce turbulence, increasing convective heat transfer (1.5)

units.name: 5.10 Tube pass configurations, erosion and S&T pros/cons
units.ov: This module covers the mechanical design features of shell-and-tube (S&T) heat exchangers: single-pass fixed/floating end plate and U-pass tube arrangements, how differential thermal expansion is accommodated, where erosion occurs, and the overall pros and cons of S&T units compared with plate exchangers. The ideas connect because tube layout determines how thermal expansion is handled, which joints and inlets are vulnerable, and what can be cleaned, repaired or expanded in service.
must: Differential thermal expansion: tubes and shell have different materials and temperatures (shell is cooler as it loses heat to atmosphere), so they expand unequally; if restrained, tubes buckle, fracture or pull out of the tube plate

Single pass end plate design: one end of the tube bundle is rigidly fixed to the shell, the other floats on two O-rings so the tube stack can slide axially; only the floating end accommodates movement
Leakage tell-tale: a connection between the two O-rings of the sliding joint that reveals leakage if one O-ring fails
Tube-to-tube-plate joints can be made by expanding the tubes, screwing and sealing, or explosion welding; the joint method affects leakage and erosion resistance
U-pass design: tube-side fluid enters and leaves at the same end, with U-shaped tubes (two tube passes) and no separate return header; the tubes are free at the bend end, which allows expansion
U-pass drawbacks: the U-bend makes the bundle hard to clean mechanically, and the shell-side flow is directed across the bundle by baffles
Baffles direct shell-side flow across the tubes, raising turbulence and heat transfer coefficient, and also support the tubes

Erosion hot spots: shell-side inlet (direct impingement on the bundle), tube-side inlet, and tube-to-sheet joints; risk is driven by high local velocity and impingement, not average flow; erosion (mechanical) is not corrosion (chemical)
S&T advantages: cheap materials, tube side cleaned easily and faster than plate units, cracked tubes easy to locate and plug, very long lifespan
S&T disadvantages: shell side hard to clean, lower heat transfer area than plate exchangers, size fixed at installation (plate units can add or remove plates)
conn: Differential expansion links to the tube arrangement: the floating O-ring end (with its tell-tale) and the U-bend both solve the same problem, but the U-pass sacrifices easy cleaning

Baffles raise shell-side heat transfer through higher velocity and turbulence, but the same high velocity at the shell inlet increases erosion risk, so there is a thermal versus mechanical durability trade-off
Joint type (expanded, screwed and sealed, explosion welded) ties together leakage, erosion at the tube sheet and the tube buckling or push-out failure under thermal stress
The pros and cons versus plate exchangers (cleaning, area, fixed size, lifespan, repair) are the context for choosing a tube configuration
exq: Explain why a fixed tube sheet at both ends would be unsuitable for a hot-tube, cooler-shell exchanger, and describe how the single pass end plate design with O-rings and a tell-tale overcomes this.
Describe a U-pass shell-and-tube exchanger with a sketch. State two advantages and two disadvantages relative to a single pass fixed/floating design, covering expansion and cleaning.
Identify the three locations most prone to erosion in a shell-and-tube exchanger, explain the mechanism, and suggest design measures to reduce it.
Compare shell-and-tube and plate heat exchangers for a fouling duty requiring a 30-year life: discuss cleaning, repair of leaks, lifespan, heat transfer area and flexibility to change capacity.
Distinguish erosion from corrosion, and explain why a high local velocity can cause failure even when average flow rate is acceptable.

notes.t: Single pass end plate configuration in heat exchangers
pts: One end of the tube bundle is rigidly fixed to the shell via the end plate, while the other end floats on two O-rings so the tube stack can expand and move within the shell.
Tubes and shell are made of different materials, so they expand at different rates; the shell is usually cooler than the tubes because it loses heat to the atmosphere.
If the tubes cannot expand freely they will buckle, fracture or push free of the tube plate, so differential thermal expansion must be allowed for in the design.
A leakage tell-tale connection is provided to reveal whether one of the O-rings in the sliding joint has failed.
Tubes can be secured to the tube plate by expanding them into position, by screwing and sealing, or by explosion welding.
defs: Single pass end plate configuration
A heat exchanger arrangement where tubes run once along the shell length, with one end fixed to the shell and the other end sealed by O-rings that permit axial thermal expansion of the tube stack.
Differential thermal expansion
Unequal expansion of components made of different materials or at different temperatures, which must be accommodated to avoid tube buckling, fracture or loss of seal.
Tell-tale (leakage tell-tale)
A small vent or drain connection between the two O-rings of the floating joint, used to detect failure of an O-ring by observing leakage.
tips: Do not forget differential expansion: materials differ, so the shell and tubes grow at different rates even at the same temperature rise.
Be clear which end is fixed and which end floats; only the floating end, sealed by O-rings, accommodates thermal movement.
rq: Why would the tubes be more likely to buckle than the shell if the free end could not move?
The tubes are hotter and expand more than the cooler shell, so the constrained tube stack is pushed into compression and buckles, fractures or pushes out of the tube plate.
What would a tell-tale reading of fluid flow indicate about the floating joint?
It indicates that one of the two O-rings has failed, so fluid is leaking past the seal and the sealing arrangement needs replacing.

notes.t: U-pass shell-and-tube heat exchanger configuration
pts: In a U-pass design the tube side fluid enters and leaves at the same end of the shell, so the tubes form a U-bend and no separate return header is needed.
The shell side (red) fluid is forced across the tube bundle by internal baffles, which increases turbulence and heat transfer coefficient.
The tube side (yellow) fluid travels through the tubes in two passes, entering at the bottom and exiting at the top on the same side.
Because the tubes are U-shaped, the bundle cannot be removed for cleaning in the usual way, which is a key mechanical design concern.
Differential thermal expansion between the shell and tubes must be accommodated, since the U-bend tubes are free at one end and the bundle is fixed at the other.
defs: U-pass configuration
A shell-and-tube heat exchanger arrangement in which the tube-side fluid makes a single U-shaped bend, returning through the same tube sheet end so both inlet and outlet are on one side.
Baffles
Plates placed inside the shell that direct the shell-side fluid across the tube bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer while supporting the tubes.
tips: Do not confuse the U-pass (single shell pass, tubes doubled back) with multi-pass designs using separate return headers; the flow arrangement and mechanical layout differ.
Remember that the mechanical concerns (thermal expansion, cleaning access, tube support) are separate from the thermal analysis of the flow.
rq: Why are baffles fitted on the shell side rather than the tube side?
Baffles force the shell-side fluid to flow across the tubes instead of along them, raising turbulence and the heat transfer coefficient, and they also support the tube bundle against vibration.
What would happen to the mechanical design if the tube bundle were rigidly fixed at both ends?

Differences in thermal expansion between tubes and shell would generate large thermal stresses, so the design would need expansion provision; the U-tube design avoids this because one end is free to expand.

notes.t: The erosion problem in shell-and-tube heat exchangers
pts: Erosion is most likely at the shell-side fluid inlet region, where the incoming fluid impinges directly on the tube bundle at high velocity.
The tube-side fluid inlet and tube sheet joints are also erosion-prone, since high-velocity flow enters the tubes and the tube-to-sheet connection is a weak point.
Tube-to-tube-sheet joints may be welded, expanded, or bolted and sealed; each method affects how well the joint resists leakage and erosion.
Seals at the tube-side inlet and outlet plenum connections prevent leakage between the tube-side and shell-side fluids.
