Free-body-diagram discipline: isolate one body, draw only forces acting on it, label the source of each (e.g. T on block), and use subscript order correctly
Resultant force is the single equivalent force that alone determines acceleration; use it, not one individual force, in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\)
conn: First Law and Second Law: equilibrium is the \(\boldsymbol{a}=0\) case of \(\sum \boldsymbol{F}=m\boldsymbol{a}\), so the same free-body diagram and component resolution serve both static and dynamic problems

Third Law and free-body diagrams: the reaction to a force on body A appears on body B's diagram, so connected-body problems (block and man on a rope) need separate diagrams linked by equal and opposite tension and contact forces

Weight, normal reaction and friction: \(W=mg\) together with the normal reaction sets the perpendicular balance, which in turn determines the friction available along the surface and hence the acceleration
Component resolution links all three laws: choose axes, sum forces in each direction, and apply equilibrium or \(ma\) per component
exq: A block of mass 20 kg is pulled by a rope along rough horizontal ground by a man. Draw free-body diagrams for the block and the man, identify all action-reaction pairs, and state which forces act on each body.

A 50 kg crate is pulled by a rope at 30° above the horizontal with tension 200 N and accelerates along the ground with friction 60 N. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration, using \(g=9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\).

A particle is acted on by three coplanar forces and is in equilibrium. Given two forces in magnitude and direction, find the third by resolving into components, and explain why the particle may still be moving.

Two carts A and B are in contact and A pushes B with 40 N. State the force of B on A, explain why these do not cancel when finding the acceleration of A, and find each cart's acceleration if the masses are 5 kg and 3 kg and an external force drives the system.
Explain the difference between mass and weight, and calculate the weight in N of a 75 kg person and the resultant force when a 10 kg body has \(a=3\,\text{m/s}^2\).

notes.t: Newton's First Law and equilibrium
pts: A particle at rest stays at rest, or moves uniformly, when no unbalanced force acts on it.
Motion with no net force is a straight line at constant velocity, so acceleration is zero.
A body in equilibrium has zero net force; the vector sum of all forces on it vanishes.
defs: Newton's First Law
A particle remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line with constant velocity if there is no unbalanced force acting on it.
Equilibrium (particle)
The state of a body where the sum of all forces acting on it is zero, so it is at rest or moving with constant velocity.
eqs: Equilibrium condition for a particle: net force is zero
\(\sum \boldsymbol{F}\) = vector sum of all forces acting on the particle (N)
tips: Equilibrium means zero net force, not zero velocity; a body moving at constant velocity is still in equilibrium.
Equilibrium equations use the vector sum, so resolve forces into components before summing; a zero magnitude sum alone is not enough.
rq: Why does a body moving at constant velocity need no net force, even though it is moving?
Newton's First Law: force changes velocity (produces acceleration), so with zero net force the acceleration is zero and velocity stays constant; motion itself does not require a force.
What if a particle is moving and the net force on it suddenly becomes zero?
It keeps moving in the same straight line at the same constant speed and direction, without slowing or curving.

notes.t: Newton's Second Law
pts: Acceleration of a particle is proportional to the resultant force acting on it.
Acceleration points in the same direction as the resultant force.
Weight of a body is its mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration.
defs: Resultant force
The single force equal to the vector sum of all forces acting on a particle, which alone determines its acceleration.
eqs: Newton's Second Law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration
\(\sum \boldsymbol{F}\) = resultant force (N); \(m\) = mass of the particle (kg); \(\boldsymbol{a}\) = resulting acceleration (m/s²)
Weight of a body of mass m
tips: Use the vector sum of all forces (resultant) in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F} = m\boldsymbol{a}\), not a single force.
Keep units consistent: mass in kg gives force in N; do not confuse weight (N) with mass (kg).
rq: Why must the resultant force, not an individual force, be used in \(\sum \boldsymbol{F} = m\boldsymbol{a}\)?
Because acceleration depends on the net effect of all forces acting on the particle; individual forces alone do not determine the motion.
What happens to the acceleration if the same resultant force acts on a body with twice the mass?
The acceleration halves, since \(\boldsymbol{a} = \sum \boldsymbol{F}/m\) is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force.

notes.t: Newton's Third Law
pts: Forces between two interacting bodies form an action–reaction pair; they are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other out when analysing a single body.
The forces are collinear: they act along the same line of action, as shown by the two arrows between the carts.
defs: Newton's Third Law
When body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts a force of equal magnitude, opposite direction and along the same line on body A.
eqs: Action–reaction force relation between bodies A and B
\(\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{B on A}}\) = force exerted by B on A (N); \(\boldsymbol{F}_{\text{A on B}}\) = force exerted by A on B (N)
tips: Do not cancel action–reaction pairs in a free-body diagram; each force appears only on the body it acts upon.
Keep the subscript order clear: \(F_{B}\) on A is the force on A exerted by B, the reverse of \(F_{A}\) on B.
rq: Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel when you analyse the motion of body A alone?
Because each force acts on a different body; only forces acting on the same body are summed in a free-body diagram.
If the two carts have different masses, which one experiences the larger acceleration, and why?
The lighter cart, because the same force magnitude produces a larger acceleration when mass is smaller (F = ma).

notes.t: Forces as the action of one body on another
pts: A force is always an action of one body on another; forces come in pairs acting on different bodies.
The rope tension acts on the block and on the man, pulling each toward the other.
Weight of each body acts vertically downward from gravity on that body.
The ground exerts a normal reaction upward on each body, and a friction force horizontally on each body.
Each force on a body is paired with an equal and opposite reaction on the other body or surface.
defs: Tension
The pulling force transmitted along a rope or cable, acting on the bodies at each end of it.
Normal reaction
The perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on a body resting on or pressed against it.
Friction force
The tangential contact force between two surfaces that opposes relative sliding or tendency to slide.
eqs: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m \(s^{-2}\))
tips: Draw each force on the body it acts on only; do not put a force on a body from itself, and always label the source (e.g. T on block).
Mass m is in kg but weight is in newtons; do not confuse m g with m.
rq: Why does the rope tension appear twice in the diagram, once on the block and once on the man?
A rope transmits tension to both bodies at its ends; each end pulls its attached body toward the rope, so the tension acts on both, in opposite directions.
If the block is stationary, why are the forces on it balanced even though the man pulls it?
The friction force on the block from the ground balances the rope tension horizontally, and the normal reaction balances the weight vertically, giving zero net force.

xq.q: A particle of mass 50 kg on a smooth horizontal surface is acted on by only two horizontal forces: 300 N due east and 400 N due north. Find the magnitude of its acceleration in m/s².
xq.a: 10 m/s²

xq.q: A block rests on the ground and is pulled by a rope. By Newton's third law, which force forms the action–reaction pair with the Earth's gravitational pull on the block (its weight)?
xq.a: The block's gravitational pull on the Earth
o: The normal reaction of the ground on the block
The tension in the rope on the block
The block's gravitational pull on the Earth
The friction force of the ground on the block
xq.w: A third-law pair acts on different bodies with equal size and opposite direction, so the partner of the Earth's pull on the block is the block's pull on the Earth; the normal reaction is the common trap since it merely balances weight on the same body.
s: Pair forces act on different bodies
Earth on block pairs with block on Earth

xq.q: Two carts A and B touch and A pushes B. Explain, using Newton's third law, why the force of A on B and the force of B on A do not cancel each other when analysing the motion of cart B.
xq.a: Newton's third law says F(B on A) = −F(A on B): equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and collinear. They act on different bodies. For cart B only the force of A on B appears in its free-body diagram, so it is part of ΣF on B and is not cancelled. The force of B on A appears only in the analysis of A.
s: State F(B on A) = −F(A on B), equal, opposite, collinear
The two forces act on different bodies
Only the force acting on B enters ΣF = ma for B
So the pair is never cancelled in a single free-body diagram

units.name: 1.3 Newton (SI unit), weight and gravitation
units.ov: This material defines the newton from Newton's second law (\(F=ma\)), then uses it to define weight as the Earth's gravitational pull on a mass (\(W=mg\)). It then generalises to Newton's law of universal gravitation, \(F=Gm_1m_2/r^2\), and shows that \(g=GM/r_e^2\) at the Earth's surface, so weight is a special case of gravitation.
must: Newton's second law uses the resultant force: \(F=ma\), with \(F\) in N, \(m\) in kg and \(a\) in m/s²
Definition: \(1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m/s^2}\), the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²; it is a derived SI unit
Weight is a force (N), not a mass (kg): \(W=mg\) with \(g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\); a 1 kg mass weighs 9.81 N
Newton's law of gravitation: \(F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\), attractive and acting along the line joining the centres
Inverse-square dependence: doubling \(r\) divides \(F\) by 4, and doubling either mass doubles \(F\)
\(G=6.673\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) is universal and very small, so gravitational forces are noticeable only when at least one body is huge
The force pair is equal and opposite (mutual attraction), so each body pulls on the other with the same magnitude of force
\(r\) is the distance between centres, not surfaces; for a body above the Earth, \(r_e=6.371\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}+\text{altitude}\)
At the surface \(mg=\dfrac{GmM}{r_e^2}\), so \(g=\dfrac{GM}{r_e^2}\approx9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\), independent of \(m\)
Convert to SI units (kg, m, s) before substituting; benchmark weights: apple ≈ 1 N, 1-tonne car ≈ 10 kN (1 tonne = 1000 kg, not 1 kN)
conn: Weight and gravitation: equating \(W=mg\) with \(F=GmM/r_e^2\) gives \(g=GM/r_e^2\), which can be used to find \(M\) or to find \(g\) at altitude
Second law and weight: a freely falling body has resultant force \(mg\), so \(a=g\); with other forces present (e.g. tension, drag) you must use the resultant in \(F=ma\)
Inverse-square scaling and unit consistency: a question may change altitude (adding the Earth's radius) and give mass in tonnes, so \(r\) and \(m\) must be converted to SI
Newton's third law and gravity: the Earth pulls on a body with force \(W\), and the body pulls on the Earth with the same force, though the Earth's acceleration is negligible because of its huge mass
exq: A 1500 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 27 m/s in 9 s against a constant 400 N resistance. Find the resultant force and the driving force, and state the car's weight in kN.
Calculate the gravitational force between two 1000 kg spheres whose centres are 2 m apart, using \(G=6.673\times10^{-11}\). Compare it with the weight of a 1 kg mass and comment.

A satellite of mass 500 kg orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface (\(r_e=6.371\times10^6\) m, \(g_{surface}=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\)). Find the gravitational force on it and the local value of \(g\), and explain why the satellite is not weightless.
Using \(g=9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\) and \(r_e=6.371\times10^6\) m, derive the mass of the Earth from Newton's law of gravitation.
At what height above the Earth's surface is the weight of a body reduced to one quarter of its surface value? Justify your answer using the inverse-square law.

notes.t: SI unit of force (the Newton)
pts: Newton's second law relates resultant force to mass and acceleration, which is used to define the SI unit of force.
One newton is the force needed to give a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
The newton is a derived SI unit, equal to kg·m/s² in base units.
defs: Newton (N)
The SI unit of force: the force that gives a body of mass 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
eqs: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²)
N = newton (force unit); kg = kilogram (mass); m/s² = metre per second squared (acceleration)
tips: Use the resultant (net) force in F = ma, not just one of several forces acting on the body.
Convert mass to kilograms and acceleration to m/s² before calculating, otherwise the result in newtons will be wrong.
rq: Why is the newton called a 'derived' unit rather than a base SI unit?
Because it is defined from the base units kilogram, metre and second through F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
If a 2 kg body accelerates at 3 m/s², how many newtons of resultant force act on it, and why?
6 N, since F = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

notes.t: Weight and gravitational force
pts: Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body due to the Earth's pull.
Weight is found by multiplying mass by the acceleration due to gravity (g = 9.81 m/s²).
A 1 kg mass has a weight of 9.81 N on Earth.
Typical everyday weights: an apple ≈ 1 N, a bag of sugar ≈ 10 N, a bag of cement ≈ 500 N, a 1-tonne car ≈ 10 kN.
defs: Weight
The force exerted on a body by the gravitational pull of the Earth.
eqs: Weight of a body from its mass
\(W\) = weight (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = acceleration due to gravity (m/s²), taken as 9.81 m/s²
tips: Weight is a force measured in newtons (N), not a mass in kilograms; always multiply mass by g to convert.
Do not confuse 1 tonne (1000 kg) with 1 kN; a car of 1 tonne weighs about 10 kN, so keep units consistent when converting.
rq: Why is a 1 kg mass's weight 9.81 N rather than 1 N, and what would change if you took it to the Moon?
Weight is mass × g, so the 9.81 m/s² gravitational acceleration scales the force; on the Moon g is about 1.62 m/s², so the same 1 kg mass would weigh roughly 1.62 N while its mass stays 1 kg.
Why do the sugar and cement examples differ so much in weight even though both are everyday bags?
Their masses differ greatly (roughly 1 kg versus 50 kg), and since weight is proportional to mass, the cement bag weighs about 50 times more.

notes.t: Newton's law of gravitation
pts: Gravity is a mutual attraction: the two bodies pull on each other with equal and opposite forces.
The force magnitude is proportional to the product of the two masses and falls off with the square of their separation.
G is a universal constant, the same everywhere in the universe, with a very small value.
defs: Gravity
The mutual attractive force between two bodies, acting along the line joining their centres, whose magnitude depends on their masses and separation.
Universal gravitational constant (G)
A constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², the same for all pairs of bodies.
eqs: Magnitude of the gravitational force between two masses

\(F\) = gravitational force magnitude (N); \(G\) = universal gravitational constant, 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ (m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²); \(m_1, m_2\) = masses of the two bodies (kg); \(r\) = distance between the bodies' centres (m)
tips: Use SI units throughout: masses in kg and r in metres, so that G's units cancel to give newtons.
r is measured between the centres of the two bodies, not between their surfaces.
rq: Why does the force on m₁ point toward m₂ and the force on m₂ point toward m₁ with the same magnitude?
Gravity is a mutual interaction; by Newton's third law the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, both along the line joining the masses.
What happens to F if the separation r is doubled?
F becomes one quarter of its original value, because F is proportional to 1/r².

notes.t: Newton's law of gravitation
pts: Gravitational force between two masses is attractive and falls off with the square of the separation distance.
Near Earth's surface the gravitational force on a mass m equals its weight, which reduces to mg with g ≈ 9.81 m/s².
Distance \(r_{e}\) is measured from the centre of the Earth to the body, not from its surface.
defs: Gravitational constant G
Universal constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, G ≈ 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².
eqs: Newton's law of gravitation (force between masses m and M)
F = gravitational force (N); G = gravitational constant (m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²); m = mass of body (kg); M = mass of Earth (kg); \(r_{e}\) = distance between centres (m)
Weight of a body at Earth's surface
F = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration ≈ 9.81 (m/s²)
tips: Use \(r_{e}\) as the distance from the Earth's centre (6.371 × 10⁶ m), not the height above the surface; forgetting to add altitude is a common error.
Keep SI units throughout: convert radius to metres and mass to kg before substituting into F = GmM/\(r_{e}\)².
rq: Why can the weight formula be written as mg, with g = GM/\(r_{e}\)² treated as a constant?
Because M, G and \(r_{e}\) are fixed for the Earth and a body near its surface, so GM/\(r_{e}\)² is a constant ≈ 9.81 m/s²; only m varies.
What would happen to the force on a body if its distance from Earth's centre doubled?
The force would fall to one quarter of its original value, since F is proportional to 1/\(r_{e}\)².

xq.q: A 20 kg mass is lifted vertically by a cable that exerts a constant upward force of 250 N. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², find the upward acceleration of the mass.

Two uniform spheres of mass 1000 kg and 2000 kg, each of radius 0.5 m, are placed with their surfaces 1.0 m apart in space. Using G = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², find the gravitational force between them in newtons.
A satellite is at a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius \(r_e\). If its weight at the surface would be W, what is the gravitational force on it at this height?
o: 4W
xq.w: The distance is measured from the Earth's centre so r = 2r_e and the force falls with r², giving W/4; the traps are forgetting the square (W/2) or using r = 3r_e (W/9).

units.name: 1.4 Vector addition of displacements
units.ov: This material introduces vector addition using displacements: a displacement is a vector, and successive displacements U and V combine tip-to-tail into a single resultant W. Addition is commutative, so the order does not change the final position. The ideas (head-to-tail, triangle/parallelogram rule, components) underpin all later vector work on forces, velocities and statics.
must: A displacement is a vector: its magnitude is the straight-line distance from start to end, and its direction points from start to end.
The resultant of successive displacements is \( \vec{W}=\vec{U}+\vec{V} \), the single displacement from the original position to the final position.
Add vectors tip-to-tail: draw V starting at the tip of U, then W runs from the tail of U to the tip of V.
Never add magnitudes arithmetically: \( |\vec{W}|\neq|\vec{U}|+|\vec{V}| \) in general. Equality holds only when U and V are parallel and in the same direction.
Vector addition is commutative: \( \mathbf{U}+\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{V}+\mathbf{U} \), which is the parallelogram rule.
Displacement (vector, net change in position) differs from distance travelled (scalar path length). Distance is at least as large as \( |\vec{W}| \).
Subtraction is not commutative: \( \mathbf{U}-\mathbf{V}=-(\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{U}) \). Treat it as adding the negative vector.
Compute the resultant with components: \( W_x=U_x+V_x,\ W_y=U_y+V_y \), then \( |W|=\sqrt{W_x^2+W_y^2} \) and \( \theta=\tan^{-1}(W_y/W_x) \), checking the quadrant.
For two vectors at angle \( \alpha \) between their tails, the triangle gives the cosine rule, \( |W|^2=U^2+V^2+2UV\cos\alpha \). Use the sine rule for the direction.
Give a resultant as magnitude, direction (angle and reference axis) and units (m).
conn: Components link to the triangle/parallelogram rule: a graphical resultant can be checked with \( W_x \) and \( W_y \), and the cosine and sine rules give the same answer.
Commutativity links to the parallelogram construction: both orders of tip-to-tail give the same diagonal, so the final position is independent of the route.
Displacement versus distance links to the magnitude warning: a path of two legs has distance \( U+V \) but net displacement \( |\vec{U}+\vec{V}| \).
Displacement addition extends directly to forces and velocities (relative velocity, equilibrium of concurrent forces), which use the same resultant method.
exq: A robot moves 30 m due east and then 40 m due north. Find the magnitude and bearing of its resultant displacement and compare it with the distance travelled.
Displacements U = 5 m at 30° above the x-axis and V = 8 m at 120° are applied in succession. Find W by components, and show that V+U gives the same resultant.
Two displacements of 6 m and 9 m have an angle of 60° between them when drawn tail to tail. Use the cosine rule to find the resultant magnitude, and the sine rule to find its angle to the 6 m vector.
A student says that the resultant of 3 m and 4 m displacements is always 7 m. Explain the error and state the range of possible resultant magnitudes, with the conditions for the maximum and minimum.
A point undergoes three successive displacements A, B and C. Find the single displacement that returns it to the start, and state what the vector sum of all four displacements equals.

notes.t: Vector addition of displacements
pts: A displacement moves a point from one position to another and can be represented by a vector.
Two successive displacements U and V are equivalent to a single displacement W from the original to the final position.
The resultant of successive displacements is found by joining them tip to tail, giving the net displacement.
defs: Displacement vector
A vector representing the change in position of a point, having magnitude equal to the straight-line distance moved and direction from the start to the end position.
Resultant vector
The single vector that has the same effect as a combination of several vectors acting in succession.
eqs: Vector addition of successive displacements (resultant displacement)
\( \vec{W} \) = resultant displacement (m); \( \vec{U} \) = first displacement (m); \( \vec{V} \) = second displacement (m)
tips: Do not add vector magnitudes arithmetically; vector addition must account for direction (e.g. use components or the triangle/parallelogram rule).
Distinguish displacement (vector, change in position) from distance travelled (scalar path length).
rq: Why is the final displacement W not simply the sum of the lengths of U and V?

Because displacement is a vector; the net result depends on both magnitude and direction, so W is the vector sum (tip-to-tail), which is generally shorter than the total distance travelled unless U and V are parallel.
What would happen to W if V were reversed in direction?
W would become the difference \( \vec{U} - \vec{V} \), with its length reduced (or changed in direction), since the second displacement now opposes the first.

notes.t: Vector addition (displacements)
pts: Adding two displacement vectors gives a resultant displacement W; the order of addition does not change the final position.
The resultant W of displacements U and V is their vector sum.
Because the order does not matter, vector addition is commutative.
defs: Commutative (vector addition)
A property where adding vectors in either order gives the same resultant, i.e. \( \mathbf{U}+\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{V}+\mathbf{U} \).
eqs: Resultant of two displacement vectors (commutative vector sum)
\( \mathbf{W} \) = resultant displacement (m); \( \mathbf{U} \) = first displacement (m); \( \mathbf{V} \) = second displacement (m)
tips: Commutativity applies to vector addition only; do not assume the order matters less or more for subtraction, which is not commutative.
Vectors add head-to-tail with direction; adding magnitudes alone ignores direction and gives wrong results.
rq: Why does the order of the two displacements not change the final position of the object?
Because vector addition is commutative: the resultant displacement is the same whether U or V is applied first, so both paths end at the same point (the diagonal W).

xq.q: A survey drone makes two successive displacements. The first is \( \vec{U} \) = 80 m due east. The second is \( \vec{V} \) = 60 m in a direction 60° north of east. Find the magnitude of the single displacement \( \vec{W} \) that takes the drone from its start point to its finish point.
s: Components of V: 60cos60° = 30 m east, 60sin60° = 51.96 m north

xq.q: A hiker walks 6 km due east and then 8 km due north. Which row correctly gives the magnitude of her net displacement from the start?
xq.a: 10 km, found by adding the vectors using Pythagoras
o: 14 km, found by adding the two magnitudes (this is the distance travelled)
2 km, found by subtracting the magnitudes
10 km, found by adding the vectors using Pythagoras
7 km, found by averaging the magnitudes
xq.w: The displacements are perpendicular, so |W| = √(6²+8²) = 10 km; adding magnitudes gives the path length, not the displacement.
s: Perpendicular vectors add by Pythagoras: √(36+64) = 10 km

xq.q: Two successive displacements \( \vec{U} \) and \( \vec{V} \) take a point from A to B. Using a sketch, show that the final position is the same whichever displacement is made first, and state the name of this property of vector addition.
xq.a: Draw U from A, then V from the tip of U to give the final point B; the resultant W = U + V runs from A to B. Now draw V first from A and then U from the tip of V. The two routes form the sides of a parallelogram with W as the common diagonal from A. Both routes end at the same point B, so W = U + V = V + U. This property is called commutativity of vector addition.
s: Sketch of U then V joined tip to tail, with resultant W from start to end
Sketch of V then U joined tip to tail, giving the parallelogram
Both routes end at the same point, so the resultant W is the same
Conclusion: U + V = V + U, i.e. vector addition is commutative

units.name: 1.5 Force as a vector: concurrent forces and transmissibility
units.ov: This material defines a force as a vector with magnitude, direction, point of application and line of action, then introduces concurrent force systems (lines of action meeting at one point). The principle of transmissibility lets a force slide along its line of action for rigid-body external effects. This justifies moving forces to a common point and replacing collinear or concurrent systems with a single resultant.
must: A force is fully specified by four properties: magnitude, direction, point of application and line of action.
Principle of transmissibility: a force can be slid anywhere along its line of action without changing the external effect on a rigid body.
Transmissibility applies to external effects only; internal stresses and deformation can change with the point of application.
Moving a force off its line of action is not allowed unless a moment is added.
Concurrent forces: the lines of action all pass through one common point, even if the forces are applied at different points on the body.
To check concurrency, extend the lines of action and see whether they meet at one point; the drawn application points are not enough.
Scalar multiples and negatives: \(\vec{F}_B = 2\vec{F}_A\) doubles the magnitude with the same direction; \(\vec{F}_C = -\vec{F}_A\) has equal magnitude and opposite direction, so \(|F_C|=|F_A|\).
Resultant of collinear forces: \(R=\sum F_i\) with a sign convention for direction; the resultant acts in the direction of the larger net force.
Equal magnitude and direction do not make forces equal if their lines of action or application points differ.
Concurrent is not the same as parallel or collinear, and does not mean the forces are equal or point the same way.
conn: Transmissibility is what allows non-coincident forces to be slid along their lines of action until they meet at a common point, turning them into a concurrent system that can be added as vectors.
Collinear addition \(R=\sum F_i\) is the one-dimensional special case of finding the resultant of concurrent forces. Sign conventions carry over to component resolution.
Transmissibility fails for internal effects (stress, deformation) and for forces moved off their line of action, which links it to moments and to rigid versus deformable body assumptions.
Identifying the point of concurrency in a structure (e.g. the Cutty Sark support) is the first step of an equilibrium analysis.
exq: Two forces of 25 N and 15 N act along the same line in opposite directions on a block. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant. A third force of 10 N is then added in the direction of the smaller force; find the new resultant.

State the principle of transmissibility. A 200 N force acts on a rigid beam at point A. Show where else it can be applied without changing the external effect, and explain why the internal stresses in the beam would differ.

Three forces act on a bracket at different application points. Their lines of action are given by their directions and positions. Determine whether the forces are concurrent and find the common point if they are.

Given \(\vec{F}_A = 30\) N to the right, find \(\vec{F}_B = 2\vec{F}_A\) and \(\vec{F}_C = -\vec{F}_A\). State their magnitudes and directions, and explain why a minus sign does not mean a negative magnitude.
Explain why two forces with the same magnitude and direction but different lines of action are not equivalent, and what must be added to move one onto the other's line of action.

notes.t: Vectors – Forces: magnitude, direction, point of application and line of action
pts: A force is fully described by four properties: magnitude, direction, point of application and line of action.
The line of action is the straight line along which the force acts, passing through its point of application.
Multiplying a force by a scalar changes its magnitude: \(F_{B}\) = 2F_A is twice as large and in the same direction as \(F_{A}\).
A negative sign reverses direction: \(F_{C}\) = -\(F_{A}\) has the same magnitude as \(F_{A}\) but acts in the opposite direction.
defs: Line of action
The straight line, extended infinitely in both directions, along which a force acts, passing through its point of application.
Point of application
The point on a body at which a force acts.
eqs: Scalar multiple of a force (doubling magnitude, same direction)
tips: A minus sign on a vector indicates direction, not a negative magnitude; the magnitude is always taken as positive (|\(F_{C}\)| = |\(F_{A}\)|).
Forces with the same magnitude and direction are not equal if they have different lines of action or points of application.
rq: Why must a force's line of action and point of application both be specified, not just its magnitude and direction?
Two forces with identical magnitude and direction but different lines of action produce different moments/rotations on a body, so their effect depends on where and along what line they act.
What happens to \(F_{C}\) if \(F_{A}\) is doubled, and why does the sign matter?
\(F_{C}\) becomes -2F_A: magnitude doubles, and the minus sign still means it points opposite to \(F_{A}\).

notes.t: Concurrent Forces
pts: Forces are concurrent when they act at the same point of application.
Forces are concurrent at a point when their lines of action intersect at that point, even if they are applied at different points on the body.
defs: Concurrent forces
A set of forces is concurrent if they all act at the same point of application, or if their lines of action all pass through a common point.
tips: Concurrency depends on lines of action, not just the drawn application point; check that the extended lines actually meet at one point.
Do not confuse concurrent forces (common point) with parallel or collinear forces, which have different geometric conditions.
rq: Why can two forces with different points of application still be treated as concurrent?

Because if their lines of action intersect at a common point, they can be slid along their lines of action to that point without changing their effect on the rigid body, so they are concurrent at that point.
In the figure, what would make the 3 kN and 2 kN forces concurrent at point O?
Their lines of action must both pass through point O, which is where the members meet; the lines of action of the forces intersect at O.

notes.t: Concurrent Forces
pts: Concurrent forces are forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point.
In the Cutty Sark support, the lines of action of the applied forces (shown as dashed lines) intersect at one point, so the forces are concurrent.
Identifying the common point of intersection of the force lines is the first step in analysing a concurrent force system.
defs: Concurrent forces
A set of forces whose lines of action all intersect at a single common point.
tips: Concurrent means the lines of action meet at one point, not that the forces are equal or act in the same direction.
Check the direction of each arrow carefully when resolving forces; the dashed lines show lines of action, not the force magnitudes.
rq: Why does it matter that the lines of action of the forces meet at one point?
Because forces acting through a common point produce no moment about that point, so the system can be reduced to a single resultant force and analysed using force equilibrium alone.
What would change if one force line did not pass through the intersection point?
The forces would no longer be concurrent; a moment would arise about the intersection point, and the system would need moment equilibrium as well as force equilibrium.

notes.t: Principle of Transmissibility
pts: The overall external effect of a force on a rigid body does not depend on where along its line of action the force is applied.
Force vectors can be slid anywhere along their line of action when modelling a body, which simplifies the problem.
The principle applies to the external effect only; internal effects (stresses, deformation) can change with the point of application.
defs: Principle of transmissibility
A force acting on a body may be applied at any point along its line of action without changing the overall external effect on that body.
Line of action
The straight line, passing through a force vector, along which the force acts; it defines the direction in which a force can be moved without changing its external effect.
tips: Transmissibility applies only to rigid-body external effects; do not move a force off its line of action (that would require adding a moment).
Do not confuse the principle with the external effect being zero: it says the effect is unchanged, not that the force disappears.
rq: Why does the principle only hold for the external effect, not for internal effects?

Moving a force along its line of action changes the internal forces and deformation within the body near the point of application, so internal stresses can differ, although the external motion and equilibrium are unchanged.
Why does the push and pull in the diagram give the same external effect when moved along the blue line?
Both forces lie on the same line of action, so sliding either one along that line does not change the net external effect on the car as a rigid body.

notes.t: Vector Addition of Parallel or Collinear Forces
pts: Forces acting along the same line (parallel or collinear) can be added or subtracted directly, taking direction into account, to give a single resultant force.
Forces in the same direction are added together; forces in opposite directions are subtracted, and the resultant takes the direction of the larger force.
Two or more collinear forces can be replaced by one equivalent force that produces the same effect on the body.
The 5N scale bar on the page is a reference length used to indicate force magnitude on the diagram; it is not a force acting on the block.
defs: Collinear forces
Forces whose lines of action lie along the same straight line, regardless of their magnitude or sense.
Resultant force
The single force that has the same external effect as a system of forces acting on a body.
eqs: Resultant of collinear forces (taking one direction as positive)
R = resultant force (N); \(F_{i}\) = individual force components along the line, with sign given by direction (N)
tips: Forgetting direction: adding 25N and 15N to get 40N when they act in opposite directions is wrong; the answer is 10N.
The resultant direction is that of the larger force; do not assume it follows the first force listed.
rq: Why must the direction of each force be considered before adding collinear forces?
Because forces are vectors; opposing forces reduce the net magnitude, so they must be assigned signs and summed algebraically.
In the diagram, why does the 25N force to the left plus the 15N force to the right give a net force to the left, and how big is it?
The larger force (25N left) dominates; net = 25 − 15 = 10N to the left, which matches the 10N equivalent force shown.

xq.q: Four collinear forces act along the x-axis on a rigid block. \( \vec{F}_A \) has magnitude 30 N in the +x direction. \( \vec{F}_B = 2\vec{F}_A \), \( \vec{F}_C = -\vec{F}_A \), and \( \vec{F}_D \) is 45 N in the −x direction. Find the magnitude of the single equivalent resultant force and state its direction.
xq.a: 15 N in the +x direction
s: \(F_{B}\) = +60 N, \(F_{C}\) = −30 N (reversed direction, same magnitude as \(F_{A}\))
Resultant = 30 + 60 − 30 − 45 = +15 N, so 15 N in the +x direction

xq.q: A 200 N force acts on a rigid beam. It is moved 1 m along its own line of action to a different point on the beam. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: The external effect on the beam is unchanged, but the internal stresses may change
o: The external effect (support reactions) is unchanged, and so are the internal stresses everywhere in the beam
The external effect on the beam is unchanged, but the internal stresses may change
The external effect is zero because the force has moved
The external effect is unchanged only if a moment is added to compensate
xq.w: Transmissibility guarantees only the overall external effect is unchanged; internal stresses and deformation depend on where the force is applied, and no moment is needed when sliding along the line of action.
s: Sliding along the line of action leaves external effects unchanged
Internal effects can change, and no moment is needed along the line of action

xq.q: Three forces are applied at three different points on a rigid bracket, and their extended lines of action all pass through one point P. Explain why the forces are concurrent, and explain how the principle of transmissibility allows them to be treated as acting at P when finding their combined external effect.
xq.a: Forces are concurrent if their lines of action all pass through a common point, even when their points of application differ. Here all three lines meet at P, so the system is concurrent. Transmissibility says a force on a rigid body can be applied anywhere along its line of action without changing its external effect. Each force can therefore be slid along its line to P, and the three forces can then be added as vectors at that single point. This is valid only for external effects on a rigid body, not for internal stresses.
s: Concurrent means lines of action meet at one point, not that application points coincide
All three lines pass through P, so the system is concurrent
Transmissibility: slide each force along its line of action to P without changing the external effect
Then add the forces as vectors at P; this applies to rigid-body external effects only

units.name: 1.6 Adding forces: parallelogram law
units.ov: This material revises vector addition and applies it to forces. Two vectors, or two concurrent forces, are added with the parallelogram law, and the resultant is the diagonal from the common tail. Its magnitude and direction are then found from the force triangle using the sine and cosine rules, so the geometry and the trigonometry are two views of the same calculation.
must: Parallelogram law: draw both vectors tail-to-tail from a common origin, complete the parallelogram, and the resultant is the diagonal from that origin.
Vector addition is commutative: \( \vec{C} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A} \), so the order of drawing does not matter.
The resultant is a single vector with the same effect as the originals combined, with the same units (N for forces).
Concurrent forces have lines of action through the same point, so their resultant is \( \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 \).
Find the resultant's magnitude with the cosine rule on the force triangle: \( F^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 - 2F_1F_2\cos\gamma \), where \( \gamma \) is the triangle's included angle.

Cosine rule trap: the included angle in the triangle is the supplement of the tail-to-tail angle \( \alpha \) between the forces, i.e. \( \gamma = 180^\circ - \alpha \). This gives \( F^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos\alpha \).
Find the direction of the resultant with the sine rule (\( \sin\beta / F_2 = \sin\gamma / F \)), then express it relative to a stated reference line.
Measure \( \theta_1 \) and \( \theta_2 \) from the same reference line (e.g. the horizontal) before combining forces.
Common errors: the resultant is the diagonal from the common origin, not the other diagonal or a side, and vectors must be drawn tail-to-tail from one origin, not from different origins.
conn: Parallelogram law and the triangle rule: the head-to-tail triangle is half the parallelogram, which is why the cosine and sine rules apply to the force triangle.
Tail-to-tail angle versus triangle angle: the supplement relationship decides the sign of the cosine term, so check it with limiting cases (0° gives \( F_1+F_2 \), 180° gives \( |F_1-F_2| \)).
Resultant and direction: the cosine rule gives the magnitude, the sine rule gives the angle, and the angle must then be tied to a reference axis using \( \theta_1 \) and \( \theta_2 \).
Concurrency and the single-force replacement: only concurrent forces can be replaced by one resultant at the common point, which is the basis for later equilibrium problems.
exq: Two concurrent forces of 80 N and 120 N act on a bracket with 50° between them. Find the magnitude of the resultant and its angle from the 120 N force, using the cosine and sine rules.

Force F1 = 500 N acts at 30° above the horizontal and F2 = 300 N acts at 110° from the same horizontal. Find the resultant's magnitude and direction by the parallelogram law, and check the result with a scale drawing.
Explain why the cosine rule on the force triangle uses the supplement of the angle between the forces placed tail-to-tail. Show the effect on the sign of the \( 2F_1F_2\cos \) term.
Show that vector addition is commutative with a parallelogram sketch, then identify which diagonal is the resultant and why the other diagonal is wrong.
Two concurrent forces have equal magnitude P. Find the angle between them for which the resultant also has magnitude P, and give the resultant's direction relative to the forces.

notes.t: Vector addition by the parallelogram law
pts: Two vectors are added by placing their tails together and completing a parallelogram; the resultant is the diagonal from the common tail.
The resultant C is the same whichever vector is drawn first, so vector addition is commutative.
The resultant is a single vector with magnitude and direction that replaces the two original vectors.
defs: Parallelogram law
Two vectors acting at a point are added by drawing them from a common origin, completing a parallelogram; the diagonal from that origin is their resultant.
Resultant vector
The single vector obtained by adding two or more vectors, which has the same effect as the original vectors combined.
eqs: Vector addition (resultant of A and B)
\( \vec{C} \) = resultant vector (same units as A and B); \( \vec{A} \) = first vector; \( \vec{B} \) = second vector
tips: Draw both vectors from a common origin (tails together) before completing the parallelogram; joining head-to-tail gives the same result but drawing from different origins is wrong.
The resultant is the diagonal starting at the common origin, not the other diagonal or a side of the parallelogram.
rq: Why does the diagonal of the parallelogram, rather than one of its sides, represent the sum of A and B?
Because the diagonal runs from the common tail to the far corner, which is reached by moving along B then A (or A then B); it therefore represents the net displacement of the combined effect.
Why does swapping the order of A and B leave the resultant unchanged?
Swapping the order produces the same parallelogram with the same diagonal, so the resultant is identical: vector addition is commutative.

notes.t: Vectors - Force Addition
pts: Two concurrent forces act at the same point of application, so their resultant can be found by vector addition.
The sum of two concurrent forces is found geometrically using the parallelogram law, with the resultant as the diagonal from the common point.
The magnitude and direction of the resultant can be found from the triangle formed by the forces using the sine rule or cosine rule.
defs: Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through the same point of application.
Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as the sum of the given forces, found by vector addition.
eqs: Resultant of two concurrent forces (vector sum)
\mathbf{F} = resultant force (N); \mathbf{F}_1 = first force (N); \mathbf{F}_2 = second force (N)
tips: Make sure the angles θ1 and θ2 are measured from the same reference line (e.g. the horizontal) before adding the forces.
When applying the cosine rule to the force triangle, remember the included angle is the supplement of the angle between the two force vectors when they are placed tail-to-tail.
rq: Why can the two forces be added using the parallelogram law only because they are concurrent?
Concurrent forces share one point of application, so their vectors can be placed tail-to-tail at P1 and the diagonal of the parallelogram gives their sum.
Which rule would you use to find the resultant magnitude F and direction θ from the triangle of forces, and why not the other?
The cosine rule gives the magnitude from the two sides and included angle, and the sine rule then gives the direction θ; both are needed to fix F and θ.

xq.q: Two concurrent forces act at a point with their tails together. \( F_1 \) = 50 N and \( F_2 \) = 70 N, and the angle between them is 120°. Use the parallelogram law with the cosine rule to find the magnitude of the resultant force.
s: Angle between the tails is 120°, so the included angle in the force triangle is 180° − 120° = 60°

xq.q: Two forces of 30 N each act at a point with their tails together, with an angle of 60° between them. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
xq.a: 52.0 N, from the parallelogram diagonal
o: 60.0 N, from adding the magnitudes
30.0 N, from using 60° directly as the included angle in the cosine rule on the force triangle
42.4 N, from treating the forces as perpendicular
52.0 N, from the parallelogram diagonal
xq.w: The diagonal gives R = 2(30)cos30° ≈ 52.0 N; the triangle's included angle is 180° − 60° = 120°, and using 60° gives 30 N.

xq.q: Two concurrent forces \( F_1 \) and \( F_2 \) act at a point with their tails together, the angle between them being \( \theta \). Using the parallelogram law and the cosine rule, show that the magnitude of the resultant is \( R=\sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2+2F_1F_2\cos\theta} \).
xq.a: Draw F1 and F2 from a common point and complete the parallelogram. The resultant R is the diagonal from the common point. Redrawing as a triangle with F1 and F2 joined tip to tail, the angle between the two sides is 180° − θ. The cosine rule gives R² = F1² + F2² − 2F1F2cos(180° − θ). Since cos(180° − θ) = −cosθ, R² = F1² + F2² + 2F1F2cosθ, so R = √(F1² + F2² + 2F1F2cosθ).
s: Parallelogram sketch with R as the diagonal from the common tail
Force triangle has included angle 180° − θ
Cosine rule: R² = F1² + F2² − 2F1F2cos(180° − θ)
Use cos(180° − θ) = −cosθ to reach the result

units.name: 1.7 Rectangular components of forces
units.ov: This material covers resolving a force into perpendicular x and y components, and rebuilding the force's magnitude and direction from those components. Signs come from the quadrant, and whether sine or cosine is used depends on which axis the angle is measured from. These ideas underpin resultants of several forces and equilibrium analysis.
must: Resolve a force from the x-axis: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\)
Rebuild the magnitude: \(F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}\)
Rebuild the direction: \(\tan\theta = F_y/F_x\), with \(\theta\) measured from the x-axis
Always identify the reference axis for \(\theta\). If it is measured from the y-axis, the roles swap: \(F_x = F\sin\theta\), \(F_y = F\cos\theta\)
Quadrant signs: I (+,+), II (−,+), III (−,−), IV (+,−). Take the sign from the direction of the component, not from the formula's magnitude
Arctan alone can give the wrong quadrant. Check the signs of \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) and add \(180^\circ\) where needed
Rectangular components are perpendicular projections whose vector sum equals the original force: \(\vec F = \vec F_x + \vec F_y\)
Set the calculator to the right angle mode (degrees or radians) before evaluating sine and cosine
Sketch a labelled force triangle every time to check that your sine/cosine choice and signs are sensible
conn: Resultant of concurrent forces: resolve each force, sum \(\Sigma F_x\) and \(\Sigma F_y\) separately, then recombine with Pythagoras and arctan
Equilibrium: set \(\Sigma F_x = 0\) and \(\Sigma F_y = 0\) to solve for unknown forces or angles, which needs correct component signs
Inclined planes and cables: the choice of axes and the angle's reference axis decides whether sine or cosine appears
Direction by arctan links with the quadrant sign table, because the calculator's principal value must be corrected
exq: A force of 500 N acts at 35° above the positive x-axis. Find \(F_x\) and \(F_y\), then check by recovering the magnitude and direction.
A force has components \(F_x = -120\) N and \(F_y = 160\) N. Find its magnitude and its direction from the positive x-axis, and state the quadrant.
Forces \(F_B\) and \(F_D\) act at a point at given angles measured from the y-axis. Resolve each into x and y components, using the quadrant signs, and find the resultant magnitude and direction.
A 800 N force acts at 30° from the y-axis in quadrant IV. Write its components with correct signs, and explain how the answer changes if the angle is measured from the x-axis.
Find the angle at which a 250 N force must act so that its x-component is 150 N, then find its y-component. Discuss the two possible quadrants.

notes.t: Components of Forces – Rectangular Components
pts: Any force F can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components along the coordinate axes.
The x-component is the force times the cosine of the angle from the x-axis.
The y-component is the force times the sine of the angle from the x-axis.
The resultant magnitude and direction can be recovered from the components using Pythagoras and the tangent ratio.
defs: Rectangular components
The perpendicular projections of a force onto the x and y coordinate axes, whose vector sum equals the original force.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = x-component of force (N); F = force magnitude (N); \theta = angle measured from the x-axis (degrees or radians)
\(F_{y}\) = y-component of force (N); F = force magnitude (N); \theta = angle measured from the x-axis (degrees or radians)
Magnitude of force from its components
Direction of force from its components
\theta = angle from the x-axis (degrees or radians); \(F_{y}\) = y-component (N); \(F_{x}\) = x-component (N)
tips: Ensure the calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) when computing cos θ and sin θ.
Using arctan alone can give the wrong quadrant; check the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\).
rq: Why must you use the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\), not just the tan ratio, to find the correct direction?
tan θ gives the same value for opposite quadrants, so the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) determine which quadrant θ lies in.
If a force is vector-added from its components, why does \(\vec F = \vec F_x + \vec F_y\) hold?
The components are perpendicular projections, so they form the two sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is F.

notes.t: Rectangular Components of Forces
pts: A force can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components that add vectorially to give the original force.
The sign of each component depends on the quadrant in which the force's direction lies.
In quadrant I both \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) are positive; in quadrant II \(F_{x}\) is negative and \(F_{y}\) positive.
In quadrant III both components are negative; in quadrant IV \(F_{x}\) is positive and \(F_{y}\) negative.
The angle θ is measured from the y-axis, so the component magnitudes use sine and cosine with that reference.
defs: Rectangular components
Two mutually perpendicular vector parts (along the x and y axes) whose vector sum equals the original force.
eqs: Vector sum of rectangular components of force \(F_{D}\)
Vector sum of rectangular components of force \(F_{B}\)
tips: Assign component signs from the quadrant table, not from the magnitude; a component pointing in the negative axis direction is negative.
Check which axis θ is measured from before using sine or cosine for the component.
rq: Why does the sign of \(F_{x}\) change between quadrants I and II while \(F_{y}\) keeps the same sign?
Moving from quadrant I to II the force points further left (negative x-direction) but still upward (positive y-direction), so \(F_{x}\) becomes negative while \(F_{y}\) stays positive.

xq.q: A force \(F_1\) of 800 N acts on a bracket, pointing left and downward (quadrant III). Its angle \(\theta = 60^\circ\) is measured from the negative y-axis. A second force \(F_2\) of 500 N acts along the positive x-axis. Taking x positive to the right, find the x-component \(R_x\) of the resultant of the two forces.
xq.a: \(R_{x}\) = -192.8 N, i.e. 192.8 N directed to the left
s: Angle is from the y-axis, so \(F_{1x} = -800\sin 60^\circ = -692.8\) N (negative: points left)

xq.q: A force \(F = 200\) N points upward and to the left. Its angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\) is measured from the positive y-axis. What is its x-component \(F_x\)?
xq.w: Because θ is measured from the y-axis, the x-component is \(200\sin30^\circ = 100\) N, and it is negative because the force points left; using cosine gives 173.2 N, and ignoring the quadrant gives the wrong sign.

xq.q: The components of a force are \(F_x = -30\) N and \(F_y = -40\) N. Find the magnitude of the force and its direction measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Explain why \(\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\) taken directly on a calculator gives the wrong direction.
xq.a: F = sqrt(30² + 40²) = 50 N. tan⁻¹(40/30) = 53.1°, but both components are negative so the force lies in quadrant III. The direction is 180° + 53.1° = 233.1° anticlockwise from +x (equivalently 53.1° below the negative x-axis). The calculator gives the same value for tan⁻¹(+40/+30), because the signs cancel in the ratio, so it cannot identify the quadrant.
s: Both components negative, so quadrant III [1]
The ratio loses the signs, so arctan alone cannot give the quadrant [1]

units.name: 2.1 Rectangular components of a force
units.ov: This material covers resolving a force into perpendicular x and y components, and recombining components to get the magnitude and direction of the resultant force. Resolution uses right-triangle trigonometry, and the signs of the components come from the quadrant the force points into. Everything depends on knowing which axis the angle is measured from, because that decides whether sine or cosine applies. The notes are inconsistent on this: page 1 measures θ from the x-axis, page 2 from the y-axis.
must: Resolve a force with θ measured from the x-axis: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\)
Always identify the axis θ is measured from. If θ is from the y-axis, the roles swap: \(F_x = F\sin\theta\), \(F_y = F\cos\theta\). Pages 1 and 2 use different conventions.
Recombine components to find the magnitude: \(F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}\)
Find the direction from \(\tan\theta = F_y/F_x\), and state which axis the angle is measured from

Set the sign of each component from the direction or quadrant, never from the magnitude alone. Left is negative \(x\) and down is negative \(y\); \(F_x>0\) in quadrants I and IV, \(F_y>0\) in quadrants I and II
A calculator's \(\tan^{-1}\) gives the wrong quadrant when \(F_x<0\). Check the signs of \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) and add \(180^\circ\) if needed
The components are vectors that sum to the original force: \(\vec F = \vec F_x + \vec F_y\), and this applies to each force (A, B, D) separately
Rectangular components are mutually perpendicular projections onto the axes, so \(F_x\) is the adjacent side and \(F_y\) the opposite side of the right triangle
Use units of N, and keep the calculator in degrees or radians consistently with the angle given
Sketch the force triangle and check the answer: each component magnitude must be \(\le F\), and the signs must match the sketch
conn: Resolving each force into components is the first step in finding a resultant: sum the \(x\) components and the \(y\) components separately, then use Pythagoras and \(\tan\theta\) to get the resultant's magnitude and direction.
Sign conventions link to equilibrium: \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) only work if every component has the correct sign from its quadrant.
The choice of angle reference (x-axis or y-axis) feeds into the sine/cosine choice and the quadrant correction for the direction, so a single error can propagate through all three.
Inclined-plane and cable problems combine these ideas: resolve along tilted axes or at given angles, then recombine to a net force.
exq: A force of 800 N acts at 35° above the positive x-axis. Find \(F_x\) and \(F_y\).
A force has \(F_x=-300\) N and \(F_y=400\) N. Find its magnitude and its direction measured from the positive x-axis, explaining the quadrant correction.
A 500 N force points down and to the left at 30° measured from the negative y-axis. Determine its rectangular components with correct signs.

Forces \(F_B\) and \(F_D\) act on a bracket at different angles, one measured from the x-axis and one from the y-axis. Resolve each, sum the components and find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
Explain with an example why \(\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\) alone can give the wrong direction, and show how to correct it.

notes.t: Components of Forces – Rectangular Components
pts: Any force F can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components using its angle θ measured from the x-axis.
Given F and θ, the components are found by trigonometry: \(F_{x}\) is the adjacent side and \(F_{y}\) the opposite side of the right triangle.
Given the components, the force is the vector sum of its parts and its magnitude follows from Pythagoras.
The direction θ is found from the ratio of the components, not from the magnitude alone.
defs: Rectangular components
The two perpendicular projections of a force onto the x and y axes, whose vector sum equals the original force.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = x-component of force (N); F = magnitude of force (N); θ = angle from the x-axis (degrees or rad)
\(F_{y}\) = y-component of force (N); F = magnitude of force (N); θ = angle from the x-axis (degrees or rad)
Magnitude of a force from its components
F = magnitude of force (N); \(F_{x}\) = x-component (N); \(F_{y}\) = y-component (N)
Direction of a force from its components
θ = angle from the x-axis (degrees or rad); \(F_{y}\) = y-component (N); \(F_{x}\) = x-component (N)
tips: Mixing up sine and cosine: always check which component is adjacent to the angle measured from the x-axis before substituting.
Using tan⁻¹ alone for direction can give the wrong quadrant; check the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) to place θ correctly.
rq: Why does \(F_{x}\) = F cos θ and not F sin θ, given that θ is measured from the x-axis?
Cosine gives the adjacent side to θ in the right triangle, and the x-axis is adjacent to θ; sine gives the opposite side, which is the y-component.
If you know \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\), why can't you simply add their magnitudes to get F?
The components are perpendicular, so they add as vectors; Pythagoras gives F = √(\(F_{x}\)² + \(F_{y}\)²), not \(F_{x}\) + \(F_{y}\).
What happens to the components if θ is increased toward 90°?
cos θ falls toward 0 so \(F_{x}\) shrinks, while sin θ rises toward 1 so \(F_{y}\) approaches F: the force becomes nearly vertical.

notes.t: Rectangular Components of Forces
pts: A force can be resolved into perpendicular x and y components that add vectorially to give the original force.
The sign of each rectangular component is set by the quadrant the force points into: Fx is positive in quadrants I and IV, Fy is positive in quadrants I and II.
The angle θ is measured from the positive y-axis, so the component magnitudes follow from sine and cosine of θ.
A force directed to the left has a negative x-component, and a force directed downward has a negative y-component.
defs: Rectangular components
Two mutually perpendicular vectors, one along the x-axis and one along the y-axis, whose vector sum equals the original force.
eqs: Vector sum of rectangular components of force \(F_{D}\)
\vec{F}_D = force D (N); \vec{F}_{Dx} = x-component of \(F_{D}\) (N); \vec{F}_{Dy} = y-component of \(F_{D}\) (N)
Vector sum of rectangular components of force \(F_{B}\)
\vec{F}_B = force B (N); \vec{F}_{Bx} = x-component of \(F_{B}\) (N); \vec{F}_{By} = y-component of \(F_{B}\) (N)
tips: Do not assign the sign of a component from the magnitude alone; always check the quadrant or direction to set the sign.
Check whether θ is measured from the x-axis or the y-axis before using sine or cosine to find the components.
rq: Why is the sign of \(F_{x}\) negative for a force in quadrant II but positive for a force in quadrant IV?
Quadrant II lies to the left of the y-axis, where x-values are negative; quadrant IV lies to the right, where x-values are positive.
If a force points straight down along the negative y-axis, which components are non-zero and what are their signs?
Only \(F_{y}\) is non-zero, and it is negative, since the force has no horizontal part.

xq.q: A force has rectangular components \(F_x = -360\) N and \(F_y = 480\) N. Find the direction \(\theta\) of the force, measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.
xq.a: θ = 126.9° from the positive x-axis (magnitude 600 N)

xq.q: A cable pulls upward with a force \(F = 1500\) N at \(\theta = 40^\circ\) above the positive x-axis. Which value is the y-component \(F_y\)? (Calculator in degree mode.)
xq.w: With θ from the x-axis, \(F_y = F\sin\theta = 964\) N; cosine gives 1149 N, tangent gives 1259 N, and radian mode gives 1118 N.

xq.q: A force \(F\) points downward and to the right (quadrant IV). Its angle \(\theta\) is measured from the positive y-axis. Write expressions for \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) including their signs. Then show that \(\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=F\).
xq.a: Since θ is measured from the y-axis, the x-component uses sine and the y-component uses cosine. The force points right, so \(F_{x}\) = +F sinθ, and it points down, so \(F_{y}\) = -F cosθ. Then \(F_{x}\)² + \(F_{y}\)² = F²sin²θ + F²cos²θ = F²(sin²θ + cos²θ) = F², so the magnitude is F.
s: θ from y-axis, so \(F_x\) uses sin and \(F_y\) uses cos [1]

units.name: 2.2 Unit vectors for force direction
units.ov: This material introduces unit vectors i, j, k as dimensionless, magnitude-1 vectors that specify direction along the +x, +y and +z axes. A force is resolved into rectangular components and written in Cartesian form \( \mathbf{F} = F_x\mathbf{i} + F_y\mathbf{j} + F_z\mathbf{k} \). The unit vectors carry direction and the coefficients carry magnitude, sign and units (N). The notes cover only this basic notation, so the wider topic (force direction from position vectors) builds on it. Anything beyond the notes below is standard theory that I have flagged as such.
must: A unit vector has magnitude 1, no units, and specifies direction only.
\( \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} \) point along the positive x, y and z axes respectively.
Cartesian form of a force: \( \mathbf{F} = F_x\mathbf{i} + F_y\mathbf{j} + F_z\mathbf{k} \), where the components are perpendicular (rectangular).
A 2D force has no k term, e.g. \( \mathbf{F} = 4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \) N.
The components carry the units (N) and the sign; unit vectors are dimensionless.
A force pointing in the negative x direction has a negative coefficient on \( \mathbf{i} \); the unit vector itself is not made negative.
Standard result (beyond the notes): magnitude \( F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2} \), so 4i + 3j gives 5 N.
Standard result (beyond the notes): the unit vector along a force is \( \hat{\mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{F}/F \), and \( \mathbf{F} = F\hat{\mathbf{u}} \).
Standard result (beyond the notes): in 2D, \( F_x = F\cos\theta \) and \( F_y = F\sin\theta \), with \( \theta \) measured from the x-axis.
conn: Resolving a force into components with trigonometry (\( F\cos\theta, F\sin\theta \)) feeds directly into writing it in i, j, k form.
Resultant of several forces: add the i, j and k coefficients separately, then find the magnitude and direction of the sum.
Equilibrium: \( \sum F_x = 0, \sum F_y = 0, \sum F_z = 0 \) means each unit-vector coefficient of the resultant must be zero, which gives equations for unknown forces.
Position vectors between two points give a direction unit vector, which is then multiplied by the force magnitude to get Cartesian components (in 3D cable problems).
exq: Write the force \( \mathbf{F} = 4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \) N in terms of its magnitude and direction angle from the x-axis, and state the units of each term.
A 200 N force acts at 30° above the negative x-axis in the x-y plane. Express it in unit-vector form, paying attention to the signs of the components.

Three forces \( \mathbf{F}_1 = 3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} \), \( \mathbf{F}_2 = -5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} \) and an unknown \( \mathbf{F}_3 \) (all in N) are in equilibrium. Find \( \mathbf{F}_3 \) and its magnitude.
A force of 500 N acts along a line from A(0,0,0) to B(2,3,6) m. Find the unit vector from A to B and write the force as \( F_x\mathbf{i} + F_y\mathbf{j} + F_z\mathbf{k} \).
Explain why the unit vector \( \mathbf{i} \) has no units while \( F_x\mathbf{i} \) is measured in newtons, and explain how a force in the -y direction is written.

notes.t: Forces - Unit Vectors
pts: A unit vector has magnitude 1 and no units, used to give direction.
Unit vectors are commonly used for forces resolved into rectangular components.
i, j and k point in the positive x, y and z directions respectively.
A 2D force is written as its x-component times i plus its y-component times j.
defs: Unit vector
A vector of magnitude 1 with no units, used to specify direction only.
Rectangular components
The perpendicular x, y (and z) components into which a force is resolved.
eqs: Force expressed in Cartesian unit-vector form
\(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\), \(F_{z}\) = force components along x, y, z (N); \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} = unit vectors in +x, +y, +z directions (dimensionless)
tips: Components can be negative: a force pointing in the negative x direction has a negative \(F_{x}\) coefficient, not a negative unit vector.
Unit vectors themselves carry no units; the force components carry the units (e.g. N).
rq: Why do we write forces with unit vectors rather than just stating a magnitude?
A magnitude alone gives no direction; unit vectors multiplied by components carry both magnitude and direction in each axis.
If F = 4i + 3j, what is the magnitude of F?
\( |F| = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5 \) N, using the Pythagorean relation for the rectangular components.

xq.q: Two forces act at a joint: \(\mathbf{F}_1 = (500\mathbf{i} - 200\mathbf{j})\) N and \(\mathbf{F}_2 = (-200\mathbf{i} + 600\mathbf{j})\) N. Here \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{j}\) are unit vectors in the +x and +y directions. Find the magnitude of the resultant force.
A force acts 30 N to the left and 40 N downward, with \(\mathbf{i}\) in the +x direction and \(\mathbf{j}\) in the +y direction. Which is its correct unit-vector form?
xq.a: \(-30\mathbf{i} - 40\mathbf{j}\) N
o: \(-30\mathbf{i} - 40\mathbf{j}\) N
\(30\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j}\) N
\(-30\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j}\) N
\(30\mathbf{i} - 40\mathbf{j}\) N
xq.w: Left is negative x and down is negative y, so both coefficients are negative; the traps are using magnitudes only or mixing up one sign.

xq.q: A force is written \(\mathbf{F} = (4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\) N. Find its magnitude, and show that it can be written as the magnitude multiplied by the unit vector \(0.8\mathbf{i} + 0.6\mathbf{j}\). Show that this vector really is a unit vector and state what units it carries.
xq.a: F = sqrt(4² + 3²) = 5 N. The vector 0.8i + 0.6j has magnitude sqrt(0.64 + 0.36) = 1, so it is a unit vector. 5 N × (0.8i + 0.6j) = (4i + 3j) N, so F equals its magnitude times that unit vector. The unit vector has no units; the 5 N carries the units of force.
s: Unit vector is dimensionless; the units belong to the force magnitude [1]

units.name: 2.3 Superposition and resultant of concurrent forces
units.ov: This module covers replacing a set of concurrent forces (lines of action through one point) with a single resultant, using vector addition by the parallelogram/triangle rule or by components. It also covers resolving a force into perpendicular components and recombining them with Pythagoras and trigonometry. The ideas connect because component resolution is the algebraic version of the graphical rule and underpins every resultant calculation.
must: The resultant is the vector sum, not the sum of magnitudes: \( \boldsymbol{R}=\sum\boldsymbol{F} \), so \( R\neq F_1+F_2 \) in general
Resolve each force into components: \( F_x=F\cos\theta,\ F_y=F\sin\theta \), with \(\theta\) measured from the x-axis (switch to sin/cos if the angle is measured from the y-axis)
Sum components with correct signs: \( R_x=\sum F_x,\ R_y=\sum F_y \) (a force in the negative x-direction has negative \(F_x\))
Magnitude of the resultant: \( R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2} \)
Direction of the resultant: \( \tan\theta=R_y/R_x \); use the quadrant signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\), since the calculator arctan gives only one of two possible angles
Parallelogram/triangle rule: two force vectors drawn tail to tail, or head to tail, give the resultant graphically; the component method is its algebraic equivalent
A force equals the vector sum of its perpendicular components, \( \boldsymbol{F}=\boldsymbol{F}_x+\boldsymbol{F}_y \), which act at the same point, so the external effect on the body is unchanged
Definition: concurrent forces have lines of action through one common point; the resultant is the single force with the same effect as the whole system
The equivalence holds only for concurrent forces or components at the same point; forces at different points can produce moments that a single concurrent resultant does not capture
Method: draw a sketch with axes, tabulate \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) for each force, sum them, then find \(R\) and \(\theta\); check the answer against the sketch
conn: Component resolution links to the parallelogram rule: the graphical construction and the \(R_x, R_y\) sums must give the same \(R\) and \(\theta\), so one can check the other
The resultant of concurrent forces leads to equilibrium: if \(R_x=0\) and \(R_y=0\) the body is in equilibrium, so unknown forces can be found by setting the sums to zero
Resolving a force into components links to the sign convention and quadrant of the angle: one sign error in \(F_x\) or \(F_y\) changes both \(R\) and \(\theta\)
Concurrency links to moments: forces at different points need a force-couple treatment, so questions may ask when a single resultant is valid
exq: Three concurrent forces act at a point: 100 N at 0°, 150 N at 60° and 200 N at 135° measured anticlockwise from the +x axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant, stating the quadrant.
Two forces of 80 N and 120 N act at a point with an angle of 50° between them. Find the resultant using the parallelogram rule (cosine rule) and check it using components.
A 500 N force acts at 30° below the horizontal pointing to the left. Resolve it into x and y components with correct signs, and explain why its magnitude is not \(F_x+F_y\).
A third force is to be added to two given concurrent forces so that the resultant is purely vertical with magnitude 300 N. Determine the magnitude and direction of the required force.
Explain why replacing a force by its components at the same point does not change the external effect on a rigid body, but moving a component to another point does.

notes.t: Superposition of Forces
pts: Any number of concurrent forces acting at a point can be replaced by one resultant force.
The resultant is the vector sum of the forces, not their arithmetic sum of magnitudes.
The parallelogram (triangle) rule graphically builds the resultant from the two force vectors drawn tail to tail.
The equivalence holds for the external effect on the body; the single resultant produces the same effect as the original set of forces.
defs: Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through the same point on a body.
Resultant force
A single force whose effect on a body is equivalent to the combined effect of a system of concurrent forces.
eqs: Resultant of two concurrent forces (vector sum)
\(\boldsymbol{R}\) = resultant force vector (N); \(\boldsymbol{F}_1\) = first force vector (N); \(\boldsymbol{F}_2\) = second force vector (N)
tips: Do not add force magnitudes arithmetically; always add them as vectors using components or the parallelogram rule.
The equivalence applies to forces concurrent at a point; forces at different points may also produce moments that a single concurrent resultant does not capture.
rq: Why must the resultant be found by vector addition rather than by simply adding the magnitudes of F₁ and F₂?
Forces have direction as well as magnitude; forces acting at different angles partly cancel or reinforce, so only vector addition gives the correct combined effect.
What would happen to the resultant if F₁ were reversed in direction while keeping its magnitude?
The resultant would change, since the vector sum depends on direction; the magnitude could drop substantially and the direction would shift.

notes.t: Superposition of Forces
pts: Any force can be resolved into two perpendicular component vectors, \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\), that together have the same effect as the original force.
The component vectors act at the same point as the original force, so the replacement does not change the external effect on the body.
The original force is the vector sum of its components, found by vector (not simple scalar) addition.
defs: Superposition of forces
The principle that a single force may be replaced by the vector sum of its perpendicular components acting at the same point, and conversely that components may be combined into one resultant force.
eqs: Vector sum of components giving the resultant force F
\boldsymbol{F} = resultant force vector (N); \boldsymbol{F}_x = component along x-axis (N); \boldsymbol{F}_y = component along y-axis (N)
tips: Forces are vectors: components must be added vectorially, so the resultant magnitude is \( \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} \), not \( F_x + F_y \).
The equivalence holds only when the components act at the same point; moving them to different points can change the effect on a rigid body.
rq: Why can the two component forces replace the single force on the block without changing its motion?
Because the components are acting at the same point and their vector sum equals F, so they produce the same net force and therefore the same external effect.
What would happen if you added \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) as ordinary numbers, ignoring direction?
You would get the wrong magnitude, since perpendicular forces combine as vectors (via Pythagoras for magnitude), not by simple arithmetic addition.

notes.t: Resultant Force of Concurrent Forces
pts: Concurrent forces act at the same point, so their resultant is simply their vector sum.
The vector sum can be found by summing the forces component by component along each axis.
The magnitude of the resultant follows from its x and y components via Pythagoras.
The direction of the resultant is found from the ratio of its components, measured from the x-axis.
defs: Resultant force
The single force (vector sum) that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting together at a point.
Concurrent forces
Forces that all act at the same point of application on a body.
eqs: Resultant as vector sum of forces
\(R_x\) = resultant x-component (N); \(F_{1x}, F_{2x}, F_{3x}\) = x-components of each force (N)
\(R_y\) = resultant y-component (N); \(F_{1y}, F_{2y}, F_{3y}\) = y-components of each force (N)
\(R\) = magnitude of resultant (N); \(R_x, R_y\) = resultant components (N)
\(\theta\) = angle of resultant measured from the x-axis (degrees or rad); \(R_x, R_y\) = resultant components (N)
tips: Use the quadrant signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) when finding θ from tan θ, since the arctangent alone gives only one of two possible angles.
Add components with their correct signs (e.g. a force acting in the negative x-direction has negative \(F_{x}\)).
rq: Why can we add the x and y components separately instead of adding the force vectors directly?
Because vector addition is linear and the x and y directions are independent, so the sum of each component gives the component of the sum.
Why must the forces be concurrent for this method to give the resultant of the system?
Concurrent forces share one point of application, so their effects combine as a simple vector sum; non-concurrent forces would also create moments that this method ignores.
If \(R_{x}\) is negative, which quadrant does θ lie in, and why does tan θ alone not tell you?
tan θ = \(R_{y}\)/\(R_{x}\) gives the same value for opposite quadrants, so you must use the signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) to find the correct quadrant.

xq.q: Three concurrent forces act at a point O. \(F_1 = 16\) N acts in the negative x-direction. \(F_2 = 50\) N acts at \(\theta = 36.87^\circ\) above the positive x-axis (\(\cos\theta = 0.8\), \(\sin\theta = 0.6\)). \(F_3 = 23\) N acts in the negative y-direction.
