Find the magnitude of the resultant force \(R\) at O.
xq.a: R = 25 N

xq.q: Two forces, each of magnitude 30 N, act at the same point with an angle of \(120^\circ\) between their lines of action (tails together). What is the magnitude of their resultant?
o: 0 N
xq.w: \(R^2 = 30^2 + 30^2 + 2(30)(30)\cos120^\circ = 900\), so \(R = 30\) N; adding magnitudes gives 60 N, and using \(60^\circ\) gives 52 N.

xq.q: Two concurrent forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) act at a point with an angle \(\theta\) between them. Take the x-axis along \(F_1\). Show that the magnitude of the resultant is \(R = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos\theta}\), and explain why \(R\) is not generally \(F_1 + F_2\).
xq.a: With the x-axis along F1, F1 has components (F1, 0) and F2 has components (F2 cosθ, F2 sinθ). Summing components gives Rx = F1 + F2 cosθ and Ry = F2 sinθ. Then R² = Rx² + Ry² = F1² + 2F1F2 cosθ + F2²cos²θ + F2²sin²θ = F1² + F2² + 2F1F2 cosθ. Forces are vectors, so they add by components. R = F1 + F2 only when θ = 0°, when the forces are in the same direction.
s: Resolve: Rx = F1 + F2cosθ, Ry = F2sinθ
Expand and use cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 to get the result
Forces add as vectors; R = F1 + F2 only for θ = 0°

units.name: 2.4 Resolving forces along perpendicular and oblique axes
units.ov: This material covers resolving a force into components, first along perpendicular x-y axes with trigonometry and unit vectors, then along any two non-parallel axes p and q using the sine law. Both methods rest on the same idea: a force is the vector sum of its components, so the same force can be described in many axis systems. The perpendicular case is the special one in which the sine law reduces to cos and sin.
must: Perpendicular components with θ from the x-axis: \(F_x=F\cos\theta\), \(F_y=F\sin\theta\)
If the angle φ is measured from the y-axis, the functions swap: \(F_x=F\sin\phi\), \(F_y=F\cos\phi\). Always check which axis the angle is measured from.
Recover the magnitude and direction from components: \(F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}\), \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\)
Use the signs of \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) to fix the quadrant, because arctan alone is ambiguous (add 180° when \(F_x<0\)).
Unit-vector form: \(\mathbf{F}=F\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i}+F\sin\theta\,\mathbf{j}\), where i and j are dimensionless unit vectors along +x and +y.
Oblique axes p and q: \(\underline{F}=F_p\underline{e}_p+F_q\underline{e}_q\), where the components are the sides of the triangle of vector addition (a parallelogram, not a perpendicular projection).
Sine law for oblique components: \(\frac{F}{\sin(180^\circ-\alpha-\beta)}=\frac{F_p}{\sin\alpha}=\frac{F_q}{\sin\beta}\)
F is opposite the angle \(180^\circ-\alpha-\beta\); each component is opposite the angle between the other component and F. Mixing these up is the most common error.
Keep vectors and scalars distinct: \(F_p\) is a signed scalar, \(\underline{F}_p=F_p\underline{e}_p\) is a vector.
Draw the force triangle or parallelogram, label the angles and sense, and check that the components add back to F.
conn: Equilibrium of a particle: resolve into x and y components and set \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\). Choosing axes along an unknown force removes it from one equation.
Resultant of several forces: resolve each force into components, sum the components, then rebuild the magnitude and direction with Pythagoras and arctan, with quadrant checking.
Oblique resolution versus perpendicular resolution: with p and q at 90° the sine law reduces to cos and sin, which is a useful check on an answer.
Inclined planes and cables or struts: choose axes along and normal to the plane or member, which means resolving along non-horizontal axes, and write the results in unit-vector form.
exq: A 500 N force acts at 35° above the negative x-axis, pointing into the second quadrant. Find \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) and write F in i-j form.
Components are \(F_x=-120\) N and \(F_y=-80\) N. Find the magnitude and the direction measured anticlockwise from +x, explaining the quadrant choice.

A 800 N force is to be resolved along axes p and q that are 70° apart, with F at 25° from the p-axis. Use the sine law to find \(F_p\) and \(F_q\), then write F as \(F_p\underline{e}_p+F_q\underline{e}_q\).
A force is given at angle φ = 30° from the y-axis with F = 1.2 kN. Find its x and y components and its angle θ from the x-axis, and show both methods agree.
Resolve a 600 N force along two oblique axes, then check by converting the answer to x-y components. Show the vector sum returns the original force.

notes.t: Resolving forces into x and y components
pts: A force can be split into orthogonal scalar components along any pair of perpendicular axes, and the components add back to the original force by vector addition.
Components can be written using either the angle θ measured from the x-axis or the angle φ measured from the y-axis; the trig function swaps accordingly.
The force magnitude and direction are recovered from its Cartesian components using Pythagoras and the arctangent.
A force can be written in unit-vector form, with i and j giving the x and y directions.
defs: Scalar Cartesian components
The signed magnitudes of a force's projections onto the x and y axes, found by resolving the force along each orthogonal axis.
Unit vectors i and j
Dimensionless vectors of unit length pointing along the positive x and y axes respectively, used to express vectors in Cartesian form.
eqs: x-component of F using angle θ from x-axis
\(F_{x}\) = x-component (N); F = force magnitude (N); θ = angle from x-axis (rad or °)
y-component of F using angle θ from x-axis
\(F_{y}\) = y-component (N); F = force magnitude (N); θ = angle from x-axis (rad or °)
Components using angle φ measured from y-axis
\(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = components (N); F = magnitude (N); φ = angle from y-axis (rad or °)
θ = angle from x-axis (rad or °); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = components (N)
F = magnitude (N); θ = angle from x-axis; i, j = unit vectors (dimensionless)
tips: Check which axis the angle is measured from: θ from x gives cos for \(F_{x}\), while φ from y gives sin for \(F_{x}\).
Use the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) to fix the quadrant when using tan⁻¹(\(F_{y}\)/\(F_{x}\)), since the arctan alone does not give the full direction.
rq: Why must you check which axis the angle is measured from before choosing sine or cosine?

Because θ measured from the x-axis gives \(F_{x}\) = F cosθ, whereas φ measured from the y-axis swaps the functions to \(F_{x}\) = F sinφ; using the wrong pairing gives components wrong by a trig swap.
Why can the arctan formula give the wrong quadrant, and how would you fix it?
tan⁻¹(\(F_{y}\)/\(F_{x}\)) returns an angle in only one half-range, so you must use the signs of \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) to place the vector in the correct quadrant.
What if the chosen axes were not perpendicular?
The sine/cosine component formulas and Pythagoras would no longer apply directly, since the procedure is only valid for orthogonal axis pairs.

notes.t: Resolving forces into components along any pair of planar axes
pts: A force can be resolved into scalar components along any two non-parallel planar axes p and q, using unit vectors along each axis.
The sine law gives the magnitudes of the components from the triangle formed by F, \(F_{p}\) and \(F_{q}\); the angles are measured between the force and the axes.
By vector addition, the two component vectors sum to the original force vector.
Each component vector is the scalar component multiplied by the unit vector along its axis.
defs: Unit vector along an axis
A vector of magnitude one pointing along a given axis, denoted by e with a subscript giving the axis label.
Scalar component of a force
The signed magnitude of a force's projection/triangle side along a specified axis, which multiplied by the axis unit vector gives the component vector.
eqs: Sine law for force components along p and q axes

\(F\) = magnitude of force (N); \(F_p\) = component along p-axis (N); \(F_q\) = component along q-axis (N); \(\alpha\) = angle between q-axis and F-triangle side (degrees); \(\beta\) = angle between p-axis and F-triangle side (degrees)
Force as sum of unit-vector components

\(\underline{F}\) = force vector (N); \(F_p\) = scalar component along p (N); \(\underline{e}_p\) = unit vector along p (dimensionless); \(F_q\) = scalar component along q (N); \(\underline{e}_q\) = unit vector along q (dimensionless)
tips: Check the angle in the sine law: the side F is opposite the angle 180° − α − β, not α or β, so using the wrong angle gives wrong components.
Keep vectors and scalars distinct: \(F_p\) is a signed scalar while \(\underline{F}_p\) is a vector equal to \(F_p\underline{e}_p\).
rq: Why does the sine law, rather than the cosine law, suit finding the components along two axes?

The force and its two components form a triangle where angles at the axes are known, and the sine law relates each side to the opposite angle directly, giving each component without needing a third angle.
What happens to the component calculation if the p and q axes are perpendicular?
Then the triangle is right-angled, the sine law reduces to the familiar trigonometric projections \(F_{p}\) = F cos(angle) and \(F_{q}\) = F sin(angle), with the sine law still valid.

xq.q: A force \(F = 100\) N is resolved into components \(F_p\) and \(F_q\) along two oblique axes p and q. The line of action of F makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the p-axis and \(30^\circ\) with the q-axis, with F lying between the axes. Use the sine law to find the component \(F_p\).
s: The angle opposite F in the force triangle is \(180^\circ - 30^\circ - 30^\circ = 120^\circ\)

xq.q: A force of magnitude \(F = 200\) N points up and to the right, at \(\phi = 30^\circ\) measured from the positive y-axis. What is its x-component \(F_x\)?
xq.w: With the angle measured from the y-axis, \(F_x = F\sin\phi = 100\) N; using cosine (as for an angle from the x-axis) gives 173 N.
s: The angle is from the y-axis, so \(F_x = F\sin\phi\)

xq.q: A force F is to be resolved along two non-perpendicular axes p and q, with unit vectors \(\underline{e}_p\) and \(\underline{e}_q\). Sketch the force triangle and explain how the sine law gives the scalar components \(F_p\) and \(F_q\). State which angle lies opposite F and how the components combine to give F.
xq.a: Draw F, then draw lines through its tail parallel to p and through its tip parallel to q, or vice versa. This closes a triangle with sides F, Fp and Fq. If α is the angle between F and the q-axis and β is the angle between F and the p-axis, then the angle opposite F is 180° − α − β. The sine law gives F/sin(180°−α−β) = Fp/sinα = Fq/sinβ, so Fp = F sinα / sin(180°−α−β) and Fq = F sinβ / sin(180°−α−β). The vector sum is F = Fp \(e_{p}\) + Fq \(e_{q}\), where Fp and Fq are signed scalars.
s: Sketch a closed triangle of F, Fp and Fq with the axes' directions marked
Angle opposite F is 180° − α − β

units.name: 2.5 Graphical addition: parallelogram, triangle and polygon methods
units.ov: This material covers finding the resultant of concurrent forces, for example two cable forces at a support, by scale drawing (parallelogram and triangle/head-to-tail methods) and exactly by trigonometry (cosine and sine rules or components). Forces are vectors, so they are added with both magnitude and direction. The graphical result is a check on the exact calculation, and the main risk in both is using the wrong angle.
must: The resultant is a single force equivalent in effect to all the forces acting: \(\vec{F}_R=\vec{F}_{AB}+\vec{F}_{AC}\). It is a vector sum, not \(F_{AB}+F_{AC}\) arithmetically.
Parallelogram method: draw both forces from a common origin, complete the parallelogram, and the diagonal from the origin is the resultant.
Triangle (head-to-tail) method: the resultant joins the tail of the first force to the tip of the last, and the order of addition does not change it.
Fix and state a scale before drawing (e.g. 1 cm = 10 kN). Convert the measured length to force, and measure the direction from a stated reference axis.
Cosine rule for the magnitude: \(R^2=F_{AB}^2+F_{AC}^2+2F_{AB}F_{AC}\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the lines of action when both are drawn from the same point.

Angle trap: in a head-to-tail triangle the included angle is the supplement, 150° rather than 30°. Then \(R^2=F_1^2+F_2^2-2F_1F_2\cos150^\circ\), which gives the same result as the formula above with \(\theta=30^\circ\).
Use the sine rule on the force triangle to find the resultant's direction. Alternatively use components: \(R_x=\sum F_x\), \(R_y=\sum F_y\), \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\), \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\).
Give a full answer: magnitude with units (kN) and direction relative to a named axis. Check the quadrant, and check that the graphical and calculated answers agree within drawing accuracy.
Each force is defined by magnitude and direction, e.g. \(F_{AB}\) at 30° above the horizontal and \(F_{AC}\) horizontal. Read the given angles carefully before drawing.
conn: Graphical and trigonometric methods are used together: the scale drawing gives an estimate and a check, and the cosine and sine rules give the exact value.
Cosine rule versus components: both give the same resultant, but components extend easily to three or more forces, while the triangle and cosine rule suit two forces.
The resultant is the basis of equilibrium: the equilibrant is equal and opposite to the resultant, so cable-support problems reduce to \(\sum F=0\).

The supplementary-angle error links the drawing, where the head-to-tail angle is 150°, to the formula, where the angle between lines of action is 30°. Questions often test whether the sign of the cosine term is right.
exq: Two cables AB and AC pull on a support A. \(F_{AB}=40\) kN at 30° above the horizontal and \(F_{AC}=30\) kN horizontal. Draw the parallelogram to a scale of 1 cm = 10 kN, measure the resultant, then calculate its magnitude and direction exactly.

Using the head-to-tail triangle for the forces in the previous question, state the included angle and use the cosine rule and then the sine rule to find \(R\) and its angle from the horizontal. Explain why the angle is not 30°.
Two forces of 50 kN and 70 kN act at a point with an angle of 60° between them. Find the resultant by the cosine rule and verify it by resolving into components.
Explain why the resultant of two forces is generally not the sum of their magnitudes. State when it equals the sum, and when it equals the difference.
A scale drawing gives a resultant of 6.2 cm at 18° to the horizontal, with 1 cm = 10 kN. Convert this to a force, compare it with a calculated value, and comment on the sources of graphical error.

notes.t: Resultant of Two Forces: Graphical and Trigonometric Methods (Example)
pts: Two cable forces acting at the same support point can be combined into a single resultant force.
The resultant can be found graphically by drawing the forces to scale and measuring the resulting vector.
The resultant can be found exactly using trigonometry (cosine and sine rules applied to the force triangle or components).
Each force is given by its magnitude and direction: \(F_{\text{AB}}\) at 30° above the horizontal and \(F_{\text{AC}}\) horizontal.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect on a body is equivalent to the combined effect of all the individual forces acting on it.
eqs: Law of cosines for the magnitude of the resultant of two forces with angle θ between them
R = magnitude of resultant (kN); \(F_{AB}\) = force in cable AB (kN); \(F_{AC}\) = force in cable AC (kN); θ = angle between the two force lines of action (°)
tips: Watch the angle: when forces are drawn head-to-tail, the included angle in the triangle is supplementary to the given angle (150° rather than 30°).
Keep units consistent (kN) and check the direction of the resultant is stated relative to a reference axis, not only its magnitude.
rq: Why must the angle used in the cosine rule be the angle between the forces placed tail-to-tail, not the 30° shown on the diagram?

Because the triangle of vectors is built head-to-tail; the included angle between the vectors is 180° − 30° = 150° when the vectors are joined head-to-tail, so using 30° would give the wrong magnitude.
What would happen to the resultant if the 30° angle were increased while both magnitudes stayed the same?
The resultant would change, since the cosine term depends on the angle; the magnitude varies with the angle between the forces.

notes.t: Graphical addition of forces (resultant by parallelogram/triangle method)
pts: Forces can be added graphically using a scale drawing; the resultant is the vector joining the tail of the first force to the tip of the last.
A scale is fixed before drawing (here 1 cm represents 10 kN), so the measured length converts directly into force magnitude.
The resultant's magnitude is read from the scaled length and its direction is measured as an angle from the horizontal reference.
Parallelogram construction: \(F_{\text{AB}}\) and \(F_{\text{AC}}\) are drawn from a common origin and completed with dashed lines to form the parallelogram whose diagonal is the resultant.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect on a body is equivalent to the combined effect of all the forces acting on it.
eqs: Resultant of two concurrent forces (graphical result, read from scaled diagram)
\vec{F}_R = resultant force (kN); \vec{F}_{AB} = force along AB (kN); \vec{F}_{AC} = force along AC (kN)
tips: Graphical answers depend on drawing accuracy; always state the scale and quote the resultant with its direction measured from a stated reference (here the horizontal).
Do not confuse the resultant with the sum of magnitudes; forces at an angle must be added as vectors, not arithmetically.
rq: Why must the force diagram be drawn to a fixed scale, and what would go wrong if the scale were ignored?
The scale (1 cm = 10 kN) converts measured lengths into forces; without it the length carries no force value, so the magnitude (155 kN) cannot be obtained.
Why does the resultant point from the common tail of the forces to the far corner of the parallelogram rather than to either individual force?
Vector addition gives the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two forces, so the resultant is the diagonal from the shared origin to the opposite corner.

xq.q: Two cables meet at a support A. Cable AC pulls with \(F_{AC} = 50\) kN horizontally and cable AB pulls with \(F_{AB} = 30\) kN at \(60^\circ\) to AC (tails together at A). Using the law of cosines for two forces with angle \(\theta\) between their lines of action, find the magnitude of the resultant \(R\).
xq.a: R = 70 kN

xq.q: Two cable forces are added graphically using a scale of 1 cm = 10 kN. The resultant, measured on the parallelogram diagonal, is 6.4 cm long. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
xq.a: 64 kN
o: 6.4 kN
640 kN
64 kN
xq.w: Force = measured length × scale = 6.4 × 10 = 64 kN; the traps are forgetting the scale or applying it the wrong way round.
s: Multiply the length by the scale factor

xq.q: Two forces of magnitudes \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) have lines of action \(30^\circ\) apart. They are added by the triangle method, drawn head to tail. Explain why the included angle in the force triangle is \(150^\circ\), and show that the cosine rule then gives \(R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos30^\circ\).
xq.a: When F2 is drawn from the tip of F1, the interior angle of the triangle between them is the supplement of the 30° between the lines of action, i.e. 180° − 30° = 150°. The resultant is the side opposite this angle. The cosine rule gives R² = F1² + F2² − 2F1F2 cos150°. Since cos150° = −cos30°, this becomes R² = F1² + F2² + 2F1F2 cos30°, which matches the parallelogram result. Taking R as the sum of magnitudes would be wrong.
s: Resultant is the side opposite the 150° angle

units.name: 2.6 Resultant of two forces by cosine and sine rules
units.ov: This module finds the resultant of concurrent forces, first for two forces with the parallelogram/triangle of forces solved by the cosine rule (magnitude) and sine rule (direction). It then extends to several forces by resolving into x and y components, or by the graphical force polygon, and to three forces by solving two triangles in sequence. The common thread is that the resultant is the single equivalent force, and the main risk is using the wrong angle or reference axis.
must: Resultant = single force with the same external effect as the system; for two forces it is the closing side of the triangle of forces
Cosine rule for magnitude: \(F^2=F_1^2+F_2^2-2F_1F_2\cos\gamma\), where \(\gamma\) is the included angle in the triangle (tail-to-head), not necessarily the angle between the lines of action as drawn
Triangle vs. parallelogram angle: using \(\cos 30^\circ\) instead of \(\cos 150^\circ\) (supplementary angle) flips the sign of the cosine term and gives a wrong magnitude
Sine rule for direction: \(\frac{\sin\beta}{F_1}=\frac{\sin\gamma}{F}\); pair each side with its opposite angle
Take the square root at the end: e.g. \(\bar F^2=24400\) gives \(\bar F=156.20\) kN
Component method for concurrent forces: \(F_x=F\cos\theta,\ F_y=F\sin\theta\) with \(\theta\) from the positive x-axis; \(F=\sqrt{(\sum F_x)^2+(\sum F_y)^2}\); left/down components are negative
Direction from components: \(\tan\theta=\sum F_y/\sum F_x\), with the quadrant fixed by the signs of the sums
Force polygon: draw forces head-to-tail; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last, with a consistent scale
Concurrent forces and transmissibility: a force can slide along its line of action without changing its external effect, so forces through a common point can be treated as acting at that point

Three or more forces by repeated triangles: combine two to get \(\bar F\), then combine with the third (e.g. \(\cos 56.33^\circ\)); convert \(\beta\) to the horizontal by adding or subtracting the known angle (e.g. 11.33°); keep units (kN vs N) and calculator in degree mode
conn: Cosine rule then sine rule: the magnitude from the cosine rule is needed as the denominator in the sine rule for direction, so an error in the first propagates to the second

Two-force triangle then third force: the resultant of the first pair becomes a known force in a second triangle, and its angle (e.g. 11.33°) must be added to the angle from the sine rule to give the final direction
Components method vs. trigonometric triangle method vs. force polygon: all give the same resultant, so one can be used as a check on another
Transmissibility and concurrency: they justify moving all forces to a common point before the resultant is found
exq: Two forces of 100 kN and 60 kN act at a point with 30° between their lines of action as drawn, so the triangle angle is 150°. Use the cosine rule to find the resultant magnitude (check: 154.9 kN) and the sine rule to find its angle to the 100 kN force.
Two forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) have a 120° included angle in the force triangle and \(\bar F^2=24400\) kN². Find \(\bar F\) (156.20 kN) and the angle \(\alpha\) between \(\bar F\) and \(F_1\).

Three concurrent forces act on a bracket: \(F_1\) at 15° below the x-axis, \(F_2\) at 45° above the x-axis to the right, and \(F_3\) at 45° above the x-axis to the left. Resolve into components, find \(\sum F_x\), \(\sum F_y\), the resultant magnitude, and its direction from the x-axis.

Combine \(\bar F=156.20\) kN (at 11.33° to the horizontal) with \(F_3\) using an included angle of 56.33°. Find the final resultant and its angle to the horizontal, stating which axis \(\beta\) is measured from.
Draw a scaled force polygon for a system of three concurrent forces, identify the resultant as the closing side, and check the measured magnitude and direction against a component calculation.

notes.t: Solving vector resultants using the cosine and sine rules
pts: The resultant of two vectors can be found by the parallelogram law, then solved using trigonometry on the resulting triangle.
The cosine rule relates the three sides of a triangle when one included angle is known; use it to find the magnitude of the resultant.
The sine rule relates each side to the sine of its opposite angle; use it to find the direction of the resultant.
eqs: Cosine rule: finds an unknown side from two sides and the included angle
\(c\) = side opposite angle \(\gamma\) (m or N); \(a,b\) = other two sides (m or N); \(\gamma\) = included angle (degrees or rad)
Sine rule: relates sides to their opposite angles in any triangle
\(a,b,c\) = side lengths (m or N); \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) = angles opposite \(a,b,c\) respectively (degrees or rad)
tips: Check whether the angle used in the cosine rule is the included angle between the two sides; using the supplementary angle flips the sign of the cosine term.
Keep the sine rule pairing consistent: each side must be paired with the angle opposite it (e.g. \(a\) with \(\alpha\)).
rq: Why must the cosine rule be used before the sine rule when finding a resultant force from two forces at an angle?
The sine rule needs a side and its opposite angle as a pair; with only two sides and an included angle, the cosine rule is the only way to find the third side (the resultant magnitude).
What if the angle between the two vectors is the angle inside the parallelogram rather than the angle in the triangle?

The angle must be the one between the vectors when tail-to-tail; the triangle's interior angle is supplementary (\(180^\circ -\theta\)), so using the wrong one changes the cosine sign and gives a wrong resultant.

notes.t: Resultant of two forces using the cosine and sine rules
pts: Two concurrent forces can be replaced by a single resultant force that has the same effect on the structure; the triangle of forces is solved with the cosine rule for magnitude.
The cosine rule gives the magnitude of the resultant from the two force magnitudes and the included angle between them.
The sine rule then gives the direction of the resultant, i.e. the angle β between one force and the resultant.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has exactly the same effect on a body as a system of forces acting on it.
eqs: Magnitude of resultant force by the cosine rule
F = resultant force (N or kN); \(F_{AB}\), \(F_{AC}\) = component forces (N or kN); γ = angle between \(F_{AB}\) and \(F_{AC}\) (degrees)
Direction of resultant by the sine rule
β = angle between \(F_{AB}\) and the resultant F (degrees); \(F_{AB}\) = force (N or kN); γ = included angle (degrees); F = resultant force (N or kN)
tips: Use the angle γ between the two forces as drawn in the triangle of forces, not the external angle; using cos 30° instead of cos 150° gives the wrong magnitude.
Keep units consistent: \(F_{\text{AB}}\) = 100 and \(F_{\text{AC}}\) = 60 are in kN, so F = 154.9 kN, not N.
rq: Why is the cosine rule used first, and the sine rule second?
The cosine rule needs only the two sides and the included angle to find the unknown third side F; once F is known, the sine rule can find an angle, β, opposite a known side.
What would change in the resultant if the included angle γ were 30° instead of 150°?
cos 30° is positive while cos 150° is negative, so the subtracted term becomes smaller and the resultant magnitude would be larger, because the forces would point more nearly in the same direction.

notes.t: Concurrent forces and resultant using trigonometry
pts: Three forces act through a common point (concurrent), so the principle of transmissibility allows each force to be treated as acting at the bracket's centre.
For a concurrent force system, the resultant is found by resolving each force into x and y components, summing them, then combining the sums by Pythagoras.

Angles must be measured consistently from the positive x-axis to determine the sign (direction) of each component; \(F_{1}\) lies 15° below the x-axis, while \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) lie 45° above it, \(F_{2}\) to the right and \(F_{3}\) to the left.
defs: Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point.
Principle of transmissibility
A force acting on a rigid body may be moved along its line of action without changing its external effect on the body.
Resultant force
A single force that has the same external effect as the whole system of forces acting on a body.
eqs: F = resultant force (kN); \(\sum F_x\) = sum of x-components (kN); \(\sum F_y\) = sum of y-components (kN)
Components of a force at angle θ
F = force magnitude (kN); θ = angle from the positive x-axis (degrees); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = components (kN)
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: components pointing left or down are negative when using the angle from the positive x-axis.
Check your calculator is in degree mode when computing \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) of the 15° and 45° angles.
rq: Why can each force be moved to the centre of the bracket before resolving?
Because the forces are concurrent and the principle of transmissibility lets a force slide along its line of action without changing its external effect on the rigid body.
Why does \(F_{1}\) contribute a negative y-component even though its magnitude is positive?
Because it points 15° below the x-axis, so its vertical component \(F_1\sin(-15^\circ)\) is negative; the sign comes from the direction, not the magnitude.

notes.t: Force polygon method for finding a resultant force
pts: Forces are added graphically by placing them head-to-tail to form an open polygon; the resultant is the closing side.
The resultant runs from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force, so its direction is reversed relative to the traversal of the polygon.
The force polygon method gives the magnitude and direction of the resultant F, which can be measured from the drawing or obtained by resolving components.
defs: Force polygon
A graphical construction in which force vectors are drawn head-to-tail in sequence; the closing side (from the start of the first vector to the end of the last) represents the resultant force.
Resultant force
The single force whose effect is equivalent to the combined effect of a system of forces; it is represented by the closing side of the force polygon.
tips: The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force, not from the tail of the last force to the head of the first.
Use a consistent scale and measure angles from the x-axis when reading direction from a graphical force polygon.
rq: Why must the forces be placed head-to-tail rather than all starting from the same point?

Head-to-tail placement makes the vector sum equal to the closing side, since each force is added to the running total; the same-start method is the parallelogram/triangle approach for only two forces at a time.
What if the polygon closes with the arrow pointing the opposite way from the traversal order?
That is correct behaviour: the resultant is directed from the start of the first force to the end of the last, so it points opposite to the closing direction of the chain of arrows.

notes.t: Resultant of two forces using the cosine and sine rules
pts: The magnitude of the resultant of two forces is found with the cosine rule (law of cosines), using the angle between the two force vectors in the triangle (120°) rather than the angle between the forces' lines of action.
Once the resultant magnitude is known, the sine rule gives the angle α that the resultant makes with one of the component forces.
The resultant F̄ = 156.20 kN is obtained by taking the square root of 24400, so the squared value must be square-rooted before use.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same external effect as a system of forces acting together on a body; found by vector addition of the individual forces.
eqs: Magnitude of resultant of two forces (cosine rule)
\(\bar{F}\) = magnitude of resultant force (kN); \(F_1\), \(F_2\) = magnitudes of the two forces (kN); 120° = included angle in the force triangle
\(\alpha\) = angle between resultant and \(F_1\) (degrees); \(F_2\) = force magnitude (kN); \(\bar{F}\) = resultant magnitude (kN)
tips: Make sure the calculator is in degree mode when evaluating cos120° and sin120°.
Take the square root of the sum after applying the cosine rule; the value 24400 is \(\bar{F}^2\), not \(\bar{F}\).
rq: Why must the angle 120° be used in the cosine rule rather than 60°?
In the force triangle the 120° angle lies between the tail-to-tail sides; using the included angle in the triangle gives the correct magnitude, and cos120° = −0.5 accounts for the sign change.
What would happen to the resultant if F2 were applied in the opposite direction?
The included angle would change to 60°, giving a smaller resultant; the magnitude depends on the angle between the vectors as drawn tip-to-tail.

notes.t: Resultant of two forces using the cosine and sine rules
pts: The resultant of two non-parallel forces is found by the triangle (cosine rule) method, using the angle between them.
The cosine rule gives the magnitude of the resultant from the two force magnitudes and the included angle.
The sine rule then gives the angle β of the resultant relative to the reference direction (the y-axis here).
The final direction is measured to the horizontal by adding the known angle of F̄ (11.33°) to β.
defs: Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as the combination of two or more forces acting on a body.
eqs: Magnitude of resultant of two forces (cosine rule)
F = resultant magnitude (kN); \bar{F} = magnitude of known force (kN); \(F_{3}\) = magnitude of force \(F_{3}\) (kN)
β = angle of resultant from the y-axis (°); \(F_{3}\) = magnitude of \(F_{3}\) (kN); F = resultant magnitude (kN)
tips: Check the included angle used in the cosine rule: it must be the angle between the two force vectors as drawn tail-to-tail, not the supplementary angle.
Keep the reference axis consistent: β is measured from the y-axis, so convert to the horizontal by adding or subtracting the given angle before giving the final answer.
rq: Why must the cosine rule be used here rather than simply adding the two force magnitudes?
Because the forces are not parallel; their vector sum depends on the angle between them, so the cosine term accounts for the non-collinear geometry.
Why is the angle β added to 11.33° to give the direction relative to the horizontal?
β is measured from the y-axis (vertical), so the reference must be converted to the horizontal, and the 11.33° offset of the known force links the two reference frames.

xq.q: Two concurrent forces act at point A: \(F_{AB}=100\) kN and \(F_{AC}=60\) kN. The angle between their lines of action, measured in the parallelogram, is 30°. Use the triangle of forces and the cosine rule to find the magnitude of the resultant force \(F\).
s: Angle in the triangle of forces is the supplement: γ = 180° − 30° = 150°

xq.q: Two forces of 80 N and 50 N act at a point with 120° between their lines of action. Using the cosine rule and then the sine rule on the triangle of forces, find the angle β between the 80 N force and the resultant.
s: The side opposite β is the 50 N force: sinβ/50 = sin60°/70

xq.q: Forces of 30 N and 40 N both act away from a point A, and the angle between their lines of action is 60°. The resultant is found with the cosine rule on the triangle of forces. What is its magnitude?
xq.w: The included angle in the force triangle is 180° − 60° = 120°, giving R² = 900 + 1600 + 1200 = 3700; using cos60° gives 36.1 N, a right angle gives 50 N, and a straight sum gives 70 N.

units.name: 3.1 Scalar components and the parallelogram law
units.ov: This material shows how to find the resultant of concurrent forces in two ways. The first is to resolve each force into signed x and y scalar components, sum them, and recover the magnitude and direction with Pythagoras and arctan. The second is the parallelogram law, which gives the resultant of two forces from the angle between them using the cosine rule. Both methods give the same answer, so each can be used to check the other. The worked example (T = 200 N at 45° to the upper left, P = 80 N along +x) runs through all three pages.
must: Resolve a force as \(F_x=F\cos\theta\) and \(F_y=F\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the +x axis. Always check which angle you have been given.
Sum components separately and algebraically: \(R_x=\sum F_x\), \(R_y=\sum F_y\). Left and down are negative.
Resultant magnitude: \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\).
Resultant direction: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\). The calculator only returns −90° to 90°, so find the quadrant from the signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\) and add 180° if \(R_x<0\).
Parallelogram law: the resultant of two concurrent forces is the diagonal of the parallelogram, from the common tail.
Magnitude from the parallelogram law: \(R=\sqrt{T^2+P^2+2TP\cos\theta}\). Here \(\theta\) is the angle between the two forces tail-to-tail, not the angle to the x-axis.
Worked example: T at 135° from +x and P at 0° gives an angle of 135° between them. \(R_x=80-141.4=-61.4\) N, \(R_y=141.4\) N, \(R\approx154\) N at about 113.5° from +x (66.5° above the −x axis).
Special angles give quick sign checks: a force at 270° has \(F_x=0\) and \(F_y=-F\), and a force along +x contributes only to \(R_x\).
Keep units consistent (all forces in N) and state the answer as magnitude plus direction, with the reference axis stated.
conn: Components and the parallelogram law are the same calculation. Use the cosine-rule result \(R=154\) N to check the component result \(\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\).
Resolving forces into components feeds directly into equilibrium. Setting \(R_x=0\) and \(R_y=0\) gives unknown forces or angles.
Quadrant checking links the signs of the components to the arctan result. A wrong sign on one component changes both the magnitude and the direction.
The angle between the forces is not the angle from the x-axis. Converting between them (for example 45° from the horizontal becomes 135° between the forces when T points up-left) is a common trap.
exq: Forces of 200 N at 45° to the upper left of the +x axis and 80 N along +x act at point A. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant using components, then verify it with the parallelogram law.
Three concurrent forces of 100 N at 30°, 150 N at 140° and 80 N at 270° (all from +x) act at a point. Find the resultant magnitude and its angle from +x, stating the quadrant.
Two forces of 60 N and 90 N have an angle of 50° between them. Find the resultant magnitude and its angle relative to the 90 N force.
A resultant has \(R_x=-61.4\) N and \(R_y=141.4\) N. Explain why \(\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\) on a calculator gives −66.5° and state the correct direction from +x.
A force P acts along +x and T = 200 N acts at 45° above −x. Find the value of P that makes the resultant purely vertical, and give that resultant.

notes.t: Addition of Forces – Scalar Components
pts: Each force is resolved into x and y scalar components using its magnitude and angle measured from the +x axis.
Resultant components are found by summing the x-components and the y-components separately (algebraically, with sign).
The resultant magnitude follows from Pythagoras applied to its components, and its direction from the arctangent of the component ratio.
Components carry sign: a force at 270° points along −y, so its y-component is negative while its x-component is zero.
defs: Scalar component
The signed magnitude of a force's projection onto a coordinate axis, equal to F cos θ along x and F sin θ along y for a force at angle θ from the +x axis.
Resultant force
The single force whose effect equals the combined effect of all forces acting on a body; found by vector addition of components.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = x-component (N); F = force magnitude (N); θ = angle from +x axis (°)
\(F_{y}\) = y-component (N); F = force magnitude (N); θ = angle from +x axis (°)
\(F_{Rx}\) = resultant x-component (N); \(F_{Ax}\), \(F_{Bx}\), \(F_{Cx}\) = x-components of each force (N)
\(F_{Ry}\) = resultant y-component (N); \(F_{Ay}\), \(F_{By}\), \(F_{Cy}\) = y-components of each force (N)
θ = angle of resultant from +x axis (°); \(F_{Ry}\), \(F_{Rx}\) = resultant components (N)
tips: Components must be added algebraically with their signs; forgetting that a negative component points in the negative axis direction is a common error.
The angle θ in F = F cos θ and F sin θ must be measured from the +x axis; using the angle from another reference gives wrong components.
rq: Why is the force at 270° assigned a zero x-component even though it has a large magnitude?
A force at 270° points straight down along the −y axis, so its projection onto the x-axis is cos 270° = 0 and it contributes only to the y-component (−2.5 N).
Why must the resultant's direction be checked against the signs of \(F_{\text{Rx}}\) and \(F_{\text{Ry}}\) rather than taken from arctan alone?
tan θ gives the same value for opposite quadrants, so the signs of \(F_{\text{Rx}}\) and \(F_{\text{Ry}}\) are needed to place the resultant in the correct quadrant.
What would change in the resultant if the 45° force were directed at 135° instead?
Its x-component would become negative (−3.5 N) while its y-component stays +3.5 N, so \(F_{\text{Rx}}\) would fall to 1.5 N and the resultant magnitude and angle would change.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces (worked example)
pts: Concurrent forces acting at a single point A can be added vectorially by resolving each force into x and y components.
The resultant is found from the sum of components: \( R_x = \sum F_x \) and \( R_y = \sum F_y \), then \( R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} \).
Force T = 200 N acts at 45° to the x-axis towards the upper left, so it has a negative x-component and a positive y-component.
Force P = 80 N acts horizontally along the positive x-direction, so it contributes only to \( R_x \).
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same effect as the combined action of all the forces acting on a body.
eqs: R = resultant force magnitude (N); \( R_x \) = sum of x-components (N); \( R_y \) = sum of y-components (N)
\( \theta \) = angle of resultant from the x-axis (°); \( R_x \), \( R_y \) = force components (N)
tips: Take care with signs: forces pointing left or down are negative in the x or y direction respectively.
Check the quadrant of the resultant angle when using \( \tan^{-1} \), since the calculator gives only angles between −90° and 90°.
rq: Why must the 45° angle be applied to the x-axis rather than the y-axis when resolving T?
The 45° is measured from the horizontal x-axis in the figure, so the cosine gives the x-component and the sine gives the y-component.
What would change in the resultant if P acted in the negative x-direction instead?
\( R_x \) would change sign and become \( -200\cos 45^\circ - 80 \), altering both the magnitude and the direction of R.

notes.t: Parallelogram Law
pts: Two forces acting at a point can be combined into a single resultant force using the parallelogram law, with the resultant being the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two force vectors.
The resultant R of forces T and P acting at point A is found by drawing a parallelogram with T and P as adjacent sides; R is the diagonal from the common origin.
Here T = 200 N acts at 45° to the horizontal and P = 80 N acts horizontally, both applied at point A.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same effect as the combination of two or more forces acting at a point.
Parallelogram law
The rule that the resultant of two concurrent forces is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides represent the two forces.
eqs: Magnitude of resultant of two concurrent forces with angle θ between them
R = resultant force (N); T = first force (N); P = second force (N); θ = angle between the two forces (°)
tips: Ensure the angle used in the cosine term is the angle between the two force vectors tail-to-tail, not the angle measured to the x-axis (e.g. the 45° shown is from the horizontal).
Keep units consistent: both forces must be in newtons before combining them.
rq: Why must both forces be drawn from the same point before applying the parallelogram law?
The parallelogram law requires the two vectors to be concurrent (tail-to-tail) so they form adjacent sides of a parallelogram; only then is the diagonal the resultant.
What would happen to R if the angle between T and P were increased from 0° to 180°?
R would decrease from T+P to |T−P| because the cosine term changes from +1 to −1, so the forces oppose each other more.

xq.q: Three concurrent forces act at a point. \(F_A=100\) N acts at 0° to the +x axis, \(F_B=150\) N at 60° and \(F_C=200\) N at 270°, all angles measured from the +x axis. Find the magnitude of the resultant.

A force T = 200 N acts at A at 45° to the x-axis towards the upper left, and a force P = 80 N acts along the +x direction. Find the direction of the resultant, measured anticlockwise from the +x axis.
xq.a: θ ≈ 113.5° from the +x axis
s: \(R_{x}\) < 0 and \(R_{y}\) > 0, so the resultant is in the second quadrant: θ = 180° − 66.5° = 113.5°

xq.q: The summed components of a resultant are \(R_x=-50\) N and \(R_y=+80\) N. What is the direction of the resultant measured anticlockwise from the +x axis?
xq.w: tan⁻¹(80/−50) = −58.0° on a calculator, but \(R_{x}\) < 0 and \(R_{y}\) > 0 puts the resultant in the second quadrant, so θ = 180° − 58.0° = 122.0°.
s: Quadrant check: \(R_{x}\) negative, \(R_{y}\) positive, so second quadrant

units.name: 3.2 Resultant of concurrent forces by x,y components
units.ov: This module covers finding the single resultant of a set of concurrent forces by resolving each force into perpendicular x and y components, summing the components algebraically, and recombining them. Resolution (trigonometry and signs) feeds into summation, then Pythagoras gives the magnitude and the arctangent, with a quadrant check, gives the direction. Accuracy depends on consistent sign conventions and on correctly identifying which axis each angle is measured from.
must: Resolve every force into rectangular components: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\) when \(\theta\) is measured from the x-axis; swap cos and sin if the angle is measured from the y-axis.
Resultant components are algebraic sums: \(R_x = \sum F_x\), \(R_y = \sum F_y\), which is the same as \(\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{F}_1+\boldsymbol{F}_2+\dots\).
Magnitude by Pythagoras: \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\).
Direction: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\); the calculator only returns −90° to 90°, so check the quadrant from the signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\).
Quadrant correction: if \(R_x<0\), add 180° to the calculator angle (or quote the angle to the negative x-axis); state clearly which axis the angle is measured from.
Sign convention: positive x or y direction is positive, left or down is negative, and it must be applied consistently to every force.
Check the angle reference for each force (e.g. 30° and 45° measured from different axes) before choosing sin or cos.
A force along an axis has a zero component on the other axis (e.g. \(F_3\) contributes only to \(R_y\)).
Definitions: the resultant is the single force with the same effect as all the forces; rectangular components are perpendicular projections whose vector sum equals the original force.
Set the calculator to degree mode and keep intermediate values unrounded, quoting the final answer in N and degrees.
conn: Resolution and sign convention feed directly into the sums: one wrong sign in a component corrupts both \(R\) and \(\theta\).
The signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\) determine the quadrant, which fixes the true direction after the arctangent.

Component resolution is the basis for equilibrium: \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) mean the resultant is zero, so a missing force is minus the resultant of the others (e.g. tension \(T\) and force \(P\) problems).
The component method is the algebraic equivalent of the graphical triangle/parallelogram law and can be used to check it.
exq: Three concurrent forces act at a point: 100 N at 30° above the +x axis, 150 N at 45° above the −x axis, and 80 N vertically downward. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant, stating the angle from the +x axis.
A tension \(T\) = 200 N at 60° to the horizontal and a horizontal force \(P\) = 120 N to the left act on a bracket. Find \(R_x\), \(R_y\), \(R\) and \(\theta\), with a sketch showing the quadrant.
The resultant of two forces has \(R_x = -45\) N and \(R_y = 30\) N. Calculate \(R\) and \(\theta\), and explain why the calculator value of \(\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\) is wrong as the direction.
Forces of 50 N, 80 N and 60 N act at angles of 20°, 135° and 250° measured anticlockwise from +x. Determine the resultant magnitude and direction.
A fourth force is added so that the system in the previous question is in equilibrium. Determine its magnitude and direction.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces using x,y components
pts: Resolve each force into x and y components before adding them; the resultant components are the algebraic sums of the component values.
A force at an angle is resolved with cosine for the x component and sine for the y component, and its sign depends on its direction.
The magnitude of the resultant is found by Pythagoras applied to its components.
The direction of the resultant is found from the tangent of the ratio of components, but the calculator result must be placed in the correct quadrant.
defs: Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as the combined action of all the forces acting at a point.
Rectangular components
The perpendicular projections of a force onto the x and y axes, whose vector sum equals the original force.
eqs: \(R_{x}\) = resultant x-component (N); \(T_{x}\) = x-component of tension (N); \(P_{x}\) = x-component of force P (N)
\(R_{y}\) = resultant y-component (N); \(T_{y}\) = y-component of tension (N); \(P_{y}\) = y-component of force P (N)
tips: Do not take the arctangent of \(R_{y}\)/\(R_{x}\) alone without checking the quadrant; the calculator returns an angle between −90° and 90°.
Keep sign conventions consistent: components along the positive x or y axis are positive, opposite directions are negative.
rq: Why is the calculator angle tan⁻¹(−2.30) = −66.5° not the final answer here?
Because \(R_{x}\) is negative and \(R_{y}\) positive, the resultant lies in the second quadrant, so 180° is added to give 113.5°.
Why is \(P_{y}\) = 0 in this problem?
Force P = 80 N acts horizontally along the x-axis, so it has no y-component.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces (worked example)
pts: The resultant of concurrent forces is found by summing their x and y components separately, then combining them.
Resolve each force into components using the angle it makes with the x or y axis; sign depends on direction.
Magnitude comes from Pythagoras on the summed components; direction from the arctangent of their ratio, quadrant checked.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect on a body is equivalent to the combined effect of all the individual forces acting on it.
eqs: Magnitude of the resultant from its components
\(F_{R}\) = resultant force magnitude (N); \sum \(F_{x}\) = sum of x-components (N); \sum \(F_{y}\) = sum of y-components (N)
Direction of the resultant from its components
\theta = angle of resultant measured from the x-axis (degrees); \sum \(F_{y}\) = sum of y-components (N); \sum \(F_{x}\) = sum of x-components (N)
tips: Watch the angle reference: 30° and 45° are measured from different axes in this figure, so resolve each force carefully.
Keep track of signs: forces pointing left or down are negative components, a common source of error.
rq: Why must the force components be added algebraically (with signs) rather than adding the magnitudes directly?
Forces act in different directions, so adding magnitudes ignores direction; signed component sums correctly cancel or reinforce effects along each axis.
If the arctangent gives an angle in the wrong quadrant, how do you correct the direction?
Use the signs of \sum \(F_{x}\) and \sum \(F_{y}\) to determine the quadrant, adding 180° when \sum \(F_{x}\) is negative.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces using rectangular components
pts: Resolve each force into x and y components, then sum the components separately to get \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).
The resultant magnitude comes from Pythagoras applied to the summed components.
The direction is found from the arctangent of the component ratio, but the quadrant must be checked from the signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).
Forces with no x-component (\(F_{3}\) here) contribute zero to \(R_{x}\) and only to \(R_{y}\).
defs: Resultant force
The single force that has the same external effect as the system of concurrent forces acting together, found as the vector sum of those forces.
Rectangular components
The orthogonal projections of a force onto the x and y axes, \(F_{x}\) = F cosθ and \(F_{y}\) = F sinθ, measured from the positive x-axis.
eqs: Resultant force vector as sum of forces
\(R_x\) = resultant x-component (N); \(F_{ix}\) = x-component of force i (N)
\(R_y\) = resultant y-component (N); \(F_{iy}\) = y-component of force i (N)
\(\theta\) = angle of resultant from x-axis (degrees); \(R_x, R_y\) = components (N)
tips: Keep sign conventions consistent: forces pointing left or down give negative components, and a negative \(R_{x}\) changes the quadrant of θ.
Make sure the calculator is in degree mode when evaluating cos, sin and tan⁻¹ of angles given in degrees.
rq: Why does \(F_{3}\) contribute nothing to the x-sum in this problem?
\(F_{3}\) acts vertically (along the y-axis), so its x-component is zero: \(F_{3x}\) = 0.
Why must you check the quadrant when finding θ from tan⁻¹(\(R_{y}\)/\(R_{x}\))?
The calculator returns an angle between −90° and 90°, so if \(R_{x}\) is negative (as here, \(R_{x}\) = −38.9 N) the true direction lies in the second quadrant and must be corrected by adding 180°.
What if the force \(F_{2}\) were given as 300 N at 45° above the horizontal instead of 45° to the vertical?
Its components would change to \(F_{2x}\) = 300cos45° and \(F_{2y}\) = 300sin45°, so the sums \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\), and therefore R and θ, would change.

xq.q: Three concurrent forces act at a point. \(F_1=300\) N acts 30° above the +x axis (up and to the right), \(F_2=250\) N acts 45° above the −x axis (up and to the left), and \(F_3=400\) N acts vertically downwards. Find the magnitude of the resultant.

Three forces act at a point. \(F_1=400\) N acts 60° above the +x axis, \(F_2=300\) N acts along the −x axis, and \(F_3=200\) N acts 30° below the −x axis (down and to the left). Find the direction of the resultant, measured anticlockwise from the +x axis.
xq.a: θ ≈ 138.0° from the +x axis
s: \(R_{x}\) < 0 and \(R_{y}\) > 0, so the resultant is in the second quadrant: θ = 180° − 42.0° ≈ 138.0°

xq.q: A resultant has components \(R_x=-30\) N and \(R_y=-40\) N. Find its magnitude and direction from the +x axis. Explain why using \(\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\) on a calculator alone gives the wrong direction here, and how you correct it.
xq.a: R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 N. The calculator gives tan⁻¹(−40/−30) = tan⁻¹(1.333) = 53.1°, because the two negative signs cancel in the ratio and the result is limited to −90° to 90°. Since both \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) are negative the resultant lies in the third quadrant, so θ = 180° + 53.1° = 233.1° anticlockwise from +x (equivalently 126.9° clockwise from +x).
s: The ratio \(R_{y}\)/\(R_{x}\) loses the signs, so the calculator returns 53.1°, a first-quadrant angle
Identify the quadrant from the signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\): both negative, so third quadrant

units.name: 3.3 Worked examples: cable and bracket forces
units.ov: This material covers finding the resultant of concurrent forces (cable forces at a support and forces on a bracket) by resolving each force into rectangular components, summing them algebraically, and recombining with Pythagoras and arctangent. The method is the same in every example: choose axes, resolve, sum with signs, then find magnitude and direction.
must: Resolve a force at angle \(\theta\) from the x-axis: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\)
Always check which axis the angle is measured from; if it is measured from the vertical, sine and cosine swap
Sum components separately in each direction: \(\sum F_x\) and \(\sum F_y\), never add magnitudes directly
Sign convention: +x right and +y up; leftward or downward components are negative
Resultant magnitude: \(R=\sqrt{(\sum F_x)^2+(\sum F_y)^2}\)
Resultant direction: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(\sum F_y/\sum F_x)\), with the quadrant checked from the signs of the components (or use atan2)
A horizontal force (0°) has no y-component, and a vertical force (90°) has no x-component
The resultant is the single force with the same effect as all the concurrent forces
Keep units consistent (kN), and state the answer with magnitude, angle, and the reference axis and sense
Sketch the force diagram and the resultant's components to verify its direction before finalising
conn: Resultant of concurrent forces leads to equilibrium: if \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\), the resultant is zero, and the same resolution finds unknown cable tensions
Quadrant checking in the arctangent links to sign conventions: the signs of \(\sum F_x\) and \(\sum F_y\) determine the direction, so a sign slip gives a wrong angle as well as a wrong magnitude
Cable and bracket resultants give the support reaction (equal and opposite to the resultant), which feeds into later structural and stress analysis
Geometry of cable layouts (given as lengths or slopes rather than angles) converts to angles via trigonometry before resolving
exq: Two cables AB and AC pull on a support at A with forces of, say, 8 kN at 30° above the horizontal and 6 kN horizontal. Find the resultant's magnitude and direction.

A bracket carries three concurrent forces at different angles, including leftward and downward components. Resolve them, find \(\sum F_x\) and \(\sum F_y\), and give the resultant's magnitude and angle from the +x axis, stating its quadrant.
A resultant has \(\sum F_x=-4\) kN and \(\sum F_y=3\) kN. Calculate its direction from the +x axis and explain why \(\tan^{-1}(3/-4)\) alone on a calculator gives the wrong angle.
A cable force is given with its angle measured from the vertical. Re-express the angle, resolve the force, and determine what support reaction is needed to balance the resultant.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent cable forces at a support
pts: Resolve each inclined cable force into horizontal and vertical components using cosine and sine of its angle.
A force at 0° has no vertical component, so the horizontal cable contributes only an x-component.
The resultant components are found by adding the components of all forces in each direction separately.
The resultant magnitude follows from the Pythagorean combination of the summed components.
defs: Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as all the given forces acting together at a point.
eqs: Horizontal component of a force F at angle θ
F = applied force (kN); θ = angle from the horizontal (degrees); \(F_{x}\) = horizontal component (kN)
Vertical component of a force F at angle θ
F = applied force (kN); θ = angle from the horizontal (degrees); \(F_{y}\) = vertical component (kN)
\sum F_x = F_{AB_x} + F_{AC_x}, \quad \sum F_y = F_{AB_y} + F_{AC_y}
tips: Check that the angle is measured from the horizontal axis; using sine for the x-component is a common error.
Keep units in kN consistently and add components with their correct signs, since leftward or downward components are negative.
rq: Why is the vertical component of cable AC zero?
Cable AC is horizontal (0° to the horizontal), so sin 0° = 0 and all of its force acts along x.
Why must components be added algebraically rather than the magnitudes of the forces?
Forces are vectors with direction; only components along the same axis can be summed directly, and summing magnitudes ignores direction.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces: magnitude and direction from components
pts: The resultant magnitude is found from the square root of the sum of the squared x and y components.
Resolve each force into x and y components, then add components of the same direction to get \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\).
The direction (angle from the x-axis) is found using the arctangent of the y component over the x component.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same effect as the combination of all the forces acting on a body, found by vector addition of their components.
eqs: F = resultant force magnitude (kN); \(F_{x}\) = sum of x-components (kN); \(F_{y}\) = sum of y-components (kN)
θ = angle of resultant from x-axis (degrees); \(F_{y}\) = sum of y-components (kN); \(F_{x}\) = sum of x-components (kN)
\(F_{x}\) = total x-component (kN); \(F_{AB_x}\) = x-component of force AB (kN); \(F_{AC_x}\) = x-component of force AC (kN)
\(F_{y}\) = total y-component (kN); \(F_{AB_y}\) = y-component of force AB (kN); \(F_{AC_y}\) = y-component of force AC (kN)
tips: Use atan2 or check the quadrant when \(F_{x}\) is negative; tan⁻¹ alone gives the wrong angle in the second and third quadrants.
Keep units consistent (kN) throughout; the resultant magnitude carries the same unit as the components.
rq: Why must the components be added separately before using the Pythagorean formula, rather than adding the forces' magnitudes directly?
Forces are vectors with direction; magnitudes cannot be added directly unless they act along the same line. Resolving into components lets you add same-direction parts correctly.
What happens to the angle θ if \(F_{y}\) were negative while \(F_{x}\) stays positive?
θ would become negative, meaning the resultant points below the x-axis (clockwise from the x-axis).

notes.t: Resultant force by rectangular components (bracket example)
pts: Resolve each force into x and y components using its angle measured from the x-axis, then sum the components algebraically.
Components are positive along +x and +y; forces pointing left or down take negative signs.
The resultant magnitude comes from Pythagoras on the summed components, and its direction from the arctangent of the component ratio.
defs: Rectangular components
Perpendicular projections of a force onto the x and y axes, found using sine and cosine of the force's angle to the axis.
eqs: Components of a force at angle θ to the x-axis
F = force magnitude (kN); θ = angle from +x axis (°); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = components (kN)
R = resultant force (kN); \(\sum F_x\), \(\sum F_y\) = summed components (kN)
tips: Measure angles from the positive x-axis consistently; using the wrong reference angle flips the sign or magnitude of components.
Keep the sign convention consistent when summing; forgetting that leftward and downward components are negative gives a wrong resultant.
rq: Why must the force \(F_{1}\) at 15° below the x-axis have a negative y-component?
Because it points downward, below the x-axis, so its vertical component is negative: \(F_{1y}\) = −100 sin15°.
Why does \(F_{3}\) at 45° above the negative x-axis contribute a negative x-component?
It points to the left, so \(F_{3x}\) = −150 cos45°, while its y-component is positive.

xq.q: Two cables are attached at a support A. Cable AB pulls with a force of 10 kN at 60° above the horizontal, towards the right. Cable AC is horizontal and pulls with a force of 8 kN, also towards the right. Resolve the forces into horizontal and vertical components and determine the magnitude of the resultant force on the support, in kN.
s: ΣFx = 10cos60° + 8 = 5 + 8 = 13 kN (cable AC has no vertical component)

xq.q: Two forces act at a bracket. F1 = 12 kN acts at 30° to the +x axis and F2 = 9 kN acts at 150° to the +x axis, both measured anticlockwise from +x. Determine the direction of the resultant, in degrees from the +x axis.
xq.a: θ ≈ 76.1° from the +x axis
s: θ = tan⁻¹(10.5/2.60) = 76.1° (Fx and Fy both positive, so first quadrant)

xq.q: The forces on a bracket sum to Fx = −3 kN and Fy = +4 kN. What is the direction of the resultant measured anticlockwise from the +x axis?
xq.w: Fx is negative and Fy positive, so the resultant lies in the second quadrant and the calculator value tan⁻¹(4/−3) = −53.1° must be corrected by adding 180°; the other options ignore the quadrant or swap the ratio.

units.name: 3.4 Summing components and resultant magnitude/direction
units.ov: This module covers finding the single resultant of a set of concurrent coplanar forces. Each force is resolved into x and y components with \(F\cos\theta\) and \(F\sin\theta\), the components are summed algebraically, and the resultant's magnitude and direction are recovered with Pythagoras and the arctangent. Careful sign and quadrant handling links all three steps.
must: Resolve each force: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the +x axis
Sign convention: the signs of the components follow the quadrant the force points into, e.g. 135° gives \(F_x<0\), \(F_y>0\), and \(-15^\circ\) gives \(F_y<0\)
Sum components algebraically: \(R_x=\sum F_{i_x}\), \(R_y=\sum F_{i_y}\). Never add the force magnitudes directly
Resultant magnitude: \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\)
Resultant direction: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\), then correct for the quadrant using the signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\)
Worked example: \(R_x=47.09\) kN and \(R_y=136.76\) kN give \(R\approx144.6\) kN at about 71° from the x-axis, i.e. 19° from the y-axis
Always state which axis the angle is measured from (x or y) and give the direction in the answer, e.g. with a sketch
For a 45° force, \(F_x=F_y=F\cos45^\circ\)
Keep the calculator in degree mode, keep units consistent (kN), and keep extra decimal places until the final answer
Sanity check: the resultant must point into the quadrant given by the signs of \(R_x\) and \(R_y\), and \(R\) is at most the sum of the magnitudes
conn: Resolving into components feeds the summation, and sign errors made there carry straight into \(R\) and \(\theta\)
The angle from \(\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\) depends on the quadrant, so it links back to the sign convention of the components
The resultant method is the basis for equilibrium: a system is in equilibrium when \(R_x=0\) and \(R_y=0\), which is also how to find an unknown force that balances the system
Angle reference: the angle is measured from the x-axis in the formulas, but answers may be quoted from the y-axis (e.g. 19° from y), so conversion between references is needed
exq: Three concurrent forces act at a point: F₁ at −15° to the x-axis, F₂ at 45° and F₃ at 135°. Resolve each into x and y components and tabulate them with correct signs, given magnitudes in kN.
Given \(R_x=47.09\) kN and \(R_y=136.76\) kN, calculate the magnitude of the resultant and its direction from both the x-axis and the y-axis.

Four coplanar forces act at a point and one has a negative x-component. Find the resultant magnitude and direction, and state which quadrant it lies in. Explain why \(\tan^{-1}\) on a calculator may give the wrong angle if \(R_x<0\).
Find the magnitude and direction of the additional force that must be applied to the three-force system to hold the point in equilibrium.
Show why adding the magnitudes of three forces gives a wrong resultant, using a numerical example to compare \(\sum F\) with \(R\).

notes.t: Resolving forces into x and y components
pts: Each force is resolved into horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components using the angle it makes with the x-axis.
Angles measured below the x-axis give negative y-components (F₁ at −15°).
Forces at 45° to the axes split equally, so both components equal F·cos45° and F·sin45°.
An angle of 135° measured from +x gives a negative x-component and positive y-component for F₃.
defs: Resolving a force
Splitting a force into perpendicular components along chosen coordinate axes, each equal to the force magnitude multiplied by the cosine (x) or sine (y) of its angle to that axis.
eqs: Horizontal component of a force F at angle θ to the x-axis
\(F_x\) = x-component (kN); \(F\) = force magnitude (kN); \(\theta\) = angle from +x axis (°)
Vertical component of a force F at angle θ to the x-axis
\(F_y\) = y-component (kN); \(F\) = force magnitude (kN); \(\theta\) = angle from +x axis (°)
tips: Check the sign of each component against the quadrant the force points into; the angle reference (from +x) determines the sign.
Make sure your calculator is in degree mode when evaluating cos and sin of angles such as 15°, 45° and 135°.
rq: Why is the y-component of F₁ negative even though its magnitude is positive?
F₁ acts at 15° below the +x axis, so its direction points downward, giving a negative sine and hence a negative \(F_{y}\).
Why must F₃ at 135° have a negative x-component?
Cos(135°) = −cos45° < 0, so the force points to the left of the y-axis, opposite to the positive x direction.

notes.t: Resultant of concurrent forces: summing components
pts: The resultant's x-component is the algebraic sum of all force x-components, with signs respecting direction.
The resultant's y-component is found the same way, summing all force y-components.
Components are added algebraically, so forces pointing in negative directions contribute negative values.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect equals the combined effect of all the forces acting on a body; its components are the sums of the corresponding components of the individual forces.
eqs: \(R_{x}\) = resultant x-component (kN); \(F_{i_x}\) = x-component of force i (kN)
\(R_{y}\) = resultant y-component (kN); \(F_{i_y}\) = y-component of force i (kN)
tips: Keep track of signs: a force pointing in the negative x or y direction must be entered as a negative component.
Keep consistent units (kN) throughout and check that each component is taken from the correct axis.
rq: Why must the x and y components be summed separately rather than adding the force magnitudes directly?
Forces act in different directions, so their magnitudes cannot be added directly; only components along the same axis can be combined algebraically.
What would happen to \(R_{x}\) if the 106.07 kN force on the negative x-axis were taken as positive?
\(R_{x}\) would be overstated by twice 106.07 kN, giving a wrong resultant direction and magnitude, because that force's negative sign must be retained.

notes.t: Resultant of Concurrent Forces: Magnitude and Direction
pts: The magnitude of the resultant is found from its rectangular components using Pythagoras.
The direction of the resultant is the arctangent of the ratio of the y- to x-component.
The resultant of concurrent forces replaces F1, F2 and F3 acting at a single point, shown as one force at 19° from the y-axis.
defs: Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as the combined action of a system of forces, found by summing their components.
eqs: Magnitude of the resultant force from its components
R = resultant magnitude (kN); \(R_{x}\) = sum of x-components (kN); \(R_{y}\) = sum of y-components (kN)
Direction of the resultant force measured from the x-axis
θ = angle of resultant from x-axis (°); \(R_{x}\) = x-component (kN); \(R_{y}\) = y-component (kN)
tips: Forces must be resolved into x and y components before adding; adding magnitudes directly is wrong.
Use the correct quadrant when converting tan⁻¹ results; the calculator value alone may give the wrong direction.
rq: Why must the quadrant of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\) be checked when using tan⁻¹(\(R_{y}\)/\(R_{x}\))?
The calculator returns an angle between −90° and 90°, so if \(R_{x}\) is negative the true direction lies in another quadrant and 180° must be added or the signs considered.
Why does the resultant here give an angle of 71° from the x-axis but 19° from the y-axis?
The two angles are complementary, since 90° − 71° = 19°, so the same direction is being described relative to different reference axes.

xq.q: Three concurrent forces act at a point. F1 = 20 kN at −15° to the +x axis, F2 = 30 kN at 45° and F3 = 40 kN at 135°, all measured from +x with anticlockwise positive. Find the magnitude of the resultant force, in kN.
The summed components of a system of concurrent forces are Rx = 47.09 kN and Ry = 136.76 kN. Determine the magnitude of the resultant, in kN, and state its direction from the x-axis.
xq.a: R ≈ 144.6 kN, at about 71.0° from the x-axis
s: θ = tan⁻¹(136.76/47.09) = 71.0° from the x-axis (19° from the y-axis)

xq.q: A force F3 = 50 kN acts at 135° measured from the +x axis. What are its components (Fx, Fy)?
xq.w: At 135° the force points up and to the left, so Fx = 50cos135° = −35.4 kN and Fy = 50sin135° = +35.4 kN; the traps are dropping the sign or using 120° values.

units.name: 4.1 Turning effect, pivots and lever distance
units.ov: This material introduces the moment (torque) of a force as its turning effect about a chosen pivot, given by force times perpendicular distance. It explains why leverage works, since a larger distance needs a smaller force, and applies the idea to levers and to loads on supports such as a TV on a wall shelf. The ideas connect through one rule: pick a pivot, find the perpendicular distance to each line of action, and compare clockwise and anticlockwise effects.
must: Moment of a force: \( M = F \times d \), where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of F
Units: moment in N·m, with force in N and distance in m (convert mm and cm first)
Always state the pivot before calculating, because the same force gives different moments about different points
The distance must be perpendicular to the line of action, not the distance along the beam or shelf to the edge of the object
A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has d = 0, so it produces no moment
Torque is the engineering term for moment; a moment is a rotational effect, distinct from the force that causes translation
Lever principle: a larger distance from the pivot means a smaller force is needed to produce the same moment, as when lifting a load with a beam
Balance: take all moments about the same pivot and compare clockwise with anticlockwise; for equilibrium \( \sum M_{cw} = \sum M_{acw} \)
Weight acts vertically through the centre of weight, so for horizontal members d is the horizontal distance from the support to that point
The turning point may be an imaginary axis, not a physical pivot, so identify it from the geometry and loading
conn: Lever balance and the moment equation: the 50 N weight at one distance is balanced by force F at another, so \( F d_F = 50\, d_{50} \) about the same pivot, which gives the mechanical advantage
Moments and support safety: the load's moment about the wall support (weight × horizontal distance) is what the support must resist, so moving the load closer reduces it
Perpendicular distance and line of action: inclined forces need resolving or the perpendicular distance found geometrically, and a force through the pivot gives zero moment
Choice of pivot and equilibrium: choosing the pivot at an unknown force removes it from the moment equation, which is then combined with force balance
exq: A uniform beam pivots at a point. A 50 N weight hangs 0.4 m to the left of the pivot. Find the downward force F needed at 1.0 m to the right to hold the beam horizontal, and state the direction of each moment.

A TV of mass 15 kg sits on a shelf with its centre of weight 0.30 m from the wall. Calculate its moment about the wall support, then find the new moment and the percentage reduction if it is moved to 0.12 m from the wall.
A 200 N force is applied to a spanner at 30° to the handle, 0.25 m from the bolt centre. Calculate the moment about the bolt, explaining which distance or component is perpendicular.

Explain why a force acting along a line through the pivot produces no rotation, and calculate the moments of the same 100 N force about two different points 0.5 m and 1.2 m perpendicular from its line of action.
A lever has a load of 500 N at 0.2 m from the fulcrum. Find the effort required at 1.5 m, and the effort if the effort arm is reduced to 0.8 m. Comment on the mechanical advantage.

notes.t: Moments of Forces
pts: A force can make a body translate along its line of action and also tend to rotate it about an axis.
The turning effect of a force is called its moment, also called torque in engineering.
The figure shows a force applied to a block pivoting about a fixed corner, producing clockwise rotation.
defs: Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about an axis or point, equal to the product of the force and its perpendicular distance from that axis or point.
Torque
The engineering term for the moment of a force, i.e. the turning effect that tends to rotate a body about an axis.
tips: Moments are about a specific point or axis; always state the pivot before calculating, since the same force gives different moments about different points.
Do not confuse the moment (rotational effect, N·m) with the force itself (N) that causes translation.
rq: Why can a single force produce both translation and rotation, and what determines whether rotation occurs?

A force has a tendency to translate the body along its line of action and to rotate it about an axis; rotation depends on the force's position relative to the pivot, so a force acting through the pivot produces no moment.

notes.t: Moments of Forces: turning points and lever distance
pts: A body rotates about a turning point, which may be a physical pivot or an imaginary axis.
Turning points go by several names, such as pivots, fulcrums, hinges and axes.
Many real systems have no obvious physical pivot, so the turning point must be identified from the geometry and loading.
The ease of rotating a body depends on both the size of the force and its perpendicular distance from the turning point, which motivates the moment.
defs: Turning point (pivot / fulcrum / hinge / axis)
The point or line about which a body rotates when acted on by a force; it may be a physical pivot or an imaginary axis.
tips: A force acting along a line through the turning point produces no rotation, so distance matters, not just magnitude.
Do not assume a physical pivot exists; in many problems the turning point is an imaginary axis chosen for analysis.
rq: Why does pushing a door near its hinge require more effort than pushing near the handle?
Rotational effect depends on the force's distance from the turning point; a smaller distance gives a smaller turning effect for the same force, so more force is needed.
If a body has no physical pivot, how can you still analyse its rotation?
Choose an imaginary axis (a point about which moments are taken) based on the geometry and the supports or contact points.

notes.t: Moments of Forces: lever and pivot
pts: A force applied further from the pivot requires a smaller force to rotate the beam and lift a load.
Pushing down further to the right of the pivot makes it easier to rotate the beam and lift the weight.
The 50 N weight on the left of the pivot tends to rotate the beam anticlockwise, and the applied force F on the right opposes it.
tips: Students often forget that the distance used in a moment must be the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Check that moments are taken about the same pivot for all forces when balancing clockwise and anticlockwise effects.
rq: Why does moving the applied force F further from the pivot reduce the force needed to lift the 50 N load?

Because the turning effect (moment) equals force × perpendicular distance from the pivot; a longer distance gives a larger moment for the same force, so a smaller F is needed to balance the 50 N moment.
