If F is placed at the same distance as the 50 N weight, what force is needed to lift the load?
Equal distances on opposite sides mean equal moments, so F must equal 50 N (ignoring the beam's own weight).

notes.t: Moments of Forces: turning effect of a load about a support
pts: A heavy item placed far from the wall produces a larger turning effect (moment) about the wall support, making the shelf less safe.
Moving the television closer to the wall reduces its moment about the wall support, which makes the arrangement safer.
The turning effect of the weight depends on how far its line of action is from the support, not just on the weight itself.
defs: Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of a force about a support (turning effect of the weight)
M = moment (N m); F = force, here the weight of the TV (N); d = perpendicular distance from the support to the line of action of the force (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance from the support to the line of action of the force, not the distance along the shelf to the object's edge, and keep units consistently in N and m to give moments in N m.
Remember that weight acts vertically downwards, so the distance used is horizontal, measured from the wall support to the TV's centre of weight.
rq: Why does a television placed at the far end of a shelf make the shelf less safe even though its weight is unchanged?
Its weight produces a larger moment about the wall support because the perpendicular distance d from the support to its line of action is greater, so the turning effect M = F × d increases.
What would happen to the moment if the same television were moved to half its distance from the wall?
The moment halves, since M = F × d and F is unchanged while d is halved.

xq.q: A television of mass 12 kg sits on a shelf with its centre of weight 0.45 m horizontally from the wall support. It is moved so that its centre of weight is 0.30 m from the wall. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², find the reduction in the moment of its weight about the wall support, in N m.
xq.a: Reduction ≈ 17.7 N m

xq.q: A beam is pivoted at a fulcrum. A 50 N weight hangs 0.40 m to the left of the pivot. A downward force F is applied 1.25 m to the right of the pivot so that the beam is just balanced. Find F in N.
xq.a: F = 16 N
s: Take moments about the pivot: anticlockwise = 50 × 0.40 = 20 N m

xq.q: A vertical force of 40 N is applied at the end of a straight arm of length 2 m, which is inclined at 30° above the horizontal and is pivoted at its other end. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?
o: 80 N m
40 N m
xq.w: The moment uses the perpendicular (horizontal) distance 2cos30° = 1.73 m, so M = 40 × 1.73 = 69.3 N m; the traps are using the full arm length, using sin30°, or dividing by cos30°.
s: Force is vertical, so perpendicular distance d = 2cos30° = 1.732 m

units.name: 4.2 Definition of a moment and line of action
units.ov: This material defines the moment of a force as its tendency to rotate a body about a point or axis, with magnitude \(M = Fd\), where \(d\) is the perpendicular distance to the line of action. It stresses that a force is fully specified by magnitude, direction and line of action, and that sliding a force along its line of action leaves its external effect and moment unchanged. Together these ideas let you choose convenient points of application and moment arms when solving problems.
must: Moment magnitude: \(M = Fd\), in N·m, where \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the axis or point to the line of action
The moment arm \(d\) is measured perpendicular to the line of action, never the straight-line distance to the point of application (unless the two are perpendicular)
A moment is a vector, so it needs a magnitude and a rotational sense (clockwise/anticlockwise, or direction along the axis by the right-hand rule)
A force is fully specified by magnitude, direction and line of action; equal forces on different lines of action can have different effects
Line of action: the infinite straight line along which the force acts
Principle of transmissibility: sliding a force along its line of action leaves the force and its moment about any point unchanged for a rigid body
Only the force component perpendicular to the position vector or moment arm produces a moment; the parallel component gives zero moment
Moment units are N·m, the same dimensions as energy, but a moment is not energy and must never be written in J
The moment depends on the chosen point O, so always state the reference point (\(M_O\)); a force through O gives \(d=0\) and zero moment
conn: Resolving a force into components links to moments: use the perpendicular component \(F\sin\theta\) with the full arm, or the full force with the perpendicular arm, and both give the same \(M\)
Transmissibility lets you slide a force to a point where one component passes through the moment centre, which simplifies calculations and leads to Varignon's theorem
Moments about a point feed into equilibrium (\(\sum M = 0\)) and into replacing a force system with an equivalent force-couple system
Choosing the moment point at an unknown force's line of action eliminates that force from the moment equation, which is useful for finding support reactions
exq: A 200 N force acts on a spanner at 30° to the handle, 0.25 m from the bolt centre. Find the moment about the bolt, first by finding the perpendicular distance and then by resolving the force, and show the results agree.

A 500 N force acts on a bracket along a line passing 0.4 m from point O. Calculate \(M_O\) and state its sense. Explain why the moment is unchanged if the force's point of application slides along its line of action.
Two equal forces of 100 N act on a rigid beam with different lines of action. Explain with moments about a pivot why their effects differ, and find the moment of each about the pivot.

A force of 80 N acts at a point 1.5 m from a hinge, directed along the line joining the hinge and the point. What is its moment about the hinge, and why? Then find the moment when the force is rotated to 90° to this line.
A student writes the moment of a 50 N force at 0.6 m as 30 J. Identify the error, give the correct units and explain the difference between a moment and energy.

notes.t: Definition of a moment
pts: A moment is a measure of a force's tendency to rotate a body about a point or axis.
A moment has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity.
The magnitude of a moment uses only the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the axis.
The perpendicular distance d is called the moment arm or lever arm.
defs: Moment of a force
The measure of the tendency of a force to rotate a body about a point or axis.
Moment arm (lever arm)
The perpendicular distance from the line of action of a force to the axis or point about which moments are taken.
eqs: Magnitude of the moment of a force about an axis or point
\(M\) = moment magnitude (N·m); \(F\) = force magnitude (N); \(d\) = perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the axis (m)
tips: Do not use the straight-line distance from the axis to the force's point of application; always use the perpendicular distance to the line of action.
A moment is a vector with units of N·m; do not confuse it with energy (joules) even though the units are dimensionally similar.
rq: Why must the distance used in the moment calculation be measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force, rather than straight-line from the axis to any point on the force?

Only the perpendicular component of the distance determines the rotational effect; the component of the lever arm parallel to the force produces no turning, so the perpendicular distance gives the correct moment magnitude.
If you double a force but halve its perpendicular distance from the axis, what happens to the moment?
The moment stays the same, since M = F·d gives 2F × (d/2) = Fd.

notes.t: Moments and the line of action of a force
pts: A force is fully specified only by its magnitude, direction and line of action.
Forces with the same magnitude and direction but different lines of action can have different effects on a body.
Forces acting along the same line of action have the same effect on a rigid body, even at different points of application.
Sliding a force along its line of action leaves both its force and its moment unchanged.
defs: Line of action
The straight line, extended infinitely in both directions, along which a force acts.
tips: Do not assume equal forces have equal effects; always check the line of action, since the moment depends on it.
The moment of a force depends on the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action, not just the point where the force is applied.
rq: Why can F1 and F2 be treated as equivalent even though they act at different points?
Because they share the same magnitude, direction and line of action, so they produce the same force and the same moment about any point on the body.
What if F3 had the same magnitude and direction as F1 but a different line of action: would the support reaction change?
Yes, the moment about the pivot would differ, so the rotational effect and the reaction distribution at the supports would change.

notes.t: Moments (moment of a force)
pts: A moment is a vector quantity whose size depends on the force and on how far its line of action is from the axis of rotation.
Only the component of force perpendicular to the moment arm produces a moment; the moment arm is measured perpendicular to the line of action.
The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.
The moment's magnitude is the product of force and moment arm, and its SI unit is the newton metre.
defs: Moment (of a force)

A vector quantity measuring the tendency of a force to cause rotation about an axis; its magnitude is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force.
Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Magnitude of the moment about point O
\(M_{0}\) = moment about O (N m); F = magnitude of perpendicular force (N); d = moment arm (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance d, not the distance from the axis to the point where the force is applied, unless the force is perpendicular to that line.
Moment units are N m, the same as work/energy units, but a moment is not energy; do not write it as J.
rq: Why does a force acting along the line through the axis of rotation produce no moment?
Its moment arm d is zero, so \(M_{0}\) = Fd = 0; the force has no perpendicular distance from the axis to act through.
If the same force is applied further from the axis, what happens to the moment, and why?
The moment increases proportionally, since \(M_{0}\) = Fd and d is larger for the same F.

xq.q: A force of magnitude \(F = 150\) N acts on a rigid bar. Its line of action is a straight line passing at a perpendicular distance of \(0.40\) m from pivot O. The point of application of the force is \(0.50\) m from O (straight-line distance). The force is then slid along its line of action to a new point of application \(0.90\) m from O. Find the moment of the force about O after sliding, and the moment about a second point P, which lies on the line of action, in the same two steps.
xq.a: Moment about O = 60 N·m; moment about P = 0 N·m. Taking the moment about O only: 60 N·m.
s: Sliding a force along its line of action leaves its moment unchanged
Use perpendicular distance d = 0.40 m, not 0.50 m or 0.90 m
About P on the line of action d = 0, so M = 0

xq.q: A 200 N force is applied to a spanner at a point 0.30 m from the nut centre O. The line of action of the force is at 30° to the spanner, so its perpendicular distance from O is \(0.30\sin 30°\). What is the magnitude of the moment about O?
xq.a: 30 N·m
o: 60 N·m
30 N·m
52 N·m
xq.w: The moment is F × perpendicular distance = 200 × 0.15 = 30 N·m; using 0.30 m gives 60 N·m, using cos gives 52 N·m, and the unit is N·m not J.

xq.q: Two forces have the same magnitude and direction but act along different parallel lines of action relative to a pivot O. Explain why they have different effects on a rigid body, and explain why moving the point of application of one force along its own line of action does not change its effect.
xq.a: The moment about O is M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action. Parallel forces of equal magnitude on different lines have different d, so different moments and different turning effects. Sliding a force along its line of action leaves F, the line, and hence d unchanged, so its moment and its effect on a rigid body are unchanged.
s: Moment M = Fd with d perpendicular to line of action
Different lines give different d, so different moments
Sliding along the line keeps F and d the same
So the moment and effect are unchanged

units.name: 4.3 Calculating moments about a point (force × perpendicular distance)
units.ov: This material introduces the moment of a force about a point as force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action, with a sign set by the sense of rotation. It then shows how an oblique force is handled by resolving it so that only the component perpendicular to the lever arm contributes. These ideas are the basis for summing moments in equilibrium problems.
must: Moment about a point: \(M_O = F\,d\), where d is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action of F; units N·m
Always use the perpendicular distance to the line of action, never the straight-line distance to the point of application
A force whose line of action passes through the pivot has zero moment (d = 0)
Sign convention: anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative, applied consistently (e.g. \(M_A = -F_4 d\) for a clockwise force)
Only the force component perpendicular to the lever arm produces a moment: \(M_O = F_y d\)
The component along the lever axis gives no turning effect; for an oblique force at angle \(\theta\) to the lever, \(F_y = F\sin\theta\)
Equal-magnitude forces can give different moments through different lever arms and senses of rotation, so the moment depends on both direction and distance
The line of action extends infinitely in both directions, so the perpendicular distance may be to an extended line rather than to the force's drawn length
Keep units consistent (N and m give N·m) and state the sense of rotation with the answer
conn: Resolving forces into components (trigonometry) feeds directly into moments: find \(F_y\), then multiply by d
Sum of moments about a point (with sign convention) leads to equilibrium conditions \(\sum M = 0\), combined with \(\sum F = 0\) to find unknown reactions
Choosing the pivot at the point where unknown forces act removes them from the moment equation because their lever arm is zero
Equivalent approaches: \(F\) times perpendicular distance equals the perpendicular component times distance along the lever, so either may be used as a check
exq: A 50 N force acts on a spanner at 60° to its axis, at 0.25 m from the nut centre. Calculate the moment about the nut centre and state its sense.
Four forces of equal magnitude F = 20 N act on a plate at perpendicular distances 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.15 m from pivot A, three anticlockwise and one clockwise. Find the net moment about A.

Explain why using the distance from the pivot to the point of application, rather than the perpendicular distance, gives the wrong moment. Illustrate with a force of 100 N inclined at 30° to a 0.5 m lever.
A force of 200 N passes through pivot A and another force of 100 N acts 0.4 m from A. Determine the moment of each about A and the total, stating the sign convention.

A lever has an oblique force F applied at its end, 0.6 m from the pivot, and a required moment of 30 N·m. Resolve the force to find the minimum F needed if it acts at 40° to the lever, and compare with a perpendicular force.

notes.t: Moments about a pivot (point A)
pts: A moment is a force times its perpendicular distance from the pivot; forces passing through A create no moment.
Forces F1, F2 and F3 are on the right or act to produce anticlockwise rotation about A, so their moments are taken as positive.
Force F4 is on the left and produces a clockwise rotation, so its moment is negative.
All forces have equal magnitude F, so the moments differ only by sign and lever arm direction.
defs: Moment about a point
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force magnitude multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of force \(F_{1}\) about pivot A
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{1}\) = force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Moment of force \(F_{4}\) about pivot A (clockwise, negative)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{4}\) = force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, and check the sign convention (anticlockwise positive) consistently.
Forces acting directly through the pivot point produce zero moment; do not include them in the distance term.
rq: Why does the sign of F4's moment differ from F1's even though all forces are equal in magnitude?
F4 acts on the opposite side of pivot A from F1, so it rotates the beam clockwise while F1 rotates it anticlockwise; the sign convention records this opposite sense.
What would happen to the moment of F3 if it were applied at the pivot A instead of distance d?
Its lever arm would be zero, so its moment about A would be zero, since a force through the pivot produces no turning effect.

notes.t: Moment of a force about a point
pts: A force tends to rotate a body about a point; this turning effect is the moment of the force about that point.
The magnitude of the moment equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
The distance used must be perpendicular to the line of action of the force, not the straight-line distance to the point.
The sense of rotation (here anticlockwise) gives the direction of the moment, which is needed when summing moments.
defs: Moment of a force about a point
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the magnitude of the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
Line of action
The straight line along which a force acts, extended infinitely in both directions.
eqs: Magnitude of the moment of force F about point O
\(M_O\) = moment of the force about O (N·m); \(F\) = magnitude of the force (N); \(d\) = perpendicular distance from O to the line of action of F (m)
tips: Using the distance from O to the point of application instead of the perpendicular distance to the line of action gives an incorrect moment.
Keep units consistent: force in N and distance in m give moments in N·m, not N/m or N alone.
rq: Why must d be measured perpendicular to the line of action rather than as the direct distance from O to the point where F is applied?
Only the perpendicular component of the distance produces turning; a force passing through a point along its line of action (d = 0) produces no moment, which the direct distance would wrongly ignore.
What happens to the moment if the same force is applied further along the wrench handle, keeping its direction fixed?
The perpendicular distance d stays the same since the line of action is unchanged, so the moment is unchanged; the moment depends on the line of action, not the point of application along it.

notes.t: Moments: resolving a force into perpendicular components
pts: A moment is produced only by the component of a force perpendicular to the lever arm.
Applying an oblique force supplies more force than needed; only its perpendicular part turns the lever.
The component along the lever axis pushes along the lever and produces no turning effect.
Resolving the force into rectangular components \(F_{x}\) and \(F_{y}\) isolates the turning part \(F_{y}\).
defs: Moment about a point O
The turning effect of a force about point O, equal to the perpendicular component of the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance d from O to the line of action.
eqs: Moment of a force about point O using the perpendicular component
\(M_{O}\) = moment about O (N·m); \(F_{y}\) = force component perpendicular to the lever arm (N); d = perpendicular distance from O to the force's line of action (m)
tips: Use only the perpendicular component \(F_{y}\) in M = \(F_{y}\) d; do not multiply the full force F by d when the force is oblique.
Check that d is the perpendicular distance to the line of action, not the distance along the lever to the point of application.
rq: Why does the component \(F_{x}\) produce no moment about O even though it is a real force acting on the lever?
\(F_{x}\) acts along the axis of the lever, passing through O, so its perpendicular distance from O is zero and it cannot rotate the lever.
If the oblique force F were applied at a smaller angle to the lever, what would happen to \(F_{y}\) and to the moment?
\(F_{y}\) would decrease, so the moment for the same F and d would decrease; the moment is largest when the force is perpendicular to the lever.

xq.q: A uniform lever pivoted at A has horizontal axis along x. Three forces act on it, all perpendicular to the lever: \(F_1 = 40\) N at 0.5 m to the right of A pushing upward (anticlockwise about A), \(F_2 = 25\) N at 1.2 m to the right of A pushing downward (clockwise), and \(F_4 = 30\) N at 0.8 m to the left of A pushing downward (anticlockwise). A fourth force of 60 N acts through A. Taking anticlockwise as positive, find the net moment about A.
xq.a: +14 N·m, i.e. 14 N·m anticlockwise
s: Force through A gives zero moment

xq.q: A force \(F = 120\) N acts on the end of a lever of length \(L = 0.60\) m pivoted at O. The force is directed at \(40°\) to the lever axis. Find the moment about O, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
A 50 N force acts at 60° to a lever of length 0.80 m, measured from the lever axis. Which is the moment about the pivot?
o: 40 N·m
20 N·m
xq.w: Only the perpendicular component 50 sin60° = 43.3 N turns the lever, giving 34.6 N·m; 40 ignores the angle, 20 uses cos60°, 69.3 divides by sin.

units.name: 4.4 Moment as a vector and cross product
units.ov: This material introduces the moment of a force about a point, first as a scalar (force times perpendicular distance, with a sign for sense) and then as a vector given by the cross product \(\underline{M}_O = \underline{r}\times\underline{F}\). In 2D problems the moment vector lies along the z-axis, so the vector and scalar descriptions are equivalent. The key link is that \(d = r\sin\alpha\), so the cross product magnitude reproduces \(Fd\).
must: Moment about O is the turning effect of a force: \(M_O = Fd\), with d the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action (not to the point of application)
Vector definition: \(\underline{M}_O = \underline{r}\times\underline{F}\), where r runs from O to any point on the line of action of F
Magnitude: \(M_O = Fr\sin\alpha = Fd\), with \(\alpha\) the angle between r and F (tail-to-tail) and \(d = r\sin\alpha\) the lever arm
Direction: \(\underline{M}_O\) is perpendicular to the plane containing r and F; for x-y plane problems it is \(\pm M_O\underline{k}\), found by the right-hand rule
Sign convention: anticlockwise = positive (+z), clockwise = negative (−z); apply it consistently when summing moments
Order matters: \(\underline{r}\times\underline{F} = -\underline{F}\times\underline{r}\), so reversing the order reverses the direction
In 2D the moment is drawn as a curved arrow showing its sense; in 3D it is a true vector along the axis of rotation
Units are N·m; r in m and F in N, and sin α needs the angle mode (degrees or radians) set correctly
Check for a quick method: the moment is unchanged if F slides along its line of action, so r can be taken to any point on that line
conn: Cross product with components: \(\underline{r}\times\underline{F}\) via the determinant gives \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\), which should match \(\pm Fd\) from geometry
Resolving a force into components, then taking moments of each (Varignon's principle), is often easier than finding d directly
Summing moments about a point links to equilibrium (\(\sum M_O = 0\)) for finding unknown forces and reactions
Sign convention ties the scalar 2D answer to the vector form: anticlockwise positive corresponds to \(+\underline{k}\)
exq: A 200 N force acts at 30° to the horizontal at the end of a 0.8 m spanner. Find the moment about the bolt using \(Fd\) and then using \(\underline{r}\times\underline{F}\), and state its sense.

Given \(\underline{r} = (3\underline{i}+2\underline{j})\) m and \(\underline{F} = (4\underline{i}-5\underline{j})\) N, compute \(\underline{M}_O = \underline{r}\times\underline{F}\), find its magnitude and direction, and the perpendicular distance d from O to the line of action.
Show that \(\underline{r}\times\underline{F}\) and \(\underline{F}\times\underline{r}\) differ, and explain the physical meaning of the difference for a force applied to a beam.
Three coplanar forces act on a plate at given positions. Using anticlockwise positive, find the resultant moment about O and the single force position that gives the same moment.
A force acts at angle α to a position vector of length r. Explain why using the angle to the normal gives the wrong moment, and find the correct moment for r = 1.5 m, F = 80 N, α = 40°.

notes.t: Representing a Moment
pts: A moment about point O can be represented as a vector along the z-axis, whose magnitude is the force times the perpendicular distance.
In 2D, the moment is shown as a curved arrow indicating its sense of rotation rather than a vector.
The sense of the moment vector is anticlockwise (along +z) or clockwise (along −z).
Sign convention: anticlockwise moments are taken as positive and clockwise moments as negative.
defs: Moment about O
The turning effect of a force about point O, equal to the force magnitude multiplied by the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of force F about O in 3D (vector form)
\underline{M}_O = moment vector about O (N·m); F = force magnitude (N); d = perpendicular distance from O to line of action of F (m); \underline{k} = unit vector along the z-axis (dimensionless)
Moment of force F about O in 2D (scalar form)
\(M_{O}\) = scalar moment about O (N·m); F = force magnitude (N); d = perpendicular distance from O to line of action of F (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance d, not the distance from O to the point of application of the force, when calculating the moment.
Keep the sign convention consistent: anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative, and check the sense before summing moments.
rq: Why does the 3D moment vector point along the z-axis when the force lies in the x–y plane?
The moment is perpendicular to both the position vector and the force, so for forces in the x–y plane it must be perpendicular to that plane, i.e. along z.
What would change if the force were moved further from O along its line of action?
Nothing: the moment depends only on the perpendicular distance d to the line of action, so moving the force along its line leaves the moment unchanged.

notes.t: Moment as a Vector: Cross Product Representation
pts: The moment about point O is the cross product of the position vector r and the force F, giving a vector perpendicular to the plane containing them.
Because r and F lie in the x-y plane, the moment points along the z-axis, so it is fully described by a magnitude and a unit vector k.
The magnitude equals force times perpendicular distance d, where d = r sin α is the lever arm.
defs: Moment about O
The vector quantity equal to the cross product of the position vector from O to the point of force application and the force vector; it measures the tendency of the force to rotate a body about O.
Moment arm (lever arm) d
The perpendicular distance from the point O to the line of action of the force; the moment magnitude is the force multiplied by this distance.
eqs: \underline{M}_O = moment vector about O (N·m); \underline{r} = position vector from O to the point of application (m); \underline{F} = force vector (N)

\(M_{O}\) = moment magnitude (N·m); F = force magnitude (N); r = distance from O to point of application (m); \alpha = angle between r and F (degrees or radians); d = perpendicular distance from O to line of action of F (m)
\underline{k} = unit vector along the z-axis (dimensionless); F = force (N); d = moment arm (m)
tips: The angle α in \(M_{O}\) = Fr sin α is measured between r and F; using the wrong angle (e.g. to the normal) gives the wrong sine.
Keep the order of the cross product: r × F is not equal to F × r; reversing it reverses the sign of the moment direction.
rq: Why does the moment vector point along the z-axis when r and F both lie in the x-y plane?
The cross product of two vectors is perpendicular to both, so for vectors in the x-y plane the result must lie along z (the normal to that plane).
What happens to the moment if the force acts along the line through O (α = 0°)?
sin 0° = 0, so \(M_{O}\) = 0; the force has no turning effect about O because its line of action passes through the point.

xq.q: A force \(\underline{F} = (30\underline{i} + 40\underline{j})\) N acts at a point with position vector \(\underline{r} = (2\underline{i} + 1\underline{j})\) m relative to O. Using \(\underline{M}_O = \underline{r}\times\underline{F}\), find the moment about O and the perpendicular distance d from O to the line of action of the force.
xq.a: \(M_{O}\) = +50 k N·m (anticlockwise); d = 1.0 m
s: M = (rx Fy − ry Fx) k = (2×40 − 1×30) k

xq.q: The position vector from O to the point of application of a force has magnitude r = 2.0 m. The force F = 80 N makes an angle α = 30° with r. What is the magnitude of the moment about O?
xq.a: 80 N·m
o: 80 N·m
40 N·m
xq.w: M = F r sinα = 80×2.0×0.5 = 80 N·m; 160 omits the sine, 138.6 uses cosα, 40 omits r.

xq.q: Show that for a force F acting at position r from O in the x–y plane, with angle α between r and F, the moment is \(\underline{M}_O = Fd\,\underline{k}\) with \(d = r\sin\alpha\). State the direction of the moment, and explain what happens to it if the cross product is written as F × r.
xq.a: The cross product r × F has magnitude rF sinα and is perpendicular to the plane of r and F. Since both lie in the x–y plane, the moment is along z: \(M_{O}\) = rF sinα k. The perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is d = r sinα, so \(M_{O}\) = Fd k. Anticlockwise gives +k, clockwise −k. Writing F × r reverses the sign (direction) of the moment, so order must be r × F.
s: Perpendicular to x–y plane, so along k
d = r sinα so M = Fd k
F × r = −(r × F), reversing the direction

units.name: 5.1 Moments 2: moments in 2D and 3D
units.ov: This material covers the moment of a force about a point and the equivalent ways of calculating it: perpendicular distance (M = Fd), Varignon's principle with components, sliding a force along its line of action (transmissibility), and the vector cross product. The same force-and-point problem is worked by four or five methods that must all agree. Choosing the easiest method and keeping signs and units consistent is the key skill.
must: Moment of a force about O: \(M_O = F d\), where d is the PERPENDICULAR distance from O to the line of action (not the distance to the point of application)
Varignon's principle: the moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components, \(M_O = M_{O,x}+M_{O,y}\); the same holds for the resultant of several forces
Sign convention: anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative; state it and apply it to every term, with the same reference point throughout

Resolve an inclined force: \(F_x = F\cos\theta\), \(F_y = F\sin\theta\); each component's arm is the perpendicular distance to ITS line of action (\(F_x\) uses the vertical distance, \(F_y\) the horizontal distance)
A component whose line of action passes through the moment point contributes zero moment (e.g. only \(F_y\) gives \(M_O=-FL\sin\alpha\) for a force at the end of a beam of length L)

Transmissibility: sliding a force along its line of action leaves its moment unchanged. Slide it to a point where one component has zero moment (Methods 3 and 4: only \(F_y d\) or only \(F_x d\) remains)
Vector form: \(\mathbf{M}_A = \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\), where r runs from A to any point on the line of action; in the x–y plane only the k component survives, \(M_k = r_xF_y - r_yF_x\)
Geometric moment arm: resolve the known length with the force angle (e.g. \(d=100\cos45^\circ=70.71\) mm), then \(M_A=Fd\); check which angle is actually between the length and the perpendicular to F
Convert mm to m before multiplying (100 mm = 0.1 m); the worked example is F = 200 N at 45°, so \(F_x=F_y=141.42\) N
Check any answer by computing it with a second method; all methods must give the same magnitude and sense
conn: Varignon's principle justifies both the component method and the sliding-force methods: choosing where to slide F is choosing which component's moment vanishes
The cross product \(r_xF_y - r_yF_x\) is Varignon's component method written with signs built in, so it checks the scalar methods and fixes the sign automatically
Moment of the resultant equals the sum of the moments of the individual forces, which leads to equivalent force systems and equilibrium (\(\sum M = 0\)) problems
Perpendicular-distance geometry (\(d=L\sin\alpha\)) and the component method are two views of the same calculation, so questions often ask you to show they agree
exq: A 200 N force acts at B at 45° to the horizontal, with A 100 mm below and 200 mm to one side of B. Find the moment about A by (a) the perpendicular moment arm, (b) rectangular components, (c) sliding F along its line of action, and (d) \(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\). State the sense of rotation.

A force F acts at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal at the free end of a cantilever of length L fixed at O. Use Varignon's principle to derive \(M_O\), give its sign and sense, and evaluate it for F = 500 N, L = 1.5 m, \(\alpha=30^\circ\).

Two forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) act at the same point. Find their resultant by the parallelogram law, and show that the moment of the resultant about B equals \(F_1d_1+F_2d_2\). Give a numerical check.

Write \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{F}\) in i, j, k form for a 200 N force at 45° acting at a point (0.2, 0.1) m from A, and compute \(\mathbf{M}_A\). Explain why only the k component is non-zero and why r may end at any point on the line of action.

Explain why, in a moment calculation about A, a force component acting through A has no effect. Where along its line of action should the force be placed to leave only one component, and what mistake occurs if it is moved sideways instead?

notes.t: Varignon's Principle
pts: The moment of a force about a point O equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point O.
Because of this principle, the moment of a force can be found in several different ways.
The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from point O to the line of action of the force, and it can be found for the original force or for its resolved components.
Either calculate the moment directly from the original force, or resolve the force into components and sum the component moments; both must give the same result.
Assign a sign to each moment: positive if anticlockwise, negative if clockwise.
defs: Moment of a force about a point O
The turning effect of a force about O, equal to the force magnitude multiplied by the perpendicular distance (moment arm) from O to the line of action of the force.
Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from the point about which moments are taken to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Varignon's principle: moment of a force equals sum of moments of its components about the same point
\(M_O\) = moment of the force about O (N·m); \(M_{O,x}\), \(M_{O,y}\) = moments of the x and y components about O (N·m)
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative, and apply it to every component moment.
Use the same reference point O for all components; mixing reference points invalidates the sum.
rq: Why must the component moments be taken about the same point O as the original force?

Varignon's principle only holds when all moments are taken about one common point; using different reference points for the components would give a sum that does not equal the moment of the original force.
If a force is resolved into components, why might the component method be easier than using the original perpendicular distance?
The perpendicular distance to the original line of action may be hard to find, whereas each component's moment arm is often a simple horizontal or vertical distance from O.

notes.t: Moment of resultant force
pts: The moment about a point can be found by summing the moments of individual forces acting at the same point of application.
Alternatively, the moment can be found from the moment of the resultant force, found by the parallelogram law.
Both representations give the same moment, so the moment of the resultant equals the sum of the individual moments (Varignon's theorem).
defs: Resultant force
The single force F obtained by vector addition of the forces acting at a point, found using the parallelogram law, having the same overall effect as the original forces.
eqs: Moment about B from individual forces
\(M_B\) = moment about point B (N·m); \(F_1, F_2\) = component forces (N); \(d_1, d_2\) = perpendicular distances from B to the lines of action of \(F_1, F_2\) (m)
Moment about B from the resultant force
\(M_B\) = moment about point B (N·m); \(F\) = resultant force (N); \(d\) = perpendicular distance from B to the line of action of \(F\) (m)
\(F_1, F_2\) = component forces (N); \(F\) = resultant force (N); \(d_1, d_2, d\) = perpendicular distances from the rotation axis B (m)
tips: Lever arms must be perpendicular distances to the line of action, not the straight-line distance from B to A.
Ensure the same reference point B is used for every moment term; mixing reference points gives wrong answers.
rq: Why must the perpendicular distances d1, d2 and d be measured from the rotation axis B rather than from point A?
The moment is always taken about the rotation axis (point B), so the lever arms are the perpendicular distances from B to each line of action.
If F1 and F2 are parallel and in the same direction, what does the equality F1d1 + F2d2 = Fd tell you about d?
The resultant F = F1 + F2 lies between them, and d is the weighted average of d1 and d2: d = (F1d1 + F2d2)/(F1 + F2).

notes.t: Calculating simple moments of forces about points
pts: The moment of a force about a point equals the force magnitude multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
Moments are signed: the sign indicates the sense of rotation about the chosen point (e.g. anticlockwise positive, clockwise negative, per the convention used in the solution).
The moment of \(F_{A}\) about C uses the perpendicular distance from C to the vertical line of action of \(F_{A}\), which is the 10 cm vertical arm height.
The moment of \(F_{E}\) about A uses the perpendicular distance from A to the vertical line of action of \(F_{E}\), which is 0.12 m.
defs: Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of a force about a point
\(M\) = moment about the point (N m); \(F\) = force magnitude (N); \(d\) = perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force (m)
tips: Use the perpendicular distance to the line of action of the force, not the distance along the beam between the point and the force's point of application.
Keep track of the sign convention: a moment in the opposite rotational sense must carry the opposite sign, and state the convention used.
rq: Why is the moment of \(F_{A}\) about C 10 Nm, and not 100 × 0.08 or 100 × 0.18 using the horizontal distances shown?

Moment depends on the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. \(F_{A}\) is horizontal, so the perpendicular distance from C is the vertical height of the arm, 0.1 m (10 cm). Horizontal distances along the beam are not the lever arm for a horizontal force.
Why does \(F_{D}\) give a negative moment about B while \(F_{E}\) gives a moment about A that is positive?

The sign depends on the direction of rotation each force produces about the chosen point; the downward force \(F_{D}\) rotates the beam clockwise about B (negative in this convention), while the solution's sign convention gives the opposite sense for the moment about A.

notes.t: Varignon's principle: moment of an inclined force about a point
pts: Resolve the inclined force into horizontal and vertical components, then take moments of each component; the perpendicular component produces the moment about O.
Varignon's principle: the moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point.
Only the vertical component \( F_y \) has a moment arm L about O, so the horizontal component contributes zero moment.
The moment is negative (clockwise) because the downward component acts to the right of the fixed support O.
defs: Varignon's principle
The moment of a force about a point is equal to the sum of the moments of its components about the same point.
Moment of a force about a point
The product of the force's perpendicular component and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of force F about O using the vertical component
\( M_O \) = moment about O (N·m); \( F_y \) = vertical component of F (N); \( F \) = magnitude of force (N); \( L \) = beam length (m); \( \alpha \) = angle of F to horizontal (degrees or rad)
\( F_y \) = vertical component (N); \( F \) = force magnitude (N); \( \alpha \) = angle to horizontal (rad)
tips: Use the perpendicular component of the force (here \( F\sin\alpha \)) with the lever arm L; using \( F\cos\alpha \) gives the wrong answer.
Keep the sign convention consistent: the result \( -FL\sin\alpha \) is clockwise, so state the direction clearly.
rq: Why does the horizontal component of F contribute nothing to the moment about O?
Its line of action passes through O (it is parallel to the beam, which lies along the line from O), so its perpendicular distance from O is zero.
What would happen to the moment if the force were applied at the same angle but the beam were twice as long?
The moment doubles, since \( M_O = -FL\sin\alpha \) is directly proportional to L.

notes.t: Different ways to calculate the moment about a point
pts: The moment of a force about a point can be found by several equivalent methods, all giving the same result for the same force and point.
Using the force components (resolving F into horizontal and vertical parts) and taking moments of each component about A is one valid method.
The perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to point A (moment arm) can be used directly as moment = F × d.
defs: Moment of a force about a point
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
eqs: Moment of a force about a point (scalar form)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); F = force magnitude (N); d = perpendicular distance from A to the line of action of F (m)
\(M_{A}\) = moment vector about A (N·m); \(r_{\text{AB}}\) = position vector from A to a point on the line of action (m); F = force vector (N)
tips: Watch units: distances given in mm must be converted to metres before computing moments in N·m.
Use the perpendicular distance to the line of action, not the distance to the point of application measured horizontally or vertically unless the component is resolved correctly.
rq: Why does the perpendicular distance, rather than the straight-line distance from A to B, determine the moment?
Only the perpendicular component of the lever arm produces turning; the component along the line of action passes through the pivot and creates no moment.
Why must the components of the force be taken relative to the same point A when using the principle of moments?
Moments must be summed about one common point; using different reference points gives inconsistent results.

notes.t: Moments: finding the moment arm from geometry
pts: The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force; here it is found from the 100 mm geometry and the 45° inclination of F.
The moment arm is obtained by resolving the 100 mm height with the 45° angle, giving d in mm, which is then converted to metres before multiplying by F.
The moment about A is the force times the perpendicular distance, giving a magnitude in N·m with the sense shown by the curved arrow.
defs: Moment arm
The perpendicular distance from a point (pivot) to the line of action of a force; it is the lever arm used to calculate the moment of the force about that point.
eqs: d = moment arm length (mm); 100 = vertical height from A to the reference line (mm); 45° = angle of F to horizontal
\(M_{A}\) = moment about point A (N·m); F = applied force (N); d = moment arm (m)
tips: Convert millimetres to metres before multiplying by force in newtons, otherwise the moment is wrongly scaled by 1000.
Check that the angle used is between the measured length and the perpendicular to the force, not simply the given angle to horizontal.
rq: Why is the 100 mm height multiplied by cos 45° rather than sin 45° to get the moment arm?

The 100 mm is measured along the vertical, and the perpendicular distance to the inclined line of action of F is obtained by projecting it with cos 45° (the angle between the vertical and the perpendicular direction).
Why must d be converted to metres before computing \(M_{A}\)?
The force is in newtons, so to obtain moment in N·m the arm must be in metres; using 70.71 mm directly would give an answer 1000 times too large.

notes.t: Moments via rectangular components (Method 2)
pts: Resolve the inclined force F at B into horizontal and vertical components, then take moments of each component about A.
Components of a 200 N force at 45° are equal, so each has magnitude F cos45° = F sin45°.
Moment about A is the sum of each component's moment; the sign depends on the direction of rotation about A.
defs: Moment of a force about a point
The product of the force component perpendicular to the lever arm and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force; positive when it tends to rotate anticlockwise.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); F = applied force (N); \theta = angle to horizontal (°)
\(F_{y}\) = vertical component (N); F = applied force (N); \theta = angle to horizontal (°)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = force components (N); \(d_{1}\) = vertical distance (m); \(d_{2}\) = horizontal distance (m)
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: a component's moment arm is the perpendicular distance, so use \(d_{1}\) for \(F_{x}\) and \(d_{2}\) for \(F_{y}\), not the other way round.
Convert distances to metres before multiplying (100 mm = 0.1 m, 200 mm = 0.2 m) to obtain the moment in N·m.
rq: Why can the moment of F about A be found by summing the moments of its components rather than the full force?
Moments are additive (Varignon's theorem): the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point, since the components together produce the same effect as F.
Why does \(F_{x}\) contribute a negative moment while \(F_{y}\) contributes a positive one here?

\(F_{x}\) acts at height \(d_{1}\) above A and tends to rotate the member clockwise, while \(F_{y}\) acts at horizontal distance \(d_{2}\) and tends to rotate it anticlockwise, so their signs are opposite.

notes.t: Moments: Method 3 – sliding a force along its line of action to eliminate a component's mo
pts: A force can be moved along its line of action without changing its moment about a point, so F can be slid to a convenient location.
Choose the point along the line of action where the moment due to the x-component is eliminated, so only the y-component produces a moment about A.
Resolve F into components; the y-component's moment about A is the product of its magnitude and the perpendicular distance d.
eqs: Vertical component of the force F at 45°
\(F_{y}\) = vertical component of force (N); 200 = magnitude of F (N); 45° = angle of line of action to horizontal
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{y}\) = vertical force component (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
tips: Ensure d is the perpendicular distance to the force's component, measured in metres (100 mm = 0.1 m) before multiplying by force in N to get N·m.
Only the component whose line of action does not pass through the reference point produces a moment; check the sign (direction) of the moment when combining with other moments.
rq: Why does sliding F along its line of action to a point directly above or in line with A remove the x-component's moment about A?
Because the x-component's line of action then passes through A (its perpendicular distance becomes zero), so its moment about A is zero; only \(F_{y}\) contributes a moment.
What would change if F were moved to a different point on its line of action without this choice?

The moment of F about A would be unchanged in total, but it would now be split between the components, making the calculation more complex; the moment of F itself is invariant along its line of action.

notes.t: Moments: Method 4 – sliding a force along its line of action to eliminate a component's mo
pts: A force can be moved along its line of action without changing its moment about any point, so the force can be slid to a convenient position to simplify the moment calculation.
Sliding F to the point where its y-component produces no moment leaves only the x-component contributing to the moment about A.
The moment about A is found from the perpendicular distance d of the remaining component's line of action from A.
eqs: Moment of the force about point A using the x-component at perpendicular distance d
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{x}\) = x-component of force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Horizontal component of a 200 N force at 45°
\(F_{x}\) = horizontal component (N); F = resultant force (N); 45° = angle to horizontal
tips: Convert d to metres before multiplying by a force in newtons so that the moment is in N·m (100 mm must become 0.1 m).
Only slide the force along its own line of action; moving it sideways changes the moment.
rq: Why does sliding F along its line of action leave the moment about A unchanged?
The moment is F multiplied by the perpendicular distance from A to the line of action, and sliding along the line keeps both the force and that perpendicular distance the same.
Why is the moment of \(F_{y}\) eliminated at the chosen point on the line of action?
The point is chosen so that the line of action of \(F_{y}\) passes through A, giving zero perpendicular distance and therefore zero moment.

notes.t: Moment of a force using the vector cross product (unit vectors)
pts: The moment about a point is the cross product of the position vector from that point to the force line of action with the force vector.
Express both the position vector and the force vector in terms of unit vectors i, j, k, then expand the cross product.
For vectors lying in the x–y plane, only the k component of the moment is non-zero, so the result is a scalar couple acting perpendicular to the plane.
defs: Position vector r
A vector from the reference point (here A) to any point on the line of action of the force.
Moment (vector form)
The moment of a force about a point equals the cross product of the position vector and the force vector, M = r × F.
eqs: Moment of force F about point A using the cross product
\underline{M}_A = moment about A (N·m); \underline{r} = position vector from A (m); \underline{F} = force vector (N)
Force vector components from magnitude and 45° angle
F = force magnitude (N); \theta = 45^\circ angle to horizontal
tips: Ensure the position vector r runs from the moment point (A) to the line of action of the force, not from the origin to the force.
Check the sign of the k component: subtract the j-term contribution from the i-term contribution correctly, since \( i \times j = k \) but \( j \times i = -k \).
rq: Why does the cross product only produce a component along k when both r and F lie in the x–y plane?
The cross product of two vectors is perpendicular to both; for vectors in the x–y plane, the result must point along the z-axis (k), so only the k component survives.
What would happen to the moment if the force acted along the line through A?
The position vector and force would be parallel, so their cross product is zero and the moment about A is zero.

xq.q: A force of \(F = 500\) N acts at point P on a bracket at 30° above the horizontal. P is 0.40 m to the right of and 0.30 m above a pivot O. Using Varignon's principle (resolve the force into horizontal and vertical components), find the moment of the force about O. Take anticlockwise as positive, and give the answer as a signed value in N·m.
s: Fy at x = +0.40 m gives anticlockwise: +250×0.40 = +100 N·m
Fx at y = +0.30 m gives clockwise: -433.0×0.30 = -129.9 N·m

xq.q: A force of 100 N acts vertically downward at a point on a beam 2 m along it from pivot A. The beam is inclined so that the straight line from A to the point makes 60° with the vertical. What is the magnitude of the moment about A?
xq.w: The moment arm is the horizontal perpendicular distance 2 sin60° = 1.73 m, so M = 173 N·m; using the full 2 m distance gives 200 N·m.
s: Perpendicular distance to vertical line of action = 2 sin60° = 1.732 m

xq.q: A force F acts at point P with position (x, y) relative to O, with components Fx and Fy. Show, using perpendicular distances, that the moment of F about O is \(M_{O}\) = xFy - yFx (anticlockwise positive), and explain why this agrees with Varignon's principle.
xq.a: Fy has line of action at perpendicular distance x from O and gives anticlockwise moment +xFy for positive x. Fx has line of action at perpendicular distance y and gives clockwise moment -yFx. Varignon states that the moment of F equals the sum of its component moments about the same point, so \(M_{O}\) = xFy - yFx, which equals F times its perpendicular distance.
s: Sum of component moments about same point O
Varignon: equals moment of F itself

units.name: 6.1 Equivalent force systems
units.ov: This material covers replacing a system of forces and couples with a simpler equivalent system, usually a single resultant force with a located line of action. The resultant's magnitude and direction come from summing components. Its position then comes from equating moments about a chosen point. The ideas connect because the force sum fixes R and the moment sum fixes where R acts.
must: Two systems are equivalent if they have the same resultant force AND the same resultant moment about any point (matching only the force gives the wrong location)
Resultant components: \(R_x=\sum F_x\), \(R_y=\sum F_y\), with signs set by direction and the chosen axes
Magnitude and direction: \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\), \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\), checking the quadrant from the signs of both components
Resolve inclined forces correctly: the 500 N at 60° gives \(500\cos60^\circ\) in x and \(500\sin60^\circ\) in y (don't swap them)
Locate the line of action with the moment equivalence \(\sum M_A = R\,d\), so \(d=M_A/R\) (for parallel forces \(d_R=M_A/F\))

Moment = force × perpendicular distance; for a horizontal beam only the vertical component of a force gives a moment about a point on the beam, but a horizontal force acting off the beam (the 100 N at 0.5 m height) also gives a moment and must be included
Use one consistent sign convention (e.g. anticlockwise positive) and the same reference point for every term; the point is arbitrary and any choice gives the same line of action
Equal and opposite forces at a point can be added or removed without changing the system (net force and moments both cancel)
Worked example: \(R_x=350\) N, \(R_y=-233\) N, \(R=420.5\) N, \(\theta=33.7^\circ\), line of action 0.9 m from A
Concurrent forces have the resultant through the common point; for non-concurrent forces the position must come from moments, not from an intersection point
conn: Component resolution feeds the moment calculation: the same \(R_x\), \(R_y\) give both the resultant magnitude and direction and the moment equation used to find \(d\)
Taking moments about a different point (A versus D) must give the same line of action, which serves as a check; resultant components at their own lever arms give \(\sum M_D=R_xd_y+R_yd_x\)
Equivalence of force systems leads into equilibrium: if \(R=0\) and the resultant moment is 0, the system is in balance, and a nonzero moment with \(R=0\) is a pure couple
Sign convention and unit consistency (N, m, N·m) affect both the resultant and its position, so one slip carries through the whole answer
exq: A beam carries a 500 N force at 60° to the beam at B (2 m from A), a 200 N vertical force at 3.5 m and a 100 N horizontal force 0.5 m above the beam. Find the resultant's magnitude and direction, and the distance from A at which its line of action crosses the beam.
Three parallel forces \(F_1\), \(F_2\), \(F_3\) act on a bar at known spacings. Replace them with a single resultant and find \(d_R=M_A/F\) from A. Then check by taking moments about a second point.
Explain why a pair of equal and opposite forces added at one point leaves a force system unchanged, and show that the moment about A of a three-force system equals \(F_1 d\).
Using the same beam loading, take moments about D rather than A to find the position of the resultant, and show that \(233\,d_x+350(0.5)\) equals the original system's moment about D.

Resolve a concurrent system with a 500 N force at 60°, a 100 N horizontal force and a 200 N vertical force. Find \(R\) and \(\theta\), and state the quadrant. Say what changes if one component's sign is wrong.

notes.t: Equivalent force systems
pts: Two force systems are equivalent if they produce the same total translational effect (net force) and the same rotational effect (moment about a point).

Adding a pair of equal and opposite forces at the same point does not change the system; here \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) are equal and opposite, so they cancel in net force, and their moments about A also cancel.
The moment about pivot A of the three-force system equals the moment of the single force \(F_{1}\) at distance d, so the single force can replace the whole system.
Moments are taken about the same point A in both systems, so the rotational comparison is valid only for that reference point.
defs: Equivalent force systems
Force systems that have the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any given point, so they produce identical translational and rotational effects on a body.
eqs: Net force of the system (translational effect)
Moment about pivot A of the single force (a)
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{1}\) = force (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Moment about pivot A of the three-force system (b)
M_A = (F_1 \times d) + (F_2 \times d) - (F_3 \times d) = F_1 \times d
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N·m); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = forces (N); d = distance from A (m)
tips: Check moment directions (clockwise vs anticlockwise) carefully when summing moments; opposing forces on opposite sides of the pivot subtract.
Equivalence of moments holds only about the same reference point; always state which point the moments are taken about.
rq: Why does the pair \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) leave the system unchanged even though they add extra forces?

They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their net force is zero, and their moments about A (\(F_{2}\) d and \(F_{3}\) d acting in opposite senses) cancel, giving no change in translation or rotation.
What would happen to the equivalence if \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\) were not equal in magnitude?
The net force would no longer equal \(F_{1}\) and the net moment about A would no longer equal \(F_{1}\) d, so the systems would not be equivalent.

notes.t: Equivalent systems of forces
pts: Any system of concurrent or non-concurrent forces on a body can be replaced by one equivalent resultant force.
For concurrent forces, the resultant acts where all lines of action intersect.
For non-concurrent forces, the resultant's location must be found by constructing an equivalent system.
An equivalent system must have the same resultant moment (rotational effect) as the original forces.
If the equivalent system is a single resultant force, the original system's moment about the point of application of that resultant must be zero, which locates its line of action.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that is statically equivalent to a system of forces, producing the same net force and the same resultant moment on a body.
Resultant moment
The net turning effect of a system of forces about a given point, equal to the sum of the moments of all forces about that point.
Concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action all pass through a single common point.
Non-concurrent forces
Forces whose lines of action do not all intersect at a single point.
tips: Do not place the resultant at the intersection point for non-concurrent forces; the line of action must be found from moment equivalence.
Ensure the equivalent system matches both the net force and the resultant moment; matching only force gives an incorrect location.
rq: Why must the resultant moment of the original forces about the resultant's point of application be zero when the system reduces to a single force?
A single force passing through a point produces no moment about that point, so the original system must produce none either to be equivalent; this condition locates the resultant's line of action.
Why can't you simply place the resultant at the centroid of the forces when they are non-concurrent?

Equivalence requires matching both force and moment; a non-concurrent system produces a moment that must be reproduced by offsetting the resultant's line of action, which the equivalent-system method determines.

notes.t: Equivalent systems: resultant force and moment about a point
pts: Equivalent force systems share the same resultant force and the same moment about any point; here the three parallel forces are replaced by one resultant F acting at distance \(d_{R}\) from A.
Take moments about any convenient point (here A) for the original system, with anticlockwise moments treated as positive according to the sign convention used.
The moment of the resultant about A must equal the total moment of the original forces about A, which fixes the line of action of the resultant.
The line of action of the resultant is found by dividing the moment by the resultant force: \(d_{R}\) = \(M_{A}\) / F.
defs: Resultant force
A single force equivalent to a system of forces, having the same net force (vector sum) and the same moment about any point as the original system.
Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from that point.
eqs: F = resultant force (N); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = individual forces (N), signed by direction
Moment of the original system about point A
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N m); \(F_{1}\), \(F_{2}\), \(F_{3}\) = forces (N); d = perpendicular distance from A (m)
Line of action of the resultant
\(M_{A}\) = moment about A (N m); F = resultant force (N); \(d_{R}\) = distance of resultant's line of action from A (m)
tips: Keep sign conventions consistent: forces and moments in one direction positive (here upwards forces and anticlockwise moments), and apply them the same way throughout the calculation.
Units trap: distances must be in metres (d = 0.5 m) so that moments come out in N m before dividing by force in N to get a distance in m.
rq: Why must the moment of the resultant about A equal the moment of the original forces about A?
Equivalent systems must have the same effect on the body; matching both net force and moment about a point ensures the resultant reproduces the original system's turning effect everywhere.
What would happen to \(d_{R}\) if \(F_{3}\) were 0 instead of 20 N, with \(F_{1}\) = \(F_{2}\) = 20 N and d = 0.5 m?
\(M_{A}\) = 20(0.5) + 20(0.5) = 20 N m and F = 20 - 20 = 0, so the resultant is a pure couple of 20 N m; no single resultant force exists and \(d_{R}\) is undefined.
Why does the choice of point A not change the final answer for the resultant force?
The resultant force F is the same regardless of point; only the moment changes with the reference point, and the line of action found from any point is the same once the moment is consistent.

notes.t: Equivalent systems: resultant of co-planar forces on a beam
pts: A resultant force R is found by summing the force components in x and y, and its line of action is located by summing moments about a chosen point.
The 500 N force acts at 60° to the beam, so it must be resolved into horizontal and vertical components before summing.
A couple/moment is created by the offset of the 100 N horizontal force 0.5 m above the beam at point D, which must be included in the moment sum.
The line of action of R is found where its moment about the reference point equals the sum of the moments of the original system.
defs: Resultant force
A single force that has the same external effect as a system of forces acting on a body, found by vector summation of the forces.
Co-planar forces
Forces whose lines of action all lie in the same plane.
eqs: Horizontal component of the resultant (sum of x-components)
\(R_{x}\) = horizontal component of resultant (N); \(F_{x}\) = component of each force in x-direction (N)
Vertical component of the resultant (sum of y-components)
\(R_{y}\) = vertical component of resultant (N); \(F_{y}\) = component of each force in y-direction (N)
Location of line of action via moment equivalence
\bar{x} = distance along beam from O to line of action of R (m); \sum \(M_{O}\) = sum of moments about O (N·m); \(R_{y}\) = vertical resultant (N)
tips: Watch units and angles: the 500 N component must use cos 60° horizontally and sin 60° vertically, not the reverse.
Do not forget the moment of the horizontal 100 N force, which acts at a height of 0.5 m above the beam.
rq: Why must the 500 N force be resolved into components rather than added directly to the 100 N force?
Forces acting in different directions cannot be added as scalars; only their components along the same axes can be summed, giving \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).
Why does the 100 N force at D contribute to the moment even though it acts horizontally?
Because it acts 0.5 m above the beam, its perpendicular distance to the beam axis produces a moment about points on the beam.

notes.t: Equivalent force systems: resultant of concurrent forces by components
pts: Resolve each inclined force into rectangular x and y components before adding.
Components of the resultant are the algebraic sums of the components of all forces, with sign set by direction.
The magnitude of the resultant follows from the Pythagorean theorem applied to its components.
The direction is the angle the resultant makes with the x-axis, found from the arctangent of the component ratio.
defs: Resultant force
A single force whose effect is equivalent to the combined effect of a system of forces acting on a body.
eqs: x-component of the 500 N force at B
y-component of the 500 N force at B
tips: Keep the sign of each component consistent with the chosen axes; a sign error changes both the magnitude and direction.
Use \( \tan^{-1} \) with the signs of both components to find the correct quadrant of θ, not just the magnitude of the ratio.
rq: Why must the 500 N force be resolved into components rather than added directly to the 100 N and 200 N forces?
Forces act in different directions, so only components along the same axis can be added algebraically; a vector sum requires component-wise addition.
Why is the y-component of the 500 N force negative while the 200 N load is taken as positive?
Signs follow the chosen axes: the 500 N force points downward (negative y), while the 200 N load at C points upward (positive y).
What happens to θ if \(R_{y}\) were positive rather than negative?
The resultant would point above the x-axis, so θ would be measured in the opposite sense; the quadrant must be checked from the signs of \(R_{x}\) and \(R_{y}\).

notes.t: Location of the Resultant (Equivalent Systems)
pts: Once the resultant force magnitude is known, its line of action must be located so the system is fully equivalent.
The line of action is found by equating moments: the moment of the resultant about a point equals the moment of the original forces about that same point.
The choice of reference point is arbitrary; any point gives the same line of action, which can be checked by using two different points.
tips: Be consistent with the sign convention for moments (clockwise vs anticlockwise) when equating the two sides.
Use the same reference point for all forces when summing moments; mixing points gives an incorrect line of action.
rq: Why must the moment of the resultant about a point equal the moment of the original forces about that same point?
Equivalent systems must produce the same force and the same moment at every point; otherwise the beam would respond differently to the two systems.
If you choose a different moment point, why does the resultant's line of action stay the same?
Because the moment condition holds for every point, so the location of the resultant derived from any point must agree with the others.

notes.t: Equivalent moment – locating the line of action of a resultant
pts: Moments about point A of the resultant equal the sum of moments of the original forces; this locates the resultant along the beam.
The resultant's moment about A is its vertical component times the perpendicular distance \(d_{A}\) from A.
A positive force-couple sign convention must be applied consistently when summing moments.
The line of action of the resultant is 0.9 m along the beam from A, so the equivalent system is the resultant at that position.
defs: Equivalent system
A simpler set of forces and/or couples that has the same resultant force and resultant moment about a point as the original system.
Line of action
The straight line along which a force acts; for a resultant it is the position at which the single force reproduces the moment of the original system.
eqs: Moment of the resultant about A
\(R_y\) = vertical component of resultant (N); \(d_A\) = distance from A to line of action of resultant (m)
\(d_A\) = distance from A (m); forces in N, distances in m
tips: Only the vertical component of inclined forces contributes to moments about A along a horizontal beam; do not use the full force magnitude.
Keep units consistent: forces in N and distances in m give moments in N·m, and sign conventions for clockwise/anticlockwise must match throughout.
rq: Why is the moment of the 500 N inclined force computed using only its vertical component, \(500\sin 60^\circ\), about A?
Because the horizontal component \(500\cos 60^\circ\) acts along the beam line through A, so its moment arm about A is zero.
What would happen to \(d_A\) if the 100 N force at E were omitted from the moment sum?
The denominator would still be −233 only if the vertical forces are unchanged; omitting the 100 N moment term changes the numerator, so \(d_A\) would change accordingly.

notes.t: Equivalent moment – replacing a force system with a resultant and moment about point D
pts: Taking moments about a point gives the moment of the resultant equal to the sum of the moments of the original forces
A resultant force R acting at distance d from a point produces the same moment as its components Rx and Ry acting at their own lever arms
Solving the moment equation for the unknown lever arm dx locates the resultant along the beam, measured from point A
defs: Equivalent system
A set of forces and moments that has the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any point as the original loading.
Moment about a point
The product of a force and its perpendicular distance from the point, equal to F × d; positive or negative depending on rotation sense.
eqs: Moment balance about point D for the resultant components
\(\Sigma M_D\) = sum of moments about D (N·m); \(R_x\) = horizontal resultant component (N); \(R_y\) = vertical resultant component (N); \(d_x\), \(d_y\) = perpendicular lever arms (m)
Solved moment equation giving the lever arm \(d_{x}\)
\(d_x\) = lever arm of resultant (m); forces in N; distances in m
tips: Ensure the 60° angle is applied correctly: horizontal component uses cos 60° and vertical uses sin 60° depending on the chosen axes, and mixing them gives wrong moments.
Convert all distances to metres before summing moments, and remember to subtract from the total span when reporting the position measured from point A.
rq: Why can we choose any point, such as D, to take moments about when finding an equivalent system?
Because an equivalent system must give the same resultant moment about every point; choosing D simply makes the unknown lever arm easy to solve for.
Why is the distance from A given as 4.5 − 3.6 rather than 3.6 m directly?
Because dx was measured from point D, so the position from A is the total length AD (4.5 m) minus dx.

xq.q: Parallel vertical forces act on a horizontal beam: 200 N downward at A (x = 0), 500 N upward at x = 2 m, and 100 N downward at x = 5 m. Replace them by a single equivalent resultant force. Find the distance of its line of action from A, in m, measured to the right of A.

Three non-concurrent forces on a body are replaced by a single resultant force with the same magnitude and direction as their vector sum. Which condition must also hold for the systems to be equivalent?
xq.a: The resultant must have the same moment about any point as the original forces
o: The resultant must act at the point where two of the forces intersect
The resultant must have the same moment about any point as the original forces
The resultant must act at the geometric centre of the body
The moment of the original forces about the resultant's point of application must be non-zero
xq.w: Equivalence needs both the same net force and the same moment, which fixes the line of action; matching force alone or choosing an intersection point is wrong.
s: Equivalent systems share force and moment
Moment equivalence locates the line of action

xq.q: A single force F1 acts at distance d from pivot A. A second system has F1, plus equal and opposite forces F2 and F3 acting at the same point (F2 = F3 in magnitude). Explain why the two systems are equivalent.
xq.a: F2 and F3 are equal and opposite and act at the same point, so their net force is zero and their moments about A are equal and opposite, so also cancel. Hence both systems have net force F1 and moment F1d about A, making them equivalent.
s: Net force of F2 and F3 is zero
Moments about A of F2 and F3 cancel
Remaining force F1 identical in both
Same force and same moment, so equivalent

units.name: 7.1 Force–couple systems
units.ov: This module covers couples (two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces giving pure moment with no net force) and equivalent force-couple systems. It then reduces a coplanar 4-force system to a single resultant R, a force-couple system at a point, and the line of action of R. Everything rests on two checks, \(\sum F\) and \(\sum M\) about the same point, which are used to move forces, replace systems, and locate the resultant.
must: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action. Net force is zero and it gives pure rotation: \(\sum F=F-F=0\).
Moment of a couple \(M=Fd\), where d is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action (not the distance from a moment centre or between the points of application).
A couple's moment is the same about every point, so it is a free vector. Check: \(M_A=F(a+d)-Fa=Fd\), and a drops out.
Moving a force F to a new point requires adding a couple \(M=Fd\), with d the perpendicular distance moved. The result is the same F at the new point plus a couple M.
Two force systems are equivalent only if both the resultant force and the resultant moment about the same point match. Matching \(\sum F\) alone is not enough.
Resolve inclined forces first: \(R_x=\sum F_x=50+250\cos45^\circ=226.8\) N and \(R_y=\sum F_y=-100-250\sin45^\circ=-276.8\) N. Down and left are negative.
Resultant magnitude \(R=\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}\approx358\) N. Direction \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)\approx50.7^\circ\) below the +x axis (down-right). Check the quadrant from the signs.
Force-couple system at A: R acts at A, plus \(M_A=\sum M_A=-(250\cos45^\circ)(1)-(100)(3.5)\approx-527\) N·m (clockwise). State the sign convention and use perpendicular arms.
Line of action of R: equate the moment of R about A to \(M_A\). Only \(R_x\) has a moment about a point on the y-axis, so \(226.8\,d=526.8\), giving \(d\approx2.32\) m.

Rigid-bar equilibrium with a couple: the two bar forces must be equal and opposite, and \(\sum M_A=0\) gives \(F_2(4)-200=0\), so \(F_2=50\) N (units N, not N·m). The bar's force pair forms an anticlockwise couple balancing the applied clockwise 200 N·m.
conn: Moving a force to another point (force-couple) is the same operation used to reduce the 4-force system to R plus \(M_A\). The added couple is the moment of the force about the new point.
The resultant R and \(M_A\) combine to give the line of action. Divide \(M_A\) by the relevant force component to get the offset d, which turns the force-couple system back into a single force.
Couples in equilibrium problems: a bar with an applied couple needs an equal and opposite couple from two equal, opposite forces. Use \(\sum F=0\) to link the forces and \(\sum M=0\) to find them.
Component resolution feeds both the force sums (R, θ) and the moments (the 45° force's moment arm). A wrong component or sign propagates into R, θ, \(M_A\) and d.
exq: A rigid weightless bar has an applied clockwise couple of 200 N·m. Forces \(F_1\) at A and \(F_2\) 4 m from A hold it in equilibrium. Find \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), state their directions, and explain why the answer is independent of the moment centre.

A 4-force coplanar system contains 50 N horizontal, 100 N downward and 250 N at 45° forces, with moment arms of 1 m and 3.5 m about A. Find \(R_x\), \(R_y\), the magnitude R and the direction θ of the resultant, and say which quadrant it lies in.
For the same system, find the equivalent force-couple system at A, giving \(M_A\) with its sense. Then find where the line of action of R crosses the y-axis, showing \(d\approx2.32\) m.

A 50 N force acts at R. Replace it with an equivalent force-couple system at a point S a perpendicular distance d away. Give the force and the couple moment with its sense, and show that \(\sum F\) and \(\sum M_A\) match the original.
