R tilts until its angle from N reaches φ_s; any further tilt would exceed the maximum friction, so motion begins.

xq.q: A 40 kg block is placed on a plank that is slowly tilted. The block just begins to slide when the plank is at 28° to the horizontal. The same block is then placed on a horizontal surface of the same material. Find the horizontal force needed to just start it sliding. Take \( g = 9.81 \) m/s².
s: At impending slip, μ_s = tan φ_s = tan 28° = 0.532

xq.q: Two dry surfaces have a coefficient of static friction \( \mu_s = 0.36 \). What is the static friction angle \( \varphi_s \), the angle between the total reaction \( R \) and the normal reaction \( N \) at impending slip?
xq.w: tan φ_s = μ_s gives φ_s = tan⁻¹ 0.36 = 19.8°; using sin⁻¹ gives 21.1°, 90° − φ gives 70.2° (the angle from the surface), and 36° wrongly treats μ as a percentage or angle.

xq.q: A block is on a rough horizontal surface and is on the point of sliding under a tangential force. Show that the angle \( \varphi_s \) between the total reaction \( R \) and the normal reaction \( N \) satisfies \( \tan\varphi_s = \mu_s \). Then explain why a block on a plane inclined at angle \( \theta \) just starts to slide when \( \theta = \varphi_s \).
xq.a: R is the resultant of N and the friction force F. At impending motion F = \(F_{\text{max}}\) = μ_s N. From the force triangle, tan φ_s = \(F_{\text{max}}\)/N = μ_s N/N = μ_s. On an incline the weight W is balanced by R, so R is vertical. N = W cos θ and F = W sin θ, so F/N = tan θ. Slip is impending when F/N = μ_s, that is tan θ = μ_s = tan φ_s, so θ = φ_s.
s: R is the resultant of N and F, and φ_s is measured from N
At impending slip, \(F_{\text{max}}\) = μ_s N, so tan φ_s = \(F_{\text{max}}\)/N = μ_s
On the incline, N = W cos θ and F = W sin θ, so F/N = tan θ
Slip is impending when tan θ = μ_s, so θ = φ_s

units.name: 10.5 Friction on inclined planes: impending motion and preventing slip
units.ov: This material covers static friction on an inclined plane. It treats impending slip, where friction is at its limiting value \(\mu_s N\), and the range of loads over which a body stays in equilibrium. The method is always the same: resolve perpendicular to the slope to get \(N\), then resolve along the slope with friction opposing the impending motion. This gives the winch tension to start motion up a slope, and the upper and lower bounds on a hanging mass \(m\) in the pulley example.
must: Resolve perpendicular to the slope first: \(N = mg\cos\theta\) (when no other load has a perpendicular component), not \(mg\).
Limiting friction at impending slip: \(F_{max}=\mu_s N\). In general \(F \le \mu_s N\), and equality holds only at the point of slipping.
Friction opposes the impending motion: it acts down the slope when the body is about to slide up, and up the slope when it is about to slide down.
Winch tension to just start motion up the slope: \(T = mg\sin\theta + \mu_s mg\cos\theta\).
Along the slope use \(\sin\theta\) for the weight component; perpendicular to the slope use \(\cos\theta\). Swapping them is the commonest error.
Frictionless pulleys mean the cable tension equals the hanging weight (\(T=mg\)) on each side.

A no-slip problem has two limiting cases, one for each direction of impending slip, and together they give a range of \(m\). Down-slope slip: \(9.81m-20(9.81)+\mu_sN-25(9.81)\sin30^\circ=0\), giving \(m_{min}\approx 24.9\) kg. Up-slope slip: the friction sign flips, giving \(m_{max}\approx 40.1\) kg.
Worked example values: \(N = 25(9.81)\cos30^\circ = 212.4\) N, so \(F_{max}=0.35\times212.4\approx74.3\) N.
Use \(\mu_s\) for impending motion or no-slip and \(\mu_k\) once the body is sliding. Keep mass in kg, forces in N and angles correct in the calculator.
Correction to the notes: '0.35 N' means \(0.35\times N\), i.e. \(\mu_s N\), not a friction force of 0.35 newtons. The notes' 'm = 25 kg' is really 24.9 kg.
conn: Free-body diagram and equilibrium (\(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0\)) feed into friction: \(N\) from the perpendicular equation sets the friction limit used in the parallel equation.
Pulley and cable systems combine with friction: tensions equal the hanging weights, and these act as the driving forces along the slope.

Impending up-slope and down-slope slip give the two bounds of one range. A question asking for the range of \(m\), or for the minimum and maximum load, needs both cases with the friction sign reversed.
The slope angle links to the friction angle: slip is impending when \(\tan\theta=\mu_s\) with no applied load. Exam questions may ask whether a body self-locks on a given slope.
exq: A crate of mass 25 kg rests on a 30° slope with \(\mu_s=0.35\) and is pulled up the slope by a winch cable parallel to the slope. Find the tension at which it is about to slide up. Use \(T=mg\sin\theta+\mu_s mg\cos\theta\).

A 25 kg block lies on a 30° slope (\(\mu_s=0.35\)). A 20 kg mass hangs from a cable pulling it down the slope and a mass \(m\) hangs from a cable pulling it up the slope, both over frictionless pulleys. Draw the free-body diagrams and find the minimum and maximum \(m\) for equilibrium (about 24.9 kg and 40.1 kg).
Explain why the direction of friction reverses between the two limiting cases in the pulley problem. Write the \(\sum F_x\) equation for each case.
Show that a block on an incline with no applied load is on the point of slipping when \(\tan\theta=\mu_s\). For \(\mu_s=0.35\), find the maximum angle at which it stays at rest (about 19.3°).
For the 25 kg block on the 30° slope, state the friction force actually acting if \(m=30\) kg, and explain why it is less than \(\mu_s N\).

notes.t: Friction on an inclined plane: winch tension to start sliding up
pts: For impending motion up the incline, static friction acts down the slope and is at its maximum value \(F_s = \mu_s N\).
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane to find the normal force; the normal force is not simply the weight.
Resolve forces parallel to the plane: winch tension balances the weight component plus maximum friction at impending motion.
defs: Coefficient of static friction
Dimensionless ratio \(\mu_s\) giving the maximum static friction force as a fraction of the normal force between two surfaces before slipping begins.
Impending motion
The state in which a body is on the verge of sliding, with static friction at its maximum value \(\mu_s N\).
eqs: \(F_s\) = maximum static friction (N); \(\mu_s\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); \(N\) = normal force (N)
\(N\) = normal force (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); \(\theta\) = incline angle (°)
Tension needed for impending motion up the incline
\(T\) = cable tension (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); \(\theta\) = incline angle (°); \(\mu_s\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless)
tips: Use \(F_s = \mu_s N\) only at the point of impending motion; for a body already sliding use kinetic friction \(\mu_k N\).
Keep angles and units consistent: \(\theta\) in degrees must be converted properly in trigonometric functions, and mass in kg gives weight in N via \(g\).
rq: Why does static friction point down the slope rather than up it when the crate is about to slide up?
Friction opposes the impending relative motion, which is up the slope, so friction acts down the slope.
What happens to the required tension if the incline angle increases, and why?

Tension increases because both the gravity component \(mg\sin\theta\) increases and the normal force \(mg\cos\theta\), hence friction, decreases only partly; the net effect is a larger required tension for steeper slopes in the sliding-up case.
Why must the normal force be found from perpendicular equilibrium rather than taken as \(mg\)?
Because the incline carries only the component \(mg\cos\theta\) of the weight perpendicular to the surface, and the winch cable's tension also has a component acting along the slope, not into it.

notes.t: Static friction on an inclined plane: impending motion
pts: At the instant before the crate slides, static friction is at its maximum value, equal to the coefficient of static friction times the normal force.
Resolving forces perpendicular to the incline gives the normal force, which equals the component of weight perpendicular to the surface.
Along the incline, the applied tension must balance the maximum friction plus the component of weight down the slope.
defs: Maximum static friction
The largest friction force that can act between two surfaces at rest, proportional to the normal force; motion begins when it is exceeded.
eqs: \(\mu_s\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); \(N\) = normal force (N); \((F_f)_{\max}\) = maximum static friction (N)
Normal force on an incline (equilibrium perpendicular to the surface)
\(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); \(\theta\) = incline angle (degrees); \(N\) = normal force (N)
Tension required to just initiate motion up the incline
\(T\) = rope tension (N); \((F_f)_{\max}\) = maximum static friction (N); \(m\) = mass (kg); \(g\) = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); \(\theta\) = incline angle (degrees)
tips: Use the normal force \(N = mg\cos\theta\), not \(mg\), when computing friction on an incline; forgetting the cosine overstates friction.
Keep angles in consistent units and ensure the friction direction opposes impending motion (down the slope when the crate is pulled up), otherwise the sign in \(\sum F_x\) will be wrong.
rq: Why does the friction force take its maximum value at the instant before motion, rather than at its value when the crate is at rest under a small load?
Static friction adjusts to match the applied force up to a limit; it reaches \(\mu_s N\) only when the applied tension is just large enough to start the crate sliding (impending motion).
Why is the normal force \(mg\cos\theta\) and not \(mg\)?
On an incline, the surface supports only the component of weight perpendicular to it; the component \(mg\sin\theta\) acts along the slope and must be balanced by tension and friction.

notes.t: Static friction on an inclined plane with pulleys (Example 2)
pts: The crate is in equilibrium, so the net force along the slope must be zero with friction acting to resist impending slip.
The 20kg mass pulls the crate one way and the mass m pulls the other way over frictionless pulleys, so cable tensions equal the hanging weights.
Limiting static friction gives the upper and lower bounds on m, one for each direction of impending slip.
Resolve the 25kg weight into components parallel and perpendicular to the 30° slope before applying friction.
defs: Coefficient of static friction
The dimensionless ratio of the maximum static friction force to the normal reaction, \(F_{\text{max}}\) = μ_s N, which must not be exceeded for no slip.
eqs: F = friction force (N); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
N = normal reaction (N); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); 30° = incline angle
tips: Do not use the kinetic coefficient; the problem gives the static coefficient, and only the static limit applies to no-slip.
Remember to use mass in kg for the normal reaction calculation with 25g cos 30°, and keep the weight term in newtons.
rq: Why does the friction force change direction when you check the two limits of m?
Friction always opposes the impending slip. If m is too light the crate slides down the slope, so friction acts up the slope; if m is too heavy it slides up, so friction acts down the slope.
Why is the tension in the cable equal to the weight of the hanging mass?
The pulleys are frictionless and the hanging masses are in equilibrium, so each cable tension equals the weight of the mass it supports (T = mg).

notes.t: Friction on an inclined plane: preventing slip
pts: Resolve forces into components parallel and perpendicular to the incline; the normal force balances the perpendicular weight component.
Equilibrium along the incline requires the friction force to balance the net driving force down the slope; the friction force is found from the limiting friction condition.
eqs: Equilibrium perpendicular to the incline (normal force)
N = normal reaction (N); m = mass (kg); 9.81 = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); 30° = incline angle
Equilibrium along the incline (solve for mass to prevent slip)
m = mass of block (kg); \(F_{f}\) = friction force (N); N = normal force (N); 0.35 = coefficient used for friction; θ = 30° incline angle
tips: Ensure consistent units: the friction force \(F_f = 0.35\ \text{N}\) and weight terms must be in newtons, using \(g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2\) throughout.
Take the sine component for forces along the incline and the cosine component for the perpendicular direction; swapping them is a common error.
rq: Why does the normal force equal the component of weight perpendicular to the incline rather than the full weight?
Because there is no acceleration perpendicular to the surface, so the normal force balances only the weight component \(W\cos\theta\), i.e. \(N = mg\cos 30^\circ\).
Why must friction act up the slope in this problem?
Friction opposes the tendency to slip, so when the block would otherwise slide down, friction acts up the incline, reducing the net down-slope force.

notes.t: Friction on an inclined plane: preventing slip up the incline
pts: Resolve forces perpendicular to the incline first (Σ\(F_{y}\) = 0) to find the normal reaction N.
Resolve forces along the incline (Σ\(F_{x}\) = 0), with friction acting down the slope when the body tends to slide up.
The weight component along the incline is W sin θ, and the perpendicular component is W cos θ, where θ = 30°.
Friction force is limited by \(F_{f}\) ≤ μN, so the friction value of 0.35 N is used directly in the equilibrium equation.
defs: Normal reaction (N)
The contact force exerted by the inclined surface on the body, acting perpendicular to the surface.
eqs: N = normal reaction (N); 25 = body mass (kg); 9.81 = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); 30° = incline angle
Equilibrium along the incline (limiting up-slope slip)
m = mass of the applied block (kg); N = normal reaction (N); 0.35 N = friction force (N); 20 and 25 = masses (kg)
tips: Keep the sign convention consistent: take the direction of the applied load as positive and the friction direction opposite to the impending motion.
Use the correct angle in the components: the weight perpendicular to the plane uses cos θ, and along the plane uses sin θ.
rq: Why is the normal reaction found before the along-slope equation is solved?
Because the friction force depends on N (\(F_{f}\) = μN), so N must be known before friction can be substituted into the x-direction equilibrium.
What would happen to the required mass range if friction were ignored?
The lower bound would be unchanged in principle, but the upper bound would be reduced, since friction contributes a restraining force that allows a larger mass to be held.

xq.q: A 50 kg crate lies on a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. A cable parallel to the plane pulls the crate up the slope. The coefficient of static friction is \( \mu_s = 0.40 \). Take \( g = 9.81 \) m/s². Find the cable tension \( T \) at which the crate is just about to slide up the slope.
s: Perpendicular to the plane: N = mg cos 25° = 490.5(0.9063) = 444.5 N
Maximum friction acts down the slope: F = 0.40(444.5) = 177.8 N
Weight component down the slope: mg sin 25° = 490.5(0.4226) = 207.3 N

xq.q: A 20 kg crate rests on a 30° incline with \( \mu_s = 0.60 \), with no other force applied (take \( g = 9.81 \) m/s²). What is the friction force acting on the crate?
xq.w: The crate is in equilibrium, so friction equals the weight component down the slope, mg sin 30° = 98.1 N, which is less than the limit 102 N; quoting μ_s N gives 102 N, μ_s mg gives 118 N, and N = mg cos θ gives 170 N.
s: Equilibrium along the slope: F = mg sin 30° = 98.1 N
98.1 N < 102 N, so there is no slip and friction is 98.1 N

xq.q: A 25 kg block rests on a rough 30° slope with \( \mu_s = 0.40 \). A light cable parallel to the slope runs up over a frictionless pulley and carries a 20 kg mass hanging at its upper end. A second cable runs down the slope over another frictionless pulley and carries a mass \( m \) (kg). Take \( g = 9.81 \) m/s². Find the largest \( m \) for which the block does not slip down the slope.
s: Cable tensions equal the hanging weights: 20g up the slope and mg down the slope
N = 25g cos 30°, so \(F_{\text{max}}\) = 0.40(25g cos 30°) = 8.66g, acting up the slope at impending slip downward

units.name: 10.6 Friction with springs and guides: limiting equilibrium examples
units.ov: This material covers limiting equilibrium of a box or block held in guide rails or clamped between two faces, loaded by a spring, its weight and an applied force P. Friction acts on both faces, so the limit is \(2\mu N\). Its direction flips between the two impending-slip cases, which gives a minimum and a maximum P. The method is a free-body diagram, a vertical force balance with friction at its limit, and then the two cases solved for the range of P.
must: Method: draw a free-body diagram, state the direction of impending slip, put friction opposing it at \(F_f=\mu N\) per face, then apply \(\sum F_y=0\). Derive the signs each time rather than memorising them.
Friction acts on both guide faces: \(F_{f,\max}=2\mu N\), where N is the normal force on each face.
Friction always opposes the impending motion. If the block tends to slide up, friction acts down; if it tends to slide down, friction acts up.
Spring force \(F_s=kx\), with x the extension from the unstretched length, always converted to metres (0.1 m, not 100). Here \(k=600\) N/m and \(x=0.1\) m give 60 N.
Weight \(W=mg\) (here 29.43 N, so m = 3 kg with g = 9.81) must appear in the vertical balance in both limiting cases.
The range of P is \(P=ky-mg\mp 2\mu_sF\). The two limits are symmetric about \(ky-mg\), and the width of the range is \(4\mu_sF\).

The case that gives the smaller P is the one in which friction helps P. Check that the result is physically sensible (for example, that \(P_{min}<P_{max}\) and the sign of P matches the arrow direction).
Static friction is an inequality, \(F_f\le\mu_s N\). Any P between the two limits holds the block in equilibrium, and the limits are the impending-slip values.

Be careful with the notes: the p18 labelling (friction down for \(P_{\text{min}}\) while the block 'tends to slide down') is internally inconsistent. Always confirm the direction of P on the diagram and re-derive.
conn: Free-body diagram with the sign of friction: the choice of impending-slip direction fixes the signs in the equilibrium equation, which fixes whether you are finding \(P_{\text{min}}\) or \(P_{\text{max}}\).

Spring mechanics with friction: spring extension changes the spring force, so the allowable range of P depends on position y. Questions may ask for the range of y that is in equilibrium for a given P.
Normal force from a clamping mechanism: N may come from a clamping force or another equilibrium (for example, a wedge or screw). It then feeds into \(2\mu N\).
Units and numerical consistency: converting mm to m, mass to weight, and a final check that the answer is in N tie together the spring, weight and friction terms.
exq: A 3 kg box slides in a vertical slot with friction on both faces (\(\mu_s\) given, clamping force F on each face). It is supported by a spring with \(k=600\) N/m stretched 100 mm. Find the minimum and maximum vertical force P for equilibrium.
For the same box, draw the free-body diagrams for impending upward and downward slip. Show the direction of friction in each and write the equilibrium equation.

Find the minimum coefficient of static friction needed for the block to stay in equilibrium with no applied force (P = 0), given \(k=600\) N/m, extension 0.1 m, m = 3 kg and clamping force F on each face.
For a given P, find the range of spring extension y over which the block remains at rest, and explain what happens at each end of the range.
A student writes \(P_{min}=ky-mg+2\mu_sF\). Identify the error, explain physically why the result is wrong, and give the corrected expression with a numerical value.

notes.t: Friction in guide rails: limiting equilibrium of a sliding box with a spring
pts: Friction in a guided slot acts on both contacting faces, so total friction capacity is the coefficient times the normal force on each face summed over both faces.
Spring force is the stiffness times the extension, and it acts upward on the box; it is not reduced by the box's own weight in the friction calculation.
Upward slip is prevented when the applied load P is large enough that friction acts downward at its limiting value; downward slip is prevented when friction acts upward at its limiting value.
Weight acts downward on the box and must be included in the equilibrium of vertical forces together with P, spring force and friction.
defs: Coefficient of static friction
The ratio of the maximum friction force that can be developed before slip begins to the normal (compressive) force pressing the surfaces together.
Limiting friction
The maximum friction force that can be generated at an impending slip condition, equal to the coefficient of static friction multiplied by the normal reaction.
eqs: \(F_{s}\) = spring force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); x = extension from unstretched length (m)
Maximum friction force for two contacting faces
\(F_{f}\) = total limiting friction force (N); \mu = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = compressive force on each face (N)
W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
tips: Convert all lengths to metres before using k = 600 N/m; a 100 mm stretch is 0.1 m, not 100.
Do not forget the box's weight (mg, with g = 9.81 m/\(s^{2}\)) when balancing vertical forces in both limiting cases.
rq: Why is the friction force doubled in the calculation even though only one coefficient is given?
Because the guide rails press on two contacting faces of the box, each face develops limiting friction \( \mu N \), so the total is \( 2\mu N \).
Which direction does friction act when the box is about to slip upward, and why does this change the sign of the friction term?
Friction acts downward, opposing upward motion, so it adds to the downward forces (weight and friction) and the minimum P must balance them against the spring force.

notes.t: Friction on a block clamped between two forces – minimum and maximum pulling force P
pts: The spring force ky opposes the block's position; with k = 0.1 × 600 = 60 N it is the largest upward term.
For the minimum P, friction acts downward on the block (block tends to slide down), so friction subtracts from the upward forces.
For the maximum P, friction acts upward (block tends to slide up), so friction adds to the upward forces.
The friction limit on each face is μ_s times the normal force F, giving the static friction bound.
The weight term mg = 29.43 N is subtracted in both cases; the range of P is between the two limits.
defs: Static friction coefficient (μ_s)
The ratio of the maximum static friction force to the normal force just before slipping begins; it sets the limiting friction force μ_s F.
eqs: Minimum applied force \(P_{\text{min}}\) (block about to slide down)

P = applied force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); y = extension (m); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); μ_s = static friction coefficient (dimensionless); F = normal (clamping) force (N)
Maximum applied force \(P_{\text{max}}\) (block about to slide up)

P = applied force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); y = extension (m); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); μ_s = static friction coefficient (dimensionless); F = normal (clamping) force (N)
tips: Keep consistent units: k in N/m multiplied by y in m gives N; check that 0.1 × 600 gives 60 N, not a unit mismatch.
Do not swap the signs: \(P_{\text{min}}\) subtracts 2μ_sF and \(P_{\text{max}}\) adds it; reversing these gives a wrong (larger minimum) answer.
rq: Why does friction subtract in the \(P_{\text{min}}\) case but add in the \(P_{\text{max}}\) case?

Friction always opposes the tendency to slip: when the block tends to slide down (\(P_{\text{min}}\)), friction acts up and reduces the required force; when it tends to slide up (\(P_{\text{max}}\)), friction acts down and increases the required force.
Why is the factor 2 present in the friction terms?
Two faces of the block are in contact with the clamping forces F, so friction acts on both faces, each contributing μ_s F.

xq.q: A box of mass m = 3 kg slides in a vertical guide slot. The slot walls touch the box on two faces, each pressed on by a clamping force F = 40 N, and the coefficient of static friction is \(\mu_s\) = 0.30. A spring of stiffness k = 600 N/m is stretched y = 100 mm and pulls the box upward. A force P acts downward on the box. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the largest P for which the box stays in equilibrium, i.e. the box is about to slide down with friction acting upward at its limit on both faces.
s: Spring force ky = 600 × 0.1 = 60 N; weight mg = 3 × 9.81 = 29.43 N
Limiting friction on both faces: 2\(\mu_s\)F = 2 × 0.30 × 40 = 24 N
Vertical equilibrium with friction up: ky + 2\(\mu_s\)F = P + mg

xq.q: For the guided box of mass 3 kg (g = 9.81 m/s²), the spring has k = 600 N/m and is stretched 100 mm, pulling the box upward. The clamping force on each of the two faces is F = 50 N and \(\mu_s\) = 0.25. P acts downward on the box. What is the minimum P for equilibrium, with the box about to slide up and friction acting downward at its limit?
xq.w: \(P_{\text{min}}\) = ky − mg − 2\(\mu_s\)F = 60 − 29.43 − 25 = 5.57 N; the traps are swapping the friction sign (55.6 N), omitting the weight (35.0 N) and counting friction on one face only (18.1 N).

xq.q: A box of mass m is held in a vertical guide slot, with clamping force F on each of its two faces. A spring of stiffness k, extended by y, pulls the box upward, and a force P acts downward. The coefficient of static friction is \(\mu_s\). Derive expressions for the minimum and maximum values of P for which the box stays in equilibrium, and explain the direction of friction in each case.
xq.a: The spring force is ky upward and the weight is mg downward. Limiting friction over both faces is 2\(\mu_s\)F. For \(P_{\text{min}}\) the box is about to slide up, so friction acts downward: ky = P + mg + 2\(\mu_s\)F, giving \(P_{\text{min}}\) = ky − mg − 2\(\mu_s\)F. For \(P_{\text{max}}\) the box is about to slide down, so friction acts upward: ky + 2\(\mu_s\)F = P + mg, giving \(P_{\text{max}}\) = ky − mg + 2\(\mu_s\)F. P can lie anywhere between these limits.
s: Identify the forces: ky up, mg down, P down, friction on two faces (1 mark)
Limiting friction is 2\(\mu_s\)F, since friction acts on both faces (1 mark)
Impending upward slip: friction acts down, giving \(P_{\text{min}}\) = ky − mg − 2\(\mu_s\)F (1.5 marks)
Impending downward slip: friction acts up, giving \(P_{\text{max}}\) = ky − mg + 2\(\mu_s\)F (1.5 marks)
Equilibrium holds for P between the two limits (1 mark)

units.name: 11.1 Trusses 1: introduction to trusses
units.ov: This introductory material frames structural design around three checks: strength (no material failure), stability (no mechanism) and stiffness (acceptably small deflection). It then introduces trusses, which are triangulated frameworks of straight members joined at their ends and idealised as frictionless pins. The pin idealisation, with axial-only member forces, is what makes truss analysis tractable and sets up the later methods (joints and sections).
must: Three separate structural checks: strength, stability, stiffness. A structure must satisfy all three, not just strength.
Strength: the ability to carry load without material failure (yielding or fracture). Failure occurs where stress or bending moment is greatest, e.g. mid-span of a beam or the base of a column.
Stability: the ability to avoid failure by instability. An unstable structure moves as a mechanism without any material failing.
Stiffness: resistance to deformation, so that deflections stay small. It is distinct from strength: a strong member can be flexible and a stiff one can still fail (Millennium Bridge example).
Truss: a rigid framework of straight members joined at their ends in a triangulated pattern. A triangle is geometrically rigid, which is why trusses resist deformation.
Ideal truss assumption: frictionless pin joints that transmit only axial force (no moment, free rotation), so each member is in pure tension or compression.
The pin joint is an idealisation. Real joints (gusset plates, welded or bolted connections, two bolts) are not true pins, and real members may carry some bending.
Long compression members buckle, so members are kept short or buckling is checked explicitly.
Use precise exam wording: a truss is 'rigid' and 'triangulated' (not just 'strong'), and it differs from a continuous beam or a rigidly jointed frame.
Statics shifts from external forces on a rigid body to internal forces within a structure, which is the basis for finding member forces.
conn: Stability and triangulation: a non-triangulated pin-jointed frame is a mechanism (an instability failure), while adding triangles gives a rigid truss. This links the definition of stability to the choice of truss geometry.

Pin-joint idealisation and axial forces: the assumption that members carry only axial force lets you use equilibrium at joints or sections. The same assumption underlies tension/compression classification and the buckling check on compression members.
Strength versus buckling: a compression member may fail by buckling (instability) before it reaches material yield, so strength and stability checks must both be applied to the same member.
Ideal versus real: gusset plates and rigid connections introduce bending that the ideal analysis ignores. Questions often ask you to justify when the ideal-truss model is acceptable.
exq: Define strength, stability and stiffness for a structure. Give an example where a structure is strong but not stiff, and one where it fails by instability without material failure.
State the assumptions of ideal truss analysis. Explain why two bolts at a joint do not behave as a frictionless pin, and discuss how this affects the validity of the member-force results.
Explain why a triangle is the basic unit of a rigid truss. Sketch a four-bar pin-jointed rectangle, show how it behaves as a mechanism, and add one member to make it rigid.
Why are truss members kept short? A long slender member in a truss is in compression: describe the likely failure mode and how it differs from yielding.

Describe the role of gusset plates in real trusses. Compare an ideal pin-jointed truss with a real bridge truss, and state the type of internal force each member is assumed to carry in the ideal case.

notes.t: Structures: strength, stability and stiffness
pts: Earlier work only considered external forces acting on a rigid body; this section shifts focus to forces internal to a structure.
Strength and stability together ensure the structure does not collapse.
Stiffness ensures the structure does not deform too much under load.
defs: Strength
The ability of a structure to carry applied loads without failing or collapsing.
Stability
The ability of a structure to maintain its equilibrium configuration without sudden collapse or unwanted movement under load.
Stiffness
The resistance of a structure to deformation under applied load, so that it does not deform too much.
tips: Do not confuse stiffness with strength: a stiff member may still fail under a large load, and a strong member may deform excessively.
Analysis of internal forces applies to structures, whereas earlier statics problems treated the body as rigid with only external forces.
rq: Why must strength and stability both be checked, rather than strength alone?
A structure can have adequate material strength yet still be unstable (e.g. buckling or tipping), which causes collapse even though no member fails in tension or compression.
What is the difference between a structure that collapses and one that deforms too much?

Collapse means failure or loss of load-carrying capacity (strength/stability); excessive deformation means the structure still carries load but moves too much (stiffness), which may still make it unserviceable.

notes.t: Structures: strength, stability and stiffness
pts: Earlier work only considered external forces acting on a rigid body; attention now shifts to forces internal to a structure.
Strength means the structure must withstand the load without material failure.
Stability means the structure must avoid failure due to instability, i.e. a mechanism.
Stiffness means the structure must not deform too much under load.
defs: Strength
The ability of a structure to carry the applied load without material failure (yielding or fracture).
Stability
The ability of a structure to avoid failure by instability; an unstable structure can move as a mechanism without material failure.
Stiffness
The ability of a structure to resist deformation under load so that displacements remain acceptably small.
tips: Do not confuse stability (instability/mechanism) with strength (material failure); they are separate checks.
Check all three attributes—strength, stability and stiffness—when assessing a structure, not just strength.
rq: Why can a structure with adequate strength still fail?
It can lack stability: if it is unstable it may collapse as a mechanism even though no material has failed.
What is the difference between strength and stiffness?
Strength concerns material failure under load; stiffness concerns how much the structure deforms. A structure can be strong but too flexible.

notes.t: Strength of structural members
pts: A beam or member must be strong enough to carry the loads applied to it without failing; left unchecked, it can break under load.
The left diagram shows a beam supported at both ends that fractures at mid-span under load, dropping the load onto the person below.
The right diagram shows a vertical column that fails at its base when a person hangs from the end of a horizontal arm, illustrating that failure occurs where bending and axial stress are greatest.
tips: Failure in a member typically occurs at the section of maximum bending moment or stress, not at a random point.
Check that the member's strength is assessed against the actual load path, including where the load is applied.
rq: Why does the beam on the left break near its middle rather than at its supports?
The bending moment is greatest at mid-span for a simply supported beam under a central load, so the tensile bending stress is highest there.
What would happen to the cantilever-type column on the right if the person hung from a point closer to the column?
The bending moment at the base would decrease, reducing the stress at the critical section and lowering the chance of failure.

notes.t: Stiffness
pts: A stiff structure resists deformation under load, so it stays nearly flat when a load is applied.
A flexible structure bends noticeably under the same load, so it deflects much more.
tips: Stiffness describes resistance to deflection, not strength; a member can be strong yet still flexible.
rq: Why does a stiff beam support a person and dog with little visible bending, while a flexible one sags a lot?
A stiff member resists deformation, so its deflection under the same load is small; a flexible member deforms much more under that load.

notes.t: Stiffness
pts: A stiff structure resists bending under load, so it deflects very little when a person walks on it.
A flexible structure bends noticeably under the same load, with a larger deflection.
The page is a movie slide illustrating these ideas using London's Millennium Bridge as the example.
tips: Stiffness describes resistance to deflection under load, not strength; a strong member can still be flexible.
rq: Why does a stiffer beam feel more solid to walk on than a flexible one carrying the same person?
A stiffer beam deflects less under the same load, so it does not sag or sway noticeably under the walker's weight.

notes.t: Pin-jointed structures - trusses
pts: A truss is a framework of members joined at their ends that forms a rigid structure.
Trusses are built from short straight elements in a stable, triangulated pattern, which is what makes them rigid.
A rigid truss only undergoes relatively minor overall deformations under load.
Trusses have a long history, with timber trusses in use since Roman times.
Common modern applications include bridges, roof supports, cranes and transmission pylons.
defs: Truss
A rigid framework of straight members interconnected at their ends, arranged in a stable triangulated pattern.
tips: A truss is defined by its members being joined at their ends (pin-jointed); do not confuse it with a continuous beam or frame with rigid joints.
Students often describe a truss as 'strong' rather than 'rigid' and 'stable'; use the terms rigid and triangulated in exam answers.
rq: Why does triangulation, rather than a rectangular arrangement of members, give a truss its rigidity?
A triangle cannot change shape without changing member lengths, so its joints cannot move freely; a rectangle can deform into a parallelogram, so it is not stable on its own.
If a truss is described as 'rigid', what does that tell you about the size of its deformations under load?
They are relatively small, so the structure keeps its overall geometry under normal loading.

notes.t: Pin-jointed structures - trusses
pts: Truss members are typically I-sections, channel sections, angle sections, or bars, joined by welding, bolting or pins.
Truss analysis assumes joints are frictionless pins, but real joints (e.g. two bolts) do not behave as ideal pins.
Real truss connections are most often made through gusset plates that join several members at a node.
Members are kept short because long elements are prone to buckling under compression.
defs: Gusset plate
A flat plate used to connect several truss members at a joint, through which welded or bolted connections are made.
Frictionless pin joint
An idealised joint assumed in truss analysis that transmits only axial force between members and carries no moment, rotation being free.
tips: Two bolts do not behave as a pin; the frictionless pin assumption is an idealisation, not a physical reality.
Long compression members can buckle, so keep element lengths short or check buckling explicitly.
rq: Why does the ideal pin-joint assumption matter for how a real truss is modelled?
Because real joints (bolts, welds, gusset connections) transmit some moment and friction, so the pin assumption is an approximation that makes analysis simpler but is not exact.
Why are truss members kept short in design?
Long slender members in compression are liable to buckle at loads well below their material yield capacity, so shortness limits buckling risk.

notes.t: Applications of trusses
pts: Trusses are used in a wide range of real structures, including bridges, cranes, towers, and aerospace structures.
Truss members are arranged in triangular units because a triangle is geometrically rigid, so the structure resists deformation under load.
Biological structures such as bone and the foot arch show truss-like load paths, with trabecular bone and the plantar aponeurosis acting as load-carrying members.
tips: Do not confuse the biological examples with engineered trusses: they illustrate similar load paths but are not ideal pin-jointed trusses.
Real structures like bridges have members that may carry bending or be rigidly connected; the ideal truss analysis assumes pin joints and axial-only forces.
rq: Why do the bridges and towers on this page use triangular arrangements of members rather than rectangular frames?
A triangle cannot change shape without changing member lengths, so it is geometrically rigid; a rectangle can deform (shear) into a parallelogram unless diagonals are added, which form triangles.
What do the trabecular bone and the foot images suggest about how natural structures carry load?
They suggest load is carried along efficient internal paths, with material concentrated along the lines of tension and compression, similar to how truss members carry axial forces.

xq.q: A footbridge carries pedestrians without any member yielding or fracturing, and it does not collapse as a mechanism. However, it bends visibly under the walkers' weight. Which attribute is inadequate?
xq.a: Stiffness, because it deflects too much under load
o: Strength, because the bridge has deformed under load
Stability, because it moves under load
Stiffness, because it deflects too much under load
None, because any bridge that stays up is satisfactory
xq.w: Excessive deflection without material failure or mechanism motion is a lack of stiffness; the traps are confusing deflection with failure (strength) or with mechanism motion (stability).
s: No material failure, so strength is adequate
No mechanism, so stability is adequate
Excessive deflection means stiffness is inadequate

xq.q: Which statement best explains why a truss is described as rigid?
xq.a: It is built from straight members joined at their ends in a triangulated pattern, so it undergoes only small overall deformation
o: It is built from heavy members that cannot break
It is built from straight members joined at their ends in a triangulated pattern, so it undergoes only small overall deformation
It is built from members rigidly welded so that bending is carried at every joint
It contains as many members as possible, whatever their arrangement
xq.w: Rigidity comes from triangulation of pin-jointed straight members; the traps are confusing rigid with strong, with rigid-jointed frames, or with simply having many members.
s: Pin-jointed straight members give only small deformation; rigid is not the same as strong

xq.q: Explain the difference between strength, stability and stiffness of a structure. For each, give one example of how a structure could be inadequate in that respect.
xq.a: Strength is the ability to carry the load without material failure, for example a beam fractures at mid-span or a column fails at its base. Stability is the ability to avoid failure by instability, where the structure moves as a mechanism without material failure, for example a pinned four-sided frame that collapses sideways. Stiffness is the resistance to deformation, so that displacements stay acceptably small, for example a flexible bridge deck that deflects a lot when people walk on it. All three must be checked, because a strong member may be flexible and a stiff one may still fail.
s: Strength: no material failure, with an example (1.5 marks)
Stability: no mechanism or instability, with an example (1.5 marks)
Stiffness: small deflection, with an example (1.5 marks)
All three need checking, and they are separate (0.5 mark)

units.name: 12.1 Triangulation and stability of pinned frames
units.ov: This material introduces plane pin-jointed trusses, whose basic rigid unit is the triangle, and explains why loads must be applied only at joints so that members carry purely axial force. It then shows that quadrilateral panels are mechanisms unless triangulated with a diagonal or upright, so stability depends on every panel being a triangle. The ideas connect through one chain: joint loading gives axial members, axial members in triangles give a rigid frame, and a rigid frame gives small displacements.
must: A truss is pin-jointed straight members arranged in triangles, loaded only at joints, so every member carries axial force only.
The triangle is the basic rigid element: three bars pinned at their ends cannot change shape without a bar changing length.
A pinned quadrilateral with no diagonal is a mechanism: it collapses into a parallelogram under load with large displacements.
Triangulation means adding a diagonal (or upright) so that every panel is a triangle. This makes the frame stable and rigid, with only very small displacements under load \(P\).
Strut = member in compression; tie = member in tension. Do not mix them up when labelling member forces.
Loads applied between joints cause bending, which invalidates the axial-force assumption of simple truss analysis.
Member count alone does not prove stability: inspect every panel and check that it is a triangle.

A partially triangulated truss still has an unbraced sub-panel that can deform or rotate about its supports, so it is not rigid. Adding the missing member, such as an upright between the bottom and top nodes, completes the triangulation.
Cross bracing (two diagonals in one panel) is not examined this year. Use a single diagonal or added member to triangulate.
conn: Joint loading and axial forces: if a load is applied between joints, the member bends and the truss model no longer holds. Questions often ask you to relocate or justify the load positions.
Triangulation and stability: identifying a mechanism, choosing where to add a member, and then stating the resulting small displacement all belong in one answer.
Stability and strut/tie identification: once a truss is triangulated and stable, the next step is to find member forces and label each as a strut (compression) or a tie (tension).
exq: Sketch a pin-jointed rectangular panel with a load \(P\) at one top corner. Explain why it is a mechanism, describe how it deforms, and add one member to make it stable.

A truss is made of several panels, and one sub-panel is not a triangle. Identify the unstable panel, state how the frame could move, and add the minimum member (e.g. an upright) to make it fully triangulated.
Define strut and tie. For a given loaded triangular truss, state which members are in compression and which are in tension, and justify each.
Explain why external loads must be applied only at joints in a truss. What happens to member forces if a load acts midway along a member?
A student claims a four-member frame is stable because it has enough members. Use triangulation to evaluate the claim, and explain why cross bracing is not needed in your answer.

notes.t: Pin-jointed structures - trusses: basic elements
pts: The basic element of a plane truss is a triangle, which forms a rigid shape when its three bars are pinned at the ends.
External loads must be applied only at the joints so that internal forces in members are purely axial, avoiding bending.
If loads act between joints, members bend and internal forces become complicated to analyse.
Members in compression are called struts; members in tension are called ties.
defs: Strut
A truss member carrying a compressive axial force.
Tie
A truss member carrying a tensile axial force.
Truss
A structure of pin-jointed straight members, with triangular elements, loaded only at joints so that members carry axial forces only.
tips: Do not confuse struts (compression) with ties (tension) when labelling member forces.
Loads applied between joints cause bending, invalidating the simple axial-force assumption of truss analysis.
rq: Why must the basic element of a plane truss be a triangle rather than, say, a four-sided quadrilateral of pinned bars?
Three pinned bars form a rigid shape, whereas a four-bar quadrilateral can deform (collapse) under load unless extra members are added.
What would happen to the internal forces if a load were applied at the middle of a horizontal member instead of at a joint?
The member would bend, so internal forces would no longer be purely axial and would become more complicated to calculate.

notes.t: Stability and triangulation of pinned panels
pts: A pinned quadrilateral panel without a diagonal is a mechanism: it is unstable and undergoes large displacements under load.
Adding a diagonal member to the quadrilateral triangulates it, making the panel stable and rigid.
A triangulated panel only undergoes very small displacements under the same applied load P.
defs: Mechanism
A pin-jointed structure that is unstable, with insufficient members to resist load, so it deforms by large displacements.
Triangulation
Adding diagonal members to a framework so that it consists of triangles, which makes it stable and rigid.
tips: Do not assume four pinned members form a stable frame; a quadrilateral needs a diagonal to be rigid.
A stable pin-jointed frame made of triangles is not guaranteed by counting members alone; check that every panel is triangulated.
rq: Why does adding a single diagonal to a square panel stop it from deforming, when the four pins alone do not?
A triangle cannot change shape without changing member lengths, so with pinned joints its three sides fix the geometry; the square can shear into a rhombus because its angles are free to change.
What if the load P were applied to only one corner of the triangulated panel instead of two?
The panel is still stable and rigid, since triangulation fixes its shape regardless of how the load is distributed; only the member forces change.

notes.t: Stability and triangulation of trusses
pts: A pin-jointed frame made of a four-sided panel is unstable (can collapse into a parallelogram) unless it is braced; a diagonal member triangulates the panel.
Cross bracing (both diagonals) adds further triangulation, but this is not examined this year, so the focus is on single diagonals and added members.
A partially triangulated truss has a sub-panel that can still deform, so it is not rigid; the partially unstable case shows the frame can rotate about its supports.
Adding an upright (vertical member) between the bottom and top nodes completes the triangulation, making the truss stable under the load P.
defs: Triangulation
Arranging members so that every panel of the truss forms triangles, which prevents the joints from moving relative to each other and makes the frame rigid.
Stable truss
A truss in which all joints are fixed relative to each other so no mechanism (collapse by rotation of panels) can occur under load.
tips: Do not assume a frame is stable just because it has the right number of members; check that every panel is a triangle.
Cross bracing (two diagonals in one panel) is not examined this year, so don't add it when asked to triangulate a panel.
rq: Why does a four-sided panel with pin joints collapse, while a triangle does not?
A quadrilateral can change shape (a mechanism) by changing its angles without changing member lengths; a triangle's shape is fixed by its three side lengths, so it cannot deform.
What if the upright in the bottom figure were removed: which panel would still be able to deform?
The central/upper sub-panel bounded by the top node and the two lower nodes would remain a quadrilateral and could deform under P, leaving the truss partially unstable.

xq.q: A pin-jointed frame is made of two adjacent square panels sharing a vertical member. A single diagonal is fitted in the left panel only, and a load P is applied at a joint. What is the state of the frame?
xq.a: Unstable: the right-hand panel is still a quadrilateral and can distort as a mechanism
o: Unstable: the right-hand panel is still a quadrilateral and can distort as a mechanism
Stable: one diagonal in the frame is enough to make everything rigid
Stable: the frame has enough members, which is all that matters
Unstable: both panels must have crossed diagonals to be rigid
xq.w: Every panel must be triangulated, and the untriangulated right panel can still collapse into a parallelogram; the traps are counting members and thinking cross bracing is required.
s: The left panel is triangulated and rigid
The right panel has no diagonal, so it is a mechanism
One diagonal per panel is enough, and cross bracing is not needed

xq.q: In a pin-jointed truss, one member shortens under load and pushes on the joints at both of its ends. What is this member called, and what must be true of how the loads are applied for it to carry only axial force?
xq.a: A strut; loads must be applied only at the joints
o: A tie; loads may act anywhere along members
A strut; loads must be applied only at the joints
A tie; loads must be applied only at the joints
A strut; loads may act anywhere along members
xq.w: A member in compression is a strut, and loads between joints would cause bending and break the axial-only assumption; the traps are mixing up strut and tie and ignoring the joint-loading rule.
s: Compression means a strut, and tension means a tie
Axial-only force needs loads at the joints, because loads between joints cause bending

xq.q: A pinned rectangular panel with four members is loaded horizontally at one top corner by a force P. Explain, with a sketch description, why it is unstable, and how adding a single member makes it stable. State what type of member force each assumption of truss analysis requires.
xq.a: A pinned quadrilateral has no member resisting change of shape, so under P it distorts into a parallelogram with large displacements. It is a mechanism. Adding one diagonal between opposite corners divides it into two triangles. A triangle with pinned ends cannot change shape without changing a member length, so the panel becomes rigid and displaces only very slightly under P. Cross bracing is not needed. For truss analysis the loads must be applied at the joints only, so that every member carries purely axial force, either tension (a tie) or compression (a strut), with no bending.
s: The quadrilateral distorts into a parallelogram: it is a mechanism with large displacements (1.5 marks)
A triangle cannot change shape, so the panel is rigid with very small displacements (1.5 marks)
Loads at joints only, so members carry axial force: tie in tension, strut in compression (1 mark)

units.name: 12.2 Static determinacy and the m = 2j − r check
units.ov: This material covers classifying pin-jointed plane trusses as unstable (a mechanism), statically determinate or statically indeterminate. The test compares the actual member count with the required count \(m = 2j - r\), using \(j\) joints and \(r\) support reaction components. The count is necessary but not sufficient, so it must always be backed by a geometric check for triangulation. Only determinate, stable trusses can be solved by statics alone.
must: The determinacy count is \(m = 2j - r\), where \(m\) is the required number of members, \(j\) the number of joints and \(r\) the number of reaction components.
Compare actual members with required: actual \(<\) required means unstable (a mechanism); actual \(=\) required means determinate if the geometry is good; actual \(>\) required means indeterminate.
Count reactions correctly: a pin gives 2 and a roller gives 1, so a pin plus a roller gives \(r = 3\).
The count is necessary but not sufficient. A matching count can still be a mechanism if the members are badly arranged, so check the geometry for triangulation and for panels that can shear.

Statically determinate means member forces and reactions follow from equilibrium equations alone. Statically indeterminate means the structure is stable but has more unknowns than equations, so compatibility of deformations is needed.
An unstable structure (a mechanism) can move or collapse under load, and statics cannot be applied to it. Add members to form triangles first.
Worked example 1: a square frame with \(j=4\), \(r=3\) needs \(m = 2(4)-3 = 5\) members but has 4, so it is unstable. Adding one diagonal gives 5 and makes it stable and determinate.
Worked example 2: for \(j=4\), \(r=3\) the required count is 5. A truss with 6 members has one redundant member, so it is statically indeterminate.
A redundant member is one whose removal leaves the truss stable. There is one redundant member for each surplus member, and the degree of indeterminacy equals actual minus required members.
Method: count \(j\), count \(r\), compute \(m\), compare with the actual count, then inspect the geometry. Choose the stable determinate form for analysis.
conn: The determinacy check comes before analysis by the method of joints or sections. If the truss is a mechanism or indeterminate, equilibrium alone will not give the member forces.
The reaction count links supports to determinacy. Changing a roller to a pin changes \(r\), and so changes the required \(m\) and the classification.

Triangulation links the geometric check to the count. A diagonal adds one member and raises the actual count to the required one, and a poorly placed or missing member can leave a mechanism even when the count matches.
Indeterminate structures lead on to compatibility and deformation methods, since a redundant member needs extra equations beyond statics.
exq: A pin-jointed truss has \(j=4\) joints supported by a pin and a roller. Calculate \(r\) and the required \(m\). Then classify it if it has (a) 4, (b) 5 and (c) 6 members, and say what the extra member does in (c).
A square pin-jointed frame is supported by a pin and a roller and loaded horizontally. Show that it is unstable, add a diagonal member, and then show that it is stable and determinate.

Explain why \(m = 2j - r\) is necessary but not sufficient for stability. Sketch a truss whose member count matches the requirement yet is a mechanism, and explain how you would detect this by inspection.

For a truss with \(j=6\) joints, a pin and a roller support, and 10 members, find the degree of indeterminacy. Identify which members could be redundant, and state what additional information is needed to solve it.
Define statically determinate, statically indeterminate and unstable structures. For each, state whether the equilibrium equations alone can give the member forces and reactions.

notes.t: Determinacy of Trusses
pts: An unstable frame (a mechanism) cannot have the equations of statics applied to it
Adding a diagonal member makes the frame stable and statically determinate, so statics can solve it
A stable frame with extra members is statically indeterminate: more information (e.g. compatibility) is needed to solve it
For typical problems, the structure chosen for analysis is the stable, determinate one (b)
The formula m = 2j − r is a useful but not foolproof test of determinacy
defs: Statically determinate
A structure whose member forces and support reactions can be found using only the equations of equilibrium of statics.
Statically indeterminate
A stable structure with more unknowns than available equilibrium equations, so additional information (such as compatibility of deformations) is needed for a solution.
Unstable structure
A structure that can move or collapse under load (a mechanism), for which the equations of statics cannot be applied.
eqs: Determinacy test for a truss: number of members needed for a statically determinate structure
\(m\) = number of members (–); \(j\) = number of joints (–); \(r\) = number of reactions (–)
tips: The test m = 2j − r is not foolproof: a count can pass while the structure is still unstable, so check stability by geometry (triangulation) too.
Do not apply statics to an unstable frame such as (a); first add members to create triangles, then check determinacy.
rq: Why can the frame in figure (a) not be analysed using the equations of statics, even though it has the same joints as (b)?
It is unstable: a square with pin joints can deform into a parallelogram, so it is a mechanism and equilibrium cannot be guaranteed. Adding a diagonal (b) makes the triangles rigid.
If a stable truss satisfies m > 2j − r, what does this tell you about how it can be solved?
It has more members than needed, so it is statically indeterminate; statics alone cannot give all member forces and compatibility conditions must be used.

notes.t: Determinacy: stability check using joints and reactions
pts: Required members for a stable pin-jointed truss equal twice the number of joints minus the number of reactions.
If actual members are fewer than required, the truss is unstable; adding a diagonal makes it stable and statically determinate.
Adding one diagonal member to the square frame raises actual members from 4 to 5, matching the requirement.
defs: Statically determinate
A structure whose member forces and support reactions can be found fully from equilibrium equations alone, with actual members equal to the required number.
Unstable structure
A structure with fewer members than required for equilibrium of its joints, so it can collapse or deform without bound under load.
eqs: Number of members required for a stable truss
\(m\) = required number of members (-); \(j\) = number of joints (-); \(r\) = number of support reactions (-)
tips: Count reactions carefully: a pin gives 2 reactions and a roller gives 1, so 3 reactions here comes from the pin plus roller arrangement.
Stability and determinacy are checked by member count alone here; a count that matches does not guarantee good geometry, so check the layout is triangulated.
rq: Why does the square frame with no diagonal fail the check even though it looks rigid?
Its 4 members are fewer than the 5 required, so it can deform into a parallelogram; a rigid-looking shape with pinned joints is not necessarily stable.
What if the truss had 4 joints but 4 reactions instead of 3?

Required members would be 2×4−4 = 4, so the 4-member square would become statically determinate, though the extra reaction makes it indeterminate in support terms only if actual members exceed required.

notes.t: Determinacy of trusses: worked example
pts: Equations of equilibrium alone are not enough to solve this truss, so it is statically indeterminate.
The example truss contains one redundant member: the number of members exceeds what is required for a stable determinate truss.
Actual member count (6) exceeds the required count (5), giving an indeterminate structure.
Determinacy should be identified by inspection or by using the member-count formula.
defs: Statically indeterminate truss
A truss whose member forces and support reactions cannot be found from equilibrium equations alone because it has more members (or reactions) than the minimum needed for stability.
Redundant member
A member whose removal does not make the truss unstable; it is extra beyond the number required for a determinate, stable truss.
eqs: Member count for a determinate planar pin-jointed truss
\(m\) = number of members (-); \(j\) = number of joints (-); \(r\) = number of support reaction components (-)
Worked check for this example truss
tips: Count reactions correctly: a pin gives 2 and a roller gives 1, so use \(r = 3\) for this example, not 4.
Using \(m = 2j - r\) only tells you the count; it does not prove stability, so check geometry by inspection too.
rq: Why does having 6 members instead of 5 make the truss statically indeterminate rather than unstable?
The extra member provides stiffness and stability; the structure is stable, but equilibrium equations (2 per joint) are insufficient to find all unknowns, so compatibility is needed.
What would happen to the classification if one support were removed from the example?
The reaction count drops and the required member count changes; the structure may become unstable or determinate depending on the new counts, so the formula must be reapplied.

notes.t: Determinacy of trusses: m = 2j − r check and its limits
pts: The count m = 2j − r is necessary but not sufficient; a count that matches does not guarantee stability.
A truss can satisfy the count yet be a mechanism if members are poorly arranged, so the count alone cannot confirm stability.
Extra members beyond the count make a truss statically indeterminate, with one redundant member per surplus member.
A truss with too few members for the joints and supports is unstable (a mechanism) even if the count is sufficient elsewhere.
defs: Mechanism
A structure that is geometrically unstable: it can deform without any change in member length, so it cannot carry load.
Statically indeterminate
A structure whose member forces and reactions cannot be found from equilibrium equations alone, because it has more members or supports than needed for stability.
Statically determinate
A stable structure whose member forces and reactions can all be found from equilibrium equations alone.
Redundant member
A member beyond the minimum needed for a stable, determinate truss; its removal does not make the structure unstable.
eqs: Member count for a pin-jointed plane truss (number of members needed for determinacy)
\(m\) = number of members (–); \(j\) = number of joints (–); \(r\) = number of support reaction components (–)
tips: Do not conclude stability from the count alone; always inspect the geometry for panels that can shear.
Count reactions r correctly: a pin gives 2, a roller gives 1 in the count.
rq: Why does the example truss with 9 members satisfy m = 2j − r yet still fail to be a sound determinate truss?
Its members are arranged such that the bottom panel is a mechanism; the count is correct overall but the local geometry lacks a diagonal, so the structure is unstable.
What if you add one more member to a determinate truss?
It becomes statically indeterminate with one redundant member, requiring compatibility conditions to solve.

xq.q: A planar pin-jointed truss has \(j = 8\) joints and 14 members. It is supported by one pin (two reaction components) and one roller (one reaction component). Using \(m = 2j - r\), where \(m\) is the number of members required for a stable determinate truss, \(j\) is the number of joints and \(r\) is the number of reaction components, find the number of redundant members.
xq.a: 1 redundant member (required m = 13, actual 14)

xq.q: A pin-jointed truss has \(j = 5\) joints and 6 members. It is supported by a pin and a roller. Using \(m = 2j - r\), what is the correct conclusion?
xq.a: Unstable (a mechanism), because it has fewer members than the 7 required
o: Statically determinate, because 6 members matches the count if r = 4 is used
Statically indeterminate with one redundant member
Unstable (a mechanism), because it has fewer members than the 7 required
Statically determinate, because any frame whose count matches is stable
xq.w: With r = 3, m = 2(5) − 3 = 7 are required but only 6 are present, so the truss is a mechanism; counting the roller as 2 reactions gives the false match of 6.

xq.q: A student checks a truss with \(m = 2j - r\) and finds that the number of members equals the required number. Explain why this does not prove the truss is stable and determinate. Describe how you would check the truss further, and say what you would do if the truss were found to be unstable.
xq.a: The count m = 2j − r is necessary but not sufficient. Members can be arranged badly, for example with one part over-braced and another part left as an unbraced quadrilateral, so the total count matches while part of the truss is still a mechanism. The geometry must therefore be checked by inspection, to see that the members form triangles. If the truss is unstable, statics cannot be applied to it. Members, such as diagonals, must be added to create triangles, and determinacy is then re-checked.
s: Count is necessary but not sufficient (1)
Poor arrangement of members can still give a mechanism while the count matches (1)
Unstable frame: statics cannot be applied, so add diagonals to form triangles and re-check (1)

units.name: 12.3 Struts and ties: compression vs tension members
units.ov: This material introduces the two kinds of axial truss member: struts, which carry internal compression and push the joints apart, and ties, which carry internal tension and pull the joints together. The central skill is to identify each member's type from joint equilibrium and to keep the sign and labelling conventions consistent. Joint-by-joint force analysis of a truss is built on this.
must: A strut carries internal compression: it tends to shorten and pushes the joints at its ends apart.
A tie carries internal tension: it tends to lengthen and pulls the joints at its ends together.
Label compression as c and tension as t consistently on every member, and state your sign convention before starting.
Member forces act on the joints: draw the force the member exerts on the joint, with a strut pushing away from the joint and a tie pulling towards the member.
Joint equilibrium (\(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0\)) determines whether each member is a strut or a tie.
Do not confuse the direction of the external load with the direction of the internal force: the internal force on the joint is opposite to the external push or pull applied at that joint.
Members are treated as two-force axial members, so the force acts along the member's line.
A negative result from equilibrium means the assumed sense was wrong (assumed tension but actually compression, or vice versa). Reverse the label rather than the working.
Check sign conventions against the equilibrium at every joint before moving to the next.
conn: Joint equilibrium (method of joints) links to strut/tie identification: the sign of each solved force tells you whether the member is in compression or tension.
Strut versus tie type links to design: compression members risk buckling and need to be stocky, while tension members are sized on stress and yield.
External loads and support reactions must be found first, since they set the joint forces from which the internal member forces follow.
Force direction on the joint links to the member's effect: a strut pushes the joints apart and a tie pulls them together, which checks the equilibrium results.
exq: Define a strut and a tie. For a simple triangular truss with a vertical load at the apex, state which members are in compression and which in tension, and justify this using joint equilibrium.
Draw the free-body diagram of a joint where three members meet and a 10 kN external load is applied. Find the member forces, labelling each as c or t and stating the sign convention used.
Explain why the internal force on a joint is opposite in sense to the external push or pull applied there, with a sketch of a strut and a tie showing the forces on the joints.
A solution of joint equilibrium gives a negative force for a member assumed to be in tension. What does this mean, and how should the member be relabelled? Illustrate with a numerical example.
Discuss why a long strut and a tie carrying the same load would be designed differently, with reference to failure modes.

notes.t: Truss members: struts (compression) and ties (tension)
pts: A strut is a truss member pushed externally, so it carries internal compression.
A tie is a truss member pulled externally, so it carries internal tension.
Member forces act on the joints: a strut pushes the joints apart, a tie pulls them together, and the joint equilibrium shows this.
The convention labels compression forces c and tension forces t on the member.
defs: Strut
A truss member in compression, loaded by external pushes so that its internal force tends to shorten it and push the joints apart.
Tie
A truss member in tension, loaded by external pulls so that its internal force tends to lengthen it and pull the joints together.
tips: Don't confuse the direction of the external load with the direction of the internal force; the internal force on the joint is opposite to the external push or pull applied at that joint.
Label strut forces as compression (c) and tie forces as tension (t) consistently, and check sign conventions against the equilibrium at each joint.
rq: Why does a strut's internal force act on its joints in the direction pushing them apart?
Because the external push compresses the member, and for equilibrium at each joint the member must push back on the joint, opposing the load and driving the joints outward.
If a member's internal force is labelled t, what can you conclude about its state, and what would a negative value of the force mean?
It is a tie in tension; a negative force would indicate the member is actually in compression, i.e. a strut, reversing the assumed sign.

xq.q: A truss member is found to be a tie. Which statement correctly describes its effect on the joints at its ends?
xq.a: It pulls the two joints towards each other, and the member is in tension
o: It pulls the two joints towards each other, and the member is in tension
It pushes the two joints apart, and the member is in tension
It pushes the two joints apart, and the member is in compression
It pulls the two joints towards each other, and the member is in compression
xq.w: A tie is pulled externally and carries tension, so it pulls its joints together; the trap is mixing up which of the two (strut or tie) pushes the joints apart.

xq.q: In a joint-equilibrium diagram, the force exerted by a member on a joint points away from the joint. How should this member be labelled?
xq.a: A strut in compression, because the force on the joint points outwards
o: A tie in tension, because the force on the joint points outwards
A strut in compression, because the force on the joint points outwards
A strut in compression, because the force on the joint points inwards
A tie in compression, because the force depends on the external load direction
xq.w: A member that pushes on the joint (force away from it) is a strut in compression; the trap is judging by the direction of the external load rather than the internal force on the joint.
s: A strut pushes the joints apart, so its force on each joint points away from the joint

xq.q: Explain, with a sketch of a single member and the two joints at its ends, the difference between a strut and a tie in terms of the forces the member exerts on the joints. State how each should be labelled.
xq.a: Sketch: a member between joints A and B. For a strut the external loads push on the ends. The member's internal force tends to shorten it and pushes the joints apart, so the force on each joint points away from the joint. The strut is in compression and is labelled c. For a tie the external loads pull on the ends. The member's internal force tends to lengthen it and pulls the joints together, so the force on each joint points towards the member. The tie is in tension and is labelled t. The internal force on the joint is opposite in sense to the external push or pull, and this must be checked against the equilibrium of each joint.
s: Sketch of member with joint forces (1)
Strut: compression, pushes joints apart, label c (1)
Tie: tension, pulls joints together, label t (1)
Internal force is not the same as the external load direction; check by joint equilibrium (1)

units.name: 12.4 Support conditions and reactions of trusses
units.ov: This module covers how pin and roller supports restrict a truss and how many reaction components each supplies. It then covers the determinacy test \(m = 2j - r\) and the use of equilibrium to find support reactions for a simply supported truss. The ideas connect because the support type fixes r, r feeds the determinacy test, and a determinate truss lets the reactions be found from statics before any member forces are analysed.
must: A pin support gives 2 reaction components (\(H\), \(V\)); a roller gives 1, perpendicular to its contact surface.
Determinacy test: \(m = 2j - r\). If the actual member count equals this, the truss is statically determinate; if it is larger, indeterminate.
Count r correctly: pin + roller gives r = 3. Two pins give r = 4, which gave m = 10 required against 11 actual members for 7 joints, so the truss is indeterminate.
If actual members exceed \(2j-r\), the truss is indeterminate (redundant), not unstable. Fewer members than required would mean a mechanism or instability.
Reactions come from three equilibrium equations: \(\sum F_x=0\), \(\sum F_y=0\), \(\sum M=0\).
With no horizontal applied load, \(\sum F_x=0\) gives \(H_A=0\) at the pin.
Take moments about the pin A to get the roller reaction directly: \(V_B = 110/6 = 18.33\ \text{kN}\). Then \(V_A = 30 - 18.33 = 11.67\ \text{kN}\).
Use the correct moment arms measured from A: loads of 5, 10 and 15 kN act at 1, 3 and 5 m, on a 6 m span. Do not use the joint spacing of 2 m.
Neglect self-weight unless the question says otherwise; only the applied joint loads enter the reactions.
Check the sign and direction of each moment, and check the result with a second equation, e.g. moments about B.
conn: Support type sets r, which sets the required member count \(m=2j-r\). A wrong r gives a wrong determinacy verdict, and that decides whether statics alone can solve the truss.

Reactions are the starting point for member forces: after finding \(V_A\), \(V_B\) and \(H_A\), method of joints or sections begins at the supports. An error in a reaction carries through to every member force.
Moment equilibrium about a support removes unknown reactions. Choosing A (pin) leaves only \(V_B\) in the equation, which links the choice of moment point to the support conditions.
Determinacy and external stability are separate checks. Three reactions are enough for the external equations, but the \(2j-r\) count includes internal members, so questions often ask for both.
exq: A truss has 7 joints, 11 members, and is supported by two pins. Calculate r and the required m, and state with justification whether it is determinate. What change (e.g. replacing one pin with a roller) would make it determinate?

A 6 m span truss is pin-supported at A and roller-supported at B, with vertical loads of 5, 10 and 15 kN at 1, 3 and 5 m from A. Find \(H_A\), \(V_A\) and \(V_B\), and verify the result by taking moments about B.
Explain, with sketches, the reaction components provided by pin and roller supports. Why does using 2 reaction components for a roller give the wrong determinacy result?

For a truss with j joints and a given number of members, use \(m=2j-r\) to classify it as determinate, indeterminate or unstable with pin-roller supports. Then state what you can and cannot calculate from equilibrium alone.
Explain how the reactions change if the roller at B is moved to a sloping surface or a horizontal load is added at a joint. Which equilibrium equations now determine \(H_A\)?

notes.t: Support reactions of a truss
pts: Support conditions (pin and roller) determine how many reaction components must be solved for before analysing member forces.
Self-weight of the members is neglected unless the problem states otherwise, so only the applied joint loads contribute to reactions.
defs: Pin support
A support that resists both horizontal and vertical translation but allows rotation; it provides two unknown reaction components.
Roller support
A support that resists only translation perpendicular to its contact surface (vertical here), allowing horizontal movement and rotation; it provides one unknown reaction component.
tips: Ignore self-weight unless the question explicitly asks for it; including it without instruction changes the reactions.
Check the geometry (here 6 m span, 1 m height) carefully when taking moments about supports.
rq: Why does the pin support provide two unknown reactions while the roller provides only one?
The pin prevents translation in both x and y directions, giving \( R_{Ax} \) and \( R_{Ay} \); the roller only prevents vertical translation, giving \( R_B \).
What if the roller were replaced by a pin—how would the reaction solution change?
It would add a second unknown (horizontal reaction), so the system would need an additional equilibrium condition or would be statically indeterminate in the simple sense.

notes.t: Support Conditions and Determinacy Test for Trusses
pts: A truss with two pin supports has four unknown reactions (\(H_{A}\), \(V_{A}\), \(H_{B}\), \(V_{B}\)), so reactions alone do not fix determinacy; the member count and joint count must be compared.
Using the determinacy test with 7 joints and r = 4 reactions gives m = 10 required members, but the truss has 11 actual members, so it is statically indeterminate.
