A pin support restrains translation in both directions but allows rotation, which is why each pin contributes two reaction components.
defs: Pin support
A support that prevents movement in both horizontal and vertical directions but permits rotation, giving two unknown reaction components.
Statically indeterminate
A structure whose number of members exceeds the number required for stability (m > 2j − r), so internal forces cannot be found from equilibrium equations alone.
eqs: Determinacy test for a pin-jointed truss (number of members required)
m = required number of members (dimensionless); j = number of joints (dimensionless); r = number of reaction components (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the determinacy test with the external reaction check: here the test uses r = 4 (two pins), not r = 3.
Remember the test gives the number of members for determinacy; a truss with more members than this is indeterminate, not unstable.
rq: Why does the test compare m with 2j − r rather than just counting supports?

Each joint gives two equilibrium equations (ΣFx and ΣFy), giving 2j equations; the r reactions are unknowns, so the members plus reactions must equal the number of equations for a determinate solution.
What would happen to the classification if one member were removed from this truss?
It would have 10 members, equal to 2j − r = 10, making it statically determinate (provided it remains stable).

notes.t: Support conditions and reactions for a simply supported truss
pts: A pin support can resist horizontal and vertical reactions, while a roller support resists only vertical reaction.
Checking the determinacy of a truss uses m = 2j − r; if the result equals the number of members the truss is statically determinate and the reactions can be found from equilibrium.
With no horizontal applied loads, horizontal equilibrium gives zero reaction at the pin support.
Taking moments about support A gives the reaction at the roller, and vertical equilibrium then gives the reaction at the pin.
defs: Statically determinate truss
A truss whose member forces and support reactions can be found using only the equations of static equilibrium, i.e. m = 2j − r.
Pin support
A support that prevents translation in both x and y directions but allows rotation; it provides two reaction components.
Roller support
A support that prevents translation in one direction only (perpendicular to its surface) and allows rotation and movement parallel to the surface; it provides one reaction component.
eqs: Determinacy check for a pin-jointed truss
m = number of members; j = number of joints; r = number of support reaction components
\(V_A\), \(V_B\) = vertical reactions at A and B (kN)
\(V_B\) = reaction at roller (kN); loads 5, 10, 15 kN at 1 m, 3 m, 5 m from A; span 6 m
tips: Check the sign and moment arm of each load: 5 kN acts at 1 m, 10 kN at 3 m and 15 kN at 5 m from A, not at the joint spacing of 2 m.
Count reaction components correctly (pin = 2, roller = 1) before applying m = 2j − r; using 2 for the roller gives the wrong determinacy result.
rq: Why is \(H_A = 0\) even though the truss has a pin support?
All applied loads act vertically, so there is no horizontal force to balance; the horizontal equilibrium equation gives zero reaction at the pin.
Why must the moments be taken about support A rather than about B to find \(V_B\) directly?
Taking moments about A eliminates \(V_A\) and \(H_A\) (their moment arms are zero), leaving only \(V_B\) as the unknown.
What would happen to determinacy if the roller were replaced by a second pin?
r would increase to 4, giving m = 2j − r = 10 ≠ 11, the truss would have one redundant reaction and would be statically indeterminate.

xq.q: A simply supported truss of span 6 m has a pin at A and a roller at B. It carries vertical loads of 5 kN, 10 kN and 15 kN at horizontal distances of 1 m, 3 m and 5 m from A. Self-weight is neglected. Find the vertical reaction \(V_A\) at the pin.
A pin-jointed truss has \(j = 7\) joints and 11 members. It is supported on two pins. Using \(m = 2j - r\), what is the correct conclusion?
xq.a: Statically indeterminate with one redundant member
o: Statically determinate, because r = 3 gives m = 11
Statically indeterminate with one redundant member
Unstable, because two pins allow movement
Statically indeterminate with two redundant members
xq.w: Two pins give r = 4, so m = 14 − 4 = 10 is required and 11 is one too many; the trap is using r = 3, which falsely gives a match.
s: m = 14 − 4 = 10 < 11 actual, so one redundant member

xq.q: A truss on a pin at A and a roller at B carries only vertical loads. Explain how you would find the support reactions: show that the horizontal reaction at A is zero and state the order of equations used to get \(V_B\) and \(V_A\). Say why self-weight can be ignored.
xq.a: The pin gives \(H_{A}\) and \(V_{A}\) and the roller gives \(V_{B}\), which makes three unknowns. They can be found from the three equations of equilibrium. With no horizontal loads, ΣFx = 0 gives \(H_{A}\) = 0. Taking moments about A, with each load multiplied by its distance from A, gives \(V_{B}\), because \(H_{A}\) and \(V_{A}\) have no moment about A. ΣFy = 0 then gives \(V_{A}\) = total load − \(V_{B}\). Self-weight of the members is neglected unless stated, so only the applied joint loads contribute.
s: Σ\(M_{A}\) = 0 gives \(V_{B}\), using load × distance from A (1)

units.name: 12.5 Numerical solution procedure for trusses
units.ov: This material sets out the standard procedure for analysing statically determinate pin-jointed trusses. First find the external support reactions from whole-truss equilibrium, then find internal member forces with the method of joints (all members) or the method of sections (selected members). Every step rests on equilibrium, and the result is expressed as tension or compression in each member.
must: Always start with a whole-truss free-body diagram and solve the reactions first: \(\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0\)
Pin supports give two reaction components (horizontal and vertical); roller supports give one reaction, perpendicular to the supporting surface
Method of joints: apply \(\sum F_x=0\) and \(\sum F_y=0\) at each pin, which gives two equations and so at most two unknowns per joint
Start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces, then move on joint by joint as each new joint has at most two unknowns
Method of sections: cut through the truss, draw a free-body of one part, and apply equilibrium to find only the selected member forces
Sign convention: a tension member pulls away from the joint and a compression member pushes into it; a negative result means the assumed direction was wrong
Choose moment centres and cuts so that unknowns are eliminated, for example by taking moments about the point where two unknown lines of action intersect
Finish by redrawing the truss with each member force labelled with its magnitude and its tension or compression state (T/C)
Use leftover equations, such as a spare joint or the overall moment equation, to check the answers
Units: forces in N (or kN), moments in N·m; keep the sign and direction conventions consistent throughout
conn: Whole-truss equilibrium gives the reactions, which act as the external loads at the support joints when starting the method of joints
Method of joints and method of sections are often combined: use sections to find a few key members quickly, then joints to find a remaining member or to check
Moment equilibrium links the geometry (angles, lengths) to the force components, so the trigonometry of member angles feeds directly into the joint equations
Tension/compression results connect to member design, since compression members can buckle and tension members can yield
exq: A simply supported truss (pin at A, roller at B) carries vertical loads at two joints. Draw the free-body diagram and calculate the reactions at A and B.
For a triangular truss with a given load and span, use the method of joints starting at a joint with two unknowns to find all member forces, and state whether each is in tension or compression.
For a Warren or Pratt truss, cut through three members and use the method of sections to find the force in a named member. Explain your choice of moment centre.
Explain why the method of joints must start at a joint with no more than two unknowns, and identify a suitable starting joint on a given truss.
Compare the method of joints and the method of sections, and state when each is more efficient. Then redraw a solved truss showing the correct direction of all member forces.

notes.t: Numerical Analysis of Trusses: Solution Procedure
pts: Start by identifying support reactions (pin, roller) and drawing a free-body diagram of the whole truss.
Apply equilibrium equations to the whole truss to solve for the unknown external reactions before analysing members.
Method of joints finds all unknown internal member forces by isolating each pin in turn.
Method of sections cuts the truss to find only a selected number of internal forces.
After solving, redraw the truss showing member forces acting in their correct direction (tension or compression).
defs: Method of joints
Truss analysis technique that applies force equilibrium (Σ\(F_{x}\) = 0, Σ\(F_{y}\) = 0) at each pin to find all internal member forces.
Method of sections
Truss analysis technique that imaginarily cuts through the truss and applies equilibrium to a free-body of one section to find selected member forces.
eqs: \(F_{x}\) = horizontal force (N); \(F_{y}\) = vertical force (N); M = moment (N·m)
tips: Redraw the truss with forces in their correct direction; tension members pull away from the joint and compression members push into it.
Check that the method of joints is started at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces.
rq: Why must the external reactions be found before using either method?
Because the joint or section equilibrium equations require the external loads and reactions as known inputs; the reactions are also needed to start at a joint with only two unknowns.
When would you choose the method of sections over the method of joints?
When only a few specific member forces are needed, since sections avoid solving every joint in the truss.

xq.q: A simple pin-jointed truss ABC has a pin support at A and a roller support at B. A and B lie on a horizontal line 6 m apart, and C is the apex, 4 m vertically above the midpoint of AB. A downward vertical load of 30 kN acts at C. Treat the members' self-weight as negligible. First find the support reactions for the whole truss. Then use the method of joints at A to find the force in member AB, in kN (tension positive).
xq.a: \(F_{\text{AB}}\) = 11.25 kN (tension)
s: Whole truss: the load is at midspan, so Σ\(M_{A}\) = 0 gives \(B_{y}\)(6) = 30(3), so \(B_{y}\) = 15 kN. Σ\(F_{y}\) = 0 gives \(A_{y}\) = 15 kN, and Σ\(F_{x}\) = 0 gives \(A_{x}\) = 0.
Member AC has length √(3²+4²) = 5 m, so its direction cosines are 3/5 horizontal and 4/5 vertical.
Joint A, Σ\(F_{y}\) = 0: 15 − (4/5)\(F_{\text{AC}}\) = 0, so \(F_{\text{AC}}\) = 18.75 kN. This is compressive because it pushes into the joint.
Joint A, Σ\(F_{x}\) = 0: \(F_{\text{AB}}\) − (3/5)(18.75) = 0, so \(F_{\text{AB}}\) = 11.25 kN. It pulls away from the joint, so it is in tension.

xq.q: You are about to analyse a loaded truss by the method of joints. Which approach is correct?
xq.a: Find the support reactions from the whole truss, then start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces.
o: Start at the joint where the external load is applied, whatever the number of unknowns.
Start at any joint, because equilibrium holds at every pin.
Find the support reactions from the whole truss, then start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces.
Start at a joint with three unknown members, because it gives the most equations.
xq.w: Each pin gives only two equations (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0), so you must start at a joint with at most two unknowns, and the reactions are found first from the whole truss; starting at a loaded joint or one with three unknowns cannot be solved directly.
s: Whole-truss equilibrium gives the external reactions first.
A pin gives only two equations, so it can resolve at most two unknowns.

xq.q: In a method of joints solution you assume every member is in tension, pulling away from the joint. For member BC you obtain \(F_{\text{BC}}\) = −24 kN. What should the redrawn truss show for BC?
xq.a: Compression of 24 kN, with the member pushing into each joint it connects.
o: Tension of 24 kN, with the arrow pulling away from the joint.
Compression of 24 kN, with the member pushing into each joint it connects.
Compression of −24 kN, because the sign must be kept in the magnitude.
A zero-force member, because the sign shows the assumption was wrong.
xq.w: A negative result for an assumed tension means the member is actually in compression with magnitude 24 kN, so it pushes into the joints; the trap is to keep the sign as a magnitude or to treat the result as an error.
s: The assumed direction was tension, and the negative sign reverses it.
The member is in compression, so it pushes into the joint, with magnitude 24 kN.

topics.topic: Equilibrium of a Statically Determinate Cantilever (Uniform Load)

formulas.name: Vertical force equilibrium (vertical reaction at fixed support A)
formulas.vars: \(R_{A}\) = vertical reaction at A (N); q = uniform load intensity (N/m); L = loaded length (m)
formulas.use: Cantilever fixed at A carrying a uniform distributed load q over length L; the resultant load qL acts downward.

formulas.name: Moment equilibrium about support A (fixed-end moment reaction)
formulas.vars: \(M_{A}\) = reaction moment at A (N·m); q = uniform load intensity (N/m); L = loaded length (m)
formulas.use: Take moments about the fixed end; the resultant qL acts at the midpoint L/2 of the uniformly loaded span.

formulas.name: Newton's second law (resultant force)
formulas.vars: ΣF = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/s²)
formulas.use: Particle with net force; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²

formulas.name: Equilibrium of a particle
formulas.vars: ΣF = vector sum of all forces on the particle (N)
formulas.use: Particle at rest or moving at constant velocity (a = 0)

formulas.name: Weight
formulas.vars: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (≈9.81 m/s²)
formulas.use: Weight of a body near Earth's surface, directed downwards

formulas.name: Newton's third law (action–reaction)
formulas.vars: \(F_{B}\) on A = force by B on A (N); \(F_{A}\) on B = force by A on B (N)
formulas.use: Forces between interacting bodies are equal and opposite

formulas.name: Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.vars: F = gravitational force (N); G = 6.673×10⁻¹¹ (m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²); m₁, m₂ = masses (kg); r = distance between centres (m)
formulas.use: Attraction between two bodies

formulas.name: Gravitational acceleration at Earth's surface
formulas.vars: g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); M = Earth's mass (kg); \(r_{e}\) = Earth's radius (m)
formulas.use: Links gravitation to weight, W = mg

formulas.name: Resultant of concurrent forces (vector sum)
formulas.vars: R = resultant force (N); \(F_{i}\) = individual forces (N)
formulas.use: Forces acting at a single point; addition is commutative (parallelogram/triangle law)

formulas.name: Resultant of collinear forces
formulas.vars: R = resultant (N); \(F_{i}\) = signed forces along the line (N)
formulas.use: All forces along one line; sign set by direction

formulas.name: Opposite and scaled force
formulas.vars: k = scalar multiplier (dimensionless); F = force (N)
formulas.use: Reversing direction or scaling magnitude of a force vector

formulas.name: Components of a force (angle θ from x-axis)
formulas.vars: F = force magnitude (N); θ = angle from +x axis (° or rad); Fx, Fy = components (N)
formulas.use: Resolving a force; if angle φ is from the y-axis, Fx = F sinφ, Fy = F cosφ

formulas.name: Magnitude from components
formulas.vars: F = magnitude (N); Fx, Fy = components (N)
formulas.use: Rebuilding a force from perpendicular components

formulas.name: Direction from components
formulas.vars: θ = angle from x-axis (° or rad)
formulas.use: Check the quadrant from the signs of Fx and Fy

formulas.name: Cartesian unit-vector form
formulas.vars: i, j, k = unit vectors along x, y, z (dimensionless); θ = angle from x-axis (2D)
formulas.use: Writing forces as vectors; the second form is for 2D

formulas.name: Oblique-axis components
formulas.vars: Fp, Fq = components along p, q (N); e = unit vectors; α, β = angles in the force triangle (°)
formulas.use: Resolving along non-perpendicular axes via the sine rule on the force triangle

formulas.name: Components of the resultant
formulas.vars: Rx, Ry = resultant components (N); Fx, Fy = components of each force (N)
formulas.use: Several concurrent forces in 2D; take signs into account

formulas.name: Magnitude of the resultant
formulas.vars: R = resultant magnitude (N)
formulas.use: After summing components

formulas.name: Direction of the resultant
formulas.vars: θ = angle from +x axis (°)
formulas.use: Check the quadrant from the signs of Rx and Ry

topics.topic: Triangle methods: cosine and sine rules

formulas.name: Cosine rule
formulas.vars: a, b, c = triangle sides (N or m); γ = angle between a and b, opposite c (°)
formulas.use: In the force triangle, γ is the interior angle, so for forces with angle θ between their lines of action from the tail, γ = 180° − θ

formulas.name: Sine rule
formulas.vars: a, b, c = sides (N or m); α, β, γ = opposite angles (°)
formulas.use: Find the direction of the resultant or an unknown force after using the cosine rule

formulas.name: Resultant of two forces, angle θ between them (tail to tail)
formulas.vars: R = resultant (N); F₁, F₂ = forces (N); θ = angle between the forces (°)
formulas.use: Direct parallelogram-law magnitude; equals the cosine rule with γ = 180° − θ

formulas.name: Moment of a force about a point/axis
formulas.vars: \(M_{O}\) = moment about O (N m); F = force magnitude (N); d = perpendicular distance from O to line of action (m)
formulas.use: Whenever the perpendicular distance is easy to find. Sign convention: anticlockwise +, clockwise − (state it)

formulas.name: Moment using force components
formulas.vars: \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = force components (N); \(d_{x}\), \(d_{y}\) = perpendicular distances from O to lines of action of \(F_{y}\), \(F_{x}\) (m)
formulas.use: When the force is inclined and the perpendicular distance is awkward; each component's sense gives its sign

formulas.name: Resolving a force into components
formulas.vars: F = force magnitude (N); \theta = angle to the x-axis (horizontal) (rad or °)
formulas.use: Resolve before taking moments; swap sin/cos if θ is measured from the vertical

formulas.name: Moment arm of an inclined force
formulas.vars: d = moment arm (m); r = distance from O to point of application (m); \alpha = angle between r and F
formulas.use: Geometric way to find the perpendicular distance

formulas.name: Varignon's principle
formulas.latex: M_O = \sum M_{O,i} = M_{O,x}+M_{O,y}, \quad F d = F_1 d_1 + F_2 d_2
formulas.vars: \(M_{O,i}\) = moments of the components about O (N m); F = resultant force (N); d = its perpendicular distance from O (m)
formulas.use: Moment of a force (or resultant) equals the sum of moments of its components about the same point

formulas.name: Vector moment (cross product)
formulas.vars: \underline{M}_O = moment vector about O (N m); \underline{r} = position vector from O to any point on the line of action (m); \underline{F} = force vector (N)
formulas.use: 3D problems or when coordinates are given; in 2D it points along \underline{k} (z-axis)

formulas.name: Magnitude of the cross-product moment
formulas.vars: r = distance from O to point of application (m); \alpha = angle between \underline{r} and \underline{F}; d = perpendicular distance (m)
formulas.use: Links vector and scalar forms

formulas.name: 2D moment in unit-vector form
formulas.vars: \underline{k} = unit vector along the z-axis; F = force (N); d = moment arm (m)
formulas.use: For planar problems; +k is anticlockwise

formulas.name: Resultant components
formulas.vars: \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\) = resultant components (N); \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = components of each force (N), signed
formulas.use: Replacing a coplanar system by a single resultant force

formulas.name: Resultant magnitude
formulas.vars: R = resultant magnitude (N)
formulas.use: After finding the components

formulas.name: Resultant direction
formulas.vars: \theta = angle from the x-axis (°)
formulas.use: Check the quadrant from the signs of \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\)

formulas.name: Position of the resultant (parallel forces)
formulas.vars: \(d_{R}\) = distance of the line of action of the resultant from A (m); \sum \(M_{A}\) = sum of moments of the original forces about A (N m)
formulas.use: Moment of the resultant about A must equal the moment of the original system about A

formulas.name: Moment equivalence for a general system
formulas.vars: \(d_{x}\), \(d_{y}\) = coordinates of a point on the line of action of R relative to A (m)
formulas.use: Locating the resultant of a non-parallel system (signs by chosen convention)

formulas.name: Moment of a couple
formulas.vars: M = couple moment (N m); F = magnitude of each force (N); d = perpendicular distance between the forces (m)
formulas.use: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces; net force zero

formulas.name: Couple moment is independent of the point
formulas.vars: a = distance from A to the nearer force (m)
formulas.use: A couple is a free vector, so it can be moved anywhere on the body

formulas.name: Equivalent force–couple system at A
formulas.vars: \(M_{A}\) = couple moment at A (N m); \underline{r} = position vector from A (m)
formulas.use: Reduce any system to a force at A plus a couple; the two systems must have the same R and the same \(M_{A}\)

formulas.name: Moving a force to a new point
formulas.vars: F = force (N); d = perpendicular distance moved (m)
formulas.use: Moving F parallel to itself by d requires adding a couple M = Fd

formulas.name: Equilibrium with an applied couple
formulas.vars: \(M_{c}\) = applied couple (N m)
formulas.use: Find forces that balance a couple

formulas.name: Equivalence of two systems
formulas.vars: (1),(2) = the two systems
formulas.use: Two systems have the same external effect if forces and moments about any point match

formulas.name: First condition (translational equilibrium)
formulas.vars: \sum\vec F = vector sum of all external forces on the body (N)
formulas.use: Body at rest or constant velocity; no net force.

formulas.name: Second condition (rotational equilibrium)
formulas.vars: \sum M = sum of moments of all forces about any chosen point (N·m)
formulas.use: Valid about any point; choose the point where unknown forces act to eliminate them.

formulas.name: Weight of a body
formulas.vars: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²)
formulas.use: Acts downward at the centre of mass; include in every free-body diagram.

formulas.name: Components of a force or cable tension at angle θ to the horizontal
formulas.vars: T = tension or force (N); \theta = angle to horizontal (deg or rad); \(T_{x}\), \(T_{y}\) = horizontal and vertical components (N)
formulas.use: Resolving cable tensions or inclined forces; check which angle is measured from the horizontal.

formulas.name: Resultant of pin reaction components
formulas.vars: \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\) = horizontal and vertical pin reaction components (N); R = resultant reaction (N)
formulas.use: A pin gives two unknown components; combine them for the total reaction.

formulas.name: Component force balance (coplanar)
formulas.vars: \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = force components along x and y axes (N)
formulas.use: Concurrent coplanar systems such as a knot with ropes; gives two equations for two unknowns.

formulas.name: Knot with two ropes at angles α (left) and β (right) supporting weight W
formulas.vars: \(T_{L}\), \(T_{R}\) = left and right rope tensions (N); \alpha, \beta = rope angles to horizontal; W = hanging weight (N)
formulas.use: Solve the simultaneous equations for the tensions. The lecture example uses α=45°, β=30°, W=98 N, giving \(T_{R}\)≈71.7 N and \(T_{L}\)≈87.8 N.

formulas.name: Hanging mass on a single rope
formulas.vars: T = rope tension (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²)
formulas.use: Simple vertical balance of a suspended mass.

formulas.name: Three independent equations for coplanar equilibrium
formulas.vars: \(F_{x}\), \(F_{y}\) = force components (N); M = moment about the chosen point (N·m)
formulas.use: Standard method for beams, frames and ladders; at most 3 unknowns can be found.

formulas.name: Alternative set: one force and two moment equations
formulas.latex: \sum F_x=0,\ \sum M_{1}=0,\ \sum M_{2}=0\quad\text{or}\quad \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M_{1}=0,\ \sum M_{2}=0
formulas.vars: \(M_{1}\), \(M_{2}\) = moments about points 1 and 2 (N·m)
formulas.use: The two moment points must not lie on a line perpendicular to the force direction used.

formulas.name: Alternative set: three moment equations
formulas.vars: \(M_{1}\), \(M_{2}\), \(M_{3}\) = moments about three points (N·m)
formulas.use: The three points must be non-collinear.

formulas.name: Fixed (built-in) support reactions
formulas.latex: \sum F_x=0\Rightarrow F_{Ax};\ \sum F_y=0\Rightarrow F_{Ay};\ \sum M_A=0\Rightarrow M_A
formulas.vars: \(F_{Ax}\), \(F_{Ay}\) = reaction force components at A (N); \(M_{A}\) = reaction moment at A (N·m)
formulas.use: A built-in support provides two forces and a moment. Example: loads 400 N at 1 m and 200 N at 2 m give \(F_{Ay}\)=600 N and \(M_{A}\)=800 N·m.

formulas.name: Pin-supported beam held by a cable at angle θ, length L, loads \(W_{i}\) at distances \(d_{i}\) from the pin
formulas.latex: T\sin\theta\,L=\sum W_i d_i,\quad R_x=T\cos\theta,\quad R_y=\sum W_i-T\sin\theta
formulas.vars: T = cable tension (N); \theta = cable angle to beam; L = distance from the pin to the cable attachment (m); \(W_{i}\) = loads (N); \(d_{i}\) = their distances from the pin (m); \(R_{x}\), \(R_{y}\) = pin reactions (N)
formulas.use: Take moments about the pin first to find T, then use the force balances. Example: θ=53°, L=8 m, loads 200 N at 4 m and 600 N at 2 m.

formulas.name: Hinged beam with a wire: moments about hinge A
formulas.vars: T = wire tension (N); \(d_{C}\) = distance from A to the wire attachment (m); \(W_{i}\) = loads (N); \(d_{i}\) = distances from A (m)
formulas.use: Take moments about A to find T, then \sum \(F_{y}\)=0 for \(R_{y}\) and \sum \(F_{x}\)=0 for \(R_{x}\). Example: \(R_{y}\)+T-60-20=0 and 0.35T-60(0.2)-20(0.6)=0.

formulas.name: Uniform inclined member (e.g. walkway or ladder) hinged at A, supported at B
formulas.vars: m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/s²); \theta = angle of the member; \(R_{A}\) = reaction at A (N)
formulas.use: Weight acts at the midpoint of a uniform member; moment arms are horizontal distances, so \cos\theta cancels. In the example m = 300 kg and the member length is 8 m.

formulas.name: Force balances for the walkway
formulas.vars: \(R_{A}\), \(R_{B}\) = reactions at A and B (N); T = rope tension (N); \theta = angle
formulas.use: After finding the reactions from moments, use these to find the remaining unknowns. Check the sign and direction of each component against the free-body diagram.

topics.topic: Dry friction: static and kinetic laws

formulas.name: Static friction condition (no slip)
formulas.vars: \(F_{f}\) = static friction force (N); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
formulas.use: Friction is whatever equilibrium requires, up to this limit; check it to decide whether a body slips.

formulas.name: Limiting (maximum) static friction, impending slip
formulas.vars: \(F_{f,\max}\) = limiting friction force (N); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
formulas.use: Use only when slip is just about to occur; friction acts opposite to the impending motion.

formulas.name: Kinetic friction force
formulas.vars: \(F_{k}\) = kinetic friction force (N); \(\mu_{k}\) = coefficient of kinetic friction (dimensionless); N = normal reaction (N)
formulas.use: Use when the surfaces are sliding; usually \(\mu_{k}\) < \(\mu_{s}\).

formulas.name: Normal reaction on a horizontal surface
formulas.vars: N = normal reaction (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
formulas.use: Block on a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces; otherwise use \sum \(F_{y}\) = 0.

formulas.name: Newton's second law for a sliding block
formulas.vars: P = applied horizontal force (N); \(F_{k}\) = kinetic friction force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
formulas.use: Use when the block slides and accelerates.

formulas.name: Static friction angle
formulas.vars: \(\varphi_{s}\) = static friction angle (rad or deg); \(F_{max}\) = limiting friction force (N); N = normal reaction (N); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless)
formulas.use: At impending slip, the resultant of N and F makes angle \(\varphi_{s}\) with the normal.

formulas.name: Kinetic friction angle
formulas.vars: \(\varphi_{k}\) = kinetic friction angle (rad or deg); \(F_{k}\) = kinetic friction force (N); N = normal reaction (N); \(\mu_{k}\) = coefficient of kinetic friction (dimensionless)
formulas.use: During sliding.

formulas.name: Normal reaction on an incline
formulas.vars: N = normal reaction (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\)); \theta = incline angle (deg)
formulas.use: Equilibrium perpendicular to the slope, with no other force components perpendicular to it.

formulas.name: Force along the incline for impending motion up the slope
formulas.vars: T = tension/pulling force parallel to slope (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\)); \theta = incline angle (deg); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Impending motion up the slope with friction acting down the slope; for impending motion down use -\(\mu_{s}\) mg\cos\theta.

formulas.name: Equilibrium along the incline (general form)
formulas.vars: T = applied force along slope (N); \(F_{f}\) = friction force (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\)); \theta = incline angle (deg)
formulas.use: Set the sign of \(F_{f}\) opposite to the impending motion; for impending slip \(F_{f}\) = \(\mu_{s}\) N.

formulas.name: Maximum friction with two contact faces
formulas.vars: \(F_{f,\max}\) = total limiting friction (N); \(\mu_{s}\) = coefficient of static friction (dimensionless); N = normal force on each face (N)
formulas.use: Block gripped between two surfaces, each with normal force N.

formulas.name: Spring force
formulas.vars: \(F_{s}\) = spring force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); x = extension or compression from natural length (m)
formulas.use: Linear spring.

formulas.name: Weight
formulas.vars: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
formulas.use: Convert mass to force.

formulas.name: Minimum applied force (block about to slide down)
formulas.vars: P = applied force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); y = spring extension (m); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\)); \(\mu_{s}\) = static friction coefficient (dimensionless); F = clamping normal force (N)
formulas.use: Friction acts up, with limiting value 2\mu_s F. This is the example geometry with spring force ky; derive from vertical equilibrium for other setups.

formulas.name: Maximum applied force (block about to slide up)
formulas.vars: P = applied force (N); k = spring stiffness (N/m); y = spring extension (m); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\)); \(\mu_{s}\) = static friction coefficient (dimensionless); F = clamping normal force (N)
formulas.use: Friction acts down, with limiting value 2\mu_s F. Same example geometry as above.

formulas.name: Member count for a statically determinate planar pin-jointed truss
formulas.vars: m = required number of members (–); j = number of joints (–); r = number of support reaction components (–)
formulas.use: Check determinacy and stability: \(m_{\text{actual}}\) > 2j - r means redundant members (indeterminate); \(m_{\text{actual}}\) < 2j - r means a mechanism (unstable). Example: j=4, r=3 gives m=5.

formulas.name: Whole-truss equilibrium for external reactions
formulas.vars: \(F_{x}\) = horizontal force (N); \(F_{y}\) = vertical force (N); M = moment about any chosen point (N·m)
formulas.use: Apply to the whole truss first to find the support reactions, before analysing joints or sections. Take moments about a support to eliminate unknowns.

rep.ov: Materials 1 (ENG1033) starts with why materials matter, classes of materials, selection and failure case studies, and the basic definitions of stress, strain and moduli. It then explains properties from the atom up: bonding and energy bands, crystal structures, defects, X-ray diffraction, electrical and optical behaviour, and diffusion. Next it moves to mechanical behaviour: modulus, yield, dislocations, strengthening, fracture, creep, viscoelasticity and fatigue. It closes with cost, sustainability and a quantitative materials-selection case study (the \( \rho^2/E \) index). Each block builds on the previous one: bonding sets structure, structure and defects set properties, and properties drive failure and selection.
must: Stress and strain: \( \sigma=F/A \), \( \varepsilon=\Delta L/L_0 \), \( E=\sigma/\varepsilon \), Poisson's ratio \( \nu=-\varepsilon_{lat}/\varepsilon_{axial} \). Know the units (Pa, strain dimensionless), the three moduli, and how to read a stress-strain curve (proportional limit, yield, UTS, necking, fracture).

Bonding types: ionic, covalent, metallic (primary) and van der Waals, hydrogen (secondary). Know the net energy curve \( E_N=-A/r+B/r^n \), with the equilibrium separation at the minimum, and how bond stiffness \( S=dF/dr \) sets modulus.

Crystal geometry: atoms per cell (SC 1, BCC 2, FCC 4); contact directions and cell edge \( a \) from atomic radius R (FCC \( a=2\sqrt2R \), BCC \( a=4R/\sqrt3 \)); close-packed stacking (FCC ABC, HCP AB); the 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices; iron allotropy (BCC–FCC–BCC at 912 and 1394 °C).
Density from structure: \( \rho=nA/(V_CN_A) \), including the cm/nm unit conversion; polymer density by the volume-fraction rule of mixtures.

Defects: vacancies, interstitials, edge/screw/mixed dislocations (Burgers vector), grain boundaries. Know why dislocation motion (slip on close-packed planes, \( \tau_R=\tau_{crss} \)) explains yield and why every strengthening method works by hindering dislocations.
Strengthening mechanisms: grain size (Hall-Petch), solid solution, precipitate (Orowan), work hardening (%CW). Know the strength-ductility trade-off.

Yield criteria and stress states: stress on inclined planes, principal stresses, Tresca (\( \sigma_1-\sigma_3=\sigma_y \)) and von Mises. Know the yield envelope comparison and the torsion example (\( T_{max}=\pi r^3\sigma_y/4 \) for Tresca, \( \pi r^3\sigma_y/\sqrt{12} \) for von Mises).

Fracture: Griffith energy balance, \( K=\sigma\sqrt{\pi a} \) with failure at \( K=K_c \), ductile vs brittle fracture (cup-and-cone, dimples), modes I–III, toughness vs resilience vs ductility (%EL, %RA), and toughening via fibres and particles.

Diffusion: Fick's first law \( J=-D\,dC/dx \), Fick's second law, Arrhenius \( D=D_0\exp(-Q_d/RT) \) (temperature in K), vacancy vs interstitial mechanisms, carburising, doping, and the Cu vs Al interconnect case.

Time-dependent failure: creep (stages I–III, significant above \( T>0.4T_m \) in K), stress relaxation vs creep, and fatigue (S-N curves, fatigue limit, \( \sigma_a \), \( \sigma_m \), high vs low cycle, Miner's rule \( \sum n_i/N_{f,i}=1 \)).

Electrical and optical properties from band theory: Ohm's law and \( \rho=RA/\ell \), \( \sigma=n|e|\mu \), metal vs semiconductor vs insulator band filling, absorption \( I=I_0e^{-\alpha L} \), Snell's law and the critical angle \( \theta_c=\arcsin(n_2/n_1) \), and dielectrics \( C=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0A/L \).

Materials selection: define the objective and constraints, derive the performance index (minimum mass for a stiffness-limited beam: minimise \( \rho^2/E \)), and weigh cost, embodied energy, recycling and availability.
conn: Bonding to modulus to selection: the bond energy curve gives bond stiffness, which sets E (high for ceramics and metals, low for polymers because of weak secondary bonds), and E and \( \rho \) then feed into the \( \rho^2/E \) selection index.

Crystal structure to slip to strengthening: FCC, BCC and HCP slip systems determine ductility. Dislocations explain yield, and every strengthening mechanism, plus the resulting loss of toughness, follows from restricting them.

Dislocation and defect density to fracture and fatigue: the strength-ductility trade-off links to Griffith/\( K_c \) (flaw size \( a \)) and to fatigue crack initiation at surface stress concentrations. Fatigue and creep combine in service cases such as the Comet and aircraft engine blades.
Temperature and diffusion to creep and processing: vacancy diffusion with Arrhenius behaviour underlies creep above \( 0.4T_m \), carburising, and dopant or metal diffusion in Si ICs.

Band theory to electrical, optical and device behaviour: the band gap determines conduction, photon absorption, the contact potential in MOSFETs, and the dielectric constant and refractive index (\( n=\sqrt{\varepsilon_r} \)), which feed into total internal reflection in fibres.
exq: Copper is FCC with atomic radius 0.128 nm and atomic weight 63.5 g/mol. Calculate the cell edge a, the number of atoms per cell, and the theoretical density in g/cm³ (and kg/m³).

A steel bar of diameter 12 mm carries 30 kN in tension. Calculate the stress and strain (given E = 200 GPa), and the lateral strain (given \( \nu=0.3 \)). Sketch the engineering stress-strain curve and mark yield, UTS, necking and fracture.

A solid shaft of radius r is loaded in pure torsion. Find the principal stresses and the maximum torque before yield by (a) Tresca and (b) von Mises, and comment on which is more conservative and by what factor.

A wide plate with a 4 mm edge crack (a) has \( K_c=50\ \text{MPa}\sqrt{m} \). Use \( K=\sigma\sqrt{\pi a} \) to find the fracture stress, and explain how Griffith's energy balance leads to this result. How do fibres or rubber particles toughen a brittle matrix?

Carbon diffuses into steel at 900 °C. Given \( D_0 \) and \( Q_d \), calculate D (remember K), then find the depth at which the carbon concentration reaches a set value using the error-function solution of Fick's second law. Explain why only the surface is carburised.

A component sees \(10^{5}\) cycles at \( \sigma_a \)=200 MPa and \(10^{6}\) cycles at 150 MPa. Using an S-N curve and Miner's rule, determine whether it fails. Define \( \sigma_a \) and \( \sigma_m \) for \( \sigma_{max} \)=300, \( \sigma_{min} \)=−100 MPa, and contrast steel with aluminium (fatigue limit).

Derive the minimum-mass index for a stiffness-limited cantilever beam of square section using \( \delta=4l^3F/(Et^4) \) and \( M=lt^2\rho \), rank steel, CFRP and wood by \( \rho^2/E \), and discuss how cost changes the choice.
weak: Crystal geometry and Miller indices, density and diffraction calculations: students mix up the contact directions (edge vs face diagonal vs body diagonal), forget the atom-sharing fractions, and slip on units (nm to cm, K vs °C). Bragg's law with \( d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2} \) adds another layer.

Stress transformations, resolved shear stress and the yield criteria: it is hard to keep sign conventions, principal stresses and the differences between Tresca and von Mises straight, and the algebra for reducing a multiaxial state to an equivalent stress is easy to get wrong.

Time-dependent and statistical failure (creep, stress relaxation, fatigue, Miner's rule) and the selection-index derivation: students confuse constant stress with constant strain, the high-cycle and low-cycle regimes, and which quantity is divided by \( N_f \), while the \( \rho^2/E \) index requires eliminating the free variable t and ranking correctly (lower is better).

units.name: 1.1 Course introduction and lecturers
units.ov: The notes cover only the administrative introduction to ENG 1033 Materials I: the lecturers and how to contact them. They contain no technical materials content (no stress, strain, crystal structure or mechanical properties), so the only real theme is engaging steadily and communicating properly so you can get help. Technical revision has to come from later lectures.
must: The course is ENG 1033 Materials I, and Lecture 1 is only an introduction, with no examinable technical content in these notes
Lecturers can be reached by email, but with 500+ enrolled students their workloads are heavy, so expect limited individual replies
Put the course name and code (ENG1033 Materials I) in every email subject line so the query can be routed and answered
Queries are normally dealt with in the next office hour, lecture or on Moodle, so use these channels first
Sustained engagement through the semester is expected, so keep up with the lectures week by week
Last-minute emails just before the exam are unlikely to get help, so ask questions early
Check the lecturer list (p2) so you know who teaches which part of the course; the notes do not give the names or topic split
conn: Early, regular engagement links to exam success: questions raised during the semester can be answered in office hours, lectures or on Moodle, while late ones cannot
Because of the class size, a clear subject line and use of shared channels (Moodle, lectures) are what let lecturers address your query at all
Learning who teaches which block of the course helps you direct each technical question to the right lecturer
exq: Unlikely to be examined directly: this lecture is administrative, so expect no calculation questions from it. Use it only to plan your semester study and support routes.
Practice: If you are unsure about a topic in ENG1033, which channels should you use and what should an email subject line include?
Practice: Why will emailing a lecturer in the final days before the exam probably not get you help, and what should you do instead?
Check later lecture notes for the real exam content, since this material gives no basis for quantitative questions.

notes.t: Lecturers: Getting in Touch
pts: Lecturers are contactable by email, but they have heavy workloads given 500+ enrolled students.
Emails should use the course name and code in the subject line so they can be addressed in the next office hour, lecture or Moodle.
Sustained engagement through the semester is expected; last-minute emails before the exam will not get help.
tips: Students who only engage in the final days before the exam are unlikely to receive help, so keep up with the course throughout the semester.
rq: Why does the subject-line convention matter for students who email the lecturers?
With 500+ students emailing, a clearly labelled subject line lets the lecturers find and address queries efficiently in the next office hour, lecture or Moodle post.
Why might emailing the night before the exam fail to get help?
Lecturers cannot reasonably support students with last-minute queries; help depends on engaging with the course throughout the semester.

units.name: 1.2 Why study materials: history from Stone Age to nanotechnology
units.ov: This introductory material traces human technology through materials-defined ages (Stone, Bronze, Iron, industrial, and the modern Materials Age extending to nanotechnology) to show that advances in materials have driven technological progress. It frames the Materials 1 module: knowledge plus practical experience yields creativity in engineering design. The notes are thin on detail for the Stone, Iron, Industrial and Nano sections, so these should be supplemented from lectures.
must: Material ages in sequence: Stone, Bronze, Iron, industrial, and the modern Materials Age extending to nano-scale materials
Bronze is an alloy of copper (Cu) and tin (Sn), harder and more useful than pure copper; use the correct symbols (Cu not Co, Sn)
Alloying improves properties: the Bronze Age example shows combining elements gives a better material than the pure metal
Advances in materials have historically driven technological progress, so materials understanding underpins engineering design
Module logic: knowledge + experience (applying knowledge in practice) → creativity and new engineering solutions
Timeline dates (e.g. 3300 BC, 1200 BC, 600 BC) are illustrative, not precise dating standards; do not confuse them with the ages themselves
'Future' materials on the timeline means nano-scale materials, not one named material
Bronze Age trade routes linked Mediterranean and Near Eastern peoples, spreading metals, goods and ideas; the Mycenaean gold mask shows advanced metalworking and wealth
Iron Age examples (Antonine Wall, iron nail) illustrate iron's use in construction and everyday objects (check lecture notes for detail)
conn: Alloying (bronze as Cu + Sn) links to later topics on how composition and structure control properties such as hardness and strength
Trade and the spread of metals links materials availability and processing to societal and technological development
Historical progression from bronze to iron to industrial materials to nanomaterials links to the engineer's need to select materials for design based on properties
Knowledge, experience and creativity link the module's theory to practical design problems
exq: Describe the sequence of materials ages from the Stone Age to the present and explain why each shift in dominant material enabled technological advances.
Define bronze, state its constituent elements with chemical symbols, and explain why it was more useful than pure copper for tools and weapons.
Explain how knowledge, experience and creativity combine in engineering, using an example of a materials-driven innovation.
Discuss what is meant by 'nano-scale materials' as future materials and why they are expected to shape future engineering.
Using the Bronze Age as a case study, discuss how trade routes and metalworking skill influenced the spread of materials technology.

notes.t: Why study Materials 1
pts: Materials 1 builds a foundation of knowledge about engineering materials.
Experience with materials is built up through applying that knowledge in practice.
Creativity emerges when knowledge and experience are combined to generate new engineering solutions.
rq: Why is knowledge alone not sufficient for a good engineer, according to this diagram?
Knowledge must be connected through experience and then combined creatively; isolated facts do not produce solutions.

notes.t: Why we need to study materials
pts: Human material use has progressed through ages defined by materials: stone, bronze, iron, and now the materials age.
Modern materials science (SciMAP Materials Age) extends into nano-scale materials that are expected to shape the future.
Advances in materials have historically driven technological progress, so understanding materials underpins engineering design.
tips: Do not confuse the historical date labels (3300 BC, 1200 BC, 600 BC) with the ages themselves; the timeline is illustrative, not a precise dating standard.
The 'Future' materials on the timeline refer to nano-scale materials, not a single named material.
rq: Why might the transition from bronze to iron have changed what engineers could build?
Iron is stronger and more abundant than bronze, enabling tougher tools, weapons and structures, so new material capabilities expand what designs are possible.
What does 'nano' in the Materials Age imply about how material properties can be controlled?
Structuring materials at the nanometre scale allows properties such as strength, conductivity or reactivity to be tailored beyond those of bulk materials.

notes.t: Bronze Age Materials
pts: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, making it harder and more useful than pure copper.
Bronze Age trade routes linked Mediterranean and Near Eastern peoples, spreading metals, goods and ideas.
The Mycenaean gold mask from Greece shows the advanced metalworking and wealth of Bronze Age societies.
defs: Bronze
An alloy of copper (Cu) and tin (Sn), used widely in the Bronze Age for tools, weapons and ornaments.
tips: Use the correct chemical symbols: copper is Cu (not Co) and tin is Sn.
rq: Why would early smiths have combined copper with tin rather than using copper alone?
Tin added to copper produces a harder, more durable alloy that holds a sharper edge and casts more easily than pure copper.

units.name: 1.3 Course topics and timetable
units.ov: These pages are an introduction to ENG1033 Materials I. They set out that the course deals mainly with solids and studies their physical, mechanical, electrical and optical behaviour. They also stress engineering materials to behave as required, understanding failure, and selecting materials for applications. The notes contain no technical content or equations; the timetable page (Weeks 1-5) gives only the schedule. Revision should therefore focus on the course framing and on how it links to later technical topics.
must: Materials in this course are mostly solids, so the structure-property ideas that follow apply to solids.
Four behaviour types are studied and must be kept distinct: physical, mechanical, electrical and optical.
Do not reduce material behaviour to mechanical properties alone; a good answer considers all relevant behaviour types.
A central aim is to engineer materials so that they behave as required, i.e. tailoring properties for a purpose.
Understanding why materials fail to meet expectations (failure) is a core topic.
Material selection for a given application is a key skill: match the required properties to the material.
Materials I is only the visible tip of a larger body of knowledge, and the field changes quickly.
Professional engineers must keep up with advances after graduating (lifelong learning).
Know the Weeks 1-5 timetable so you can place each topic in the course sequence (the notes give no detail beyond the title).
conn: Selection links to all four behaviour types: a choice must satisfy mechanical, physical, electrical and optical requirements together, often with trade-offs.
Engineering a material to behave as required is the reverse of failure analysis: failure shows which property or condition was mis-specified, and that informs better design.
Behaviour in all four categories ultimately depends on the material's structure, so later topics on structure and processing explain why properties differ and how they can be changed.
exq: List the four types of material behaviour studied in Materials I and give one engineering example of a property in each.
A component failed in service even though the material appeared suitable. Discuss why materials may fail to meet expectations and what information you would need to select a better material.

For an application of your choice, such as a bicycle frame or an electrical cable, outline the properties you would require and justify a material choice. Include at least two non-mechanical properties.
Explain why materials engineering requires continued learning after graduation, with reference to the pace of change in the field.
Describe how the aims of 'engineering materials to behave as required' and 'selecting the right material' differ and how they complement each other.

notes.t: Topics covered in Materials I
pts: Materials in this course are mostly solids.
Materials are studied for their physical, mechanical, electrical and optical behaviour.
A central aim is to engineer materials so they behave as required.
Understanding why materials fail to meet expectations is a core topic.
Selecting the right material for a given application is a key skill.
tips: Keep the four behaviour types (physical, mechanical, electrical, optical) distinct; do not reduce material behaviour to mechanical properties alone.
rq: Why is the course's focus on solids rather than all materials?
Solids are the most widely used engineering materials, so the course concentrates on them.
Why must a material's physical, mechanical, electrical and optical behaviour all be considered when selecting it?
A material may meet one requirement but fail another, so the application's demands across all four properties determine suitability.

notes.t: University Courses – why so much to cover?
pts: Materials I is only the visible tip of a much larger body of knowledge in materials engineering.
Materials engineering sits at the frontier of science and technology, so the field changes quickly.
As a professional engineer you must keep up with fast-moving advances after graduating.
rq: Why does the iceberg analogy suggest that first-year courses cover only a small part of what an engineer needs?
Like an iceberg, most of the knowledge lies below the surface; the course introduces the visible tip, and further learning builds the rest.
Why might a foundational course still be essential even though the field keeps advancing?
Fundamentals provide the underlying principles needed to understand and evaluate new materials and technologies as they emerge.

units.name: 1.4 Laboratories and tutorials

must: Lab 1 = mechanical testing: it compares the mechanical properties of two alloys, iron and copper
Lab 2 = electrical and thermal testing: it compares how different materials behave electrically and thermally
Do not mix up the labs: mechanical properties (Lab 1) vs electrical and thermal properties (Lab 2)
Lab 1 answers should stay on mechanical properties such as strength and ductility, not chemical composition or corrosion
Lab 2 has two parts: Part 1 uses a coil/sample apparatus and Part 2 uses a circuit board test rig; check the lab manual for each part's purpose
Each lab requires a graded report or worksheet submitted via Moodle within 2 weeks of completing the lab
Missing a report or worksheet for any lab gives credit withheld (CW)
Attending a lab does not earn credit; the submitted report or worksheet does
The 2-week deadline runs from when the lab was completed, not from the start of term or the release of instructions
Lab instructions and video demonstrations are on Moodle; use them to prepare
conn: Lab 1 and Lab 2 both compare materials by testing, so the same approach applies: state the test, the property measured, and the difference between materials
Mechanical, electrical and thermal properties all follow from material structure and composition, so iron and copper can be contrasted across both labs
Lab work feeds the assessment: the testing in each lab produces the data for the report or worksheet, and failing to submit it means CW
exq: State which lab covers mechanical testing and which covers electrical and thermal testing, and name the materials compared in Lab 1.
Describe the purpose of Lab 1 and explain which properties of iron and copper alloys you would compare, such as strength and ductility.
Outline the two parts of Lab 2 and the apparatus used in each (coil/sample apparatus, circuit board test rig), and say what is compared in each.
A student attended a lab but did not submit the worksheet. What is the consequence, and within what time must it be submitted?
Compare how two different materials might behave in electrical and thermal testing, and explain why a comparison of materials is made in each lab.

notes.t: Laboratories overview
pts: Lab 1 introduces mechanical testing and compares mechanical properties of iron and copper alloys.
Lab 2 introduces electrical and thermal testing and compares how different materials behave electrically and thermally.
tips: Do not confuse Lab 1 (mechanical properties) with Lab 2 (electrical and thermal properties) when recalling which lab covers which property.
rq: Why are iron and copper compared in the mechanical testing lab rather than just one metal?
Comparing two metals with different structures and properties shows how material type changes mechanical behaviour, making the differences in test results meaningful.

notes.t: Laboratories: Lab 1 mechanical testing of iron and copper
pts: Lab 1 introduces mechanical testing of two different alloys, iron and copper, to compare their mechanical properties.
The purpose of the lab is to introduce students to mechanical testing and the mechanical properties of different metals.
tips: The lab is about mechanical testing and mechanical properties, not chemical composition or corrosion; keep answers focused on strength, ductility and similar properties.
rq: Why compare iron and copper specimens in the same mechanical test rather than testing one metal alone?
Comparing two metals under identical test conditions shows how composition and bonding change mechanical properties such as strength and ductility.

notes.t: Laboratories: Lab 2 Electrical and Thermal properties of materials
pts: Lab 2 introduces students to electrical and thermal testing of materials.
Lab 2 compares the electrical and thermal behaviour of different materials.
The lab is split into two parts, shown by a coil/sample apparatus (Part 1) and a circuit board test rig (Part 2).
tips: Lab 2 is about testing and comparing different materials; do not confuse the two parts' purposes without checking the lab manual.
rq: Why would a materials engineer test both electrical and thermal behaviour of the same material?

Because a material's suitability for an application (e.g. insulation, conductor, heat sink) depends on both how it conducts electricity and how it conducts heat, which are often related but not identical.

notes.t: Laboratories
pts: Lab instructions and video demonstrations are accessed through Moodle.
Each lab requires a graded report or worksheet, submitted via Moodle within 2 weeks of completing the lab.

Attendance alone is not enough; each lab must also have its graded report/worksheet submitted on Moodle by the deadline, otherwise CW (credit withheld) applies.
If a lab was completed on 1 March, what is the submission deadline and why does timing matter?
