xq.w: E = σ/ε and ε is a ratio of lengths with no units, so E carries the units of stress; calling E dimensionless confuses it with strain.
s: ε has no units so E is in Pa

xq.q: Explain why the metre is not an independent base unit in the SI system, whereas the second is. Then explain why the pascal is a derived unit and express it in terms of the base units kg, m and s.
xq.a: The metre is defined using the speed of light, which is a fixed number of metres per second, so defining the metre requires the definition of the second. The second is defined independently of the other base units. The pascal is N/m², and the newton is kg·m/s², so Pa = kg·\(m^{-1}\)·\(s^{-2.}\) It is built from base units and is not one of the seven.
s: Metre defined via speed of light, so depends on second

units.name: 3.1 Why bonding matters: mechanical and electrical properties
units.ov: This lecture introduces why the way atoms are bonded and arranged controls a material's bulk behaviour. Interatomic bonds, which come from electron-nucleus interactions, together with atomic packing set stiffness, strength and density. In a solid, discrete atomic energy levels broaden into bands, and how electrons fill these bands decides whether the material is a metal, semiconductor or insulator.
must: Bonding type and atomic arrangement together determine a material's properties; composition alone does not
Interatomic bonds are attractive and repulsive forces between neighbouring atoms, and they set stiffness and strength
Atomic packing (the positions of atoms) is distinct from bonding (the forces between atoms), and both affect mechanical behaviour
Stiffness, strength and density all follow from how atoms are interconnected, so the strength-to-weight ratio depends on bond type
Compare strength and weight using density consistently, e.g. specific strength \(\sigma/\rho\); a stronger but much denser material may not be the better choice
Isolated atoms have discrete energy levels; in a solid, many interacting atoms broaden these into energy bands
Band filling by electrons decides whether a material is a metal, semiconductor or insulator
Do not classify a material as a conductor or insulator from its elements alone; the band structure and electron filling decide it
Exam answers should link bond type to observable properties rather than just listing bond types
conn: Bond type fixes both mechanical properties (stiffness, strength, density) and electrical properties (band structure), so one bonding model explains both
Atomic packing and bonding combine to set density, and density feeds into strength-to-weight ratio comparisons
Atomic energy levels lead to bands through the interaction of many atoms, which then leads to electrical classification by filling
Electron-nucleus interactions give rise to bonds, which give interatomic forces, which give stiffness and strength
exq: Explain how interatomic bonding determines stiffness and strength, distinguishing the role of bonding from that of atomic packing.

Two materials have strengths of 400 MPa and 250 MPa and densities of 7800 and 2700 kg/m³. Calculate the specific strength of each and state which is better for a lightweight component, justifying your answer.
Describe how discrete atomic energy levels become energy bands when atoms form a solid, and why isolated atoms do not have bands.
Explain how the filling of energy bands distinguishes a metal, a semiconductor and an insulator, and why composition alone cannot predict this.
Discuss why the type of atomic bonding governs the strength-to-weight ratio of a material, using examples of different material classes.

notes.t: Introduction to atomic bonding and energy bands in solids
pts: Types of bonding between atoms in a solid strongly influence its physical properties.
Electron–nucleus interactions within an atom give rise to the various types of bonds between atoms.
Discrete atomic energy levels spread into energy bands when atoms come together in a solid.
tips: Do not confuse the atomic energy levels of an isolated atom with the energy bands that form in a solid; bands arise only from many interacting atoms.
Remember that this page is introductory: exam answers should link bonding type to observable physical properties rather than just listing bond types.
rq: Why would the type of bonding in a solid affect properties such as melting point or electrical conductivity?

Bonding determines how strongly atoms are held together and how electrons are shared or localised, which governs cohesive energy (melting point) and the availability of mobile electrons (conductivity).
What happens to a single sharp atomic energy level when many atoms are brought together to form a solid?
It splits into many closely spaced levels that merge into a continuous energy band, due to interactions between neighbouring atoms.

notes.t: Mechanical properties: stiffness, strength and density
pts: Stiffness, strength and density of a material are governed by how its atoms are interconnected.
Mechanical properties arise from the forces acting between atoms, i.e. the interatomic bonds.
The arrangement (position) of atoms, i.e. atomic packing, also controls mechanical behaviour.
The key strength-to-weight ratio is determined by the type of atomic bonding.
defs: Interatomic bond
The attractive and repulsive force linking neighbouring atoms, which determines a material's stiffness and strength.
Atomic packing
The spatial arrangement of atoms in a material's structure, which affects its mechanical properties.
tips: Do not confuse atomic packing (arrangement of atoms) with interatomic bonding (forces between atoms); both influence properties but are different factors.
Strength-to-weight comparisons must use density consistently; a stronger material is not always the better choice if it is much denser.
rq: Why would two materials with identical atomic packing still have very different stiffness?
Because stiffness depends on the forces between atoms (the type of interatomic bonding), not only on their arrangement.
Why does the atomic bonding matter for strength-to-weight ratio rather than strength alone?
Because a light material with strong bonds can be strong yet low in density, so the ratio of strength to density is what makes it efficient.

notes.t: Electrical properties: metal, semiconductor or insulator
pts: Electrical behaviour depends on how atoms are interconnected, not just on the atoms themselves.
Atomic bonds merge to form bands, and how those bands are filled with electrons determines whether a material conducts, is a semiconductor, or is an insulator.
tips: Do not classify a material as a metal, semiconductor or insulator by its atomic composition alone; the band structure and electron filling decide it.
rq: Why would two materials made of the same atoms behave differently as a metal and as an insulator?
Because the way the atoms are interconnected and bonded affects how the bands form and how they are filled with electrons, which sets the electrical behaviour.
What determines whether a band-filled material conducts electricity?
Whether the electrons can move into empty states within a partly filled band (metal) or whether the band gap separating filled and empty bands is large (insulator) or small (semiconductor).

xq.q: Two solids contain the same type of atom, yet one is an electrical conductor and the other an insulator. Explain how this is possible, referring to atomic energy levels and bonding.
xq.a: In an isolated atom electrons occupy discrete energy levels. When atoms bond in a solid, the levels spread into energy bands. Electrical behaviour depends on how these bands are filled with electrons: a partly filled band gives a metal (conductor), while filled bands separated from empty ones give an insulator or semiconductor. Different bonding or arrangement of the same atoms changes the band structure, so the composition alone does not decide conductivity.
s: Discrete atomic levels broaden into bands in a solid
Band filling determines metal, semiconductor or insulator
Composition alone does not decide it

xq.q: A designer proposes material A because its strength is 20% higher than material B. Material A has a density 60% higher than B. What is the correct engineering conclusion for a weight-critical part?
xq.a: A has a lower strength-to-weight ratio than B, so B is better on this criterion
o: A has a lower strength-to-weight ratio than B, so B is better on this criterion
A is better because it is stronger
A is better because higher density means stronger bonding
The materials are equal because density and strength cancel
xq.w: Specific strength is 1.2/1.6 = 0.75 of B's, so A is worse per unit weight; the trap is comparing strength without density.
s: So A is lower per unit weight

xq.q: Which statement best explains why stiffness and strength of a material depend on bonding?
xq.a: They arise from the forces between atoms, together with how the atoms are packed
o: They arise from the forces between atoms, together with how the atoms are packed
They depend only on the mass of the individual atoms
They depend only on the packing, not on interatomic forces
They depend on the number of electrons in an isolated atom only
xq.w: Mechanical properties come from interatomic bond forces and atomic packing; the wrong options ignore one factor or treat atoms in isolation.
s: Bond forces and packing both control properties

units.name: 3.2 Periodic table and atomic spectra
units.ov: This material covers how the periodic table organises elements by atomic number into groups (similar chemistry) and periods (same number of electron shells), and how atoms produce discrete line spectra. Both ideas rest on quantised electron energy levels: the electron configuration sets chemical behaviour, while transitions between levels set emitted and absorbed photon energies, as seen in hydrogen's Balmer series.
must: Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number; groups (columns) share chemical properties, periods (rows) share the number of electron shells
Photon energy: \(E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\), with \(h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\) J·s and \(c = 3.00\times10^{8}\) m/s
Gases emit and absorb only at specific wavelengths, giving line spectra; hot solids and liquids give continuous spectra
Emission: an electron falls to a lower level and releases a photon with energy equal to the level difference, \(\Delta E = E_{upper}-E_{lower}\)
Absorption: an electron is excited by a photon of exactly matching energy; absorption and emission lines occur at the same wavelengths
Emission spectrum = bright lines on a dark background; absorption spectrum = dark lines on a continuous coloured background
Balmer series: hydrogen transitions ending at \(n = 2\), which give the visible lines
Alkali metals (Group 1) have one valence electron and are highly reactive; noble gases (Group 18) have full outer shells and are largely unreactive
Transition metals (groups 3–12) have partially filled d shells, giving coloured compounds and multiple oxidation states
Lanthanides and actinides are displayed separately beneath the table, not in the main body; do not mix up groups and periods
conn: Electron energy levels link the two halves: the outer-shell configuration determines a group's chemistry, and transitions between levels determine its spectral lines
Level difference \(\Delta E\) links to photon wavelength through \(E = hc/\lambda\), so a Balmer transition's energy gives its visible colour and vice versa

Emission and absorption are the reverse of one another, so a cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs the same wavelengths that the hot gas would emit (used to identify elements, e.g. in stars)
Valence electron count (one for alkali metals, full shell for noble gases) explains both reactivity trends and an element's position in the table
exq: Calculate the energy in joules and in eV of a photon of wavelength 656 nm (the red Balmer line), and state which transition produces it.
Explain, with sketches, the difference between the emission and absorption spectra of hydrogen, and state how their line positions compare.
An electron in hydrogen drops from \(n=3\) to \(n=2\), releasing a photon of energy \(3.03\times10^{-19}\) J. Find the photon's frequency and wavelength, and say whether it is visible.
Why do isolated gas atoms give line spectra while a hot solid gives a continuous spectrum? Relate your answer to quantised energy levels.
Distinguish between groups and periods, and explain why alkali metals are highly reactive while noble gases are inert, using their valence electrons.

notes.t: The Periodic Table
pts: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, with groups (columns) sharing similar chemical properties.
Elements are colour-coded by class: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, rare earths, radioactive rare earths, other metals, semimetals, non-metals, noble gases and hydrogen.
The lanthanide (rare earth) and actinide (radioactive rare earth) series are shown separately beneath the main table.
defs: Alkali metals
Group 1 metals (e.g. Li, Na, K) that are highly reactive, with one valence electron.
Transition metals
Elements in the central block (groups 3–12) with partially filled d-electron shells, typically forming coloured compounds and multiple oxidation states.
Noble gases
Group 18 elements (e.g. He, Ne, Ar) with full outer electron shells, making them largely chemically unreactive.
tips: Do not confuse the groups (columns, sharing chemical behaviour) with the periods (rows, sharing electron shell count).
Remember that the lanthanide and actinide series are displayed separately, not inserted into the main table body.
rq: Why do elements in the same group tend to behave chemically alike?
They have the same number of valence (outer-shell) electrons, which determines how they bond.
Why are the noble gases so unreactive compared with the alkali metals?
Noble gases have full outer electron shells and no tendency to gain or lose electrons, whereas alkali metals readily lose their single valence electron.

notes.t: Atomic spectra and the Balmer series in hydrogen
pts: Gases of elements emit and absorb light only at specific wavelengths, producing line spectra rather than continuous spectra.
Hydrogen's Balmer series is the classic example: transitions ending in the n = 2 level produce visible lines.
Emission spectra show bright coloured lines on a dark background, while absorption spectra show dark lines on a continuous coloured background; the lines occur at the same wavelengths.
Emission occurs when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, releasing a photon of energy equal to the level difference.
Absorption occurs when an electron is excited from a lower level (here n = 2) to a higher level by absorbing a photon of exactly the matching energy.
defs: Emission spectrum
The set of discrete wavelengths of light emitted by an excited gas as electrons drop to lower energy levels.
Absorption spectrum
The set of discrete wavelengths removed from a continuous light source when passed through a cool gas, as electrons are excited to higher levels.
Balmer series
The set of visible spectral lines of hydrogen produced by electron transitions to the n = 2 energy level.
eqs: Energy of a photon emitted or absorbed during an electron transition
E = photon energy (J); h = Planck's constant (J·s); \nu = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (m/s); \lambda = wavelength (m)
tips: Do not confuse the positions of emission and absorption lines: they coincide, but emission gives bright lines on dark while absorption gives dark lines on coloured background.
Remember that spectral lines are discrete; a continuous spectrum is produced by hot solids or liquids, not by isolated gas atoms.
rq: Why does a hot gas emit only certain colours, rather than a continuous rainbow like a hot solid?
Electrons in an isolated atom can occupy only discrete energy levels, so only photons matching the differences between those levels are emitted.
Why do the dark absorption lines appear at the same wavelengths as the bright emission lines?
The same energy level gaps govern both processes: an electron absorbs only photons matching a gap it can jump across, and emits photons matching the same gap when falling back.

xq.q: A hydrogen gas discharge tube emits a Balmer line of wavelength 656 nm, produced when an electron falls to the n = 2 level. Using Planck's constant h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s and speed of light c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s, calculate the energy of one emitted photon in electron-volts (1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J).
White light passes through a cool hydrogen gas and the transmitted light is viewed through a spectrometer. Which observation is correct, compared with the emission spectrum of hot hydrogen?
xq.a: Dark lines on a continuous coloured background, at the same wavelengths as the emission lines
o: Bright lines on a dark background, at the same wavelengths as the emission lines
Dark lines on a continuous coloured background, at the same wavelengths as the emission lines
Dark lines on a continuous coloured background, at different wavelengths from the emission lines
A fully continuous spectrum with no lines, because the gas is cool
xq.w: Atoms absorb exactly the photon energies they emit, so dark lines appear at the emission wavelengths; confusing the line appearance or position is the trap.
s: Absorption removes discrete wavelengths from the continuous source

xq.q: Explain why an excited hydrogen gas produces a line spectrum rather than a continuous spectrum, and explain why the wavelength of a Balmer line is related to the energy levels involved.
xq.a: Electrons in atoms occupy only discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level to n = 2 it emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two levels. Since only certain differences exist, only certain photon energies, and so wavelengths (E = hc/λ), are emitted, giving discrete lines. A continuous spectrum comes from hot solids or liquids, not isolated gas atoms.
s: Photon energy equals the level difference
E = hc/λ gives a specific wavelength for each transition
Only a finite set of transitions gives discrete lines; Balmer lines end at n = 2 and are visible

units.name: 3.3 Bohr model, atomic number and isotopes
units.ov: This material introduces the Bohr model of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons carrying almost all the mass, with electrons in discrete orbits that absorb or emit photons when they jump. It then uses atomic number Z to define element identity and isotopes as same-Z, different-neutron-number variants (e.g. U-235 and U-238). The ideas connect through counting particles (protons, neutrons, electrons) and using the fundamental charge and mass constants.
must: Atomic number \(Z\) = number of protons; it alone defines the element
Mass number \(A = Z + N\) (protons + neutrons); neutron number \(N = A - Z\), e.g. U-235: \(N = 235 - 92 = 143\), U-238: \(N = 146\)
Isotopes: same \(Z\), different \(N\), so different mass number and atomic mass; changing protons changes the element
Neutral atom: electrons = protons; ions have unequal numbers (the exception)
Bohr model: nucleus of protons and neutrons, electrons in discrete orbits, held by electrostatic attraction
Electron jumps between orbits absorb or emit energy as a photon (optical photon)
Elementary charge \(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\): proton +, electron −, neutron 0
Masses: \(m_p \approx m_n = 1.67\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\), \(m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\) (protons are ~1800× heavier than electrons), so the nucleus holds almost all the mass
Use SI units (kg, C); Mg has \(Z = 12\), so 12 protons and 12 electrons when neutral
The Bohr model is a simplification: orbits are not exact physical trajectories; Bohr received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 (born 1885, died 1962)
conn: Atomic number and mass number: counting protons, neutrons and electrons for an isotope or ion, then using Z to identify the element
Particle counts with the charge and mass constants: net charge of an ion (\((N_p - N_e)e\)) and atomic mass from \(Z m_p + N m_n + Z m_e\)
Isotopes with the nuclear mass fraction: isotopes differ only in neutron mass, while electron mass is negligible, so mass changes are due to the nucleus
Electron orbit jumps with electrostatic attraction and photons: energy changes in the electron's orbit correspond to emitted or absorbed light
exq: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 both have Z = 92. Calculate the number of neutrons in each and explain why they are the same element but different isotopes.
Estimate the mass of a neutral magnesium atom (Z = 12, A = 24) using \(m_p\), \(m_n\) and \(m_e\), and calculate the fraction of this mass contributed by the electrons.
Calculate the total charge, in coulombs, of the protons in a magnesium nucleus and of the electrons in a neutral atom. What is the net charge? What would it be for an Mg\(^{2+}\) ion?
Describe the Bohr model of the atom, including what happens when an electron jumps between orbits, and state two limitations of the model.
Distinguish between atomic number and mass number, and explain why changing the number of neutrons produces an isotope whereas changing the number of protons produces a different element.

notes.t: Nils Bohr and atomic structure
pts: Bohr was a Danish physicist (1885–1962) and a key figure in understanding atomic structure.
Bohr helped develop quantum mechanics, which underpins modern understanding of how electrons behave in atoms.
Bohr was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922 for investigating atomic structure and the radiation atoms emit.
tips: Do not confuse the 1922 Nobel Prize date with his birth or death years (1885–1962); exam questions often test the date of the award, not his lifespan.
rq: Why is understanding atomic structure important for a materials engineer?

Atomic structure (electron arrangement and bonding) determines a material's properties such as strength, conductivity, and melting point, so it is the foundation for explaining and designing materials.

notes.t: Bohr model of the atom: nucleus and electron orbits
pts: The simple Bohr model places protons and neutrons in a central nucleus.
Protons and neutrons have almost identical masses, far greater than the electron mass.
Neutrons carry no electric charge, while protons and electrons carry equal and opposite charges.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in defined, discrete orbits rather than continuous paths.
In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons; ions are the exception.
defs: Bohr model
A simple model of the atom in which a nucleus of protons and neutrons is orbited by electrons in defined, discrete orbits.
eqs: Charge of a proton or electron (elementary charge)
Mass of a proton or neutron
tips: Use the electron charge 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C with sign only for electrons (−) and protons (+); the magnitude is the same.
Keep SI units: masses must be in kg (e.g., 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, not grams) and charges in Coulombs.
rq: Why does the electron's mass contribute almost nothing to the atom's total mass?
The electron mass (9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) is roughly 1800 times smaller than a proton or neutron mass (1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg), so almost all atomic mass is in the nucleus.
If an atom has 8 protons and 8 neutrons but gains 2 electrons, what is its charge and why?
Charge is −2e: the 8 protons give +8e and the 10 electrons give −10e, so the net charge is −2e; it is a negative ion.

notes.t: Bohr model of the atom
pts: The nucleus, made of protons and neutrons, carries almost all of the atom's mass.
Electrons occupy orbits and can jump between them, gaining or losing energy.
Energy change during an electron jump is absorbed or emitted as an optical photon.
Electrons carry negative charge while protons carry positive charge, so the atom is held together by electrostatic attraction.
The atomic number gives the number of protons; this diagram shows magnesium (Mg) with atomic number 12.
defs: Atomic number
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, which identifies the element.
Nucleus
The dense central core of an atom containing protons and neutrons, which provides almost all of the atom's mass.
tips: Do not confuse the atomic number (protons) with the mass number (protons plus neutrons); the mass is mainly from the nucleus, not the electrons.
The Bohr model is a simplified picture; electrons are not in fixed circular paths in reality, so avoid stating orbits as exact physical trajectories in exam answers.
rq: Why does a photon get emitted when an electron drops to a lower orbit, rather than the energy simply disappearing?
Energy is conserved: the difference between the two orbit energy levels is released as a photon of that energy (in the optical range for visible light).
If magnesium has 12 protons, how many electrons does a neutral Mg atom have, and why?
12 electrons, because a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative) so the charges cancel.

notes.t: Atomic number and isotopes
pts: Chemical identity of an element is set by the number of protons in the nucleus (atomic number Z).
Isotopes are variants of the same element with the same proton count but different neutron counts, giving different atomic masses.
Uranium-235 and uranium-238 both have 92 protons; they differ only in neutron number (143 vs 146).
defs: Atomic number (Z)
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus; it determines which chemical element the atom is.
Isotopes
Variants of a chemical element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and hence different atomic masses.
tips: Do not confuse atomic number (protons only) with mass number (protons + neutrons); e.g. U-235 has mass number 235, not 92.
Isotopes differ in neutron number, not proton number; changing protons would change the element itself.
rq: Why do isotopes of the same element behave almost identically in chemical reactions?

Chemical behaviour depends on the electron configuration, which is set by the number of protons (and hence electrons); neutrons do not change the electron count, so chemistry is essentially unchanged.
If an atom has 92 protons and 146 neutrons, what is its mass number and which isotope is it?
Mass number is 92 + 146 = 238, so it is uranium-238.

xq.q: A uranium-235 atom has atomic number Z = 92. Taking the proton and neutron mass as 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg and the electron mass as 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, calculate the total mass of the neutral atom in kg, and the percentage of that mass contributed by the electrons.
xq.a: Mass ≈ 3.92×10⁻²⁵ kg; electrons contribute ≈ 0.021 %

xq.q: Uranium-238 and uranium-235 are isotopes of uranium (Z = 92). How many neutrons does U-238 have, and why is it the same element as U-235?
xq.a: 146 neutrons; both have 92 protons
o: 238 neutrons; both have the same mass number
146 neutrons; both have 92 protons
92 neutrons; both have the same number of neutrons
143 neutrons; both have 92 electrons only
xq.w: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 238 − 92 = 146, and the element is fixed by the proton count; the trap is treating mass number as neutrons.

xq.q: A neutral magnesium atom has atomic number 12. Describe its structure in the Bohr model, state the numbers of each particle if the isotope has mass number 24, and explain why the nucleus accounts for almost all of the atom's mass.
xq.a: The nucleus has 12 protons and 12 neutrons (24 − 12), with 12 electrons in discrete orbits, since a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons. Protons and neutrons each have mass about 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, about 1800 times the electron mass of 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, so the nucleus carries nearly all the mass.
s: 12 electrons in discrete orbits, charge balance
Nucleon mass ≫ electron mass, so nucleus holds nearly all mass

units.name: 3.4 Wave-mechanical model, quantum numbers and orbitals
units.ov: This material introduces the wave-mechanical model, in which electrons occupy atomic orbitals (probability distributions) with discrete energies set by four quantum numbers (n, l, \(m_{l}\), \(m_{s}\)). It covers how the quantum numbers determine shell and subshell capacity, how the Pauli exclusion principle and lowest-energy-first filling fix electron configurations, and how orbital shapes (s spherical, p directional) underlie the directionality of covalent bonds.
must: Electrons are described by orbitals, i.e. probability distributions, not fixed orbits; never write 'electrons orbit in paths'
Energy levels are discrete (quantised); electrons cannot have energies between levels
Four quantum numbers: \(n=1,2,3,\dots\) (shell), \(l=0\) to \(n-1\) (subshell: s, p, d, f = 0, 1, 2, 3), \(m_l=-l\) to \(+l\) (orientation), \(m_s=\pm\tfrac12\) (spin)
Orbitals per subshell \(=2l+1\) (s=1, p=3, d=5, f=7); max electrons per subshell \(=2(2l+1)\) (2, 6, 10, 14)
Shell n contains n subshells and holds a maximum of \(2n^2\) electrons (K=2, L=8, M=18, N=32)
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin
Aufbau: lowest energy filled first; within a shell s < p < d < f, and shells overlap so 4s fills before 3d
Shell labels: K (n=1, 1s), L (n=2, 2s and 2p), M, N, O
s orbital is spherical with no directional lobes; p subshell has three mutually perpendicular dumbbell orbitals \(p_x, p_y, p_z\), each with two lobes
Orbital shape and orientation give covalent bonds their directionality
Common errors: forgetting \(m_l=0\) (giving 2l instead of 2l+1), and confusing the orbital count with the electron count
conn: Quantum number ranges (l up to n−1, \(m_{l}\) from −l to +l) lead to orbital counts 2l+1, then subshell capacity, then shell capacity \(2n^2\)
The Pauli principle (two electrons per orbital with opposite \(m_{s}\)) combined with energy ordering (4s below 3d) gives electron configurations
Orbital shape (s spherical, p directional) links to bonding: overlap of orbitals forms covalent bonds with specific directions
Quantised energy states connect to the wave-particle duality of electrons, and to why orbitals are probabilities rather than paths
exq: List all allowed sets of quantum numbers (n, l, \(m_{l}\), \(m_{s}\)) for electrons in the n=3 shell, and show that the total is 18 = 2n².
Explain why a d subshell holds 10 electrons and an f subshell 14, using the allowed values of \(m_{l}\) and \(m_{s}\).
State the Pauli exclusion principle and use it, with the energy ordering of subshells, to write the electron configuration of an atom such as Fe (26 electrons), explaining why 4s fills before 3d.
Why is it incorrect to say an electron orbits the nucleus in a fixed path? Define an atomic orbital and describe the shapes of the s and p orbitals.
Which of these quantum-number sets is not allowed, and why: (3, 3, 0, +½), (2, 1, −1, −½), (1, 0, 0, +½)?

notes.t: Atomic structure: a wave-mechanical model
pts: Electrons have both wave-like and particle-like properties according to quantum mechanics.
Electrons around the nucleus occupy atomic orbitals, described by a spatial probability distribution rather than fixed orbits.
Each orbital corresponds to a discrete energy level, and these levels are defined by quantum numbers.
defs: Atomic orbital
A region around the nucleus described by a spatial probability distribution, in which an electron is likely to be found, defined by quantum numbers.
Quantum numbers
A set of numbers that specify the discrete energy level and properties of an electron in an atomic orbital.
tips: Do not describe electrons as orbiting in fixed paths; orbitals give the probability of finding an electron, not its exact position.
Energy levels are discrete, not continuous; do not describe electron energies as varying smoothly.
rq: Why can't we assign electrons fixed circular orbits around the nucleus as in the Bohr model?
Because electrons have wave-like properties, so their position is described probabilistically by an orbital (a spatial probability distribution) rather than a definite path.
Why are only certain energy levels allowed for an electron in an atom?
Because the wave-like behaviour of electrons bound to the nucleus leads to standing-wave solutions, and each allowed solution is a discrete energy level defined by quantum numbers.

notes.t: Wave-mechanical atomic model: quantum numbers and electron capacity
pts: Four quantum numbers (n, l, \(m_{l}\), \(m_{s}\)) fully describe each electron's state in an atom.
The principal quantum number n sets the energy level (shell); the angular number l sets the subshell type (s, p, d, f).
The number of orbitals in a subshell is 2l+1, and each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
Subshells in a given shell n run from l = 0 to l = n−1, so shell n contains n subshells.
Total electrons per shell is 2n², which follows from summing orbitals × 2.
defs: Principal quantum number (n)
Integer (1, 2, 3, …) giving the energy level or shell (K, L, M, N, O) an electron occupies.
Angular (azimuthal) quantum number (l)
Integer from 0 to n−1 defining the orbital shape and subshell (s = 0, p = 1, d = 2, f = 3).
Magnetic quantum number (\(m_{l}\))
Integer from −l to +l specifying the orientation of an orbital within a subshell.
Spin quantum number (\(m_{s}\))
Electron spin of +½ (spin up) or −½ (spin down); two electrons with opposite spins can share an orbital.
eqs: Number of orbitals in a subshell
\(N_{orb}\) = number of orbitals (dimensionless); l = angular quantum number (dimensionless)
\(N_{e}\) = maximum electrons (dimensionless); l = angular quantum number (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the number of orbitals (2l+1) with the number of electrons (2(2l+1)); the table gives electrons, so double the orbital count.
Count \(m_{l}\) values from −l to +l including zero; forgetting zero gives 2l instead of 2l+1 orbitals.
rq: Why does the 3d subshell hold 10 electrons but the 3p subshell holds only 6?
d subshells have l = 2, giving 2l+1 = 5 orbitals; p subshells have l = 1, giving 3 orbitals. Each orbital holds 2 electrons, so 5×2 = 10 and 3×2 = 6.
What if the shell n = 2 allowed l = 2? What would break in the table?
The rule l ≤ n−1 would be violated, since l = 2 requires n ≥ 3; a 2d subshell would not exist and the shell's electron count would no longer match 2n².
Why does the \(m_{l}\) column for 4f list seven values rather than four?
For l = 3, \(m_{l}\) runs from −3 to +3, giving 7 values, one per orbital in the f subshell.

notes.t: Electron energy states and electron filling
pts: Electrons can only occupy discrete (quantised) energy states, not any energy value.
Electrons tend to fill the lowest available energy state first, so higher subshells are filled only after lower ones.
Electrons are fermions and obey the Pauli exclusion principle: at most two electrons per energy level, one spin up and one spin down.
Energy increases with shell number n, and within a shell subshells differ in energy (s < p < d), with overlap between shells such as 4s lying below 3d.
defs: Discrete energy states
Fixed, quantised energy levels that an electron in an atom may occupy; electron energies cannot take values between these levels.
Pauli exclusion principle
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.
K-shell (n = 1)
The principal energy shell closest to the nucleus, containing the 1s subshell.
L-shell (n = 2)
The second principal shell, containing the 2s and 2p subshells.
tips: Do not assume 4s fills after 3d simply because 4 > 3; the 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d and fills first.
Remember the two-electron limit applies per energy level (per orbital), with opposite spins, not per shell as a whole.
rq: Why does a 3d orbital sit above the 4s orbital in energy even though 3d has a lower principal number?
Because subshell energy depends on both n and l; 4s (n+l = 4) has a lower energy than 3d (n+l = 5), so 4s fills before 3d.
What would happen to electron filling if electrons were not restricted to two per energy level?
Many electrons would crowd into the lowest state, so atomic structure and the periodic table's shell filling would not follow the observed pattern.

notes.t: Atomic orbitals: s and p shapes and bonding
pts: The s orbital is spherical and centred on the nucleus.
The p subshell has three orbitals (px, py, pz) oriented mutually perpendicular along the x, y and z axes.
Orbital shape describes the probability of finding an electron relative to the nucleus at the centre.
Atomic orbitals combine to form bonds between atoms and give covalent bonds their directionality.
defs: Atomic orbital
A region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron, described by its shape and orientation.
p subshell
An electron subshell containing three mutually perpendicular p orbitals (px, py, pz).
tips: Do not confuse orbital shape with the electron's path; orbitals describe probability, not orbits.
The s orbital is spherical and has no directional lobes, whereas each p orbital has two lobes along one axis.
rq: Why do the three p orbitals point along x, y and z rather than in the same direction?
Each p orbital is a distinct spatial solution that is orthogonal to the others, so they lie mutually perpendicular, giving three independent orientations.
Why does the directionality of orbitals matter for covalent bonds in materials?
Overlap of orbitals is strongest along specific directions, so covalent bonds have fixed angles that determine the geometry and properties of the material.

xq.q: For the principal quantum number n = 3 (the M shell), use the rules for l and the number of orbitals in a subshell, 2l+1, to find the total number of orbitals and the maximum number of electrons in the shell. Show the maximum number of electrons in each subshell.
xq.a: 9 orbitals; 18 electrons (s: 2, p: 6, d: 10)

xq.q: Which is the correct order of filling for the 3d and 4s subshells in an isolated atom, and why?
xq.a: 4s fills before 3d because 4s is lower in energy
o: 3d fills before 4s because n = 3 is less than 4
4s fills before 3d because 4s is lower in energy
They fill simultaneously because both hold ten electrons
4s fills before 3d because it holds more electrons
xq.w: Subshell energies overlap so 4s lies below 3d; assuming order by n alone is the trap.

xq.q: Explain how the Pauli exclusion principle limits the number of electrons in a p subshell, and hence show that the L shell (n = 2) holds at most 8 electrons.
xq.a: For a p subshell l = 1, so \(m_{l}\) = −1, 0, +1, giving 3 orbitals (2l+1). Each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin (\(m_{s}\) = ±½) as no two electrons share all four quantum numbers, so p holds 6. The L shell has 2s (1 orbital, 2 electrons) and 2p (6 electrons), total 8 = 2n².
s: Pauli: max 2 electrons per orbital with opposite spin, so 6

units.name: 3.5 Electron configurations and stability
units.ov: This material covers how electrons occupy discrete energy states (shells K, L, M, N and sub-levels s, p, d) according to the filling order and the Pauli limit of two electrons per orbital. It links the resulting configurations to valence electrons and to stability: a full outer shell, as in the noble gases, gives stability, while an incomplete outer shell makes an element reactive and determines its bonding. Some of the source notes contain errors, which are flagged below so they are not memorised.
must: Filling order (Aufbau): \(1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,4p,5s,4d,5p\ldots\). Note that \(4s\) fills before \(3d\); the notes' list stops at 4p and omits where 3d goes.
Capacity rules: at most 2 electrons per orbital with opposite spins; s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10; shell \(n\) holds \(2n^2\) (K 2, L 8, M 18).
Always check that the superscripts sum to the atomic number \(Z\). For example, Fe (\(Z=26\)) is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^6\).

Krypton (\(Z=36\)) is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^6\). The p15 tip says 3d¹⁰ is filled before 4s², which contradicts the filling order. Fill 4s first; when writing by shell, 3d is listed before 4s.
Stability means a full valence shell (noble gases: He \(1s^2\), Ne, Ar, Kr). It does not depend on the number of electrons: Na (\(Z=11\), \(\ldots 3s^1\)) is not stable.
Valence electrons are those in the outermost (highest-\(n\)) shell, and they control bonding and chemical and electrical behaviour. Elements with 1 valence electron (H, Li, Na) are highly reactive.
Shell labels: K (\(n=1\)), L (\(n=2\)), M (\(n=3\)), N (\(n=4\)). Each contains sub-levels up to \(s,p,d\) (and \(f\) for \(n\ge4\)).
Electrons occupy the lowest available energy state first. 4s lies lower in energy than 3d even though 4s has the higher \(n\). The notes' wording that 3d has the 'higher principal number' is wrong.

Fe valence: by the strict outermost-shell definition only \(4s^2\) are valence electrons. The 3d⁶ electrons are also involved in bonding, which is why transition metals show variable valence. The notes' '4s² 3d⁶' conflicts with their own definition.
conn: Configuration to valence electrons to reactivity: write the configuration, identify the outer shell, then judge whether the shell is full (stable) or incomplete (reactive, bond-forming).

Filling order to transition metals: 4s filling before 3d explains the Fe configuration, the variable valence of transition metals, and why a configuration is written in shell order (3d before 4s) but filled in energy order.

Electron configuration to bonding type to material properties: valence electron count leads to ionic, covalent or metallic bonding, which affects electrical conductivity, strength and stiffness in engineering materials.
Shell capacities (\(2n^2\)) to the total electron count check: use \(Z\) to validate any configuration.
exq: Write the full electron configuration of Fe (\(Z=26\)) and Kr (\(Z=36\)), stating the filling order and checking each sums to \(Z\). Explain why 4s is filled before 3d.
Explain why Ne and Ar are stable while Na (\(Z=11\)) and Li (\(Z=3\)) are reactive. State the valence configuration of each.
Define valence electrons. Identify the shell and number of valence electrons in Fe, and discuss whether the 3d electrons should count as valence.
State the maximum number of electrons in the K, L, M and N shells and in each of the s, p and d sub-levels. Show that shell \(n\) holds \(2n^2\) electrons for \(n=1\)–3.
Predict the electron configuration and number of valence electrons of an element with \(Z=20\) (Ca) and \(Z=29\) (Cu), and comment on how they would behave chemically.

notes.t: Electron configurations and stability of elements
pts: Most elements do not have stable electron configurations because their valence (outer) shell is not completely filled.
Noble gases such as helium, neon, argon and krypton have completely filled outer shells and are stable.
Filling of orbitals follows the sequence 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s, 4p, so the outer shell is filled in stages.
Hydrogen (1s¹) and lithium (1s² 2s¹) have a single electron in their outermost shell, making them reactive.
defs: Valence shell
The outermost electron shell of an atom, whose electrons determine its chemical bonding behaviour.
tips: Do not confuse the subshell filling order: 4s fills before 3d, so krypton's configuration includes 3d¹⁰ before 4s² and 4p⁶.
Stability refers to a full outer (valence) shell, not simply to having many electrons; sodium with 11 electrons is not stable.
rq: Why is helium (1s²) considered stable while hydrogen (1s¹) is not?
Helium's 1s shell is completely filled with two electrons, which is the full capacity of the first shell, whereas hydrogen has only one electron, leaving its shell incomplete.
What do neon, argon and krypton have in common in their electron configurations?
Each has a completely filled outermost shell (e.g. 2s²2p⁶ for neon, 3s²3p⁶ for argon, 4s²4p⁶ for krypton), which gives them stability.

notes.t: Electron energy states and electron configuration (Fe example)
pts: Electrons occupy discrete energy states grouped into shells (K, L, M, N for n = 1 to 4), with sub-levels s, p, d within each shell.
Electrons fill the lowest available energy states first, with at most two electrons per orbital of opposite spin.
For Fe (atomic number 26) the configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶, so 26 electrons in total.
The valence electrons are those in the outermost shell (here 4s² 3d⁶), which control bonding and chemical behaviour.
The 4s sub-level is filled before 3d even though 3d has a higher principal number, because 4s has lower energy in the sequence shown.
defs: Valence electrons
Electrons in the outermost (highest-n) shell of an atom; they participate in chemical bonding and determine the atom's chemical and electrical behaviour.
K-shell (n = 1)
The innermost electron shell, containing the 1s sub-level holding up to two electrons.
L-shell (n = 2)
The second shell, containing the 2s and 2p sub-levels (up to 8 electrons).
M-shell (n = 3)
The third shell, containing 3s, 3p and 3d sub-levels (up to 18 electrons).
N-shell (n = 4)
The fourth shell, containing 4s, 4p and 4d sub-levels among others.
tips: Count total electrons from the atomic number and check the configuration sums to that number; 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²3d⁶ gives 26.
Do not assume the highest-n sub-level is always filled last; 4s fills before 3d, so writing 3d⁶4s² incorrectly for the order of filling loses marks.
rq: Why does Fe's configuration end in 4s² 3d⁶ rather than 3d⁸, even though the 3d orbitals are in the M-shell?
The 4s sub-level is lower in energy than 3d in the filling order, so electrons fill 4s before 3d; the outer 4s² electrons are therefore counted as valence electrons.
If an atom had 26 electrons but its outer configuration were 4s² 3d⁶ with the 3d orbitals half-filled, how would the number of unpaired electrons change?
Unpaired electrons in 3d depend on Hund's rule: 3d⁶ has 4 unpaired electrons, which is why iron is ferromagnetic-capable; the count changes with the number of 3d electrons.

xq.q: Which of the following ground-state configurations belongs to an atom with a completely filled valence shell, and is therefore chemically stable?
xq.a: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶
o: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵
1s² 2s² 2p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
xq.w: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (neon) has a full n = 2 outer shell; the trap is to treat any atom with many electrons or a filled s sub-level, like Na (11 electrons) or Ca, as stable.
s: Stability needs a completely filled outermost shell
Only 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ has a full outer shell (2s² 2p⁶); the others have 3s¹, 3p⁵ or 4s² as outer electrons

xq.q: Iron (atomic number 26) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶. How many electrons does an Fe atom have in the M shell (n = 3)?
xq.w: The M shell holds 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ = 14 electrons; the traps are to count only 3s and 3p (8), to quote the M-shell capacity (18), or to include the 4s² electrons (16).
s: M shell (n = 3) contains the 3s, 3p and 3d sub-levels
Count 2 + 6 + 6 = 14; the 4s² electrons belong to the N shell

xq.q: Write out the ground-state configuration of krypton (atomic number 36) in the order in which the sub-levels are filled. Explain why krypton is chemically stable, and why sodium (11 electrons) is not.
xq.a: Kr: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶. The electron count is 2+2+6+2+6+2+10+6 = 36. Here 4s fills before 3d because it has lower energy. Kr has a completely filled outer shell (4s² 4p⁶), so it is stable and unreactive like the other noble gases. Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ and has a single electron in its outer shell, so it is reactive. Stability depends on a full valence shell, not on the number of electrons.
s: Correct filling order with 4s² before 3d¹⁰ (1 mark)
Kr has a full outer shell 4s² 4p⁶, so it is stable (1 mark)
Na has one 3s¹ valence electron, so its outer shell is not full (1 mark)
Stability is a full valence shell, not a large number of electrons (1 mark)

units.name: 3.6 Types of bonds: primary overview
units.ov: This material classifies interatomic bonds into primary (strong) bonds (ionic, covalent, metallic) and secondary (weaker) bonds (van der Waals, hydrogen). The key ideas are the classification itself and the relative strengths: secondary bonds are weaker than primary bonds, and hydrogen bonds are stronger than van der Waals forces but still secondary. These categories underpin later explanations of material properties and behaviour.
must: Primary (strong) bonds are of three types: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Secondary (weaker) bonds are of two types: van der Waals and hydrogen bonds.
Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals bonds are secondary; they are NOT covalent or ionic, so do not confuse them with primary bonds.
'Strong' and 'weaker' are relative terms; the primary/secondary split is a classification of bond type, not just a measure of strength.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than van der Waals forces yet are still classed as secondary bonds.
Total count: 5 bond types (3 primary + 2 secondary).

Give the general strength ordering: primary bonds > hydrogen bonds > van der Waals forces (the notes only state that hydrogen bonds exceed van der Waals forces, and that both are weaker than primary bonds).
conn: Bond type (primary vs secondary) links to material properties such as strength and melting behaviour: stronger bonding generally means a stiffer, higher-melting material.

Classification of materials (metals, ceramics, polymers) links to their dominant bond types: metallic for metals, ionic/covalent for ceramics, covalent within polymer chains with secondary bonds between them.
The 'relative strength' idea links hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces: a question may ask why a hydrogen bond is secondary despite being stronger than van der Waals.
exq: List the three types of primary bond and the two types of secondary bond.
Explain why hydrogen bonds are classed as secondary bonds even though they are stronger than van der Waals bonds.
A student states that van der Waals forces are a type of covalent bond. Identify and correct the error.
Rank hydrogen, van der Waals and primary bonds in order of relative strength and comment on the meaning of 'strong' and 'weaker' in this classification.

notes.t: Types of bonds
pts: Primary (strong) bonds come in three types: ionic, covalent and metallic.
Secondary (weaker) bonds come in two types: van der Waals and hydrogen bonds.
tips: Do not confuse secondary bonds with primary bonds: van der Waals and hydrogen bonds are secondary, not covalent or ionic.
Remember 'strong' and 'weaker' are relative terms; hydrogen bonds are classed as secondary even though they are stronger than van der Waals forces.
rq: Why are primary bonds described as 'strong' while secondary bonds are 'weaker', and what physical property would you expect this difference to affect?

Primary bonds involve transfer or sharing of electrons between atoms (large bond energies), whereas secondary bonds are weak electrostatic/dipole attractions between molecules. The difference mainly affects melting point, boiling point, stiffness and strength; e.g. polymers held by van der Waals forces soften at much lower temperatures than ionic or metallic solids.
Which bond type would you expect to hold together water molecules in ice, and why does this matter for ice being less dense than liquid water?
Hydrogen bonds. They are directional and form an open hexagonal lattice in ice, which occupies more volume than the more tightly packed liquid.

units.name: 3.7 Ionic bonding and energy curves
units.ov: This material covers ionic bonding: electron transfer from metal to non-metal gives oppositely charged ions held together by Coulomb attraction. It builds the Coulomb force and potential energy, adds a short-range repulsive term to give the net energy curve with a minimum at the equilibrium separation r₀, and applies this to ceramics such as NaCl, MgO, CaF₂ and CsCl. The key chain is electron configuration → ion charge → Coulomb attraction → repulsion → energy minimum → bond energy and stability.
must: Ion formation: a metal loses valence electrons and a non-metal gains them. Charge comes from electrons only, e.g. Na (1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹) → Na⁺ and Cl (…3s²3p⁵) → Cl⁻, both with full outer shells.
Coulomb force: \( F = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \), which falls as \(1/r^2\).

Potential energy from force: \( U=\int_r^\infty F\,dr = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} \), which falls as \(1/r\), more slowly than the force. For oppositely charged ions the attractive term is negative: \( -\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} \).
Net pair energy: \( U(r)=U_i-\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}+\frac{B}{r^n} \), with an attractive Coulomb term, a repulsive term and a constant offset \(U_i\).
Repulsion \(B/r^n\) is short-range and very steep (n ~ 6–12, typically ~12) because electron clouds overlap. B and n are material-specific.

The net curve has a minimum at the equilibrium separation \(r_0\), where attraction and repulsion balance (net force zero, \(dU/dr=0\)) and the bond is most stable. Attraction dominates at large r, repulsion at small r.
Bond (dissociation) energy is the depth of the well: the energy needed to separate the ions to infinity. Keep the reference zero (separated ions at infinity) clear.
Ionic bonds are non-directional, with no fixed bond angles. They are strong electrostatic bonds between ions of opposite charge.
Ionic bonding dominates in ceramics and arises from a large electronegativity difference (Na 1.0 / Cl 2.9; Cs 0.9 / Cl 2.9). Compounds must be charge balanced, e.g. CaF₂ has 2 F per Ca.
Use SI units throughout: q in C, r in m, \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\) F/m. Do not mix nm or eV without converting.
conn: Force vs energy: U is the integral of F (1/r² → 1/r), and F = −dU/dr. Setting dU/dr = 0 gives r₀, so the equilibrium separation comes from the energy minimum.
Electron configuration → ion charge → q in Coulomb's law: the valence electrons transferred (Na⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺, O²⁻) set the magnitude of q and hence the bond strength.
Electronegativity difference → ionic character → ceramics: bonding type determines material behaviour, and charge balance sets the stoichiometry (CaF₂).
Energy curve → bond energy and stability: well depth and r₀ link to the strength of the bond, with the reference zero at infinite separation.
exq: Explain, using electron configurations, how NaCl forms from Na (1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹) and Cl (1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵). State the ions formed and why the bond is non-directional.
Calculate the Coulomb force and the potential energy between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ at r = 0.28 nm (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m). Comment on the units and the sign.
Sketch the net potential energy curve U(r) for an ion pair, showing the attractive term, the repulsive term, r₀ and the bond energy. Explain what happens at r < r₀ and r > r₀.
Given U(r) = −q²/(4πε₀r) + B/rⁿ, derive an expression for B in terms of r₀ and n by setting dU/dr = 0. Then find the energy at r₀.
Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed between Ca and F, and explain using electronegativity and charge balance why CaF₂ and CsCl are ionic.

notes.t: Ionic bonds
pts: An ion is an atom that has acquired charge by losing or gaining electrons.
Ionic bonding involves both positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Sodium (Na) has 11 electrons with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹, so it can lose its single outer 3s electron easily.
Chlorine (Cl) has 17 electrons with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵, so it needs one more electron to complete its outer shell.
In NaCl, one electron transfers from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
defs: Ion
An atom that has acquired a net electrical charge by losing (becoming positive) or gaining (becoming negative) electrons.
tips: Ions carry charge from electron transfer only; protons and neutrons do not change, so do not count neutrons when determining ion charge.
Make sure to write Na⁺ and Cl⁻ with the charge superscript, and balance electron transfer (one electron lost equals one gained).
rq: Why does sodium lose an electron rather than gain seven to fill its shell?
Losing its single 3s electron requires far less energy than gaining seven electrons, and leaves a stable, full inner shell (neon-like configuration).
Why is NaCl described as an ionic compound rather than a covalent one?
Electrons are fully transferred from Na to Cl, forming oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction, not shared between atoms.

notes.t: Ionic bonds
pts: In ionic bonding, a valence electron transfers from the metal atom (Na) to the non-metal atom (Cl), forming oppositely charged ions that attract each other.
Na (+11 nucleus) loses one outer electron to Cl (+17 nucleus), which gains it, producing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ with full outer shells.
The ions are held together by electrostatic (Coulomb) attraction; the bond strength depends on the interatomic distance r between the ion centres.
defs: Ionic bond
A bond formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, created when electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
Interatomic distance (r)
The separation between the centres of two neighbouring atoms or ions, which determines the strength of the bonding force.
tips: Do not confuse the nuclear charge (+11, +17) with the ion charge; the ion charge is determined by the electrons gained or lost (Na⁺, Cl⁻).
Ionic bonds are non-directional, so do not describe them as having fixed bond angles like covalent bonds.
rq: Why does sodium lose its outer electron rather than gain seven electrons to complete its shell?
Losing one electron is energetically far easier, leaving a stable full inner shell; Na has only one valence electron, so removing it costs much less energy than adding seven.
What would happen to the attractive force between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ if the interatomic distance r doubled?
Electrostatic attraction falls off with distance (roughly as 1/r²), so the force would drop to about one quarter of its original value.

notes.t: Ionic bonds: Coulomb's law and potential energy
pts: The force between two charged particles follows Coulomb's law: it grows with the product of charges and falls off with the square of their separation.
The force depends on the charge on each particle, the permittivity of vacuum, and the separation between them.
Potential energy and force are linked mathematically: potential energy is the integral of force with respect to separation, giving an energy that falls off as 1/r.
Potential energy is sometimes written as E in other texts, such as Callister 10e, so students should recognise the symbol change.
defs: Coulomb's law
The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
eqs: Coulomb force between two charged particles
F = electrostatic force (N); q = charge on each particle (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of vacuum (F/m); r = separation between particles (m)
Potential energy of two charged particles from force
U = potential energy (J); F = force (N); r = separation (m); q = charge (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of vacuum (F/m)
tips: Watch the unit of permittivity: \(\varepsilon_{0}\) must be in F/m, and r must be in metres, not nanometres or angstroms, when substituting.
Do not confuse force (1/\(r^{2}\)) with potential energy (1/r); the energy falls off more slowly than the force.
rq: Why does the potential energy curve approach zero as r tends to infinity, and what does this choice of reference imply?
The integral is taken from r to infinity, so energy is defined as zero when particles are infinitely far apart (no interaction); the bonded state therefore has negative energy.
What happens to the force and potential energy if the separation doubles?
The force falls to one quarter (1/\(r^{2}\)), while potential energy halves (1/r).

notes.t: Ionic bonds: attraction, repulsion and optimal separation
pts: When ions approach each other, electrostatic attraction lowers the potential energy, but if they get too close, repulsion rises sharply, so the energy has a minimum at an optimal separation.
The potential energy curve is the sum of an attractive Coulomb term (negative) and a repulsive term that grows steeply at short range; the balance point defines the equilibrium bond distance.
\(U_{i}\) is the initial energy needed to create the ions, which is a constant offset in the energy expression.
The constants B and n depend on the specific ionic system; the repulsive exponent n is typically around 12, so repulsion falls off very rapidly with distance.
defs: Ionic bond
A bond formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, produced when electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
Optimal (equilibrium) distance
The interatomic separation at which the attractive and repulsive contributions to the potential energy balance, giving the minimum potential energy.
eqs: Potential energy of an ionic pair as a function of separation r

U(r) = potential energy of the ion pair (J); \(U_{i}\) = initial energy to create the ions (J); q = ionic charge (C); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of free space (F \(m^{-1}\)); r = interionic separation (m); B = material-specific repulsion constant (J \(m^{n}\)); n = repulsion exponent (dimensionless, typically ~12)
tips: The attractive Coulomb term carries a minus sign in U(r); forgetting it reverses the physical meaning of the curve.
Keep q in coulombs and r in metres with ε_0 in SI units; mixing in nm or eV without conversion gives wrong energies.
rq: Why does the energy curve need both an attractive and a repulsive term rather than attraction alone?
Attraction alone would let ions collapse to zero separation with energy going to minus infinity; the short-range repulsive term stops this and creates a minimum at a finite equilibrium distance.
What would happen to the equilibrium separation if the repulsive exponent n were made larger?
The repulsive term would fall off more steeply with r, so the repulsion would act over a shorter range and the equilibrium separation would tend to be slightly smaller.

notes.t: Ionic bonds: Lennard-Jones potential energy curve
pts: The net energy of an ionic bond is the sum of an attractive electrostatic term and a short-range repulsive term; the net curve has a minimum at the stable inter-ion distance.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions makes the energy fall (more negative) as the ions approach, so it dominates at large separations.
At very small separations the repulsion curve rises steeply because electron clouds overlap, so the bond becomes unstable if ions are pushed closer than r₀.
The bond energy \(U_{i}\) is the energy needed to separate the ions into separate ions, measured from the energy of the bonded state at the minimum.
The most stable bond occurs at the equilibrium inter-ion distance r₀, where the net energy is at its minimum.
defs: Inter-ion distance r₀
The equilibrium separation between the centres of two bonded ions, at which the net potential energy of the ionic bond is at its minimum (most stable).
Bond dissociation energy \(U_{i}\)
The energy required to separate a bonded pair of ions into separate, neutral-free ions at infinite distance, measured from the minimum of the net energy curve.
eqs: Electrostatic (Coulomb) attraction energy between two ions
U = potential energy (J); q = ion charge magnitude (C); \(\epsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of free space (F/m); r = inter-ion distance (m)
U = repulsive potential energy (J); B = constant (J·mⁿ); r = inter-ion distance (m); n = repulsion exponent (dimensionless, typically 6–12)
tips: Watch the sign convention: the attractive Coulomb energy is negative, so U decreases (becomes more negative) as r decreases.
Do not confuse \(U_{i}\) (energy to separate ions) with the energy at r₀; keep track of the reference zero (separated atoms/ions) when quoting bond energies.
rq: Why does the net energy curve have a minimum rather than continuing to fall as the ions get closer?
Because the attractive Coulomb term falls off as −1/r while the repulsive B/rⁿ term (with n large) rises much more steeply at short range; at r₀ the two balance, giving the minimum energy.
What would happen to r₀ if the ion charges q were doubled, and why?
The attraction would increase by a factor of 4 (q²), pulling ions closer; the equilibrium distance r₀ would decrease until balanced by repulsion.

notes.t: Examples: Ionic Bonding in Ceramics
pts: Ionic bonding is the predominant bonding type in ceramics.
Ionic bonds form between elements that give up electrons (left side, low electronegativity) and elements that acquire electrons (right side, high electronegativity).

Electronegativity increases from left to right across the periodic table, and the electronegativity difference between the two bonding partners drives ionic character; e.g. Na (1.0) with Cl (2.9) gives NaCl, and Cs (0.9) with Cl (2.9) gives CsCl.
Example compounds shown: NaCl, MgO, CaF₂ and CsCl, each pairing a metal from the left with a non-metal from the right.
defs: Ionic bonding

Bonding formed by the complete transfer of valence electrons from a metal (electron donor) to a non-metal (electron acceptor), creating oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of electron transfer: metals (left) give up electrons and non-metals (right) acquire them.
Ionic compounds need charge balance, so CaF₂ requires two F atoms per Ca, not one.
rq: Why does Mg form MgO with oxygen rather than a compound with a different stoichiometry?
Mg (group IIA) gives up two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and O (group VIA) acquires two electrons to become O²⁻, so charges balance 1:1.
What would happen to the ionic character of a bond if the electronegativity difference between the partners were reduced?
Ionic character decreases and the bond becomes more covalent, since electrons are shared more equally.

xq.q: In an NaCl ion pair the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions each carry a charge of magnitude q = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C and their centres are separated by r = 0.282 nm. Treat the ions as point charges, with ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m. Calculate the magnitude of the Coulomb attractive force between them in newtons.
s: Convert r = 0.282×10⁻⁹ m, so r² = 7.95×10⁻²⁰ m²

xq.q: The separation r between a Na⁺ and a Cl⁻ ion is doubled. What happens to the magnitude of the Coulomb force F and to the magnitude of the electrostatic potential energy U between them?
xq.a: F falls to a quarter and U halves
o: F halves and U halves
F halves and U falls to a quarter
F falls to a quarter and U falls to a quarter
F falls to a quarter and U halves
xq.w: F varies as 1/r² and U as 1/r, so doubling r divides F by 4 and U by 2; the trap is to apply the same power of r to both.
s: F = q²/(4πε₀r²) ∝ 1/r², so F becomes F/4
U = q²/(4πε₀r) ∝ 1/r, so U becomes U/2

xq.q: Sketch the net potential energy against interatomic separation r curve for an ionic pair such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻, showing the attractive and repulsive contributions. Explain why the net curve has a minimum and what that minimum represents.
xq.a: The sketch shows three curves against r. The attractive Coulomb term is negative and rises towards zero as 1/r. The repulsive term is positive and increases very steeply at small r (B/rⁿ with n about 12). The net curve is their sum: it is zero at large r, falls to a minimum and then rises sharply. At large r attraction dominates, so bringing the ions closer lowers the energy. At small r the steep repulsion dominates and raises the energy. The minimum is at the equilibrium (optimal) separation r₀, the stable ionic bond length, where attraction and repulsion balance. Its depth gives the bond energy.
s: Sketch with labelled axes, a negative attractive curve and a positive repulsive curve (2 marks)
Net curve is the sum, with a minimum (1 mark)
Attraction dominates at large r and steep repulsion (n about 12) at small r (1 mark)
Minimum is the equilibrium bond distance, where forces balance (1 mark)

units.name: 3.8 Covalent bonding, hybridisation and carbon structures
units.ov: This material covers covalent bonding as electron sharing, described by an interatomic potential energy curve with an attractive and a repulsive term. It then explains how carbon's orbital hybridisation (sp³ and sp²) sets bond geometry in methane, diamond, graphite and graphene. The central idea is that bond strength and directionality determine structure, and structure determines properties such as hardness, stiffness, melting point and lubricity.
must: A covalent bond forms when atoms share valence electrons to attain full outer shells; it is typically strong and directional, unlike ionic or metallic bonds
Bond potential energy: \( U = -\frac{A}{r^{m}} + \frac{B}{r^{n}} \) with \( m<n \); the attractive term is negative and the repulsive term is positive
Equilibrium bond length is at the minimum of the net U–r curve (most negative U), not where the attractive term is zero; \( U\to 0 \) at large r (isolated atoms)
Repulsion (exponent n) dominates at small r and rises steeply, while attraction (exponent m) dominates at larger r; A and B are found empirically
sp³ hybridisation: promote one 2s electron to 2p, then mix one s and three p orbitals to give four equivalent orbitals directed tetrahedrally at 109.5°
sp² hybridisation: one s and two p orbitals give three trigonal-planar orbitals at 120°, leaving one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane for π bonding
Number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed; promotion costs energy, but bond formation releases more
Methane CH₄: C has 4 valence electrons and H has 1, so there are four equivalent C–H σ bonds (4 bonding pairs, 8 shared electrons) in a tetrahedral molecule
Diamond: a 3D network of sp³ bonds, each C bonded to 4 neighbours, gives very high hardness, stiffness and melting point
Graphite/graphene: sp² in-plane σ bonds form a strong hexagonal sheet, and weak van der Waals forces between layers let them slide easily
conn: The potential energy curve links to material properties: a deep, narrow minimum means high bond energy, so high stiffness and high melting point, as in diamond
Hybridisation determines geometry (sp³ at 109.5°, sp² at 120°), and geometry determines network dimensionality (3D diamond vs layered graphite) and hence hardness vs lubricity
Electronegativity difference decides covalent vs ionic character, which links bond type to directionality and to the properties of the resulting solid
Strong in-plane covalent bonding combined with weak interlayer van der Waals bonding gives strongly anisotropic properties in graphite
exq: Sketch the net potential energy vs separation curve for a covalent bond, showing the attractive and repulsive terms, and label the equilibrium separation and bond energy. Explain the sign of each term and why m < n.
Describe step by step how carbon's ground-state configuration (1s² 2s² 2p²) leads to four sp³ hybrid orbitals. State the bond angle and explain why promotion is energetically worthwhile.
Explain the bonding in methane in terms of sp³ hybrid overlap with H 1s orbitals. How many bonding pairs and shared electrons are there, and why is the bonding covalent rather than ionic?
Compare diamond and graphite in terms of hybridisation, bond angle, and bonding between atoms or layers. Explain why diamond is extremely hard while graphite is soft and a dry lubricant.
Given \( U = -A/r^{m} + B/r^{n} \), find the equilibrium separation \( r_0 \) by setting \( dU/dr = 0 \), and show that the bond energy at \( r_0 \) is negative.

notes.t: Covalent Bonding
pts: In covalent bonding, two atoms combine by sharing valence electrons so each can achieve a full outer shell.
Each hydrogen atom has one valence electron but needs one more, so the pair shares electrons to form H₂.
The shared electron pair is attracted to both nuclei, holding the two atoms together.
The bond energy vs. separation is described by an attractive term and a repulsive term; equilibrium occurs at the energy minimum.
defs: Covalent bond
A chemical bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons so that each attains a stable electron configuration.
Valence electron
An electron in the outermost shell of an atom that participates in chemical bonding.
eqs: Potential energy of a covalent bond as a function of atomic separation r
U = potential energy (J); r = interatomic separation (m); A = empirical attractive constant (J·\(m^{m}\)); B = empirical repulsive constant (J·\(m^{n}\)); m, n = exponents with m < n
tips: The constants A and B are specific to each covalent system and must be found empirically, not calculated from first principles.
Remember the condition m < n; reversing the exponents gives the wrong shape of the potential energy curve.
rq: Why must the exponent m be smaller than n in the bond energy equation?

The attractive term must decay more slowly with distance than the repulsive term, so attraction dominates at larger separations and repulsion dominates at very short separations, producing an energy minimum at equilibrium.
Why does hydrogen form H₂ rather than remaining as single atoms?
Each H atom has one electron and needs one more to fill its 1s shell; sharing an electron pair with another H atom lowers the system's total energy.

notes.t: Covalent bonds: potential energy versus atomic separation
pts: Net potential energy is the sum of an attractive electron-overlap term and a repulsive term; the minimum of the net curve marks the stable equilibrium separation.
The repulsion curve rises steeply at small separations because the atomic cores repel one another, with U = B/rⁿ.
At large separations both terms vanish and the energy approaches zero, corresponding to isolated atoms.
The stable region is where the net energy is at its lowest (most negative) value, i.e. the bond length.
defs: Stable bond separation
The interatomic distance at which the net potential energy is minimum; the atoms sit at this separation in equilibrium.
Electron overlap attraction
The attractive contribution to the potential energy arising from shared electron density between neighbouring atoms, varying as −A/rᵐ.
Repulsion curve
The positive (repulsive) potential energy term due to overlap of atomic cores/electron shells, varying as B/rⁿ.
eqs: Net interatomic potential energy of a covalent bond
U = potential energy (J); r = atomic separation (m); A, B = material/bond constants (J·mᵐ, J·mⁿ); m, n = exponents with m < n (dimensionless)
tips: Remember that the stable separation corresponds to the minimum of the net curve, not the point where the attractive curve is zero.
Keep the sign convention clear: the attractive term is negative and the repulsive term is positive.
rq: Why must the attractive exponent m be smaller than the repulsive exponent n?

Because the attraction must dominate at larger separations and decay more slowly, while repulsion must dominate at very small separations by falling off more steeply; with m < n the net curve gives a single energy minimum.
What happens to the net energy if the atoms are pushed closer than the equilibrium separation?
The repulsive term grows faster than the attractive term, so U rises sharply, resisting further compression.

notes.t: Bond Hybridization (sp³ orbitals in carbon)
pts: Carbon's ground state has 2 unpaired electrons, but it needs 4 bonding orbitals; one 2s electron is promoted into the empty 2p orbital.
The one 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, each holding one electron.
The four sp³ hybrids point towards the corners of a regular tetrahedron, giving the bond angle between them.
Because the four hybrid orbitals are identical, carbon forms four equivalent bonds (as in methane).
defs: Hybridization
The mixing of atomic orbitals of similar energy on the same atom to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals suited to bonding.
sp³ hybrid orbital
One of four equivalent orbitals formed from one s and three p orbitals, directed tetrahedrally at 109.5° to each other.
tips: Do not confuse the 2s→2p promotion (which happens within the atom, costing energy) with bond formation (which releases energy).
Hybrid orbitals number equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: one s plus three p gives four sp³ orbitals, not three.
rq: Why must an electron be promoted from 2s to 2p before carbon can bond with four atoms?
Ground-state carbon has only two unpaired electrons (in 2p); promotion creates four singly occupied orbitals, allowing four bonds. The energy cost is recovered by forming four bonds.
What would the bond angle be if carbon used unhybridized p orbitals (90°) instead?
The angle would be 90° between mutually perpendicular p orbitals; sp³ hybridization instead gives the tetrahedral 109.5°, which minimises electron-pair repulsion.

notes.t: Covalent bonding in carbon: sp³ hybridisation in methane (CH₄)
pts: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to fill its outer shell, so it forms four covalent bonds.
Hydrogen has 1 valence electron and needs 1 more, so each H forms one covalent bond with carbon.
Electronegativities of C and H are comparable, so electrons are shared rather than transferred, giving covalent bonds.
In CH₄ the carbon sp³ hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron, each overlapping with an H 1s orbital.
defs: Covalent bond
A bond formed when atoms share valence electrons, typically because their electronegativities are comparable.
sp³ hybridisation
Mixing of one s and three p atomic orbitals on carbon to form four equivalent hybrid orbitals directed tetrahedrally.
Valence electrons
Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom that take part in chemical bonding.
tips: Do not confuse valence electron count with the number of bonds: carbon needs 4 more electrons, so it forms 4 bonds, not 8.
Covalent sharing applies only when electronegativities are comparable; large differences indicate ionic character.
rq: Why does carbon form exactly four bonds in methane rather than two or three?
Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its outer shell, so it shares electrons with four H atoms, each contributing one electron.
What would change if electronegativities of the two atoms differed greatly?
Electrons would be transferred rather than shared, producing an ionic bond instead of a covalent bond.

notes.t: Covalent bonding in methane (CH₄)
pts: In covalent bonding, atoms share electrons rather than transferring them, so each shared pair holds the atoms together.
Carbon has four valence electrons, each shared with one hydrogen atom, so each hydrogen completes its outer shell with two electrons.
Methane forms four equivalent C–H covalent bonds, giving a stable molecule with carbon at the centre and hydrogens at the corners of a tetrahedron.
defs: Covalent bond
A chemical bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that each atom attains a stable outer electron configuration.
tips: Do not confuse covalent bonding (sharing electrons) with ionic bonding (transfer of electrons); methane is a molecule held together by shared pairs, not ions.
Count valence electrons correctly: carbon has 4 and hydrogen has 1, so CH₄ has 8 shared electrons in total (4 bonding pairs).
rq: Why does each hydrogen atom in methane share exactly one electron with carbon?
Hydrogen has one valence electron and needs two to fill its 1s shell, so sharing one electron with carbon (a shared pair) completes it.
How many covalent bonds can carbon form, and what determines this number?
Four, because carbon has four valence electrons in its outer shell and needs four more to reach an octet.

notes.t: Linear combination of atomic orbitals and the covalent bond
