pts: A covalent bond can be modelled as a linear combination (summation) of atomic orbitals.
Mixing one s orbital with three p orbitals (2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z) gives four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals.
The sp³ hybrids point to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving the basic tetrahedral unit of diamond.
defs: Linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO)
A method of describing a molecular or covalent bonding orbital as a weighted sum of atomic orbitals on the bonded atoms.
sp³ hybrid
A set of four equivalent orbitals formed by combining one s and three p atomic orbitals, directed tetrahedrally (109.5°).
tips: Do not confuse hybridisation (mixing orbitals within one atom) with bonding (overlap between atoms); hybrids are the orbitals that overlap to form bonds.
An sp³ hybrid set always contains four orbitals, so counting must total one s plus three p.
rq: Why does combining one s and three p orbitals produce a tetrahedral arrangement rather than the original s and p directions?
The four hybrids are equivalent mixtures of s and p character that spread their lobes as far apart as possible, which places them at the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5° between bonds).
What would happen to the geometry if only s and \(p_{x}\) orbitals were mixed?
Only two sp hybrids would form, lying along a line (180°), and the remaining \(p_{y}\) and \(p_{z}\) orbitals would be unhybridised, so the tetrahedral diamond structure would not result.

notes.t: sp³ covalent bonds in diamond
pts: Each carbon atom in diamond forms four sp³ hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron.
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four neighbouring carbon atoms, producing a continuous three-dimensional network.
The strong, directional sp³ covalent bonds explain diamond's very high hardness and high melting point.
defs: sp³ hybridisation
Mixing of one s orbital and three p orbitals of an atom to form four equivalent orbitals directed tetrahedrally (≈109.5° apart), used to form four σ covalent bonds.
tips: Do not confuse diamond's tetrahedral sp³ network (bond angle ≈109.5°) with the planar sp² bonding of graphite (≈120°).
Diamond's hardness comes from covalent bonding throughout the whole network, not from van der Waals or metallic bonding.
rq: Why does the tetrahedral arrangement of sp³ bonds make diamond so hard?
Each carbon is strongly and directionally bonded to four neighbours in a rigid 3D network, so breaking the structure requires breaking many strong covalent bonds.
What would change if carbon atoms formed only sp² bonds instead?
Atoms would be planar with bond angles of about 120°, giving layered structures (as in graphite) that are softer and conduct electricity along the layers.

notes.t: sp² Covalent Bonds in Graphite & Graphene
pts: In sp² hybridisation, one s and two p orbitals mix to form three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals lying in a plane at 120° to each other.
The unhybridised p orbital lies perpendicular to the plane of the sp² orbitals and is available for π bonding.
Each carbon in graphene forms three strong in-plane σ covalent bonds, giving a hexagonal honeycomb sheet.
Weak van der Waals forces hold the stacked graphene layers together in graphite, which is why layers slide apart easily (e.g. the pencil-tape demonstration).
defs: sp² hybridisation
Mixing of one s and two p atomic orbitals to form three equivalent trigonal planar hybrid orbitals separated by 120°, leaving one unhybridised p orbital per atom.
tips: Do not confuse sp² (three hybrids, 120°) with sp³ (four hybrids, 109.5°) when describing carbon bonding.
Remember that the inter-layer bonding in graphite is weak van der Waals, not covalent, so it does not explain the strength within a layer.
rq: Why does the sp² geometry give hexagonal rather than square or linear sheets?
The 120° bond angles between sp² orbitals in a plane allow six carbon atoms to form a closed hexagonal ring with minimal strain.
Why is graphite soft and graphene-based layers easy to separate, even though the in-plane bonds are very strong?
Layers are held by weak van der Waals forces rather than covalent bonds, so little energy is needed to slide them apart.

notes.t: Covalent bonds summary
pts: Covalent bonds can be very strong, giving high bond energies.
Strong covalent bonding leads to stiff materials with high melting points, such as diamond.
Covalent bonds are generally sp³ hybridised, so they are directional (fixed bond angles in space).
defs: Covalent bond
A bond formed by the sharing of electron pairs between atoms, which is typically strong and directional.
sp³ hybridisation
Mixing of one s and three p atomic orbitals to form four equivalent hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron (bond angle about 109.5°).
tips: Do not confuse directional covalent bonding with the non-directional metallic or ionic bonding; covalent bonds have fixed angles.
Remember that high stiffness and high melting point are consequences of strong bonds, not separate properties.
rq: Why does the directionality of sp³ bonds make diamond so stiff and hard?
Each carbon bonds to four neighbours in fixed tetrahedral directions, forming a rigid three-dimensional network that resists bending and deformation of the bond angles.
Why would a material with strong covalent bonds have a high melting point?
A large amount of thermal energy is needed to break many strong bonds, so the material only melts at high temperature.

xq.q: A simple model of a covalent bond gives the potential energy U = −A/r + B/r², where r is the interatomic separation in m, A = 2.0×10⁻²⁸ J·m and B = 1.6×10⁻³⁸ J·m². Calculate the net potential energy U at r = 0.20 nm, and state whether the net energy is attractive or repulsive at this separation.
xq.a: U = −6.0×10⁻¹⁹ J (net attractive, since U is negative)

xq.q: In forming sp³ hybrid orbitals in carbon, one 2s orbital is mixed with three 2p orbitals. How many hybrid orbitals result and what is the angle between them?
xq.a: 4 orbitals at 109.5°
o: 3 orbitals at 120°
4 orbitals at 109.5°
3 orbitals at 109.5°
4 orbitals at 90°
xq.w: The number of hybrids equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed (1 + 3 = 4), and they point to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°; the traps are counting only the p orbitals or using the 90° angle between unhybridised p orbitals.
s: One s plus three p orbitals gives four equivalent sp³ hybrids
The four hybrids point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart

xq.q: Explain how sp³ hybridisation allows carbon to form four equivalent covalent bonds in methane (CH₄). Refer to the ground-state electron configuration of carbon and the energy changes involved.
xq.a: Ground-state carbon (1s² 2s² 2p²) has only two unpaired electrons, but it needs four bonds to fill its outer shell. One 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2p orbital, which costs energy. The 2s and three 2p orbitals then mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, each holding one electron. These point to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°. Each overlaps with a hydrogen 1s orbital, and the two atoms share the electron pair. C and H have comparable electronegativities, so the electrons are shared rather than transferred and the bonds are covalent. Bond formation releases energy, which more than compensates for the promotion energy. All four C–H bonds are equivalent because the hybrids are identical.
s: Ground state has only 2 unpaired electrons, but 4 bonds are needed (1 mark)
One s and three p orbitals mix to give four equivalent sp³ orbitals (1 mark)
Each sp³ overlaps with an H 1s orbital and the electron pair is shared, giving covalent bonds (1 mark)

units.name: 3.9 Metallic bonds
units.ov: This module covers metallic bonding: valence electrons detach from atoms and form a delocalised 'sea' around positive ion cores, and the electrostatic attraction between the two holds the solid together. Because the electrons are shared by the whole solid and the bonding is non-directional, this one model explains the characteristic properties of metals: ductility and high electrical and thermal conductivity.
must: Metallic bond: electrostatic attraction between positive metal ion cores and a sea of delocalised electrons
Delocalised electrons are weakly bound outer (valence) electrons that leave their atoms and move freely, shared by all atoms in the solid
Metallic bonding occurs in metals and alloys, and only to some extent in semiconductors (not in all solids)
Bonding electrons are not localised between specific pairs of atoms, so the bond is non-directional
Non-directional bonding lets atoms slide past one another, which gives metals their ductility and malleability
Mobile delocalised electrons give high electrical conductivity and high thermal (heat) conductivity
Structure: ion cores (positive nuclei plus inner electrons) sit immersed in the negative electron sea, which holds the structure together
Common error: describing metallic bonds as electron sharing between specific atom pairs (that is covalent bonding)
conn: Delocalisation links bonding to properties: free electrons explain electrical and heat conductivity, and non-directionality explains ductility

Contrast with covalent bonding (localised, directional electron pairs, which resists sliding) and ionic bonding (fixed electrons transferred between ions), to explain why metals deform plastically rather than fracture in a brittle way
Metallic bonding in alloys and semiconductors: partial metallic character connects bonding type to conductivity behaviour and to material selection in mechanical design
exq: Describe the metallic bonding model, defining delocalised electrons and the role of the ion cores, and use a labelled sketch to illustrate it.
Explain, in terms of bonding, why metals are good electrical and thermal conductors but a covalently bonded ceramic is not.
Why can metals be bent or drawn into wire without shattering, whereas ionic or covalent solids tend to be brittle? Refer to directionality of the bond.

A student says 'metallic bonds are electrons shared between neighbouring atom pairs.' Identify and correct the error, and state in which other class of material metallic bonding occurs to some extent.
Compare metallic, ionic and covalent bonding in a table covering electron behaviour, directionality, conductivity and ductility.

notes.t: Metallic bonds
pts: Metallic bonding occurs in metals and metal alloys, and to some extent in semiconductors.
Outer electrons are weakly bound to their atoms, leave the nuclei and wander through the solid; these electrons are delocalised.
The metal ion cores (positive nuclei) sit immersed in a sea of negative delocalised electrons, which holds the structure together.
Because the bonding electrons are not localised between specific atoms, metallic bonds have no directionality, allowing atoms to slide past one another.
The mobile delocalised electrons give metals high electrical and heat conductivity.
defs: Delocalised electrons
Outer (valence) electrons that are only weakly bound to individual atoms and move freely throughout the solid, shared by all the atoms rather than belonging to any one of them.
Metallic bond
The bonding in metals arising from the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ion cores and a sea of delocalised electrons.
tips: Do not describe metallic bonds as involving electrons shared between specific pairs of atoms; the electrons are delocalised across the whole solid.
Remember that metallic bonding also occurs only to some extent in semiconductors, not in all solids.
rq: Why does the non-directional nature of metallic bonding make metals ductile?

Because the electron sea surrounds the ions equally in all directions, layers of atoms can slide over one another without breaking discrete bonds, so the structure deforms plastically rather than fracturing.
Why are metals good conductors of electricity and heat, while the same delocalisation explains both?

Delocalised electrons are free to move through the solid, carrying electric charge and transferring thermal energy between atoms, so both conduction processes are enabled by the same mobile electrons.

xq.q: A copper wire is bent repeatedly without fracturing. Which statement best explains this in terms of its bonding?
xq.a: The bonding electrons are delocalised, so the bond has no directionality and ion cores can slide past each other while the electron sea keeps them bonded.
o: Electrons are shared between specific pairs of neighbouring atoms, and these bonds re-form after each bend.
The bonding electrons are delocalised, so the bond has no directionality and ion cores can slide past each other while the electron sea keeps them bonded.
Copper ions of opposite charge attract each other, and bending only rotates these ion pairs.
Weak dipole–dipole attractions between neutral copper atoms break and re-form easily.
xq.w: Metallic bonds are non-directional because the electrons are delocalised across the whole solid; the traps are describing metallic bonding as pair-wise sharing (covalent) or as a secondary bond.
s: Delocalised electron sea surrounds the ion cores
No directionality, so atoms can slide without breaking the bonding

xq.q: Which of the following correctly describes the structure and properties of a metallic solid such as aluminium?
xq.a: Positive ion cores in a sea of delocalised electrons; the mobile electrons give high electrical and thermal conductivity.
o: Positive ion cores in a sea of delocalised electrons; the mobile electrons give high electrical and thermal conductivity.
Neutral atoms held by temporary induced dipoles; conductivity arises from the vibrating dipoles.
Atoms sharing electrons in fixed directions between pairs; conductivity arises because the shared pairs are free to move.
Positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attraction; electrical conductivity arises from the fixed anions.
xq.w: The conduction comes from mobile delocalised electrons around positive cores; the other options describe van der Waals, covalent and ionic bonding.
s: Identify metallic bonding as ion cores plus electron sea

xq.q: Explain, in terms of metallic bonding, why metals are good conductors of electricity and heat and why metals can be deformed by atoms sliding past one another. Explain also why describing the metallic bond as electrons shared between specific pairs of atoms is incorrect.
xq.a: Outer electrons are weakly bound and leave their atoms, becoming delocalised and wandering freely through the solid, while the positive ion cores sit in this negative electron sea, which holds the structure together by electrostatic attraction. The mobile electrons carry charge and energy through the solid, giving high electrical and thermal conductivity. Because the electrons are not localised between particular atoms, the bond has no directionality, so atoms can slide past each other without bonds being broken, and the electron sea continues to bond the ions. The pair-sharing description is wrong because the electrons belong to the whole solid, not to a specific pair; pair sharing is covalent bonding.
s: Valence electrons delocalised; ion cores in electron sea (1)
Mobile electrons give electrical and thermal conduction (1)
Non-directional bonding allows atoms to slide (1)
Electron sea maintains bonding during sliding (1)
Electrons are shared across the whole solid, not between specific pairs (1)

units.name: 3.10 Secondary bonds: van der Waals and hydrogen bonds
units.ov: This material covers secondary (van der Waals) bonding, in which weak, non-directional attraction arises between neutral atoms or molecules through temporary, induced or permanent dipoles. Hydrogen bonding is a stronger special case, in which an exposed positive hydrogen nucleus attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule. Together these bonds explain macroscopic behaviour such as gecko adhesion, the open structure of ice and the high boiling point of water.
must: Secondary bonds arise from dipole–dipole attraction between electrically neutral atoms or molecules; they are weak and non-directional, unlike primary (ionic, covalent, metallic) bonds.
Mechanism of the van der Waals bond: vibration makes the electron distribution fluctuate, so a temporary dipole forms even though the time-averaged distribution is symmetric.
A temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring symmetric atom, and the two dipoles attract. The attraction relies on time-varying, not time-averaged, asymmetry.
Definitions: a dipole is a separation of positive and negative charge (charge separation plus direction). An induced dipole is created by the field of a nearby dipole.

Hydrogen bond: the hydrogen electron is shared, leaving a bare positive nucleus that attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule. It is a secondary bond, far weaker than primary bonds, and must not be called covalent.
Ice has an open hexagonal crystal structure set by hydrogen bonding, so it is less dense than water and floats. Water expands on cooling below 4ºC.
Hydrogen bonding gives water a relatively high boiling point of 100ºC = 373 K. Convert to kelvin with \(T(\text{K}) = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273\) in calculations.
Real-world example: the gecko sticks to surfaces by van der Waals forces, which are individually weak but add up over very many contacts.

Bond-strength hierarchy: primary bonds (ionic, covalent, metallic) are much stronger than hydrogen bonds, which are in turn stronger than ordinary van der Waals bonds. Be able to justify this ordering.
conn: Bond type and properties: weak, non-directional van der Waals bonding, or hydrogen bonding, leads to low melting and boiling points and soft solids, whereas primary bonds give high-strength, high-melting-point materials.
Hydrogen bonding, crystal structure and density: the open hexagonal arrangement in ice links bonding to packing, so density is lower than in the liquid and ice floats.

Dipole mechanism and adhesion: temporary dipole, induced dipole and attraction explain the gecko effect. Many weak bonds sum to a large total force, linking atomic bonding to engineering surface adhesion.
Hydrogen bonding, boiling point and unit conversion: the high boiling point of water (373 K) is attributed to hydrogen bonds, and exam calculations need the correct temperature units.
exq: Explain, with sketches, how a temporary dipole arises in a neutral atom and how it induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom to form a van der Waals bond. Why is the bond weak and non-directional?
Define a dipole and an induced dipole. Why do neutral atoms with a symmetric time-averaged electron distribution still attract each other?
Describe the hydrogen bond in water. Use it to explain (a) the open hexagonal structure of ice, (b) why ice floats, and (c) the relatively high boiling point of 100ºC (373 K).
Compare secondary bonds with primary bonds in terms of strength, directionality and mechanism. Why is a hydrogen bond not classed as covalent?
Explain how a gecko can adhere to a smooth wall using secondary bonding, and say why the individual bonds are weak yet the overall adhesion is strong.

notes.t: van der Waals secondary bonds
pts: Secondary bonds arise from dipole–dipole attraction between electrically neutral atoms or molecules.
Atoms are never still; constant vibrational motion makes the electron distribution fluctuate in time.
Although the time-averaged electron position is symmetrical, instantaneous asymmetry creates a temporary dipole.
A temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring symmetric atom, so the two attract, forming a van der Waals bond.
The bond is weak and non-directional; it explains the gecko's ability to stick to surfaces.
defs: van der Waals (secondary) bond
A weak, non-directional bond between atoms or molecules caused by attraction between temporary or induced dipoles arising from fluctuating electron distributions.
Dipole
A separation of positive and negative charge within an atom or molecule, characterised by its charge separation and direction.
Induced dipole
A dipole created in an electrically symmetric atom or molecule by the electric field of a nearby dipole.
tips: Van der Waals bonds are weak and non-directional; do not confuse them with primary (ionic, covalent, metallic) bonds.
Do not assume neutral atoms have no attraction: the mechanism relies on time-varying, not time-averaged, electron asymmetry.
rq: Why does an electrically neutral argon atom attract another argon atom even though its average charge distribution is symmetrical?

Because electron motion makes the instantaneous charge distribution asymmetric, creating a fluctuating dipole that induces a dipole in the neighbour, giving attraction. Time-averaging hides this transient asymmetry.
What would happen to van der Waals bond strength if atoms vibrated less (e.g. at very low temperature)?

Fluctuations would be reduced, weakening induced dipoles; the attraction is sensitive to the dipole fluctuations, so bonding would generally weaken, though quantum fluctuations persist at absolute zero.

notes.t: Hydrogen bonds as secondary bonds
pts: In hydrogen-containing molecules the hydrogen electron is shared, leaving a bare hydrogen nucleus that is positive.
The exposed positive hydrogen nucleus attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule, forming a hydrogen bond.
Hydrogen bonds determine the open hexagonal crystal structure of ice.
Ice is less dense than water, so it floats; water expands below 4ºC.
Hydrogen bonding gives water a relatively high boiling point of 100ºC (373K).
defs: Hydrogen bond

A secondary (van der Waals-type) bond in which a hydrogen atom, bonded to an electronegative atom, is attracted to the negative end of a neighbouring molecule, arising from a shared hydrogen electron that leaves a bare positive nucleus.
tips: Hydrogen bonds are secondary (weak) bonds, far weaker than primary ionic/covalent/metallic bonds; do not describe them as covalent.
Remember that the boiling point of 100ºC equals 373K; convert units correctly when used in calculations.
rq: Why does ice float on water even though both are the same substance?
Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open hexagonal lattice in ice, which occupies more volume, so ice is less dense than liquid water.
Why is water's boiling point unusually high for such a small molecule?
Hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken as well as covalent bonds, requiring extra energy, so boiling occurs at a higher temperature (100ºC).

xq.q: Two neutral, spherically symmetric argon atoms attract each other weakly. What is the origin of this attraction?
xq.a: Instantaneous electron asymmetry gives a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in the neighbouring atom, and the two dipoles attract.
o: The time-averaged electron cloud of each atom is asymmetric, giving permanent dipoles that attract.
Instantaneous electron asymmetry gives a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in the neighbouring atom, and the two dipoles attract.
Argon atoms share a pair of electrons, forming a directional covalent bond.
Argon atoms transfer an electron, forming oppositely charged ions that attract.
xq.w: Time-averaged symmetry does not mean zero attraction, because fluctuations create temporary and induced dipoles; the traps are permanent dipoles and primary bonding.
s: Vibration makes the electron distribution fluctuate
Temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighbour, giving attraction

xq.q: Ice floats on liquid water, and water has a boiling point of 100 °C. Which statement correctly explains these observations and gives the boiling point in kelvin?
xq.a: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal structure that is less dense than water, and also raise the boiling point to 373 K.
o: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal structure that is less dense than water, and also raise the boiling point to 373 K.
Hydrogen bonds are strong covalent bonds that pack ice more densely than water; the boiling point is 373 K.
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal structure that is less dense than water; the boiling point is 173 K.
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal structure that is less dense than water; the boiling point is 273 K.
xq.w: The open hexagonal hydrogen-bonded structure makes ice less dense, and 100 + 273 = 373 K; the traps are calling hydrogen bonds covalent and mis-converting the temperature.
s: Open hexagonal ice structure is less dense so it floats

xq.q: Describe how a hydrogen bond forms between two water molecules and explain two consequences of hydrogen bonding in water. State how hydrogen bonds compare in strength with primary bonds.
xq.a: In a water molecule the hydrogen electron is shared, which leaves the hydrogen nucleus bare and positive. This exposed positive nucleus is attracted to the negative end of a neighbouring molecule, forming a hydrogen bond. It is a secondary bond, much weaker than ionic, covalent or metallic bonds, and should not be called covalent. Consequences: hydrogen bonding gives ice an open hexagonal crystal structure, so ice is less dense than water and floats; and it gives water a relatively high boiling point of 100 °C (373 K).
s: Shared hydrogen electron leaves a bare positive nucleus (1)
Nucleus attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule (1)
Secondary bond, far weaker than primary bonds (1)
Open hexagonal ice structure, so ice floats (1)

units.name: 3.11 Conclusions, further reading and Lecture 4 prep
units.ov: This short wrap-up closes the bonding lecture and previews Lecture 4. The main message is that bonding type (ionic, covalent, metallic, van der Waals) sets the band structure and so the basic physical properties of a solid. How the bands fill with electrons then determines electrical and optical behaviour, which Lecture 4 develops. The notes are thin: they contain a conclusion, a further-reading slide with no detail, and a pointer to PhET simulations. Any detail must therefore come from the main lecture content.
must: Bonding type determines the physical properties of solids (hardness, melting point, conductivity, brittleness or ductility).
Bonding sets the band structure, while band filling sets whether the material conducts. Both are needed to explain conductivity, and the two must not be confused.
Atomic energy levels broaden into bands when many atoms bond. Allowed bands are separated by forbidden gaps, and the number of states per band is tied to the number of atoms.
Conductor: the highest occupied band is partially filled, or a filled band overlaps an empty one, so there are free states just above the Fermi level.
Insulator and semiconductor: the valence band is full and the conduction band is empty, separated by a gap \(E_g\). Insulators have a large gap and semiconductors a small one (about 1 eV for Si).
Optical properties follow from the band gap: a photon is absorbed only if \(h\nu \ge E_g\), where \(\lambda = hc/E_g\) gives the cutoff wavelength.

Qualitative link between each bond type and its properties: metallic bonding gives delocalised electrons and high conductivity, ionic and covalent bonding give localised electrons and (usually) insulating or semiconducting behaviour, and van der Waals bonding is weak with a low melting point.
Lecture 4 preparation: the PhET simulations on band structure and conductivity should be used to see how bands fill.
conn: Bond type, then band structure, then band filling, then electrical and optical properties. This is the chain a full answer should follow.
Band gap links conductivity to optical absorption and transparency: a wide-gap insulator is transparent to visible light, while a metal absorbs or reflects it.
Bond strength and atomic spacing affect band width and gap size, which links mechanical and thermal properties to electronic ones.
Temperature affects band filling, since thermal excitation across a small gap gives semiconductors higher conductivity as temperature rises, unlike metals.
exq: Explain why bonding type alone cannot tell you whether a material conducts, and what extra information is needed. Give one example each of a conductor, a semiconductor and an insulator.
Silicon has \(E_g \approx 1.1\) eV. Calculate the longest wavelength of light it can absorb, using \(\lambda = hc/E_g\). Is it transparent to visible light? Is diamond (\(E_g \approx 5.5\) eV)?
Sketch band diagrams (valence band, conduction band, gap and filling) for a metal, a semiconductor and an insulator, and explain how each fills with electrons.
Compare ionic, covalent, metallic and van der Waals solids in terms of bonding, melting point, and electrical conductivity, linking each to its band picture.
Describe how electrons in a semiconductor are excited across the gap as temperature rises, and why this makes conductivity increase, unlike in a metal.

notes.t: Conclusions: types of bonding and preview of band filling
pts: The bonding types covered in this lecture fundamentally determine the physical properties of solids.
The next lecture extends the concept of bands to explain electrical and optical properties through how bands fill with electrons.
tips: Do not confuse bonding type (which sets the band structure) with band filling (which sets whether a material conducts); both are needed to explain conductivity.
rq: Why would the way electrons occupy bands, rather than the bonding type alone, govern electrical conductivity?
Conduction needs partially filled bands or a small gap to nearby empty states so electrons can gain energy and move; a full band with a large gap (insulator) cannot carry current.

units.name: 5.1 Bonding energy and dense packing
units.ov: This material explains why atoms bond and why they pack in ordered arrays. The net potential energy of an ion pair is an attractive term plus a repulsive term, and its minimum fixes the equilibrium separation (bond length) and the bond energy \(E_0\). Dense, ordered packing lets each atom sit near its energy minimum with many neighbours, so it has lower energy and is more stable than random packing.
must: Net energy: \(E_N = E_A + E_R = -\frac{A}{r} + \frac{B}{r^n}\), with attraction negative and repulsion positive
Equilibrium separation \(r_0\) is the minimum of \(E_N\), found from \(\frac{dE_N}{dr}=0\); it is not where the attractive and repulsive curves cross
Bond energy \(E_0 = E_N(r_0)\) is the depth of the well and is negative; more negative means a stronger bond
Bond length (the r value at the minimum) and bond energy (the E value there) are different quantities, so check which one is asked for
Repulsion is short-range and steep (large \(n\)), while attraction is longer-range; at large \(r\), \(E_N \to 0\) (unbonded)
Derivation: setting \(dE_N/dr=0\) gives \(r_0=\left(\frac{nB}{A}\right)^{1/(n-1)}\); substitute back to get \(E_0\) (re-derive and check this yourself)
Dense, ordered packing has lower energy and greater stability than non-dense, random packing
Units: \(A\) in J·m, \(B\) in J·mⁿ, \(n\) dimensionless, \(r\) in m, \(E\) in J (convert to eV where needed)
Lower energy means more stable; at \(r_0\) the attractive and repulsive forces balance, giving zero net force
conn: Energy minimum to bond length and strength: \(dE_N/dr=0\) gives \(r_0\), and substituting back gives \(E_0\), so one calculation answers both questions
Bond energy to packing: a deeper well per bond, multiplied over many close neighbours, gives lower total energy, which explains why crystals favour dense ordered packing
Force and energy: net force is \(F=-dE_N/dr\), so zero force at \(r_0\) links the energy curve to the equilibrium picture and to stiffness (curvature of the well)
Sign convention and curve sketching: a sign error in the attractive or repulsive term inverts the curve, which then gives a wrong minimum and wrong \(E_0\)
exq: Sketch \(E_A\), \(E_R\) and \(E_N\) against \(r\) for an ion pair. Label \(r_0\) and \(E_0\), and state why the minimum is not where \(E_A\) and \(E_R\) cross.
Given \(E_N=-\frac{A}{r}+\frac{B}{r^n}\), derive \(r_0\) in terms of \(A\), \(B\) and \(n\), then \(E_0\). Evaluate both for \(A=1.44\times10^{-28}\) J·m, \(B=\) a given value and \(n=9\).
Explain, using energy arguments, why dense ordered packing is more stable than random packing, and distinguish bond energy from bond length.
Two materials have energy wells of different depth and position. Which has the stronger bond and which the larger bond length? Justify from the curves.
Using \(F=-dE_N/dr\), show the net force is zero at \(r_0\) and describe the sign of the force for \(r<r_0\) and \(r>r_0\).

notes.t: Ionic Bonding: Energy Balance and Equilibrium Separation
pts: Bonding stability is set by the net potential energy between two ions, which is the sum of an attractive and a repulsive term.
The most stable state is the interatomic separation at which the net energy is at its minimum; the energy E₀ at this point is the bond energy.
Attractive energy is negative and grows in magnitude as ions approach, while repulsive energy is positive and rises steeply at very small separations.
At large separations the net energy tends to zero, so the ions are effectively unbonded.
defs: Net potential energy \(E_{N}\)
The sum of attractive and repulsive potential energies between two ions; its minimum with respect to separation defines the stable equilibrium bond.
Bond energy E₀
The depth of the minimum of the net energy curve, i.e. the energy released when the ions form a bond at equilibrium separation.
eqs: Net potential energy between two ions (attractive plus repulsive contributions)

\(E_N\) = net potential energy (J); \(E_A\) = attractive energy (J); \(E_R\) = repulsive energy (J); \(r\) = interatomic separation (m); \(A\) = attractive constant (J·m); \(B\) = repulsive constant (J·mⁿ); \(n\) = repulsion exponent (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the sign convention: the attractive term \(-A/r\) is negative and the repulsive term \(B/r^n\) is positive; mixing these up reverses the energy curve.
The minimum of the net energy curve gives the equilibrium separation, not the point where the attractive and repulsive curves cross.
rq: Why does the net energy curve have a minimum rather than simply decreasing to negative infinity as ions approach each other?

Because the repulsive term \(B/r^n\) grows rapidly at small \(r\) and eventually outweighs the attractive term \(-A/r\), so the sum turns upward; the balance creates the minimum at equilibrium separation.
What would happen to the equilibrium separation and bond energy if the repulsive exponent n were increased?

The repulsive term would become steeper at short range, so the equilibrium separation would shift to a slightly smaller r, and the well would tend to be sharper; the bond energy magnitude depends on A, B and n together.

notes.t: Energy and Packing
pts: Dense, ordered packed structures tend to have lower energies than non-dense, random packing.
The interatomic energy curve has a minimum at the typical neighbour bond length, where the bond energy is most stable.
The depth of the energy well (typical neighbour bond energy) is what makes a bonded structure stable; ordered packing gives a deeper, more favourable well.
defs: Dense, ordered packing
An arrangement of atoms in a regular, repeating pattern in which atoms sit close together, giving low total energy.
Non-dense, random packing
An arrangement of atoms with no long-range order and lower packing density, which corresponds to higher energy.
Typical neighbour bond length
The equilibrium separation between neighbouring atoms, at which the interatomic energy is at its minimum.
tips: Do not confuse the bond energy (the depth of the energy minimum, usually negative) with the bond length (the r value at that minimum); the question may ask for either.
Lower energy means more stable; a more negative energy at the minimum indicates a stronger bond.
rq: Why do dense, ordered structures have lower energy than random ones?
Ordered packing lets each atom sit at or near the equilibrium bond length with all its neighbours, so more of the energy well is exploited and total energy is lower.
What would happen to the energy minimum if neighbours were pushed closer than the typical bond length?
Energy rises steeply because of strong repulsion, so the structure would be unstable at that spacing.

xq.q: The net potential energy between two ions is \(E_N = -A/r + B/r^n\), where \(r\) is the separation (m), \(A = 2.3\times10^{-28}\) J·m, \(B = 2.875\times10^{-38}\) J·m² and the repulsion exponent is \(n = 2\). Find the equilibrium separation \(r_0\) from the condition \(dE_N/dr = 0\), and hence the bond energy \(E_0\), the value of \(E_N\) at \(r_0\).
For ions with \(E_N = -A/r + B/r^2\), \(A = 2.3\times10^{-28}\) J·m and \(B = 2.875\times10^{-38}\) J·m², what is the net potential energy at \(r = 0.50\) nm?
xq.w: Attractive term is −4.6×10⁻¹⁹ J and repulsive term is +1.15×10⁻¹⁹ J, so the sum is −3.45×10⁻¹⁹ J; the traps are omitting the repulsion or giving it the wrong sign.

xq.q: Sketch the attractive energy, repulsive energy and net potential energy curves against interatomic separation \(r\) for two ions. Mark the equilibrium separation and the bond energy \(E_0\), and explain why ordered, dense packing of atoms is more stable than random, non-dense packing.
xq.a: Sketch: the attractive curve is negative and grows in magnitude as r decreases; the repulsive curve is positive and rises steeply at small r; the net curve is their sum, tends to zero at large r, and has a single minimum. The r value at the minimum is the equilibrium separation (bond length), not where the two curves cross. The depth of the minimum, a negative energy, is the bond energy E₀. Ordered dense packing places atoms at the typical neighbour bond length so that each sits in the energy well, giving a lower, more negative total energy; non-dense random packing has higher energy. Lower energy means more stable.
s: Attractive negative, repulsive positive and steep at small r (1)
Net curve with a minimum, tending to zero at large r (1)
Equilibrium r at the minimum and E₀ as the well depth, labelled (1)
Ordered dense packing keeps neighbours at the bond length, giving lower total energy (1)
Lower energy means more stable, so a deeper well means a stronger bond (1)

units.name: 5.2 Crystalline vs amorphous solids
units.ov: This material classifies solids by atomic arrangement: crystalline (long-range periodic order, e.g. metals and ceramics), amorphous (only short-range order, e.g. glasses and polymers) and semicrystalline (a mixture of both, e.g. high modulus polymers). The key idea is that structure, not chemistry, determines the type: the same SiO₂ can be crystalline sand or amorphous silica gel/glass, depending on atomic arrangement and cooling or complexity. These structural differences underlie differences in properties such as melting behaviour and deformation.
must: Crystalline solid: atoms in a periodic, repeating 3D array with long-range order (typically metals and ceramics)
Amorphous solid: no long-range periodic order, though short-range order remains (typically glasses and polymers)
Semicrystalline solid: crystalline regions interspersed with amorphous regions (typically high modulus polymers); it is not the same as amorphous
Same composition can be crystalline or amorphous: SiO₂ is crystalline in silica sand and amorphous in silica gel/glass, so the difference is structural, not chemical
Noncrystalline structures form when the structure is complex or cooling is rapid, which stops atoms arranging periodically
Amorphous does not mean liquid or structureless: amorphous solids are rigid and keep local bonding and short-range order, such as a fixed number of neighbours
Soda glass: a continuous random Si–O network with Na⁺ ions sitting in the gaps
Polymers: long chains of repeating units with strong covalent intramolecular bonds along the backbone but weak secondary bonds between chains
Amorphous and polymer solids have no regular unit cell, so they lack sharp melting points and simple slip-based deformation like crystalline metals
Glasses are amorphous even though they are ceramic-based; do not classify them as crystalline ceramics
conn: Processing and structure: rapid cooling or structural complexity gives amorphous solids, while slow cooling allows periodic packing. This links to why the same SiO₂ gives sand or glass, and to semicrystalline polymers.

Structure and bonding to properties: the absence of a unit cell means no simple slip planes and no sharp melting point, and weak inter-chain bonding in polymers explains their different mechanical and thermal behaviour compared with metals.

Classification by material class: metals and ceramics are crystalline, polymers and glasses are amorphous, and high modulus polymers are semicrystalline. Exceptions such as glass (a ceramic that is amorphous) are commonly tested.
exq: Define crystalline, amorphous and semicrystalline solids and give a typical material class for each.
Silica sand and silica gel both have composition SiO₂. Explain why they are different types of solid and sketch the atomic arrangement of each.
Describe the structure of soda glass, including the role of sodium ions, and explain why it is classified as amorphous rather than crystalline.
Explain how bonding in a polymer differs along a chain and between chains, and why polymers lack a regular unit cell and a sharp melting point compared with a metal.
Under what conditions do noncrystalline solids form, and why does a semicrystalline polymer have different properties from a fully amorphous one?

notes.t: Types of solids
pts: Crystalline solids have atoms packed in an organised, repeating structure; typically metals and ceramics.
Amorphous solids have atoms packed together randomly, with no long-range order; typically polymers and glasses.
Semicrystalline solids contain both crystalline regions and amorphous regions; typically high modulus polymers.
defs: Crystalline solid
A solid in which atoms are arranged in an organised, periodically repeating structure (long-range order).
Amorphous solid
A solid in which atoms are packed together randomly, with no long-range order.
Semicrystalline solid
A solid containing regions that are crystalline interspersed with regions that are amorphous.
tips: Do not confuse semicrystalline with amorphous: semicrystalline materials contain ordered crystalline regions as well as amorphous ones.
Glasses are amorphous even though they look solid; do not classify them as crystalline ceramics just because they are ceramic-based.
rq: Why are metals and ceramics typically crystalline, while polymers and glasses are typically amorphous?

Metals and ceramics bond in ways that favour ordered, close packing as atoms solidify, whereas polymer chains and glass network structures tend to freeze in a disordered state, and their long molecules or rapid cooling hinder ordering.
What might a semicrystalline polymer's properties look like compared with a fully amorphous one?
The crystalline regions add stiffness and a higher modulus, so semicrystalline polymers are generally stiffer and stronger than fully amorphous polymers of the same type.

notes.t: Types of solids: crystalline vs noncrystalline
pts: Crystalline materials have atoms packed in periodic, 3D arrays, typical of metals, many ceramics and some polymers.
Noncrystalline materials have atoms with no periodic packing; they form for complex structures or rapid cooling.
Noncrystalline materials occur for complex structures and under rapid cooling, which stops atoms arranging periodically.
Crystalline and noncrystalline SiO₂ share the same Si and O atoms but differ in long-range order: the crystalline form is periodic, the noncrystalline (glass) form is random.
defs: Crystalline material
A solid whose atoms are packed in a periodic, repeating three-dimensional array.
Noncrystalline (amorphous) material
A solid in which atoms have no periodic, long-range packing; also called amorphous.
tips: Do not confuse 'noncrystalline' with 'no atoms bonded': noncrystalline solids are still solids with local bonding, lacking only long-range periodic order.
Crystalline and noncrystalline forms of the same compound (e.g. SiO₂) have identical chemistry; the difference is structural, not compositional.
rq: Why does rapid cooling tend to produce a noncrystalline solid rather than a crystalline one?
Rapid cooling gives atoms too little time to diffuse and settle into periodic positions, so they freeze in a disordered arrangement.
Both crystalline and noncrystalline SiO₂ contain the same atoms, so what distinguishes them?
Their atomic arrangement: crystalline SiO₂ has a repeating 3D order, while noncrystalline SiO₂ has a random network with no long-range periodicity.

notes.t: Types of solids: crystalline vs noncrystalline (amorphous) SiO₂
pts: Silica sand is crystalline SiO₂, with Si and O atoms arranged in a regular, repeating long-range pattern.
Silica gel is noncrystalline (amorphous) SiO₂: the same Si–O building blocks form a disordered network with no long-range repeating order.
Both forms have the same chemical composition (SiO₂); the difference lies in atomic arrangement, not chemistry.
Crystalline solids show ordered, periodic atomic packing, whereas amorphous solids lack this long-range order despite being solid.
defs: Crystalline solid
A solid in which atoms are arranged in a regular, periodic, long-range repeating pattern.
Noncrystalline (amorphous) solid
A solid whose atoms lack long-range periodic order, though short-range order may exist between neighbouring atoms.
tips: Do not assume that different materials are needed for crystalline and amorphous forms; the same chemical composition can give both, depending on atomic arrangement.
Amorphous does not mean liquid or 'no structure': amorphous solids still have short-range order between neighbouring atoms.
rq: Why can silica sand and silica gel both be made of SiO₂ yet behave as different materials?

Because the atomic arrangement differs: sand is crystalline with ordered repeating structure, while silica gel is amorphous with a disordered network, changing properties such as packing and water adsorption.
What would happen to the regular order if the crystalline SiO₂ were melted and rapidly cooled?
The atoms would be frozen in a disordered arrangement, forming a noncrystalline (amorphous) solid such as glass, since there is insufficient time for periodic ordering.

notes.t: Types of solids: amorphous and polymer structures
pts: Amorphous solids such as soda glass have no long-range periodic arrangement of atoms; the silicon-oxygen network is randomly connected with sodium ions sitting in gaps.
In soda glass the silicon and oxygen atoms form a continuous random network, with sodium atoms held within the open spaces of the network.
A polymer molecule is a long chain of repeating carbon and hydrogen atoms, bonded covalently along the backbone, which gives strong intramolecular bonding but weaker bonding between chains.
Unlike crystalline metals, amorphous and polymer solids lack a regular repeating unit cell, so they do not show sharp melting points or simple slip-based deformation in the same way.
defs: Amorphous solid
A solid whose atoms lack long-range periodic order, having only short-range order such as a fixed number of neighbours around each atom.
Polymer
A large molecule built from many repeating units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds, forming long chains.
tips: Do not confuse amorphous solids with crystalline solids: amorphous materials have no repeating unit cell, even though they are rigid.
Polymer chains are held together by strong covalent bonds along the chain but only weak secondary forces between chains; do not treat the whole polymer as a single strongly bonded network.
rq: Why can soda glass be solid yet still lack a crystal structure?
Its atoms are linked into a rigid, continuous three-dimensional network, so it is held together strongly, but the network has no repeating unit cell or long-range periodicity.
What would happen to the properties of soda glass if sodium oxide were removed from the network?
The network would be more tightly cross-linked, giving a higher melting/softening temperature and greater hardness, while sodium ions (which break Si–O–Si bonds) would no longer modify the structure.

xq.q: A sample of SiO₂ is cooled very rapidly from the melt and forms a glass. A second sample of SiO₂ of identical chemical composition is cooled slowly and forms quartz. Which statement correctly explains the difference between them?
xq.a: The glass has the same Si and O atoms but no long-range periodic order, because rapid cooling prevents the atoms arranging into a repeating array.
o: The glass contains a different ratio of Si to O atoms, because rapid cooling drives off oxygen.
The glass has the same Si and O atoms but no long-range periodic order, because rapid cooling prevents the atoms arranging into a repeating array.
The glass has no bonds between atoms, so it is not a true solid, while quartz is bonded.
The glass has no order at all, including between neighbouring atoms, whereas quartz has only short-range order.
xq.w: Crystalline and amorphous SiO₂ differ in structure, not composition, and the glass still has short-range order and bonding; rapid cooling stops long-range periodic arrangement.
s: Rapid cooling gives no time for periodic arrangement

xq.q: A polymer is found to contain ordered crystalline regions embedded within disordered regions, and it has a high modulus. How should it be classified?
xq.a: Semicrystalline
o: Amorphous, because the polymer chains are randomly tangled overall.
Crystalline, because it contains some regions of long-range order.
Semicrystalline
Noncrystalline, because polymers have no unit cell.
xq.w: It contains both crystalline and amorphous regions, which defines semicrystalline; calling it amorphous or crystalline ignores one of the two region types.
s: Ordered regions present, so not fully amorphous
Disordered regions present, so not fully crystalline

xq.q: Silica sand and silica gel are both SiO₂. Explain why they have different structures despite identical chemistry, and state what type of order remains in silica gel. Explain why soda glass, though rigid, is not classed as a crystalline ceramic.
xq.a: Silica sand is crystalline: Si and O atoms form a periodic, repeating long-range pattern. Silica gel has the same Si–O building blocks but joined in a disordered network with no long-range repeat. The difference is atomic arrangement, not composition. Silica gel still has short-range order (fixed number of neighbours around each atom). Soda glass is a randomly connected Si–O network with Na ions in the gaps and has no repeating unit cell, so it is amorphous even though rigid.
s: Sand: periodic long-range order; gel: disordered network
Soda glass has no repeating unit cell so it is amorphous despite being rigid

units.name: 5.3 Carbon polymorphs: fullerenes, nanotubes, graphene
units.ov: This module surveys the polymorphs of carbon: diamond, graphite, amorphous carbon black, fullerenes (C60), carbon nanotubes and graphene. All share the same chemistry, and their very different properties come from how the atoms are arranged and bonded. Graphene (a single hexagonal sheet) is the building block that links graphite (stacked sheets), nanotubes (rolled sheets) and fullerenes (curved, closed sheets with pentagons).
must: Polymorphs have the same chemical composition but different atomic arrangements, and structure (not chemistry) determines properties.
Diamond is cubic, with each C atom tetrahedrally bonded to four neighbours, so it is very hard.
Graphite is stacked hexagonal-ring layers with weak (van der Waals) bonding between layers, so the layers slide easily.
Graphene is a single one-atom-thick honeycomb layer of graphite; it was isolated by Geim and Novoselov (Manchester, Nobel Prize in Physics 2010).
Fullerenes (e.g. C60, 'bucky balls') are discrete closed hollow cages of pentagons and hexagons, like a football. They are molecular solids, not extended networks.
Carbon nanotubes are rolled graphene sheets capped by half-buckyball hemispheres. They can be single-walled (SWNT, one layer) or multiwalled (MWNT, concentric layers).
Carbon black is amorphous, with no long-range crystalline order despite being pure carbon.
Name origin: fullerenes honour R. Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes use the same design principle. Spell it 'fullerene'.
Do not confuse graphene (single sheet) with graphite (many stacked sheets), or nanotubes (rolled sheet) with graphite (stacked layers).
conn: Graphene is the parent structure: stacked gives graphite, rolled gives a nanotube, and curved with pentagons gives a fullerene.
Bonding and structure explain properties: tetrahedral 3D bonding makes diamond hard, while weak interlayer bonding makes graphite slippery and soft.
Crystalline versus amorphous: diamond and graphite have long-range order, whereas carbon black lacks it, so composition alone cannot predict properties.
Molecular versus extended solids: C60 is a discrete molecule, whereas diamond and graphite are extended networks, which affects how each is described and used.
exq: Define a polymorph and explain, using diamond and graphite, why two materials of identical composition can have very different hardness.
Describe the structure of C60, stating the types of faces in the cage and the origin of the name 'bucky ball'.
Distinguish between single-walled and multiwalled carbon nanotubes, and explain how a nanotube is related to graphene and to fullerenes.
Compare graphene and graphite in terms of structure, thickness and interlayer bonding, and state who isolated graphene and when they were recognised.
Explain why carbon black is described as amorphous and how its structure differs from that of diamond.

notes.t: Carbon polymorphs
pts: Carbon exists in several polymorphic forms, each with different atomic arrangements and therefore different properties.
Diamond has a cubic crystal structure in which each carbon atom is bonded tetrahedrally to four neighbours, making it very hard.
Graphite consists of stacked layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings, with weak bonding between layers, so the layers slide over each other.
Fullerenes (bucky balls) and nanotubes are closed-cage or extended carbon structures, while graphene is a single layer of graphite.
Carbon black is an amorphous form of carbon, lacking long-range crystalline order.
defs: Polymorph
A material that can exist in more than one crystal structure (or atomic arrangement) while having the same chemical composition.
Fullerene
A closed-cage molecule of carbon atoms, such as C60, arranged in pentagons and hexagons (bucky ball).
Amorphous carbon
A form of carbon with no long-range crystalline order, such as carbon black.
tips: Do not confuse polymorphs (same composition, different structure) with allotropes-only terms; state clearly that the structure, not the chemistry, determines the properties.
Remember that carbon black is amorphous, so it has no regular crystal structure despite being made of carbon.
rq: Why can graphite be used as a lubricant and pencil lead, while diamond cannot?
In graphite, layers are bonded weakly to each other (van der Waals forces), so they slide easily; in diamond, every atom is strongly covalently bonded in 3D, so no easy slip plane exists.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. What explains their very different hardness?
The difference lies in the atomic arrangement and bonding: diamond's rigid tetrahedral 3D covalent network versus graphite's layered structure with weak interlayer bonding.

notes.t: Carbon: Fullerenes (Bucky Balls)
pts: Fullerene C60 is a carbon allotrope whose molecules form closed hollow cages.
The C60 cage is built from a mixture of pentagonal (5-sided) and hexagonal (6-sided) faces, like a football.
The name 'Bucky Balls' honours Richard Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes share the same design principle.
defs: Fullerene
A molecular form of carbon (e.g. C60) consisting of closed, hollow cages of carbon atoms arranged in pentagonal and hexagonal rings.
tips: Do not confuse fullerenes (discrete molecules, C60) with graphite or diamond (extended networks); fullerenes are molecular solids.
Remember the spelling and the name origin: 'fullerene' after R. Buckminster Fuller, not 'fullerine' in exam answers.
rq: Why must a closed carbon cage contain exactly 12 pentagons regardless of its size?
Euler's polyhedron theorem for a closed sphere of trivalent carbon atoms requires 12 pentagonal faces (with any number of hexagons) to close the surface; C60 has 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
What would happen to the cage if pentagons were replaced entirely by hexagons?
The surface would be flat (like graphene) and could not close into a sphere, so no hollow cage would form.

notes.t: Carbon nanotubes
pts: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical structures with half-buckyball caps at each end joined by tubular walls.
Carbon nanotubes can exist as a single wall or as multiple concentric walls.
defs: Carbon nanotube
A nanoscale cylinder of rolled-up graphene sheets capped at each end by half-buckyball (fullerene-like) hemispheres.
Single-walled nanotube
A carbon nanotube consisting of one cylindrical layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
Multiwalled nanotube
A carbon nanotube made of several concentric cylindrical layers of carbon atoms.
tips: Do not confuse carbon nanotubes (tubes with fullerene-type caps) with simple graphite; the structure is a rolled graphene sheet, not stacked layers.
rq: Why does a nanotube need hemispherical caps at its ends rather than simply open ends?
Open ends leave dangling bonds that are unstable; half-buckyball caps close the structure so every carbon atom is bonded to three neighbours, lowering energy.
How would the properties of a multiwalled nanotube differ from a single-walled one of the same diameter?

Multiwalled tubes have more layers, interlayer van der Waals interactions and typically larger overall diameter, usually making them less uniform and with different electrical behaviour than a single-walled tube.

notes.t: Carbon: graphene
pts: Graphene is a two-dimensional sheet of carbon atoms, essentially a single layer of graphite.
Graphene was isolated and studied experimentally by Geim and Novoselov at Manchester, recognised with the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
defs: Graphene
A two-dimensional sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice, one atom thick, forming the basic layer of graphite.
tips: Do not confuse graphene (single sheet) with graphite (many stacked sheets bonded by weak van der Waals forces).
Graphene is a single layer; quoting its thickness as a bulk-material value is a common error.
rq: Why is graphene described as two-dimensional even though it is made of carbon atoms that have three-dimensional bonding in diamond?

In graphene each carbon bonds in-plane to three neighbours (sp² bonding) and is only one atom thick, so the sheet has no thickness in the third dimension; diamond's sp³ tetrahedral network is three-dimensional.
What would happen to graphene's properties if you stacked many sheets together?
Stacking sheets gives bulk graphite, where weak van der Waals forces between layers allow them to slide, making graphite soft and lubricating.

xq.q: Why does graphite act as a solid lubricant whereas diamond is extremely hard, given both are pure carbon?
xq.a: Graphite has strongly bonded hexagonal layers held together weakly, so layers slide; diamond has tetrahedral bonding to four neighbours in 3D.
o: Graphite contains a different element from diamond, which is softer.
Graphite is amorphous, whereas diamond is crystalline.
Graphite has strongly bonded hexagonal layers held together weakly, so layers slide; diamond has tetrahedral bonding to four neighbours in 3D.
Graphite has tetrahedral bonding and diamond has hexagonal layers with weak bonding between them.
xq.w: Both are polymorphs of carbon, so the difference is structure: weak interlayer bonding in graphite versus a 3D tetrahedral network in diamond.
s: Graphite layers weakly bonded so slide
Diamond tetrahedral covalent network is hard

xq.q: Which description of a single-walled carbon nanotube is correct?
xq.a: A rolled-up graphene sheet forming one cylindrical layer, capped by half-fullerene hemispheres.
o: Stacked graphite layers bonded by weak forces, curved into a tube.
A rolled-up graphene sheet forming one cylindrical layer, capped by half-fullerene hemispheres.
Several concentric cylinders of carbon atoms with no caps.
A hollow cage of 60 carbon atoms in pentagons and hexagons.
xq.w: A nanotube is rolled graphene with fullerene-type caps; confusing it with graphite, a multiwalled tube or C60 are the traps.

xq.q: Describe the structures of C60 fullerene, graphene and graphite, and explain how graphene relates to both graphite and carbon nanotubes.
xq.a: C60 is a discrete molecule, a closed hollow cage of carbon atoms in pentagonal and hexagonal rings like a football. Graphene is a single one-atom-thick sheet of carbon atoms in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice. Graphite is many graphene layers stacked and bonded weakly by van der Waals forces. A carbon nanotube is a graphene sheet rolled into a cylinder and capped with half-fullerene ends.
s: C60: closed cage of pentagons and hexagons, molecular
Graphite: stacked graphene with weak bonding
Nanotube: rolled graphene with fullerene caps

units.name: 5.4 Crystal structure basics and assumptions
units.ov: This material introduces crystal structure as the way atoms pack in space, modelled with hard spheres joined by spring-like bonds and arranged to minimise energy. It builds from 2-D close packing to the three common metallic structures (BCC, FCC, HCP), and frames perfect lattices as a reference from which real defects and their effects on properties are later understood.
must: Crystal structure = arrangement of atoms in space; microstructure = grains and phase distribution. Do not confuse them.
Hard-sphere model: atoms are rigid spheres of fixed size, and only the bonds (spring-like) deform, at an energy cost.
Packing is driven by minimising the energy of the bonded atoms, not simply by maximising density. State this reasoning explicitly.
Packing depends on bond type and relative atomic size; structure can change with temperature (allotropy/polymorphism).
In 2-D, hexagonal packing leaves less empty space than square packing; close-packed layers stack to build 3-D structures.
There are 14 Bravais lattices, but most metals use only BCC, FCC or HCP.
BCC: atoms at 8 corners plus 1 at the centre, giving \(2\) atoms per unit cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+1\)).
FCC: atoms at 8 corners plus 6 face centres, giving \(4\) atoms per cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+6\times\tfrac12\)).
HCP is hexagonal (not cubic) with ABAB layer stacking and is close packed; FCC is also close packed (ABCABC stacking).
Real crystals always contain defects; the perfect lattice is only a reference model, and defects explain real properties.
conn: Energy minimisation and bond type determine the packing, which determines the structure (BCC/FCC/HCP) and so properties such as density and packing efficiency.
2-D close packing leads to 3-D stacking sequences: ABAB gives HCP, while ABC stacking gives FCC.
Unit-cell atom counting links to density calculations: \(\rho = nA/(V_c N_A)\), together with atomic radius and cell edge length \(a\).
Perfect lattice versus defects: the ideal structure is the baseline, and deviations (defects) explain deviations in mechanical behaviour.
exq: Calculate the number of atoms per unit cell for BCC and FCC, showing the corner and face contributions, and state which is more densely packed.
Explain why atoms adopt ordered crystal structures, referring to the hard-sphere and spring-bond assumptions and to energy minimisation.
Compare square and hexagonal 2-D packing and describe how close-packed layers are stacked to give HCP and FCC structures.
Distinguish between crystal structure and microstructure, and explain why a real crystal differs from the ideal lattice and why this matters.
Describe the unit cells of BCC, FCC and HCP, and explain why HCP is not classed as a cubic structure even though it is close packed.

notes.t: Crystal structure
pts: Crystal structure describes how atoms in a crystal are packed together in space.
The packing arrangement is governed by the type of interatomic bonds present.
The relative sizes of the atoms strongly influence the resulting packing arrangement.
Real crystals may be perfect or contain distortions from the ideal lattice.
A material can change between different crystal structures as temperature changes.
tips: Do not confuse crystal structure (arrangement of atoms) with microstructure (grain size and phase distribution).
Remember that real crystals are often imperfect, so ideal lattice descriptions are approximations.
rq: Why would two metals with similar bonding but very different atomic radii adopt different crystal structures?
Atomic size ratio changes how atoms can pack; different radii allow or prevent close packing in a given geometry, so the structure changes.
What might happen to a crystal structure when it is heated, and why?
It may transform to a different structure (polymorphism/allotropy) because the stable arrangement depends on temperature, as thermal energy changes the balance of packing and bonding.

notes.t: Crystal structure: assumptions for atomic packing
pts: Atoms are modelled as hard, spherical particles with fixed size.
Atoms themselves cannot change shape; only the bonds between them can deform.
Bonds act like springs: they deform easily but deforming them costs energy.
Crystal structures form because atoms arrange themselves to minimise the energy needed to hold them together.
tips: Do not confuse the assumptions: atoms are rigid, but the bonds between them are the deformable part that costs energy.
Packing is driven by minimising energy, not by maximising density alone; state this reasoning explicitly in exam answers.
rq: Why does treating atoms as non-deformable spheres still allow realistic crystal structures to be predicted?

Because the rigid-sphere packing sets the geometry, while the deformable bonds let the structure relax slightly; the energy-minimising arrangement is the one that packs spheres most efficiently with the least bond strain.
What would happen to packing if bonds were infinitely stiff?
Atoms could not adjust their separation to lower energy, so the structure would be fixed by the initial geometry and energy minimisation would have little effect on arrangement.

notes.t: Crystal structure: perfect structures, defects and their effects
pts: Study crystal structure in a logical sequence: first the ideal (perfect) lattice, then deviations from it, then how those deviations affect properties.
Real crystals always contain imperfections (defects), so the perfect structure is a reference model rather than an everyday reality.
Defects in the crystal structure change material behaviour, so their effects must be understood, not just their existence.
tips: Do not treat the perfect crystal as realistic; real materials always contain defects, which are essential to explaining their properties.
Remember that this slide is only an outline: the defects and their effects are developed in the following slides.
rq: Why do engineers begin with the perfect crystal structure before studying defects?
The perfect lattice provides a reference model; deviations from it (defects) can then be described and their effects on properties understood systematically.
If a metal's crystal contains no defects at all, what would you expect its strength to be compared with a real metal, and why?
Ideal, defect-free crystals are far stronger than real metals in theory, because defects such as dislocations are what allow plastic deformation at low stresses.

notes.t: Crystal structure: stacking atoms to minimize empty space
pts: In 2-D, atoms packed in a hexagonal arrangement leave less empty space than a square arrangement.
Close-packed 2-D layers can be stacked on top of each other to build 3-D crystal structures.
tips: Do not confuse the 2-D packing comparison with the full 3-D crystal: this slide only shows layers, not the stacking sequence of the 3-D structure.
Remember that the square arrangement is less dense; avoid claiming it is the most efficient packing.
rq: Why does the hexagonal arrangement of atoms leave less empty space than the square arrangement?

Each circle in the hexagonal layer touches six neighbours, so the circles nest into the gaps between one another, whereas in the square layer each circle touches only four neighbours, leaving larger gaps between them.
Why is stacking close-packed 2-D layers the natural next step toward a 3-D crystal?
Because the layers that already minimise empty space in 2-D can be repeated vertically, so the packing efficiency is preserved in three dimensions.

notes.t: Crystal structure: common packing arrangements
pts: There are 14 possible (Bravais) lattice arrangements for packing atoms in crystals.
Despite 14 possibilities, most common metallic structures are two cubic and one hexagonal.
The three common structures are BCC, FCC and HCP.
defs: Body Centred Cubic (BCC)
A cubic crystal structure with atoms at the 8 corners of the unit cell plus one atom at the cube centre.
Face Centred Cubic (FCC)
A cubic crystal structure with atoms at the 8 corners plus one atom at the centre of each of the 6 faces.
Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP)
A hexagonal crystal structure in which atoms are closely packed in layers with ABAB stacking, giving the highest packing efficiency of the common structures.
tips: Do not confuse BCC (2 atoms per cell) with FCC (4 atoms per cell) when counting atoms.
HCP is a hexagonal structure, not a cubic one, even though it is close packed.
rq: Why are only three of the 14 possible packing arrangements commonly found in metals?

Metals bond non-directionally (metallic bonding), so atoms pack to maximise density and coordination; BCC, FCC and HCP give high packing efficiency and are energetically favourable, unlike the other lattices.
What would change if the BCC structure were replaced by simple cubic packing?
Simple cubic has only 1 atom per cell and a packing fraction of about 0.52 versus 0.68 for BCC, so it is less dense and rarely occurs in metals.

xq.q: A metal unit cell contains atoms at the 8 corners and one atom at the centre of each of the 6 faces. Each corner atom is shared among 8 cells and each face atom between 2 cells. Find the number of atoms per unit cell, then the total number of atoms in a crystal made of 2500 such cells.
xq.a: 4 atoms per cell; 10000 atoms in 2500 cells.

xq.q: A student says: 'Crystal structures form because atoms pack to achieve the maximum density.' What is the best correction?
xq.a: Structures form because atoms arrange to minimise the energy needed to hold them together; bonds act like springs and deforming them costs energy.
o: Atoms are soft and change shape to fill space, so density is maximised.
Structures form because atoms arrange to minimise the energy needed to hold them together; bonds act like springs and deforming them costs energy.
Structures form because square 2-D packing leaves least empty space.
Structures form randomly and do not depend on bonding or atom size.
xq.w: Packing is driven by energy minimisation with rigid atoms and deformable bonds, not density alone.

xq.q: Explain why a hexagonal arrangement of atoms in 2-D is preferred over a square arrangement, how such layers lead to 3-D structures, and name the three most common metallic crystal structures, stating how many atoms BCC and FCC cells contain.
xq.a: Hexagonal packing of hard spheres leaves less empty space than square packing, so it is denser and lower in energy. Close-packed layers can be stacked to build 3-D structures, such as HCP with ABAB stacking. The common metallic structures are BCC, FCC and HCP. BCC has 2 atoms per cell (8×1/8 + 1) and FCC has 4 (8×1/8 + 6×1/2).
s: Hexagonal leaves less empty space than square
Close-packed layers stack to form 3-D crystals

units.name: 5.5 Close-packed structures: FCC vs HCP stacking
units.ov: This material covers close-packed crystal structures, in which atoms are modelled as hard spheres packed as densely as possible in layers. FCC (ABCABC stacking) and HCP (ABAB stacking) are built from identical close-packed layers and differ only in stacking sequence. Both have the same packing fraction (0.74), and which one a metal adopts is energy-driven but not examinable here.
must: FCC = Face Centred Cubic and HCP = Hexagonal Close Packed; give the full names when defining them
FCC stacking is \(ABCABC\), repeating every third layer, so layer 3 sits in a different position from layer 1
HCP stacking is \(ABAB\), repeating every second layer, so layers alternate between two positions
Both are close packed with the same packing fraction \(0.74\); HCP is not denser than FCC
The two structures differ only in stacking sequence, not in the close-packed layers themselves; identify the sequence before naming the structure
Atoms are modelled as hard spheres touching their nearest neighbours; this is a packing model, not real atomic overlap or bonding geometry
Each new layer sits in one of two hollow positions on the layer below; it cannot sit in any position and still be close packed
FCC unit cell has atoms at each corner and at the centre of each face; FCC is close packed but BCC is not
Examples: FCC metals are Al, Cu, Ni; HCP metals are Mg, Zn, Ti
Structure selection is energy-driven; the detailed reasons are not covered in this course
conn: The two-hollow-position rule produces both stacking sequences: ABAB if the third layer returns to the first position, ABCABC if it takes the other hollow
Same close-packed layers imply the same packing fraction (0.74), so stacking sequence alone cannot change density
Stacking sequence links to structure name and then to material examples (ABC gives FCC gives Al, Cu, Ni; AB gives HCP gives Mg, Zn, Ti)
The hard-sphere model links packing fraction to why FCC and HCP are contrasted with the non-close-packed BCC
exq: Define a close-packed structure and state the full names of FCC and HCP. (3 marks)
Sketch the stacking sequences of FCC and HCP, labelling the layer positions A, B and C, and state after how many layers each repeats.
A student claims HCP is more densely packed than FCC. Explain with reference to packing fraction (0.74) and stacking why this is wrong.
Explain why a new close-packed layer cannot sit in an arbitrary position on the layer below, and how the two hollow sites lead to FCC or HCP.
Classify aluminium, magnesium, copper and titanium as FCC or HCP, and state the stacking sequence of each.

notes.t: Close packed structures
pts: Atoms are modelled as hard spheres when describing crystal packing.
Atoms are packed in layers as closely as geometrically possible to minimise empty space.
Each new close-packed layer sits in one of two possible hollow positions on the layer below, so stacking sequences such as ABAB or ABCABC arise.
defs: Close packed structure
A crystal arrangement in which spherical atoms are packed as closely as possible, with each layer nestling into the hollows of the layer beneath it.
tips: Atoms are treated as hard spheres touching their nearest neighbours; do not confuse this model with real atomic overlap or bonding geometry.
Do not state that a close-packed layer can sit in any position; only the two hollow positions give close packing.
rq: Why does each new layer have only two possible positions rather than any position?

Each close-packed layer's atoms sit in the hollows formed by three neighbours in the layer below; of the two sets of hollows available (B and C relative to A), a new layer must occupy one of them to achieve close packing, giving two choices.
What would happen to packing efficiency if the spheres were stacked in a simple square array directly on top of each other?
Packing would be less efficient because the spheres would not nest into hollows, leaving more empty space, so the structure would not be close packed.

notes.t: Close packed structures
pts: Close packed structures are the two crystal structures in which atoms pack together as densely as possible.
There are two types of close packed structure: FCC and HCP.
FCC stands for Face Centred Cubic, a cubic close packed arrangement.
HCP stands for Hexagonal Close Packed, a hexagonal close packed arrangement.
defs: Close packed structure
A crystal structure in which atoms are arranged to fill space as efficiently as possible, giving the maximum packing density for equal-sized spheres.
FCC (Face Centred Cubic)
A close packed cubic crystal structure with atoms at each corner and at the centre of each face of the unit cell.
HCP (Hexagonal Close Packed)
A close packed hexagonal crystal structure with an ABAB stacking sequence of close packed layers.
tips: Do not confuse FCC with BCC; FCC is close packed, BCC is not.
Give the full names (Face Centred Cubic, Hexagonal Close Packed) rather than only the abbreviations when asked to define them.
rq: Why are FCC and HCP both called close packed, even though their unit cells have different shapes?

Both place atoms in layers that pack as densely as possible, giving the same maximum packing fraction (about 74%); they differ only in the stacking sequence of those layers (ABCABC for FCC, ABAB for HCP).
What would you expect to change if the close packed layers were stacked in a different sequence?
The crystal structure would change, but the packing density would stay the same, since the close packed layers themselves are unchanged.

notes.t: FCC versus HCP crystal structures
pts: FCC and HCP are both close-packed structures built from stacked close-packed layers; they differ only in the stacking sequence of those layers.
In FCC, the layer stacking repeats in an ABCABC sequence, so the third layer sits in a different position from the first.
In HCP, the layer stacking repeats in an ABAB sequence, so the layers alternate between two positions.
The diagrams show close-packed layers of spheres sitting in the hollows of the layer below, with the layers shown as coloured rows of spheres.
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence with the crystal lattice: FCC and HCP both have the same close-packed layers, so identifying the stacking pattern (ABC versus AB) is what distinguishes them.
rq: Why do FCC and HCP have the same packing density even though their stacking sequences differ?

Both are close-packed arrangements: each layer of spheres sits in the hollows of the layer below, giving the maximum packing fraction of about 0.74, and the stacking variant does not change the local arrangement within each layer.

notes.t: FCC versus HCP stacking
pts: FCC and HCP are two close-packed structures that differ only in how successive layers of atoms are stacked.
FCC stacking repeats every third layer, giving the sequence ABCABC.
HCP stacking repeats every second layer, giving the sequence ABABAB.
Different metals adopt one stacking or the other depending on their atoms.
Common FCC metals include aluminium, copper and nickel; common HCP metals include magnesium, zinc and titanium.
tips: Do not confuse the stacking sequence with the crystal name: ABC gives FCC and AB gives HCP, so check the sequence before naming the structure.
FCC and HCP are both close-packed with the same packing fraction (0.74), so do not claim HCP is more densely packed than FCC.
rq: Why does the ABAB stacking give a hexagonal structure while ABCABC does not?
