notes.t: The 14 Bravais lattices
pts: There are 14 distinct crystal lattice types, grouped into 7 crystal systems by their lattice parameter relationships and angles.
The 14 lattices are also called Bravais lattices; each differs in cell edge lengths, angles, and where extra lattice points sit (simple, base/body/face centred).
Cubic lattices (simple, body-centred, face-centred) have all edges equal and all angles 90°.
Hexagonal lattice has a ≠ c with a 120° angle in the basal plane (only one hexagonal lattice type).
Triclinic is the lowest-symmetry system with α, β, γ all ≠ 90°, and a ≠ b ≠ c.
defs: Bravais lattice

One of the 14 distinct three-dimensional arrangements of lattice points that cannot be transformed into one another by symmetry-preserving operations; each describes a unique translational periodicity of a crystal.
Crystal lattice
An infinite periodic array of points in space, where each point has identical surroundings, used as the framework on which atoms or molecules are placed to form a crystal structure.
tips: Do not confuse the 7 crystal systems with the 14 lattices: the systems are groupings, and the 14 Bravais lattices are the distinct centring variants within them.
Check the angle conditions carefully: monoclinic requires only β (or α, γ) ≠ 90°, while triclinic needs all three angles different from 90°.
rq: Why does a body-centred cubic lattice have a different number of atoms per unit cell than a simple cubic lattice, even though both are cubic?
Simple cubic has 8 corner atoms each shared by 8 cells (1 atom per cell); body-centred adds a full atom at the cube centre, giving 2 atoms per cell.
What is the key difference between a monoclinic simple and a monoclinic centred lattice?
Monoclinic simple has lattice points only at the corners, while monoclinic centred adds extra lattice points at the centre of two opposite faces (a base-centred arrangement).

notes.t: 14 types of crystal lattices (Bravais lattices)
pts: There are 14 distinct ways to arrange lattice points in 3D, grouped into 7 crystal systems (cubic, triclinic, monoclinic, rhombohedral, hexagonal, orthorhombic, tetragonal).
Each lattice type is named by its crystal system plus its centring: simple (P), body centred (I), face centred (F), or base centred (C).
Cubic lattices come in three forms: simple, body centred and face centred.
Monoclinic and orthorhombic systems have simple, centred variants, while rhombohedral and hexagonal lattices have no centring variants listed.
Tetragonal lattices occur only as simple and body centred forms.
defs: Crystal lattice
A regular, periodic three-dimensional arrangement of points in space that repeats throughout a crystal; each point has identical surroundings.
Simple (primitive) lattice
A lattice in which lattice points occur only at the corners of the unit cell.
Body centred lattice
A lattice with an additional lattice point at the centre of the unit cell.
Face centred lattice
A lattice with additional lattice points at the centres of all six faces of the unit cell.
Base centred lattice
A lattice with additional lattice points at the centres of one pair of opposite faces of the unit cell.
tips: Do not confuse the 7 crystal systems with the 14 lattice types; the 14 arise from centring variants within those systems.
Remember that triclinic, rhombohedral and hexagonal appear with only one listed type, so do not assume every system has three centring options.
rq: Why can there be only 14 lattice types when there are 7 crystal systems?

Each crystal system can accommodate different centring arrangements (simple, body, face or base centred) that keep the symmetry of that system; only the combinations that are not equivalent to a smaller cell are counted, giving 14 in total.
What would happen to the number of lattice types if you added a lattice point at the centre of a hexagonal cell?
That arrangement is equivalent to a simpler hexagonal lattice, so it is not a new Bravais lattice; this is why the hexagonal system has only one listed type.

notes.t: Simple vs Centred Cubic Unit Cells
pts: Simple cubic cells have atoms only at the corners of the cube or rhomboid.
Body centred cells add one extra atom at the centre of the cube.
Face centred cells add one extra atom at the centre of each face of the cube.
defs: Simple cubic (SC) unit cell
A cubic unit cell with atoms located only at the eight corners.
Body centred cubic (BCC) unit cell
A cubic unit cell with atoms at the eight corners plus one atom at the cube centre.
Face centred cubic (FCC) unit cell
A cubic unit cell with atoms at the eight corners plus one atom at the centre of each of the six faces.
tips: Do not count corner atoms as full atoms per cell; each corner atom is shared by eight cells.
Remember the centred labels refer to the position of the extra atom, not the number of cubes in the lattice.
rq: Why does a face-centred cubic cell contain more atoms per cell than a simple cubic cell, even though both have the same cube shape?
Each corner atom is shared by 8 cells, giving 1 atom from corners in SC; FCC adds 6 face atoms each shared by 2 cells (3 atoms), giving 4 atoms per cell versus 1 for SC.
What would happen to the atom count if the body-centred atom were moved onto a face?
The structure would no longer be body centred; it would become face centred only if all faces received atoms, so a single face atom alone does not define either named cell.

notes.t: BCC Unit Cell (VMSE Screenshot)
pts: The body-centred cubic (BCC) unit cell has atoms at each of the eight cube corners plus one atom at the centre of the cube.
The VMSE tool lets you view unit cells for the seven crystal systems and for FCC, BCC and HCP metal structures in three dimensions.
The screenshot shows the BCC structure as a cube with atoms at the corners and one central atom, drawn with a ball-and-stick style representation.
defs: Body-centred cubic (BCC) structure
A cubic crystal structure in which one atom sits at each corner of the cube and one atom sits at the body centre of the cube.
tips: Do not count all eight corner atoms as belonging entirely to one cell; each corner contributes only 1/8 to the cell.
Confusing the BCC body-centre atom with a face-centre atom (as in FCC) leads to wrong atom counts and packing calculations.
rq: Why does the BCC unit cell contain two atoms in total even though the cube has eight corners?
Each corner atom is shared by eight adjacent cells, so eight corners contribute 8 × 1/8 = 1 atom, and the single body-centre atom lies wholly inside the cell, giving 2 atoms per cell.
How does the BCC structure differ from FCC in terms of atoms per cell and packing?
BCC has 2 atoms per cell with a lower atomic packing factor (about 0.68) than FCC, which has 4 atoms per cell and a packing factor of about 0.74.

xq.q: A BCC metal has cubic lattice constant a = 0.287 nm. Atoms touch along the body diagonal, which has length √3 a. Using that each corner atom is shared by 8 cells, find the number of atoms per unit cell, and hence the atomic radius R in nm.
xq.a: R = 0.124 nm (2 atoms per cell)

xq.q: How many atoms belong to one FCC unit cell (corners shared by 8 cells, face atoms shared by 2 cells)?
o: 14, counting every atom in the drawing
xq.w: 8×1/8 + 6×1/2 = 4; counting all atoms (14) ignores sharing, and 7 or 6 miscount corner or face contributions.

xq.q: Explain why there are 14 Bravais lattices but only 7 crystal systems. Use the cubic system to illustrate, and state which systems have only one lattice type.
xq.a: The crystal systems are shape classes defined by the relations between a, b, c and α, β, γ. Within a system, lattice points can be placed in different ways: simple (corners only), body centred, face centred or base centred, giving distinct lattices. The 14 Bravais lattices are these centring variants. The cubic system has three: simple, body centred (extra point at centre) and face centred (extra points at six face centres). Triclinic, rhombohedral and hexagonal have only one type each.
s: Lattices are centring variants (P, I, F, C)
Triclinic, rhombohedral, hexagonal have one each

units.name: 6.5 Drawing SC, BCC, FCC and HCP unit cells
units.ov: These notes cover how to draw SC, BCC, FCC and HCP unit cells in two ways: the reduced radius model (small atoms joined by lines, so positions are clear) and the full radius model (touching spheres, so atomic contact and packing are clear). The same atoms are drawn in both. The choice depends on whether you need to show atom positions or how atoms touch, and the full radius model is the one that links atomic radius to lattice parameter. The notes give no numerical relations, so the quantitative results below come from standard background knowledge.
must: Reduced radius model: small atoms joined by lines, shows atom centres and the spaces between them; it is a visual aid only, not true atomic size
Full radius model: atoms drawn at true size and touching, shows contact and how much of the cell is filled
Atom radius is identical in both models; only the drawing changes, so never read the reduced picture as a smaller atom
Always state which model you used, since the same structure looks very different in each
BCC: atoms at the 8 corners plus 1 at the body centre (never corners only); atoms touch along the body diagonal, not the cube edges, so \(\sqrt{3}a=4R\)
FCC: atoms at the 8 corners plus the centre of each of the 6 faces; atoms touch along the face diagonal, so \(\sqrt{2}a=4R\)
SC (standard background): atoms at the 8 corners only and touching along the cube edge, so \(a=2R\)
HCP: hexagonal prism with atoms at corners, at the centres of the top and bottom faces, and 3 atoms in the mid-plane; atoms at the cell boundary are partly cut away in the full radius model
Use the full radius model when relating atomic radius \(R\) to lattice parameter \(a\); the touching direction differs for each structure
conn: Touching direction (edge for SC, face diagonal for FCC, body diagonal for BCC) links the full radius drawing to the geometry that gives \(a\) in terms of \(R\)
The full radius model shows how much of the cube is filled, which leads to atomic packing factor and coordination number
Atoms cut by the cell boundary in the full radius drawing link to counting the effective number of atoms per cell (SC 1, BCC 2, FCC 4)
Choice of model links to the purpose of the drawing: positions and lattice points use reduced, contact and density or packing use full
exq: Sketch a BCC unit cell using both the reduced and full radius models. Label the atom positions and mark the direction along which atoms touch.
Draw an FCC unit cell in the full radius model, show the face diagonal, and derive \(a\) in terms of atomic radius \(R\). Find \(a\) for \(R=0.128\) nm.
Explain why the reduced radius model must not be taken as showing true atomic size, and state when each model is the more appropriate one.
Sketch an HCP unit cell, identifying the atom positions at the corners, the face centres and the mid-plane. Why do some atoms appear only partly inside the cell?
A student draws a BCC cell with atoms only at the corners and touching along the cube edges. Identify and correct both errors.

notes.t: Drawing crystal cells: reduced vs full radius models
pts: The reduced radius model draws small atoms joined by lines, so the spaces between atoms are visible.
The full radius model draws full-sized atoms touching and filling all the space, showing how atoms interact.
The choice of drawing model depends on what you are trying to show about the structure.
tips: Do not confuse the two models: the reduced radius model shows spaces, while the full radius model shows atom contact.
State which model you used when drawing a cell, since the same structure looks very different in each.
rq: Why would you choose the reduced radius model when showing a unit cell's geometry?
Because its small atoms and joining lines make the cell's edges, angles and empty spaces between atoms easy to see.
If you want to show which atoms touch each other in a close-packed structure, which model is more suitable and why?
The full radius model, because full-sized atoms show their contact and interaction directly.

notes.t: Drawing BCC unit cells: reduced vs full radius models
pts: The reduced radius model shows atom centres at the cube corners plus one atom at the body centre, drawn as small spheres joined by lines for clarity.
The full radius model shows atoms as touching spheres, revealing how much of the cube is filled and that atoms touch along the body diagonal.
In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal, not along the cube edges.
tips: Do not confuse the reduced radius model (atoms shown smaller, for visibility) with a real change in atom size; the atoms have the same radius in both pictures.
Remember the BCC cell contains a centre atom plus corner atoms, so it is not drawn with atoms only at the corners.
rq: Why does the reduced radius model draw spheres smaller than the full radius model?
So that the atom centres and the lattice geometry remain visible; the full model would overlap and obscure the cube edges and the body-centre atom.
In the full radius model, which direction do the touching atoms lie along, and why does this matter for the packing?
The body diagonal; this contact fixes the relation between atomic radius and cube edge length, which is needed to calculate the packing factor.

notes.t: Drawing FCC unit cells: reduced vs full radius models
pts: The FCC unit cell is drawn as a cube with atoms at each of the 8 corners and at the centre of each of the 6 faces.
The reduced radius model shows atom centres shrunk so the cube's atom arrangement is visible; atoms do not appear to touch.
The full radius model shows atoms at their true size, so neighbouring atoms touch along the face diagonal of the cube.
tips: Do not confuse the reduced radius model (atoms shrunk for clarity) with the true geometry; use the full radius model when relating atomic radius to lattice parameter.
rq: Why does the reduced radius model show gaps between atoms even though atoms in FCC are in contact?
The reduced radius model shrinks each atom so the lattice positions are clearly visible; in the full radius model the atoms touch along the close-packed face diagonal.

notes.t: Drawing HCP unit cells: reduced vs full radius models
pts: HCP cells are drawn in two ways: reduced radius models show atom centres clearly, while full radius models show atoms touching their neighbours.
The full radius model shows the hexagonal prism with atoms at corners, face centres and three mid-plane sites, with spheres partly cut away by the cell boundary.
tips: Do not confuse the two drawing models: the reduced radius model is a visual aid for atom positions, not a true representation of atomic size.
rq: Why does the reduced radius model use smaller spheres than the full radius model?
So that the atom centres and the arrangement of the lattice are visible, rather than the spheres overlapping and hiding the structure.
Why are only parts of some spheres shown in the full radius model?
Atoms on the cell faces, edges and corners are shared with neighbouring cells, so only the portion inside the cell is drawn.

units.name: 6.6 FCC cell size from atomic radius
units.ov: This material derives the FCC cubic cell edge length from the atomic radius using hard-sphere contact along the face diagonal (not the cube edge). The result \(a = 2\sqrt{2}\,R\) then gives the cell volume \(16\sqrt{2}\,r^3\), which is the basis for later packing-factor and density calculations.
must: In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, not along the cube edge.
The face diagonal contains 4 atomic radii: a corner atom (r), the face-centre atom (2r), and a corner atom (r), so the length is \(4r\).
Pythagoras on one face gives \(a^2 + a^2 = (4r)^2\), i.e. \(\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r\).
Solving gives \(a = \dfrac{4r}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\,r \approx 2.83\,r\).
Cell volume is \(V_{cell} = a^3 = (2\sqrt{2}\,r)^3 = 16\sqrt{2}\,r^3 \approx 22.6\,r^3\).
FCC has 4 atoms per cell: \(6\times\tfrac12 + 8\times\tfrac18 = 4\).
Atomic radius is half the centre-to-centre distance of touching neighbours (hard-sphere model).
Common errors: using \(a = 2r\) (simple cubic only), \(a = 4r\), or \((2\sqrt{2})^3 = 8\sqrt{2}\) instead of \(16\sqrt{2}\).
Keep units consistent (nm or m) for \(a\) and \(r\); convert before substituting (1 nm = \(10^{-9}\) m).
conn: Face diagonal geometry, Pythagoras and atom counting (4 atoms per cell) combine to give atomic packing factor: \(4\cdot\tfrac43\pi r^3 / (16\sqrt{2}\,r^3) = \pi/(3\sqrt{2}) \approx 0.74\).
Cell volume from \(a(r)\) plus atoms per cell and atomic mass gives theoretical density \(\rho = nA/(V_{cell}N_A)\).
Comparing contact directions across structures (SC along edge \(a=2r\), BCC along body diagonal \(a=4r/\sqrt{3}\), FCC along face diagonal) tests understanding of which direction is close-packed.
Unit conversions (nm to m, cm³ to m³) are needed when cubing \(a\) to get volume.
exq: Derive the relationship between the FCC cell edge \(a\) and atomic radius \(r\) from the face diagonal, stating clearly where the atoms touch.
Aluminium is FCC with \(r = 0.143\) nm. Calculate the lattice parameter \(a\) and the unit cell volume in \(\text{m}^3\).
Copper (FCC) has \(a = 0.361\) nm. Calculate its atomic radius and the centre-to-centre distance of nearest neighbours.
Show that the volume of an FCC cell is \(16\sqrt{2}\,r^3\) and use it with 4 atoms per cell to find the atomic packing factor.
Explain why \(a = 2r\) is wrong for FCC, and compare the \(a\)-\(r\) relations for simple cubic and FCC.

notes.t: Cell size for FCC
pts: For FCC, assume atoms touch so the cell size can be calculated from the atomic radius.
In FCC, atoms touch each other along the face diagonal, not along the cube edge.
defs: Atomic radius (R)
Half the distance between the centres of two neighbouring touching atoms in the crystal structure.
eqs: Cell edge length a for FCC from atomic radius R
a = cubic cell edge length (m); R = atomic radius (m)
tips: Do not use a = 2R for FCC; that relation applies only to simple cubic. Using the face diagonal gives a = 2√2 R.
Keep units consistent: R and a must be in the same unit (e.g. nm or m) before comparing or substituting.
rq: Why is the face diagonal, rather than the cube edge, used to relate cell size to atomic radius in FCC?
Because atoms touch along the face diagonal, which contains four atomic radii (4R); along the edge atoms do not touch, so the edge is not 2R.

notes.t: Cell size for FCC (face diagonal geometry)
pts: Looking across one face diagonal of an FCC cube, the atoms touching along that diagonal are one full sphere plus two half-spheres at the corners, giving a total diagonal length of 4r.
The face diagonal contains one whole atom (diameter 2r) at the face centre and two corner atoms each contributing a radius r, so the sphere contacts run along the diagonal.
Atoms in FCC touch along the face diagonal, not along the cube edge, so this diagonal is used to relate the cell edge length a to the atomic radius r.
eqs: Relation between FCC cell edge length and atomic radius (from face diagonal)
a = cubic unit cell edge length (m); r = atomic radius (m)
tips: Use the face diagonal \(\sqrt{2}\,a\), not the edge length a, when relating a and r; using a = 4r is a common error.
Keep units consistent (m or nm) when substituting a and r into \(\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r\).
rq: Why does the face diagonal, rather than the cube edge, give the correct relation between a and r in FCC?
Atoms touch along the face diagonal (close-packed direction), so the diagonal length \(\sqrt{2}\,a\) equals four atomic radii \(4r\); along the edge the atoms do not touch.
If the diagonal contains 4r of atomic spacing, how many atoms lie along it and why do the corner atoms count as half?
Two corner atoms and one face-centre atom: the corner atoms each contribute only r (half of their diameter) because only half of each lies within the diagonal line.

notes.t: FCC unit cell size: relating lattice parameter a to atomic radius r
pts: An FCC unit cell has one half atom on each face (6 faces) and one eighth atom at each corner (8 corners), giving 4 atoms per cell.
Atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the diagonal length equals four atomic radii.
Solving the Pythagorean relation gives the cell edge length in terms of the atomic radius.
defs: Atomic radius (r)
Radius of an atom treated as a hard sphere; in close-packed structures neighbouring atoms touch, so r sets the spacing between atom centres.
eqs: Lattice parameter of an FCC cell in terms of atomic radius
a = cube edge length (m); r = atomic radius (m)
Face diagonal condition for touching atoms in FCC
a = cube edge length (m); r = atomic radius (m)
tips: Do not use a = 2r for FCC; atoms touch along the face diagonal, giving a = 2√2 r.
Remember the diagonal contains four radii, not two, when converting between a and r.
rq: Why does the face diagonal, not the cube edge, determine the FCC cell size?
Atoms touch along the face diagonal (close-packed direction), which contains four radii (corner atom, face atom, face atom, corner atom); along the edge atoms do not touch.
Why is the atom count 4 and not 8 per FCC cell?
Corner atoms contribute 1/8 each (8 corners → 1 atom) and face atoms contribute 1/2 each (6 faces → 3 atoms), totalling 4.

notes.t: Unit cell size of FCC structure
pts: In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the diagonal length equals four atomic radii, giving the cell edge a in terms of r.
The cell edge a is linked to the atomic radius r, so the cell volume can be written purely in terms of r.
eqs: Volume of FCC unit cell in terms of atomic radius r
\(V_{cell}\) = volume of unit cell (\(m^{3}\)); \(a\) = cell edge length (m); \(r\) = atomic radius (m)
tips: Do not use a = 2r for FCC; atoms touch along the face diagonal, so a = 2√2·r.
Cubing the factor 2√2 gives 16√2·r³ (since (2√2)³ = 16√2), not 8·√2·r³.
rq: Why is the cell edge a = 2√2·r rather than a = 2r for FCC?
Atoms touch along the face diagonal, not the edge. The face diagonal is √2·a and equals 4r, so a = 4r/√2 = 2√2·r.

xq.q: A metal has an FCC structure in which atoms are treated as hard spheres touching along the face diagonal of the cubic cell. The atomic radius is \(R = 0.125\) nm. Calculate the volume of the unit cell, \(V_{cell}\), in m³.
s: Face diagonal gives √2·a = 4R, so a = 2√2·R = 2.828 × 0.125 = 0.3536 nm
Convert: 1 nm³ = 10⁻²⁷ m³, so V = 4.42 × 10⁻²⁹ m³

xq.q: An FCC metal has a cubic cell edge \(a = 0.360\) nm. Assuming hard spheres touching along the face diagonal, what is the atomic radius \(r\)?
xq.w: The face diagonal \(\sqrt{2}a = 4r\) gives \(r = \sqrt{2}a/4 = 0.127\) nm; the traps are using a/4 or a/2 (edge contact), or the BCC body-diagonal formula \(\sqrt{3}a/4\).

xq.q: Using a sketch of one face of an FCC unit cell, show that the cell edge length is \(a = 2\sqrt{2}\,R\), where \(R\) is the atomic radius. Explain why the relation \(a = 2R\) cannot be used for FCC.
xq.a: In FCC the atoms touch along the face diagonal. Along this diagonal there are two corner atoms (each contributing a radius R) and the whole face-centre atom (diameter 2R), so the diagonal length is 4R. By Pythagoras on the face, the diagonal is \(\sqrt{a^2+a^2} = \sqrt{2}a\). Hence \(\sqrt{2}a = 4R\), so \(a = 4R/\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}R\). The relation a = 2R would require atoms to touch along the cube edge, which only happens in simple cubic. In FCC the corner atoms along an edge do not touch, since they are separated by a gap.
s: Sketch of the face with corner atoms and a face-centre atom touching along the diagonal
a = 2R requires contact along the edge (simple cubic), not true in FCC

units.name: 6.7 BCC cell size from atomic radius
units.ov: This material derives the BCC lattice parameter from the atomic radius using hard-sphere contact along the cube body diagonal, which holds four atomic radii. Pythagoras applied twice gives a body diagonal of \(\sqrt{3}a\), so \(a = 4R/\sqrt{3}\). The same geometry then gives the cell volume and underpins atom counting and packing calculations.
must: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal, not along the cube edge or the face diagonal.
The body diagonal is \(\sqrt{3}a\). It comes from the face diagonal \(\sqrt{2}a\) combined with the edge \(a\) by Pythagoras: \(a^2+a^2+a^2=(4r)^2\).
The body diagonal contains four atomic radii: one full centre atom (2r) plus a radius from each of the two corner atoms.
Lattice parameter: \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\), equivalent to \(r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a\).
Cell volume: \(V=a^3=\frac{64}{3\sqrt{3}}r^3\), not \(64r^3/\sqrt{3}\). Cube the \(\sqrt{3}\) as well: \((\sqrt{3})^3=3\sqrt{3}\).
BCC has 2 atoms per cell: 8 corners × 1/8 plus 1 centre atom.
Do not use \(a=2r\). That is the simple cubic contact condition, and FCC is also not \(a=2r\), since FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal (\(a=4r/\sqrt{2}\)).
Derive the result from geometry rather than memorising it, and sketch the diagonal to check the count of 4r.
Convert the radius to metres (1 nm = 1e-9 m, 1 Å = 1e-10 m) before calculating, and keep units consistent through volume calculations.
conn: Cell size links to atoms per cell (2 for BCC): the volume of atoms in the cell is \(2\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), which gives the atomic packing factor \(\approx 0.68\).
Lattice parameter and atoms per cell give theoretical density: \(\rho = \frac{nA}{V_c N_A}\) with \(V_c=a^3\), where \(A\) is the atomic mass and \(N_A\) is Avogadro's number.
The close-packed direction \(\langle111\rangle\) is the body diagonal, so the same geometry gives the linear density along that direction and is relevant to slip.
Comparing BCC (diagonal contact, \(a=4r/\sqrt{3}\)) with FCC (face diagonal contact, \(a=4r/\sqrt{2}\)) shows how the contact direction sets \(a\) and the packing efficiency.
exq: Iron is BCC at room temperature with atomic radius 0.124 nm. Calculate the lattice parameter and the unit cell volume.
Derive from first principles the relation between \(a\) and \(r\) for BCC, explaining why atoms touch along the body diagonal and how many atomic radii it contains.
Show that the BCC cell volume is \(\frac{64}{3\sqrt{3}}r^3\), and identify the error in the answer \(64r^3/\sqrt{3}\).
Tungsten is BCC with \(a=0.3165\) nm. Calculate its atomic radius, then its theoretical density given \(A=183.84\) g/mol.
Compare the lattice parameters of BCC and FCC metals of the same atomic radius, stating the touching direction in each. Which has the larger cell, and what does the answer show about packing?

notes.t: Cell size of BCC structure
pts: In BCC, atoms touch along the cube body diagonal, not along the cube edge.
The cell size is found by relating the atom radius to the body diagonal length, so the packing geometry sets the lattice parameter.
The same cell size calculation is repeated here, so it should be done by geometry rather than memorised.
eqs: Lattice parameter of BCC from atomic radius (body diagonal contact)
a = cube edge length (m); R = atomic radius (m)
tips: Do not use the cube edge for contact in BCC; using \( a = 2R \) is the FCC-style mistake and gives the wrong cell size.
Keep units consistent: convert the radius to metres before calculating the cell edge in m.
rq: Why do atoms in BCC touch along the body diagonal rather than along the cube edge?

The body diagonal runs through the centre atom and the two corner atoms, so it is longer than the edge; atoms touch along the longest line through the cell, which is the body diagonal of length \( \sqrt{3}\,a \).
If the body diagonal contains 4 atomic radii, what happens to the cell edge if the radius increases?
The edge length increases in proportion, since \( a = 4R/\sqrt{3} \), so a larger radius gives a larger cell.

notes.t: BCC cell size and atomic radius
pts: In BCC, the body diagonal of the cube contains one full atom at the centre and two corner atoms cut into one-eighth each, so the close-packed direction runs through four atomic radii.
Atoms touch along the body diagonal, so the diagonal length equals 4r, which links the cube edge a to the atomic radius r.
The body diagonal is found by Pythagoras applied twice: the face diagonal \(\sqrt{2}a\) combined with the edge a gives \(\sqrt{3}a\).
defs: Atomic radius (r)
Radius of an atom treated as a hard sphere; in BCC, half the length of the close-packed body diagonal.
eqs: Body diagonal relation for BCC (atoms touch along the diagonal)
Atomic radius in terms of lattice parameter for BCC
tips: Do not use the face diagonal (\(\sqrt{2}a\)) to relate a and r in BCC; the touching direction is the body diagonal, \(\sqrt{3}a\).
Count atom contributions correctly: corner atoms contribute 1/8 each and the centre atom contributes 1, giving 2 atoms per BCC cell.
rq: Why does a BCC cell contain only two atoms even though it has eight corners?
Each corner atom is shared by eight cells, so it contributes one-eighth; eight corners give 8 × 1/8 = 1, plus one full atom at the centre, totalling 2.
Why is the body diagonal, rather than the face diagonal, the close-packed direction in BCC?

The body diagonal is the longest direction along which atoms touch (length 4r), while the face diagonal contains only corner and face atoms that do not touch in BCC; atoms touch only along the body diagonal.

notes.t: BCC unit cell size: relating lattice parameter a to atomic radius r
pts: In BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal (close-packed direction), so the diagonal length equals four atomic radii.
The body diagonal of the cube has length \( \sqrt{3}\,a \), which gives the relation between lattice parameter and atomic radius.
Rearranging gives the lattice parameter in terms of r, and cubing it gives the cell volume in terms of r.
The BCC cell volume is the cube of the lattice parameter, \( V = a^3 \).
defs: Lattice parameter (a)
The edge length of the cubic unit cell.
Atomic radius (r)
Radius of an atom, taken as half the distance between touching atoms in the close-packed direction.
eqs: Atomic radius in terms of lattice parameter for BCC
r = atomic radius (m); a = lattice parameter (m)
Lattice parameter in terms of atomic radius for BCC
a = lattice parameter (m); r = atomic radius (m)
Cell volume of BCC cube in terms of atomic radius
a = lattice parameter (m); r = atomic radius (m)
tips: Do not use the edge length a = 2r (which is the FCC/simple cubic-type touching assumption); for BCC the touching condition is along the body diagonal, giving a = 4r/√3.
Remember that the volume formula a³ must be expressed consistently: substituting a = 4r/√3 gives a³ = 64r³/(3√3), not 64r³/√3.
rq: Why is the body diagonal, rather than an edge or face diagonal, used to relate a and r in BCC?
Atoms touch along the body diagonal (the close-packed direction) in BCC, not along the edges, so the diagonal length of \( \sqrt{3}\,a \) equals 4r.
If a BCC cell has a = 0.3 nm, what is the atomic radius?
\( r = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(0.3\text{ nm}) \approx 0.13\text{ nm} \)

xq.q: Iron at room temperature has a BCC structure with cubic lattice parameter \(a = 0.2866\) nm. Atoms touch along the body diagonal of the cube. Calculate the atomic radius \(r\) of iron in nm.
Two metals have the same atomic radius \(R\). One is FCC (\(a = 2\sqrt{2}R\)) and the other is BCC (\(a = 4R/\sqrt{3}\)). What is the ratio \(V_{FCC}/V_{BCC}\) of their unit cell volumes?
xq.w: The ratio of edges is 2.828/2.309 = 1.225, but volume scales as \(a^3\), so the ratio is 1.225³ = 1.84; 1.22 forgets to cube, and 0.54 is the inverted ratio.

xq.q: Starting from the fact that atoms touch along the body diagonal in BCC, show that the lattice parameter is \(a = 4r/\sqrt{3}\), where \(r\) is the atomic radius. Hence show that the cell volume is \(a^3 = 64r^3/(3\sqrt{3})\).
xq.a: The face diagonal is √2·a. The body diagonal forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides a and √2·a, so its length is √(a² + 2a²) = √3·a. The body diagonal passes through the corner atom (radius r), the whole centre atom (2r) and the other corner atom (radius r), so its length is 4r. Therefore √3·a = 4r and a = 4r/√3. Cubing: a³ = 64r³/(√3)³ = 64r³/(3√3).
s: Contact along diagonal: length = r + 2r + r = 4r

units.name: 6.8 HCP cell size and volume
units.ov: This material derives the volume of the HCP unit cell as a hexagonal prism, with base area from six equilateral triangles multiplied by the height c. The volume can be written in terms of atomic radius r or lattice parameter a, using r = a/2 for touching atoms. Cell volume matters because it links crystal geometry to atoms per unit volume and hence to density.
must: HCP cell volume is base area times height: \(V_{cell} = A_{base} \times c\)
Base area from six equilateral triangles of side a: \(A_{base} = 6\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}a^2\)
Volume in terms of a and c: \(V_{cell} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}a^2 c\)
Volume in terms of atomic radius: \(V_{cell} = 6\sqrt{3}\,r^2 c\)
Touching atoms in the basal plane give \(a = 2r\), so \(r = a/2\)
Triangle of side 2r has height \(\sqrt{3}\,r\) and area \(\sqrt{3}\,r^2\); six of them give \(6\sqrt{3}\,r^2\)
Common errors: using side r instead of 2r (area 4× too small), using \(\frac12 a^2\) for the triangle area, and writing \((a/2)^2\) as a/4 instead of \(a^2/4\)
c is the cell height, the repeat distance perpendicular to the basal plane, and is independent of a unless the ideal c/a ratio is given
Use consistent units (nm vs m) and convert to \(m^3\) (\(1\,nm^3 = 10^{-27}\,m^3\)) before density calculations
Count only the atoms belonging to one cell, using fractional shares at corners, edges and faces, when linking volume to density
conn: Cell volume with atoms per cell (fractional counting) gives density: \(\rho = nA/(V_{cell}N_A)\), the standard route to a numerical answer
The r = a/2 relation links the two volume forms \(6\sqrt{3}r^2c\) and \(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}a^2c\); check by substitution
Volume combined with atoms per cell gives the atomic packing factor, and comparison with FCC or BCC shows why HCP is close-packed
Geometry of equilateral triangles (height from Pythagoras) underlies the base area, so geometric slips propagate to volume and density
exq: Derive the volume of the HCP unit cell in terms of a and c, starting from the area of an equilateral triangle, and show that it equals \(6\sqrt{3}\,r^2c\) when a = 2r.
Zinc is HCP with a = 0.266 nm and c = 0.495 nm. Calculate the unit cell volume in nm³ and in m³.
Using the cell volume from the previous question and 6 atoms per cell, calculate the density of the metal given its atomic mass, stating your assumptions.
A student calculates the HCP base area using triangle side r and gets an answer four times too small. Explain the error and give the correct base area for r = 0.125 nm.
Explain why the unit cell volume is important for linking crystal structure to density, and why only fractional atom contributions are counted for a single cell.

notes.t: HCP unit cell size: volume derivation
pts: The HCP cell is treated as a rectangular prism whose volume equals base area times height.
The height of the hexagonal prism is the lattice parameter c.
The hexagonal base is made of six equilateral triangles, each with side a.
defs: Lattice parameter c
The height of the HCP unit cell, i.e. the repeat distance along the close-packed stacking direction.
Lattice parameter a
The edge length of the hexagonal base of the HCP unit cell, equal to the side of each of the six equilateral triangles.
eqs: Volume of the HCP unit cell (rectangular-solid approximation of hexagonal prism)
\(V_{cell}\) = unit cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); \(A_{base}\) = area of hexagonal base (\(m^{2}\)); c = cell height (m)
Area of hexagonal base from six equilateral triangles
\(A_{base}\) = base area (\(m^{2}\)); a = triangle side / basal edge (m)
tips: Use the area of an equilateral triangle, \( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 \), not \( \frac{1}{2}a^2 \), when computing the hexagonal base area.
Keep units consistent: a and c must be in the same length unit before forming the volume.
rq: Why can the hexagonal base be split into six equilateral triangles?
Each triangle has its apex at the centre of the hexagon and two vertices on adjacent corners; all sides equal a, so each triangle is equilateral with side a.
If c were doubled but a kept the same, how would the cell volume change?
It doubles, since volume is linear in c while the base area depends only on a.

notes.t: HCP cell size: base area of the hexagonal close-packed unit cell
pts: In HCP, each equilateral triangle formed by three atom centres has side length equal to twice the atomic radius.
The area of one equilateral triangle is found from the standard base × height / 2 formula, using height = √3·r.
The hexagonal base of the HCP cell is made of six such triangles, so its total area is six times the single-triangle area.
eqs: Area of one equilateral triangle with side 2r (base × height / 2)
r = atomic radius (m); base = 2r (m); height = \sqrt{3}\,r (m); Area (m²)
Total area of the hexagonal base of the HCP cell (six triangles)
\(A_{base}\) = total base area (m²); r = atomic radius (m)
tips: Use the side length 2r (not r) when calculating triangle dimensions; using r gives an area four times too small.
Check that the height of the equilateral triangle is √3·r (not √3·r/2 or 2r) before substituting into the area formula.
rq: Why is the triangle side length 2r rather than r?
Touching atoms have centres separated by the sum of their radii, 2r, so adjacent centres (the triangle vertices) are 2r apart.
Why does the height of the triangle equal √3·r?
For an equilateral triangle of side 2r, Pythagoras gives height² = (2r)² − r² = 3r², so height = √3·r.

notes.t: Cell size of HCP (hexagonal close-packed) unit cell
pts: The HCP unit cell volume can be written in terms of the atomic radius r or the lattice parameter a, using the cell height c.
For ideal close packing the atoms touch along the basal edge, so the atomic radius is half the lattice parameter a.
defs: Lattice parameter a
The edge length of the hexagonal base of the HCP unit cell, i.e. the distance between neighbouring atom centres in the basal plane.
Lattice parameter c
The height of the HCP unit cell, measured perpendicular to the basal plane.
eqs: Volume of the HCP unit cell in terms of atomic radius r and height c
\(V_{\text{cell}}\) = unit cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); r = atomic radius (m); c = unit cell height (m)
Volume of the HCP unit cell in terms of lattice parameters a and c
\(V_{\text{cell}}\) = unit cell volume (\(m^{3}\)); a = basal edge length / lattice parameter (m); c = unit cell height (m)
Relation between atomic radius and lattice parameter a for touching atoms
r = atomic radius (m); a = lattice parameter (m)
tips: Substitute r = a/2 correctly: \((a/2)^2 = a^2/4\), not a/2 squared as a/4 — a common algebra slip.
Keep units consistent: if a and c are in nm, the volume is in \(nm^{3}\); convert to \(m^{3}\) before using atomic density calculations.
rq: Why does substituting r = a/2 into 6√3 r² c give (3√3/2) a² c?
What physical assumption links a and r in HCP, and what would change if the atoms did not touch along the basal edge?
Ideal close packing: atoms touch along the basal edge so \( a = 2r \). If they did not touch, a would be larger than 2r and the relation r = a/2 would no longer hold.

notes.t: Why the volume of the unit cell matters
pts: The unit cell volume governs how many atoms fit per unit volume, linking crystal geometry to density.
Two cubic cells are compared: atoms shown as full spheres at the centre and fractional spheres at corners and faces, so the packing arrangement differs between them.
tips: Do not confuse the unit cell with the whole crystal: count only the atoms belonging to one cell, using fractional shares for atoms on faces, edges and corners.
rq: Why would two crystal structures with the same atom size have different densities?
Because they pack different numbers of atoms into a unit cell of different volume, so atoms per unit volume (and mass per unit volume) differ.

xq.q: A magnesium HCP unit cell has basal lattice parameter \(a = 0.320\) nm and cell height \(c = 0.520\) nm. Treating the cell as a hexagonal prism whose base is made of six equilateral triangles of side \(a\), calculate the unit cell volume in m³.
s: Area of one equilateral triangle = (√3/4)a², so \(A_{\text{base}}\) = 6(√3/4)a² = (3√3/2)a²

xq.q: In an HCP metal the atomic radius is \(r = 0.160\) nm and atoms touch along the basal edge. Each of the six equilateral triangles forming the hexagonal base has side \(2r\). What is the base area of the hexagon?
xq.w: Each triangle has area ½(2r)(√3 r) = √3 r², so the base is 6√3 r² = 0.266 nm²; using side r gives 0.0665 (four times too small), using ½a² gives 0.307, and using height √3r/2 gives 0.133.

xq.q: For an HCP unit cell the volume is \(V = 6\sqrt{3}\,r^2 c\), where \(r\) is the atomic radius and \(c\) is the cell height. Show that, in terms of the basal lattice parameter \(a\), this becomes \(V = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}a^2 c\). Explain how the factor \(6\sqrt{3}r^2\) arises.
xq.a: Each equilateral triangle in the hexagonal base has side 2r and height √3·r, so its area is ½(2r)(√3 r) = √3 r². Six triangles give a base area 6√3 r², and multiplying by height c gives V = 6√3 r² c. Atoms touch along the basal edge, so a = 2r, i.e. r = a/2 and r² = a²/4. Substituting: V = 6√3 (a²/4) c = (3√3/2) a² c.
s: Triangle side 2r, height √3 r, area √3 r²
Touching atoms: r = a/2, so r² = a²/4

units.name: 6.9 Density calculations from crystal structure
units.ov: This module shows how to predict a material's density from its crystal structure: mass of the atoms in one unit cell divided by the cell volume. The calculation is applied to FCC (Cu), BCC (W) and HCP (Zn), each needing a different geometric link between atomic radius and cell dimensions. The results are then used to explain why metals, ceramics, polymers and composites occupy different density ranges.
must: Core formula: \(\rho = \frac{nA}{V_C N_A}\), with \(n\) = atoms per cell, \(A\) in g/mol, \(V_C\) in cm³, \(N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\) mol⁻¹
Atoms per cell from shared-atom counting: SC 1, BCC 2, FCC 4 (8×1/8 + 6×1/2); use \(n\), not the atoms drawn
FCC geometry: atoms touch along the face diagonal, \(a=2\sqrt{2}\,r\), so \(V_C=a^3=16\sqrt{2}\,r^3\)
BCC geometry: atoms touch along the body diagonal (4r), so \(a=\frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(V_C=a^3\)
HCP: needs r, A and the c/a ratio to get the cell dimensions and volume, and the correct atom count per cell
Unit trap: convert nm or Å to cm before cubing (1 nm = 10⁻⁷ cm); an error here gives a factor of about 10²¹
Unit consistency: 1 g/cm³ = 1 Mg/m³ = 1000 kg/m³; use A in g/mol, not kg
Worked check: Cu (FCC, r = 0.1278 nm, A = 63.54) gives about 8.93 g/cm³, against 8.94 g/cm³ in the literature; always compare with the literature value
Density ordering: metals > ceramics > polymers, with composites in between, explained by close-packing, atomic mass and amorphous structure
Density charts use a log axis, and classes overlap (e.g. zirconia overlaps titanium); density is not hardness or strength
conn: Atomic radius to cell edge geometry (face diagonal for FCC, body diagonal for BCC) feeds directly into \(V_C\), so a density question often starts with crystal geometry and packing
Atoms per cell and atomic packing link to why close-packed metals are dense and why polymers with amorphous structures and light atoms (C, H, O) are not
Unit conversions (nm to cm or m, g/cm³ to kg/m³) combine with the formula, so a correct method can still give a wrong numerical answer
Calculated versus literature density can be compared to judge accuracy, and differences point to real-world defects such as vacancies or impurities
exq: Tungsten is BCC with atomic radius 0.1371 nm and atomic weight 183.85 g/mol. Calculate the theoretical density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³, and compare it with the literature value.
Show that the FCC unit cell volume is \(16\sqrt{2}\,r^3\), then calculate the density of copper (r = 0.1278 nm, A = 63.54 g/mol).
Zinc is HCP with r, atomic weight and c/a given. Find the unit cell volume and the theoretical density, stating the number of atoms per cell used.
A student calculates a density that is about 10²¹ times too large or too small. Identify the likely error and correct it, using a worked example.
Explain, in terms of bonding, packing and atomic mass, why metals are generally denser than ceramics and polymers, and give one example where classes overlap.

notes.t: Calculation of density from crystal structure
pts: Density is mass per unit volume, so for a crystal it is the mass of atoms in one unit cell divided by the unit cell volume.
Number of atoms per unit cell, atomic weight and Avogadro's number convert the atomic mass into grams; the cell volume for a cubic cell is a cubed.
Avogadro's number converts moles of atomic weight into individual atoms, so the mass per cell uses n·A/\(N_{A}\).
defs: Density (ρ)
Mass of atoms contained in one unit cell divided by the total volume of that unit cell.
Avogadro's number (\(N_{A}\))
The number of atoms in one mole of a substance, 6.022 × \(10^{23}\) atoms/mol.
Atomic weight (A)
The mass of one mole of atoms of an element, used to find the mass of atoms in a unit cell.
eqs: Density of a crystalline material from unit cell parameters
\rho = density (g/\(cm^{3}\)); n = number of atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); A = atomic weight (g/mol); \(V_{C}\) = unit cell volume (\(cm^{3}\)); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (atoms/mol)
Unit cell volume for a cubic cell
\(V_{C}\) = unit cell volume (\(cm^{3}\)); a = lattice parameter / cell edge length (cm)
tips: Unit trap: convert the lattice parameter to cm before cubing; using nm or Å directly gives a density wildly wrong in g/\(cm^{3.}\)
Use the number of atoms per unit cell n (e.g. 2 for BCC, 4 for FCC), not the number of atoms visible in the drawing, and make sure A is in g/mol.
rq: Why must the atomic weight be divided by Avogadro's number rather than used directly to find the mass of a unit cell?
A is the mass of one mole (\(N_{A}\) atoms), so dividing by \(N_{A}\) gives the mass of a single atom in grams; multiplying by n then gives the mass of the atoms in one unit cell.
What would happen to the calculated density if the lattice parameter a were measured in nm rather than cm without conversion?
\(V_{C}\) = \(a^{3}\) would be off by a factor of \(10^{21}\) (1 \(nm^{3}\) = \(10^{-21}\) \(cm^{3}\)), giving a grossly wrong density; all lengths must be converted to cm to match g/\(cm^{3.}\)
If two metals have the same crystal structure and lattice parameter, what determines which is denser?
The density depends on n·A: the metal with the larger product of atoms per cell and atomic weight is denser.

notes.t: Calculation of density for an FCC metal (copper)
pts: Density can be calculated from atoms per unit cell, atomic mass, cell volume and Avogadro's number.
For FCC, the atomic radius is related to the cell edge via the face diagonal, giving a cell volume of 16√2 r³.
FCC unit cell contains 4 atoms; use this count with the atomic weight of copper to get density.
Worked result for copper is about 8.93 g cm⁻³, close to the literature value of 8.94 g cm⁻³.
defs: Atoms per unit cell (FCC)
The number of equivalent atoms belonging to one FCC unit cell, equal to 4 (8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2).
Atomic radius (metallic)
Half the distance between nearest-neighbour atom centres in a close-packed metal structure.
eqs: Theoretical density of a crystalline material
\(\rho\) = density (g cm⁻³ or kg m⁻³); \(n\) = atoms per unit cell (–); \(A\) = atomic weight (g mol⁻¹); \(V_c\) = unit cell volume (cm³ or m³); \(N_A\) = Avogadro's number (atoms mol⁻¹)
Unit cell volume for FCC in terms of atomic radius
\(\rho\) = density (g m⁻³ then converted to Mg m⁻³ or g cm⁻³); \(r = 0.1278\times10^{-9}\) m; \(N_A = 6.023\times10^{23}\) mol⁻¹
tips: Use SI units consistently: convert the radius from nm to m (×10⁻⁹) and cube it before substituting; mixing nm and cm gives wrong answers.
Give density in g cm⁻³ or Mg m⁻³ with the correct conversion (1 g cm⁻³ = 1 Mg m⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³).
rq: Why does the FCC cell volume use 16√2 r³ rather than a³ with a = 2r?
Because in FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the diagonal √2·a = 4r, giving a = 2√2·r and a³ = 16√2·r³.
What would happen to the calculated density if you used the cell edge length a = 2r instead of the correct relation?
The volume would be underestimated (a³ = 8r³ instead of 16√2 r³), so the calculated density would be overestimated, roughly by a factor of about 2.8.
Why is the calculated value (8.93) slightly different from the literature value (8.94)?
Because the atomic radius is a measured, rounded value and the calculation assumes a perfect, defect-free FCC lattice.

notes.t: Calculation of density for BCC tungsten
pts: Density is found from mass of atoms per unit cell divided by unit cell volume; BCC has 2 atoms per cell.
In BCC, the atomic radius is linked to the cube edge length through the body diagonal, which contains 4 radii.
Compare the calculated density with the literature value to check the result.
defs: BCC (body-centred cubic)
A crystal structure with atoms at the corners of a cube plus one atom at the cube centre, giving 2 atoms per unit cell.
Atomic weight
The mass of one mole of atoms of an element, in g mol\(^{-1}\).
eqs: Density of a crystalline material from unit cell properties

\( \rho \) = density (g cm\(^{-3}\)); \( n \) = atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); \( A \) = atomic weight (g mol\(^{-1}\)); \( V_C \) = unit cell volume (cm\(^3\)); \( N_A \) = Avogadro's number (mol\(^{-1}\))
Edge length of a BCC unit cell from atomic radius
\( a \) = cube edge length (nm or cm); \( R \) = atomic radius (nm or cm)
tips: Unit trap: convert nm to cm (1 nm = 10\(^{-7}\) cm) before calculating unit cell volume, or the density will be wrong by a factor of about 10\(^{21}\).
Use the atomic weight in g mol\(^{-1}\) with Avogadro's number, not the atomic mass in kg, to keep units consistent in g cm\(^{-3}\).
rq: Why does a BCC cell contain 2 atoms rather than 1 or 8?
Eight corner atoms each contribute 1/8 to the cell, giving 1; the central atom lies wholly inside, giving 1; total = 2.
Why must the atomic radius be converted before computing volume?
Volume must be in cm\(^3\) to give density in g cm\(^{-3}\); 1 nm = 10\(^{-7}\) cm, so the radius must be converted first.

notes.t: Calculation of density for an HCP metal (zinc)
pts: Density of a crystalline metal can be calculated from its unit cell: mass of atoms in the cell divided by the cell volume.
HCP zinc is specified by its atomic radius, atomic weight and c/a ratio, which are all needed to find the unit cell dimensions.
The calculated density should be compared with the literature value to check the result.
eqs: Theoretical density of a crystalline solid from unit cell properties

\rho = density (g \(cm^{-3}\)); n = number of atoms per unit cell (dimensionless); A = atomic weight (g \(mol^{-1}\)); \(V_{C}\) = unit cell volume (\(cm^{3}\)); \(N_{A}\) = Avogadro's number (\(mol^{-1}\))
tips: Unit trap: convert the atomic radius from nm to cm before calculating volume, since density is in g \(cm^{-3}\).
Do not count the full atom in the unit cell; corner and face atoms are shared, so use the correct number of atoms per cell.
rq: Why must the HCP unit cell contain 6 atoms rather than 2 when calculating density, and how does this relate to the c/a ratio?

Atoms on corners and face centres are shared between cells, giving 6 atoms per HCP cell; the c/a ratio (1.856 here, ideal is about 1.633) fixes the cell height c relative to the base edge a, which is needed for the cell volume \( V_C = 6\sqrt{3}\,a^2c/2 \) type calculation.
If the calculated density is noticeably lower than 7.1 g \(cm^{-3}\), what might be wrong with the inputs?
The atomic radius, the number of atoms per cell, or the unit conversion from nm to cm (\( 1\,\text{nm} = 10^{-7}\,\text{cm} \)) may have been applied incorrectly.

notes.t: Material density comparison
pts: Density is mass per unit volume; among the options, gold is the densest of the listed materials.
defs: Density
Mass per unit volume of a material, usually expressed in kg/m³ or g/cm³.
tips: Do not confuse density with hardness or strength; a hard material is not necessarily dense.
Keep units consistent when comparing densities (e.g. g/cm³ vs kg/m³ differ by a factor of 1000).
rq: Why does diamond, despite being very hard, not have the highest density among these options?

Diamond's density (about 3.5 g/cm³) is much lower than gold's (about 19.3 g/cm³); hardness and density are independent properties, since hardness depends on bonding strength and density depends on atomic mass and packing.

notes.t: Densities of material classes
pts: Metals are generally the densest class, because their atoms are close-packed held by metallic bonding and often have large atomic masses.
Ceramics are intermediate in density, with less dense packing and often lighter elements than metals.
Polymers are the least dense class, having low packing density, often amorphous structures, and light elements (C, H, O).
Composites fall between the pure classes, with intermediate density values depending on their fibre and matrix content.
Overall ordering of density is metals > ceramics > polymers, which is shown by the ranges plotted on the log-scale chart.
defs: Close-packing
An atomic arrangement in which atoms are packed as tightly as possible, giving high density; typical of metals.
Amorphous
A material lacking long-range ordered atomic arrangement, typical of many polymers, which gives them lower packing density.
Density (ρ)
Mass per unit volume of a material, expressed in g/cm³ on this chart.
tips: Density values are in g/cm³ on a logarithmic axis; do not read the chart linearly when comparing values.
Do not assume all ceramics are less dense than all metals: some ceramics such as zirconia overlap with lower-density metals like titanium on the chart.
rq: Why would a polymer be less dense than a metal even when both have similar atomic masses per atom?
Polymers have low packing density and are often amorphous, so atoms occupy more volume per unit mass; metals are close-packed, giving higher density.
If a composite is made from a dense metal matrix versus a light polymer matrix, how would its density change?
A metal matrix would give a higher composite density and a polymer matrix a lower one, since the composite density lies between the constituent values.

xq.q: Copper is face-centred cubic with atomic radius r = 0.128 nm and atomic weight A = 63.5 g/mol. Taking Avogadro's number \(N_{A}\) = 6.022 × \(10^{23}\) mol⁻¹, calculate the theoretical density of copper in g/cm³. The atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the cell edge is a = 2√2 r.
xq.a: ≈ 8.89 g/cm³

xq.q: Tungsten is body-centred cubic with atomic radius R = 0.1371 nm and atomic weight A = 183.85 g/mol. The atoms touch along the body diagonal, so the cell edge is a = 4R/√3. Use \(N_{A}\) = 6.022 × \(10^{23}\) mol⁻¹ to calculate the density of tungsten in g/cm³.
xq.a: ≈ 19.2 g/cm³

xq.q: A hypothetical FCC metal has lattice parameter a = 0.400 nm and atomic weight A = 27 g/mol (\(N_{A}\) = 6.022 × \(10^{23}\) mol⁻¹). Which value is its density?
xq.a: 2.80 g/cm³
o: 1.40 g/cm³
0.70 g/cm³
2.80 g/cm³
9.81 g/cm³
xq.w: An FCC cell contains n = 4 atoms, so ρ = 4(27)/(6.022×10²³ × 6.4×10⁻²³ cm³) = 2.80 g/cm³; the traps are using the wrong atom count (2 for BCC, 1, or the 14 atoms visible in the drawing).

units.name: 6.10 Allotropy and phase transformation in iron
units.ov: This module covers allotropy, the ability of a solid to exist in more than one crystal structure, using iron as the key example. Pure Fe is BCC (α) at low temperature, FCC (γ) from 912 to 1394 °C, and BCC (δ) up to melting at 1538 °C. The BCC/FCC difference in packing and carbon solubility underlies the heat treatment of steel.
must: Definition: allotropy (polymorphism) is the existence of a solid in more than one distinct crystal structure, depending on temperature (and pressure).
Sequence on heating at 1 atm: α-Fe (BCC) \(\rightarrow\) γ-Fe (FCC) at 912 °C \(\rightarrow\) δ-Fe (BCC) at 1394 °C \(\rightarrow\) liquid at 1538 °C.
The structure is not monotonic with temperature: BCC appears twice with FCC in between.
α and δ are both BCC but are different phases, since they occupy different temperature ranges. The Greek labels denote structures of the same element, not different materials.
Unit cell contents: BCC has 2 atoms per cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+1\)); FCC has 4 atoms per cell (\(8\times\tfrac18+6\times\tfrac12\)).

Transformation temperatures are fixed at atmospheric pressure, so they appear as horizontal boundaries on the phase diagram. 912 and 1394 °C are solid-state transitions, while 1538 °C is melting; δ-Fe is still solid.
Pressure has a negligible effect on the solid-state boundaries over the range shown, which remain near-vertical in the solid region.
The α→γ change at 912 °C is the basis of steel heat treatment, because FCC γ-Fe dissolves far more carbon than BCC α-Fe.
Other materials show allotropy too, for example titanium (α-Ti and β-Ti).
Be able to sketch the unit cells and state which atoms sit at the corners, face centres and body centre.
conn: Crystal structure and atoms per cell link to packing: with the lattice parameter \(a\), the atomic radius is \(R=\sqrt3a/4\) (BCC) or \(R=\sqrt2a/4\) (FCC), and the packing factor is 0.68 (BCC) or 0.74 (FCC). Hence density and volume change at the 912 °C transformation.
Allotropy and carbon solubility: the BCC→FCC change at 912 °C allows more carbon to dissolve in γ-Fe, which leads to the Fe–C phase diagram, austenite/ferrite, and heat treatment.
Phase diagram reading: horizontal boundaries (temperature-fixed transitions) versus the pressure axis connect to the Gibbs phase rule and to why pressure is neglected for solids.
Allotropy in other metals (Ti) links to property changes, since a change of structure alters density, slip systems, ductility and strength.
exq: List the allotropic forms of pure iron with their crystal structures and transformation temperatures at atmospheric pressure, and state which transitions are solid-state and which is melting.
Define allotropy. Explain why α-Fe and δ-Fe are both BCC yet are regarded as different phases.

Calculate the number of atoms per unit cell for BCC and FCC. Using the atomic radius, find the lattice parameter and packing factor of each, and comment on the volume change when α-Fe transforms to γ-Fe at 912 °C.
Explain why the α→γ transformation in iron is the basis for heat treating steel, referring to carbon solubility in BCC and FCC iron.
Sketch the pressure–temperature diagram of iron, marking the α, γ, δ and liquid regions, and explain why the solid-state boundaries are nearly vertical.

notes.t: Phase transformation and allotropy in iron
pts: A material can exist in two or more distinct crystal structures; this is called allotropy (or polymorphism).
Allotropic forms change with temperature: iron is BCC at low temperature (α-Fe), FCC at intermediate temperature (γ-Fe), and BCC again at high temperature (δ-Fe) before melting.
Iron's transformation temperatures on cooling/heating are 912 °C (α↔γ), 1394 °C (γ↔δ) and 1538 °C (melting point of δ-Fe, liquid above).
Titanium also shows allotropy, with α-Ti and β-Ti phases.
defs: Allotropy / polymorphism
The ability of a solid material to exist in more than one distinct crystal structure, depending on temperature (and pressure).
BCC (body-centred cubic)
A crystal structure with atoms at the cube corners and one atom at the body centre (e.g. α-Fe, δ-Fe).
FCC (face-centred cubic)
A crystal structure with atoms at the cube corners and at the centre of each face (e.g. γ-Fe).
tips: Do not confuse the phase labels: α, γ and δ denote different crystal structures of the same element, not different materials.
Remember that the BCC structure appears twice in iron (α and δ) with FCC in between; the structure is not monotonic with temperature.
rq: Why does the same iron atom arrangement change from BCC to FCC as it is heated from 912 °C to 1394 °C?
Atoms gain thermal energy; the FCC structure is more densely packed/lower energy at this temperature range, so it becomes the stable form.
If you cool pure iron from the liquid state, what sequence of crystal structures do you pass through?
Liquid → δ-Fe (BCC) at 1538 °C → γ-Fe (FCC) at 1394 °C → α-Fe (BCC) at 912 °C.

notes.t: Phase transformations in iron (allotropy of Fe)
pts: Pure iron changes crystal structure with temperature: BCC (α) at room temperature, FCC (γ) between 912 and 1394 °C, then BCC (δ) up to melting.
Each allotropic transformation occurs at a fixed temperature at atmospheric pressure, shown as horizontal boundaries on the phase diagram.
The α-Fe to γ-Fe transformation at 912 °C is the basis for heat treating steel, since FCC γ-Fe can dissolve carbon far more than BCC α-Fe.
Pressure has a negligible effect on these solid-state boundaries at the pressures shown, which span many orders of magnitude but remain near-vertical in the diagram's solid region.
defs: Allotropy (polymorphism)
The ability of a solid element to exist in more than one crystal structure depending on temperature and pressure.
BCC (body-centred cubic)
Cubic crystal structure with one atom at each corner and one at the cube centre; 2 atoms per unit cell.
FCC (face-centred cubic)
Cubic crystal structure with atoms at the corners and at the centre of each face; 4 atoms per unit cell.
tips: Do not confuse the allotropic transition temperatures (912 °C, 1394 °C) with the melting point (1538 °C); δ-Fe is still a solid.
Remember that both α-Fe and δ-Fe are BCC but are different phases (different temperature ranges), so BCC does not imply the same phase.
rq: Why does α-Fe (BCC) change to γ-Fe (FCC) on heating past 912 °C, even though both are solids?

The FCC structure has a lower free energy at that temperature range, so the more stable phase changes; the entropy term from atomic vibration favours the more open/close-packed FCC arrangement above 912 °C.
What would happen to the transformation temperatures if the iron were heated at very high pressure, e.g. \(10^{4}\) bar?
The phase boundaries shift; pressure changes the transition temperatures, and the diagram shows the boundaries are nearly horizontal at these pressures, so the effect is small in this range.

xq.q: A sample of pure iron is heated slowly from 20 °C to 1500 °C at atmospheric pressure. Which sequence of solid crystal structures does it pass through?
xq.a: BCC → FCC → BCC
o: BCC → FCC only, then it melts at 1394 °C
FCC → BCC → FCC
BCC → FCC → BCC
BCC → FCC → liquid at 1394 °C
xq.w: Iron is BCC (α) below 912 °C, FCC (γ) from 912 to 1394 °C and BCC (δ) from 1394 °C up to melting at 1538 °C; the trap is confusing the 1394 °C transformation with melting.

xq.q: Pure iron is held at 1450 °C at atmospheric pressure. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: It is solid δ-Fe with a BCC structure.
o: It is liquid, because 1450 °C is above the 1394 °C transformation.
It is solid γ-Fe with an FCC structure.
It is solid α-Fe, since BCC means the same phase at any temperature.
It is solid δ-Fe with a BCC structure.
xq.w: 1450 °C lies between 1394 °C and the melting point of 1538 °C, so iron is solid BCC δ-Fe; the traps are mistaking 1394 °C for melting and treating all BCC iron as α-Fe.
s: This is the δ-Fe range, which is BCC and solid

xq.q: Explain what is meant by allotropy, using pure iron as the example, and explain why the α→γ transformation at 912 °C is the basis for the heat treatment of steel. Also explain why the transformation temperatures appear as near-vertical boundaries on an iron pressure–temperature diagram.
xq.a: Allotropy is the ability of a solid to exist in more than one crystal structure depending on temperature (and pressure). Iron is BCC (α) below 912 °C, FCC (γ) between 912 and 1394 °C and BCC (δ) from 1394 °C to melting at 1538 °C. Heating steel through 912 °C changes BCC α-Fe into FCC γ-Fe, which can dissolve far more carbon than α-Fe. Cooling back through the transformation lets the structure and properties be controlled, which is what heat treatment exploits. The boundaries are near-vertical because pressure has a negligible effect on these solid-state transformation temperatures over the pressures shown.
s: Definition of allotropy: more than one crystal structure with temperature/pressure (1)
Sequence BCC α, FCC γ, BCC δ with 912 and 1394 °C (1)
γ-Fe (FCC) dissolves much more carbon than α-Fe (BCC) (1)
This is used to control the structure when cooling through the transformation (1)
Pressure has a negligible effect on the solid-state boundaries (1)
