Electrical conductivity: \(\sigma = n e \mu\) (more generally \(\sigma=\sum n_i q_i\mu_i\)), with resistivity \(\rho=1/\sigma\) and Ohm's law \(J=\sigma E\)
Metals: resistivity rises with temperature (more phonon scattering), roughly \(\rho(T)=\rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]\); impurities add a temperature-independent term (Matthiessen's rule)
Semiconductors: carrier concentration is thermally activated, \(n\propto \exp(-E_g/2k_BT)\), so conductivity increases with temperature; doping (n-type, p-type) creates extrinsic carriers
Thermal conductivity: in metals mainly electrons, in insulators mainly phonons; Wiedemann-Franz law \(\kappa/(\sigma T)=L\approx 2.44\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,\Omega\,K^{-2}}\)
Fourier's law \(q=-\kappa\,dT/dx\); thermal expansion \(\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T\) and thermal stress \(\sigma=E\alpha\Delta T\) when constrained
Optical behaviour: photon absorbed if \(h\nu\ge E_g\), with \(E=hc/\lambda\); metals are opaque and reflective, wide-gap insulators are transparent, semiconductors absorb above their gap energy
Light at an interface: \(n=c/v\), reflectivity \(R=\left(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\right)^2\), and \(T+R+A=1\) with Beer-Lambert attenuation \(I=I_0e^{-\beta x}\)
Colour and transparency arise from which wavelengths are absorbed, transmitted or reflected (impurities and defects can introduce gap states)
conn: Band gap links all three property types: it sets carrier density (electrical), the absorption edge (optical), and, via free electrons, the electronic part of heat conduction (thermal)
Wiedemann-Franz ties electrical and thermal conductivity in metals, so alloying that raises resistivity also lowers thermal conductivity
Temperature affects everything: phonon scattering lowers metal conductivity, thermal activation raises semiconductor conductivity, and thermal expansion gives thermal stress in design
Optical absorption by electron excitation across \(E_g\) underlies photoconductivity, LEDs and solar cells, combining optical and electrical ideas
exq: Using band diagrams, explain why copper, silicon and diamond have very different electrical conductivities, and why silicon's conductivity changes with temperature in the opposite way to copper's.
Calculate the longest wavelength of light that can excite an electron across the gap in silicon (\(E_g=1.1\) eV) and state whether silicon is transparent to visible light.
A copper wire has conductivity \(5.96\times10^7\) S/m at 20 °C. Estimate its thermal conductivity at 300 K using the Wiedemann-Franz law, and explain why the value differs for an alloy such as brass.
A 2 m steel rail (\(\alpha=12\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\), \(E=200\) GPa) is rigidly constrained and heated by 40 K. Find the expansion if free and the thermal stress if constrained.

Glass with refractive index 1.5 transmits light through a 5 mm thickness. Calculate the reflection loss at each surface and the overall transmitted fraction given an absorption coefficient \(\beta=10\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\).

units.name: 9.2 Electrical conduction in metals: Ohm's law and electron scattering
units.ov: This material develops electrical conduction in metals from the macroscopic Ohm's law (V = IR, resistivity, conductivity) to the geometry-independent form J = σε. It then gives a microscopic picture: electrons accelerate in a field but are scattered by defects and thermal vibrations, so they reach an average drift velocity \(v_{D}\) = μ_eε. Scattering is what produces resistance, and it links the microscopic model back to the macroscopic quantities.
must: Ohm's law \(V = IR\), and \(R\) depends on geometry while \(\rho\) does not
Resistivity \(\rho = RA/\ell\) in Ω·m, and conductivity \(\sigma = 1/\rho\) in S/m
Current density \(J = I/A\) (A/m²) and electric field \(\varepsilon = V/\ell\) (V/m)
Ohm's law in field form \(J = \sigma\varepsilon\), which holds for a uniform field and constant σ (fixed T and material)
Force on an electron \(F = e\mathcal{E}\) with \(e=-1.6\times10^{-19}\) C, so the force is opposite to the field; use \(F = ma\) for acceleration
In a perfect crystal at T = 0 K the electron wave is not scattered, so there is no resistance (Bragg-like reflection gives the energy gap)
Scattering centres are dislocations, impurities, surfaces and thermally displaced ions; thermal scattering occurs in a perfect crystal at any T > 0 K
Drift velocity is the average carrier velocity superimposed on random thermal motion: \(v_D = \mu_e\varepsilon\), with μ in m²/V·s
Scattering must be included to get Ohm's law; more scattering means lower mobility, lower σ and higher ρ
Unit discipline: convert lengths to m and areas to m², and distinguish A (area) from A (amperes)
conn: Macroscopic to field form: \(R = \rho\ell/A\) with \(V=\varepsilon\ell\) and \(I=JA\) turns \(V=IR\) into \(J=\sigma\varepsilon\)
Microscopic to macroscopic: \(v_D=\mu_e\varepsilon\) combined with \(J=\sigma\varepsilon\) gives \(\sigma = n e \mu_e\) (carrier density times charge times mobility)
Scattering sources link to resistivity: defects (impurities, dislocations) and temperature (thermal vibrations) both raise ρ by lowering mobility
Newton's law and scattering: free acceleration \(a = e\mathcal{E}/m\) is interrupted by collisions, giving a constant average drift velocity rather than ever-increasing speed
exq: A copper wire of length 2.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm carries 5 A with a 0.34 V drop across it. Calculate R, ρ, σ, J and the electric field.
Explain why a perfect crystal at 0 K would have zero resistivity, and give three reasons why real metals have non-zero resistivity at room temperature.
An electron sits in a 0.5 m bar with 1.5 V across it. Calculate the field, the force (with direction) and the initial acceleration. Why does it not keep accelerating?
Given μ_e = 4.3×10⁻³ m²/V·s for copper and a field of 0.05 V/m, find the drift velocity. Then, using σ = 5.9×10⁷ S/m, find J and the electron density n.
Distinguish resistance from resistivity, and show how \(V=IR\) is converted into \(J=\sigma\varepsilon\), stating the assumptions.

notes.t: Electrical Conduction: Ohm's Law, Resistivity and Conductivity
pts: Ohm's law relates voltage drop across a conductor to the current flowing through it and its resistance.
Resistivity is an intrinsic material property, so it does not depend on the sample's size or shape.
Resistivity is found from the measured resistance scaled by cross-sectional area and divided by the current flow path length.
Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, so it measures how readily a material conducts current.
defs: Resistivity (ρ)
An intrinsic material property giving the resistance of a unit-area, unit-length sample; independent of sample size and geometry.
Conductivity (σ)
The reciprocal of resistivity; a measure of a material's ability to conduct electric current.
eqs: Ohm's law: voltage drop across a conductor
\(V\) = voltage drop (V = J/C); \(I\) = current (A = C/s); \(R\) = resistance (Ω)
Resistivity from resistance, area and length
\(\rho\) = resistivity (Ω·m); \(R\) = resistance (Ω); \(A\) = cross-sectional area of current flow (m²); \(\ell\) = current flow path length (m)
tips: Keep units consistent: resistivity uses \(\ell\) in metres and \(A\) in m², giving Ω·m, not Ω.
Do not confuse resistance (\(R\), depends on geometry) with resistivity (\(\rho\), intrinsic); only \(\rho\) is a material property.
rq: Why is resistivity useful for comparing materials when resistance is not?

Resistance depends on sample length and cross-sectional area, whereas resistivity is an intrinsic material property independent of geometry, so it allows fair comparison between different samples and materials.
What would happen to the resistance of a wire if its length doubled while its cross-sectional area stayed the same, and why?
Using \(R = \rho\ell/A\), resistance doubles because resistance is directly proportional to path length.

notes.t: Current density, electric field and Ohm's law in current form
pts: Ohm's law can be written in terms of current density J, conductivity σ and electric field ε, showing J is proportional to ε
Current density is current per unit cross-sectional area, so it behaves like a flux
Electric field potential (voltage gradient) is voltage drop per unit length of the conductor
Charge carriers are mainly electrons in most solids, while ions can also carry charge, particularly in liquid solutions
defs: Current density (J)
Current per unit cross-sectional area, J = I/A, a flux-like quantity measuring how much charge flows through a given area.
Electric field potential (ε)
Voltage drop per unit length along a conductor, ε = V/ℓ (or ΔV/Δℓ).
Conductivity (σ)
A material property describing how readily the material conducts electric current under an applied electric field.
eqs: Ohm's law in current density form
J = current density (A/\(m^{2}\)); \sigma = conductivity (S/m); \varepsilon = electric field potential (V/m)
J = current density (A/\(m^{2}\)); I = current (A); A = cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
\varepsilon = electric field potential (V/m); V = voltage (V); \ell = length (m)
tips: Watch units: current density is A/m² (per area), not A; electric field potential is V/m, so convert lengths to metres.
Ohm's law J = σε assumes a uniform field and constant conductivity (temperature and material held constant); ions, not just electrons, may carry current in liquids.
rq: Why does a larger conductivity σ give a larger current density J for the same electric field ε?
Since J = σε, J is directly proportional to σ; a more conductive material lets more charge flow per unit area for the same driving field.
If the same voltage is applied across a conductor twice as long, what happens to the electric field potential and the current density?
ε = V/ℓ halves, so J = σε halves (assuming σ is unchanged).

notes.t: Microscopic model of conduction: electron in a perfect crystal
pts: An electron in an applied field experiences a force pulling it toward the positive end of the bar, so it accelerates per Newton's law.
In a perfect crystal at T=0 the electron behaves as a wave that is not scattered by the periodic array of Cu ions, so it does not collide with atoms.
The energy gap arises because electron waves that would propagate are reflected by the planes of atoms, analogous to Bragg reflection of X-rays.
defs: Electric field
Voltage gradient across a conductor, equal to the applied voltage divided by length; it produces a force on charge carriers.
eqs: Force on an electron in an electric field
F = force (N); e = electron charge (C), e = -1.6\times10^{-19} C; \mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m)
\mathcal{E} = electric field (V/m); V = applied voltage (V); L = bar length (m)
Newton's second law for the electron
F = force (N); m = electron mass (kg); a = acceleration (m/\(s^{2}\))
tips: The electron charge is negative (\( e = -1.6\times10^{-19}\) C), so the force points opposite to the field direction; keep the sign when writing F = eE.
Use the field \( \mathcal{E} = V/L \) with V in volts and L in metres; mixing mm and m gives errors of 1000.
rq: If electrons accelerate freely in a perfect crystal, why does the bar not show infinite current under constant voltage?
Real crystals are not perfect: at T>0 thermal vibrations and defects scatter electrons, limiting drift velocity and giving finite resistance. The perfect-crystal picture applies at T=0 only.
Why does the electron wave not collide with the positive Cu ions even though they attract it?
Electrons behave as waves in a periodic lattice; waves at certain energies are Bragg-reflected by atomic planes, so they propagate without scattering from individual atoms.

notes.t: Scattering from Defects and Drift Velocity
pts: The simple free-electron model J = σε alone does not predict Ohm's law; electron scattering must be included.
Defects such as dislocations, impurities and surfaces scatter electrons, which stop, deflect and restart, giving resistance.
Even a perfect crystal scatters electrons above 0 K because thermal vibrations displace the ions from their periodic positions.
The stop-go motion of electrons is described by an averaged velocity called the drift velocity, proportional to the applied field.
defs: Scattering
The process by which electrons collide with defects or lattice imperfections, changing their direction and/or stopping, thereby limiting their velocity under an applied field.
Scattering centre
A defect or irregularity in a crystal (dislocation, impurity, surface, or thermally displaced ion) that deflects conduction electrons.
Drift velocity
The average velocity of charge carriers in a material under an applied electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion.
eqs: Drift velocity of electrons in an electric field
\(V_{D}\) = drift velocity (m/s); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (\(m^{2}\)/V·s); \varepsilon = electric field (V/m)
Current density (simple model, fails to give Ohm's law without scattering)
J = current density (A/\(m^{2}\)); \sigma = conductivity (S/m); \varepsilon = electric field (V/m)
tips: Mobility μ_e has units m²/V·s, not m/s; check units when combining μ_e with the field ε (V/m) to get drift velocity in m/s.
Scattering occurs even in perfect crystals when T > 0 K; do not assume defects are the only source of resistance.
rq: Why does a perfect crystal at absolute zero have no electrical resistance, but one at room temperature does?
At 0 K ions sit exactly on their periodic lattice positions, so electrons are not scattered; above 0 K thermal vibrations displace ions, breaking periodicity and scattering electrons.
What would happen to the drift velocity if the mobility of electrons doubled while the applied field stayed the same?
The drift velocity would double, since \(V_{D}\) = μ_e ε is directly proportional to mobility at fixed field.

xq.q: A straight copper wire of length \( \ell = 5.0\ \mathrm{m} \) and uniform cross-sectional area \( A = 2.5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2} \) is measured to have a resistance \( R = 0.40\ \Omega \). Find the electrical conductivity \( \sigma \) of the copper, in S/m.

A wire of conductivity \( \sigma = 5.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{S/m} \) and cross-sectional area \( A = 2.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2} \) carries a steady current \( I = 10\ \mathrm{A} \). Using the current-density form of Ohm's law \( J=\sigma\varepsilon \), where \( J \) is current density and \( \varepsilon \) is the electric field, find the voltage drop across a 3.0 m length of the wire, in V.
A uniform copper bar is cut to half its original length, keeping the same cross-sectional area and temperature. Which statement about its resistance \( R \) and resistivity \( \rho \) is correct?
xq.a: R halves and ρ is unchanged
o: R halves and ρ halves
R halves and ρ is unchanged
R doubles and ρ is unchanged
R and ρ are both unchanged
xq.w: R = ρℓ/A is proportional to length so it halves, while ρ is an intrinsic material property and does not depend on size; the trap is treating ρ as geometry-dependent like R.

units.name: 9.3 Heat transport and the Wiedemann-Franz law
units.ov: Heat in metals is carried mainly by free (Fermi-gas) electrons, which are scattered by the same mechanisms that cause electrical resistance. Kinetic theory of the electron gas gives \(\kappa_{Elec}\) and the Drude \(\sigma\); their ratio cancels \(n\) and \(\tau\), giving the Wiedemann-Franz law \(\kappa/\sigma = LT\) with a universal Lorenz number that experiment confirms to within about 15%.
must: Wiedemann-Franz law: \(\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\left(\frac{k_B}{e}\right)^2T = LT\), so \(\kappa/\sigma\) is proportional to \(T\)
Lorenz number: \(L=\frac{\kappa}{\sigma T}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\left(\frac{k_B}{e}\right)^2=2.45\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,\Omega\,K^{-2}}\); be able to compute it from \(k_B\) and \(e\)
Electronic thermal conductivity: \(\kappa_{Elec}=\frac13 C_e\langle vl\rangle=\frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T\tau}{3m}\)
Electrical conductivity (Drude): \(\sigma=\frac{ne^2\tau}{m}\); dividing gives \(\kappa/\sigma\) with \(n,\tau,m\) cancelling, which is why the result is universal
Mean free path: \(l=v_F\tau\), where \(v_F\) is the Fermi velocity, not the thermal velocity
Electronic specific heat \(C_e=\frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T}{2E_F}=\frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T}{m v_F^2}\), which gives the \(\frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2T}{3mv_F^2}v_Fl\) form of \(\kappa\)
Physical reason for the law: the same electrons and same scattering carry both charge and heat, so good electrical conductors are good thermal conductors
Validity: needs electrons to dominate heat transport (metals); it fails where phonons carry heat (insulators, semiconductors, and metals when phonon contribution is significant)
Experiment: Ag, Au, Cd, Cu and Mo have \(L\) within about 0-15% of theory (Mo deviates most), and \(L\) rises slightly from 273 K to 373 K, so the law is approximate, not exact
Units: \(L\) in W Ω K⁻², \(\sigma\) in S m⁻¹ = Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹, \(\tau\) in seconds, and \(T\) in kelvin
conn: Drude electrical conductivity with kinetic-theory thermal conductivity: both depend on \(\tau\) and \(n\), and the ratio removes them, so measuring \(\sigma\) lets you predict \(\kappa\) at a given \(T\)
Fermi-gas electronic specific heat (linear in \(T\)) with \(\kappa=\frac13 C_e v_F l\): the linear \(T\) in \(C_e\) is the origin of the \(T\) in \(\kappa/\sigma\)
Mean free path \(l=v_F\tau\) with scattering mechanisms (phonons, impurities): temperature-dependent \(\tau\) changes both \(\kappa\) and \(\sigma\), but \(L\) stays roughly constant
Electron versus phonon heat transport: deviations of \(L\) from 2.45×10⁻⁸ indicate a lattice contribution or inelastic scattering
exq: Derive the Wiedemann-Franz law from \(\kappa_{Elec}=\pi^2 n k_B^2T\tau/3m\) and \(\sigma=ne^2\tau/m\), and evaluate \(L\) numerically using \(k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\) J/K and \(e=1.60\times10^{-19}\) C.

Copper has \(\sigma=5.9\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}\) at 300 K. Use the Wiedemann-Franz law to estimate \(\kappa\), and compare it with the measured value of about 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, with the percentage difference.
A metal has \(v_F=1.5\times10^6\) m/s and \(\tau=2.5\times10^{-14}\) s. Calculate the mean free path, and then \(\kappa_{Elec}\) if \(n=8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) at 300 K.
Explain why the Wiedemann-Franz law works well for metals but fails for insulators, and give two reasons why experimental \(L\) values differ from 2.45×10⁻⁸ and vary with temperature.
The electrical conductivity of a metal halves when it is heated from 273 K to 373 K. Assuming the Wiedemann-Franz law holds, predict the new thermal conductivity relative to the old one.

notes.t: Heat Transport in Metals
pts: Mean free path of electrons equals Fermi velocity times scattering time.
In metals, heat is carried mainly by free electrons, dominating over phonon (lattice vibration) contribution.
Thermal resistance arises from the same electron scattering mechanisms that cause electrical resistance, so thermal and electrical conductivity are linked.
The ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity is proportional to temperature, giving the Wiedemann-Franz law.
defs: Mean free path (l)
The average distance an electron travels between scattering events, given by the Fermi velocity multiplied by the scattering time.
Fermi velocity (\(v_{F}\))
The velocity of electrons at the Fermi energy; the speed of scattered electrons in the thermal conductivity expression.
Phonon
A quantum of lattice vibration that carries heat in materials; a minor heat carrier in metals compared with free electrons.
Lorenz number (L)
The ratio of thermal conductivity to electrical conductivity times temperature, L = K/(σT); constant for metals per the Wiedemann-Franz law.
eqs: Mean free path of free electrons
l = mean free path (m); \(v_{F}\) = Fermi velocity (m/s); \tau = scattering time (s)
\kappa_{Elec} = \frac{1}{3} C_e \langle v l \rangle = \frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T}{3 m v_F^2} v_F l = \frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T \tau}{3m}

\(\kappa_{Elec}\) = electronic thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)); \(C_{e}\) = electronic specific heat (J/(m³·K)); v = electron speed (m/s); l = mean free path (m); n = electron number density (m⁻³); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (J/K); T = temperature (K); m = electron mass (kg); \tau = scattering time (s)
Wiedemann-Franz law (ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity)
\kappa = thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)); \sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (J/K); e = electron charge (C); T = temperature (K)
L = Lorenz number (W·Ω/K²); \kappa = thermal conductivity (W/(m·K)); \sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); T = temperature (K)
tips: Watch units: the Lorenz number L = κ/(σT) has units W·Ω/K², and τ must be in seconds, not as a frequency.
The Wiedemann-Franz relation only approximates behaviour; it applies when electrons dominate heat and charge transport (typically metals), not in insulators where phonons dominate.
rq: Why does the Wiedemann-Franz law make κ/σ independent of the scattering time τ?
Both κ and σ are proportional to τ (the same scattering processes limit both), so τ cancels in the ratio.
Why are free electrons, rather than phonons, the dominant heat carriers in metals?
Free electrons have high velocities and long mean free paths and large numbers, so their contribution to heat transport far exceeds that of lattice vibrations.

notes.t: Wiedemann-Franz Law: comparison with experiment
pts: Wiedemann-Franz law predicts a fixed ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity for metals, the Lorentz number L, which is nearly independent of metal and temperature.
The theoretical value of L from free-electron theory is 2.45 × 10⁻⁸ WΩK⁻².
Experimental L values for Ag, Au, Cd, Cu and Mo lie close to the theoretical value, typically within about 0–15%, with Mo deviating most.
Experimental L values generally rise slightly from 0 °C (273 K) to 100 °C (373 K), showing a small temperature dependence not captured by the simple law.
defs: Lorentz number (L)
The ratio of thermal conductivity to the product of electrical conductivity and absolute temperature, L = K/(σT); for free electrons it is a universal constant of about 2.45 × 10⁻⁸ WΩK⁻².
eqs: L = Lorentz number (W Ω K⁻²); K = thermal conductivity (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹); σ = electrical conductivity (S m⁻¹ or Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹); T = absolute temperature (K); \(k_{B}\) = Boltzmann constant (J K⁻¹); e = elementary charge (C)
tips: Check units: L is in W Ω K⁻², not W m⁻¹ K⁻¹; mixing conductivity units (S vs Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹) gives wrong results.
The law is only approximate; experimental L values differ from 2.45 × 10⁻⁸ and vary with temperature, so do not state it as exact.
rq: Why does the Lorentz number come out nearly the same for different metals, even though their conductivities differ greatly?
Both thermal and electrical conduction are carried by the same free electrons, so their ratio depends only on fundamental constants (\(k_{B}\) and e), not on the material.
Why might the measured L for molybdenum (2.61 at 273 K) exceed the free-electron value?
Deviations arise because real electrons are not perfectly free: scattering by phonons and imperfections affects thermal and electrical transport differently, and band structure matters.

xq.q: Copper at \( T = 300\ \mathrm{K} \) has electrical conductivity \( \sigma = 6.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{S/m} \). Assuming electrons dominate heat transport and using the free-electron Lorentz number \( L = 2.45\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,\Omega\,K^{-2}} \), estimate the thermal conductivity \( \kappa \) in W/(m·K).

A metal sample has thermal conductivity \( \kappa = 367.5\ \mathrm{W/(m\,K)} \) and electrical conductivity \( \sigma = 5.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{S/m} \). Assuming the Wiedemann-Franz law with \( L = 2.45\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,\Omega\,K^{-2}} \), find the absolute temperature \( T \) of the sample, in K.

Electrons carry both charge and heat in a metal. Using \( \kappa = \frac{\pi^2 n k_B^2 T\tau}{3m} \) and \( \sigma = \frac{n e^2 \tau}{m} \), where \( n \) is electron density, \( \tau \) scattering time, \( m \) electron mass, \( k_B \) Boltzmann constant, \( e \) electron charge and \( T \) temperature, show that \( \kappa/\sigma \) is proportional to \( T \) and independent of the metal. Explain why this ratio fails for insulators.
xq.a: Dividing: κ/σ = (π² n \(k_{B}\)² T τ/3m)/(n e² τ/m). The n, τ and m cancel, leaving κ/σ = (π²/3)(\(k_{B}\)/e)² T. Everything except T is a universal constant, so the ratio (Lorentz number L = κ/σT = 2.45×10⁻⁸ W Ω K⁻²) is the same for all metals. It cancels because the same electron scattering controls both thermal and electrical resistance. In insulators heat is carried mainly by phonons, not free electrons, so the electron-based derivation does not apply.
s: Result (π²/3)(\(k_{B}\)/e)²T, so κ/σ ∝ T with universal constant L
Same scattering limits heat and charge transport
Insulators: phonons dominate heat, law invalid

units.name: 9.4 Conductivity of metals and semiconductors: intrinsic and extrinsic
units.ov: This module covers how electrical conductivity arises in metals and semiconductors, using the common form \(\sigma = \sum n|e|\mu\) (carrier concentration × charge × mobility). It contrasts metals (fixed n, mobility falling with T) with intrinsic semiconductors (electron-hole pairs, n = p) and extrinsic doped semiconductors (majority carriers set by dopants). The temperature dependence ties these together: freeze-out, extrinsic plateau, then intrinsic dominance.
must: Metal conductivity: \(\sigma = n|e|\mu_e\); semiconductor conductivity: \(\sigma = n|e|\mu_e + p|e|\mu_h\), and never omit the hole term in intrinsic material
Intrinsic semiconductor: electron-hole pairs are created thermally, so \(n = p\); the hole is a valence-band vacancy acting as a positive carrier
Temperature trends differ: metal \(\sigma\) falls with T (more scattering, lower \(\mu\)); semiconductor \(\sigma\) rises because the increase in carrier concentration outweighs the fall in mobility
Mobility is drift velocity per unit field (m²/V·s); it is reduced by scattering (phonons, defects, dislocations) and depends on effective mass; \(\mu_e \neq \mu_h\) in general

n-type doping (e.g. P, 5 valence electrons, donors) gives \(n \gg p\) and \(\sigma \approx n|e|\mu_e\); p-type doping (e.g. B, 3 valence electrons, acceptors) gives \(p \gg n\) and \(\sigma \approx p|e|\mu_h\)

Three temperature regimes in extrinsic material: freeze-out (below about 100 K, dopants not ionised, low \(\sigma\)), extrinsic plateau (about 150–450 K, n fixed by dopant level), intrinsic (above about 450 K, band-gap excitation dominates and doped and undoped curves converge)

Doping creates donor or acceptor levels that lower the activation energy for carriers, so \(\sigma\) rises with doping level; the regime boundaries shift with dopant concentration (the notes' ranges are for about \(10^{21}\,\text{m}^{-3}\))
Compound semiconductors (III-V such as GaAs and InSb, II-VI such as CdS and ZnTe): a larger electronegativity difference between the elements gives a wider band gap
Unit discipline: n and p in \(\text{m}^{-3}\) (convert from \(\text{cm}^{-3}\) by ×10⁶), \(\mu\) in \(\text{m}^2/(\text{V·s})\), giving \(\sigma\) in S/m
Periodic table context: Si and Ge are Group IV semimetals/semiconductors on the metal/non-metal boundary; Group IV are the intrinsic examples, while Group III and V elements act as dopants
conn: Conductivity equation and temperature: \(\sigma\) depends on both n(T) and \(\mu(T)\). In metals n is constant so \(\mu\) controls the trend; in semiconductors n(T) wins, except on the extrinsic plateau, where n is fixed and the fall in \(\mu\) can slightly reduce \(\sigma\).

Doping and temperature regimes: dopant valence (5 or 3) determines the majority carrier, which then fixes which mobility to use. At high T the intrinsic contribution restores \(n \approx p\) and the doped material loses its extrinsic character.

Effective mass links band structure to mobility: a lighter effective mass gives a higher mobility, which explains why \(\mu_e \neq \mu_h\) and why mobility differs between materials, feeding into both the metal and semiconductor \(\sigma\) formulae.
Periodic table position and electronegativity difference determine band gap and the type of semiconductor, which sets the carrier generation and the intrinsic conductivity.
exq: Explain why the electrical conductivity of copper decreases with temperature while that of silicon increases. Why does a heavily deformed (dislocation-rich) piece of pure Cu have lower conductivity than an annealed one?

An intrinsic semiconductor has \(n = p = 1.5\times10^{16}\,\text{m}^{-3}\), \(\mu_e = 0.14\,\text{m}^2/\text{V·s}\) and \(\mu_h = 0.05\,\text{m}^2/\text{V·s}\). Calculate \(\sigma\), and the fraction due to holes.

Silicon is doped with \(10^{21}\,\text{m}^{-3}\) phosphorus atoms. State the type of semiconductor, the majority carrier, and estimate \(\sigma\) in the extrinsic region (take \(\mu_e = 0.14\,\text{m}^2/\text{V·s}\)). How would it change if boron were used instead, and which mobility would you use?

Sketch log carrier concentration (or \(\sigma\)) against temperature for n-type Si and for undoped Si. Label freeze-out, extrinsic and intrinsic regions, give approximate temperature ranges, and explain what happens physically in each. How would the curve shift if the doping were increased?
Explain why GaAs and CdS have wider band gaps than Si or Ge, referring to electronegativity difference, and state what type of compound semiconductor each is.

notes.t: Electrical conductivity of metals and semiconductors
pts: In metals, conductivity depends on electron concentration and electron mobility; mobility falls as temperature rises because scattering increases.
Mobility in metals depends on scattering centres and the effective mass of electrons in the conduction band.
Sample defects such as dislocations reduce a metal's conductivity even if it is pure Cu.
In semiconductors both electrons (conduction band) and holes (valence band) carry charge, and their mobilities differ between materials.
Semiconductor conductivity increases with temperature because the increase in carrier concentration outweighs the drop in mobility.
defs: Mobility
The average drift velocity of charge carriers per unit electric field; reduced by scattering centres and influenced by effective mass.
Effective mass
The apparent mass of an electron or hole in a crystal lattice, determining how readily it responds to an applied field.
Holes
Vacancies in the valence band that behave as positive charge carriers in semiconductors.
eqs: \sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); n = concentration of electrons (\(m^{-3}\)); |e| = magnitude of electron charge (C); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (\(m^{2}\)/(V·s))

\sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); n = electron concentration (\(m^{-3}\)); p = hole concentration (\(m^{-3}\)); |e| = electron charge magnitude (C); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (\(m^{2}\)/(V·s)); \(\mu_{h}\) = hole mobility (\(m^{2}\)/(V·s))
tips: Do not assume mobility is the same for electrons and holes or across semiconductors; they differ due to effective mass.
Metal conductivity decreases with temperature, but semiconductor conductivity increases; do not apply the same trend to both.
rq: Why does metal conductivity fall as temperature rises, even though the electron concentration stays roughly constant?
Higher temperature increases lattice vibrations (phonons) and thus scattering of electrons, lowering their mobility \(\mu_e\).
Why does semiconductor conductivity rise with temperature when mobility also falls?
Thermal excitation greatly increases the concentrations \(n\) and \(p\) of carriers, and this increase dominates the mobility reduction.
What would happen to the conductivity of a semiconductor if only electrons, not holes, were present?
Conductivity would be \(\sigma = n|e|\mu_e\) only, so the hole term is lost and conductivity would be smaller for the same total carriers.

notes.t: Intrinsic Semiconductors
pts: Pure (intrinsic) semiconductors such as silicon and germanium are Group IV materials.
Compound semiconductors are formed from combinations of elements, commonly III-V (e.g., GaAs, InSb) or II-VI (e.g., CdS, ZnTe).
A larger electronegativity difference between the constituent elements gives a wider energy gap.
defs: Intrinsic semiconductor
A pure semiconductor material with no deliberate impurities, whose electrical properties are determined by the material itself (e.g., silicon or germanium).
Compound semiconductor
A semiconductor made from two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio, such as III-V (GaAs) or II-VI (CdS) compounds.
tips: Do not confuse intrinsic (pure) semiconductors with extrinsic (doped) ones; the examples here are all undoped materials.
Remember the trend is electronegativity difference, not the absolute electronegativity values, when relating to energy gap.
rq: Why does a larger electronegativity difference between the elements in a compound semiconductor lead to a wider energy gap?

A larger electronegativity difference means more ionic character in the bonding, with electrons more strongly localised on one atom. This increases the separation between bonding (valence) and antibonding (conduction) states, widening the band gap.
Why are silicon and germanium called Group IV materials, and what does that imply about their bonding?
They have four valence electrons, so each atom forms four covalent bonds with neighbours, giving a tetrahedral covalent structure.

notes.t: The Periodic Table
pts: Elements are arranged by atomic number and grouped by shared chemical properties, with colour-coded classes such as alkali metals, transition metals, non-metals and noble gases.
Groups 1 and 2 are the alkali metals and alkaline earth metals; these are highly reactive metals on the left of the table.
Transition metals occupy the central block, and the rare earths (lanthanides and actinides) are shown as separate rows below the main table.
Non-metals and noble gases lie on the right of the table, with noble gases being the chemically inert group in the final column.
Semimetals (metalloids) such as silicon and germanium sit on the boundary between metals and non-metals, which is relevant to electrical behaviour.
defs: Alkali metals
Group 1 elements (e.g. Li, Na, K) that are soft, highly reactive metals with a single valence electron.
Transition metals
Elements in the central block of the periodic table (e.g. Fe, Cu, Ni) with partially filled d-electron shells, typically forming strong, hard metals.
Noble gases
Group 18 elements (e.g. He, Ne, Ar) with full outer electron shells, making them chemically inert.
Semimetals
Elements (e.g. B, Si, Ge) with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, often acting as semiconductors.
tips: Do not confuse alkali metals (Group 1) with alkaline earth metals (Group 2); the former have one valence electron, the latter two.
Rare earths shown below the main table are not placed in the transition metal block; remember they are separate series in exams.
rq: Why are noble gases chemically inert while alkali metals are highly reactive?
Noble gases have full outer electron shells and so need no electrons gained or lost, whereas alkali metals have one valence electron they readily lose to form stable ions.
Why are semimetals such as silicon useful in electronic devices?
Their electrical conductivity lies between metals and insulators and can be controlled by doping, making them semiconductors.

notes.t: Electron and hole migration in intrinsic semiconductors
pts: In an intrinsic semiconductor, thermal energy breaks a covalent bond, creating a free electron and a hole as an electron-hole pair.
Under an applied electric field, electrons move toward the positive terminal while holes effectively move toward the negative terminal, both contributing to current.
Total conductivity is the sum of electron and hole contributions, each proportional to carrier concentration and mobility.
Electrons and holes are created in equal numbers in an intrinsic semiconductor, so n equals p.
defs: Hole
A vacancy left in the valence band when an electron is excited across the band gap; it behaves as a positive charge carrier with mobility μ_h.
Intrinsic semiconductor
A pure semiconductor (e.g. Si) in which conduction arises only from thermally generated electron-hole pairs, with no dopant atoms.
Valence electron
An outer-shell electron of an atom that participates in covalent bonding and, when freed, becomes a conduction electron.
Electron mobility
The ratio of the drift velocity of electrons to the applied electric field, indicating how easily electrons move through the lattice.
eqs: Electrical conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor (electron plus hole contributions)

\sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); n = electron concentration (electrons/\(m^{3}\)); p = hole concentration (holes/\(m^{3}\)); |e| = elementary charge magnitude (C); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (\(m^{2}\)/V·s); \(\mu_{h}\) = hole mobility (\(m^{2}\)/V·s)
tips: Do not forget the hole term: σ includes p|e|μ_h as well as n|e|μ_e; omitting it underestimates conductivity.
Mobility units are \(m^{2}\)/V·s and concentrations are per \(m^{3}\); keep SI units consistent when calculating σ in S/m.
rq: Why do both electrons and holes contribute to conduction in an intrinsic semiconductor, and what would happen to the hole term if no holes existed?

Each thermally created pair gives one free electron and one hole; the hole is filled by a neighbouring valence electron moving the vacancy, so both carriers carry current. Without holes, the p|e|μ_h term would be zero and only electron conduction would remain.
If electron mobility is much larger than hole mobility, which carrier dominates conductivity, and why?
Electrons dominate, because the term n|e|μ_e is larger when μ_e >> μ_h and n = p, so the electron contribution outweighs the hole contribution.

notes.t: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Conduction in Semiconductors
pts: In pure (intrinsic) Si, electrons and holes are generated in equal numbers, so n = p.
In extrinsic semiconductors, impurities introduce excess carriers so that n ≠ p, and electrical behaviour is controlled by the dopants.
n-type doping (e.g. phosphorus, 5 valence electrons) donates extra conduction electrons, so electrons are the majority carriers (n ≫ p).
p-type doping (e.g. boron, 3 valence electrons) creates holes, so holes are the majority carriers (p ≫ n).
Conductivity is the product of carrier concentration, electron charge and carrier mobility, so the majority carrier dominates conduction.
defs: Intrinsic semiconductor
A pure semiconductor in which conduction electrons and holes are created in equal numbers, so n = p.
Extrinsic semiconductor
A semiconductor whose electrical behaviour is governed by deliberately added impurities that introduce excess electrons or holes, so n ≠ p.
n-type semiconductor
An extrinsic semiconductor doped with donor atoms (e.g. P in Si) where electrons are the majority carriers.
p-type semiconductor
An extrinsic semiconductor doped with acceptor atoms (e.g. B in Si) where holes are the majority carriers.
Hole
A vacancy in the valence band left by a missing electron that behaves as a positive charge carrier.
Conduction electron
A free electron in the conduction band able to move under an applied electric field.
eqs: \sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); n = electron concentration (\(m^{-3}\)); |e| = magnitude of electron charge (C); \(\mu_{e}\) = electron mobility (\(m^{2}\)/(V·s))
\sigma = electrical conductivity (S/m); p = hole concentration (\(m^{-3}\)); |e| = magnitude of electron charge (C); \(\mu_{h}\) = hole mobility (\(m^{2}\)/(V·s))
tips: Use the correct majority carrier: σ ≈ n|e|μ_e applies to n-type, σ ≈ p|e|μ_h to p-type; do not swap μ_e and μ_h.
Keep units consistent: concentrations in \(m^{-3}\) and mobility in \(m^{2}\)/(V·s) give conductivity in S/m; quoting \(cm^{-3}\) without conversion is a common error.
rq: Why does adding phosphorus to silicon make it n-type rather than p-type?
Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, so only 4 bond with neighbouring Si atoms; the spare electron becomes a free conduction electron.
Why must n = p in pure silicon but not in doped silicon?
In intrinsic Si, each thermally excited electron leaves exactly one hole, so carriers are created in pairs; dopants add one carrier type without creating its partner, breaking the balance.
If boron-doped Si has p ≫ n, why is its conductivity mainly due to holes even though electrons are present?
Conductivity scales with carrier concentration times mobility, and the majority carrier (holes, p) dominates the sum, so the small electron population contributes negligibly.

notes.t: Extrinsic Semiconductors: Conductivity vs. Temperature
pts: Doping adds imperfection sites that lower the activation energy needed to produce mobile electrons, so conductivity rises with doping level.
Below about 100 K there is freeze-out: thermal energy is insufficient to excite electrons, so few carriers are available and conductivity is low.
In the extrinsic region (about 150 K to 450 K) the donor impurities supply essentially all conduction electrons, so the carrier concentration plateaus at the dopant level.
At high temperature (T ≫ 450 K) intrinsic conduction dominates; thermally generated electron-hole pairs swamp the dopant contribution, and doped and undoped curves converge.
Intrinsic conduction is the comparison case: the undoped material's carrier concentration rises sharply with temperature because electrons must be thermally excited across the full band gap.
defs: Extrinsic semiconductor
A semiconductor whose conduction is controlled by deliberately added impurity (dopant) atoms, which supply the majority of charge carriers over a useful temperature range.
Freeze-out
The low-temperature regime in which thermal energy is too small to ionise dopant atoms, so donor electrons remain bound and the carrier concentration falls.
Intrinsic conduction
Conduction in a pure semiconductor where charge carriers come from thermal excitation of electrons across the band gap, dominating at high temperature.
n-type donor impurity
A pentavalent dopant (e.g. phosphorus in silicon) that contributes an extra, weakly bound electron to the conduction band.
tips: Do not confuse the regimes: extrinsic means carriers come from dopants (flat plateau), intrinsic means carriers come from band-gap excitation (steep rise at high T).
Temperature ranges given are approximate guides for this doping level (\(10^{21}\) /\(m^{3}\)); the boundaries shift with dopant concentration.
rq: Why does the doped curve plateau in the extrinsic region while the undoped curve keeps rising?

In the extrinsic region the donors have all been ionised, so the electron concentration is fixed at the dopant level (≈\(10^{21}\) /\(m^{3}\)). The undoped material has no such fixed supply, so thermal excitation across the band gap makes its carrier concentration grow rapidly with temperature.
What would happen to the freeze-out region if the material were cooled further, and why?
The carrier concentration would drop further towards zero, because even the weakly bound donor electrons lack enough thermal energy to be excited into the conduction band.

xq.q: An intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature has equal electron and hole concentrations \( n = p = 1.5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} \), electron mobility \( \mu_e = 0.15\ \mathrm{m^2/(V\,s)} \) and hole mobility \( \mu_h = 0.045\ \mathrm{m^2/(V\,s)} \). Take \( |e| = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C} \). Calculate its electrical conductivity \( \sigma \) in S/m.
s: σ = n|e|μe + p|e|μh = n|e|(μe+μh) since n = p

xq.q: Copper has electron concentration \( n = 8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} \) and conductivity \( \sigma = 5.44\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{S/m} \). Take \( |e| = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C} \). Find the electron mobility \( \mu_e \), then the average drift velocity of the electrons in an electric field of \( 0.050\ \mathrm{V/m} \), in m/s.
xq.a: μe = 4.0×10⁻³ m²/(V·s); drift velocity = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m/s

xq.q: A pure copper wire and a silicon sample are both heated from 300 K to 350 K. Which description of the change in conductivity is correct?
xq.a: Copper decreases because mobility falls with more scattering, while silicon increases because the rise in carrier concentration outweighs the mobility drop
o: Both increase, because more thermal energy frees more carriers in each
Copper increases and silicon decreases, because copper has more scattering centres at low temperature
Copper decreases because mobility falls with more scattering, while silicon increases because the rise in carrier concentration outweighs the mobility drop
Both decrease, because mobility falls with temperature in every material
xq.w: In a metal n is fixed so greater scattering lowers mobility and σ; in a semiconductor the carrier concentration rises strongly enough to outweigh the mobility drop, so applying one trend to both is the trap.

units.name: 9.5 Contact potential and transistors (MOSFET)
units.ov: This material covers contact potential (Fermi level alignment when dissimilar conductors touch) and the MOSFET, the field-effect transistor at the heart of digital electronics. It runs from the first transistor and modern FinFET/gate-all-around scaling, through the source-gate-drain switch picture, to MOSFET structure, n/p polarity and CMOS. The unifying idea is that electron energy levels, Fermi energy and electric fields set carrier density and hence conduction, so a gate field can switch a channel on or off.
must: Contact potential: dissimilar conductors have different Fermi energies; electrons flow until the Fermi levels equalise, leaving a potential difference across the junction (\(V_c=\Delta E_F/e\))
Fermi energy is the highest occupied electron level at absolute zero; contact potential is a voltage, not an energy, so convert eV to V by dividing by \(e\)
The contact potential comes from Fermi energy differences alone and must not be confused with an externally applied voltage

MOSFET = Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor: the gate, insulated by SiO\(_2\), uses an electric field (not injected current) to control carrier density in the channel between source and drain
Roles of terminals: source supplies carriers, drain collects them, gate switches OFF (path blocked) or ON (path open); the gate draws essentially no DC current
Polarity: a p-type MOSFET is switched off by a positive gate voltage and an n-type by a negative gate voltage (as stated in the notes); do not mix these up
Structure in the notes' diagram: metal contacts on SiO\(_2\), a p-type channel between p-type Si regions in an n-type substrate, so channel and substrate types are opposite
CMOS pairs n-type and p-type MOSFETs and is the dominant electronic technology

Scaling: planar to FinFET (Intel 2011, gate on three sides) to gate-all-around nanowire/nanosheet (IBM/IMEC 2017) for better electrostatic control and less leakage; high-k dielectrics allow a thicker layer with the same capacitance and lower leakage, and work-function metals set the threshold voltage
Silicon TEM spacing along \(\langle110\rangle\) is \(a/\sqrt2=3.84\) Å, not \(a\); 1 nm = 10 Å; the first transistor was made at Bell Labs in 1947 by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley (Nobel Prize 1956)
conn: Fermi level equalisation links to MOSFET operation: the gate field shifts energy levels and carrier density in the channel, much as charge transfer shifts levels at a contact
Conductivity and carrier density (\(\sigma=ne\mu\)) from earlier lectures explain why changing the carrier number in the channel switches the current
Gate-oxide capacitance, dielectric constant and thickness connect high-k materials to leakage and drive current, and to why scaling needs FinFET/GAA geometries
n-type and p-type polarity rules combine in CMOS: complementary devices are switched oppositely by the same gate voltage
exq: Two metals have Fermi energies of 4.3 eV and 5.1 eV. Describe what happens when they are brought into contact, state the direction of electron flow and calculate the contact potential in volts.
Explain why a MOSFET is called a field-effect device. Why does the gate draw essentially no DC current, and what role does the SiO\(_2\) layer play?
Sketch a MOSFET cross-section labelling source, gate, drain, oxide, channel and substrate, and state the gate voltage polarity that turns off an n-type and a p-type device.
Compare planar, FinFET and gate-all-around transistors in terms of electrostatic control and leakage. What are the roles of a high-k dielectric and a work-function metal?
A TEM image of silicon along \(\langle110\rangle\) shows column spacing of 3.84 Å. Calculate the lattice constant \(a\) and express the spacing in nm.

notes.t: Contact potential
pts: Different conductors (metals or semiconductors) generally have different Fermi energies, so their electron energy levels are not aligned.
When dissimilar conductors touch, electrons flow from one to the other, lowering the total energy of the system.
Charge transfer shifts the energy levels until the Fermi energy is equal on both sides, producing a measurable contact potential across the junction.
defs: Fermi energy
The highest occupied electron energy level in a material at absolute zero; it characterises the electron energy distribution in a conductor.
Contact potential
The voltage difference that develops between two dissimilar conductors in contact once electrons have flowed to equalise their Fermi energies.
tips: Do not confuse the contact potential with an externally applied voltage; it arises from Fermi energy differences alone.
Remember that the contact potential is a voltage (V), not an energy; convert energy differences in eV to volts by dividing by the electron charge.
rq: Why does electron flow stop once the two conductors are in contact?

Flow stops when the Fermi energies equalise; at that point the system energy is minimised and no net energy is gained by further transfer, with the built-up contact potential balancing the driving force.
What would happen to the contact potential if both conductors had identical Fermi energies?
No net electron flow would occur, so no contact potential would develop.

notes.t: The first transistor (historical context)
pts: The first transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs (USA) by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley.
The inventors were awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1956, recognising the invention's importance.
rq: Why was the 1947 point-contact transistor considered a breakthrough compared with the vacuum tube?
It performed amplification and switching using a solid semiconductor, with no heated filament, so it was smaller, more robust, lower power and more reliable.

notes.t: Transistors: FinFET and nanowire device scaling
pts: Modern transistors have evolved from planar designs to 3D fin-based and nanowire structures to control current better at very small sizes.
Intel's 2011 FinFET design uses vertical silicon fins, with the gate wrapping around the fin on three sides for better electrostatic control.
IBM's 2017 5 nm technology stacks horizontal nanosheet channels, increasing the gate-channel contact area and drive current per footprint.
IMEC's 2017 device uses silicon nanowires surrounded by a high-k gate dielectric (RMG-HK) and work-function metal, giving gate-all-around control.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) reveals the atomic lattice of silicon, showing how crystal orientation affects the spacing of atoms seen on images.
defs: FinFET
A non-planar transistor in which the channel is a thin vertical silicon fin wrapped by the gate on multiple sides, improving control of leakage at small dimensions.
Gate-all-around (GAA)
A transistor architecture where the gate completely surrounds the channel (nanowire or nanosheet), giving the best electrostatic control of the channel.
High-k dielectric
A gate insulator material with a dielectric constant higher than SiO₂, allowing a physically thicker layer with the same capacitance and lower leakage.
Work-function (WF) metal
A gate metal whose work function is chosen to set the threshold voltage of the transistor.
eqs: Silicon lattice spacing along the <110> direction (from the TEM schematic)
a = lattice constant (Å); a/√2 = projected spacing between atomic columns (Å)
tips: Do not confuse the projected spacing a/√2 with the lattice constant a; they differ by a factor of √2.
Keep units consistent: lattice dimensions are in Ångströms (Å) or nanometres, and 1 nm = 10 Å.
rq: Why does wrapping the gate around more sides of the channel reduce leakage current when the transistor is off?
More gate surface gives stronger electrostatic control over the channel, so the channel is fully depleted when off and fewer carriers leak through, reducing short-channel effects.
Why are high-k dielectrics used in the IMEC gate stack rather than simply thinning SiO₂?
Thinning SiO₂ further causes large tunnelling leakage; a high-k material gives the same capacitance with a thicker, lower-leakage physical layer.

notes.t: Transistor Analogy (Water Tank Model)
pts: The gate controls whether current can flow from source to drain, acting as a switch.
In the OFF state the gate blocks the pipe, so no flow reaches the drain.
In the ON state the gate opens the pipe, letting flow reach the drain.
defs: Source
The terminal from which charge carriers (current) originate in a transistor; the water reservoir in the analogy.
Drain
The terminal to which charge carriers flow from the source; the collecting reservoir in the analogy.
Gate
The control terminal whose voltage switches the transistor between OFF (no conduction) and ON (conduction) states.
tips: Do not confuse the OFF and ON states: OFF means the path is blocked, ON means the path is open.
The analogy shows switching behaviour only; it does not explicitly represent voltages or currents quantitatively.
rq: Why is the transistor analogy a switch rather than a simple pipe?
Because the gate, when actuated, changes the flow path between source and drain, turning conduction on or off rather than just passing flow continuously.
What would happen to the drain in the OFF state if the source tank were full?
Nothing reaches the drain; the source is full but the blocked gate prevents flow, showing that a high source level alone does not produce current.

notes.t: MOSFET: structure and field-effect operation
pts: The MOSFET is the most important device of the 20th–21st century and the foundation of digital electronics; engineers make more MOSFETs than any other device.
A MOSFET's cross section comprises source, gate and drain metal contacts on top of an SiO₂ insulating layer, with a p-type channel between p-type Si regions in an n-type Si substrate.
The gate is separated from the semiconductor by an insulating oxide, so it controls the channel by electric field rather than by current injection.
It is called a Field Effect device because the electric field at the gate controls the number of charge carriers flowing through the channel.
Conduction principles from earlier lectures (charge carriers and conductivity) give a basic understanding of how the MOSFET works.
defs: MOSFET

Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor: a transistor in which a gate electrode, insulated by an oxide layer, uses an electric field to control the density of charge carriers in a semiconductor channel between source and drain.
tips: Do not confuse the MOSFET's p-type channel with the n-type Si substrate; the channel type and the substrate type are opposite in this diagram.
The key mechanism is the electric field from the gate, not direct current injection through the gate, which is insulated by SiO₂.
rq: Why is the MOSFET called a 'field effect' device, and why does the insulating SiO₂ layer matter?

The gate's electric field controls the number of charge carriers in the channel; the SiO₂ insulator separates the gate from the channel so no DC gate current flows while the field still modulates conduction.
What would happen to control of the channel if the SiO₂ layer were replaced by a conductor?
The gate would short to the channel, so the field could not be used as a voltage-controlled switch; the insulating oxide is essential to the field-effect action.

notes.t: The MOSFET: gate control, p-type vs n-type, and CMOS
pts: The gate voltage controls (switches on and off) the current flowing between source and drain.
A p-type MOSFET is switched off by a positive gate voltage; an n-type MOSFET is switched off by a negative gate voltage.
Pairing n-type and p-type MOSFETs forms CMOS integrated circuits, the dominant electronic technology.
defs: MOSFET
Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor: a transistor in which a gate electrode, insulated by an oxide layer (SiO₂), controls current flow between source and drain through a channel.
CMOS
Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor: integrated circuit technology that combines n-type and p-type MOSFETs, the dominant electronic technology.
tips: Check the polarity: p-type switches off with positive gate voltage and n-type with negative gate voltage; mixing these up is a common error.
Remember that the gate is insulated from the channel by SiO₂, so the gate draws essentially no DC current.
rq: Why does a p-type MOSFET switch off with a positive gate voltage but an n-type switch off with a negative one?

The gate voltage sets the polarity of the field that controls the channel; a positive gate repels the holes forming a p-type channel (turning it off), while a negative gate does the same for electrons in an n-type channel.
Why is it useful to combine n-type and p-type MOSFETs in one circuit?
Complementary pairs mean one device is on while the other is off in a steady state, so little static current flows and power consumption is low, which is why CMOS dominates.

xq.q: A TEM image of silicon viewed along the <110> direction shows atomic columns with a projected spacing of \(a/\sqrt{2} = 3.84\) Å, where \(a\) is the lattice constant. Find \(a\) in nm, and hence the distance in nm spanned by 20 consecutive projected spacings is not needed; give only \(a\). (1 nm = 10 Å.)
Two metals in contact have Fermi energies differing by 0.45 eV before contact. Electrons flow until the Fermi energies are equal. What is the contact potential across the junction?
xq.w: Contact potential is a voltage, so divide the energy difference in eV by the electron charge to get 0.45 V; quoting eV or converting to joules and calling it volts is a unit slip, and halving has no basis.

xq.q: Two dissimilar metals with different Fermi energies are brought into contact. Explain how a contact potential arises and why it does not depend on any externally applied voltage.
xq.a: Before contact the Fermi energies differ, so the electron energy levels of the two metals are not aligned. On contact, electrons flow from one conductor to the other because this lowers the total energy of the system. The charge transfer shifts the energy levels until the Fermi energy is the same on both sides. The charge left on each side leaves a voltage difference across the junction, which is the contact potential. It is set only by the original Fermi energy difference (divided by e to give volts), so no external source is involved.
s: Fermi energies differ, so levels are misaligned
Electrons flow to lower the total energy
Levels shift until Fermi energies are equal
Resulting voltage across the junction is the contact potential
It arises from the Fermi energy difference alone, not an applied voltage

units.name: 9.6 Dielectrics: capacitance, polarisation and breakdown
units.ov: This module introduces dielectrics as insulators that store charge by polarisation rather than conduction, using SiO₂ on a MOSFET as the example. Relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r\) determines capacitance through the parallel-plate formula, and the microscopic picture (bound charges forming dipoles) explains both charge storage and the limit of breakdown when the band gap is overcome.
must: Parallel-plate capacitance with a dielectric: \(C=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0\frac{A}{L}\)
Charge stored: \(Q=CV\); capacitance is charge per unit volt, in farads (F)
\(\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\) F/m (absolute, with units); \(\varepsilon_r\) is dimensionless and a multiplier on \(\varepsilon_0\), never a replacement for it
\(\varepsilon_r\) is the ratio of the material's permittivity to that of vacuum; SiO₂ has \(\varepsilon_r\approx3\) (the notes' value)
Dielectric: insulator with bound charges (electrons in the valence band) that does not conduct DC but can be polarised
An applied voltage creates electric dipoles with \(\mu=qr\) (C·m); total stored charge is the sum of all the dipoles
Dielectric breakdown: a very large voltage gives bound charges enough energy to cross the band gap, so the insulator conducts
SiO₂ has a large gap (~9 eV), so it withstands large fields; it also grows easily on Si by hot O₂ exposure, hence its use in MOSFETs
Unit consistency: convert A to m² and L to m (and r to m for dipoles), or answers are off by orders of magnitude
Lightning is breakdown of air, not conduction by free electrons in a solid
conn: \(\varepsilon_r\) links the microscopic and macroscopic pictures: more polarisation (larger dipole sum) gives larger \(\varepsilon_r\), hence larger \(C\) and \(Q=CV\) at a given voltage
Band gap links to breakdown: a larger gap means a higher breakdown field, so a thinner dielectric (smaller \(L\), larger \(C\)) can be used safely
Geometry and material trade-off: increasing \(C\) via bigger \(A\), smaller \(L\) or larger \(\varepsilon_r\) is limited by the breakdown voltage across \(L\)
Combining \(C=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0A/L\) with \(Q=CV\) gives the charge stored for a given device geometry, as in a MOSFET gate oxide
exq: A parallel-plate capacitor has SiO₂ (\(\varepsilon_r=3\)) between plates of area 1 mm² separated by 10 nm. Calculate \(C\), and the charge stored at 1 V.
Explain, in terms of bound charges and dipoles, how a dielectric stores charge but does not conduct DC. Why is the stored charge the sum of the dipoles?
Define dielectric breakdown and use band-gap arguments to explain why SiO₂ (~9 eV gap) is a good gate dielectric on a MOSFET.
A dipole consists of charges \(\pm1.6\times10^{-19}\) C separated by 0.2 nm. Calculate the dipole moment, stating units.
How does the capacitance change if the plate separation is halved and the dielectric is replaced by one with twice the \(\varepsilon_r\)? What practical limit might apply?

notes.t: Dielectrics – SiO₂ on the MOSFET and capacitance
pts: Dielectrics are insulators that do not conduct DC electricity, so they can separate charged plates.
A dielectric's behaviour is quantified by its relative permittivity (dielectric constant), εr; for SiO₂ εr ≈ 3.
SiO₂ is used on MOSFETs because it forms easily on silicon by exposing the Si surface to hot O₂, and it has good dielectric properties.
Relative permittivity relates to a material's capacity to store charge, Q.
A parallel-plate capacitor stores charge Q between two metal plates with dielectric in between; capacitance C is measured in Farads.
defs: Dielectric
An insulating material that does not conduct DC electricity and can be polarised to store charge between electrodes.
Relative permittivity (dielectric constant), εr
Ratio of a material's permittivity to the permittivity of vacuum; indicates how well it stores electric charge.
Capacitance, C
Charge stored per unit voltage across a capacitor, measured in Farads (F).
eqs: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with dielectric

C = capacitance (F); \(\varepsilon_{r}\) = relative permittivity (dimensionless); \(\varepsilon_{0}\) = permittivity of vacuum, 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m; A = area of plates (m²); L = distance between plates (m)
Q = charge (C); C = capacitance (F); V = voltage across plates (V)
tips: Keep units consistent: convert area to m² and distance to m before using C = εrε₀A/L, otherwise C will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
Do not confuse εr (relative, dimensionless) with ε₀ (absolute, F/m); εr is a multiplier, not a substitute for ε₀.
rq: Why does increasing εr increase the charge a capacitor can store, and what does this mean for a thin SiO₂ gate?
Higher εr raises C = εrε₀A/L, so for a given voltage more charge Q = CV is stored; SiO₂ with εr ≈ 3 gives a useful capacitance while remaining an insulator.
If plate separation L doubles and everything else stays the same, what happens to C?
C halves, since C is inversely proportional to L.

notes.t: Dielectric polarisation and breakdown
pts: In a dielectric charges are bound and cannot move; electrons sit in the valence band.
Applying a voltage forms electric dipoles; dipole moment depends on charge and separation.
Total charge stored is the sum of all dipoles in the material.
A very large voltage can give bound charges enough energy to cross the energy gap, making the dielectric conducting (dielectric breakdown).
SiO₂ has a large energy gap (~9 eV), so it withstands large electric fields before breaking down.
defs: Dielectric
An electrically insulating material whose charges are bound, so it can store charge through polarisation rather than conduct current.
Electric dipole
A pair of equal and opposite charges separated by a distance, produced in a material when a voltage is applied.
Dielectric breakdown
The point at which a very large applied voltage gives bound charges enough energy to cross the band gap, so the insulator becomes conducting.
eqs: Dipole moment of a charge pair
\mu = dipole moment (C·m); q = magnitude of charge (C); r = separation between charges (m)
tips: Dipole moment μ = qr uses separation r in metres; mixing units (e.g. nm or µm) gives wrong values.
Lightning is dielectric breakdown of air, not conduction through a solid; don't confuse bound-charge polarisation with free-electron conduction.
rq: Why does a dielectric store charge even though it cannot conduct?
Applied voltage displaces bound charges slightly, forming dipoles; the sum of these dipoles stores charge without any free charge carriers moving through the material.
What would happen to the stored charge if the dipole separation doubled for the same charge q?
The dipole moment μ = qr doubles, so each dipole's moment doubles, increasing the material's stored polarisation for the same charge.

xq.q: A MOSFET gate is modelled as a parallel-plate capacitor with an SiO₂ dielectric of relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r = 3\), plate area \(A = 1.0\times10^{-12}\) m² and thickness \(L = 2.0\) nm. Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\) F/m. Calculate the charge \(Q\) stored when the gate voltage is \(V = 1.5\) V, using \(C=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0A/L\) and \(Q=CV\).
A parallel-plate capacitor has its dielectric thickness halved and its plate area doubled, with the same dielectric. By what factor does the capacitance change?
o: ×1 (unchanged)
xq.w: C ∝ A/L, so doubling A gives ×2 and halving L gives another ×2, a total of ×4; the traps are applying only one change or inverting the dependence on L.
s: New C = ε A(2)/(L/2) = 4 × old C

xq.q: Explain why SiO₂ can withstand a large applied voltage as a gate dielectric, and describe what happens physically at dielectric breakdown. Refer to bound charge and the energy gap.
xq.a: In a dielectric the charges are bound, with electrons in the valence band, so an applied voltage only forms dipoles (polarisation) and stores charge rather than driving a current. SiO₂ has a large energy gap (~9 eV), so bound electrons need a lot of energy to reach the conduction band. At very large voltage the bound charges gain enough energy to cross the gap. The material then becomes conducting; this is dielectric breakdown.
s: Bound charges: voltage forms dipoles, no conduction
Large gap (~9 eV) means large fields can be withstood
At very high voltage charges gain enough energy to cross the gap

units.name: 9.7 Refractive index, dispersion and Snell's law
units.ov: This material covers how light slows in a transparent material (n = c/v), how that slowing makes rays bend at an interface (Snell's law), and how n varies with wavelength (dispersion). Dispersion explains why prisms and raindrops split white light into colours. The link to microscopic behaviour is that electron clouds distort and dipoles form, which ties n to relative permittivity.
must: Definition of refractive index: \( n = c/v \), dimensionless, always \( \ge 1 \); higher n means slower light in the medium
Snell's law: \( n_1\sin\theta_i = n_2\sin\theta_r \), with angles measured from the normal, not the surface
Glass to air (\( n_2=1 \)): \( \sin\theta_r = n_1\sin\theta_i \); the ray bends away from the normal, so \( \theta_r>\theta_i \)
Direction of bending: into a higher-n medium the ray bends toward the normal; into a lower-n medium it bends away
Dispersion: n depends on wavelength or photon energy; in glass n is larger for blue (short wavelength, high energy) than red
Consequence of dispersion: blue is deviated more than red by a prism, giving a spectrum; the same effect in water droplets produces rainbows
Physical origin: light distorts the electron clouds of atoms, forming dipoles that slow the light; n is related to relative permittivity \( \varepsilon_r \)
Adding heavy ions such as lead raises n, because it slows light further (high-index glass)
Common errors: swapping \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \), inverting \( c/v \), using angles from the surface, putting units on n
conn: \( n=c/v \) with Snell's law: speed change at the boundary sets the bending, so you can find v from measured angles, or the angle from known speeds
Dispersion with Snell's law: apply Snell's law separately for \( n_{blue} \) and \( n_{red} \) to get the angular spread of colours after a prism
Permittivity with refractive index: dipole formation under an applied field links the electrical property \( \varepsilon_r \) to the optical property n, and both vary with frequency
Composition with refractive index: heavy ions such as lead raise n, so glass choice controls bending and dispersion
exq: Light travels at \( 2.0\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1} \) in a glass. Calculate n, then the angle of refraction in air for a ray inside the glass hitting the surface at 25° to the normal (\( c=3.0\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1} \)).
A ray in glass with n = 1.52 meets an air boundary at 30° from the normal. Find \( \theta_r \), state whether it bends towards or away from the normal, and explain why.
Explain, using the idea of dispersion, why a glass prism splits white light and why blue is deviated more than red. Sketch the ray paths.
Glass has \( n_{blue}=1.53 \) and \( n_{red}=1.51 \). For a 20° angle of incidence inside the glass at a glass-air surface, calculate the angular separation of the two emerging colours.
Describe how electron-cloud distortion and dipoles in a material cause light to slow, relate this to relative permittivity, and explain why adding lead to glass raises n.

notes.t: The refractive index and dispersion
pts: The refractive index changes with wavelength, so different colours bend by different amounts; this is why a prism splits white light into a spectrum.
Blue light is deflected more than red light by a prism, producing the spread of colours.
The refractive index is an optical property related to the relative permittivity of the material.
Both refractive index and relative permittivity depend on the dipoles that form in a material when an electric field is applied.
The same wavelength-dependent effect in water produces the colours of the rainbow.
defs: Refractive index (n)
An optical property of a material, related to its relative permittivity, that describes how much light slows down and bends on entering the material.
Dispersion
The change in refractive index with photon energy (or wavelength), which causes white light to separate into its component colours.
tips: Do not confuse refractive index n with the symbol for number or other quantities; n here is the optical refractive index.
Remember that the blue light is deflected more than red light: the higher-energy (shorter wavelength) light bends more.
rq: Why does a prism split white light into colours rather than just bending it?
Because the refractive index depends on wavelength, so each colour is bent by a different amount (blue more than red), spreading white light into a spectrum.
What links the refractive index to the speed at which dipoles respond to an electric field?
Dispersion: the dispersion of the material relates to how quickly the dipoles form when the electric field is applied, so the frequency-dependent response sets the wavelength dependence of n.

notes.t: Refraction and the index of refraction
pts: Light passing through a transparent material distorts the electron clouds of the atoms, which slows the light down.
Light travels more slowly in a material than in a vacuum, and this reduction in speed is what causes refraction (bending).
Adding large, heavy ions such as lead to glass increases the refractive index by further slowing light in the glass.
Light is bent as it passes through a transparent prism because its speed changes on entering and leaving the material.
defs: Index of refraction (n)
The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in a given medium; a larger n means light travels more slowly in the material.
eqs: Index of refraction of a medium
n = index of refraction (dimensionless); c = speed of light in vacuum (m \(s^{-1}\)); v = speed of light in the medium (m \(s^{-1}\))
tips: Remember that n = c/v means a higher index gives a lower speed in the material; do not invert the ratio.
The index of refraction is dimensionless, so do not attach units to n.
rq: Why does adding lead ions to glass give it a higher refractive index?
Large, heavy ions distort the electron clouds more strongly, slowing light further and so increasing n.
Diamond has n = 2.41 while typical glass has n ≈ 1.5–1.7. What does this imply about light speed in each?
Light travels more slowly in diamond than in glass, since n = c/v is larger for diamond.

notes.t: Snell's law and dispersion at a glass-air surface
pts: Light passing from a high refractive index material (glass) into a low refractive index material (air) is bent away from the normal according to Snell's law.
The refracted angle depends on the ratio of the refractive indices, with the angles measured from the normal to the surface.
Refractive index of glass (mostly SiO2) is wavelength dependent, being larger for blue light than for red light.
Because blue light is refracted more strongly than red, a prism spreads white light into its component colours (dispersion).
defs: Angle of incidence (θ_i)
The angle between the incoming ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence.
Angle of refraction (θ_r)
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal to the surface, measured on the far side of the boundary.
Normal
The line drawn at right angles to a surface at the point where a ray meets it; angles of incidence and refraction are measured from it.
Refractive index (n)
The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a material; a higher n means light slows more and bends more on refraction.
eqs: Snell's law at a glass-to-air surface, giving the angle of refraction

\(\theta_r\) = angle of refraction (degrees or radians); \(\theta_i\) = angle of incidence (degrees or radians); \(n_1\) = refractive index of glass (dimensionless); \(n_2\) = refractive index of air = 1 (dimensionless)
tips: Angles in Snell's law are measured from the normal, not from the surface; using the surface gives wrong answers.
Remember that \(n_1\) is the glass (incident side) and \(n_2\) is air here; swapping them reverses the ratio and the bending direction.
rq: Why does blue light bend more than red light when leaving the prism, even though both start at the same angle of incidence?
Glass has a larger refractive index for blue than for red, \(n_1(\text{Blue}) > n_1(\text{Red})\), so by Snell's law \(\sin(\theta_r)\) is larger for blue, giving a larger \(\theta_r\).
What would happen to the angle of refraction if light travelled from air into glass instead?
The refractive index ratio would be inverted, so the light would bend towards the normal, with \(\theta_r\) smaller than \(\theta_i\).

xq.q: Light travels in a glass at speed \(v = 2.00\times10^{8}\) m s⁻¹, with \(c = 3.00\times10^{8}\) m s⁻¹ in vacuum. A ray inside the glass meets a glass–air surface at an angle of incidence of 30° to the normal. Find the refractive index of the glass and hence the angle of refraction in air, in degrees.
xq.a: n = 1.5, so sin θr = 1.5 sin 30° = 0.75 and θr ≈ 48.6°

xq.q: A glass has refractive index n = 1.60. Taking c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is the speed of light in the glass?
xq.w: Since n = c/v, v = c/n = 1.88×10⁸ m s⁻¹; multiplying by n inverts the ratio and gives a speed above c.

xq.q: Explain why a glass prism splits white light into a spectrum, and say which of blue and red light is deviated more. Refer to what happens to the light inside the glass.
xq.a: Light passing through glass distorts the electron clouds of the atoms, which slows the light, giving n = c/v. The refractive index depends on wavelength (dispersion) and is larger for blue light than for red. By Snell's law, the larger n means blue light is bent more at each surface. So the different colours leave the prism at different angles and the white light spreads out, with blue deflected more than red.
s: Light slows in the glass because of electron cloud distortion, n = c/v
n depends on wavelength (dispersion), larger for blue
Snell's law: larger n gives more bending
Colours emerge at different angles; blue is deviated more than red

units.name: 9.8 Total internal reflection and optical fibres
units.ov: This module explains how optical fibres guide light using total internal reflection (TIR), which follows from Snell's law and the critical angle at a core/cladding boundary. It then covers how fibres carry data: pulses of light, limited by attenuation and dispersion, restored by 3R repeaters and multiplied in capacity by wavelength division multiplexing. The physics of the interface (refractive indices) sets the fibre design, and the fibre's loss and pulse spreading set the practical link limits.
must: TIR needs light going from higher index \(n_1\) to lower index \(n_2\) (\(n_1>n_2\)) with incidence angle greater than the critical angle
Critical angle: \(\theta_c=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)\), where \(n_1\) is the denser medium the light is in; e.g. \(n_1=1.5, n_2=1\) gives \(\theta_c\approx 42^\circ\)
Snell's law: \(n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_r\); at \(\theta_c\) the refraction angle is \(90^\circ\) (ray grazes the boundary)
All angles are measured from the normal, not from the boundary surface
Fibre structure: high-index glass core inside lower-index cladding; the relative index difference is tiny, \((n_2-n_1)/n_1\approx10^{-3}\) in magnitude, so \(\theta_c\) is close to \(90^\circ\)
Sizes: fibre diameter about 125 µm (\(125\times10^{-6}\) m), single-mode core about 8 µm; flexible despite being thin
Attenuation (power loss, dB/km) is distinct from dispersion (pulse broadening in time, from different wavelengths/modes travelling at different speeds); both limit data rate and range
Best transmission is near 1550 nm (near infrared), with loss about 0.2 dB/km, so repeaters are needed roughly every 30 km
3R repeaters Regenerate, Reshape and Retime pulses to counter attenuation and dispersion
WDM: each channel is a separate wavelength on the same fibre (about 40 channels at about 10 Gb/s each in undersea cables, i.e. about 400 Gb/s total)
conn: Snell's law leads directly to the critical angle (set \(\theta_r=90^\circ\)), which determines whether a ray in the core is guided by TIR
