Check that \(\nu\) is dimensionless and that moduli are consistent in units (Pa or GPa) before substituting values.
rq: Why does the bulk modulus expression have the denominator \(3(1-2\nu)\), and what happens as \(\nu\) approaches 0.5?

The factor \(1-2
u\) reflects volumetric response; as \(
u 	o 0.5\) the material becomes incompressible, so \(1-2
u 	o 0\) and \(K 	o \infty\).
If you know E and \(\nu\) only, how would you find G without memorising a new formula?
Rearrange \(E = 2G(1+\nu)\) to give \(G = E/[2(1+\nu)]\).

xq.q: A steel bar of original length \(l_0 = 400\) mm and original width \(w_0 = 25.0\) mm is loaded in tension along z and stays elastic. Its length increases by 0.60 mm and its width decreases by 0.00500 mm. Find Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) for the steel. Then, treating the steel as isotropic with Young's modulus \(E = 200\) GPa, find its shear modulus \(G\) in GPa.

An isotropic alloy has Young's modulus \(E = 70\) GPa and shear modulus \(G = 26\) GPa. A rod of this alloy, of diameter 20.0 mm, is stretched elastically to an axial strain of \(2.0\times10^{-3}\). Find Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) and the change in diameter in mm (negative for a decrease).
xq.a: \(\nu = 0.346\); change in diameter = \(-0.0138\) mm

xq.q: A rectangular specimen is stretched elastically along z with axial strain \(+0.0040\). Its Poisson's ratio is \(\nu = 0.35\). What is the lateral strain \(\varepsilon_x\)?
xq.w: \(\varepsilon_x = -\nu\varepsilon_z = -0.35\times0.0040\); the lateral strain is negative in tension, so the sign must not be dropped, and one must multiply rather than divide by \(\nu\).

units.name: 11.5 Isotropic vs anisotropic materials
units.ov: This module contrasts isotropic materials, whose properties are the same in every direction, with anisotropic materials, whose properties depend on direction. It shows how this changes the elastic description: isotropic materials need only E, G and ν, linked by one relation, while anisotropic (orthotropic) materials need direction-labelled moduli and Poisson's ratios, nine independent constants in total. Careful use of subscripts and the cube-face stress notation ties it all together.
must: Isotropic: properties identical in all directions; anisotropic: properties vary with direction, so always state the direction when quoting a value.
Isotropic materials are described by E, G and ν, but only two are independent because \( G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} \).
Do not apply \( G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} \) to anisotropic materials; it fails when moduli depend on direction.

Anisotropic notation: normal moduli \( E_{11}, E_{22}, E_{33} \); shear moduli \( G_{12}, G_{23}, G_{31} \); Poisson's ratios \( 
u_{12}, 
u_{23}, 
u_{31} \) (axes 1, 2, 3 = x, y, z).

Orthotropic form needs nine independent elastic constants. Note that the notes' 'three values each of E, G, ν' count is the three-per-type listing, not the independent total, so be ready to explain both.
Stress and strain components have two indices: the first is the face normal and the second is the direction of the component. Do not confuse the two.
Isotropic is not the same as homogeneous: a material can be homogeneous (uniform throughout) yet anisotropic.
Anisotropy concerns direction, not size or temperature; isotropic does not mean simple or weak.
Isotropic properties include stiffness, strength and thermal expansion, all direction-independent.
conn: Isotropic relation \( G = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)} \) with Hooke's law: you can find the third constant from two, but only for isotropic materials.
Anisotropic subscript notation with the stress cube: matching face normal and component direction to the correct \( E_{ii} \), \( G_{ij} \) or \( \nu_{ij} \).
Material choice (e.g. fibre composites or timber, which are anisotropic) with loading direction: the same load gives different strain depending on orientation.
Homogeneity versus isotropy in classifying real materials such as metals, wood and composites.
exq: Define isotropic and anisotropic materials, and explain with an example why a material can be homogeneous but anisotropic.
An isotropic steel has \( E = 200 \) GPa and \( \nu = 0.3 \). Calculate the shear modulus G and state how many independent constants describe it.
List the elastic constants needed for an orthotropic material using correct subscripts, and state how many are independent.
A student uses \( G = E/(2(1+\nu)) \) with \( E_{11} \) and \( \nu_{12} \) for a unidirectional composite. Explain why this is invalid.
On a stress cube, explain the meaning of the two indices in a component such as \( \sigma_{12} \), identifying the face normal and the direction of the component.

notes.t: Anisotropy
pts: Isotropic materials have the same physical properties in every direction.
Anisotropic materials have physical properties that depend on the direction of measurement.
The name comes from ancient Greek: 'iso' meaning same and 'an' meaning not, so anisotropic means 'not the same'.
defs: Isotropic
A material whose physical properties (e.g. stiffness, strength, thermal expansion) are identical in all directions.
Anisotropic
A material whose physical properties vary with the direction in which they are measured.
tips: Do not confuse 'isotropic' (same in all directions) with 'homogeneous' (same throughout the material); a material can be homogeneous yet anisotropic.
Anisotropy is a property of direction, not of size or temperature; always state the direction when quoting an anisotropic value.
rq: Why does a wooden beam bend more easily across the grain than along it?
Wood is anisotropic: its fibres (grain) give much higher stiffness and strength along the grain than across it, so properties depend on loading direction.
Would a single tensile test in one direction be enough to fully characterise an anisotropic material?
No; properties differ with direction, so tests in several orientations are needed to describe the material fully.

notes.t: Isotropic vs Anisotropic materials
pts: Isotropic materials have the same properties in all directions, so one value each of Young's modulus, shear modulus and Poisson's ratio describes them.
Anisotropic materials have properties that depend on direction, so three values are needed for each of Young's modulus, shear modulus and Poisson's ratio.
defs: Isotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties are identical in all directions, described by a single Young's modulus, shear modulus and Poisson's ratio.
Anisotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties vary with direction, requiring three values each of Young's modulus, shear modulus and Poisson's ratio.
tips: Do not confuse the number of constants: isotropic needs one value each, anisotropic needs three values each for E, G and ν.
Isotropic does not mean the material is weak or simple; it only means its properties are the same in all directions.
rq: Why does an anisotropic material need three Young's moduli rather than one?
Its stiffness differs along each of the three orthogonal axes, so a separate Young's modulus is needed for each direction.
Would a fibre-reinforced composite be expected to be isotropic or anisotropic, and why?
Anisotropic, because the fibres give much greater stiffness and strength along their length than across it.

notes.t: Isotropic vs Anisotropic Materials
pts: An isotropic material has the same properties in all directions, so only three constants (E, G and ν) are needed to describe it.
An anisotropic material has properties that depend on direction, so separate moduli and Poisson's ratios are needed for each axis pair.
Anisotropic moduli are labelled with direction subscripts: normal moduli E11, E22, E33; shear moduli G12, G23, G31; Poisson's ratios ν12, ν23, ν31.
Stress and strain components on the cube faces are labelled with two indices, the first giving the face normal and the second the direction of the component.
defs: Isotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties are identical in all directions at a point, described by E, G and ν.
Anisotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties vary with direction, requiring nine independent elastic constants (in orthotropic form) to describe its behaviour.
eqs: Relation between shear modulus, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio for an isotropic material
G = shear modulus (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); ν = Poisson's ratio (dimensionless)
tips: Do not use isotropic relations such as G = E/(2(1+ν)) for anisotropic materials, since they do not hold when the moduli depend on direction.
Match the subscripts to the correct axes (1, 2, 3 = x, y, z) when reading the cube diagram; confusing the face normal with the force direction is a common error.
rq: Why does an isotropic material need only three elastic constants while an anisotropic one needs more?

Isotropy means properties are the same in every direction, so one E, G and ν describe all directions; anisotropy makes each direction distinct, so separate constants are needed for each axis and pair of axes.
What would change if you cut a fibre-reinforced composite along a different axis?
Its stiffness and strength would change, because it is anisotropic and E11, E22 and G12 differ, so the moduli used must match the loading direction.

xq.q: A carbon-fibre composite plate has different Young's moduli along its length and across its width. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: It is anisotropic, so the isotropic relation \(G = E/[2(1+\nu)]\) cannot be used and direction must be stated with each modulus.
o: It is isotropic, because it is the same material throughout.
It is anisotropic, but \(G = E/[2(1+\nu)]\) still holds using the average E.
It is anisotropic, so the isotropic relation \(G = E/[2(1+\nu)]\) cannot be used and direction must be stated with each modulus.
It is isotropic, because it has a single Poisson's ratio.
xq.w: Properties depending on direction means anisotropic; the trap is confusing homogeneous (same throughout) with isotropic and applying isotropic relations.

xq.q: Explain the difference between an isotropic and an anisotropic material. State how many independent values of E, G and \(\nu\) are needed to describe each, and explain why a material can be homogeneous yet anisotropic. Give an example of how the subscripts are used for the anisotropic case.
xq.a: An isotropic material has the same properties in every direction, so one value each of E, G and \(\nu\) describes it. An anisotropic material has direction-dependent properties, so three values each are needed, labelled by direction: normal moduli E11, E22, E33, shear moduli G12, G23, G31 and Poisson's ratios ν12, ν23, ν31. Homogeneous means the same at every position, while isotropic means the same in every direction; a material uniform throughout (e.g. aligned-fibre composite) can still be stiffer along one axis, so it is homogeneous but anisotropic.
s: Isotropic: same in all directions, one E, G, ν
Anisotropic: three values each, direction subscripts (E11, G12, ν12 etc.)
Homogeneous = same throughout position; isotropic = same in direction
Example of homogeneous but anisotropic material

xq.q: An isotropic polymer has \(E = 2.4\) GPa and \(\nu = 0.40\). Find its shear modulus G. Then explain briefly why the same calculation would not be valid for a fibre-reinforced polymer in which E differs along the three axes.
xq.a: \(G = 2.4/(2\times1.40) = 0.857\) GPa. The relation holds only for isotropic materials; for an anisotropic material the moduli depend on direction, so no single E and \(\nu\) define G.
s: Relation valid only when properties are direction independent

units.name: 11.6 Polymer stiffness, chain entanglement and crosslinking
units.ov: Polymers have strong covalent C–C backbones, yet their bulk stiffness is low because loading makes chains slide past one another against weak secondary (van der Waals) bonds. Stiffness rises as covalent crosslinks replace this sliding with backbone deformation. The effect of crosslinking depends on temperature relative to \(T_G\), with diamond as the limiting fully covalent network.
must: Backbone bond strength does not set bulk polymer stiffness; inter-chain bonding and chain mobility do
Under load, chains slide and uncoil past each other; the covalent C–C backbone is not stretched in uncrosslinked polymers
Van der Waals bonds are weak, short-range secondary forces, so polymers with only these have \(E \lesssim 1\) GPa
Entanglement is physical, temporary and involves no bonds; crosslinking is chemical, covalent and permanent. Do not confuse them
Crosslink: a covalent bond joining two chains into a 3D network that prevents sliding
Increasing crosslink density raises modulus because more covalent bonds carry the load and deformation is reduced
In crosslinked polymers, deformation is by movement of the backbone itself, not chain sliding (sliding describes thermoplastics)
\(T_G\): below it the polymer is glassy and hard; above it a lightly crosslinked polymer is rubbery with a much lower modulus. Always state the regime
Diamond is the 100% crosslinked limit (all covalent), with \(E\approx10^{3}\) GPa; heavily crosslinked thermosets (epoxy, alkyds) lie at intermediate-to-high modulus
Read modulus charts on a log scale: one tick is a factor of 10
conn: Bond type (covalent vs van der Waals) links to deformation mechanism (backbone deformation vs chain sliding) and hence to modulus
Crosslink density combines with temperature relative to \(T_G\) to determine whether a polymer is glassy, rubbery or rigid
Comparing polymers with metals and ceramics needs the distinction between intra-chain covalent bonds and inter-chain secondary bonds
Diamond as a fully crosslinked network sets the upper bound on the modulus-versus-crosslink-density trend
exq: Polymer backbones contain strong C–C covalent bonds, yet polyethylene has \(E \approx 1\) GPa or less while diamond has about \(10^{3}\) GPa. Explain this using deformation mechanisms and bond types.
Distinguish chain entanglement from crosslinking, giving the bond type, permanence and effect on chain sliding for each.
Sketch log modulus against crosslink density for a polymer above and below \(T_G\). Explain the shape and why a lightly crosslinked polymer is rubbery above \(T_G\).
A chart shows a thermoset at 3 GPa and a rubber at 0.003 GPa. By what factor do their moduli differ, and what difference in crosslinking and bonding explains it?
Describe how the deformation mechanism changes from a thermoplastic to a heavily crosslinked epoxy, and predict the effect on stiffness and extensibility.

notes.t: Polymers: strong backbone bonds do not imply high stiffness
pts: Polymer backbones are C–C chains with strong covalent bonds, which might suggest high stiffness.
Despite strong covalent bonds, polymer stiffness is not high, so bond strength alone does not determine stiffness.
Stiffness of a bulk polymer depends on more than backbone bond strength, e.g. chain entanglement, secondary (van der Waals/hydrogen) bonding between chains, and crystallinity.
tips: Do not assume that strong primary (covalent) bonds in the chain mean a high Young's modulus; bulk stiffness is governed by inter-chain interactions and chain mobility.
Distinguish intra-chain (covalent) bond strength from inter-chain (secondary) bonding when comparing polymers with metals or ceramics.
rq: Why does a strong covalent backbone not guarantee a stiff polymer?
Stiffness of the bulk material depends on how chains interact and deform, not just intra-chain bond strength; chains are held together only by weak secondary bonds and can slide or uncoil under load.
What would you expect to change if the polymer chains were cross-linked?
Cross-linking adds strong covalent links between chains, restricting chain sliding and increasing stiffness (as in thermosets).

notes.t: Polymers: deformation mechanism and bonding
pts: Polymer chains are entangled, so loading moves chains past one another rather than stretching the covalent backbone.
The stretching/deformation under load is resisted by secondary bonds between chains, not by the strong C-C backbone bonds.
Van der Waals forces are weak, which is why polymers are generally compliant and low-stiffness compared with metals or ceramics.
defs: Van der Waals forces
Weak, short-range secondary intermolecular attractions between polymer chains (or molecules) arising from transient/induced dipoles, much weaker than covalent bonds.
tips: Do not assume the C-C covalent backbone stretches under load in polymers; the deformation is governed by the weak secondary bonds between chains.
Remember that van der Waals forces are secondary bonds, far weaker than primary covalent or metallic bonds.
rq: Why does a polymer's stiffness depend far more on inter-chain bonding than on the strength of its C-C backbone?
Under load, chains slide and move relative to each other; the resisting bonds are the weak van der Waals forces between chains, so the strong covalent C-C backbone is hardly stretched.
What would happen to the stiffness of a polymer if chains were cross-linked by strong covalent bonds?
Chains could no longer slide freely, so the material would become much stiffer and stronger (as in thermosets), since load would be carried by strong covalent links.

notes.t: Polymers: crosslinking and chain entanglement
pts: Non- or low-crosslinked polymers rely on chain entanglement, since chains have limited connection to one another.
Because inter-chain connections are limited, the chains can slide past each other, which governs the polymer's deformation behaviour.
Crosslinked polymers have chains that are joined to one another by covalent bonds (crosslinks), restricting relative chain movement.
defs: Crosslinking
The formation of chemical bonds joining neighbouring polymer chains together into a network, restricting chains from sliding past one another.
Chain entanglement
The physical interlocking of long polymer chains that acts as a temporary connection between chains in non- or low-crosslinked polymers, without chemical bonding.
tips: Do not confuse chain entanglement (physical, temporary, no bonds) with crosslinking (chemical covalent bonds between chains).
Remember that low crosslinking still allows sliding, so it does not make a polymer rigid like a fully crosslinked network.
rq: Why can non- or low-crosslinked polymers deform by sliding while crosslinked polymers cannot?

In low-crosslinked polymers chains are only physically entangled with limited chemical links, so they can slide past one another; in crosslinked polymers the chains are chemically joined into a network, which stops them sliding.
What would happen to the stiffness and the ability to flow when crosslink density is increased?
Higher crosslink density restricts chain movement more, making the polymer stiffer, harder and less able to flow or be reshaped, as in thermosets.

notes.t: Crosslinked Polymers
pts: Increasing crosslink density means more covalent bonds carry load, so the material is stiffer and deforms less.
In crosslinked polymers, deformation occurs by movement of the polymer backbone itself, rather than chains sliding past one another as in thermoplastics.
defs: Crosslink
A covalent bond joining two polymer chains, forming a three-dimensional network that prevents chains from sliding past each other.
tips: Crosslinks are covalent bonds, not secondary (van der Waals or hydrogen) bonds; confusing them loses marks.
Do not describe crosslinked polymers as having chains sliding past each other; that describes uncrosslinked thermoplastics.
rq: Why does a higher crosslink density make a polymer stiffer and less able to creep?
Crosslinks join chains into a network, so applied load is transferred through covalent bonds and chains cannot slide relative to each other, limiting movement.
What is the difference in deformation mechanism between a crosslinked polymer and an uncrosslinked thermoplastic under load?
Crosslinked polymers deform by backbone movement (bond stretching/rotation) because chains are locked together, whereas thermoplastic chains slide past one another.

notes.t: Effect of crosslinks on polymer modulus
pts: Increasing the number of covalent crosslinks raises the elastic modulus of a polymer.
Diamond is an extreme case: every bond is covalent, so it can be treated as a fully (100%) cross-linked network with modulus near \(10^{3}\) GPa.

Below the glass transition temperature \(T_{G}\), the modulus rises steeply with crosslink density, whereas above \(T_{G}\) a lightly crosslinked polymer behaves as a rubber with a much lower modulus.
Polymers with only van der Waals bonding (no crosslinks) have low moduli of about 1 GPa or less, which is why rubbers are compliant.
Heavily crosslinked thermosets such as epoxy, nylon and alkyds lie in the intermediate-to-high modulus region of the chart.
defs: Covalent crosslink density
The number of covalent bonds linking adjacent polymer chains per unit volume (or per monomer), which controls how stiff and rigid the network is.
Crosslink
A covalent bond joining two separate polymer chains, forming a three-dimensional network that resists chain slippage.
Glass transition temperature (\(T_{G}\))
The temperature below which an amorphous polymer is hard and glassy and above which it becomes rubbery; the modulus changes sharply across it.
tips: Read the chart's log scales carefully: modulus is in GN \(m^{-2}\) (GPa) on a log axis, so a gap of one tick means a factor of 10, not a small difference.
Don't apply the modulus trend without noting temperature: the curve for polyethylene differs above and below \(T_{G}\), so state which regime you are considering.
rq: Why does polyethylene drop by about two orders of magnitude in modulus when heated above \(T_{G}\), while heavily crosslinked epoxy hardly changes?

Polyethylene is only weakly bonded by van der Waals forces between chains, so above \(T_{G}\) the chains slide freely and the modulus falls sharply; epoxy's covalent crosslinks hold the network together, so its modulus is largely unaffected by moderate heating.
What would you expect to happen to the modulus if you crosslinked a rubber lightly, and why?
The modulus would increase as crosslink density rises, because more covalent junctions restrict chain movement and stiffen the network, moving the material up the chart toward plastics.

xq.q: Polyethylene has strong covalent C–C backbone bonds, yet its Young's modulus is only about 1 GPa or less. What is the main reason?
xq.a: Loading mainly makes entangled chains slide past each other against weak van der Waals bonds, rather than stretching the backbone.
o: The C–C covalent bonds in the backbone are intrinsically weak.
Loading mainly makes entangled chains slide past each other against weak van der Waals bonds, rather than stretching the backbone.
Crosslinks between the chains stretch easily under load.
The covalent backbone stretches but van der Waals bonds carry no load, so the modulus is zero.
xq.w: Deformation is governed by weak secondary inter-chain bonds, not the strong backbone; the trap is assuming bond strength within the chain sets bulk stiffness.

xq.q: Explain how increasing covalent crosslink density changes the deformation mechanism and Young's modulus of a polymer. Contrast this with a non-crosslinked thermoplastic, and explain why diamond lies at the extreme.
xq.a: In a non- or low-crosslinked polymer, chains are held only by physical entanglement and weak van der Waals bonds, so chains slide past one another and the modulus is low (≲1 GPa). Crosslinks are covalent bonds joining chains into a 3D network that prevents sliding, so deformation requires movement of the backbone itself and more covalent bonds carry load. Hence the modulus increases with crosslink density, steeply below the glass transition temperature. Diamond, with every bond covalent, is effectively 100% crosslinked, with a modulus near \(10^{3}\) GPa.
s: Thermoplastic: entanglement and van der Waals, chains slide, low E
Crosslinks are covalent and prevent sliding
More covalent bonds carry load so E rises with density
Diamond is fully covalent network, E about \(10^{3}\) GPa

xq.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes chain entanglement from crosslinking in polymers?
xq.a: Entanglement is a physical, temporary interlocking without bonds; crosslinks are covalent bonds between chains.
o: Both are covalent bonds, but crosslinks are longer.
Entanglement is a physical, temporary interlocking without bonds; crosslinks are covalent bonds between chains.
Entanglement is covalent and crosslinks are van der Waals bonds.
Crosslinked chains slide past each other more easily than entangled chains.
xq.w: Crosslinks are covalent bonds that restrict sliding, whereas entanglement is only physical; the trap is calling crosslinks secondary bonds.

units.name: 11.7 Composites: load transfer and rule of mixtures bounds
units.ov: This module defines composites as multi-phase materials whose phases stay distinguishable, and shows how their stiffness is bounded by two limiting load-transfer models. Iso-strain (parallel, longitudinal loading) gives the Voigt upper bound, an arithmetic volume-weighted mean of the moduli. Iso-stress (series, transverse loading) gives the Reuss lower bound, a harmonic mean. Real composites, especially particulate ones, lie between the bounds, so fibre orientation, volume fraction and interfacial bonding decide where a given composite sits.
must: Iso-strain (parallel, longitudinal) upper bound: \(E_{cl}=E_mV_m+E_fV_f=E_m(1-V_f)+E_fV_f\), a straight line in \(V_f\)
Iso-stress (series, transverse) lower bound: \(\frac{1}{E_{ct}}=\frac{V_m}{E_m}+\frac{V_f}{E_f}\); sum the \(V/E\) terms, then invert at the end
Iso-strain gives the upper bound and iso-stress the lower bound; real composites lie between them, and particulate data sit closer to the lower bound
Iso-strain: \(\varepsilon_c=\varepsilon_m=\varepsilon_f\), \(F_c=F_m+F_f\), \(\sigma_c=\sigma_mV_m+\sigma_fV_f\) (stress is volume-averaged, and phase stresses differ)
Iso-stress: \(\sigma_c=\sigma_m=\sigma_f=F/A\), \(\varepsilon=\sigma/E\) in each layer, \(\varepsilon_c=\varepsilon_mV_m+\varepsilon_fV_f\) (strain is volume-averaged), \(\delta=\sigma t/E\)
Always use volume fractions, not weight fractions, with \(V_m+V_f=1\); convert percentages to fractions and keep moduli in consistent units
Area fraction equals volume fraction only when all phases have equal length (\(V_f=A_f/A_c\))

Definition of a composite: two or more phases that remain distinguishable under a microscope, engineered to optimise properties (GFRP, CFRP, filled polymers, wood). It differs from an alloy, whose phases are usually not separately visible
Reinforcement depends on good interfacial bonding and effective load transfer from matrix to filler; poor bonding gives a weaker composite than predicted
On the property chart, stiffness is on a log scale, so each division is a factor of 10; the wide composite bubbles reflect the spread between the bounds and the anisotropy
conn: Force equilibrium \(F_c=F_m+F_f\) combined with equal strain and \(\sigma=E\varepsilon\) gives the Voigt modulus, so questions often ask you to derive it and then find the load share \(F_f/F_c=E_fV_f/E_cl\)
Deformation \(\delta=\sigma t/E\) per layer ties the series model to the Reuss formula: total \(\delta\) is the sum over layers, giving the harmonic average of the moduli
Comparing the two bounds at the same \(V_f\) shows anisotropy: longitudinal stiffness is high and transverse stiffness is low, and this links to the property chart and to fibre orientation
Volume fraction versus weight fraction links to density: convert weight to volume using \(\rho\) before applying either rule of mixtures
exq: A GFRP has a polymer matrix with \(E_m=3\) GPa and glass fibres with \(E_f=72\) GPa at \(V_f=0.3\). Calculate the upper-bound and lower-bound composite moduli and state the loading direction for each.
Derive the iso-strain rule of mixtures \(E_{cl}=E_mV_m+E_fV_f\) starting from \(F_c=F_m+F_f\). State the assumptions and why it fails for transverse loading.
For a CFRP under longitudinal load with \(V_f=0.6\), \(E_f=230\) GPa and \(E_m=3.5\) GPa, find the fraction of the load carried by the fibres.
A composite contains 40 wt% glass fibre in a polymer. Given the densities, convert to volume fraction and estimate both bounds on the modulus.
Sketch modulus against \(V_f\) showing both bounds. Explain where experimental particulate-composite data lie and why, and why stiffness is plotted on a log scale in the property chart.

notes.t: Composites
pts: A composite is made from two or more distinct phases, which remain separable under a microscope.
Composites are generally engineered to optimise the combined properties of the constituent phases.
Glass-fibre and carbon-fibre reinforced polymers (GFRP, CFRP) are common engineered composites in which fibres are embedded in a polymer matrix.
Polymers filled with glass powder or silica flour are composites, and wood is a naturally occurring composite of lignin and cellulose fibres.
defs: Composite
A material made from two or more phases that remain distinguishable (visible as separate phases under a microscope), combined to optimise the properties of the phases.
tips: Do not confuse a composite with an alloy: alloy phases are usually not separately visible, whereas composite phases are.
Wood counts as a natural composite (lignin plus cellulose fibres), so do not assume composites are only man-made.
rq: Why does a composite need its phases to be visibly separate under a microscope to count as a composite?
Because a composite is defined by having distinct phases; a single-phase material (e.g. a homogeneous alloy) has no separate phases to combine, so it is not a composite.
What would you expect to happen to stiffness and strength if the fibres in a GFRP were aligned with the principal stress direction, compared with random orientation?

Properties are highest along the fibre direction when fibres align with the principal stress, since the stiff fibres carry the load; random orientation gives more uniform but lower directional properties.

notes.t: Mechanical Properties of Composites – factors to control
pts: Filler and matrix choice set the composite's baseline properties.
Filler amount should be specified by volume fraction rather than weight, since volume governs the mechanical contribution.
Good contact (interfacial bonding) between filler and matrix is needed for the composite to behave as one material.
Effective load transfer from matrix to filler is what gives reinforcement its strengthening effect.
tips: Do not quote filler content by weight when comparing mechanical properties; convert to volume fraction first.
Poor interfacial bonding can make a reinforced composite weaker than expected, so bonding must be considered alongside filler choice.
rq: Why is filler content specified by volume rather than weight?

Mechanical behaviour depends on the volume each phase occupies; fillers of different densities give different volume fractions for the same weight, so volume fraction gives comparable, meaningful properties.
What would happen to a composite with poor filler–matrix contact under load?
The matrix cannot transfer stress to the filler, so the filler does not carry load; the composite fails at lower strength, often by debonding at the interface.

notes.t: Load transfer in composites
pts: How load is shared between phases depends on how stress is transferred, so bounding models are used.
The extreme-case models assume stress is uniform throughout the composite (iso-stress).
The other extreme assumes strain is uniform throughout the composite (iso-strain).
Composite stiffness from these bounds lies between the two extremes, which is why the chart shows wide ranges for composites such as CFRC, GFRC and wood.
defs: Iso-stress assumption
Model in which the stress is the same in every phase of a composite, so the composite modulus follows a rule-of-mixtures in compliance (lower-bound stiffness estimate).
Iso-strain assumption
Model in which the strain is the same in every phase of a composite, so the composite modulus follows the rule of mixtures (upper-bound stiffness estimate).
tips: Do not mix up the two bounds: iso-strain gives the upper (stiffer) estimate, iso-stress gives the lower estimate.
Stiffness is plotted on a logarithmic scale in GPa, so differences of one division represent a factor of 10 in modulus, not a fixed addition.
rq: Why does the iso-strain model give an upper bound on composite stiffness rather than a lower bound?

Iso-strain forces every phase to deform equally, so stiffer phases carry proportionally more stress; this maximises the load-carrying contribution of the stiff reinforcement and so gives the highest predicted modulus.
If a real composite has fibres aligned at an angle to the load, what would you expect for its stiffness relative to the two bounds?
It should lie below the iso-strain (upper) bound, because the fibre cannot be strained equally along its full length in the loading direction, reducing its effective load share.

notes.t: Strain constant (parallel sheet model of composites)
pts: In the simplest composite model, filler and matrix are assumed to deform by the same strain under longitudinal loading.
The simplest model represents the composite as alternating sheets of filler and matrix arranged in parallel to the load.
Because the phases act in parallel, the total load carried by the composite is the sum of the loads carried by matrix and filler.
defs: Strain constant (isostrain) condition
Assumption that matrix and filler experience identical strain when loaded in parallel, so the composite strain equals each constituent's strain.
eqs: Load carried by the composite under isostrain (parallel) loading
\(F_c\) = total load on composite (N); \(F_m\) = load carried by matrix (N); \(F_f\) = load carried by filler (N)
tips: The rule \(F_{c}\) = \(F_{m}\) + \(F_{f}\) applies only to the parallel (isostrain) model with load along the longitudinal direction; do not use it for transverse loading.
Remember that equal strain, not equal stress, is the defining assumption; stresses in the two phases generally differ.
rq: Why does assuming equal strain in filler and matrix allow the loads to be simply added?
Because the sheets are parallel and must stretch together; equilibrium of the applied force divides it between the two phases, so total force is the sum of each phase's force.
What would change if the filler and matrix were arranged in series instead of parallel?
The stresses would be equal rather than strains, so the isostrain rule \(F_{c}\) = \(F_{m}\) + \(F_{f}\) would no longer apply.

notes.t: Strain constant: rule of mixtures for composite stress
pts: In a composite under equal strain, the total load is shared between matrix and fibre, so the composite stress is the area-weighted sum of phase stresses.
When phase lengths are equal, area fractions equal volume fractions, so the weighting uses the volume fractions of fibre and matrix.
The area fractions \(A_{m}\)/\(A_{c}\) and \(A_{f}\)/\(A_{c}\) must sum to 1 because the composite area is the sum of matrix and fibre areas.
defs: Area fraction
The ratio of the cross-sectional area of a phase to the total composite cross-sectional area, used to weight phase stresses.
Volume fraction
The fraction of the composite volume occupied by a phase; equal to its area fraction when all phases have the same length.
eqs: Load balance for the composite (force equilibrium)

\(\sigma_{c}\) = composite stress (Pa); \(A_{c}\) = composite cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \(\sigma_{m}\) = matrix stress (Pa); \(A_{m}\) = matrix area (\(m^{2}\)); \(\sigma_{f}\) = fibre stress (Pa); \(A_{f}\) = fibre area (\(m^{2}\))
Rule of mixtures for composite stress (area-weighted)

\(\sigma_{c}\) = composite stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{m}\) = matrix stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{f}\) = fibre stress (Pa); \(A_{m}\)/\(A_{c}\) = matrix area fraction (dimensionless); \(A_{f}\)/\(A_{c}\) = fibre area fraction (dimensionless)
Volume fractions from area fractions (equal phase lengths)

\(V_{f}\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless); \(V_{m}\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(A_{f}\) = fibre area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_{m}\) = matrix area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_{c}\) = composite area (\(m^{2}\))
tips: Area fractions only equal volume fractions when all phases have equal lengths; otherwise the volume weighting must be used.
Ensure the fractions sum to 1 (\(A_{m}\)/\(A_{c}\) + \(A_{f}\)/\(A_{c}\) = 1) and keep stresses in consistent units (Pa or MPa).
rq: Why can the area fractions be used directly as volume fractions here?
Because the composite, matrix and fibre phase lengths are equal, so volume = area × length reduces to a ratio of areas.
What is the composite stress if the matrix carries 20 MPa over 0.6 of the area and the fibre carries 200 MPa over 0.4 of the area?

notes.t: Strain Constant – Rule of Mixtures for Composite Stiffness (Longitudinal Loading)
pts: Stress in the composite is the volume-fraction-weighted sum of matrix and fibre stresses.
Assuming equal strain in matrix and fibre (iso-strain), the composite stiffness is the volume-weighted average of the constituent moduli.
Because the volume fractions sum to one, the composite modulus depends on a single fibre volume fraction.
eqs: Composite stress (rule of mixtures for stress)

\(\sigma_c\) = composite stress (Pa); \(\sigma_m\) = matrix stress (Pa); \(\sigma_f\) = fibre stress (Pa); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
Longitudinal composite modulus (iso-strain rule of mixtures)

\(E_{cl}\) = longitudinal composite modulus (Pa); \(E_m\) = matrix modulus (Pa); \(E_f\) = fibre modulus (Pa); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
Longitudinal composite modulus in terms of fibre fraction
\(E_{cl}\) = longitudinal composite modulus (Pa); \(E_m\) = matrix modulus (Pa); \(E_f\) = fibre modulus (Pa); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
tips: Volume fractions must be dimensionless and sum to one; using percentages without converting to fractions gives wrong moduli.
This rule of mixtures assumes equal strain (longitudinal loading); it does not apply directly to transverse loading.
rq: Why does assuming equal strain in fibre and matrix lead to a simple addition of moduli?
Since \(\varepsilon_c=\varepsilon_m=\varepsilon_f\), dividing the stress relation by the common strain turns each stress/strain ratio into a modulus, so \(E_{cl}=E_mV_m+E_fV_f\).
What if the fibre volume fraction doubled while the constituent moduli stayed the same?
The composite modulus would move closer to the fibre modulus, because \(E_{cl}=E_m(1-V_f)+E_fV_f\) is linear in \(V_f\).

notes.t: Stress constant model for layered filler-matrix composites
pts: In the transverse (layered) model, stress is the same in the filler and matrix layers, so each layer carries the same stress F/A.
The simplest model stacks alternating layers of filler and matrix, with the load applied transverse to the layers.
Because stress is shared and each layer has its own modulus, each layer's strain is σ/E, giving different strains in filler and matrix.
Total deformation of each layer equals its strain multiplied by its own thickness.
defs: Stress constant (transverse model)
A composite model in which the same stress acts in every filler and matrix layer when the load is applied perpendicular to the layers.
eqs: \(\varepsilon\) = strain (dimensionless); \(\sigma\) = stress (Pa); \(E\) = Young's modulus of that layer (Pa)
\(\delta\) = deformation (m); \(\sigma\) = stress (Pa); \(E\) = Young's modulus of the layer (Pa); \(t\) = layer thickness (m)
tips: Do not assume equal strain in filler and matrix; equal stress means strains differ according to each E.
Deformation requires multiplying strain by layer thickness; using strain alone gives the wrong units (m versus dimensionless).
rq: Why does the stress stay the same in every layer under transverse loading, while the strain does not?
The layers are in series under the same force and area, so σ = F/A is common; strain σ/E depends on each layer's modulus E, which differs between filler and matrix.
What would happen to the layer deformations if the filler were much stiffer than the matrix?
The filler layers would strain less (σ/\(E_{\text{filler}}\) is small) while matrix layers strain more, so most of the total deformation occurs in the matrix.

notes.t: Isostress state and rule of mixtures for strain in composites
pts: In an isostress state, stress is the same in the composite, matrix and fibre, so the load is shared as a common stress.
The composite strain is the volume-fraction-weighted average of the matrix and fibre strains.
Volume fractions of matrix and fibre must add to one.
defs: Isostress state
A condition in a composite where the stress in the composite, matrix and fibre are all equal (σ_c = σ_m = σ_f = σ), so each constituent carries the same stress.
eqs: Composite strain under isostress (rule of mixtures for strain)

\(\varepsilon_c\) = composite strain (dimensionless); \(\varepsilon_m\) = matrix strain (dimensionless); \(\varepsilon_f\) = fibre strain (dimensionless); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
tips: Do not mix up isostress (equal stress, strain averaged) with isostrain (equal strain, stress averaged); the rule of mixtures for strain applies only under isostress.
Volume fractions must sum to one; check \(V_m + V_f = 1\) before substituting values.
rq: Why does the isostress condition lead to a strain that is a weighted average of matrix and fibre strains?

Because the stress is equal in both phases, the constituents deform according to their own stiffness; the overall strain is the volume-weighted sum of the phase strains, so each phase contributes in proportion to its volume fraction.
What if the matrix volume fraction were 0.7 and the fibre volume fraction were not adjusted to match?
The constraint \(V_{m}\) + \(V_{f}\) = 1 would be violated, so the strain calculation would be invalid; the fibre fraction must be 0.3 to keep the volume fractions consistent.

notes.t: Stress constant in composite rule of mixtures (iso-stress)
pts: Under equal stress in matrix and fibre, the composite modulus relates to each phase's modulus weighted by its volume fraction.
Dividing the stress-strain relation through by the common stress σ gives the reciprocal form of the composite modulus, which is the iso-stress (Reuss-type) rule of mixtures.
defs: Iso-stress condition
Assumption that the matrix and fibre carry the same stress σ, so the composite modulus is the volume-fraction-weighted sum of the reciprocal phase moduli.
eqs: Reciprocal composite modulus under iso-stress (rule of mixtures)
\(E_{ct}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(E_m\) = matrix modulus (Pa); \(E_f\) = fibre modulus (Pa); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
tips: Volume fractions must sum to 1 (\(V_{m}\) + \(V_{f}\) = 1) and the result is for the reciprocal of \(E_{\text{ct}}\), not \(E_{\text{ct}}\) itself — take the inverse at the end.
This iso-stress form assumes equal stress in each phase; it is not the equal-strain (simple rule of mixtures) result \(E_{\text{ct}}\) = \(E_{m}\) \(V_{m}\) + \(E_{f}\) \(V_{f}\).
rq: Why does dividing through by σ turn the stress-based form into a sum of reciprocal moduli, and what physical assumption makes that valid?
Dividing by σ converts each term σ/E into 1/E-type terms; the sum holds because σ is the same in matrix, fibre and composite (iso-stress), so the strain contributions add by volume fraction.
If the fibre is much stiffer than the matrix, which term dominates the reciprocal sum and what does that imply for \(E_{\text{ct}}\)?
The \(V_{m}\)/\(E_{m}\) term dominates because \(E_{m}\) is small; \(E_{\text{ct}}\) is then limited by the matrix, approaching the lower value rather than the fibre modulus.

notes.t: Composite modulus bounds (rule of mixtures)
pts: Constant strain (iso-strain) assumption gives the upper bound on composite modulus, computed as a volume-weighted arithmetic average.
Constant stress (iso-stress) assumption gives the lower bound on composite modulus, computed via a harmonic-type (inverse) average.
Real composites lie between these two bounds; other models give intermediate values.
defs: Upper bound (iso-strain)
The maximum possible composite modulus, obtained by assuming matrix and fibre experience the same strain under load.
Lower bound (iso-stress)
The minimum possible composite modulus, obtained by assuming matrix and fibre carry the same stress under load.
eqs: Upper bound composite modulus (constant strain / Voigt rule of mixtures)

\(E_{cl}\) = upper-bound composite modulus (Pa); \(E_m\) = matrix modulus (Pa); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(E_f\) = fibre modulus (Pa); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
Lower bound composite modulus (constant stress / Reuss rule of mixtures)

\(E_{ct}\) = lower-bound composite modulus (Pa); \(E_m\) = matrix modulus (Pa); \(V_m\) = matrix volume fraction (dimensionless); \(E_f\) = fibre modulus (Pa); \(V_f\) = fibre volume fraction (dimensionless)
tips: Do not mix the two formulas: the upper bound is a direct weighted sum, while the lower bound requires summing \(V/E\) terms and then taking the reciprocal.
Check that volume fractions sum to 1 and that moduli are in consistent units (e.g. GPa) before substituting.
rq: Why does the iso-strain (upper bound) model give a higher modulus than the iso-stress (lower bound) model for the same fibre and matrix?

Iso-strain forces the stiffer fibre to share the same strain, so it carries more load in parallel with the matrix; iso-stress forces equal stress, so the compliant matrix must deform more, reducing overall stiffness (series arrangement).
If \(V_f = 0\), what do both bound equations predict, and why does this check validate them?
Both reduce to \(E = E_m\), the matrix modulus, since with no fibres the composite is pure matrix; this confirms the equations are consistent at the limit.

notes.t: Simplest models for composite stiffness (rule of mixtures bounds)
pts: Composite modulus lies between an upper bound (constant strain, iso-strain) and a lower bound (constant stress, iso-stress) as a function of fibre/particle volume fraction.

The upper bound is a straight line from \(E_{m}\) at \(V_{f}\) = 0 to \(E_{f}\) at \(V_{f}\) = 1, representing the constant-strain (Voigt) model, which overestimates stiffness for particulate composites.
The lower bound is a curve that stays close to \(E_{m}\) at low volume fraction and rises steeply near \(V_{f}\) = 1, representing the constant-stress (Reuss) model.
Experimental data for particulate composites lie between the two bounds, closer to the lower limit, showing that the simple models only bracket real behaviour.
The region between the bounds is labelled as anisotropy, reflecting that the real stiffness depends on fibre orientation and loading direction.
defs: Constant strain (iso-strain) model
Assumes matrix and reinforcement experience the same strain under load, giving an upper bound on composite modulus.
Constant stress (iso-stress) model
Assumes matrix and reinforcement carry the same stress, giving a lower bound on composite modulus.
Anisotropy
Direction-dependent properties of a composite; the spread between the bounds reflects how stiffness varies with fibre orientation.
eqs: \(E_{\text{composite}}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(V_{f}\) = volume fraction of reinforcement (–); \(E_{f}\) = fibre/filler modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\) = matrix modulus (Pa)
\(E_{\text{composite}}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(V_{f}\) = volume fraction of reinforcement (–); \(E_{f}\) = fibre/filler modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\) = matrix modulus (Pa)
tips: Keep the rule of mixtures straight: the constant-strain (Voigt) form is linear in \(V_{f}\), whereas the constant-stress (Reuss) form uses reciprocals; mixing these up swaps the bounds.
Ensure volume fractions are used (not mass fractions) and that moduli share the same units (Pa or GPa) before substituting.
rq: Why does the constant-strain model overestimate the stiffness of particulate composites?

It assumes the matrix and particles deform equally, ignoring that the softer matrix can deform more and the load is not shared as the strain-equal condition requires; real particles do not carry the full strain-compatible load.
What happens to the bounds as \(V_{f}\) approaches 0, and why does it matter?
Both bounds converge to \(E_{m}\), since a pure matrix has only the matrix modulus; this is a necessary consistency check on any composite model.
Which bound would you use as a conservative design estimate, and why?
The lower bound (constant stress), because it gives the smallest modulus and so avoids overestimating stiffness.

xq.q: A unidirectional glass-fibre/epoxy composite contains a fibre volume fraction \(V_f = 0.30\). The fibre modulus is \(E_f = 70\) GPa and the matrix modulus is \(E_m = 3\) GPa. The composite is loaded parallel to the fibres, and fibre and matrix are assumed to have the same strain. Calculate the composite modulus \(E_c\) and the fraction of the total load carried by the fibres.
xq.a: \(E_c = 23.1\) GPa; the fibres carry 90.9% of the load.
s: Equal strain gives the rule of mixtures: \(E_c = V_f E_f + V_m E_m\), with \(V_m = 0.70\).
Load fraction in fibre: \(F_f/F_c = V_f E_f/E_c = 21/23.1 = 0.909\), i.e. 90.9%.

xq.q: A composite consists of 50% by volume of a stiff filler (\(E_f = 200\) GPa) in a polymer matrix (\(E_m = 4\) GPa). Assuming the stress is the same in both phases (iso-stress), calculate the composite modulus \(E_c\). State whether this is an upper or lower bound on stiffness.
xq.a: \(E_c \approx 7.84\) GPa, which is the lower bound.
s: Iso-stress gives the lower bound; the iso-strain value (102 GPa) is the upper bound.

xq.q: A composite has 50% by volume of fibres with \(E_f = 100\) GPa in a matrix with \(E_m = 5\) GPa. What is the lower-bound (iso-stress) modulus of the composite?
xq.a: 9.52 GPa
o: 52.5 GPa
9.52 GPa
22.4 GPa
xq.w: The iso-stress bound is \(E_c = [V_f/E_f + V_m/E_m]^{-1} = 1/0.105 = 9.52\) GPa; 52.5 GPa is the iso-strain upper bound, 0.105 forgets to invert, and 22.4 is a geometric mean that belongs to neither model.

units.name: 11.8 Composite examples: concrete and dental fillings
units.ov: This material introduces composites as two-phase materials in which a continuous matrix binds a dispersed filler, using concrete (cement matrix, gravel/stone aggregate) and white dental fillings (polymer matrix, silica/quartz glass filler) as examples. Both show the same principle: the matrix binds and transfers load, the filler reinforces, and the combination outperforms either constituent alone. Performance depends on the matrix-filler bond and on loading conditions, for example concrete's compressive strength and tensile weakness.
must: Composite: two or more distinct constituents (matrix + filler) combining to give properties superior to either alone
Matrix = continuous phase that binds the filler and transfers load; filler = dispersed reinforcing phase (do not mix these up)
Concrete: cement matrix (hardens by mixing with water and recrystallising) + aggregate filler (gravel, small stones)
Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so non-reinforced structures rely on compressive geometry such as domes
Pantheon, Rome (126 A.D.): largest non-reinforced concrete structure, dome 43 m high; concrete was invented by the Romans and re-invented in the mid 18th century
Dental composites (developed in the 1980s): tooth-coloured polymer matrix, typically set by UV light
Dental filler particles (silica or quartz glass) provide strength, stiffness and wear resistance
Composite properties depend on the matrix-filler bond; poor bonding weakens the material
Both examples are particulate composites: filler particles dispersed in a continuous matrix
conn: Matrix/filler roles link both examples: cement and polymer bind and transfer load, while aggregate and glass particles reinforce
Concrete's compression/tension asymmetry links to structural design (domes, arches) and to why reinforcement is added in tension zones
Interfacial bonding links to failure: poor matrix-filler adhesion causes weak concrete or a worn or failed filling
Processing/setting (cement hydration versus UV curing of polymer) links to how the matrix forms and so to final properties
exq: Define a composite and identify the matrix and filler in (a) concrete and (b) a white dental filling, stating the function of each.
Explain why the Pantheon's non-reinforced concrete dome has survived, referring to concrete's compressive and tensile behaviour.
Describe how the matrix hardens in concrete and in a dental composite, and compare the two setting mechanisms.
Discuss how poor bonding between filler and matrix would affect the performance of a dental filling and of concrete.
Why are silica or quartz glass particles added to the polymer in a dental composite? State the property improvements and why the polymer alone is inadequate.

notes.t: Composites – Concrete
pts: Concrete is a composite whose matrix is cement, which hardens by mixing with water and recrystallising.
The filler (reinforcement phase) in concrete is aggregate such as gravel and small stones.
Concrete was invented by the Romans and re-invented in the mid 18th century.
The Pantheon in Rome (126 A.D.) is the world's largest non-reinforced concrete structure, with a dome 43 m high.
defs: Concrete
A composite material in which a cement matrix binds a particulate aggregate filler such as gravel or small stones.
Matrix
The continuous phase that binds the filler together in a composite; in concrete this is cement mixed with water.
Aggregate
The filler phase in concrete, typically gravel or other small stones, dispersed within the cement matrix.
tips: Do not confuse the matrix (cement) with the filler (aggregate): cement binds, aggregate is the dispersed phase.
Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so 'non-reinforced' structures rely on compressive geometry such as domes.
rq: Why does concrete need aggregate filler rather than being made of cement paste alone?
Aggregate reduces the amount of cement needed, lowers shrinkage and cost, and provides bulk and load-bearing particles within the matrix.
Why is the Pantheon's dome able to stand without steel reinforcement?
Concrete is strong in compression; the dome's curved shape carries loads as compressive stresses, so no reinforcement is needed to resist tension.

notes.t: Composite materials – white dental fillings
pts: Dental composites were developed in the 1980s as tooth-coloured restorative materials.
The matrix of a dental composite is a polymer that is typically hardened (set) by ultraviolet light.
The filler particles, typically silica or quartz glasses, are dispersed in the polymer matrix and provide strength and wear resistance.
defs: Composite
A material made from two or more distinct constituents (a matrix and a filler) that combine to give properties superior to either alone.
Matrix (composite)
The continuous phase, here a polymer, that binds the filler particles together and transfers load to them.
Filler (composite)
The dispersed reinforcing phase, typically silica or quartz glass particles, which improves stiffness, strength and wear resistance of the matrix.
tips: Do not confuse the matrix (continuous polymer) with the filler (dispersed particles); the filler is the reinforcement, not the binder.
Remember that the composite's properties depend on the matrix–filler bond; poor bonding weakens the filling.
rq: Why is a filler such as silica added to the polymer matrix rather than using the polymer alone?
The polymer alone is weak, wears easily and shrinks more; silica/quartz filler increases stiffness, strength and wear resistance and reduces polymerisation shrinkage.
Why is ultraviolet light used to set the matrix rather than heat?
UV light triggers photo-initiators that start polymerisation at room temperature in the mouth, allowing the filling to be shaped and hardened on demand without heating tooth tissue.

xq.q: The Pantheon in Rome (126 A.D.) has a large non-reinforced concrete dome that has survived for nearly two thousand years. Which statement best explains why a non-reinforced concrete structure can work in this form?
xq.a: The dome geometry keeps the concrete mostly in compression, where concrete is strong, rather than in tension, where it is weak.
o: Concrete is strong in tension, so the dome resists the bending loads in its walls.
The dome geometry keeps the concrete mostly in compression, where concrete is strong, rather than in tension, where it is weak.
The aggregate is the continuous matrix, which carries tensile load around the dome.
The cement matrix recrystallises into a single crystal, which removes the need for reinforcement.
xq.w: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, so a compressive geometry such as a dome suits it; the trap is assuming it is strong in tension or mixing up matrix and aggregate.
s: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension.
A dome loads the material mainly in compression.

xq.q: A dental filling is a polymer matrix hardened by ultraviolet light and filled with silica or quartz glass particles. Tests show the filling wears and fractures much faster than expected for its filler content, and the filler particles are seen to pull cleanly out of the polymer. What is the most likely cause?
xq.a: Poor interfacial bonding between filler and matrix, so load is not transferred to the particles.
o: The filler is the continuous phase, so it cannot transfer load to the matrix.
The filler volume fraction is too high because it was quoted by weight.
Poor interfacial bonding between filler and matrix, so load is not transferred to the particles.
The polymer matrix has hardened, which always weakens a composite.
xq.w: Particles pulling cleanly out indicate a weak filler–matrix bond, so the matrix cannot transfer load to the filler; the trap is blaming the phase roles or the hardening step.
s: The matrix must transfer load to the filler.
Clean pull-out indicates a weak interface.

xq.q: For a white dental filling, explain the roles of the polymer matrix and the silica/quartz glass filler particles. Explain why the bond between them matters for the performance of the filling.
xq.a: The matrix is the continuous polymer phase. It is set by ultraviolet light, binds the particles together and transfers load to them. The filler is the dispersed silica or quartz glass particles. It is the reinforcement and improves stiffness, strength and wear resistance. For the composite to behave as one material, the interface must transfer load from matrix to filler. If the bond is poor, the particles do not share the load, and the filling is weaker than expected and wears or fails early.
s: Matrix: continuous polymer, binds and transfers load (1)
Filler: dispersed silica/quartz particles giving strength, stiffness and wear resistance (1)
Good bond needed for load transfer from matrix to filler (1)

units.name: 12.1 Elastic vs plastic deformation and shear in yield
units.ov: This lecture separates elastic deformation (reversible, bonds stretch but stay intact) from plastic deformation (permanent, bonds break and reform through slip of atomic planes). It then shows that yield is driven by shear stress, which is greatest on planes at 45° to a uniaxial load in isotropic materials. The unifying idea is that yielding is a shear-driven, slip-based process, not a normal-stress one.
must: Elastic deformation is reversible: bonds stretch but do not break, and the original shape is fully recovered on unloading.
Plastic deformation is permanent: bonds fail and new ones form, and the shape is not recovered after unloading.
The discriminator is recovery after unloading, not whether the shape changes under load, since both types change shape under load.
Metals are typically elastic only up to about 0.5% strain (\( \varepsilon \approx 0.005 \)). This is a typical value, not a universal constant.
Yield is the onset of permanent deformation and is driven by shear stress on atomic planes, not by normal stress alone.
Shear means forces parallel to a surface, so layers of atoms slide over one another. Elastically the planes spring back; plastically they slip to a new lattice arrangement.
Failure favours the planes of greatest shear stress. In an isotropic material under uniaxial tension or compression these lie at \( \theta = 45^\circ \) to the load.
Planes of maximum shear (45° to the load) are different from planes of maximum normal stress (perpendicular to the load).
Isotropic means properties are the same in all directions. The 45° result may not hold for anisotropic materials such as single crystals.
Strain is dimensionless, so 0.005 equals 0.5%. State which form you use to avoid errors.
conn: Slip of atomic planes (microscopic mechanism) links to the 45° maximum shear plane (continuum stress analysis), which explains the angled shear bands seen in yielded tensile specimens.
The elastic limit and the strain at which bonds start to fail link to the start of plastic deformation on a stress-strain curve, and so to the definition of yield strength.
Isotropy underlies the 45° result, so questions may ask how anisotropy or crystal orientation changes the critical slip plane.
Uniaxial tension and compression give the same 45° plane, linking the loading mode to the shear that causes yield, which leads on to Mohr's circle and the Tresca criterion.
exq: Define elastic and plastic deformation at the atomic level. Using sketches of atomic planes under shear, explain what the lattice looks like after unloading in each case.

A metal rod is loaded in uniaxial tension. State the angle of the plane of maximum shear stress to the load axis and explain why yielding occurs on this plane rather than the plane of maximum normal stress.

A metal has an elastic strain limit of about 0.5%. A 200 mm specimen is stretched by 0.8 mm and unloaded. Is it permanently deformed? Justify your answer with the strain value and state any assumptions.
Explain why the statement 'elastic deformation involves no change in shape' is wrong. What actually distinguishes elastic from plastic deformation?
Under what conditions does the 45° maximum shear plane result apply? Discuss how it might differ for an anisotropic material.

notes.t: Elastic deformation
pts: Elastic deformation is reversible: atomic bonds stretch but stay intact, so the material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
For metals, elastic behaviour typically holds only up to about 0.5% strain (0.005).
Beyond the elastic limit, plastic deformation begins: bonds fail and new ones form, so the deformation is permanent.
defs: Elastic deformation
Reversible deformation in which atomic bonds stretch without breaking, so the material returns to its original shape once the load is removed.
Plastic deformation
Permanent deformation that occurs after the elastic limit, in which atomic bonds fail and new bonds form, so the shape is not recovered on unloading.
tips: Do not confuse the elastic limit with the yield strength in general; the 0.5% figure is a typical value for metals, not a universal constant.
Strain is dimensionless: 0.005 and 0.5% are the same value, so state the form used clearly to avoid unit or percentage errors.
rq: Why does unloading a metal within its elastic range return it exactly to its original length, while unloading it beyond that range does not?

Within the elastic range the atomic bonds only stretch and remain intact, so the stored energy is recovered and the structure springs back. Beyond it, bonds fail and reform in new positions, so the displacement is permanent.
What would you expect to happen to the elastic limit of a metal if its strain were limited to 0.2% during loading?
The metal would remain entirely elastic, since 0.2% is below the typical elastic limit of about 0.5% for metals, so it would fully recover on unloading.

notes.t: Elastic and Plastic Deformation
pts: Elastic deformation is reversible: the material changes shape under load and fully recovers its original shape once the load is removed.
Plastic deformation is permanent: the material changes shape under load but does not return to its original shape after the load is removed.
Under shear loading, atomic planes slide relative to one another; in the elastic case the planes spring back when the load is removed, leaving the lattice unchanged.
In plastic deformation, the atomic planes are displaced permanently by slip, so the lattice is left in a new, shifted arrangement after unloading.
defs: Elastic deformation
A reversible change in shape that occurs when a load is applied and disappears completely when the load is removed, the material returning to its original shape.
Plastic deformation
An irreversible change in shape that persists after the load is removed; the material does not return to its original shape.
Shear
A loading mode in which forces act parallel to a surface, causing layers of atoms to slide relative to one another.
tips: Do not confuse elastic deformation with plastic deformation: the key discriminator is whether the shape is recovered after the load is removed, not whether shape changes under load (both change shape under load).
Elastic deformation is not 'no deformation': the shape does change under load; only the recovery distinguishes it from plastic deformation.
rq: Why does an elastically deformed metal spring back to its original shape, while a plastically deformed one does not?

In elastic deformation atomic bonds are stretched or displaced but not permanently broken or rearranged, so they restore the original configuration when unloaded. In plastic deformation planes of atoms slide past one another permanently (slip), so the new arrangement persists after unloading.
What would you expect to observe on a stress–strain curve if a material is loaded beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded?
The unloading curve is roughly parallel to the elastic slope but does not return to zero strain; a permanent (plastic) strain remains.

notes.t: Yield and maximum shear stress
pts: Yielding is driven by shear acting on planes of atoms within the material.
Failure favourably occurs along the planes where shear stress is greatest.
For isotropic materials in uniaxial tension or compression, the maximum shear plane is inclined at 45° to the load.
defs: Yield
Onset of permanent (plastic) deformation in a material, driven by shear stress acting on planes of atoms rather than by normal stress alone.
Isotropic material
A material whose mechanical properties are the same in all directions.
eqs: Maximum shear stress under uniaxial load (plane angle)
\theta = angle between maximum shear plane and applied load (degrees)
tips: Do not confuse the planes of maximum shear (45° to the load) with the planes of maximum normal stress (perpendicular to the load).
This 45° result applies to isotropic materials under uniaxial loading; anisotropic materials may have different critical planes.
rq: Why does yielding occur on 45° planes in a tensile test rather than on the plane perpendicular to the load?
On the plane perpendicular to the load the shear stress is zero; the shear stress is maximised at 45° to the load, so yielding by shear is favoured there.
What would happen to the orientation of the maximum shear planes in a brittle material that fails by normal stress?
Brittle materials fail by normal (tensile) stress on planes perpendicular to the load, so the 45° shear-plane argument does not govern their failure.

xq.q: A steel wire of length 2.0 m behaves elastically up to a typical metal elastic-limit strain of 0.5%. What is the largest extension it can undergo while still returning fully to its original length when unloaded?
xq.a: 10 mm
o: 1.0 mm
100 mm
10 mm
xq.w: Strain 0.5% = 0.005, so extension = 0.005 × 2000 mm = 10 mm; the traps are treating 0.5% as 0.5 or 0.05, and unit slips.

xq.q: An isotropic cylindrical metal specimen is loaded in uniaxial tension and begins to yield by slip. At what angle to the loading axis do the planes of maximum shear stress lie?
xq.w: For isotropic materials under uniaxial load, maximum shear acts on planes at 45° to the load; the trap is confusing these with planes of maximum normal stress, which are perpendicular (90°) to the load.
s: Maximum shear plane is at 45° to the load for an isotropic material.

xq.q: Explain, in terms of atomic planes under shear loading, the difference between elastic and plastic deformation. Say why yielding in a uniaxially loaded isotropic metal is expected on planes at 45° to the load.
xq.a: In elastic deformation the bonds stretch but stay intact. The atomic planes shift slightly under shear and spring back when the load is removed, so the original shape and lattice are recovered. In plastic deformation, beyond the elastic limit (about 0.5% strain in metals), bonds fail and new ones form as planes slip. The planes end up permanently displaced, so the shape is not recovered. Both change shape under load, and recovery is the difference. Yielding is driven by shear on atomic planes, and slip occurs where shear stress is greatest. For an isotropic material under uniaxial load this is on planes at 45° to the load, not on the planes of maximum normal stress.
s: Elastic: bonds stretch, planes spring back, shape recovered (1)
Plastic: bonds break and re-form, planes permanently displaced by slip (1)
The difference is recovery after unloading (1)
Yield is driven by shear on atomic planes (1)
Maximum shear is at 45° to the load for an isotropic material (1)

units.name: 12.2 Slip mechanisms and slip systems in FCC, BCC, HCP
units.ov: This material explains yield in crystalline metals as dislocation glide (slip) on specific crystallographic planes and in specific directions, which are set by the crystal structure. A slip system is a slip plane plus a slip direction within it. The number of slip systems in FCC, BCC and HCP then explains the differences in ductility between them.
must: Yield in crystalline metals is dislocation motion; slip needs far less stress than moving whole planes of atoms at once (theoretical shear strength)
Slip plane = the plane of highest atomic packing density (largest interplanar spacing, lowest resistance); slip direction = the close-packed direction within that plane
A slip system = one slip plane + one slip direction; the number of systems is planes × directions per plane, and you must give both
FCC: slip on {111} planes along ⟨110⟩ face diagonals (not cube edges), giving 12 slip systems (4 planes × 3 directions), so FCC is highly ductile
BCC: slip along ⟨111⟩ cube diagonals, with many systems (up to 48 in the notes), so it is generally ductile
HCP: slip is restricted to directions parallel to the basal plane, giving only 3 slip systems, so it is less ductile and tends towards brittleness
More slip systems means easier plastic deformation and greater ductility; this is not the same as higher or lower yield strength
Slip is driven by shear stress resolved onto the slip plane and direction; the applied tensile stress alone does not give the slip direction
Slip family = a group of symmetry-equivalent slip systems with the same plane and direction type
HCP ductility is a trend only: Ti and Zn can become ductile at elevated temperature as extra slip systems activate
conn: Packing density links to slip: the densest planes have the largest spacing and the lowest shear resistance, so they are the slip planes. The densest direction within them has the smallest Burgers displacement, so it is the slip direction.
Crystal structure sets the number of slip systems, and that number sets ductility (FCC/BCC ductile, HCP less so). Temperature can modify this by activating extra systems.

Dislocation motion links to resolved shear stress: yield occurs when the shear stress on a slip system reaches a critical value, so the orientation of the plane and direction relative to the load matters.

Unit-cell geometry links to the Miller indices of slip: face diagonals in FCC and body diagonals in BCC give the ⟨110⟩ and ⟨111⟩ directions, and confusing these with cube edges gives the wrong slip system.
exq: Define slip plane, slip direction and slip system. For an FCC crystal, state the slip plane family and slip direction family and show how the 12 slip systems arise (4 planes × 3 directions).
Explain why slip occurs on the most densely packed planes and along close-packed directions, referring to interplanar spacing, atomic spacing and Burgers displacement.

Compare the number of slip systems in FCC (12), BCC (up to 48) and HCP (3). Explain how this accounts for their relative ductility, and why HCP metals such as Ti or Zn can become more ductile at high temperature.

A single FCC crystal is loaded in tension. Explain why the tensile stress must be resolved onto the slip plane and slip direction, and state what the resolved shear stress must reach for yield to begin.
Sketch an FCC unit cell and mark one {111} slip plane and one ⟨110⟩ slip direction within it. Explain why cube edges are not slip directions in FCC.

notes.t: Mechanisms of Yield
pts: Yield in crystalline metals occurs when dislocations move through the material, allowing permanent (plastic) deformation.
Atoms move preferentially along specific slip planes and in specific slip directions, which requires far less energy than moving everything at once.
The available slip planes and directions are set by the crystal structure (e.g. FCC, BCC, HCP), so they differ between materials.

Slip generally occurs on the planes with the highest atomic packing density, since atoms there are spaced furthest apart and the interplanar spacing is largest, giving the lowest resistance to motion.
defs: Slip plane
A crystallographic plane, usually of highest atomic packing density, along which atoms preferentially glide during plastic deformation.
Slip direction
The close-packed crystallographic direction within a slip plane along which atoms move during slip.
Dislocation
A line defect in a crystal lattice whose movement through the material carries plastic deformation at stresses far below the theoretical shear strength.
tips: Slip systems depend on the crystal structure, so do not assume every metal slips on the same planes.
Slip planes are the highest packing density planes; do not confuse them with the lowest density planes.
rq: Why is slip on the highest packing density planes easier than on sparsely packed planes?
Closely packed planes have larger interplanar spacing and fewer bonds to break per unit displacement, so the lattice resistance (Peierls stress) to dislocation motion is lower.
If a metal has few slip systems, what does this imply for its ductility?
Fewer independent slip systems limit the ability to accommodate arbitrary deformation, so the metal tends to be less ductile (e.g. HCP metals).

notes.t: Mechanisms of Yield: Slip in FCC Crystals
pts: In FCC metals, plastic deformation by slip occurs on the most densely packed planes, since these require the smallest shear force to move.
Slip proceeds along the close-packed direction, the line of highest linear atomic density, because the atomic spacing is smallest and the Burgers displacement is minimal.
In an FCC cell, the slip direction lies along the face diagonals (⟨110⟩-type directions) within the close-packed {111} planes.
tips: Do not confuse the slip plane (the most densely packed plane) with the slip direction (the close-packed line within it); both must be identified.
Slip in FCC is along face diagonals, not cube edges; using edge directions gives the wrong slip system.
rq: Why do slip planes and slip directions both favour the most densely packed arrangements?

Closely packed planes have the largest interplanar spacing and weakest bonding between them, so less shear stress is needed; the close-packed direction has the smallest slip displacement, minimising lattice distortion and energy.
What would happen to the number of slip systems if the crystal were not FCC but had only one close-packed plane family?
Fewer independent slip systems would be available, so the material would be less ductile, since plastic deformation requires enough systems to accommodate arbitrary shape change.

notes.t: FCC slip directions and slip systems
pts: Slip occurs when one plane of atoms (red) moves over the adjacent plane (blue) under shear stress.
During slip, atoms in the slipping plane shift to neighbouring equivalent lattice sites: a top corner atom moves to a mid back face position.
Slip proceeds along close-packed directions, so the atoms move between mid-face and corner positions that are the same type of site.
An FCC crystal has 12 slip systems, which makes FCC metals generally highly ductile.
defs: Slip plane
The crystallographic plane on which one part of a crystal slides over another under shear stress, producing plastic deformation.
Slip system
A combination of a slip plane and a slip direction within it; the number of slip systems determines how easily a metal deforms plastically.
Shear stress
A stress acting parallel to a plane, which causes layers of atoms to slide relative to each other and drives dislocation motion/slip.
tips: Slip occurs in close-packed planes and close-packed directions, not on arbitrary planes; do not count the 12 slip systems without including both plane and direction.
Shear stress must be resolved onto the slip plane and slip direction; the applied tensile stress alone does not indicate the slip direction.
rq: Why does FCC have more slip systems than BCC or HCP metals, and what does this mean for ductility?

FCC has 4 close-packed {111} planes each with 3 close-packed <110> directions, giving 12 slip systems; more systems allow slip to occur under many orientations of applied stress, so FCC metals are generally more ductile.
What would happen to slip if the shear stress acted in the opposite direction to the arrows shown?
Slip would occur in the opposite sense (the red plane would move the other way); the slip plane and slip direction are unchanged, only the sense of motion reverses.

notes.t: Slip directions in BCC and HCP crystal structures
pts: In BCC metals, slip occurs along the cube diagonal <111> directions, giving many available slip systems.
BCC structures have up to 48 slip systems, which makes them generally more ductile than HCP metals.
In HCP metals, slip directions lie only parallel to the basal plane, so slip is restricted.
HCP structures have only 3 slip systems, limiting plastic deformation and making them less ductile.
defs: Slip system
A combination of a slip plane and a slip direction along which dislocations move to produce plastic deformation.
tips: Do not confuse slip directions with slip planes; the count of slip systems depends on both.
Remember that the HCP restriction to the basal plane is why HCP metals are typically less ductile than BCC or FCC metals.
rq: Why does having fewer slip systems make HCP metals less ductile?
Fewer slip systems means fewer independent ways for dislocations to move, so the metal cannot easily accommodate arbitrary plastic strain without fracturing.
Why are BCC slip directions along cube diagonals rather than cube edges?
The cube diagonal <111> directions have the closest atomic packing and shortest Burgers vector in BCC, so they are the preferred slip directions.

notes.t: Slip systems
pts: Slip planes are the crystallographic planes on which dislocation glide (slip) can occur; the slip plane set gives the number of possible planes for slip.
