Comparing strengthening mechanisms: work hardening vs solid-solution vs grain-size strengthening, each acting on dislocation motion differently.
exq: Define work hardening and explain, in terms of dislocation density and spacing, why a metal's flow stress increases during cold working.
A copper wire of diameter 10 mm is drawn to 8 mm diameter at room temperature. Calculate the percent cold work and estimate the yield strength and ductility change using the cold-work charts.

Explain why percent cold work is defined using cross-sectional area rather than length, and show how an incorrect length-ratio calculation would give a different value for a bar reduced from 20 mm to 15 mm diameter.
Sketch how yield strength, tensile strength and ductility vary with percent cold work for brass, and comment on why yield strength levels off while tensile strength continues to rise.
Why does work hardening not occur in elastic loading or in brittle materials, and how does it differ from solid-solution and grain-size strengthening?

notes.t: Work hardening
pts: Work hardening is the process by which a ductile metal becomes harder and stronger as it is plastically deformed.
Work hardening is also called strain hardening or cold working, since the deformation occurs at relatively low temperature.
The charts show that yield strength and tensile strength rise as percent cold work increases, for 1040 steel, brass and copper.
Strengthening is rapid at low cold work and levels off at high cold work for yield strength, whereas tensile strength keeps rising in brass and steel over the range shown.
Ductility decreases as the metal is work hardened, which is the trade-off for the gain in strength.
defs: Work hardening
The increase in hardness and strength of a ductile metal caused by plastic deformation at temperatures where recrystallisation does not occur.
Strain hardening
Another name for work hardening; strengthening produced by plastic strain (dislocation multiplication and interaction).
Cold working
Plastic deformation of a metal below its recrystallisation temperature, which causes work hardening.
Percent cold work
The percentage reduction in cross-sectional area of a metal produced by plastic deformation at room temperature.
eqs: \(\%CW\) = percent cold work (%); \(A_0\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_d\) = cross-sectional area after deformation (\(m^{2}\))
tips: Percent cold work is based on area reduction, not length change; using the wrong ratio gives incorrect values.
Work hardening only applies to plastic deformation of ductile metals; it does not describe elastic loading or brittle materials.
rq: Why does the yield strength of 1040 steel rise steeply at small amounts of cold work but flatten at large amounts?
Dislocation density increases rapidly at first, so dislocations impede each other more; at high density the additional obstruction per unit strain diminishes, so the curve levels off.
Why must a metal be ductile for work hardening to be useful in forming?
Ductility allows large plastic deformation without fracture; a brittle metal would crack before achieving meaningful strain hardening.
What would you expect to happen to the strength of a work-hardened copper component if it were heated above its recrystallisation temperature?
The strength would drop back toward its original value because new strain-free grains form and dislocation density falls (annealing).

notes.t: Work hardening
pts: Dislocations impede each other's motion, so increasing their number makes further plastic deformation harder.
Plastic deformation raises dislocation density, which is the mechanism behind work hardening.
As dislocations multiply, the mean spacing between them shrinks, increasing interaction and blocking.
Higher dislocation density raises the resistance to dislocation motion, strengthening the metal.
Consequently, the flow stress needed to keep deforming the metal rises as work hardening proceeds.
tips: Work hardening is caused by increasing dislocation density, not by the dislocations moving more easily; do not confuse it with solid-solution or grain-size strengthening.
Work hardening occurs during plastic deformation (above the yield point); it does not occur in purely elastic loading.
rq: Why does cold working a metal make it stronger but less ductile?

Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations; their mutual interference (tangling and blocking) raises the stress needed for further slip, so strength rises while the remaining capacity for slip, and hence ductility, falls.
What would happen to the flow stress if dislocation spacing were halved?
Dislocation density roughly quadruples for a given area, so interactions and resistance to motion increase, and the flow stress rises accordingly.

xq.q: A cylindrical copper wire of diameter 6.0 mm is cold drawn through a die to a diameter of 4.5 mm at room temperature. Calculate the percent cold work, using \(\%CW=(A_0-A_d)/A_0\times100\), where \(A_0\) is the original and \(A_d\) the final cross-sectional area.
s: A is proportional to d², so %CW = (1 − (4.5/6.0)²) × 100

xq.q: A brass rod of diameter 12.0 mm is cold worked by 36% (percent reduction in cross-sectional area) by drawing it to a smaller circular cross-section. Calculate the final diameter in mm.
xq.a: 9.6 mm

xq.q: Explain, in terms of dislocations, why a ductile metal becomes stronger but less ductile as it is cold worked. State why this effect does not occur during purely elastic loading.
xq.a: Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, so the dislocation density rises and the mean spacing between dislocations falls. Dislocations interact with and impede each other's motion, so with more of them present, each is blocked more often. A higher stress is therefore needed to keep the metal deforming, which raises the flow stress, yield strength and hardness. Because dislocations are increasingly blocked, there is less capacity for further plastic flow, so ductility falls. In purely elastic loading the atoms are only stretched and no dislocations are generated, so the dislocation density does not change and there is no work hardening.
s: Dislocation spacing falls and they impede each other's motion.
The flow stress needed to continue deformation rises, so strength and hardness increase.
Ductility decreases because further slip is harder.
Elastic loading does not multiply dislocations, so there is no hardening.

units.name: 15.7 Stopping cracks: fibres and rubber particles in composites
units.ov: This module covers how obstacles in a crack's path deflect or arrest it, using fibres in brittle matrices (e.g. SiC in glass) and rubber particles in polymers (e.g. RTPMMA). Both rely on absorbing energy so that less is available to create new fracture surfaces. Fibres do this by debonding, pull-out and bridging; rubber particles do it by stretching and tearing. Design trade-offs such as interface strength and transparency determine how well each works.
must: Deflection changes the crack path, whereas arrest stops growth completely. Do not use the terms interchangeably.
Fibre toughening in a brittle matrix works through three mechanisms: interfacial debonding, fibre pull-out, and crack-tip blunting that reduces the driving force until the crack arrests.
Debonding is driven by the crack-tip stress field separating fibre from matrix along the interface, and it consumes energy.
A fibre–matrix interface must be weak enough to debond. A too-strong bond removes the toughening mechanism.
In SiC/glass ceramic composites, toughening comes from fibre pull-out and crack bridging, not plastic deformation. Fracture surfaces show pulled-out fibres rather than clean breaks.
Stiffness of the glass/SiC composite: the fibres (\(E\approx 400\) GPa) are much stiffer than the glass (\(E\approx 76\) GPa), so they carry a large share of the load. Do not mix up the two moduli.

Rubber particles toughen a polymer by stretching and tearing when the crack reaches them, absorbing energy so less remains for new surface. Elastic particles also pull the crack faces together, resisting opening.
Rubber particles raise toughness, not stiffness or strength. Do not claim they make the polymer stronger.
RTPMMA needs small, narrowly distributed particles whose refractive index matches PMMA, to avoid light scattering and keep it clear. Strong particle–matrix adhesion is needed for stress transfer.
Be clear about structure: PMMA is the continuous matrix and the rubber is the dispersed phase. Do not confuse the fibre as crack stopper with the fibre as the load-bearing phase.
conn: Interface strength links the fibre and rubber cases: fibres need a relatively weak interface to debond, while rubber particles need strong adhesion to transfer stress. Be ready to explain why the two differ.
Stiffness versus toughness: fibres are stiff and load-bearing as well as crack stoppers, while rubber particles add toughness without adding stiffness or strength.
Energy-absorption arguments (debonding, pull-out, stretching) link to the energy balance for fracture: more energy absorbed means less available for new crack surface, so toughness rises.
Optical design constraints (particle size, refractive-index matching) compete with toughening in RTPMMA, so a glass-replacement question combines both.
exq: Describe step by step what happens when a crack in a brittle glass matrix meets a SiC fibre. Name the energy-absorbing mechanisms and explain how the crack is arrested rather than merely deflected.
Explain why a very strong fibre–matrix bond can reduce the toughness of a ceramic matrix composite. What interface property is desirable?
Using \(E_{glass}=76\) GPa and \(E_{SiC}=400\) GPa, estimate the composite modulus for a given fibre volume fraction, and comment on which phase carries more of the load.
Explain how rubber particles toughen a polymer, and why they do not increase its strength or stiffness.

Rubber-toughened PMMA is proposed to replace glass in a transparent shatter-resistant panel. State the requirements on particle size, size distribution, refractive index and adhesion, and justify each.

notes.t: Stopping crack growth
pts: Cracks can be deflected or arrested by placing an obstacle in their path
The guiding question is how to deflect or arrest a crack
tips: Deflection and arrest are different outcomes: deflection changes the crack path, while arrest stops growth completely; do not use the terms interchangeably.
rq: Why might placing a second phase or obstacle ahead of a crack make it harder for the crack to continue growing?
The obstacle can deflect the crack path, forcing it to change direction and consume more energy, or arrest it by blunting the tip and reducing the local stress intensity at the crack front.

notes.t: Fibres as crack stoppers in composites
pts: In a brittle matrix, a crack runs until it meets a fibre, where it is stopped or deflected.
The crack-tip stress field separates (debonds) the fibre from the matrix at the interface.
Energy is absorbed by debonding and by pulling the fibres out of the matrix, toughening the composite.
The crack tip is blunted and its driving force reduced until the crack is arrested.
defs: Crack stopper (fibre reinforcement)
A fibre that intercepts a propagating crack in a brittle matrix, causing interfacial debonding, fibre pull-out and crack-tip blunting that absorb energy and arrest the crack.
Debonding
Separation of the fibre from the surrounding matrix along the interface, caused by the crack-tip stress field, which consumes energy.
tips: Do not confuse the fibre acting as a crack stopper with the fibre being the load-bearing phase; here the emphasis is on energy absorption and crack arrest.
Toughening relies on a weak-enough fibre–matrix interface to allow debonding; a too-strong bond removes this mechanism.
rq: Why does debonding at the fibre–matrix interface increase the toughness of the composite rather than simply weakening it?
Creating the new debonded surfaces and frictionally pulling the fibre out consumes energy that would otherwise drive the crack forward, so more work is needed to propagate it.
What would happen to the crack-stopping ability if the fibre were strongly bonded to the matrix?
Strong bonding prevents debonding and pull-out, so the crack would pass through the fibre (or the interface would not absorb energy), losing the toughening mechanism.

notes.t: Fibers in ceramic matrix composites (glass reinforced with SiC fibers)
pts: SiC fibres are much stiffer than the glass matrix, so they carry a large share of the load in the composite.
The composite is formed by infiltrating/mixing the fibres with a glass slurry, then consolidating it.
The fracture surface shows fibres pulled out and bridging the crack rather than fracturing cleanly, which absorbs energy and toughens the ceramic.
defs: Ceramic matrix composite
A brittle ceramic (here glass) reinforced with stiff, strong fibres (here SiC) that improve toughness by bridging cracks and enabling fibre pull-out.
tips: Do not confuse the glass matrix modulus (76 GPa) with the SiC fibre modulus (400 GPa) when computing composite stiffness.
Ceramic composites are toughened by fibre pull-out and crack bridging, not by plastic deformation as in metals.
rq: Why does the much higher modulus of SiC (400 GPa) versus glass (76 GPa) matter for load sharing?
Under equal strain the stiffer SiC fibres carry a proportionally larger stress and load, so they bear most of the applied load and the composite stiffness is raised.
Why does fibre pull-out in the fracture surface make the composite tougher than monolithic glass?
Cracks are bridged by intact fibres and pulling them out requires frictional work, dissipating energy and preventing sudden brittle failure.

notes.t: Rubber particles in composites: toughening mechanism
pts: Rubber particles in a polymer matrix toughen it because they stretch when a crack reaches them.
Stretching the particles absorbs energy, so less energy remains to create new fracture surfaces.
Each rubbery particle requires more energy to tear before it breaks, raising the composite's toughness.
Elastic rubber particles also act to pull the crack faces back together, resisting crack opening.
defs: Toughening (by rubber particles)
Increasing a polymer's fracture resistance by dispersing rubbery particles that stretch and absorb energy as a crack passes, and bridge/close the crack faces.
tips: Rubber particles toughen the polymer by absorbing energy; they do not increase its stiffness or strength, so don't claim they make it stronger.
Remember that the energy is absorbed by stretching and tearing the particles, not by the crack simply stopping at them.
rq: Why does stretching a rubber particle make the polymer tougher rather than just weaker?
The energy spent stretching and tearing the particle is taken from the energy available for creating new fracture surfaces, so more total energy is needed for the crack to propagate.
What would happen to toughness if the rubber particles were bonded very weakly to the matrix?
They would debond rather than stretch and tear, absorbing less energy, so the toughening effect would be reduced.

notes.t: Applications of rubbery particles: rubber-toughened PMMA (RTPMMA)
pts: RTPMMA is a possible replacement for glass where high toughness and shatter resistance are needed.
Transparency must be preserved, so the dispersed rubber phase is carefully controlled rather than just added for toughness.
Small, narrowly distributed rubber particles avoid light scattering that would make the material cloudy.
The rubber particles' refractive index should match the PMMA matrix so light passes through without scattering.
Strong particle-matrix adhesion lets the rubber transfer stress and absorb energy, improving toughness.
defs: RTPMMA
Rubber-toughened polymethylmethacrylate: a transparent PMMA matrix containing dispersed rubber particles that increase toughness and shatter resistance while retaining optical clarity.
tips: Transparency and toughness are competing requirements: small, index-matched, narrowly distributed particles are needed to keep the material clear.
Do not confuse the rubber phase (dispersed particles) with the PMMA matrix (continuous phase) when describing the structure.
rq: Why would a mismatch in refractive index between rubber particles and the PMMA matrix make the material opaque even if the particles are small?
Light is scattered at each interface where the refractive index changes; a mismatch causes scattering that makes the material cloudy or translucent, so index matching is needed for transparency.
What would happen to toughness if the rubber particles did not adhere strongly to the matrix?
Stress could not be transferred to the particles, and debonding at the interface would occur, so the rubber would not effectively absorb energy and toughness would be poor.

xq.q: A brittle glass matrix is reinforced with SiC fibres. A crack running through the matrix meets a fibre. Which statement best explains why the composite is tougher than the unreinforced glass?
xq.a: The crack-tip stress field debonds the fibre from the matrix and the fibre is then pulled out, absorbing energy and blunting the crack tip
o: The fibre bonds very strongly to the matrix, so the crack cannot cause any debonding and the fibre fractures cleanly at the crack plane
The crack-tip stress field debonds the fibre from the matrix and the fibre is then pulled out, absorbing energy and blunting the crack tip
The fibre deforms plastically like a metal, absorbing energy through dislocation motion
The fibre makes the glass stiffer, so the crack tip stress is simply halved and the crack stops because the material is stronger
xq.w: Toughening comes from debonding, pull-out and crack bridging that absorb energy; a too-strong interface removes this, and ceramic fibres do not toughen by plasticity.
s: Crack meets fibre and the interface debonds

xq.q: Rubber particles are dispersed in a brittle polymer to raise its fracture toughness. What is the main toughening mechanism?
xq.a: The particles stretch and tear as the crack passes, absorbing energy and pulling the crack faces together
o: The particles raise the modulus of the polymer so the crack needs a higher stress to start
The particles stretch and tear as the crack passes, absorbing energy and pulling the crack faces together
The crack stops at each particle without any energy being absorbed by the particle
The particles bond strongly to nothing and create voids that blunt the crack by plastic flow of the matrix only
xq.w: Energy is absorbed by stretching and tearing the particles, which also bridge the crack; they do not make the polymer stiffer or stronger.
s: Stretching absorbs energy, leaving less for new surface
Elastic particles close the crack faces

xq.q: Rubber-toughened PMMA (RTPMMA) is proposed as a shatter-resistant replacement for window glass. Explain how the rubber particles toughen the PMMA, and describe the requirements on the particles that allow the material to remain transparent.
xq.a: Rubber particles stretch and tear when a crack reaches them, absorbing energy so less is available to create new fracture surface, and they bridge the crack faces. Good adhesion lets stress transfer into the particles. To remain transparent, the particles must be small and narrowly distributed to avoid light scattering, and their refractive index must match that of the PMMA matrix.
s: Strong particle-matrix adhesion for stress transfer (1)
Small, narrow size distribution to avoid scattering (1)

units.name: 16.1 Time effects and viscoelasticity basics
units.ov: This material introduces time-dependent mechanical behaviour. Metals and ceramics are treated as essentially time-independent, while polymers, composites, powders and soils show significant time effects. Viscoelasticity combines recoverable elastic and fluid-like viscous responses, and the clearest way to tell elastic, viscous and viscoelastic materials apart is to compare their strain-time curves under a step stress.
must: Definition: viscoelastic materials combine elastic (recoverable, solid-like) and viscous (time-dependent, fluid-like) behaviour, so stress or strain changes with time under load
Which materials are viscoelastic: polymers, polymer composites, powders and soils show significant time effects; metals and ceramics show only very limited ones
Elastic response to a step stress: strain is instantaneous, constant while the stress is held, and fully recovered on unloading, \(\varepsilon=\sigma/E\)
Viscous response to a step stress: strain rises linearly with time, \(\varepsilon\propto t\) (constant strain rate), and is not recovered on unloading (permanent flow)
Viscoelastic response to a step stress: instantaneous elastic jump, then creep (strain increasing at a decreasing rate) under constant stress
Viscoelastic response on unloading: an instant elastic recovery, then gradual decay of strain (delayed elasticity). Recovery is partial or slow, and any remaining strain is permanent
Viscoelastic materials do not have a single constant modulus; the response depends on loading rate and duration, so always check whether loading rate matters
Reading strain-time graphs: flat strain under constant stress means elastic only; rising strain means viscous flow or creep; a gradual return after unloading means viscoelastic
Definitions: 'elastic' means spontaneously returning to the original bulk or shape after contraction, distortion or dilation; 'visco' means fluid-like and rate/time dependent
conn: Step-stress strain-time graphs link the three material types: elastic (instant, fully recovered), viscous (linear rise, no recovery) and viscoelastic (a mixture of both)
Material classes link to modelling choices: polymers and soils need time-dependent analysis, while metals and ceramics can usually be treated as time-independent elastic solids
Time-dependent strain under constant load (creep) links to the loss of a fixed modulus: apparent stiffness depends on loading duration and rate
Recovery behaviour links to permanent deformation: the viscous part is not recovered, so unloading curves show how much flow occurred
exq: Define viscoelasticity and state which classes of material (polymers, metals, ceramics, composites, soils) show significant time effects, and which do not.

Sketch strain-time curves for an elastic, a viscous and a viscoelastic material subjected to a step stress that is applied and later removed. Label the instantaneous jump, creep, delayed recovery and any permanent strain.

A material under constant stress shows strain increasing linearly with time and no recovery on unloading. Classify its behaviour and justify your answer. How would the curve differ for a viscoelastic material?
Explain why a single constant Young's modulus is inadequate for a polymer loaded at two different rates, and discuss how the measured response would change.
Explain the terms 'visco' and 'elastic' in viscoelasticity, and describe what happens to the strain of a viscoelastic material immediately after unloading and at long times afterwards.

notes.t: Time effects in materials
pts: Time and rate of loading are usually assumed to have little effect on material response in basic analysis.
In metals and ceramics, time effects exist but are very limited.
In polymers, polymer composites, powders and soils, time effects can be significant and must be considered.
Materials whose behaviour depends substantially on time are classed as viscoelastic.
defs: Viscoelastic
A class of materials in which the mechanical response depends substantially on time and rate of loading, combining elastic (recoverable) and viscous (time-dependent) behaviour.
tips: Do not assume time-independent (purely elastic) behaviour for polymers, composites, powders or soils; check whether loading rate matters.
Viscoelastic does not mean metals or ceramics: those show only very limited time effects.
rq: Why can the rate of loading be ignored for steel but not for a polymer?
Steel and metals show only very limited time dependence, so elastic analysis is adequate; polymers have significant time-dependent (viscous) behaviour, so loading rate changes their response.
What would you expect to happen to a viscoelastic material under rapid versus slow loading?
Under rapid loading it tends to behave stiffer and more elastically; under slow loading it deforms more by viscous flow, so its apparent stiffness is lower.

notes.t: Viscoelasticity
pts: Viscoelastic materials combine viscous (fluid-like) and elastic (solid-like) behaviour.
The 'visco' part means the material's response is fluid-like, involving flow over time.
The 'elastic' part means the material spontaneously returns to its original bulk or shape after contraction, distortion or dilation.
Because of viscoelasticity, stress or strain in the material changes with time under load.
defs: Viscoelasticity
A material property where the mechanical response combines viscous (time-dependent, fluid-like) and elastic (recoverable, solid-like) behaviour, so stress or strain changes with time.
Elastic
The ability of a material to spontaneously return to its original bulk or shape after being contracted, distorted or dilated.
Visco (viscous)
Fluid-like behaviour in which deformation depends on rate and time; the prefix denotes fluid character.
tips: Do not treat viscoelastic materials as having constant modulus; their response is time-dependent, so results depend on loading rate and duration.
Remember 'visco' means fluid-like and 'elastic' means recoverable; both must be present for viscoelasticity.
rq: Why does a viscoelastic material's stress change over time even when its strain is held constant?
The viscous component causes stress to relax gradually as the material flows internally, so stress decays with time at constant strain (stress relaxation).
How does a viscoelastic material differ from a purely elastic one when unloaded?
An elastic material recovers instantly, whereas a viscoelastic material recovers gradually over time, with some residual deformation possible.

notes.t: Viscoelasticity: elastic, viscous and viscoelastic responses to a step stress
pts: An elastic material's strain follows the applied stress instantaneously and is fully recovered when the stress is removed.
A viscous material under constant stress shows strain that increases linearly with time (flow) and does not recover after unloading.
A viscoelastic material shows time-dependent strain: an instantaneous elastic jump, then gradual creep under constant stress, and partial recovery (delayed elasticity) after unloading.
For the viscoelastic response, the strain does not return to zero immediately on unloading; it decays gradually.
defs: Viscoelasticity
Material behaviour combining elastic (stress-proportional, recoverable) and viscous (time-dependent, flowing) responses, so strain depends on both the magnitude and the duration of loading.
Elastic material
A material whose strain is instantaneous and fully recoverable on unloading, with no time dependence.
Viscous material
A material whose strain increases linearly with time under constant stress and is not recovered after the load is removed.
tips: Do not assume a viscoelastic strain recovers fully on unloading; only the elastic part returns instantly, while the rest recovers slowly or not at all.
Read the strain-time graph carefully: a flat strain under constant stress indicates elasticity only, whereas a rising strain indicates viscous flow.
rq: Why does the strain in the viscoelastic case jump on loading but then keep increasing while the stress stays constant?
The instantaneous jump is the elastic (spring-like) component; the continued increase is the time-dependent viscous (dashpot-like) flow, i.e. creep under constant stress.
If a viscoelastic specimen is unloaded and the strain only partly drops, what does the remaining strain tell you?
The partly recovering part is the delayed elastic response; the remaining strain is permanent viscous flow that does not recover.

xq.q: A polymer rod is held under a constant tensile stress for 1 hour and then unloaded. Which strain-time response is characteristic of a viscoelastic material?
xq.a: An instantaneous jump, then gradual increase while loaded, and after unloading an instant drop followed by gradual partial recovery
o: Strain is constant while loaded and falls instantly to zero on unloading
Strain rises linearly with time while loaded and stays at its final value after unloading
An instantaneous jump, then gradual increase while loaded, and after unloading an instant drop followed by gradual partial recovery
Strain jumps instantly and falls to zero gradually only after a long delay with no strain increase during loading
xq.w: Viscoelasticity combines an elastic jump, creep and delayed recovery; option A is purely elastic and B is purely viscous.
s: Elastic part recovers instantly, rest slowly

xq.q: A strain-time graph for a material under constant stress shows strain increasing in a straight line with time, and on removing the stress the strain stays at its final value. The material is best described as:
xq.a: Viscous
o: Elastic
Viscoelastic with full recovery
Viscous
Elastic with a lower modulus
xq.w: Linear strain growth with no recovery is viscous flow; a flat line would indicate elasticity.

xq.q: Sketch strain against time for a viscoelastic polymer subjected to a constant stress applied at t = 0 and removed at a later time t1. Label the features and explain why it differs from an elastic and a viscous material.
xq.a: On loading, strain jumps instantly (elastic part), then increases gradually at constant stress (creep). At t1 the strain drops instantly by the elastic jump, then decays gradually (delayed elasticity), not fully returning to zero immediately and possibly leaving permanent strain. An elastic material would show a flat strain while loaded and instant full recovery; a viscous material would show linear strain rise and no recovery.
s: Sketch with instantaneous jump and rising creep (2)
Instant drop and gradual decay on unloading (1)
Elastic comparison: flat, full instant recovery (1)
Viscous comparison: linear rise, no recovery (1)

units.name: 16.2 Physical origins of viscoelasticity: creep vs stress relaxation
units.ov: This material explains why materials show time-dependent mechanical behaviour and distinguishes the two classic manifestations: creep (constant stress, strain rises) and stress relaxation (constant strain, stress falls). The physical origin is molecular motion in polymers (random, stress-biased movement of chains past one another) and dislocation motion with grain shape change in metals and ceramics. Both tests probe the same underlying process, with a different variable controlled.
must: Creep = constant applied stress, strain increases with time (strain is the measured quantity).
Stress relaxation = constant imposed strain, stress decays with time (stress is the measured quantity).
The controlled variable determines the phenomenon: creep is a constant-stress test, relaxation is a constant-strain test, and the two are complementary views of the same process.
Viscoelasticity = time-dependent behaviour combining viscous (flow) and elastic (recoverable) responses.
Polymer origin: molecules move randomly past one another; applied stress biases the direction of motion, changing shape (creep) or letting internal stress dissipate (relaxation).
Metal/ceramic origin: dislocation motion changes the shape of individual grains, giving time-dependent deformation; this is a different mechanism from polymer chain motion.
The instantaneous strain on loading is elastic and not creep; only the subsequent time-dependent rise in strain counts.
Creep strain-time curve: instantaneous elastic strain, then continued rise, typically accelerating towards failure.
Creep can cause fracture even at stresses below short-term yield or strength, so time-dependent failure must be considered in design.
In relaxation the load needed to hold fixed deformation falls as the material slowly deforms viscously/plastically.
conn: Molecular or dislocation motion (microscopic cause) leads to macroscopic time-dependence, appearing as creep or relaxation depending on the test control.
Creep links to design and failure: time-dependent strain growth links to fracture below nominal yield strength, so safe stress depends on service time.
Elastic vs viscous response: the instantaneous elastic strain plus time-dependent viscous strain combine in viscoelastic models and in separating the creep curve into parts.
Relaxation and creep as complementary tests: a question may give one test and ask for the expected behaviour in the other.
exq: Define creep and stress relaxation. For each, state which variable is held constant, which is measured, and sketch the response against time.
Sketch a creep strain-time curve for a polymer under constant stress, labelling the instantaneous elastic strain and the time-dependent portion, and explain why the instantaneous part is not creep.
Explain at the molecular level why a polymer shows creep and stress relaxation, and contrast this with the mechanism in metals and ceramics.

A polymer component is held at a fixed strain in a bolted joint and the clamping load falls over months. Identify the phenomenon, explain its origin, and say what would happen if the load rather than the strain were fixed.
Why might a component loaded below its short-term yield strength still fracture after a long time? Discuss in terms of creep.

notes.t: Why Viscoelasticity? (polymer molecular motion, creep and stress relaxation)
pts: In polymers, molecules move randomly past one another, which underlies time-dependent behaviour.
Applied stress organises the direction of molecular motion, producing a change in shape.
Under constant stress, distortion increases over time and may eventually lead to specimen fracture (creep).
Under constant strain, molecular movement allows the stress to decrease over time (stress relaxation).
defs: Viscoelasticity
Time-dependent mechanical behaviour in which a material shows both viscous (flow) and elastic (recoverable) responses, arising from random, stress-driven movement of polymer molecules.
Creep
Increase in strain over time in a material held under constant stress, which may ultimately lead to fracture.
Stress relaxation
Decrease in stress over time in a material held at constant strain, as molecular movement allows the internal stress to dissipate.
tips: Do not confuse creep (constant stress, strain increases) with stress relaxation (constant strain, stress decreases); the controlled variable determines which occurs.
Creep can lead to fracture, so time-dependent failure must be considered even when the applied stress is below the short-term yield or strength value.
rq: Why does a polymer under constant load keep deforming over time, whereas a metal under the same load typically does not?

Polymer molecules can slide and reorient past one another over time (viscous flow), so strain grows under constant stress (creep); metals deform elastically and their strain stays essentially fixed at constant stress.
What would you expect to happen to the stress in a stretched polymer strip held at fixed length, and why?
The stress would fall over time (stress relaxation) because molecular rearrangement lets the material accommodate the imposed strain with less internal stress.

notes.t: Creep vs Stress Relaxation
pts: Creep: under a constant applied stress, strain increases with time; the strain-time curve starts with an instantaneous elastic strain and then keeps rising, typically accelerating towards failure.
Stress relaxation: under a constant imposed strain, the stress required to maintain that strain decays with time, as the material slowly deforms plastically/viscously and the load reduces.
The two phenomena are complementary: creep is a constant-stress test with strain measured, while stress relaxation is a constant-strain test with stress measured.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent increase in strain in a material held under a constant stress, often at elevated temperature.
Stress relaxation
Time-dependent decrease in stress in a material held at a constant strain, as viscoelastic or creep processes relieve the stress.
tips: Do not confuse the controlled variable: creep = constant stress (strain measured); stress relaxation = constant strain (stress measured).
The instantaneous strain on loading is elastic and is not itself creep; only the time-dependent increase counts as creep.
rq: Why does the stress fall during stress relaxation even though the total strain is held constant?
Part of the elastic strain is gradually converted to inelastic (creep/plastic) strain over time, so the elastic component and hence the stress decreases while the total strain stays fixed.
If a bolt is tightened to a fixed strain and the clamping force drops over months, which phenomenon is occurring and why does it matter?
Stress relaxation; the clamping force can fall below the required preload, risking joint loosening or leakage.

notes.t: Why viscoelasticity: dislocation motion and grain shape change
pts: In metals and ceramics, viscoelastic-type time-dependent behaviour arises because dislocations move through the material.
As dislocations move, individual grains change shape, so the material deforms over time rather than instantaneously.
Time-dependent response appears either as a change in shape under constant load (creep) or as a change in load needed to hold a constant deformation (relaxation).
defs: Creep
Time-dependent change in shape of a material under constant load.
tips: Creep means change in shape at constant load; do not confuse it with a change in load at constant deformation (relaxation).
Dislocation-based time dependence applies to metals and ceramics; polymers are viscoelastic for different molecular reasons.
rq: Why does dislocation motion make a metal's response time-dependent rather than instantaneous?
Dislocations need time to move through the lattice and grains, so the shape change accumulates gradually under load.
If a specimen is held at constant deformation, what time-dependent quantity changes, and why?
The load required to maintain the deformation decreases over time (stress relaxation), as dislocation motion relieves the internal stress.

xq.q: A polymer clip is stretched to a fixed extension and held there. Over several days the force it exerts falls. Which phenomenon is this, and what is the controlled variable?
xq.a: Stress relaxation, with constant strain
o: Creep, with constant stress
Stress relaxation, with constant strain
Creep, with constant strain
Stress relaxation, with constant stress
xq.w: Fixed extension means constant strain with decaying stress, which is stress relaxation; creep is the constant-stress case.
s: Stress falls with time so relaxation

xq.q: A polymer pipe carries a constant stress well below its short-term yield strength. Why can it still fail after a long time?
xq.a: Creep strain accumulates over time under constant stress and can eventually lead to fracture
o: Creep strain accumulates over time under constant stress and can eventually lead to fracture
Stress relaxation increases the stress in the pipe until it exceeds yield
Viscoelastic materials have a constant modulus, so stresses build up
The initial elastic strain slowly grows back until fracture
xq.w: Creep continues to increase strain at constant stress and may cause fracture; relaxation lowers stress rather than raising it.
s: Strain rises over time to failure

xq.q: Explain the physical origin of time-dependent behaviour in polymers, and use it to distinguish creep from stress relaxation. State what is held constant and what is measured in each case.
xq.a: Polymer molecules move randomly past one another; an applied stress organises this motion in a direction, changing the shape over time. In creep the stress is held constant and strain is measured: after the instantaneous elastic strain, strain keeps increasing and may lead to fracture. In stress relaxation the strain is held constant and stress is measured: molecular movement lets the stress needed to hold the strain decay with time.
s: Random molecular motion past one another (1)
Stress directs motion, causing shape change (1)

units.name: 16.3 Creep testing and creep curves
units.ov: Creep is the time-dependent increase in strain of a material held under constant stress, usually at elevated temperature and measured in a furnace with a constant load. Results are plotted as strain against (log) time and split into primary, secondary and tertiary stages, each with a characteristic strain rate and mechanism. The key ideas are that creep happens at constant stress, that it differs from stress relaxation and from a tensile test, and that the log plot changes how the curve is read.
must: Definition: creep is the time-dependent increase in strain under constant applied stress, a viscoelastic effect, and it can occur below yield stress
Creep test setup: constant load on a specimen in a furnace at controlled high temperature, with extension measured against time
Creep curves plot strain (\(\varepsilon\)) against time, not stress against strain; state that strain increases with time
Primary (I) creep: strain rate starts high and decreases as the material work-hardens
Secondary (II) creep: roughly constant minimum strain rate, the steady-state stage, which is a straight line on the plot
Tertiary (III) creep: strain rate accelerates through necking/damage until fracture
Creep vs stress relaxation: creep is strain rising at constant stress; relaxation is stress falling at constant strain
Creep vs tensile test: creep has constant load and time-dependent strain; a tensile test has increasing load and gives a stress-strain curve
Log axes: creep timescales are long, so log time spreads out the early events; on a log\(\varepsilon\)-log\(t\) plot a straight line means a power law, not strain linear in time
Example: lead creeps at ambient temperature (sagging sheet and pipework), and irradiated HDPE shows a sharp upturn near \(10^{5}\) s, which is tertiary-like
conn: Three creep stages and the log-log plot: the secondary stage appears as a straight line on log\(\varepsilon\)-log\(t\), so slope gives the power-law exponent, whereas on linear axes it is a constant strain rate
Creep versus stress relaxation: both show viscoelastic time dependence, but with opposite controlled and measured variables, so questions ask you to identify which is occurring
Creep test design and the plotted output: constant load and furnace temperature link to the strain-time plot, and changing stress or temperature shifts the curve and the time to tertiary failure
Material examples (lead, polymers such as HDPE) link creep to the idea that low-melting or viscoelastic materials creep at ambient temperature
exq: Define creep and sketch a typical strain-time curve. Label primary, secondary and tertiary stages and describe the strain rate in each.
Explain why creep data is often plotted against log time, and what a straight line on a log\(\varepsilon\)-log\(t\) plot indicates about the relationship between strain and time.
Describe how a creep test is carried out, including the load, temperature control and measurements. State how it differs from a tensile test and from a stress relaxation test.
A lead pipe sags under its own weight at room temperature. Explain this in terms of creep and viscoelasticity, and state which creep stage would end in failure.

From a creep curve, identify the minimum (secondary) strain rate and estimate it for a given strain change over a given time. Explain what the sharp upturn at about \(10^{5}\) s in irradiated HDPE shows.

notes.t: Creep as an effect of viscoelasticity
pts: Creep is the time-dependent increase in strain under a constant applied stress.
Creep is a viscoelastic effect: the material's strain keeps changing over time even though the load does not.
Lead, at ambient temperature, creeps noticeably, as shown by lead sheet hung vertically at Stokesay Court sagging over time and lead pipework deforming under its own weight.
defs: Creep
The change in strain with time in a material held under constant stress; a viscoelastic effect.
tips: Creep occurs under constant stress, not constant strain; do not confuse it with stress relaxation, which is stress decreasing under constant strain.
Creep is time-dependent: always state that strain increases with time, not just that the material deforms.
rq: Why does lead sheet on a historic building sag over decades even though its weight never changes?
Because lead is viscoelastic: under a constant stress its strain increases with time (creep), so the sheet slowly deforms even though the load is constant.
What would you expect to happen to creep rate if the same lead component were in a hotter environment?
Creep rate would increase, since creep is strongly temperature-dependent and accelerates as temperature rises toward the material's melting point.

notes.t: Creep testing
pts: A constant load is applied to a specimen held in a furnace at elevated temperature.
Creep is monitored by measuring how the displacement (extension) of the specimen changes over time under the constant load.
The test is run inside a furnace so the specimen is held at a controlled high temperature while the load acts.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent permanent deformation of a material under a constant stress, typically at elevated temperature, measured as increasing strain with time.
tips: Do not confuse creep (constant load, time-dependent strain at high temperature) with a tensile test (increasing load, strain measured against stress).
Creep results are plotted as strain against time, not stress against strain.
rq: Why must the load be kept constant during a creep test rather than increasing the load as in a tensile test?

Creep is defined as time-dependent deformation under constant stress; a constant load keeps the stress constant so the change in displacement reflects creep alone, not elastic response to rising stress.
Why is a furnace required for creep testing?
Creep is significant at elevated temperatures (typically above about 0.4 of the absolute melting temperature), so the furnace holds the specimen at the temperature of interest.

notes.t: Plotting creep data on a log time axis
pts: Creep is plotted as the strain produced by an applied stress against time.
Creep timescales are normally very long, so the interesting early events are compressed; plotting against log time spreads them out.

The example compares HDPE and 40 HA/PE, irradiated and non-irradiated; the curves show strain rising with log time, then a sharp upturn at around \(10^{5}\) s (tertiary-like behaviour) in the irradiated HDPE.
Both axes are logarithmic: strain on a log scale spanning about 0.001 to 0.01, time on a log scale from 10 s upward.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent increase in strain under a constant applied stress, occurring at a steady load and typically over long timescales.
tips: Creep is plotted as strain against time at constant stress, not stress against time; check which variable is on each axis.
Remember the axis is log time because creep timescales are long; state that both log axes are used in the example graph.
rq: Why is a logarithmic time axis used for creep data rather than linear time?
Creep timescales are very long, while the important early changes happen quickly; log time spreads these early events out so they can be seen clearly.
What would you expect the strain-time curve to look like on linear axes for the same data, and why would that hide information?
Early strain changes would be squeezed into a tiny region near the origin, so the rate differences between materials at short times would be hard to distinguish.

notes.t: Creep: strain increasing with time under constant stress
pts: Creep is time-dependent strain that grows under constant applied stress, even when the stress is below yield.
Primary (I) creep: strain rate starts high and decreases as the material work-hardens.
Secondary (II) creep: roughly constant, minimum strain rate; the straight line on a log-log plot.
Tertiary (III) creep: strain rate accelerates (necking/damage) until fracture, marked by the cross.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent plastic deformation of a material under a constant (sustained) stress, typically at elevated temperature, where strain increases with time.
tips: Creep is time-dependent: it occurs at constant stress, unlike plastic deformation under a rising load in a tensile test; don't confuse the two curves.
Note the axes: the right-hand plot is log(ε) against log(time), so the linear region is a power-law relationship, not a linear time relationship.
rq: Why does the strain rate fall in primary creep but stay constant in secondary creep?
In primary creep work hardening dominates, reducing dislocation mobility; in secondary creep hardening is balanced by recovery (dynamic softening), giving a steady minimum strain rate.
What is happening in tertiary creep that causes acceleration toward the cross?
Cavitation/void formation at grain boundaries and reduction of effective load-bearing area raise the true stress, so strain rate increases until rupture.

units.name: 16.4 Stages, mechanisms and failure in creep
units.ov: Creep is time-dependent permanent deformation under sustained stress at elevated temperature, typically a significant fraction of the melting temperature. It passes through primary, secondary and tertiary stages, read from the slope of the strain-time curve. The mechanisms (dislocation motion in metals and ceramics, chain sliding in polymers) and the failure modes (grain boundary voiding versus fibril drawing) depend on material class.
must: Definition: creep is time-dependent, permanent deformation under constant load or stress at elevated temperature, typically a significant fraction of the melting temperature \(T_m\)
Creep rate is the gradient of the creep strain vs time curve, \(\dot{\varepsilon}=d\varepsilon/dt\), at constant stress and temperature
Primary creep: the rate decreases with time as the material work-hardens. Strain still increases; only the slope falls
Secondary (steady-state) creep: the rate is roughly constant, so strain is linear in time. This minimum creep rate is the one used in design
Tertiary creep: the rate accelerates because voids form between grains and grow, ending in rupture
Primary and secondary mechanism in metals and ceramics: dislocation motion
Primary and secondary mechanism in polymers: molecular chains sliding past one another
Failure in metals: voids open and grow at grain boundaries (intergranular), and the remaining material between voids fractures
Failure in polymers: fibrils are drawn out and then break, with no grain boundary voiding
Common mistakes: confusing slope with strain, saying creep happens only at high stress at room temperature, and applying one mechanism to all materials
conn: Stage shape ties to mechanism: work-hardening in primary slows the rate, the balance in secondary gives a constant rate, and void growth in tertiary accelerates it to failure
Material class links mechanism and failure: metals show dislocation motion then grain boundary voiding, while polymers show chain sliding then fibril drawing
Design use of the minimum (secondary) creep rate links to service life: a lower steady rate means longer time to reach a strain limit or rupture
Temperature relative to \(T_m\) and stress duration determine whether creep matters, so questions often combine operating conditions with the stage reached
exq: Sketch a creep strain vs time curve at constant stress and temperature. Label the three stages and describe the creep rate in each, explaining the physical cause.

Explain why the secondary creep rate is used in design. A component's steady creep rate is \(10^{-8}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) and the allowable strain is 1%. Estimate the time in secondary creep, ignoring primary strain.
Compare the creep mechanisms and failure modes of a metal turbine blade and a polymer component. Name the process at the microscopic level in each case.
A student says that in primary creep the strain decreases with time. Identify and correct the error, and state what actually decreases and why.
Describe how voids lead to creep failure in metals and why this produces tertiary creep. Where do the voids form?

notes.t: Stages of creep
pts: Primary creep: the creep rate (slope of strain vs time) decreases with time as the material work-hardens.
Secondary creep is the steady-state stage where the creep rate is roughly constant, so strain grows linearly with time.
Tertiary creep: the creep rate accelerates with time and leads to failure, driven by void formation between grains and their growth.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent, permanent deformation of a material under a constant load (or stress) at elevated temperature, typically a significant fraction of its melting temperature.
Creep rate
The gradient of the creep strain versus time curve, i.e. the rate at which strain accumulates under constant stress and temperature.
Steady-state creep
The secondary stage of creep in which the creep rate is approximately constant, giving a minimum creep rate that is often used in design.
Tertiary creep
The final stage of creep in which the creep rate accelerates due to void formation and growth, leading to rupture.
tips: Do not confuse the slope (creep rate) with the strain itself: primary creep has a decreasing slope, not decreasing strain; strain always increases.
Creep is time-dependent at elevated temperature; do not describe it as occurring only under high stress at room temperature.
rq: Why does the creep rate decrease during primary creep but then become constant in secondary creep?

In primary creep, work hardening (dislocation build-up) makes further deformation harder, lowering the rate. Secondary creep occurs when hardening is balanced by recovery (dynamic softening), so the rate settles to a constant steady value.
What would you expect to happen to the creep life if the stress were increased at the same temperature?
Creep rate increases and the time to reach tertiary creep and failure shortens, because higher stress accelerates dislocation motion and void growth.

notes.t: Mechanisms of creep in primary and secondary phases
pts: In primary and secondary creep, the deformation mechanism differs by material class: dislocation motion in metals and ceramics.
In polymers, deformation during primary and secondary creep occurs because molecular chains slide past one another.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent permanent deformation of a material under a sustained load, typically at elevated temperature, occurring over primary, secondary and tertiary stages.
tips: Do not assume the creep mechanism is the same for all materials; dislocations apply to crystalline metals and ceramics, chain sliding applies to polymers.
Creep at tertiary stage (necking/cavitation) is not covered by this page; keep the mechanisms for primary and secondary stages distinct.
rq: Why does creep in metals and ceramics depend on dislocations moving through the crystal, whereas in polymers it depends on chains sliding past each other?

Metals and ceramics are crystalline, so plastic flow is carried by dislocation glide and climb through the lattice; polymers are made of long molecular chains whose entanglements and weak intermolecular bonds allow chains to slide relative to one another.
What would you expect to happen to the creep rate of a metal if dislocation motion were hindered, for example by fine precipitates?
The creep rate would decrease, because dislocations must overcome obstacles, reducing the steady dislocation movement that drives secondary (steady-state) creep.

notes.t: Creep failure
pts: In metals, creep failure occurs by cracking/failure along grain boundaries, where voids open up under sustained stress.
Voids form and grow at grain boundaries, and the material between the voids eventually fails, leading to fracture.
Polymers fail under creep differently: by drawing out fibrils that then break, rather than by grain boundary voiding.
defs: Creep failure
Time-dependent fracture of a material held under sustained stress, typically at elevated temperature, where strain accumulates slowly until rupture.
tips: Do not confuse creep failure in metals (intergranular voiding) with polymer creep failure (fibril drawing); the mechanisms are different.
Creep is a time- and temperature-dependent process; state that failure occurs under sustained stress over time, not instantly.
rq: Why does creep failure in metals tend to start at grain boundaries rather than within the grains themselves?
Grain boundaries are regions of atomic mismatch and higher diffusion rates, so voids nucleate and grow there more easily under applied stress, especially at high temperature.
How does the failure mechanism of a polymer under creep differ from that of a metal, and why?
Polymers fail by drawing out fibrils that then break, whereas metals form voids along grain boundaries; the difference stems from polymer chain/fibril structure versus crystalline grain structure.

xq.q: A constant-load creep test on a metal at elevated temperature gives a strain–time curve whose slope decreases at first, then stays constant for a long period, then increases until rupture. Which statement about the first stage is correct?
xq.a: Strain keeps increasing but the creep rate (slope) falls as the material work-hardens.
o: Strain decreases with time because the material recovers elastically.
Strain keeps increasing but the creep rate (slope) falls as the material work-hardens.
The creep rate is constant because voids have not yet formed.
Strain keeps increasing and the creep rate rises because voids open at grain boundaries.
xq.w: Primary creep has a decreasing slope due to work-hardening while strain still rises; the trap is confusing slope with strain, or mixing in tertiary void growth.
s: Primary creep: rate decreases, strain still increases.

xq.q: Explain how the mechanism of creep deformation and the mode of creep failure differ between a polycrystalline metal and a polymer. Refer to the primary/secondary stages and to the final failure.
xq.a: In a metal, primary and secondary creep occur by dislocation motion. In a polymer they occur by molecular chains sliding past one another. In the tertiary stage a metal develops voids at grain boundaries, which grow until the material between them fails, giving intergranular fracture. A polymer fails by drawing out fibrils, which then break.
s: Metals (and ceramics): dislocation motion in primary/secondary creep (1)
Metal failure: voids form and grow at grain boundaries, causing intergranular fracture (1.5)
Polymer failure: fibrils drawn out then break, no grain boundary voiding (1.5)

xq.q: A creep curve shows a long region where strain increases linearly with time at \(2\times10^{-8}\) s\(^{-1}\). A designer uses this value as the design creep rate. Which stage and why?
xq.a: Secondary (steady-state) creep, because the rate is roughly constant and is the minimum creep rate.
o: Primary creep, because the rate is decreasing and so is safest.
Tertiary creep, because the rate is constant just before rupture.
Secondary (steady-state) creep, because the rate is roughly constant and is the minimum creep rate.
Secondary creep, because strain stops increasing once steady state is reached.
xq.w: Steady-state creep has constant slope (the minimum rate used in design); strain does not stop, and tertiary is accelerating.
s: Linear strain means constant rate: secondary stage.

units.name: 16.5 Temperature effects and homologous temperature
units.ov: This material covers how temperature controls creep, using the homologous temperature T/Tm (absolute temperatures) with a rule-of-thumb threshold of about 0.4 Tm. Above this threshold, a material under constant stress shows time-dependent permanent deformation through primary, steady-state and tertiary stages ending in rupture. Higher temperature speeds up the whole process and shortens life, which is why low-melting metals such as lead creep at room temperature.
must: Creep is time-dependent permanent deformation under constant stress, significant when \(T > 0.4\,T_m\)
Homologous temperature is \(T/T_m\), with both temperatures in kelvin; creep matters above about 0.4
Always convert first: \(T(\text{K}) = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273\). Using °C gives a wrong ratio and is the classic error
Threshold temperature is \(T_{\text{creep}} = 0.4\,T_m\); compute it in K, then convert back to °C if asked
Creep curve stages: primary (strain rate decreasing), steady-state (roughly constant rate), tertiary (accelerating rate) leading to rupture
Increasing temperature makes creep strain grow faster and brings failure (×) in much shorter time
Below 0.4 Tm there is only the instantaneous elastic strain, which levels off with no continuing creep strain
Do not confuse instantaneous elastic strain at loading with creep strain, which accumulates over time
Lead has a low Tm, so room temperature is already above 0.4 Tm and it creeps in all normal climates
0.4 Tm is a rule of thumb, not an exact onset, so state that creep is 'significant above' it
conn: Homologous temperature and unit conversion: any threshold question needs °C to K, then the ratio T/Tm, then a judgement on creep
Creep curve stages and temperature: higher T shifts the curve up and left, giving a higher steady-state rate and shorter rupture time, which links to component life and design
Elastic strain and creep strain: total strain is instantaneous elastic strain plus accumulating creep strain, so read off curves carefully
Material choice and service conditions: low-Tm metals like lead, tin and solder creep at ambient, whereas high-Tm alloys are chosen for turbines and boilers
exq: Lead melts at 327 °C. Calculate its homologous temperature at 20 °C and at -30 °C, and state whether creep is significant in each case.
Steel with Tm of about 1500 °C operates at 650 °C. Find T/Tm using kelvin and decide whether creep must be considered. Then find the threshold temperature in °C.
Sketch a creep curve, labelling elastic strain, primary, steady-state and tertiary stages and rupture. Show how the curve changes as temperature increases.
Explain why a student who uses °C instead of K for the 0.4 Tm criterion reaches the wrong conclusion. Illustrate with a numerical example.
Define homologous temperature and explain why lead creeps at room temperature while a high-melting-point material does not.

notes.t: Effect of temperature on creep
pts: Creep becomes significant when the absolute operating temperature exceeds about 0.4 of the material's melting temperature, so the threshold is set on the Kelvin scale.
Below 0.4 Tm the material shows only an initial elastic strain that levels off, with no continuing creep strain over time.
As temperature increases, creep strain grows faster with time and the material reaches failure (marked ×) in a much shorter time.
Creep curves show a primary (transient) stage where strain rate decreases, followed by steady-state and tertiary stages leading to rupture.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent permanent deformation of a material under a constant stress, occurring significantly above about 0.4 of its absolute melting temperature.
eqs: T = absolute operating temperature (K); \(T_{m}\) = absolute melting temperature (K)
tips: Always convert temperatures to Kelvin before applying the 0.4 Tm criterion; using degrees Celsius gives a wrong ratio.
Do not confuse the elastic strain shown at loading (instantaneous) with creep strain, which accumulates over time.
rq: Why must temperatures be expressed in Kelvin when applying the 0.4 Tm rule?
The rule is a ratio of absolute temperatures; Celsius values have an arbitrary zero, so ratios would be meaningless and the threshold would give wrong results.
What would you expect to happen to the time to rupture if the operating temperature is raised while stress stays constant?
The time to rupture decreases, because higher temperature increases the creep rate and the curves reach the failure point sooner.

notes.t: Effect of temperature on creep (homologous temperature)
pts: Creep occurs at ambient temperature for lead because its melting point is low, so room temperature is already a large fraction of the absolute melting temperature.
Creep becomes significant once the operating temperature exceeds about 0.4 of the absolute melting temperature, which is measured in kelvin.
Even in very cold climates, lead's operating temperature stays above 0.4Tm, so lead creeps in all normal service conditions.
defs: Homologous temperature
The ratio of an operating absolute temperature to the material's absolute melting temperature, T/Tm; creep becomes significant above about 0.4 Tm.
eqs: Threshold temperature for creep (0.4 homologous temperature)
\(T_m\) = absolute melting temperature (K); \(T_{\text{creep}}\) = threshold temperature above which creep is significant (K)
tips: Always convert temperatures to kelvin before forming the homologous temperature ratio; using °C gives wrong results.
The 0.4Tm threshold is a rule of thumb, so creep is considered significant above it rather than starting at an exact temperature.
rq: Why must the melting temperature be converted to kelvin before applying the 0.4Tm rule?
The homologous temperature rule uses absolute temperature; Celsius values give meaningless ratios, so 327°C becomes 600 K and 0.4Tm = 240 K.
Why does lead creep at ambient temperature while steel typically does not?
Lead has a very low melting point (600 K), so room temperature (~293 K) exceeds 0.4Tm; steel's much higher melting point keeps room temperature well below its creep threshold.

xq.q: A nickel alloy has melting temperature \(T_m = 1728\) K. Using the rule that creep is significant above \(0.4T_m\), find the lowest operating temperature in °C at which creep becomes significant. Use K = °C + 273.
Lead melts at 327 °C. At room temperature of 20 °C, what is the homologous temperature \(T/T_m\) and does lead creep? (K = °C + 273)
xq.a: 0.49; yes, it is above 0.4
o: 0.06; no, it is below 0.4
0.49; yes, it is above 0.4
0.92; yes, it is above 0.4
0.49; no, because 20 °C is well below the melting point
xq.w: 293/600 = 0.49 > 0.4 so lead creeps; the traps are using °C (20/327 = 0.06) or concluding from being far below melting.

xq.q: A steel component is tested at constant stress at two temperatures, one below \(0.4T_m\) and one well above it. Sketch and describe the two strain–time curves, explaining the differences.
xq.a: Below 0.4Tm the curve shows only an initial instantaneous elastic strain that then levels off, with no continuing strain over time. Above 0.4Tm the curve has the initial elastic strain followed by primary (decreasing rate), secondary (constant rate) and tertiary (accelerating) stages ending in rupture. At higher temperature, strain accumulates faster and rupture occurs after a much shorter time.
s: Low T: elastic strain then flat, no creep (1.5)
High T: elastic jump, then primary, secondary, tertiary to rupture (2)
Higher temperature gives a steeper curve and earlier failure (1)

units.name: 16.6 Creep in aircraft engine blades
units.ov: This module explains why aircraft engine blades suffer creep (time-dependent permanent deformation under centrifugal stress at about 850 °C, roughly 0.74 of the melting temperature) and how it is controlled. Control comes from alloy choice (high-melting nickel-based alloys) and from grain-structure engineering: conventional equiaxed casting, then directional solidification, then single crystals. Each step removes more grain boundaries, the sites of creep sliding and cavitation, at higher cost.
must: Creep: time-dependent, permanent (irreversible) deformation under sustained stress at high temperature, significant above about \(0.4T_m\); it is not elastic or rate-independent plastic strain
Homologous temperature \(T/T_m\) with both temperatures in kelvin (K = °C + 273); at 850 °C (1123 K) it is about 0.74, well above the 0.4 threshold

Blade specification: withstand 250 MPa at 850 °C with under 0.1% irreversible strain after 30 h, and also be impact resistant (foreign object ingestion); keep stress, temperature and strain units distinct
Cause and trade-off: centrifugal force gives high stress; conventional blades must be undersized to limit creep, which lowers engine efficiency, so better alloys and processing are needed
Because engines run far above \(0.4T_m\), creep resistance must be engineered in (high-\(T_m\) Ni-based alloys plus microstructure control) rather than avoided by lowering temperature
Conventional casting gives equiaxed, randomly oriented polycrystals with many grain boundaries, so grain boundary sliding and cavitation weaken the blade at high temperature

Directional solidification: the mould is slowly withdrawn from the furnace, giving columnar grains along the blade length; there are no transverse boundaries, so boundaries parallel to the stress carry no shear (no sliding) and no tensile stress across them (no cavities)
Single-crystal blades: a spiral (pigtail) grain selector lets only one grain survive, so there are no grain boundaries and no boundary sliding; the selector is discarded after casting
Directional solidification still has multiple aligned grains, whereas a single crystal has one; moving from conventional to directional to single crystal improves creep performance at increasing cost
Explain benefits through grain boundary mechanisms at high temperature, not just 'stronger'
conn: Homologous temperature links to the choice of material: a high \(T_m\) lowers \(T/T_m\), so Ni alloys delay creep, but 850 °C is still about 0.74 \(T_m\), so grain-structure control is also needed
Centrifugal stress direction links to grain boundary orientation: boundaries perpendicular to the load slide and cavitate, so directional solidification aligns them parallel to the stress axis
The creep-resistance and efficiency trade-off links to processing cost: better creep resistance allows larger blades and higher efficiency, but single-crystal casting costs more
The spec (creep strain under 0.1% in 30 h) links to the definition of creep as irreversible strain, so it is judged on permanent strain, not elastic deformation
exq: Calculate the homologous temperature of a blade alloy at 850 °C if its melting temperature is 1500 °C (convert to K). Is creep expected to be significant? Justify using the 0.4 \(T_m\) rule.
Explain with a labelled sketch how directional solidification and a spiral grain selector produce columnar-grain and single-crystal blades. Why is the spiral discarded afterwards?

Compare conventional cast, directionally solidified and single-crystal blades in terms of grain boundaries, creep mechanisms (sliding and cavity formation) and cost, and say which suits the most demanding turbine stages.
A blade must carry 250 MPa at 850 °C with under 0.1% irreversible strain after 30 h. Interpret each number, explain why elastic strain is excluded, and state what else the material must resist.
Why do designers of conventional blades have to undersize them, and how does improved creep resistance recover engine efficiency?

notes.t: Aircraft engine blades: operating conditions and creep
pts: Turbine/compressor blades run at up to about 850°C at very high rotational speed, a harsh thermal environment.
Centrifugal forces from rotation generate high stresses in the blade, which drives the need for creep-resistant materials.
Conventional blades undergo creep (slow permanent deformation under sustained stress at high temperature) during flight.
To limit creep, blades must be undersized, which reduces engine efficiency; this is the design trade-off motivating better alloys.
defs: Creep
Time-dependent, permanent deformation of a material under a constant stress, occurring mainly at high temperatures (typically above about 0.4–0.5 of the absolute melting temperature).
tips: Creep is a time-dependent deformation under constant load at high temperature; do not confuse it with elastic or plastic (rate-independent) deformation.
Quote temperatures in °C and convert to K (add 273) when using temperature-dependent creep relations.
rq: Why does reducing blade size to avoid creep lower engine efficiency?
A smaller blade sweeps less area and extracts/compresses less gas per revolution, so less work or thrust is produced for the same fuel burned.
Why does creep become a problem during flight rather than at room temperature?
Creep is thermally activated; at ~850°C atoms diffuse fast enough that sustained centrifugal stress causes continuous deformation over flight time.

notes.t: Aircraft engine blade material specification
pts: Blade materials must resist creep at high temperature: 250 MPa at 850 °C with under 0.1% irreversible strain after 30 h.
Creep performance is judged by the permanent (irreversible) strain accumulated under sustained load, not by instantaneous elastic deformation.
Besides creep resistance, blade materials must also be impact resistant (e.g. from foreign object ingestion).
defs: Creep
Time-dependent plastic deformation of a material under constant stress, usually at elevated temperature (typically above about 0.4 of its absolute melting temperature).
tips: Keep the units straight: 250 MPa is stress and 850 °C is temperature; the 0.1% is a strain (dimensionless), not a stress.
Creep strain is irreversible, so do not confuse it with recoverable elastic strain when answering spec questions.
rq: Why is the specification given as a stress at a fixed temperature with a limit on strain after a fixed time, rather than as a yield strength at room temperature?

Blades operate at high temperature under sustained load, where creep governs failure; room-temperature yield strength does not capture time-dependent deformation, so the spec tests creep strain over a set duration.
What would happen to the creep requirement if the operating temperature rose by 100 °C?
Creep rates increase rapidly with temperature, so the material would accumulate far more strain in 30 h and would likely fail the 0.1% limit unless a more creep-resistant alloy were used.

notes.t: Preventing creep in high-temperature alloys
pts: Creep is avoided by using alloys with very high melting temperatures, such as some nickel-based alloys.
A useful rule of thumb: creep becomes significant above roughly 0.4 of the absolute melting temperature.
Aircraft engines run well above this threshold, so creep resistance must be engineered in rather than avoided by temperature alone.
At 850 °C (1123 K) an engine operates at about 0.74 of the alloy's melting temperature, showing how demanding the conditions are.
defs: Homologous temperature
The ratio of an operating temperature to the absolute melting temperature of a material, T/\(T_{m}\), with both temperatures in kelvin; creep becomes significant above about 0.4 \(T_{m}\).
eqs: T = operating temperature (K); \(T_{m}\) = absolute melting temperature (K)
tips: Always convert to kelvin (K = °C + 273) before calculating T/\(T_{m}\); using °C gives wrong ratios.
Do not confuse the 0.4 \(T_{m}\) creep threshold with the melting point itself; the operating temperature can be far below \(T_{m}\) and still cause creep.
rq: Why must temperatures be converted to kelvin before computing T/\(T_{m}\)?
Because the homologous temperature is a ratio of absolute temperatures; Celsius has an arbitrary zero, so the ratio would be meaningless (e.g. 0 °C is not zero thermal energy).
Why is 850 °C a problem even though it is below the melting point of the nickel alloy?
Creep is driven by thermally activated diffusion, which becomes significant at around 0.4 \(T_{m}\); at 0.74 \(T_{m}\) diffusion is fast, so the alloy deforms slowly under stress despite not melting.

notes.t: Directional solidification of aircraft engine blades
pts: Directional solidification is used to improve turbine blade performance by controlling grain growth direction during casting.
The blade is gradually withdrawn from the furnace so solidification proceeds progressively from one end to the other.
Grains nucleated at the top grow longitudinally along the blade, producing columnar grains spanning its full length.
Removing transverse grain boundaries prevents creep failure at grain interfaces that lie perpendicular to the centrifugal load.
Eliminating perpendicular grain boundaries means the centrifugal stress does not act across weak boundaries, extending blade life at high temperature.
defs: Directional solidification
A casting process in which a metal is solidified progressively in one direction (e.g. by withdrawing the mould from a furnace), producing elongated columnar grains aligned along that direction.
Creep
Time-dependent, permanent deformation of a material under sustained stress at high temperature, often concentrated at grain boundaries.
tips: Do not confuse directional solidification with single-crystal casting; directional solidification still leaves aligned grain boundaries, just none transverse to the load.
Remember the aim is to eliminate boundaries perpendicular to the centrifugal stress, not to eliminate all grain boundaries.
rq: Why does a grain boundary perpendicular to the centrifugal stress matter more than one parallel to it?
A perpendicular boundary carries the full tensile stress across the interface, where atomic sliding and void formation (creep) are easiest, so it is the critical weak point.
What would happen to creep resistance if the blade were cast with equiaxed grains instead?
Equiaxed grains would produce many transverse boundaries across the load path, increasing grain-boundary creep and reducing creep life at high temperature.

notes.t: Directional solidification
pts: Directional solidification withdraws the mould slowly from the furnace so solidification proceeds in one direction, producing elongated columnar grains aligned along the solidification direction.
Grain boundaries aligned parallel to the applied tensile stress carry no shear stress, so there is no grain-boundary sliding.
Grain boundaries lie parallel to the tensile axis, so no tensile stress acts across them, which prevents cavity formation at the boundaries.
defs: Directional solidification

A casting process in which the melt solidifies progressively in one direction (controlled by slow withdrawal from a furnace with heated windings), giving columnar grains aligned with the growth direction.
tips: Do not confuse the grain alignment: boundaries must be parallel to the stress axis, not perpendicular, to avoid sliding and cavities.
Directional solidification is used for turbine blades to improve creep resistance; quote the mechanism (no sliding, no cavities) rather than just stating it is 'stronger'.
rq: Why does aligning grain boundaries parallel to the applied tensile stress improve high-temperature performance?
Because there is no shear stress on the boundaries (no sliding) and no tensile stress across them (no cavity opening), so creep-related boundary failure is suppressed.
What would happen to boundary-related failure if grain boundaries were transverse to the load axis instead?
Tensile stress would act normal to the boundaries and shear would act along them, promoting cavitation and grain-boundary sliding, and reducing creep life.

notes.t: Single-crystal aircraft engine turbine blades via spiral grain selection
pts: Directional solidification is used to grow the blade so grains align along one direction, improving high-temperature performance.
A spiral (pigtail) selector at the base of the mould lets only one grain survive, as competing grains are blocked by its winding path.
