Fatigue tests are long-duration, lasting days, weeks or even months.
For metals there is a practical maximum test frequency of about 100 Hz, because localised heating occurs at higher frequencies.
tips: The 100 Hz limit applies specifically to metals; the limit for other materials is not given on this page and should not be assumed the same.
rq: Why can't fatigue tests on metals simply be run faster to save time?
Above about 100 Hz, localised heating effects arise, which alter the material's behaviour and invalidate the test, so the frequency is practically limited to about 100 Hz for metals.

notes.t: Random loading cycles in fatigue testing
pts: Random loading better represents real service conditions than constant amplitude loading.
Random loading makes it hard to compare stress levels and fatigue lives between materials, because the load history varies.
For this reason, standard materials fatigue testing is normally carried out using constant amplitude tests, which give directly comparable results.
tips: Do not confuse the realism of random loading with its suitability for material comparison; standard materials data come from constant amplitude tests.
rq: Why would engineers use constant amplitude tests to rank materials even though random loading is more realistic?

Constant amplitude tests keep stress range and mean stress fixed, so fatigue lives and stress levels from different materials can be compared directly; random histories vary, making such comparison difficult.

notes.t: Stress vs Strain Control in Material Testing
pts: The choice between stress and strain control depends on what behaviour is being modelled.
Under stress control the applied stress is held constant, so strain grows as the material fails.
Under strain control the strain is held constant, so the stress falls as the material fails.
defs: Stress control
A loading mode in which the stress is kept constant during the test, so the resulting strain increases as the material fails (e.g. creep-type behaviour).
Strain control
A loading mode in which the strain is kept constant during the test, so the resulting stress decreases as the material fails (e.g. softening/post-peak behaviour).
tips: Do not confuse the two: in stress control it is the strain that increases, in strain control it is the stress that decreases.
Always state which variable is held constant and which one responds, linked to the real loading condition being modelled.
rq: Why would a strain-controlled test be needed to capture the post-peak softening of a brittle material?
Under stress control the specimen would fail suddenly once peak stress is reached; holding strain constant lets the stress fall gradually, so the softening branch can be measured.
If you want to model creep of a component under constant service load, which control mode should you use and why?
Stress control, because the load (stress) is constant in service, so the strain is allowed to increase over time.

notes.t: Stress Control in Cyclic (Fatigue) Testing
pts: Under stress control, a sinusoidal stress of fixed amplitude is applied cyclically to the specimen.
The strain response is measured; for a stress-controlled test, strain may increase with time (ratcheting/creep-type behaviour) rather than remaining constant.
The strain amplitude envelope widens over time, showing progressive increase in strain for constant stress amplitude.
Hysteresis loops and cycle-by-cycle strain changes can be compared between early and late cycles to characterise material behaviour.
defs: Stress control
A cyclic test mode in which the applied stress amplitude is held constant and the resulting strain is measured as a function of time or cycles.
tips: Do not confuse stress control with strain control: in stress control the strain amplitude is the response, not the input.
Check whether the question asks about amplitude (envelope) or mean value when interpreting the strain–time trace.
rq: Why does the strain envelope increase with time under constant stress amplitude?
Because the material accumulates permanent (plastic or creep) deformation each cycle, so the same stress produces progressively larger strain.
What would you expect to see in the strain trace if the material were purely elastic?
A strain waveform exactly in phase with the stress and of constant amplitude, with no envelope growth.

notes.t: Strain-controlled cyclic loading and stress response
pts: In strain control, a sinusoidal strain is imposed on the specimen over time, and the resulting stress is measured.
With a sinusoidal strain input, the stress response lags behind the strain in a viscoelastic material.
Under constant strain amplitude, the stress amplitude decreases over successive cycles, indicating stress relaxation or cyclic softening.
tips: Do not confuse strain control (strain imposed, stress measured) with stress control (stress imposed, strain measured).
rq: Why does the stress amplitude decrease over successive cycles under constant strain amplitude?
The material relaxes or softens cyclically (e.g. viscoelastic relaxation, microstructural change), so the same strain produces a smaller stress.

xq.q: A sinusoidal fatigue test is run on a metal specimen in a servo-hydraulic machine. The applied stress amplitude is held fixed, and the measured strain amplitude envelope widens steadily over the test. Which statement correctly describes the test?
xq.a: Stress control: stress amplitude is the input and the strain amplitude is the response, which grows
o: Strain control: strain is held constant and the stress amplitude falls as the material fails
Stress control: stress amplitude is the input and the strain amplitude is the response, which grows
Strain control: the strain amplitude is the input and it grows as the material fails
Stress control: the strain stays constant and the stress amplitude rises over successive cycles
xq.w: The fixed variable is stress, so strain is the response and it increases; the trap is mixing up which variable is imposed and which responds.
s: Fixed stress amplitude means stress control
Strain is then the measured response and increases

xq.q: A fatigue test on a steel specimen must be completed within a 5-day slot. The metal's practical maximum test frequency is 100 Hz. Roughly how many cycles can be applied at most in 5 days of continuous running at this frequency?
xq.a: 4.3 × 10⁷ cycles
o: 4.3 × 10⁷ cycles
7.2 × 10⁵ cycles
4.3 × 10⁴ cycles
1.8 × 10⁶ cycles
xq.w: N = 100 × 5 × 24 × 3600 = 4.32×10⁷; the traps are using minutes instead of seconds or forgetting the hours per day.

xq.q: Explain why standard materials fatigue data are obtained from constant amplitude tests even though random loading better represents service conditions. Also explain why a test frequency of 100 Hz is a practical upper limit for metals.
xq.a: Random loading is more realistic, but the varying load history makes it hard to compare stress levels and lives between materials. Constant amplitude tests give directly comparable results, so they are used for standard data. For metals, testing above about 100 Hz causes localised heating of the specimen, which would change the material behaviour and invalidate the results.
s: Random loading is more realistic for service
Varying history makes comparison of stress levels and lives difficult
Constant amplitude gives directly comparable results
Above about 100 Hz metals heat locally, so the frequency is limited

units.name: 17.6 S-N curves, fatigue limit and scatter
units.ov: This module covers how fatigue life is characterised: S-N (Wöhler) curves of stress amplitude against log cycles to failure, the distinction between a true fatigue limit (steels, titanium) and an endurance limit at a stated cycle count (Al, Cu, Mg), and the scatter in results handled by P-S-N curves and Weibull analysis. It also contrasts stress-controlled and strain-controlled testing, using bone cements as an example. The common thread is that fatigue life is a statistical, test-condition-dependent property, so any quoted value needs its conditions stated (mean stress, cycle count, probability, control mode).
must: S-N (Wöhler) curve: stress amplitude \(\sigma_a\) on the vertical axis against cycles to failure \(N_f\) on a log horizontal axis; read it either way (allowable stress for a required life, or life at a given stress)

Stress amplitude is the semi-range: \(\sigma_a=(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2\); S-N curves normally assume fully reversed cycling (zero mean stress), and a non-zero mean stress changes the allowable amplitude

Fatigue limit (steels, titanium alloys): the curve plateaus, and below this stress amplitude failure is not expected at any number of cycles; for most steels it is about \(0.5\,\sigma_{UTS}\) (mild steel ≈ 200 MN/m² in the notes)
Endurance limit (Al, Cu, Mg and their alloys, with no true plateau): the stress amplitude giving failure at a stated number of cycles, conventionally \(10^7\); always quote the cycle count
Never quote a fatigue limit for aluminium (e.g. 24S-T3), whose curve keeps falling with N
The log N axis means equal spacing is equal ratios of cycles, and a difference of 1 in log N is a factor of 10 in life; do not read it linearly
Fatigue results scatter even for nominally identical specimens, so a single S-N line is insufficient and a probabilistic treatment is needed

P-S-N curves: a family of S-N curves, each for a probability of failure P (e.g. 0.1, 0.5, 0.9); at a given stress a higher P means failure at fewer cycles, so the curve is lower in life; Weibull analysis is the statistical model behind this

Stress-controlled testing holds the stress amplitude constant, while strain-controlled testing holds the strain amplitude constant; material rankings can differ between the two (bone cements: Simplex lasts longest under stress control, Boneloc does best at low strain under strain control)
Always state which method you are using (S-N vs Weibull) and check the axes and units: stress in MPa or MN/m², strain dimensionless
conn: Fatigue limit versus endurance limit: identifying the material class (steel/Ti versus Al/Cu/Mg) decides whether you read a plateau stress or the stress at \(10^7\) cycles
Scatter leads to P-S-N: a design stress from a mean S-N curve (P = 0.5) gives a 50% failure chance, so safe design needs a low-P curve, linking to safety factors and Weibull analysis
Mean stress and stress amplitude: S-N data apply only to zero mean stress, so a loaded component with a non-zero mean needs the cycle converted to an amplitude and corrected before using the curve

Control mode and material ranking: comparing materials requires the same control mode, because stiffness and strain differ, so stress-controlled and strain-controlled curves can rank materials differently
exq: Sketch S-N curves for mild steel and for an aluminium alloy on axes of \(\sigma_a\) versus \(\log N_f\) from \(10^4\) to \(10^8\). Explain why one has a fatigue limit and the other needs an endurance limit, and state the conventional cycle count.

A steel has UTS = 600 MPa. Estimate its fatigue limit. A component sees a fully reversed stress of ±250 MPa. Is infinite life expected? Then give the stress amplitude for a cycle with \(\sigma_{max}=300\) MPa and \(\sigma_{min}=-100\) MPa, and comment on the mean stress.

Explain why fatigue data scatter and how a P-S-N diagram represents this. For P = 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 at a fixed stress amplitude, state which gives the shortest life and which curve you would use to design for a 10% failure risk.

On an S-N plot a specimen at 300 MPa fails at \(10^5\) cycles and another at 250 MPa fails at \(10^6\) cycles. Calculate the factor increase in life and explain why equal spacing on the log axis does not mean equal cycle increments.

Distinguish stress-controlled from strain-controlled fatigue testing using the bone cement data. Why might Simplex Vacuum Mix outperform Boneloc under stress control while Boneloc does best at low strain under strain control?

notes.t: Analysis of fatigue data
pts: Fatigue data can be analysed by testing at multiple stress levels and plotting an S-N curve of stress against cycles to failure.
The S-N curve is also known as the Wöhler curve.
Alternatively, fatigue data can be analysed in terms of probability of failure using Weibull analysis.
defs: S-N curve (Wöhler curve)
A plot of applied stress amplitude S against the number of cycles to failure N, used to characterise a material's fatigue behaviour.
Weibull analysis
A probability-of-failure based statistical analysis of fatigue data that models the distribution of failure stresses or lifetimes.
tips: Do not confuse the S-N (Wöhler) curve, which uses multiple stress levels, with Weibull analysis, which is probability based; state which one you are using.
Remember the S-N curve axes: stress on the vertical axis and number of cycles to failure N on the horizontal axis, often on a log scale.
rq: Why might an engineer choose Weibull analysis instead of an S-N curve for fatigue data?
Weibull analysis gives the probability of failure at a given stress or life, capturing scatter in fatigue results, whereas an S-N curve gives a single characteristic stress-life relationship.
What does each point on an S-N curve represent?
The number of cycles to failure obtained when a specimen is cycled at a particular stress amplitude.

notes.t: The S-N curve (fatigue life)
pts: An S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to fatigue fracture, and is used to predict fatigue life under cyclic loading.
Read from the curve in one direction, it gives the maximum stress amplitude that can be sustained for a required number of cycles.
Read in the other direction, it gives the number of cycles to failure for a given stress amplitude.
Mild steel shows a clear fatigue limit: its curve levels off at about 200 MN/m² so, at this stress, failure is not expected at very high cycle counts.
The aluminium alloy (24S-T3) has no distinct endurance limit; its stress amplitude keeps falling as cycles increase, so a fatigue strength at a stated cycle count (e.g. 10⁸) must be quoted.
defs: Stress amplitude (σₐ)
Half the range of cyclic stress, i.e. the semi-range of stress about the mean stress, in MN/m² (Pa).
Cycles to failure (\(N_{f}\))
The number of load cycles a component endures at a given stress amplitude before fatigue fracture occurs.
Fully reversed (zero mean stress) cycling
Cyclic loading in which the mean stress is zero, so the stress alternates equally between tension and compression.
tips: Ensure the curve applies to fully reversed (zero mean stress) cycling; with a non-zero mean stress the allowable amplitude changes.
Use the log scale for cycles: the axis runs 10⁴ to 10⁸, so do not read values as linear increments.
rq: Why does the mild steel curve flatten out while the aluminium curve keeps falling?

Mild steel has a fatigue (endurance) limit below which it can survive indefinitely, around 200 MN/m²; aluminium alloys lack a true limit, so failure eventually occurs at any stress amplitude given enough cycles.
What would happen to the cycles-to-failure for an aluminium component if the stress amplitude were reduced from 250 to 150 MN/m²?
\(N_{f}\) would increase greatly (from roughly 10⁵ towards 10⁷ cycles or more), since fatigue life rises steeply as stress amplitude falls.

notes.t: The S-N curve: fatigue limit vs endurance limit
pts: Steels and titanium alloys show a fatigue limit: stress amplitude stops decreasing with cycles to failure once a plateau is reached.
The fatigue limit is also called the fatigue strength; for most steels it is about 50% of the UTS.
Non-ferrous metals and alloys (Al, Cu, Mg) show no realistic lower limit, so an endurance limit must be specified for a chosen number of cycles.
The endurance limit is the stress amplitude that gives failure at a stated cycle count, here taken as \(10^{7}\) cycles.
On the S-N plot the stress amplitude σ_a falls as the number of cycles to failure \(N_{f}\) increases, with \(N_{f}\) on a log scale.
defs: Fatigue limit (fatigue strength)
The stress amplitude below which a material (typically steel or titanium) does not fail, regardless of the number of cycles applied.
Endurance limit
For materials with no true fatigue limit (e.g. Al, Cu, Mg), the stress amplitude at which failure occurs after a specified number of cycles, conventionally \(10^{7.}\)
tips: Do not quote a fatigue limit for aluminium, copper or magnesium; quote an endurance limit and state the cycle count (\(10^{7}\)) it applies to.
Remember that \(N_{f}\) is plotted on a logarithmic axis, so equal spacing corresponds to equal ratios of cycles, not equal numbers of cycles.
rq: Why can't aluminium alloys be given a fatigue limit in the same way as steel?

Their S-N curve keeps falling with increasing cycles with no flat plateau, so no realistic stress exists below which they never fail; hence an endurance limit at a stated cycle count (\(10^{7}\)) is specified.
If a steel component is designed to operate at 50% of its UTS, what should you expect for its fatigue life?
Roughly at or below its fatigue strength, so it should survive a very large (effectively infinite) number of cycles, since the rule of thumb puts the fatigue limit near 50% of UTS.

notes.t: Probabilistic fatigue data: the P-S-N curve
pts: Fatigue test results scatter, even between nominally identical samples, so a single S-N line is insufficient.
A probabilistic approach is therefore useful for fatigue design, giving the chance of failure at a given stress amplitude and life.
The P-S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure with one curve per probability of failure P (e.g. P = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9).
For a given stress amplitude, a higher probability of failure corresponds to a curve lying higher, i.e. failure at fewer cycles is more likely.
The diagram shown is for zero mean stress, with cycles to failure plotted on a logarithmic scale.
defs: P-S-N curve
A family of stress amplitude versus cycles-to-failure curves, each labelled with a probability of failure P, showing the statistical scatter of fatigue life.
Probability of failure (P)
The fraction of test specimens expected to fail at a given stress amplitude and number of cycles.
tips: Do not confuse P (probability of failure) with stress or life; P is a fraction or percentage labelling each curve.
Remember the x-axis is cycles to failure on a logarithmic scale, so curves appear straight-ish and spacing is not linear.
rq: Why does a 90% failure-probability curve lie above the 10% curve on a P-S-N plot?
At a given stress amplitude, a specimen is more likely to fail, so fewer cycles are needed; the curve for higher P sits at higher stress for the same life.
Why is a deterministic S-N curve alone risky for design?
It ignores scatter between samples, so it may not reflect the failure risk at chosen stress and life; a probabilistic curve quantifies that risk.

notes.t: Stress-controlled vs strain-controlled fatigue of bone cements
pts: Strain-controlled fatigue curves plot applied strain against log cycles to failure; higher strain gives fewer cycles to failure.
Stress-controlled fatigue curves plot applied stress (MPa) against log cycles to failure; the same material shows different ranking and scatter than under strain control.
Under stress control, Simplex Vacuum Mix lasts longest at each stress level, while Boneloc has the shortest fatigue life.
Under strain control, Boneloc achieves the most cycles at low strain, so the material ranking differs between control modes.
defs: Log cycles to failure
The base-10 logarithm of the number of load cycles a specimen sustains before fracturing at a given stress or strain amplitude.
Strain-controlled fatigue
Fatigue testing in which the strain amplitude is held constant and the number of cycles to failure is recorded.
Stress-controlled fatigue
Fatigue testing in which the stress amplitude is held constant and the number of cycles to failure is recorded.
tips: Check which axis is stress (MPa) and which is strain (dimensionless) before comparing curves; they are not interchangeable.
Log cycles to failure means the exponent, so a difference of 1 on the axis is a factor of 10 in cycles.
rq: Why can the material ranking differ between stress-controlled and strain-controlled fatigue tests?
Because the two tests fix different variables; a material that deforms less under a given stress may not deform less under a given strain, so the failure order can change.
What would you expect to happen to log cycles to failure if the applied stress amplitude is increased?
It decreases: higher stress amplitude causes failure after fewer cycles, giving a downward-sloping S-N type curve.

xq.q: A fully reversed fatigue test cycles a specimen between a maximum stress of +260 MPa and a minimum stress of −260 MPa. A mild steel has a fatigue limit of 200 MPa, and for most steels the fatigue limit is about 50% of the UTS. (a) Find the stress amplitude and the stress range. (b) Estimate the UTS of this steel from its fatigue limit. Give the UTS in MPa.
xq.a: UTS ≈ 400 MPa (amplitude 260 MPa, range 520 MPa)
s: Amplitude = half the range = (260−(−260))/2 = 260 MPa; range 520 MPa
Fatigue limit ≈ 0.5 UTS so UTS ≈ 200/0.5 = 400 MPa
The amplitude of 260 MPa exceeds the 200 MPa limit so finite life is expected

xq.q: An aluminium alloy bracket is to be designed against fatigue. Which statement is correct for this material?
xq.a: It has no true fatigue limit, so an endurance limit must be quoted at a stated number of cycles such as 10⁷
o: It has a fatigue limit, below which it never fails, as for steel
It has no true fatigue limit, so an endurance limit must be quoted at a stated number of cycles such as 10⁷
Its fatigue limit is about 50% of its UTS
Its S-N curve levels off, so the endurance limit applies at any number of cycles
xq.w: Non-ferrous alloys such as Al show continually falling S-N curves, so the stress must be quoted at a stated life; applying the steel behaviour is the trap.
s: Al, Cu, Mg show no plateau
Quote endurance limit at a stated cycle count, e.g. 10⁷

xq.q: Explain why a single S-N line is insufficient for fatigue design, and describe how a P-S-N diagram addresses this. State how the curves for P = 0.1 and P = 0.9 are positioned relative to each other.
xq.a: Fatigue results scatter, even for nominally identical specimens, so one line cannot give the chance of failure. A P-S-N diagram plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure (log scale) with a separate curve for each probability of failure P, e.g. 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, for zero mean stress. At a given stress amplitude, the higher probability curve (P = 0.9) lies higher than the P = 0.1 curve, since failure at fewer cycles is more likely.
s: P-S-N has one curve per probability of failure
Gives chance of failure at a given stress and life
P = 0.9 curve lies above the P = 0.1 curve

units.name: 17.7 High vs low cycle fatigue and application examples
units.ov: This material separates high cycle fatigue (elastic, stress-based, long life) from low cycle fatigue (plastic strain each cycle, strain-based, short life). It then applies the classification to real components (engine blades, steel bridges, suspension bolts, aircraft wings) by identifying mechanical, thermal and chemical sources of cyclic loading. The link is that the yield criterion decides the regime, the regime decides the test and analysis method, and the loading sources decide the stress cycle.
must: High cycle fatigue (HCF): peak stress below yield (\(\sigma_{max}<\sigma_y\)), elastic deformation, long life (more than about \(10^4\) to \(10^5\) cycles)
Low cycle fatigue (LCF): peak stress exceeds yield (\(\sigma_{max}>\sigma_y\) or \(|\sigma_{min}|>\sigma_y\)), plastic strain every cycle, short life (fewer than about \(10^4\) to \(10^5\) cycles)
The deciding criterion is stress relative to yield, not cycle count; the boundary is approximate and the notes quote both \(10^4\) and \(10^5\), so state which figure you use and say it is typical
LCF needs a strain-based life parameter and cyclic strain-controlled testing; HCF uses stress-based analysis and cyclic stress-controlled testing
Fatigue is progressive, localised damage from repeated fluctuating stress, and it can cause failure well below static yield or tensile strength
Only the varying (cyclic) component of stress drives fatigue; a steady mean load such as bridge dead weight sets the mean stress but is not itself the fatigue driver
Fatigue sources fall into three categories, mechanical, thermal and chemical, and they often act together
Engine blades: thermal cycling (ground vs cruise), centrifugal tensile stress that varies with each start-stop cycle, and bird strike impact
Bridges: traffic (main dynamic load) and wind are mechanical, weather cycles are thermal, de-icing chemicals are chemical; dead weight is the mean load

Suspension bolts and wings: bolt loads from vehicle weight, cornering and speed bumps plus road salt; wing loads from ground vs in-air weight, storms and turbulence plus de-icing fluid and temperature change
conn: Yield criterion, regime, method: \(\sigma_{max}\) vs \(\sigma_y\) decides HCF or LCF, which decides stress-based or strain-based analysis and stress-controlled or strain-controlled testing
Mean vs alternating stress: dead weight (mean) combined with traffic (cyclic) gives the stress cycle, linking the bridge example to the idea that only the fluctuating part drives fatigue
Environment and mechanics together: salt or de-icer accelerates crack initiation and growth under cyclic mechanical load, so thermal, chemical and mechanical sources must all be listed
Classification of an application: for a component like an engine blade, identify every cyclic source, then judge whether peak stress exceeds yield to assign HCF or LCF
exq: Define high and low cycle fatigue, giving the stress condition relative to yield and the typical cycle counts (\(10^4\) to \(10^5\)). Why is the cycle count only a guide?

A component has \(\sigma_y = 350\) MPa and sees a cyclic stress between +400 MPa and -400 MPa. Classify the fatigue regime, justify it, and state the appropriate test control and life-prediction parameter.
Explain why a strain-based approach is used for low cycle fatigue but a stress-based approach is adequate for high cycle fatigue.
List and classify (mechanical, thermal, chemical) the fatigue loading sources on an aircraft engine blade, and explain why centrifugal load is not purely static.
For a steel bridge, distinguish the mean load from the fatigue loads, identify the sources of each, and name the chemical and thermal contributions.

notes.t: High vs low cycle fatigue
pts: High cycle fatigue: applied stresses stay below yield, so no plastic deformation occurs in the cycles.
High cycle fatigue typically fails after more than about \(10^{4}\) cycles.
Low cycle fatigue: applied stresses exceed yield, so plastic deformation is included in each cycle.
Low cycle fatigue typically fails in fewer than about \(10^{4}\) cycles.
defs: High cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure under cyclic stresses below the yield strength, with no macroscopic plastic deformation, typically lasting more than \(10^4\) cycles.
Low cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure under cyclic stresses above the yield strength, where plastic deformation occurs in each cycle, typically failing in fewer than \(10^4\) cycles.
tips: Do not confuse the regimes: high cycle means below yield (elastic), low cycle means above yield (plastic); the \(10^{4}\) cycle figure is typical, not an exact cut-off.
State the cycle count with the power of ten (\(10^{4}\)) and the stress condition relative to yield in your answer.
rq: Why does the \(10^{4}\)-cycle boundary separate the two regimes rather than the stress magnitude alone?

The boundary reflects the stress level relative to yield: stresses below yield give long lives (>\(10^{4}\) cycles) with elastic-only behaviour, while stresses above yield cause plastic strain each cycle and failure within fewer cycles; the cycle count is a typical indicator of this behaviour.
What would happen to the fatigue regime of a component if its cyclic stress amplitude is raised from below yield to above yield?
It moves from high cycle to low cycle fatigue, because plastic deformation is introduced each cycle and the life drops below about \(10^{4}\) cycles.

notes.t: Distinction between high and low cycle fatigue
pts: Low cycle fatigue occurs at fewer than about \(10^{5}\) cycles, where peak stress exceeds yield so plastic strain occurs every cycle.
Because plastic strain occurs each cycle in low cycle fatigue, a strain-based parameter should be used for life prediction in metals.
High cycle fatigue occurs at more than about \(10^{5}\) cycles, where peak stress is generally below yield, i.e. in the elastic range.
For high cycle fatigue a stress-based analysis is adequate and a cyclic stress-controlled test is most appropriate.
Low cycle fatigue is tested with cyclic strain-controlled tests, while high cycle fatigue uses cyclic stress-controlled tests.
defs: Low cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure at fewer than about \(10^{5}\) cycles (\(N_{f}\) < \(10^{5}\)), where the maximum stress exceeds the yield strength so plastic strain occurs in every cycle.
High cycle fatigue
Fatigue failure at more than about \(10^{5}\) cycles (\(N_{f}\) > \(10^{5}\)), where the stress is generally below yield so deformation is elastic and stress-based analysis is adequate.
eqs: \(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
\(\sigma_{max}\) = maximum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{min}\) = minimum stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
tips: The \(10^{5}\) cycle boundary is approximate; the deciding condition is whether the maximum stress exceeds yield.
Check whether stress exceeds yield (plastic, strain-based) or stays below it (elastic, stress-based) rather than judging by cycle count alone.
rq: Why must a strain-based parameter rather than a stress-based one be used for low cycle fatigue in metals?
Because peak stress exceeds yield, so permanent plastic strain accumulates every cycle; strain describes this deformation and governs life better than stress.
What would happen to the appropriate analysis if a high cycle fatigue component were loaded so its maximum stress rose above yield?
Plastic strain would occur each cycle, so the regime would become low cycle fatigue and a strain-based approach and strain-controlled testing would be needed.

notes.t: Fatigue loading in aircraft engine blades
pts: Aircraft engine blades experience fatigue from both thermal cycling and mechanical loading.
Thermal fatigue arises from temperature swings between airport ground level and cruise altitude.
Centrifugal force from rotation imposes a steady and cyclic tensile stress on each blade.
Bird strike is a sudden mechanical impact that can initiate or grow fatigue cracks.
tips: Do not treat centrifugal load as purely static; it fluctuates with each start-stop cycle, so it contributes to fatigue.
Identify all sources of cyclic loading (thermal, centrifugal, impact) when classifying the fatigue type, not just the dominant one.
rq: Why is a blade's fatigue life affected by flights to 30,000 feet even if the blade is never loaded at full power on the ground?
Each flight cycle takes the blade through a large temperature change, so thermal stresses are repeatedly applied and removed, accumulating fatigue damage regardless of mechanical load.
Why does the centrifugal stress in a rotating blade count as fatigue loading rather than a static load?
The engine starts, runs, and stops on every flight, so the centrifugal stress rises and falls cyclically, producing repeated stress reversals/fluctuations that cause fatigue.

notes.t: Fatigue loading types in steel bridges
pts: Fatigue in a steel bridge can be driven by thermal, chemical and mechanical sources; weather cycles cause thermal fatigue.
De-icing chemicals act as a chemical source of degradation contributing to fatigue damage.
Dead weight of the bridge gives a steady mean load, which is not itself the fatigue-driving component.
Traffic weight produces dynamic, fluctuating loads that are the main source of mechanical fatigue loading.
Wind loads are a further mechanical source of cyclic stress.
defs: Fatigue
Progressive, localised structural damage caused by repeated fluctuating stresses, leading to crack initiation and failure at stresses well below the static strength.
Mean load (dead weight)
The steady, permanent load from the structure's own weight, which sets the mean stress about which cyclic stresses vary.
Dynamic (fatigue) loads
Time-varying loads from moving traffic that cause cyclic stress ranges responsible for fatigue damage.
tips: Do not confuse mean (dead) load with fatigue load: only the varying component of stress drives fatigue.
Remember that fatigue can be triggered by thermal, chemical and mechanical sources together, not just by traffic.
rq: Why does the dead weight of the bridge not by itself cause fatigue, even though it is a large load?
Because it is essentially constant, so it produces a mean stress with no cyclic stress range; fatigue requires fluctuating stress, supplied by traffic and wind.
Why might thermal weather cycles cause fatigue in a steel bridge even without any traffic?
Daily and seasonal temperature changes cause repeated expansion and contraction; if restrained, this produces cyclic thermal stresses.

notes.t: Fatigue types: service loading and environment
pts: Fatigue in a car suspension bolt is driven by cyclic stress from mechanical loads such as vehicle weight, cornering and speed bumps.
Thermal cycling from weather can also cause fatigue damage in components through repeated expansion and contraction.
A chemical environment, such as road salt, can accelerate crack initiation and growth under cyclic loading.
The stress σ shown on the bolted joint is a fluctuating (alternating) stress, which is the signature of fatigue loading.
defs: Fatigue
Progressive, localised cracking and failure of a material under repeated or fluctuating stresses, usually at levels well below the static yield or tensile strength.
tips: Classify each loading source correctly: mechanical (weight, cornering, speed bumps), thermal (weather) and chemical (salt) fatigue are distinct categories.
Do not confuse fatigue with simple overload: fatigue involves repeated loading, so the stress need not exceed the static strength to cause failure.
rq: Why can a bolt fail by fatigue even when the static load it carries is well below its yield strength?
Because repeated fluctuating stresses initiate and grow cracks progressively, so failure occurs at stress amplitudes far below the static strength.
Why would salt from roads matter for a suspension bolt that is loaded purely mechanically?
A corrosive environment combined with cyclic stress promotes crack initiation and growth (corrosion-fatigue), lowering the fatigue life compared with dry conditions.

notes.t: Fatigue types in aircraft wings
pts: Aircraft wings experience fatigue from several environmental and loading sources, not just one.
Thermal fatigue arises from temperature cycling due to weather and from the change between ground and flying height.
Chemical environment fatigue can be driven by de-icing fluids that come into contact with the wing structure.
Mechanical fatigue comes from cyclic loads such as the on-ground weight of the wings, in-air weight of the aircraft, storms and clear air turbulence.
tips: Do not treat fatigue as only mechanical; thermal and chemical environments also contribute and should be listed when asked for fatigue types.
Distinguish the on-ground weight of the wings from the in-air loading of the aircraft, since they produce different stress cycles.
rq: Why is clear air turbulence a fatigue concern even though it is not a severe single-event load?

Its repeated, fluctuating gust loads cause many stress cycles over the aircraft's life, and fatigue damage accumulates from repeated cycling even when each individual load is well below the static strength.
How could de-icer contribute to fatigue of a wing structure?
A chemical environment can cause corrosion or environmentally assisted crack growth, so combined chemical attack and cyclic stress accelerates fatigue cracking compared with cycling in air alone.

xq.q: A steel component is cycled between σ_max = +380 MPa and σ_min = −380 MPa. Its yield stress is σ_y = 350 MPa. (a) State whether this is high cycle or low cycle fatigue and which test control is appropriate. (b) The yield stress is raised by heat treatment to 420 MPa. Find the percentage margin by which σ_y then exceeds σ_max, to the nearest whole percent.
xq.a: Initially low cycle (strain control); after heat treatment margin = 10.5% ≈ 11%
s: 380 > 350 MPa so yield is exceeded: low cycle fatigue, strain-controlled test
New σ_y = 420 > 380 so the cycling is elastic (high cycle)

xq.q: A component fails after 2 × 10⁵ cycles, but its peak stress in every cycle was above the yield stress. How should the failure be classified and analysed?
xq.a: Low cycle fatigue, because plastic strain occurs every cycle, so a strain-based analysis is used
o: High cycle fatigue, because the life exceeds 10⁵ cycles, using stress-based analysis
Low cycle fatigue, because plastic strain occurs every cycle, so a strain-based analysis is used
High cycle fatigue, because stress above yield is elastic
Low cycle fatigue, but tested using stress control because life exceeds 10⁴
xq.w: The deciding condition is whether the maximum stress exceeds yield, not the cycle count, which is only approximate.
s: σ_max > σ_y means plastic strain each cycle
So low cycle fatigue with strain-based parameter

xq.q: Identify the sources of cyclic loading that cause fatigue in an aircraft engine blade, and explain why the centrifugal load should not be treated as purely static.
xq.a: Thermal fatigue arises from temperature swings between ground level and cruise altitude. Mechanical loading comes from centrifugal force due to rotation, giving a tensile stress on each blade, and bird strike impact can initiate or grow cracks. The centrifugal load is not purely static because it varies with every start-stop cycle, so it fluctuates and contributes to fatigue.
s: Thermal cycling: ground to cruise temperature
Bird strike impact can initiate or grow cracks
Centrifugal stress changes with each start-stop so is cyclic

units.name: 17.8 Fatigue limit and factors affecting fatigue life
units.ov: This material covers how S–N curves describe fatigue and which materials show a fatigue (endurance) limit. It then looks at factors that change fatigue life: mean stress, loading frequency (especially in viscoelastic polymers), and surface compressive treatments. The common thread is that tensile stress and heat shorten life, while anything that suppresses surface crack growth lengthens it.
must: S–N curve: stress amplitude (MPa) against cycles to failure N on a log axis; read the fatigue limit as the flat plateau value, not the stress at a low cycle count
Fatigue limit = stress amplitude below which failure never occurs (about \(10^7\) cycles in testing); steels and titanium alloys have one
Aluminium alloys have no clear fatigue limit, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated N (e.g. \(10^7\) or \(10^8\) cycles)
Stress amplitude \(\sigma_a=(\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2\) and mean stress \(\sigma_m=(\sigma_{max}+\sigma_{min})/2\); do not confuse the two
Tensile mean stress lowers the S–N curve and so shortens life at a given amplitude; zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest life
Polymers: PMMA, PP, PE, PTFE level off, with fatigue limits of roughly 10, 5, 3 and 2 MPa; nylon (dry), PET and PS keep falling; all are far weaker than metals (plotted up to about 25 MPa)
Frequency has little effect on metals below yield, since they are purely elastic and return the energy each cycle; in polymers it matters a lot
Polymers are viscoelastic, so each cycle dissipates energy \(W_d=\oint\sigma\,d\varepsilon\) (the hysteresis loop area); this appears as heat and causes self-heating and early failure
PMMA at ±30 MPa: 5 Hz gave log N ≈ 3.3 and 2 Hz gave log N ≈ 4.1, so higher frequency means more heating and shorter life; remember the axis is log10 N
Improve fatigue life with surface compressive stress, which suppresses surface crack growth: shot peening (plastic deformation of the surface) and carburizing (carbon diffusion plus hardening)
conn: Mean stress and surface treatments: shot peening and carburizing work by imposing a compressive residual (mean) stress at the surface, which shifts the S–N curve upward

Hysteresis and frequency: energy loss per cycle × number of cycles per second gives the heating rate, so higher frequency means a higher temperature rise and a shorter life in polymers, but not in elastic metals
Material type and S–N shape: deciding whether to quote a fatigue limit (steel, PP) or a fatigue strength at N cycles (aluminium, nylon) depends on whether the curve plateaus
Log axis and quantitative reading: the S–N plot, the log N frequency comparison and the amplitude/mean-stress definitions are often combined in one calculation
exq: Sketch S–N curves for a steel and an aluminium alloy. Explain why a fatigue limit can be specified for one but not the other, and state how you would specify the design stress for the aluminium.

A component cycles between +200 MPa and −40 MPa. Calculate the stress amplitude and mean stress, and explain how this mean stress affects life compared with fully reversed loading of the same amplitude.

PMMA bone cement tested at ±30 MPa lasts log N ≈ 4.1 at 2 Hz and ≈ 3.3 at 5 Hz. Calculate the ratio of cycles to failure and the time to failure at each frequency, and explain the difference using hysteresis.
Explain why frequency has little effect on the fatigue of metals below yield but a large effect on polymers. Define the hysteresis loop area and say what happens to the dissipated energy.
Describe how shot peening and carburizing improve fatigue life. Relate your answer to the effect of mean stress on the S–N curve and to surface crack growth.

notes.t: Fatigue limit (endurance limit)
pts: Some materials (e.g. steel, titanium alloys) have a stress amplitude below which fatigue failure does not occur, however many cycles are applied.
The fatigue limit is typically defined at about \(10^{7}\) load cycles in testing; beyond this the S–N curve becomes flat.
Aluminium alloys show no clear endurance limit; their S–N curve keeps falling, so they will eventually fail at any stress level.
The vertical axis is the peak value of repeated tensile stress (MPa) and the horizontal axis is the number of cycles to failure on a log scale.
defs: Fatigue limit (endurance limit)
The stress amplitude below which a material can withstand an infinite (practically ~\(10^{7}\) or more) number of load cycles without fatigue failure.
S–N curve
A plot of stress amplitude against number of cycles to failure; for materials with an endurance limit it levels off horizontally, while for others it keeps decreasing.
tips: Do not assume every metal has a fatigue limit; aluminium alloys do not, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated number of cycles instead.
Check units: the stress axis is in MPa (N/mm²), and the cycle count is dimensionless but must be given on a log scale.
rq: Why can't aluminium alloys be designed using an endurance limit like steel?
Their S–N curve has no horizontal plateau, so failure eventually occurs at any stress level; a finite fatigue life must be specified instead (e.g. at \(10^{8}\) cycles).
Why is the horizontal axis plotted on a logarithmic scale?
Fatigue lives span many orders of magnitude (\(10^{4}\) to \(10^{8}\) cycles), so a log scale displays the whole range clearly and makes the knee and plateau visible.

notes.t: Fatigue limit of polymers (S-N curves)
pts: Some polymers show a fatigue limit: stress amplitude below which they survive indefinitely, as the curve flattens at high cycle counts.
Nylon (dry), PET and PS have curves that keep falling with cycles, so they show no clear fatigue limit in this range.
PMMA, PP, PE and PTFE curves level off, indicating a fatigue limit at roughly 10 MPa, 5 MPa, 3 MPa and 2 MPa respectively.
Polymers generally have much lower fatigue strengths than metals, with the highest plotted stress amplitude around 25 MPa.
defs: Fatigue limit
The maximum stress amplitude below which a material does not fail under cyclic loading, however many cycles are applied.
Stress amplitude
Half the difference between maximum and minimum stress in a cyclic loading cycle.
tips: Read the fatigue limit as the plateau value of stress amplitude, not the stress at a low cycle count such as \(10^{3.}\)
Check units: the vertical axis is stress amplitude in MPa, not total stress or strain.
rq: Why do the nylon, PET and PS curves not flatten within the range shown, and what does that imply for design?
They keep decreasing with cycles, so no safe stress exists for infinite life in this range; a design must assume a finite fatigue life or use a conservative stress.
What would happen to the fatigue limit of PMMA if the test environment were humid rather than dry?
Water absorption typically reduces polymer fatigue strength, so the plateau would likely shift to a lower stress amplitude (nylon is noted as dry for this reason).

notes.t: Effect of mean stress on fatigue life
pts: Increasing the mean (tensile) stress reduces the number of cycles to failure at a given stress amplitude.
Curves shift downward as mean stress becomes more tensile, so fatigue life is shorter for the same stress amplitude.
Near-zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest fatigue life for the same stress amplitude.
On an S–N (stress amplitude vs cycles to failure) plot, a horizontal line at fixed amplitude crosses each curve at a different N, showing the reduction in life.
defs: Mean stress (\( \sigma_m \))
The average of the maximum and minimum stresses in a fatigue cycle; tensile mean stress is harmful to fatigue life.
Stress amplitude (\( \sigma \))
Half the range of stress in a cyclic loading, plotted on the vertical axis of an S–N diagram.
Cycles to failure (\( N \))
The number of load cycles a material withstands before fatigue fracture at a given stress level.
tips: Do not confuse stress amplitude with mean stress; the graph holds amplitude on the vertical axis and changes the mean stress as the curve parameter.
Remember that the effect applies to fatigue (cyclic) loading only; mean stress does not change the static tensile strength of the material.
rq: Why does a tensile mean stress shorten fatigue life even when the stress amplitude is unchanged?
A tensile mean stress raises the peak stress in each cycle, so crack initiation and growth occur more readily, reducing the cycles to failure.
If two components have the same stress amplitude but one has compressive mean stress, which will last longer and why?
The compressive-mean-stress component, because compressive mean stress tends to keep cracks closed and lowers the effective tensile stress at the crack tip.

notes.t: Effect of frequency on fatigue/cyclic loading
pts: In metals, loading frequency has only a limited effect on behaviour.
Below yield, metals respond purely elastically, so no hysteresis losses accumulate.
In metals each load cycle returns all the energy put in, so little energy is retained in the material.
In polymers, frequency can have a substantial effect because they are viscoelastic and dissipate energy.
tips: Do not assume frequency is irrelevant for all materials: the 'limited effect' statement applies to metals below yield, not to polymers.
Remember the metal result holds only for purely elastic loading; above yield, plastic work makes frequency relevant again.
rq: Why does loading frequency matter much more for polymers than for metals below yield?

Polymers are viscoelastic: part of the input energy is dissipated as heat each cycle (hysteresis), and the response depends on time/rate. Metals below yield are purely elastic, so energy in equals energy returned and little is retained.
What would happen to the heat generated in a polymer component if the loading frequency were increased?
More energy is dissipated per unit time, so the temperature rises faster, which can soften the polymer, change its stiffness and accelerate fatigue or creep damage.

notes.t: Effect of loading frequency on fatigue life of polymers (PMMA bone cement)
pts: Polymers rarely show purely elastic behaviour, so energy input per cycle is not fully recovered on unloading.
Energy put in per load cycle is not equal to energy got out, so some is absorbed (hysteresis) each cycle.
Absorbed energy that cannot escape is retained as heat, raising specimen temperature and accelerating failure.
At ±30 MPa in air, PMMA specimens tested at 5 Hz failed after far fewer cycles than at 2 Hz (about log10 N ≈ 3.3 vs ≈ 4.1).
5 Hz specimens were warm to the touch after testing, evidence of self-heating due to energy absorption.
defs: Hysteresis (in polymers)
Energy dissipated per load cycle as the stress–strain loading and unloading paths do not coincide, shown as an enclosed loop area; the dissipated energy typically appears as heat.
eqs: Energy dissipated per cycle (area of hysteresis loop)
\(W_{d}\) = energy dissipated per cycle (J/\(m^{3}\)); \sigma = stress (Pa); \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless)
tips: Plot is log10 of cycles to failure: a value of 4 means \(10^{4}\) cycles, not 4 cycles; don't confuse the logarithmic axis with linear.
Frequency alone is not a material property; results only apply to the stated stress amplitude, environment (in air) and material (PMMA), and heating effects depend on specimen size and heat loss.
rq: Why does a higher testing frequency reduce fatigue life of PMMA even though the stress amplitude is the same?
More cycles per second means more energy absorbed per unit time, causing more self-heating that cannot be released; the heat softens/degrades the polymer and reduces cycles to failure.
What would you expect to happen to the temperature of a PMMA specimen if the loading frequency were lowered to 0.5 Hz at the same stress amplitude?
Less heat generated per unit time, so the specimen would stay cooler and its fatigue life would be longer, since heat can be lost to surroundings between cycles.

notes.t: Improving Fatigue Life: Surface Compressive Stress
pts: Imposing a compressive surface stress suppresses the growth of surface cracks, which are the usual starting points of fatigue failure.
A near-zero or compressive mean stress gives the highest stress amplitude for a given number of cycles to failure, so fatigue life is longest; increasing tensile mean stress lowers the S–N curve.
Shot peening bombards the surface with small shot particles, plastically deforming the surface layer so it is left in compression.
Carburizing diffuses carbon into the surface from a C-rich gas, producing a surface layer that is put into compression on treatment, which suppresses crack growth.
defs: Mean stress (\(\sigma_m\))
The average of the maximum and minimum stresses in a fatigue cycle; tensile mean stress reduces fatigue life, while zero or compressive mean stress improves it.
Stress amplitude (S)
Half the range of cyclic stress in a fatigue test, plotted against cycles to failure on an S–N curve.
Shot peening
A surface treatment in which small hard particles are fired at a component to introduce residual compressive stress in the surface layer, improving fatigue resistance.
Carburizing
A surface hardening process in which carbon diffuses into low-carbon steel from a carbon-rich atmosphere, creating a hard, compressively stressed surface layer.
tips: Do not confuse the direction of the mean stress effect: tensile mean stress reduces fatigue life, so the curves shift down as \(\sigma_m\) increases.
Carburizing creates compression only after the treatment combined with hardening (quenching); carbon diffusion alone does not give the compressive layer.
rq: Why does a compressive surface stress improve fatigue life even when the applied load cycles are unchanged?

Fatigue cracks nucleate and grow at the surface; compressive residual stress offsets the applied tensile stress there, so the effective stress range driving crack growth is reduced and cracks are suppressed.
Two components have the same stress amplitude, but one is operated with a large tensile mean stress. Which will fail first and why?
The component with the large tensile mean stress fails first, because its S–N curve lies lower, so fewer cycles are needed to reach failure at the same amplitude.

xq.q: A wing bracket made from an aluminium alloy must survive \(10^{8}\) load cycles. A designer reads the flat part of a steel S–N curve and argues that the alloy will last indefinitely below some endurance stress. Which statement is correct?
xq.a: The aluminium S–N curve keeps falling, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated number of cycles (e.g. \(10^{8}\)).
o: Aluminium alloys have a fatigue limit at about \(10^{7}\) cycles, so any stress below it is safe forever.
The aluminium S–N curve keeps falling, so quote a fatigue strength at a stated number of cycles (e.g. \(10^{8}\)).
Aluminium fails at any stress above its yield stress only, so fatigue is irrelevant below yield.
Aluminium has a fatigue limit, but it is reached only after \(10^{3}\) cycles.
xq.w: Aluminium alloys show no clear endurance limit and eventually fail at any stress, so a fatigue strength at a stated life is needed; the trap is assuming every metal behaves like steel.
s: Aluminium S–N curve has no plateau
Use fatigue strength at a stated N

xq.q: The S–N curves of several polymers flatten at high cycle counts with plateau stress amplitudes of about 10 MPa (PMMA), 5 MPa (PP), 3 MPa (PE) and 2 MPa (PTFE). Dry nylon and PET show curves that keep falling. Which polymers could carry a cyclic stress amplitude of 4 MPa indefinitely?
xq.a: PMMA and PP
o: PE and PTFE
Dry nylon and PET
PMMA and PP
PMMA, PP, PE and PTFE
xq.w: Only polymers whose fatigue limit (plateau) exceeds 4 MPa survive indefinitely; the trap is choosing those with the lower plateau values or assuming all flat curves qualify.
s: PE (3) and PTFE (2) are below it; nylon and PET have no limit

xq.q: A steel specimen is cycled at a constant stress amplitude \(\sigma_a\) with a tensile mean stress \(\sigma_m\). Using a sketch of S–N curves (stress amplitude against \(\log N\)) for three different mean stresses, explain how the mean stress affects the number of cycles to failure, and state whether it changes the static tensile strength.
xq.a: Sketch: stress amplitude on the vertical axis, log N on the horizontal axis, with three falling curves. The curve for zero or compressive mean stress is highest, and curves for increasingly tensile mean stress lie lower. A horizontal line at fixed amplitude cuts the curves at different N: the more tensile the mean stress, the smaller N is, so fatigue life is shorter. Zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest life. Mean stress affects fatigue (cyclic) behaviour only; the static tensile strength is unchanged.
s: Sketch with labelled axes and three curves
Curves shift down as mean stress becomes more tensile
Horizontal line at fixed amplitude gives smaller N for higher mean stress
Zero or compressive mean stress gives the longest life

units.name: 17.9 Miner's rule for cumulative damage
units.ov: This material covers Miner's rule, a linear cumulative-damage model for predicting fatigue failure under variable-amplitude loading. Each block of cycles at a stress amplitude uses up a fraction \(n_i/N_i\) of life, with \(N_i\) read from the S–N curve, and failure is predicted when the fractions sum to 1. The rule is used both to find life from a repeating load spectrum (e.g. damage per week) and to find the remaining cycles at a new stress level after prior damage.
must: Miner's rule: failure when \(\sum_i n_i/N_{f,i}=1\), where \(n_i\) is applied cycles and \(N_{f,i}\) is cycles to failure at the same stress amplitude
Each ratio \(n_i/N_{f,i}\) is the fraction of life consumed; never sum raw cycle counts, always divide by \(N_{f,i}\) first
\(N_{f,i}\) is read from the S–N curve or table at the matching stress amplitude (or range). Mismatching \(n_i\) and \(N_i\) is the commonest error
Life from a repeating spectrum: \(T = 1/(\text{damage per week})\). Worked example: \(0.001+0.01=0.011\) per week gives \(T\approx 91\) weeks
Remaining life at a new stress: \(X = N_4\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^{3} n_i/N_i\right)\), i.e. the remaining damage fraction multiplied by \(N_f\) at the new stress (Example 2, 480 MN/m²)
Damage fractions are dimensionless; time units enter only through the per-week (or per-unit-time) damage rate
Assumptions: damage accumulates linearly and is independent of load sequence, and the rule is empirical, not exact
Because sequence effects are ignored, predictions can be non-conservative for some orderings (e.g. high-to-low versus low-to-high loading)
The tabulated S–N data assume zero mean stress; a non-zero mean stress needs correction first. Do not interpolate unless told to
conn: S–N curve reading feeds Miner's rule: an error in \(N_f\) at any stress level propagates directly into the damage sum
Stress amplitude, range and mean stress definitions determine which S–N data apply (mean stress corrections such as Goodman come before Miner)
Repeating load spectrum plus Miner's rule gives life in weeks, hours or km, linking cycle counting to service life and inspection intervals
Remaining-life problems combine prior damage (a partial Miner sum) with the S–N value at a new stress level
exq: A component sees \(10^{5}\) cycles at 100 MPa and \(10^{4}\) cycles at 300 MPa each week. Given \(N_f=10^8\) and \(10^6\) respectively, compute the damage per week and the predicted life in weeks.

A specimen is cycled at 510 MN/m² for \(n_1\) cycles, 450 MN/m² for \(n_2\) cycles and 380 MN/m² for \(n_3\) cycles, using the S–N table to find each \(N_f\). How many further cycles at 480 MN/m² can it survive under Miner's rule?
Explain why summing raw cycle counts is wrong, and state the physical meaning of a Miner sum of 0.4.
Discuss two limitations of Miner's rule, including load sequence effects, and say when its predictions may be non-conservative.

A load spectrum has three stress levels with given block cycle counts per year. Calculate the annual damage, the life in years, and the effect on life of increasing the highest stress block by 20% if \(N_f\) falls from \(2\times10^5\) to \(1\times10^5\).

notes.t: Minor's Rule: cumulative fatigue damage under varying stress cycles
pts: Real components see varying stress waveforms, so life predictions must handle changing stress amplitudes rather than a single constant waveform.
Damage from each series of cycles at one stress level is the fraction of endured cycles to cycles to failure at that level.
Minor's Rule assumes damage accumulates linearly; total damage from all series of cycles must sum to 100% (failure).
defs: Minor's Rule
Linear cumulative damage rule stating that failure occurs when the sum of fractional damages \(n_{i}\)/\(N_{f}\),i over all stress levels equals one.
Cycles to failure \(N_{f}\),i
Number of cycles at stress amplitude σ_a,i needed to fail the component at that stress level, read from the S–N (failure) curve.
eqs: Minor's Rule: condition for fatigue failure under varying stress amplitudes
\(n_{i}\) = number of cycles endured at stress level i (dimensionless); \(N_{f,i}\) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless); m = number of stress levels (dimensionless)
tips: Do not sum raw cycle counts \(n_{i}\); each term must be divided by the cycles to failure \(N_{f}\),i at that specific stress amplitude before summing.
Minor's Rule assumes linear damage accumulation and ignores load sequence effects, so predictions can be non-conservative for some orderings of cycles.
rq: Why does Minor's Rule sum fractions of damage rather than simply counting total cycles endured?

Because cycles at high stress amplitude cause far more damage than cycles at low amplitude; each cycle is weighted by its share of the cycles to failure at that stress level, so the sum of fractional damages indicates how close the component is to failure.
If a component has \(n_{1}\)/\(N_{f}\),1 = 0.4 at one stress level, what must the rest of the load history contribute for failure to be predicted?
The remaining damage fractions must sum to 0.6, i.e. the other stress levels together must account for 60% of the damage.

notes.t: Adding sets of cycles (Miner's rule)
pts: Miner's rule is an empirical rule for cumulative fatigue damage from several loading regimes.
Each set of cycles consumes a fraction of the total fatigue life.
Failure is predicted when the summed fractional damage reaches one.
defs: Miner's rule
Empirical linear damage rule stating that fatigue failure occurs when the sum of cycle ratios applied to cycles-to-failure at each loading level equals one.
Cycles to failure (\(N_{\text{fi}}\))
The number of cycles at a given loading regime (stress range) that would cause fatigue failure if applied alone.
Cycles applied (\(N_{i}\))
The number of cycles actually applied at loading regime i.
eqs: Miner's cumulative damage criterion (failure when sum equals 1)
\(N_{i}\) = number of cycles applied at regime i (dimensionless count); \(N_{fi}\) = cycles to failure at regime i (dimensionless count); \(\sum_{i}\) = sum over all loading regimes
tips: Miner's rule is empirical and ignores load sequence effects; do not claim it is exact for variable-amplitude loading.
\(N_{i}\) and \(N_{\text{fi}}\) must be counts at the same stress range; mixing different stress ranges in one ratio is a common error.
rq: Why does Miner's rule assume damage adds linearly, and what does a sum less than 1 tell you about remaining life?

It is an empirical simplification that each cycle at a level uses a fixed fraction of life, independent of order. A sum below 1 means the component has not yet failed and remaining life is the unused fraction (1 minus the sum) of the total fatigue life.
What if the same number of cycles is applied at a high stress range versus a low stress range?
High stress range cycles have a much smaller \(N_{\text{fi}}\), so they consume a larger fraction of life (\(N_{i}\)/\(N_{\text{fi}}\) is larger), contributing more damage per cycle.

notes.t: Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage
pts: Each load level contributes a damage fraction equal to applied cycles divided by cycles to failure at that stress; damage fractions are summed.
Failure is predicted when the summed damage fraction reaches 1 (100% damage); the time to failure is the reciprocal of the damage accumulated per week.
Weekly damage here is 0.001 from the 100 MPa loading plus 0.01 from the 300 MPa loading, giving 0.011 per week.
defs: Damage fraction (Miner's rule)
The fraction of fatigue life consumed by a given number of cycles at a given stress amplitude, equal to \(n_i/N_i\); failure is expected when the sum of these fractions equals 1.
eqs: Miner's rule cumulative damage at failure
\(n_i\) = applied cycles at stress level i (dimensionless count); \(N_i\) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless count)
Predicted life in weeks from weekly damage
\(T\) = expected life (weeks); \(\sum n_i/N_i\) per week = damage fraction accumulated per week (dimensionless)
tips: Keep consistent units: damage fractions are dimensionless, so the life result in weeks comes only from the per-week damage rate, not from mixing cycles and weeks.
Use cycles to failure at each specific stress amplitude (\(N_i\)) rather than the cycles applied, and do not forget to sum all stress levels before taking the reciprocal.
rq: Why can the damage fractions from 100 MPa and 300 MPa simply be added together?
Miner's rule assumes linear damage accumulation, so each stress level's cycles consume a fixed share of life independent of the order of loading, and the total damage is their sum.
What would happen to the predicted life if the 300 MPa loading were doubled to 1000 cycles per week?
Its damage fraction doubles to 0.02, so weekly damage becomes 0.021 and life falls to about 1/0.021 ≈ 47.6 weeks.

notes.t: Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage (Example 2)
pts: Miner's rule sums the fraction of life used at each stress amplitude; failure is predicted when the sum equals 1.
Each term is the applied cycles n divided by the cycles to failure N at that stress amplitude, read from the S-N data.
Remaining life is found by subtracting the damage already accumulated from 1, then multiplying by the cycles to failure at the new stress.
Stress amplitudes not in the table are not interpolated here; the data points used are 510, 450 and 380 MN/m² plus 480 MN/m² for the final block.
defs: Cumulative damage
The fraction of fatigue life consumed by a sequence of cycles at different stress amplitudes, taken as the sum of \( n_i/N_i \) over all stress levels.
eqs: \( n_i \) = applied cycles at stress level i (dimensionless count); \( N_i \) = cycles to failure at stress level i (dimensionless count)
Additional cycles to failure at a new stress level
\( X \) = remaining cycles at 480 MN/m² (cycles); \( N_4 \) = cycles to failure at 480 MN/m² (cycles)
tips: Use the \( N_f \) column for the same stress amplitude as each \( n_i \); mismatching stress levels is a common error.
Miner's rule assumes zero mean stress, as stated; with mean stress the tabulated data would need correction.
rq: Why does the specimen survive the 380 MN/m² block of 80 000 cycles yet still fail at 480 MN/m²?
The 380 MN/m² stress is close to the endurance limit, so its 275 000 cycles to failure is large; the 80 000 cycles contribute only about 0.29 of damage, leaving 0.17 for 480 MN/m².
What would happen to the answer if the cycles were applied in a different order?
Miner's linear rule predicts the same total damage regardless of sequence, so the answer is unchanged; real materials can show sequence effects, which the rule ignores.
Why is the 380 MN/m² term given as 80 000/275 000 rather than using the 380 entry in the table directly?
Each term needs the cycles to failure \( N_i \) at that exact stress amplitude, and 275 000 is the tabulated \( N_f \) for 380 MN/m².

xq.q: A bracket sees each week \(2\times10^{4}\) cycles at a stress amplitude of 100 MPa and \(3\times10^{3}\) cycles at 300 MPa. From the S–N curve, the cycles to failure are \(2\times10^{7}\) at 100 MPa and \(3\times10^{5}\) at 300 MPa. Using Miner's rule, estimate the life of the bracket in weeks.
xq.a: About 90.9 weeks

xq.q: A component has already endured \(1.0\times10^{5}\) cycles at 250 MPa (cycles to failure \(4\times10^{5}\)) and \(2.0\times10^{5}\) cycles at 150 MPa (cycles to failure \(1\times10^{6}\)). It is then run at 350 MPa, for which the cycles to failure are \(2\times10^{5}\). Using Miner's rule, how many cycles at 350 MPa can it endure before failure is predicted?
xq.a: \(1.1\times10^{5}\) cycles
s: Total so far 0.45, so remaining damage 0.55

xq.q: A part is cycled \(n_1=1\times10^{4}\) times at a stress with \(N_{f,1}=1\times10^{5}\) and \(n_2=5\times10^{4}\) times at a lower stress with \(N_{f,2}=1\times10^{6}\). What is the Miner's rule damage sum \(\sum n_i/N_{f,i}\)?
xq.w: Each ratio is calculated at its own stress level (0.10 + 0.05 = 0.15); the traps are summing raw counts (0.0545), giving the remaining life (0.85), or inverting the ratios (30).

units.name: 18.1 Material selection criteria and the materials cycle
units.ov: This module introduces the criteria used to choose engineering materials and places that choice within the materials cycle. Properties are split into intrinsic (bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical, surface) and attributive (price, availability, production, aesthetics) groups, and good selection weighs all of them together. The materials cycle shows that this choice affects the whole product life from extraction to disposal or recycling, which links selection to cost and sustainability.
must: Intrinsic properties are inherent to the material: bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical and surface properties.
Attributive properties are assigned by external factors: price and availability, production properties (ease of manufacture and fabrication) and aesthetics (appearance, texture).
Material selection must draw on all branches of the property diagram, not only bulk mechanical properties such as strength and stiffness.
Materials cycle order: raw materials → synthesis and processing → engineered materials → design, manufacture and assembly → products → use (construction, transport, energy, health) → waste.
At the waste stage, material is either recycled/reused or discarded to the environment, which closes the loop back to raw materials.
Recycle/reuse feeds back into synthesis and processing, not directly into product manufacture, so the cycle is a loop and not a straight line.
Raw materials (ores, minerals) are extracted from the Earth; engineered materials are the result of synthesis and processing to give specific properties. Do not mix these up.
Recycling reduces the demand for new raw materials, which is the main link between the cycle and sustainability.
Material choice affects the whole product life cycle (manufacture, use, end of life), not just performance in service.
conn: Attributive properties such as cost, availability and manufacturability constrain which materials with suitable intrinsic properties can actually be used, so selection is a trade-off between the two groups.
Material choice at the design stage determines how easily the product can be recycled or reused at end of life, which links selection to the sustainability loop.
Recycling and availability are linked: higher recycling rates reduce demand for raw material extraction, which affects price and supply security.
Production properties (ease of fabrication) connect the 'manufacture and assembly' stage of the cycle to the attributive branch of the property diagram.
exq: Define intrinsic and attributive properties. Classify each of these as intrinsic or attributive and justify your answers: yield strength, price per kg, thermal conductivity, surface hardness, surface finish appearance, ease of welding.
Sketch the materials cycle, labelling raw materials, engineered materials, products, use, waste, and the recycle/reuse path. Explain where recycled material re-enters the cycle and why.

A company is choosing a material for a consumer product. Discuss why bulk mechanical properties alone are not sufficient, and list the other property groups that must be considered with an example of each.
Explain the difference between raw materials and engineered materials, giving one example of each, and describe how recycling reduces the need for raw material extraction.
Discuss how the choice of material at the design stage can influence sustainability across the whole product life cycle, referring to the materials cycle.

notes.t: Choosing Materials: Properties Considered in Design
pts: Material properties split into intrinsic properties (inherent to the material itself) and attributive properties (depend on cost, supply and how the material is made or looks).
Intrinsic properties include bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical and surface properties.
Attributive properties include price and availability, production properties (ease of manufacture, fabrication) and aesthetic properties (appearance, texture).
Material selection for design draws on all these property groups together, not on mechanical properties alone.
defs: Intrinsic property
A property inherent to the material itself, such as bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical or surface properties, independent of how or where it is used.
Attributive property
A property attributed to a material by external factors such as price, availability, ease of production and aesthetics, rather than by its inherent physics.
tips: Do not confuse intrinsic properties (inherent to the material) with attributive properties (cost, production, appearance), which depend on external factors.
Design selection should consider all branches of the property diagram, not only bulk mechanical properties.
rq: Why might a material with excellent bulk mechanical properties still be rejected for a consumer product?
Because attributive properties such as price, availability, ease of manufacture or aesthetic appearance and texture can outweigh intrinsic performance in the design decision.
Which property group would determine whether a component's surface resists wear, and why is it classed as intrinsic?
Surface properties; they belong to the intrinsic group because they are a physical characteristic of the material's surface itself.

notes.t: The Materials Cycle
pts: Materials flow in a closed cycle: raw materials are synthesised and processed into engineered materials, which are designed, manufactured and assembled into products.
Products are used across many application areas such as construction, transportation, energy and health before they become waste.
Waste can be recycled or reused and fed back into synthesis and processing, reducing the need for new raw materials.
Materials that are not recycled are discarded as waste and ultimately returned to the environment, closing the loop back to raw materials extracted from the Earth.
The cycle links materials science to engineering design, manufacturing and sustainability, showing that material choice affects the whole product life cycle.
defs: Raw materials
Naturally occurring substances extracted from the Earth (e.g. ores, minerals) that are the starting point for engineered materials.
Engineered materials
Materials produced by synthesis and processing of raw materials to achieve specific properties for an intended application.
Recycle/reuse
Recovering used material from waste and returning it to synthesis and processing, either as the same material or a new one.
tips: Do not treat the cycle as a straight line: recycle/reuse feeds back into synthesis and processing, not directly into product manufacture.
Remember that 'raw materials' are extracted from the Earth, while 'engineered materials' have been synthesised or processed; mixing these up is a common error.
rq: Why does recycling reduce environmental impact compared with always extracting new raw materials?
It reduces demand for mining and extraction, lowering energy use, emissions and the depletion of finite natural resources, and it reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill.
What would happen to the cycle if no waste were recycled or reused?
Every product would need fresh raw materials, so the loop would become a linear 'extract–make–dispose' flow, increasing resource depletion and waste accumulation.

xq.q: In a design review for a bicycle frame, which property is an attributive property rather than an intrinsic one?
xq.a: Ease of fabrication (e.g. welding or forming)
o: Yield strength
Surface hardness
Thermal conductivity
Ease of fabrication (e.g. welding or forming)
xq.w: Attributive properties depend on external factors such as cost, availability, production and appearance; the trap is treating all measurable properties as intrinsic.
s: Ease of fabrication: production property, attributive

xq.q: On the materials cycle, a manufacturer collects scrap aluminium cans. Where does recycled material re-enter the cycle?
xq.a: Back into synthesis and processing, reducing the need for new raw materials
o: Directly into product manufacture, skipping processing
Into raw materials extracted from the Earth
Back into synthesis and processing, reducing the need for new raw materials
Into waste, where it is returned to the environment
xq.w: Recycle/reuse feeds back into synthesis and processing; the trap is treating the cycle as a straight line or confusing recycled stock with raw materials.
s: Waste is recovered and returned to synthesis and processing
This reduces the demand for newly extracted raw materials

xq.q: Explain why choosing a material for a product should consider more than its bulk mechanical properties. In your answer, distinguish intrinsic from attributive properties and use the materials cycle to show how material choice affects the whole product life.
xq.a: Intrinsic properties are inherent to the material: bulk mechanical, bulk non-mechanical and surface properties. Attributive properties come from external factors: price and availability, production (ease of manufacture and fabrication) and aesthetics. A material with excellent strength may still be unsuitable if it is too costly, unavailable or hard to process, so all property groups must be considered together. In the materials cycle, raw materials are processed into engineered materials, then designed, manufactured and assembled into products, used, and become waste. Waste can be recycled or reused back into synthesis and processing, or discarded to the environment. The material chosen therefore affects manufacture, use, recyclability and environmental impact across the whole life.
s: Selection needs both groups, not mechanical alone
Cycle stages: raw material, processing, product, use, waste
Recycle/reuse feeds back to processing, so material choice affects the whole life

units.name: 18.2 Sources and abundance of raw materials
units.ov: This module covers where engineering materials come from (mining, synthesis from oil, growing, processing) and how abundant the elements are in the crust, oceans and atmosphere. The key link is that abundance by weight percent determines which elements are plentiful, and so which raw materials (metal ores, ceramics, polymers) are available. A side page on diamond carats provides a unit-conversion example that is not core materials content.
must: Around 15 billion tonnes of raw material are extracted worldwide each year
Metals come from mining ores; ceramics come from mined raw materials, either used directly or after processing (never say all ceramics are simply mined)
Polymers are artificial (from oil or other raw products) or natural (grown, e.g. rubber)
Composites are mixtures of other material classes, so their source depends on their constituents
Do not confuse natural materials (e.g. wood) with natural polymers: both are grown but belong to different material classes
Crust by weight: oxygen 47 wt%, silicon 27 wt%
Oceans: oxygen 85 wt%, hydrogen 10 wt% (water, H₂O). Atmosphere: nitrogen 79 wt%, oxygen 19 wt%, argon 2 wt%
Oxygen is the only element abundant in all three reservoirs; carbon is scarce in all (0.02 wt% crust, 0.002 wt% oceans, 0.04 wt% CO₂ in air)
Wt% is a mass fraction of the reservoir, not an atomic percentage; listed values do not sum to 100, and atmospheric CO₂ is a compound so it should not be compared directly with elemental carbon
Carat conversion: \(m_g = m_{ct}/5\) since 1 ct = 200 mg; e.g. 16.08 ct ≈ 3216 mg ≈ 3.2 g (carat is mass, not karat gold purity)
conn: Abundance and source: the dominance of oxygen and silicon in the crust explains why many mined raw materials are oxides and silicates, which relates to ceramics and to metal ores
Material class and source: classification (metal, polymer, ceramic, composite) determines the extraction route, and composites inherit the sources of their constituents

Wt% and compounds: the oceans' 85 wt% oxygen and 10 wt% hydrogen arise from water, and atmospheric carbon appears as CO₂, so interpreting a table requires distinguishing elements from compounds and mass from atomic fractions
Scarcity versus importance: carbon is rare in every reservoir yet underpins polymers (oil-based), so low abundance does not imply low engineering use
