formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.vars: n₁, n₂ = refractive indices of first and second media; θ_i = incidence angle; θ_r = refraction angle
formulas.use: Refraction at an interface (air: n = 1).

formulas.name: Critical angle
formulas.vars: θ_c = critical angle; n₁ = denser medium index; n₂ = less dense medium index
formulas.use: Total internal reflection when n₁ > n₂ and θ_i > θ_c; fibre core/cladding.

formulas.name: Fibre core–cladding index difference
formulas.vars: n₁ = core index; n₂ = cladding index
formulas.use: Typical fibre index contrast.

formulas.name: Fick's first law
formulas.vars: J = flux (mol/m²·s); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); C = concentration (mol/m³); x = position (m)
formulas.use: Steady-state diffusion with linear concentration profile.

formulas.name: Diffusion flux definition
formulas.vars: M = mass or moles transferred; A = area (m²); t = time (s)
formulas.use: Flux from measured mass transfer.

formulas.name: Permeation flux through polymer membrane
formulas.vars: J = flux (cm³STP/cm²·s); \(P_{M}\) = permeability coefficient; ΔP = pressure difference (Pa); Δx = thickness (cm)
formulas.use: Gas diffusion through polymer membranes.

formulas.name: Arrhenius equation for D
formulas.vars: D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s); D₀ = pre-exponential factor (m²/s); \(Q_{d}\) = activation energy (J/mol); R = 8.314 J/mol·K; T = temperature (K)
formulas.use: D at temperature T; use two temperatures to find \(Q_{d}\) or D₀.

formulas.name: Pre-exponential factor from known D
formulas.vars: D₁ = known D at T₁
formulas.use: Find D₀, then compute D at another T.

formulas.name: Fick's second law
formulas.vars: C = concentration; t = time (s); x = position (m); D = diffusion coefficient (m²/s)
formulas.use: Non-steady-state diffusion.

formulas.name: Constant surface concentration solution
formulas.vars: \(C_{s}\) = surface concentration; C₀ = initial uniform concentration; x = depth (m); D = diffusion coefficient; t = time (s)
formulas.use: Semi-infinite solid with fixed surface concentration (e.g. carburising, doping).

formulas.name: Error function
formulas.vars: z = argument; y = dummy variable
formulas.use: Evaluate with tables.

formulas.name: Theoretical Young's modulus from bond stiffness
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium atomic separation (m)
formulas.use: Estimate theoretical modulus from the bond; follows from \sigma = N \(S_{0}\) \varepsilon \(r_{0}\) with N = 1/\(r_{0}^{2.}\)

formulas.name: Bond stiffness from force or energy
formulas.vars: \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); F = bond force (N); U = bond energy (J); r = atomic separation (m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium separation (m)
formulas.use: Slope of the force–separation curve at equilibrium, or curvature of the energy curve.

formulas.name: Force from bond energy
formulas.vars: F = force (N); U = bond energy (J); r = separation (m)
formulas.use: Convert an energy–separation curve to force (sign convention as in lectures).

formulas.name: Linear bond force for small displacement
formulas.vars: F = force (N); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); r = separation (m); \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium separation (m)
formulas.use: Small displacements about equilibrium (linear elastic region).

formulas.name: Stress from N bonds per unit area
formulas.latex: \sigma = N S_0 (r - r_0) = N S_0 r_0 \varepsilon
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); N = bonds per unit area (\(m^{-2}\)); \(S_{0}\) = bond stiffness (N/m); \varepsilon = strain; \(r_{0}\) = equilibrium bond length (m)
formulas.use: Derivation step linking atomic bonds to macroscopic stress.

formulas.name: Bond areal density
formulas.vars: N = bonds per unit area (\(m^{-2}\)); \(r_{0}\) = bond spacing (m)
formulas.use: Simple cubic-type atomic packing assumption.

formulas.name: Engineering stress
formulas.vars: \sigma = stress (Pa); F = applied force (N); \(A_{0}\) = original cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Stress from the load on the original area.

formulas.name: Engineering strain
formulas.vars: \varepsilon = strain (dimensionless); \Delta L = change in length (m); \(L_{0}\) = original length (m)
formulas.use: Strain from the change in length relative to the original length.

formulas.name: Young's modulus (Hooke's law)
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \sigma = normal stress (Pa); \varepsilon = normal strain
formulas.use: Linear elastic region, slope of the stress–strain curve.

formulas.name: Poisson's ratio
formulas.vars: \nu = Poisson's ratio; \(\varepsilon_{x}\) = lateral strain, \Delta w/\(w_{0}\); \(\varepsilon_{z}\) = axial strain, \Delta l/\(l_{0}\)
formulas.use: Lateral contraction under axial tension.

formulas.name: Shear modulus
formulas.vars: G = shear modulus (Pa); \tau = shear stress (Pa); \gamma = shear strain
formulas.use: Elastic response to shear.

formulas.name: Relation between E, G and \nu (isotropic)
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); G = shear modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (\(m^{3}\)); \Delta V/V = relative volume change (sign: V falls as P rises)
formulas.use: Hydrostatic compression.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus from E and \nu
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus from G and \nu
formulas.vars: K = bulk modulus (Pa); G = shear modulus (Pa); \nu = Poisson's ratio
formulas.use: Isotropic materials only.

formulas.name: Longitudinal modulus, iso-strain (Voigt, upper bound)
formulas.latex: E_{cl} = E_m V_m + E_f V_f = E_m(1-V_f) + E_f V_f
formulas.vars: \(E_{cl}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\), \(E_{f}\) = matrix and fibre moduli (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions (\(V_{m}\) + \(V_{f}\) = 1)
formulas.use: Load applied parallel to fibres; equal strain in both phases.

formulas.name: Transverse modulus, iso-stress (Reuss, lower bound)
formulas.vars: \(E_{ct}\) = composite modulus (Pa); \(E_{m}\), \(E_{f}\) = moduli (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Load applied perpendicular to layers/fibres; equal stress in both phases.

formulas.name: Composite stress (iso-strain)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{c}\), \(\sigma_{m}\), \(\sigma_{f}\) = composite, matrix and fibre stresses (Pa); \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Follows from force balance \(\sigma_{c}\) \(A_{c}\) = \(\sigma_{m}\) \(A_{m}\) + \(\sigma_{f}\) \(A_{f}\), with V = A/\(A_{c}\) for equal lengths.

formulas.name: Composite strain (iso-stress)
formulas.vars: \(\varepsilon_{c}\), \(\varepsilon_{m}\), \(\varepsilon_{f}\) = composite, matrix and fibre strains; \(V_{m}\), \(V_{f}\) = volume fractions
formulas.use: Layers in series under equal stress.

formulas.name: Load sharing and layer response
formulas.vars: F = load (N); \sigma = stress (Pa); E = layer modulus (Pa); t = layer thickness (m); \delta = layer deformation (m)
formulas.use: Layer-by-layer analysis in iso-strain and iso-stress problems.

topics.topic: Yield, slip and resolved shear stress

formulas.name: Normal stress on an inclined plane
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{n}\) = normal stress on the plane (Pa); \(\sigma_{x}\) = uniaxial stress (Pa); \theta = angle between the plane normal and the load axis
formulas.use: Uniaxial loading; derived from \(F_{n}\) = F\cos\theta and A' = A\sec\theta.

formulas.name: Shear stress on an inclined plane
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{s}\) = shear stress on the plane (Pa); \(\sigma_{x}\) = uniaxial stress (Pa); \theta = plane angle
formulas.use: Uniaxial loading; maximum \(\sigma_{x}\)/2 at \theta = 45^\circ (sign shows direction only).

formulas.name: Yield on a slip plane (critical resolved shear stress)
formulas.vars: \(\tau_{R}\) = resolved shear stress (Pa); \(F_{s}\) = shear force along slip direction (N); \(A_{s}\) = slip plane area (\(m^{2}\)); \(\tau_{crss}\) = critical resolved shear stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Single-crystal slip begins when the resolved shear stress reaches \(\tau_{crss}\).

formulas.name: Inclined section area
formulas.vars: A' = inclined plane area (\(m^{2}\)); A = cross-section normal to load (\(m^{2}\)); \theta = inclination angle
formulas.use: Used when deriving stresses on inclined planes.

formulas.name: True stress
formulas.vars: F = force (N); \(A_{i}\) = instantaneous cross-sectional area (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Needed beyond necking, where area has changed appreciably.

formulas.name: True strain
formulas.vars: \(l_{i}\) = instantaneous length (m); \(l_{0}\) = original length (m)
formulas.use: Large plastic strains; \(\varepsilon_{true}\) = \ln(1+\(\varepsilon_{eng}\)).

formulas.name: Hall–Petch relation
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{y}\) = yield stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{i}\) = friction stress (Pa); k = grain-boundary constant (Pa \(m^{1/2}\)); D = mean grain diameter (m)
formulas.use: Yield strength increases as grain size decreases.

formulas.name: Percent elongation
formulas.vars: \(l_{f}\) = gauge length at fracture (m); \(l_{0}\) = original gauge length (m)
formulas.use: Ductility measure.

formulas.name: Percent reduction in area
formulas.vars: \(A_{0}\) = original area (\(m^{2}\)); \(A_{f}\) = area at fracture (\(m^{2}\))
formulas.use: Ductility measure.

formulas.name: Dislocations in a pile-up
formulas.vars: n = number of dislocations; \alpha = constant; \tau = shear stress (Pa); d = grain size (m); G = shear modulus (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m)
formulas.use: Pile-up at a grain boundary; larger grains give larger n and stress concentration.

topics.topic: Yield criteria: Tresca and von Mises

formulas.name: Tresca yield criterion
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\),\(\sigma_{3}\) = principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = uniaxial yield stress (Pa); \(\tau_{max}\) = maximum shear stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield when the maximum shear stress reaches \(\sigma_{Y}\)/2; hexagonal yield locus.

formulas.name: Von Mises yield criterion
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\),\(\sigma_{3}\) = principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = uniaxial yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Ductile yield; elliptical locus, which encloses the Tresca hexagon.

formulas.name: Von Mises equivalent stress
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{e}\) = equivalent stress (Pa); \(\sigma_{i}\) = principal stresses (Pa)
formulas.use: Yield occurs when \(\sigma_{e}\) = \(\sigma_{Y}\).

formulas.name: Plane stress special cases (Tresca)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\) = in-plane principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Reading the Tresca hexagon with \(\sigma_{3}\) = 0.

formulas.name: Von Mises, plane stress (\(\sigma_{3}\) = 0)
formulas.vars: \(\sigma_{1}\),\(\sigma_{2}\) = in-plane principal stresses (Pa); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Biaxial or torsion problems.

topics.topic: Yield of a shaft in torsion

formulas.name: Shear stress and principal stresses in a solid shaft
formulas.vars: T = torque (N m); r = shaft radius (m); \tau = surface shear stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Pure torsion gives principal stresses equal and opposite to the shear stress.

formulas.name: Yield torque (Tresca)
formulas.vars: \(T_{max}\) = yield torque (N m); r = radius (m); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = tensile yield stress (Pa)

formulas.name: Yield torque (von Mises)
formulas.vars: \(T_{max}\) = yield torque (N m); r = radius (m); \(\sigma_{Y}\) = tensile yield stress (Pa)
formulas.use: From 3\tau^2 = \(\sigma_{Y}^{2}\), i.e. \(\tau_{Y}\) = \(\sigma_{Y}\)/\sqrt{3}; about 15% above Tresca (ratio 2/\sqrt{3} \approx 1.155).

formulas.name: Griffith fracture stress (internal crack of length 2c)
formulas.vars: σ_f = fracture stress (Pa); γ_s = surface energy per unit area (J/m²); E = Young's modulus (Pa); c = half-length of internal crack (m)
formulas.use: Brittle fracture of a plate with an internal crack. The refined result. The earlier rough version gave 4γ_sE/(πc) in place of 2γ_sE/(πc) (check which one your course uses). For a surface crack, c is the full crack length.

formulas.name: Elastic energy released by crack
formulas.vars: \(U_{E}\) = elastic energy released (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); σ = applied stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Energy-balance derivation: the elastic energy term, which falls as the crack grows.

formulas.name: Surface energy of crack
formulas.vars: \(U_{s}\) = surface energy (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); γ_s = surface energy per unit area (J/m²)
formulas.use: Energy-balance derivation: two crack faces, each of area 2ct.

formulas.name: Energy balance condition for crack growth
formulas.vars: U = \(U_{E}\)+\(U_{s}\) = total energy (J); c = half crack length (m); t = thickness (m); σ = stress (Pa); E = Young's modulus (Pa); γ_s = surface energy (J/m²)
formulas.use: Setting dU/dc = 0 gives the critical crack size or fracture stress.

formulas.name: Critical crack length (from the energy balance)
formulas.vars: 2c = critical crack length (m); γ_s = surface energy (J/m²); E = Young's modulus (Pa); σ = applied stress (Pa)
formulas.use: Crack length above which the crack grows unstably at stress σ.

formulas.name: Stress intensity factor
formulas.vars: K = stress intensity factor (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); σ = applied stress (MPa); a = crack length (m)
formulas.use: Gives the crack-tip loading. A geometry factor Y is often included for real specimens.

formulas.name: Fracture criterion
formulas.vars: \(K_{c}\) = fracture toughness (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); σ_f = fracture stress (MPa); a = crack length (m)
formulas.use: Fracture occurs when K reaches \(K_{c}\). Use it for the critical stress or critical crack size.

formulas.name: Hall–Petch equation
formulas.vars: σ_Y = yield strength (MPa); σ_0 = friction stress opposing dislocation motion (MPa); \(k_{y}\) = strengthening coefficient (MPa \(m^{1/2}\)); d = grain size (m)
formulas.use: Smaller grains give higher yield strength.

formulas.name: Orowan bowing stress (precipitate strengthening)
formulas.vars: τ_Y = critical shear stress (Pa); T = dislocation line tension (N); b = Burgers vector (m); L = precipitate spacing (m)
formulas.use: Dislocations bow between non-shearable precipitates. Closer spacing gives higher strength. Often T ≈ Gb²/2.

formulas.name: Percent cold work
formulas.vars: %CW = percent cold work (%); \(A_{0}\) = original cross-sectional area (m²); \(A_{d}\) = area after deformation (m²)
formulas.use: Quantifies work hardening. More cold work gives higher strength and lower ductility.

formulas.name: Force balance on bowing dislocation
formulas.vars: τ = applied shear stress (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m); L = precipitate spacing (m); T = line tension (N); \(f_{0}\) = force per unit length (N/m)
formulas.use: Origin of the Orowan stress.

formulas.name: Dislocations in a pile-up
formulas.vars: n = number of dislocations; α = constant; τ = shear stress (Pa); d = grain size (m); G = shear modulus (Pa); b = Burgers vector (m)
formulas.use: Explains Hall–Petch: larger grains give longer pile-ups and a larger stress concentration at the boundary. (The slide's definition of G was garbled.)

formulas.name: Creep threshold (homologous temperature)
formulas.vars: T = operating temperature (K); \(T_{m}\) = melting temperature (K)
formulas.use: Creep becomes significant above about 0.4 \(T_{m}\). Use absolute temperatures.

formulas.name: Celsius to Kelvin
formulas.vars: T = temperature
formulas.use: Always convert before computing T/\(T_{m}\).

formulas.name: Relaxation modulus
formulas.vars: \(E_{r}\) = relaxation modulus (Pa); σ(t) = stress at time t (Pa); ε_0 = constant applied strain
formulas.use: Stress relaxation test at constant strain.

formulas.name: Stress ratio
formulas.vars: R = stress ratio; σ_min = minimum stress (MPa); σ_max = maximum stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Characterises the cycle. R = −1 is fully reversed tension–compression. (One source line inverted this; the standard form is min/max.)

formulas.name: Stress amplitude
formulas.vars: σ_a = stress amplitude (MPa); σ_max, σ_min = maximum and minimum stress (MPa); σ_r = stress range (MPa)
formulas.use: Used for S–N data.

formulas.name: Mean stress
formulas.vars: σ_m = mean stress (MPa); σ_max, σ_min = maximum and minimum stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Describes the cycle's offset from zero stress.

formulas.name: Stress range
formulas.vars: σ_r = Δσ = stress range (MPa); σ_max, σ_min = maximum and minimum stress (MPa); σ_a = stress amplitude (MPa)
formulas.use: Used in ΔK and the Paris law.

formulas.name: Low-cycle fatigue condition
formulas.vars: σ_max, σ_min = maximum and minimum stress (MPa); σ_y = yield stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Plastic deformation each cycle gives low-cycle fatigue, with a short life.

formulas.name: High-cycle fatigue condition
formulas.vars: σ_max, σ_min = maximum and minimum stress (MPa); σ_y = yield stress (MPa)
formulas.use: Stresses stay elastic, giving a long life.

formulas.name: Energy dissipated per cycle
formulas.vars: \(W_{d}\) = energy dissipated per cycle (J/m³); σ = stress (Pa); ε = strain
formulas.use: Equals the area of the hysteresis loop.

formulas.name: Paris law
formulas.vars: da/dN = crack growth per cycle (m/cycle); ΔK = stress intensity range (MPa√m); A, m = material constants
formulas.use: Stable (Stage II) crack growth. The notes omit A, but it is required for correct units.

formulas.name: Stress intensity range
formulas.vars: ΔK = stress intensity range (MPa√m); Δσ = stress range (MPa); a = crack length (m)
formulas.use: The notes give ΔK ∝ Δσ√a. Include Y or π for calculations, as appropriate.

formulas.name: Miner's rule
formulas.vars: \(n_{i}\) = cycles applied at stress level i; \(N_{f,i}\) = cycles to failure at stress level i
formulas.use: Linear damage summation. Failure is predicted when the sum reaches 1.

formulas.name: Remaining cycles at a new stress level
formulas.vars: X = remaining cycles at the new level; \(N_{\text{new}}\) = cycles to failure at the new level; \(n_{i}\), \(N_{i}\) = applied cycles and cycles to failure at earlier levels
formulas.use: Use when part of the life is already used up.

formulas.name: Life from damage per block
formulas.vars: T = expected life (weeks); (\(n_{i}\)/\(N_{i}\))_per week = damage fraction per week
formulas.use: Repeating load schedules. Use any block unit, not only weeks.

formulas.name: Relative cost of a material
formulas.vars: \bar{c} = relative cost (dimensionless); $/kg = price per kg of the material ($/kg); (\$/kg)_ref = price per kg of reference material, rolled A36 plain carbon steel ($/kg)
formulas.use: Compare material prices on a common scale relative to the reference steel.

formulas.name: Carats to grams
formulas.vars: \(m_{g}\) = mass (g); \(m_{\text{ct}}\) = mass (carats, ct)
formulas.use: Convert gem mass in carats to grams (1 ct = 0.2 g).

topics.topic: Cantilever beam: deflection, mass and geometry

formulas.name: Tip deflection of square-section cantilever under end load
formulas.vars: \delta = tip deflection (m); l = beam length (m); F = end load (N); E = Young's modulus (Pa); t = side of square section (m)
formulas.use: Stiffness constraint for a square-section cantilever; rearrange for t.

formulas.name: Beam mass
formulas.vars: M = mass (kg); l = length (m); t = section side (m); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: Objective function: mass to be minimised for a square-section beam.

formulas.name: Thickness required for stiffness (constraint rearranged)
formulas.vars: t = section side (m); l = length (m); F = force (N); E = Young's modulus (Pa); \delta = allowable deflection (m)
formulas.use: Eliminate the free variable t using the stiffness constraint.

formulas.name: Thickness from mass (rearranged)
formulas.vars: t = section side (m); M = mass (kg); l = length (m); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\))
formulas.use: Substitute into the stiffness constraint to eliminate t.

formulas.name: Mass of beam meeting stiffness requirement
formulas.vars: M = beam mass (kg); l = length (m); F = load (N); \delta = allowable deflection (m); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Final result: the first bracket is the load/geometry term, the second is the material term. Minimise M by minimising \(\rho^{2}\)/E.

formulas.name: Material performance index for light stiff beam
formulas.vars: \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\), or Mg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa, or GPa)
formulas.use: Rank materials for minimum mass at given stiffness (beam in bending, square section); units must be consistent.

formulas.name: Relation after eliminating t
formulas.latex: t^{4} = \frac{4 l^{3} F}{E\delta} = \left(\frac{M}{l\rho}\right)^{2}\;\Rightarrow\; M^{2} = \frac{4 l^{5} F\rho^{2}}{E\delta}
formulas.vars: symbols as above
formulas.use: Intermediate step for deriving the mass expression.

formulas.name: Guide line: beam, stiffness-limited, minimum mass
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); C = constant
formulas.use: Slope 2 line on log E–log \rho chart; beams in bending (equivalent to minimising \(\rho^{2}\)/E).

formulas.name: Guide line: tie, stiffness-limited, minimum mass
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); C = constant
formulas.use: Slope 1 line on log E–log \rho chart; for ties/rods in tension.

formulas.name: Guide line: panel/plate, stiffness-limited, minimum mass
formulas.vars: E = Young's modulus (Pa); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); C = constant
formulas.use: Slope 3 line on log E–log \rho chart; panels/plates in bending.

formulas.name: Cost of a stiffness-limited beam
formulas.vars: Price = cost of beam (currency); l = length (m); F = load (N); \delta = allowable deflection (m); \bar{p} = relative price per kg (dimensionless); \rho = density (kg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (Pa)
formulas.use: Minimum cost for given stiffness: minimise \bar{p}\(\rho^{2}\)/E (equivalently maximise \(E^{1/2}\)/(\bar{p}\rho)).

formulas.name: Cost-weighted performance index
formulas.vars: C = relative cost index; \rho = density (Mg/\(m^{3}\)); E = Young's modulus (GPa); \(p^{*}\) = relative price per unit mass (dimensionless)
formulas.use: Rank materials for minimum cost; smaller C is better.
